sectionTitles: A changing country on a coarse map
Books, classrooms and a Persian writing sample
Care, water and the everyday work of staying well
Discovering and protecting a deeper past

passages.text: Afghanistan’s modern history grew out of the Durrani realm founded in 1747 and its gradual contraction into a territorial state. This card follows a country through changing monarchies, republics and Taliban governments. It also follows the people who baked bread, taught children, cared for patients and protected collections through those changes. The map’s 1783 start is a coverage date, not the country’s founding.

passages.title: A changing country on a coarse map
passages.text: The map’s Afghanistan outline changes sharply: its 1783 and 1800 snapshots extend much farther west or east than its later outline. One later snapshot covers 1960 to 1994, crossing several governments. These shapes cannot show every change of control, and the imported name “Islamic State of Afghanistan” fits only part of this long history.

passages.title: A changing country on a coarse map
passages.text: Ahmad Shah Durrani established his realm in 1747. At its height it reached from Central Asia toward the Indian Ocean and northern India, but tribute and allegiance did not make every district equally obedient. Sikh expansion, local resistance and succession struggles weakened this enormous inheritance.

passages.title: A changing country on a coarse map
passages.text: Abdur Rahman’s reign, from 1880 to 1901, strengthened central power through troops, taxation and controls on local leaders. This came at a severe human cost: campaigns in Hazarajat caused repression and exile, while the conquest of Kafiristan imposed conversion to Islam and the new name Nuristan.

passages.title: A changing country on a coarse map
passages.text: State-building also brought roads, bridges, caravanserais and small industries employing foreign technical specialists. A public clinic opened in 1895. These changes were concentrated in Kabul, so a new machine or clinic in the capital did not mean every village suddenly had one.

passages.title: A changing country on a coarse map
passages.text: After the Third Anglo-Afghan War, the 1919 settlement secured independence in foreign affairs. Amanullah introduced a constitution in 1923, but resistance to his reforms helped force his abdication in 1929. Independence and domestic agreement were very different achievements.

passages.title: A changing country on a coarse map
passages.text: In 2001 a United States-led campaign against al-Qaeda and the Taliban removed the first Taliban government. The internationally supported government that followed made uneven gains while a Taliban insurgency continued. In August 2021, as foreign forces withdrew and government forces collapsed, the Taliban entered Kabul and President Ashraf Ghani fled.

passages.title: Books, classrooms and a Persian writing sample
passages.text: Writing history was itself political work. Fayz Muhammad compiled Siraj al-Tawarikh in Kabul under Emir Habibullah’s supervision. Its early volumes covered earlier rulers; the third drew closely on government orders, letters and documents. Such books preserve valuable evidence while also showing what a ruler allowed an author to say.

passages.title: Books, classrooms and a Persian writing sample
passages.text: A short Persian writing sample is the title سراج التواریخ, transliterated Sirāj al-tawārīkh, meaning “Lamp of history.” This is modern typesetting of the title in Fayz Muhammad’s early-1910s history, also visible in the Library of Congress text. It is a dated example of written Persian used for Afghan history, among Afghanistan’s many languages.

passages.title: Books, classrooms and a Persian writing sample
passages.text: One small schoolbook makes education tangible: the Library of Congress holds a 28-page Persian Islamic-education textbook prepared for Afghan elementary pupils. Its catalog tentatively dates the Lahore printing to about 1913 and records approval by Afghan religious and education authorities. School knowledge could travel across a border in a very thin book.

passages.title: Books, classrooms and a Persian writing sample
passages.text: The Islamic Republic’s 2004 constitution recognized gender equality and reserved parliamentary seats for women. UN Women reports that women held 69 of 249 parliamentary seats by 2021. These were institutions of that former republic; the change of government later that year profoundly altered women’s public lives.

passages.title: Books, classrooms and a Persian writing sample
passages.text: UNESCO reported in August 2026 that about 2.4 million girls were excluded from secondary education under Taliban restrictions, while women were barred from university. Nearly one million girls had been enrolled in secondary education in 2021. This reversal concerns real classrooms, friendships and ambitions, not just a number on a chart.

passages.title: Books, classrooms and a Persian writing sample
passages.text: Learning efforts continued under these restrictions. UNESCO’s August 2026 account describes community literacy, skills classes and psychosocial support, while emphasizing that these alternatives cannot replace normal access to school. The primary-school examples below therefore should not be mistaken for evidence that older girls could freely continue their education.

passages.title: Homes, hospitality and skilled hands
passages.text: Nancy Hatch Dupree’s 1993 account links hospitality and family celebrations with cooking, while stressing regional diversity and the simplicity of many everyday meals. A feast for guests could be much more elaborate than supper on an ordinary evening. Bread and sweetened black or green tea were central staples in her account.

passages.title: Homes, hospitality and skilled hands
passages.text: Bread did not always need a kitchen oven. Dupree describes dough baked against a clay oven’s walls, nomadic groups using a curved iron griddle, and shepherds wrapping dough around heated stones beside a fire. A hot rock could be useful cooking equipment, though rather awkward to put in a kitchen drawer.

passages.title: Homes, hospitality and skilled hands
passages.text: Food could also express thanks. Dupree describes sweets distributed after prayers were answered and rice dishes given to people visiting religious shrines. Some shrines kept enormous cooking vessels and employed cooks for these gatherings. These are documented late-twentieth-century practices, not a claim that every Afghan household observed the same customs.

passages.title: Homes, hospitality and skilled hands
passages.text: Restorers in Kabul’s Murad Khani district had to remove so much accumulated garbage that street levels fell by as much as two metres. Some families had been confined to upper floors. As the debris came out, old houses reappeared: restoring a neighborhood began with the decidedly unglamorous work of hauling rubbish.

passages.title: Homes, hospitality and skilled hands
passages.text: Murad Khani’s nineteenth-century courtyards also became classrooms for craft. Turquoise Mountain reports training builders in woodwork and mud plaster, restoring carved cedar panels, and converting buildings into a library and spaces for ceramics, calligraphy and miniature painting. One restored serai received a UNESCO conservation award in 2013.

passages.title: Care, water and the everyday work of staying well
passages.text: In a 2015 WHO report, Dr Aziza worked as a midwife in a mobile clinic serving 450 displaced families in Kabul’s Nasaji-Bagrami camp. The clinic was operated by an Afghan organization, SHRDO. Her account describes more women seeking family-planning and hygiene advice: medical care included conversation and trust as well as treatment.

passages.title: Care, water and the everyday work of staying well
passages.text: At Malik Sheer Ahmed school in Logar, a teacher recalled children leaving to relieve themselves in fields or missing lessons to fetch water. UNICEF’s July 2025 report describes new toilets and handwashing facilities. Six-year-old Malika especially liked having soap and a place to wash indoors. A usable school toilet can be an educational improvement.

passages.title: Care, water and the everyday work of staying well
passages.text: In Bamyan’s Qafila Bashi village, a 2025 water project supplied a reservoir for 130 households, with taps shared by four or five families. Safoora’s children, Zahra and Abdul Ahad, could attend primary school without the old task of fetching water from a stream four kilometres away. Household chores and classroom time were closely connected.

passages.title: Discovering and protecting a deeper past
passages.text: In 1978, excavators at Tillya Tepe uncovered six richly furnished ancient graves. Among the finds was a first-century CE gold crown that could be folded for transport. The discovery belongs to modern archaeological history; the crown belongs to people who lived long before the modern Afghan state. Royal luggage apparently needed practical solutions too.

passages.title: Discovering and protecting a deeper past
passages.text: Museum workers later protected important collections by moving objects into safer storage and keeping valuable pieces hidden. Their survival was publicly announced in 2003; authentication and inventory followed in 2004. The Art Gallery of New South Wales records the work of Afghan curators and archaeologists alongside foreign specialists. Preservation was an achievement of people, not only institutions.

passages.title: Discovering and protecting a deeper past
passages.text: That survival was incomplete. A rocket attack badly damaged the National Museum in 1993, and looting removed many objects and records. In 2001 the Taliban destroyed museum sculptures and the great Bamiyan Buddhas. Conservators later helped reassemble damaged pieces; an old fragment could become evidence again instead of remaining rubble.

Afghanistan continues through changes of government. The Islamic Republic collapsed in August 2021 and the Taliban returned to power; that political ending did not mean the disappearance of Afghanistan’s people.

sectionTitles: Communities and families around the map’s period
Earlier Ife: skilled makers and food discoveries
Floors, rain and a family’s archaeological site

passages.text: The imported label “Africa” is misleading: this 1783 to 1815 outline covers a small area of southwestern Nigeria containing Ife and Ondo, not the continent. It does not identify one kingdom or people. This card offers selected local histories, with earlier archaeology and later community evidence clearly dated. Neighboring Oyo, Benin, Lagos and Ijebu histories remain distinct.

passages.title: Communities and families around the map’s period
passages.text: Ondo incorporated older communities rather than starting with an empty landscape. Nolte’s study describes Idoko, a settlement that retained its identity within the city, and compares Ife’s traditions of conquest and negotiation among earlier settlements. A town could contain several histories of belonging.

passages.title: Communities and families around the map’s period
passages.text: Family connections could change a town’s celebrations. A tradition discussed by Nolte links Ondo’s Eku festival to Terere’s reign, 1770 to 1795, and to his mother’s home at Ile-Oluji. Mothers brought knowledge and practices into royal households; their influence could reach beyond the household walls.

passages.title: Communities and families around the map’s period
passages.text: Nwaokoro’s historical account describes Ondo markets selling farm produce, chickens, goats, locally made textiles, oil and pottery. People carried goods on foot, sometimes using enslaved labor. The account does not provide trade volumes or date every practice precisely; it shows the range of work behind a market, rather than a fixed shopping list for 1783.

passages.title: Communities and families around the map’s period
passages.text: That history also connects eighteenth-century Ondo traders, including women, with slave trading near the coast at Okitipupa. Enslaved people were exchanged for goods including salt, beads and cloth. Commerce brought useful materials, but also depended on coercion and the breaking of families; it cannot be described only as prosperity.

passages.title: Earlier Ife: skilled makers and food discoveries
passages.text: Centuries before this map window, Igbo Olokun at Ife was a glassworking center. Excavations in 2011 and 2012 recovered almost 13,000 glass beads and more than 800 glass-lined crucible fragments. Charcoal dates placed the investigated deposits between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries. Workshop waste can be just as revealing as a finished jewel.

passages.title: Earlier Ife: skilled makers and food discoveries
passages.text: Chemical analysis found distinctive glass rich in lime and alumina, consistent with a local recipe using regional raw materials. This supports making glass from ingredients, rather than only reshaping imported glass. The evidence concerns medieval Ife; it does not prove that the same workshops were still operating in 1800.

passages.title: Earlier Ife: skilled makers and food discoveries
passages.text: A 2024 study identified 48 wheat grains from a medieval Ife pit. Direct dating places the wheat broadly in the late thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. Researchers argue that it was imported because local growing conditions were unsuitable. They suggest porridge-like preparations as a possibility, but no surviving recipe tells us exactly what dinner looked like.

passages.title: Earlier Ife: skilled makers and food discoveries
passages.text: The same project found cotton seeds dating to the late twelfth and early thirteenth centuries. Broken seeds and seed coats are consistent with fiber processing. Cotton may have been grown locally or brought in for working into cloth. Tiny charred fragments help reconstruct skilled textile work that usually leaves little surviving fabric.

passages.title: Floors, rain and a family’s archaeological site
passages.text: At Lujumo Compound in Ife, excavators in 2022 found three successive levels of pavement made from pottery fragments. The earlier deposits date to the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Broken pots could become patterned surfaces underfoot: a household object might have a second life as part of the ground.

passages.title: Floors, rain and a family’s archaeological site
passages.text: Such pavements helped protect surfaces from erosion in heavy tropical rain. Their different patterns may also have marked social or ritual spaces. This is evidence of managing the built environment, although it does not establish a citywide sewer network or tell us where every household’s toilet was.

passages.title: Floors, rain and a family’s archaeological site
passages.text: The excavation lay under a ruined family house, probably built in the late nineteenth century. The building had protected medieval layers while exposed ground nearby eroded. Family memories and photographs could therefore be studied alongside archaeology. Surprisingly, a later house helped preserve a much older neighborhood beneath it.

passages.title: Knowledge, language and later changes
passages.text: Nwaokoro’s 2013 account records girls learning to sweep rooms and kitchens, fetch water and care for younger children. Toys called omolangi helped them practice carrying a baby on the back. This describes remembered training, not a dated observation from 1783.

passages.title: Knowledge, language and later changes
passages.text: UNESCO’s modern account of Ifa describes a living Yoruba knowledge tradition organized into 256 odu, with verses recited by specialists. Palm nuts or a divining chain generate signs that guide interpretation. Learning includes remembering and performing poetry. This describes a continuing tradition, not an excavated eighteenth-century classroom or an alphabet used by everyone.

passages.title: Knowledge, language and later changes
passages.text: Here is a small written-language example: “ìdímì”, an Ondo Yoruba word for town quarters or wards, printed in Nolte’s study first published in 2025. It uses modern Latin-based Yoruba spelling. This is a documented regional term, not an inscription dated to 1783 or a language sample for all Africa.

passages.title: Knowledge, language and later changes
passages.text: After this map ends, new commercial routes changed eastern Yoruba communities. Akintoye’s study explains how the Ondo Road, developed from around 1870, stimulated farming and local manufacture and brought mission stations and schools. A transport route could alter both a family’s work and the kinds of education available nearby.

passages.title: Knowledge, language and later changes
passages.text: School access remained unequal. Nwaokoro’s study places the start of Western-style schooling in Ondo in 1875 and reports that girls made up less than one fifth of primary pupils through 1906. This later school system did not begin all learning: family instruction and specialist knowledge had their own histories.

Nothing called an “Africa civilization” ended in 1815. The date only closes this imported map record. The communities discussed here continued through later changes in trade, colonial authority and education, and Yoruba traditions remain living practices. Those changes belong to distinct local and regional histories, not a single continental rise and fall.

sectionTitles: Architecture and the work of skilled makers

passages.text: The Aghlabids governed Ifriqiya, centred on Kairouan in present-day Tunisia, while acknowledging the Abbasid caliph. Their court, towns and Mediterranean connections supported distinctive architecture, craftsmanship and learning.

passages.title: Water engineering for daily needs
passages.text: Kairouan’s reservoirs receive runoff and water from tributaries of the Merguellil valley. Water first enters a settling basin, then passes through an outlet into a larger storage basin and covered cisterns. The sequence separates sediment removal from storage and drawing, showing how the builders organized a practical response to unreliable rainfall.

passages.title: Water engineering for daily needs
passages.text: Rubble masonry, thick plaster and buttresses helped the basins retain water and withstand its pressure. The heritage account explains their use for people facing shortages, including poorer residents, as well as caravans and livestock. Public storage supplemented household wells and cisterns rather than replacing every private supply.

passages.title: Architecture and the work of skilled makers
passages.text: The Great Mosque’s pillared prayer hall reuses Roman and Byzantine columns and capitals. New arrangements brought older building materials into an Islamic place of worship. A fluted dome and carved supports emphasize the area before the mihrab, showing that reuse and new design were combined rather than being separate architectural choices.

passages.title: Architecture and the work of skilled makers
passages.text: The mihrab combines carved marble, painted wood and lustre-glazed ceramic tiles. These different surfaces create a layered setting for prayer. The catalogue links the ninth-century tiles with Iraq; the building also contains later restorations, so not every surviving feature should be attributed to Aghlabid builders.

passages.title: Architecture and the work of skilled makers
passages.text: Raqqada museum’s teak fragment BS 200 came from the Great Mosque’s minbar, the preacher’s pulpit. Its carved vine leaves and grape clusters belonged to the stair’s upper edge. Joining separately carved components produced an elaborate furnishing whose craftsmanship served the weekly act of public preaching.

passages.title: Architecture and the work of skilled makers
passages.text: The fragment is dated through historical accounts and comparison with other ninth-century decoration. Its workshop remains debated: references to Baghdad do not settle where it was carved. Removal during restoration around 1920 explains how this component entered the museum record; it was not excavated from Raqqada’s palaces.

passages.title: Ceramics, inscriptions and exchange
passages.text: Bowl C 34, recovered at Raqqada, combines green, brown and yellow glaze with repeated kufic lettering for al-Mulk, or sovereignty. Its surface shows how calligraphy could become part of vessel decoration. The catalogue associates the colours with copper, manganese and antimony or iron compounds, connecting the appearance to material choices.

passages.title: Ceramics, inscriptions and exchange
passages.text: The bowl is usually assigned to the late ninth-century Aghlabid repertoire, but its 1960s excavation lacked a detailed record. Similar forms and techniques continued under the Fatimids. Style therefore supports an approximate attribution, while the missing archaeological context prevents a securely dated manufacturing year.

passages.title: Ceramics, inscriptions and exchange
passages.text: Gold dinar M 200 carries the date 192 AH, rendered by the museum as 808 CE. Its kufic inscriptions include the dynastic emblem ghalaba within a layout related to Abbasid coinage. Unlike a vessel dated mainly by style, this coin contains direct written evidence for its issue date.

passages.title: Ceramics, inscriptions and exchange
passages.text: The museum attributes the dinar to Kairouan and describes Aghlabid gold coinage circulating in Mediterranean commerce. That connects a small object with government and exchange. The catalogue does not provide this specimen’s excavation findspot, so its present museum location cannot reconstruct a particular merchant’s route.

passages.title: Learning, livelihoods and political change
passages.text: Sahnun’s compilation of Maliki teachings in the Mudawwana became a major reference for North African law. Kairouan’s scholarship was an achievement alongside its buildings and objects.

passages.title: Learning, livelihoods and political change
passages.text: Farmers and artisans supplied grain, olive oil and textiles to exchange networks. Those networks also trafficked enslaved people across the Mediterranean and Sahara. Prosperity depended on unequal relationships as well as productive work.

The Fatimids conquered Aghlabid Ifriqiya in 909, ending the dynasty’s rule. Local building practices and infrastructure continued under the new rulers. The map has no Fatimid geometry at 909, so a successor link would give a misleading location for the event.

sectionTitles: Care for country and new enterprises

passages.text: Ewamian people are Traditional Owners around northern Queensland’s Gilbert and Einasleigh rivers. Their history connects river livelihoods, colonial resistance and continuing cultural responsibilities.

passages.title: River livelihoods and material evidence
passages.text: Rivers and lagoons provided food and routes through country. Ewamian accounts describe fish, shellfish, water birds and water plants, with fishing spears, finely woven nets and stone traps. These methods combined knowledge of particular waters with skills in making tools and working fibres.

passages.title: River livelihoods and material evidence
passages.text: At Talaroo Station, Ewamian heritage officers, rangers and an archaeologist recorded scars on Cooktown ironwood trees. Brickey and Buhrich’s 2014 report identifies these as sugarbag scars, made by cutting into heartwood with a stone axe to reach native bees’ honey and wax. The altered living trees preserve evidence of harvesting.

passages.title: River livelihoods and material evidence
passages.text: The same Talaroo survey recorded grinding grooves beside the Einasleigh River, together with fishing places and story places. Their shared landscape links material traces with travel, food and cultural memory. The conference abstract does not date individual grooves or identify everything ground there, so those details remain unspecified.

passages.title: Names, records and language renewal
passages.text: Agwarmin is the imported map spelling. The State Library lists Agwamin, Wamin and other related names, while noting disagreement over whether they name a people, a language or dialects. Ewamian is the community’s own organizational spelling. A shared label should not erase these distinctions.

passages.title: Names, records and language renewal
passages.text: Language documentation survives in records associated with Tindale, Sutton and Roth, but the State Library describes the evidence as limited. Its 2020 account also identifies community revival with Pama Language Centre. Archival survival and renewed teaching are separate parts of the language’s history; an old speaker assessment is not a current census.

passages.title: Names, records and language renewal
passages.text: Ewamian rangers organize language workshops and camps on country with Elders and young people. This work places language learning beside the identification and protection of cultural sites. Knowledge is passed through relationships and activities as well as through written records.

passages.title: Displacement, rights and collective decisions
passages.text: The community’s history records resistance to miners at Gilberton and later dispossession as more miners and pastoralists arrived. Elders were forced onto missions and reserves. Work as ringers, cooks and domestic workers could keep people on their cultural estate, but did not undo the loss of control over land.

passages.title: Displacement, rights and collective decisions
passages.text: The 2013 determination recognized continuing native title rights. The community explains these through activities including access, camping, fishing, gathering, teaching and caring for important places. Different rights apply to different land interests; recognition should not be described as unrestricted ownership of every parcel in the region.

passages.title: Displacement, rights and collective decisions
passages.text: Ewamian People Aboriginal Corporation represents native title holders, but decisions affecting rights require agreement by the holders at community meetings. This is a living institution for collective responsibility. Its role connects land negotiations with the authority of the wider community.

passages.title: Care for country and new enterprises
passages.text: At Talaroo Hot Springs, ranger work includes removing damaging infrastructure to restore natural water flows and controlling weeds. Elsewhere, prescribed burns protect ecological and cultural places, and surveys guide heritage management. These are specific applications of environmental knowledge, supported by monitoring and collaboration with park managers.

passages.title: Care for country and new enterprises
passages.text: Talaroo is managed as an Indigenous Protected Area and a nature refuge. The community combines protection of important habitats with compatible uses and economic aspirations. Different management zones permit different activities, allowing conservation responsibilities and community needs to be considered together.

passages.title: Care for country and new enterprises
passages.text: The CSIRO collaboration assessed natural and cultural resources against Ewamian enterprise aspirations. Its tasks included choosing development pathways, preparing investment prospectuses and producing guidance for other Indigenous groups. The achievement lies in linking technical assessment to community priorities; an assessment alone does not prove that every proposed business was established.

Ewamian people continue to care for country and exercise recognized rights through community institutions. Native title recognition and collective governance document this continuity. The map’s final snapshot in 1815 is not an extinction or conquest date.

sectionTitles: What records preserve and leave out

passages.text: The Ahantchuyuk, also called the Pudding River or French Prairie people, were a Kalapuya community in Oregon’s Willamette Valley. Champoeg connected their food gathering, travel and exchange with neighbouring peoples.

passages.title: Food, movement and practical knowledge
passages.text: Families moved seasonally between food sources, including camas prairies and acorn-gathering areas. Yampah grew near Champoeg. David Lewis’s reconstruction also describes trade for preserved salmon and lamprey at the falls. Food knowledge included storage and exchange as well as knowing when and where to gather.

passages.title: Food, movement and practical knowledge
passages.text: Alexander Henry’s January 1814 account describes local hunters wearing a deer’s head and imitating the animal’s movements to approach deer. Lewis places this observation in Ahantchuyuk country. It records skill in reading animal behaviour, but remains a visitor’s account of a particular encounter rather than a complete description of every hunt.

passages.title: Food, movement and practical knowledge
passages.text: Grand Ronde Elder Greg Archuleta explains that Kalapuya cooks baked camas bulbs, mashed them into cakes and dried them for storage and trade. Prolonged cooking changes the bulbs’ inulin. This account connects food processing with portable provisions; it describes a broader Kalapuya practice rather than an excavated Ahantchuyuk household.

passages.title: Food, movement and practical knowledge
passages.text: Archuleta’s account also connects plant management with basketry: flexible hazel supplied useful material, while seed fans and baskets helped harvest tarweed. Such technologies depended on selecting suitable plants and maintaining productive gathering places. The account concerns regional traditions and does not establish identical methods in every village.

passages.title: What records preserve and leave out
passages.text: The Grand Ronde Reservation log book, catalogued as Mss555_F3, includes a March 1856 census naming the French Prairie band. It lists household heads and family sizes alongside other communities. This is concrete evidence of people living after removal, not support for treating the map’s 1500 endpoint as their disappearance.

passages.title: What records preserve and leave out
passages.text: The same volume records supplies issued to arriving households and property left by earlier settlers. These accounts reveal the administrative organization of reservation life. Their scope is limited: a government distribution ledger cannot by itself describe all household food, possessions, work or continuing cultural practices.

passages.title: What records preserve and leave out
passages.text: The 1855 treaty text promises payments, clothing, provisions, tools and agricultural support, with a physician, teacher and blacksmith after removal. Reading its clauses shows what the United States undertook to provide. The promises should be distinguished from what families actually received and from their own existing skills.

passages.title: What records preserve and leave out
passages.text: The treaty also allowed land to be divided into household allotments and tied continued possession to residence and cultivation. These provisions sought to reorganize land use and work under federal supervision. They help explain why removal meant a transformation of institutions as well as a change of location.

passages.title: Continuity, restoration and renewed access
passages.text: Grand Ronde families remained connected after termination. Tribal leaders organized, raised funds and testified before Congress to restore federal recognition, achieved in 1983. This was the work of the wider confederation, within which Ahantchuyuk history continues. The campaign restored legal recognition of an existing community.

passages.title: Continuity, restoration and renewed access
passages.text: Yampah has been restored at Champoeg with Tribal input, according to Archuleta’s public account. Restoring an important food plant makes the site more than a monument to settler government. It connects a named place with continuing knowledge about the plants that supported its earlier community.

passages.title: Continuity, restoration and renewed access
passages.text: The Lifeways program offers cultural classes that recognize the different tribes and bands within Grand Ronde. Reconnecting people with particular homelands and practices is an achievement in teaching and community life. The confederation’s shared institutions do not require every constituent history to be treated as identical.

Removal to Grand Ronde transformed Ahantchuyuk community life. Their history continues within the Confederated Tribes of Grand Ronde. Federal termination in 1954 ended recognition, not the people; recognition was restored in 1983. No historical disappearance in 1500 is established by the map.

sectionTitles: Documents, loss and the defence of continuity

passages.text: Ahé is the self-name of the Karipuna of Rondônia, a Tupi-Kawahib people associated with Brazil’s Jacy-Paraná and Mutum-Paraná rivers. They are distinct from the Karipuna of Amapá.

passages.title: Skills remembered and practised
passages.text: In his 2022 oral-history interview, Adriano Karipuna recalls learning to make arrows and catching fish with them as a child. His mother roasted the catch and kept it in banana or babassu leaves for the next day. The recollection connects skilled fishing, household food preparation and avoiding waste.

passages.title: Skills remembered and practised
passages.text: Adriano also remembers a palm-thatched house near the river. He describes the roof’s cool interior alongside its need for regular replacement as insects weakened the material and rain entered. This is a particular household’s experience of building and maintenance, rather than a claim that every Karipuna house was identical.

passages.title: Skills remembered and practised
passages.text: Forest loss affects more than the availability of food. In the same interview, Adriano explains that clearing and burning destroyed places supplying material for bows and arrows. He still fished with surviving arrows, while making new ones had become difficult. Environmental damage therefore interrupted the practice of a learned craft.

passages.title: Food, work and learning
passages.text: In his 2017 account, Adriano describes fishing, cassava flour, Brazil nuts and açaí as sources of subsistence and income. Produce was sold to buyers in town. The combination shows that forest and river livelihoods could support exchange with urban markets while remaining important to life in the village.

passages.title: Food, work and learning
passages.text: Studying in town brought transport costs, living expenses and racist treatment from classmates, Adriano reports. He described education as a way to gain skills useful to his people. His account makes the journey between village and city part of community history, rather than treating urban residence as the loss of Indigenous identity.

passages.title: Food, work and learning
passages.text: A 2023 field study at Panorama records garden plots and a flour-processing house, with flour used at home and sold in Porto Velho. These working spaces connect cultivation, processing and income. The report also identifies difficulties transporting and packaging produce for sale.

passages.title: Food, work and learning
passages.text: The field study records an Indigenous teacher passing the language to children. Community concerns included aligning school activities with the Brazil-nut harvest. This joins classroom learning with seasonal work, rather than assuming that education happens only inside a school building.

passages.title: Documents, loss and the defence of continuity
passages.text: Funai reports from the 1970s describe visits between the contact post and large communal houses on the Contra and Mutum-Paraná waterways. ISA’s historical account contrasts official descriptions of successful contact with the illnesses and deaths that followed. Administrative records need to be read alongside their consequences for families.

passages.title: Documents, loss and the defence of continuity
passages.text: The 2023 study combined interviews, field notes and questionnaires with community members and health workers. Its findings are a dated account of conditions and priorities, not a timeless description of Karipuna culture or a current census of everyone belonging to the people.

passages.title: Documents, loss and the defence of continuity
passages.text: Greenpeace’s account of its work in 2019 describes combining aerial observations and satellite images with Karipuna reports of invasion. These different forms of evidence made forest clearing visible beyond the territory. They document particular monitoring efforts; a short-term change in clearing does not establish lasting protection.

passages.title: Documents, loss and the defence of continuity
passages.text: Karipuna leaders also spoke in international forums and built solidarity with other Indigenous peoples. These public interventions carried community demands beyond Rondônia. Protecting land, communicating its significance and insisting on continued existence are achievements in political organization as well as responses to danger.

The Karipuna continue as a living people. Recent fieldwork documents food production, language teaching and collective demands, despite invasion and barriers to services. Their recognized territory and continuing community life cannot be reduced to the map’s 1492 to 1500 interval.

sectionTitles: Rulers, families and a contested kingdom
Travel, learning and a small piece of writing
Pictures, memory and the end of independence

passages.text: Ahmadnagar was a major Deccan sultanate ruled by the Nizam Shahi dynasty, conventionally dated 1490 to 1636. Its courts supported painting, scholarship and monumental building. The imported map runs from 1492 to 1700 and repeats a broad outline across several snapshots. That outline cannot represent unchanged borders or continuing Nizam Shahi independence after 1636; later dates belong to Mughal and Maratha history.

passages.title: Rulers, families and a contested kingdom
passages.text: Ahmad Nizam Shah, the dynasty’s founder, ruled around 1490 to 1510. His tomb at Bagh Rauza is a surviving anchor for this early court. Its square chamber, arched openings and decorative niches connect the new dynasty with the architectural traditions of the earlier Bahmani realm.

passages.title: Rulers, families and a contested kingdom
passages.text: Husain Nizam Shah joined the Deccan alliance that defeated Vijayanagara’s forces in January 1565. The illustrated Persian Tarif-i Husain Shahi praised both him and Queen Khanzada Humayun. Historians date it close to that victory because it celebrates the triumph but does not mention Husain’s death a few months later.

passages.title: Rulers, families and a contested kingdom
passages.text: Chand Bibi’s family connected two rival courts. A daughter of Ahmadnagar’s ruler, she married the sultan of Bijapur. After her husband’s murder in 1580, she helped protect a child successor and served as regent. She later returned to Ahmadnagar and became a leader during its struggle against the Mughals.

passages.title: Rulers, families and a contested kingdom
passages.text: Malik Ambar was born in Ethiopia, enslaved and taken through Baghdad before reaching India. After gaining freedom, he rose to command armies and became Ahmadnagar’s effective ruler. His daughter’s marriage to Sultan Murtaza II joined military power to a royal family alliance. His extraordinary career also exposes the coercive trade in people behind some courtly success stories.

passages.title: Water, baths and comfortable buildings
passages.text: The state gazetteer records fifteen Nizam Shahi water channels supplying Ahmadnagar from deep wells near surrounding hills. Builders combined excavated channels with earthen pipes. The Vadgaon supply reached palaces, the Jama Mosque and city wells: keeping a capital alive required much more than a strong fort.

passages.title: Water, baths and comfortable buildings
passages.text: Two conduits from Nepti and Nimbgaon fed a reservoir beside a noble’s audience hall and a nearby hamam, or bath, during Burhan I’s reign. Their broken ends survived side by side inside masonry. Water engineering could support washing as well as display, although this particular evidence describes an elite establishment.

passages.title: Water, baths and comfortable buildings
passages.text: Royal gardens also made room for sociability. The gazetteer associates Murtaza I with playing chess with the singer Fateh Shah at Behisht Bagh and providing him a residence there. Music, companionship and a difficult chess move could all belong to the same courtly afternoon.

passages.title: Water, baths and comfortable buildings
passages.text: Modern analysis of Farah Bagh palace found lime plaster containing broken pottery and brick, together with plant fibers. The researchers suggest these porous materials helped manage moisture and cool the interior. A smashed pot could still have a useful second career in a wall. The proposed cooling function is an interpretation of the materials, not a surviving temperature measurement.

passages.title: Travel, learning and a small piece of writing
passages.text: Nizam Shahi roads had durable directions. A Persian inscription dated 1591 to 1592 records an order to put signposts where roads divided so travelers would not be confused. Another stone at Bir, now Beed, gave the route toward Ahmadnagar in Persian and Marathi. Finding the correct road mattered to people who were not kings, too.

passages.title: Travel, learning and a small piece of writing
passages.text: A small written sample is راه احمدانگر, meaning “road to Ahmadnagar.” It comes from the published Persian transcription of the Bir direction-stone of 1591 to 1592. The editor notes the unusual spelling of the city’s name. Its Persian line uses Naskh script, while the accompanying Marathi lines use Nagari: one roadside object preserves two written languages.

passages.title: Travel, learning and a small piece of writing
passages.text: Medicine crossed languages at Burhan I’s court. Rostam Gorgani adapted an Arabic work on medicinal substances into Persian and dedicated it to the sultan; another physician translated Ibn Jazla’s medical handbook. Such books helped learned practitioners compare inherited knowledge. They do not establish that every household had access to a court physician.

passages.title: Travel, learning and a small piece of writing
passages.text: Firishta, famous for writing history, also studied medicine with an Indian teacher and compiled a work on Indian medicines, diseases and treatments. He lived in both Ahmadnagar and Bijapur. His career connects personal teaching with book learning, and shows why scholarship at these courts cannot be divided neatly into isolated language traditions.

passages.title: Pictures, memory and the end of independence
passages.text: An Ahmadnagar drawing of a royal picnic, made around 1590 to 1595, includes hunters, a falcon and attendants at an outdoor feast. One servant covers his lower face with cloth. The catalogue suggests this protected the food from pollution. It is a fascinating detail of an elite scene, rather than proof of a universal dining custom.

passages.title: Pictures, memory and the end of independence
passages.text: The Mughals captured Ahmadnagar’s fort in 1600. Malik Ambar and other leaders continued to govern and fight in its remaining territories, supporting Nizam Shahi claimants. Resistance lasted for decades after the capital fell, and the struggle repeatedly changed who could collect revenue and command the kingdom’s surviving forces.

passages.title: Pictures, memory and the end of independence
passages.text: Inscribed rocks at forts in the Satmala hills provide physical evidence of the final campaigns. An archaeological report describes inscriptions dated 1636 that name fourteen captured forts and credit the Mughal commander Allah Vardi Khan Turkman. These are victory records made for conquerors, so their confident voice belongs to the victorious side.

passages.title: Pictures, memory and the end of independence
passages.text: After the 1636 settlement, the Mughals joined the governments of Ahmadnagar and Khandesh and appointed Aurangzeb viceroy. During the following decades, Shahaji’s son Shivaji built a competing Maratha power in the region. The city, its inhabitants and its waterworks belonged to this changing political landscape long after Nizam Shahi sovereignty ended.

passages.title: Pictures, memory and the end of independence
passages.text: Chand Bibi’s memory outlived her kingdom. A Deccan painting made around 1700 shows her hawking with attendants, about a century after her death. Its confident rider celebrates an admired woman ruler. The picture records later remembrance, so it should not be mistaken for an eyewitness portrait of her daily outings.

Ahmadnagar lost its capital to the Mughals in 1600, while resistance continued elsewhere. In 1636, Shahaji surrendered the remaining Nizam Shahi claimant and entered Bijapur’s service as Mughal conquest and settlement ended the sultanate. Its communities continued under subsequent governments. The imported 1700 cutoff is a map boundary, not the dynasty’s historical ending.

passages.text: Ahtna communities continue to care for their lands and waters in Alaska. Their history connects skilled fishing and copper working with living Tribal institutions, resource stewardship and the transmission of knowledge.

passages.title: Tools, materials and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: Excavations at Ringling near Gulkana recovered copper pieces, tools and hearths. The association suggested heating during metalworking; analysis of the metal’s crystal structure subsequently supported annealing. Heating made worked copper easier to shape again, showing a controlled manufacturing technique rather than simply the collection of attractive nuggets.

passages.title: Tools, materials and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: Ringling’s rolled copper cones have several possible explanations. A Gulkana resident described their use as detachable fishing-spear tips; comparable forms could also serve as rattles or unfinished tool components. The finds reveal skilled sheet-metal work, but their shape alone does not settle every object’s purpose.

passages.title: Tools, materials and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: Museum knife 2/2661 is attributed to Ahtna people of the Copper River. Its catalogue records hammered metal and hide, but does not identify the metal as copper. George Heye acquired it around 1909 from an unknown source. The acquisition date therefore cannot establish when it was made or an excavated context.

passages.title: Tools, materials and archaeological discoveries
passages.text: A 1954 photograph identifies a dip net made by Grandma McKinley for Tenas Charley at Copper Center. Willow and spruce roots formed its frame and mesh. The record preserves a named maker and the practical transformation of plant materials into fishing equipment.

passages.title: Seasonal work and changing access
passages.text: Ben Neeley’s childhood recollections describe summer salmon fishing on the Copper River followed by travel toward Tangle Lakes for large-game hunting. Winter trapping and spring fishing and trapping fitted into a seasonal round. Movement linked different food sources rather than indicating an absence of established homes and knowledge.

passages.title: Seasonal work and changing access
passages.text: Miller’s winter-access study used interviews with experienced Copper River Basin residents, including Ahtna trappers. Most recalled more reliable river ice in earlier decades. Shorter periods of usable ice could reduce access to trapping grounds and other resources. This is a study of particular people’s observations, not a forecast of safe crossing conditions.

passages.title: Seasonal work and changing access
passages.text: Interviewees described variable snow, wetter conditions and thicker brush affecting winter routes. Miller also records changes in employment and transport. These factors worked together: altered trapping patterns cannot be explained by temperature alone, and the experiences of selected residents should not be treated as a census of all Ahtna households.

passages.title: Seasonal work and changing access
passages.text: Dry Creek families were forced out for an army airfield in the winter of 1942 to 1943. At Gulkana, road and bridge works divided the village and disrupted fishing. The ethnographic account uses residents’ recollections to recover losses that official construction histories could overlook.

passages.title: Living institutions and new research
passages.text: The Ahtna Intertribal Resource Commission brings together Tribal governments and Native corporation landholders, which are distinct institutions. Its work combines ecological knowledge, research and advocacy for continued access to subsistence resources. Organization across communities makes knowledge useful in collective decisions about fish, wildlife and plants.

passages.title: Living institutions and new research
passages.text: At Tanada Creek, a seasonal weir guides salmon through a camera-equipped passage before they continue upstream. Staff record passage and maintain the structure through the run. Repeated observations help track abundance and timing, making everyday fieldwork part of long-term stewardship and Tribal participation in management.

passages.title: Living institutions and new research
passages.text: The Tanada project also collects ear stones, or otoliths, from sockeye carcasses at Tanada Lake. Their growth layers help researchers estimate fish ages. Combining age information with counts offers a fuller picture of the returning population than either measurement alone. This is a documented research method, not an ancient archaeological find.

Ahtna people and Tribal institutions continue. Contemporary resource stewardship expresses ongoing relationships with the land. The map’s 1492 to 1500 interval does not establish an ending or a disappearance.

passages.text: The atlas’s Annam record covers 1000 to 1100, followed by Đại Việt from 1100 to 1815. These labels join a history of successive Vietnamese courts, beginning here with Early Lê and Lý rule; they do not name one unchanged dynasty. The medieval outline broadly covers northern and central Vietnam, but its southern edge is not a verified frontier for every year. Later outlines also conceal rival governments, especially after 1530. Colonial-era Annam is a separate record. Events and objects below retain their own dates.

passages.title: The earlier Annam window: 1000 to 1100
passages.text: At the start of this map window, the Early Lê court ruled from Hoa Lư. Lý Công Uẩn’s accession in 1009 began a new dynasty. Royal succession could transform the court without creating a new population. The name Đại Cồ Việt continued until the adoption of Đại Việt in 1054.

passages.title: The earlier Annam window: 1000 to 1100
passages.text: In 1010, Lý Thái Tổ moved his capital from Hoa Lư to Đại La, renamed Thăng Long. The heritage authority reconstructs a river journey through connected waterways toward the Red River. Moving a government involved boats as well as buildings: the exhibition follows a travel route, not just an arrow between two dots.

passages.title: The earlier Annam window: 1000 to 1100
passages.text: Vietnamese rulers exchanged tribute, envoys and titles with the Song court while maintaining their own government. These relationships could alternate with armed conflict. A title bestowed by a neighboring emperor expressed a diplomatic hierarchy; it should not be confused with Song officials routinely running the Lý kingdom’s towns.

passages.title: The earlier Annam window: 1000 to 1100
passages.text: The Temple of Literature was founded in 1070, a court examination followed in 1075, and the Imperial Academy was established in 1076. Learning could open a route into royal service. These institutions were major developments in elite education, not evidence that every child attended school or sat an examination.

passages.title: The earlier Annam window: 1000 to 1100
passages.text: A short line in the capital-relocation edict attributed to Lý Thái Tổ in 1010 reads 其地廣而坦平: “Its land is broad and level.” The Sino-Vietnamese reading is Kỳ địa quảng nhi thản bình. This Classical Chinese text explains a choice of site. Here it follows a modern institutional edition of a transmitted work, not a surviving document in the king’s own handwriting.

passages.title: Capitals, wars and changing governments
passages.text: The name Đại Việt was adopted under Lý Thánh Tông in 1054, within the earlier Annam map interval. It survived several dynastic changes, although the Hồ rulers used Đại Ngu. A familiar country name could outlast a ruling family; it should not make the many changes of government disappear.

passages.title: Capitals, wars and changing governments
passages.text: Thăng Long’s Lý citadel was built on reclaimed ground in the Red River Delta, above remains of an earlier Chinese fortress. Excavations at 18 Hoàng Diệu reveal successive layers of buildings and objects. Archaeologists have to separate those layers: a seventh-century foundation and an eleventh-century palace tell different chapters of the same place.

passages.title: Capitals, wars and changing governments
passages.text: In 1288, Trần commanders helped defeat a Yuan invasion by attacking its food supply and using the tidal waterways. The invaders temporarily occupied Thăng Long, but their retreating fleet met obstacles and ambushes on the Bạch Đằng River. The historical account describes submerged stakes exposed as the tide fell. Geography and supplies mattered as much as fighting strength.

passages.title: Capitals, wars and changing governments
passages.text: After Ming occupation, Lê Lợi’s forces negotiated the withdrawal of the opposing army at Đông Quan in late 1427. The agreement included provisions for food, horses and boats so troops could leave. The last contingent departed in early 1428, and the Lê dynasty followed. The resolution involved negotiation and transport as well as battlefield victory.

passages.title: Capitals, wars and changing governments
passages.text: The Mạc replaced the Lê court in 1527, but later Lê and Nguyễn histories often treated the Mạc as illegitimate usurpers. Museum historian Nguyễn Ngọc Chất points out that even hostile accounts preserve evidence of their examinations and administration. A dynasty’s reputation depends partly on who wrote its history afterward.

passages.title: Capitals, wars and changing governments
passages.text: Trịnh lords ruled the north in the Lê kings’ name, while Nguyễn lords governed the south. Warfare from 1627 to 1672 left a lasting division near the Gianh River. Tây Sơn forces overthrew Trịnh power in 1786; their leader Nguyễn Huệ, Emperor Quang Trung, defeated a Qing intervention in 1789. These upheavals were far more complicated than the map’s single colored outline.

passages.title: Water, dishes and skilled hands
passages.text: Lý builders reused earlier wells at Thăng Long rather than starting every water supply from scratch. Archaeologists recognized Lý bricks above older well structures. That is a practical household lesson on a royal scale: if a useful well is already there, rebuilding the whole thing may be unnecessary. These finds come from the palace area, not a survey of every village.

passages.title: Water, dishes and skilled hands
passages.text: Trần-period wells at the citadel used bricks arranged diagonally in a herringbone pattern. The interlocking arrangement held the lining together without mortar. Some much smaller wells are interpreted by the heritage authority as ritual features rather than drinking-water sources. Shape and construction help archaeologists ask what a feature was actually for.

passages.title: Water, dishes and skilled hands
passages.text: Potters working at Thăng Long made glazed vessels as well as architectural materials. Among the workshop waste preserved by the National Museum are bowls and plates fused together during firing. A stuck stack could be a potter’s disappointment and an archaeologist’s lucky find: it locates the work of making things, not just their later use.

passages.title: Water, dishes and skilled hands
passages.text: An eleventh- to fourteenth-century white-glazed bowl in the museum’s study measures 16.5 centimeters across and has raised plant decoration inside. Five small support marks remain in its bowl. Such traces preserve how objects were supported in the kiln. Even an attractive dish can carry the fingerprints of its manufacturing process, although these are firing marks rather than actual fingers.

passages.title: Water, dishes and skilled hands
passages.text: A fifteenth- or sixteenth-century Vietnamese dish in Singapore’s Asian Civilisations Museum shows a duck flying among water reeds, painted in cobalt blue beneath the glaze. Vietnamese ceramics reached buyers in places now called Indonesia, the Philippines and Malaysia. A familiar bird could travel across the sea on a plate, carried through trading networks far beyond its maker’s workshop.

passages.title: Water, dishes and skilled hands
passages.text: Palace excavations also revealed drainage in Lý-period layers, alongside wells and building foundations. Water had to be brought into a busy royal complex and carried away again. These are tangible traces of managing a built environment; the identified drains alone do not establish that houses throughout the kingdom had toilets.

passages.title: Water, dishes and skilled hands
passages.text: Betel-chewing utensils offer another glimpse of social life. The museum exhibition includes lime containers, trays and spittoons, and identifies surviving equipment from the Lý period onward. Later traditions connect betel with hospitality and weddings, but the objects should not make every later ceremony an eleventh-century custom. A small container can be evidence of conversation as well as craftsmanship.

passages.title: Examinations and a voice carved in stone
passages.text: At Hanoi’s Temple of Literature, 82 stone steles record royal examinations held from 1442 to 1779. They were erected between 1484 and 1780, so the date of an examination is not always the date its stone was carved. Their inscriptions preserve successful candidates, examiners and the officials who prepared the monuments. The Tiến sĩ qualification belonged to this historical examination system.

passages.title: Examinations and a voice carved in stone
passages.text: A small writing sample is “人才國家之元氣,” meaning “talented people are the vital force of the state.” This is Classical Chinese in the scholarly transcription of Đào Cử’s inscription for the 1463 examination, carved in 1484. The phrase explains why the ruler should cultivate talent. It is an official written language here, not a claim that ordinary conversation sounded like the inscription.

passages.title: Examinations and a voice carved in stone
passages.text: That same inscription remembers about 1,400 candidates and 44 selected scholars in the 1463 examination. Names were announced and displayed, and successful candidates received clothing and a banquet. Passing was a public achievement, not merely a private mark on a sheet of paper. The inscription also warns graduates to live up to their reputations and serve the people.

passages.title: Later port households and medical learning
passages.text: Hội An’s historic townscape preserves a clever arrangement for merchant households: buildings faced the street for customers and opened toward the river behind for loading boats. Timber houses stood close together, alongside markets and family worship buildings. The surviving pattern reflects the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, though many structures were repaired or renewed in the nineteenth. The river was effectively a delivery entrance.

passages.title: Later port households and medical learning
passages.text: The eighteenth-century physician Lê Hữu Trác came from a scholarly family, but left military life and returned to care for his elderly mother and his brother’s orphaned children. He became known as Hải Thượng Lãn Ông, the “lazy old man” of Hải Thượng. The nickname described his rejection of the race for status, rather than a lack of effort in studying and treating patients.

passages.title: Later port households and medical learning
passages.text: Lê Hữu Trác taught students who copied his medical writings by hand. His collected work covered childbirth, children’s illnesses, eye problems, injuries and medical ethics, alongside other subjects. He also organized opportunities for practitioners to exchange experience. These manuscripts reveal a culture of medical learning and concern for families; listing a historical treatment does not establish that it worked.

The Annam record’s 1100 endpoint falls within continuing Lý rule, not a conquest or disappearance. In the longer sequence, Gia Long reunited the country in 1802 and Việt Nam became the state name in 1804. The Đại Việt record’s 1815 endpoint is another map cutoff during Nguyễn rule. Dynasties, capitals and official names changed while communities, crafts, learning and family life continued.

sectionTitles: Places, records and discoveries about language

passages.text: The Aikanã are a living people of Rondônia, Brazil. Their own name identifies both people and language. Older records use several other names, including Huari, which must not be confused with the distinct Wari people.

passages.title: Making, growing and sharing
passages.text: Vasconcelos describes an elder making bows and different arrows for particular targets, including animals of different sizes and fish. The account records design choices connected to use. It documents a living craft observed during fieldwork, not an excavated weapon or a securely dated practice in 1492.

passages.title: Making, growing and sharing
passages.text: The Aikanã belong to a wider regional network associated with marico bags made from palm-leaf fibres. Transforming leaves into durable carrying equipment required selecting and preparing material as well as skilled construction. Shared technologies link neighbouring peoples without making their languages or identities interchangeable.

passages.title: Making, growing and sharing
passages.text: Regional food practices combine cultivated gardens, hunting and gathering. Chicha is prepared from cultivated or gathered ingredients through processing, fermentation and straining. The documentation project places these practices in a history of intercommunity contact; the regional pattern should not be read as an identical menu for every Aikanã family.

passages.title: Making, growing and sharing
passages.text: Craftwork also enters exchange with the surrounding society. Vasconcelos records ear ornaments, bracelets, necklaces, bags, rings and wooden objects being made for sale. Production for a market is part of the documented history of work and adaptation; it does not make the makers less Aikanã.

passages.title: Places, records and discoveries about language
passages.text: Cascata preserves pottery remains and rock paintings near an old village and burial area, according to Grund. Aikanã memories identify it as a place of residence and meeting. These traces matter alongside oral history, but the article does not date every object or establish that all were made by one people.

passages.title: Places, records and discoveries about language
passages.text: Aikanã and Kwaza are distinct languages with no demonstrated membership in a larger language family. Similar grammatical features can reflect long contact between speakers. Calling a language an isolate describes what has been established about linguistic relationships; it does not mean its speakers lived without neighbours or exchange.

passages.title: Places, records and discoveries about language
passages.text: Aikanã speakers can link a sequence of actions while marking whether the person doing the next action changes. Van der Voort illustrates this with recorded speech and discusses exceptions in narrative use. This detailed grammar is part of the community’s intellectual heritage, rather than evidence that one language is more advanced than another.

passages.title: Places, records and discoveries about language
passages.text: The study prints a story told by Raimunda Dadü Kwã’ĩ at Barroso on May 6, 1996, with linguistic analysis and translation. Naming the narrator, place and recording date makes the evidence traceable. The recording date documents one performance of an older story; it does not date the story’s origin.

passages.title: Teaching and maintaining community knowledge
passages.text: The DOBES project records everyday activities, personal histories, conversations and environmental knowledge, alongside word lists and grammatical work. Its multimedia record recognizes that a language lives in social use. Cooking, building and knowing plants belong in its documentation as much as isolated dictionary entries.

passages.title: Teaching and maintaining community knowledge
passages.text: The 2018 teaching book Nós Kwazá Aikanã was created from cultural-mediator workshops for schools in Kwazá do Rio São Pedro. Named Aikanã and Kwazá authors and illustrators connect community knowledge with climate and territorial education. This is a concrete educational work produced with community participation.

passages.title: Teaching and maintaining community knowledge
passages.text: The same book asks pupils to speak with elders, retell histories and explain pictures. Its authors describe a shared Kwazá Aikanã identity while recognizing different languages and family histories. These exercises make younger learners participants in transmission rather than passive recipients of an account written only by outsiders.

The Aikanã continue despite epidemic losses, forced labour and dispossession. Grund’s fieldwork records living narrators preserving the history of places transformed by colonization. The map’s 1500 endpoint is not a historical disappearance or the end of the people.

sectionTitles: Later documented households, food and practical skills

passages.text: The Ainu are an Indigenous people associated with Hokkaido, Sakhalin, the Kuril Islands and northern Honshu. These three map labels describe regional communities, not a single kingdom. The imported beginning at 4000 BCE and early outlines extending deep into Honshu conflate predecessor archaeology with later Ainu identity. The phases below distinguish that earlier background from medieval Ainu history; the map’s final date of 1715 does not mark the disappearance of Ainu people.

passages.title: Archaeology before the medieval Ainu
passages.text: Okhotsk communities reached Hokkaido from Sakhalin during the fifth century. Their coastal settlements supported fishing and marine hunting, with some pentagonal or hexagonal pit houses more than ten metres long. These are an earlier archaeological setting, rather than a description of every later Ainu household.

passages.title: Archaeology before the medieval Ainu
passages.text: In eighth-century Satsumon settlements near river mouths, people combined salmon and trout fishing with wild plants, millet and barley cultivation. Square pit houses had cooking stoves. Iron tools and smithing skills arriving through exchanges with Honshu changed what people could make and repair.

passages.title: Archaeology before the medieval Ainu
passages.text: Tenth-century Tobinitai pottery combines forms and decoration associated with Okhotsk and Satsumon traditions. Houses also show mixed features. Archaeologists can follow cultural exchange in a cooking pot as well as in a trade route.

passages.title: Archaeology before the medieval Ainu
passages.text: An eighth-century pottery steamer from the Yura site at Iwamizawa had holes in its base and lower sides. Set above a water-filled pot, it let steam rise through cloth to cook grain. Its holes were useful kitchen engineering, not evidence that somebody had broken the bowl.

passages.title: Archaeology before the medieval Ainu
passages.text: The steamer’s discovery has a school connection: in 1959, Sapporo West High School’s local-history club excavated a pit dwelling at Yura. Their find now helps museum researchers investigate how mainland cooking techniques reached Hokkaido more than a thousand years earlier.

passages.title: Medieval exchange, objects and power
passages.text: Between the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries, above-ground dwellings increasingly replaced pit houses, while iron pots and traded lacquerware displaced locally made earthenware. Changes in trade were therefore changes at home too: a household’s cooking equipment could connect it to distant workshops.

passages.title: Medieval exchange, objects and power
passages.text: Japanese-speaking Wajin traders established fortified dwellings called tate in southern Hokkaido. Their growing settlements brought exchange but also threats to Ainu livelihoods and armed conflict. The Kakizaki family, later named Matsumae, consolidated power among these settlers and obtained privileged access to Ainu trade.

passages.title: Medieval exchange, objects and power
passages.text: Ainu traders exchanged salmon and animal pelts for rice, sake and iron goods. Rice entered meals and ceremonies, while Matsumae’s economy depended on the exchange. This was a relationship with valuable goods on both sides, although the domain increasingly imposed unfair terms to increase its profits.

passages.title: Medieval exchange, objects and power
passages.text: Libation sticks called ikupasuy excavated beside the Miyanosawa River at Kaminokuni are dated to the late sixteenth or early seventeenth century. These small ritual objects give archaeologists a tangible connection with Ainu practices during the map’s later centuries.

passages.title: Medieval exchange, objects and power
passages.text: In 1669, a dispute over fishing and hunting rights in Hidaka widened into Shakushain’s resistance against Matsumae oppression. Shakushain was killed at a feast celebrating a peace agreement. His defeat strengthened the domain’s hold; it did not erase Ainu communities or their knowledge.

passages.title: Medieval exchange, objects and power
passages.text: At Tokoro, an Ainu chashi, or fort, occupied a river terrace near the sea around the early eighteenth century. The same archaeological complex also contains much older pit houses. University excavations distinguish these layers: sharing a hill does not make every building the same age.

passages.title: Later documented households, food and practical skills
passages.text: Museum accounts of nineteenth- and early twentieth-century life describe houses with a central hearth and an entrance used for storage. Grass, reed screens and mats covered floors; some homes had low sleeping platforms. Materials and arrangements varied between regions and households.

passages.title: Later documented households, food and practical skills
passages.text: Some households in these later accounts designated an outdoor rubbish area and separated hearth ash and rice bran from other waste. Nearby racks dried fish and meat, and rods held laundry. Keeping a home working required unglamorous jobs as well as skilled craftwork.

passages.title: Later documented households, food and practical skills
passages.text: Later meals commonly combined soup and grain porridge. Wild plants, meat, fish or seaweed could enrich soup; food was dried and stored for winter shortages. Rataskep mixed vegetables, wild plants or beans with oil and salt. Preparation varied with local resources.

passages.title: Later documented households, food and practical skills
passages.text: Fish could provide clothing as well as dinner. In documented later garments, pieces of salmon or trout skin were stitched into clothing with narrow sleeves and a wider hem. Other textiles used soft inner bark from elm or linden trees: the forest supplied fibres as well as firewood.

passages.title: Later documented households, food and practical skills
passages.text: Hokkaido Museum restored a dwelling with guidance from Yaichiro Hama, born in Shiraoi in 1916. Its hearth warmed the earth while reed walls and roofing held in heat. The reconstruction records knowledge carried by a named person, including places for sleeping, sitting and keeping treasured objects.

passages.title: Later documented households, food and practical skills
passages.text: A saranip basket could carry millet, gathered plants or fish. Makers combined tree bark and climbing-plant stems, changing the weave to make different shapes and sizes. The museum’s examples show a practical design problem familiar to any family: how to bring dinner home without dropping it.

passages.title: Stories, written language and teaching
passages.text: Ainu oral literature includes heroic epics, mythic epics and prose tales. A mythic narrator might be an animal or another kamuy, a spiritual being. Such stories teach ways of behaving toward people and the living world; an entertaining tale could also carry serious lessons.

passages.title: Stories, written language and teaching
passages.text: Chiri Yukie, who lived from 1903 to 1922, recorded and translated thirteen mythic epics. Her Ainu Shin’yoshu appeared in 1923 with Roman-letter Ainu and Japanese translations. It preserves a named Ainu author’s work, rather than treating oral tradition as anonymous material without its own interpreters.

passages.title: Stories, written language and teaching
passages.text: A short writing sample from Chiri Yukie’s 1923 collection is “Shirokanipe ranran pishkan”: “Silver droplets fall all around.” It opens the owl spirit’s song. This is the book’s attested Roman-letter Ainu spelling, with an English rendering of its Japanese translation, not an inscription from the ancient map period.

passages.title: Stories, written language and teaching
passages.text: In her preface dated March 1922, Chiri remembered storytelling gatherings on rainy evenings and snowy nights. She wanted readers to know her people through the words inherited from their ancestors. The preface turns a printed book into evidence of family and community transmission.

passages.title: Stories, written language and teaching
passages.text: Ainu was traditionally transmitted through speech; later writers used Roman letters and katakana to record it. Upopoy explains that it is distinct from Japanese. The survival of recordings, books and learners makes language history an ongoing activity, not simply a display of old objects.

passages.title: Stories, written language and teaching
passages.text: For present-day learners, Hokkaido Museum offers coloured blocks that assemble into Ainu sentences. Moving words and grammatical pieces around turns language structure into something a child can handle. These are modern teaching tools, showing one way museums support learning alongside books and performances.

passages.title: Later disruption and continuing communities
passages.text: After the Meiji government renamed Ezochi Hokkaido in 1869, settler expansion and state policies restricted Ainu language, customs, salmon fishing and deer hunting. Loss of land damaged the basis of family livelihoods. These nineteenth-century changes occurred long after the atlas’s 1715 endpoint.

passages.title: Later disruption and continuing communities
passages.text: A photograph from around 1930 records a poster advertising speeches by Ainu young people at Sapporo’s Clock Tower. The poster challenged Japanese prejudice and policies affecting Ainu people. Young people were publicly arguing about their future, not merely preserving memories of the past.

passages.title: Later disruption and continuing communities
passages.text: Living traditions include dance, embroidery, woodcarving and new music. Upopoy describes people recovering dances from older records while also creating new forms. Cultural continuity can involve both careful reconstruction and invention by today’s artists; it does not require every generation to live in the same kind of house.

The map stops in 1715, but Ainu history continues through later coercion, resistance and cultural renewal. Ainu people remain living communities; the National Ainu Museum presents their language, work, exchanges and contemporary perspectives, rather than the remains of an extinct kingdom.
