passages.text: The Appamattuck, also called Appomattoc, lived along the lower Appomattox River in Virginia. They belonged to the core of Powhatan’s paramount chiefdom while maintaining local leaders and communities. River foods, cultivated land, skilled travel and diplomacy shaped their history, which continued through repeated colonial attacks and restrictions.

passages.title: Water, food and ordinary work
passages.text: The Appomattox delta supplied fish such as shad and sturgeon, waterfowl and edible wetland plants. Upland ground provided garden soils, deer and other game. Moving among river, marsh and woodland gave households access to different resources across the seasons; fishing was one part of a broader food system.

passages.title: Water, food and ordinary work
passages.text: Timber from the river’s uplands could become dugout canoes and house frames, while ravines connected freshwater springs with landing places. These details explain how settlement depended on more than fertile fields. Woodworking, water access and routes between houses and river landings were connected parts of everyday life.

passages.title: Water, food and ordinary work
passages.text: A Charles City County payment recorded in 1658 compensated Appomattuck people for killing wolves. This small administrative trace shows hunting skills entering a colonial economy that valued protection of livestock. It documents particular paid work, not the disappearance of Indigenous hunting for food or the wholesale adoption of a new livelihood.

passages.title: Authority, ornaments and historical evidence
passages.text: Opossunoquonuske ruled one Appamattuck town and was the sister of the chief Coquonasum. English visitors called her a queen, but her local title was weroansqua. At her reception of Newport’s party in May 1607, attendants and rules about approaching her made authority visible in the arrangement of people and space.

passages.title: Authority, ornaments and historical evidence
passages.text: The same account describes copper ornaments at her head, ears and neck. These were observed objects of status, rather than treasures recovered from her burial. The description preserves evidence of adornment and political display, filtered through English observers’ unfamiliarity with the community.

passages.title: Authority, ornaments and historical evidence
passages.text: A copper badge inscribed for the King of Appomattock was reported found in Dinwiddie County in the early twentieth century. The NPS study suggests that it may be a colonial identification insignia. Its inscription is evidence of an official designation; the proposed function remains an interpretation, and the account gives no secure excavation context.

passages.title: Authority, ornaments and historical evidence
passages.text: Within Powhatan’s political world, leadership followed the female line, and chiefs consulted councillors rather than acting entirely alone. Tribute could include food, skins, beads and copper. This regional system helps explain Appamattuck institutions, but an individual town’s decisions and relationships cannot all be reconstructed from a general description.

passages.title: Travel knowledge and encounters
passages.text: Percy’s entry for 8 May 1607 describes armed residents challenging the English landing at Apamatica before accepting signs of peace. His hostile vocabulary belongs to a colonist’s account. Read carefully, the episode also records Indigenous people controlling access to their country and deciding whether visitors could come ashore.

passages.title: Travel knowledge and encounters
passages.text: Bland’s 1651 pamphlet names Pyancha as the Appamattuck guide on a journey made the previous year. He describes Pyancha explaining river branches and neighboring settlements and advising a different return route after receiving a warning through a local relationship. The expedition’s knowledge came through Indigenous expertise and social connections.

passages.title: Travel knowledge and encounters
passages.text: At a path marked by two trees, Bland observed Pyancha clear one side before continuing. Another guide supplied a political story explaining different groups’ use of the route. The passage reveals a landscape carrying remembered relationships and conflict; it also shows the limits of an outsider’s account when Pyancha himself declined to explain.

passages.title: Treaties, petitions and what followed
passages.text: The 1677 treaty’s final memorandum says that Pericuhtah sought to join but was excluded because English officials accused him or his people of killings. The document records an accusation and exclusion, not a demonstrated verdict of guilt. Its own text therefore qualifies modern catalogue headings that simply list Appomattoc among the original signatories.

passages.title: Treaties, petitions and what followed
passages.text: The treaty promised land protection and access to fishing and gathering, while requiring submission to the English Crown and permission for some travel. These terms joined recognition with control. Their wording describes obligations and promises, not proof that colonial settlers respected every protected right after Appamattuck participation in the expanded agreement.

passages.title: Treaties, petitions and what followed
passages.text: A petition dated 24 April 1691 was made by an Appamattuck female ruler for herself and her people to live among English settlers. A later ferry-payment record names Appamattuck travelers to Jamestown. Such documents preserve collective representation and movement after the earlier devastation, even when they tell us little about individual households.

Colonial warfare, land loss and dependent treaty relations transformed Appamattuck political life. Families remained identifiable in Beverley’s 1705 account. These sources do not establish the later fate of every family or a single extinction date. The imported map’s endpoint of 1500 is not a historical ending.

sectionTitles: More of everyday and national life

passages.text: The Apsáalooke, widely called Crow, are a living nation of the Yellowstone and Bighorn country. The map uses both names for overlapping homeland outlines: Apsaalooké (Crow) in 1492 to 1500 and Crow in 1500 to 1783. Those imported intervals describe map coverage, not a founding or disappearance. Migration traditions, horse expertise, extended families and self-government connect their past and present.

passages.title: Food, families and movement
passages.text: Smaller winter villages could come together in the warmer part of the year, when the major bands gathered and hunted. Dried meat, roots and berries helped sustain households in winter. Food preservation mattered alongside the hunt: the ability to store and share provisions supported community life through seasons with very different opportunities.

passages.title: Food, families and movement
passages.text: Matrilineal clans and an extended network of relatives shaped responsibility for children. A mother’s sisters were also mothers, and a father’s brothers were also fathers in the kinship system described by the college. These relationships made care and belonging broader than the small household model familiar to many outsiders.

passages.title: Food, families and movement
passages.text: Horses increased the loads families could move and the distances hunters could cover. Larger tipi loads became practical as transport changed. The approximate early eighteenth-century adoption date describes a transformation in an existing society, not its beginning; horse expertise was developed through learning, use and exchange.

passages.title: Objects as records of knowledge
passages.text: The NMAI’s robe 1/2558 combines bison hide, pigment, trade cloth, beads and porcupine quillwork. Its approximately 1850 date is a museum attribution; acquisition at Fort Benton in 1861 is a separate event. Bringing different materials together required hide preparation, painting and decorative skills, and also reflects access to traded goods.

passages.title: Objects as records of knowledge
passages.text: Apsáalooke historian Patrick J. Hill and Timothy P. McCleary interpret the robe’s six scenes as a public account of martial accomplishments. They explain its pictorial conventions as narrative writing. The object is therefore evidence of a way to communicate remembered deeds, rather than merely an ornamental surface.

passages.title: Objects as records of knowledge
passages.text: Tipi liner 18/9242 preserves cotton canvas, deer hooves, glass beads and porcupine quills, with bead stitching and quill wrapping recorded in its catalogue. The museum bought it from a New York dealer in 1936. Its maker, manufacture date and earlier ownership are not supplied, so that purchase cannot be presented as an excavation or a date of invention.

passages.title: Objects as records of knowledge
passages.text: Liners helped manage drafts, dampness and ventilation inside tipis. During the reservation period, some families carried their use into log houses. Crow house interiors could retain a central stove, an east-facing entrance and decorated wall linings. New construction materials did not automatically erase established ways of organizing domestic space.

passages.title: Land, education and adaptation
passages.text: The 1868 treaty made a reservation the prescribed permanent home while retaining specified hunting rights on unoccupied United States land, subject to conditions in its text. Reading both provisions matters: reservation boundaries did not by themselves describe every place the agreement allowed Crow people to use. These are the treaty’s historical terms.

passages.title: Land, education and adaptation
passages.text: Boarding schools separated children from their families as part of federal assimilation policy. Families established camps near reservation missions, keeping themselves closer to children attending those schools. This response shows parents working within severe constraints to preserve relationships; attendance cannot be read simply as willing abandonment of Crow social life.

passages.title: Land, education and adaptation
passages.text: Plenty Coups’ preserved homestead near Pryor includes a log house, farm and store. Montana’s state park account dates his residence there from 1884 until his death in 1932. The buildings provide concrete evidence of a leader negotiating new economic conditions through farming and commerce, alongside his public responsibilities.

passages.title: Continuing institutions and achievements
passages.text: Crow Fair brings people together in a large gathering that includes a tipi encampment and public cultural activities. In the college’s account it belongs to continuing social life, alongside smaller family and community relationships. A historical card should place such gatherings in the present as well as discuss nineteenth-century objects.

passages.title: Continuing institutions and achievements
passages.text: In March 2016, Apsáalooke researchers at the Smithsonian examined beadwork and horn-reinforced bows, documenting construction for possible recreation and teaching. They treated museum holdings as resources for living knowledge. The project’s proposed digital archive was a goal described at the time, not a product whose completion this account establishes.

passages.title: Continuing institutions and achievements
passages.text: The same visitors viewed a film of the 1908 Crow Fair and listened to later commentary recorded by Dean Bear Claw. Their own explanations added another layer of knowledge. This work connects community interpretation with museum records; collecting an old film alone does not preserve all the meanings that knowledgeable viewers can recognize.

passages.title: Continuing institutions and achievements
passages.text: The tribe’s official website describes executive, legislative and judicial branches under its 2001 Constitution. Tribal government is a continuing institution, with public responsibilities extending beyond cultural representation. Its existence makes it particularly misleading to treat the final year of an imported historical map polygon as the disappearance of a people.

passages.title: More of everyday and national life
passages.text: Crow oral tradition follows Shiipdeetash on a sacred journey in search of tobacco, linking places from Chief Mountain to Cloud Peak. The tribal tourism office presents these places as a spiritual geography that still matters. A migration story can preserve relationships with a landscape as well as memories of travel.

passages.title: More of everyday and national life
passages.text: In 1851, Sits In The Middle Land compared Crow country to four tipi poles: Wind River, Black Hills, the Yellowstone-Missouri meeting place and Three Forks. A familiar home explained a vast homeland.

passages.title: More of everyday and national life
passages.text: Elk-tooth dresses celebrate sewing skill and family achievement. The Smithsonian explains that especially elaborate examples can carry hundreds of teeth, traditionally the bull elk’s two canine teeth. Modern makers also use substitutes. Its featured dress, dated around 1930, combines cotton, beads, bone, skin and wool: an outfit with considerable craftsmanship behind it.

passages.title: More of everyday and national life
passages.text: For its Apsáalooke exhibition, the Field Museum worked with Crow curator Nina Sanders. Seven historic war shields formed part of the display. Men traditionally made these shields, while women kept them; their protective meaning included spiritual power. The museum account treats them as objects with living community relationships.

passages.title: More of everyday and national life
passages.text: The college’s 1995 tipi account records “ashé,” meaning “home,” and “ashtáale,” meaning “real home.” The latter term followed government-built houses. These documented modern spellings provide a small written sample of the language.

passages.title: More of everyday and national life
passages.text: A modern tribal-college lesson turns kinship vocabulary into a matching game. Students receive cards, find the person whose card matches their relationship term, and discuss the connections in their own families. Learning a family vocabulary can therefore involve getting out of a chair and finding a relative on paper.

passages.title: More of everyday and national life
passages.text: Crow community members formed an environmental-health steering committee in 2005. A study published in 2015 describes a Crow project coordinator and Little Big Horn College science students collecting well-water samples and interviewing families. Local knowledge helped decide what questions the research should ask.

passages.title: More of everyday and national life
passages.text: The same study followed thirty families whose wells had especially high contamination. All had begun obtaining better water for drinking, and many also changed the water used for cooking. It is a concrete household detail behind environmental research: a safe meal can depend on where the water jug was filled.

The Apsáalooke continue as a people and a self-governing tribe. Treaties and reservation policies profoundly restricted land and reshaped institutions, but did not end their community. Neither the earlier outline’s 1500 cutoff nor the later Crow record’s 1783 cutoff marks their disappearance.

sectionTitles: Featherwork and the evidence in collections

passages.text: The Apyãwa, widely known as Tapirapé, are an Indigenous people of the middle Araguaia region of Brazil. Their history connects forest gardens, fishing places and village ceremonies with struggles to recover land. Apyãwa is their own name; Tapirapé remains common in historical writing and museum catalogues.

passages.title: Gardens, villages and sharing food
passages.text: Villages combine access to non-flooding forest suitable for gardens with streams, fishing places and seasonally useful open country. Houses traditionally surround a central takara. Farming, hunting, fishing and collecting require knowledge of different environments, so a village’s livelihood cannot be represented by a single crop or occupation.

passages.title: Gardens, villages and sharing food
passages.text: Koria Valdvane Tapirapé’s research records Imakopy’s account of collective garden work and distribution of the harvest among families. Cassava, beans, squash, yams and maize appear among the crops he discusses. The account connects agricultural work with education and ceremonial responsibilities, rather than treating cultivation as an isolated economic activity.

passages.title: Gardens, villages and sharing food
passages.text: The same researcher describes tataopãwa eating groups through Korako’s explanations. Family affiliations, participation in a shared fish meal and remembered group names connect food with belonging. The study distinguishes groups maintained at the time of research from those recalled in ceremonial knowledge; it does not describe every historical arrangement as unchanged.

passages.title: Gardens, villages and sharing food
passages.text: His 2020 dissertation also examines the increasing place of industrially produced foods. Using field notes, photographs and recordings in Tapi’itãwa, he asks how communities can draw on their territory’s resources while maintaining knowledge and relationships around eating. This is an Apyãwa investigation of contemporary change.

passages.title: Featherwork and the evidence in collections
passages.text: The Met’s mask 2017.100 is dated to 1950 to 1965. Its semicircular wooden structure carries feather mosaics in yellow and green, a central blue-green division and shell details around the face. Combining wood, feathers, shells and bindings required several kinds of material knowledge. The catalogue does not identify the individual artist.

passages.title: Featherwork and the evidence in collections
passages.text: The mask entered the Met as a gift in 2017. That acquisition date is different from the museum’s earlier date for the work itself. Its description makes the construction visible: shaped wooden elements frame the face, while individual feathers radiate above it and decorated fibre pendants hang below.

passages.title: Featherwork and the evidence in collections
passages.text: Madrid’s Museo de América holds another example, 1993/02/007, catalogued as made before 1993. It combines a wooden support, stitched feathers, vegetable fibres and shell. Eyes and mouth are cut through the support. The two collections show related forms with different arrangements; their accession records are not archaeological excavation dates.

passages.title: Featherwork and the evidence in collections
passages.text: Objects can also be chosen to explain history by the people who made and used them. At the NMAI consultation, Apyãwa representatives selected palm baskets, body-painting tools, feather headdresses and masks. The selection linked everyday making and ceremonial life with migrations, land and the struggle to return to it.

passages.title: Featherwork and the evidence in collections
passages.text: The museum’s report names Xywaeri José Pio, Ararawytygi Paulo Tapirapé and Xario Domingos Tapirapé among the participants. Discussion of a flour basket concerned its selection and display, not simply its appearance. Their participation supplied knowledge that a materials list alone could not convey.

passages.title: Teaching, research and new institutions
passages.text: Teacher Nivaldo Korira’i Tapirapé describes a 2014 project in which pupils learned words while studying practical knowledge. Kaxowari’i and his class drew a fish and worked on names for its parts, including fins and gills. The lesson joined literacy with close knowledge of animals familiar to the community.

passages.title: Teaching, research and new institutions
passages.text: Yrywaxã researched a flat canoe with a knowledgeable community member, then worked with children on its construction and use. Other classes studied different arrow types. A gathering brought pupils, parents and grandparents together. These activities made observing, making and speaking parts of the same educational work.

passages.title: Teaching, research and new institutions
passages.text: Gilson Ipaxi’awyga Tapirapé entered UFG’s intercultural education course in 2007 and became a university professor in 2023. The university identifies this as its first Indigenous faculty appointment. His path connects education in the community with teaching in a university, while bringing Apyãwa experience into academic work.

passages.title: Teaching, research and new institutions
passages.text: A 2024 paper coauthored by Koria Valdvane Tapirapé describes plans for a museum in Tapi’itãwa. The design drew on the form of a large-face mask and a feather diadem. The authors also discuss recording songs, managing collections and protecting territory. Their paper documents a collaborative project in progress, not proof that the building had opened.

The Apyãwa continue as communities with their own language, schools, researchers and territorial responsibilities. Severe losses and displacement were followed by recovery and renewed institutions. The map’s 1492 to 1500 coverage does not mark their disappearance, and recognition of Indigenous lands does not mean that every land conflict has ended.

sectionTitles: What objects and archaeological camps reveal
Continuing achievements and care for Country

passages.text: Arabana Country lies around Kati Thanda, also known as Lake Eyre, in northern South Australia. Springs, waterholes and the knowledge needed to care for them connect livelihoods, family histories and cultural responsibilities. Arabana people continue to maintain those relationships through community institutions, teaching and work on Country.

passages.title: Water, food and everyday knowledge
passages.text: The 2015 water report describes creeks and waterholes as places for longer stays, fishing and gathering. The value of a water place includes its history and relationships as well as its immediate supply. Meeting, washing and harvesting connect practical needs with remembered journeys and responsibilities.

passages.title: Water, food and everyday knowledge
passages.text: Soakages can be recognized through soil colour, texture, cracks and vegetation that indicate water below the surface. Elders and parents teach younger people how to recognize and use water places. This is learned knowledge of particular landscapes, not a single technique that can be assumed to work throughout Australia.

passages.title: Water, food and everyday knowledge
passages.text: The research employed Arabana co-researchers and included field visits. Indicators considered plants, animals, soil, use and pressures on water. Community participation shaped what counted as evidence of environmental condition and why a place mattered.

passages.title: Water, food and everyday knowledge
passages.text: The corporation’s Kutha work connects water management with Arabana decision-making. Its project account describes partnerships involving Rangers, Elders, conservation volunteers and environmental researchers. Considering the health of plants and animals alongside water conditions helps turn knowledge of Country into practical monitoring and management priorities.

passages.title: What objects and archaeological camps reveal
passages.text: The Museums Victoria ornament is a netted form made from hand-spun string. Its catalogue tentatively identifies animal fur and human hair among the fibres. The object records skilled work with flexible materials, but the uncertain identification should remain visible: a museum description is not a laboratory confirmation of every component.

passages.title: What objects and archaeological camps reveal
passages.text: The museum associates the ornament with Arabana people near Lake Eyre and records Spencer’s collecting in 1917. It does not name its maker. Collection history therefore gives one point in the object’s journey, while leaving important questions about manufacture, ownership and use unanswered.

passages.title: What objects and archaeological camps reveal
passages.text: At Strangways Springs, archaeologists identified flaked, thick amethyst glass derived from telegraph battery containers in Arabana camps. Reworking these materials shows people selecting and reshaping new supplies for their own uses. The finds document technological choices in a colonial setting, not simply the passive receipt of imported goods.

passages.title: What objects and archaeological camps reveal
passages.text: Camp S355 contained buttons, pipe fragments, cooking vessels and other household goods. Broken shears may have been reused as knives, although the authors present that interpretation cautiously. Such finds help reconstruct activities around work and home; the presence of purchased goods alone cannot establish the abandonment of Arabana identity.

passages.title: What objects and archaeological camps reveal
passages.text: Colonial employment could be paid in food and clothing rather than cash. Ration distribution also gave outsiders power over access to necessities. Archaeological evidence of new goods must be read alongside these unequal working conditions.

passages.title: Families, photographs and language
passages.text: David Moore’s 1959 photograph at Finniss Springs depicts Old Finke Bob and his wife Jessie. The gallery identifies Bob as Southern Arrernte, with an Arabana mother, Kantyara Nhuka. That specific family history matters: a photograph taken on Arabana Country does not make every person in it exclusively Arabana.

passages.title: Families, photographs and language
passages.text: The gallery catalogue connects Finniss Springs with Francis Warren and Laura Paralta, an Arabana woman. It describes the mission’s protection of children from removal and its eventual closure amid drought, water shortages and fire. The photograph survives as a record of people within that wider history; the museum print was made in 2000.

passages.title: Families, photographs and language
passages.text: The 2022 exhibition Arabana Yanhi! Tanganekald Yan! brought together two distinct language communities. For Arabana, Elders’ knowledge and memories were connected with archival spoken and written records. Artwork and word cards supported teaching. The exhibition’s Tanganekald materials belong to their own language history and should not be relabelled as Arabana evidence.

passages.title: Continuing achievements and care for Country
passages.text: Arabana Rangers monitor springs, care for threatened species and address feral animals and weeds. Cultural heritage work and learning from Elders are part of the same program. Training and employment help community members practise this knowledge on Country while developing skills needed for long-term management.

passages.title: Continuing achievements and care for Country
passages.text: The November 2025 burn targeted excessive reed growth around springs associated with the threatened salt pipewort, Eriocaulon carsonii. Arabana Elders and Rangers participated with partners. The project was a trial intended to protect spring habitat; its announcement does not establish that the plant had already recovered or that every spring needs burning.

passages.title: Continuing achievements and care for Country
passages.text: The Arabana Aboriginal Corporation represents community responsibilities for land, water and culture. Its public account links those responsibilities to native title recognition and to continuing family connections. These institutions give contemporary form to relationships whose significance extends beyond the dates displayed by a historical map.

Arabana people and their relationships with Country continue. Colonial stations, mission closure and changes in work altered community life without bringing it to an end. The map’s 1600 to 1815 interval is a coverage range, not a founding date, disappearance or transfer of Arabana identity to another people.

passages.text: The Arabela are an Indigenous people living around the Arabela River in Peru’s Loreto region. Their language belongs to the Zaparoan family. Tapueyocuaca, meaning family or siblings, is another name recorded for the people.

passages.title: Work, homes and materials
passages.text: A minga brings neighbours together for substantial jobs such as clearing a garden or building a house. The ILV account describes collective work followed by food, drink and conversation. Production therefore includes relationships of cooperation as well as the household that requested help.

passages.title: Work, homes and materials
passages.text: The Ministry of Culture describes an earlier pattern of related families sharing a maloca, followed by greater use of separate family houses. This is a history of changing domestic arrangements, not evidence that all households followed one permanent design.

passages.title: Work, homes and materials
passages.text: Historical clothing descriptions record women’s tubular bark garments with painted hexagonal designs and men’s woven ornaments with feather tassels. Cotton and chambira fibres, bark, feathers and beeswax appear in these accounts. They show the selection and combination of forest materials; they do not date the invention of those techniques.

passages.title: Work, homes and materials
passages.text: ILV describes hunting, fishing and collecting alongside cultivation. Its missionary account records customary divisions of work as well as collaboration, rather than demonstrating that all households followed an identical pattern.

passages.title: Coercion, trade and schooling
passages.text: Rubber extraction and patronage subjected Arabela people to exploitation. ILV describes goods advanced against labour and forest products at valuations that kept workers indebted. It connects literacy and arithmetic with households’ ability to track transactions and challenge abuse. Schooling had practical consequences within an unequal trading system.

passages.title: Coercion, trade and schooling
passages.text: The 1999 dictionary’s stated purpose was reciprocal communication: helping Arabela speakers learn Spanish and helping Spanish speakers communicate with them. Its listed contents include Arabela-to-Spanish entries, a Spanish-to-Arabela section, grammatical notes and guidance on the alphabet. The publication documents substantial linguistic work rather than the creation of a previously nonexistent language.

passages.title: Coercion, trade and schooling
passages.text: The 2016 alphabet resolution provides a different kind of evidence: a dated administrative record concerning a standardized way to write Arabela. Official recognition and the earlier dictionary are separate milestones. Neither establishes that language transmission was secure or that every speaker used the same written conventions beforehand.

passages.title: Recorded voices and continuing knowledge
passages.text: Casa de la Literatura credits Alfredo Pacaya Torrejón, Edgar Pastor Rosero and Ester Rosero Vásquez in the 2012 Buena Vista recording, with Vivian Wauters and Alfredo Pacaya as collectors. Naming these participants makes visible the people behind a recording that might otherwise appear only as an anonymous language sample.

passages.title: Recorded voices and continuing knowledge
passages.text: In the published translation’s opening, the narrator frames the account through writing and knowledge from elders, then tells of a child emerging from the earth and being welcomed into a household. This is a particular recorded narrative, not a statement that all Arabela people share one unchanging religious interpretation.

passages.title: Recorded voices and continuing knowledge
passages.text: Berkeley’s 2019 update describes more than 36 hours of Arabela recordings, along with field notes and a lexical database. These preserve different kinds of evidence: spoken examples, research observations and organized vocabulary. The announced deposit documents preservation work; it does not demonstrate that the entire collection was transcribed or that every recording is unrestricted.

passages.title: Recorded voices and continuing knowledge
passages.text: The 2023 classroom resource contains eight illustrated sheets intended for children aged three to five. Its catalogue says the scenes concern community calendars, including activities of other Indigenous peoples and Afro-Peruvian communities. The resource therefore should not be read as eight ethnographic photographs of Arabela life.

passages.title: Recorded voices and continuing knowledge
passages.text: Publishing materials for children is one part of the work of sustaining language and knowledge. A catalogue can establish that a resource was produced and whom it was designed for; it does not by itself establish how widely teachers used it or measure changes in children’s fluency.

Arabela communities continue, despite coercion, displacement and serious pressure on their language. Changes in housing, schooling and multilingual life do not mean the people disappeared. The map’s 1492 to 1500 interval is only imported coverage.

sectionTitles: Rulers, alliances and people on the move
A loud telephone and a language sample

passages.text: This Arabia record spans 1878 to 1914 and represents a broad interior region, not a unified kingdom or all Arab peoples. Its nearly unchanged outline includes Riyadh, Ha’il and Tayma but excludes Mecca, Medina, Hofuf and Muscat. It cannot track shifting Saudi, Rashidi and Ottoman authority. The southern extent is broad geographic context; the detailed evidence here concerns named northern and central communities.

passages.title: Rulers, alliances and people on the move
passages.text: The Second Saudi State ended in 1891, when the Rashidis prevailed. Abdulaziz Ibn Saud returned from exile and captured Riyadh in 1902. These changes affected rulers and allegiances, not the continued existence of Arabia’s communities.

passages.title: Rulers, alliances and people on the move
passages.text: The Rashidi rulers of Ha’il built a mutually useful partnership with the Ottoman Empire. Imperial money, grain and prestigious robes supported their position, while their regional influence helped Ottoman interests. Local rulers were active negotiators: imperial influence did not always mean direct administration from Istanbul.

passages.title: Rulers, alliances and people on the move
passages.text: War could alter a family’s livelihood far from the battlefield. Between 1901 and 1904, many pilgrims avoided dangerous inland routes and traveled to the Hijaz by sea. The loss of caravan traffic reduced income for Shammar communities whose economy depended partly on those journeys.

passages.title: Water, workshops and houses
passages.text: Lorimer’s 1908 gazetteer reports drinking-water wells in and around Riyadh about 40 to 50 feet deep, roughly 12 to 15 meters. The same groundwater irrigated date plantations. After good spring rains, Wadi Hanifah could flow for months. A town’s water supply depended on both underground stores and seasonal weather.

passages.title: Water, workshops and houses
passages.text: Riyadh workshops made coffee mortars and pestles from local marble, according to the same gazetteer. Its trade connections brought goods chiefly from al-Hasa, with others from Kuwait and the Hijaz. Even preparing coffee could connect a local craftsperson with trading routes reaching beyond the city.

passages.title: Water, workshops and houses
passages.text: In Ha’il in 1879, Anne Blunt’s lodging had wooden doors, wooden locks and wooden keys. Its small courtyard could hold the visitors’ three mares. The walls carried pale patterns scratched through a brown coating. Security, animals and decoration all fitted within one compact household compound.

passages.title: Water, workshops and houses
passages.text: At the map’s 1914 endpoint, Bell stayed in a former summer palace at Ha’il. A widow whom she called Lu.lu.ah cared for the house and lived with an enslaved woman and that woman’s son. This small household record preserves both women’s work and the unequal freedoms within elite society.

passages.title: Food, learning and care
passages.text: On 7 March 1914, Bell saw Bedouin women selling milk, butter and semneh, clarified butter, in Ha’il’s market. Their stalls connected pastoral production with town customers. Women appear here as sellers doing public economic work, quite different from the secluded palace life described elsewhere in travel accounts.

passages.title: Food, learning and care
passages.text: Scholarship required support as well as determination. In nineteenth- and early twentieth-century Najd, students could depend on teachers, wealthy donors and religious endowments. Some left after learning basic reading and writing to enter commerce or help with farming. Family income and labor needs shaped how long study continued.

passages.title: Food, learning and care
passages.text: Near Jebel Shammar in January 1879, Blunt noted a thick-leaved plant she recorded as “gheyseh”. Her companions said it benefited the eyes. This preserves a reported medicinal belief, not a proven treatment; the account does not securely identify the plant or establish that it worked.

passages.title: A loud telephone and a language sample
passages.text: At Ha’il’s court in 1879, Blunt saw two enslaved attendants demonstrate a telephone toy, one shouting from the courtyard. Her 1881 book prints the spoken Arabic in Roman letters: “Ya Abdallah weyn ente? yeridak el Emir.” Her translation is “O Abdallah, where are you? the Emir wants you”. This is a traveler’s transcription, not original Arabic script. Early telephone practice could be very loud!

passages.title: Discoveries, pictures and surviving evidence
passages.text: The Tayma stele entered archaeological study after being found reused in a house in 1884. The Louvre dates its Aramaic inscription to the fifth century BCE and records acquisition in 1885. Its text concerns a priest and a religious foundation. This was discovery of a much older past, not the language or religion of nineteenth-century Tayma.

passages.title: Discoveries, pictures and surviving evidence
passages.text: Bell’s 7 March 1914 diary records permission to photograph Ha’il’s palace. She described a columned courtyard, wall decoration, old artillery and very large coffee pots. Photographs and written notes can preserve different clues about the same place, although neither provides a complete picture of its people’s lives.

passages.title: Discoveries, pictures and surviving evidence
passages.text: Blunt’s journey survives in a separate sketchbook, catalogued by the British Library for 13 December 1878 to 20 February 1879. This working record lets researchers compare a traveler’s original documentation with her later published account.

The 1914 endpoint marks a map change and the beginning of a new wartime setting, not the end of Arabia. Saudi expansion and Rashidi resistance continued, while Britain and the Ottoman Empire became more involved. The region’s settlements and communities outlasted these changing political arrangements.

sectionTitles: Oasis kitchens, farms and local government
Homes, learning and the work of staying healthy
Messages, equipment and a surviving letter

passages.text: This 1914 to 1920 record covers an Arabian interior region, not one unified state. Its outline includes Riyadh and rival Ha’il, which Ibn Saud conquered only in 1921, plus an erroneous detached Musandam-area fragment. It cannot represent his borders. The evidence below follows particular Najdi towns and journeys, without treating all Arabian communities as alike.

passages.title: Power, borders and distant connections
passages.text: Before this map interval, Abdulaziz Ibn Saud took Riyadh in 1902 and al-Ahsa from Ottoman control in 1913. His expanding state gained an eastern outlet. Yet Ha’il remained a rival center: a single color spread across the interior hides important political divisions.

passages.title: Power, borders and distant connections
passages.text: The treaty signed at Darin on 26 December 1915 recognized Ibn Saud as an independent ruler, while leaving territorial limits for later discussion. It also restricted his agreements with foreign powers and transfers of land. Recognition came with conditions, rather than a neatly settled modern border.

passages.title: Power, borders and distant connections
passages.text: The same treaty required protection for pilgrims and the roads through Ibn Saud’s territories toward the holy places. Keeping a route open mattered to travelers as well as rulers. This was a written obligation; the clause alone cannot tell us how safe each journey actually was.

passages.title: Power, borders and distant connections
passages.text: Faisal represented his father in a Najdi delegation to Britain in October and November 1919; Ahmad Ibn Thunayan handled the negotiations. The mission carried Ibn Saud’s letter and presented two gilded swords to George V. Written messages, experienced diplomats and ceremonial objects all helped communicate authority abroad.

passages.title: Oasis kitchens, farms and local government
passages.text: Philby’s 1918 southern journey produced a detailed report and map of routes between Riyadh, Kharj, Aflaj, Sulayyil and Wadi Dawasir. These records help historians recover fields, wells and settlements. They were also British political intelligence about places whose inhabitants already knew their own landscape.

passages.title: Oasis kitchens, farms and local government
passages.text: At Sulayyil, Philby recorded date palms, wheat, vegetables, grapes, peaches and citrons. He saw a little cotton, including one small field. An oasis garden could offer much more variety than a desert-colored map suggests: the crop list has room for both dinner and something sweet.

passages.title: Oasis kitchens, farms and local government
passages.text: In Wadi Dawasir, Philby described wheat irrigated from wells in the valley bed, with houses and palm groves often on opposite sides. He also reported serious agricultural damage from the previous year’s flood. Water needed careful management whether too little arrived or far too much.

passages.title: Oasis kitchens, farms and local government
passages.text: Sulayyil’s hamlet leaders managed much local business; a district leader intervened when rival settlements quarreled. Philby also described repeated invitations for coffee and meals from his hosts. Government and hospitality operated through local relationships, alongside the larger rulers whose names fill political histories.

passages.title: Homes, learning and the work of staying healthy
passages.text: Hamilton’s wartime diary describes well-traveled people in Unaizah who knew Kuwait, Bahrain, Basra, Karachi and Bombay; some had reached Damascus, Beirut or Constantinople. He also recorded stocked shops. This inland oasis participated in wide commercial networks, rather than living entirely on what its gardens produced.

passages.title: Homes, learning and the work of staying healthy
passages.text: In one Unaizah house, Hamilton saw a coffee room about 18 by 30 feet, roughly 5.5 by 9 meters. A screened gallery near the roof let women see and hear the gathering below. Painted Quranic texts decorated the walls. This particular room combined hospitality, decoration and controlled privacy.

passages.title: Homes, learning and the work of staying healthy
passages.text: For nineteenth- and early twentieth-century Najdi scholars, legal learning helped settle disputes and divide inheritances. Books and writing materials were expensive, so copyists prioritized useful law texts. Copying a book was substantial work; a small collection could still serve important needs in a community.

passages.title: Homes, learning and the work of staying healthy
passages.text: During the influenza crisis in late 1918, Ibn Saud urgently requested the physician Paul Harrison from Bahrain. Harrison stayed in Riyadh for almost three months and offered free care. His work belonged to an American missionary enterprise with religious ambitions, alongside the immediate task of helping sick people.

passages.title: Homes, learning and the work of staying healthy
passages.text: Local chronicles describe another terrible effect of the 1918 to 1919 epidemic: sick households could no longer feed, herd or water their animals. Camels and other livestock were neglected. Caring for people and caring for animals were closely connected parts of keeping families alive.

passages.title: Messages, equipment and a surviving letter
passages.text: Philby’s mission needed messengers supplied through Abdullah al-Nafisi, a Najdi commercial agent in Kuwait, as well as photographic film and other equipment. In November 1917 Philby requested twelve gold and twelve silver watches, probably for diplomatic gifts. Even serious negotiations could involve a rather sparkly shopping list.

passages.title: Messages, equipment and a surviving letter
passages.text: A letter from Ibn Saud to George V dated 1 August 1919 survives with the mission’s papers. Its published English translation includes “our son Faisal ibn Abdulaziz”. This identifies the ruler’s representative. The original was Arabic; this excerpt is a translation, not a verified transcription of its handwriting.

The map stops in 1920, but Najd’s communities and Ibn Saud’s state continued. Ha’il fell to him in 1921. Further conquests and political changes led to the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932. Neither date marks the disappearance of local families, towns or regional identities.

sectionTitles: Water, animals and a place to return to
A neighboring desert camp: people and animals at Timna
Later voices of herders and families

passages.text: This label covers varied mobile herding communities, not one Arabian nation or kingdom. Its broad outline and 1500 to 500 BCE interval are atlas conventions, not established ethnic boundaries. Temporary camps could connect with villages, markets and workshops. Examples below distinguish southeastern Arabia from neighboring Timna in the Arabah and much later Jordanian inscriptions, both outside this outline. Arabia, Nejd and particular ancient kingdoms have separate histories.

passages.title: Water, animals and a place to return to
passages.text: Saruq al-Hadid, now in Dubai’s desert, was repeatedly used rather than simply abandoned after one visit. Researchers identify water, vegetation and fuel as attractions. Shallow water may have come from wells or collected beneath dunes; nearby grazing supported sheep and goats while wild animals also drew hunters.

passages.title: Water, animals and a place to return to
passages.text: Its bone midden, deposited around 1750 to 1300 BCE, overlaps the beginning of this map period. Excavators recovered more than a tonne of animal-bone fragments, with oryx, gazelle and wild camel prominent. Hearths and other finds show that hunting and food preparation shared space with toolmaking.

passages.title: Water, animals and a place to return to
passages.text: The desert gathering place was connected to settled communities. Chemical analysis of Saruq al-Hadid pottery found both continuity and changes across the Bronze and Iron Ages, suggesting participation in wider regional economies. Moving with animals did not mean living beyond the reach of other people’s goods and skills.

passages.title: Tools, craft knowledge and ingenuity
passages.text: Late Bronze Age stoneworkers at Saruq al-Hadid sometimes picked up much older discarded stone cores and struck off new flakes. Archaeologists distinguish weathered old scars from fresher cuts. Recycling was practical: an ancient toolmaker could recognize useful material that another person had left behind long before.

passages.title: Tools, craft knowledge and ingenuity
passages.text: The same workers produced small backed stone implements through a sequence of flaking and trimming. Unfinished pieces and mistakes reveal the risks in making a consistent shape from irregular stone. Such debris records practiced technical knowledge, although it cannot identify a particular teacher, apprentice or classroom.

passages.title: Tools, craft knowledge and ingenuity
passages.text: By the Iron Age, Saruq al-Hadid also had sophisticated goldworking. A study of finds excavated in 2015 to 2017 examined about 450 gold items and identified casting and shaping techniques, including lost-wax casting. Desert communities participated in craft networks capable of producing much more than basic survival equipment.

passages.title: A neighboring desert camp: people and animals at Timna
passages.text: At tenth-century BCE Timna, outside this map outline in the neighboring Arabah, dung preserved seeds and pollen from animal feed. Researchers concluded that donkeys or mules ate grape pomace and good hay brought from wetter regions. These essential transport animals received a carefully supplied menu of their own.

passages.title: A neighboring desert camp: people and animals at Timna
passages.text: Timna’s camp managers piled dung against the inside of the wall, probably to help start the copper furnaces. A later soil-chemistry study located more refuse and penning traces there. Animal waste could become a useful resource; this evidence concerns camp organization, not a known toilet system or medical treatment.

passages.title: A neighboring desert camp: people and animals at Timna
passages.text: Cloth from Timna’s late eleventh- and tenth-century BCE copper camp included wool decorated with red and blue bands. Chemical tests identified madder-based red and plant-derived blue dye. The fabrics demonstrate skilled spinning, weaving and dyeing, and access to colorful clothing in an exceptionally dry landscape.

passages.title: A neighboring desert camp: people and animals at Timna
passages.text: Animal bones at Timna also suggest unequal access to food. Better meat cuts occurred in industrial areas associated with specialist metalworkers, compared with domestic areas used by support workers. Researchers interpret this as evidence of valued expertise: the furnace specialist’s dinner could be better than a colleague’s.

passages.title: Camels, rulers and vulnerable camps
passages.text: Camel transport changed desert connections, but camels should not be added automatically to every camp in 1500 BCE. A study of Aravah Valley bones places their first substantial domestic appearance there no earlier than the final third of the tenth century BCE. Other Arabian regions require their own evidence and chronology.

passages.title: Camels, rulers and vulnerable camps
passages.text: In the eighth century BCE, the Assyrian ruler Tiglath-pileser III described defeating Samsi, a queen of the Arabs. His inscription lists camels, cattle and aromatics among seized wealth, then describes tribute and an Assyrian representative placed over her. This is evidence for female political leadership and imperial pressure.

passages.title: Camels, rulers and vulnerable camps
passages.text: The same hostile account describes Samsi’s tents as protection for people within her camp, then boasts of burning them. Portable homes were vital shelter and property, not evidence that their owners lacked an organized society. The king’s victory language gives us his perspective, not Samsi’s own account.

passages.title: Later voices of herders and families
passages.text: A later Safaitic inscription from Wadi Salma, Jordan, includes w rʿy h-ḍʾn, “and he pastured the sheep.” This is scholarly transliteration of KRS 41. Safaitic is conventionally dated from the first century BCE to fourth century CE, with some earlier evidence; this undated example is not testimony from 1500 BCE.

passages.title: Later voices of herders and families
passages.text: Another later Safaitic writer, at Wadi Miqat in Jordan, recorded pasturing sheep, encountering older writing, and longing for his brothers. These personal concerns survive beside prayers for safety. His words offer a family voice from a later pastoral world, not a description of every community in ancient Arabia.

The label ends in 500 BCE without a collective conquest or disappearance. Later pastoral inscriptions show continuing, changing desert lives. Particular communities encountered states and new languages over time; neither mobility nor herding defines one unchanging people, and these records are not aliases for modern Arabian states.

sectionTitles: A region of communities and rulers

passages.text: The atlas uses “Arabs” for a broad Arabian area from about 200 to 100 BCE. This was no single kingdom. Ancient authors applied the name to different communities, and neither residence in Arabia nor a particular script identifies everyone as Arab. This card explores regional examples at Thaj and Mleiha, while keeping Saba, the Nabataean kingdom and later Arabian states distinct.

passages.title: A region of communities and rulers
passages.text: The imported outline reaches across much of Arabia, but it cannot show the boundaries of an ancient ethnic identity. “Arab” could mean different things to different writers. The towns discussed here are securely located regional examples; their artifacts do not establish that all their residents shared one language, ancestry or political allegiance.

passages.title: A region of communities and rulers
passages.text: Before this map interval, Gerrha negotiated with Antiochus III around 205 BCE. Polybius reports an interpreted letter requesting freedom, followed by gifts of silver and aromatics.

passages.title: A region of communities and rulers
passages.text: Gerrha’s merchants connected eastern Arabia with incense-producing southern regions and customers farther north. Potts discusses Strabo’s report of a forty-day journey to Hadramawt. That is weeks of transport and provisioning behind a pleasant smell. Gerrha’s exact location is debated; identifying it automatically with excavated Thaj would hide an important uncertainty.

passages.title: A region of communities and rulers
passages.text: Mleiha in today’s Sharjah participated in a southeastern Arabian kingdom named Oman. Its coins drew on Hellenistic models, and its position linked overland and maritime commerce. Excavator Bruno Overlaet describes Mleiha as a proposed capital: a substantial political center, but not proven ruler of the entire Arabian polygon.

passages.title: Building, cooking and family work
passages.text: At Thaj, a fortified town covered roughly forty hectares. Excavations exposed residential blocks and a monumental gateway flanked by towers. Repairs and additions eventually made part of the defenses nearly ten meters thick. Those dimensions belong to the town’s long history, rather than one construction campaign in 200 BCE.

passages.title: Building, cooking and family work
passages.text: Thaj depended on groundwater as well as trading routes. Masonry wells around the site reach a lasting karst aquifer, replenished by deeper water and rainfall. Drawing and maintaining water supplies was essential work for residents; the excavated wells make that need tangible, without supplying an invented ancient toilet system.

passages.title: Building, cooking and family work
passages.text: Thaj’s workshop landscape changed over time. At Tall al-Zayir, a pottery workshop operating in the fourth or third century BCE preceded an aristocratic cemetery of the first or second century CE. The same ground could move from making everyday vessels to commemorating the dead as the town changed.

passages.title: Building, cooking and family work
passages.text: A Mleiha farmhouse complex dated broadly to 200 BCE through 100 CE contained ovens and grinding stones for preparing cereals and bread. Its neighboring kitchen included steps descending to a chamber with two large ovens. Before a loaf reached the table, somebody had to grind, mix, tend the heat and clean up.

passages.title: Building, cooking and family work
passages.text: These kitchen remains are also evidence of learned skill: grinding grain and managing an oven required practice. They do not identify the teacher or establish a formal school. A stone grinder gives us a firmer glimpse of everyday work than guessing which family member had to do the washing up.

passages.title: Building, cooking and family work
passages.text: One Mleiha tomb preserves an unusually personal political record. An inscription names Amud and says his son built the monument for him; both appear as inspectors serving the king of Oman. Its damaged year probably corresponds to 222/221 or 215/214 BCE. It links kinship, commemoration and royal service shortly before the mapped century.

passages.title: Objects that preserve connections
passages.text: At Thaj, archaeologists used pottery to untangle layers of settlement. Thin Seleucid-style vessels and Greek black-glazed fragments helped date early levels to the third century BCE. Comparable fragments beneath the wall’s foundations linked a building project to that sequence. Broken dishes can act as archaeological clocks, though they rarely give an exact year.

passages.title: Objects that preserve connections
passages.text: A handle from a Mleiha tomb carries the scholarly transcription “ʾby / bn / hnʾyn”: “(Belonging to) ʾBY son of HNʾYN.” Written in South Arabian cursive zabūr, it marks ownership. The chamber dates to the middle second century BCE; the Rhodian-type jar was manufactured between 225 and 125 BCE. This is an ancient regional witness, not modern Arabic script.

passages.title: Objects that preserve connections
passages.text: The owner’s mark makes writing an ordinary possession-management tool, not only something kings displayed. Stein also identified related cursive writing on a silver plaque from Mleiha. He suggests that writing had broader practical uses there, while noting that everyday correspondence itself has not yet been recovered. The evidence does not tell us how many residents could read.

passages.title: Objects that preserve connections
passages.text: Mleiha’s burials also connect families with long-distance exchange. Excavations recovered imported wine containers among funerary offerings. These were deliberate choices about what accompanied the dead, rather than a census of ordinary meals. Goods traveling across seas could become part of a deeply local act of remembrance.

passages.title: Objects that preserve connections
passages.text: Fish bones show that inland Mleiha was supplied from the sea. Tuna relatives recur in well-sampled phases from the third century BCE onward. A much later example, building H in the second to mid-third century CE, contained processed fish with heads removed; researchers interpret the stock as probably salted and sun-dried for storage and transport.

passages.title: Objects that preserve connections
passages.text: The burned fish stock in building H was a discovery about both food and a building’s final days. The researchers distinguish heat from the house fire from cooking marks. That distinction matters: an accidental archaeological “roast” cannot be turned into a recipe. Nor does evidence for a burned building identify who caused the fire.

There was no collective “fall of the Arabs” in 100 BCE. That is this imported record’s endpoint. Arabian settlements and communities continued through distinct local political and economic changes; the ancient label cannot be treated as one state with one conqueror.

sectionTitles: Reading the map and its local societies
Nearby Medina: food, schooling and washing

passages.text: This atlas label covers varied Arabian communities from 1492 to 1530, including parts of the central interior and the eastern al-Ahsa oasis region. It is not the name of a single state. Oasis settlements, mobile groups and regional rulers had different institutions; the Jabrids were one important eastern dynasty, not rulers of every place colored here.

passages.title: Reading the map and its local societies
passages.text: The imported outline includes Hofuf and Diriyah but excludes Mecca, Medina, Jeddah, Julfar and Muscat. It therefore cannot show either all Arab-speaking populations or a unified Arabian kingdom. Examples below name their locations; the pilgrimage-city and seafaring sections describe neighboring connections outside this polygon.

passages.title: Reading the map and its local societies
passages.text: Al-Ahsa was an oasis region with a long agricultural history. Its name is linked to underground accumulations of water. That helps explain why a landscape surrounded by desert could support settled communities as well as connections with mobile neighbors.

passages.title: Reading the map and its local societies
passages.text: The Jabrids were a ruling family centered on al-Ahsa. Ajwad ibn Zamil expanded their influence along the Gulf and exacted tribute from some neighboring rulers. Tribute relationships and local family power made a more complicated political map than one tidy block of color.

passages.title: Homes, harvests and skilled work
passages.text: Diriyah’s settlement story begins before this map window: in 1446, Mani al-Muraydi moved with his family to Wadi Hanifa. A relative granted him Mulaybid and Ghusaybah. The account distinguishes farmland at Mulaybid from the walled residence and governing center at Ghusaybah: fields and homes were planned together.

passages.title: Homes, harvests and skilled work
passages.text: Wadi Hanifa’s seasonal floods left fertile silt and replenished groundwater. Traditional agriculture at Diriyah used shallow wells to support orchards and palm groves. A dry-looking valley could thus store part of its usefulness underground, where a farmer with a well could reach it.

passages.title: Homes, harvests and skilled work
passages.text: Ibn Zayd’s poetry for the Jabrid ruler Ajwad describes camping in al-Dahna after rain and moving to al-Ahsa when dates ripened. This is a court poet’s picture of seasonal life, preserved in later scholarship. It connects desert movement with cultivated palm gardens, rather than treating herding and farming as separate worlds.

passages.title: Homes, harvests and skilled work
passages.text: The same discussion of Jabrid poetry describes hunting with falcons and cheetahs. These were elite pursuits celebrated in verse, not every child’s afternoon entertainment. The poems offer a lively window into how rulers wanted their outdoor skill and status to be remembered.

passages.title: Homes, harvests and skilled work
passages.text: At Hofuf, the official heritage account dates al-Jabri Mosque to 1475 and identifies clay and limestone as its building materials. Later repairs repeatedly replaced damaged parts. Its survival is also a story of maintenance: a historic building can carry centuries of careful mending alongside its older fabric.

passages.title: Homes, harvests and skilled work
passages.text: Al-Ahsa’s broader craft heritage includes pottery made from local clay and ceilings or furniture made with palm trunks and fronds. These are documented regional traditions, not precisely dated inventories of a house in 1500. They show how an oasis could provide building materials as well as food.

passages.title: Learning, families and travel
passages.text: Learning could travel with a family. Under Ajwad, Shaykh Nasrullah settled in al-Ahsa to serve as an imam, while the scholarly Abdulqadir family also migrated there. Patronage helped draw teachers into the oasis; political influence was built with books and religious institutions as well as armed followers.

passages.title: Learning, families and travel
passages.text: Ahmad ibn Atwa, born at al-Uyaynah in 1456, grew up in a prosperous family that supported his studies. His early education included reading, writing, arithmetic and Quranic recitation. This named scholar’s experience gives us a concrete curriculum, while also reminding us that family resources affected educational opportunities.

passages.title: Learning, families and travel
passages.text: Ibn Atwa studied in Damascus, where he lived at al-Umariyah School in 1475 and donated books. He later taught in Najd, including Diriyah at its rulers’ invitation. A student’s journey could therefore become a route by which books, qualifications and teaching practices returned to an Arabian town.

passages.title: Learning, families and travel
passages.text: Pilgrimage also carried political connections. In 1520, the Jabrid ruler Muqrin traveled to Mecca, outside this polygon, where Egyptians visited and honored him as an eastern Bedouin leader.

passages.title: Nearby Medina: food, schooling and washing
passages.text: A neighboring example comes from Medina, outside the outline. Sultan Qaytbay’s foundation, completed in the 1480s, linked a hostel with eighty cells to a larger religious complex. Its endowment records also describe wheat storage, a mill, bakery and kitchen: supporting visitors required a food supply system, not just a doorway.

passages.title: Nearby Medina: food, schooling and washing
passages.text: At the same Medina foundation, a public water dispenser had a primary school above it. Wheat storerooms and living units shared another building. Lessons, drinking water, supplies and accommodation were brought close together, a very practical arrangement for a busy pilgrimage city.

passages.title: Nearby Medina: food, schooling and washing
passages.text: The Medina hostel complex included an ablution fountain and a small bath. These are specific documented washing facilities, rather than evidence for identical sanitation across Arabia. For a dusty traveler, somewhere to wash was a useful part of hospitality alongside somewhere to sleep.

passages.title: Arabic knowledge beyond the interior
passages.text: The navigator Ahmad ibn Majid came from Julfar, outside this polygon, and was associated with the southern Arabian port of al-Shihr. His sailing knowledge belonged to a maritime network. His father and grandfather were also sailors, giving another example of expertise linked to family experience.

passages.title: Arabic knowledge beyond the interior
passages.text: Ibn Majid composed both prose manuals and verse about sailing. Historian A. C. S. Peacock suggests that verse helped captains remember instructions. This was practical knowledge about routes, landmarks and stars: rhyme could serve as a memory aid long before a navigator could tap a phone.

passages.title: Arabic knowledge beyond the interior
passages.text: An Arabic writing sample is علم البحر, transliterated ʿilm al-baḥr, meaning “knowledge of the sea.” It appears within the Library of Congress’s Arabic title for Ibn Majid’s navigational collection, originally assembled in 1490. The library’s manuscript was copied on 18 June 1926: this is a catalogued later witness to the older work, not a surviving autograph from 1490.

The atlas stops this label in 1530, but Arabian communities did not end then. Diriyah’s later history, for example, continued through successive generations and eventually its role as a Saudi capital in the eighteenth century. That later state belongs to a separate historical phase.

sectionTitles: City life, care and a very practical writing sample

passages.text: Aragon developed from a Pyrenean county into a kingdom and became the name of a wider crown linking distinct territories around the western Mediterranean. A common ruler did not make their laws, languages or institutions identical. The atlas’s 1000 to 1530 record spans that changing scale; examples from Barcelona belong to the later crown, not the early mountain kingdom.

passages.title: Dynasties, laws and knowledge
passages.text: Petronila was still a child when the 1137 betrothal agreement joined her future to Ramon Berenguer IV, count of Barcelona. Their wedding occurred in 1150. Keeping those dates separate avoids turning a dynastic arrangement made for a baby into an adult marriage ceremony.

passages.title: Dynasties, laws and knowledge
passages.text: The crown incorporated territories with different legal traditions. Aragon was both a particular kingdom and part of this larger monarchy. Calling every inhabitant “Aragonese” without explaining the scale would erase important Catalan, Valencian and other local identities.

passages.title: Dynasties, laws and knowledge
passages.text: James I commissioned a systematic legal compilation in 1247. The Getty’s Vidal Mayor, c. 1290 to 1310, preserves a Navarro-Aragonese translation of a lost Latin version. Law had to be organized, copied and understood through particular languages.

passages.title: Dynasties, laws and knowledge
passages.text: The Vidal Mayor deals with Christians of different ranks, Muslims and Jews. It reveals a society whose law distinguished status and religion. Sharing cities and markets did not mean enjoying identical legal rights.

passages.title: Dynasties, laws and knowledge
passages.text: The medieval Llibre de Sent Soví survives within a manuscript that also contains medical, grammatical, astrological and devotional texts. One volume could be a small collection of useful knowledge. Its recipes cannot simply be treated as the usual meals of every household.

passages.title: Dynasties, laws and knowledge
passages.text: The Council of Aragon, created in 1494, organized work through offices for different territories. Records of those offices show the continued complexity of the crown after the dynastic union with Castile. A shared monarch was not the same thing as a single uniform administration.

passages.title: City life, care and a very practical writing sample
passages.text: In Barcelona in 1401, municipal and church authorities united six hospitals into the Hospital de la Santa Creu. The new institution served poor people, orphans and the sick. Care was a civic and religious undertaking as well as a medical one.

passages.title: City life, care and a very practical writing sample
passages.text: Barcelona’s council also regulated and subsidized food supplies as part of its social policy. Feeding the city and supporting vulnerable residents helped authorities seek stability. Hospital buildings alone cannot tell us whether every person who needed assistance received it.

passages.title: City life, care and a very practical writing sample
passages.text: By about 1303, Barcelona had written rules against throwing dirty water and other waste into streets through windows or doorways. The existence of a ban suggests an unwelcome practice worth regulating, not evidence that every resident did it every day.

passages.title: City life, care and a very practical writing sample
passages.text: The ordinance’s Catalan begins “que ninguna persona no gos gitar en carrers”: “that no person dare throw into the streets.” This sample is quoted in the museum’s transcription. Some medieval writing was less about heroic battles and more about preventing an unpleasant surprise from upstairs.

passages.title: City life, care and a very practical writing sample
passages.text: The museum’s history identifies chamber pots and latrines as household solutions and notes medieval names for toilets such as necessaria. Those facilities varied by building. They should not be imagined as modern flushing toilets connected to one complete citywide system.

passages.title: City life, care and a very practical writing sample
passages.text: Part of Barcelona’s Rambla drainage channel was covered in 1364 to 1366. Public fountains also needed drains. Water supply and waste disposal required continuing labor and construction; the later crown’s impressive buildings rested on many less glamorous maintenance jobs.

The 1530 atlas endpoint is not the end of Aragon. Its crown continued within the Spanish monarchy. Much later, the Nueva Planta changes dismantled key separate institutions: the 1707 decree affected Aragon and Valencia, and the Council of Aragon was suppressed that year. Regional communities, languages and identities continued.

sectionTitles: What the early label can and cannot tell us
Discoveries that clarify the later landscape

passages.text: This imported Arakan outline covers 200 BCE to 200 CE. It does not establish a kingdom lasting exactly those years. The better-documented cities and inscriptions discussed below are mostly later; their rulers and customs should not be moved backward into this early interval.

passages.title: What the early label can and cannot tell us
passages.text: Dhanyawadi is a real archaeological site, but its starting date remains unevenly reported. Mya Oo’s historical introduction mentions evidence from the first century CE; archaeologist Elisabeth Moore generally dates the city from the fourth to sixth centuries. Neither source establishes this map’s 200 BCE beginning.

passages.title: What the early label can and cannot tell us
passages.text: The imported polygon includes Dhanyawadi but leaves Vesali beyond its southeastern edge, judging from published site coordinates. Its boundary should not be read as an exact ancient frontier.

passages.title: What the early label can and cannot tell us
passages.text: The later Anandacandra pillar looks far back into the past. Its early royal list includes extraordinarily long reigns, and Johnston regarded that opening sequence as at least partly mythical. Such a royal account tells us how a later court imagined its ancestry; it cannot independently certify centuries of earlier kings.

passages.title: What the early label can and cannot tell us
passages.text: We have not verified a written-language sample securely belonging to this record’s 200 BCE to 200 CE span. The Sanskrit and Pali inscriptions central to studies of early Arakan belong to later contexts. Printing one of those without its date would give this early map a misleading voice.

passages.title: Discoveries that clarify the later landscape
passages.text: Modern fieldwork corrected Dhanyawadi’s archaeological plan: earth banks once drawn as part of an oddly shaped city wall proved to be a separate feature. Brickwork underneath helped reveal the older wall’s course. This is a lesson in checking maps on the ground; it does not date those walls to 200 BCE.

passages.title: Discoveries that clarify the later landscape
passages.text: For the much later Vesali, excavators in 1980 to 1984 uncovered a monastery and a hall interpreted as a place for monastic ordinations, measuring 21 by 15 meters. Such buildings show organized religious communities. Their existence should not become a claim that children in this earlier map interval attended the same institutions.

passages.title: Discoveries that clarify the later landscape
passages.text: Household meals, family routines, remedies and toilets cannot be reconstructed for this exact early interval from the sources checked here. Later inscriptions illuminate donors and religious institutions far better than ordinary homes. Leaving those gaps visible is preferable to giving an ancient family a menu borrowed from people living centuries afterward.

passages.title: Discoveries that clarify the later landscape
passages.text: The famous pillar now at Mrauk U carries writing from several later periods on different faces. Much is worn away. Its present location is also later than its inscriptions: local history says a sixteenth-century king moved it from Vesali. An artifact can have a long traveling life, quite apart from the story written on it.

The year 200 CE is the end of this map fragment, not a demonstrated conquest or disappearance. Later cities developed in the region, but the evidence checked here does not supply an uninterrupted sequence of rulers connecting this early outline to them.
