passages.text: Arma families descended from soldiers who remained after Morocco invaded the Songhay Empire in 1591. Their locally rooted garrisons and pashas, or governors, became increasingly independent. This map shows a late slice, 1715 to 1783, of a much longer history around Timbuktu and the Niger River.

passages.title: Soldiers, families and government
passages.text: The name Arma is associated with an Arabic word for musketeers. Yet their story soon became about households as well as armies: descendants of the invaders established families and communities in the Niger towns, rather than remaining a temporary force sent from Morocco.

passages.title: Soldiers, families and government
passages.text: Garrisons occupied river towns between Kukya and Jenne. Their commanders collected tribute and supervised navigation. Control of a river landing mattered because merchants, supplies and tax payments moved through it: government depended on boats and trading towns as well as soldiers.

passages.title: Soldiers, families and government
passages.text: Old military divisions associated with Fez and Marrakesh became lasting family groups. Names such as Fasi and Marrakshi preserved memories of these origins even as the communities became part of local society. A surname could carry a much longer journey than its owner.

passages.title: Books, learning and ordinary concerns
passages.text: A Timbuktu library manuscript copied in 1733 charts the stars and connects their movements with seasons. Its astronomy also includes astrological ideas. The diagram offers a concrete glimpse of what a scholar might study during this map period.

passages.title: Books, learning and ordinary concerns
passages.text: An eighteenth-century arithmetic commentary by al-Rasmuki explains addition, subtraction, multiplication and division with charts. Books used in Timbuktu and North Africa made calculation a teachable skill. Even among desert manuscripts, somebody still had to do the sums.

passages.title: Books, learning and ordinary concerns
passages.text: A poem by al-Mukhtar al-Kunti discusses the rights of orphans and married women. Verse helped readers remember legal instruction. Another manuscript treats contracts and loans in verse: rhyme could help carry serious rules about money and responsibility.

passages.title: Books, learning and ordinary concerns
passages.text: A medical manuscript from the same library collection describes illnesses, plant, animal and mineral preparations, and prayers or protective amulets. It records historical approaches to healing, rather than advice to follow today. These collections preserve the city’s wider scholarly life, not only Arma authors.

passages.title: Books, learning and ordinary concerns
passages.text: A small Arabic sample is “الباب الاول”, meaning “the first chapter”, from the 1898 printed edition of al-Sadi’s seventeenth-century history of the region. Arabic was a language of historical scholarship. This is a later printed witness, not a surviving page in the author’s own handwriting.

passages.title: A city maintained, authority transformed
passages.text: Timbuktu’s Djingareyber, Sankore and Sidi Yahia mosques are older than the Arma map interval. Their earthen architecture depended on repeated care. UNESCO emphasizes surviving construction techniques and maintenance: keeping a famous building standing is itself a skilled, continuing achievement.

passages.title: A city maintained, authority transformed
passages.text: Timbuktu was never simply a military headquarters. Its scholars and prominent families maintained institutions of learning and asserted local autonomy under successive rulers. Their influence helps explain why a change of soldiers did not automatically replace the city’s intellectual and civic life.

passages.title: A city maintained, authority transformed
passages.text: The Kel Tadamakkat defeated the pashalik in 1737, but Arma authority briefly recovered after 1755. Further attacks followed. Historian Ariela Marcus-Sells places the decisive Iwellemmedan capture of Timbuktu in 1787, illustrating a long erosion of power rather than a single neat collapse in the map’s last year.

passages.title: A city maintained, authority transformed
passages.text: Arma communities continued after the pashalik. In a February 2023 justice meeting, an Arma community leader from Gao described helping settle minor land and family disputes and referring larger matters to formal courts. This is a dated modern example of community life, not a claim that eighteenth-century government survives unchanged.

Arma political supremacy weakened through eighteenth-century warfare; the 1787 capture of Timbuktu is one scholarly endpoint for the pashalik. The map’s 1783 cutoff is not an established fall date. Arma families and communities continued.

sectionTitles: Kingdoms, diplomacy and a short-lived empire
Families, coins and words that survive

passages.text: Ancient Armenia was a succession of highland kingdoms, not one unchanging dynasty. These two map records cover 323 to 200 BCE and 1 BCE to 400 CE; the gap is an atlas omission, not a disappearance of Armenia. Orontid, Artaxiad and Arsacid rulers connected the country with Iranian and Mediterranean worlds.

passages.title: Kingdoms, diplomacy and a short-lived empire
passages.text: The Orontids linked Armenian kingship to the earlier Iranian imperial world while operating among Hellenistic powers. Their history survives unevenly in Greek authors, inscriptions and coins. A dynasty could adopt new diplomatic partners without replacing every local institution or family.

passages.title: Kingdoms, diplomacy and a short-lived empire
passages.text: Artaxias I set up inscribed boundary stones on the lands of towns and estates. Such markers made royal authority visible where a dispute could be painfully practical: whose field, and whose harvest? Archaeologists have recovered multiple stones bearing Aramaic inscriptions.

passages.title: Kingdoms, diplomacy and a short-lived empire
passages.text: Tigranes II, ruling approximately 95 to 55 BCE, expanded Armenia into a major power between Rome and Parthia. His conquests included Sophene and Syria. The imperial maximum belongs between the two imported map intervals, so neither outline should be treated as a picture of his whole empire.

passages.title: Kingdoms, diplomacy and a short-lived empire
passages.text: Conquest did not guarantee a permanent empire. After wars against Roman commanders, Tigranes reached a settlement with Pompey in 66 BCE. He lost his wider conquests but retained the Armenian kingdom and continued to rule. Losing an empire was not the same event as the disappearance of Armenia.

passages.title: Kingdoms, diplomacy and a short-lived empire
passages.text: Arsacid government involved bargaining with hereditary princely houses. Kings tried to strengthen their own authority; powerful nobles defended inherited positions and possessions. Palace politics therefore depended on regional families as well as on relations with Rome and Iran.

passages.title: Inside a working city
passages.text: Artaxata became an Armenian royal capital in the second century BCE. Its buildings used earth as well as stone. Researchers examined mudbrick with microscopes and material analyses, turning apparently ordinary lumps of soil into evidence for how builders organized their work.

passages.title: Inside a working city
passages.text: The mudbrick study suggests that Hellenistic builders remade material from older Urartian bricks. Old earth could be broken down, mixed with water and fresh temper, and shaped again. Recycling here meant manufacturing new bricks from old material: a much older idea than the modern recycling bin.

passages.title: Inside a working city
passages.text: Pottery from Artaxata’s Hill XIII records a change in how buildings were used. Early complexes, dating to the second and first centuries BCE, contained many fine vessels and may have served public or sanctuary functions. Later domestic occupation brought more cooking pots and storage jars.

passages.title: Inside a working city
passages.text: A study of 53 ceramic samples found that most of the examined pottery was made locally. Fine tableware, coarse vessels and turquoise-glazed wares involved different recipes or workshops. A household’s dishes could therefore connect it with several specialized producers within the same city.

passages.title: Inside a working city
passages.text: Cooking and storage vessels give archaeologists a route into household work that royal histories often ignore. At Artaxata, the increased number of such pots is evidence for domestic activity; the shapes alone do not supply a complete dinner menu or tell us exactly who cooked.

passages.title: Inside a working city
passages.text: Excavations in 1979 and 1980 recovered roughly 8,000 seal impressions on Artaxata’s Hill V, with a much smaller group on Hill VIII. These small clay marks outlasted the documents they once helped secure. For archaeologists, administrative paperwork can survive as its packaging.

passages.title: Inside a working city
passages.text: Were those seals from private business or a public archive? A modern reassessment compares their size, imagery and administrative character and argues for a city archive. The interpretation remains an archaeological argument, but it makes the collection important evidence for organized record keeping.

passages.title: Water, buildings and religious change
passages.text: An aqueduct discovered outside Artaxata was a water project that never reached completion. Excavators connect its foundations with Trajan’s Roman occupation, approximately 114 to 117 CE. After Trajan died, Hadrian relinquished the province and construction stopped. These pillars are evidence of an interrupted plan, not proof of running taps.

passages.title: Water, buildings and religious change
passages.text: The aqueduct first appeared to investigators as a dotted line in a magnetic survey. Excavation, drilling, drone imagery and mortar analysis helped explain the pattern. The broad scientific dating was less precise than the historical attribution: archaeology combines several clues rather than producing a date stamped on every stone.

passages.title: Water, buildings and religious change
passages.text: At Artaxata, a church announced in 2024 has an octagonal plan with cross-shaped extensions. Surviving wooden platforms were radiocarbon-dated to the middle of the fourth century. The building provides physical evidence for an early Christian community, alongside the written traditions about Armenia’s conversion.

passages.title: Water, buildings and religious change
passages.text: The church measured about 30 metres across and had mortar flooring, terracotta tiles and fragments of imported Mediterranean marble. Its builders and patrons invested in a substantial shared religious space. The excavators had not yet established its dedication: finding a church does not automatically reveal its name.

passages.title: Families, coins and words that survive
passages.text: A copper coin from Artaxata names Queen Erato alongside a King Tigranes. Oxford’s catalogue leaves the attribution uncertain between Tigranes III and V, with possible dates around 10 or 5 BCE or 6 CE. A royal woman is visible here through money, even when the exact reign remains debated.

passages.title: Families, coins and words that survive
passages.text: The coin’s Greek reverse reads Ἐρατὼ βασιλέως Τιγράνου ἀδελφή, transliterated Eratō basileōs Tigranou adelphē: “Erato, sister of King Tigranes.” This is a catalogue transcription of an ancient coin legend, not Armenian script. It shows how a royal family relationship could become a public message.

passages.title: Families, coins and words that survive
passages.text: An earlier writing sample comes from Artaxias’s boundary stones: MLK RWNDKN, translated by the scholar James Russell as “Orontid king.” This is scholarly transliteration of Aramaic, with an alternative reading noted in the publication. Artaxias advertised inherited legitimacy even while establishing a new dynasty.

passages.title: Families, coins and words that survive
passages.text: Armenian is an Indo-European language with extensive Iranian influence, but it is not simply a form of Persian. Its own alphabet was created by Mesrop Mashtots around 405, just after these map records end. Surviving Armenian literary writing therefore belongs to a later phase than the Aramaic and Greek witnesses shown here.

Neither 200 BCE nor 400 CE marks Armenia’s disappearance. After partition around 387, an eastern Armenian monarchy survived until its abolition in 428 under Sasanian authority. Armenian communities, aristocratic families and the church continued through the political change.

sectionTitles: A highland crossroads, not one unchanged kingdom
Cities, households and the work behind trade

passages.text: This map record covers 1000 to 1279 in the Armenian highlands, across several changing political orders. It includes the final decades of the Bagratid kingdom of Ani, followed by Byzantine, Seljuk, Georgian and Mongol rule in different places and periods. The repeated outline and its 1100 to 1200 gap are atlas limitations, not a continuous independent kingdom or an empty century.

passages.title: A highland crossroads, not one unchanged kingdom
passages.text: A new Bagratid monarchy emerged in the 880s. Its capital moved from Bagaran to Kars and then to Ani in 961. The record’s start at 1000 picks up a kingdom already more than a century old.

passages.title: A highland crossroads, not one unchanged kingdom
passages.text: Different branches of the ruling family established kingdoms at Kars and Lori, while other Armenian dynasties also claimed royal titles. Ani’s king could bear the title “king of kings,” but the highlands contained multiple courts and competing interests. Family connections did not guarantee political unity.

passages.title: A highland crossroads, not one unchanged kingdom
passages.text: In 1045, Gagik II of Ani was pressured into surrendering his kingdom to the Byzantine emperor. This ended Ani’s Bagratid monarchy; it did not end Armenian society. The date matters because much of this map interval lies after that royal state had ceased to exist.

passages.title: A highland crossroads, not one unchanged kingdom
passages.text: The Armenian kingdom of Cilicia developed separately near the Mediterranean, with a king crowned in 1198 or 1199. Its capital at Sis lay outside this imported highland outline. A shared language and religious tradition connected Armenian communities without making their different states interchangeable.

passages.title: Cities, households and the work behind trade
passages.text: Ani stood on a defensible plateau above river valleys and grew wealthy through a branch of the Silk Roads. Its remains include houses, a market, fortifications, churches, a mosque and a bridge. These structures accumulated under different rulers: the city was more than a royal monument or a single religious community.

passages.title: Cities, households and the work behind trade
passages.text: Architects and stoneworkers at Ani brought together Armenian, Georgian and Islamic building traditions. Its surviving religious, domestic and military structures show a long exchange of ideas in design and decoration. The ruined city is an archaeological record of those interactions, rather than a perfectly preserved snapshot of one year.

passages.title: Cities, households and the work behind trade
passages.text: At Ambroyi village, thirteenth- and fourteenth-century excavated spaces contained clay ovens, storage pits and cooking rubbish. Nearby Arai-Bazarjul caravanserai had closely matching cooking jars and red bowls. Archaeologist Kate Franklin argues that village households helped feed travelers. This evidence straddles the map’s 1279 endpoint.

passages.title: Cities, households and the work behind trade
passages.text: The same thirteenth- and fourteenth-century caravanserai yielded wheat, barley, millet, fruit remains and chopped animal bones. Franklin interprets the combination as evidence for grain-and-meat dishes, perhaps resembling herisa porridge. That is a reconstruction from rubbish, not a surviving menu; the cooks did not leave recipe cards in the drain.

passages.title: Cities, households and the work behind trade
passages.text: Small finds from Arai-Bazarjul’s medieval gutters included iron nails, fragments of horse or donkey shoes, needles and beads. Trade required repairs and animal care as well as buying and selling. These thirteenth- and fourteenth-century objects reveal everyday maintenance around the caravan routes.

passages.title: Bath time required engineering
passages.text: Excavations at Lore fortress uncovered two bathhouses associated with its eleventh- to thirteenth-century development. One had a heater, bathing area and dressing room. Later builders apparently enlarged the bathing space by taking over part of the dressing room and constructing a replacement: even medieval buildings needed remodeling.

passages.title: Bath time required engineering
passages.text: Lore’s second bathhouse stood beside the gorge. A reservoir supplied water, and differences in height allowed it to flow through the bath by gravity. Clay pipes and waterproof surfaces reveal the practical work behind a warm wash. The arrangements belong to this complex, not necessarily to every home.

passages.title: Bath time required engineering
passages.text: Getting used water out mattered as much as bringing clean water in. At Lore, the gorge-side location made wastewater disposal easier than at the bathhouse in the citadel’s center. This was useful engineering, although draining toward a gorge was not the same thing as modern wastewater treatment.

passages.title: Schools, books and named people
passages.text: Haghpat and Sanahin were important centers of learning during the tenth to thirteenth centuries. Sanahin became known for illuminators and calligraphers: specialists who painted and wrote books by hand. Their work joined education, religious devotion and skilled craft in the same monastic setting.

passages.title: Schools, books and named people
passages.text: Sanahin’s library-scriptorium was built in 1063 with funds from Hranush, daughter of King David Anhoghin, under Abbot Dioskoros. Her patronage made a royal woman part of the history of learning. Books and religious valuables were stored in deep niches in the walls, not in modern library stacks.

passages.title: Schools, books and named people
passages.text: A medieval Armenian manuscript could preserve a small social history in its colophon, the note recording its creation or ownership. Such notes name scribes, donors and sometimes painters or later owners, and may mention personal or political events. These people help historians see beyond the name of a king.

passages.title: Schools, books and named people
passages.text: Bookmaking was physical work as well as scholarship. Medieval Armenian images show paper being polished and texts copied from model books. Such illustrations, some from later centuries than this map interval, help explain the continuing craft tradition. A beautiful page began with prepared materials and many patient movements of the hand.

passages.title: Memory carved into stone
passages.text: At Dadivank, a building inscription dated 1211 identifies Grigoris, son of Hassan, as the patron of a hall. Its wording ties a construction project to family identity and remembrance of the donor’s soul. This is a named medieval person asking future visitors to remember him.

passages.title: Memory carved into stone
passages.text: A short Armenian sample from that inscription is ՅԻՇԵՑԷՔ, transliterated yišecʿēkʿ, meaning “Remember.” It is the final word of the published Armenian transcription, shown here in modern type rather than copied stone lettering. In context, the donor asks to be remembered in prayer.

passages.title: Memory carved into stone
passages.text: Armenian stoneworkers developed khachkars, carved cross stones placed at significant sites and used as grave markers. They turned faith and commemoration into a durable public art. Unlike a book that could be carried away, a standing stone also marked a particular place in the landscape.

The Bagratid kingdom of Ani ended in 1045, long before this map record stops. Armenian communities and institutions continued under later rulers. Ani’s decline unfolded over centuries, shaped by conquest, changing trade routes and the 1319 earthquake; the city was not suddenly erased at the map’s 1279 boundary.

sectionTitles: A university and an Armenian sentence
Remaking a city and remembering its costs

passages.text: This map record combines a troubled era rather than one state lasting from 1914 to 1938. The independent Armenian Republic existed from 1918 to 1920, followed by Soviet rule. The imported “Sasanian E” alias is wrong. Its 1930 outline lies far west across much of present-day eastern Turkey; it must not be read as Soviet Armenia’s border or proof that a proposed postwar Armenian frontier became reality.

passages.title: War, survival and public responsibility
passages.text: In 1914, Armenian society was divided across imperial borders. Russian forces and Ottoman forces fought through the Caucasus and eastern Anatolia. The modern country and the Ottoman Armenian communities affected by that war were connected, but they were not identical territories or populations.

passages.title: War, survival and public responsibility
passages.text: The Armenian genocide destroyed Ottoman Armenian communities in 1915 and 1916 through mass killing, deportation and deliberately lethal conditions. Survivors and refugees carried memories, skills and family ties into new places. Their later lives belong to this history alongside the violence inflicted on them.

passages.title: War, survival and public responsibility
passages.text: The First Republic’s 1919 election sent three women to an eighty-member parliament. Katarine Zalyan-Manukyan, Perchuhi Partizpanyan-Barseghyan and Varvara Sahakyan participated in a new public institution during an emergency. Voting rights and elected office opened possibilities beyond traditional household responsibilities.

passages.title: War, survival and public responsibility
passages.text: Katarine Zalyan-Manukyan worked on the Medical-Sanitary Commission, including refugees’ needs. Varvara Sahakyan also worked with people left homeless by the genocide. Medicine, shelter and family survival were immediate political tasks, not subjects that could wait until borders and governments settled down.

passages.title: A university and an Armenian sentence
passages.text: A law of 16 May 1919 established the university. Because Yerevan lacked a suitable building, the opening took place at Alexandropol’s trade school on 31 January 1920. A national university began by borrowing space: an ambitious idea did not arrive with a ready-made campus.

passages.title: A university and an Armenian sentence
passages.text: For the opening, a one-day newspaper presented professors’ speeches and the first semester’s timetable. Its sales supported a fund for students with little money. Publishing, public celebration and practical help for students were brought together in the same small object.

passages.title: A university and an Armenian sentence
passages.text: Written Armenian: Գիտութիւնն ոյժ է ,  Gitutʿiwnn oyž ē, “Science is power.” This is the university museum’s transcription of the motto in the newspaper issued on 31 January 1920. Its historical spelling is preserved; the museum’s English account supplies the translation.

passages.title: A university and an Armenian sentence
passages.text: Teaching required books as well as buildings. The university’s history records professors translating textbooks in 1922. Students attended laboratory work and seminars alongside lectures, making scientific education a matter of things to handle and test as well as words to hear.

passages.title: A university and an Armenian sentence
passages.text: Laboratories obtained microscopes and other costly equipment from abroad. In 1926, physiologist Leon Orbeli helped purchase laboratory equipment. Scientific work depended on these networks of people and instruments; declaring a faculty was only the start of making it function.

passages.title: Children, food and ordinary pleasures
passages.text: At Alexandropol’s relief orphanages, schooling and vocational training shared the day with organized play. An archive photograph shows girls doing gymnastics in the yard around 1920. These institutions served children affected by catastrophe; their routines were not a description of every Armenian childhood.

passages.title: Children, food and ordinary pleasures
passages.text: The orphanage gardens supplied practical lessons, but children also filled them with little mud houses and play spaces. Archived photographs show children building and inspecting these miniature structures. A gardening lesson could apparently acquire its own tiny neighborhood.

passages.title: Children, food and ordinary pleasures
passages.text: Food relief could begin far away in a grocery shop. In 1921, American shopkeepers displayed flour barrels and collected contributions for Near East Relief. Alexandropol’s orphanages used flour in large quantities for bread, although the surviving account does not identify the exact bread recipe.

passages.title: Remaking a city and remembering its costs
passages.text: Alexander Tamanyan’s 1924 plan imagined Yerevan for about 150,000 residents. Broad streets and open squares reorganized the capital. The plan shows how a government could try to shape daily movement, public gatherings and future growth through the layout of a city.

passages.title: Remaking a city and remembering its costs
passages.text: During the 1930s, Yerevan gained electricity, sewers, running water and paved streets. These works changed practical city life, from lighting to moving water and waste. The evidence describes urban infrastructure, not a promise that every home immediately had its own bathroom.

passages.title: Remaking a city and remembering its costs
passages.text: Modernization also removed older places. Yerevan’s ruined fortress, the old ruler’s palace and open bazaar were cleared away during rebuilding. A new capital gained facilities while losing parts of its earlier streetscape; progress and preservation did not always travel together.

passages.title: Remaking a city and remembering its costs
passages.text: Educational growth existed alongside Stalinist repression. University rector Kamsar Arakelyan was arrested on 8 January 1938, later imprisoned and exiled. He was cleared in 1955 when the case was found to lack a crime. Political terror could overturn a scholarly career and a family’s life.

The independent republic ended in 1920 amid Turkish attacks and the Soviet takeover. Armenian institutions continued in a different political system. The map’s 1938 cutoff ends this imported interval, not Soviet Armenia or Armenian society; Soviet rule lasted until 1991.

passages.text: This is the modern Republic of Armenia, whose independence referendum took place on 21 September 1991, before this map record begins in 1994. It is distinct from Soviet Armenia and the First Republic of 1918 to 1920. The imported “Sasanian E” alias is erroneous. Coarse outlines from 1994, 2000 and 2010 cannot establish present legal borders or resolve the changing history of the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict.

passages.title: Government and public words
passages.text: Armenia entered the United Nations on 2 March 1992. Membership offers a clear milestone in the republic’s international history, separate from the date when a particular atlas happens to begin drawing its outline.

passages.title: Government and public words
passages.text: The 2015 constitutional text gives the National Assembly a role in choosing the prime minister, who directs government policy and coordinates ministers. These written rules describe the organization of public power; the text itself is not evidence that every constitutional promise is always fulfilled.

passages.title: Government and public words
passages.text: Written Armenian: իշխանությունը պատկանում է ժողովրդին ,  išxanutʿyunə patkanum ē žołovrdin, “power belongs to the people.” These words come from Article 2 of the official constitutional text adopted on 6 December 2015. The excerpt preserves the Armenian spelling; the official English version provides the translation.

passages.title: Bread, relatives and creative skills
passages.text: UNESCO’s 2014 description of lavash shows bread-making as coordinated work. Bakers stretch a thin sheet of flour-and-water dough over an oval cushion and slap it onto a clay oven’s inner wall. It bakes in roughly thirty seconds to one minute: this bread requires close attention!

passages.title: Bread, relatives and creative skills
passages.text: The same account describes women baking together, younger girls helping and learning, and men making cushions or building ovens. These are documented patterns of sharing skills, not rules for every household. A loaf depends on tools, building knowledge and teamwork as well as a baker.

passages.title: Bread, relatives and creative skills
passages.text: Lavash can wrap cheese, greens or meat. In the wedding practice described by UNESCO, it is also placed on newlyweds’ shoulders with wishes for fertility and prosperity. Bread can be both food for a meal and part of how a family marks a new beginning.

passages.title: Learning and modern discoveries
passages.text: TUMO describes a free educational program where teenagers combine self-directed activities, workshops and project laboratories. Its founders, Sam and Sylva Simonian, grew up in Beirut and later moved to the United States. Their educational project is one concrete link between Armenia and its wider diaspora.

passages.title: Learning and modern discoveries
passages.text: Armenian letters can become art as well as sentences. UNESCO’s 2019 record describes ornamental letters shaped like birds, animals, knots and imaginary creatures, used by craftspeople including embroiderers, sculptors and jewelers. Learning to recognize a letter might occasionally involve spotting its beak!

passages.title: Learning and modern discoveries
passages.text: Modern archaeological research brought an ancient shoe back into view. In 2008, a team at Areni-1 cave found a complete leather shoe in a prehistoric pit. Published analysis dated its leather to approximately 3627 to 3377 BCE. This was a modern discovery of ancient life, not an invention by the modern republic.

passages.title: Learning and modern discoveries
passages.text: The Areni shoe was made from one piece of leather and had taken the shape of a right foot. Grass packed inside may have helped it keep its shape in storage. The researchers could not securely identify the wearer’s sex: even a well-preserved shoe does not tell its owner’s whole story.

passages.title: School toilets and healthcare that travels
passages.text: A UNICEF assessment begun in 2023 examined 350 schools and preschools in Lori, Syunik, Gegharkunik and Yerevan. Among assessed schools, 86 percent lacked sanitation accessible to students with disabilities. This is a finding about the surveyed institutions, not a census of every school in Armenia.

passages.title: School toilets and healthcare that travels
passages.text: In January 2025, accessible mobile restroom units arrived at schools in Hovk and Hermon. Hovk’s earlier toilet had a rocky access path, and its washing pipe was attached to a tree. The new model addressed privacy, handwashing and access together rather than simply adding another door.

passages.title: School toilets and healthcare that travels
passages.text: The mobile toilet design solves an unusual problem: a school may need decent bathrooms now even when its building will later be replaced. UNICEF explains that the unit can move to another site after a rebuilt school gains indoor facilities. Even a bathroom can have a second assignment.

passages.title: School toilets and healthcare that travels
passages.text: WHO’s March 2024 account describes mobile mental-health teams visiting communities affected by the refugee influx. A social worker from Karabakh worked with a psychiatrist and psychologists. Care involved helping people with grief, stress and longer-term conditions, bringing services closer to families rather than expecting everyone to travel.

passages.title: School toilets and healthcare that travels
passages.text: Between November 2023 and February 2024, outreach teams also brought consultations and flu vaccination to older people and people with chronic conditions in shelters and care facilities. WHO describes a 75-year-old woman receiving vaccination alongside her family in a former kindergarten used as a shelter.

passages.title: Conflict, displacement and continuity
passages.text: A joint statement by Armenia, Azerbaijan and Russia declared a ceasefire effective on 10 November 2020 in the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict zone. Its provisions addressed military positions, peacekeeping and movement. This is a dated agreement; its terms should not be mistaken for a description of today’s situation.

passages.title: Conflict, displacement and continuity
passages.text: In September 2023, more than 100,000 refugees arrived in Armenia from Karabakh within one week, according to UNHCR. Receiving communities had to find housing, classroom places and services at extraordinary speed. Refugee experience is part of the republic’s recent history, not an interchangeable label for all its residents.

passages.title: Conflict, displacement and continuity
passages.text: On 11 August 2025, Armenia’s foreign ministry published the initialed Armenia-Azerbaijan peace agreement by mutual agreement of the parties. Publication and initialing are specific diplomatic steps. This dated record alone does not establish that every provision had been ratified or put into effect.

The Republic of Armenia continues as a state and United Nations member. Its modern history includes constitutional change, cultural work, scientific research and the demands of caring for displaced families. Neither a map snapshot ending in 2020 nor this card’s historical phases mark the country’s disappearance.

sectionTitles: Everyday objects and practical water supplies
Talin: two brothers, a cathedral and an inscription
Learning, books and food in a mathematics lesson

passages.text: This map’s Armenia represents part of the region during caliphal rule, not a restored Armenian kingdom. Dvin served as a caliphal governor’s seat until 789. The imported outline covers a northern and eastern slice: Talin is inside it, while Dvin is just outside. The map’s “Sasanian E” alias is misleading for this period; neither the outline nor its 700 to 800 interval defines the whole historical province.

passages.title: Rulers, obligations and changing power
passages.text: Armenian princes still mattered under outside rule. Ghewond describes governor Marwan appointing Ashot Bagratuni as presiding prince in the 730s. Ashot then sought overdue cavalry pay from Caliph Hisham: political cooperation involved money for mounted soldiers as well as titles.

passages.title: Rulers, obligations and changing power
passages.text: Christian Armenian communities belonged to the caliphate’s protected but subordinate non-Muslim population. Church life could continue, while liability for the jizya poll tax marked an unequal legal position. Religious protection did not mean equal citizenship in the modern sense.

passages.title: Rulers, obligations and changing power
passages.text: Power also rested on family estates. The Kamsarakans held principalities in Shirak and Arsharunik. Following a failed late eighth-century revolt, they sold these lands to the Bagratids. A dynasty could lose its regional power without its descendants or cultural connections disappearing.

passages.title: Everyday objects and practical water supplies
passages.text: Dvin’s excavated pottery, broadly dated to the fifth through eighth centuries, includes jars, pitchers, cups and small perfume containers. These reveal different jobs for different vessels: storing, pouring, drinking and keeping a small valuable liquid. A kitchen cupboard already needed more than one shape.

passages.title: Everyday objects and practical water supplies
passages.text: Oil lamps and an inkpot appear among Dvin’s broadly dated fifth- to eighth-century finds. Lighting a room and writing required physical equipment, not just skill. An excavated object can preserve a small working detail that a story about kings leaves out.

passages.title: Everyday objects and practical water supplies
passages.text: Glass vessels also survive from fifth- to eighth-century Dvin. Their fragments widen the household picture beyond clay: people used different materials for containers. This evidence identifies objects, without telling us that every family could afford the same possessions.

passages.title: Everyday objects and practical water supplies
passages.text: The Dvin excavation report identifies water mains as part of a complex urban water-supply system in its fifth- to eighth-century material. Moving water through a town required planned infrastructure. These remains do not establish that every home had a tap or a toilet.

passages.title: Talin: two brothers, a cathedral and an inscription
passages.text: At Talin, monk Uxtaytur and his brother Tuti endowed the cathedral with a water source. Their inscription dates the gift to Armenian year 232, corresponding to 15 May 783 through 13 May 784. Here, family cooperation left a particularly practical monument.

passages.title: Talin: two brothers, a cathedral and an inscription
passages.text: The donors protected their gift with a written curse against anyone who destroyed the water source. An ordinary “please do not break this” sign apparently did not feel strong enough. The warning tied damage to spiritual responsibility for the donor’s sins.

passages.title: Talin: two brothers, a cathedral and an inscription
passages.text: Talin’s cathedral was probably built in the later seventh century, so it already had a history by the time of the water gift. Black and red tufa stone formed its walls; surviving painted decoration includes an open book resting on a cushioned throne.

passages.title: Talin: two brothers, a cathedral and an inscription
passages.text: Written Armenian: ՏՈՒՏԻ ԵՂԲԱՅՐ ԻՄ ,  Tuti ełbayr im, “Tuti, my brother.” This is a modern scholarly transcription of three surviving words in line 3 of Talin’s water inscription, dated 783/784. The family relationship is recorded on stone, not supplied by a modern storyteller.

passages.title: Learning, books and food in a mathematics lesson
passages.text: A useful earlier background is the seventh-century scholar Anania of Shirak. His autobiography describes eight years studying with Tychikos at Trebizond. The teacher could translate Greek into Armenian and owned scientific, historical and medical books: education crossed linguistic and political boundaries.

passages.title: Learning, books and food in a mathematics lesson
passages.text: Anania’s arithmetic gives food a starring role. Its seventh-century problems involve garden lettuce, river fish and wine measured into jars. These are imaginary exercises built around recognizable activities, preserved in later manuscripts; they are glimpses of a teaching world rather than a menu for every Armenian household.

passages.title: Learning, books and food in a mathematics lesson
passages.text: One problem has a student bringing apples to his teacher. Three groups of jesters successively take three-quarters of the remaining fruit. Only five apples arrive. Working backward gives 320 at the start: a surprisingly expensive mathematics lesson, at least in apples!

passages.title: Learning, books and food in a mathematics lesson
passages.text: The same arithmetic collection includes entertaining puzzles intended for social gatherings. Fractions and number tricks could be a form of amusement as well as instruction. This is evidence for the book’s purpose, not a claim that every eighth-century dinner came with a compulsory mathematics quiz.

passages.title: How we know
passages.text: Ghewond wrote in the late eighth century, drawing on older informants and events closer to his own lifetime. His Christian outlook and Bagratid patronage shaped the story. The surviving manuscript tradition is later, so his text is neither a neutral government report nor an original eighth-century notebook.

passages.title: How we know
passages.text: Dvin became a major archaeological project in the twentieth century, with excavations running from 1937 apart from the wartime interruption. Much of the uncovered material belongs to later centuries. Dating each find matters: an impressive medieval ruin cannot automatically describe life in the year 700.

The map’s cutoff at 800 is not the disappearance of Armenian society. Dvin’s role as the caliphal governor’s seat had ended in 789, but the city continued through later struggles involving Arab rulers and Armenian dynasties. This card’s century is one phase within that longer history.

sectionTitles: Kingdoms, diplomacy and a short-lived empire
Families, coins and words that survive

passages.text: Ancient Armenia was a succession of highland kingdoms, not one unchanging dynasty. These two map records cover 323 to 200 BCE and 1 BCE to 400 CE; the gap is an atlas omission, not a disappearance of Armenia. Orontid, Artaxiad and Arsacid rulers connected the country with Iranian and Mediterranean worlds.

passages.title: Kingdoms, diplomacy and a short-lived empire
passages.text: The Orontids linked Armenian kingship to the earlier Iranian imperial world while operating among Hellenistic powers. Their history survives unevenly in Greek authors, inscriptions and coins. A dynasty could adopt new diplomatic partners without replacing every local institution or family.

passages.title: Kingdoms, diplomacy and a short-lived empire
passages.text: Artaxias I set up inscribed boundary stones on the lands of towns and estates. Such markers made royal authority visible where a dispute could be painfully practical: whose field, and whose harvest? Archaeologists have recovered multiple stones bearing Aramaic inscriptions.

passages.title: Kingdoms, diplomacy and a short-lived empire
passages.text: Tigranes II, ruling approximately 95 to 55 BCE, expanded Armenia into a major power between Rome and Parthia. His conquests included Sophene and Syria. The imperial maximum belongs between the two imported map intervals, so neither outline should be treated as a picture of his whole empire.

passages.title: Kingdoms, diplomacy and a short-lived empire
passages.text: Conquest did not guarantee a permanent empire. After wars against Roman commanders, Tigranes reached a settlement with Pompey in 66 BCE. He lost his wider conquests but retained the Armenian kingdom and continued to rule. Losing an empire was not the same event as the disappearance of Armenia.

passages.title: Kingdoms, diplomacy and a short-lived empire
passages.text: Arsacid government involved bargaining with hereditary princely houses. Kings tried to strengthen their own authority; powerful nobles defended inherited positions and possessions. Palace politics therefore depended on regional families as well as on relations with Rome and Iran.

passages.title: Inside a working city
passages.text: Artaxata became an Armenian royal capital in the second century BCE. Its buildings used earth as well as stone. Researchers examined mudbrick with microscopes and material analyses, turning apparently ordinary lumps of soil into evidence for how builders organized their work.

passages.title: Inside a working city
passages.text: The mudbrick study suggests that Hellenistic builders remade material from older Urartian bricks. Old earth could be broken down, mixed with water and fresh temper, and shaped again. Recycling here meant manufacturing new bricks from old material: a much older idea than the modern recycling bin.

passages.title: Inside a working city
passages.text: Pottery from Artaxata’s Hill XIII records a change in how buildings were used. Early complexes, dating to the second and first centuries BCE, contained many fine vessels and may have served public or sanctuary functions. Later domestic occupation brought more cooking pots and storage jars.

passages.title: Inside a working city
passages.text: A study of 53 ceramic samples found that most of the examined pottery was made locally. Fine tableware, coarse vessels and turquoise-glazed wares involved different recipes or workshops. A household’s dishes could therefore connect it with several specialized producers within the same city.

passages.title: Inside a working city
passages.text: Cooking and storage vessels give archaeologists a route into household work that royal histories often ignore. At Artaxata, the increased number of such pots is evidence for domestic activity; the shapes alone do not supply a complete dinner menu or tell us exactly who cooked.

passages.title: Inside a working city
passages.text: Excavations in 1979 and 1980 recovered roughly 8,000 seal impressions on Artaxata’s Hill V, with a much smaller group on Hill VIII. These small clay marks outlasted the documents they once helped secure. For archaeologists, administrative paperwork can survive as its packaging.

passages.title: Inside a working city
passages.text: Were those seals from private business or a public archive? A modern reassessment compares their size, imagery and administrative character and argues for a city archive. The interpretation remains an archaeological argument, but it makes the collection important evidence for organized record keeping.

passages.title: Water, buildings and religious change
passages.text: An aqueduct discovered outside Artaxata was a water project that never reached completion. Excavators connect its foundations with Trajan’s Roman occupation, approximately 114 to 117 CE. After Trajan died, Hadrian relinquished the province and construction stopped. These pillars are evidence of an interrupted plan, not proof of running taps.

passages.title: Water, buildings and religious change
passages.text: The aqueduct first appeared to investigators as a dotted line in a magnetic survey. Excavation, drilling, drone imagery and mortar analysis helped explain the pattern. The broad scientific dating was less precise than the historical attribution: archaeology combines several clues rather than producing a date stamped on every stone.

passages.title: Water, buildings and religious change
passages.text: At Artaxata, a church announced in 2024 has an octagonal plan with cross-shaped extensions. Surviving wooden platforms were radiocarbon-dated to the middle of the fourth century. The building provides physical evidence for an early Christian community, alongside the written traditions about Armenia’s conversion.

passages.title: Water, buildings and religious change
passages.text: The church measured about 30 metres across and had mortar flooring, terracotta tiles and fragments of imported Mediterranean marble. Its builders and patrons invested in a substantial shared religious space. The excavators had not yet established its dedication: finding a church does not automatically reveal its name.

passages.title: Families, coins and words that survive
passages.text: A copper coin from Artaxata names Queen Erato alongside a King Tigranes. Oxford’s catalogue leaves the attribution uncertain between Tigranes III and V, with possible dates around 10 or 5 BCE or 6 CE. A royal woman is visible here through money, even when the exact reign remains debated.

passages.title: Families, coins and words that survive
passages.text: The coin’s Greek reverse reads Ἐρατὼ βασιλέως Τιγράνου ἀδελφή, transliterated Eratō basileōs Tigranou adelphē: “Erato, sister of King Tigranes.” This is a catalogue transcription of an ancient coin legend, not Armenian script. It shows how a royal family relationship could become a public message.

passages.title: Families, coins and words that survive
passages.text: An earlier writing sample comes from Artaxias’s boundary stones: MLK RWNDKN, translated by the scholar James Russell as “Orontid king.” This is scholarly transliteration of Aramaic, with an alternative reading noted in the publication. Artaxias advertised inherited legitimacy even while establishing a new dynasty.

passages.title: Families, coins and words that survive
passages.text: Armenian is an Indo-European language with extensive Iranian influence, but it is not simply a form of Persian. Its own alphabet was created by Mesrop Mashtots around 405, just after these map records end. Surviving Armenian literary writing therefore belongs to a later phase than the Aramaic and Greek witnesses shown here.

Neither 200 BCE nor 400 CE marks Armenia’s disappearance. After partition around 387, an eastern Armenian monarchy survived until its abolition in 428 under Sasanian authority. Armenian communities, aristocratic families and the church continued through the political change.

sectionTitles: A small word for the stars

passages.text: Early medieval Armorica became a meeting place of local communities and migrants from Britain. Broërec was a particular region around Vannes within this wider story, not another name for the whole peninsula. The imported Broërec outline is misplaced far to the northwest; it should not be used as a reliable border.

passages.title: People crossing the Channel
passages.text: Similarities among Breton, Welsh and Cornish place names and languages support migration from Britain in the late fifth and sixth centuries. Its scale is debated: newcomers could influence existing communities without every family arriving on a boat.

passages.title: People crossing the Channel
passages.text: The council of Tours in 567 distinguished Romans and Bretons living in Armorica. That is unusually clear evidence in a period with few written records. The peninsula contained interacting communities rather than a single population with one simple origin story.

passages.title: Broërec and its neighbours
passages.text: Broërec belonged to the country around Vannes, between the Ellé and Vilaine rivers. The name is associated with Waroc. Geography mattered: this southeastern Breton region faced different neighbours and political pressures from communities at the peninsula’s western tip.

passages.title: Broërec and its neighbours
passages.text: Under Carolingian rule, Vannes, Rennes and Nantes formed parts of a frontier march. Broërec later entered the larger Breton political world. The county’s territory eventually passed into the ducal domain, while its bishopric and regional identity continued.

passages.title: Keeping a farm fed
passages.text: At Lenn Sec’h in Caudan, archaeologists uncovered a farm used during the sixth to ninth centuries. Its enclosure covered about 5,300 square metres, bounded by substantial ditches. These traces give us a household landscape beyond the better-known stories of rulers and saints.

passages.title: Keeping a farm fed
passages.text: Pits at the Caudan farm were used to dry grain before it went into underground storage. A large, deep silo also survived. Getting the harvest safely through the year required planning after the cutting and gathering were finished.

passages.title: Keeping a farm fed
passages.text: One medieval building at Caudan was constructed on ground-level timber sills. The surrounding ditches reached roughly two metres in width and depth. Most of the building itself has disappeared, but the excavated layout still reveals how the farm was organised.

passages.title: A monastery grows
passages.text: At Landévennec, excavation found a small early oratory surrounded by a cemetery. The monastery’s beginnings belong around the turn of the fifth and sixth centuries. The traditional story of Guénolé and eleven disciples is a founding legend, while the buildings provide physical evidence.

passages.title: A monastery grows
passages.text: By the ninth century, after the earlier map phases, Landévennec’s monks copied books and followed the Rule of Benedict. A religious community could also be a centre of learning and a substantial landholder. Copying a book meant sustained skilled work by hand.

passages.title: A monastery grows
passages.text: The excavated ninth-century monastery included a church, living buildings and a courtyard edged by a covered gallery. A Viking raid in 913 interrupted its flourishing life. Its long history helps connect the small early foundation with the more elaborate institutions that followed.

passages.title: A small word for the stars
passages.text: In Pierre-Yves Lambert’s reading, the Old Breton word “nimer” means “constellation”. It appears above a Latin star-name in Angers manuscript 477, folio 14b. This is the scholarly transcription of an attested word in Latin letters; another scholar interpreted it as “number”.

passages.title: A small word for the stars
passages.text: The relevant part of Angers 477 was written in 897 and contains many Breton notes beside Latin learning. Scholars identify Breton scribes but debate where they worked. The book therefore illustrates later Breton scholarship and its connections, rather than a securely located school in early Broërec.

Armorica and Broërec did not vanish when these map intervals ended. Local political structures became part of wider Breton kingdoms and the duchy. The Vannes region retained a recognisable identity through those changes.

sectionTitles: Ovens, workshops and the archaeology of ordinary life
Stories and a real line of Persian

passages.text: Here Arran means a medieval Caucasian region between the Kura and Aras rivers, not the Scottish island. The map covers 1000 to 1200, across changing rulers. Its simplified outline includes Barda and Baylaqan but cuts off the Ganja urban area discussed here. This is neither a complete map of ancient Caucasian Albania nor an uninterrupted kingdom; Armenia, Artsakh and later regional identities remain distinct.

passages.title: Cities between competing powers
passages.text: The Shaddadids established themselves at Ganja in 969 or 970 with local support. Fadl I expanded their territory and took Barda and Baylaqan in 993, shortly before this map begins. Their dynasty probably had Kurdish origins, but its subjects belonged to a much more varied regional population.

passages.title: Cities between competing powers
passages.text: In 1075 the Seljuq commander Sav Tegin took the Ganja branch’s territories. Peacock favors the account connecting this transfer to Sultan Malik Shah, rather than the already deceased Alp Arslan. The Shaddadids of Ani followed a separate political history; their survival does not mean their old Arran government survived unchanged.

passages.title: Cities between competing powers
passages.text: An earthquake devastated Ganja in 1139, and a Georgian army raided the damaged city. The governor Qara Sonqor rebuilt it, and Ganja again flourished under later rulers, including the Ildegizid atabegs. Rebuilding a city meant restoring a place where people worked and lived, as well as a seat of power.

passages.title: Cities between competing powers
passages.text: One iron gate preserves a craftsman’s name. Its Arabic inscription dates its manufacture to AH 455, about 1063, and names the blacksmith Ibrahim son of Uthman. Georgian forces carried the gate away in 1139; a surviving leaf is now at Gelati. A city entrance became a war trophy, but the maker’s credit survived the journey.

passages.title: Ovens, workshops and the archaeology of ordinary life
passages.text: Excavations at Barda in 2015 uncovered settlement from the eleventh through fourteenth centuries. This challenged the idea that everyone had abandoned the city for nearby Ganja. Pottery and building remains can correct a story of urban decline: losing political importance is not the same as losing every household.

passages.title: Ovens, workshops and the archaeology of ordinary life
passages.text: Barda’s earliest medieval layers in the 2016 report were dated by pottery to the eleventh through early thirteenth centuries. One hearth reused large fired bricks or floor tiles and retained ash from its last use. A useful old building material could begin another career beside somebody’s fire.

passages.title: Ovens, workshops and the archaeology of ordinary life
passages.text: Nearby, archaeologists found a clay-lined tandir oven on a brick foundation and a pot buried in the ground, probably for cooking or storage. They tentatively interpreted the setting as an outdoor domestic area. These are practical traces of preparing and keeping food; the remains do not identify a particular family or recipe.

passages.title: Ovens, workshops and the archaeology of ordinary life
passages.text: The 2017 Barda report records iron blades and tools, reworked glazed pottery, faience beads, cowrie shells and a worked bone handle. These finds come from a range of medieval contexts, some beyond this map’s endpoint. They reveal skilled hands cutting, shaping and reusing small objects as well as building monuments.

passages.title: Ovens, workshops and the archaeology of ordinary life
passages.text: Small scale pans and coins from the same excavation suggest trading activity. The report cannot turn them into a named shop with a price list, but weighing equipment makes the business of exchange tangible. A tiny balance could matter as much to a transaction as a large city gate.

passages.title: Food, neighbors and families
passages.text: Tenth-century geographers, describing Baylaqan just before this map’s window, praised a flourishing town on the route between Ardabil and Barda. It produced textiles and a confection called natef. The report preserves a tempting trace of regional food, although it does not supply a recipe or tell us how often children ate it.

passages.title: Food, neighbors and families
passages.text: Letters and documents associated with the official Masud ibn Namdar in 1111 and 1112 illuminate Baylaqan’s ethnically and religiously mixed society. Such paperwork offers a view of people living under government, alongside the chronicles that mostly follow rulers and campaigns. Arran was not a place where everyone shared one language or faith.

passages.title: Food, neighbors and families
passages.text: David of Gandzak, writing around the early twelfth century, criticized Christian women at Ganja who married Kurdish men. Yet his account also describes priests baptizing their children and continuing religious care. Read critically, his disapproval reveals actual mixed families and mothers passing on traditions across boundaries that religious authorities wanted to maintain.

passages.title: Stories and a real line of Persian
passages.text: Nizami of Ganja became famous for five long narrative poems, later collected as the Khamsa, or quintet. He drew on earlier Persian writing, oral traditions and Arabic stories while reshaping them into new works. Later poets imitated both individual poems and the five-part collection, carrying Ganja’s literary influence far beyond Arran.

passages.title: Stories and a real line of Persian
passages.text: A modern scholarly printing of Nizami’s Layli and Majnun, completed in 1188, gives this Persian opening: “ای نام تو بهترین سرآغاز” (ey nām-e to behtarīn sarāghāz). Zahra Taheri translates it “O your name the most rightful beginning.” This is a devotional address. The sample is Persian literary writing from a named poet, not a claim that all Arran’s inhabitants spoke Persian or could read it.

passages.title: Stories and a real line of Persian
passages.text: The five poems were gathered into manuscripts after Nizami’s death. The oldest dated surviving copy of the whole collection is from 1362, although earlier incomplete copies survive. This later manuscript history matters: the writing sample above is transmitted literature, not a photograph of a page in the poet’s own handwriting.

The atlas stops in 1200, before further political upheaval. Mongol forces devastated Baylaqan in the early 1220s, but survivors returned and rebuilt; later attempts to revive the town also followed. Arran’s cities and regional names changed over time. Neither the map endpoint nor the destruction of a town marks the disappearance of all its inhabitants.

sectionTitles: The historical region and the imperfect outline
Books, learning and a voice in Armenian

passages.text: This 1100 to 1200 map record represents the historical Artsakh region and the world of Khachen’s local princes, monasteries and settlements. It is not a modern state boundary. Archaeology at Tigranakert and dated Armenian inscriptions reveal both ordinary work and the institutions of powerful families.

passages.title: The historical region and the imperfect outline
passages.text: The imported outline includes Tigranakert, Handaberd and Amaras, but excludes Dadivank and Gandzasar. Those excluded monasteries still provide evidence for historical Khachen. Their examples are located explicitly below. This coarse polygon is neither a verified medieval frontier nor evidence for modern sovereignty, and neighboring Armenia and Arran have separate records.

passages.title: The historical region and the imperfect outline
passages.text: At Dadivank, outside this outline, Hasan son of Vakhtang left an inscription dated 1182. He names six sons and says he gave them his fortresses and districts before becoming a religious in the monastery near his brother Grigores. Family inheritance and religious retirement appear in the same political document.

passages.title: Homes, bread and useful tools
passages.text: Tigranakert’s Central Quarter changed repeatedly. Houses built between the eleventh and mid-twelfth centuries had clay floors, substantial pits and clay-lined tonir ovens as much as 1.5 metres across. The remains bring us into working rooms, where preparing food and storing supplies occupied real space.

passages.title: Homes, bread and useful tools
passages.text: By the late twelfth and early thirteenth centuries, another Tigranakert complex had partly sunken rooms, narrow passages and light reed roofs supported on wooden posts. Its smaller ovens and shallow hearths show a different arrangement of domestic work. A town’s houses did not all follow one timeless plan.

passages.title: Homes, bread and useful tools
passages.text: An iron chopping knife from Tigranakert is dated to the eleventh or twelfth century and interpreted as a tool for gardening and cutting bushes. Excavators also found worn whetstones for sharpening blades. Keeping a useful edge was part of the job; a tool needed care between its turns at work.

passages.title: Homes, bread and useful tools
passages.text: A mill’s upper runner stone from Tigranakert is also dated to the eleventh or twelfth century. The excavation report describes mortars whose bases were worn down through repeated grinding. Grain processing left its mark on the stone itself, turning a household chore into something archaeologists can recognize centuries later.

passages.title: Containers, decoration and water
passages.text: A complete storage jar was found on a twelfth-century floor at Tigranakert. Excavators interpret it as a grain container. Large pottery vessels helped households keep provisions together; alongside the ovens and grinding tools, this jar supplies another piece of the journey from harvested grain to a meal.

passages.title: Containers, decoration and water
passages.text: Some Tigranakert plates from the twelfth and thirteenth centuries carry birds, animals and plant ornament under their glaze. Not every table was plain brown pottery. One fragment shows a bird that researchers identify cautiously as an eagle or peacock: even a fancy broken plate can keep a small mystery.

passages.title: Containers, decoration and water
passages.text: Glass bracelets from Tigranakert’s broader ninth- to thirteenth-century layers include blue, green and black examples, with occasional multicolored pieces. Their fragments record personal adornment as well as the practical vessels of a household. They cannot tell us the names, ages or genders of all the people who wore them.

passages.title: Containers, decoration and water
passages.text: Tigranakert’s canal combined open channels with rock-cut passages and tunnels. Investigators excavated a 300-metre rock-cut stretch and found limestone laid to reduce water loss. They interpret the older canal as remaining in use into the thirteenth century for irrigation and domestic needs. This was inherited water infrastructure, not a newly invented twelfth-century system.

passages.title: Books, learning and a voice in Armenian
passages.text: The scholar Mkhitar Gosh spent several years with Prince Vakhtang and his brothers in Khachen. He had studied in different centers and later taught others. His career shows how a princely household could support a traveling scholar, connecting this region with a much wider Armenian intellectual world.

passages.title: Books, learning and a voice in Armenian
passages.text: Gosh began his Lawcode in 1184. It addressed secular as well as church matters and influenced later Armenian legal collections, including those in Cilicia and communities farther away. Writing rules down was a major intellectual project; the existence of a code does not mean every local dispute was settled exactly as its author wished.

passages.title: Books, learning and a voice in Armenian
passages.text: A manuscript associated with Gosh’s legal work was made for Haterk’s Prince Vakhtang and his wife Arzukhatun in 1184. A later inscription from Khadavank, dated 1204 and preserved in the Matenadaran, records a manuscript library. This small step beyond the map’s endpoint shows the continuation of organized book collecting.

passages.title: Books, learning and a voice in Armenian
passages.text: A short Armenian sample from Dadivank’s 1182 stone is ԵՍ ՀԱՍԱՆ, transliterated Es Hasan, meaning “I, Hasan.” These are the opening words after its date in the published transcription. Modern type preserves the wording, rather than reproducing the shape of the carved letters.

passages.title: Teaching through stories
passages.text: In Gosh’s fable 168, gold declares itself king and expects other materials to bow. Wheat refuses: in a famine, even gold must come asking for food. This is a story, not an account of talking crops, but it makes the value of farmers’ work wonderfully difficult to overlook.

passages.title: Teaching through stories
passages.text: Another Gosh fable tells of a healthy man who mocks physicians, then changes his mind after becoming ill. Gosh compares bodily care with listening to spiritual teachers. The tale shows medicine as a familiar subject for moral instruction; it does not document a particular clinic or treatment in Khachen.

passages.title: What followed the map’s endpoint
passages.text: The celebrated Gandzasar church belongs to the following century, outside both this record’s dates and its coarse outline. Hasan Jalal commissioned it between 1216 and 1238, and it was consecrated in 1240. Its inscriptions name family members and patrons, preserving the relationships behind an ambitious building project.

passages.title: What followed the map’s endpoint
passages.text: Under Mongol pressure in the thirteenth century, Hasan Jalal combined resistance, submission and diplomacy to preserve his position. He traveled to Mongol rulers, but was ultimately killed in 1260 or 1261. His descendants continued as patrons and builders. Political accommodation could preserve institutions for a time without making their leaders secure.

The atlas stops this label in 1200, not at the disappearance of Khachen’s communities. Princely patronage and Armenian religious and literary life continued into later centuries, under changing rulers and pressures. The thirteenth-century story of Hasan Jalal demonstrates continuity alongside a major loss of political security.

passages.text: Asante architecture joined construction skill with visual language and religious practice. Surviving shrine buildings near Kumasi preserve parts of a tradition that remained meaningful beyond the period of imperial power.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Builders arranged timber and bamboo structures around courtyards, applying mud plaster to walls and originally roofing them with thatch.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Wall reliefs combine spirals with animal, bird and plant forms. Motifs related to Adinkra convey meanings as well as decorate surfaces.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Shrines are places for consultation with deities before important decisions. Their symbolic features belong to continuing religious practice.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Maintaining earthen buildings requires responding to heavy rain, humidity and damage to organic materials. Architectural survival depends on repeated care.

passages.text: Ashaninka communities connect forests and rivers of Peru’s central Amazon, with related communities in Brazil. They have maintained far-reaching alliances without forming a single empire. The imported 1492 to 1500 outline is an approximate map snapshot, not their lifetime or a precise ancestral border. This card preserves the distinction between Ashaninka and the separately recognized Asheninka people.

passages.title: Exchange, resistance and survival
passages.text: Salt helped connect a large region. The Cerro de la Sal was an important meeting place in central Peru, where Ashaninka and neighbouring peoples exchanged goods. Forest products also moved toward the Andes, while cloth and metal tools travelled back through trading and family networks.

passages.title: Exchange, resistance and survival
passages.text: Franciscan expansion included the Quimiri mission in 1635. Ashaninka joined other peoples in Juan Santos Atahualpa’s rebellion beginning in 1742; victories over Spanish forces helped keep much of the central forest beyond colonial control for more than a century. This was a broad alliance, not an exclusively Ashaninka kingdom.

passages.title: Exchange, resistance and survival
passages.text: From the 1870s, rubber extraction reached Ashaninka in the upper Ucayali. Employers used debt systems that kept workers dependent: supplies created obligations, and the employer controlled the prices. The rubber boom brought coercion and territorial disruption rather than a simple new opportunity to sell forest products.

passages.title: Exchange, resistance and survival
passages.text: Peru’s 2003 Truth and Reconciliation Commission estimated that the internal conflict had displaced about 10,000 Ashaninka and killed about 6,000; it explicitly warned that precise totals were unavailable. Families also endured captivity under Shining Path. Refuge communities struggled to provide food and room for people forced from their homes.

passages.title: Family life and remarkable cloth
passages.text: Ethnographic accounts describe small, dispersed settlements and different household spaces: the intómoe was a family house for cooking and sleeping, while the káapa served men or guests. Visits connected households separated by long distances. Hosts offered visitors masato, a cassava drink, and a chance to rest.

passages.title: Family life and remarkable cloth
passages.text: Rojas Zolezzi’s 1999 study describes cotton being beaten gently on stacked palm mats so the fibres spread without breaking. A spinner could then rotate her spindle inside a little gourd while controlling the thread with her big toe. Textile production called for skilled hands and a very useful foot.

passages.title: Family life and remarkable cloth
passages.text: In the same study, a husband made wooden loom parts while his wife arranged the threads. A strap around the weaver’s waist let her own body keep the loom taut. Moving her weight changed the tension: the craftworker was part of the machine.

passages.title: Family life and remarkable cloth
passages.text: A surviving cushma, or tunic, in the Museum of International Folk Art is catalogued as Ashaninka, made in Peru around 1970. It combines cotton and paint and measures 122 by 104 centimetres. The object preserves a particular recent garment; its catalogue does not name the maker or village.

passages.title: Learning, food and care today
passages.text: The Ashaninka producers of Kemito Ene explain why they organised around cacao: selling beyond low-paying intermediaries could bring more income into households. Their account also describes technical advice that improved cultivation and bean quality. Chocolate here is connected to families’ efforts to pay for transport, schooling and other needs.

passages.title: Learning, food and care today
passages.text: CARE’s 2024 strategy identified a serious school transition problem: only half of primary-school graduates in its Ene context reached secondary education. Its programme to 2030 calls for better teacher preparation and wider educational access. These are community priorities and targets, not a claim that every child already receives them.

passages.title: Learning, food and care today
passages.text: The Ministry of Culture describes healing knowledge passed through elders and specialist practitioners. Families cultivate or exchange plants, while some women known as vaporeadoras conduct steam treatments. These accounts explain a system of care and relationships; they do not establish that the treatments cure the illnesses attributed to them.

passages.title: Learning, food and care today
passages.text: In July 2025, CARE reported that SAVIA was supporting more than 300 families in fourteen Ene communities, focusing on pregnancy, nursing mothers and children under three. Home visits and digital contact were linked with the Satipo health network. Community care could combine local language and organisation with access to health services.

passages.title: Learning, food and care today
passages.text: A small written sample appears in TVPerú’s 2022 documentary title: “Pasonki Quipatsi”, translated there as “Gracias Madre Tierra”, or “Thank you, Mother Earth”. The announcement explicitly identifies the words as Ashaninka. This is modern published writing associated with a food-security documentary, not an inscription surviving from 1492.

The map’s cutoff in 1500 does not mark an Ashaninka disappearance. Colonial expansion and the late twentieth-century conflict caused profound losses, while communities continued to rebuild. CARE’s current planning shows continuing institutions pursuing territory, education, health and livelihoods; these goals do not erase the unequal conditions or unfinished work.
