sectionTitles: School, work and a letter home
Water, toilets, medicine and war food

passages.text: Austria-Hungary was a dual monarchy created by the 1867 Compromise: the Austrian and Hungarian halves had separate governments, while Franz Joseph, the army and foreign policy linked them. Its many peoples spoke more than ten languages, but political rights and schooling were uneven. Some families worked in crowded brickworks or fields; others strolled Vienna’s Ringstrasse, read in cafés or experimented with new cars. The First World War brought hunger, hospitals and separation. Defeat and national movements ended the monarchy in 1918. The imported map interval, about 1878 to 1914, misses both the real beginning and end.

passages.title: Two governments under one crown
passages.text: In 1867 Franz Joseph agreed to the Compromise with Hungary. Austria and Hungary each had its own government and parliament, while the monarch, army and foreign policy joined them. This was not a single parliament ruling everyone.

passages.title: Two governments under one crown
passages.text: German-speaking and Magyar elites held more power than many other groups. Czechs, South Slavs, Romanians, Ruthenians and others pressed for greater representation and language rights. Hungarian authorities promoted Magyar language and identity.

passages.title: Two governments under one crown
passages.text: An 1867 basic law for the Austrian half said “Alle Volksstämme des Staates sind gleichberechtigt,” meaning “All peoples of the state have equal rights.” Its promise about languages in schools and offices did not settle daily discrimination, and it did not govern Hungary’s separate domestic policy.

passages.title: Two governments under one crown
passages.text: After the 1914 assassination of heir Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie in Sarajevo, Austria-Hungary chose war against Serbia. The resulting world war strained an already divided empire; its imported 1914 map endpoint is not the empire’s end.

passages.title: Two governments under one crown
passages.text: By autumn 1918 military defeat and national councils dismantled the monarchy. Czechoslovakia, Austria, Hungary and a South Slav state emerged among its successors. The inhabitants and their languages did not vanish with the imperial flag.

passages.title: School, work and a letter home
passages.text: An Austrian law called for eight years of primary schooling, yet in 1900 only about three quarters of school-age children attended. Czech and German schools in Bohemia had high literacy; peripheral regions had far fewer classrooms. A law and a school desk were not the same thing.

passages.title: School, work and a letter home
passages.text: Women campaigned for access to education and a vote. A 1869 law widened Austrian girls’ secondary schooling, but social class, region and family resources still shaped who could keep studying.

passages.title: School, work and a letter home
passages.text: Bohemian and Moravian migrants making bricks near Vienna slept in company barracks, sometimes dozens in a room. After a 1895 strike, families gained separate accommodation and shorter workdays. The Ringstrasse’s handsome buildings rested in part on exhausting labor.

passages.title: School, work and a letter home
passages.text: Mathilde Hübner studied to become a teacher in Vienna. She and mathematics tutor Ottokar Hanzel courted by letter, married in 1910 and raised two daughters while she kept teaching. “Wir” (“We”) was the title of their shared letter notebook.

passages.title: School, work and a letter home
passages.text: When war separated families, letters carried news about children, meals, weather and sleep. Ordinary details became precious because a reply meant someone was still alive and thinking of home.

passages.title: School, work and a letter home
passages.text: In Vienna cafés, patrons played chess or billiards and argued about politics and art. Some writers practically lived at their favorite table. Women could visit some cafés, but the public space was far from equally open to them.

passages.title: School, work and a letter home
passages.text: A Moravian carriage and railway-wagon factory at Nesselsdorf displayed the Präsident motorcar in 1898. It was an early factory-built car in the monarchy, though most children still encountered feet, carts and trains rather than a family automobile.

passages.title: Water, toilets, medicine and war food
passages.text: Empress Elisabeth’s Hermes Villa had running water in its bathrooms, a luxury novel enough that she enjoyed turning the taps on and off. She first worried that pipes might cost bathing attendants their jobs. A palace bathroom tells us almost nothing about a brickworker’s washroom.

passages.title: Water, toilets, medicine and war food
passages.text: Franz Joseph had a private lavatory at Schönbrunn Palace. Meanwhile clean water connections reached Vienna homes gradually. The emperor’s toilet was real, but it should never stand in for everyone else’s.

passages.title: Water, toilets, medicine and war food
passages.text: War overwhelmed medical services. Vienna’s university became a temporary hospital; nurses were trained quickly and women doctors took on work often denied them in peacetime. Patients came from many parts of the monarchy.

passages.title: Water, toilets, medicine and war food
passages.text: In wartime Vienna, queues, food and fuel shortages changed cooking and heating. Some residents grew vegetables on vacant ground, and schoolchildren helped tend war plots. For a hungry child, a patch of potatoes mattered more than an imperial parade.

Austria-Hungary’s dual monarchy ended in 1918 after military defeat and national independence movements. Austria, Hungary, Czechoslovakia and other successor states formed, often with their own minority disputes. Communities and languages continued across new borders. The imported map interval from about 1878 to 1914 omits both the 1867 Compromise and the empire’s actual end.

sectionTitles: An empire remade more than once

passages.text: The Austrian Empire was a Habsburg state founded in 1804, during the wars with Napoleon. It linked many lands and languages, with great differences between a Viennese parlor and a rural village. The court tried to preserve its power after 1815, but people pressed for constitutions, national rights and social change in 1848. Families encountered changing schools, crowded cities, polluted water and new medical ideas. In 1867 a compromise with Hungary remade the polity as Austria-Hungary. The imported “austrian-empire” border stretches from about 1650 to 1878, crossing earlier and later Habsburg systems; it is not this empire’s historical lifespan.

passages.title: An empire remade more than once
passages.text: In 1804 Francis took an Austrian imperial title while Napoleon dominated Europe; the Holy Roman Empire ended in 1806. The imported map begins in 1650, when these Habsburg lands existed but the Austrian Empire by that name did not.

passages.title: An empire remade more than once
passages.text: The Congress of Vienna in 1814 and 1815 set a new balance among major European powers. The city’s famous dancing was real social display, but the diplomats were also negotiating borders and war’s aftermath.

passages.title: An empire remade more than once
passages.text: The monarchy joined German, Hungarian, Czech, Polish and many other language communities. A family’s school, market and political hopes could depend on which language it spoke and where it lived; “Austrian” was not one everyday tongue.

passages.title: An empire remade more than once
passages.text: In 1848 protesters in Vienna and elsewhere demanded constitutions and political voice. Workers, farmers, women and national movements did not all want exactly the same reforms, but they challenged the old order together.

passages.title: An empire remade more than once
passages.text: The 1867 compromise gave Hungary its own government under the same monarch, with some affairs kept in common. It transformed this empire into Austria-Hungary; the Habsburg people did not disappear or all become one nationality.

passages.title: Lessons, homes and written language
passages.text: Compulsory elementary-school policy dated back to the eighteenth century and aimed to teach reading, writing and arithmetic. Secondary schools and universities remained much harder to enter; a rule about all children was not an equal path for all children.

passages.title: Lessons, homes and written language
passages.text: Private girls’ schools in Vienna taught some pupils reading, arithmetic, science and geography, though many families and schools still expected girls to prepare for marriage and motherhood. Access varied sharply by class and city.

passages.title: Lessons, homes and written language
passages.text: A middle-class Viennese parlor could display furniture and family status, with visitors welcomed to admire it. Some families took railway excursions after 1842. This was not the daily rhythm of farm workers or poorer city households.

passages.title: Lessons, homes and written language
passages.text: An 1807 imperial decree began “Wir Franz der Erste, von Gottes Gnaden Kaiser von Oesterreich,” meaning “We Francis the First, by God’s grace Emperor of Austria.” The old spelling “Oesterreich” is a tiny sample of written German from imperial government.

passages.title: Lessons, homes and written language
passages.text: Vienna’s Ringstrasse, opened in part in 1865, looked splendid. Its brick and stone came through long, poorly paid work by migrants from Bohemia, including women. A child admiring the boulevard should know who built it.

passages.title: Water, toilets and health
passages.text: Vienna had water shortages in 1835 even beside the Danube. Polluted groundwater and inadequate sewers brought disease risks. A future Alpine pipeline did not open until 1873, after this empire had become Austria-Hungary.

passages.title: Water, toilets and health
passages.text: Paintings of imperial bedrooms included water closets, but that does not mean ordinary apartment families had private indoor toilets. Even later in the century, such facilities were more likely in inner districts than outer working-class areas.

passages.title: Water, toilets and health
passages.text: At Vienna’s General Hospital, Ignaz Semmelweis introduced hand cleaning in 1847 to reduce childbed fever. It was an important medical insight for mothers and newborns, not an instant cure for every hospital or village.

passages.title: Water, toilets and health
passages.text: The state’s schools and hospitals could reach some families while language, wealth and distance limited others. “What would a child learn?” or “Where would a mother give birth?” had many answers across this enormous empire.

The Austrian Empire as a pre-compromise political system ended in 1867, when the Habsburg lands were reorganized as the Dual Monarchy of Austria-Hungary. The dynasty, territories and populations continued in a changed constitutional arrangement. The imported 1878 endpoint belongs to map coverage, not this transition.

sectionTitles: School, work and a fountain with a wardrobe
Words used to challenge a ruler

passages.text: The Austrian Netherlands were southern Low Countries provinces governed by the Austrian Habsburgs during much of the eighteenth century. Their institutions and local privileges differed; they were not simply modern Belgium under an earlier name. The map samples only the late phase and continues its label beyond the French conquest of 1794.

passages.title: Mapping a busy landscape
passages.text: The Ferraris mapping project of the 1770s produced 275 detailed sheets covering the Austrian Netherlands and the neighboring principality of Liège. Including Liège matters: the mapped area was not exactly the same thing as Habsburg territory. A historical map has a purpose and extent of its own.

passages.title: Mapping a busy landscape
passages.text: The cabinet map used a scale of 1:11,520 and depicted settlements, streets, gardens and other landscape details. It served officials and military planners. Today those details can help researchers reconstruct older surroundings, although a drawn feature still needs to be read with the mapmaker’s methods in mind.

passages.title: Mapping a busy landscape
passages.text: Maria Theresa granted a charter to the Brussels academy in 1772, building on a society established in 1769. It supported work in the sciences and letters. This was one way government and learned investigation became connected without turning every resident into a scholar.

passages.title: Mapping a busy landscape
passages.text: Governor Charles of Lorraine began building his Brussels palace in 1757. The rotunda’s floor incorporated specimens of regional marbles. A fashionable interior could also display curiosity about materials and their origins: even the floor could participate in a collector’s world.

passages.title: School, work and a fountain with a wardrobe
passages.text: Brussels accounts from 1720 describe dressing Manneken-Pis for festivities and distinguished visitors. In 1756 a paid dresser appears in the surviving record. Keeping a small fountain figure properly outfitted became a real civic job; the bronze boy had an unusually well-organized wardrobe.

passages.title: School, work and a fountain with a wardrobe
passages.text: In 1747 Louis XV provided a costume for Manneken-Pis after French soldiers attempted to steal the statue. The gift turned a diplomatic embarrassment into a lasting item of clothing. This particular fountain story should not be confused with evidence about domestic toilets or household plumbing.

passages.title: School, work and a fountain with a wardrobe
passages.text: The royal college at Herve was founded in 1777 and opened in 1778, after the suppression of the Jesuits had prompted educational reorganization. Its history makes reform visible in a specific school. It does not establish that every child in the provinces attended school.

passages.title: School, work and a fountain with a wardrobe
passages.text: The 1777 education reforms used competitive recruitment for teachers, open to clergy and lay applicants, and introduced government inspection. They also changed curricula and fees. Expanding state oversight should not be mistaken for universal free schooling in the modern sense.

passages.title: School, work and a fountain with a wardrobe
passages.text: Maria Theresia Borrekens and her husband had thirteen children. After his death in 1768, she directed the Moretus printing business for twenty-nine years. The museum records both her leadership and the firm’s difficulties. Family responsibilities and commercial authority could overlap, without making business success inevitable.

passages.title: School, work and a fountain with a wardrobe
passages.text: In January 1776, fifteen-year-old Frans Jozef Moretus sent his grandmother a New Year letter in French from boarding school in Mons. She complimented his French. A surviving family letter preserves both language learning and the very recognizable pleasure of impressing a relative.

passages.title: School, work and a fountain with a wardrobe
passages.text: Ghent’s Rasphuis was built in 1772 to 1775 under Maria Theresa. Prisoners rasped wood used to make dyes, which explains the institution’s name. The city museum preserves a print dated 1800 depicting it; that later image should not be mistaken for a drawing made during its construction.

passages.title: Words used to challenge a ruler
passages.text: A 1789 publication by Van der Noot bears the French title “Le manifeste du peuple brabançon”: “The manifesto of the Brabant people.” The wording survives in the national library’s catalogue of the original printed work. It is a short example of the language used in political argument during the revolt.

passages.title: Words used to challenge a ruler
passages.text: Opponents of Austrian government did not all want the same future. Rival groups cooperated temporarily, while provinces responded differently to the upheaval. The United Belgian States of 1790 should therefore be understood as a particular revolutionary experiment, rather than as an already unified modern national state.

French forces conquered the provinces in 1794 after the battle of Fleurus. Formal annexation followed on 1 October 1795. These changes ended Austrian government here; the atlas’s persistence of the label to 1815 should not be read as continued Habsburg rule.

sectionTitles: How a rice harvest leaves clues
More than a bowl of rice
Homes, floors and the work of keeping house
Changing technology, status and living languages

passages.text: This atlas label combines ancient farming horizons with a language-family hypothesis; it names no single people or state. Its 2000 to 323 BCE window is approximate. The earliest outline even reaches Afghanistan, while later shapes spread across mainland Southeast Asia and southern China. These are not verified language boundaries; some examples lie outside particular snapshots. Named Vietnamese and Thai sites below illustrate regional lives, without identifying every resident as an Austroasiatic speaker.

passages.title: How a rice harvest leaves clues
passages.text: At An Son and Loc Giang in southern Vietnam, early Neolithic potters mixed rice-processing remains into clay. A 2017 study scanned small pottery samples in three dimensions and found husks and grain-attachment parts inside. An everyday broken pot had become a tiny archive of farming.

passages.title: How a rice harvest leaves clues
passages.text: The telling detail was a rough, deeply recessed scar at the base of a rice spikelet. Wild rice usually releases its grains naturally; domesticated plants hold on until people remove them. These scars helped identify cultivated rice, rather than merely proving that someone had collected a wild plant.

passages.title: How a rice harvest leaves clues
passages.text: These southern settlements also yielded stone adzes, bone tools, decorated pottery and remains of domestic pigs and dogs. Postholes and prepared floors locate wooden buildings on mounds above low-lying landscapes. Food production belonged to a wider household world of building, making tools and tending animals.

passages.title: More than a bowl of rice
passages.text: Around 2000 BCE, the Trang Kenh community near Ha Long Bay used rice and foxtail millet. Researchers identified microscopic plant traces, including silica bodies called phytoliths and starch grains. These little survivors can reveal food processing even when no recognizable meal remains on a plate.

passages.title: More than a bowl of rice
passages.text: Nearby island sites Bai Ben and Bai Cat Don tell a different food story. Traces include taro, yams, acorns, palm, ginger and beans, as well as millet. Their inhabitants continued using diverse plants while incorporating cereals. The neighbors did not all receive the same prehistoric dinner menu.

passages.title: More than a bowl of rice
passages.text: At Rach Nui, around 1500 to 1300 BCE, rice and millet occurred alongside abundant remains of other plants. Researchers also found evidence of fishing, hunting and gathering. Living permanently in a village did not require everyone to become a specialist rice farmer.

passages.title: More than a bowl of rice
passages.text: Rach Nui stood beside a salty, tidal environment, a difficult setting for rice cultivation. Archaeologists propose that residents acquired cereals from other communities while drawing heavily on local resources. Rice-processing debris shows handling at the settlement; it does not by itself locate the fields where the crop grew.

passages.title: Homes, floors and the work of keeping house
passages.text: At Loc Giang, floor builders probably burned shells to make lime, then prepared hard mortar surfaces. Excavators found more than thirty stacked surfaces, dating roughly from 1560 to 1200 BCE. This was skilled construction with recipes for materials, not simply packing down whichever dirt happened to be underfoot.

passages.title: Homes, floors and the work of keeping house
passages.text: Microscopic study of Loc Giang floors found little accumulated debris, while worn areas had been repaired. Researchers interpret this as regular cleaning and maintenance, perhaps sweeping or using mats. Someone had to keep the household floor usable; the evidence does not preserve a chore chart assigning the job.

passages.title: Homes, floors and the work of keeping house
passages.text: At Lo Gach in southern Vietnam, woven mats left impressions on clay floors about 2750 years before 1950, roughly 800 BCE. The mat itself could decay while its pattern survived. Such traces bring weaving and furnishings into view alongside the more durable stone and pottery.

passages.title: Care and living together
passages.text: Man Bac in northern Vietnam preserves an unusually personal story from around 2000 to 1700 BCE. A man known to archaeologists as Burial 9 developed severe physical disabilities during childhood and survived into his twenties. Researchers infer sustained assistance from others over approximately a decade.

passages.title: Care and living together
passages.text: His movement restrictions imply help obtaining food and water, and probably assistance with eating and drinking. The study also argues that maintaining his cleanliness required bathing and help with toileting. These are reasoned reconstructions of care needs, not proof of a particular toilet, hospital or medical profession.

passages.title: Care and living together
passages.text: The same case makes cooperation visible: moving him safely and keeping him sheltered took repeated attention. Archaeology cannot tell us the names or family relationships of his helpers. It can show why a community’s achievements include care for a person, as well as the tools and buildings it made.

passages.title: Changing technology, status and living languages
passages.text: Bronze brought new expertise in combining and casting metals. A 2015 radiocarbon study favored an eleventh-century BCE Bronze Age transition at Ban Non Wat in northeastern Thailand, substantially later than some older chronologies. The timing is an archaeological argument, not a birthday shared by all the communities in this atlas shape.

passages.title: Changing technology, status and living languages
passages.text: At Ban Non Wat, some early Bronze Age graves held striking quantities of valuables, including rich infant burials. Researchers interpret this as evidence for inherited status. Burial 197 also contained a pottery vessel decorated with dancers: a lively little scene among the axes and other offerings.

passages.title: Changing technology, status and living languages
passages.text: A later language glimpse: modern Khmer writes ទឹក, transcribed tɨk, meaning “water.” This is a SEAlang dictionary witness checked in 2026, from a resource based mainly on 1977 and 1997 dictionaries. It is not prehistoric writing. The ancient sites here have no securely identified inscription establishing their residents’ languages.

The atlas stops this label in 323 BCE, not at a documented collective collapse. Austroasiatic languages continue in diverse communities, including Khmer, Vietnamese, Mon and several Indian language groups. Later states have their own histories; neither rice cultivation nor a language family makes them one continuing empire.

passages.text: Austria-Hungary was a dual monarchy created by an agreement in 1867: Austrian and Hungarian halves shared a Habsburg ruler and certain common affairs, yet had distinct governments and policies. Its residents spoke many languages and lived in very different cities, villages and classes. A Vienna tram, Czech-language school collection tin, worker's shared bed and palace chamber pot reveal different worlds under one crown. War, shortages and national movements ended Habsburg rule in 1918, before the imported map interval ends.

passages.title: Two halves and many peoples
passages.text: The 1867 compromise created Austrian and Hungarian political halves with a common ruler and some shared affairs. It improved the power of Hungarian elites but left Czechs and many South Slav groups seeking greater influence. The label “Austria-Hungary” hides political differences within the state.

passages.title: Two halves and many peoples
passages.text: The Habsburg Monarchy recognized nine official languages, including German, Hungarian, Czech, Polish and others. A family's home language, a school's teaching language and an office's paperwork could differ. There was never one everyday “Austro-Hungarian language.”

passages.title: Two halves and many peoples
passages.text: Vienna's Czech-speaking residents began organizing a vocational school in their own language in 1868 and raised money through a school association. A surviving collection tin reminds us that classrooms could depend on families and neighbors collecting coins, not simply a decree from the palace.

passages.title: Two halves and many peoples
passages.text: The Austrian half promised language equality in its 1867 basic law, while the Hungarian half pursued stronger Hungarian-language policies. Rights on paper and the language actually heard in a classroom could be different, and communities contested both.

passages.title: Work, family and social life
passages.text: A photograph around 1900 shows a working family in cramped accommodation. Some urban households had only a room and kitchen and rented a bed to a “Bettgeher,” someone who slept there when the usual occupant was away at work. Even a bed might have a timetable.

passages.title: Work, family and social life
passages.text: Many working families relied on women's earnings to pay rent and buy food. The middle-class ideal of a private home for only parents and children was a luxury for some laborers. Rural farm and artisan households often combined home and workplace differently.

passages.title: Work, family and social life
passages.text: A film of Vienna streets around 1908 shows horse-drawn vehicles, electric trams and early automobiles sharing space. Bicycles offered some people a cheaper way to explore beyond their daily route. Modern transport appeared in layers rather than replacing every older journey at once.

passages.title: Work, family and social life
passages.text: Vienna's Ringstrasse displayed new parliament, university and museum buildings in historical styles. Those monumental facades were meant to project imperial confidence, but a worker in a crowded rented room lived far from the postcard view.

passages.title: Work, family and social life
passages.text: The imperial court employed many servants. A valet who served Franz Joseph remembered helping him dress, while chamber staff ironed laundry and emptied his chamber pot. The kingly version of “doing the dishes” required quite a payroll; it tells us about one palace, not a farm kitchen.

passages.title: School, water and health
passages.text: Schooling in a child's first language could become a political struggle. Vienna's Czech school organizers wanted that option, while policies differed greatly across the Austrian and Hungarian halves. The language printed in a textbook mattered to families as well as politicians.

passages.title: School, water and health
passages.text: Vienna opened an Alpine water pipeline in 1873 to bring water from springs about 80 kilometers away. It aimed to serve suburbs as well as palaces, but water fees and uneven household plumbing meant the benefit did not arrive equally at every sink.

passages.title: School, water and health
passages.text: Inside toilets and bathrooms were more common in Vienna's central districts than in outer working-class areas. A second Alpine pipeline opened in 1910. The emperor had a private lavatory at Schönbrunn and staff to empty a chamber pot: sanitation could be a question of both pipes and privilege.

passages.title: School, water and health
passages.text: Schoolrooms also met epidemics. A teacher in Edelsbach wrote in 1898 that childhood illness disrupted school repeatedly, and later archives record closures in 1918. Medicine, clean water and hygiene improved over time, but an ordinary school day could still be interrupted by disease.

passages.title: A line of written German
passages.text: Article 19 of an 1867 Austrian basic law begins “Alle Volksstämme des Staates sind gleichberechtigt”. In English: “All ethnic groups of the state are equal.” It is a short sample of written German preserved in Austria's official legal information system, concerning the Austrian half of the dual monarchy.

passages.title: A line of written German
passages.text: The sentence was a promise of equality, not proof that the empire treated every language group equally. Families also wrote and spoke Hungarian, Czech, Polish, Romanian, Slovenian and other languages; one German legal line is only a glimpse of a multilingual state.

passages.title: War and many endings
passages.text: Austria-Hungary occupied Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1878 and formally annexed it in 1908. Bosnians had their own communities and claims; the change triggered an international crisis and disputes inside the dual monarchy over who would administer the territory.

passages.title: War and many endings
passages.text: The assassination of heir Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie at Sarajevo in June 1914 was followed by leaders choosing war against Serbia. The crisis did not make global war automatic; government decisions and alliances turned it into a wider catastrophe.

passages.title: War and many endings
passages.text: Wartime teachers set children essays and drawings about the conflict, and propaganda entered lessons. A 1915 school essay imagined a night attack on London by Zeppelin. It was one documented classroom exercise, not evidence that every child wanted war.

passages.title: War and many endings
passages.text: In wartime Vienna, women, children and young people queued for food and soup kitchens served tens of thousands daily. War work brought more women into factories, while household care and shortages continued at home. The queue, not a parade, was part of civilian war life.

passages.title: War and many endings
passages.text: On 11 November 1918, Emperor Karl renounced further participation in state affairs. Other national governments and movements were already claiming authority. Austria-Hungary ended as a political arrangement; its families and many languages carried on through new borders.

Military defeat, shortages and national movements broke the dual monarchy apart in autumn 1918. Emperor Karl renounced participation in state affairs on 11 November. Different governments and states emerged from its lands; no one successor inherited all its people or languages. The imported 1914 to 1920 polygon extends past Habsburg rule and does not verify the borders of any successor.

sectionTitles: Food, cloth and places to live
A stone can travel farther than its maker
Pacific communities beyond the highlighted islands

passages.text: Austronesian names a language family and many peoples, not one kingdom or uniform culture. The atlas shows 4000 to 323 BCE, with broad shapes across western Indonesia and sometimes the Philippines. These are not reliable migration fronts: they omit Taiwan and the Pacific, and their earliest spread is too broad to treat as established history. Examples here distinguish particular places, periods and later traditions.

passages.title: Connections without a single empire
passages.text: Related languages eventually connected communities from Madagascar to Rapa Nui, but people formed very different societies. A language family is a historical relationship between languages, not a test of someone’s appearance, ancestry or citizenship.

passages.title: Connections without a single empire
passages.text: A widely supported model places a major movement from Taiwan into Island Southeast Asia about 4,000 to 4,500 years ago. Wallacea, including Sulawesi and the islands farther east, already had inhabitants with histories stretching back tens of thousands of years. Migration brought encounters and exchange, not a discovery of universally empty land.

passages.title: Connections without a single empire
passages.text: A 2022 study of ancient DNA from 16 people in Wallacea found different histories in northern and southern islands, with repeated population mixing. Its samples span roughly the last 2,600 years, mostly later than this map. The result cautions against a single arrow representing every voyage, family or language change.

passages.title: Food, cloth and places to live
passages.text: At Nagsabaran in northern Luzon, a small excavation trench produced 79 rice grains or fragments and 224 examples of Job’s tears, another edible cereal, in its Neolithic layer. These tiny charred remains turn “farming” into identifiable crops. The regional Neolithic began roughly 4,200 to 4,000 years ago, among people already living in the Cagayan valley.

passages.title: Food, cloth and places to live
passages.text: Nagsabaran’s Neolithic finds also include clay spindle whorls, polished stone adzes and a jade bracelet fragment. Whorls helped a spindle turn while fibers became thread; adzes shaped wood. The assemblage joins food production, making useful things and personal adornment in the same community.

passages.title: Food, cloth and places to live
passages.text: At Peinan in eastern Taiwan, excavation plans and museum reconstructions show dwellings oriented toward the Taitung plain, away from the mountains. Finds include tools for farming, fishing, hunting, carpentry, weaving and food preparation. These homes belonged to a particular archaeological community; they are not a universal Austronesian house plan.

passages.title: Food, cloth and places to live
passages.text: Peinan’s late Neolithic jade use peaked roughly 3,500 to 2,500 years ago. More than 5,000 jade objects have been excavated, mostly as offerings in slate coffins. Yet there is little jade-working waste. Researchers therefore suspect many finished pieces arrived from specialist workshops near Taiwan’s Fengtian jade source.

passages.title: Food, cloth and places to live
passages.text: The Peinan cemetery contains more than 2,000 slate coffins. Carefully made jade and pottery accompanied some burials. These are records of how communities treated the dead across generations, as well as valuable objects; the richness of a burial cannot tell us every detail of the person’s household.

passages.title: A stone can travel farther than its maker
passages.text: A jade bracelet from Nagsabaran, dated about 1800 to 1500 BCE, was traced to Fengtian nephrite in eastern Taiwan. Its size resembles older Taiwanese bracelets. The stone gives evidence of a sea connection even when no ship survives. It does not reveal whether the wearer, trader or craftsperson spoke a particular language.

passages.title: A stone can travel farther than its maker
passages.text: From around 500 BCE, near this map’s end, jade exchange expanded widely around the South China Sea and continued for centuries afterward. Unfinished ornaments and offcuts show manufacture in several places. At Khao Sam Kaeo in Thailand, an older Taiwanese jade adze was being reshaped into a pendant: a stone tool could enjoy a second career as jewelry.

passages.title: Pacific communities beyond the highlighted islands
passages.text: Lapita is an archaeological label for a distinctive Pacific material tradition, not a synonym for every Austronesian-speaking society. Its potters combined small toothed-stamp impressions into elaborate geometric patterns, sometimes including faces. The name comes from a site in New Caledonia, far outside this atlas record’s shapes.

passages.title: Pacific communities beyond the highlighted islands
passages.text: At Teouma in Vanuatu, bones of 49 adults buried around 3,000 years ago indicate protein from reef foods, domestic animals and fruit bats. Their diets combined sea and land resources.

passages.title: Pacific communities beyond the highlighted islands
passages.text: Later movements into Vanuatu brought substantial new ancestry from Near Oceania while Austronesian languages continued. Researchers compared ancient DNA with linguistic history to identify this contrast. Languages can survive major demographic changes; a community’s speech and its family tree do not have to follow identical paths.

passages.title: Later voices and living skills
passages.text: A much later Amis example shows why boats were also working places. Taiwan’s National Museum of Prehistory describes an 1803 castaway account of bamboo craft used by two or three fishers, with woven bamboo sails and a rear platform for preparing food. A fishing trip needed room for lunch as well as the catch. This is not a reconstruction of a Neolithic voyage.

passages.title: Later voices and living skills
passages.text: For a securely dated language sample, the 2026 Nanshi Amis learning list gives wawa, meaning “child.” These Roman letters are the modern written form used in that teaching resource. This is one living Austronesian language in Taiwan, not a surviving prehistoric inscription or a phrase spoken identically by all Austronesian peoples.

passages.title: Later voices and living skills
passages.text: Modern language learning also uses songs, picture books and games. An Indigenous Languages Research and Development Foundation report covering resources in 2024 describes touch games, audiobooks, animations and classroom videos. This is present-day educational work helping children and other learners use their languages, not evidence of ancient schools.

The atlas stops in 323 BCE, but Austronesian-speaking communities did not disappear. Their languages and institutions kept changing through distinct island histories, later kingdoms, colonial encounters and modern states. There is no single fall, ruler or successor for this language family.

sectionTitles: A capital connected by water and trade
Learning, health and a royal message

passages.text: This Ava record spans 1650 to 1783: the later restored Toungoo or Nyaungyan kingdom, its fall in 1752, and early Konbaung rule. It does not represent medieval Ava. The imported outline stays identical through three map snapshots, including the southern coast, despite major political changes. Read it as broad geographic context, not a reliable border throughout these years.

passages.title: A capital connected by water and trade
passages.text: Ava stood where the Myitnge meets the Irrawaddy, near the irrigated rice lands of Kyaukse. A canal linked the rivers around the city. Water helped connect royal government, farming and transport: feeding a capital depended on much more than what grew inside its walls.

passages.title: A capital connected by water and trade
passages.text: In 1752 forces from Pegu captured Ava and ended the Nyaungyan dynasty. Their victory did not secure lasting obedience from Upper Burma’s local leaders. Aung Zeya, later called Alaungpaya, organized resistance from Moksobo and founded the Konbaung dynasty. The city’s familiar name outlasted the defeated royal house.

passages.title: A capital connected by water and trade
passages.text: Dutch East India Company records open an unusually detailed window onto seventeenth-century commerce. Its main Burma office was at Syriam, with a subsidiary at Ava. Surviving inventories and accounts record fabrics, prices and wages. These business papers preserve traces of customers and workers who rarely appear in royal monuments.

passages.title: A capital connected by water and trade
passages.text: Many buyers wanted affordable Indian cloth of medium or coarse quality, rather than only royal luxuries. Imported red cotton yarn was valued for its lasting color and could be mixed with local yarn in weaving. A thread in a household’s clothing could therefore connect local work with distant Indian producers.

passages.title: A capital connected by water and trade
passages.text: Large glazed Martaban jars carried water, rice and even gunpowder aboard ships. A pot could be part of the shipping equipment, not merely something sold at the destination. Before standardized metal containers, a very big jar could do a surprisingly important transport job.

passages.title: Food, families and obligations
passages.text: An order dated 16 March 1680 demanded rice or paddy from more than 200 villages in an irrigated district. Religious and service lands had exemptions. Such documents show government tracking fields and households while claiming a share of the harvest.

passages.title: Food, families and obligations
passages.text: A 1691 order addressed which hereditary service groups children of marriages between different groups should enter. Family relationships could shape compulsory duties to rulers and institutions. These classifications remind us that royal society included severe restrictions on personal freedom.

passages.title: Food, families and obligations
passages.text: In 1715 Hla Myat San, formerly of the palace entertainment group, received a title after marrying a royal uncle. She was permitted gold containers for betel and pickled tea. Even the snack dishes could announce someone’s newly elevated rank.

passages.title: What buildings and paintings preserve
passages.text: The seventeenth-century Leidatgyi temple borrowed from Bagan’s Ananda temple. Its builders used radial vaulting, tiers of windows and elaborate stucco; seated lions guarded a doorway. Looking backward could be a creative choice: earlier religious architecture remained a model for later craftspeople.

passages.title: What buildings and paintings preserve
passages.text: Across the river, the Kaunghmudaw pagoda was already standing when this map interval begins: it was founded in 1636. Its great rounded dome is surrounded by 812 stone pillars with niches for oil lamps. Imagine preparing that many little places for light.

passages.title: What buildings and paintings preserve
passages.text: Religious murals can contain a bustling world of ordinary work. The Ava-period survey identifies people fishing, plowing and making pots, as well as contemporary clothing and houses. Painters placed sacred stories in recognizable surroundings, leaving clues about the material world around their viewers.

passages.title: What buildings and paintings preserve
passages.text: Dating a painted building takes detective work. Tilokaguru’s murals were long discussed using a 1672 date. Later research challenged that chronology and connected the paintings with early seventeenth-century evidence, before this record begins. A building’s foundation story and the date of its paintings must be checked separately.

passages.title: Learning, health and a royal message
passages.text: Late eighteenth-century Upper Burmese monasteries taught boys, novices and junior monks through Pali and bilingual texts. Regular study included grammar, monastic discipline and Buddhist philosophy. Learning involved mastering languages and categories, not simply hearing stories; the evidence describes particular institutions rather than schooling available equally to every child.

passages.title: Learning, health and a royal message
passages.text: In 1783 a minister asked the scholar Ñāṇābhivaṃsa which works of worldly knowledge could no longer be found in Burma. He identified 48 previously available titles. This was a serious missing-books list: rulers and scholars were trying to recover texts through wider Indian Ocean connections.

passages.title: Learning, health and a royal message
passages.text: A history published by Myanmar’s traditional-medicine department identifies U Myat Tun of Khwe Saung village, south of Ava, as the author of a prose medical manual dated 1133 Myanmar Era, in the early 1770s. Its subjects included childbirth, infant illnesses, fever and diarrhea. The list records the family health problems its author sought to address.

passages.title: Learning, health and a royal message
passages.text: Alaungpaya’s Golden Letter of 7 May 1756 names Ava as “Ratanā-pūra-Aṅwa-prañ-krī,” translated as “royal city of Ratanapura-Ava.” This is the scholarly Roman transliteration of Burmese written on the surviving gold letter, not a modern phrase invented for this page. Its royal voice belongs to the new Konbaung dynasty.

The Nyaungyan dynasty ended in 1752, but Konbaung rule continued beyond this map record. In 1783 Bodawpaya moved the royal residence from Ava to Amarapura. A change of dynasty and capital did not erase the region’s communities.

sectionTitles: Work, water and the longer urban sequence
Learning, households and bodily care in Buddhist accounts
Later writing and families from Ujjain

passages.text: Avanti was an important early kingdom around Ujjain and the Narmada valley, competing with other large states in northern India. This map shows an approximate Malwa outline for 500 to 400 BCE, not surveyed ancient borders or exact founding and conquest dates. Later Ujjain discoveries below are explicitly separated from this century; the city’s long history is not one uninterrupted Avanti dynasty.

passages.title: A kingdom among competing powers
passages.text: Avanti’s strength rested on fertile agricultural land, access to iron resources and routes bringing trade from the south. Ujjain and Mahishmati appear as its important centers. It belonged to a world of several powerful monarchies, rather than an already united India.

passages.title: A kingdom among competing powers
passages.text: The Buddhist discourse Majjhima Nikaya 108 opens with Magadha’s King Ajatasattu strengthening Rajagaha because he feared King Pajjota, also known as Pradyota. That remembered anxiety gives Avanti a place among serious rivals. The passage reports preparations, without describing a battle between those kings.

passages.title: Finding the city beneath Ujjain
passages.text: In the 1950s, N. R. Banerjee’s archaeological team excavated the Garh-Kalika mound on Ujjain’s northern edge. A massive earth rampart and moat emerged. The ancient city used both the Shipra River and an artificial water barrier in its defenses, combining earth-moving work with the local landscape.

passages.title: Finding the city beneath Ujjain
passages.text: The river was also a dangerous neighbor. Excavators recognized repeated flood breaches during Ujjain’s Period II, followed by repairs and extra brick protection. Sand and silt reached habitation areas. A big wall could discourage an army, but it still needed maintenance after the river paid an unwelcome visit.

passages.title: Finding the city beneath Ujjain
passages.text: Pottery drawings from the excavation show bowls and vessels from Ujjain’s earliest phases, including black-slipped and black-and-red wares. Archaeologists compare rims, surfaces and layers to reconstruct a sequence. A broken pot is therefore useful evidence, even when nobody can put dinner back into it.

passages.title: Work, water and the longer urban sequence
passages.text: In the broader urban phase conventionally placed around 500 to 200 BCE, Ujjain had a tile-roofed mud building used as a workshop. Raw materials and unfinished objects reveal the making of agate beads and bone needles and arrowheads. The half-finished pieces let us follow work in progress rather than merely admire finished ornaments.

passages.title: Work, water and the longer urban sequence
passages.text: A brick water tank at Ujjain measured about 34 by 26 feet, roughly 10 by 8 meters. It belongs to the excavated urban sequence, much of which extends beyond independent Avanti. Stored water required considerable building work; this tank alone does not identify a public bath or prove that every home had a toilet.

passages.title: Work, water and the longer urban sequence
passages.text: Period II also produced a deep brick well, while small finds included ivory combs and dice, bangles and grinding stones. These discoveries bring grooming, games and food preparation into the picture. The phase spans roughly 500 to 200 BCE, so individual objects cannot all be assigned to the map’s single century.

passages.title: Work, water and the longer urban sequence
passages.text: For a much earlier regional food glimpse, excavators at Navdatoli found charred wheat, rice and several pulses. Their report assigned that Chalcolithic settlement roughly to 1200 to 700 BCE. These seeds show farming traditions in the Narmada region before this map interval; they are not a recovered menu from King Pradyota’s kitchen.

passages.title: Learning, households and bodily care in Buddhist accounts
passages.text: The Udana tells of Sona, a lay supporter of the teacher Maha Kaccana in Avanti, repeatedly asking to become a monk. His teacher first recommends religious practice while remaining a householder. The story recognizes that household duties and a life of renunciation made different demands on someone’s time.

passages.title: Learning, households and bodily care in Buddhist accounts
passages.text: The same account has Sona travel to meet the Buddha and recite all sixteen sections of the Atthaka Vagga. Clear delivery and remembering the teaching earn praise. This is a vivid literary picture of education through listening, memorizing and speaking, rather than evidence of a universal school system.

passages.title: Learning, households and bodily care in Buddhist accounts
passages.text: The Vinaya describes Avanti and the southern region as places where people valued frequent bathing. It also mentions rough, hoof-marked soil and permits monks thicker footwear. Even a religious rulebook had to make room for sore feet and local washing habits.

passages.title: Learning, households and bodily care in Buddhist accounts
passages.text: Another Vinaya story sends the doctor Jivaka to treat Pajjota’s jaundice. The king detests ghee, so the physician disguises it in medicine. This is a tale of royal medical patronage and an awkward patient, not proof that its remedy worked.

passages.title: Later writing and families from Ujjain
passages.text: A later witness, from Sanchi outside this map outline and its second- and first-century BCE donation inscriptions, reads “Ujeniya Muladataye dānaṁ”: “The gift of Muladatā (Mūladattā) from Ujeni (Ujjayini).” This is the published Roman transliteration of Prakrit written in Brahmi on a stone crossbar, inscription 76. It names a donor from Ujjain centuries after the mapped kingdom; it is not a fifth-century BCE Avanti document.

passages.title: Later writing and families from Ujjain
passages.text: Nearby inscriptions identify Vayadata as Upedadatta’s wife and Himadata as his sister, each making a gift. These later donors give us specific women and family relationships, rather than only royal names. Sponsoring part of a Buddhist monument made a personal contribution visible well beyond the household.

Historical tradition credits Shishunaga of Magadha with defeating Avanti’s Pradyota ruling house. The precise chronology is uncertain; the map’s 400 BCE cutoff is not a securely dated conquest. Ujjain continued as an inhabited center, with workshops, waterworks and later donors surviving in the archaeological record.

sectionTitles: Treasure, craft and careful detective work

passages.text: Avar rulers and their followers established a powerful, diverse realm in the Carpathian Basin after arriving in 567-568. Its history includes settled villages, skilled metalworkers and extensive family networks as well as mounted armies. The map continues the label later than the independent khaganate.

passages.title: Families, neighbours and food
passages.text: A study of four fully excavated Hungarian cemeteries reconstructed family trees extending as far as nine generations. Some 300 of the 424 sampled people had identifiable close relatives in the same cemetery: a family album assembled from ancient DNA.

passages.title: Families, neighbours and food
passages.text: In those communities, male family lines tended to remain locally rooted while women arrived from other communities. Marriage helped connect settlements. This describes the studied cemeteries, not an inflexible rule for every Avar household.

passages.title: Families, neighbours and food
passages.text: Researchers found little evidence of unions between close biological relatives. They suggest that remembering ancestry mattered across generations. DNA can reveal biological connections; adoption, affection and other social bonds require different evidence.

passages.title: Families, neighbours and food
passages.text: Leobersdorf and Modling, two seventh- and eighth-century communities near Vienna, used similar material culture but had different ancestry and marriage networks. Matching clothes or ornaments do not automatically mean that two families shared the same origins.

passages.title: Families, neighbours and food
passages.text: Environmental and archaeological research indicates expanding settlement and farming into the mid-700s. The familiar image of an entire population permanently on horseback misses the people growing food and maintaining villages.

passages.title: Treasure, craft and careful detective work
passages.text: The Vrap treasure was discovered in Albania in 1901 inside a copper cauldron. Its vessels, gold belt fittings and pieces of precious metal were gathered together, but that does not tell us who buried them or why.

passages.title: Treasure, craft and careful detective work
passages.text: Some Vrap belt fittings show griffins and curling vines. Casting such small, elaborate objects required careful metalworking. The museum interprets decorated belts as statements of rank, rather like formal clothing with an exceptionally expensive buckle.

passages.title: Treasure, craft and careful detective work
passages.text: The treasure includes drinking vessels, a pouring ewer and a bucket. They reveal an elite world of serving and displaying precious metal; they are not a picture of the tableware in every village home.

passages.title: Treasure, craft and careful detective work
passages.text: The Met now labels the ensemble Avar or Byzantine. Proposed explanations include a leader's wealth or a craftworker's materials, and scholars disagree over where some pieces were made. Those uncertainties are part of the discovery.

passages.title: Treasure, craft and careful detective work
passages.text: The eighth-century Ewer of Zenobius has five marks imitating Byzantine official stamps. Examination shows they were engraved, not struck. A convincing-looking quality mark is a clue to investigate, not automatic proof of origin.

passages.title: Writing and what survived
passages.text: The Zenobius ewer carries a Greek inscription, possibly copied from a Byzantine model by an Avar craftworker. Greek letters on a valued object do not establish the language spoken in the owner's household.

passages.title: Writing and what survived
passages.text: Other Avar-period objects have short runiform inscriptions. Their readings remain disputed, including the Szarvas example. A confidently translated sentence in an imagined Avar language would conceal how much is still unresolved.

Charlemagne's campaigns in the 790s and early 800s dismantled Avar political power. People and local traditions continued within neighbouring societies. The map's later Avar label is not evidence that an independent khaganate survived to 1000.

sectionTitles: An oasis with a complicated political past
Later family life in the lower Awash

passages.text: Awsa centred on the lower Awash valley, where a Muslim imamate was followed by an Afar sultanate. The imported 1650 to 1815 span crosses political phases; its broad outline should not imply uniform rule over every Afar community.

passages.title: An oasis with a complicated political past
passages.text: In 1577, Imam Muhammad Jasa moved his seat from Harar to Awsa, seeking greater security amid regional conflict. The desert surroundings helped make the oasis attractive as a refuge. Awsa’s political history therefore began before this record first appears on the map.

passages.title: An oasis with a complicated political past
passages.text: The ruling Aydahiso lineage belonged to the Mudaito grouping. Succession usually privileged the ruler’s family, but choosing a successor could still cause argument. Nineteenth-century traditions about Mohammed Hanfare’s preference for a nephew show that a royal family tree did not settle every political decision.

passages.title: Growing food and managing herds
passages.text: Awsa could mean the cultivated area beside the Awsa canal as well as the wider sultanate. Settled farmers lived along the canal, while neighbouring areas supported herding. Calling everyone a nomad would miss the farmers whose fields helped sustain this political centre.

passages.title: Growing food and managing herds
passages.text: Officials known as malokti coordinated irrigation and controlled flooding, managed access to pasture and organized responses to cattle disease, including isolating sick animals. Keeping herds healthy and arranging who could graze where were practical responsibilities of government, alongside taxation.

passages.title: Growing food and managing herds
passages.text: Farmers had practised irrigation here for centuries before large modern plantations arrived. River water supported a concentration of people and political authority in otherwise dry surroundings. In Awsa, understanding channels and seasonal water was part of the foundation of state power.

passages.title: Changes after the map ends
passages.text: Menelik’s forces defeated Awsa in 1895, but direct Ethiopian administration did not immediately follow. In the 1960s, the British company Mitchell Cotts still had to negotiate with the sultan over land for Tendaho cotton development. Military defeat and everyday control of territory were different things.

passages.title: Changes after the map ends
passages.text: Cotton brought income to some Afar landholders, while plantation expansion and water regulation reduced grazing access for pastoralists. These twentieth-century changes created winners and losers within the region. A project that increased crop output could also make it harder for a herding family to feed its animals.

passages.title: Changes after the map ends
passages.text: The sultanate established an education fund and sent twenty-five Afar students to Egypt via Yemen in 1964. Historian Maknun Ashami, who later studied in Cairo himself, describes the scheme. It connected local political resources with opportunities to attend schools and universities abroad.

passages.title: Later family life in the lower Awash
passages.text: Research published in 2024 describes women bargaining with highland merchants at Asaita’s Tuesday market. Transactions included animals, grain, salt, flour, spices and detergents. The market linked household supplies with livestock income, and women’s commercial work mattered even where formal leadership remained dominated by men.

passages.title: Later family life in the lower Awash
passages.text: The same study records women’s work in managing water sources and moving homes when families followed pasture. A move could mean loading household structures onto camels or donkeys, then rebuilding. Packing for a trip was substantial work when the house came along too.

passages.title: Later family life in the lower Awash
passages.text: Interviewees also described relatives contributing to weddings and sharing resources during emergencies. Women helped organize these exchanges and household decisions. These are observations from recent Lower Awash communities, showing continuing family networks without treating modern arrangements as a complete picture of life in 1700.

passages.title: A small written sample
passages.text: “áh roóbu” means “This is rain” in Afar. Linguist Richard Hayward prints the phrase in his modern grammar chapter, using accents to mark high tone. This is an attested linguistic transcription from the 1998/2001 handbook, not a manuscript from the early sultanate. It gives a short example of the region’s living language.

The map’s 1815 endpoint is not Awsa’s fall. Sultan Ali Mirah fled during violent conflict with Ethiopia’s military government in 1975, a major rupture in the sultanate’s political power. Afar people, language and community institutions continued.

passages.text: Aymara-speaking communities built several powerful highland societies around Lake Titicaca and beyond. They were never one timeless kingdom. The linked map records span 1279 to 1500; their outlines simplify overlapping peoples and territories, especially the southern extension toward the Atacama. Aymara history continues today.

passages.title: Highland power and stone memorials

passages.text: Across the cold Andean highlands, farmers make chuño by letting potatoes freeze at night and dry during sunny days. Trampling removes moisture and skins. Properly dried potatoes can keep for years: winter weather becomes part of the pantry’s equipment.

passages.title: Food, clothing and learning
passages.text: A museum’s evidence for that food need not be ancient. Michigan’s collection includes chuño bought in a Cusco grocery in 1966. Such specimens help document a living food technology alongside the much older accounts of Andean potato preservation.

passages.title: Food, clothing and learning
passages.text: An Aymara tunic from Bolivia in the Metropolitan Museum dates to the late eighteenth century. It is woven from camelid hair and measures roughly 67 by 89 centimeters. A surviving garment makes the skilled handling of animal fibers tangible.

passages.title: Food, clothing and learning
passages.text: A twentieth-century Aymara tupu in Chile’s pre-Columbian museum combines silver and glass. This large pin fastened or adorned women’s clothing at the chest. Everyday dress can carry metalworking skill and an enduring emblem of identity.

passages.title: Food, clothing and learning
passages.text: María Choque told an interviewer in 2023 that she began making thread at six, taught by her grandmother. Socks and hats came before more demanding garments. Her account gives one family’s learning sequence, from watching an elder to mastering difficult work.

passages.title: Food, clothing and learning
passages.text: The same reporting describes October shearing that leaves wool on the animals for warmth. During February festivities, families attach wool flowers and pompoms to camelids. Even the suppliers of the wool can end up wearing some of the decoration.

passages.title: Words and survival
passages.text: A modern Chilean schoolbook prints “Kamisaraki jilata”, meaning “How are you, brother?” It appears in Estela Gamero’s bilingual greeting song. These Latin letters record living Aymara; the sample is from a present-day teaching resource, not an ancient inscription.

passages.title: Words and survival
passages.text: Spanish authorities forced Karanqas communities into concentrated towns and demanded labor for the Potosí mines. These policies separated people from land and strained households. Colonial rule transformed local institutions, but Aymara communities kept rebuilding relationships and practices across the region.

Inca conquest and Spanish colonization changed Aymara political autonomy and landholding. Neither ended the people or their language. passages.text: Ayutthaya, founded on an island in the Chao Phraya in 1351, ruled Siam for four centuries and was one of the great trading cities of Asia. Its kings took the Khmer idea of divine kingship, and its port welcomed Chinese, Japanese, Persian, Dutch, Portuguese and French merchants.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Rice, deer hides, sappanwood and tin left through the royal warehouses; Chinese junks and, from 1511, Portuguese ships came to buy them.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Foreign quarters ringed the city: Japanese, Portuguese, Dutch from 1608, French and Persian; the Greek Constantine Phaulkon rose to chief minister under King Narai.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: King Narai sent an embassy to Louis XIV at Versailles in 1686.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Prang towers in the Khmer manner and the tall chedis of Wat Phra Si Sanphet, with gilded Buddhas.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Court poetry, the Ramakien, the Thai Ramayana, and masked dance drama.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Theravada Buddhism with royal patronage and hundreds of temples in the capital.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Khmer court ritual and the devaraja idea of the king as a god shaped kingship; the law code of 1805 preserves Ayutthaya's laws.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Historic City of Ayutthaya was listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Thai kingship, law and court culture descend from Ayutthaya.
A Burmese army took and burned the city in April 1767. Within the year Taksin had rallied Siam from a new capital at Thonburi.

sectionTitles: Several kingdoms, not one medieval empire

passages.text: The Azande formed several connected kingdoms in central Africa. This record’s 900 to 1000 dates and enormous outline are unreliable for those states: the histories discussed here concern the much later kingdoms and their communities. The evidence does not establish a medieval Azande empire.

passages.title: Several kingdoms, not one medieval empire
passages.text: Nineteenth-century Azande rulers belonged to the Avongara aristocracy. Kings appointed governors to smaller areas, and princes could fight over succession. Political connections did not make every Zande community part of a single centralized state.

passages.title: Several kingdoms, not one medieval empire
passages.text: In the first half of the nineteenth century, Zande expansion crossed the Congo-Nile watershed from the Mbomu valley. Gbudwe established a kingdom around Yambio while confronting slave traders and neighboring powers.

passages.title: Several kingdoms, not one medieval empire
passages.text: Colonial borders divided Zande lands among Anglo-Egyptian Sudan, French Equatorial Africa and the Belgian Congo. Communities and ruling families survived those partitions, but their political autonomy and connections were profoundly disrupted.

passages.title: Food, homes and practiced skills
passages.text: A photograph from Yambio, taken between 1927 and 1930, shows a large soro granary reached by a ladder. Grain was stored upstairs; woven reeds or grass enclosed additional storage below. This family’s pantry had its own upper floor.

passages.title: Food, homes and practiced skills
passages.text: In another Yambio photograph from 1927 to 1930, women sit together beating finger millet with sticks. The grain supplied porridge and beer. Preparing food could be a shared task long before it reached a cooking pot.

passages.title: Food, homes and practiced skills
passages.text: A potter photographed between 1927 and 1930 stands beside coil-built earthenware vessels used in everyday life. Evans-Pritchard admitted that learning pottery from Zande men went badly for him. Expertise did not transfer just because the visitor owned a notebook.

passages.title: Food, homes and practiced skills
passages.text: A 1927 photograph records wives and children in Prince Rikita’s homestead, with crops beside the approach and houses behind them. This is a particular aristocratic family, showing how a royal lineage continued after Gbudwe’s defeat.

passages.title: Games, learning and written voices
passages.text: The game abanga could use a carved board or holes in the earth. A photograph dated 1927 to 1930 shows the ground version tucked under a hut’s eaves, with a stool ready nearby. No game box was required.

passages.title: Games, learning and written voices
passages.text: A kundi harp collected between 1927 and 1930 has five strings, wooden tuning pegs and a hide-covered soundbox. Plant materials form the strings and their attachments. Musicians and makers combined different natural materials to control tension and sound.

passages.title: Games, learning and written voices
passages.text: Colonial schooling could mix instruction with coercion. At Wau’s technical school, established in 1905 to teach carpentry, reading and writing, Rikita’s son Rumba was among pupils held as guarantees of their families’ submission.

passages.title: Games, learning and written voices
passages.text: A Zande written sample is “Rikita ni-fu-re na kporo.” The researchers translate it as “Rikita gave me a district to administer.” Published in their 2011 study, it comes from a historical narrative published in 1963, using a modern Latin-script transcription.

passages.title: Games, learning and written voices
passages.text: When researchers shared these older recorded stories with Zande speakers in Bangassou, participants wanted copies to take home. Language research could also return accounts of ancestors and political life to people whose heritage the stories preserved.

Gbudwe was killed in 1905 and colonial rule replaced autonomous kingship. In 2022, a new Azande monarchy was established within South Sudan, combining four historical kingdoms as a modern institution. It was not a return of their former sovereign powers.
