Soviet power remade politics, borders and farms
Work, homes and an oil city under construction
At home: relatives, rugs, iceboxes and no universal “normal”

passages.text: This card covers the atlas’s approximate 1914-1938 Azerbaijan record, not all Azerbaijani history and not the separate modern azerbaijan-1994 card. Its first shape has a detached Nakhchivan polygon and covers 1914-1920; its second covers 1930-1938, joins the western area to the mainland and even contains the tested point for Yerevan. No feature covers 1920-1930 although the index continues through those years. The label spans Russian imperial collapse, a short independent republic, Red Army takeover, a Transcaucasian federation, rapid Soviet change and Stalinist terror. Neither 1914 nor 1938 is a true national beginning or ending, and the polygons cannot settle borders or control.

passages.title: First, decode the atlas label
passages.text: The 1914 feature is a two-part multipolygon with 165 vertices. Its main part contains the tested points for Baku, Ganja, Lankaran, Shaki, Quba, Shusha and Khankendi/Stepanakert; a detached western part contains Nakhchivan. Tested Yerevan, Tbilisi, Tabriz and Derbent fall outside. These tests only describe what the imported shape draws. They cannot prove who governed a village, where an army stood or which community lived there.

passages.title: First, decode the atlas label
passages.text: The 1930 feature behaves very differently. It is one 115-vertex polygon stretching much farther west, joining the Nakhchivan area to the mainland and swallowing the tested point for Yerevan, while still excluding Tbilisi, Tabriz and Derbent. The atlas also has no azerbaijan polygon at all from 1920 to 1930. A border that changes this strangely is a warning label: use it to find the region, never to settle a territorial argument.

passages.title: First, decode the atlas label
passages.text: Names need care too. “Azerbaijan” had long named a historical region in northwestern Iran. In 1918 leaders north of the Aras adopted it for their new republic, whose territory had usually been described through places such as Arran, Shirvan, Baku, Ganja, Karabakh and Nakhchivan. Scholars still debate the politics of that choice. This card means the northern state and Soviet republic; it does not quietly annex Iranian Azerbaijan into the story.

passages.title: First, decode the atlas label
passages.text: The separate modern card begins only in 1994, while this one stops in 1938. Those are database seams. Azerbaijan did not disappear in 1938, and modern independence did not begin in 1994. Keeping the IDs separate prevents the cleaner modern outline and present-day institutions from being projected backward into revolution, civil war and early Soviet rule.

passages.title: Oil city, revolution and a twenty-three-month republic
passages.text: Baku entered the period as one of the world’s great oil centers. The boom had made fortunes for Azerbaijani, Armenian, Russian and foreign industrialists and drawn a multinational workforce into drilling, refining, shipping and rail work. Labor politics mattered: oil workers won what Ronald Suny describes as the first general labor contract in Russian history in 1904, then returned to major strikes just before World War I. Oil made Baku powerful, crowded, unequal and strategically irresistible.

passages.title: Oil city, revolution and a twenty-three-month republic
passages.text: After the 1917 revolutions, no single government smoothly inherited the region. Baku’s soviet, Bolsheviks, the Armenian Dashnak party, Muslim political organizations, oil employers and armed groups competed inside the city while Ottoman, British and Russian forces pursued it from outside. The Baku Commune held power from April to July 1918; a different coalition followed, then Ottoman forces took the city in September and British troops arrived after the armistice. “Who ruled?” could change within months.

passages.title: Oil city, revolution and a twenty-three-month republic
passages.text: Civilians paid terribly. Bolshevik and Armenian forces killed large numbers of Azerbaijani Muslims during the March 1918 fighting in Baku. After Ottoman and Azerbaijani forces captured the city in September, Armenian civilians were massacred. Donald Bloxham reports a very high estimate for the September killings but also stresses the complicated background and wider reciprocal violence; other scholarship disputes exact totals. The honest lesson is clear without scoreboard history: armed movements on several sides murdered civilians, and casualty numbers remain contested.

passages.title: Oil city, revolution and a twenty-three-month republic
passages.text: On 28 May 1918 the National Council proclaimed the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic. Its declaration chose a democratic republican government and promised civil rights regardless of nationality, religion, class, estate or sex, plus room for ethnic groups to develop independently. That sex-equality clause gave women political rights in law, a striking achievement for the period. A promise on paper did not erase war, displacement, class hierarchy or practical barriers to participation, so the card treats it as a constitutional commitment rather than instant equality.

passages.title: Oil city, revolution and a twenty-three-month republic
passages.text: The provisional parliament opened in Baku on 7 December 1918 in the former Taghiyev girls’ school. Its planned 120 seats allocated places to Muslims, Armenians, Russians, a German, a Jew, trade unions and business bodies; by late 1919, 96 members represented eleven factions. This was broader than a one-party chamber, although many members were co-opted through organizations rather than elected in a completed nationwide ballot. It met 145 times before its final sitting on 27 April 1920.

passages.title: Oil city, revolution and a twenty-three-month republic
passages.text: The republic also founded Baku State University. A September 1919 law planned faculties of history-philology, physics-mathematics, law and medicine, required Azerbaijani language study and admitted women and men on equal terms. Classes began on 15 November; the first year enrolled 877 students plus 217 auditors. Instruction initially relied heavily on Russian and recruited professors, which prompted debate, but the university survived every later regime change. Two Azerbaijani women were among its first physician graduates in 1922.

passages.title: Soviet power remade politics, borders and farms
passages.text: Late on 27 April 1920, with the Red Army approaching, parliament voted to transfer power under written conditions: Azerbaijan’s sovereignty was supposedly to remain, the communist government would be temporary, officials and property would be protected, and fighting in Baku would be avoided. Those words are useful because they show what deputies feared and hoped to preserve. They were not a freely negotiated guarantee between equal powers; independent government ended as Soviet forces entered.

passages.title: Soviet power remade politics, borders and farms
passages.text: Soviet Azerbaijan did not keep one constitutional position. In 1922 it was joined with Soviet Armenia and Georgia in the Transcaucasian federation, which entered the new USSR. The 1936 Soviet constitution dissolved that federation and listed Azerbaijan as its own union republic. “Republic” therefore did not mean sovereign democracy: Communist Party power and decisions from Moscow constrained every phase, even while Azerbaijani-language institutions and local cadres expanded.

passages.title: Soviet power remade politics, borders and farms
passages.text: The early Soviet border was not drawn once by a ruler with a perfect map. Officials bargained over transport, pasture, population, security and administrative convenience, often leaving ambiguity. Later, collectivization made those lines painfully real. In 1930 the Azerbaijani secret police arrested and deported more than a thousand alleged kulaks with their families; officials then pressed others into collective farms. Across the Armenian-Azerbaijani borderland, more than 12,000 rural households were abandoned from 1930 to 1934 as people fled toward cities, neighboring republics or Turkey.

passages.title: Soviet power remade politics, borders and farms
passages.text: The Great Terror reached far beyond famous politicians. From 1936 through 1938, secret-police troikas processed cases without ordinary trials while numerical quotas encouraged executions, imprisonment and banishment. In Azerbaijan, targets included party officials, former non-Bolshevik activists, professionals, peasants and border residents. Wives could be exiled merely for being married to a condemned “enemy,” and children could be sent to orphanages and branded for their parents’ alleged crimes. Published totals vary, so this card does not turn one disputed estimate into a fact.

passages.title: Work, homes and an oil city under construction
passages.text: Baku’s first Soviet planners inherited a dense center, oil works beside homes, poor worker housing and weak transport. From 1924 to 1927 they tested small houses, converted industrial buildings and denser apartment blocks at settlements such as Stepan Razin and Armenikend. Plans bundled housing with services, green space and shorter trips to work, and hundreds of units were built. Yet the need was much larger. A handsome plan did not guarantee every oil worker a sunny room, sewer connection or nearby clinic.

passages.title: Work, homes and an oil city under construction
passages.text: One visible innovation arrived in 1926: an electrified railway joined Baku’s oil districts to the center. The Presidential Library calls it the first electric railway line in the USSR. New worker settlements and constructivist clubs grew along the industrial landscape, while three successive general plans tried to organize the whole Absheron peninsula. Kid version: the oil fields got an electric commute before most families got anything resembling a modern bathroom.

passages.title: Work, homes and an oil city under construction
passages.text: Clean water was a major engineering achievement, but it arrived unevenly. Construction of the 187-kilometer Shollar-Baku pipeline began in 1911; water reached Baku in February 1917 at roughly one-third of planned flow. Extra wells, reservoirs and stronger pumps raised delivery to the stated design capacity in the 1930s. A city pipeline still does not tell us which flat had a tap, sewer or flush toilet. The sources support expanding supply, not a magical overnight conversion of every outhouse.

passages.title: Work, homes and an oil city under construction
passages.text: Sewage was part of the planning problem, not an already solved detail. The 1927 city plan called for unobstructed sewer and storm-water systems, and experimental blocks paid attention to ventilation and open space. Surviving evidence does not give a trustworthy republic-wide toilet percentage for 1914-1938. Urban apartments, older courtyard houses, oil settlements and villages had very different arrangements. When a source says “hygienic housing,” ask whether it describes a design drawing, a finished block or the home where most people actually lived.

passages.title: At home: relatives, rugs, iceboxes and no universal “normal”
passages.text: In early twentieth-century villages, both small households of parents and children and larger joint households of parents, married sons, spouses and grandchildren existed. Work, property and childcare could be shared across generations. Collectivization transferred land and animals into collective ownership and helped break up many large-household arrangements in the 1930s. The evidence comes from censuses, archives and much later fieldwork, so it reveals patterns rather than one rule followed by every Azerbaijani, Armenian, Lezgin, Talysh, Tat, Jewish or Russian family.

passages.title: At home: relatives, rugs, iceboxes and no universal “normal”
passages.text: Wedding preparations could fill a home with useful art. Museum collections preserve carpets, embroidered curtains, bedcovers, tablecloths, clothing cases, copper utensils and jewelry associated with late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century interiors and dowries. A bride’s handiwork could be both skill and household wealth. Region, class, religion and family choice changed the bundle, and Soviet campaigns later tried to remake marriage customs. So imagine many traditions in motion, not one costume party repeated identically from Baku to mountain villages.

passages.title: At home: relatives, rugs, iceboxes and no universal “normal”
passages.text: Khadija Aghabeyli, born in Baku’s Old City in 1910, remembered waking to ice sellers. Wealthier homes bought blocks for wooden iceboxes; people with less money often bought small amounts of meat, fish or milk day by day. Her family prized freshly cooked piti, dolma, kebab and dushbara and considered yesterday’s food embarrassing for a guest. This is a vivid memory from one prosperous Muslim household, not a menu for the whole country. Still, “the ice vendor is coming” is a wonderfully pre-refrigerator morning sound.

passages.title: At home: relatives, rugs, iceboxes and no universal “normal”
passages.text: Clothing and household goods also changed with place and income. The national history museum’s ethnographic fund preserves regional men’s and women’s garments, decorated copper vessels, felt, carpets, woven shopping bags and other everyday objects. Its own home is the lavish former mansion of oil magnate Haji Zeynalabdin Taghiyev, whose restored bedroom, dining room and boudoir show elite life. A museum visitor must not mistake those rooms for an oil worker’s lodging or a farmer’s house.

passages.title: School, writing, medicine and children
passages.text: Literacy and schooling became a huge Soviet project. A republic-wide education commission began work in 1921; officials promoted free schooling, Azerbaijani-language administration and textbooks, and general compulsory education was adopted in 1928 and approved in 1929. Access still depended on teachers, buildings, language, gender and location. A decree could reach a village faster than a classroom, but the expansion created new paths for children whose parents had never attended school.

passages.title: School, writing, medicine and children
passages.text: Written-language sample: `Yeni yol` (roughly “New Way”). That is the cataloged Azerbaijani title of a newspaper launched on 21 September 1922 by the New Turkic Alphabet Committee to promote a Latin-based script. It is a publication title, not a sentence overheard at breakfast. Readers were living through a real script transition: Arabic-derived and experimental Latin writing overlapped before the 1929 official switch, and a later Cyrillic change would again make family papers hard for grandchildren to read.

passages.title: School, writing, medicine and children
passages.text: Medical training grew from a thin base. The 1919 university opened a medical faculty; a pharmacy technical school followed in 1925, Azerbaijan Medical University in 1930 and a pediatrics faculty in 1936 because child-health specialists were scarce. A specialized higher pharmacy institute opened at the atlas endpoint in 1938. These dates show institution building, not universal access. Rural patients might still face distance, few specialists and very different mixtures of household care, local healers, pharmacies and state medicine.

passages.title: School, writing, medicine and children
passages.text: Children gradually gained dedicated services. A health-epidemiology department founded in 1924 monitored infectious disease; three sanatoria with 252 places operated in 1928; the medical university opened in 1930 and an independent pediatrics faculty in 1936. The same review says specialized healthcare had been extremely limited before 1917. The change was meaningful, yet a clinic in Baku did not mean a mountain child could see a pediatrician. Capacity, geography and political upheaval kept care unequal.

passages.title: School, writing, medicine and children
passages.text: The new state museum was another classroom. Founded in 1920 and opened in 1921, it collected archaeology, coins, clothing, tools and household crafts; related museums and a manuscript fund grew during the 1920s and 1930s. Those collections helped scholars study the region’s past while Soviet institutions also decided which pasts to celebrate, secularize or condemn. Discovery here was not treasure hunting alone: cataloging a cooking vessel, textile or old document could preserve ordinary lives that political histories often miss.

The 1938 endpoint is an atlas cutoff, not a collapse. The Azerbaijan Soviet Socialist Republic continued inside the USSR, endured World War II and later Soviet decades, and restored independence in 1991 while explicitly claiming legal succession from the 1918-1920 republic. The project’s separate modern card begins in 1994, so the missing years are a catalog gap rather than a historical void. People, families, languages, institutions and memories crossed every one of these political seams, even when governments changed the alphabet, economy and permitted version of the past.

sectionTitles: Water at home and a continuing country

passages.text: This card follows the modern Republic of Azerbaijan, including mainland territory and the separate Nakhchivan component shown by the atlas. Independence returned in 1991, before this record begins in 1994. The older map outlines remain unchanged through 2020 despite war and displacement; a later outline replaces them. These shapes cannot show who controlled every place at a particular moment. Earlier khanates, the Soviet republic and the separate 1914 to 1938 Azerbaijan record have their own histories.

passages.title: Government, conflict and rebuilding
passages.text: Azerbaijan regained independence as the Soviet Union broke up in 1991. The United States recognized it that December and established diplomatic relations in February 1992. This was a new international setting for a republic whose earlier independence had ended with the Red Army’s arrival in 1920. The atlas’s 1994 start is therefore a display boundary, not the country’s birthday.

passages.title: Government, conflict and rebuilding
passages.text: Voters adopted a constitution on 12 November 1995. Its text describes a secular, unitary republic and divides state power among legislative, executive and judicial institutions. It also sets out rights to education and use of a native language. These are constitutional commitments; how government worked in practice also requires evidence about elections and public services.

passages.title: Government, conflict and rebuilding
passages.text: In the 2003 election, Heydar Aliyev withdrew in favor of his son Ilham, who was declared the winner. International observers found serious shortcomings, including intimidation and unequal campaign conditions. The succession preserved a powerful presidency. Two decades later, OSCE observers described the February 2024 election as efficiently prepared but lacking genuine pluralism, with critical voices suppressed.

passages.title: Government, conflict and rebuilding
passages.text: Nagorno-Karabakh was internationally recognized as part of Azerbaijan, while Armenian-backed forces controlled it after the war ending in 1994. Azerbaijan regained parts of the region and surrounding territory in the 2020 war. A further Azerbaijani offensive in September 2023 defeated the remaining Armenian forces there. These different military situations should not be read from one unchanged atlas outline.

passages.title: Government, conflict and rebuilding
passages.text: The human consequences crossed borders. UNHCR and partners recorded that more than 100,000 ethnic Armenians fled Nagorno-Karabakh to Armenia during the last week of September 2023. Families urgently needed housing, healthcare and schooling. This refugee movement is central to the period’s history, alongside the earlier displacement of Azerbaijanis, rather than a small footnote to changes on a map.

passages.title: Government, conflict and rebuilding
passages.text: The December 2020 ICRC report describes damaged homes, schools and hospitals across the conflict region. Its response included new showers and latrines for 66 families living in shelters. A working toilet and a place to wash could matter immediately to people forced from home. These are regional aid figures, not a claim that every family in Azerbaijan lacked sanitation.

passages.title: Work, heritage and time together
passages.text: In June 2006, the tanker British Hawthorn left Ceyhan in Turkey with the first cargo delivered by the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline. The route carried Caspian oil from Azerbaijan through Georgia to the Mediterranean. Thousands of workers from the three countries helped build this connection. A ship leaving one port could mark the result of years of work far inland.

passages.title: Work, heritage and time together
passages.text: Modern Baku also had to look after its older buildings. UNESCO removed its walled city, Shirvanshah’s Palace and Maiden Tower from the Danger List in 2009 after preservation improved. Earthquake damage and poorly controlled development had threatened the historic area. Repairing and protecting inherited buildings is an achievement of the modern city, even though the monuments themselves are much older.

passages.title: Work, heritage and time together
passages.text: Dolma can be a tiny edible parcel: a filling of ingredients such as meat, onion, rice and spices wrapped in leaves or tucked into vegetables. UNESCO’s 2017 description emphasizes sharing within families and communities, with recipes varying between them. Children can learn alongside parents, while vocational schools teach the craft too. There is more than one way to make dinner fit inside its own wrapper.

passages.title: Work, heritage and time together
passages.text: Carpet weaving joins skilled hands across generations. UNESCO describes girls learning from mothers and grandmothers in weaving families, often during winter. Some carpets use knotted pile; others have a flatter woven surface. Finishing one can be an occasion for a solemn celebration when it is cut from the loom. A floor covering may contain a great many patient afternoons.

passages.title: Work, heritage and time together
passages.text: Tea makes room for conversation. A joint UNESCO listing for Azerbaijan and Türkiye describes freshly brewed tea served in pear-shaped cups, with accompaniments such as sweets, lemon or jam. Hospitality is part of the practice: the cup helps mark a welcome and sustain social ties. This is shared regional heritage, with room for different household habits.

passages.title: Children, language and health
passages.text: Preschool access grew, although it remained far from universal. UNICEF reported that enrollment rose from 14 percent in 2015 to 35 percent in 2024, following national investment in early learning. For families, such programs create places where young children can play, learn and prepare for school. The figures describe those years, not a promise that every child already has a place.

passages.title: Children, language and health
passages.text: Support for a small child can begin at home. UNICEF describes a home-visiting model in which health workers help families with vaccination, developmental checks and early concerns. Such visits connect child health with the people doing everyday care. They can help a parent notice a difficulty sooner instead of waiting until a child reaches school.

passages.title: Children, language and health
passages.text: The constitution’s Article 42 begins: “Hər bir vətəndaşın təhsil almaq hüququ vardır.” Its official English version says: “Every citizen has the right to education.” This is Azerbaijani in its modern Latin alphabet, including the letter ə. The sample comes from the government’s current consolidated text of the 1995 constitution, shown here in modern type, rather than a photograph of its original publication.

passages.title: Children, language and health
passages.text: A 2024 WHO and European Observatory review describes mandatory health insurance covering residents for a range of emergency, primary and hospital services. Important gaps remained: most outpatient medicines and dental care were outside the package. Rural shortages of staff and facilities also limited access. Having a right to treatment and finding nearby, affordable treatment are related but different challenges.

passages.title: Children, language and health
passages.text: In Shamakhi, three mobile clinics brought equipped medical vehicles and trained workers to rural communities in a WHO-supported project reported in 2021. The team included family doctors and pediatricians, with drivers trained for the outreach work. Sometimes getting care closer to home meant putting part of the doctor’s office on wheels.

passages.title: Water at home and a continuing country
passages.text: For some families, a water project changed an everyday chore. A World Bank account from Siyazan describes a resident who previously carried buckets and later could use water from taps for washing and cleaning. Across eight selected districts, project results through 2019 recorded over 46,000 household connections to new piped water. These improvements were substantial, but the eight districts were not the entire country.

passages.title: Water at home and a continuing country
passages.text: The same project connected 43,000 households to new sewer networks and invested in wastewater treatment. Water arriving at a tap is only half the job: used water also needs somewhere safe to go. These figures document infrastructure, not a count of particular toilet designs in every home. Sanitation improvements often happen underground, where visitors never see the work.

passages.title: Water at home and a continuing country
passages.text: Diplomacy remained a process. Armenia and Azerbaijan signed a joint declaration at the August 2025 Washington summit, while their foreign ministers initialed a draft interstate agreement. A joint statement with the United States dated 10 August 2026 reported border stability and continuing normalization and boundary work. Signing a declaration, initialing a draft and implementing a lasting settlement are different steps.

Azerbaijan continues as a state; the atlas gives this record no historical end date. Its modern polygon’s 2100 endpoint is a rendering horizon, not a prediction. The August 2026 trilateral statement described continuing work on relations and borders with Armenia. That dated account cannot guarantee future peace or turn the map into a live record of control. Communities, family traditions and public services continue to change within this political history.

passages.text: Tenochtitlan brought canals, markets, workshops and ceremonial architecture into a large lake city. This card focuses on the capital's civic and artistic life within the Aztec imperial world.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Canals and raised causeways connected the capital to surrounding lakeshore towns. Canoes carried people and goods through the urban network.

passages.title: Water and daily life
passages.text: Aqueducts supplied fresh water, while neighborhood communities maintained local temples and markets.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Stone carvers used stone and hardwood tools, fiber cords, water and sand to shape even hard materials into detailed sculpture.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: The Templo Mayor paired shrines to Tlaloc and Huitzilopochtli. Successive rulers enlarged the complex, sometimes also responding to flooding and unstable ground.

passages.title: Craft and exchange
passages.text: The capital's markets offered food and luxury goods. Its neighborhoods included potters, weavers, sculptors, lapidaries and featherworkers.
Tenochtitlan fell in 1521. Spanish rulers built a new colonial capital over the devastated city.

sectionTitles: Kingdoms, wars and things they built

passages.text: Babylonia was a southern Mesopotamian region centred on Babylon, not one dynasty with a thousand-year reign. Its cities, temples and written records survived Kassite rule, Assyrian domination and a brief Neo-Babylonian empire. The atlas shows only selected snapshots from 1500 to 500 BCE; it omits Babylon’s earlier rise under Hammurabi and continues after Persian conquest in 539 BCE. The map dates describe coverage, not uninterrupted independence.

passages.title: Kingdoms, wars and things they built
passages.text: Babylon had become a major capital under Hammurabi in the eighteenth century BCE, before this map’s first Babylonian snapshot. The Hittite raid of 1595 BCE ended his dynasty, but did not erase the city. Kassite rulers later adopted many Babylonian political and religious traditions while governing a new territorial state.

passages.title: Kingdoms, wars and things they built
passages.text: Around the late fifteenth or early fourteenth century BCE, Kurigalzu I built Dur-Kurigalzu, a city with temples and a palace. Kassite rulers exchanged messages and goods with courts from Egypt to Anatolia. Their artisans experimented with molded and glazed brick, a technique later used spectacularly at Babylon.

passages.title: Kingdoms, wars and things they built
passages.text: Kassite kings recorded land gifts on stone monuments called kudurrus. A later example shows a dragon associated with Marduk and symbols of several gods. Despite the modern nickname ‘boundary stones,’ these records were probably kept in temples rather than planted in farm fields. Ancient paperwork could be impressive stonework.

passages.title: Kingdoms, wars and things they built
passages.text: An Elamite army ended Kassite rule around 1155 BCE and carried away sacred objects, including Marduk’s statue. Nebuchadnezzar I later recovered that statue. In the following centuries Assyrian kings dominated Babylonia; uprisings continued, and Sennacherib sacked Babylon in 689 BCE.

passages.title: Kingdoms, wars and things they built
passages.text: Nabopolassar’s dynasty broke Assyrian power and built the Neo-Babylonian empire. Nebuchadnezzar II raised walls, gates and temples at Babylon. The Ishtar Gate’s approach was lined with bright glazed lions; those striking animals were part of a ceremonial route, not evidence that real lions wandered the street on festival day.

passages.title: People behind the monumental walls
passages.text: Clay archives from Babylonian cities record land, goods and agreements from temples and private households. They make everyday economic life visible far beyond royal monuments. The surviving sample favours people whose transactions were written down, so it cannot describe every worker or family equally.

passages.title: People behind the monumental walls
passages.text: At Borsippa, priests’ archives name bakers, brewers, butchers and oxherds who supplied four meals a day for the god Nabû. The oxen were managed by a family actually called the Oxherds. Even the divine menu required very human work: preparing food, caring for animals and guarding gates.

passages.title: People behind the monumental walls
passages.text: Borsippa’s temple jobs could belong to families for generations, with a share in temple service and rules of lineage and ritual purity. That tells us about one privileged, well-documented social world, not every Babylonian household. The tablets also reveal personal lives behind the official work rosters.

passages.title: People behind the monumental walls
passages.text: Babylonia’s New Year festival brought Marduk’s statue from the Esagila temple along the Processional Way, accompanied by visiting gods’ statues. A king ceremonially took the god’s hand. The event linked religious devotion with public power and turned the decorated city route into a stage for a major gathering.

passages.title: School, healing and written words
passages.text: One small Old Babylonian school tablet fits in a hand. A teacher wrote a cuneiform model and a student copied it on the other side; on this tablet, the name of the god Urash appears six times. A student who had to repeat a sign has something in common with children practising handwriting today.

passages.title: School, healing and written words
passages.text: Old Babylonian trainee scribes also copied model contracts covering loans, land sales, marriage and adoption. These were practice pieces, not legally binding deals. Learning to write meant learning the formulas that made business and family agreements work in a document-heavy society.

passages.title: School, healing and written words
passages.text: Mesopotamian medical texts included lists of symptoms and predicted outcomes as well as instructions using plants and minerals. Healers could combine practical treatments with religious ideas. Surviving tablets tell us what specialists wrote, not how often remedies helped or whether every family could obtain them.

passages.title: School, healing and written words
passages.text: A royal inscription of Nebuchadnezzar II contains ‘LUGAL KÁ.DINGIR.RA.KI,’ meaning ‘king of Babylon.’ These are the editor’s Roman-letter signs for Akkadian cuneiform, not a claim that the king wrote in Latin letters. The original wedge marks were impressed or inscribed into a physical object; the transliteration lets us see the words accurately here.

Cyrus II of Persia captured Babylon in 539 BCE, ending the Neo-Babylonian empire. The city and its temples continued under Persian rule, while scholars still wrote religious, literary and scholarly works in Akkadian. The atlas’s 500 BCE cutoff is a map limit, not the disappearance of Babylonian people or learning.

sectionTitles: Building a state and a capital
A constitution in its own words
Light, water and the awkward business of toilets

passages.text: Baden grew from divided margraviates into a much larger grand duchy along the Upper Rhine. Karlsruhe became an important capital, while Mannheim and other towns developed manufacturing and new transport. The imported 1715 to 1878 outline is misleading at its early dates: it projects a later, enlarged territory backward over lands Baden acquired much later. The grand duchy itself continued until 1918.

passages.title: Building a state and a capital
passages.text: In 1771, Karl Friedrich of Baden-Durlach inherited Baden-Baden, joining Protestant and Catholic territories under one ruler. Further acquisitions between 1802 and 1810 included Heidelberg, Mannheim and lands farther south. The familiar long shape of Baden emerged through these changes, rather than existing unchanged in 1715.

passages.title: Building a state and a capital
passages.text: Karlsruhe’s founding offer in 1715 welcomed settlers of different Christian denominations. Such promises helped a new town attract inhabitants, but everyday equality remained contested: religious communities still argued over their treatment and public rights. A ruler’s invitation was the beginning of negotiations about living together.

passages.title: Building a state and a capital
passages.text: Baden’s expanded territory brought together places with different legal traditions. Johann Niklas Friedrich Brauer adapted the French civil code into a Baden law book. Announced in 1808, a uniform civil law finally took effect in 1810. Governing a bigger state required more than drawing a larger border.

passages.title: A constitution in its own words
passages.text: Writing sample: section 14 of the constitution of 22 August 1818 says, “Die Gerichte sind unabhängig innerhalb der Grenzen ihrer Competenz.” It means “The courts are independent within the limits of their jurisdiction.” This German wording, including the spelling Competenz, comes from a modern transcription of the historical document.

passages.title: A constitution in its own words
passages.text: The same constitution protected property and personal liberty and provided two parliamentary chambers. Its rights were unequal: eligibility for the second chamber required being Christian, at least thirty, and meeting financial qualifications. Reading both the promises and the exclusions helps explain why constitutional reform did not finish the struggle for political rights.

passages.title: Light, water and the awkward business of toilets
passages.text: Karlsruhe’s first public oil lamps appeared in 1759. They burned rapeseed oil and were lit only on moonless nights when the margrave was present. The moon had a surprisingly important job in the lighting budget, and a ruler’s absence could leave everyone relying on it.

passages.title: Light, water and the awkward business of toilets
passages.text: In 1764, a new Karlsruhe waterworks used horses to drive wooden pumping machinery. It lifted groundwater from about three metres below ground. Keeping water moving required animals, mechanisms and maintenance long before electric pumps could be switched on.

passages.title: Light, water and the awkward business of toilets
passages.text: After the map’s 1878 cutoff, but still during the grand duchy, Karlsruhe expanded its sewers from 1883. Toilets did not immediately join them: water closets were expensive for working families, and officials worried about fouling the river. Cesspits remained part of the system; in 1893 officials permitted sewer expansion for flushing away human waste. Underground pipes alone did not solve the toilet question.

passages.title: Wheels, bread and stories
passages.text: On 12 June 1817, Karl von Drais rode his running machine from Mannheim toward Schwetzingen and back, covering about fourteen kilometres in a little over an hour. Riders pushed against the ground with their feet. Pedals were still in the future: the engine was the person sitting on top.

passages.title: Wheels, bread and stories
passages.text: These early machines were largely wooden, with a few iron parts. Drais sold construction plans that craftsmen turned into vehicles. A wheelwright’s workshop, rather than a modern bicycle factory, supplied the skills behind this invention’s first examples.

passages.title: Wheels, bread and stories
passages.text: Food prices made 1817 much harder for families than the bicycle story suggests. After the disastrous harvest of 1816, a one-kreuzer bread roll in Mannheim shrank from seven Loth to two and a half Loth, roughly 112 grams to 40 grams. The price stayed the same while the portion became much smaller.

passages.title: Wheels, bread and stories
passages.text: Johann Peter Hebel turned calendar writing into memorable literature. His 1811 Schatzkästlein collected 127 short pieces from earlier issues of the Rheinländischer Hausfreund. He revised expressions for readers beyond the local dialect area. A calendar could offer stories and observations alongside its practical job of marking the year.

passages.title: Revolution reached ordinary streets
passages.text: When Prussian troops bombarded Rastatt in July 1849, civilians took shelter in cellars, the palace and fortifications. The revolutionary stronghold surrendered on 23 July. Captivity and disease followed for prisoners. The struggle over government reached homes and families as well as soldiers and political leaders.

Grand Duke Friedrich II definitively renounced the throne on 22 November 1918, after a provisional government had formed. Baden changed from a monarchy into a republic. Its people, towns and institutions continued; the imported map endpoint of 1878 does not mark the end of the state.

passages.text: Baekje held the southwest of the Korean peninsula and was the most refined of the Three Kingdoms, trading by sea with China and Japan. Its monks, scholars and craftsmen carried Buddhism, Chinese learning and temple architecture to the Yamato court.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Sea routes linked Baekje to the southern Chinese dynasties and to Japan, and possibly further south.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: King Seong sent a Buddha image, sutras and monks to the Yamato court, the official introduction of Buddhism to Japan; Japanese sources date it to 538 or 552.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Baekje smile, the gentle expression of its stone and bronze Buddhas, as on the rock-cut triad at Seosan.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Gilt-bronze Buddhas, reliquaries and roof tiles stamped with lotus designs.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Gilt-bronze Incense Burner of Baekje, found at Neungsan-ri in 1993, a mountain of peaks, musicians and animals on a lotus base.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The monk Marananta arrived from Eastern Jin and the court adopted Buddhism, building temples and monastic communities.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Confucian learning and the Chinese classics were taught to the aristocracy; Baekje scholars such as Wang In took the classics to Japan.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Baekje Historic Areas were listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Baekje's transmission of Buddhism, writing and craft shaped early Japanese civilization.
A Silla army and a Tang fleet took the capital Sabi in 660; a restoration movement was crushed at the Baekgang river in 663, and Silla absorbed the land by 676.

sectionTitles: A capital built by many kinds of work
Meals, relatives, skilled work and unequal lives
A traveler’s gift and words carved in stone

passages.text: Bagan, also called Pagan, was the center of a powerful kingdom in the Ayeyarwady valley of present-day Myanmar. This atlas record isolates 1200 to 1279, part of its late flourishing, rather than the kingdom’s whole lifetime. The imported polygon actually excludes Bagan and Kyaukse while including Mrauk U and Chittagong. It is geographically misleading and cannot establish the kingdom’s borders. Earlier Pagan and the later Pagan map record remain separate here; the change of label in 1279 was not the disappearance of the city.

passages.title: A capital built by many kinds of work
passages.text: Bagan’s kings connected religious patronage with the organization of land, labor and building. Agricultural production helped support monasteries and monuments, while royal sponsorship also shaped trade. Historian Rila Mukherjee emphasizes these connections: a glittering temple depended on fields and workers as well as a generous donor.

passages.title: A capital built by many kinds of work
passages.text: The early thirteenth-century Htilominlo Temple rises in two storeys around a massive solid core. Its builders combined brickwork with sandstone blocks. A big temple had to solve a very practical puzzle: how to carry the weight of the upper shrine without squashing the spaces beneath it.

passages.title: A capital built by many kinds of work
passages.text: The walls enclosed Bagan’s royal and religious center, not its entire population. Archaeologists study a surrounding mixture of homes, farmland and religious buildings. Timber and other perishable domestic materials leave fainter traces than brick temples, which helps explain why spectacular monuments long received more attention than ordinary households.

passages.title: A capital built by many kinds of work
passages.text: At Shwe Creek, excavators found plastered and tamped-earth floors, postholes and objects lying on former living surfaces. Radiocarbon results place early and middle activity within 1045 to 1216 and later activity within 1254 to 1295. These ranges overlap this card’s century but do not date every floor to one precise year.

passages.title: A capital built by many kinds of work
passages.text: Shwe Creek also produced pottery-making tools, including ceramic anvils and a spacer, alongside many broken pots. The excavators interpret the place as a possible combination of residence and pottery production. For some occupants, getting to work may have involved a very short commute.

passages.title: Meals, relatives, skilled work and unequal lives
passages.text: Bagan-period inscriptions name parents, spouses, children, stepmothers and in-laws. They distinguish a mother’s older sister from her younger sister. A short stone record can contain quite a family tree.

passages.title: Meals, relatives, skilled work and unequal lives
passages.text: The records distinguish rice cooks from curry cooks, as well as household cooks, fish suppliers and honey suppliers. Preparing a communal meal could involve several specialized jobs. Communal cooking required teamwork.

passages.title: Meals, relatives, skilled work and unequal lives
passages.text: Occupational names also include midwives, laundresses and water carriers. Singers, dancers, drummers and cymbal players appear among the musical professions. These inscriptions preserve childbirth care and entertainment alongside the better-known labor of building temples.

passages.title: Meals, relatives, skilled work and unequal lives
passages.text: This work was not always freely chosen. Inscriptions describe people inherited, bought or transferred to settle debts. Than Tun records a palm-leaf preparer whose bankruptcy in 1227 brought his family into enslavement under a minister. Religious monuments also belonged to this unequal society.

passages.title: Meals, relatives, skilled work and unequal lives
passages.text: A later record, from 1291, required monks to care for people dedicated to a monastery when they became sick or old. It records an obligation, not proof that everyone received good treatment. The date also falls beyond this map interval.

passages.title: Meals, relatives, skilled work and unequal lives
passages.text: Food archaeology reaches further back. At Otein Taung, pigs’ teeth and ruminant bones came from an ash layer dated to 880 to 1030. The excavators suggested meals were cooked on the hot ashes. This is a glimpse of earlier activity near Bagan, not a menu securely dated to the thirteenth century.

passages.title: Water, toilets and learning
passages.text: Bagan’s waterworks linked seasonal channels, ponds and reservoirs in a dry landscape. The excavated moat stood above the nearby river’s level, so rainwater was important to filling it. Managing the arrival and storage of water mattered as much as standing beside a great river.

passages.title: Water, toilets and learning
passages.text: Possible ancient toilets are among the less glamorous discoveries. At Old Bagan, excavators found earthenware tubes stacked vertically, sometimes eight deep, interpreted as latrine linings. Similar fragments occurred at Otein Taung. The report does not securely date these installations to this card’s century; a clay-lined pit is also not evidence for a citywide sewer network.

passages.title: Water, toilets and learning
passages.text: More than fifty spouts from ritual water-pouring pots were collected on Otein Taung’s surface. Smaller numbers were excavated below. Such vessels connected pottery manufacture to Buddhist offerings. A broken spout can tell archaeologists what sort of pot it belonged to, even when most of the pot has vanished.

passages.title: Water, toilets and learning
passages.text: Writing and religious learning were not confined entirely to men. Rachelle Saruya’s review identifies Bagan-period inscriptions describing some literate enslaved women and nuns learned in Buddhist ritual. Later chronicles praise women’s study of Pali grammar, but those stories cannot establish how many medieval girls attended school.

passages.title: Water, toilets and learning
passages.text: At Payathonzu, probably a thirteenth-century temple, paintings display an elaborate late Bagan style. The museum catalogue describes compositions with the Buddha inside a structure resembling the temple at Bodh Gaya. Artists used recognizable sacred settings to connect a local place of worship with a much wider Buddhist world.

passages.title: A traveler’s gift and words carved in stone
passages.text: A sandstone inscription found at Myinpagan records a donor from Magodayarpattanam on India’s Malabar coast. He provided a hall, a door and a lamp to burn continually in a Vishnu temple at Bagan. Its Sanskrit verse and Tamil prose reveal a specific South Indian religious connection within this predominantly Buddhist city.

passages.title: A traveler’s gift and words carved in stone
passages.text: The same inscription begins “Svasti śrî,” translated by its editor as “Hail! Prosperity!” These are the published Roman-letter transliteration of Sanskrit words carved in Grantha script, not a facsimile of the letters. The Tamil letterforms date the stone approximately to the thirteenth century. This witness represents one donor’s dedication, not everyone’s everyday language.

The 1279 map seam is not a fall date. Bagan’s kingdom fragmented in the late thirteenth century and other centers gained power. Mongol pressure belonged to this upheaval, but a story of total destruction of the city is not supported by the evidence. Bagan continued as a place of worship, with later rebuilding and living Buddhist communities.

sectionTitles: A capital of earth and brick

passages.text: Bagirmi developed southeast of Lake Chad around Massenya in the sixteenth century. Its rulers negotiated, fought and sometimes paid tribute to Bornu and Wadai. Both Bagirmi labels on this map refer to phases of this kingdom, with imperfect imported borders.

passages.title: A kingdom between neighbors
passages.text: Bagirmi’s rulers used the title mbang. Conversion at court did not make the entire population religiously uniform. Bornu’s influence included scholars as well as armies, and periods of tribute alternated with renewed independence.

passages.title: A kingdom between neighbors
passages.text: In the eighteenth century Bagirmi raided southern and southeastern communities and profited from selling captives. Later invasions also carried Bagirmi’s own inhabitants into slavery. Royal prosperity and ordinary people’s security could move in opposite directions.

passages.title: A kingdom between neighbors
passages.text: Historian Viviana Pâques compared oral traditions and written evidence during research in 1966 and 1967. The sources did not always agree on reigns or dates. A royal list is historical evidence to investigate, rather than a ready-made calendar immune to disagreement.

passages.title: A capital of earth and brick
passages.text: Archaeologist Annie Lebeuf located the old capital, Boum Massenya, east of the Chari. By her 1967 report, its great earth enclosure survived as a low, uneven trace. An almost vanished wall can still reveal where a city once organized its defenses.

passages.title: A capital of earth and brick
passages.text: Fired-brick remains marked the palace, mosque and houses of prominent residents. Some old bricks had been reused for road fill. Archaeologists therefore had to read both surviving buildings and displaced materials, rather than expecting a complete abandoned city waiting untouched.

passages.title: A capital of earth and brick
passages.text: Lebeuf describes Massenya chiefly as a royal and administrative centre. A capital need not also be the kingdom’s busiest trading town. Its palace and officials gave it importance even when the most active buying and selling happened elsewhere.

passages.title: A capital of earth and brick
passages.text: In 1898 Sultan Gaorang ordered the old capital burned and abandoned as Rabih threatened it. The later settlement called Massenya occupied a different location. Keeping those places separate helps explain why a modern town and an archaeological capital share a name.

passages.title: Scholars, crafts and continuing language
passages.text: In 1852 Barth met Faki Sambo, a blind Fula scholar educated at al-Azhar in Cairo. They discussed books and distant places. The encounter connects a Bagirmi scholarly household with an intellectual network stretching well beyond the Lake Chad region.

passages.title: Scholars, crafts and continuing language
passages.text: Sambo served Barth a cold rice pudding with dates from Kanem; Barth offered coffee. Manuscripts and conversation shared the scene with refreshments. Even a meeting that later becomes historical evidence may have begun with something good to eat.

passages.title: Scholars, crafts and continuing language
passages.text: Barth described weavers and dyers, including Kanuri craftspeople producing dark cloth. His account also names officials responsible for pasture, woods and waters. Running a kingdom involved regulating useful resources as well as issuing commands at court.

passages.title: Scholars, crafts and continuing language
passages.text: Barth recorded the language name as “tar Bágrimma”. This is his nineteenth-century Roman transcription, not a surviving text written by a Bagirmi court scribe. It offers a small linguistic trace alongside the much richer spoken knowledge of the people he met.

passages.title: Scholars, crafts and continuing language
passages.text: A modern Bagirmi book supplies an attested writing sample: “Kup an Duniya”, translated by its publisher as “The Beginning of Creation”. This illustrated Christian publication demonstrates continuing use of the language in print; it is not a text from the Muslim sultanate.

French protection in 1897 and further restrictions in 1903 ended Bagirmi’s independent position. Its rulers continued under colonial control, and Bagirmi communities remained part of the region’s history. Neither imported map cutoff marks their disappearance.

sectionTitles: Discoveries: clay, weaving and island food
Making music, costumes and public memory

passages.text: The Bahamas became independent in 1973 after a much longer history of Lucayan communities, colonial settlement, slavery and struggles for political rights. Pottery, house yards and living craft traditions reveal how people worked, raised families and made things together across the islands.

passages.title: Discoveries: clay, weaving and island food
passages.text: A pottery recipe began with a surprising ingredient: dust blown across the Atlantic from the Sahara. Researchers sampled red deposits on Long Island and experimented with Palmetto Ware, the Lucayan pottery containing burned, crushed conch shell. The shell helped difficult local material hold its shape. Experiments indicate relatively low firing temperatures, showing careful adaptation to the islands’ available resources.

passages.title: Discoveries: clay, weaving and island food
passages.text: At Long Bay on San Salvador, impressions preserved in pottery reveal woven materials that have largely decayed. Hutcheson’s study compares these with other Late Lucayan sites; at Palmetto Grove, impressions even preserve evidence of woven spun thread. Clay kept a record of fibre work. Different patterns suggest variation in craft, but do not automatically identify a specific ethnic group.

passages.title: Discoveries: clay, weaving and island food
passages.text: At Clifton on New Providence, excavators distinguished two Lucayan settlements using radiocarbon dates and objects, rather than assuming all nearby remains belonged to one village. Griddles, hollow vessels, shell beads and tools differed between the sites. Marine remains show the importance of conch and other seafood. The researchers favoured successive settlement over a long-lived pair of simultaneous villages.

passages.title: Household work and family knowledge
passages.text: Laundry left clues at early nineteenth-century Clifton. Buttons, beads and fasteners clustered between houses and outdoor kitchens; the excavators interpreted them as losses during washing and drying. Food remains and cooking tools marked other activity areas. The yards supported sewing, childcare and conversation as well as chores, within the constrained lives of enslaved households.

passages.title: Household work and family knowledge
passages.text: On Cat Island, Iva Thompson passed skills to her family, including Sheena Woodside and Peggy Johnson. The tourism ministry’s family profile describes Woodside plaiting dried palm leaves into bags, baskets and rugs from childhood. Ordinary plants became useful household objects through learned patterns and patient hands. This is one documented family’s story, not a rule for every Bahamian home.

passages.title: Household work and family knowledge
passages.text: The same Cat Island family remembers bush teas made from local plants, including cerasee, breadfruit and guava. Peggy Johnson describes this knowledge as part of an inherited tradition of care. The account tells us what this family practised and valued; it does not demonstrate that a tea cures an illness.

passages.title: Making music, costumes and public memory
passages.text: For Junkanoo, families and groups transform cardboard and crepe paper into towering costumes. Skills pass between generations in preparation spaces called shacks and at home. A child can learn by helping someone who already knows the craft. UNESCO’s 2023 inscription recognizes the shared work and creativity behind the spectacle.

passages.title: Making music, costumes and public memory
passages.text: The street music of Junkanoo includes whistles, cowbells, horns and goatskin drums. A 2022 postal-service account describes months of preparation and costumes whose materials changed over time, from cloth and natural materials to elaborate cardboard constructions. The exact origin remains debated. The parade is the part you see; much of the work happens beforehand.

passages.title: Making music, costumes and public memory
passages.text: At Clifton, Antonius Roberts carved female figures from unwanted casuarina tree trunks, leaving them in place as a memorial. Tyrone Ferguson added metal bells. The work, called Sacred Space, connects art, ancestry and the landscape. These contemporary sculptures commemorate history; they are not excavated Lucayan statues.

passages.title: Work, votes and independence
passages.text: The Burma Road unrest of 1942 grew from workers’ anger over unequal pay at an airfield construction project. Bahamian labourers learned that Americans received more for comparable work. The dispute helped connect workplace demands with the wider struggle over racial inequality and political power.

passages.title: Work, votes and independence
passages.text: Mary Ingraham, Doris Johnson, Eugenia Lockhart and other campaigners pressed for women’s voting rights through organizing and petitions. Women voted in the general election of 26 November 1962. That achievement widened participation before majority rule in 1967.

passages.title: Work, votes and independence
passages.text: After the September 1972 election, the Bahamas legislature requested independence and government and opposition delegates attended a London conference. The resulting settlement fixed 10 July 1973 as independence day. This was a negotiated end to British colonial rule, not a conquest or the disappearance of an island community.
British colonial rule ended with independence in 1973. The Bahamas continues as a country. The map’s separate entries represent coverage of the same islands, not vanished and refounded societies.

Nawabs, ministers, soldiers, and negotiated power
Forts, towns, routes, money, and exchange
Farms, herds, rivers, and the desert environment
Families, women, marriage, celebration, and unequal voices
Children, learning, scripts, and a written-language sample
