passages.text: Bahawalpur here means the historical state, not the present Pakistani city described by the imported summary. The atlas gives this id one coarse six-point polygon from 1800 to 1815. It includes Derawar, Uch Sharif, Ahmadpur East, desert and riverine towns, and even sampled Sukkur; astonishingly, it excludes Bahawalpur city, Multan, Dera Ghazi Khan, Khairpur, Shikarpur, Jaisalmer, Bikaner, and Jodhpur. Those results expose a display shape, not a surveyed border. No modern border should be inferred. The polity already had an eighteenth-century history; Punjab's official account dates a new phase of princely independence to 1802. Derawar, regained in 1804, anchored a fort network built around scarce water and caravan routes. Nawabs, viziers, jagirdars, religious specialists, merchants, cultivators, herders, artisans, servants, women, and children did not experience one uniform life. Evidence is richest for courts, forts, and later observers, so household chapters mark what is later, local, or unknown. In 1815 every audited point flips to an enormous atlas “maratha” layer, although Bahawalpur continued. That endpoint is a software seam, not Maratha conquest, state extinction, or population replacement.

passages.title: Read the atlas shape before trusting its color
passages.text: The exact index contains one generated id, “bahawalpur,” displayed as “Bahawalpur” from approximately 1800 to 1815. Its coverage record points to one border file and one observed interval. This is the historical-state target, even though the imported prose talks only about today's city and its population.

passages.title: Read the atlas shape before trusting its color
passages.text: The 1800 target is one Polygon with one ring and only six coordinate positions. Derawar, Uch Sharif, Ahmadpur East, Yazman, Khanpur, Rahim Yar Khan, Sadiqabad, Liaquatpur, and the sampled Cholistan interior fall inside. The tiny vertex count alone warns against reading it as a surveyed border.

passages.title: Read the atlas shape before trusting its color
passages.text: The shape excludes sampled Bahawalpur city itself, assigning that point to “sikhs.” It also excludes Multan, Dera Ghazi Khan, Khairpur, Shikarpur, Jaisalmer, Bikaner, and Jodhpur, yet includes sampled Sukkur. Those oddities are atlas artifacts, not claims about uniform Sikh or Bahawalpur ownership.

passages.title: Read the atlas shape before trusting its color
passages.text: Directly reused topology arcs touch atlas layers called “sindh-1800,” “rajputs,” and “sikhs.” These are technical neighbors in this file. They do not certify diplomatic frontiers, ethnic blocks, or control on the ground, and they cannot settle disputes that surviving treaties and chronicles describe more carefully.

passages.title: Read the atlas shape before trusting its color
passages.text: In 1783 the same target-region probes sit inside a broad “multan-1783” layer; in 1815 all audited points switch to “maratha”; by 1878 they switch to “british-raj.” Bahawalpur neither began nor ended at those JSON seams. The sequence measures changing atlas labels, not three sudden conquests.

passages.title: Nawabs, ministers, soldiers, and negotiated power
passages.text: Bahawalpur rule centered on a Nawab from the Daudputra elite, but power ran through relatives, jagirdars, commanders, religious figures, accountants, scribes, and town or fort officers. A ruler needed allegiance, revenue, armed retainers, and negotiation; one palace order did not automatically become everyday reality across river lands and desert.

passages.title: Nawabs, ministers, soldiers, and negotiated power
passages.text: The vizier was far more than a ceremonial adviser. Research based on Persian chronicles and state records describes viziers managing diplomacy with the Sikh Empire, Talpur Sindh, and the East India Company while overseeing administration and military affairs. Their personal influence could stabilize government and also create dangerous dependence.

passages.title: Nawabs, ministers, soldiers, and negotiated power
passages.text: The 1809 ministry distributed work among a keeper of the privy seal, vizier, commander-in-chief, military paymaster, general accountants, chief justice, councillors, and a preceptor for the ruler's children. This list reveals specialization at court; it does not tell us how effectively each office reached every village or camp.

passages.title: Nawabs, ministers, soldiers, and negotiated power
passages.text: Naseer Khan Gurgaij's career joined military command, tribal leadership, land development, and the vizierate. The same study records campaigns, rivalry, and violent intrigue. Offices were embedded in personal and kin networks, so “the state” often acted through people whose loyalty and private power could shift.

passages.title: Nawabs, ministers, soldiers, and negotiated power
passages.text: Colonial travelers praised or condemned Nawabs according to changing British interests. A modern source study shows how the same court could be painted hospitable, backward, loyal, or threatening. Read vivid descriptions as situated testimony: useful details need corroboration, and an outsider's insult is never a neutral portrait of a whole population.

passages.title: Forts, towns, routes, money, and exchange
passages.text: Derawar stood at a Cholistan crossroads and served at different times as fortress, refuge, capital, and treasury site. Its strategic value came from location as much as walls: controlling a defensible watering and caravan node connected desert movement with dynastic survival. One fort's importance still does not map every nearby settlement.

passages.title: Forts, towns, routes, money, and exchange
passages.text: Pakistan's archaeology record identifies Derawar as a protected monumental site, while specialist study places it among contested desert strongholds. Together they support a physical fort, not a fantasy castle. The card avoids assigning every visible repair to 1804 because the fabric accumulated across many centuries and rulers.

passages.title: Forts, towns, routes, money, and exchange
passages.text: Uch Sharif's surviving tombs and mosque preserve carved timber, cut brick, painted ceilings, and blue-and-white glazed tile. These monuments predate 1800, yet they show the inherited sacred and artistic landscape through which residents and travelers moved. They are evidence for Uch, not a universal Bahawalpur house style.

passages.title: Forts, towns, routes, money, and exchange
passages.text: Daulat Rai and Suba Rai appear as court-connected writers and diplomats in regional records. Their movement among Bahawalpur, Shah Shuja's camp, Multan, and Ranjit Singh's orbit shows that a munshi's skill could travel with letters, memory, and verse. Political work depended on literate intermediaries as well as cavalry.

passages.title: Forts, towns, routes, money, and exchange
passages.text: The 1802 mint produced gold, silver, and copper currency under authority linked to Mahmud Shah of Kabul. Coinage made claims portable: metal carried names and legitimacy through payments and markets. Later Bahawalpur coins survive in museums, but an 1858 specimen demonstrates continuity, not the exact design in a child's hand in 1802.

passages.title: Farms, herds, rivers, and the desert environment
passages.text: Research on Bahawalpur's later agrarian economy shows how cultivation became entangled with canals, settlement, and state administration after 1866. Because that study begins decades after 1815, it cannot supply an unchanged farm calendar for our interval. It gives comparison while early acreage, yields, and tenancy remain poorly quantified.

passages.title: Farms, herds, rivers, and the desert environment
passages.text: A later agrarian study begins in 1866, after this card ends. Its very date is useful: major canal, settlement, and administrative changes in later Bahawalpur cannot be copied backward into 1800. Early chronicles mention irrigation and cultivation, but acreage, yields, and tenancy varied and remain poorly quantified here.

passages.title: Farms, herds, rivers, and the desert environment
passages.text: Modern Cholistan research finds that livestock, grazing, temporary settlement, and rainwater still organize many desert livelihoods. This helps children see why water matters, but technology, markets, borders, and population changed enormously. It is environmental comparison, not proof that an 1805 herding family followed today's schedule.

passages.title: Farms, herds, rivers, and the desert environment
passages.text: A 2015 field survey found temporary communities gathering with animals around rain-filled tobas and moving when water failed. That is powerful evidence about modern vulnerability in the same desert. It cannot identify an 1800 household, yet it explains why rulers who guarded wells and water routes held practical power.

passages.title: Farms, herds, rivers, and the desert environment
passages.text: The fort chain linked security with access to water and caravan traffic. Deep water near Derawar made the site useful when surrounding sands were harsh. Fort walls therefore guarded more than soldiers: they could organize movement, tolls, shelter, and survival, although actual access would differ for elites, merchants, herders, and travelers.

passages.title: Families, women, marriage, celebration, and unequal voices
passages.text: Sairistan-i Mubaraz ud Daula grew from a Persian writer's fourteen years of later residence in Bahawalpur and records society as well as politics. It can help recover people court annals neglect, but it postdates this interval and speaks from one observer. Its families and women cannot be copied wholesale into 1800.

passages.title: Families, women, marriage, celebration, and unequal voices
passages.text: A later nineteenth-century observer recorded mahr marriage payments, divorce before a qazi, a waiting period, and wedding processions with music and shared meals. These are valuable direct observations, but they come after the mapped interval and may reflect normative claims as well as practice; local communities differed.

passages.title: Families, women, marriage, celebration, and unequal voices
passages.text: A study spanning 1727 to 1947 describes Muslim and Hindu communities, festival visits, gifts, sweets, alms, shrine fairs, and livestock shows as social and economic gatherings. Many cited examples are late nineteenth or twentieth century, so the card uses the study to show long regional themes, never to date each custom to 1800.

passages.title: Families, women, marriage, celebration, and unequal voices
passages.text: Murad Bakhsh's travel narrative preserves a woman performer's mobility, honor claims, defiance, and negotiations in late eighteenth-century Multan, linked to courtiers who also served Bahawalpur. It gives one extraordinary named voice, not a template for all women. Its value is showing that women could act in political-literary networks.

passages.title: Families, women, marriage, celebration, and unequal voices
passages.text: Modern agro-pastoral research treats households as working units whose members combine livestock, farming, gathering, migration, and wage strategies. That division of labor has changed with policy and technology. For 1800 to 1815, we can safely say family labor mattered, but not assign today's measured tasks or authority to historical mothers and children.

passages.title: Children, learning, scripts, and a written-language sample
passages.text: In 1809 the court appointed Mawlawi Shir Ali as preceptor to the Nawab's children. That is secure evidence of elite household education and a named teacher. It says nothing about how many village children learned letters, and it cannot turn royal tutoring into a state school system.

passages.title: Children, learning, scripts, and a written-language sample
passages.text: A history of Bahawalpur primary education starts in 1866, more than fifty years after this atlas interval. Organized state schooling from that later era must stay later. Children in 1800 may have learned at home, in religious settings, workshops, fields, and herding camps, but exact participation rates are not securely documented here.

passages.title: Children, learning, scripts, and a written-language sample
passages.text: Later observers found some higher-status children taught Persian and Arabic and some commercial writers literate, while describing widespread illiteracy. That evidence is unequal and judgment-laden. It supports restricted access to formal literacy, not a precise 1800 rate, and it leaves oral teaching, practical skill, and girls' learning underrecorded.

passages.title: Children, learning, scripts, and a written-language sample
passages.text: Written-language sample: “مرآت دولت عباسی” (Mirʾāt-i Daulat-i ʿAbbāsī), translated “Mirror of the Abbasi State.” It is the Persian title of Lala Daulat Rai Gehi's court-sponsored political history of Bahawalpur. This is a book title, not a sentence of ordinary conversation or every resident's spoken language.

passages.title: Children, learning, scripts, and a written-language sample
passages.text: The British Museum catalogue describes manuscript Or. 1631 as 586 folios written by different hands in nastaʿlīq and shikasta-amiz. One section was finished at Bahawalpur in AH 1224 and the work in AH 1227, about 1809 to 1812. Spelling and transliteration vary, and the displayed title is a secure sample, not universal speech.

passages.title: Food, homes, clothing, crafts, and ordinary work
passages.text: A broad Bahawalpur food study tracks meat, fish, pulses, vegetables, and changing attitudes toward lentils across a long period. It is not a menu for every 1800 table. One memorable later insult treated “pulse-eater” as rude, which is a strange fate for a perfectly respectable lentil.

passages.title: Food, homes, clothing, crafts, and ordinary work
passages.text: During the 1808 embassy, the Nawab's court sent abundant provisions and hosted the travelers at public expense. That is a spectacular diplomatic welcome, recorded from inside the visiting mission. It is useful precisely because it was exceptional, not evidence for an average child's Tuesday dinner.

passages.title: Food, homes, clothing, crafts, and ordinary work
passages.text: Later descriptions mention lungis, turbans, long coats, trousers, shawls, locally made silk, gold or silver ornaments, and enameled work. Dress signaled wealth, setting, gender, and occasion. One gently human detail: hair oil could keep locks glossy and also leave shoulder cloth noticeably greasy. Fashion has always had tradeoffs.

passages.title: Food, homes, clothing, crafts, and ordinary work
passages.text: A modern Cholistan survey records gopas made from branches and leaves at temporary toba settlements. Such light materials suit mobility, but this 2015 evidence cannot reconstruct an 1800 house. Town dwellings, fort rooms, tents, village compounds, and river settlements would have offered very different spaces and levels of permanence.

passages.title: Food, homes, clothing, crafts, and ordinary work
passages.text: Later cultural research lists pottery, textile work, embroidery, woodwork, tents, animal-skin curtains, and hearth-centered household gathering. These traditions help identify skills worth investigating, but the study ranges broadly across Bahawalpur history. It cannot date every tool or claim that every family gathered around the same hearth in 1805.

passages.title: Medicine, illness, healers, and the limits of care
passages.text: Bahawal Khan II's final illness is described through stomach and liver pain, swelling, a medicinal plaster, pulse-taking, and named physicians. It gives rare exact-period medical detail at court. It does not prove diagnosis, treatment effectiveness, or that farmers, artisans, servants, women, and children could reach comparable care.

passages.title: Medicine, illness, healers, and the limits of care
passages.text: A modern ethnobotanical field study interviewed herbalists, landowners, and other knowledgeable residents and recorded seventy medicinal plants. Leaves, stems, fruits, flowers, seeds, bark, and pods entered remedies. This documents living knowledge and possible research leads; it cannot demonstrate that the same species, recipes, or claims were used in 1800.

passages.title: Medicine, illness, healers, and the limits of care
passages.text: A separate comparative study recorded sixty-seven medicinal plant species in modern Cholistan and warned that old knowledge is disappearing. Agreement between recent surveys strengthens evidence for a rich present tradition, while still leaving a two-century gap. “Traditional” is not a time machine, and medicinal use is not automatic proof of clinical efficacy.

passages.title: Medicine, illness, healers, and the limits of care
passages.text: Modern researchers also document animal-derived remedies in Cholistan. That zootherapy study belongs to present ethnomedicine, not the Nawabs' court. It helps explain the range of knowledge historians might seek in oral histories and material culture, but this card does not assign a current remedy to an 1800 patient without period evidence.

passages.title: Medicine, illness, healers, and the limits of care
passages.text: Another medical survey sought to conserve knowledge of common Cholistan plants. Its purpose matters: researchers were recording practice, not verifying an early nineteenth-century pharmacy. For 1800 to 1815, secure evidence supports named court physicians and treatments; access, childbirth care, epidemic response, and village practitioners remain incompletely documented.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets, and what the sources do not show
passages.text: Modern water research distinguishes shallow rain-fed tobas from constructed kunds that store drinking water longer. The terms help explain Cholistan's enduring water problem, but today's brick, mortar, pipes, pumps, and management rules are not evidence for 1800 technology. Period sources securely show forts, wells, rivers, canals, and caravan water needs.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets, and what the sources do not show
passages.text: PCRWR reports that rainwater in natural depressions or man-made ponds remains Cholistan's main fresh-water source and that current storage falls short of estimated human and livestock demand. This is a modern crisis measure, not a historical statistic, but it makes clear why water quality, distance, and drought belong in any honest daily-life chapter.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets, and what the sources do not show
passages.text: A Punjab drought plan says people and animals may use the same turbid toba water and notes a lack of disinfection. That is present evidence of health risk, not a claim about 1805. It warns us against romantic desert scenes: a sparkling map symbol cannot reveal microbes, labor spent carrying water, or unequal access.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets, and what the sources do not show
passages.text: A 2015 survey found sanitation and drinking-water provision rudimentary or absent at sampled temporary toba settlements. Conditions and infrastructure have changed, so the finding must remain modern. It still teaches a sound historical question: where people and animals gathered seasonally, safe separation of drinking water, waste, and manure would matter.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets, and what the sources do not show
passages.text: No secure source reviewed for 1800 to 1815 describes a Bahawalpur household toilet, latrine design, sewer, or routine waste collector. The detailed later history discusses food, dress, education, trades, rivers, and canals but stays silent here. A missing privy is missing evidence, not permission to invent palace plumbing.

passages.title: Faith, literature, art, achievements, discoveries, and continuity
passages.text: Uch Sharif's Sufi monuments joined worship, memory, architecture, and craft. Carved wooden pillars, molded brick, painted floral ceilings, and faience mosaics preserve work by designers and makers whose names often vanish from political chronicles. Their survival is an achievement of inherited skill, repeated repair, and community attachment, not one Nawab's invention.

passages.title: Faith, literature, art, achievements, discoveries, and continuity
passages.text: Daulat Rai's Mirat-i Daulat-i Abbasi is itself an achievement and a discovery source: a Persian political history commissioned under Bahawal Khan II that records people, works, and events. Historians still compare its manuscript, later lithograph, and other chronicles because copying and publication introduced omissions and additions.

passages.title: Faith, literature, art, achievements, discoveries, and continuity
passages.text: The festival study places Uch at the center of religious, educational, and social activity and describes Muslim and Hindu communities in the state. Its long 1727 to 1947 scope combines manuscripts, printed records, and oral interviews. That breadth reveals plural traditions while preventing any single late example from becoming universal 1800 practice.

passages.title: Faith, literature, art, achievements, discoveries, and continuity
passages.text: Bahawalpur's textual life continued to change after this card: later Persian political manuscripts survive, a press opened in 1866, and official correspondence eventually shifted toward Urdu. Those later milestones belong after 1815. They show continuity and transformation in learning without pretending mass print or later language policy already existed under Bahawal Khan II.

passages.title: Faith, literature, art, achievements, discoveries, and continuity
passages.text: In 1815 the exact id disappears and every audited probe becomes atlas “maratha.” Yet the Nawab was still petitioning about territorial protection, and Bahawalpur continued as a state long afterward. The seam is therefore continuity with no historical conqueror successor: the atlas successor label is “maratha,” but the polity and people did not become Maratha overnight.

The atlas removes the Bahawalpur id in 1815 and assigns every audited point to “maratha.” Bahawalpur's Nawab was still seeking protection for threatened territory, and the state continued. This is an atlas handoff, not a Maratha conquest or a population's disappearance.

sectionTitles: Stories, money and a written wish

passages.text: Founded in 1347 after a revolt against Delhi, the Bahmani sultanate became a major Deccan power, ruling first from Gulbarga and then Bidar. This map shows only 1500 to 1530, during its fragmentation. Its very narrow southern outline misses both capitals and must not be read as the kingdom’s full territory.

passages.title: Markets, languages and government
passages.text: Russian merchant Afanasy Nikitin visited the Deccan in the late fifteenth century. His account describes trade in horses, cloth, silk and pepper, and busy trading gatherings. Bidar’s inland court depended on commercial routes reaching the coast, including the port of Dabhol.

passages.title: Markets, languages and government
passages.text: Nikitin noticed sharp differences between poor rural people and wealthy nobles carried in silver palanquins, accompanied by horses and attendants. His eye-catching description helps reveal inequality, though a visitor’s contrast does not describe every merchant, craft worker or household in the kingdom.

passages.title: Markets, languages and government
passages.text: The kingdom was multilingual: Persian, Marathi, Kannada, Telugu and Dakhni were used in different settings and regions. Court culture connected local families with migrants from Iran, Central Asia and elsewhere. A single royal dynasty did not mean everyone spoke the same language.

passages.title: Markets, languages and government
passages.text: Minister Mahmud Gawan ordered land measurements and the fixing of village and town boundaries. These practical surveys helped officials assess revenue. For people cultivating the land, government involved fields, boundaries and tax demands as well as distant ceremonies at court.

passages.title: Children, learning and care
passages.text: When Humayun died in 1461, his young son’s government was entrusted to a regency council that included the queen mother and Mahmud Gawan. Royal women could participate directly in state affairs; this council’s responsibilities went well beyond arranging palace ceremonies.

passages.title: Children, learning and care
passages.text: Yazdani’s history, drawing on earlier chronicles, records schools for orphans at Bidar and other Deccan towns under Muhammad Shah II, who ruled from 1378 to 1397. This is a specific example of organized provision for children, rather than evidence that every child attended school.

passages.title: Children, learning and care
passages.text: Alauddin Ahmad II’s Bidar hospital employed Hindu and Muslim physicians, according to the historical accounts summarized by Yazdani. Endowed land supplied income for medicines, food and drink. Care required a continuing budget, not just a building with an impressive entrance.

passages.title: Children, learning and care
passages.text: Gawan’s madrasa, built at Bidar in 1472, gathered lecture rooms, a prayer hall, a library and living quarters around a large court. Teachers and students could live within the institution. His surviving letters show his efforts to recruit learned people from Iran and Iraq.

passages.title: Children, learning and care
passages.text: The college courtyard contained a twelve-sided cistern. Yazdani thought an underground channel probably supplied it from a well outside the main building. Students’ surroundings therefore combined lessons, residence and a carefully planned water supply: geometry was useful beyond the classroom.

passages.title: Buildings with practical jobs
passages.text: The madrasa’s facade was covered with glazed tiles arranged into flowers and inscriptions in vivid colors. Two minarets originally framed the entrance, although only one survives. Its decoration connected a Deccan school with architectural traditions also seen in Iran and Central Asia.

passages.title: Buildings with practical jobs
passages.text: Gulbarga’s congregational mosque, built in 1367, covered its courtyard rather than leaving the central space open to the sky. Its roofed gathering space is one of the distinctive features noted in India’s heritage submission. The surviving building makes a design choice visible centuries later.

passages.title: Buildings with practical jobs
passages.text: Bidar’s fortifications incorporated gates and sluices that could flood selected portions of the moat while conserving water. Managing defenses required controlling water as well as moving soldiers. The surviving fort also includes later alterations, so every wall should not be assigned to one Bahmani building campaign.

passages.title: Buildings with practical jobs
passages.text: At Ashtur, the royal tombs preserved a different kind of craftsmanship: painted and gilded ceilings inside large domed chambers. These were carefully decorated memorials. Their surviving color helps counter the impression that old stone monuments always looked plain and grey.

passages.title: Stories, money and a written wish
passages.text: Bidar attracted musicians, storytellers, dancers and reciters of the Persian Shahnameh, alongside poets and historians. Adhari composed the Bahman-nama, a dynastic history in verse. At court, listening to a story could also mean hearing a carefully shaped account of royal identity.

passages.title: Stories, money and a written wish
passages.text: Bahmani mints produced copper, silver and gold coins carrying Arabic names, titles and dates. Commerce also crossed political borders: Vijayanagara gold coins circulated within Bahmani territories. A market stall did not necessarily require every coin to carry the name of the local ruler.

passages.title: Stories, money and a written wish
passages.text: A silver coin struck at Bidar in 1471 to 1472 for Muhammad Shah III ends its inscription “khallada mulkahu”: “May God preserve the kingdom.” This is the museum catalogue’s Roman transliteration of the original Arabic. A small coin could carry both a ruler’s identity and a prayer.

The kingdom fragmented into Ahmadnagar, Berar, Bidar, Bijapur and Golconda. Nominal Bahmani rulers lingered: Iranica ends the dynasty in 1528, while the Met uses 1538. Neither makes 1530 a secure single fall date. Successor courts continued Deccan artistic and intellectual traditions.

passages.text: Balhae was founded in 698 by Dae Joyeong, a former Goguryeo general, in the hills of eastern Manchuria, and grew into a power that Tang writers called the Flourishing State of the East. Its capitals were laid out on the Tang model and its envoys sailed regularly to Japan.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Embassies went to Tang China and, more than thirty times, across the sea to Japan, carrying furs, ginseng and horses.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Balhae sat on the routes between Manchuria, the Korean peninsula, north China and the steppe.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Buddhism was practiced in the capitals, alongside the native beliefs of the Mohe majority.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: A Tang-style government of three chancelleries and six ministries ran a state of many peoples; the capital Sanggyeong copied the grid of Chang'an.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Korea, China and Russia each claim Balhae's story in their national histories.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Excavations of its walled capitals and tombs show a state that mixed Goguryeo, Mohe and Tang traditions.
The Khitan under Yelü Abaoji, founder of what became the Liao dynasty, took the capital Sanggyeong in 926 after a campaign of a few weeks. Refugees from the ruling class moved south into Goryeo.

sectionTitles: Neighbours and people on the move
A wooden world preserved by water
Words that survive from a later century

passages.text: Balts is a broad name for related Baltic-speaking peoples east and southeast of the Baltic Sea, not one kingdom. These two map labels cover 700 to 1100, with local examples from different centuries. Their outlines are overbroad, extending into areas inhabited by Finnic-speaking communities. They should not be read as exact ethnic borders or as the borders of modern Lithuania and Latvia.

passages.title: Neighbours and people on the move
passages.text: The lower Daugava was home to Livonians, who spoke a Finnic language. The Daugava Museum dates their settlement there from the tenth century and describes a culture shaped by Baltic, Scandinavian and other contacts. Living beside the same river did not make everyone speak the same language.

passages.title: Neighbours and people on the move
passages.text: At Grobiņa in western Latvia, Curonian communities encountered settlers from Scandinavia during the seventh to ninth centuries. The Ālande River connected the area with the Baltic Sea, while nearby farmland helped support people. This was a place of agriculture and exchange as well as overseas travel.

passages.title: Neighbours and people on the move
passages.text: Some jewellery from Scandinavian-style graves at Grobiņa also shows Baltic influences. Archaeologists compare objects and burial practices to investigate contact between communities. A borrowed design can reveal an exchange of ideas, although it cannot tell us every detail of its wearer’s identity.

passages.title: A wooden world preserved by water
passages.text: Ninth- and tenth-century Āraiši was a fortified Latgalian settlement in a lake. Waterlogged layers preserved timber buildings and objects that usually rot away. Excavators studied a thick accumulation of occupation remains, allowing them to reconstruct much more than the outline of a few postholes.

passages.title: A wooden world preserved by water

passages.text: Balts is a broad name for related Baltic-speaking peoples east and southeast of the Baltic Sea, not one kingdom. These two map labels cover 700 to 1100, with local examples from different centuries. Their outlines are overbroad, extending into areas inhabited by Finnic-speaking communities. They should not be read as exact ethnic borders or as the borders of modern Lithuania and Latvia.

passages.title: Neighbours and people on the move
passages.text: The lower Daugava was home to Livonians, who spoke a Finnic language. The Daugava Museum dates their settlement there from the tenth century and describes a culture shaped by Baltic, Scandinavian and other contacts. Living beside the same river did not make everyone speak the same language.

passages.title: Neighbours and people on the move
passages.text: At Grobiņa in western Latvia, Curonian communities encountered settlers from Scandinavia during the seventh to ninth centuries. The Ālande River connected the area with the Baltic Sea, while nearby farmland helped support people. This was a place of agriculture and exchange as well as overseas travel.

passages.title: Neighbours and people on the move
passages.text: Some jewellery from Scandinavian-style graves at Grobiņa also shows Baltic influences. Archaeologists compare objects and burial practices to investigate contact between communities. A borrowed design can reveal an exchange of ideas, although it cannot tell us every detail of its wearer’s identity.

passages.text: Bangladesh became independent in 1971 after the liberation war. Its earlier twentieth-century history includes British Bengal and the eastern wing of Pakistan. This imported record starts in 1945, before Bangladesh was a sovereign state, and projects a later outline backward. Its available polygons skip 1960 to 1994 and stop at 2020 despite an open-ended index. Those gaps do not represent independence or disappearance. Bengal, British Raj and Pakistan have separate cards.

passages.title: Independence and a changing republic
passages.text: Partition in 1947 placed the eastern and western parts of Pakistan on opposite sides of India, more than a thousand miles apart. Governmental and economic power was concentrated in the west. Being part of one country did not remove the distance or disagreements over how resources and political authority should be shared.

passages.title: Independence and a changing republic
passages.text: The language movement made everyday speech a constitutional issue. Activists demanded recognition for Bangla alongside Urdu. On 21 February 1952 police killed demonstrators in Dhaka. Their deaths became central to the movement’s memory and to a broader struggle over whose language and voice would count in public institutions.

passages.title: Independence and a changing republic
passages.text: Sheikh Mujibur Rahman’s Awami League won the majority in Pakistan’s 1970 national election, but power was not transferred to it. A Pakistani military crackdown in March 1971 was followed by the liberation war. Bengali resistance forces and Indian troops entered Dhaka in December; Pakistan’s forces there surrendered on 16 December 1971.

passages.title: Independence and a changing republic
passages.text: The constitution took effect in December 1972, establishing parliamentary institutions. Independence did not bring stable government immediately: Mujib was killed in a 1975 military coup, and military rule followed through successive changes of leadership. A constitutional change in 1991 restored parliamentary government, with executive authority centred on the prime minister.

passages.title: Independence and a changing republic
passages.text: Article 3 of the 1972 constitution reads “প্রজাতন্ত্রের রাষ্ট্রভাষা বাংলা৷” in the official online Bangla edition. A simplified Latin reading is “prajatantrer rashtrabhasha Bangla”; the official English meaning is “The state language of the Republic is Bangla.” This is a modern digital reproduction of the constitutional text, not a photograph of its original page.

passages.title: Independence and a changing republic
passages.text: The constitution describes the national emblem using familiar plants: a water lily, ears of rice and jute leaves, together with stars. Fields and wetlands thus appear in the country’s official imagery. A symbol on a government document can also be a miniature lesson about the landscape people work in.

passages.title: Work, gardens and household skills
passages.text: Jamdani weavers around Dhaka create fine cotton cloth on handlooms, inserting patterns as they weave. The designs are built into the fabric through an additional discontinuous weft, rather than printed afterward. UNESCO describes home workshops where skills pass from parents to children, supported by spinners, dyers and people who prepare the looms.

passages.title: Work, gardens and household skills
passages.text: In Sylhet, Shital Pati makers split murta stems into strips and weave them into mats used for sitting, sleeping or prayer. UNESCO’s account describes both men and women preparing materials, with women particularly involved in weaving. Learning happens in families and cooperatives. Furniture can begin as a bundle of carefully prepared plant strips.

passages.title: Work, gardens and household skills
passages.text: In parts of Gopalganj, Pirojpur and Barisal, farmers grow vegetables on floating beds called dhap. Layers of water hyacinth and other plant material support the beds, with bamboo helping their structure and decomposing upper layers feeding the crops. Okra, gourds, spinach and aubergines can grow above flooded ground. The vegetable patch has learned to float.

passages.title: Work, gardens and household skills
passages.text: A floating garden changes with the seasons. When floodwaters recede, farmers dismantle the beds and spread the decomposed material on land for winter cultivation. The old garden becomes food for the next one. FAO’s account documents a cycle linking flood-season vegetables, compost and dry-season farming, rather than a permanent floating island.

passages.title: Work, gardens and household skills
passages.text: Factory clothing became a major part of Bangladesh’s economy alongside older weaving skills. An ILO report records that ready-made garments supplied more than 80 percent of export earnings in 2013 to 2014, employing about four million people, a majority women. These are dated figures, but they show how strongly overseas wardrobes became linked to Bangladeshi workplaces.

passages.title: Work, gardens and household skills
passages.text: The Rana Plaza building collapse in 2013 exposed deadly failures in workplace safety. Inspections and training followed. In a 2018 ILO account, a garment-factory manager describes changing how chemicals were stored after safety training, then helping train colleagues. Safer work involved buildings, electrical systems and everyday practices, with further improvements still needed.

passages.title: Learning, health and everyday ingenuity
passages.text: Research in Dhaka and Calcutta helped establish oral rehydration therapy during the 1960s. Carefully measured fluids containing glucose and salts could help patients replace water lost through severe diarrhoea. A Dhaka study published in 1968 greatly reduced the need for intravenous fluid in its adult cholera patients. This was an international research achievement with important work in what was then East Pakistan.

passages.title: Learning, health and everyday ingenuity
passages.text: BRAC began in 1972 with relief and rehabilitation in Sulla, helping communities rebuild after the war. During the 1980s its oral therapy extension programme taught women about treating diarrhoeal dehydration. Sharing medical knowledge with families was part of the achievement: a laboratory discovery had to reach the people caring for sick children.

passages.title: Learning, health and everyday ingenuity
passages.text: BRAC’s education programme began in 1985 with twenty-two one-room schools. Its three-year primary course aimed to reach children who had missed school or dropped out, with particular attention to girls. A small classroom close to a community could open a route back into learning.

passages.title: Learning, health and everyday ingenuity
passages.text: In 1993 Bangladeshi television introduced UNICEF’s fictional nine-year-old Meena in Count Your Chickens, a story about her wish to attend school. Her brother Raju and pet parrot Mithu joined the adventures. Children helped shape the character through extensive consultation. A cartoon girl and a bird became a way for families to discuss education and fair treatment.

passages.title: Learning, health and everyday ingenuity
passages.text: A 2022 UNICEF story follows sixteen-year-old Eti in Monohorpur, Satkhira. Her family moved their toilet closer to the house and upgraded its concrete rings, slab and water seal. The 3,300-taka cost was paid in instalments. Eti felt safer using it at night: sanitation also involved privacy, location and whether someone needed to accompany her.

passages.title: Learning, health and everyday ingenuity
passages.text: At a Pirojpur school described by UNICEF in 2022, girls could obtain free menstrual pads from a hygiene corner. An honesty shop also sold pads and stationery, with pupils expected to leave the correct payment themselves. These practical arrangements helped make menstruation something students could discuss and manage while attending lessons.

passages.title: Learning, health and everyday ingenuity
passages.text: After the devastating 1970 cyclone, the Cyclone Preparedness Programme began in 1972 and became a joint government and Red Crescent programme in 1973. Volunteers carry official weather warnings into communities and help people evacuate, reach shelters and receive first aid. Preparing together turns a forecast into actions that neighbours can actually take.

Bangladesh continues as an independent republic. Coups and constitutional changes concern its government, not the disappearance of its people. The imported record’s missing 1960 to 1994 polygons and last snapshot in 2020 are gaps in this map dataset, not the country’s beginning or ending.

sectionTitles: Food and homes in the Congo basin
A later language sample and storytelling

passages.text: Bantu names a large family of languages and the many societies that speak them, not a single empire. The map’s early “Bantu” and later “Bantu peoples” labels are broad historical approximations. This shared account follows the wider history; its dated examples do not all belong to either displayed interval or polygon.

passages.title: Languages, movement and exchange
passages.text: Early Bantu-speaking communities expanded from western Africa over many generations, with movement into forest and savanna regions. They met and mixed with other populations. This long history produced hundreds of languages and diverse communities; it was not one army marching across an empty continent.

passages.title: Languages, movement and exchange
passages.text: Urewe pottery around the Great Lakes illustrates how ideas can travel between neighbors. Scholars caution that its makers need not all have spoken the same language, or have introduced farming and ironworking together. Pots preserve skilled choices about clay and design, but they do not come with a spoken-language label.

passages.title: Food and homes in the Congo basin
passages.text: At Iyonda in today’s DR Congo, charred millet grains survived in early Iron Age pits. The Imbonga phase is broadly dated around 400 to 200 BCE, although individual grain dates span wider ranges. Such tiny remains make real crops visible in a rainforest history once known mainly through pottery.

passages.title: Food and homes in the Congo basin
passages.text: Plant tissue from Iyonda, Mbandaka and Bolondo also points to tubers. Charring suggests that some were roasted in hot ash. Around 1350 at Mbandaka, grains showing germination may reflect malting for beer: a plausible interpretation, rather than a surviving recipe.

passages.title: Food and homes in the Congo basin
passages.text: At Bolondo, house platforms were repeatedly raised from the settlement’s beginnings around the mid-fourteenth century. Over time they joined into an artificial island. Building upward helped people live beside the Tshuapa River through changing water levels: floors could be part of a family’s flood strategy.

passages.title: Food and homes in the Congo basin
passages.text: Fish bones are abundant at Bolondo, and chemical traces in human remains show the importance of forest and freshwater foods. Millet was present, but researchers caution against imagining a diet dominated by cereal farming. Living by a river could mean a very different dinner from life on a dry plateau.

passages.title: Regional skills, courtyards and toilets
passages.text: At Kalundu in Zambia, excavators recovered finger millet and a sorghum grain dated between 1320 and 1415. Finger millet can supply porridge, malt and other foods, and stores well. Researchers therefore suggest that nearby Isamu Pati’s grain bins may have held millet, an important household reserve.

passages.title: Regional skills, courtyards and toilets
passages.text: Fourteenth-century Great Zimbabwe shows another regional achievement: carefully laid granite enclosure walls surrounding living spaces made with clay and granitic sand. UNESCO describes family areas with kitchens, living huts and courts. Behind the monumental stonework were people cooking, resting and sharing the work of a household.

passages.title: Regional skills, courtyards and toilets
passages.text: At the coastal Swahili town of Songo Mnara, House 44 had coral-and-lime walls, plaster floors in most rooms and shaped coral around its doorways. The house belonged to the late fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. Even comparatively simple urban homes involved specialized building materials and careful finishing.

passages.title: Regional skills, courtyards and toilets
passages.text: House 44 also had a latrine in the back room’s southwest corner. Archaeologists found that it was filled in during a change when a fresh sand layer covered accumulated deposits. Toilets leave evidence too, which is fortunate for historians, if less glamorous than finding gold.

passages.title: A later language sample and storytelling
passages.text: Swahili provides one written example from the much later history of a Bantu language. In an 1870 collection of Zanzibari tales, a lion asks, “Nani ninyi?” The facing English text reads, “Who are you?” These are the book’s Latin letters, not a reconstruction of prehistoric Bantu speech.

passages.title: A later language sample and storytelling
passages.text: In that tale, a hare finds honey and invites companions to share it, then tries to escape when its owner, the lion, appears. The collector noted that narrators could add touches as they told stories. Such performances reveal creativity and humor; they are literature, not literal reports of talking animals.

Neither 1500 BCE nor 1530 CE marks the end of Bantu-speaking peoples. These are endpoints of imported map labels. Their languages and communities continued to change, form states, exchange ideas and develop new histories; there was never one Bantu empire with a single fall.

sectionTitles: Work, homes and the struggle for freedom

passages.text: Barbados’s island history long predates the plantation colony. Archaeology records shell tools, pottery and fishing, while Bridgetown’s buildings reveal the organization of colonial trade and slavery. Independence in 1966 and the republic established in 2021 are distinct political changes within a continuing society.

passages.title: Discoveries and earlier island life
passages.text: At Heywoods, a conch-shell adze from archaeological Context 7 produced a calibrated date range of 2530 to 2200 BCE. The shaped shell is evidence of toolmaking before pottery became common on the island. The dating study also discusses contamination and marine-shell problems, so this evidence does not establish an exact arrival year for the first islanders.

passages.title: Discoveries and earlier island life
passages.text: Excavators at Heywoods washed deposits through fine mesh to recover small fish bones. Elizabeth Wing identified an assemblage dominated by open-water fish, especially flying fish and tuna, alongside fewer reef fish. Shell remains also point to collecting around mangroves and the shore. These finds reveal varied coastal food gathering in the precolonial settlement landscape.

passages.title: Discoveries and earlier island life
passages.text: The later Heywoods settlement produced footed bowls, animal and human pottery ornaments, and a spindle whorl. Shell adzes, beads and cut conch added evidence of manufacture. These finds connect food preparation, ornament and textile-related work; pottery classifications describe material traditions rather than proving a single ethnic identity.

passages.title: Work, homes and the struggle for freedom
passages.text: The 1661 slave code tried to control movement through written passes and ordered overseers to search enslaved people’s houses twice weekly for fugitives. It also specified an annual clothing allowance. These provisions expose intrusion into domestic life and mobility; a written requirement does not demonstrate that clothing was actually supplied or that people complied.

passages.title: Work, homes and the struggle for freedom
passages.text: The rebellion that began on 14 April 1816 was organized across estates. Participants included Bussa, an estate ranger, the carpenter King Wiltshire and Nanny Grigg, a literate domestic worker. Colonial forces defeated the uprising, but its organization shows enslaved people using occupational contacts and knowledge in their struggle for freedom.

passages.title: Work, homes and the struggle for freedom
passages.text: Much surviving documentation of the rebellion comes from officials who suppressed it. The National Archives presents governors’ letters and military reports for critical reading, alongside a sketch of an insurgent flag. These sources preserve evidence of resistance through the language and interests of colonial authorities; their viewpoint requires interpretation.

passages.title: Work, homes and the struggle for freedom
passages.text: For some Barbadian families, moving house meant moving the actual house. Wooden chattel houses stood on blocks and could be taken apart and relocated. Residents might own the building but rent plantation land beneath it, so portability helped preserve their home when a landowner required them to leave. A clever building method answered a very real insecurity.

passages.title: Buildings, representation and creative achievement
passages.text: Bridgetown’s winding streets, warehouses and dock facilities record a port built around commerce. Buildings adapted European forms to tropical conditions, including storage designed against storms and damage to goods. The same harbour infrastructure supported the traffic in enslaved people, so architectural achievement and the coercive economy that sustained it must be considered together.

passages.title: Buildings, representation and creative achievement
passages.text: Samuel Jackman Prescod entered the House of Assembly in 1843, after free men of colour meeting property requirements had gained voting rights. More than a century later, Edna Bourne became the first woman elected to the House in the 1951 adult-suffrage election. These changes broadened institutions whose early membership had been tied to property.

passages.title: Buildings, representation and creative achievement
passages.text: Crop Over developed from end-of-harvest celebrations and was revived as a national festival in 1974. The decorated cart parade recalled plantation transport and drew extensive local participation. Other early events attracted criticism for favouring visitors and wealthier audiences, making the festival’s development a debate about who could take part and whose culture it represented.

passages.title: Buildings, representation and creative achievement
passages.text: Kamau Brathwaite made Barbadian places central to works including Mother Poem, Sun Poem and Barabajan Poems. The editors of Poui describe his attention to beaches, villages, canefields and threatened landscapes, as well as experiments in rhythm and language. His writing gave these environments literary importance while questioning how they were being transformed.

passages.title: Buildings, representation and creative achievement
passages.text: In a 2021 interview, spoken-word artist Adrian Green emphasized differences among the speech of Barbadian parishes and neighbourhoods. His performances use the language he speaks in daily life. Rather than treating the island as having one uniform voice, he describes local variation as a resource for artistic expression and communication.

British colonial rule ended with independence in 1966. Becoming a republic in 2021 changed the head of state of an already independent country. Barbados continues as a nation, and its separate map records represent coverage intervals rather than successive disappearances and refoundings.

sectionTitles: Living with a river that changes its address
A table with ducks and baskets with animals
A living language and later everyday life

passages.text: Barotse refers here to the Lozi kingdom and its many communities around the upper Zambezi floodplain in western Zambia. The imported 1878 to 1914 window covers a late phase of royal and colonial history. Its polygon lies mainly north of the floodplain heartland described below and should not be treated as a verified kingdom boundary.

passages.title: Living with a river that changes its address
passages.text: Families raised earth into settlement mounds above the surrounding plain. Seasonal flooding still required movement to higher ground. The Kuomboka journey carries the Litunga from Lealui toward Limulunga; other households also relocate. Moving season follows the river’s timetable.

passages.title: Living with a river that changes its address
passages.text: The Mwayowamo canal, dated 1887 to 1889 in Zambia’s heritage account, connected Lealui and Limulunga and supplied Lealui with water. Other channels drained fields or carried boats. These were useful engineering works with several jobs, rather than a decorative moat around a palace.

passages.title: Living with a river that changes its address
passages.text: Fishers built malelo weirs to retain water as floods receded. Opening a gap let water pass into a waiting basket and helped catch fish. Temporary maongo shelters of reeds, grass or branches served people at fishing camps and during seasonal moves.

passages.title: A table with ducks and baskets with animals
passages.text: A wooden food bowl now in the British Museum has six swimming ducks carved on its lid. Dated about 1891 to 1901, it carried a collector’s label saying it was used by headmen. A remarkable serving dish, but not a census of everyone’s dinnerware.

passages.title: A table with ducks and baskets with animals
passages.text: Court objects drew on different communities’ skills. The museum identifies Kwangwa and Mbunda carvers among those meeting demand for wooden vessels at the Lozi court. The kingdom’s artistic achievements belonged to people with distinct identities, not to one ruler working alone.

passages.title: A table with ducks and baskets with animals
passages.text: Women made tightly coiled baskets for storing valuable goods. A surviving example from about 1900 to 1920 uses Makenge root fibre and pigment. Its orderly woven surface turns a flexible plant material into a carefully shaped, lidded container.

passages.title: A table with ducks and baskets with animals
passages.text: Overseas demand changed basket decoration during Lewanika’s reign. The Metropolitan Museum contrasts earlier geometric designs with animal figures made for European customers. On this basket, figures march around lid and body: a procession you could carry under your arm.

passages.title: Power, work and learning
passages.text: The canal-building story also includes coercion. Historian Jack Hogan’s archival research identifies enslaved labour as central to major royal public works. Admiring the engineering should leave room for the workers whose effort was demanded rather than freely offered.

passages.title: Power, work and learning
passages.text: Slavery was formally abolished in 1906, but Hogan follows its slow decline over the next two decades. A proclamation did not instantly free every person from a master’s control. The difference between a law and everyday freedom is part of the kingdom’s history.

passages.title: Power, work and learning
passages.text: Barotse National School opened in March 1907 with seven pupils, according to the education history summarized by Peggy Mwanza. An agreement with Lewanika allocated a share of local tax revenue to education. The tiny opening class belonged to a much larger argument about who should fund schooling.

passages.title: A living language and later everyday life
passages.text: “Bà-shímànì bà-ká-sèh-à” means “The boys will laugh.” This Silozi example was published by linguists in 2025 from work with speaker Mubiana Liswaniso in 2022 to 2024. The Latin letters, tone marks and hyphens reproduce their notation. It is a modern language witness, not a royal document from 1878.

passages.title: A living language and later everyday life
passages.text: A 2015 canals report describes a continuing practical problem: sandy ground and scarce building stone made durable latrines difficult. It also records boreholes serving schools and health centres. These are dated modern observations, showing why water management includes safe drinking water and sanitation as well as boat routes.

Colonial agreements gradually reduced independent royal power; 1914 is only this map record’s endpoint. In 1964 a new agreement addressed Barotseland’s place within independent Zambia and replaced earlier British obligations. That political change did not end Lozi communities or royal traditions. The parliamentary explanation records the settlement’s intended framework, not a guarantee that every later dispute was resolved.

sectionTitles: Evidence close to the map’s century
Food and farming in the wider medieval period

passages.text: The Basques are a continuing people, not a kingdom that existed only from 500 to 600. This map’s outline spreads too far across northern Iberia to serve as a reliable linguistic or political border. The early medieval western Pyrenees were a region of movement, exchange and competing powers. Archaeology illuminates local communities, while their exact languages and identities cannot simply be read from their belongings.

passages.title: Evidence close to the map’s century
passages.text: A drought in 1987 exposed human remains and objects on the shore of the Ullibarri-Gamboa reservoir. The discovery led to excavation of Aldaieta’s sixth- and seventh-century cemetery. Lower water had briefly opened a window into a much older landscape.

passages.title: Evidence close to the map’s century
passages.text: At San Pelayo in Dulantzi, a sixth- or seventh-century burial preserved amber necklace beads. Their forms resemble those found at Aldaieta. Small personal ornaments help archaeologists compare communities across the region, even when the people themselves left no written biography.

passages.title: Evidence close to the map’s century
passages.text: Another San Pelayo burial retained metal fittings from a wooden bowl, alongside rounded pottery vessels. The bowl fittings resemble examples from cemeteries around the Rhine and Loire. Wood often disappears underground, while its metal parts keep a clue to the missing object’s shape.

passages.title: Food and farming in the wider medieval period
passages.text: A study of fifth- to ninth-century rural communities found that the sampled Basque-region diets relied heavily on plants, including substantial amounts of millet. Researchers investigated chemical signals in bones. These reveal broad food patterns rather than the recipe for a particular family’s supper.

passages.title: Food and farming in the wider medieval period
passages.text: The same study found no simple rule that a grander burial meant a richer diet. Even people buried in silos or wells often ate the same broad kinds of food as other community members. A grave’s location and the meals of a lifetime tell different parts of a person’s story.

passages.title: Food and farming in the wider medieval period
passages.text: At Zornoztegi and Aistra, researchers tested 50 samples of charred seeds spanning the fourth to fourteenth centuries. Wheat and barley generally grew with low or moderate water availability and little evidence of manure. The burnt seeds preserve traces of farming decisions long after the fields have changed.

passages.title: Food and farming in the wider medieval period
passages.text: The seed study also suggests that farmers may have rotated crops with legumes to replenish soil. This remains an interpretation to test with more evidence. A field could need a change of crop, just as a household needed more than one kind of food.

passages.title: Food and farming in the wider medieval period
passages.text: Medieval Zornoztegi appears as a farming village without obvious differences between family groups, while Aistra has evidence of local elites and may have collected dues. Comparing their crops helps researchers ask who grew food, who received it and how much work households invested.

passages.title: Later words, books and ships
passages.text: In 1545, Bernat Etxepare published the first printed Basque book in Bordeaux. Its fifteen poems include religious verse, love poetry and reflections on his imprisonment. The language comes from the Garazi area of Lower Navarre, giving a particular regional voice a place in print.

passages.title: Later words, books and ships
passages.text: Writing sample: “Euskara, jalgi hadi mundura” means “Euskara, go forth into the world.” The Etxepare Institute prints this as its motto, echoing the poet’s invitation to his language. This attested modern spelling is used in the Institute’s publication; Etxepare’s sixteenth-century spellings differed.

passages.title: Later words, books and ships
passages.text: Etxepare’s book used spellings such as “heuscara” for the language’s name and “beçala” for “like” or “similar to.” The sole known surviving copy is held in France’s national library. A whole literary milestone now depends on the survival of one small book.

passages.title: Later words, books and ships
passages.text: For the later Basque whaling ship San Juan, historian Selma Huxley followed documentary clues in Spanish archives before underwater archaeologists found the wreck at Red Bay in 1978. Written records and surviving ship timbers could then be studied together, connecting names on paper with the craft of shipbuilding.

passages.title: Later words, books and ships
passages.text: Basque cultural life continues through writers, filmmakers, musicians and language learning. The Etxepare Institute supports this work internationally. The map’s sixth-century endpoint is therefore a limit of this particular imported record, not the end of Basque people or their language.
Basque communities and their language continue. Their histories passed through many political institutions and borders; the map’s 600 endpoint is not a collective conquest or extinction date.

sectionTitles: A mountain in history and memory
Homes that are works of art
Music at work, at home and in healing

passages.text: Lesotho’s national story took shape around Moshoeshoe I’s mountain stronghold at Thaba Bosiu. Clay sculptures of parents, children and musicians bring everyday lives into this history alongside rulers and political events.

passages.title: A mountain in history and memory
passages.text: Thaba Bosiu became Moshoeshoe I’s political centre in 1824. Lesotho’s heritage account describes stone walls, gateways and lookout posts strengthening the plateau’s natural defences. It also records an oral tradition that the mountain grew taller at night. That story belongs to how the place was remembered and understood; it is not a measurement of a mountain changing height.

passages.title: Homes that are works of art
passages.text: Writing in 2020, artist ‘Matsooana Sekokotoana explains how Basotho women decorated homes with litema. Designs were worked into damp earth plaster, sometimes with coloured stones making a mosaic. Cow dung helped bind the mud. The wall was a surface for skilled pattern-making as well as shelter. Her account describes a practice that has become less common as building methods change.

passages.title: Homes that are works of art
passages.text: Sekokotoana also describes a ceramic plate she made using two litema designs: boliba, associated with deep water, and lihlaba, with hills or mountains. She arranged them to evoke Lesotho’s landscape. She recalls her father encouraging patience, a lesson she connected with the careful painting. Family advice and the patterns of home found another life on a plate.

passages.title: Getting dressed for the mountains
passages.text: A blanket made around 2012 and held by the British Museum combines black and turquoise with four red vertical stripes. Its feather design belongs to the Victoria England range. The catalogue identifies wool and cotton, and manufacture at Aranda’s mill in Randfontein, South Africa. An object associated with Basotho dress can also reveal production and trade across the border.

passages.title: Getting dressed for the mountains
passages.text: The museum explains that wearing blankets are wrapped around the body and secured at the shoulders, providing warmth in Lesotho’s cold mountain conditions. The familiar stripes usually run vertically when worn. A blanket can be part of getting dressed as well as going to bed. The catalogue describes a living clothing tradition with different designs, rather than one outfit worn by everyone.

passages.title: Little sculptures, everyday people
passages.text: Samuele Makoanyane, who lived from 1909 to 1944, made small clay figures of people around him. Iziko’s collection includes a woman feeding a baby and another rolling a sleeping mat. These are an artist’s representations, not photographs of every household. Their subjects put childcare and ordinary work into a museum collection alongside portraits of kings and warriors.

passages.title: Little sculptures, everyday people
passages.text: In 1935, collector Percival Kirby commissioned Makoanyane to model musicians and their instruments. Seven figures were completed, including a herdboy playing the lesiba and a woman with a drum. The exhibition lets viewers examine these fragile sculptures as digital models. Close attention to the tiny players helps preserve evidence of performance as well as the sculptor’s individual skill.

passages.title: Music at work, at home and in healing
passages.text: A lesiba combines a stick, a stretched string and a quill. Pusetso Nyabela’s 2022 museum report describes players using their breath to make the quill vibrate, rather than simply plucking a tune. Associated with shepherds, the instrument also supplied a familiar sound before Radio Lesotho’s news. Small materials can make a very distinctive voice.

passages.title: Music at work, at home and in healing
passages.text: A revival project in 2007 and 2008 found older women in Leribe who still played the lekope, with instruments hanging on their house walls. The report describes a string stretched along a reed and a player’s mouth shaping the sound. Skills that seemed to be disappearing were still present in particular homes.

passages.title: Music at work, at home and in healing
passages.text: Recordings from the late 1950s and early 1960s documented the lekope in hlophe, a ritual healing dance. Nyabela discusses music, singing, clapping and beliefs about ancestral help. These recordings preserve accounts of healing and performance; they do not test the medical effectiveness of a treatment.

passages.title: Reading, learning and remembering families
passages.text: Morija’s archives preserve Leselinyana, a newspaper first published in 1863, alongside church registers, letters, government reports and Sesotho hymnals. French, Sesotho and English all appear in the collections. Such records let researchers follow reading, music and public debate through time. A newspaper’s small notices can open questions quite different from those answered by a royal portrait.

passages.title: Reading, learning and remembering families
passages.text: The Hub at Morija opened in 2015 as a place for digital creativity. The museum describes internet access and training in photography, film, writing and information technology. It connects a town known for historical collections with new ways of making and sharing stories. Learning about the past can happen in the same community as learning to use a camera or computer.

passages.title: Reading, learning and remembering families
passages.text: David-Frédéric Ellenberger collected oral histories and genealogies from 1866 to 1905. His interview notes, letters and maps survive at Morija, and a British Library project digitised the archive. The notes offer evidence about families and remembered events, but they also reflect what a missionary asked and chose to record. Preserving a source includes understanding the viewpoint through which it was made.

passages.title: Paintings older than the kingdom
passages.text: A 2013 heritage evaluation describes Sehlabathebe’s rock paintings in shelters and overhangs: human figures, animals including eland, and colours from earthy yellow to dark red and white. These works belong to San histories that extend beyond the later story of the Basotho kingdom. Interpreting their spiritual meanings takes research; a painted animal is not automatically a literal record of a hunting trip.

British rule ended on 4 October 1966. Lesotho continues as an independent kingdom, with later changes of government forming part of its history. The map’s Basutoland and Lesotho records do not represent the extinction and replacement of three separate peoples.

sectionTitles: Who could shape the new state?
A written ideal and its limits

passages.text: The Batavian Republic replaced the old Dutch Republic in 1795 with French military support. It experimented with national representation and a centralized state before becoming the Kingdom of Holland in 1806. The atlas’s 1800 to 1815 label runs beyond the republic’s life and covers only its European outline.

passages.title: Who could shape the new state?
passages.text: The National Assembly first met in 1796 after indirect elections in 126 districts. Voters chose electors, who chose representatives. Men had to meet age and other qualifications, including limits on recent poor relief and a political declaration. Revolutionary citizenship still had gates to pass through.

passages.title: Who could shape the new state?
passages.text: The 1798 constitutional project replaced the old provincial confederation with a stronger national framework. The National Archives preserves a handsome parchment record of the referendum result. Its calligraphy and expensive material show how the new authorities made a vote into a public founding document.

passages.title: Who could shape the new state?
passages.text: Jewish campaigners in the Felix Libertate club pressed for equal citizenship. On 2 September 1796 the National Assembly formally granted Jews the same civil rights as other citizens. Religious barriers were challenged, though eligibility for political participation remained restricted.

passages.title: Who could shape the new state?
passages.text: Historian Myriam Everard traced a women’s newspaper launched in Amsterdam in 1796 through advertisements in another publication. No issues were known to her. Those notices reveal women as an audience in revolutionary political culture, even where the newspaper itself has disappeared.

passages.title: Celebrations, classrooms and useful objects
passages.text: In January 1795 people danced around a liberty tree on Amsterdam’s Dam square, renamed the Square of the Revolution. A small twig survives in the Rijksmuseum. A branch saved as a souvenir can carry evidence of a political celebration just as a grand monument can.

passages.title: Celebrations, classrooms and useful objects
passages.text: The 1801 school law made education a national concern. Municipal governments were to provide enough schools and adequately paid teachers so children could attend. This was an ambitious administrative program; a law’s promise did not mean every child instantly had an equal school experience.

passages.title: Celebrations, classrooms and useful objects
passages.text: School inspectors served on departmental education boards appointed by the national executive. Teaching was becoming something that officials could inspect and organize across regions. The surviving inspection archive lets historians follow the machinery behind a classroom reform.

passages.title: Celebrations, classrooms and useful objects
passages.text: A 1799 iron standard metre in the Rijksmuseum sits in a wooden case lined with red velvet. It has no little centimetre marks: the important thing was the exact length of the whole bar. This unusually pampered ruler helped define a shared unit of measurement.

passages.title: Celebrations, classrooms and useful objects
passages.text: A colored drawing dated September 1799 records a coastal signal mast at Scheveningen. Its semaphore communicated through visible signals before electrical telegraphs. The drawing makes military communication equipment part of the republic’s surviving material record.

passages.title: Celebrations, classrooms and useful objects
passages.text: French and Dutch troops camped near Kraantje Lek at Overveen and were also lodged with local people. Several hundred soldiers could change the rhythm of a quiet district even without a battle there. In 1803 troops from the camps were sent to nearby Zandvoort during a British bombardment.

passages.title: A written ideal and its limits
passages.text: A draft of the 1798 constitution begins “Alle menschen zijn, als menschen, aan elkander gelijk”: “All people, as people, are equal to one another.” This is Dutch from the surviving draft; the final printed constitution used different wording in Article 3. Even constitutional sentences have revision histories.

passages.title: A written ideal and its limits
passages.text: The liberty proclaimed in Europe did not automatically free enslaved people in Dutch colonies. On Curaçao in 1795, Tula drew on revolutionary ideas to demand freedom. The museum connects his resistance with the same slogans celebrated around Dutch liberty trees, exposing the unequal reach of those promises.

French pressure replaced the republic with the Kingdom of Holland under Louis Napoleon in 1806. National institutions and reform projects outlasted individual constitutions, while the inhabitants continued through another change of government. The 1815 map endpoint is not the republic’s fall date.
