passages.text: The British Raj was Crown rule in the Indian subcontinent from 1858 to 1947. The map covers only 1878 to 1938. Its outline mixes political authorities and includes Burma across changes in status, as explained below.

passages.title: Government, borders and resistance
passages.text: The viceroy and provincial governors governed through councils dominated by appointed officials. Indian participation expanded slowly, but early elected council members could advise without making the governor answerable to them. Holding a seat therefore did not mean sharing the power of an elected government.

passages.title: Government, borders and resistance
passages.text: Princely states had a different relationship to British power from directly administered provinces. A February 1947 policy draft explicitly distinguished Britain’s powers over the Indian states from the government of British India. The single colored outline hides these different political arrangements.

passages.title: Government, borders and resistance
passages.text: The map’s Burmese extension needs particular care. British forces invaded Upper Burma in 1885; annexation followed in 1886. Burma became separately administered in 1937. The imported outline already includes Upper Burma in 1878 and still includes Burma after separation, so those edges should not be treated as reliable borders for each year.

passages.title: Government, borders and resistance
passages.text: The Congress organization created in 1885 became an important forum for Indian political demands. Indians also disagreed about empire: Dadabhai Naoroji criticized British rule, while another Indian MP in London, M. M. Bhownaggree, supported the Raj. Shared origins did not produce identical political opinions.

passages.title: Government, borders and resistance
passages.text: On 13 April 1919, troops fired on an unarmed crowd at Jallianwala Bagh in Amritsar, killing hundreds. The exact total remains disputed. The massacre deeply damaged trust in British government and strengthened the independence movement. This was a turning point in relations between rulers and ruled.

passages.title: Government, borders and resistance
passages.text: In March 1930, Gandhi told the viceroy in advance that he intended to break the salt law. He announced a march to Dandi, then left Sabarmati Ashram with followers on 12 March. An ordinary substance used in food became the focus of a carefully announced challenge to colonial authority.

passages.title: Clothes, travel and everyday dignity
passages.text: Imported factory cloth put intense pressure on Indian spinning and weaving. The V&A describes unemployment and hardship as Lancashire goods displaced much handmade production. A piece of fabric could carry a long chain of work behind it: growers, spinners, weavers and sellers all depended on what customers bought.

passages.title: Clothes, travel and everyday dignity
passages.text: Gandhi urged people to spin, weave and wear khadi, cloth made from hand-spun thread. The spinning wheel appeared on a nationalist flag in 1921. Surviving Gujarat khadi dated about 1867 also reminds us that the material preceded that campaign. Political protest could begin with the clothes in someone’s cupboard.

passages.title: Clothes, travel and everyday dignity
passages.text: Gandhi’s 1917 railway account describes a Bombay-to-Madras carriage labeled for 22 passengers that held as many as 35. Travelers spent two nights without sleeping bunks; some stood or slept on a dirty floor. Railways connected distant places, but a ticket could buy a very uncomfortable journey.

passages.title: Clothes, travel and everyday dignity
passages.text: The same account says the carriage toilet went uncleaned and its water tank was empty. Gandhi asked senior officials to try third-class travel without warning the railway first. His proposed inspection had a practical sting: if important passengers needed water and a clean seat, so did everyone else.

passages.title: Families, learning and discoveries
passages.text: Anandibai Joshee, born in 1865, married as a child and later lost an infant. She described the need for better medical care as a reason to study medicine. In 1886 she graduated from Woman’s Medical College of Pennsylvania. Her story connects family experience with a determined effort to open a professional path for women.

passages.title: Families, learning and discoveries
passages.text: Studying abroad also meant negotiating food and clothing. Joshee continued wearing a sari to classes, and the college dean housed her so she could obtain familiar food. She accepted a hospital post caring for women in Kolhapur, but died in 1887 before beginning practice. Her college preserved correspondence and course records.

passages.title: Families, learning and discoveries
passages.text: Rabindranath Tagore founded a residential school at Santiniketan in 1901. Its learning included nature, music and art, with classrooms outdoors beneath trees. A university followed in 1921. Imagine looking up from a lesson and finding leaves overhead: the setting was part of an educational vision linking Indian traditions with human fellowship across cultural boundaries.

passages.title: Families, learning and discoveries
passages.text: In a 1928 scientific letter from Calcutta, C. V. Raman and K. S. Krishnan reported experiments on light scattered by dust-free liquids and gases. Alongside light of the original frequency, they detected a changed component. Tiny differences in scattered light could reveal behavior of molecules too small to watch directly.

passages.title: Families, learning and discoveries
passages.text: A Gujarati writing sample is “હિન્દ સ્વરાજ”, the title Hind Swaraj, translated as “Indian Home Rule”. Gandhi wrote the work in 1909 and translated it into English in 1910. The Gujarati spelling here comes from a modern digital edition. It preserves one influential Indian voice in a society with many languages and scripts.

passages.title: World wars, hunger and independence
passages.text: The Raj drew Indian people into distant wars. In Mesopotamia in October 1918, medical officer Heerajee Cursetjee and fellow medics treated and evacuated wounded men under fire. His medal citation recorded exhausting work across two days. Armies depended on medical skill and care as well as weapons; Indian service helped sustain Britain’s global military power.

passages.title: World wars, hunger and independence
passages.text: By August 1943, an American diplomatic report described starving villagers arriving in Calcutta and dying there. It recorded an appeal for hospitals to admit people who had collapsed and urged rice shipments if transport could be found. These documents show officials receiving urgent warnings during Bengal’s famine, while food and care failed to reach many families.

passages.title: World wars, hunger and independence
passages.text: In July 1942, Jawaharlal Nehru explained that the demand for independence required British withdrawal. He proposed a provisional government representing major groups, including Congress and the Muslim League. Such proposals show that anti-colonial politics also involved a difficult question: how would different political communities govern together after Britain left?

passages.title: World wars, hunger and independence
passages.text: Independence in August 1947 came with Partition into India and Pakistan. Millions crossed new borders, while violence devastated many communities. A contemporary officer’s account recorded Indian soldiers desperately worrying about relatives in Punjab. Political independence and family catastrophe could occur at the same time; both belong in this history.

Crown rule ended in August 1947 with independent India and Pakistan. The map’s 1938 cutoff is not the Raj’s ending. Communities, languages and cultural institutions continued through Partition’s upheaval.

sectionTitles: A small word for the stars

passages.text: Early medieval Armorica became a meeting place of local communities and migrants from Britain. Broërec was a particular region around Vannes within this wider story, not another name for the whole peninsula. The imported Broërec outline is misplaced far to the northwest; it should not be used as a reliable border.

passages.title: People crossing the Channel
passages.text: Similarities among Breton, Welsh and Cornish place names and languages support migration from Britain in the late fifth and sixth centuries. Its scale is debated: newcomers could influence existing communities without every family arriving on a boat.

passages.title: People crossing the Channel
passages.text: The council of Tours in 567 distinguished Romans and Bretons living in Armorica. That is unusually clear evidence in a period with few written records. The peninsula contained interacting communities rather than a single population with one simple origin story.

passages.title: Broërec and its neighbours
passages.text: Broërec belonged to the country around Vannes, between the Ellé and Vilaine rivers. The name is associated with Waroc. Geography mattered: this southeastern Breton region faced different neighbours and political pressures from communities at the peninsula’s western tip.

passages.title: Broërec and its neighbours
passages.text: Under Carolingian rule, Vannes, Rennes and Nantes formed parts of a frontier march. Broërec later entered the larger Breton political world. The county’s territory eventually passed into the ducal domain, while its bishopric and regional identity continued.

passages.title: Keeping a farm fed
passages.text: At Lenn Sec’h in Caudan, archaeologists uncovered a farm used during the sixth to ninth centuries. Its enclosure covered about 5,300 square metres, bounded by substantial ditches. These traces give us a household landscape beyond the better-known stories of rulers and saints.

passages.title: Keeping a farm fed
passages.text: Pits at the Caudan farm were used to dry grain before it went into underground storage. A large, deep silo also survived. Getting the harvest safely through the year required planning after the cutting and gathering were finished.

passages.title: Keeping a farm fed
passages.text: One medieval building at Caudan was constructed on ground-level timber sills. The surrounding ditches reached roughly two metres in width and depth. Most of the building itself has disappeared, but the excavated layout still reveals how the farm was organised.

passages.title: A monastery grows
passages.text: At Landévennec, excavation found a small early oratory surrounded by a cemetery. The monastery’s beginnings belong around the turn of the fifth and sixth centuries. The traditional story of Guénolé and eleven disciples is a founding legend, while the buildings provide physical evidence.

passages.title: A monastery grows
passages.text: By the ninth century, after the earlier map phases, Landévennec’s monks copied books and followed the Rule of Benedict. A religious community could also be a centre of learning and a substantial landholder. Copying a book meant sustained skilled work by hand.

passages.title: A monastery grows
passages.text: The excavated ninth-century monastery included a church, living buildings and a courtyard edged by a covered gallery. A Viking raid in 913 interrupted its flourishing life. Its long history helps connect the small early foundation with the more elaborate institutions that followed.

passages.title: A small word for the stars
passages.text: In Pierre-Yves Lambert’s reading, the Old Breton word “nimer” means “constellation”. It appears above a Latin star-name in Angers manuscript 477, folio 14b. This is the scholarly transcription of an attested word in Latin letters; another scholar interpreted it as “number”.

passages.title: A small word for the stars
passages.text: The relevant part of Angers 477 was written in 897 and contains many Breton notes beside Latin learning. Scholars identify Breton scribes but debate where they worked. The book therefore illustrates later Breton scholarship and its connections, rather than a securely located school in early Broërec.

Armorica and Broërec did not vanish when these map intervals ended. Local political structures became part of wider Breton kingdoms and the duchy. The Vannes region retained a recognisable identity through those changes.

sectionTitles: A royal book, a baby and learning
Homes, food and looking after people

passages.text: Brunei is a continuing sultanate on northern Borneo whose maritime influence once reached far beyond its present territory. This record begins in 1650, long after its emergence, and follows changing sovereignty through British protection to independence. The imported outlines barely change from 1650 to 2020, concealing major territorial losses; they cannot reconstruct the old sultanate’s reach. A different modern outline appears after 2020.

passages.title: Sovereignty, conflict and commerce
passages.text: A royal genealogy describes a civil war between Sultan Abdul Mubin and Sultan Muhyiuddin. An added manuscript note dates Muhammad Ali’s killing to 4 February 1662. The defeated faction’s wealthy families survived: political defeat did not erase an entire community.

passages.title: Sovereignty, conflict and commerce
passages.text: Brunei became a British protectorate in 1888. From 1906, a British Resident advised the sultan in most affairs, with exceptions for Malay customs and Islam. The 1959 constitution established internal self-government; a 1971 revision left defence and external affairs outside that internal independence.

passages.title: Sovereignty, conflict and commerce
passages.text: Diplomacy could arrive with a bundle of cloth. In a letter of 15 July 1820, Singapore official William Farquhar acknowledged 100 katis of wax from Pengiran Muda Muhammad Alam and sent patterned cotton and handkerchief cloth in return. Named ship captains carried both goods and correspondence between the courts and ports.

passages.title: Sovereignty, conflict and commerce
passages.text: War interrupted these longer histories. Allied forces landed around Brunei Bay on 10 June 1945 and took Brunei town from Japanese occupation. Their advance continued toward Seria’s oilfields. Engineers extinguished burning wells and repaired damaged roads and bridges, practical work needed after the fighting.

passages.title: Sovereignty, conflict and commerce
passages.text: An armed uprising began on 8 December 1962. The sultan requested British help, and troops secured government buildings, communications and oil installations while suppressing the revolt. This crisis belongs to the contested politics of decolonisation, before Brunei’s later full independence.

passages.title: Objects that reveal wider connections
passages.text: The Brunei shipwreck offers an earlier glimpse of maritime commerce. Dating to the late fifteenth century, before this map record begins, it held Chinese blue-and-white ceramics and jars from China, Thailand and Vietnam. Glass bracelets, bronze gongs, metal ingots and cooking pots travelled alongside the fashionable tableware.

passages.title: Objects that reveal wider connections
passages.text: Recovering that cargo was a large underwater investigation. After a 1997 survey, archaeologists excavated for three months in 1998 at about 65 metres depth. They recorded roughly 14,000 significant objects. A broken cooking pot can be as useful to this history as a beautiful vase: both were part of the shipment.

passages.title: Objects that reveal wider connections
passages.text: Commercial oil was found at Seria in 1929. The first well, S-1, became an industrial landmark; a monument built nearby in 1991 commemorated the field’s billionth barrel. Brunei’s material history includes drilling equipment and petroleum infrastructure as well as royal buildings and old ceramics.

passages.title: A royal book, a baby and learning
passages.text: A Malay royal genealogy copied probably in the 1820s uses Jawi, an Arabic-derived script. Gallop quotes its opening in Roman transliteration: “Bahwa inilah silsilah segala raja2”, meaning “This is the genealogy of the rulers”. The numeral 2 marks a repeated word. This is an editor’s transliteration, not a facsimile of the handwriting.

passages.title: A royal book, a baby and learning
passages.text: The same manuscript also became a family notebook. Its final birth notice records Abdul Rajad on 22 January 1831, after an earlier draft gave another date. Protective writings for children’s crying and convulsions appear nearby. They preserve parental worries and historical beliefs, not evidence that the charms cured illness.

passages.title: A royal book, a baby and learning
passages.text: Brunei’s modern school system expanded in several languages. A Malay-medium primary school opened in 1912, a Chinese school in 1916, and a nongovernment English primary school at Seria in 1931. The ministry records 32 primary schools by 1941. These dates concern school institutions, not the beginning of religious or family learning.

passages.title: A royal book, a baby and learning
passages.text: Secondary schooling came later: the first English-medium secondary school opened in 1953, with Malay-medium secondary education following in 1966. The inclusive education policy introduced in 1997 supported pupils with special educational needs in mainstream classrooms through collaboration with specialist teachers.

passages.title: Homes, food and looking after people
passages.text: A royal letter from 28 April 1822 reports a severe epidemic. The sultan apologised that requested weights and measures were below standard because the town was suffering. The letter links illness with interrupted skilled work and overseas exchange; it does not identify the disease well enough for a confident modern diagnosis.

passages.title: Homes, food and looking after people
passages.text: Living over water still requires plumbing. A Kampong Ayer pilot housing project completed in 2012 included sewage treatment, a pumping station toward Sungai Kebun, water pipes and firefighting equipment. Its roofed bridges and leisure platforms connected homes and shared spaces. These improvements belong to a named project, not every historic water-village house.

passages.title: Homes, food and looking after people
passages.text: The same new houses used concrete floors and columns with flame-retardant wooden walls. That combination kept wood in the home while addressing fire and structural safety. Kampong Ayer’s built heritage is continually adapted for the people living there, rather than consisting only of buildings preserved unchanged.

passages.title: Homes, food and looking after people
passages.text: Today’s ambuyat begins with starch from the inside of a sago palm and water. Its sticky texture is twirled onto candas, paired bamboo sticks joined at one end, then dipped in sour, spicy cacah. Dinner gives the chopsticks a workout. This is a documented living food tradition, not a dated seventeenth-century menu.

passages.title: Homes, food and looking after people
passages.text: Food also marks family celebrations. Brunei Tourism describes kelupis, glutinous-rice parcels wrapped in nyirik leaves, as refreshments at Bisaya weddings and special occasions. Some versions include dried shrimp or anchovies. The leaf is part of the packaging, making each portion a small edible present once unwrapped.

Brunei did not disappear when its territory contracted or British protection ended. It became fully independent on 1 January 1984 and assumed responsibility for its own defence. The sultanate continues; 1650 is merely this map record’s starting point, not its foundation date.

sectionTitles: Learning, numbers and a letter about triangles
Railways and vegetables with longer journeys

passages.text: Brunswick, or Braunschweig, was a northern German duchy ruled by the Welf family, earlier commonly called Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel. This record covers 1783 to 1878, including the interruption of ducal rule under Napoleon’s Kingdom of Westphalia from 1807 to 1813. Its imported outline is seriously incomplete: it shows southern pieces while omitting the capital, Braunschweig, and the northern core. The narrative describes the historical duchy, whose monarchy survived until 1918.

passages.title: Rulers and a restless capital
passages.text: In 1830 angry townspeople drove Duke Karl II from Braunschweig and set his palace on fire. The replacement residence was a nineteenth-century building, not the same palace restored unchanged. The palace museum preserves a history in which relations between ruler and residents could become a crisis in the streets.

passages.title: Rulers and a restless capital
passages.text: The constitution issued on 12 October 1832 kept hereditary monarchy but established a representative chamber. The State Archives preserve a large file of drafts, additions and discussions from its preparation. A constitution emerged through argument and revision; the surviving paperwork lets historians examine that process instead of relying only on a duke’s portrait.

passages.title: Learning, numbers and a letter about triangles
passages.text: In 1835 the Collegium Carolinum divided teaching into technical, commercial and humanistic departments. The commercial course prepared future merchants, while the humanistic section helped students prepare for university. A school serving a small state could connect literary education with the practical needs of business and engineering.

passages.title: Learning, numbers and a letter about triangles
passages.text: The institution became a polytechnic school in 1862. Applicants had to be at least sixteen and demonstrate adequate knowledge before enrolling. Subjects included engineering, mechanical construction, chemical technology, pharmacy and forestry. Some specialized courses later closed when they proved uneconomic, so even an ambitious technical school had to balance its plans against its resources.

passages.title: Learning, numbers and a letter about triangles
passages.text: The duke supported Carl Friedrich Gauss with a scholarship that continued after his return to Braunschweig in 1798. In 1801 Gauss’s calculations helped astronomers find Ceres again after observations of the small planet had been interrupted. His work joined abstract mathematics with the practical problem of knowing where to point a telescope.

passages.title: Learning, numbers and a letter about triangles
passages.text: Writing sample: in a letter sent from Braunschweig to Wilhelm Olbers on 8 April 1803, Gauss hoped “einst das ganze Land mit einem Dreiecksnetz zu beziehen,” meaning “one day to cover the whole country with a network of triangles.” This German sentence, transcribed in the university library’s catalog, describes his plan to map the land through measured angles and connected survey points.

passages.title: Railways and vegetables with longer journeys
passages.text: A state railway linked Braunschweig and Wolfenbüttel in 1838. When agreement with neighboring states over joint planning proved difficult, the duchy built its own line. Railway workshops and manufacturers followed. Trains needed more than rails: repairs, machines and eventually signaling equipment helped create work around the new transport system.

passages.title: Railways and vegetables with longer journeys
passages.text: Sugar-beet cultivation expanded around 1850, supplying factories in the surrounding countryside. By the 1870s Braunschweig had a school for the sugar industry. Making sugar involved farming, machinery and technical learning as well as boiling something sweet. Local machine builders adapted their work to the needs of sugar processing.

passages.title: Railways and vegetables with longer journeys
passages.text: Asparagus was difficult to ship fresh over long distances. Around 1850, preserving it in tins helped growers sell it beyond its short harvest season, and local cultivation expanded. A vegetable that had to be eaten quickly could now wait on a shelf. Braunschweig’s fields and canning businesses grew together.

passages.title: Water, crowded homes and toilets
passages.text: An older water system brought spring water into Braunschweig through wooden pipes, following the slope of the ground. It supplied public fountains on market squares and remained in use into the nineteenth century, until the new central waterworks took over in 1865. Water infrastructure could be centuries old while still serving everyday needs.

passages.title: Water, crowded homes and toilets
passages.text: The new waterworks entered full operation on 1 January 1865. It treated Oker river water in settling and filter basins, then used steam pumps to send it into a cast-iron network. Industrial wastewater had helped make the old arrangements inadequate. Growing industry created jobs and also forced the city to rethink its water supply.

passages.title: Water, crowded homes and toilets
passages.text: The waterworks’ 54-metre tower, roughly 177 feet, resembled a Gothic church tower. Inside, it concealed a chimney and tall water pipes that helped balance pressure when pumping changed. The impressive exterior housed a very practical job: making the flow in the pipes steadier.

passages.title: Water, crowded homes and toilets
passages.text: A report from the second half of the nineteenth century describes severe crowding in the Klint neighborhood, a date range that may extend beyond this map’s 1878 cutoff. In some buildings twenty to thirty people shared one toilet, and cesspits stood near water outlets. These were documented conditions in a poor district, not the arrangements of every home in the duchy.

The revolution of 8 November 1918 ended ducal rule and Brunswick became a Free State. Some institutions continued: the regional court kept working under its new republican name without an immediate replacement of its staff. The imported cutoff at 1878 therefore predates the monarchy’s actual end by forty years.

passages.text: Buganda grew around the Kabaka, chiefs and clans in the Lake Victoria region. Its history can also be read in barkcloth workshops, the wooden architecture of Kasubi and recordings of court musicians. Royal government changed under colonial rule and was later abolished; Baganda cultural life and a restored royal institution continue.

passages.title: Buildings that preserve knowledge
passages.text: Kasubi's palace became a royal burial ground in 1884. The main building, Muzibu Azaala Mpanga, used a circular plan, a domed thatched roof and wooden supports. Monumental architecture here depended on skilled work with plant materials, rather than masonry.

passages.title: Buildings that preserve knowledge
passages.text: The documented interior combined palm-frond structural rings with long poles wrapped in barkcloth. A drum house and gatehouse faced the courtyard. These details connect construction, textile work and ceremonial movement within one royal compound.

passages.title: Buildings that preserve knowledge
passages.text: After the destructive 2010 fire, restoration drew on surviving building knowledge as well as documentation. Kasubi left UNESCO's danger list in 2023. Conservation work announced in 2026 addresses disaster preparation, site management and community participation.

passages.title: Barkcloth and household work
passages.text: Craftspeople harvest the Mutuba tree's inner bark in the wet season and beat it with wooden mallets. Working under an open shed keeps it from drying too quickly. Repeated skilled handling produces a soft sheet from bark, without weaving threads.

passages.title: Barkcloth and household work
passages.text: Barkcloth served as bedding, curtains, storage material and clothing as well as ceremonial dress. Its household uses place the craft within ordinary work and comfort, alongside the royal and funerary settings in which it remains especially visible.

passages.title: Barkcloth and household work
passages.text: UNESCO identifies Ngonge clan craftspeople and a hereditary chief craftsman as custodians of this knowledge. Imported cotton reduced demand during the nineteenth century. Continued ceremonial use and later promotion helped sustain skills through a changing textile economy.

passages.title: Listening to musicians across generations
passages.text: The 2021 album Buganda Royal Music Revival places archival sessions beside recordings made in 2017. Its credits name recordists and dates, allowing listeners to distinguish historical documentation from later performances rather than treating all tracks as one ancient sound.

passages.title: Listening to musicians across generations
passages.text: The collection includes the endongo lyre, the large akadinda xylophone and an entenga ensemble of tuned drums. These are different approaches to melody, resonance and ensemble coordination, not interchangeable examples of drumming.

passages.title: Listening to musicians across generations
passages.text: Performers credited include lyre player Albert Bisaso Ssempeke and royal harpist Temutewo Mukasa. Naming musicians preserves individual artistic work within a court tradition too often described only through kings and ceremonies.

passages.title: Councils and changing authority
passages.text: The Lukiiko developed from advisory councils of chiefs and clan heads. Its organization changed during the nineteenth century and under the 1900 agreement. Its present cultural and consultative role should not be projected unchanged onto earlier royal government.

passages.title: Councils and changing authority
passages.text: Article 118 of Uganda's 1967 constitution explicitly abolished royal offices. For Buganda it made that provision effective from 24 May 1966. This distinction explains why histories mention both years when describing the suppression of the kingdom.

Buganda's royal political institutions were suppressed during the 1966 crisis and the constitutional changes of 1967. Their restoration in 1993 established a cultural role within Uganda. Baganda communities, crafts and music continued across that interruption; the map's final snapshot is not their disappearance.

passages.text: Bukhara’s state linked oasis towns, irrigated farms and caravan routes in Central Asia. The map’s “Bukara” entry covers 1530 to 1600, during Shaybanid rule; “Bokhara” covers 1878 to 1900, during the Manghit emirate under Russian protection. They represent different phases, not one unchanging dynasty. Both imported outlines miss Bukhara city: the earlier one lies too far east, the later one too far south. Their dates are map coverage, not the state’s lifetime.

passages.title: Work, trade and water
passages.text: Property records from the mid-sixteenth-century Molla Amiri Mosque quarter name grocers, a shoemaker, a grain broker, a bath attendant and a cart driver. They bring ordinary occupations into view beside rulers: a neighborhood needed shoes repaired and grain delivered as well as government.

passages.title: Work, trade and water
passages.text: The same neighborhood included streets named for mats and rope-makers. These occupational clues come from documents about people and property, rather than a modern reconstruction of a perfect bazaar. Shops and workshops were part of the city’s residential fabric.

passages.title: Work, trade and water
passages.text: Water helped organize Bukhara’s geography. Districts followed major canals, while smaller quarters were commonly associated with a mosque and a communal reservoir; one reservoir could serve several quarters. A water source was therefore a shared neighborhood responsibility, not simply a private household possession.

passages.title: Work, trade and water
passages.text: In 1585 Abdullah Khan’s delegation to the Mughal emperor Akbar brought horses, camels, garments and prized pigeons, together with a specialist pigeon-handler. Diplomacy also advertised valuable goods. Even a bird could travel with its own expert companion.

passages.title: Work, trade and water
passages.text: Bukhara’s covered commercial buildings included Taki Sarafon, the Dome of the Moneychangers, and Taki Tilpak Furushan, associated with headgear sellers. Their names preserve different kinds of commercial work. The historic city was a network of markets, routes and monumental crossroads, not just a collection of royal buildings.

passages.title: Work, trade and water
passages.text: For 1848, the heritage evaluation records thirty-eight caravanserais and sixteen public baths in Bukhara, alongside bazaars and trading arcades. Visitors needed lodging, and urban residents had institutions for washing. These counts describe that nineteenth-century city, not every settlement or every earlier century.

passages.title: Learning and public institutions
passages.text: Under the Manghit rulers, Bukhara attracted students from across Central Asia. Historical estimates count roughly ten thousand students among its many madrasas, though the number of institutions varies by source. Islamic learning gave the city influence beyond the territory its amirs directly controlled.

passages.title: Learning and public institutions
passages.text: The wealthy Juybari family endowed schools, mosques, canals, bridges and caravanserais. Surviving purchase records and endowment deeds show property income being assigned to maintain institutions and pay their employees. Buildings needed continuing revenue: a splendid opening ceremony could not fund centuries of repairs by itself.

passages.title: Learning and public institutions
passages.text: Ay Padshah Bibi’s name and seal appear on endowment deeds. In 1671 she provided madrasas and a water tank on the street of Abd al-Aziz Khan’s mosque. The written record preserves a woman’s substantial public patronage even where the buildings themselves have disappeared.

passages.title: Learning and public institutions
passages.text: In the sixteenth-century Bukhara book workshop of Abd al-Aziz Khan, the calligrapher Mir Hosayn Kolangi worked with other scribes. He helped copy four works by Jami in 1548 to 1549; that manuscript is now Chester Beatty Per 213. A finished book could be a coordinated team achievement.

passages.title: Family work, money and change
passages.text: An early nineteenth-century embroidered cover at the Metropolitan Museum is attributed to Bukhara. Such suzanis decorated homes and formed part of a bride’s dowry. The museum’s example has silk embroidery on linen, with bold flowers along its border and more delicate curling stems inside.

passages.title: Family work, money and change
passages.text: The museum describes a usual suzani technique: a specialist drew a design across loosely joined strips, which were separated for the bride’s relatives to embroider and then sewn together again. Slight mismatches at the seams could reveal shared handiwork. Family teamwork did not always produce perfect alignment.

passages.title: Family work, money and change
passages.text: A gold coin struck for Nasr Allah at Bukhara in the Islamic year 1257 weighs 4.55 grams in Charles Torrey’s catalogue. Its border includes an interlaced dotted design. The date, mint inscription and measured metal turn a tiny object into evidence for nineteenth-century monetary production.

passages.title: Family work, money and change
passages.text: In the later emirate, promises of reform did not necessarily bring reform. Alim Khan announced changes against corruption and in education but generally followed conservative policies. Young Bukharan reformers challenged the regime. Debates about schools were part of a larger struggle over who could change public life.

passages.title: Family work, money and change
passages.text: After losing his throne, Alim Khan wrote a Persian account of Bukhara’s suffering. Its text is dated 1921, but the surviving edition includes a map with information after 1925. A former ruler’s memoir is valuable evidence of his perspective; it is not a neutral account of everyone’s experience.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: “ضرب بخارا” means “struck at Bukhara.” This short mint phrase is printed in Torrey’s transcription of Nasr Allah’s gold coin dated AH 1257, from the nineteenth-century emirate. It uses the Arabic script employed for Persian. Here writing identified where money was made, rather than telling a long royal story.

The emirate survived the map’s 1900 endpoint. The Red Army overthrew Alim Khan in September 1920, ending Manghit rule; he went into exile. A new Bukharan republic replaced the monarchy. The city’s inhabitants, languages, religious traditions and crafts continued through profound political change.

passages.text: These map labels span several phases: Bulgars on the Black Sea steppe, a Danube state formed among Slavic and other communities, and medieval Bulgarian kingdoms. They do not describe one unchanging population. Volga Bulgaria followed a separate history. Later Balkan art and books belong to the explicitly dated periods below.

passages.title: A state takes shape
passages.text: The early-eighth-century Madara Rider shows a horseman above a fallen lion on a high rock face. Its setting made a ruler's image part of the landscape. It is a royal monument, not evidence that villagers routinely went lion hunting.

passages.title: A state takes shape
passages.text: Inscriptions beside the rider record events associated with rulers including Tervel and Omurtag. Text and image together provide evidence for early Bulgarian political memory; the cliff is more than a giant picture frame.

passages.title: A state takes shape
passages.text: Boris I's adoption of Christianity in the 860s transformed official religious institutions. It did not instantly replace every household practice or erase the older histories of the people living in the state.

passages.title: Pots, work and getting dressed
passages.text: Early Bulgar cemeteries at Balchik, Novi Pazar, Kyulevcha and Topola contained ceramic jugs, bowls and other table vessels. Scholars compare their shapes with metal, glass and wooden examples from wider Eurasian traditions. Similar shape alone does not prove a pot was imported.

passages.title: Pots, work and getting dressed
passages.text: Four pottery kilns at the early medieval settlement of Topola demonstrate production, not just consumption. The study associates these vessel traditions especially with the first half and middle of the 700s. Someone had to make the dishes before anyone could argue about washing them.

passages.title: Pots, work and getting dressed
passages.text: Preslav excavations recovered agricultural and craft tools alongside pots, cups, bowls and amphoras. These ordinary objects connect the capital to food production and skilled work, rather than only to the activities of its rulers.

passages.title: Pots, work and getting dressed
passages.text: The Preslav museum distinguishes locally produced pottery from vessels imported from Byzantium. A household could use objects with different production histories; an imported container does not by itself tell us who lived in the house.

passages.title: Pots, work and getting dressed
passages.text: Earrings, bracelets and rings at Preslav include copper, bronze and silver examples, with glass, amber and other materials also represented. Dressing up had a much wider material range than gold treasure alone suggests.

passages.title: Pots, work and getting dressed
passages.text: A gold ring found at Pliska has a split and thinned ends that may reflect resizing. Its human portrait cannot be securely named. The wear and adjustments suggest an object with a history of use, not simply an untouched badge of a famous king.

passages.title: Artists, hosts and readers
passages.text: At Patleina near Preslav, excavations in 1909 found fragments of a tenth-century ceramic portrait of St Theodore. Its large face was assembled from square tiles about 12 centimetres across: a carefully planned image made from separate fired pieces.

passages.title: Artists, hosts and readers
passages.text: Monastic workshops around Preslav made painted tiles for churches and palaces. The saint portrait uses dark outlines, coloured slips and glaze. Archaeological workshop discoveries support local production, rather than assuming that every impressive object came from Byzantium.

passages.title: Artists, hosts and readers
passages.text: Early Bulgarian inscriptions describe elite gifts and feasting. A recent study interprets these occasions as ways to display rank and strengthen personal ties. Royal hospitality was political work; it is not a menu for the average family.

passages.title: Artists, hosts and readers
passages.text: In 1355-1356 the monk Simeon copied a lavish Gospel book for Tsar Ivan Alexander. Its parchment pages carry Slavonic text in Cyrillic. The manuscript's named scribe gives us a specific person behind the broad label “medieval learning.”

passages.title: Artists, hosts and readers
passages.text: The same book uses gold for chapter titles in its margins and red for directions used in worship. Colour helped readers navigate the text. These are features of an expensive royal commission, not evidence that every household owned illustrated books.

passages.title: Artists, hosts and readers
passages.text: A royal family portrait opens the Gospel book, while a word puzzle on folio 273v encodes Ivan Alexander's name. A medieval book could combine sacred reading, family image-making and an elaborate puzzle.

passages.title: A short written sample
passages.text: Κανα συβιγι Ωμουρταγ is the ruler's title and name, conventionally rendered “Kan sybigi Omurtag.” It begins a ninth-century Greek funerary inscription for Turdatzis on limestone. The sample follows the scholarly transcription, joining a line break. The title is Bulgar vocabulary written in Greek letters, not modern Bulgarian.

passages.title: A short written sample
passages.text: The inscriptions studied by Matilde Casas Olea preserve forms of ninth-century everyday Greek rather than only polished literary language. They show how Bulgarian rulers used a neighbouring written language in their new Balkan setting.

Byzantine conquest ended the first Bulgarian kingdom in 1018. Renewed Bulgarian rule emerged in the 1180s, and Ottoman conquest ended the later medieval kingdoms in the late 1300s. Bulgarian communities, religious life and literary traditions continued. Neither the map's 1000 change of label nor its 1400 boundary is a disappearance of a people.

passages.text: This record covers modern Bulgaria from the state established in 1878 through monarchy, communist government and parliamentary democracy. It is distinct from the medieval Bulgar labels. Buildings, scientific work and living community traditions show how political change intersected with education, food and daily life.

passages.title: Institutions and difficult changes
passages.text: The Tarnovo Constitution of 1879 set the framework for Bulgaria's early parliamentary institutions. Its operation was interrupted during authoritarian periods, so the existence of a constitution did not mean uninterrupted democratic government.

passages.title: Institutions and difficult changes
passages.text: The National Assembly building, designed by Constantin Jovanovic and constructed in 1884-1886, made the new institutions physically visible in Sofia. Its neo-Renaissance design belongs to a wider European architectural conversation.

passages.title: Institutions and difficult changes
passages.text: Bulgaria and Eastern Rumelia united in 1885; Ferdinand declared independence in 1908. These were separate steps, which is why the map's 1878 beginning should not be read as the date when every question of sovereignty was settled.

passages.title: Institutions and difficult changes
passages.text: In March 1943, Bulgarian authorities deported more than 11,000 Jews from occupied Macedonia, Thrace and Pirot into German custody; almost all were murdered at Treblinka. This responsibility is part of the country's wartime history.

passages.title: Institutions and difficult changes
passages.text: Public and political protests helped stop deportations from Bulgaria's core provinces, but Jews there still endured discriminatory laws, forced labour, dispossession and internal expulsion. Survival and persecution must both be remembered.

passages.title: Institutions and difficult changes
passages.text: After the Second World War, the communist government nationalized businesses and forced farmland into cooperatives. Changes of ownership and work reached into family routines, rather than remaining only a story about leaders.

passages.title: Learning and celebrating together
passages.text: Chitalishta are community cultural centres, first established in 1856, before modern statehood. Communities created places for learning and cultural activities; older members continue to pass knowledge and skills to younger participants.

passages.title: Learning and celebrating together
passages.text: These centres organize performances, celebrations, exhibitions and local documentation. Their collaboration with schools joins formal lessons with skills learned by doing. Learning continues outside the classroom through community activities.

passages.title: Learning and celebrating together
passages.text: For the beginning of March, people exchange and wear red-and-white thread ornaments associated with wishes for a safe spring. The tradition is shared across several neighbouring countries, not exclusively Bulgarian.

passages.title: Learning and celebrating together
passages.text: A first blossom, swallow or stork can signal that it is time to remove the thread. Families, teachers and craftworkers pass on the making skills. Nature gets a say in the calendar: the stork does not need a smartphone reminder.

passages.title: Food, science and washing
passages.text: Stamen Grigorov investigated the microbes in Bulgarian yogurt in 1905. The achievement was explaining fermentation already practiced by food makers, not inventing yogurt from nothing.

passages.title: Food, science and washing
passages.text: The Serdica dairy in Sofia introduced mechanized pasteurization for industrial yogurt production in 1960. The producer's history describes earlier cauldrons, starter cultures and reusable containers, connecting laboratory knowledge with the practical work of feeding people.

passages.title: Food, science and washing
passages.text: Sofia's Central Mineral Baths were built in 1906-1913, with colourful majolica decoration. Their architects treated a place for washing as an important civic building. The former bath now houses the regional history museum: the building itself is one of its historical objects.

passages.title: A small sample of Bulgarian
passages.text: България е република с парламентарно управление. This means “Bulgaria is a republic with a parliamentary form of government.” It is Article 1(1) of the 1991 Constitution, written in modern Bulgarian using Cyrillic, not a medieval inscription.

Bulgaria continues as a sovereign parliamentary republic. The monarchy's end in 1946 and the transition from communist rule beginning in 1989 were changes of government, not the disappearance of the country. It joined the European Union in 2007.

passages.text: Bundelkhand is a central Indian region with several states and communities, rather than one continuous kingdom. Around 1800, Bundela rulers and Maratha interests faced expanding East India Company power. The atlas shows 1800 to 1815, but its outline is misplaced: it excludes Jhansi, Orchha, Banda, Panna and Khajuraho while reaching Kolkata and Dhaka. It must not be read as Bundelkhand’s historical border. This card follows the named region; earlier Chandela and Bundela achievements and later community evidence are clearly dated.

passages.title: Several centers of power
passages.text: The Chandelas of medieval Khajuraho and the later Bundelas of Orchha were different ruling lineages. Orchha became a Bundela capital in the sixteenth century and remained a capital until 1783. Its palaces already had long histories when this atlas window begins; the region was not newly founded in 1800.

passages.title: Several centers of power
passages.text: Chhatrasal’s rebellion against Mughal authority began in 1671. His alliance with the Marathas helped reshape Bundelkhand’s politics, and Maratha interests expanded during the eighteenth century. Royal families and local chiefs retained different positions within this changing landscape. A regional name cannot tell us that every town obeyed one ruler.

passages.title: Several centers of power
passages.text: British control arrived through separate agreements and military operations. Kalpi passed to the British in 1806, while Kalinjar fort was occupied in 1812. These were changes affecting particular places, not a single moment when all Bundelkhand was conquered. Banda became the headquarters of a southern Bundelkhand district in 1819, after this map interval.

passages.title: Several centers of power
passages.text: A surviving 23-page handwritten account is titled Memoir on the Situation of Bundelcund in 1803. It includes royal family trees and annual revenue statements. Alexander Gerard presented it in 1828, but had not been in India in 1803. The archive therefore identifies it as a retrospective history, not his eyewitness diary.

passages.title: Palaces, pictures and reading
passages.text: Orchha’s Raja Mahal, Jahangir Mahal and Rani Mahal use square plans divided around open courtyards. Higher pavilions rise around these spaces. Gardens combined Mughal-style divisions, fort gardens and sacred groves with water management. Builders arranged views from above and open spaces below: the courtyards were as important to the design as the walls.

passages.title: Palaces, pictures and reading
passages.text: A small painted page now at LACMA shows Krishna and Radha meeting. Dated 1634, its image measures about 11 by 14 centimeters and uses opaque watercolor, gold and ink on paper. The museum cautiously attributes it to Orchha with a question mark. It illustrates poetry about relationships, rather than documenting an ordinary couple’s home.

passages.title: Palaces, pictures and reading
passages.text: Keshav Das’s Rasikapriya was composed in 1591 as a guide to poetry and feelings. A manuscript catalogued in 1899 preserves an eighteenth-century copy on European paper bearing a J. Whatman watermark. Books could carry ideas across generations, while even the paper records a connection beyond the local court.

passages.title: Palaces, pictures and reading
passages.text: A short language sample is the title “रसिकप्रिया” (Rasikapriyā), translated by the Smithsonian as “Connoisseur’s Delights.” The work dates to 1591 and belongs to Braj literary culture. The Devanagari spelling shown here is the modern transcription printed by IGNCA, not a claim to reproduce the handwriting of a surviving sixteenth-century page.

passages.title: Water, food and shared work
passages.text: Traditional haveli farming could turn the same land into a shallow reservoir during the monsoon and a field afterward. Earthen banks held runoff; after the rains, water was released and crops grew in the moist soil. A 2022 research account traces this system back several centuries. A field could temporarily become a pond without ceasing to be a farm.

passages.title: Water, food and shared work
passages.text: Keeping a haveli working required neighbors to repair banks and outlets and agree when water should be released. Water draining from one area could irrigate fields farther downhill. The study’s modern photographs show wheat on a drained reservoir bed. Food production depended on shared timing as well as individual effort.

passages.title: Water, food and shared work
passages.text: Bundela reservoirs could include broad stairways down to the water and adjoining orchards. A 2014 national disaster-management study describes these elaborate tanks alongside simpler ponds and embankments. Waterworks served agriculture and displayed royal power, but they also needed continuing labor and money for maintenance.

passages.title: Water, food and shared work
passages.text: IGNCA’s modern cultural account lists foods such as bara and fara and describes making little figures for festivals. It also records children’s games including marbles, gilli-danda and kabaddi. These are examples of remembered regional life, not a fixed menu or timetable for every child in 1800. Play did not require a palace full of toys.

passages.title: Families, care and later changes
passages.text: A much later account reproduced in the 2014 drought study describes women fetching water while also cooking, farming and tending livestock. Girls sometimes cared for younger siblings while mothers searched for water, or spent hours fetching it themselves. Water shortages could therefore take time from both school and play. This describes modern conditions, not a measured household survey from 1800.

passages.title: Families, care and later changes
passages.text: In Tikamgarh villages, research conducted from July 2011 to June 2012 recorded farmers’ and healers’ use of 41 plant species in livestock healthcare. The researcher interviewed knowledgeable elders, collected plants and preserved identified specimens. This documents care for animals and the transmission of practical knowledge; it neither establishes which remedies work nor proves that the same practices existed in 1800.

passages.title: Families, care and later changes
passages.text: A modern Orchha homestay project reports two houses with composting toilets and another household, which keeps buffaloes, with a toilet linked to a biogas digester. The gas is used for cooking. Bathwater passes through a sand filter before irrigation. These are documented recent experiments in handling waste, not toilets reconstructed for the Bundela palaces.

passages.title: Families, care and later changes
passages.text: The region’s political changes continued after 1815. In 1817 the Peshwa ceded his claims in British Bundelkhand; further annexations followed at different dates. Directly administered districts and princely states developed different relationships with colonial power. Bundelkhand’s communities and regional identity did not disappear when a treaty changed who collected revenue or claimed authority.

The atlas’s 1815 endpoint is not a fall date. Maratha claims, individual princely states and British districts changed separately. Bundelkhand continued as a region, and Orchha remains a living town whose residents help maintain its monuments. Political sovereignty changed; communities, buildings and cultural practices carried on.

passages.text: Bunyoro in western Uganda connected royal institutions with farming, exchange and specialist production. At Kibiro, pottery and living salt-working practices reveal a history beyond royal genealogies. British conquest reshaped the kingdom; later abolition and cultural restoration of the monarchy are separate from the continuing lives of Banyoro communities.

passages.title: What Kibiro's archaeology reveals
passages.text: Excavations at Kibiro on Lake Albert uncovered abundant pottery associated with a salt-producing settlement. In his 1991 report, Graham Connah placed the origins of this important economic center early in the second millennium CE. This is evidence about a settlement and livelihood, not a secure founding date for Bunyoro.

passages.title: What Kibiro's archaeology reveals
passages.text: Many Kibiro pots carried patterns impressed with roulettes, including carved rollers. Connah interpreted these as connections toward the upper Nile or regions farther west. Similar decoration supports comparison and contact; it does not by itself identify the makers' language or ethnicity.

passages.title: What Kibiro's archaeology reveals
passages.text: Uganda's heritage submission identifies pottery used in leaching and boiling salt. Broken vessels therefore preserve traces of an industrial process as well as decorative choices. Its broad dates are less precise than a dated excavation context and should be used cautiously.

passages.title: Women's work and salt-making skill
passages.text: At Kibiro, workers spread and recycle earth over salt gardens so saline water rises into it. They collect the salty material, leach it and boil the resulting liquid to crystallize salt. The sequence combines knowledge of soil, water and heat.

passages.title: Women's work and salt-making skill
passages.text: Women carry out the salt work and inherit rights to garden plots through female relationships. These arrangements tie expertise to access to a productive place. Fishing complements salt production in the lakeshore economy.

passages.title: Women's work and salt-making skill
passages.text: Kibiro was proposed on Uganda's World Heritage Tentative List in 2025. That proposal documents a living workplace, not simply an abandoned ruin. Tentative status is distinct from inscription on the World Heritage List.

passages.title: Names, meals and social ties
passages.text: Empaako is an additional name used among Banyoro and neighboring communities. Addressing someone by this name can express affection and respect or ease tension. It identifies a relationship between people rather than merely distinguishing one individual from another.

passages.title: Names, meals and social ties
passages.text: In UNESCO's documented naming ceremony, paternal aunts consider the child's resemblance to relatives and the clan head announces the name. A meal of millet and smoked beef, gifts and a planted tree follow. Household ritual joins kinship with food and obligations of care.

passages.title: Names, meals and social ties
passages.text: The tradition entered UNESCO's Urgent Safeguarding List in 2013 because transmission and use of its associated language were weakening. Recognition concerns support for a living practice; it does not mean that the community or naming tradition had ended.

passages.title: Political change and its consequences
passages.text: The British-Buganda coalition defeated and deported Kabarega in 1899. Colonial incorporation and the transfer of territory changed the scale and authority of Bunyoro. These events concerned a political kingdom whose people and dynasty continued afterward.

passages.title: Political change and its consequences
passages.text: Historian G. N. Uzoigwe interprets Bunyoro's contraction through interacting causes: decisions by rulers, disease affecting people and animals, and violent British conquest. This is a historical argument about a long crisis, not evidence for one battle explaining every loss.

passages.title: Political change and its consequences
passages.text: In the 1964 referendum, voters in Buyaga and Bugangaizi chose a return to Bunyoro after their earlier transfer to Buganda under colonial rule. The vote shows that territorial change also involved local political choices, not only decisions made at royal courts.

Conquest in the late nineteenth century ended Bunyoro's independent political power. Uganda abolished kingship in 1967, and the monarchy returned with cultural functions in 1994. Banyoro communities and practices continued through those changes. Neither the salt village's age nor the map's last snapshot establishes a single lifetime for the kingdom.

sectionTitles: A lakeside community around the year 1000
Royal women and a growing monastery

passages.text: This map label fits the kingdom of Burgundy and Arles, linking the Rhône valley with lands around western Switzerland and Alpine passes. It is distinct from the duchy centred on Dijon. The imported outline is approximate and continues long after the independent royal dynasty ended.

passages.title: Ruling a country of routes
passages.text: Control of Alpine passes made Burgundy valuable to emperors travelling toward Italy. Royal estates lay among counties, while bishops received political powers. The kingdom was held together through relationships, land and strategic roads rather than one uniform administration.

passages.title: A lakeside community around the year 1000
passages.text: At Colletière beside Lake Paladru, early eleventh-century families lived inside a timber enclosure. Three wooden buildings, a workshop and livestock facilities survive archaeologically. Waterlogged conditions preserved wood, seeds and leather that would normally rot away, giving this small community an unusually clear material record.

passages.title: A lakeside community around the year 1000
passages.text: Cereal grains, sickles, hooks, net floats and fish scales reveal farming and fishing. Animal bones show different foods in the main house and smaller buildings. Researchers interpret those differences as signs of social rank within the settlement, rather than a single menu shared by everyone.

passages.title: A lakeside community around the year 1000
passages.text: Colletière also produced chess pieces and musical instruments, including a bowed instrument called a vielle. Its inhabitants had tools for weaving, carpentry and metalworking. Work filled much of life, but the surviving objects leave room for music and a board-game argument too.

passages.title: Small feet, skilled hands
passages.text: A tiny leather shoe from Colletière belonged to a child. A small maple shoemaker’s last helped shape footwear for very young children. These objects put families into a story otherwise easily crowded with kings, mounted warriors and abbots.

passages.title: Small feet, skilled hands
passages.text: Leather offcuts show that shoes were made locally. Oak cutting templates, metal awls and tools for threading laces reveal the stages of the craft. Different models and stitching methods suggest that medieval shoemakers cared about variety as well as keeping feet covered.

passages.title: Royal women and a growing monastery
passages.text: At Payerne, the Burgundian royal family supported a religious community before the year 1000. Adelaide, daughter of Queen Bertha and herself an empress, connected it with the monastery of Cluny. Women in the dynasty helped shape institutions as well as royal family relationships.

passages.title: Royal women and a growing monastery
passages.text: Builders began Payerne’s great Romanesque church in the eleventh century. Later priors altered and embellished it. The standing building is therefore a layered achievement of masonry and patronage, not a church completed in one royal building season.

passages.title: Help at a mountain crossing
passages.text: The Great Saint Bernard hospice is securely documented from 1125, with an earlier foundation traditionally placed around 1050. Its religious community assisted pilgrims crossing the Alps. Food, shelter and spiritual care belonged together at a route where reaching the other side was a serious undertaking.

passages.title: Help at a mountain crossing
passages.text: By 1177 the hospice’s wider network counted 78 hospices, houses, priories and churches. Gifts and properties supported the work. The famous rescue dogs belong to much later evidence, so a medieval traveller should not automatically be pictured meeting one.

passages.title: A royal gift in Latin
passages.text: A charter dated 24 April 1011 names Neuchâtel as “Novum castellum”, meaning “new castle”. This is a Latin phrase preserved in the published transcription of Rudolf III’s gift to Queen Ermengarde. The original parchment survives in the Isère archives, with a royal wax seal.

passages.title: A royal gift in Latin
passages.text: The gift transferred revenues from royal estates, including the work of unfree peasants attached to them. A later note records Ermengarde’s donation to the church of Saint-Maurice in Vienne. The document links affection, property, labour and religion in one royal household’s decisions.

Rudolf III died in 1032, ending the dynasty. Incorporation into the Empire unfolded through 1038. Burgundy retained a royal title, while regional lordships increasingly shaped everyday government. Its people and settlements continued beyond this political transition.

sectionTitles: Families, work and the rules of ordinary life
What graves and an abbey reveal
A few words from their legal world

passages.text: Burgundian rulers first established a kingdom near the Rhine, then governed a new realm around the western Alps and Rhône after Roman authorities settled survivors in Sapaudia in 443. Their subjects included established Roman provincial communities. This is the fifth- and early sixth-century kingdom, centuries before the famous medieval duchy of Burgundy.

passages.title: Families, work and the rules of ordinary life
passages.text: A Roman-law collection compiled in the Burgundian kingdom borrowed from earlier Roman legislation rather than starting law from scratch. Modern scholarship places it in the early sixth century. Its subjects include inheritance, sales, contracts and guardianship: royal government reached into household affairs.

passages.title: Families, work and the rules of ordinary life
passages.text: Its guardianship rules gave a willing mother priority over other prospective guardians. This concerns legal management for children, especially their property. It recognizes a maternal role without establishing equal legal standing for all women.

passages.title: Families, work and the rules of ordinary life
passages.text: The collection required a seller to stand by a completed sale. Market exchanges could become courtroom arguments when someone wanted a bargain undone. These rules reveal lawmakers’ intentions, rather than how every village transaction worked.

passages.title: Families, work and the rules of ordinary life
passages.text: One provision required compensation when someone deliberately frightened a horse so badly that it died. Denying an offense and then being proved responsible increased the payment. Working animals mattered enough for a very particular dispute to enter a legal handbook.

passages.title: Families, work and the rules of ordinary life
passages.text: The courts’ calendar made room for harvesting and grape gathering as well as Christian festivals. Ordinary lawsuits were forbidden during these breaks, although fiscal business had an exception. Even legal paperwork had to reckon with the farming year.

passages.title: What graves and an abbey reveal
passages.text: The cemetery at Sézegnin near Geneva contained more than 700 burials spanning the late fourth to eighth centuries. That long sequence crosses the Burgundian kingdom’s rise and conquest. It lets archaeologists investigate communities over generations rather than treating every grave as a separate incoming people.

passages.title: What graves and an abbey reveal
passages.text: Regional excavations distinguish earth graves, wooden burial containers and later stone constructions. Changes in materials and arrangement help date funerary practices. A stone-lined grave tells us about burial choices and labor; by itself it does not identify the language spoken by the person buried there.

passages.title: What graves and an abbey reveal
passages.text: At Geneva’s Saint-Antoine cemetery, researchers examined people of different ages but found some of the youngest children underrepresented. A separate burial area is one possible explanation. Archaeologists cannot simply count the surviving graves and assume they represent every child born in the community.

passages.title: What graves and an abbey reveal
passages.text: Sigismund founded the monastery at Agaune, now Saint-Maurice, in 515. Royal support linked the dynasty to an important Christian shrine. The foundation also created an institution whose daily routines and surviving records outlasted the independent kingdom.

passages.title: What graves and an abbey reveal
passages.text: Agaune became known for continual praise, with groups of monks taking turns singing. Think of a choir relay: the aim was continuity of worship, not requiring one exhausted singer to carry on forever. It was a demanding organized routine within this monastery.

passages.title: What graves and an abbey reveal
passages.text: The abbey stood on an important Rhône route toward Alpine crossings. Its 515 inauguration is associated with a sermon by Bishop Avitus. Travel, royal ceremony and religious learning met at a specific place, rather than belonging to separate worlds.

passages.title: A few words from their legal world
passages.text: The Latin heading “De tutelis minorum” means “On the guardianship of minors.” It appears as title 36 of the Roman-law collection transmitted from the kingdom. This is administrative Latin preserved through manuscript copying, not a reconstructed sentence in the poorly documented Burgundian vernacular.

Frankish armies defeated the kingdom in 532, and Frankish rulers divided it in 534. Communities, laws and religious institutions continued after royal independence ended. The map’s 600 endpoint is a coverage boundary, not the date of the conquest.

passages.text: The imported record starts in 1945, when this area was under French rule. Upper Volta had been dissolved as a separate colony in 1932 and was restored in 1947, so the 1945 outline is not evidence of an independent Burkina Faso. Independence followed in 1960; the present name dates to 1984.

passages.title: Names, writing and political change
passages.text: Upper Volta became independent on 5 August 1960. Its name referred to the river system; in 1984 it became Burkina Faso. The change belonged to Thomas Sankara’s revolutionary government, which had taken power the previous year.

passages.title: Names, writing and political change
passages.text: A dated French writing sample survives in the legislature’s report of 29 October 2024: “Unité-Progrès-Justice,” meaning “Unity-Progress-Justice.” The report quotes this as the former motto while approving its replacement. Words on official documents can change with politics, just as flags and country names do.

passages.title: Names, writing and political change
passages.text: Sankara was killed in the October 1987 coup that brought Blaise Compaoré to power. Much later, two coups in 2022 removed first the elected president Roch Kaboré, then the military leader Paul-Henri Damiba. These are changes of regime within a continuing country.

passages.title: Buildings that teach
passages.text: Francis Kéré’s first building, Gando Primary School, was completed in his home community in 2001. It tackled the practical problems of dark, overheated classrooms using locally available clay mixed with cement for stronger bricks, with an overhanging roof protecting the walls from rain.

passages.title: Buildings that teach
passages.text: At Gando, the metal roof sits above a separate brick ceiling. Air enters through windows and warm air escapes through openings overhead. The building does some of the cooling work itself: a lesson in engineering before the teacher has even written on the board.

passages.title: Buildings that teach
passages.text: Community members helped build the school, combining familiar construction skills with the architect’s engineering. Kéré’s account emphasizes methods that could also simplify future maintenance. A school building needs people who can repair it, as well as people who can design it.

passages.title: Buildings that teach
passages.text: At the living royal court of Tiébélé, Kasena house shapes have social meanings. Figure-of-eight mother houses accommodate elderly residents, widows, unmarried women and children; young married people occupy rectangular houses, and adolescent or unmarried men circular ones. UNESCO documented this arrangement when the site was inscribed in 2024.

passages.title: Buildings that teach
passages.text: Tiébélé’s buildings use earth, wood, straw and cow dung. Men construct the houses, while women preserve and teach the knowledge of symbolic wall decoration. Older motifs coexist with new ones, learned through observation and practice: these walls belong to an active community, not an abandoned stage set.

passages.title: Soil, stories and household water
passages.text: Farmer Yacouba Sawadogo improved traditional zaï planting pits after the droughts around 1980. Compost goes into the pits before seeds; rows of stones slow rainwater running away. He also put water pots in trees for birds that could bring seeds. Small holes helped produce very large changes.

passages.title: Soil, stories and household water
passages.text: From 1984, Sawadogo organized seed-sharing gatherings. Farmers brought crop samples after harvest; seeds were stored at his homestead, then selected before the rains. This was experimentation shared across villages, with the next season’s meals depending on the results.

passages.title: Soil, stories and household water
passages.text: Ouagadougou hosts FESPACO, a festival of African cinema and television. Its 2021 edition ran in October after the pandemic forced a delay. Film selection and screenings made the capital a meeting place for storytellers across borders, adding a different kind of public gathering to markets and ceremonies.

passages.title: Soil, stories and household water
passages.text: In Dori in 2024, teenager Djeneba Dicko described how a nearby water point reduced the exhausting search for water for her family. UNICEF reported eight solar-powered supply systems. Displaced resident Nafissa Sanou managed one at Petit Paris, cleaning the collection area and reminding users about hygiene.

Burkina Faso continues as a state despite repeated changes of government and armed conflict. The two coups of 2022 ended particular governments; they did not end the country’s communities, farms, schools or cultural institutions.
