sectionTitles: A powerful kingdom with complicated borders
Letters, learning and books you could not carry
Families, games and useful beautiful things

passages.text: This record represents Burma under the Konbaung dynasty, founded in 1752, rather than every people or kingdom of present-day Myanmar. Its imported dates, 1783 to 1878, cover only part of the dynasty. The outline also keeps southern territory long after British conquests in 1826 and 1852-53, so it should not be read as an accurate border for every selected year. The monarchy survived until the British invasion of 1885.

passages.title: A powerful kingdom with complicated borders
passages.text: The dynasty began with U Aungzeya, better known as Alaungpaya, who organized resistance from Shwebo in 1752. Shwebo was also called Konbaung, the name later given to his dynasty. His victories over the southern Mon kingdom established a new royal house; the map’s 1783 starting point comes decades into that story.

passages.title: A powerful kingdom with complicated borders
passages.text: Conquest moved skills and stories under brutal circumstances. After Burmese armies sacked Ayutthaya in 1767, large numbers of people were taken to central Myanmar. Thai theatrical performers helped popularize the Ramayana at the Burmese court, and travelling actors spread its stories more widely. Artistic exchange here was bound up with forced displacement.

passages.title: A powerful kingdom with complicated borders
passages.text: Shan rulers were not simply provincial officials inside a tidy national border. Some paid tribute to Burmese kings and hosted soldiers; others had only nominal obligations. A state could acknowledge Burma, China or Siam at the same time. These overlapping relationships help explain why a single solid outline can exaggerate a king’s everyday control.

passages.title: A powerful kingdom with complicated borders
passages.text: In 1882, after this map record ends, Thibaw issued two gold-foil commissions appointing Twek Nga Lu over Mong Nai and Kengtawng. The surviving documents carry royal seals. Their troubled history, amid rebellion and competing claimants, reveals how the court tried to turn a royal appointment into authority on the ground.

passages.title: A powerful kingdom with complicated borders
passages.text: Rank could determine which objects and buildings an official was allowed to use. A painted folding book from about 1880, associated with minister U Shwe Maung, recorded such privileges. The British Museum interprets it as a guide issued after his promotion. His new job therefore came with an illustrated guide to its visible signs of status.

passages.title: Letters, learning and books you could not carry
passages.text: Alaungpaya sent George II an extraordinary letter in 1756, engraved on gold and decorated with rubies. It offered a site for English ships at Pathein and proposed friendship between their descendants. The letter travelled inside an ivory container, with further wrappings and boxes: diplomacy came with quite a lot of packaging.

passages.title: Letters, learning and books you could not carry
passages.text: A tiny Burmese sample from that Golden Letter is ဆင်ဖြူ, meaning “white elephants.” It occurs in the second line among the king’s claims to precious resources and magnificent animals. Historian Jacques Leider supplies both the Burmese transcript and an English translation. This is royal ceremonial language from a surviving 1756 document.

passages.title: Letters, learning and books you could not carry
passages.text: At Mandalay, Mindon’s scripture project produced a library whose pages were stone. Craftsmen carved the Buddhist Pali canon in Burmese script onto 729 marble slabs, completed in 1868 and housed in individual shrines. The language and alphabet are different things: these particular texts are Pali, even though their letters are Burmese.

passages.title: Letters, learning and books you could not carry
passages.text: Making that stone book required both scholarship and patient handwork. Senior monks and officials checked palm-leaf texts before the lettering was cut. The nomination records a carver completing roughly ten to twelve lines in a day. A spelling correction was considerably less convenient than reaching for an eraser.

passages.title: Letters, learning and books you could not carry
passages.text: Buddhist monasteries taught boys and helped sustain a strong tradition of literacy. Education also reached outward during Mindon’s reign: members of the royal family sent children to schools in India and farther afield, supported English-language newspapers, and explored science and technology. Royal schooling and village monastic learning offered very different kinds of opportunity.

passages.title: Families, games and useful beautiful things
passages.text: A son entering a monastery could be an important family occasion. Relatives commissioned a decorated Kammavaca manuscript as a gift and an act of religious merit. Eighteenth- and nineteenth-century examples survive on lacquered and gilded palm leaves. The ordination texts are Pali written in Burmese script, linking family generosity with the community’s religious learning.

passages.title: Families, games and useful beautiful things
passages.text: Burmese folding-book paintings show chinlone players entertaining a royal audience while musicians perform nearby. The ball is woven from cane or rattan, and the challenge is to keep it airborne without using the hands. One painted performer handles three balls. It is a striking reminder that impressive footwork could be entertainment as well as exercise.

passages.title: Families, games and useful beautiful things
passages.text: A Shan women’s lacquer box dated about 1840-1850 has two shallow trays above a deeper compartment, for jewellery, cosmetics or small clothing. Its painted story includes horsemen, swordsmen and a woman archer. The container organized possessions while putting a lively miniature drama around its sides.

passages.title: Families, games and useful beautiful things
passages.text: A small Shan lacquered basket from about 1850 probably held betel-chewing ingredients. Its compact size suited personal use; larger containers served groups. The inside tray even hides an ogre in the decoration. A useful everyday object could reward a closer look after its lid was lifted.

passages.title: Families, games and useful beautiful things
passages.text: Another lacquer set, made about 1850-1865, contains six boxes nested inside one another and a tray. Cylindrical containers commonly stored betel ingredients or pickled tea, but this particular arrangement may have been intended for European customers. Its uncertainty is interesting: the shape survives, while the original owner’s precise habits do not.

passages.title: Families, games and useful beautiful things
passages.text: Medical learning also lived in books. A Burmese manuscript dated 1878 gathers seven medical works on 255 palm-leaf folios, with nine lines of writing on each side. Its edges and binding boards are gilded. This substantial, carefully protected collection shows sustained investment in recording medical knowledge; the catalogue does not establish whether its treatments worked.

passages.title: Conquest and what continued
passages.text: The late kingdom shared the region with expanding British possessions. The 1826 settlement removed Arakan and Tenasserim from royal control; the war of 1852-53 brought British rule to the lower Irrawaddy. Upper Burma remained a separate monarchy until 1885. The coastal areas inside this atlas outline were therefore no longer all governed from the Burmese court.

passages.title: Conquest and what continued
passages.text: The fall of the palace did not instantly settle the country. After Thibaw’s removal, resistance continued across Upper Burma and the Shan, Kachin and Chin hills. British officers then tried to convert former tributary relationships into colonial territorial borders, discovering that some rulers had acknowledged more than one powerful neighbour.

British forces took Mandalay in November 1885 and exiled Thibaw and his family to India. Annexation of Upper Burma followed in 1886, ending the Konbaung monarchy. The imported 1878 cutoff is not that ending. Burmese and neighbouring communities continued under colonial rule, and armed resistance outlasted the loss of the court.

sectionTitles: Culture, writing and a country still changing

passages.text: Myanmar’s atlas record begins in 1945 and remains open-ended, crossing the end of colonial rule, independence, parliamentary governments, military and socialist regimes, partial reform and renewed war. Independence came in 1948. The outline is a coarse country boundary, not a map of each armed group’s control. Earlier Burmese kingdoms have separate cards. This country contains many ethnic, linguistic and religious communities; its history cannot be reduced to one people or one uninterrupted government.

passages.title: Independence and changing political orders
passages.text: Burma became independent on 4 January 1948 and joined the United Nations on 19 April that year. Independence also changed people’s legal nationality: British regulations provided procedures by which certain eligible people could elect to remain British subjects. Such documents reveal how a political transition could reach into the paperwork of individual families.

passages.title: Independence and changing political orders
passages.text: The early republic had elected leaders and fierce political divisions. After a split in the governing alliance, Ne Win’s army headed a caretaker government from 1958 to 1960. U Nu then returned through an election. On 2 March 1962, another military intervention arrested the civilian leadership and set aside the constitution. These were distinct changes, not one continuous government from 1948.

passages.title: Independence and changing political orders
passages.text: Under the 1974 constitution, the Burma Socialist Programme Party formally ruled a one-party state. Its ambitious long-term plan promised industrial development and greater equality. Historian Tin Maung Maung Than describes a system strained by excessive state control and resource constraints; its promised transformation did not materialize. The socialist order ended amid the crisis of 1988.

passages.title: Independence and changing political orders
passages.text: Demonstrators demanded political change in 1988 and faced severe military repression. The NLD won the 1990 election, but the military authorities did not hand over government. Historians can follow this struggle through leaflets, reports and periodicals: the International Institute of Social History’s archive guide describes a collection of Burmese political movements’ documents from this period.

passages.title: Independence and changing political orders
passages.text: The 2011 transition opened a new legislature, but the 2008 constitution reserved a quarter of legislative seats and key ministries for the military. The elected government could not simply order the army out of politics.

passages.title: Independence and changing political orders
passages.text: The NLD’s 2015 electoral victory brought a civilian-led administration in 2016. Htin Kyaw became president and Aung San Suu Kyi became State Counsellor. A contemporary UN report welcomed the transition while warning that more than a million people, mainly Muslims in Rakhine and other minorities, had been excluded from voting. Electoral progress and exclusion existed together.

passages.title: Independence and changing political orders
passages.text: In 2017, military crackdowns in Rakhine drove hundreds of thousands of Rohingya into Bangladesh. UNHCR describes a population suffering discrimination and statelessness. Families lost homes, livelihoods and access to ordinary civic protections. This mass displacement is central to modern Myanmar’s history, including during the years when an elected civilian administration was in office.

passages.title: Independence and changing political orders
passages.text: On 1 February 2021, the military detained civilian leaders and seized power. Protesters banged pots and pans; health workers, teachers and other employees joined strikes. Armed resistance expanded, involving newer People’s Defence Forces and established ethnic armed organizations with different goals and alliances. The conflict cannot be represented as just two uniform sides.

passages.title: Families, learning and public health
passages.text: Living standards improved before the recent crises, although gains were unequal. A World Bank-supported survey found that the share below the national poverty line fell from 48.2 percent in 2005 to 24.8 percent in 2017. Rural poverty remained much higher than urban poverty, and many households were vulnerable to setbacks. These historical figures should not be read as today’s poverty rate.

passages.title: Families, learning and public health
passages.text: A major health achievement came in September 2020, when WHO validated Myanmar’s elimination of trachoma as a public-health problem. The eye-disease campaign had begun in 1964 and combined treatment with clean water, sanitation, hygiene education and rural access to eye care. Elimination at this public-health threshold does not mean every future infection became impossible.

passages.title: Families, learning and public health
passages.text: After the March 2025 earthquake, one family in Bandar village near Amarapura had to share a neighbour’s toilet with others because their own was destroyed. UNICEF’s July 2026 account describes repairs that brought a solar-powered water supply and a fly-proof household latrine. A private, nearby toilet reduced a daily burden on the mother caring for three children.

passages.title: Families, learning and public health
passages.text: The same family received a 20-liter water container and hygiene supplies. Seven-year-old Jue Jue San learned handwashing routines from her mother, who attended community hygiene sessions. Water that once required exhausting collection could be obtained by turning a tap. The story connects engineering with children’s time for chores, play and homework, without pretending every displaced family had received the same help.

passages.title: Families, learning and public health
passages.text: Keeping education going during conflict and disaster requires much more than replacing textbooks. UNICEF and partners reported supporting 854,401 children’s access to formal and non-formal education during 2025, including early learning. They established or maintained 1,328 temporary learning spaces and supported literacy, numeracy and social-emotional learning. These were reported assistance results, not proof that the national school system had fully recovered.

passages.title: Culture, writing and a country still changing
passages.text: Thanakha paste is made by grinding tree bark with water on a round stone. UNESCO’s 2021 account describes children and adults wearing circles, leaves or flower shapes on their faces. Applying it can also be family teaching time: elders pass on manners and values while caring for young children. This describes a documented cultural practice, not a claim that the paste cures disease.

passages.title: Culture, writing and a country still changing
passages.text: The traditional New Year festival Thingyan can arrive with a splash. UNESCO’s 2024 listing describes five days of activities, usually in mid-April: people pour water, donate food, reunite with family and care for elders, sometimes by giving manicures and pedicures. Flowers and leaves can be arranged in a vase at the house entrance. Communities celebrate differently, and war can disrupt ordinary festivities.

passages.title: Culture, writing and a country still changing
passages.text: A small modern Burmese writing sample is မင်္ဂလာပါ, meaning “Hello.” It appears on the British Council’s Burmese page for its 2026 Yangon summer classes. United World Schools gives the approximate Roman spelling “Maingalarpar.” The letters shown here are modern type, not an ancient inscription, and Burmese is one of many languages used by Myanmar’s communities.

passages.title: Culture, writing and a country still changing
passages.text: In a report released on 11 August 2026, UN investigators described a pattern of deliberate military attacks on civilians, including homes, schools and medical facilities. Their reporting period ended on 30 June 2026. They said attacks continued after elections completed that January. These are attributed investigative findings, not a declaration that conflict ended or a claim to show today’s front lines.

Myanmar continues as a country, but the atlas’s open-ended record does not mean one regime or peaceful control has continued since 1945. The August 2026 UN investigative report still documented severe conflict-related harm. Families, community organizations and cultural traditions continue amid displacement and political uncertainty; no final outcome to the conflict is assigned here.

passages.text: The atlas paints a region “Burmese” from 1500 to 500 BCE, but the label arrives too early. Its polygon reaches from Chittagong, Assam and northern Myanmar to Kunming and Dali, while excluding Beikthano, Sri Ksetra, Yangon and most lower Myanmar. It cannot be one people, language or state. Archaeology offers a better close-up at Oakaie and Nyaunggan in the central dry zone. Between 1300 and 700 BCE, communities made coiled pots, shaped stone beads, managed pigs, dogs, cattle and water buffalo, and obtained copper across astonishing distances. Burials preserve family care, ornaments and food offerings, though they cannot tell us everyone’s identity. Children learned by watching skilled hands; an injured adolescent’s survival shows sustained help from others. Food evidence includes mixed plant pathways, managed animals and collected resources, but no preserved prehistoric menu. Published excavations identify no standard toilet, so claiming one would be make-believe. Bead-making scraps are a fun clue: ancient workshop “trash” lets researchers rebuild each production step. Bamar identity, written Burmese and the Pyu cities belong centuries later. No responsible written sample exists for this layer. When the map color disappears in 500 BCE, communities and exchange continue; only an unsupported atlas category ends.

passages.title: A label stretched across incompatible places
passages.text: The live index calls this record Burmese, marks it as a culture and dates it approximately 1500 to 500 BCE. The category is an atlas drawing, not evidence for Bamar ethnicity, a Burmese-speaking population, a capital, government or politically surveyed frontier a thousand years long.

passages.title: A label stretched across incompatible places
passages.text: The polygon’s bounds run roughly 89.68 to 105.67° east and 20.44 to 29.41° north. It includes audited points at Chittagong, Guwahati, Imphal, Myitkyina, Bagan, Mandalay, Kunming and Dali. That enormous reach crosses distinct archaeological landscapes and several modern countries.

passages.title: A label stretched across incompatible places
passages.text: Beikthano, Sri Ksetra, Taungoo, Bago, Yangon, Thaton and most lower Myanmar sit outside the target in every exact snapshot; the atlas assigns them to Austro-Asiatic rice cultures. A “Burmese” layer that omits them cannot stand for Myanmar’s prehistory or later Pyu geography.

passages.title: A label stretched across incompatible places
passages.text: Historical linguistics places attested Burmese with Pagan, and the oldest surviving Burmese document dates to 1113 CE. Another historical study places substantial Burmese-speaking lowland entry around the ninth century CE. Both are more than a millennium after this card ends.

passages.title: A label stretched across incompatible places
passages.text: Glottolog identifies Burmese as a documented Sino-Tibetan language. A language family is not a skeleton shape, a bronze style or a genetic cluster. Archaeology, linguistics and ancient DNA answer different questions; lining up their maps without dates creates a false prehistoric ethnicity.

passages.title: How archaeologists build a timeline from difficult evidence
passages.text: At Oakaie and Nyaunggan, fifty-two AMS determinations finally provided a radiometric framework. Researchers still combined dates with layer order, pottery technology and burial relationships. A laboratory number is powerful, but disturbed soil, contamination and unsuitable material can make it misleading.

passages.title: How archaeologists build a timeline from difficult evidence
passages.text: Human bone collagen often failed to preserve, so researchers tested mineral apatite and recognized that it can yield dates that are too young. Charcoal from occupation layers proved more helpful. Publishing those problems lets children see science as careful correction rather than instant certainty.

passages.title: How archaeologists build a timeline from difficult evidence
passages.text: Myanmar and French teams excavated cemeteries, living surfaces and industrial deposits together. Recording body position can reveal coffins, shrouds or jar burial even after organic material disappears. Collaboration also matters because local archaeologists, collections and communities are not background helpers to foreign discovery.

passages.title: How archaeologists build a timeline from difficult evidence
passages.text: Badah-lin’s red-ochre rock images, stone tools, unfinished pieces and ancient charcoal belong mostly thousands of years before this card. They prove deep creative and technical history in the wider region, but cannot be relabeled “Burmese Bronze Age art” merely because modern borders overlap.

passages.title: How archaeologists build a timeline from difficult evidence
passages.text: Halin provides a rare sequence from prehistoric occupation toward a much later Pyu city. Long stratigraphy can test change through time, but later walls, inscriptions and Buddhism must remain later. Archaeologists do not pour the top layer backward into every older pit beneath it.

passages.title: River valleys, dry country, mountains and changing monsoons
passages.text: The atlas merges the Brahmaputra world, northern river valleys, Myanmar’s central dry zone and Yunnan highlands. Mountains guide routes and rainfall; rivers can connect settlements yet also flood or shift. One environmental story cannot fit a polygon stretching sixteen degrees of longitude.

passages.title: River valleys, dry country, mountains and changing monsoons
passages.text: Oakaie to Nyaunggan lies in a semi-arid zone near the Chindwin, with drought risk unlike humid coasts. Food, grazing and water choices responded to local soils and season. Calling all ancient Myanmar a lush rice bowl would erase the ecology actually tested at these sites.

passages.title: River valleys, dry country, mountains and changing monsoons
passages.text: Pollen, charcoal and diatoms from Inle Lake record changing forest, burning and lake levels through the Holocene. Inle lies outside the target polygon, so the core is a regional comparison rather than a local weather diary. It shows why climate cannot be assumed constant.

passages.title: River valleys, dry country, mountains and changing monsoons
passages.text: The Ayeyarwady, Chindwin, Salween and upland passes could move people, stories, stone and metals, but transport required local knowledge and labor. Similar copper in distant places may reveal a chain of exchanges rather than one merchant traveling end to end or one empire policing the road.

passages.title: River valleys, dry country, mountains and changing monsoons
passages.text: Later Myanmar cities built tanks, canals, walls and drains suited to dry or flood-prone settings. Those examples help formulate questions about earlier water needs, but their structures are centuries later. No Bronze Age reservoir should be invented because a Pyu or Bagan one survives.

passages.title: Food, animals, farming and the missing prehistoric menu
passages.text: Stable carbon isotopes from human and animal teeth suggest both C3 and C4 food pathways at Oakaie to Nyaunggan. Rice is C3 and millet often C4, but isotope values do not print a recipe. People or animals may eat several plants, so conclusions remain probabilistic.

passages.title: Food, animals, farming and the missing prehistoric menu
passages.text: Despite extensive flotation, excavators recovered no secure prehistoric plant remains from these sites. That absence blocks confident lists of grains, greens, spices or cooking methods. A responsible card says “we do not know the menu” rather than copying modern Burmese dishes backward three thousand years.

passages.title: Food, animals, farming and the missing prehistoric menu
passages.text: Animal remains indicate management of pigs, dogs, cattle and water buffalo, alongside collected local resources and limited fish remains. Bones can reveal species and butchery, yet not every use: cattle might provide meat, labor, social value or several things across their lives.

passages.title: Food, animals, farming and the missing prehistoric menu
passages.text: Regional food-production research shows domesticated plants and animals arriving and spreading on different schedules. Yunnan archaeobotany documents its own mixtures of rice, millets and later wheat. Because the atlas includes Yunnan, that diversity refutes the idea of one Burmese subsistence package across the shape.

passages.title: Food, animals, farming and the missing prehistoric menu
passages.text: Food was also social: pots and animal parts placed with some dead suggest funerary giving or feasting, but cannot tell us a precise belief. A cattle skull, turtle, dog burial or vessel must be interpreted by context, not turned automatically into a universal favorite food.

passages.title: Pots, beads, bronze and exchange across long distances
passages.text: Potters built many vessels with coils, then shaped medium and large forms using paddle and anvil techniques. Decoration and vessel shape changed through the sequence. A pot records gestures and learned choices, but pottery similarity alone does not reveal the maker’s language or ethnic name.

passages.title: Pots, beads, bronze and exchange across long distances
passages.text: Bead researchers counted rough stone, blanks, preforms, broken drill attempts, ejected cones and finished pieces. That workshop debris is an ancient instruction manual in reverse. The fun surprise is that a snapped bead can reveal more about making than a perfect necklace.

passages.title: Pots, beads, bronze and exchange across long distances
passages.text: Copper and bronze objects include axes, points, bracelets, rings and small tools, but stone remained useful. “Bronze Age” does not mean everyone replaced stone overnight or owned metal. Materials overlapped, and burial goods may exaggerate objects chosen for display or remembrance.

passages.title: Pots, beads, bronze and exchange across long distances
passages.text: Microscopy and elemental analysis reveal alloy recipes; lead isotopes compare metal with possible ore sources. Some copper signatures fit production zones in Thailand or Laos rather than nearby Monywa. The result is evidence for far-reaching networks, not proof that foreign miners ruled Nyaunggan.

passages.title: Pots, beads, bronze and exchange across long distances
passages.text: Yunnan bronzes sometimes resemble objects farther south, and late-second-millennium interaction is real. Yet comparative archaeology warns against turning shapes into migrating races. Jicha, Dian-area traditions, Oakaie and Nyaunggan each need their own contexts, dates and production evidence before connections are named.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, work, movement and play
passages.text: Oakaie occupation deposits preserve living surfaces and postholes, evidence that people built structures near their work. Walls and roofs rarely survive, so the exact floor plan and materials remain uncertain. A few holes cannot justify one standard “Burmese house” for the entire millennium.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, work, movement and play
passages.text: Work included shaping clay, drilling stone, tending animals, obtaining food, fetching water, maintaining buildings and handling the dead. Metal exchange added mining, transport and casting somewhere along the chain. Archaeological deposits show tasks, while names, wages and daily schedules mostly remain silent.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, work, movement and play
passages.text: No cloth survives in the cited local deposits, so we cannot responsibly specify fibers, colors, wrapped garments or loom types. Perishable clothing may vanish while stone beads endure, creating a dressed-in-jewelry illusion. Preservation bias is not evidence that people wore beads and nothing else.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, work, movement and play
passages.text: Strontium in teeth records geological environments encountered while enamel formed. Studies suggest many Bronze Age individuals were local, with a few different life histories, while goods traveled far. People can stay near home while copper moves through many hands; mobility has more than one scale.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, work, movement and play
passages.text: Children certainly played, but no securely identified toy from this exact context appears in the sources. Bead chips, clay scraps or pebbles might have become playthings, yet that remains imagination. The honest fun is methodological: what wear mark would convince an archaeologist something was a toy?

passages.title: Families, women, children and learning by doing
passages.text: Burial groups and tooth chemistry let researchers test kinship and residence, but the Oakaie to Nyaunggan isotope sample is only eighteen people. Preliminary sex-pattern differences are intriguing, not a universal marriage rule. The dead sampled in cemeteries never equal the whole living population.

passages.title: Families, women, children and learning by doing
passages.text: Ancient DNA from two Oakaie individuals contributes to a wider picture of multiple population movements. Two genomes cannot define a Burmese people, and genes do not speak a language. Tropical preservation also leaves large gaps, so claims must remain proportional to the tiny sample.

passages.title: Families, women, children and learning by doing
passages.text: Underfloor newborn burials at Oakaie place some very young children within lived spaces and ritual decisions. They show care and belonging, not how every family mourned. Other children may have been buried elsewhere or left no recoverable trace, making cemetery comparisons essential.

passages.title: Families, women, children and learning by doing
passages.text: Children could learn pottery pressure, bead drilling, animal care, food collection and route knowledge by watching, helping and practicing. This is an inference from complicated skills, not a recovered school timetable. Expertise requires teaching even when no classroom, alphabet or named teacher survives.

passages.title: Families, women, children and learning by doing
passages.text: Neither tools nor grave goods carry a simple gender label. Isotopes can compare biological sex in a small sample, but social roles remain harder to reconstruct. Women’s, men’s and non-adults’ labor should not be assigned from modern stereotypes or from one object placed beside one body.

passages.title: Health, injury, care, death and cautious belief
passages.text: One Nyaunggan adolescent survived a serious head injury sustained earlier in childhood and later lived with a dislocated jaw and possible bone disease. Healing and survival imply sustained assistance. Their community provided care, although bones cannot name the caregivers or every treatment.

passages.title: Health, injury, care, death and cautious belief
passages.text: Skeletons can reveal age, injury, stress, some disease and individual life histories, but diagnoses remain probabilities. Tropical soil destroys evidence unevenly, and cemetery samples exclude people buried elsewhere. Bioarchaeology reconstructs individual lives most responsibly when uncertainty travels beside every medical-sounding label.

passages.title: Health, injury, care, death and cautious belief
passages.text: Food, rest, wound cleaning, splinting, massage, plant knowledge or ritual may have formed part of care, but the cited deposits do not securely identify a medicine chest. Naming modern remedies would be invention. The adolescent’s remodeled bone proves survival and help, not a specific prescription.

passages.title: Health, injury, care, death and cautious belief
passages.text: Bodies were buried with varying orientations and combinations of pots, beads, animal parts and metal. Archaeologists can document repeated actions and differences, yet “belief in an afterlife” is only one interpretation. Grief, status, memory, kin duty and community identity may overlap.

passages.title: Health, injury, care, death and cautious belief
passages.text: Later Iron Age graves in the Samon valley include different coffins, shrouds, jars, metals and glass. They help track change after parts of this card, not reconstruct a timeless religion. Burial customs can shift while communities remain connected, and similar rites can spread without population replacement.

passages.title: Water, ash, rubbish and the honest toilet gap
passages.text: Dry-zone households needed reliable drinking water through strong seasonality, while river and upland communities faced different problems. The exact source, well, stream, stored rain or river, for each Oakaie household is not established. Environmental necessity does not license an invented water system.

passages.title: Water, ash, rubbish and the honest toilet gap
passages.text: Living surfaces accumulated broken pots, animal bone, ash, stone-working debris and discarded tools. Archaeologists read those deposits as activity evidence, but sweeping, reuse and later disturbance move rubbish around. A workshop dump is not automatically the spot where someone sat and drilled.

passages.title: Water, ash, rubbish and the honest toilet gap
passages.text: Published Oakaie to Nyaunggan reports identify postholes, living floors, industrial deposits and burials but no standard toilet. People certainly relieved themselves; where and how is not securely recovered. Claiming a latrine, wiping material or universal rule would turn an evidence gap into fiction.

passages.title: Water, ash, rubbish and the honest toilet gap
passages.text: Later Pyu and other Myanmar sites preserve moats, tanks, canals and drainage, showing sophisticated responses to water. They postdate this card and often lie outside its polygon. They are useful comparison for questions, not permission to install a Pyu bathroom in 1000 BCE.

passages.title: Water, ash, rubbish and the honest toilet gap
passages.text: Cleaning vessels, carrying water, controlling animals and moving refuse were essential work even when histories ignore them. Children likely learned safety through participation, but exact task divisions are unknown. Sanitation is best presented as recurring labor, not a single spectacular invention or ethnic trait.

passages.title: Conflict, writing, achievements and what continues
passages.text: Axes, points and blades could serve practical, hunting, display or violent purposes; burial placement alone cannot decide. The cited sites do not reveal a Burmese army, king or war. Metal objects must not be drafted automatically into a conquest story just because modern labels sound political.

passages.title: Conflict, writing, achievements and what continues
passages.text: Later first-millennium BCE glass and metal links connected Myanmar with India, Thailand and beyond. These networks grow near or after this layer’s end. Exchange can spread technologies and prestige without erasing local practices, and an imported bead never provides its owner’s ethnicity by itself.

passages.title: Conflict, writing, achievements and what continues
passages.text: Written-language sample: none can responsibly be shown. No text is securely attributable to this atlas category between 1500 and 500 BCE. Pyu inscriptions belong centuries later, and the oldest surviving Burmese document is from 1113 CE; borrowing either would fabricate a voice.

passages.title: Conflict, writing, achievements and what continues
passages.text: Achievements visible in evidence include building durable settlements, shaping and firing pots, drilling tiny stone beads, managing animals, sustaining injured people and maintaining exchange over immense distances. These belong to particular communities and networks; calling them “Burmese achievements” would repeat the atlas’s anachronism.

passages.title: Conflict, writing, achievements and what continues
passages.text: At 500 BCE the exact target disappears; the 500 BCE map supplies no local replacement, and by 400 BCE a huge Austro-Asiatic rice-culture layer covers nearly every audited point. Neither change records extinction. Pyu cities emerge later, while Bamar identity and written Burmese are later still.

At about 500 BCE the exact Burmese id disappears, and the live 500 BCE snapshot provides no mapped local successor. By 400 BCE the atlas assigns almost every audited Myanmar and Yunnan point to a broad Austro-Asiatic rice-culture layer. This is an editorial reset, not cultural replacement or extinction. Local communities, craft, food production and exchange continued; Pyu urbanism appears later, while Bamar identity and written Burmese are later again.

passages.text: This imported label covers changing kingdoms in and around Upper Myanmar between 1492 and 1650. It includes the rise of Toungoo power, but the outline leaves southern Pegu separately labelled and cannot display Bayinnaung’s far larger empire. Pegu examples below explain the northern kingdoms’ imperial connections beyond the shading. Regional rivals, a vast sixteenth-century empire and a smaller restored kingdom followed one another; 1492 and 1650 are map seams, not founding and extinction dates.

passages.title: Kingdoms, empire and government
passages.text: Toungoo grew from a regional power into an empire reaching far beyond the Irrawaddy valley. Conquered Tai kingdoms on both sides of the Salween entered its political orbit. Its reach extended from Manipur in the west to Sipsong Panna and Laos in the east.

passages.title: Kingdoms, empire and government
passages.text: Tabinshwehti conquered Pegu in 1539 and moved his capital there. Burmese, Mon and Shan people participated in the resulting court and administration. He married a Mon queen and adopted a Mon hairstyle: royal identity could be deliberately mixed, even amid violent conquest.

passages.title: Kingdoms, empire and government
passages.text: Royal edicts studied by Toru Ohno describe a palace divided by brick walls. Administrative rooms lay east; queens, princesses and women servants occupied the western household. Movement between these areas was restricted. A palace was both a seat of government and a large, carefully controlled place of work and residence.

passages.title: Kingdoms, empire and government
passages.text: Government needed skilled readers and writers. Chief secretaries recorded council decisions for submission to the king through the privy council. Royal orders were written down and relayed through royal reporters to the council. The edicts let us follow this paperwork trail without assuming that every subject could read.

passages.title: Objects, buildings and discoveries
passages.text: Bayinnaung donated a bronze bell at Shwezigon in Bagan on 23 May 1557. Its inscription has 43 lines in Burmese, 35 in Mon and five in Pali. The same object brought royal commemoration, Buddhist devotion and several written languages together; it survives at the pagoda.

passages.title: Objects, buildings and discoveries
passages.text: The bell is about 165 centimetres high, with two hamsa birds decorating its hanging hook. Its text recounts victories and religious works. Read it as a king’s public account of his reign: a beautifully made bronze monument can also be a political argument.

passages.title: Objects, buildings and discoveries
passages.text: Excavation of Kanbawzathadi Palace in Bago began in 1991 and continued into 1997. Archaeologists recovered burnt teak posts, brick remains and religious objects. Some posts carry sixteenth-century inscriptions naming court officers. The report distinguishes possible Bayinnaung-era remains from later building work.

passages.title: Objects, buildings and discoveries
passages.text: The striking palace buildings now seen at the site are reconstructions informed by archaeology, historical descriptions and traditional craftsmanship. Burnt posts are displayed beside them. Comparing the surviving wood with the reconstructed halls is a useful detective exercise: which parts are evidence, and which show an informed attempt to rebuild?

passages.title: Objects, buildings and discoveries
passages.text: Elizabeth Howard Moore identifies a roughly 571-hectare walled and moated sixteenth-century Bago, beside an older settlement. Researchers compared a 1942 aerial photograph with a 2002 satellite image to trace features such as walls and the palace area. Sometimes a city’s buried plan becomes clearer from above.

passages.title: Homes, markets and everyday work
passages.text: A chronicle examined by U Thaw Kaung describes Bayinnaung standardizing trading weights shaped like hamsa ducks. It also lists port imports including cloth, perfume, spices and colourful parrots. Buying and selling could involve a metal bird on the scales and a live bird among the cargo!

passages.title: Homes, markets and everyday work
passages.text: Ralph Fitch’s published account of his late-1580s journey describes families living aboard riverboats and markets held on the water. Boat traders sheltered beneath broad umbrellas made from leaves, compared to cartwheels. Your shop, transport and home could share one hull.

passages.title: Homes, markets and everyday work
passages.text: The same account describes merchants’ bamboo houses with straw roofs in old Pegu. Brick storerooms protected goods when fires swept through the flammable neighbourhood. A warehouse could be a household’s most important fire precaution.

passages.title: Homes, markets and everyday work
passages.text: Fitch’s account also describes water jars at temple entrances for washing feet. Monks collected rice, fish and herbs in covered pots, receiving food from households along their route. People also gathered to hear monks preach, connecting religious teaching with household giving. These are an outsider’s descriptions of local practices.

passages.title: Homes, markets and everyday work
passages.text: A law report set at Bayinnaung’s court tells of a Tai noble family disputing inheritance. An elder son had entered royal service. Was money previously given to him support while he served, or his inheritance paid early? Judge Kyaw Thu ruled in his favour, interpreting the family’s obligations and intentions. The surviving text reaches us through much later copies.

passages.title: Writing, learning and political change
passages.text: A short Burmese sample, in Huxley’s scholarly Roman transliteration, is “Shin kyaw thu pyatton”, translated “Lord Kyaw Thu’s Precedent”. It names the inheritance report preserved in an 1870 printed edition. This is a later witness to a text about the sixteenth-century court, not a surviving sixteenth-century autograph; the Roman letters represent Burmese words rather than reproducing Burmese script.

passages.title: Writing, learning and political change
passages.text: Fitch’s published account describes petitions written on long strips of leaves with a pointed iron stylus and submitted to the king. Important writing did not have to begin with a sheet of paper: a prepared leaf could carry a request to court.

passages.title: Writing, learning and political change
passages.text: In the 1590s, unsuccessful warfare in Siam and demands for service and taxes helped break the empire apart. The restored dynasty built a smaller Irrawaddy-centred kingdom, curtailed princely autonomy and used appointed governors. Its rulers sought more manageable government instead of recovering every distant dependency.

The map stops in 1650, but the restored Toungoo dynasty continued until Pegu’s conquest of Upper Myanmar in 1752. Alaungpaya then led the movement that established the Konbaung dynasty. These were changes of ruling institutions; the region’s households, languages, trade and Buddhist traditions did not disappear at the map seam.

passages.text: This imported label spans a kingdom, colonial administration and the modern republic. The 1815 to 1878 map outline is displaced south of Burundi and should not be read as its historical frontier. Burundi regained independence as a kingdom in 1962; the monarchy ended in 1966, while the country continued.

passages.title: Kingdom, colonization and republic
passages.text: The kingdom had its own political traditions before colonial rule. At Kiganda in June 1903, King Mwezi Gisabo retained his kingship but accepted German sovereignty under coercive terms. A surviving king therefore did not mean that the kingdom remained fully independent.

passages.title: Kingdom, colonization and republic
passages.text: On 1 July 1962, the UN trusteeship administered by Belgium ended and Burundi became an independent kingdom. Four years later, Michel Micombero’s coup abolished the monarchy. These are two different turning points: the end of external rule and the end of a royal institution.

passages.title: Kingdom, colonization and republic
passages.text: The assassination of the first democratically elected president in 1993 was followed by widespread civil war and displacement. The Arusha agreement of August 2000 was a major peace effort, but it did not instantly stop every armed group. The UN was still condemning attacks on civilians in 2001.

passages.title: Kingdom, colonization and republic
passages.text: The 2018 constitution’s cover reads “REPUBURIKA Y’UBURUNDI,” Kirundi for “Republic of Burundi.” The French equivalent appears beside it. This is a sample from a particular written state document, in the Latin alphabet, within a society where spoken traditions also remain important.

passages.title: Royal architecture and living drums
passages.text: Burundi’s heritage submission associates the Gishora royal residence with King Ntare Rugamba in the early nineteenth century. It describes separate spaces for the drum sanctuary, royal dwelling, servants and royal granaries. The annual sorghum-sowing ceremony connected political authority with the farming year.

passages.title: Royal architecture and living drums
passages.text: Gishora’s roof structure was woven like an upside-down basket, then raised and supported with poles. Papyrus bindings, timber and thatch turned skilled plant work into architecture. The 2026 heritage account describes these construction techniques; it does not establish that every piece of the surviving building is nineteenth-century material.

passages.title: Royal architecture and living drums
passages.text: The royal drum performance combines synchronized percussion with dance, poetry and song. Drums form a semicircle around a central drum; some maintain a continuous beat while others follow its changing rhythm. Two or three performers dance in turn. Coordination is part of the achievement, not merely volume.

passages.title: Royal architecture and living drums
passages.text: Drum-making and performance skills pass on through practice and teaching. UNESCO describes many bearers as descendants of sanctuary keepers, with performances at public celebrations and for visitors. A tradition once connected with kings can remain meaningful after the monarchy itself has ended.

passages.title: Family knowledge and everyday health
passages.text: In Ruyigi in 2022, trained community workers and “Light Mothers” weighed children, recorded their growth and visited households. Their equipment included scales, height gauges, arm-measuring tapes and registers. Those small tools allowed concerns to be noticed near home and referred to a health facility.

passages.title: Family knowledge and everyday health
passages.text: The same programme paired measurement with practical food discussions. Parents learned how to combine available foods rather than receiving only a number on a chart. Health workers followed up with families, showing how local experience, record-keeping and professional care could work together.

passages.title: Family knowledge and everyday health
passages.text: At Kagari School in 2025, thirteen-year-old Jeannette participated in a hygiene club. She told UNICEF that reusable sanitary pads and what she learned in the club helped her stop missing lessons during her period. Privacy and ordinary supplies can affect education as directly as a textbook.

passages.title: Family knowledge and everyday health
passages.text: At Gashoho Health Center, the same report found new women’s and men’s latrine blocks under construction after older facilities became unusable. Staff had hygiene supplies including soap, chlorine, protective clothing and bins. A health centre needs a clean environment around treatment rooms as well as care inside them.

Burundi’s monarchy ended on 28 November 1966, but Burundi did not disappear. The republic continues, and royal drumming survives as a living cultural practice. Political institutions, community traditions and the lives of ordinary people follow different timelines.

passages.text: The Buyids were a Daylamite ruling family whose related principalities dominated much of Iran and Iraq in the tenth and eleventh centuries. The two imported map labels share this history, but their dates and outlines contain serious errors explained below.

passages.title: A ruling family and its subjects
passages.text: The Buwayhid Emirates outline in 1000 broadly covers Iran and Iraq, but its repeated appearance in 1200 is too late. The Buyid dynasty label has a different, misplaced 1200 outline around Afghanistan and Pakistan. Neither record establishes accurate borders; both extend to 1279, long after Buyid power ended. These cards describe the historical dynasty.

passages.title: A ruling family and its subjects
passages.text: The founding brothers, Ali, Hasan and Ahmad, built related principalities rather than one consistently united state. Their descendants competed over provinces and seniority. In 945 Ahmad entered Baghdad and received the title Muizz al-Dawla. The Abbasid caliph remained, while military and political power rested heavily with the Buyid rulers.

passages.title: A ruling family and its subjects
passages.text: A silver dirham struck at Fasa in 959 or 960 names three authorities: the caliph al-Muti, Rukn al-Dawla and Adud al-Dawla. Their names fit on a coin less than three centimeters across. Money could carry a compact statement about layered authority, alongside the religious declarations familiar to those who handled it.

passages.title: A ruling family and its subjects
passages.text: Buyid patronage supported Shiite scholars in Baghdad, especially around the commercial district of Karkh. The vizier Sabur ibn Ardashir established a major library there in 991 or 992. Sunni institutions and the Abbasid caliphate continued too. Religious life was diverse, and competition between communities could also produce serious tension and violence.

passages.title: A ruling family and its subjects
passages.text: Governing involved offices as well as armies. Buyid administration retained finance, correspondence and military departments, drawing on Abbasid practice. Officials had to collect and account for revenue, transmit decisions and manage soldiers. A change of ruling family did not mean that every ledger, letter-writing practice or office was thrown away.

passages.title: A ruling family and its subjects
passages.text: Royal households could shape government directly. After Fakhr al-Dawla died in 997, his widow Sayyeda governed Ray on behalf of their young son Majd al-Dawla. She came from the Bavandid ruling family. Her position shows a particular woman exercising political authority through dynastic relationships; it is not a description of every woman’s opportunities.

passages.title: Water, markets and celebrations
passages.text: The Band-e Amir weir across the Kor River raised water for irrigation near Shiraz. Medieval accounts describe ten waterwheels lifting water to supply hundreds of villages. Stone blocks, mortar and masonry foundations formed a structure that also carried a bridge. It joined farming and transport in one engineering project; the surviving work also has a long history of repairs.

passages.title: Water, markets and celebrations
passages.text: Adud al-Dawla built markets, caravanserais, cisterns and hospitals. The geographer Muqaddasi describes bazaars at Ramhormoz and a Shiraz palace with water channels and wind towers. These projects supplied places to trade, stay and store water. Their benefits depended on the work of builders, merchants, maintenance crews and water managers as well as royal funding.

passages.title: Water, markets and celebrations
passages.text: At the new town of Kard-e Fanna Khusraw, two annual celebrations marked its foundation and the arrival of aqueduct water. Biruni reports the occasions, while another account links the idea to Nowruz celebrations Adud remembered from childhood in Isfahan. A reliable water supply was important enough to earn its own day of celebration.

passages.title: Homes, food and streets at Siraf
passages.text: Siraf linked the Persian Gulf with Indian Ocean trade. Its excavated houses and pottery open a window onto life around the Buyid age, with some evidence also predating Buyid rule. Luxury imports mattered, but daily survival depended on water brought from surrounding mountains and food supplied from plains and valleys beyond them.

passages.title: Homes, food and streets at Siraf
passages.text: At Siraf, the excavators called one building House N. It had nine ground-floor rooms around a courtyard and evidence of an upper floor. The whole building occupied only about half the area of two larger neighboring houses. Families did not all inhabit one standard floor plan, even within the same excavated neighborhood.

passages.title: Homes, food and streets at Siraf
passages.text: Better houses had carved plaster decoration, including stars and rosettes. The excavator thought these might have stood over doors, but that placement was uncertain. Pieces fallen from upper stories also help archaeologists reconstruct buildings whose roofs and upper walls have vanished. A decorative fragment can reveal more about a home than an empty doorway.

passages.title: Homes, food and streets at Siraf
passages.text: Siraf’s roofs drained through earthenware pipes into stone-lined pits, often beside the houses. Some pits also received household waste and may have received waste from latrines. The streets themselves were unpaved. These discoveries reveal practical efforts to handle rain and rubbish, while the possible connection to toilets remains an archaeological interpretation.

passages.title: Homes, food and streets at Siraf
passages.text: A British Museum catalogue group records cooking pots made in India and excavated at Siraf, including object 2007,6001.4038, dated to the ninth or tenth century. Long-distance connections could therefore reach the cooking equipment used in a coastal town. The catalogue tells us where this pot was made and found, but not whose dinner it cooked.

passages.title: Care, books and looking at the sky
passages.text: The Adudi hospital in Baghdad was founded in 982. Ibn Marzuban, trained in religious law and the sciences, became a hospital superintendent as well as a judge. His exact clinical role is uncertain; his administrative work is clearer. Running a place for the sick required organization as well as people who knew treatments.

passages.title: Care, books and looking at the sky
passages.text: The physician al-Majusi dedicated his Complete Book of the Medical Art to Adud al-Dawla. He wanted better organization and fuller attention to anatomy and surgery than he found in an earlier medical compilation. A surviving copy at the National Library of Medicine was made in 1208, showing the work’s later use without pretending that this particular manuscript came from the Buyid court.

passages.title: Care, books and looking at the sky
passages.text: Adud al-Dawla studied Arabic and supported works on subjects including grammar, medicine, astronomy and geometry. Muqaddasi describes his large Shiraz library as having a separate list for each subject. Finding a book therefore involved some organization rather than rummaging through every volume. Royal patronage supported learned specialists, though it does not establish schooling for every child.

passages.title: Care, books and looking at the sky
passages.text: The astronomer al-Sufi worked closely with Buyid rulers. His Book of the Fixed Stars combined classical constellations, Arabic star traditions and his own observations. Drawings accompanied tables of individual stars, with coordinates calculated for 964. Readers could compare a pictured pattern with measured positions in the sky, turning familiar stars into material for careful observation and criticism.

passages.title: Care, books and looking at the sky
passages.text: An astrolabe made by al-Khujandi in 984 or 985 survives in Doha’s Museum of Islamic Art. Its rotating star map has 33 pointers, six shaped like birds’ beaks. Tiny metal birds could point to stars! The maker worked in Buyid court circles; the catalogue gives Ray or Baghdad as possible places of manufacture, rather than one certain workshop.

passages.title: Objects, discoveries and a written sample
passages.text: A tenth-century gold ewer in the Smithsonian bears an inscription naming the Buyid prince Bakhtiyar. Its relief decoration required skilled metalworking. The museum judges the inscription apparently genuine but identifies the handle as a likely later addition and records debate about authenticity. This luxurious vessel belongs to elite consumption, not a reconstruction of an ordinary family’s table.

passages.title: Objects, discoveries and a written sample
passages.text: A textile associated with the label “Buyid” in the Metropolitan Museum illustrates the hazards of dating beautiful objects. The museum now dates textile 30.67 probably to the early twentieth century. It should not be used to reconstruct Buyid clothing. Historical detective work includes recognizing that an object’s apparent age may be misleading.

passages.title: Objects, discoveries and a written sample
passages.text: On the Fasa dirham, the Arabic words “الامير العدل” (al-amīr al-ʿadl) mean “the Just Amir”. They form part of Adud al-Dawla’s title in the reverse inscription. This sample follows the Ashmolean catalogue’s transcription of a coin dated 348 AH, or 959 to 960 CE. It shows Arabic lettering used to announce a ruler’s authority on an everyday medium of exchange.

Seljuk entry into Baghdad in 1055 ended Buyid rule there. Remaining power in Fars was lost during subsequent struggles involving the Shabankara and Seljuks, by the early 1060s. The family’s political rule ended, while its cities, medical writings and scientific traditions continued under new rulers.

sectionTitles: The atlas under a magnifying glass
A family confederation, not one solid block
Food, markets and things that traveled
Water, baths and the toilet question
Stars, art and words on metal and stone
How Buyid rule ended and what continued

passages.text: Picture a map with two Buyid shapes at once, and one of them is in the wrong neighborhood. The atlas id buyid-emirate exists only from 1000 to 1100, yet its polygon lies across coastal Balochistan and Sindh, far east of Baghdad, Ray and Shiraz. The separate buwayhid-emirates shape covers those real Buyid centers. History is clearer than the artwork: three Daylamite brothers built related principalities in the 930s, and Ahmad entered Baghdad in 945. The Abbasid caliph remained a revered religious leader, while Buyid amirs commanded armies and government. Their courts supported libraries, hospitals, astronomers, builders and busy trade ports. Their family confederation was never one tidy, permanently united empire; cousins and brothers competed, and local rulers gained ground. Seljuk forces ended Buyid control of Baghdad in 1055, while the last southern branch fell by about 1062. People did not vanish with the dynasty: farmers, merchants, scholars, craftspeople and city neighborhoods continued under new rulers.

passages.title: The atlas under a magnifying glass
passages.text: The exact target is id “buyid-emirate,” labeled Buyid Emirate and indexed circa 1000 to 1100. Its only feature is one Polygon with one ring and 32 coordinate positions. Its decoded bounds run from about 63.600° to 71.405° east and 23.675° to 32.532° north.

passages.title: The atlas under a magnifying glass
passages.text: No tested historical Buyid center falls inside the target polygon: Baghdad, Basra, Ahvaz, Shiraz, Siraf, Fasa, Isfahan, Hamadan, Ray and Kerman are all outside. Karachi, Hyderabad in Sindh, Thatta and Khuzdar are inside, exposing a severe placement error rather than a forgotten eastern Buyid capital.

passages.title: The atlas under a magnifying glass
passages.text: A different feature called buwayhid-emirates appears in the same 1000 snapshot. Its two-part MultiPolygon contains every tested Buyid center from Baghdad to Kerman. Because the two geometries coexist and disagree, this card does not silently alias buyid-emirate to the separately carded Buwayhid record.

passages.title: The atlas under a magnifying glass
passages.text: The target is absent in 900 and 1100. At 900 the atlas assigns many western test points to the Abbasid Caliphate; at 1100 it assigns the same region to the Seljuk Empire. These century snapshots are display layers, not exact conquest dates or proof of uniform control.

passages.title: The atlas under a magnifying glass
passages.text: The identity problem gets stranger in 1200: buwayhid-emirates reappears over Iran and Iraq, while buyid-dynasty appears as a six-point polygon near Afghanistan and Pakistan. Both are centuries too late. The existing shared card remains separate; this target receives its own audited card and no appliesTo list.

passages.title: A family confederation, not one solid block
passages.text: The founders were three sons of Buya from the mountainous Daylam region south of the Caspian. They first served other commanders, then seized different territories. Their shared family identity helped cooperation, but each brother built a regional court with its own soldiers, officials and ambitions.

passages.title: A family confederation, not one solid block
passages.text: Ray, Shiraz and Baghdad functioned as principal capitals, with Isfahan and other cities serving related courts. A messenger could not walk into one permanent Buyid capital and find every decision-maker there. Authority moved through a network of relatives whose rank and territory changed with inheritance and war.

passages.title: A family confederation, not one solid block
passages.text: When Ahmad entered Baghdad in 945, the Abbasid caliph did not disappear. The caliph retained religious prestige and granted titles, while the Buyid amir held military and political power. This layered arrangement explains why the names of both caliph and amirs could appear in public ritual and on coins.

passages.title: A family confederation, not one solid block
passages.text: After Fakhr al-Dawla died in 997, his widow Sayyida governed Ray for their four-year-old son. Her authority grew from a particular royal household and alliance network. It proves that one woman exercised sustained high power, not that women of every rank had the same choices.

passages.title: A family confederation, not one solid block
passages.text: Family ties could also sharpen conflict. Adud al-Dawla fought a cousin for Iraq, and later branches disputed seniority and provinces. The word dynasty can sound orderly, but succession meant negotiations, banquets, signed acknowledgments, rebellions and sometimes violence among people who were close relatives.

passages.title: Governing soldiers, taxes and cities
passages.text: Buyid governments kept older administrative offices for finance, official correspondence and the army. Clerks still had to assess revenue, write orders and record military obligations. A new ruling family changed who commanded the system, but it did not erase every office or skill inherited from Abbasid government.

passages.title: Governing soldiers, taxes and cities
passages.text: Many soldiers received an iqta, an assignment to collect revenue from land as pay. Under Buyid rules these grants were normally reassigned and did not automatically give the soldier legal authority over local residents. The army office estimated their fiscal value, turning fields and taxes into military accounts.

passages.title: Governing soldiers, taxes and cities
passages.text: A Fasa silver dirham from 959 or 960 names the caliph al-Muti, Rukn al-Dawla and Adud al-Dawla. Three authorities fit on a coin only 25.7 millimeters wide and weighing 2.91 grams. Money carried a miniature chart of layered rule into markets and purses.

passages.title: Governing soldiers, taxes and cities
passages.text: Court rank was performed as well as written. Thrones, audiences, titled amirs, viziers, commanders and attendants made hierarchy visible. Surviving court descriptions tell us far more about elite ceremony than about a porter’s workday, so this evidence should not be mistaken for everyone’s social life.

passages.title: Governing soldiers, taxes and cities
passages.text: Buyid Baghdad depended on mixed expertise. Early rulers used Turkish soldiers, locally recruited bureaucrats and workers brought from Ahvaz and Isfahan for palace construction. Government was therefore not a single ethnic team; military households, scribes, builders and city communities met within one changing political system.

passages.title: Households, neighborhoods and belief
passages.text: Excavated houses at Siraf often placed rooms around an open courtyard and used stairs to reach an upper story. Some windowless ground floors stored goods or may have been rented to poorer residents. Architecture hints at wealth differences, but it does not reveal every household’s kinship or sleeping arrangements.

passages.title: Households, neighborhoods and belief
passages.text: Building space at Siraf was tight, so residents often repaired existing houses and adjusted facades to neighboring streets. Some homes were large and decorated; nearby shops could be only about three by two meters. A wealthy port still contained cramped work spaces and households with unequal resources.

passages.title: Households, neighborhoods and belief
passages.text: Buyid rulers favored Shiite scholars, especially in Baghdad’s Karkh district, and a vizier founded a major library there in 991 or 992. Sunni institutions, the Abbasid caliph, Jewish communities and others continued. Patronage encouraged learning, while sectarian rivalry could also bring intimidation and violence.

passages.title: Households, neighborhoods and belief
passages.text: Medieval Shiraz included Sunni Muslims, Shiite patrons, Jews, Christians and Zoroastrians, and residents also celebrated Iranian festivals. Labels at court cannot describe every neighbor’s practice. Religion shaped law, calendars, study and public ceremonies, but city life joined communities with different traditions and unequal political protection.

passages.title: Households, neighborhoods and belief
passages.text: The evidence reviewed here does not provide a typical Buyid family size or a rule that every home followed. Royal genealogies show strategic marriages and inheritance; courtyard houses show shared domestic space; neither tells us exactly who cooked, cared for children or controlled money in an ordinary household.

passages.title: Food, markets and things that traveled
passages.text: The province around Arrajan sent date and grape syrups, olive oil, soap and cloth into long-distance trade. Sources also list dates, nuts, olives, grapes, oranges and lemons. These products make a vivid regional pantry, though a trade list cannot reconstruct one child’s breakfast or every family’s diet.

passages.title: Food, markets and things that traveled
passages.text: British Museum records identify ninth- and tenth-century cooking pots made in India and excavated at Siraf. A sturdy kitchen vessel could cross the Indian Ocean before holding food in a Gulf port. The catalogue establishes origin, date and findspot, but not the cook, recipe or household that used it.

passages.title: Food, markets and things that traveled
passages.text: Siraf’s elegant houses stood beside a bazaar that survived for centuries, while ships connected the port with East Africa and the Far East. Merchants depended on sailors, pack animals, warehouse workers, brokers and craftspeople. Imported luxury was visible, but most of the labor behind it remains unnamed.

passages.title: Food, markets and things that traveled
passages.text: Excavation found small bazaar lockups, some with ovens, as well as imported raw material, metalworking and a pottery complex with thirty kilns. Markets were places of making as well as buying. Heat, smoke, tools, clay and repeated skilled motions filled workdays that court chronicles rarely describe.

passages.title: Food, markets and things that traveled
passages.text: A tenth-century gold ewer names the Buyid ruler Bakhtiyar, but its handle is probably later. A silk once labeled Buyid is now dated by the Met to the early twentieth century. Museum research can rewrite an object’s story, so neither luxury piece should become automatic evidence for ordinary Buyid tables or clothing.

passages.title: Water, baths and the toilet question
passages.text: The Band-e Amir weir crossed the Kor River near Shiraz. Masonry foundations and stonework raised water for irrigation, while ten waterwheels reportedly lifted it toward hundreds of villages; the structure also carried a bridge. Royal funding mattered, but builders, farmers and repair crews made the system work.

passages.title: Water, baths and the toilet question
passages.text: Shiraz drew drinking water from mountain springs, and Rokn al-Dawla built a subterranean channel carrying spring water about ten kilometers to the city. Gardens produced fruits, flowers and vegetables. Water linked daily drinking, food growing, prestige and maintenance long before anyone could turn a tap.

passages.title: Water, baths and the toilet question
passages.text: At Siraf, earthenware pipes carried roof water into stone-lined pits, and excavators found stone-lined drains. Streets were unpaved, alleys could fill with rubbish, and even rich houses sometimes had weak sewage arrangements. Medieval sanitation was practical in places and seriously limited in others.

passages.title: Water, baths and the toilet question
passages.text: A public bath at Siraf, built before 1050, had an entry or changing room, an unheated room, warm rooms over hypocaust floors and a hot room heated by a furnace. It also included drains and a latrine. Bathing required fuel, water, engineering and staff, not just a pool.

passages.title: Water, baths and the toilet question
passages.text: The Great Mosque at Siraf gained rooms for ablution, latrines and storage during repeated rebuilding. That is direct toilet evidence for a public institution, not proof that every home had the same facilities. Archaeology gives us particular drains and rooms, while household habits remain unevenly visible.

passages.title: Medicine, books and learning
passages.text: Adud al-Dawla founded endowed hospitals, including a famous institution in Baghdad and another in Shiraz. One Shiraz complex taught medicine, astronomy, philosophy and mathematics. Hospitals were organized institutions with staff and funding, though the sources do not give a patient diary or survival rate.

passages.title: Medicine, books and learning
passages.text: Ibn Marzuban studied religious law and sciences and became superintendent of the Adudi hospital as well as a judge. His administrative role is clearer than his treatment of patients. The record reminds us that caring for the sick required budgets, supplies and supervision alongside medical knowledge.

passages.title: Medicine, books and learning
passages.text: The physician al-Majusi dedicated the Complete Book of the Medical Art to Adud al-Dawla. A surviving National Library of Medicine copy was made in 1208 by a Christian scribe, centuries after the dedication. It proves the work’s later transmission, not that this manuscript sat in a Buyid hospital.

passages.title: Medicine, books and learning
passages.text: Adud al-Dawla studied Arabic, geometry and astronomy, and his Shiraz library kept a separate list for each subject. That sounds almost like a catalog search before computers. It documents elite and specialist learning; it does not show that every child attended school or could read.

passages.title: Medicine, books and learning
passages.text: Abu Said al-Sirafi, born at the Gulf port, became a leading grammarian in Baghdad. His father came from a Zoroastrian family and converted to Islam. A scholar’s path could cross religion, language, port trade and capital-city teaching, but one famous career is not a literacy rate.

passages.title: Stars, art and words on metal and stone
passages.text: Al-Sufi’s Book of the Fixed Stars combined inherited constellation knowledge with his own observations. It paired drawings with tables giving star coordinates calculated for 964. Readers could compare a picture in a book with measured positions overhead, and later astronomers continued to use the work.

passages.title: Stars, art and words on metal and stone
passages.text: A brass astrolabe signed by al-Khujandi in 984 or 985 has pointers for thirty-three stars; some end in little birds’ heads. The portable instrument could help tell time, find prayer direction and study the sky. Its signature survives, but its exact first owner does not.

passages.title: Stars, art and words on metal and stone
passages.text: Adud al-Dawla left a commemorative inscription at Persepolis in 955 or 956 that included Persian names in Arabic writing. Choosing an ancient royal site connected new power with an older landscape. The inscription records elite memory-making, not a return to the language or government of ancient Persia.

passages.title: Stars, art and words on metal and stone
passages.text: An authentic Buyid written sample is “الامير العدل” (al-amīr al-ʿadl), translated by the Ashmolean as “the Just Amir.” It appears in Arabic script on the reverse of Adud al-Dawla’s silver Fasa dirham from 959 or 960. This is coin titulature, not an ordinary person’s spoken sentence.

passages.title: Stars, art and words on metal and stone
passages.text: Putting a ruler’s name on a dirham announced political autonomy, while keeping the Abbasid caliph’s name signaled religious allegiance. The same coin could therefore speak in more than one political voice. Readers should treat its formula as an official message, not neutral reporting.

passages.title: How Buyid rule ended and what continued
passages.text: In 1029 Ghaznavid Sultan Mahmud seized Ray, deposed Majd al-Dawla and ended the northern Buyid principality. A related Kakuyid ruler still maneuvered around Isfahan and Hamadan. Political change happened branch by branch, so one dramatic “fall of the empire” date would hide the real sequence.

passages.title: How Buyid rule ended and what continued
passages.text: Seljuk forces captured Isfahan in 1051 after a destructive siege. The city then recovered as people returned, taxes were suspended temporarily and buildings were repaired. A conquest could end one political arrangement while the streets, workshops and resident communities became part of another.

passages.title: How Buyid rule ended and what continued
passages.text: Tughril Beg entered Baghdad in 1055 and the last Buyid amir there was imprisoned. The Abbasid caliph remained, now under Seljuk power. The atlas’s clean 1100 Seljuk shape compresses this transition, but the political handoff in Baghdad has a specific historical date.

passages.title: How Buyid rule ended and what continued
passages.text: A Buyid branch survived in Fars until about 1062. Shabankara forces took the province before it passed under Seljuk control, so the structured successor link points to the atlas’s Seljuk id while the prose preserves the intermediate conquest. That distinction prevents a neat but false one-step story.

passages.title: How Buyid rule ended and what continued
passages.text: Dynasties end more quickly than daily systems. Buyid patrons disappeared, yet Arabic scholarship, hospitals, irrigation works, markets, coins, cultivated land and mixed city populations continued to change under Ghaznavid, Kakuyid, Shabankara and Seljuk rulers. Continuity belonged to people and places, not an atlas label.

Buyid rule ended in stages rather than on the atlas boundary. Ghaznavids took Ray in 1029, Seljuks captured Isfahan in 1051 and Tughril Beg ended Buyid government in Baghdad in 1055. A southern line held Fars until about 1062, when Shabankara forces conquered it before Seljuk control followed. The successor link therefore points to the atlas’s Seljuk Empire id while preserving that intermediate step. Abbasid caliphs, city residents, farms, markets, hospitals, books, waterworks and craft traditions continued under new political masters. The eastern buyid-emirate polygon and the late 1200 Buyid labels are map errors, not surviving states.
