passages.text: The Cape Colony joined an Atlantic port to an expanding southern African frontier. Its communities included Khoikhoi, San, Xhosa, enslaved people and their descendants, and settlers. British rule, slavery, trade and wars made daily life profoundly unequal.

passages.title: Power, freedom and dispossession
passages.text: A parliament did not mean everyone had equal power. The Cape obtained representative government in 1853 and responsible government in 1872, allowing local ministers more control within British imperial rule. These changes concerned colonial institutions in a society already divided by ownership and coercion.

passages.title: Power, freedom and dispossession
passages.text: On the eastern frontier, successive wars between 1779 and 1878 brought conquest and dispossession. Xhosa and Khoikhoi communities lost land and livestock as colonial settlement advanced. The map’s expanding outline therefore represents upheaval in people’s homes and livelihoods.

passages.title: Power, freedom and dispossession
passages.text: Cape slavery legally ended on 1 December 1834, but most formerly enslaved people had to serve another four years as unpaid apprentices. Full release from that compulsory system came in December 1838. A declaration of freedom and the ability to leave a master were different milestones.

passages.title: Meals, marbles and washing up
passages.text: An inspection of Cape Town’s Slave Lodge in 1803 described dark, unhealthy rooms where even daytime inspection needed a lantern. In 1807 officials decided to sell its enslaved residents and reuse the building as government offices. A change of building use did not free those people.

passages.title: Meals, marbles and washing up
passages.text: The Slave Lodge excavation found a well, cobbled floors and the edge of a latrine. Its preliminary animal-bone sample included sheep, cattle, fowl and pig, alongside fish and shellfish. These mixed historical deposits help researchers investigate food and water without supplying a complete household menu.

passages.title: Meals, marbles and washing up
passages.text: Other Slave Lodge finds include scissors, pins, buttons, beads and stoneware marbles. Small things bring sewing, dress and play into view beside official records. A marble is a welcome reminder that history also happened near the floor.

passages.title: Meals, marbles and washing up
passages.text: At Koopmans-de Wet House, a Cape buffet made around 1780 to 1800 has a zinc basin, folding shelves and fold-out leaves. Glasses and porcelain could be washed in the dining room. This sideboard had a much busier job than merely looking elegant.

passages.title: Meals, marbles and washing up
passages.text: The house museum displays Chinese, Japanese and British ceramics in a reconstruction of a wealthy Cape home. Its dining service and other furnishings need their own collection histories: some were later donations. They show the goods reaching the Cape, rather than an untouched family dinner table.

passages.title: Meals, marbles and washing up
passages.text: A pantry trapdoor once connected to the kitchen below; its ladder or stair was removed during restoration. Such a practical opening reveals how serving and cooking were organized. Behind an impressive dining room lay the work of carrying, preparing and clearing meals.

passages.title: Reading, stars and shared time
passages.text: A surviving newspaper title gives a short Xhosa writing sample: “Imvo zabantsundu”. Its English section was called “Native opinion”, the historical wording recorded in the library catalogue. John Tengo Jabavu published the paper at King William’s Town from November 1884, creating a printed forum for readers.

passages.title: Reading, stars and shared time
passages.text: The Royal Observatory was authorized in 1820 to improve knowledge of southern stars and navigation. Fearon Fallows initially worked from a prefabricated hut; his 1824 catalogue listed 273 southern stars. Careful measuring could begin before the impressive permanent building arrived.

passages.title: Reading, stars and shared time
passages.text: The observatory also helped ships keep time. Visible time balls gave captains a signal for checking their clocks; electrical connections later coordinated signals across several towns. Astronomy here was useful to sailors deciding where they were, not only to people admiring the night sky.

The Cape Colony ended as a separate colony when it joined the Union of South Africa on 31 May 1910. Its peoples continued, but Black South Africans had been excluded from the negotiations establishing the Union. The imported map interval ending in 1914 runs beyond this constitutional change.

sectionTitles: Homes, work and food: evidence from Kınık Höyük
Gathering places and the limits of household evidence
What continued after the map ends

passages.text: The atlas labels a broad northern Anatolian outline “Cappadocia” from 323 to 200 BCE. It excludes tested points at Mazaca, Tyana and Kınık Höyük, which are central to the historical context below, while including Ankara and Bursa. Treat the color as a problematic imported outline, not a verified kingdom boundary. This card explains the early Cappadocian kingdom and clearly located evidence from the wider region; neither the map’s beginning nor its endpoint marks the whole history.

passages.title: From imperial province to kingdom
passages.text: Cappadocia had more than one meaning. A large geographical region had contained two Persian provinces; in the third century BCE, Pontus and the southern Cappadocian kingdom developed separately. A shared regional name did not make their courts, rulers or borders identical.

passages.title: From imperial province to kingdom
passages.text: The early Ariarathid family operated first under Persian and then Macedonian power. Scholars know relatively little about Ariarathes I and II. Independent kingship is associated with Ariaramnes or his son and co-ruler Ariarathes III in the middle of the third century BCE, so a neat uninterrupted royal timeline would hide uncertainty.

passages.title: From imperial province to kingdom
passages.text: Royal family relationships were political connections. Ariaramnes arranged marriages linking his daughter and his son with the Seleucid ruling house. These were decisions about powerful households and alliances, not evidence that ordinary Cappadocian families organized marriages in the same way.

passages.title: From imperial province to kingdom
passages.text: Horse breeding supported both wealth and military power in the region’s Persian background. Horses required grazing, care and training before a rider ever appeared in battle. Cappadocian royal names and traditions also preserved Iranian connections while rulers participated in the Greek-speaking political world.

passages.title: Homes, work and food: evidence from Kınık Höyük
passages.text: Kınık Höyük lies in southern Cappadocia, outside this imported outline. In its early to middle Hellenistic quarter, excavators uncovered small, single-room houses about 4.5 meters square, with stone foundations and mudbrick walls. These modest buildings offer a useful counterweight to a history told only through kings.

passages.title: Homes, work and food: evidence from Kınık Höyük
passages.text: An earlier room in the same Hellenistic sequence held a large storage jar, clay-tray fragments and ash. Researchers interpret it as a place for storing and preparing food. Pots and deposits help reconstruct practical household tasks even when the names and relationships of the people using them are lost.

passages.title: Homes, work and food: evidence from Kınık Höyük
passages.text: Next door, fire installations, cooking vessels, glass and iron slag, and a glass bead led excavators to interpret another room as a metal- and glass-working space. Making things and preparing food occupied closely connected rooms. A few crumbs of industrial waste can be more revealing than a beautiful finished object.

passages.title: Homes, work and food: evidence from Kınık Höyük
passages.text: The Hellenistic investigation also recovered many textile-production tools from both the citadel and lower town. They point toward the repeated skilled work behind cloth. Clothes did not begin in a shop: someone had to prepare fibers and turn them into thread and fabric.

passages.title: Homes, work and food: evidence from Kınık Höyük
passages.text: Charred grape seeds, stalks and vine wood from Kınık Höyük reveal a substantial grape-growing economy. One studied phase spans 500 to 200 BCE, overlapping the atlas years. Vine wood used as fuel particularly supports nearby vineyards: these remains are evidence of cultivation, not just a traveler dropping a grape.

passages.title: Homes, work and food: evidence from Kınık Höyük
passages.text: What happened to the harvest? Grapes could be eaten fresh, dried or processed. The study suggests that some seed-and-stalk deposits may include winemaking waste, but does not identify every product with certainty. A charred seed is an excellent clue; it is not a labeled ancient menu.

passages.title: Homes, work and food: evidence from Kınık Höyük
passages.text: Vine-growing also generated fuel. Pruning produced branches that could feed fires, and grapevine charcoal survives at the site. The same cultivated plant could provide food or drink and material for heating or craftwork. This connection makes tiny burned fragments valuable evidence for a much larger working landscape.

passages.title: Gathering places and the limits of household evidence
passages.text: The sanctuary’s earlier occupation, dated from the late Persian to middle Hellenistic period, produced vessels shaped like birds, often birds of prey. These objects connect skilled ceramic work with religious activity. A drinking or pouring vessel could be a sculpted creature rather than a plain pot.

passages.title: Gathering places and the limits of household evidence
passages.text: In a Hellenistic mudbrick building, excavators found a large vessel placed in a wall niche and proposed a connection with ritual wine drinking. Its placement makes a social or ceremonial interpretation plausible. The report does not let us reconstruct a complete guest list, seating plan or family celebration.

passages.title: Gathering places and the limits of household evidence
passages.text: The excavated food and workshop rooms preserve floors, walls, ash and equipment. They do not supply a documented household toilet or medical routine for this period. Those parts of daily life remain gaps in this evidence, rather than an invitation to borrow practices from much later cave settlements.

passages.title: A name written on money
passages.text: A copper-alloy coin in the British Museum, dated about 280 to 230 BCE and attributed to Tyana, shows Ariaramnes wearing a leather helmet on one side and a galloping spearman on the other. At only 19 millimeters across, it carried a ruler’s image in a remarkably small space.

passages.title: A name written on money
passages.text: An authentic Greek name appears on a bronze coin recorded in the Berlin collection: ΑΡΙΑΡΑΜΝΟΥ, Ariaramnou, meaning “of Ariaramnes.” This is a modern typographic transcription of the catalogue’s coin legend, dated broadly to his third-century BCE rule. The name sits beside a horseman, tying writing and royal imagery together.

passages.title: A name written on money
passages.text: The coin’s Greek spelling also helps historians identify a ruler whom written narratives sometimes call Ariamnes. Comparing texts and objects can correct a name rather than merely decorate a story. It shows Greek use in a royal setting, without telling us how many children learned to read or what language each family spoke.

passages.title: What continued after the map ends
passages.text: Later Hellenistic layers at Kınık Höyük, after the atlas’s 200 BCE endpoint, contain evidence for larger public religious displays. Excavators reconstructed fragments from ceramic bulls, some over a meter long, and proposed a sanctuary connected with Dionysus. These are later developments at a continuing site, not furnishings for a scene in 300 BCE.

passages.title: What continued after the map ends
passages.text: The monarchy outlasted the map by centuries. In 17 CE, under Emperor Tiberius, Cappadocia became a Roman province after King Archelaus died in Rome. Tacitus recounts the summons, charges and royal humiliation. The administrative outcome is clear even though his account leaves the exact manner of death uncertain.

passages.title: What continued after the map ends
passages.text: The famous rock-cut Christian dwellings and churches belong to still later regional history. UNESCO places early monastic communities in the fourth century CE and many richly painted churches after 842. They are remarkable achievements, but treating them as homes of the early Cappadocian kings would move them backward by many centuries.

The atlas stops at 200 BCE, while Cappadocian monarchy continued until Roman annexation in 17 CE. Royal government ended; the region and its inhabitants did not disappear. This administrative transformation must be kept separate from the much earlier endpoint of the imported map record.

sectionTitles: Discoveries and methods build local stories
Sea, weather, movement and other neighbors
Food was gathered, caught, grown and shared
Tools, art and exchange were major achievements
Homes, families, women and social life
Children learned by living and doing
Health, healing, water and the toilet question

passages.text: “Caribbean hunter-gatherers” is the atlas’s map label, not one people. From 1500 BCE to 700 CE its polygon bundles parts of Cuba, Hispaniola, Puerto Rico, the Lesser Antilles, Barbados, Venezuela and the Guianas. Then it shrinks, splits, disappears from most islands, returns in 1500, and ends as a tiny mainland patch in 1700. Those jumps reflect changing atlas categories, Ciboney, Arawaks, Taíno, Kalinago, Lokono and colonial states, not synchronized migrations or extinctions. Real Caribbean communities had different histories. Some fished, gathered shellfish, hunted, gardened and used pottery in changing combinations; none stayed frozen as “hunter-gatherers” for 3,200 years. Canoes connected islands, while ornaments, stone, food and stories traveled through overlapping networks. Archaeologists recover postholes, hearths, burials, food residues, teeth, bones, ancient DNA and even coprolites. Yes, ancient poo can become scientific treasure: it preserves plant fragments, parasites and microbes. Homes could be rebuilt quickly after hurricanes, children learned skilled work by watching and practicing, and families cared for babies with locally specific feeding traditions. European invasion brought warfare, enslavement, epidemic disease, forced labor and displacement, yet Indigenous people resisted and survived. Taíno, Kalinago, Lokono and other descendant communities remain living peoples. The map’s 1700 deletion is not their ending.

passages.title: First read the map’s seams
passages.text: The live index calls this a culture, dates it approximately from 1500 BCE to 1700 and supplies no historical summary. Coverage finds thirty consecutive intervals and thirty border files but no card. The exact id is preserved for software compatibility; the label itself needs a warning.

passages.title: First read the map’s seams
passages.text: From 1500 BCE through 700 CE, the same MultiPolygon has 25 parts, 596 coordinate positions and bounds reaching from roughly 84.71°W to 48.40°W and 1.74°S to 23.14°N. A perfectly frozen border for 2,200 years signals editorial geometry, not surveyed territory.

passages.title: First read the map’s seams
passages.text: At 800 the shape drops to four parts and at 1000 to three. Tested island points change to Ciboney, Arawaks and Taíno owners, while Barbados and Paria remain here. These are layer-to-layer classification changes; the coordinates do not document an invasion, language frontier or mass departure.

passages.title: First read the map’s seams
passages.text: The 1400 file contains two exact features with the same id: a 92-position Paria polygon and a separate 25-position Amazon-mouth polygon. In 1492 only the smaller one remains; in 1500 three components return. That duplicate-and-return sequence is an atlas oddity, not a recoverable ancient border.

passages.title: First read the map’s seams
passages.text: By 1530, tested islands and Paria carry colonial or named Indigenous layers while this id retreats to untested mainland remnants. At 1650 only one small polygon remains; at 1700 it vanishes. No evidence supports treating that deletion as a people’s conquest, migration or extinction.

passages.title: Discoveries and methods build local stories
passages.text: Caribbean archaeology combines stratigraphy, artifacts, plant and animal remains, burials, settlement plans and direct dates. Its basic achievement is regional comparison without assuming islands were isolated. Canoe travel connected them to one another and to surrounding mainlands for millennia before European arrival.

passages.title: Discoveries and methods build local stories
passages.text: At eight Cuban sites, researchers measured carbon, nitrogen, sulfur and strontium isotopes in 146 people. Results show varied diets and movement among communities often lumped into an “Archaic” label. Isotopes describe sampled lives and childhood geology; they do not reveal a person’s language or self-name.

passages.title: Discoveries and methods build local stories
passages.text: A 2026 preprint reports early genome-wide data from four people on Hispaniola’s Samaná Peninsula and compares them with Cuba and later Caribbean samples. It suggests long pre-Ceramic continuity plus local structure, but remains unreviewed and sparsely sampled. Genetics cannot turn an atlas polygon into one population.

passages.title: Discoveries and methods build local stories
passages.text: A larger ancient-DNA study analyzes 174 people, detects multiple movements and even relatives buried on different islands. Such work can illuminate ancestry and mobility, never culture by itself. Researchers must also respect descendant communities, destructive sampling limits and the uneven survival of tropical human remains.

passages.title: Discoveries and methods build local stories
passages.text: Colonial writers called very different people “Carib,” often to mark enemies or justify enslavement. Ancient DNA from the Lesser Antilles shows why modern researchers must test, rather than inherit, those labels. Pottery style, ancestry, political alliance and spoken language are separate questions with different evidence.

passages.title: Sea, weather, movement and other neighbors
passages.text: The first island voyagers crossed water beyond sight of land, and later communities maintained routes through currents, winds and seasonal seas. Boats rarely survive, so archaeologists infer travel from island settlement, transported stone, animals, plants and human movement. “Island” never meant “alone.”

passages.title: Sea, weather, movement and other neighbors
passages.text: Montserrat’s early deposits and Antigua’s valuable chert sources help date movement through the eastern Caribbean. Direct radiocarbon results can overturn old migration diagrams, while stone sourcing traces journeys. A tool’s rock may tell where material began, though not who paddled it or why.

passages.title: Sea, weather, movement and other neighbors
passages.text: Hurricanes, storm surges, drought and scarce freshwater repeatedly challenged settlements. Archaeology suggests flexible food systems and houses built from local materials could favor quick recovery. That was skilled resilience, not proof that storms were harmless; different islands and households faced unequal risks.

passages.title: Sea, weather, movement and other neighbors
passages.text: Human communities altered island ecologies by moving plants and animals, clearing or burning land and harvesting coasts, but impacts varied. Some fish or shellfish records show sustained use over centuries; others indicate pressure. “People damaged nature” and “people lived perfectly sustainably” are both too simple.

passages.title: Sea, weather, movement and other neighbors
passages.text: Hutia bones are not just leftover dinner. Isotope work in the Dominican Republic compares rodent diets across habitats and asks whether animals fed within human-made niches. The result reveals changing proximity between people, gardens and endemic animals without assuming every hutia was domesticated or eaten.

passages.title: Food was gathered, caught, grown and shared
passages.text: No single “hunter-gatherer menu” fits this layer. Fish, shellfish, crabs, birds, rodents, fruits, roots, maize, beans, peppers and other plants appear in different combinations. Gardens and wild foods could coexist, so archaeologists increasingly describe mixed food systems instead of forcing every site into farmer-versus-forager boxes.

passages.title: Food was gathered, caught, grown and shared
passages.text: DNA and starch from Puerto Rican coprolites identify maize, sweet potato, chili, peanut, papaya, tomato and other plants, yet absence is not proof a food was never eaten. Cooking, digestion, season and tropical decay destroy traces. Ancient poo is gross-looking scientific gold, but it is still a tiny sample.

passages.title: Food was gathered, caught, grown and shared
passages.text: Cassava needs careful language. Toxic varieties require grating, squeezing and cooking, but starch studies also find sweet potato, maize and beans, sometimes where cassava was expected. Flat ceramic griddles are clues, not automatic “cassava labels”; residue, tool use-wear and context must agree.

passages.title: Food was gathered, caught, grown and shared
passages.text: Organic molecules absorbed into Isla de Mona pottery show plant processing during early colonial occupation. Historical and archaeological evidence indicates cassava bread production intensified for Spanish supply under coercive labor. A familiar Indigenous food thus became entangled with an imposed export economy, without losing local knowledge.

passages.title: Food was gathered, caught, grown and shared
passages.text: Dental calculus, the hardened plaque nobody wants at the dentist, can trap plant particles, proteins and microbial DNA. Puerto Rican samples reveal diet and oral ecology, but contamination and preservation require strict controls. One mouth records one life; it cannot supply a menu for every island.

passages.title: Tools, art and exchange were major achievements
passages.text: Stone flakes, ground tools, shell implements, fiber, wood and pottery supported fishing, gardening, cooking and repair. Labels such as Lithic, Archaic, Saladoid or Ostionoid organize changing assemblages; they are research tools, not passports carried by one fixed people from island to island.

passages.title: Tools, art and exchange were major achievements
passages.text: Lesser Antillean exchange operated at several scales. Everyday stone and pottery, visible ornaments and rare ceremonial valuables moved in different rhythms. Sourcing raw materials and studying manufacture let archaeologists rebuild relationships; an imported bead signals a connection, not necessarily a merchant, tribute or migration.

passages.title: Tools, art and exchange were major achievements
passages.text: Before 1492, polished wood, greenstone, shell, guanín metal and food already circulated in systems of value. European beads and bells initially entered those networks, then became entangled with tribute and extraction. Indigenous participants evaluated strange shiny objects through existing ideas of beauty, status and obligation.

passages.title: Tools, art and exchange were major achievements
passages.text: Dominican settlements preserve ornaments in homes, refuse and burials. Following an object from manufacture through wear, repair, gifting and final deposit shows that adornment could build identity and memory. It also guards against calling every beautiful item elite treasure merely because museums prize it today.

passages.title: Tools, art and exchange were major achievements
passages.text: A carved wooden duho from Hispaniola shows extraordinary woodworking and polished surface treatment. Its human-animal imagery and seat form connect leadership and ceremony, while its collection history and broad date demand caution. One museum object cannot define the beliefs or furniture of an entire archipelago.

passages.title: Homes, families, women and social life
passages.text: Circular and oval post patterns reveal houses built with flexible organic materials. Caribbean examples differ from continental reconstructions and from colonial descriptions, so diameter, post spacing, rebuilding and storm exposure matter. A missing wall does not mean people lived outdoors; leaves, fiber and wood usually decay.

passages.title: Homes, families, women and social life
passages.text: At El Flaco in the Dominican Republic, leveled house areas, surrounding mounds, ash, garbage, gardens and burials show domestic spaces repeatedly remade. Ancestors and daily work could share one landscape. Archaeologists read soil layers and postholes; they cannot simply copy a chronicler’s village sketch.

passages.title: Homes, families, women and social life
passages.text: Jamaican house sizes and hillside terraces suggest some late communities used smaller residential groups, possibly nuclear-family households, while Puerto Rican sequences show different changes. Kinship remains debated because a roof group, work team, descent group and political community need not have identical membership.

passages.title: Homes, families, women and social life
passages.text: Women appear in colonial stories filtered through European agendas, and objects cannot be assigned a gender automatically. Household archaeology at En Bas Saline instead compares activity areas, class and change after conquest. It finds persistence as well as disruption, warning against a single tale of instant social collapse.

passages.title: Homes, families, women and social life
passages.text: Families cooked, repaired tools, cared for children, tended plants, fished, exchanged news and honored the dead, but tasks varied by household and life stage. Archaeology can locate hearths and work debris more securely than it can label “men’s work” or “women’s work” across 3,200 years.

passages.title: Children learned by living and doing
passages.text: At Canímar Abajo, carbon and nitrogen isotopes from children and adult women support a local model: milk supplied most protein through about age two, plant supplements grew in importance, and weaning likely ended near three. This describes sampled Cuban burials, not a Caribbean-wide parenting rule.

passages.title: Children learned by living and doing
passages.text: Children probably learned swimming, paddling, fishing, plant knowledge, cooking, pottery and craft through observation, stories and practice. Finished objects prove expertise, while mistakes and small tools may hint at learners; no surviving timetable tells us lesson ages. Education was broader than a classroom.

passages.title: Children learned by living and doing
passages.text: Clothing rarely survives tropical soil, but cotton, fiber tools, ornaments and early accounts show bodies were dressed and decorated in varied ways. A bead or pendant could mark beauty, relationship, age or status. Researchers should not turn one contact-era description into everyone’s daily outfit.

passages.title: Children learned by living and doing
passages.text: Work and play can overlap. Swimming, racing, dancing, music, storytelling and ball games built skill and community, while formal plazas and carved boulders anchor some events archaeologically. We can identify a ball-court setting more confidently than the jokes, rules or cheers heard there.

passages.title: Children learned by living and doing
passages.text: A warm daily-life fact: people who grew up among islands likely learned the sea as a moving landscape, currents, cloud shapes, winds and familiar silhouettes mattered. Archaeology proves repeated voyaging and exchange, though it cannot recover each teaching rhyme. Skilled navigation was learned knowledge, not lucky drifting.

passages.title: Health, healing, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Bones and teeth can reveal injury, infection, anemia, diet and workload, but most illnesses leave no trace. Dental calculus adds oral microbes and food particles. Researchers describe patterns in specific cemeteries rather than diagnosing every community, and care by relatives often remains archaeologically invisible.

passages.title: Health, healing, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Vieques coprolites preserve parasite eggs and DNA consistent with exposure through fish, rodents, dogs and contaminated surroundings. That evidence documents real health burdens without proving people understood microbes. Parasites also connect diet, animal proximity, water and waste in ways a single artifact cannot.

passages.title: Health, healing, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Coprolite metagenomics can reconstruct gut microbes and foods even in a humid tropic, but Caribbean samples are rare and degraded. Differences between sampled Huecoid and Saladoid deposits are intriguing, not timeless biological traits. Laboratory controls matter because modern microbial contamination is everywhere, including on scientists.

passages.title: Health, healing, water and the toilet question
passages.text: No toilet type is securely attributable to this atlas umbrella. People could use peripheral places, pits, middens or fields, and tropical decay erases waste. Archaeologists need concentrated fecal chemistry, parasite eggs and convincing feature context before calling a hole a latrine rather than storage or rubbish.

passages.title: Health, healing, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Plants certainly served food and other needs, but identifying medicine requires context, residue or careful historical evidence. A Smithsonian guide to Guiana medicinal plants is useful later comparison for nearby living knowledge, not a prescription book for ancient islanders. Freshwater access likewise varied sharply by island.

passages.title: Belief, leadership, conflict and coercion
passages.text: Burials under or near household spaces, carved zemí figures, cave imagery, duhos and plazas show that ancestors, powerful beings and ceremony shaped some communities. Meanings changed across time and place. Similar-looking objects may participate in different stories, and descendant interpretations deserve space beside museum labels.

passages.title: Belief, leadership, conflict and coercion
passages.text: Petroglyphs and pictographs are meaningful images, not automatically writing. Around the Jacaná ball court, recording each boulder’s placement helps connect imagery with movement and ceremony. Without a demonstrated sign system tied to speech, no honest transliteration or sentence-level translation can be supplied.

passages.title: Belief, leadership, conflict and coercion
passages.text: Leadership ranged from household influence to powerful caciques, while alliances and obligations crossed islands. Rich objects and plazas can indicate rank, yet chroniclers filtered Indigenous politics through European categories. “Chiefdom” is a model to test locally, not a title for every society inside the polygon.

passages.title: Belief, leadership, conflict and coercion
passages.text: Spanish invasion brought organized violence, fort building, tribute demands and campaigns against resistance. Indigenous people fought, fled, negotiated, sabotaged and formed new alliances. Calling the outcome “contact” alone hides force; calling islanders passive victims hides their decisions and the colonizers’ incomplete control.

passages.title: Belief, leadership, conflict and coercion
passages.text: Raiding and enslavement reshaped coasts and islands. Colonial officials could label opponents “Caribs” to make capture appear legal, and enslavement continued through exceptions even after the New Laws. Those categories served power; they cannot be projected backward as clean ethnic borders on this map.

passages.title: Languages, invasion and living continuity
passages.text: The atlas label supplies no language. Taíno and Lokono belong to Arawakan histories, while Kalinago language history, multilingualism and colonial naming are more complex. Shared words, pottery or ancestry cannot prove everyone spoke alike. “Arawakan” is a language-family relationship, not one timeless Caribbean nation.

passages.title: Languages, invasion and living continuity
passages.text: Contemporaneous written-language sample: none can be responsibly attributed to this exact record. Indigenous Caribbean communities carried rich oral, musical and visual traditions, but no securely deciphered local script yields original text, transliteration and translation. Borrowing nearby Maya glyphs or later European spellings would fabricate an umbrella voice.

passages.title: Languages, invasion and living continuity
passages.text: At LaSoye Point in Dominica, Cayo pottery beside European goods records early commerce in a place exposed by storm erosion. Indigenous people selected, reused and reinterpreted imports. Trade did not make the encounter equal: plantation settlement and war soon narrowed the choices available to island communities.

passages.title: Languages, invasion and living continuity
passages.text: A Lucayan genome shares ancestry with present-day Puerto Rican people, and broader studies also find Indigenous biological continuity. Genetics is only one strand: survival also lives in family memory, food, craft, place names, activism and community belonging. No DNA percentage can certify or cancel an identity.

passages.title: Languages, invasion and living continuity
passages.text: Kalinago people in Dominica maintain their territory, governance, farming, basketry, canoe knowledge and public cultural life. Taíno and other descendants likewise organize across the Caribbean and diaspora. The atlas ends this catchall in 1700 because its taxonomy changes; living communities make extinction language both false and harmful.

At 1700 the exact atlas id disappears after shrinking to one small Amazon-mouth polygon. That endpoint does not match a single defeat, migration, language death or cultural extinction. Colonial states expanded through war, disease, slavery and displacement, while Indigenous people resisted, moved, formed new alliances and maintained families, knowledge and identities. Taíno, Kalinago, Lokono and other descendant communities remain living peoples, so this card records editorial continuity rather than a fall and names no automatic successor.

sectionTitles: Court life, including the awkward bits
What buildings, books and fields reveal

passages.text: Charlemagne’s imperial coronation in 800 gave a new Roman title to a large Frankish monarchy. Its rulers joined conquest with Christian government and support for learning. The realm divided among his grandsons in 843; later Carolingian kings and emperors did not continuously govern one united empire. The map’s label through 1000 combines different political phases.

passages.title: Court life, including the awkward bits
passages.text: Einhard, a writer close to Charlemagne’s court, says the ruler enjoyed the warm baths at Aachen and invited sons, nobles and attendants to join him. The royal bath could be a social occasion. This describes a privileged court, not bathing facilities in every village.

passages.title: Court life, including the awkward bits
passages.text: According to Einhard, Charlemagne had his sons and daughters taught the liberal arts. Boys also practiced riding and hunting, while girls learned textile work. The account reveals a royal educational ideal with different expectations for boys and girls, rather than universal schooling.

passages.title: Court life, including the awkward bits
passages.text: Einhard says the aging ruler disliked doctors who urged him to exchange roasted meat for boiled meat. Even an emperor could be an uncooperative patient. The anecdote preserves a court writer’s portrait, not evidence that its dietary advice was effective medicine.

passages.title: Court life, including the awkward bits
passages.text: Charlemagne reportedly practiced writing on tablets kept beneath his pillow, but began late and made little progress. The same biography praises his interest in learned subjects. Being a powerful patron of books did not automatically make handwriting easy.

passages.title: What buildings, books and fields reveal
passages.text: Aachen’s palace chapel organized worship around an eight-sided central space, with an upper gallery and a dome. Ancient columns were reused in the building. Its architecture connected the Carolingian court with prestigious Roman and Christian traditions through materials as well as ceremony.

passages.title: What buildings, books and fields reveal
passages.text: The chapel’s surviving bronze gates belong to its early history, but the brilliant mosaic decorating today’s dome was installed in 1880 to 1881. A beautiful old building can contain several centuries at once. Archaeologists and architectural historians separate those layers before reconstructing Charlemagne’s surroundings.

passages.title: What buildings, books and fields reveal
passages.text: Scholars such as Alcuin helped develop court learning and the copying of books. Carolingian minuscule used clearer, more regular letter forms that made manuscripts easier to read. This was a major scribal achievement, although producing a book still required skilled labor and expensive materials.

passages.title: What buildings, books and fields reveal
passages.text: A Gospel book made around 825 to 850, probably at Metz, survives on parchment with ink and painted decoration. Its arcaded canon tables cross-reference passages in the four Gospels. They are both attractive pages and practical finding aids: a manuscript could help readers navigate as well as impress them.

passages.title: What buildings, books and fields reveal
passages.text: The famous plan sent from Reichenau to St Gall around 820 consists of five pieces of parchment sewn together. It was prepared for Abbot Gozbert as a framework for thinking about a monastery. It is evidence for planning and ideals, not a photograph proving every building existed exactly as drawn.

passages.title: What buildings, books and fields reveal
passages.text: The plan’s Latin dedicatory letter invites its readers to “perscrutinare,” meaning “examine closely,” and “sollertiam exercere,” meaning “exercise ingenuity.” These short phrases are transcribed in the abbey library’s scholarly catalogue. The designers expected the recipient to think about the plan, not simply copy it without judgment.

passages.title: What buildings, books and fields reveal
passages.text: At Mérigest near modern Sénart, archaeologists identified a ninth-century rural unit with two timber-post buildings, a well and three successive cooking ovens. One building was probably a house. Successive ovens show replacement over time; they should not be imagined as three simultaneous kitchens in one family home.

passages.title: What buildings, books and fields reveal
passages.text: Pits at the same site contained a millstone and iron objects including a cowbell, spur and key. Archaeologists suggest the metal may have been gathered for recycling. Grinding grain, managing animals and salvaging useful material become visible through objects whose owners’ names are lost.

passages.title: What buildings, books and fields reveal
passages.text: Imperial expansion also involved coercion. A law issued during Charlemagne’s Saxon wars threatened death for refusing baptism. It shows rulers using severe penalties to impose Christianity. A legal threat is evidence of policy, however, not a record of how often a punishment was carried out.

The partition of 843 created distinct kingdoms, though imperial titles and Carolingian dynasties continued. Charles the Fat’s later reunion collapsed in 887 to 888. The atlas’s 1000 endpoint is therefore not the fall of a continuously united empire.

sectionTitles: A house with water close at hand
A small clue to caring for children
An ancient rulebook and an agricultural book

passages.text: Founded by Phoenician settlers on the Gulf of Tunis, Carthage became the centre of a powerful Punic network linking North Africa, western Mediterranean islands and Iberia. Ports, inscriptions and archaeological remains show a place of traders, craftspeople and families as well as generals. The map uses “Carthaginian Empire” and “Carthage” for successive slices of this same history; the later Roman city on the site was a different political phase.

passages.title: A port that connected worlds
passages.text: The archaeological site preserves Punic harbour remains. They anchor Carthage’s maritime story in physical infrastructure, although the surviving basins cannot by themselves tell us the cargo or crew of every voyage. Ships and ports connected communities around the western Mediterranean.

passages.title: A port that connected worlds
passages.text: A British Museum gallery describes silver coins that Carthage minted in Sicily between about 400 and 300 BCE to pay armies. Some carry short Punic inscriptions meaning “in the land,” “of the paymaster” or “in the camp.” Even an army needed accountants; these coins are evidence of organized payments, not of what every sailor or soldier earned.

passages.title: Who made decisions?
passages.text: Carthage was governed through elected chief officials often called suffetes or shofetim, councils and public assemblies. Our picture comes mainly from later Greek and Roman writing, checked against inscriptions, so the precise powers and who could participate are debated. It was a city with institutions, not simply Hannibal giving orders to everyone.

passages.title: Who made decisions?
passages.text: The Louvre’s Punic stelae and an Ohio State edition of a Carthaginian temple tariff also preserve names of dedicators and rules for offerings. They show people making vows and priests administering a sanctuary. Those records are narrow windows into religious life; they do not tell us what every family believed.

passages.title: A house with water close at hand
passages.text: At Kerkuane, a separate Punic town on Cape Bon, excavators found houses entered through corridors into courtyards. Some plans included wells, washbasins and baths, with rooms arranged around the open centre. That gives a concrete glimpse of domestic space in Carthage’s wider Punic world; it is not a floor plan of every Carthaginian home.

passages.title: A house with water close at hand
passages.text: Kerkuane also preserves streets, shops and workshops. Its visible ruins mostly belong to the late fourth and early third centuries BCE; the town was abandoned around the middle of the third century and not built over by a Roman city. That is why these ordinary workspaces survive more clearly than much of Punic Carthage.

passages.title: Yes, there were toilets
passages.text: Excavations at Bir Massouda in Carthage found two structures interpreted as household latrines and a third as a public latrine. Their construction dates to about the late fifth or early fourth century BCE. The evidence is unusually specific: archaeology can reveal where people dealt with the least glamorous part of city life.

passages.title: Yes, there were toilets
passages.text: Those three latrines help researchers study waste collection, but they do not prove every home had a toilet or that Carthage had modern plumbing. If you are wondering whether ancient history includes toilet questions: the archaeologists were wondering too.

passages.title: A small clue to caring for children
passages.text: A spouted Punic pottery vessel from Carthage, dated to the first half of the third century BCE, is catalogued as a feeding bottle. Its shape offers a rare object connected with caring for young children. The object does not reveal who held it, what was inside, or how common such vessels were.

passages.title: Punic words in stone
passages.text: A limestone stela catalogued by the Louvre as AO 5175 begins with the Punic words 𐤋𐤓𐤁𐤕 𐤋𐤕𐤍𐤕 (LRBT LTNT): “to the Lady, to Tanit.” This is a modern Unicode rendering of the attested consonant letters, not a photograph of the carving. Punic is the language; the Phoenician-derived alphabet is its script. The stone records a dedication, not the literacy of every Carthaginian.

passages.title: Punic words in stone
passages.text: The same stela names Baal Hammon and its dedicator, with his father and grandfather. The Louvre says its final words are not yet understood. A family name on a stone can outlast an empire, but historians must still leave unread words unread.

passages.title: An ancient rulebook and an agricultural book
passages.text: A surviving Carthaginian inscription, known as KAI 74, sets out what priests received from different offerings. One clause exempts a worshipper poor in livestock from a priestly share. It is a rule on a stone, not proof that every sanctuary followed it in every century.

passages.title: An ancient rulebook and an agricultural book
passages.text: Roman writers admired an agricultural work associated with the Carthaginian Mago. Later Greek and Latin versions carried its farming advice, including guidance on trees, into Roman literature. The Punic original does not survive intact, and modern scholars debate whether “Mago” was a single author or a name attached to collected knowledge.

passages.title: Defeat did not erase everyone
passages.text: Hannibal’s crossing of the Alps in 218 BCE was a startling military feat, but it did not win the second war. Roman victory in 201 weakened Carthage; the city still existed for more than fifty years before the third war and the siege that ended in 146 BCE.

passages.title: Defeat did not erase everyone
passages.text: In 146 BCE Rome destroyed the Punic capital and enslaved its surviving inhabitants. The Roman city built later on the site is part of Carthage’s long history, but its monuments are not evidence that Punic Carthage possessed Roman theatres or baths. People and Punic cultural practices elsewhere in North Africa continued through political change.

Rome captured and destroyed Punic Carthage in 146 BCE, ending it as an independent capital. Survivors faced enslavement, while a Roman city later rose on the same ground. The political power ended; this was not the extinction of everyone with a Punic language or tradition. The map’s two imported labels and rounded years describe coverage, not two different Carthaginian civilizations or a historical end in 100 BCE.

sectionTitles: Books, learning and things people made

passages.text: Castile grew from a northern Iberian lordship into a kingdom and, after its permanent union with León in 1230, a much larger crown. Its history includes nuns with judicial authority, traveling flocks, manuscript workshops and Atlantic expansion. The atlas spellings Castilla, Castile and Castille label successive map segments, not three unrelated peoples. Their 1279, 1492 and 1530 boundaries are coverage limits.

passages.title: Books, learning and things people made
passages.text: A court manuscript completed in Seville in 1283 explains chess, dice and tables. Its compiler associated chess with calculation, dice with chance, and tables with a mixture. The book drew on games transmitted through Arabic sources; Alfonso X did not invent chess.

passages.title: Books, learning and things people made
passages.text: The Book of Games survives on 97 parchment leaves with abundant paintings. A game manual could be a major artistic commission: considerably more elaborate than the instructions that disappear from a board-game box.

passages.title: Books, learning and things people made
passages.text: The Cantigas de Santa María joined poetry, music and pictures in Alfonso X’s court. The Códice Rico, c. 1280 to 1284, illustrates miracles in sequences of scenes. These are religious stories, though their artists also pictured clothing, instruments and everyday activities.

passages.title: Books, learning and things people made
passages.text: A short Galician-Portuguese sample from Cantiga 10 reads “Rosa das rosas e Fror das frores”: “Rose of roses and Flower of flowers,” praising Mary. This is a scholarly transcription of a medieval song in Latin letters, not proof that everyone spoke or read the court’s literary languages.

passages.title: Books, learning and things people made
passages.text: Salamanca’s 1254 university staffing included teachers of law, grammar, logic and medicine, as well as an apothecary and librarian. These named posts show organized advanced study, not universal schooling or evidence that medieval medical treatments worked.

passages.title: Books, learning and things people made
passages.text: Nebrija’s Castilian grammar was printed in Salamanca in 1492. One section taught the language to people with another mother tongue. Red and black ink and empty spaces for decorative initials preserve a moment when printed books still borrowed habits from manuscripts.

passages.title: Households, work and royal women
passages.text: At Burgos, Alfonso VIII and Eleanor founded Las Huelgas in 1187 as a community of Cistercian nuns and royal burial place. Its abbess exercised unusually extensive authority, including jurisdiction over dependent properties. This was a powerful particular institution, not the position of all Castilian women.

passages.title: Households, work and royal women
passages.text: The 1187 founding charter of Las Huelgas survives as a large parchment document with a circular royal sign and witnesses. Its Latin words “Facta carta in burgis” mean “The charter was made in Burgos.” Official writing made royal gifts and obligations durable.

passages.title: Households, work and royal women
passages.text: Clothes from the tomb of Prince Fernando de la Cerda, who died in 1275, include a fitted laced garment, an open-sided outer garment and a fur-lined mantle. Castles and lions advertised royal identity. These costly burial clothes reveal elite fashion, not a peasant’s wardrobe.

passages.title: Households, work and royal women
passages.text: The Mesta received royal privileges under Alfonso X in 1273. Its livestock owners and shepherds depended on grazing and passage rights. Moving animals across the landscape was skilled work with legal consequences, not simply letting sheep wander wherever they liked.

passages.title: Households, work and royal women
passages.text: The Hospital del Rey in Burgos was founded in 1195 to assist pilgrims and sick poor people. Its later connection with Las Huelgas linked hospitality, religious endowment and care. “Hospital” could include shelter and food as well as treatment.

passages.title: Households, work and royal women
passages.text: The 1492 expulsion decree disrupted Jewish households and communities. Archival records track the property and debts they left behind. A crown’s expansion could therefore coincide with families losing their homes; cultural exchange should not be mistaken for continuous equality or safety.

Castile did not fall in 1492 or 1530. Dynastic union with Aragon from 1479 helped form the Spanish monarchy, while the crowns retained separate institutions. Castilian communities and institutions continued, even as conquest and religious coercion transformed many people’s lives.

passages.text: Clothes from the tomb of Prince Fernando de la Cerda, who died in 1275, include a fitted laced garment, an open-sided outer garment and a fur-lined mantle. Castles and lions advertised royal identity. These costly burial clothes reveal elite fashion, not a peasant’s wardrobe.

passages.title: Households, work and royal women
passages.text: The Mesta received royal privileges under Alfonso X in 1273. Its livestock owners and shepherds depended on grazing and passage rights. Moving animals across the landscape was skilled work with legal consequences, not simply letting sheep wander wherever they liked.

passages.title: Households, work and royal women
passages.text: The Hospital del Rey in Burgos was founded in 1195 to assist pilgrims and sick poor people. Its later connection with Las Huelgas linked hospitality, religious endowment and care. “Hospital” could include shelter and food as well as treatment.

passages.title: Households, work and royal women
passages.text: The 1492 expulsion decree disrupted Jewish households and communities. Archival records track the property and debts they left behind. A crown’s expansion could therefore coincide with families losing their homes; cultural exchange should not be mistaken for continuous equality or safety.

Castile did not fall in 1492 or 1530. Dynastic union with Aragon from 1479 helped form the Spanish monarchy, while the crowns retained separate institutions. Castilian communities and institutions continued, even as conquest and religious coercion transformed many people’s lives.

sectionTitles: Books, learning and things people made

passages.text: Castile grew from a northern Iberian lordship into a kingdom and, after its permanent union with León in 1230, a much larger crown. Its history includes nuns with judicial authority, traveling flocks, manuscript workshops and Atlantic expansion. The atlas spellings Castilla, Castile and Castille label successive map segments, not three unrelated peoples. Their 1279, 1492 and 1530 boundaries are coverage limits.

passages.title: Books, learning and things people made
passages.text: A court manuscript completed in Seville in 1283 explains chess, dice and tables. Its compiler associated chess with calculation, dice with chance, and tables with a mixture. The book drew on games transmitted through Arabic sources; Alfonso X did not invent chess.

passages.title: Books, learning and things people made
passages.text: The Book of Games survives on 97 parchment leaves with abundant paintings. A game manual could be a major artistic commission: considerably more elaborate than the instructions that disappear from a board-game box.

passages.title: Books, learning and things people made
passages.text: The Cantigas de Santa María joined poetry, music and pictures in Alfonso X’s court. The Códice Rico, c. 1280 to 1284, illustrates miracles in sequences of scenes. These are religious stories, though their artists also pictured clothing, instruments and everyday activities.

passages.title: Books, learning and things people made
passages.text: A short Galician-Portuguese sample from Cantiga 10 reads “Rosa das rosas e Fror das frores”: “Rose of roses and Flower of flowers,” praising Mary. This is a scholarly transcription of a medieval song in Latin letters, not proof that everyone spoke or read the court’s literary languages.

passages.title: Books, learning and things people made
passages.text: Salamanca’s 1254 university staffing included teachers of law, grammar, logic and medicine, as well as an apothecary and librarian. These named posts show organized advanced study, not universal schooling or evidence that medieval medical treatments worked.

passages.title: Books, learning and things people made
passages.text: Nebrija’s Castilian grammar was printed in Salamanca in 1492. One section taught the language to people with another mother tongue. Red and black ink and empty spaces for decorative initials preserve a moment when printed books still borrowed habits from manuscripts.

passages.title: Households, work and royal women
passages.text: At Burgos, Alfonso VIII and Eleanor founded Las Huelgas in 1187 as a community of Cistercian nuns and royal burial place. Its abbess exercised unusually extensive authority, including jurisdiction over dependent properties. This was a powerful particular institution, not the position of all Castilian women.

sectionTitles: Homes, crops and a potter’s toolbox

passages.text: The Catawba are a living Native nation whose homeland lies along the Catawba River in the Carolina Piedmont. Farming villages and trading paths made this region an important meeting place. The imported 1492 to 1715 outline is a broad historical approximation; those dates neither establish when the people began nor mark their disappearance.

passages.title: A powerful river crossroads
passages.text: Early eighteenth-century observers distinguished the Catawba from nearby Iswa communities. As war and epidemic disease battered the region, survivors from several communities came together within the Catawba Nation. Its later history includes this rebuilding of relationships, rather than an unchanged population enclosed by one permanent border.

passages.title: A powerful river crossroads
passages.text: By the late seventeenth century, Catawba villages connected traders from Virginia and Carolina. Deerskins could be exchanged for metal kettles, knives, cloth and firearms. A household’s cooking equipment and clothing thus belonged to a much wider network of hunting, bargaining and travel.

passages.title: A powerful river crossroads
passages.text: In the Yamasee War beginning in 1715, Catawba and other Native forces fought Carolina colonists. The war brought severe losses and enslavement across the region. Later Catawba alliances with the British were made in this changing political world, not inherited from an eternal friendship.

passages.title: A powerful river crossroads
passages.text: After the devastating smallpox epidemic of 1759, the 1760 Treaty of Pine Tree Hill exchanged extensive Piedmont claims for a reservation fifteen miles on each side. Catawba communities established new settlements near its southern edge. Archaeologists study Old Town, Ayers Town and New Town to trace how people rebuilt.

passages.title: A powerful river crossroads
passages.text: Catawba scouts supported the American revolutionaries. When British forces entered South Carolina in 1780, Catawba families withdrew toward Virginia and returned after the 1781 Battle of Guilford Courthouse. Returning home meant another round of rebuilding after armies had disrupted everyday life.

passages.title: Homes, crops and a potter’s toolbox
passages.text: The Nation’s historical account describes palisaded villages with a council house, a sweat lodge and an open plaza for gatherings and games. Extended families shared small bark-covered houses with rounded roofs. Riverbank fields, fishing and hunting supplied food beyond the village wall.

passages.title: Homes, crops and a potter’s toolbox
passages.text: Charred corn cobs can tell a surprisingly detailed farming story. Researcher Mary Elizabeth Fitts measured 171 cob sections from thirteen eighteenth-century Catawba smudge pits. Differences in size and rows suggest that women maintained more than one variety of maize, even through drought and repeated community relocation.

passages.title: Homes, crops and a potter’s toolbox
passages.text: Many of those smudge pits lay in outdoor work areas near houses, and most contained mainly corn cobs rather than wood. At Ayers Town, their circular arrangement partly reflects the buildings around them. Tiny burned leftovers help archaeologists reconstruct a neighborhood’s working spaces.

passages.title: Homes, crops and a potter’s toolbox
passages.text: Traditional Catawba pots begin with clay dug beside the river and prepared by hand. Potters shape the vessel without a wheel, let it dry, then scrape and polish it. Their tools may include shells, smooth river stones and old snuff cans. An excellent tool does not have to come from a fancy shop.

passages.title: Homes, crops and a potter’s toolbox
passages.text: Pottery tools can pass from parents to children and grandchildren. For firing, a pot is warmed beside an open fire and gradually moved closer before entering it. Clay, wood and heat create the finished colors. Knowledge of timing and temperature matters as much as the shape of the vessel.

passages.title: Homes, crops and a potter’s toolbox
passages.text: Pottery also helped households earn a living. The Nation recalls women traveling to settler communities to sell their work, with some buyers reserving favorite pots for particular dishes. Today, children’s programs and adult classes continue the teaching: a cooking vessel can carry family knowledge as well as dinner.

passages.title: Writing, learning and survival
passages.text: A short written Catawba example is “Suuk Hinu,” translated by the Nation as “Seed House.” It names its contemporary childcare center, whose curriculum includes movement, early learning and social skills. This is documented modern language use, not an inscription from the map’s fifteenth-century starting point.

passages.title: Writing, learning and survival
passages.text: At the Cultural Center’s present-day teaching trail, visitors can encounter a replica dwelling, a bark house and a story circle. Its demonstration garden grows corn, beans, squash, pumpkins and sunflowers. These reconstructions help explain older lifeways while living plants make the lesson grow in front of you.

passages.title: Writing, learning and survival
passages.text: The 1840 land agreement with South Carolina became the subject of a long Catawba legal struggle. Federal policy later terminated the Nation’s recognized status in 1959. Catawba people reorganized, petitioned in 1973 and regained federal recognition through the 1993 settlement act. A government’s label had never erased the people themselves.

The map’s 1715 cutoff coincides with a regional war, not the end of the Catawba. The Nation survived later dispossession and federal termination, and regained federal recognition in 1993. It continues as a self-governing community.

sectionTitles: Agreements, money and a surviving word

passages.text: Celtiberians were communities of inland Iberia, with cities, distinct local identities and a Celtic language. This imported outline covers far too much of the peninsula, and its 1500 to 500 BCE interval precedes the best documented Celtiberian towns. The examples below are explicitly later Iron Age and Roman-period evidence, not a picture of a single Bronze Age kingdom.

passages.title: Homes that did several jobs
passages.text: The archaeological reconstruction at Numantia presents a rectangular house with three rooms. The front room combines grain grinding and weaving, with a hatch down to a cellar. This is a model of later Celtiberian domestic space, not an intact ancient house with its original furniture.

passages.title: Homes that did several jobs
passages.text: In the same reconstruction, the central hearth room was used for eating, sleeping and family gatherings. Storage occupied the back, and a side door led to an animal pen. Household space had to accommodate people, provisions, tools and livestock, sometimes very close together.

passages.title: Homes that did several jobs
passages.text: A 2024 study examined four storage contexts from the Celtiberian town destroyed in 133 BCE: an attached storeroom, part of an underground cellar and two cupboards. These protected spaces preserve pottery used for storing, cooking and serving. Archaeologists can distinguish kitchen tasks without finding a written shopping list.

passages.title: Homes that did several jobs
passages.text: The storage deposits also contained evidence of textile work and brooch manufacture. A room used to keep supplies could hold craft equipment too. These finds connect ordinary domestic storage with the production of clothing and the metal fasteners that kept it together.

passages.title: Plants and painted pots
passages.text: Researchers sampled six grinding tools and fourteen pottery vessels from Numantia, spanning the Late Iron Age and Roman occupations. Starch traces revealed cereals, oats, acorns and legumes. The tiny residues preserve food evidence that a spectacular weapon or jewel cannot provide.

passages.title: Plants and painted pots
passages.text: The plant study found evidence for both cultivation and seasonal gathering. Acorns linked households to nearby oak woodland; altered starch also indicated heating during preparation. The results show continuity across political changes, although they do not give us an exact ancient recipe or a complete menu.

passages.title: Plants and painted pots
passages.text: Numantia’s especially distinctive painted pottery series belongs to the first century BCE, after the famous siege. Potters painted black designs on red clay using iron oxide, and also made multicolored vessels. Their birds, fish and human figures show that artistic traditions continued after military defeat.

passages.title: Agreements, money and a surviving word
passages.text: A bronze hospitality token from La Caridad at Caminreal dates to the late second or early first century BCE. Such objects recorded agreements with reciprocal obligations between people, family groups or communities. A portable piece of metal could preserve a relationship extending beyond its owner’s household.

passages.title: Agreements, money and a surviving word
passages.text: The Museo de Zaragoza preserves a silver coin from Turiasu, modern Tarazona, dated 100 to 50 BCE. Local minting gave a city a recognizable presence in everyday exchange. This is later evidence for urban institutions, not proof that the map’s vast earlier territory shared one currency.

passages.title: Agreements, money and a surviving word
passages.text: A first-century BCE bronze text from Contrebia Belaisca records a dispute about land sold for an irrigation channel. Salduie wanted the canal; Alaun objected, and the judges ruled for Salduie. Getting water to crops required negotiation and legal decisions as well as digging.

passages.title: Agreements, money and a surviving word
passages.text: Writing sample: the Novallas bronze has “LITANOM” in line 3, interpreted by its editors as a form meaning “wide.” The Celtiberian text uses Latin capital letters and dates around the late Roman Republic or early Augustus. This short, qualified translation is possible even though the complete fragment remains incompletely understood.

passages.title: Agreements, money and a surviving word
passages.text: Scipio’s army surrounded Numantia with camps and barriers in 134 to 133 BCE, aiming to force surrender through hunger. The town fell in 133 BCE, and survivors were taken captive. This was a devastating local conquest; it must not be described as the instant disappearance of every Celtiberian community.

Roman conquest and administration gradually transformed Celtiberian communities. Numantia’s fall in 133 BCE was a major event, but later pottery and written Celtiberian demonstrate continuing local life. The map’s 500 BCE endpoint is much too early to mark the end of these communities.

sectionTitles: Strathclyde: a rock, a river and royal stones
Welsh courts needed more than a throne
Ireland: farms, towns and powerful households
Children, learning and a very focused cat

passages.text: Celtic kingdoms is a shifting medieval map label, not one empire. In 800 and 900 the outline covers Strathclyde and Cumbria; from 1000 it switches to Ireland, Wales and a small Kintyre area. These regions had different rulers and histories. The broad outlines conceal rival kingdoms, Norse-linked towns and later English-controlled lands; the dates 800-1279 describe map coverage.

passages.title: Strathclyde: a rock, a river and royal stones
passages.text: Dumbarton Rock was a formidable stronghold, but in 870 the Viking rulers Olaf and Ivar of Dublin besieged it for four months. The attackers took treasure and captives. The Irish Sea connected competing courts and also exposed communities to raiding and enslavement.

passages.title: Strathclyde: a rock, a river and royal stones
passages.text: At Govan, ninth- to eleventh-century sculptured stones include crosses, grave slabs, five hogback monuments and an elaborate stone coffin. The concentration suggests royal patronage and burial. Archaeologists think political importance shifted upriver after Dumbarton’s defeat, rather than the British kingdom simply vanishing.

passages.title: Strathclyde: a rock, a river and royal stones
passages.text: Near Govan church once stood the huge earthen Doomster Hill, interpreted as an assembly and justice site. It was demolished in the nineteenth century. Modern researchers use three-dimensional imaging of the surviving stones to recover worn carving and investigate how carvers worked.

passages.title: Welsh courts needed more than a throne
passages.text: The thirteenth-century princes of Gwynedd used a network of courts. Excavation at Llys Rhosyr on Anglesey in 1992-1996 revealed remains later used to design the museum reconstruction at St Fagans. The reconstructed hall is a modern interpretation of archaeological evidence, not a surviving medieval palace.

passages.title: Welsh courts needed more than a throne
passages.text: Gwynedd’s 22 recorded courts included halls, kitchens, stables, barns, kennels and a privy, or toilet. Governing meant feeding people, storing supplies, caring for horses and handling waste. Even a prince needed somewhere to go when the meeting ran long.

passages.title: Welsh courts needed more than a throne
passages.text: Welsh law books attributed their tradition to Hywel Dda, who died in 950, but the earliest surviving copies are thirteenth-century. Peniarth MS 28 is a Latin copy made around that century’s middle. Its laws combine older material with later rules, so the manuscript is not Hywel’s own handbook.

passages.title: Welsh courts needed more than a throne
passages.text: Peniarth 28 pictures hair-pulling as an insult or injury requiring compensation and introduces rules concerning women with a woman holding a dish. Its animal pictures include a cat whose green pigment ate through the parchment. This particular cat has become a cat-shaped hole.

passages.title: Ireland: farms, towns and powerful households
passages.text: Brian Boru became Ireland’s high-king but faced powerful opponents. At Clontarf in 1014 he died during his side’s victory over Irish and Scandinavian enemies. Historians debate the balance between a rebellion against his supremacy and a wider conflict; a simple Irish-versus-Viking story misses important alliances.

passages.title: Ireland: farms, towns and powerful households
passages.text: Cattle were a major measure of wealth in early medieval Ireland. From the eighth century, cereal farming became increasingly important: watermills and improved grain-drying kilns helped process surplus harvests. Political power rested partly on very practical questions about livestock, grain and who controlled their production.

passages.title: Ireland: farms, towns and powerful households
passages.text: Ballinderry crannog in County Westmeath was probably a wealthy Irish household’s island home. Its late ninth- to early eleventh-century finds include spinning, weaving and sewing tools, leather goods and wooden utensils. A decorated gaming board was probably used for hnefatafl, a game associated with the Viking world.

passages.title: Ireland: farms, towns and powerful households
passages.text: Later medieval Irish finds, overlapping this map’s closing decades and continuing beyond them, include wooden churns used for butter-making, sickles for harvesting grain and quern stones for grinding flour. Preparing food required tools, time and skilled hands long before anyone sat down to eat.

passages.title: Ireland: farms, towns and powerful households
passages.text: Viking-age Dublin’s houses had woven wooden walls, probably sealed with mud or dung. Craftspeople made wooden bowls, cups, toys and board games as well as tools and furniture. Rural households and Norse-linked towns exchanged goods and influences; they were not sealed cultural compartments.

passages.title: Children, learning and a very focused cat
passages.text: Medieval Irish fosterage could build lasting relationships between children and another household. Legal and literary evidence includes care beginning in infancy, sometimes with wet-nursing. Arrangements varied: it is misleading to say that every child left home at seven or that foster parents always had one social rank.

passages.title: Children, learning and a very focused cat
passages.text: Irish legal writers even considered injuries suffered by children at play. The Old Irish tract Mellbretha distinguished stages of youth ending at seven, twelve and seventeen. Those categories show attention to changing responsibility, although legal rules cannot tell us exactly how every family managed a scraped knee.

passages.title: Children, learning and a very focused cat
passages.text: Messe ocus Pangur Bán, “I and white Pangur,” opens an Old Irish poem dated about 800-850, preserved in the continental Codex Sancti Pauli. Modern Roman type presents a scholar’s comparison of study with cat-hunting.

passages.title: Children, learning and a very focused cat
passages.text: In 1169 Anglo-Norman forces arrived in Ireland after an invitation from the displaced king of Leinster, Diarmait Mac Murchada. Conquest, settlement and new castles followed. This was a transformation of an already contested political landscape, not the replacement of one unified Celtic empire.

There was no shared fall in 1279. Strathclyde became part of Scotland; English expansion transformed Ireland while Gaelic communities and institutions continued. In Wales, Llywelyn ap Gruffudd’s death in 1282 and the conquest ended Rhosyr’s princely role. These different transitions belong to different kingdoms, not the disappearance of their peoples.
