sectionTitles: Homes and the work of feeding a family

passages.text: This imported “Celts” layer mostly covers Iron Age Britain and Ireland, where many distinct communities shared some artistic traditions and connections with continental Europe. They were not one Celtic empire, and classical authors did not explicitly call the islanders Celts. The map also adds a continental patch in its 200 BCE snapshot. These changing shapes are an unreliable cultural shorthand, not precise ethnic or political borders.

passages.title: Homes and the work of feeding a family
passages.text: At Danebury in Hampshire, roundhouses housed people while separate store buildings and pits held grain. Keeping a harvest safe mattered as much as growing it: the site’s interpretation identifies grain as a particularly valuable resource. The hillfort enclosed a working farming community, not merely a refuge for soldiers.

passages.title: Homes and the work of feeding a family
passages.text: Danebury’s inhabitants kept sheep and cattle, wove woollen cloth and made leather goods. They needed other areas for iron, tin, copper, salt, shale and stone. The site’s interpreters suggest grain and woollen products went out in exchange. A defended hilltop could still depend on its neighbours.

passages.title: Homes and the work of feeding a family
passages.text: At Glastonbury Lake Village, in the last centuries BCE, houses stood on wet ground among reeds and open water. Preserved willow or hazel wall posts were surprisingly slim, about 38 millimetres across. Their woven construction seems to have helped the houses hold together, rather like the strength of a basket.

passages.title: Homes and the work of feeding a family
passages.text: Some Glastonbury walls were decorated by pressing an ammonite fossil into wet daub, the clay mixture covering the walls. The floors had wooden foundations beneath layers of clay. A prehistoric household could have patterned walls, even though its decorating supplies looked rather different from a modern tin of paint.

passages.title: Homes and the work of feeding a family
passages.text: Glastonbury homes had central hearths, sometimes with a small bread oven beside them. Wooden buckets, turned bowls and bentwood boxes joined pottery containers. Looms and rotary querns belonged to household work: cloth and ground grain required skill, equipment and repeated effort close to home.

passages.title: Homes and the work of feeding a family
passages.text: Around Maiden Castle in Dorset, people grew wheat, barley, peas or beans and plants of the cabbage family. Managed woodland provided fuel and building materials. The settlement’s impressive banks depended on a surrounding landscape of fields and useful trees to keep its households going.

passages.title: Homes and the work of feeding a family
passages.text: Dogs at Maiden Castle helped with herding, guarding, hunting and protecting sheep from wolves. Some people also owned horses and perhaps carts. Animals were part of work and security as well as food production; a household’s useful equipment could include a very alert pair of ears.

passages.title: Roads, craftsmanship and personal appearance
passages.text: At Doogarrymore in County Roscommon, two wooden cart wheels dating to the fourth century BCE were found with a bog trackway. Wet ground preserved things that usually decay. Travelling across difficult country could require a deliberately built route, not just a driver hoping the wheels would stay above the mud.

passages.title: Roads, craftsmanship and personal appearance
passages.text: Two gold collars deposited at Ardnaglug in County Roscommon came from the Rhineland during the third century BCE. Local makers then developed their own versions of the flowing La Tène style. Imported ornaments and regional craftsmanship show that Ireland participated in wider artistic networks while producing distinctive work.

passages.title: Roads, craftsmanship and personal appearance
passages.text: The Broighter hoard from County Derry includes a richly decorated gold collar, other neck ornaments, and miniature models of a boat and cauldron. Such precious objects reveal extraordinary metalworking. Their deposition may have had a religious purpose, but the particular intentions of the people who left them are not written down.

passages.title: Roads, craftsmanship and personal appearance
passages.text: The preserved people found at Oldcroghan and Clonycavan in Ireland date broadly to 400 to 200 BCE. Museum researchers used scans and dietary, tissue and disease analyses to investigate them. The bog preserved evidence about individual bodies that is usually missing from ordinary graves.

passages.title: Roads, craftsmanship and personal appearance
passages.text: Clonycavan’s surviving hair was piled high and held with imported resin, according to archaeologist Melanie Giles’s discussion of the research. Personal appearance could involve carefully prepared materials from far away. This is evidence about one person’s hairstyle, rather than a compulsory haircut for everyone labelled Celtic.

passages.title: A short piece of writing
passages.text: A gold coin from southern England, dated by the British Museum to about 40 to 25 BCE, reads “COMMIOS”. This is the Celtic form of the ruler’s name, usually written “Commius” in English, using Roman letters. It is a name rather than a sentence, but it is an actual surviving inscription from before Rome’s conquest.

The map’s endpoint just before the Common Era marks no general disappearance. Rome invaded Britain in 43 CE and transformed the areas it conquered, while Ireland and northern Scotland remained outside lasting Roman control. Communities, languages and artistic traditions changed over centuries; modern Celtic identities have their own continuing histories.

sectionTitles: Water, school messages and medical information

passages.text: The map begins this record in 1945, during French colonial rule, but the Central African Republic became independent in 1960. This card follows the modern state and examples from its diverse communities, rather than treating all Central Africa as one people.

passages.title: Independence, names and conflict
passages.text: On 13 August 1960, the Central African Republic gained independence from France. A US recognition message addressed Prime Minister David Dacko that day. The 1945 map date belongs to the colonial period, not to the republic’s independence.

passages.title: Independence, names and conflict
passages.text: Jean-Bédel Bokassa turned the republic into an empire in December 1976. In September 1979, a French-backed coup brought David Dacko back to power and ended the imperial regime. The country’s inhabitants did not begin again from scratch when the state’s title changed.

passages.title: Independence, names and conflict
passages.text: The Séléka coalition seized Bangui in March 2013 after a rebellion begun in late 2012. Further violence, including attacks by anti-Balaka groups, devastated civilian communities. In 2014, the UN established MINUSCA with civilian protection at the centre of its mandate. These events describe a crisis within a continuing country.

passages.title: Independence, names and conflict
passages.text: A short Sango writing sample is “zo kwe zo,” translated by linguist William Samarin as “everyone’s a human being.” His scholarly account identifies it as Barthélemy Boganda’s slogan and notes its appearance on an early national stamp. The spelling here follows that published transcription in the Latin alphabet.

passages.title: Music learned by joining in
passages.text: Aka singers in the southwest developed music in which four voice parts intertwine. Individual singers can vary their contributions while the group continues: the result is intricate collective improvisation. UNESCO recognized this tradition in 2003 and placed it on its representative list in 2008.

passages.title: Music learned by joining in
passages.text: Instruments include the enzeko drum, the harp-like geedale-bagongo and the single-string mbela bow. Clapping accompanies dancing, and particular instruments suit particular occasions. An orchestra does not need dozens of identical instruments to create a complex sound.

passages.title: Music learned by joining in
passages.text: Children learn Aka music by participating in community occasions from an early age. Songs and dances accompany events such as new camps, hunting and funerals, transmitting knowledge and relationships through participation. This is a specific community’s practice, not a musical description of every Central African household.

passages.title: Water, school messages and medical information
passages.text: Irène Ndende returned to Bangui’s Castors neighbourhood after displacement. In a 2025 interview, she described the difference made by a home water connection installed in 2023: after working in distant fields, she no longer had another water-fetching journey waiting. Infrastructure can change the shape of an ordinary evening.

passages.title: Water, school messages and medical information
passages.text: At a public water point in Benz-Vi, nineteen-year-old Benisia Agdugebo sold porridge and fritters to neighbours arriving with containers. UNICEF’s reporter watched the place become a setting for greetings and conversation. The tap supplied water, but the gathering also supported a small breakfast business.

passages.title: Water, school messages and medical information
passages.text: EduTrac launched in Bangui in December 2015 to collect school information by text message. Headteachers could report attendance and security incidents without waiting for paper reports to travel. One described reports previously taking months to bring a response; faster information was the goal, not a guarantee that every problem was solved.

passages.title: Water, school messages and medical information
passages.text: The rollout needed patient teaching of its own. Some headteachers had to learn how to send SMS messages, and telephone companies had to connect the service number. French and Sango radio announcements helped explain the project. Even useful technology begins with people understanding how to use it.

passages.title: Water, school messages and medical information
passages.text: A 2016 trial in twenty-one Mambéré Kadéi health centres used the Argus app to send disease reports by SMS. Reporting became more complete and timely in the study. Where phones had no signal, the project paid for motorcycle taxis to a connected village: digital medicine sometimes still needed a road journey.

The imperial regime ended in 1979; the Central African Republic continued. Later rebellions and peacekeeping changed authority and everyday security without erasing the state or its communities. Families, teachers and cultural practitioners continued rebuilding connections through these disruptions.

sectionTitles: Learning within families and beyond them
Objects, skilled hands and written words

passages.text: This atlas label groups Central Asian khanates across 1530 to 1914, but its polygons are misplaced or conflated: the earliest lies in the Arctic, and later outlines combine widely separated regions. They cannot show reliable state boundaries. This regional account focuses on the separate states of Bukhara, Khiva and, from the eighteenth century, Kokand. Their rulers governed oasis cities, farms and pastoral communities through changing dynasties and alliances. They never formed one khanate lasting throughout the map interval.

passages.title: Separate states and regional power
passages.text: Sixteenth-century government often rested on a ruling family sharing authority. Princes controlled territories called appanages, including Bukhara, Samarkand, Tashkent and Balkh. A khan had to manage powerful relatives and military supporters. An impressive title did not automatically make every cousin obey.

passages.title: Separate states and regional power
passages.text: Bukhara’s rulers also invested in city life. In the 1530s and 1540s, Abd al-Aziz rebuilt walls and supported religious buildings; the Mir Arab madrasa was completed in 1535. A school, a shrine and a defensive wall served different needs within the same urban landscape.

passages.title: Separate states and regional power
passages.text: The khanates did not collect taxes in identical ways. In nineteenth-century Bukhara, provincial governors handled collection. In Khiva’s more centralized system, officials sent by the central government collected taxes once or twice a year. Irrigation, local authority and royal revenue were closely connected.

passages.title: Separate states and regional power
passages.text: Kokand grew partly through migration. During the eighteenth century, people arriving from Samarkand, Kashgar, nearby mountains and the steppe brought labor and skills into Ferghana. Some fled violence elsewhere. The expanding state depended on a mixture of settled farmers and townspeople, pastoral groups and merchants.

passages.title: Separate states and regional power
passages.text: Kokand’s dealings with Qing China combined diplomacy, military pressure and trade. Rulers sought economic advantages for merchants in Xinjiang. Officials on each side could interpret their relationship differently, so diplomatic language sometimes left room for negotiation rather than settling exactly who answered to whom.

passages.title: Water, homes and everyday work
passages.text: In the 1810s, Omar Khan ordered canals near Namangan and in southeastern Ferghana. A new town, Shahrikhan, followed in 1815 to 1816. Irrigation helped create farmland for a growing population, while rulers hoped that migrants and refugees would become tax-paying subjects.

passages.title: Water, homes and everyday work
passages.text: Khiva’s surviving domestic architecture includes enclosed courtyards, private rooms and reception areas with carved wooden posts. UNESCO describes versions spanning the eighteenth to twentieth centuries. These houses preserve places for family life and receiving visitors alongside the city’s much more conspicuous palaces.

passages.title: Water, homes and everyday work
passages.text: Bukhara had sixteen public baths in 1848, according to its heritage evaluation. Washing therefore had a place in the city’s shared institutions. The number belongs to this particular nineteenth-century city, not every oasis settlement.

passages.title: Water, homes and everyday work
passages.text: An early nineteenth-century Bukhara embroidered cover introduces a family project. Relatives could embroider separate strips of a bride’s suzani, then sew them together. Slightly mismatched joins preserved the teamwork: beautiful decoration did not require every flower to line up perfectly.

passages.title: Water, homes and everyday work
passages.text: A photograph catalogued by the Library of Congress shows tea stalls along a Samarkand street, with a ruined mosque behind them. Dated between 1865 and 1872, it records everyday commerce around the transition to Russian rule. The city’s history included places to buy a drink as well as royal monuments.

passages.title: Learning within families and beyond them
passages.text: Delshad Barna’s life makes the costs of expansion personal. In her own account, she lost her parents as a child and was taken from Ura Tepe to Kokand during a military assault in 1816. Her later writing combined memories of displacement with the history of the khanate.

passages.title: Learning within families and beyond them
passages.text: After marrying in 1820, Delshad taught at her mother-in-law’s girls’ school in Kokand. Her mother-in-law also introduced her to Chaghatay language and literature; Delshad said she had previously spoken only Persian. Education could pass between adult family members as well as from teachers to children.

passages.title: Learning within families and beyond them
passages.text: In 1830, Delshad opened her own girls’ school, teaching reading and writing over a long career. Her surviving works include poetry in Persian and Chaghatay and a historical memoir. These records preserve a woman’s contribution to education beyond the better-known literary circles at court.

passages.title: Objects, skilled hands and written words
passages.text: A nineteenth-century Kokand horse outfit in the Metropolitan Museum combines leather, silver, turquoise, carnelian, enamel and textile. Its bridle and other fittings brought several crafts together. This was elaborate equipment: the horse could arrive wearing rather more jewelry than its rider’s spectators.

passages.title: Objects, skilled hands and written words
passages.text: Visiting Kokand in 1873, Eugene Schuyler found mint workers making silver ornaments for bridles and harnesses. He was told that the mint master also served as court jeweller. The same workshop skills could turn precious metal into money or an impressive horse accessory.

passages.title: Objects, skilled hands and written words
passages.text: Schuyler also described Khudayar Khan’s palace front covered in white, blue and green glazed tiles. He saw only the facade briefly and was not admitted inside. His account preserves a contemporary impression of architectural display while making the limits of his visit unusually clear.

passages.title: Objects, skilled hands and written words
passages.text: “ضرب بخارا”, transliterated zarb Bukhara, means “struck at Bukhara”. Torrey prints this mint phrase on Nasr Allah’s gold coin dated AH 1257. It uses Arabic script in the Persian coinage tradition. The lettering here follows a modern transcription of the nineteenth-century object.

Russian conquest eliminated Kokand’s khanate in 1876. Bukhara and Khiva survived as subordinate monarchies beyond the map’s 1914 endpoint, until 1920. Their cities, families, languages and crafts continued under profoundly changed governments.

sectionTitles: How to read this map record
Homes, families, food, clothing and social life
Learning, print, language and historical evidence
Representation, organizing and the end of colonial rule

passages.text: This atlas record is best read as British colonial Ceylon after the 1815 takeover of the Kandyan kingdom, not as the birth of an island or a single civilization. A British Crown colony already existed on the coasts from 1802; islandwide British control followed in 1815. The eight imported polygons trace one coarse island outline through 1945. That endpoint is an atlas shortcut: colonial rule legally ended on 4 February 1948. Within this state lived many communities whose languages, religions, family systems, livelihoods and political aims differed. Roads, railways, schools, medicine, plantations and archives expanded unevenly, often through coercion and unequal labour; resistance and organizing accompanied them. The people and their histories continued beyond both atlas dates.

passages.title: How to read this map record
passages.text: The atlas record is a state-shaped label, not the name of one ancient people. Coverage marks Ceylon from 1815 to 1945 with approximate dates and eight consecutive polygons. This card therefore follows British colonial administration after the Kandyan takeover without treating a government name as one culture or a complete biography of the island's people.

passages.title: How to read this map record
passages.text: The 1800 atlas geometry makes the transition unusually visible. Its feature called ceylon-dutch-1800 is the island outline with a hole; that hole is exactly the separate Kandy polygon. In 1815 the hole disappears and the new ceylon-1815 record uses the same outer ring. This encodes a coastal-plus-interior merger, not proof that every community accepted the Convention.

passages.title: How to read this map record
passages.text: Each colonial snapshot is a single 35-position island polygon. Across all eight intervals there are only three exact coordinate variants, with about 0.001 degrees of edge jitter from first to last. Those tiny shifts are basemap redrawing, not changing coastlines, battle fronts or administrative borders.

passages.title: How to read this map record
passages.text: At 1815 the mainland British East India Company polygon has a bounding box that reaches the island's latitude; later British Raj and a 1938 United Kingdom occurrence do too. Polygon intersection tests are false in every snapshot. Mysore and Travancore are nearby mainland records, not overlapping Ceylon. A bounding box is a filing cabinet, not a border.

passages.title: How to read this map record
passages.text: The 1945 Sri Lanka polygon has the same 35-point broad outline but is not coordinate-identical to the 1938-1945 Ceylon ring. More important, the label change is three years early: the colony did not become independent until 4 February 1948. Map handoffs are navigation aids, not constitutional documents.

passages.title: Conquest, government and resistance
passages.text: The March 1815 Convention transferred the Kandyan kingdom's sovereignty to Britain in Article 4 and promised protection of Buddhism and its customs in Article 5. It was an agreement among British authorities and Kandyan chiefs amid political manoeuvring. It must not be retold as a vote by the island's whole population.

passages.title: Conquest, government and resistance
passages.text: John D'Oyly shows how scholarship could become an instrument of conquest. He learned Sinhala language and literature from respected teachers and built relationships with monks, poets and nobles; British authorities also employed him as a spy to split the Kandyan court. Knowing a language is not the same as respecting its speakers' political freedom.

passages.title: Conquest, government and resistance
passages.text: Resistance spread through the Kandyan regions in 1817-1818. British forces captured leaders and recovered the Tooth Relic, whose custody was treated as political legitimacy; the archive also calls the suppression ruthless. A colonial proclamation branded nineteen chiefs traitors, a designation formally invalidated in 2016.

passages.title: Conquest, government and resistance
passages.text: The 1833 reforms created Executive and Legislative Councils, divided the island into five provinces and proposed one judicial structure. They also abolished rajakariya compulsory labour. These were large administrative changes, but the appointed colonial councils did not amount to self-government or equal political power.

passages.title: Conquest, government and resistance
passages.text: In 1848 Dumbara residents said a road ordinance had brought compulsory labour back. Around 3,000 unarmed people gathered at the Kandy Kachcheri to petition against road, shop, gun and dog taxes; ancestral land loss under an 1840 Crown Lands ordinance may also have mattered. Violence followed, and the British imposed martial law.

passages.title: Conquest, government and resistance
passages.text: The 1915 crisis involved riots as well as severe colonial repression. Martial law authorized shooting alleged rioters without trial or showing cause; Edward Henry Pedris was court-martialled and executed, and Sinhala leaders were jailed. The National Archives page foregrounds that repression, so it should not be treated as a complete account of violence suffered by Muslim communities during the riots.

passages.title: Plantations, work, transport and technology
passages.text: Coffee expansion was an imperial project as well as a crop story. Governors supported planters, sold central-hill land cheaply, financed experiments and roads, and cleared forest for estates. Coffee rust appeared in 1869 and destroyed the industry over roughly a decade. Colonial profits and infrastructure came with environmental transformation and little local political control.

passages.title: Plantations, work, transport and technology
passages.text: James Taylor was processing tea leaves on a bungalow veranda by 1866, planted twenty acres and sent an early shipment of just 23 pounds. That is small enough to imagine lifting, although nobody should try carrying a tea industry in a school backpack. The Tea Board credits the first successful Ceylon planter while acknowledging earlier attempts.

passages.title: Plantations, work, transport and technology
passages.text: Tea and coffee relied heavily on migrant workers from South India. A peer-reviewed study describes export monocultures dependent on imported wage labour and a kangany system that recruited and coordinated workers while colonial regulation remained weak. Families who made lives on estates were people and communities, not simply a labour supply.

passages.title: Plantations, work, transport and technology
passages.text: Rail began in 1864 chiefly to move coffee from Kandy's highlands to Colombo; tea then drove further construction. Trains also carried workers, machinery, fertilizer, rice and other food, and later more passengers. The engineering connected places, but its first routes followed the export economy's priorities rather than an equal islandwide travel plan.

passages.title: Plantations, work, transport and technology
passages.text: A Central Bank retrospective separates the plantation export economy from rural subsistence farming. More than 90 percent of exports were plantation products, while rural communities received negligible benefit from plantation growth and the colony imported many consumer goods, including food. A booming export graph could therefore coexist with a struggling household budget.

passages.title: Plantations, work, transport and technology
passages.text: Colonial governments renovated many irrigation works, and that mattered to farming. Yet the island's reservoir and canal traditions were already more than two millennia old. Calling every repaired tank a British invention would be like fixing an old bicycle and claiming you invented wheels; renovation and origin are different achievements.

passages.title: Homes, families, food, clothing and social life
passages.text: A museum in Gampola uses line rooms more than a century old to reconstruct estate-worker life. One roughly 100-square-foot room represents a whole home, with clay walls, hanging pots and pans, and a basic hearth. It conveys crowding and domestic work on plantations, but it is a modern reconstruction and cannot stand for every worker, estate or decade.

passages.title: Homes, families, food, clothing and social life
passages.text: Under older Kandyan law, household location could shape inheritance. A later court explained binna marriage as the husband joining the wife's parental home so she retained parental-property rights; in diga she moved to his home and usually lost them, with exceptions. This is a Kandyan legal pattern, not a rule for Tamil, Muslim, low-country or every Kandyan family.

passages.title: Homes, families, food, clothing and social life
passages.text: Meals differed by ecology, income, religion and community. A later FAO study describes a dry-zone pattern of rice on irrigated land mainly for home use and other foods on dry land for home and market. Combined with the colonial plantation-versus-subsistence split, it suggests why an export crop tells us little about what any particular child ate for dinner.

passages.title: Homes, families, food, clothing and social life
passages.text: A shore-seine boat model preserves clever coastal engineering: full-size planks were literally sewn together with coconut-fibre rope, with leaves used to waterproof the seams. Variants worked along western, southern and northeastern coasts. Boats could need stitches without being sick, but the museum label cannot tell us the lives of every fisher who used one.

passages.title: Homes, families, food, clothing and social life
passages.text: A nineteenth-century painted wood mask from the island's interior has coiled-cobra forms dramatic enough to win a staring contest. Its 1886 purchase from a dealer leaves major gaps: the catalog does not name its maker, exact community or performance. The object documents skilled carving and colonial collecting, not one islandwide belief.

passages.title: Homes, families, food, clothing and social life
passages.text: Clothing cannot responsibly be reduced to a single Ceylon costume. Museum catalogues include Buddhist robes and cloths acquired in Sri Lanka, but often provide little production date, maker or wearing context. Dress varied with community, religion, occupation, gender, wealth, weather and occasion; a monk's robe is evidence of a robe, not everyone's wardrobe.

passages.title: Homes, families, food, clothing and social life
passages.text: A nineteenth-century betel-nut cutter associated with Kandy also records a collecting relationship. The British Museum says colonial official Hugh Nevill assembled objects with sparse provenance and likely obtained this cutter through the Kandyan Society of Arts. The little tool shows craft and social practice, while its museum journey warns how much maker information empire could discard.

passages.title: Learning, print, language and historical evidence
passages.text: Learning did not begin with colonial schools. A UNESCO-hosted history describes oral teaching and memorization around Buddhist temples, later ola-leaf manuscripts and libraries, and pirivena colleges for clergy and some male lay students. It also shows a limit: these institutions did not provide the same access to every child, gender or religious community.

passages.title: Learning, print, language and historical evidence
passages.text: British rule expanded schooling through an unequal dual structure. Church-assisted English schools attracted elites, while state vernacular schools served common people; pirivenas continued beside them. A Department of Public Instruction began in 1869. More schools mattered, but language, class, gender, religion and place still shaped who could attend and what schooling promised.

passages.title: Learning, print, language and historical evidence
passages.text: A period Tamil sample is உதய தாரகை, transliterated utayatārakai and translated “Morning Star.” It is the title on a bilingual Tamil-English issue printed in the Jaffna mission world on 15 April 1841. Tamil is a Brahmi-derived abugida. This is a verified newspaper title, not a spoken sentence, not Sinhala, and not proof that every Tamil person read mission print.

passages.title: Learning, print, language and historical evidence
passages.text: Writing also appeared on objects, but not every inscription can be translated from a catalog. A hinged brass box acquired in Kandy in 1895 is labelled as carrying Tamil writing; the museum gives neither its production date nor the inscription text. It is evidence of an inscribed object and of missing documentation, so this card does not invent a reading.

passages.title: Learning, print, language and historical evidence
passages.text: Archives make colonial government visible, but their silences matter. Holdings include Kandyan commissioners, Kachcheri offices, inquiries, newspapers, maps, the 1818 rebellion and political organizations. These files are powerful evidence about administration and petitions; they preserve far less of conversations at a hearth, a child's game or a worker's unrecorded complaint.

passages.title: Learning, print, language and historical evidence
passages.text: Government archaeology took shape through surveys, photographs and inscription work from the 1860s, with an official department from 1890. Work at Anuradhapura, Sigiriya and Polonnaruwa documented buildings, inscriptions and murals, including mural finds reported in 1897. The department organized research; it did not create the ancient sites or the knowledge local communities held about them.

passages.title: Learning, print, language and historical evidence
passages.text: The Archaeology Department now hosts scholarship criticizing its own colonial inheritance. One conference paper says early institutions privileged Western ideas and excluded local voices, and urges comparison with local texts and traditions. So “discovery” in this card means something entered an official survey or archive, not that Sri Lankans had forgotten their own heritage.

passages.title: Medicine, water and toilets
passages.text: People used more than one medical system. Sri Lanka's Department of Ayurveda names Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani and Deshiya Chikitsa as distinct living traditions. Its 2024 policy is modern evidence for plurality and continuity, not a time machine telling us exactly which remedy every nineteenth-century family used.

passages.title: Medicine, water and toilets
passages.text: Early British medical services mainly served the military and kept civil institutions under military control. A separate Civil Medical Department in 1858 marked a civilian administrative phase. That institutional milestone did not erase local healers, guarantee equal rural access or make colonial health policy purely benevolent.

passages.title: Medicine, water and toilets
passages.text: Colonial institutions trained more health workers over time: Colombo Medical College opened in 1870, a local nursing school in 1878, and women entered the medical college in 1892. Civil birth and death registration began in 1867 and a bacteriology laboratory in 1900. These were durable institutions, though the timeline alone does not prove equal service.

passages.title: Medicine, water and toilets
passages.text: Colombo planned sewers from 1896, started construction in 1906 and completed much of the system by 1925. This was city infrastructure, not an islandwide flush-toilet switch. The municipal page says even a 1972 plan found many residents using on-site systems and some with no facility, which makes broad claims about colonial household plumbing especially unsafe.

passages.title: Medicine, water and toilets
passages.text: A 1917 Colombo health report urged connecting latrines to sewers and controlling flies, refuse and manure near homes to reduce enteric fever, dysentery and infant diarrhoea. It shows officials linking toilets, waste, water and disease. It also speaks in a colonial inspector's voice, so residents' constraints and knowledge are mostly absent.

passages.title: Medicine, water and toilets
passages.text: School toilets and water were still inadequate in 1928. Colonial inspectors counted 3,106 schools serving 554,595 children, but only 2,649 schools with latrines, 493 with urinals and 991 with protected wells. Even those totals do not prove every fixture worked or every child could use it safely; a toilet count is not the same as a good toilet.

passages.title: Medicine, water and toilets
passages.text: The 1934-1935 malaria epidemic affected about 1.5 million people and killed nearly 80,000. Responses used quinine, mobile medical units, drainage and other environmental work, oiling and larvicides such as Paris green; DDT came later. The scale makes this a history of loss and organized public health, not a cheerful tale of one miracle chemical.

passages.title: Medicine, water and toilets
passages.text: Help also came through political and community organizing. The Suriya-Mal movement brought medicine, food and supplies to distant communities during the malaria crisis and supported education for children treated as lower caste. Its 1933 founding and welfare work show young activists linking anti-imperial politics to daily survival.

passages.title: Representation, organizing and the end of colonial rule
passages.text: The “elective principle” of 1910 was a narrow opening. Of ten non-official Legislative Council members, only four were elected, and those seats used ethnic categories; eleven officials remained. Ponnambalam Ramanathan's selection mattered, but this was a long way from one adult, one vote.

passages.title: Representation, organizing and the end of colonial rule
passages.text: The Ceylon National Congress began in 1919 with Ponnambalam Arunachalam as president and aimed at a common reform movement. Disagreement over a Colombo seat, withdrawal of Tamil leaders and later departures weakened it. Independence organizing crossed communities, but unity was argued over and could fracture.

passages.title: Representation, organizing and the end of colonial rule
passages.text: Workers organized on their own terrain. The Ceylon Labour Union formed in 1922 and helped lead a general strike in 1923. Its suffrage demand explicitly crossed gender, race, religion and caste. The record also recalls resistance to a contribution that could require adult men to spend six days working on roads.

passages.title: Representation, organizing and the end of colonial rule
passages.text: Universal adult suffrage arrived with the Donoughmore system in 1931, along with territorial representation and a State Council. Women did not receive the vote as a gift dropped from a government desk: Agnes de Silva and other members of the Society for Women's Suffrage testified before the commission and helped make the case.

passages.title: Representation, organizing and the end of colonial rule
passages.text: Plantation labour politics reached the highest colonial offices in the 1937 Bracegirdle case. Bracegirdle opposed twelve-hour days and described brutality toward workers, women and children; the governor ordered him deported, prompting a political battle and commission. One manager's protest does not substitute for workers' own voices, but it exposed conditions to official scrutiny.

passages.title: Representation, organizing and the end of colonial rule
passages.text: Representation changed by stages: Legislative Council from 1833, State Council from 1931 and a Soulbury Westminster model from 1944. Those forms should not be collapsed into full sovereignty. The first two operated under colonial rule, and even the 1944 redesign preceded legal independence.

passages.title: Representation, organizing and the end of colonial rule
passages.text: The Ceylon Independence Act passed in 1947, and Ceylon became independent on 4 February 1948. The country later took the name Sri Lanka. The end of colonial Ceylon was a constitutional transition, not the disappearance of its peoples, languages, religions, labour struggles, family histories or memories of resistance.

The map changes from ceylon-1815 to sri-lanka in 1945, but British colonial rule continued until 4 February 1948. Independent Ceylon inherited institutions, debts, inequalities, infrastructure and debates shaped during the colonial period; it later became the republic named Sri Lanka. Sinhala, Tamil and other communities did not begin in 1815 or end in 1945 or 1948. This card ends a colonial state period, not a people.

sectionTitles: Modern discoveries of a much older past

passages.text: This record represents independent Chad from 1960, following French colonial rule. Its borders enclose many communities with distinct histories; the modern republic is not interchangeable with earlier Kanem, Wadai or other states.

passages.title: Republic, justice and writing
passages.text: Chad’s independence was proclaimed on 11 August 1960. Diplomatic records also preserve an older capital name: the American embassy opened at Fort Lamy in 1961, in the city now called N’Djamena. Names on old letters can reveal political changes that a modern map conceals.

passages.title: Republic, justice and writing
passages.text: Hissène Habré ruled from 1982 to 1990. In 2016, the Extraordinary African Chambers in Senegal convicted him of torture, war crimes and crimes against humanity. Survivors’ efforts to secure a trial are part of Chad’s history alongside the rulers whose actions they challenged.

passages.title: Republic, justice and writing
passages.text: A small writing sample comes from the 2020 children’s comic title “Lafya,” which UNICEF translates from Ngambaye as “peace.” Its eight-year-old heroine learns about life during school closures. Versions in French, Arabic and Ngambaye show that public education can use several languages within one country.

passages.title: Modern discoveries of a much older past
passages.text: The Franco-Chadian research mission found a nearly complete skull, jaw material and teeth at Toros-Menalla site TM 266. Scientists assigned them to Sahelanthropus tchadensis, around seven million years old. Published work identifies them as evidence relevant to early human evolution, not the remains of a Chadian nation millions of years ago.

passages.title: Modern discoveries of a much older past
passages.text: Other fossils make the setting more surprising than today’s desert suggests. Fish, crocodiles and water-associated mammals occur alongside animals linked to woodland and savannah. In 2002, researchers used these remains and sediments to reconstruct a lakeside environment near sandy desert. Ancient landscapes can hide inside modern dry ground.

passages.title: Food, cattle and learning together
passages.text: Around Lake Chad, dihé is a food harvested from blue-green microorganisms in shallow waters. FAO’s account describes women straining it through palm baskets, letting water drain in sand basins, cutting the thickened material into pieces and drying them in the sun. Harvesting and processing require learned skill.

passages.title: Food, cattle and learning together
passages.text: In field notes from March 2002 near Boudou Andja, women’s leader Harita Cierom asked for sturdy clothing, gloves, boots and support for a producers’ association. Salty water made the work hard on skin and clothes. Her request puts the workers, rather than only the finished food, into the historical record.

passages.title: Food, cattle and learning together
passages.text: Massa communities live on both sides of the Logone River in Chad and Cameroon. In the annual Guruna retreat, boys and men take cattle to a camp away from home. Elders teach cattle care alongside community history, music, dance, handicrafts and wrestling: school can happen far from a classroom.

passages.title: Food, cattle and learning together
passages.text: UNESCO’s Guruna account describes girls helping prepare food and decorations without staying overnight. Older women transmit those skills, while fathers, elders and specialist masters guide other instruction. Public ceremonies and performances let participants demonstrate what they have learned; the learning involves the wider community.

passages.title: Health services that travel
passages.text: Between 2000 and 2005, researchers and health teams tested combined visits for nomadic families and their livestock. Physicians and veterinarians shared transport and equipment while providing their separate vaccinations. Bringing both services together reduced costs and reached more women and children per day than human-only rounds in the study.

passages.title: Health services that travel
passages.text: A later study in Danamadji found that pastoralists valued combined vaccination, but keeping the programme running required dependable funding and coordination. Even livestock enclosures mattered for safe, workable vaccination days. The useful invention here was organizing services around mobile families rather than expecting families to fit a distant clinic.

passages.title: Health services that travel
passages.text: During the pandemic, Chad used radio, television and phones for lessons. UNICEF’s May 2021 case study also reported handwashing kits, soap and bleach delivered to at least 1,083 primary schools. Reopening involved water and hygiene as well as books; a classroom timetable alone could not do the job.

Chad continued after Idriss Déby’s death in 2021 and the military takeover led by his son. The 2023 constitution again described a sovereign republic. These institutional changes do not mark an ending for Chad’s many peoples or their cross-border connections.

sectionTitles: Personal objects, disease and a queen’s monument
Languages and short pieces of writing

passages.text: The Chagatai Khanate grew from the Central Asian lands and peoples assigned to Chagatai, a son of Chinggis Khan. Its history joined mobile courts, pasturelands and established towns from Transoxiana toward the Ili valley and Xinjiang. The atlas’s 1279 to 1530 interval covers several political phases. Its later outline wrongly stretches far into eastern Asia, beyond this khanate’s historical territories.

passages.title: Inheritance, queens and changing governments
passages.text: Chagatai’s inheritance included people and pasture, not just land within a neat border. At first, urban tax officials answered to the Great Khan. During the imperial civil wars of the 1260s, Alghu drew that administration under his own authority, making the regional khanate more independent.

passages.title: Inheritance, queens and changing governments
passages.text: Ergene Khatun governed as regent for her son Mubarak Shah during the 1250s. She negotiated amid struggles between Mongol princes and later married Alghu. Royal women could act as rulers and brokers of alliances; family relationships were central to political power, not merely background to it.

passages.title: Inheritance, queens and changing governments
passages.text: An agreement at Talas in 1269 called for princes to keep to seasonal pasturelands, keep their herds away from cultivated fields and leave town administration alone. These rules reveal a practical problem: grazing animals and growing crops could bring neighbours into conflict. An agreement records what leaders wanted, not guaranteed compliance.

passages.title: Inheritance, queens and changing governments
passages.text: Tarmashirin, whose reign Michal Biran dates to 1331 to 1334, was a Muslim ruler within a dynasty with varied religious histories. Other khans and commanders had converted earlier. His policies drew on existing Muslim networks; the population did not change its beliefs all at once when one ruler changed his.

passages.title: Inheritance, queens and changing governments
passages.text: From the 1340s, western and eastern governments increasingly followed separate paths. Powerful commanders dominated the west, where Timur became the effective ruler in 1370. Eastern Chagatai rulers retained power in Moghulistan. One dynasty’s name therefore appears across histories of several competing governments.

passages.title: Clothes, water, gardens and money
passages.text: In 1221, before the separate khanate emerged, the traveller Chang Chun stayed in Almaliq’s fruit gardens. His account describes locally grown cotton made into thread, rope, cloth and padding. His party bought it for winter clothing. Cotton could look like wool, but no sheep needed shearing.

passages.title: Clothes, water, gardens and money
passages.text: The same account describes farmers irrigating fields through canals and people carrying water in pitchers on their heads. Almaliq’s surroundings supported both orchards and pasture. Keeping a household supplied meant skilled cultivation, maintaining water channels and repeated carrying, rather than turning on a kitchen tap.

passages.title: Clothes, water, gardens and money
passages.text: Kebek’s government issued silver dinars and dirhams in the early fourteenth century, and his name became associated with the money. Coinage helped connect the khan’s authority with everyday exchange. A small piece of silver could travel much farther than the person who first earned it.

passages.title: Clothes, water, gardens and money
passages.text: A coin hoard found at Kultobe in Kazakhstan contained money from many mints, including Bukhara, Samarkand, Kashgar and Almaliq. The Azret Sultan Museum holds only a surviving transferred subset: 24 silver coins and two copper ones. Such finds connect a local hiding place with much wider networks of exchange.

passages.title: Clothes, water, gardens and money
passages.text: Ibn Battuta’s account of his 1330s journey describes riverside pleasure gardens at Samarkand alongside damaged buildings. A traveller noticed both ruin and places to relax. His story adds a human glimpse of the city, though historians check his inconsistent chronology and other claims against independent evidence.

passages.title: Personal objects, disease and a queen’s monument
passages.text: At Kara-Djigach in the Chüy valley, Qutluq Tärim was buried in 1338 or 1339 with a bracelet, a ring and a gold earring carrying four pearls. Archaeologists recorded these objects with her grave. They reveal personal adornment and access to valued materials, although one burial cannot tell us what every woman owned.

passages.title: Personal objects, disease and a queen’s monument
passages.text: Researchers studying teeth from the same cemetery identified plague-bacterium DNA in three people buried during the 1338 to 1339 epidemic. Inscriptions also recorded an unusual surge of deaths. Combining documents, graves and ancient DNA identified a local health disaster and helped investigate its relationship to the later Black Death.

passages.title: Personal objects, disease and a queen’s monument
passages.text: At Almaliq, Tughluq Temur’s tomb preserves impressive tilework and calligraphy. His widow Tini Khatun financed it, probably some years after his death in the fourteenth century. Its exact construction date is uncertain. A queen’s patronage helped turn mourning into a durable building that visitors can still study.

passages.title: Languages and short pieces of writing
passages.text: A Christian gravestone for Sanmaq at Kara-Djigach includes the Syriac word “mawtānā”, meaning “pestilence”. This is the researchers’ Roman transcription of the inscription, dated around 1338. It preserves how a community described a terrible loss. The gravestone is distinct from the individuals whose teeth supplied the DNA evidence.

passages.title: Languages and short pieces of writing
passages.text: Chagatai also names an influential Turkic literary language. Its later classical literature flourished in Timurid centres such as Herat and Samarkand, and borrowed extensively from Persian and Arabic. Language history crossed political borders: a book called Chagatai was not necessarily written for a Chagatai khan.

passages.title: Languages and short pieces of writing
passages.text: A Samarkand silver coin from 1399 to 1400 reads “السلطان محمود خان”, or “Sultan Mahmud Khan”. It also names Timur. This later western example belongs to the era when Timur held real power while a khan supplied formal legitimacy. The Arabic lettering shows how two layers of authority could fit on one small coin.

The khanate divided during the fourteenth century. Timur’s rise transformed western rule, while eastern Chagatai dynasties continued in Moghulistan and later Kashgar and Yarkand. Sultan Said established a new Kashgar-centred state in 1514; eastern branches lasted beyond 1530 into the seventeenth century. The atlas cutoff is not one conquest or the disappearance of Central Asia’s communities.

passages.text: Choctaw history connects southeastern homelands with communities that endured removal and built new institutions. The linked Oklahoma outline is wrongly displayed in 1492: it belongs to a much later removal history. The Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma and Mississippi Band are distinct continuing governments.

passages.title: Homelands and evidence
passages.text: Nanih Waiya in Mississippi is central to Choctaw origin traditions. The earthen mound stands about 25 feet high and over 200 feet long. Its meaning reaches beyond its size: Choctaw accounts identify this place as a heart of their people’s history.

passages.title: Homelands and evidence
passages.text: Nanih Waiya returned to the Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians in 2008. That transfer brought a place lost during the removal era back into community care. An ancient monument can be part of a very present-day political and cultural relationship.

passages.title: Homelands and evidence
passages.text: Tribal archaeologist Ken Carlton describes pottery fragments as important clues to ancestral Choctaw history. Tempering materials, construction and decoration help compare sites, but he also emphasizes a difficult gap in seventeenth-century evidence. A recognizable pot is useful evidence, not a person’s identity card.

passages.title: Warm houses and busy kitchens
passages.text: The Nation’s Historic Preservation Department reconstructed a winter home from around three centuries ago with thick plastered walls and a curved entrance that reduced drafts. A central fire warmed the room; the drawing is a researched reconstruction rather than a photograph of an excavated house.

passages.title: Warm houses and busy kitchens
passages.text: In that reconstruction, cane platforms worked as couches by day and beds by night. Food could be stored underneath; cane containers held clothes and possessions. The space beneath the bed had a useful job long before anyone invented a plastic storage box.

passages.title: Warm houses and busy kitchens
passages.text: Choctaw food traditions include banaha bread and fruit dumplings. The Nation’s food history emphasizes that ingredients and recipes changed over time. Families can preserve a recognizable tradition while adapting what grows nearby and what is available in the kitchen.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: Choctaw stickball uses two wooden sticks with cupped, laced ends to handle a small ball. Traditional scoring involved hitting a goal post. Shaping the sticks and weaving the ball are skills in their own right, alongside the speed and teamwork needed on the field.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: The Choctaw Nation now uses stickball to teach children cooperation and family values, and offers workshops in making equipment. The game has survived changes in clothes, rules and organization. Learning a sport can also mean learning how to make the things needed to play.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: A short written sample on the Nation’s modern language page is “yakoke”, meaning “thank you”. The same page supplies recorded lessons and a dictionary. This is contemporary Choctaw written with Latin letters, not a claim that this spelling appeared on a 1492 artifact.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: The 1830 Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek preceded the largest waves of forced migration west. Poor supplies and planning contributed to devastating losses, particularly among elders and children. Choctaw accounts describe the journey through the institutions and relationships families struggled to preserve.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: In 1834, Choctaws adopted a new constitution in Indian Territory and organized three districts. Their council house was called Nanih Waiya, carrying the name of the Mother Mound into a new homeland. Rebuilding included laws and meeting places as well as houses and farms.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: Some Choctaw families stayed in Mississippi despite pressure to leave, then faced dispossession and difficult working conditions. Their descendants organized the Mississippi Band’s 1945 constitution. Their history is related to Oklahoma Choctaw history, but their government is not simply a branch of it.

Removal changed Choctaw landholding and institutions; it did not end Choctaw history. Distinct Choctaw governments and communities continue in Oklahoma and Mississippi. Neither the 1650 map endpoint nor its anachronistic 1492 Oklahoma outline dates the beginning or disappearance of these nations.

sectionTitles: A few words from the period

passages.text: The map’s two entries from 1000 to 1200 represent the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani, a Deccan dynasty established by Taila II around 973. They are distinct from the earlier Chalukyas of Badami. Kalyani, today Basavakalyan, became their political center. The imported outlines are coarse snapshots, not frontiers that stayed fixed for two centuries; the map endpoints are not the dynasty’s beginning or end.

passages.title: Government, merchants and patrons
passages.text: A Dambal inscription dated 1095 to 1096 names Queen Lakshmadevi governing the Eighteen Agraharas and the city of Dharmapura, identified with Dambal. Its praise is ceremonial, but the administrative role is specific: a royal woman appears as a regional governor.

passages.title: Government, merchants and patrons
passages.text: The same record credits sixteen merchants of Dambal with building a Buddhist vihara, and Sangavayya of Lakkundi with a second foundation dedicated to Tara. These were named townspeople financing religious institutions, alongside the royal government described above them.

passages.title: Government, merchants and patrons
passages.text: The Dambal endowment assigned levies on bags traveling to and from the south to its two Buddhist establishments. Passing trade could therefore support worship and upkeep. The edition cannot confidently identify some commodities, so we cannot turn those bags into a precise shopping list.

passages.title: Government, merchants and patrons
passages.text: At Lakkundi, the noblewoman Attimabbe sponsored the Brahma Jinalaya in 1007. She was the wife of Nagadeva and a major Jain patron. The building makes her contribution visible in stone: women could commission institutions remembered long after the rulers whose dates organize our timelines.

passages.title: Government, merchants and patrons
passages.text: Attimabbe also supported Kannada literature, including the poet Ranna. She is celebrated for distributing a thousand copies of Ponna’s Shantipurana. These were handwritten manuscripts: supporting a book meant paying for the work of copying it, not pressing a print button.

passages.title: School days and meals
passages.text: A Kannada inscription at Nagai dated 1058 describes a school with 200 students of the Veda and 52 studying other established disciplines. This was a Brahman teaching institution, not universal schooling. Its unusually detailed endowment lets us count an actual scholarly community.

passages.title: School days and meals
passages.text: Nagai’s school employed six librarians alongside nine teachers. Each librarian received thirty mattars of land as remuneration. Keeping a manuscript collection working was a recognized job, supported by agricultural property rather than a modern monthly bank transfer.

passages.title: School days and meals
passages.text: The school’s bell-ringer received the same land allowance as each librarian and the commentator teaching logic. Other senior scholars received larger plots. Remembering when to assemble mattered enough to appear beside scholarship in the institution’s financial arrangements.

passages.title: School days and meals
passages.text: Nagai’s endowment also covered food and accommodation for scholars and students, including the librarians. Teaching required lodging and meals as well as learned books. The inscription’s budget preserves that practical side of keeping a school alive.

passages.title: School days and meals
passages.text: A 1008 grant from the Konkan chief Ratta Raja assigned the village of Krishnamandi to Avveshvara’s temple to support meals for ascetics, learned people and visitors. The donor was a tributary ruler within the Chalukya political world. A religious endowment could also feed travelers.

passages.title: Useful knowledge and skilled work
passages.text: Chavundaraya II’s Lokopakara, composed in Kannada in 1025, assembled practical knowledge about subjects including cookery, perfumes, plants, animal medicine and building. It shows that learned writing could concern kitchens and the care of animals as well as royal victories. Its medical material records historical ideas, not tested modern treatments.

passages.title: Useful knowledge and skilled work
passages.text: Lokopakara’s eighth chapter gives cookery in fifty-seven verses. Its instructions discuss ingredients and techniques without precise measurements or cooking times. A reader still needed experience: the manuscript was not going to beep when dinner was ready. These prescriptions cannot tell us what every family ate.

passages.title: Useful knowledge and skilled work
passages.text: Lakkundi’s builders worked chloritic schist, using smaller blocks than the sandstone familiar from earlier Badami monuments. They filled temple surfaces with miniature towers, niches, pilasters and cornices. Choosing stone and carving intricate detail were practical achievements of workshops, not simply ideas in a royal order.

passages.title: Useful knowledge and skilled work
passages.text: Look closely at Lakkundi’s sculpture and grand architecture becomes a collection of small discoveries: a griffin at the Jain temple and a horseman at Kashi Vishveshvara. The surviving carvings show how makers combined sacred buildings with lively animal and human figures.

passages.title: Useful knowledge and skilled work
passages.text: Medieval Lakkundi’s surviving water architecture includes stepwells, particularly Musukina Bhavi beside Manikeshwar Temple. Steps made the water accessible below ground level. The heritage description does not supply an exact construction year, so this is a regional example rather than an event dated to a particular king.

passages.title: A few words from the period
passages.text: “Namo Buddhāya” means “Reverence to Buddha!” This Sanskrit opening comes from the Dambal inscription of 1095 to 1096, which also contains Old Kannada. The sample uses normalized Roman transliteration of the published reading; the stone’s letters belong to the contemporary Kannada script tradition.

The dynasty continued beyond the map’s first boundary in 1100. Kalachuri rulers displaced its authority in the twelfth century; Someshvara IV briefly restored it before Yadava and Hoysala expansion ended its wider power. Kannada literary, religious and craft traditions continued under changing rulers.

sectionTitles: Water, work and places to gather

passages.text: The early Chalukyas ruled a major Deccan kingdom from Vatapi, today’s Badami. Their history includes expansion, invasion, recovery and remarkable building projects. This map’s 600 to 800 window begins after their rise and extends beyond their loss of imperial power. The later Chalukya kingdom centered on Kalyani is a different phase.

passages.title: Power, rivalry and royal families
passages.text: Badami’s capital occupied a dramatic setting between sandstone hills, beside a large reservoir. Pulakeshin I fortified the place in the sixth century. The landscape offered cliffs as well as built defenses, although much surviving masonry belongs to later rebuildings. A present-day fort wall cannot all be dated from one founding inscription.

passages.title: Power, rivalry and royal families
passages.text: Pulakeshin II expanded Chalukya authority across much of the Deccan and resisted Harsha’s advance from northern India. His success did not make the kingdom invulnerable: the Pallavas later captured Badami. The dynasty’s story includes recovery after this seventh-century disaster as well as its better-advertised victories.

passages.title: Power, rivalry and royal families
passages.text: Queen Lokamahadevi commissioned Pattadakal’s Virupaksha temple around 740 to commemorate her husband’s victories in the south. Monumental patronage gave a queen a lasting public presence. Her name and purpose survive alongside the king’s military reputation.

passages.title: Power, rivalry and royal families
passages.text: An inscription at Badami’s Jambulinga temple records Queen Vinayavati installing images of Brahma, Vishnu and Maheshvara in 699, during the reign of her son Vijayaditya. This is a specific mother-and-son royal setting in which the queen undertook her own religious foundation.

passages.title: Water, work and places to gather
passages.text: Badami’s Agastya Thirtha reservoir depended on a larger water-catching landscape. A modern study identifies cliff-cut and open masonry channels from the Chalukyan period that helped direct runoff. Supplying a settlement required attention to the hills above it, not just the impressive pool at its center.

passages.title: Water, work and places to gather
passages.text: Researchers combined satellite imagery with digital models of the terrain to trace this water network. Their study separates Chalukyan channels from a much later Vijayanagara aqueduct. Small walls and channels, easily overlooked beside decorated temples, reveal how generations kept water moving where it was needed.

passages.title: Water, work and places to gather
passages.text: At Shankaralingana Gundu quarry near Pattadakal, an unfinished stone shows stages of preparation: mark a line, locate the holes, outline them, then cut them. A steel wedge and hammer found at a nearby quarry support the explanation that workers split blocks by pounding wedges into the prepared holes.

passages.title: Water, work and places to gather
passages.text: Early Chalukya stonecutters often left lens-shaped holes and U-shaped marks when blocks split. Kuppa and Menon compare these with more angular marks from later Vijayanagara work. Their proposed method helps untangle Badami’s rebuilt walls. Even the builders’ leftover dents can become historical evidence.

passages.title: Water, work and places to gather
passages.text: At Jambulinga, the porch’s outer pillars are linked by a stone bench. This small architectural feature makes a temple more than a sculpture to view from a distance: its builders provided a place to sit within the entrance space. The bench survives alongside the royal dedication.

passages.title: Water, work and places to gather
passages.text: An eighth-century Pattadakal pillar records a land transaction behind temple worship. Jnanasivacharya bought thirty nivarttanas from Aryabhatta and endowed the Vijayesvara temple. Such a record names people, a measured resource and its purpose. There is no reason to identify this landowner with the famous earlier mathematician of the same name.

passages.title: Artists, stories and learned words
passages.text: Badami Cave III was dedicated in 578, before the map’s first year, by Mangalesha during Kirtivarman I’s reign. Its inscription also records the gift of a village. Carving the shrine was only one part of the project: an endowment helped connect a religious institution to resources outside its walls.

passages.title: Artists, stories and learned words
passages.text: A surviving painted fragment in Cave III depicts a royal couple watching a dance. Craftsmen also left names on the cave’s facade, including Kolimanchi and Singimanchi. These details bring performers and makers into view beside the patrons; the painted court scene is not a description of every family’s entertainment.

passages.title: Artists, stories and learned words
passages.text: Virupaksha’s great building project names two master architects, Gunda-Anivaritachari and Sarvasiddhi-Achari, who received royal honors. Its walls and pillars preserve stories from the Ramayana, Mahabharata and Panchatantra. Skilled workers turned stone surfaces into places where familiar narratives could be recognized and retold.

passages.title: Artists, stories and learned words
passages.text: Ravikirti composed the Aihole inscription of 634 or 635 and founded the Jain temple it commemorates. His Sanskrit poem praises Pulakeshin II and compares his own literary reputation with Kalidasa and Bharavi. The learned references reveal literary training; the royal praise also reminds readers that this author wanted to impress his patron.

passages.title: Artists, stories and learned words
passages.text: The inscription opens jayati bhagavāñ jinendro, “Victorious is the holy Jinendra.” This is Sanskrit in scholarly Roman transliteration; the stone uses an early southern script ancestral to Kannada-Telugu writing. The short invocation comes from Ravikirti’s actual inscription, not an invented sentence for the court.

passages.title: What lasted beyond the dynasty
passages.text: Pattadakal’s temples brought northern and southern architectural forms into the same landscape during the seventh and eighth centuries. Comparing their towers and ground plans reveals builders trying different solutions. Their contribution was a body of experiments that later architects could study and adapt.

passages.title: What lasted beyond the dynasty
passages.text: The present monument group also contains the Jaina Narayana temple, probably built in the ninth century under the Rashtrakutas above an earlier brick Jain shrine. Its later date matters: religious construction continued after Badami Chalukya rule, and today’s cluster preserves several historical layers.

The Rashtrakutas displaced the Badami Chalukyas as the leading Deccan power in the 750s. Political histories commonly mark 753, while ASI describes Badami’s royal phase continuing to 757. The imported 800 cutoff is later still. This transition ended a dynasty’s imperial supremacy; it did not erase the region’s communities or building traditions.

passages.text: Champa was a string of Cham kingdoms along the coast of what is now central Vietnam, first recorded by the Chinese as Lin-yi in 192 CE. Seafarers and traders, the Chams built brick towers to Shiva and fought the Khmer and the Vietnamese for more than a thousand years.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Brick tower temples at My Son, built from the seventh to the thirteenth century, with sandstone carving of a fineness that rivals Angkor.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Sandstone images of Shiva, Vishnu, Ganesha and dancing apsaras in the Cham styles of Tra Kieu and Dong Duong.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Cham ports sold agarwood, ivory, gold and cinnamon to China and the archipelago and sheltered ships waiting for the monsoon.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Cham sailors traded and raided across the South China Sea and up the Mekong; they sacked Angkor in 1177.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Shaivism was the royal cult, with Buddhism strong at Dong Duong in the ninth century; Islam reached the Chams from the fifteenth century.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Sanskrit and Cham inscriptions record kings and gifts to temples; the Dong Yen Chau stone of the fourth century is the oldest text in any Southeast Asian language.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: My Son Sanctuary was listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Cham communities in Vietnam and Cambodia keep the language and, in Cambodia, Islam.
The Vietnamese took the capital Vijaya in 1471; the last Cham principality, Panduranga, was absorbed by the Nguyen emperor Minh Mang in 1832.

sectionTitles: Discoveries and a sentence carved in stone

passages.text: In the thirteenth century, Cham rulers governed several coastal and river-valley centers in what is now central and southern Vietnam. Their alliances, rivalries and temple networks crossed the neat divisions suggested by a map. This card focuses on the atlas’s 1200 to 1279 interval, separately from the longer Champa history. Neither endpoint marks its founding or disappearance. The coarse imported outline even omits relevant coastal places such as Po Nagar at Nha Trang; it cannot establish precise borders or a single unified state.

passages.title: Rulers, fields and people
passages.text: Champa’s important centers grew beside rivers and useful sea approaches. Around Quy Nhon, temple remains belong especially to the eleventh through thirteenth centuries. Vickery also identifies apparently competing royal claims in 1244. A king’s boast about ruling all Champa therefore needs checking against the inscriptions of other rulers.

passages.title: Rulers, fields and people
passages.text: The Phan Rang inscription C4 recalls Khmer departure for Angkor and Cham movement to Vijaya in 1220/1. It then records a royal consecration in 1226/7 and renewed temples. This is a ruler’s account of restoration after warfare, preserved on a sandstone doorway.

passages.title: Rulers, fields and people
passages.text: The same doorway lists named rice fields dedicated to Svayamutpanna, including fields bounded by a dyke. It also records gold and silver. Religious institutions depended on agricultural resources as well as impressive buildings; these inscriptions preserve the accounting behind royal generosity.

passages.title: Rulers, fields and people
passages.text: At Po Nagar in Nha Trang, a thirteenth-century inscription lists 55 enslaved people alongside temple property. They include Cham, Khmer, Paganese and Siamese people. This stark record shows that temples could command coerced labor, and that political and commercial connections also moved people against their will.

passages.title: A trading visitor’s notebook
passages.text: Zhao Rugua’s account, compiled around 1225 from reports and earlier texts, describes officials boarding merchant ships. They recorded cargo in white characters on folded black material, translated as leather. Goods were inspected before unloading, and the government claimed two tenths. Even a sea voyage ended with paperwork.

passages.title: A trading visitor’s notebook
passages.text: The same account describes ploughing with two buffaloes and lists beans, millet, sugar cane, bananas and coconuts. Scented wood cut in the mountains was taxed before private trading. Farming and forest products both supported exchanges with overseas merchants.

passages.title: A trading visitor’s notebook
passages.text: Zhao reports frequent bathing, fragrant body preparations and clothing perfumed with scented smoke. He also describes a procession of fishing boats in the fourth lunar month. These are reported customs, not proof that every household washed or celebrated identically, and they do not establish a sewer or toilet system.

passages.title: A trading visitor’s notebook
passages.text: For Panduranga around Phan Rang, Zhao describes palm-leaf roofs and protective wooden palisades. That short account offers a glimpse of ordinary dwellings alongside the region’s surviving stone and brick monuments.

passages.title: Discoveries and a sentence carved in stone
passages.text: At Thap Mam in Binh Dinh, excavation in 1934 uncovered tower foundations inside a walled compound and a reported 58 tons of stone sculpture and architectural decoration. The complex is dated to the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Its remains helped scholars define a distinctive sculptural style; another excavation followed in 2011.

passages.title: Discoveries and a sentence carved in stone
passages.text: One earlier masterpiece from Thap Mam, dated to the twelfth century, is a sandstone dragon with raised hind legs and a gem in its mouth. The museum guide suggests a combination with the Hindu sea creature makara. Artists could combine familiar creatures into something entirely new: quite a balancing act in stone.

passages.title: Discoveries and a sentence carved in stone
passages.text: C4, dated 1226/7 at Phan Rang, reads “humā parik· 155 jāk·”: “the rice-fields of Parik: 155 jāk.” This is the editors’ Latin transliteration of Old Cham, not a reproduction of its carved script. The land unit jāk is left unconverted.

passages.title: Discoveries and a sentence carved in stone
passages.text: Domestic archaeology is harder to date than famous temple sculptures. In his 2022 research overview, archaeologist William Southworth stresses how limited the ceramic sequence after the fourth century still is. A potsherd can be real evidence while its date remains uncertain. These sources do not establish thirteenth-century school routines, medical treatments or household toilets.

passages.title: Beyond the atlas endpoint
passages.text: Champa was still a political actor after 1279. In 1283, Khubilai Khan demanded passage and supplies from the Tran rulers of Dai Viet for a campaign against their southern neighbor. They refused. The ensuing wars connected Cham, Vietnamese and Mongol decisions, rather than ending neatly when this atlas layer changes.

passages.title: Beyond the atlas endpoint
passages.text: Living Cham communities also remain. UNESCO’s 2022 pottery record describes women shaping household vessels by walking around them instead of turning a wheel. Pots stay put while the potter moves! This is documented modern craft, not proof that the same technique made every medieval Cham vessel.

passages.title: Beyond the atlas endpoint
passages.text: In that modern practice, children learn through hands-on family teaching, while women exchange skills and conversation during work. Unglazed vessels are fired outdoors with wood and straw for seven to eight hours at about 800°C. Keeping a craft alive involves everyday practice, materials and livelihoods as well as preserving museum objects.

The map’s 1279 cutoff is not Champa’s fall: it remained involved in regional diplomacy and warfare afterward. Later political losses require their own dates and local histories. Cham communities and living crafts continue, without implying that their present practices are unchanged copies of thirteenth-century life.
