passages.text: Chile declared independence in 1818, decades before this map record begins. Industrial towns, family work and public-health debates reveal a republic whose institutions were interrupted by dictatorship and restored in 1990.

passages.title: Work, homes and health
passages.text: At Santa Laura, surviving saltpeter-processing equipment includes a leaching shed and a grinder. These are traces of the machinery that turned desert deposits into fertilizer traded overseas. Industrial achievement depended on workers and transport as well as mineral wealth.

passages.title: Work, homes and health
passages.text: Humberstone preserves living quarters and communal spaces around its square, while railway remains link it to Santa Laura. The two sites together show a workplace and a settlement. A factory did not stop affecting family life when a shift ended.

passages.title: Work, homes and health
passages.text: Workers from Chile, Peru and Bolivia built the shared Pampino culture of the nitrate towns. Former workers and descendants later returned for commemorations such as Saltpeter Week. The industry declined, but its communities retained memories and connections.

passages.title: Work, homes and health
passages.text: In late nineteenth-century Santiago, overcrowded housing and inadequate drinking-water and sewer systems helped infections spread. Elegant mansions and new public works existed alongside these conditions. A growing city could look prosperous while many residents lacked basic services.

passages.title: Work, homes and health
passages.text: A 1872 decree introduced hygiene teaching in schools, but training and implementation lagged. Physician Isaac Ugarte criticized its shortcomings in 1884. Declaring a subject compulsory did not instantly produce teachers equipped to teach it.

passages.title: Work, homes and health
passages.text: In many urban working households during 1900 to 1950, mothers combined paid employment with domestic work. Older daughters could take over childcare and cleaning; sons often assisted fathers in their trades. Childhood responsibilities varied sharply with class and gender.

passages.title: Work, homes and health
passages.text: Long working hours, insecure wages and illness placed working families under strain. Social workers and public-health nurses increasingly entered this domestic world as the state expanded assistance. The evidence concerns a changing social policy, not a claim that every household received help.

passages.title: Craft, writing and political change
passages.text: Quinchamalí and Santa Cruz de Cuca pottery uses black surfaces with white accents. Makers produce useful pots and dishes alongside decorative figures. These living traditions turn everyday materials into objects that can serve a meal or tell a local story.

passages.title: Craft, writing and political change
passages.text: One recognizable figure is the guitarrera: a rural woman holding a guitar. It connects pottery with local people and music. The 2022 UNESCO safeguarding record identifies a particular regional tradition, not a pottery style shared by all Chileans.

passages.title: Craft, writing and political change
passages.text: The Spanish sentence “Las personas nacen libres e iguales en dignidad y derechos” means “People are born free and equal in dignity and rights.” It opens Article 1 of the consolidated constitution consulted in its 2023 version. This is a legal principle, not proof that equality has always been achieved.

passages.title: Craft, writing and political change
passages.text: After the 1973 coup, the military authorities dissolved Congress and assumed legislative functions. The interruption changed where laws were made and who could participate. It belongs in the same national history as factories, schools and artistic work.

passages.title: Craft, writing and political change
passages.text: The 1988 plebiscite rejected extending Augusto Pinochet’s presidency. Congress resumed on 11 March 1990. Voting and the rebuilding of institutions were parts of a transition; the country and its communities did not begin from scratch that day.

Chile continues. Independence was declared in 1818; the 1973 dictatorship interrupted representative government, and Congress returned in 1990. The map’s 1878 start is a coverage date, not the birth of Chile or its diverse peoples.

passages.text: The Chimu kingdom made Chan Chan a major center on Peru's north coast. Its earthen compounds, craft production and water systems show how a large city organized resources in a dry coastal environment.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Canals and irrigation supported agriculture around Chan Chan. Roads helped connect the kingdom along the northern coast.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: Large walled compounds contained open courts, temples, dwellings, storage spaces, reservoirs and funerary platforms.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Earthen walls carried relief decoration with abstract patterns and human or animal subjects.

passages.title: Craft and work
passages.text: Specialized production areas supported weaving, woodworking and metalworking. These activities were part of the city's planned fabric.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Storage and water-management installations supported the city alongside agricultural land beyond its monumental center.

passages.title: Change over time
passages.text: The kingdom reached its height in the fifteenth century before incorporation into the Inca Empire. The source used here does not establish a precise conquest year.

passages.text: This record begins in 1945, when the Republic of China still governed and civil war was about to resume. The People’s Republic was proclaimed on 1 October 1949. These are distinct political phases. The imported outline spans changing governments and territorial control; it cannot resolve sovereignty disputes or substitute for the separate Taiwan record.

passages.title: Governments, campaigns and changing lives
passages.text: Japan’s defeat in 1945 did not bring lasting peace to China. Nationalists and Communists returned to full-scale civil war. Mao Zedong proclaimed the People’s Republic in October 1949, while the Nationalist government retreated to Taiwan. This was a change of government on the mainland, not the disappearance of Chinese people or culture.

passages.title: Governments, campaigns and changing lives
passages.text: The Communist Party became the leading institution of the People’s Republic. A 2025 Congressional Research Service account explains that Party authorities outrank government counterparts, while the State Council handles administration and the National People’s Congress passes laws and budgets. The Party’s influence extends through national and local institutions.

passages.title: Governments, campaigns and changing lives
passages.text: The Great Leap Forward tried to transform production rapidly. Communal farming and dining changed everyday routines, but the famine of 1959 to 1961 brought catastrophic hunger and deaths. Research identifies state grain procurement and failures to respond to real conditions as major causes; abundant grain in an area did not guarantee food for its residents.

passages.title: Governments, campaigns and changing lives
passages.text: During the Cultural Revolution, schools and universities suffered major interruptions. Researchers have traced differences in later educational attainment to the disruption experienced by different cities and age groups between 1966 and 1976. A child’s chance to keep studying could depend on political upheaval well beyond the classroom.

passages.title: Governments, campaigns and changing lives
passages.text: A 1967 poster preserved by the Library of Congress shows Red Guard youths destroying symbols of older traditions, including books and religion. It reveals how propaganda encouraged cultural destruction. An image intended to recruit enthusiasm has become evidence for historians examining a damaging political campaign.

passages.title: Governments, campaigns and changing lives
passages.text: Reforms associated with the turn beginning in 1978 experimented with markets, rural enterprises and overseas investment. The first four special economic zones were created in 1980. Change developed through experiments and adjustments rather than a single moment when the whole economy switched systems.

passages.title: Governments, campaigns and changing lives
passages.text: In June 1989, troops violently suppressed protests in Beijing, killing civilians. Declassified documents collected by the National Security Archive show military attacks and officials’ fear that dissent threatened Party rule. Economic change did not automatically produce freedom to challenge the government.

passages.title: Families, work and the table
passages.text: The 1950 Marriage Law promoted choosing one’s own spouse, monogamy and equal legal rights for women and men. Couples were required to register marriages with state offices. Posters advertised happy families, but the law also met resistance and generated disputes: a new rule did not instantly rearrange every household.

passages.title: Families, work and the table
passages.text: Family size also became a matter of government policy. Birth restrictions changed over time; UNFPA recorded a universal two-child policy in 2016 and a three-child policy announced in 2021. Its 2021 discussion stressed reproductive rights and support for families, rather than treating parents simply as tools for population targets.

passages.title: Families, work and the table
passages.text: Under the household responsibility system, farm families gained more control over production and could keep output after meeting agreed delivery and tax obligations. They received land-use rights, not unrestricted private ownership of farmland. The rules changed the relationship between daily effort, household decisions and income.

passages.title: Families, work and the table
passages.text: Jobs could also separate families. In a February 2026 UNICEF account, Zhang Qin in rural Guizhou was caring for grandchildren while their parents worked in Jiangsu. Video calls helped keep them connected. Grandparents’ daily work included play, comfort and learning, as well as food and clothes.

passages.title: Families, work and the table
passages.text: Spring Festival preparations include cleaning homes, laying in provisions and making food for reunion dinners. Families may stay awake to welcome the new year and visit relatives and neighbours. Skills pass between generations through cooking, decorations and performance: celebrations can be a lively family classroom.

passages.title: Families, work and the table
passages.text: Tea is both a craft and a way to welcome people. Producers make varieties such as green, white, oolong and black tea, while families and apprentices pass on processing skills. UNESCO also records the pastries served alongside tea. One plant can lead to a surprisingly complicated drinks menu.

passages.title: School, health and practical ingenuity
passages.text: At Doujiang Primary School in Guangxi, a 2009 UNICEF report described a “My Voice” noticeboard where pupils posted requests and criticism. They asked for dance lessons and more trees, and even complained about boring lectures. The children also managed sports equipment: responsibility could start with making sure the next class got its ball back.

passages.title: School, health and practical ingenuity
passages.text: Cold-weather sanitation needed its own engineering. At Taizi Township Central School in Qinghai, new facilities reported in 2023 used solar energy to warm handwashing water. Private stalls, more provision for girls and an accessible room addressed dignity and access as well as cleanliness. A warm tap can be an important school improvement.

passages.title: School, health and practical ingenuity
passages.text: Rural health care expanded through community workers often called barefoot doctors. They combined farming with short medical training, prevention and basic treatment. The name became popular in the 1960s; WHO’s 2008 history also describes later examinations through which workers could qualify as village doctors. Training and responsibilities changed over time.

passages.title: School, health and practical ingenuity
passages.text: Tu Youyou’s team searched for a new treatment for malaria. Her first-person Nobel account describes an effective wormwood extract in 1971 and the isolation of artemisinin in 1972. This required laboratory tests, clinical research and cooperation between institutes; an old medical clue became part of a modern drug-development programme.

passages.title: School, health and practical ingenuity
passages.text: Even a promising medicine could fail because of how its tablets were made. Tu recalled that early artemisinin tablets were too hard to break apart properly. The team investigated and tested capsules in 1973. The useful discovery was not just the molecule: how to deliver it mattered too.

passages.title: Connections, discoveries and continuing challenges
passages.text: China joined the World Trade Organization on 11 December 2001 after a long negotiation process. Membership connected its economy more formally to a system of international trade agreements. This milestone belongs to modern economic history, rather than to the much earlier Silk Roads.

passages.title: Connections, discoveries and continuing challenges
passages.text: A World Bank study published in 2019 documented more than 25,000 kilometres of high-speed railway by the end of 2017. These lines linked major cities and helped change passenger travel. The number is a dated snapshot of a rapidly expanding network, not its present-day length.

passages.title: Connections, discoveries and continuing challenges
passages.text: The Chang’e-6 mission returned the first samples from the Moon’s far side on 25 June 2024. Its lander also carried a small laser reflector developed by Chinese and Italian researchers. Collecting rocks and providing a reflector for future precision measurements were different scientific jobs aboard the same mission.

passages.title: Connections, discoveries and continuing challenges
passages.text: The returned lunar material gave researchers direct evidence of ancient volcanic activity on the far side. A November 2024 report described rock evidence for episodes roughly 2.8 and 4.2 billion years ago. Small samples can answer questions about a world far larger than the container that holds them.

passages.title: Connections, discoveries and continuing challenges
passages.text: Economic growth brought enormous reductions in severe poverty. A 2022 World Bank report estimated that almost 800 million fewer people lived below its then-used international threshold of $1.90 a day than forty years earlier. That specific measure does not mean hardship or inequality had disappeared.

passages.title: Two short written witnesses
passages.text: A 1950 marriage-law poster is catalogued as “拥护婚姻法” (Yonghu hunyinfa), translated “Support the marriage law.” These are the catalogue’s modern-character transcription and romanization. The poster shows a couple shaking hands, with the law’s twenty-seven articles printed on the back: public information came on both sides of the paper.

passages.title: Two short written witnesses
passages.text: Tu Youyou’s 2015 Nobel biography writes “青蒿素” (qīnghāosù), the Chinese name for artemisinin. This short scientific term is an attested modern Chinese writing sample tied to the malaria research described above. It names the purified drug compound, not simply a cup of herbal tea.

The People’s Republic continues; this record has no historical fall date. Political institutions and everyday conditions keep changing, so modern examples here are dated. The map’s changing outlines should not be used to settle the status of Taiwan or other contested territories.

sectionTitles: Making a living beside the desert
Care for the dead and clues to life
What survives and what remains unknown

passages.text: Chinchorro identifies ancient fishing and gathering communities of the Atacama coast, famous for carefully prepared human mummies. The map’s linked 2000 to 400 BCE intervals capture only a late slice and extend beyond the chronology of the UNESCO sites, approximately 5450 to 890 BCE. These are archaeological labels, not a kingdom’s borders.

passages.title: Making a living beside the desert
passages.text: The World Heritage sites include the slopes of Arica’s Morro, Colón 10 and the Camarones river mouth. Dense accumulations of discarded shells sit alongside settlement and burial evidence. Generations of meals helped leave an archaeological record of sustained coastal life.

passages.title: Making a living beside the desert
passages.text: Fishers shaped shell into hooks, using stone files to smooth the material. They also made hooks from plant spines. Cords and stone weights completed equipment assembled from several different parts of the landscape; a shell could help catch tomorrow’s dinner.

passages.title: Making a living beside the desert
passages.text: Sea-lion rib bones became tools for opening shellfish. Hunting equipment included detachable harpoon heads. These objects document specialized ways of obtaining food rather than a population simply picking up whatever washed onto the beach.

passages.title: Making a living beside the desert
passages.text: Plants such as rushes supplied material for mats and cords, while food came from coastal and inland environments. Permanent structures and cemeteries suggest communities could remain in favored places while people still traveled to use different resources.

passages.title: Care for the dead and clues to life
passages.text: Some bodies survived because the desert dried them naturally. Others show deliberate preparation, with internal supports, modeled surfaces and pigments. Distinguishing those processes matters: a preserved person is not automatically evidence that someone performed artificial mummification.

passages.title: Care for the dead and clues to life
passages.text: The so-called black mummies used dark manganese-rich coatings, with wooden supports and plant-fiber ties beneath modeled surfaces. Red examples used red ochre and often dark faces. The colors identify materials and techniques; they are not names of separate peoples.

passages.title: Care for the dead and clues to life
passages.text: Elaborate preservation was applied to children as well as adults. UNESCO describes people across the social spectrum among the prepared bodies.

passages.title: Care for the dead and clues to life
passages.text: Researchers examined arsenic in hair from 45 ancient people from the Arica region, spanning several archaeological periods. Some Chinchorro individuals had high values. The findings help investigate environmental exposure and movement, but cannot diagnose every member of an ancient community.

passages.title: Care for the dead and clues to life
passages.text: A 2012 study proposed that more reliable freshwater and abundant marine food supported population growth and cultural innovation. Its explanation for mummification combines archaeological dates, environmental evidence and a model of learning. It is a tested proposal about processes, not a recovered Chinchorro account.

passages.title: What survives and what remains unknown
passages.text: No deciphered Chinchorro writing is available in the evidence used here. Tools, pigments and burial arrangements convey choices and meanings, but cannot supply a reliable original-language quotation. We cannot translate the spoken words of these ancient communities.

passages.title: What survives and what remains unknown
passages.text: Conservators found that changes in humidity could encourage microbes to damage preserved skin. Harvard and Chilean researchers studied samples to understand the process. Caring for an ancient burial today therefore involves microbiology and careful storage as well as archaeology.

passages.title: What survives and what remains unknown
passages.text: In 2014, archaeologists brought specially prepared materials about Colón 10 to an Azapa school class. Children asked about food, habits and mummification before being invited to the site museum. Local heritage includes learning about how people lived, alongside respectful care for their remains.

Elaborate mummification changed and eventually ceased; its ending is not a dated military conquest. Researchers have proposed changing water supplies, marine resources and population patterns as contributing factors. The map’s 400 BCE endpoint should not be treated as a proven disappearance date for the people themselves.

sectionTitles: Making a living beside the desert
Care for the dead and clues to life
What survives and what remains unknown

passages.text: Chinchorro identifies ancient fishing and gathering communities of the Atacama coast, famous for carefully prepared human mummies. The map’s linked 2000 to 400 BCE intervals capture only a late slice and extend beyond the chronology of the UNESCO sites, approximately 5450 to 890 BCE. These are archaeological labels, not a kingdom’s borders.

passages.title: Making a living beside the desert
passages.text: The World Heritage sites include the slopes of Arica’s Morro, Colón 10 and the Camarones river mouth. Dense accumulations of discarded shells sit alongside settlement and burial evidence. Generations of meals helped leave an archaeological record of sustained coastal life.

passages.title: Making a living beside the desert
passages.text: Fishers shaped shell into hooks, using stone files to smooth the material. They also made hooks from plant spines. Cords and stone weights completed equipment assembled from several different parts of the landscape; a shell could help catch tomorrow’s dinner.

passages.title: Making a living beside the desert
passages.text: Sea-lion rib bones became tools for opening shellfish. Hunting equipment included detachable harpoon heads. These objects document specialized ways of obtaining food rather than a population simply picking up whatever washed onto the beach.

passages.title: Making a living beside the desert
passages.text: Plants such as rushes supplied material for mats and cords, while food came from coastal and inland environments. Permanent structures and cemeteries suggest communities could remain in favored places while people still traveled to use different resources.

passages.title: Care for the dead and clues to life
passages.text: Some bodies survived because the desert dried them naturally. Others show deliberate preparation, with internal supports, modeled surfaces and pigments. Distinguishing those processes matters: a preserved person is not automatically evidence that someone performed artificial mummification.

passages.title: Care for the dead and clues to life
passages.text: The so-called black mummies used dark manganese-rich coatings, with wooden supports and plant-fiber ties beneath modeled surfaces. Red examples used red ochre and often dark faces. The colors identify materials and techniques; they are not names of separate peoples.

passages.title: Care for the dead and clues to life
passages.text: Elaborate preservation was applied to children as well as adults. UNESCO describes people across the social spectrum among the prepared bodies.

passages.title: Care for the dead and clues to life
passages.text: Researchers examined arsenic in hair from 45 ancient people from the Arica region, spanning several archaeological periods. Some Chinchorro individuals had high values. The findings help investigate environmental exposure and movement, but cannot diagnose every member of an ancient community.

passages.title: Care for the dead and clues to life
passages.text: A 2012 study proposed that more reliable freshwater and abundant marine food supported population growth and cultural innovation. Its explanation for mummification combines archaeological dates, environmental evidence and a model of learning. It is a tested proposal about processes, not a recovered Chinchorro account.

passages.title: What survives and what remains unknown
passages.text: No deciphered Chinchorro writing is available in the evidence used here. Tools, pigments and burial arrangements convey choices and meanings, but cannot supply a reliable original-language quotation. We cannot translate the spoken words of these ancient communities.

passages.title: What survives and what remains unknown
passages.text: Conservators found that changes in humidity could encourage microbes to damage preserved skin. Harvard and Chilean researchers studied samples to understand the process. Caring for an ancient burial today therefore involves microbiology and careful storage as well as archaeology.

passages.title: What survives and what remains unknown
passages.text: In 2014, archaeologists brought specially prepared materials about Colón 10 to an Azapa school class. Children asked about food, habits and mummification before being invited to the site museum. Local heritage includes learning about how people lived, alongside respectful care for their remains.

Elaborate mummification changed and eventually ceased; its ending is not a dated military conquest. Researchers have proposed changing water supplies, marine resources and population patterns as contributing factors. The map’s 400 BCE endpoint should not be treated as a proven disappearance date for the people themselves.

sectionTitles: Governments, armies and a misleading single color
Families, food and photographs that survived
Learning, clinics and the unglamorous work of sanitation
Printed words and a university on the move

passages.text: “Chinese Warlords” is an atlas umbrella for a divided country, not one government or civilization. Its 1920 to 1945 interval covers competing military regimes, Nationalist consolidation and war with Japan. The imported outline stays unchanged across its snapshots: it cannot show shifting fronts, occupation or rival administrations. The examples below describe particular communities and institutions, whose achievements should not simply be credited to warlords.

passages.title: Governments, armies and a misleading single color
passages.text: After Yuan Shikai died in 1916, military factions struggled to control the republic. Duan Qirui led the Anhui clique, named for his home province; the Zhili clique was a rival. These were networks of officers and supporters, not different ancient civilizations that happened to share a map.

passages.title: Governments, armies and a misleading single color
passages.text: The Northern Expedition began in 1926 to defeat warlord armies and reunify China. Its revolutionary coalition included people with sharply different political ideas. Soldiers mattered, but so did civilian organizing and political alliances. The campaign’s success cannot be reduced to one commander marching through an empty landscape.

passages.title: Governments, armies and a misleading single color
passages.text: In 1927 the coalition broke apart. Chiang Kai-shek attacked Communist organization in Shanghai and established his government at Nanjing. Beijing, Wuhan and Nanjing each housed a rival national government. One map color conceals this contest.

passages.title: Governments, armies and a misleading single color
passages.text: By 1928 the Nanjing government had international recognition and nominal national authority. This did not mean that every provincial army or Communist base obeyed it. During the following decade, government projects pursued railway, road, banking and legal reform alongside continued political conflict.

passages.title: Governments, armies and a misleading single color
passages.text: Japanese forces seized Manchuria in 1931, outside much of this record’s outline. Full-scale war followed fighting near Beijing’s Marco Polo Bridge in July 1937. Japanese armies advanced along the coast and into Nanjing. This was foreign invasion superimposed on internal conflict, not merely another change of warlord.

passages.title: Families, food and photographs that survived
passages.text: Sidney Gamble photographed urban and rural China during visits between 1917 and 1932. Long afterward, his daughter Catherine Curran found negatives stored in rosewood boxes in a family closet. Preserving and digitizing them recovered thousands of small details of everyday life that political histories can miss.

passages.title: Families, food and photographs that survived
passages.text: An early twentieth-century Beijing photograph shows women buying and selling eggs from baskets on the street, with other people watching. The photographer’s shadow enters the scene. Even a seemingly ordinary shopping picture reminds us that someone chose where to stand and what to show; it is not a census of every household.

passages.title: Families, food and photographs that survived
passages.text: A photograph dated 1924 to 1927 shows smiling boys waiting for porridge distribution, with a school honor list behind them. Food relief and schooling could share the same visual world. Their smiles do not tell us how secure their next meal would be.

passages.title: Families, food and photographs that survived
passages.text: In Dingxian, reformers wanted to change childbirth care, infant care and household arrangements. Families accepted some proposals and rejected others. Historian Kate Merkel-Hess finds that people weighed questions of authority, expertise and whether a practice worked. Rural parents had their own judgments; they were not simply waiting to be instructed.

passages.title: Learning, clinics and the unglamorous work of sanitation
passages.text: James Yen’s Mass Education Movement used reading books built around about a thousand Chinese characters. In Dingxian, literacy teaching was connected with agricultural work and social surveys. Its staff were Chinese, and its 1930 report described the organization as independent of political factions. These achievements belonged to educators and their communities.

passages.title: Learning, clinics and the unglamorous work of sanitation
passages.text: Dingxian’s public-health work began in 1929. A dispensary and clinics opened at the county seat, and smallpox vaccination followed in spring 1930. Investigators also began collecting health and birth-and-death information. Building a service meant learning what was happening to people, as well as treating an individual patient.

passages.title: Learning, clinics and the unglamorous work of sanitation
passages.text: The same project proposed research on clean water, safer food and disinfecting human waste used as fertilizer. It also proposed studying supplementary foods such as soybean milk. The 1930 document is a plan, not proof of universal implementation or flush toilets. Public health reached right into the water jar, kitchen and field.

passages.title: Learning, clinics and the unglamorous work of sanitation
passages.text: Agricultural demonstration sites linked university researchers with rural work during the 1930s. The Rockefeller-supported program joined farming, education and health, but researchers and field workers did not always agree. Land reform remained a central difficulty that an outside foundation could not resolve. Better crops alone could not settle who owned the land.

passages.title: Learning, clinics and the unglamorous work of sanitation
passages.text: War disrupted these efforts. After the 1937 invasion, participating rural-reconstruction organizations closed or moved to southwestern China. Some support continued there through 1946. Carrying knowledge and institutions elsewhere was a form of survival, even when a carefully planned local experiment could no longer continue.

passages.title: Printed words and a university on the move
passages.text: The Chinese title 新青年, in modern Mandarin Romanization Xīn qīngnián, means “New Youth.” Qingdao Museum holds the issue dated 1 April 1920, volume 7, number 5. This is a normalized transcription of an attested magazine title, not a reproduction of its printed letter shapes. The journal preserves one strand of a lively and divided intellectual world.

passages.title: Printed words and a university on the move
passages.text: During the invasion, Tsinghua, Peking and Nankai universities combined in Changsha, then moved to Kunming in 1938 as the Southwest Associated University. A university could survive without staying on its original campus. Teachers, students and scholarly work continued under extremely difficult wartime conditions.

passages.title: Printed words and a university on the move
passages.text: One university history recounts that student Zha Liangzheng carried a small English-Chinese dictionary on the 1938 journey, tearing out pages after memorizing them. He later became the poet and translator Mu Dan. In this remembered episode, the book grew lighter as the student’s vocabulary grew heavier.

The map stops in 1945, when the war against Japan ended, not when China’s political conflicts disappeared. Nationalists and Communists returned to large-scale civil war. The People’s Republic was proclaimed in 1949, while the Republic of China government retreated to Taiwan. Communities and institutions continued through these upheavals; this umbrella has no single ruler’s fall date.

sectionTitles: Households, archaeology and working with cedar
Dispossession, rebuilding and a language sample

passages.text: Chinook communities made the lower Columbia River and its Pacific coast a busy center of river life. Today the Chinook Indian Nation joins five constituent groups. The map’s 1492 to 1500 outline covers part of this region, not every Chinookan community or the full span of Chinook history.

passages.title: Households, archaeology and working with cedar
passages.text: The present Chinook Indian Nation identifies Lower Chinook, Clatsop, Kathlamet, Wahkiakum and Willapa as its constituent groups. Their communities lie around the river mouth and neighboring shores. This modern political association should not be mistaken for a single ancient empire governing every Chinookan-speaking village upriver.

passages.title: Households, archaeology and working with cedar
passages.text: Cedar plankhouses could shelter several related families, each with its own fire. In a 1902 account, Catherine George remembered houses at Gray’s Bay with several household fires. Seasonal movement could also involve lighter summer shelters. A village was therefore a community of households whose living arrangements changed with work and season.

passages.title: Households, archaeology and working with cedar
passages.text: Household society had inequalities. The community-reviewed history describes leading families toward the back of a plankhouse and commoners and enslaved people nearer the front. Large shared houses were places of kinship and cooperation, but also of unequal power and, for enslaved residents, a lack of freedom.

passages.title: Households, archaeology and working with cedar
passages.text: Cathlapotle, farther upriver near modern Ridgefield, offers a regional Chinookan comparison outside this map outline. Excavators recorded house depressions, hearths and post traces. These buried features preserve the layout of wooden buildings even when their walls have disappeared; they do not establish a coastal Chinook capital.

passages.title: Households, archaeology and working with cedar
passages.text: Cathlapotle’s fish remains include salmon, sturgeon and smelt, with smaller fish also represented. Some excavated deposits held dense concentrations of bones. Archaeologists can study discarded meals to learn about fishing and processing: yesterday’s kitchen rubbish becomes tomorrow’s research material.

passages.title: Households, archaeology and working with cedar
passages.text: Trade beads and pieces of Chinese porcelain at Cathlapotle connect a river town to the overseas fur-trade era. One porcelain fragment had been reshaped into a scraper. Imported objects were not simply stored as curiosities; someone could give a broken piece a new working life.

passages.title: Households, archaeology and working with cedar
passages.text: Canoes carried people and goods through networks linking the coast and the interior. Small gathering boats served short trips, while larger craft carried cargo and traveled coastal waters. A canoe could be everyday transport, a fishing platform and a connection to relatives in another settlement.

passages.title: Households, archaeology and working with cedar
passages.text: Carver Tony Johnson describes placing depth pegs in a canoe hull so that hollowing could stop at the intended thickness. Hot stones and water then produced steam to soften and spread the sides. A graceful wooden boat required careful measuring as well as strength and patience.

passages.title: Households, archaeology and working with cedar
passages.text: Cedar supplied much more than boat hulls. The project’s account describes bark made into water-resistant clothing, roots used for baskets and shredded material used for baby diapers. The same tree could help a family travel, carry supplies and look after its smallest members.

passages.title: Dispossession, rebuilding and a language sample
passages.text: An epidemic in 1830 and 1831 killed many lower Columbia people, including the influential leader Comcomly. Survivors regrouped in communities along the river and Willapa Bay. The loss of relatives and neighbors altered settlement and family life; it did not erase Chinook people from their homeland.

passages.title: Dispossession, rebuilding and a language sample
passages.text: At Tansy Point in 1851, Native leaders resisted removal east of the Cascades. Treaties negotiated there promised provisions and continuing residence in their homeland, but were never ratified. Chinook scholar Rachel Cushman connects this failure with family memories of a hungry winter when promised food did not arrive.

passages.title: Dispossession, rebuilding and a language sample
passages.text: A modern Cathlapotle plankhouse opened in 2005 after more than a hundred volunteers worked on the reconstruction. Archaeology informed the building, which became a setting for education and tribal events. This is a new structure supporting living communities, not a surviving wooden house from the fifteenth century.

passages.title: Dispossession, rebuilding and a language sample
passages.text: In 2019 the Chinook Indian Nation completed the purchase of ten acres at Tansy Point. Cushman describes the fundraising and community effort that made it possible. Recovering land at the treaty site created a place for commemoration and future restoration work, turning historical memory into a practical commitment.

passages.title: Dispossession, rebuilding and a language sample
passages.text: Chinuk Wawa developed as a language of communication among different peoples, drawing on Chinookan languages and other sources. The nation recommends resources in it today. It must be distinguished from the older Chinookan languages and from the assumption that everyone in this coastal region spoke identically.

passages.title: Dispossession, rebuilding and a language sample
passages.text: A short written sample is “kakwa nsayka ulman-tilixam laska munk-kemteks nsayka”, translated “As Our Elders Teach Us to Speak It”. This is the parallel title of Grand Ronde’s 2012 Chinuk Wawa dictionary, in the spelling recorded by Smithsonian’s catalogue. It is a modern teaching witness, not a sentence dated to 1492.

passages.title: Dispossession, rebuilding and a language sample
passages.text: Federal acknowledgement granted in 2001 was reversed in 2002. The Bureau of Indian Affairs still describes the Chinook Indian Nation as non-federally recognized on its current historical-background page. That administrative status concerns the relationship with the United States; Chinook families and national cultural life continue.

There was no Chinook ending in 1500. Despite epidemic loss, land dispossession and the continuing recognition struggle, the nation maintains stories, language and community traditions. The imported date marks the end of this map record only.

sectionTitles: Schools, a written sentence and care

passages.text: The Chitimacha are a living people of southern Louisiana’s bayous and the Atchafalaya Basin. Their reservation is near Charenton. This narrative also serves the map’s “Chtimacha” label: overlapping outlines dated 1492 to 1500 and 1530 to 1783 are imported coverage phases, not separate nations or the people’s beginning and end.

passages.title: Families and waterways
passages.text: Bayou Teche and neighboring waterways were routes for trading and visiting, as well as sources of food. Heritage interpreters describe village buildings made with timber, rivercane and palmetto leaves. People adapted journeys and settlement to changing seasons and water levels, using detailed knowledge of their watery surroundings.

passages.title: Families and waterways
passages.text: The wetlands offered fish, shellfish and other foods alongside edible plants. Traveling through channels required knowing where water led and how conditions changed. The heritage account describes Chitimacha people sharing knowledge of local food, housing and navigation with Acadian newcomers after their arrival in 1765.

passages.title: Families and waterways
passages.text: Clans documented in the early twentieth century included wolf, bear, dog and lion. Membership passed through the mother’s line. The Tribe’s historical account also describes differences in social rank and forms of address, showing that manners and family connections helped organize community life.

passages.title: Families and waterways
passages.text: French slave raids helped provoke a war lasting from 1706 to 1718. French forces and Native allies attacked Chitimacha communities; many people were enslaved. Peace ended the fighting, but survivors had been pushed from eastern settlements toward Grand Lake and Bayou Teche.

passages.title: Families and waterways
passages.text: Landownership remained contested after Louisiana became part of the United States. Lawsuits, pressured sales and tax judgments reduced the land base. In 1916, remaining tribal land entered federal trust. Chitimacha voters later approved a constitution in 1970, with federal approval following in 1971.

passages.title: Baskets built for real jobs
passages.text: Chitimacha baskets begin with local rivercane, a kind of bamboo. Weavers work with red, black and yellow as well as the cane’s natural color. Earlier dyes came from plants; the Tribe also describes later use of commercial dyes. Careful preparation makes a tough stalk into flexible weaving material.

passages.title: Baskets built for real jobs
passages.text: Basket shapes suit different jobs: trays and sifters help with food preparation, while elbow baskets are used to gather berries. Double-woven baskets with lids store belongings, and some can even hold water. That is an impressive assignment for a container made from strips of a plant.

passages.title: Baskets built for real jobs
passages.text: Ada Thomas learned basketry around age twelve from her grandmother Christine Paul, who taught at the reservation school. Her aunt Pauline Paul continued the teaching. Grades one through eight shared one room, so classroom learning and the passing on of family skills could happen close together.

passages.title: Baskets built for real jobs
passages.text: Thomas prepared cane by selecting, splitting, peeling, curing and drying it. For a double-woven basket she formed the inside first, then turned the strips back to build the outside in a continuous weave. The two surfaces are connected parts of one planned structure, rather than a lining dropped into a finished container.

passages.title: Baskets built for real jobs
passages.text: A lidded basket Thomas made in 1989 is preserved at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Its rivercane sides carry the pattern called Alligator Entrails, while small track-like motifs decorate the lid. Named patterns let the viewer recognize a design vocabulary alongside the precision of the weaving.

passages.title: Baskets built for real jobs
passages.text: After eighth grade, Thomas could attend neither the local white nor the local Black high school. She moved to New Orleans to continue studying. Following years away, she returned to basketmaking in the mid-1970s and became a National Heritage Fellow in 1983. Her achievement grew through both family teaching and personal persistence.

passages.title: Schools, a written sentence and care
passages.text: In the early twentieth century, some Chitimacha children were sent far away to Carlisle’s boarding school, where they were forbidden to use their language. At home, exclusion from public schools led the community to hold classes in a tribal member’s house in 1932. Families had to struggle for education on their own terms.

passages.title: Schools, a written sentence and care
passages.text: The state supplied a condemned school building in 1934, and tribal members repaired it for their children. It remained in use until a new school opened in 1978 with funding mainly from the Bureau of Indian Affairs. The history of a classroom can also be a history of community labor.

passages.title: Schools, a written sentence and care
passages.text: A recorded Chitimacha sentence is “we haksigam hix siksi his nuytiqi,” meaning “the young man answered the eagle.” Linguist Daniel Hieber prints it from Benjamin Paul’s recorded narrative material. This example uses the modern practical spelling of a documented utterance, rather than an invented ancient inscription.

passages.title: Schools, a written sentence and care
passages.text: Benjamin Paul and Delphine Decloux Stouff helped preserve Chitimacha through work with linguist Morris Swadesh. Paul died in 1932 and Stouff in 1940, but their documentation later supported language revival in the tribal school and early learning center. Written records and remembered knowledge became resources for new learners.

passages.title: Schools, a written sentence and care
passages.text: The contemporary RiverCane elder program combines independent housing with practical support. Its published services include meals, grocery trips, social activities and checks of blood pressure and blood sugar. Meals can also reach people unable to travel. Looking after a community includes the ordinary work of helping neighbors eat, meet and stay well.

Neither imported map cutoff marks the end of the Chitimacha. The Tribe continues in Louisiana, and children can learn from language documentation preserved by earlier generations. The older record and later “Chtimacha” label belong to this continuing history.

passages.text: Choctaw history connects southeastern homelands with communities that endured removal and built new institutions. The linked Oklahoma outline is wrongly displayed in 1492: it belongs to a much later removal history. The Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma and Mississippi Band are distinct continuing governments.

passages.title: Homelands and evidence
passages.text: Nanih Waiya in Mississippi is central to Choctaw origin traditions. The earthen mound stands about 25 feet high and over 200 feet long. Its meaning reaches beyond its size: Choctaw accounts identify this place as a heart of their people’s history.

passages.title: Homelands and evidence
passages.text: Nanih Waiya returned to the Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians in 2008. That transfer brought a place lost during the removal era back into community care. An ancient monument can be part of a very present-day political and cultural relationship.

passages.title: Homelands and evidence
passages.text: Tribal archaeologist Ken Carlton describes pottery fragments as important clues to ancestral Choctaw history. Tempering materials, construction and decoration help compare sites, but he also emphasizes a difficult gap in seventeenth-century evidence. A recognizable pot is useful evidence, not a person’s identity card.

passages.title: Warm houses and busy kitchens
passages.text: The Nation’s Historic Preservation Department reconstructed a winter home from around three centuries ago with thick plastered walls and a curved entrance that reduced drafts. A central fire warmed the room; the drawing is a researched reconstruction rather than a photograph of an excavated house.

passages.title: Warm houses and busy kitchens
passages.text: In that reconstruction, cane platforms worked as couches by day and beds by night. Food could be stored underneath; cane containers held clothes and possessions. The space beneath the bed had a useful job long before anyone invented a plastic storage box.

passages.title: Warm houses and busy kitchens
passages.text: Choctaw food traditions include banaha bread and fruit dumplings. The Nation’s food history emphasizes that ingredients and recipes changed over time. Families can preserve a recognizable tradition while adapting what grows nearby and what is available in the kitchen.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: Choctaw stickball uses two wooden sticks with cupped, laced ends to handle a small ball. Traditional scoring involved hitting a goal post. Shaping the sticks and weaving the ball are skills in their own right, alongside the speed and teamwork needed on the field.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: The Choctaw Nation now uses stickball to teach children cooperation and family values, and offers workshops in making equipment. The game has survived changes in clothes, rules and organization. Learning a sport can also mean learning how to make the things needed to play.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: A short written sample on the Nation’s modern language page is “yakoke”, meaning “thank you”. The same page supplies recorded lessons and a dictionary. This is contemporary Choctaw written with Latin letters, not a claim that this spelling appeared on a 1492 artifact.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: The 1830 Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek preceded the largest waves of forced migration west. Poor supplies and planning contributed to devastating losses, particularly among elders and children. Choctaw accounts describe the journey through the institutions and relationships families struggled to preserve.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: In 1834, Choctaws adopted a new constitution in Indian Territory and organized three districts. Their council house was called Nanih Waiya, carrying the name of the Mother Mound into a new homeland. Rebuilding included laws and meeting places as well as houses and farms.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: Some Choctaw families stayed in Mississippi despite pressure to leave, then faced dispossession and difficult working conditions. Their descendants organized the Mississippi Band’s 1945 constitution. Their history is related to Oklahoma Choctaw history, but their government is not simply a branch of it.

Removal changed Choctaw landholding and institutions; it did not end Choctaw history. Distinct Choctaw governments and communities continue in Oklahoma and Mississippi. Neither the 1650 map endpoint nor its anachronistic 1492 Oklahoma outline dates the beginning or disappearance of these nations.

passages.text: Choctaw history connects southeastern homelands with communities that endured removal and built new institutions. The linked Oklahoma outline is wrongly displayed in 1492: it belongs to a much later removal history. The Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma and Mississippi Band are distinct continuing governments.

passages.title: Homelands and evidence
passages.text: Nanih Waiya in Mississippi is central to Choctaw origin traditions. The earthen mound stands about 25 feet high and over 200 feet long. Its meaning reaches beyond its size: Choctaw accounts identify this place as a heart of their people’s history.

passages.title: Homelands and evidence
passages.text: Nanih Waiya returned to the Mississippi Band of Choctaw Indians in 2008. That transfer brought a place lost during the removal era back into community care. An ancient monument can be part of a very present-day political and cultural relationship.

passages.title: Homelands and evidence
passages.text: Tribal archaeologist Ken Carlton describes pottery fragments as important clues to ancestral Choctaw history. Tempering materials, construction and decoration help compare sites, but he also emphasizes a difficult gap in seventeenth-century evidence. A recognizable pot is useful evidence, not a person’s identity card.

passages.title: Warm houses and busy kitchens
passages.text: The Nation’s Historic Preservation Department reconstructed a winter home from around three centuries ago with thick plastered walls and a curved entrance that reduced drafts. A central fire warmed the room; the drawing is a researched reconstruction rather than a photograph of an excavated house.

passages.title: Warm houses and busy kitchens
passages.text: In that reconstruction, cane platforms worked as couches by day and beds by night. Food could be stored underneath; cane containers held clothes and possessions. The space beneath the bed had a useful job long before anyone invented a plastic storage box.

passages.title: Warm houses and busy kitchens
passages.text: Choctaw food traditions include banaha bread and fruit dumplings. The Nation’s food history emphasizes that ingredients and recipes changed over time. Families can preserve a recognizable tradition while adapting what grows nearby and what is available in the kitchen.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: Choctaw stickball uses two wooden sticks with cupped, laced ends to handle a small ball. Traditional scoring involved hitting a goal post. Shaping the sticks and weaving the ball are skills in their own right, alongside the speed and teamwork needed on the field.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: The Choctaw Nation now uses stickball to teach children cooperation and family values, and offers workshops in making equipment. The game has survived changes in clothes, rules and organization. Learning a sport can also mean learning how to make the things needed to play.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: A short written sample on the Nation’s modern language page is “yakoke”, meaning “thank you”. The same page supplies recorded lessons and a dictionary. This is contemporary Choctaw written with Latin letters, not a claim that this spelling appeared on a 1492 artifact.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: The 1830 Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek preceded the largest waves of forced migration west. Poor supplies and planning contributed to devastating losses, particularly among elders and children. Choctaw accounts describe the journey through the institutions and relationships families struggled to preserve.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: In 1834, Choctaws adopted a new constitution in Indian Territory and organized three districts. Their council house was called Nanih Waiya, carrying the name of the Mother Mound into a new homeland. Rebuilding included laws and meeting places as well as houses and farms.

passages.title: Games, words and political survival
passages.text: Some Choctaw families stayed in Mississippi despite pressure to leave, then faced dispossession and difficult working conditions. Their descendants organized the Mississippi Band’s 1945 constitution. Their history is related to Oklahoma Choctaw history, but their government is not simply a branch of it.

Removal changed Choctaw landholding and institutions; it did not end Choctaw history. Distinct Choctaw governments and communities continue in Oklahoma and Mississippi. Neither the 1650 map endpoint nor its anachronistic 1492 Oklahoma outline dates the beginning or disappearance of these nations.

passages.text: This record represents the early Chola world of the Kaveri valley around 200 to 300 CE, centuries before the medieval Imperial Cholas. Uraiyur and the port of Puhar were important centers. The imported outline is misleading: it includes Madurai and Karur, associated with neighboring Pandya and Chera powers, but omits the sampled coastal Puhar and Vanagiri locations. Their evidence below is historical context outside that outline. Neither the boundaries nor the century-long map interval should be read as the kingdom’s exact extent or lifetime.

passages.title: Kings and the evidence for their world
passages.text: Early Tamil politics involved Chola, Chera and Pandya kings alongside smaller chiefs. The Cholas’ principal territory lay in the Kaveri region. Warfare, alliances and royal patronage connected these powers; the map should not turn them into one southern Indian empire.

passages.title: Kings and the evidence for their world
passages.text: Sangam poems preserve praise, conflict, love and descriptions of places. Their oral background and later compilation make their internal chronology difficult. They help us understand the early Chola world, but cannot be treated as dated eyewitness reports of every event.

passages.title: Making a living in Uraiyur
passages.text: Uraiyur’s early layers contained black-and-red pottery, other red and black wares, and dishes decorated with rouletted patterns. Excavators dated this broad Period I from roughly the first century BCE to the fourth century CE. These are everyday vessels from a long-lived settlement, not one king’s dinner service.

passages.title: Making a living in Uraiyur
passages.text: Floor levels with postholes were also found in Uraiyur’s early occupation. Such traces matter because timber-supported structures can vanish while holes and prepared ground survive. Archaeology can recover the footprint of ordinary building work even when no palace wall remains standing.

passages.title: Making a living in Uraiyur
passages.text: A brick installation at Uraiyur, interpreted as a dyeing vat, had square and rectangular chambers set diagonally opposite each other with paved floors. It belongs to the site’s early period. The structure gives physical substance to the town’s association with textiles: cloth production involved wet, messy work as well as skilled weaving.

passages.title: Making a living in Uraiyur
passages.text: Early Uraiyur yielded beads of colored glass, shell, terracotta and semiprecious stone. Bone points and needles were interpreted as weaving implements or possible writing tools. These small objects bring ornament and skilled handwork into view, although finished beads alone do not establish a bead factory.

passages.title: Water and a working port landscape
passages.text: At Vanagiri near Puhar, beyond this map’s coastline, excavators found a substantial brick inlet sluice. Its widening curved outlet and projecting brick courses helped control flowing water and erosion. The report places this engineering in the early-historic port landscape, rather than proving that one famous king personally built it.

passages.title: Water and a working port landscape
passages.text: Kilayur’s port works near Puhar developed in stages: wooden poles preceded a brick platform and channel. The old timber phase predates the atlas century. This distinction matters: a port could inherit, rebuild and adapt its waterfront rather than spring into existence with a single ruler.

passages.title: Water and a working port landscape
passages.text: The lowest deposits at Vellayan Iruppu included an early-historic ring well and black-and-red pottery. Such finds document water infrastructure in the Puhar area. They do not establish a complete sewer network, universal clean drinking water or a particular medical system for the Chola population.

passages.title: Poetic glimpses of families and the shore
passages.text: In Paṭṭiṉappālai’s extravagant picture of wealthy Puhar homes, women throw heavy earrings to chase hens away from drying food, obstructing children’s three-wheeled toy carts. It is praise poetry, not sensible poultry advice: even the imaginary traffic jams advertise the city’s riches.

passages.title: Poetic glimpses of families and the shore
passages.text: The poem celebrates large kitchens with tiger-marked doors, imagining rice water running like a river while passing carts soil painted walls. Feeding people becomes a picture of abundance and generosity. This vivid scene should not be mistaken for a measured survey of street drainage.

passages.title: Poetic glimpses of families and the shore
passages.text: Fishing households appear with small roofs, long fishing rods and nets drying in sandy front yards. Here the poem’s attention shifts from splendid goods to equipment that had to be tended between trips. A net on land was still part of the day’s work.

passages.title: Poetic glimpses of families and the shore
passages.text: Another seaside scene describes people swimming in the ocean, rinsing in river water, playing with crabs and making sand dolls. The poem links washing, ritual and enjoyment. Its families are literary figures, but their beach-day pleasures are wonderfully recognizable.

passages.title: Writing, learning and what survives
passages.text: A Uraiyur potsherd inscription contains antāṉaṉ, here copied in the catalogue’s scholarly Roman transcription. The authors interpret it, probably, as “Brahmana”, and associate the person with Mūlāṉpēdu. The inscriptions are dated broadly to the first three centuries CE. This is writing on excavated pottery, not a surviving schoolbook or a royal proclamation.

passages.title: Writing, learning and what survives
passages.text: Tamil-Brahmi writing survives on pottery, coins, seals and rings as well as rock shelters across the wider Tamil region. Learning letters therefore had practical settings beyond monumental inscriptions. The evidence does not tell us that everyone could read, or that every Tamil inscription belonged to the Chola kingdom.

passages.title: Changes after the mapped century
passages.text: Early Chola political history becomes difficult to reconstruct after the Sangam horizon. Later accounts describe a Kalabhra interval, but the evidence for its rulers and sequence is limited. A precise fall in 300 CE would give the map’s convenient cutoff more certainty than the sources support.

passages.title: Changes after the mapped century
passages.text: By the middle of the sixth century, Pallavas, Pandyas and Chalukyas were important regional powers. That later political setting should remain separate from this early Chola snapshot. Tamil-speaking communities, agriculture, crafts and literary traditions outlasted changes in which court held power.

passages.title: Changes after the mapped century
passages.text: Puhar’s excavations also reveal later occupation and a Buddhist monastic phase. Those layers help explain the place’s continuing life, but they cannot all be used to furnish a scene set in 250 CE. A single archaeological town can contain many centuries of different households and institutions.

The 300 CE endpoint is an atlas boundary, not a securely dated conquest or the disappearance of a people. Early Chola rule gave way within a changing regional order whose details remain unevenly documented. The later Imperial Chola kingdom has its own history and a separate card.

passages.text: The Cholas of the Kaveri delta, restored under Vijayalaya in 848, ruled the Tamil south for four centuries and sent fleets across the Bay of Bengal. Their bronze Natarajas, the great temples of Thanjavur and Gangaikonda Cholapuram and their village assemblies are the high point of Tamil civilization.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Rajaraja I finished the Brihadisvara temple at Thanjavur, its granite tower about 66 meters high.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bronze images of Shiva Nataraja, cast by the lost-wax method, reached their classic form in the tenth and eleventh centuries.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Rajendra I sent a fleet against Srivijaya in 1025 and sacked its ports along the Strait of Malacca.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Merchant guilds such as the Ayyavole Five Hundred traded across the Indian Ocean, and Chola embassies reached Song China in 1015 and 1077.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Tanks, sluices and the Kaveri's old anicuts irrigated the delta's rice fields.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Ocean-going ships carried armies to Sri Lanka, the Maldives and Sumatra.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Village assemblies chose their committees by lot from eligible landholders, as the Uttaramerur inscriptions of the 920s record.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Great Living Chola Temples were listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Chola bronzes and temple styles were carried to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.
The Pandyas of Madurai defeated the Cholas repeatedly from the 1210s and absorbed the last of the kingdom by 1279.

sectionTitles: Schools, a written sentence and care

passages.text: The Chitimacha are a living people of southern Louisiana’s bayous and the Atchafalaya Basin. Their reservation is near Charenton. This narrative also serves the map’s “Chtimacha” label: overlapping outlines dated 1492 to 1500 and 1530 to 1783 are imported coverage phases, not separate nations or the people’s beginning and end.

passages.title: Families and waterways
passages.text: Bayou Teche and neighboring waterways were routes for trading and visiting, as well as sources of food. Heritage interpreters describe village buildings made with timber, rivercane and palmetto leaves. People adapted journeys and settlement to changing seasons and water levels, using detailed knowledge of their watery surroundings.

passages.title: Families and waterways
passages.text: The wetlands offered fish, shellfish and other foods alongside edible plants. Traveling through channels required knowing where water led and how conditions changed. The heritage account describes Chitimacha people sharing knowledge of local food, housing and navigation with Acadian newcomers after their arrival in 1765.

passages.title: Families and waterways
passages.text: Clans documented in the early twentieth century included wolf, bear, dog and lion. Membership passed through the mother’s line. The Tribe’s historical account also describes differences in social rank and forms of address, showing that manners and family connections helped organize community life.

passages.title: Families and waterways
passages.text: French slave raids helped provoke a war lasting from 1706 to 1718. French forces and Native allies attacked Chitimacha communities; many people were enslaved. Peace ended the fighting, but survivors had been pushed from eastern settlements toward Grand Lake and Bayou Teche.

passages.title: Families and waterways
passages.text: Landownership remained contested after Louisiana became part of the United States. Lawsuits, pressured sales and tax judgments reduced the land base. In 1916, remaining tribal land entered federal trust. Chitimacha voters later approved a constitution in 1970, with federal approval following in 1971.

passages.title: Baskets built for real jobs
passages.text: Chitimacha baskets begin with local rivercane, a kind of bamboo. Weavers work with red, black and yellow as well as the cane’s natural color. Earlier dyes came from plants; the Tribe also describes later use of commercial dyes. Careful preparation makes a tough stalk into flexible weaving material.

passages.title: Baskets built for real jobs
passages.text: Basket shapes suit different jobs: trays and sifters help with food preparation, while elbow baskets are used to gather berries. Double-woven baskets with lids store belongings, and some can even hold water. That is an impressive assignment for a container made from strips of a plant.

passages.title: Baskets built for real jobs
passages.text: Ada Thomas learned basketry around age twelve from her grandmother Christine Paul, who taught at the reservation school. Her aunt Pauline Paul continued the teaching. Grades one through eight shared one room, so classroom learning and the passing on of family skills could happen close together.

passages.title: Baskets built for real jobs
passages.text: Thomas prepared cane by selecting, splitting, peeling, curing and drying it. For a double-woven basket she formed the inside first, then turned the strips back to build the outside in a continuous weave. The two surfaces are connected parts of one planned structure, rather than a lining dropped into a finished container.

passages.title: Baskets built for real jobs
passages.text: A lidded basket Thomas made in 1989 is preserved at the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Its rivercane sides carry the pattern called Alligator Entrails, while small track-like motifs decorate the lid. Named patterns let the viewer recognize a design vocabulary alongside the precision of the weaving.

passages.title: Baskets built for real jobs
passages.text: After eighth grade, Thomas could attend neither the local white nor the local Black high school. She moved to New Orleans to continue studying. Following years away, she returned to basketmaking in the mid-1970s and became a National Heritage Fellow in 1983. Her achievement grew through both family teaching and personal persistence.

passages.title: Schools, a written sentence and care
passages.text: In the early twentieth century, some Chitimacha children were sent far away to Carlisle’s boarding school, where they were forbidden to use their language. At home, exclusion from public schools led the community to hold classes in a tribal member’s house in 1932. Families had to struggle for education on their own terms.

passages.title: Schools, a written sentence and care
passages.text: The state supplied a condemned school building in 1934, and tribal members repaired it for their children. It remained in use until a new school opened in 1978 with funding mainly from the Bureau of Indian Affairs. The history of a classroom can also be a history of community labor.

passages.title: Schools, a written sentence and care
passages.text: A recorded Chitimacha sentence is “we haksigam hix siksi his nuytiqi,” meaning “the young man answered the eagle.” Linguist Daniel Hieber prints it from Benjamin Paul’s recorded narrative material. This example uses the modern practical spelling of a documented utterance, rather than an invented ancient inscription.

passages.title: Schools, a written sentence and care
passages.text: Benjamin Paul and Delphine Decloux Stouff helped preserve Chitimacha through work with linguist Morris Swadesh. Paul died in 1932 and Stouff in 1940, but their documentation later supported language revival in the tribal school and early learning center. Written records and remembered knowledge became resources for new learners.

passages.title: Schools, a written sentence and care
passages.text: The contemporary RiverCane elder program combines independent housing with practical support. Its published services include meals, grocery trips, social activities and checks of blood pressure and blood sugar. Meals can also reach people unable to travel. Looking after a community includes the ordinary work of helping neighbors eat, meet and stay well.

Neither imported map cutoff marks the end of the Chitimacha. The Tribe continues in Louisiana, and children can learn from language documentation preserved by earlier generations. The older record and later “Chtimacha” label belong to this continuing history.

sectionTitles: Homes, meals and a very practical boat
Living knowledge and a language greeting

passages.text: Chumash communities lived along the California coast, in nearby inland valleys and on the northern Channel Islands. Their villages were connected through fishing, trade and kinship, rather than one empire with a single capital. The map’s 1492 to 1650 dates cover only a slice of their history. Chumash people and distinct communities continue today; modern Santa Ynez examples below belong to that particular community.

passages.title: Homes, meals and a very practical boat
passages.text: Builders bent willow poles into domes, tied smaller branches across them and covered the framework with overlapping reeds or cattails. A roof opening let air circulate and could be covered during rain. In good weather families cooked outdoors, keeping smoke out of the house.

passages.title: Homes, meals and a very practical boat
passages.text: Acorns needed patient preparation: shelling, grinding and rinsing to remove bitter tannins. Cooks then heated the meal and water in tightly woven baskets by adding hot stones. The cooking vessel could stay away from the flames while the stones supplied the heat.

passages.title: Homes, meals and a very practical boat
passages.text: A tomol combined wooden planks, plant-fiber stitching and a sealant of pine pitch with natural asphalt. Builders smoothed the boat with sandstone and shark skin. Some seawater still seeped in, so a crew member had the essential job of bailing it out.

passages.title: Homes, meals and a very practical boat
passages.text: Historical sweathouses stood partly underground and were entered by a roof ladder. Heated stones kept the interior hot. The museum describes cleansing and purification uses, mostly among men, and larger buildings serving as meeting places. Social space could also be a very sweaty space.

passages.title: Trade, leadership and colonial upheaval
passages.text: Shell beads carried considerable economic importance. Archaeologist Lynn Gamble argues that highly standardized saucer beads were already used as money about 2,000 years ago. Her evidence includes labor-intensive manufacture and wide distribution. Archaeologists test that interpretation by comparing likely currency with beads made chiefly for adornment.

passages.title: Trade, leadership and colonial upheaval
passages.text: On Anacapa, shells, fish and marine-mammal bones, hooks and other tools reveal visits extending back thousands of years. Its limited fresh water helps explain the archaeological interpretation of seasonal camps. A good fishing place did not automatically provide everything needed for a permanent village.

passages.title: Trade, leadership and colonial upheaval
passages.text: The Santa Ynez Band’s historical account describes a society containing skilled makers, laborers, chiefs and religious specialists. Women could hold leadership and religious offices. Village politics and expertise mattered alongside the fishing boats and finely worked baskets that visitors often notice first.

passages.title: Trade, leadership and colonial upheaval
passages.text: In February 1824, a soldier’s beating of a Chumash person at Santa Inés sparked a revolt that spread to other missions. This happened after Mexican independence. Forced labor for the army and payment in promises rather than ready money had intensified resentment.

passages.title: Living knowledge and a language greeting
passages.text: In September 2004, Chumash paddlers crossed 21 miles to Santa Cruz Island in the tomol called ‘Elye’wun. The trip took over ten hours, with young people aged 14 to 22 joining the paddlers. Reviving a boat tradition meant sustained teamwork as well as skilled construction.

passages.title: Living knowledge and a language greeting
passages.text: The Santa Ynez Band began its language program in 2008 with six apprentices and expanded it in 2013. Language workers developed teaching materials and a speaking curriculum. These efforts help knowledge move from archival documentation into conversations between living people.

passages.title: Living knowledge and a language greeting
passages.text: The same community offers basket-making and cooking workshops, family archery and cultural activities for children. Basket students work with juncus and an awl, learning through their hands. Such programs bring relatives and different generations together while building practical skills.

passages.title: Living knowledge and a language greeting
passages.text: Writing sample: “haku tikaliʼ” means “Hello, how are you?” in the Santa Ynez Band’s Samala magazine of November to December 2022. This is a modern written greeting in Samala, a Chumash language. It is an attested community teaching example, not an invented ancient inscription.

passages.title: Living knowledge and a language greeting
passages.text: That magazine’s language class encouraged students to keep a lesson binder somewhere handy at home and teach their families what they learned. Introductions and short conversations gave learners something to use between lessons. The homework was a chance to talk together.

Mission colonization brought disease, forced labor and displacement; land loss continued after secularization in 1834. Chumash people survived these upheavals. The Santa Ynez Band maintains cultural and language programs, while other Chumash communities also preserve their identities. The map’s 1650 endpoint is not an extinction date.
