sectionTitles: Rulers, towns and people at work

passages.text: This map label refers to medieval Croatia, including the later native kings and the kingdom’s association with Hungarian rulers from 1102. Coastal towns, monasteries and inland communities had different connections and institutions. It is a different historical entry from the modern Republic of Croatia.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and people at work
passages.text: Zvonimir’s royal authority was linked to the papacy, while his marriage connected him to Hungary’s ruling family. After his death, competing claims helped reshape the kingdom. Medieval succession could turn a family relationship into a question affecting towns, nobles and armies.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and people at work
passages.text: Two wooden boats found in Nin’s harbor are dated to the eleventh and twelfth centuries. The surviving remains measure roughly seven and eight meters long. Their ribs and planking give physical evidence for the small craft that moved along the Adriatic coast.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and people at work
passages.text: The boat type known as a kondura combined rowing with square sails when winds were favorable. Oars offered another way to move when the breeze was unhelpful. Conserved remains and modern replicas help researchers explore these practical arrangements, though a replica is not the medieval boat itself.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and people at work
passages.text: Čika, a widow from a prominent Zadar family, founded the Benedictine convent of St Mary in 1066. Her daughters were connected with the community, and Vekenega later became abbess. Women could hold lasting responsibilities for a religious institution, its property and its records.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and people at work
passages.text: The Zadar convent preserved a parchment cartulary containing records from 1066 to 1236. Its writing includes Beneventan, Carolingian and Gothic forms. Across generations, the book kept track of the community’s affairs while handwriting styles changed around it.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and people at work
passages.text: Béla IV’s Golden Bull of 1242 granted privileges to Gradec, now part of Zagreb. The charter addressed local government, courts, taxes, markets and boundaries. A royal document could shape ordinary questions such as who judged a dispute and how a town organized trade.

passages.title: Stone, buildings and small treasures
passages.text: The Baška tablet came from St Lucy’s church at Jurandvor on the island of Krk. Carved around 1100, it formed part of a stone screen near the altar. Its thirteen lines of Glagolitic writing preserve a record of land given to the church by King Zvonimir.

passages.title: Stone, buildings and small treasures
passages.text: The tablet’s account names witnesses and records that Abbot Dobrovit built the church with nine brothers. This is unusually personal information preserved in a heavy piece of limestone. The stone combines a record of property with the memory of a small religious community.

passages.title: Stone, buildings and small treasures
passages.text: The main doorway of Trogir’s Cathedral of St Lawrence carries a date of 1240 and the name of its sculptor, Radovan. The inscription also names Bishop Treguan. A signed architectural sculpture can connect a surviving building with particular people and a specific year.

passages.title: Stone, buildings and small treasures
passages.text: Earrings with hollow metal beads survive from medieval sites including Biskupija near Knin. Gold and silver examples belong to forms used in the tenth and eleventh centuries. Jewelry records skilled metalworking and contacts with wider Mediterranean fashions, alongside the more familiar history of kings and churches.

passages.title: Stone, buildings and small treasures
passages.text: Zagreb’s twelfth-century cathedral had three aisles and Romanesque architecture. It suffered severe destruction during the Mongol invasion of 1242, followed by rebuilding in a Gothic style. The later building therefore carries a history of damage and reconstruction within its fabric.

passages.title: Two small samples of writing
passages.text: Latin on Radovan’s portal, 1240: “Per Raduanum”, meaning “by Radovan”. The phrase is quoted in art historian Vladimir Peter Goss’s discussion of the inscription. It preserves a medieval maker’s name in the Latin language and alphabet used for this public church inscription.

passages.title: Two small samples of writing
passages.text: The Baška tablet includes “Zvanimir kralj hrvatskij”, meaning “Zvonimir, the Croatian king”. These are medieval Croatian words shown in Branko Fučić’s scholarly Latin-alphabet transcription. The original stone uses Glagolitic letters; this excerpt is a transcription of that script, not a reproduction of its letter shapes.

The change of monarchy in 1102 joined Croatia and Hungary under a ruler, while Croatia retained a distinct kingdom and institutions. Medieval Croatian history continued beyond this map label’s 1279 endpoint. The later Pacta conventa text cannot be treated as a surviving original treaty from 1102.

passages.text: The modern Republic of Croatia declared independence from Yugoslavia in 1991. War and territorial disputes marked its first years, with peaceful reintegration of the remaining eastern region completed in January 1998. It later joined the European Union and adopted the euro. This entry is distinct from the medieval Croatian kingdom.

passages.title: Rebuilding services and connecting places
passages.text: Peaceful reintegration in eastern Croatia involved more than transferring offices. UN reporting discussed pensions, welfare payments, policing, returning residents and protection of rights. Restoring daily routines and trust was part of the work of bringing a war-affected region back under Croatian administration.

passages.title: Rebuilding services and connecting places
passages.text: The Pelješac Bridge opened in July 2022. Its approximately 2.4-kilometer crossing carries four lanes of road traffic, while its height allows ships to pass below. Roads and sea routes meet at the same structure, so engineers had to make room for both.

passages.title: Rebuilding services and connecting places
passages.text: The Zagreb earthquake of March 2020 damaged hundreds of education buildings. Schools were already closed because of the pandemic, so pupils were not in classrooms when it struck. The damage assessment estimated that thousands would need different teaching locations while buildings were repaired.

passages.title: Rebuilding services and connecting places
passages.text: Croatia joined the European Union in 2013 and began using euro coins and banknotes in January 2023. Currency change affected ordinary shopping and household budgets as well as banks. A familiar price tag now had a different unit printed beside the number.

passages.title: Rebuilding services and connecting places
passages.text: Primary schooling is compulsory and free, lasting at least eight years. Children can also attend separate music or dance programs alongside general school. A pupil’s week may therefore include both ordinary classroom subjects and time learning an instrument or practicing dance.

passages.title: Conservation, toys and gifts
passages.text: A bronze statue of an ancient athlete was raised from the seabed near Lošinj in 1999. Croatian and Italian specialists spent six years conserving it. The statue belongs to antiquity, but recovering, studying and displaying it was a modern achievement in archaeological conservation.

passages.title: Conservation, toys and gifts
passages.text: Researchers found a rodent’s nest inside the hollow bronze, probably made by a field mouse, along with laurel leaves and fruit remains. These small traces became part of the statue’s story. For a while, an artwork that would eventually receive its own museum had also served as somebody’s very unusual mouse house.

passages.title: Conservation, toys and gifts
passages.text: Wooden toy makers in Hrvatsko Zagorje use local woods such as willow, lime, beech and maple. UNESCO’s account describes family production, with men traditionally carving and women painting. Each toy is handmade, so matching horses or whistles may have small differences.

passages.title: Conservation, toys and gifts
passages.text: The toy repertoire has expanded to include cars, airplanes and other modern forms, alongside horses and miniature furniture. Some toys are tuned musical instruments used in children’s learning. A living craft can keep familiar techniques while changing what children get to play with.

passages.title: Conservation, toys and gifts
passages.text: Decorated gingerbread hearts from northern Croatia often carry a little mirror and a written message. They can be gifts expressing affection or respect. The decoration matters as much as the dough: this is a craft of making a keepsake for another person.

passages.title: Conservation, toys and gifts
passages.text: Gingerbread makers have passed their skills through family workshops, historically connected with candle making and honey drinks. Metal molds gradually replaced wooden ones, but individual decoration remained important. A shared outline could still become a distinctive gift in a maker’s hands.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: Croatian, article 1 of the constitution: “Republika Hrvatska jedinstvena je i nedjeljiva demokratska i socijalna država.” Translation: “The Republic of Croatia is a unified and indivisible democratic and social state.” This is the Constitutional Court’s 2014 consolidated witness of the constitution first enacted in 1990.

The Republic of Croatia continues. The map’s 1994 starting point falls after independence and during the war, not at the state’s founding. Peaceful reintegration of the eastern region concluded on 15 January 1998, while rebuilding lives and institutions extended beyond that administrative milestone.

sectionTitles: Titles, records and what remains uncertain

passages.text: Medieval Croatian kingship developed among communities whose lives survive in inscriptions, church buildings, tools and human remains. Royal titles and land grants show relationships between rulers and religious institutions; archaeology adds evidence of riding, food and health. The accession of an Arpad ruler in 1102 changed the dynasty while Croatian kingship and local society continued.

passages.title: Titles, records and what remains uncertain
passages.text: Tomislav's royal title survives through copies of papal letters associated with the Split councils, preserved in a much later compilation. The source tradition matters: a copied title is evidence to assess, not a surviving contemporary coronation record.

passages.title: Titles, records and what remains uncertain
passages.text: The familiar coronation at Duvno in 925 arose from later historical reconstruction. The Croatian Encyclopedia explains why that location claim was rejected and why a precise ceremony cannot be confidently reconstructed from the surviving evidence.

passages.title: Titles, records and what remains uncertain
passages.text: The Baska Tablet is a limestone slab originally belonging to the church screen at St Lucy's near Jurandvor on Krk. Carved around 1100, it placed a written record within a building used by a religious community.

passages.title: Titles, records and what remains uncertain
passages.text: Its text records King Zvonimir's gift of land, witnesses and an abbot's account of church construction. The inscription links property, prayer and patronage; damage and difficult readings prevent every personal name and clause from being treated as certain.

passages.title: Titles, records and what remains uncertain
passages.text: The tablet uses Croatian Church Slavonic and Glagolitic letters between rounded and angular forms. Its later reuse in the church floor damaged the surface. Both its script and its wear are part of the evidence for how the stone was used.

passages.title: Objects and ordinary lives
passages.text: A bronze fitting from the cemetery near St George at Putalj was first catalogued as a Gothic buckle. Petrinec reidentified it as part of an early Carolingian spur set, dating to the late eighth or early ninth century.

passages.title: Objects and ordinary lives
passages.text: The Putalj fitting has parallels in the Solin area and graves at Biskupija. It documents connections in riding equipment before the later royal-title evidence, but one imported style cannot establish every rider's birthplace or a whole community's identity.

passages.title: Objects and ordinary lives
passages.text: Bone-collagen analysis at sites including Glavice-Gluvine and Radasinovci-Vinogradine suggests millet contributed to early medieval diets. This is a chemical inference about food consumed, not a surviving meal or proof that everyone followed the same menu.

passages.title: Objects and ordinary lives
passages.text: The later Sibenik-Sveti Lovre sample differs from the other early medieval groups in that study. Its chemistry suggests a different protein mix, possibly including freshwater fish. The researchers' uncertainty is more informative than a single supposed national diet.

passages.title: Objects and ordinary lives
passages.text: At the ninth- to eleventh-century Konjsko cemetery, researchers recorded dental and skeletal signs of stress and disease. Their comparisons help recover the lives of people absent from royal documents, while the small sample limits conclusions about the wider population.

passages.title: Dynastic change and continuing institutions
passages.text: St Mary's cartulary at Zadar records Coloman's 1102 coronation at Biograd. An inscription at St Mary's also supports Zadar's recognition of his rule in 1105, connecting written accounts with a surviving architectural setting.

passages.title: Dynastic change and continuing institutions
passages.text: Pacta conventa survives as a note appended to a manuscript from the 1380s. Most recent scholarship rejects it as an authentic contemporary treaty. A possible agreement with nobles should be distinguished from accepting this later text as its original record.

In 1102 Coloman became king of Croatia and Dalmatia, bringing Croatian kingship under an Arpad ruler. This marks dynastic change rather than the extinction of Croatian society or the royal title. The terms of any contemporary agreement with nobles cannot simply be read from the much later Pacta conventa.

sectionTitles: More of everyday and national life

passages.text: The Apsáalooke, widely called Crow, are a living nation of the Yellowstone and Bighorn country. The map uses both names for overlapping homeland outlines: Apsaalooké (Crow) in 1492 to 1500 and Crow in 1500 to 1783. Those imported intervals describe map coverage, not a founding or disappearance. Migration traditions, horse expertise, extended families and self-government connect their past and present.

passages.title: Food, families and movement
passages.text: Smaller winter villages could come together in the warmer part of the year, when the major bands gathered and hunted. Dried meat, roots and berries helped sustain households in winter. Food preservation mattered alongside the hunt: the ability to store and share provisions supported community life through seasons with very different opportunities.

passages.title: Food, families and movement
passages.text: Matrilineal clans and an extended network of relatives shaped responsibility for children. A mother’s sisters were also mothers, and a father’s brothers were also fathers in the kinship system described by the college. These relationships made care and belonging broader than the small household model familiar to many outsiders.

passages.title: Food, families and movement
passages.text: Horses increased the loads families could move and the distances hunters could cover. Larger tipi loads became practical as transport changed. The approximate early eighteenth-century adoption date describes a transformation in an existing society, not its beginning; horse expertise was developed through learning, use and exchange.

passages.title: Objects as records of knowledge
passages.text: The NMAI’s robe 1/2558 combines bison hide, pigment, trade cloth, beads and porcupine quillwork. Its approximately 1850 date is a museum attribution; acquisition at Fort Benton in 1861 is a separate event. Bringing different materials together required hide preparation, painting and decorative skills, and also reflects access to traded goods.

passages.title: Objects as records of knowledge
passages.text: Apsáalooke historian Patrick J. Hill and Timothy P. McCleary interpret the robe’s six scenes as a public account of martial accomplishments. They explain its pictorial conventions as narrative writing. The object is therefore evidence of a way to communicate remembered deeds, rather than merely an ornamental surface.

passages.title: Objects as records of knowledge
passages.text: Tipi liner 18/9242 preserves cotton canvas, deer hooves, glass beads and porcupine quills, with bead stitching and quill wrapping recorded in its catalogue. The museum bought it from a New York dealer in 1936. Its maker, manufacture date and earlier ownership are not supplied, so that purchase cannot be presented as an excavation or a date of invention.

passages.title: Objects as records of knowledge
passages.text: Liners helped manage drafts, dampness and ventilation inside tipis. During the reservation period, some families carried their use into log houses. Crow house interiors could retain a central stove, an east-facing entrance and decorated wall linings. New construction materials did not automatically erase established ways of organizing domestic space.

passages.title: Land, education and adaptation
passages.text: The 1868 treaty made a reservation the prescribed permanent home while retaining specified hunting rights on unoccupied United States land, subject to conditions in its text. Reading both provisions matters: reservation boundaries did not by themselves describe every place the agreement allowed Crow people to use. These are the treaty’s historical terms.

passages.title: Land, education and adaptation
passages.text: Boarding schools separated children from their families as part of federal assimilation policy. Families established camps near reservation missions, keeping themselves closer to children attending those schools. This response shows parents working within severe constraints to preserve relationships; attendance cannot be read simply as willing abandonment of Crow social life.

passages.title: Land, education and adaptation
passages.text: Plenty Coups’ preserved homestead near Pryor includes a log house, farm and store. Montana’s state park account dates his residence there from 1884 until his death in 1932. The buildings provide concrete evidence of a leader negotiating new economic conditions through farming and commerce, alongside his public responsibilities.

passages.title: Continuing institutions and achievements
passages.text: Crow Fair brings people together in a large gathering that includes a tipi encampment and public cultural activities. In the college’s account it belongs to continuing social life, alongside smaller family and community relationships. A historical card should place such gatherings in the present as well as discuss nineteenth-century objects.

passages.title: Continuing institutions and achievements
passages.text: In March 2016, Apsáalooke researchers at the Smithsonian examined beadwork and horn-reinforced bows, documenting construction for possible recreation and teaching. They treated museum holdings as resources for living knowledge. The project’s proposed digital archive was a goal described at the time, not a product whose completion this account establishes.

passages.title: Continuing institutions and achievements
passages.text: The same visitors viewed a film of the 1908 Crow Fair and listened to later commentary recorded by Dean Bear Claw. Their own explanations added another layer of knowledge. This work connects community interpretation with museum records; collecting an old film alone does not preserve all the meanings that knowledgeable viewers can recognize.

passages.title: Continuing institutions and achievements
passages.text: The tribe’s official website describes executive, legislative and judicial branches under its 2001 Constitution. Tribal government is a continuing institution, with public responsibilities extending beyond cultural representation. Its existence makes it particularly misleading to treat the final year of an imported historical map polygon as the disappearance of a people.

passages.title: More of everyday and national life
passages.text: Crow oral tradition follows Shiipdeetash on a sacred journey in search of tobacco, linking places from Chief Mountain to Cloud Peak. The tribal tourism office presents these places as a spiritual geography that still matters. A migration story can preserve relationships with a landscape as well as memories of travel.

passages.title: More of everyday and national life
passages.text: In 1851, Sits In The Middle Land compared Crow country to four tipi poles: Wind River, Black Hills, the Yellowstone-Missouri meeting place and Three Forks. A familiar home explained a vast homeland.

passages.title: More of everyday and national life
passages.text: Elk-tooth dresses celebrate sewing skill and family achievement. The Smithsonian explains that especially elaborate examples can carry hundreds of teeth, traditionally the bull elk’s two canine teeth. Modern makers also use substitutes. Its featured dress, dated around 1930, combines cotton, beads, bone, skin and wool: an outfit with considerable craftsmanship behind it.

passages.title: More of everyday and national life
passages.text: For its Apsáalooke exhibition, the Field Museum worked with Crow curator Nina Sanders. Seven historic war shields formed part of the display. Men traditionally made these shields, while women kept them; their protective meaning included spiritual power. The museum account treats them as objects with living community relationships.

passages.title: More of everyday and national life
passages.text: The college’s 1995 tipi account records “ashé,” meaning “home,” and “ashtáale,” meaning “real home.” The latter term followed government-built houses. These documented modern spellings provide a small written sample of the language.

passages.title: More of everyday and national life
passages.text: A modern tribal-college lesson turns kinship vocabulary into a matching game. Students receive cards, find the person whose card matches their relationship term, and discuss the connections in their own families. Learning a family vocabulary can therefore involve getting out of a chair and finding a relative on paper.

passages.title: More of everyday and national life
passages.text: Crow community members formed an environmental-health steering committee in 2005. A study published in 2015 describes a Crow project coordinator and Little Big Horn College science students collecting well-water samples and interviewing families. Local knowledge helped decide what questions the research should ask.

passages.title: More of everyday and national life
passages.text: The same study followed thirty families whose wells had especially high contamination. All had begun obtaining better water for drinking, and many also changed the water used for cooking. It is a concrete household detail behind environmental research: a safe meal can depend on where the water jug was filled.

The Apsáalooke continue as a people and a self-governing tribe. Treaties and reservation policies profoundly restricted land and reshaped institutions, but did not end their community. Neither the earlier outline’s 1500 cutoff nor the later Crow record’s 1783 cutoff marks their disappearance.

sectionTitles: Discoveries: houses, handles and carved seats
Toilets, rubbish and traces of leisure

passages.text: Cuba’s history lives in household objects as well as public events. Wooden tools, discarded dishes, readers at work and music shared between generations reveal different kinds of knowledge. The examples below distinguish particular communities and periods across the island’s changing political history.

passages.title: Discoveries: houses, handles and carved seats
passages.text: At Los Buchillones on Cuba’s north coast, archaeologists recovered palm thatch and wooden parts of collapsed buildings. A 2006 study placed occupation before 1220 CE through 1640 or later. One partly excavated structure appeared to stand on pilings over water. The surviving pieces let researchers investigate how homes were built; the precise arrangement of every building is still a matter of reconstruction.

passages.title: Discoveries: houses, handles and carved seats
passages.text: The Los Buchillones wood collection includes axe handles with holes prepared for stone heads, and two grooved fragments interpreted as knife handles. The grooves could hold stone blades. Woodworking supplied the part that fitted a tool to a human hand. The collection combines excavated finds and earlier collected objects, so individual pieces do not all have equally precise find records.

passages.title: Discoveries: houses, handles and carved seats
passages.text: Carved seats called dujos also survive from Los Buchillones. Some were made from a single piece of wood, with sculpted human or animal features and supporting legs. Researchers classify them as ceremonial seats. Their careful carving shows skilled work, but they should not be treated as a sample of every household’s everyday furniture.

passages.title: Toilets, rubbish and traces of leisure
passages.text: At Habana 958 in Old Havana, a latrine cut into bedrock held pottery, glass, bones and seeds from the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Excavators distinguished waste left during use from later rubble used to fill it. An old toilet can preserve clues to meals and household possessions. Archaeology sometimes finds its best reading material in very unglamorous places.

passages.title: Toilets, rubbish and traces of leisure
passages.text: Excavations in 1999 and 2000 at El Padre, a nineteenth-century coffee plantation near Madruga, recovered two circular pieces cut from discarded crockery. The report interprets them as game counters. Such small objects offer glimpses of activities beyond imposed plantation work. They do not establish which game was played or who used each piece.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and family knowledge
passages.text: In a tradition traced to nineteenth-century Cuba, a lector read aloud to cigar workers as they worked. Reading brought literature and political information into the workshop. Historian Araceli Tinajero studied newspapers and interviewed readers to investigate the practice. It is a little like sharing an audiobook with the whole workplace, except the person doing the reading is actually there.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and family knowledge
passages.text: In 1881, Cuban physician Carlos Finlay proposed that mosquitoes carried yellow fever between people. The Yellow Fever Board led by Walter Reed confirmed mosquito transmission in 1900. Finlay’s insight helped change how people investigated and prevented the disease. The distinction between proposing an explanation and testing it is part of the story of scientific discovery.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and family knowledge
passages.text: A photograph taken by the Kaweiro Group in 2015 shows a mother and daughter joining other Native families in eastern Cuba for a workshop about local medicinal plants. The Smithsonian included it in its 2018 Taíno exhibition announcement. It records knowledge being discussed across generations and challenges the idea that Indigenous people vanished. The photograph does not establish whether a particular remedy works.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and family knowledge
passages.text: Cassava bread connects Cuban households with a wider Caribbean tradition. UNESCO’s 2024 account describes variations in thickness, texture and flavour across Cuba and four other countries, with skills commonly passed on at home and within communities. Learning to make a familiar food can also mean learning from an older relative or neighbour. There is no single recipe that represents every family.

passages.title: Music and neighbourhood surprises
passages.text: Rumba combines singing, movement and percussion, with roots in communities including Havana and Matanzas. Instruments can include household or workplace utensils, and the audience joins the exchange through clapping and response. UNESCO’s 2016 account describes children and adults learning through imitation within families and neighbourhoods. A musical education can begin by watching someone nearby and joining in.

passages.title: Music and neighbourhood surprises
passages.text: Punto brings poetry and melody together. Singers perform ten-line stanzas, sometimes learned in advance and sometimes made up as they sing. UNESCO’s 2017 account describes learning by imitation and workshops in Houses of Culture. Improvising a rhyme while keeping a tune takes practice. It gives thinking on your feet a very musical meaning.

passages.title: Music and neighbourhood surprises
passages.text: For Las Parrandas in central Cuba, competing neighbourhoods spend months preparing floats, costumes, lights and decorations. UNESCO’s 2018 account even mentions people trying to discover the other side’s surprise before the celebration. The preparations combine craft skills with friendly suspense: imagine keeping a spectacular float secret from the neighbours. Participation and practices vary between communities.

Spanish sovereignty ended after the 1898 war, followed by U.S. occupation and the republic in 1902. Batista’s government ended in the 1959 revolution. These political transitions did not end Cuban communities or culture, including Indigenous descendants and traditions shared across generations.

sectionTitles: An early center with a distinctive shape
Water, maize and the earth underfoot
Carved signs and an uncertain ending

passages.text: Cuicuilco was an important early center in the southern Basin of Mexico, now within Mexico City. Its monumental and residential remains belong principally to a much earlier history than this map’s imported 1492 to 1500 interval. The outline locates the archaeological site; it should not be read as an independent fifteenth-century kingdom. Its early urban development preceded Teotihuacan’s regional prominence.

passages.title: An early center with a distinctive shape
passages.text: Cuicuilco occupied a strategic area where streams descended from the Tlalpan uplands. Nearby lakes and oak-pine woodland supplied different resources, while routes connected the basin with the Toluca Valley. Its surroundings help explain why people gathered here.

passages.title: An early center with a distinctive shape
passages.text: The great circular platform grew through at least eight enlargements, according to INAH. Its builders packed an earthen core inside a covering of volcanic stone. A monument could be a long series of community building projects rather than one construction day.

passages.title: An early center with a distinctive shape
passages.text: A ceremonial structure conventionally called the Kiva preserves red linear decoration made with hematite, an iron-oxide pigment. Andesite slabs and river stones formed its construction. The surviving red lines offer a glimpse of buildings as painted spaces, not simply bare ruins.

passages.title: An early center with a distinctive shape
passages.text: Potters made tripod vessels with lids shaped like bird heads. INAH places the ceramic examples it describes within roughly 600 to 200 BCE. Practical containers could be carefully designed objects, with an animal form waiting on top of the lid.

passages.title: An early center with a distinctive shape
passages.text: An E1 building burial included pottery, a necklace and two figurines representing a man and a woman. Such a particular set of offerings records choices made for one burial; it does not establish a standard funeral kit for every household.

passages.title: Water, maize and the earth underfoot
passages.text: Investigators documented irrigation channels predating the lava. At Cuicuilco D, a reconstructed channel system incorporates smaller channels and a dam. Moving water was part of creating a productive settlement, not merely a concern for its ceremonial buildings.

passages.title: Water, maize and the earth underfoot
passages.text: A 2026 soil study argues that builders selectively dug up, transported and reused older soils near the Estela monument. Microscopic observations, chemistry and conflicting soil ages support that interpretation. Old carbon in reused earth can be older than the building that contains it.

passages.title: Water, maize and the earth underfoot
passages.text: Charred maize plants were found near the great platform and the Estela. Researchers relate the context to agricultural themes in ceremonial life. These traces show maize’s place in the settlement’s material world, although they do not give us a complete family menu.

passages.title: Water, maize and the earth underfoot
passages.text: The Xitle eruption began with ash and later produced lava flows over Cuicuilco and nearby farmland. The damage affected the means of growing food as well as buildings. Geological layers preserve this environmental upheaval even where its exact timing remains debated.

passages.title: Carved signs and an uncertain ending
passages.text: The Estela is an andesite column about 3.9 meters tall with carved circles and diamond shapes. Interpretations connect it with ritual or astronomical recording, but the checked research supplies no deciphered sentence. A translated greeting in its builders’ language would be invented.

passages.title: Carved signs and an uncertain ending
passages.text: The date of the eruption remains a research problem. A 2016 archaeomagnetic study proposed roughly 90 BCE to 20 CE; a recent geochemical paper follows radiocarbon recalibrations placing the onset shortly after 380 to 400 CE. These estimates should not be blended into a falsely precise fall year.

passages.title: Carved signs and an uncertain ending
passages.text: Ramírez and Pastrana describe evidence of later visits and some habitation after the eruption. Parts of the landscape that escaped the lava remained usable. The end of Cuicuilco’s greatest importance was therefore different from everyone vanishing permanently from the site.

Cuicuilco lost its earlier regional importance, and Xitle lava covered much of its built and agricultural landscape. The precise sequence of decline, eruption and migration remains debated. Later activity continued; neither a single unquestioned fall year nor the map’s 1500 endpoint explains the site’s history.

passages.text: The Cuman-Kipchak confederation linked regional steppe powers without one centralized state. This card covers the atlas’s 1100-1200 confederation and 1200-1279 Cuman Khanates records. The earlier outline extends into Mongolia, beyond the core range supported here, and is not a verified border. Neither cutoff marks the disappearance of the people. Mongol conquest broke up independent power in the 1230s.

passages.title: Power through people and alliances
passages.text: The wider confederation contained several regional groupings: western Cumans, Central Asian Kipchak-Qangli and western Siberian Kipchaks. Their leaders could make different alliances. A single coloured map region should not suggest one capital issuing orders to every camp.

passages.title: Power through people and alliances
passages.text: Family connections carried political weight. The Georgian king David was the son-in-law of the Cuman leader Otrok, whose followers sought refuge in Georgia after campaigns by Vladimir Monomakh. Cuman soldiers helped the Georgian crown become a stronger regional power.

passages.title: Power through people and alliances
passages.text: Trade routes linked Khwarazm, Volga Bulgaria, Rus’ lands and Black Sea markets. Cuman leaders and communities could profit from exchange or tribute, while raiding and captive-taking also brought wealth at others’ expense. Peaceful business and warfare were closely entangled.

passages.title: Power through people and alliances
passages.text: Mongol pressure pushed some Cuman groups west. Khan Kuthen sought asylum in Hungary in 1239, where King Bela IV wanted military allies. Suspicion and violence led to Kuthen’s killing and a Cuman departure; groups later returned. Migration was a difficult negotiation over safety, land and power.

passages.title: Households, food and clothing
passages.text: Herding was central to steppe livelihoods, but life varied across the enormous region. Some communities appear to have made winter camps more permanent and added cultivation. Keeping animals required practical knowledge of pasture and seasons, rather than simply wandering wherever the horses wished.

passages.title: Households, food and clothing
passages.text: External writers describe felt homes that could travel, and both texts and archaeology attest wagons. Yet chronicles also name Cuman strongholds such as Sharukan and Sugrov. Portable dwellings, settled places and political centres could coexist; owning a wagon did not make someone homeless.

passages.title: Households, food and clothing
passages.text: Food accounts need their dates attached. In the fourteenth century, after Mongol conquest, Ibn Battuta described Kipchak-region meals of millet soup with meat and fermented mare’s milk. It is a vivid later snapshot, not proof that every earlier Cuman household ate the same things.

passages.title: Households, food and clothing
passages.text: A stone woman from Stadnytsya, dated around the twelfth or thirteenth century, wears a long caftan, a tall hat, earrings and a necklace. Her belt carries a pouch. The sculpture preserves details of clothing and accessories that normally decay much faster than stone.

passages.title: Households, food and clothing
passages.text: Behind that statue’s head are hornlike decorations made as fabric-covered rolls of felt. They are part of her headgear, not animal horns growing from her head! Her hands hold a vessel. The museum does not know why someone later removed the face’s details.

passages.title: Archaeology, craft and remembered ancestors
passages.text: At the Chungul Kurgan in southern Ukraine, a rich medieval burial was inserted into an older Bronze Age mound. Researchers date this burial to the early thirteenth century. Its imported luxury objects reveal far-reaching contacts, though they do not securely identify the deceased by name.

passages.title: Archaeology, craft and remembered ancestors
passages.text: Clothing from that burial was assembled from different silks, gold decoration and reused textiles; two preserved caftans had marten-fur linings. Researchers interpret the garments as combining a riding coat’s familiar form with the prestigious decoration of neighbouring courts. Even a magnificent coat could contain carefully reused cloth.

passages.title: Archaeology, craft and remembered ancestors
passages.text: Cuman stone figures show both women and men, sometimes with weapons or armour, holding vessels in front of their bodies. The Neues Museum interprets these cups as signs of the dead joining a shared drink. That reading connects sculpture with remembrance and communal ritual.

passages.title: Language and a puzzle to try
passages.text: The Codex Cumanicus survives in Venice as a fourteenth-century manuscript. Its vocabulary records Cuman alongside Latin and Persian, while another section contains grammar, word lists and Christian religious texts. It shows people working across languages in the post-conquest Black Sea and lower Volga world.

passages.title: Language and a puzzle to try
passages.text: Here is a later Cuman riddle in modern scholarly transcription of its Latin-script text: “Ak küyməniŋ avzu yox. Ol, yumurtka.” It means: “A white tent has no mouth. It’s an egg.” The comparison turns an ordinary shell into a tiny house with no entrance.

passages.title: Language and a puzzle to try
passages.text: This was also a tool for language learning: the compilers arranged word lists and grammatical forms, and translated texts for religious services. It documents a particular multilingual teaching effort, rather than a school system attended by all Cuman children.

passages.title: Language and a puzzle to try
passages.text: The surviving codex is about 20 by 14 centimetres and has 82 paper leaves. Its opening carries an older date, 1303, but the manuscript was copied and expanded; the Veneto catalogue dates the copy to 1330. A date at a book’s beginning is not automatically every page’s birthday.

passages.title: Later community life in Hungary
passages.text: At the later medieval Cuman village of Orgondaszentmiklos in Hungary, excavators found house plots with bases interpreted as yurts nearby. Families could use buildings and tentlike structures together. This evidence belongs to settled descendants in Hungary, not automatically to the earlier Black Sea camps.

passages.title: Later community life in Hungary
passages.text: Animal bones from that village carry traces of butchery and dogs’ teeth, suggesting food refuse lay where dogs could reach it. A horse’s pelvic injury with signs of healing also suggests people kept it alive after a serious accident. The bones do not reveal a specific treatment.
Mongol conquest in the 1230s ended independent Cuman-Kipchak power across much of the steppe. Communities continued under Mongol rule and in Hungary and elsewhere, contributing to later societies.

passages.text: This map uses “Curonians” for 500 BCE to 200 CE, centuries before the fifth- to early sixth-century formation described by Lithuania’s National Museum. The label is therefore retrospective and its outline is not a secure ethnic border. This card explores earlier coastal communities in western Lithuania and southwestern Latvia, using archaeology rather than projecting medieval Curonian sailors into the distant past.

passages.title: Houses, hearths and the landscape
passages.text: At Paplaka in southwestern Latvia, excavators found a building partly sunk into the ground. Its oval hollow measured about 2 by 3 metres, with clay-lined sides and a lower approach to the entrance. Radiocarbon analysis places the building and its finds between 361 and 204 BCE.

passages.title: Houses, hearths and the landscape
passages.text: About 600 pieces of clay daub came from the Paplaka building. Impressions preserved the shapes of wooden elements, and the excavator suggests clay protected wood near the hearth from fire. A building that disappeared can still leave the imprint of its timbers in a handful of baked clay.

passages.title: Houses, hearths and the landscape
passages.text: Paplaka also yielded fragments of at least 32 pots, mostly with scratched surfaces. The same building contained pieces of bronze ornaments, an iron hook, a fire-lighting stone and a grooved sandstone whetstone. These small finds place pottery, metal objects and sharpening equipment together in an ordinary working space.

passages.title: Houses, hearths and the landscape
passages.text: Researchers studying the Akmena River near Kurmaičiai propose that three neighbouring communities used this landscape during the later first millennium BCE and early first millennium CE. They suggest a division between living and farming areas on one bank and burial places on the other. This is a model built from scattered archaeological sites.

passages.title: Houses, hearths and the landscape
passages.text: Finding a cemetery does not automatically reveal the village beside it. Five test pits on the Akmena’s left bank failed to locate the proposed prehistoric settlement. Ancient field remains nevertheless suggest activity there. Archaeology sometimes produces a useful unanswered question: where exactly did the people who used these graves live?

passages.title: Food, animals and family traces
passages.text: Regional plant research offers a glimpse of changing farming. Evidence from Lithuania places the arrival of rye and oats around 100 to 200 CE. The study draws largely on inland sites, so these are regional comparisons rather than a shopping list for every coastal household. Charred grains can preserve information that a vanished meal cannot.

passages.title: Food, animals and family traces
passages.text: Horse remains from Kurmaičiai, Kveciai and Ėgliškės show that animals also had a place in burial ceremonies. A study of Late Bronze and Early Iron Age graves found unburnt parts of horses alongside cremated people. The researchers interpret this as evidence of horses’ special importance, though the bones cannot tell the complete story of each ceremony.

passages.title: Food, animals and family traces
passages.text: A young person buried at Šlikiai was remembered with an urn and a circle of stones. Radiocarbon testing placed this grave between 396 and 206 BCE. The report identifies a non-adult, rather than claiming an exact age. Even without a surviving name, this carefully recorded grave gives a child or adolescent a place in the story.

passages.title: Food, animals and family traces
passages.text: At Dauglaukis, a child’s grave contained an iron pin and an amber bead near surviving teeth and skull fragments. Its published date, 70 to 260 CE, extends beyond this map’s endpoint. The excavator also noted possible disturbance. Small ornaments survive here as fragile traces of a particular child, whose name and sex remain unknown.

passages.title: Connections and discoveries
passages.text: By the late first and second centuries CE, some western Lithuanian cemeteries used flat graves surrounded by connected stone circles. Earlier burial mounds and cremation traditions had different arrangements. Changes in burial practice help archaeologists distinguish phases, although a new grave style alone cannot prove that an entirely new people arrived.

passages.title: Connections and discoveries
passages.text: The long-used Ėgliškiai-Anduliai cemetery yielded Roman coins, including issues of Emperor Hadrian, who ruled from 117 to 138 CE. Such objects connect this Baltic region with wider exchange networks. The date stamped into a ruler’s coin history is not necessarily the date when that coin reached the coast or entered a grave.

passages.title: Connections and discoveries
passages.text: Modern laboratory work has tested old assumptions about the burial mounds. A 2022 study dated twelve bone samples from six cemeteries. One supposed prehistoric grave at Kveciai actually dated to 1047 to 1260 CE. People had reused an ancient place much later, a reminder to check the age of each burial separately.

passages.title: What can we quote?
passages.text: There is no securely identified local written sentence to quote from these early communities. Even the much later Curonian language left no surviving written monuments, according to Lithuania’s language encyclopedia. Archaeological objects help reconstruct daily activities, but cannot supply an ancient child’s exact words. Modern Lithuanian or Latvian would not be a substitute.

The year 200 is the end of this imported map record, not a documented destruction. Coastal communities continued changing, and the recognisable medieval Curonian cultural formation emerged centuries later. The early record and medieval Kurs therefore need separate histories.

passages.text: The imported labels “Kushites” in 700 to 800 and “Cushites” in 900 to 1000 cover the Somali Horn. They are broad regional labels, not the Nile kingdom of Kush or a documented united empire. Cushitic is a family of related languages that includes Somali. This card follows regional communities through archaeology, with earlier and later examples clearly dated; it does not assign every ancient object to a modern people.

passages.title: Trade before the map labels
passages.text: At Xiis on the Gulf of Aden, excavators found imported pottery and glass in stone burial mounds. Goods came through connections reaching Roman territories, southern Arabia and Mesopotamia. The early centuries CE therefore reveal coastal people participating in far-reaching exchange, even without a large local city or imperial government.

passages.title: Trade before the map labels
passages.text: One Xiis child, estimated to have been about eight or nine years old, was buried with beads, an iron anklet and a glass flagon dated to the third century CE. The vessel probably came from Roman Syria or Cyprus. A small grave can preserve both personal care and a remarkably long journey.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: In the later medieval settlements surveyed around Borama, many houses used flat stones bound with mud. Typical examples had two or three rooms within about 20 to 40 square metres. At Fardowsa, two much larger six-room houses suggest that some households had considerably more space.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: The same survey found grinding stones and digging-stick weights near farming land. These are clues to daily work: preparing ground and turning grain into food. Some settlements had few imported luxuries, so their history cannot be told only through merchants and distant ships.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: Mosques were important gathering places in these later towns. At Abasa and Hasadinle, pillars helped support the roof. Their builders worked with the same stone-and-mud techniques used in houses, linking public religious spaces to skills also useful around the home.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: A StateHorn account of historically documented pastoral life explains why movement mattered: rain could make a grazing area usable for a season, while dry months depleted wells. Along the Guban plain, shallow wells reached water beneath sandy ground. Knowing when and where to travel was a practical skill, not aimless wandering.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: At Siyaara near Berbera, archaeologists found thousands of local and imported pottery fragments dated from the tenth to sixteenth centuries. Seasonal fairs connected arriving ships with caravans and mobile herding communities. A place could become an important meeting ground without being a busy town every month of the year.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: A milk pot collected in southern Somalia in 1934 to 1935 combines wood, woven plant fibre and a lid with a central knob. It is a much later example of household craftsmanship from within this broad region. The ordinary job of carrying and protecting milk required careful work with several materials.

passages.title: Homes, work and water
passages.text: An Issa head-rest catalogued to about 1910 to 1912 is carved from wood, with a conical base and ornament. It stands just 14.5 centimetres high. This later Somali object offers a different answer to the bedtime equipment question: a pillow need not be a bag of feathers.

passages.title: Language, learning and continuing voices
passages.text: Here is a modern Somali writing sample: “𐒍𐒖𐒇 𐒈𐒝𐒑𐒛𐒐𐒘”, far Soomaali, meaning “Somali writing”. These are Osmanya letters, from a script devised in 1920 to 1922. The sample is printed in the Unicode Standard; it is not medieval writing from either map interval.

passages.title: Language, learning and continuing voices
passages.text: Getting Osmanya onto computers involved cooperation across generations. Michael Everson described how Osman Abdihalim Osman Yusuf Keenadiid and his family supplied a photocopied book that helped the encoding project. Their collaboration produced a revised proposal in 2001: preserving writing can involve family books as well as software.

passages.title: Language, learning and continuing voices
passages.text: In 2015 to 2016, ten young adults from London’s Somali community worked with the British Museum’s Somali collections. They explored objects, contributed knowledge and developed new ways to tell their stories. Descendant communities are participants in explaining this heritage, not merely people described by old collection labels.

Neither 800 nor 1000 marks the disappearance of the Horn’s peoples. Later regional trade and settlement changed, including disruption around the end of the Adal sultanate in the sixteenth century. That was a transformation of particular political and commercial networks, not an ending for Cushitic-speaking communities.

sectionTitles: A busy building site and a later town

passages.text: Cycladic describes the prehistoric societies of the Aegean islands, famous for marble figures, seafaring and later prosperous towns. These islands shared contacts and crafts without forming one known island-wide kingdom. The map’s 4000 to 1500 BCE span begins before the conventional Early Cycladic period and stops before the end of Cycladic Bronze Age history; its outlines are a cultural envelope.

passages.title: Island households and shared skills
passages.text: Early Cycladic homes used stone and clay walls, with floors of packed earth or stone slabs. Roofs combined timber, reeds and clay. Small settlements near anchorages, and later on hillsides, placed families close to fields, animals and the sea. Most wooden furnishings have not survived.

passages.title: Island households and shared skills
passages.text: Cereals, pulses, olives, fruit and nuts supplied everyday food, supplemented by fish, shellfish and hunted animals. Sheep, goats, cattle and pigs provided food and other useful materials. Feeding a household meant tending crops and animals as well as watching the water for a catch.

passages.title: Island households and shared skills
passages.text: Clay spindle whorls and sewing needles reveal household textile work during the third millennium BCE. Impressions of woven mats remain on the bottoms of pots. A mat that rotted away thousands of years ago can still leave its pattern behind, stamped into someone’s crockery.

passages.title: Island households and shared skills
passages.text: Many marble figures originally wore colour. Surviving traces show dark blue or black hair, eyebrows and eyes, with red used for jewellery and decorative patterns. Their pale appearance today can hide an important part of the artist’s work: these sculptures were not always all-white faces staring silently back.

passages.title: Island households and shared skills
passages.text: Sculptures show people playing harps and wind instruments, alongside figures drinking or embracing. They offer a glimpse of music and gatherings in the third millennium BCE. The instruments can be recognised, but the tunes have not survived. We cannot responsibly supply an ancient Cycladic playlist.

passages.title: Island households and shared skills
passages.text: Pictures of many-oared boats and small lead boat models preserve evidence of early island navigation. Obsidian, marble and metals circulated across the Aegean. The water between islands could connect workshops and communities, even when carrying a heavy load required a demanding sea journey.

passages.title: A busy building site and a later town
passages.text: At Dhaskalio beside Keros, third-millennium builders created terraces and substantial structures using stone brought from Naxos, about ten kilometres away. Stairs and drainage were planned into the buildings. Transporting the stone itself was a major achievement before a wall could even begin to rise.

passages.title: A busy building site and a later town
passages.text: Burnt plant remains at Dhaskalio include pulses, grapes, olives, figs, almonds, emmer wheat and barley. The excavators thought Keros probably could not supply all its own food, so boats may have carried provisions as well as prestigious objects. Feeding a busy settlement depended on its wider connections.

passages.title: A busy building site and a later town
passages.text: The excavators reported five metalworking hearths at Dhaskalio, alongside moulds, crucibles, blowpipes and copper spills. Craftspeople shaped metal through heat and carefully controlled equipment. These finds preserve the tools and mess of production, not just the polished objects that eventually left the workshop.

passages.title: A busy building site and a later town
passages.text: Much later, at Akrotiri on Thera, paved streets covered a drainage network, and sanitary rooms inside buildings connected directly to it. This was a densely built town with multistorey houses and public buildings. Plumbing had become part of urban planning long before modern bathrooms.

passages.title: A busy building site and a later town
passages.text: Volcanic deposits at Akrotiri preserved the shapes of wooden furnishings after the wood decayed. Archaeologists could make plaster casts from those empty spaces. Household equipment, bronze vessels and tools survive alongside them, allowing researchers to study furniture and chores rather than only monumental buildings.

passages.title: A busy building site and a later town
passages.text: Akrotiri’s wall paintings include fishermen, boys and saffron gatherers. The museum reconstructs complete arrangements from the West House and Xesti 3, so figures can be understood within their rooms. These carefully composed pictures reveal what painters chose to show; they are not candid photographs of every family’s day.

passages.title: Their marks and words
passages.text: The early communities that made the famous marble figures left no written accounts known to the museum’s educational survey. By the later Bronze Age, Akrotiri used Linear A. That script remains undeciphered, so a fluent translation of an islander’s sentence would be guesswork.

passages.title: Their marks and words
passages.text: A broken pot sherd catalogued as 2839 carries Linear A signs and quantities. One is “𐘎”, shown here in a modern standardised form called AB20, followed on the sherd by the number nine. The quantity is readable; what the sign counts is uncertain. The exact findspot was not recorded, though Akrotiri is considered its likely source.

passages.title: Their marks and words
passages.text: The inscription was scratched into the pot after firing, when it was probably already a fragment. A piece of broken crockery had become a writing surface. Michailidou places this note most probably in the final occupation period before Akrotiri’s burial by the eruption, rather than in the much earlier age of marble figurines.

The eruption buried Akrotiri, but it did not end all Cycladic communities. The map stops at 1500 BCE; later island centres became closely integrated into the Mycenaean world. Cycladic Bronze Age history continues to about 1100 BCE in the National Archaeological Museum’s chronology.

sectionTitles: An island with several political histories
Ports, workshops and things on the table

passages.text: This record follows the island of Cyprus from about 800 to 1530, across Byzantine connections, the Lusignan kingdom and Venetian government. It is not one unchanged state. The island-wide outline hides changes of ruler and local control, including Genoese-held Famagusta. Its 1530 endpoint is a map cutoff, before the Ottoman conquest.

passages.title: An island with several political histories
passages.text: The early part of this timeline belongs to an unusual frontier situation between Byzantium and Arab powers, often called a Byzantine-Arab condominium. The arrangement changed over time and should not be imagined as two modern governments peacefully sharing an office. Byzantine reconquest in 965 established a new phase of imperial control.

passages.title: An island with several political histories
passages.text: Nicosia probably became the island’s administrative capital in the tenth century. Much later, Isaac Komnenos governed Cyprus from 1184 to 1191 as a self-proclaimed emperor. Richard I captured the island in 1191; a brief Templar interlude preceded the Lusignans. Medieval Cyprus therefore changed political identity within the same coastline.

passages.title: An island with several political histories
passages.text: Lusignan Nicosia housed a royal court and a Latin archbishop. Work on the Gothic cathedral of Saint Sophia began in 1209, while palaces, churches and streets reshaped the city. The Pediaios River ran through it, crossed by wooden and stone bridges. The kingdom also distinguished a High Court of knights from a lower court serving the bourgeoisie.

passages.title: Ports, workshops and things on the table
passages.text: After Acre fell in 1291, Christian refugees reached Famagusta. The port connected Mediterranean trade routes, while Cyprus exported cotton, sugar and wine. A Barcelona merchant’s notes describe selling silver coins to a mint agent there in 1343. Trade involved useful raw metal as well as finished goods, and the mint’s demand could draw money across the sea.

passages.title: Ports, workshops and things on the table
passages.text: Local potters supplied glazed tableware. Paphos workshops are associated with the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, Engomi near Famagusta with the fourteenth, and Lapithos with the fifteenth. Potters scratched designs into a pale clay coating and added brown, yellow or green decoration. Production also took place in Nicosia, giving the island several ceramic centres.

passages.title: Ports, workshops and things on the table
passages.text: A fourteenth-century bowl in the Leventis Museum has a sun with a human face. Another bowl, from the middle of the thirteenth century, shows a fish. Medieval table decoration could be playful: the sun might look back at you from the dish. These museum objects show decorative choices, without identifying the particular families who used them.

passages.title: Ports, workshops and things on the table
passages.text: Grain needed grinding before it could become flour. University of Cyprus researchers document medieval mule-driven mills in Famagusta and Nicosia, and watermills on the island from the twelfth century. Different power sources connected town work to animals, rivers and local conditions. The much later mills that still survive should not all be mistaken for medieval buildings.

passages.title: Ports, workshops and things on the table
passages.text: Excavations at Kouklia-Stavros in 1980 to 1982 and 1987 to 1995 uncovered a sugar-making complex with milling and refining installations. Built in the late thirteenth century, it remained in operation into the late sixteenth, beyond this map. Archaeologists recorded more than 30,000 sugar moulds and molasses pots. Sweetness required a remarkable amount of industrial pottery.

passages.title: Health, families and books
passages.text: A toilet at Saranda Kolones castle near Paphos preserved tiny clues to illness. Researchers found roundworm and whipworm eggs in its cesspit; comparison soil lacked them. The castle was used after 1191 and before an earthquake in 1222. This is evidence about its toilet users, whose origins are uncertain, rather than a health survey of every Cypriot household.

passages.title: Health, families and books
passages.text: Family plans and a young person’s wishes could clash. Neophytos the Recluse escaped a marriage his parents had arranged and eventually carved a hermitage into rock near Paphos. His unusual religious life left an unusually rich record. It offers one personal story about family pressure, without making his choices typical of all medieval sons or daughters.

passages.title: Health, families and books
passages.text: Neophytos’s final rules for his community survive in a small original manuscript, completed on 9 May 1214 and carrying his own signatures. It measures 16.8 by 12.8 centimetres and now has 85 leaves. Restored and digitised in 2020 to 2022, this portable book preserves an individual writer’s voice across the change from Byzantine to Latin rule.

passages.title: Health, families and books
passages.text: A married couple left another kind of record at Galata. An inscription dates the founding of Panagia Podithou to 1502 and names the officer Demetrios de Coron and his wife Helen. Their portraits appear on the church. Its wooden screen carries the family arms and Venice’s winged lion, putting family patronage, worship and government in the same building.

passages.title: Health, families and books
passages.text: At Asinou, the surviving monastery church preserves paintings from several centuries. Its earliest important group dates to 1105 or 1106, before the Lusignan conquest, while later painters added new layers. The small, barrel-vaulted church has a protective timber roof above it. Looking carefully can reveal several generations of artistic work in one modest village building.

passages.title: Words, money and changing rulers
passages.text: A copper coin of Henry I, dated to his reign from 1218 to 1253, carries the Latin words “REX CYPRI”, meaning “king of Cyprus”. This is the catalogue’s transcription of the original coin inscription. The 20-millimetre coin shows a crowned royal bust and a cross. A short message about authority could travel in somebody’s pocket even when its owner could not read it.

passages.title: Words, money and changing rulers
passages.text: Venice compelled Queen Catherine Cornaro to give up Cyprus in 1489. A Venetian governor and two advisers administered the island, while Famagusta’s captain held military authority. Grain, salt, cotton and sugar mattered to the new rulers. The wealth of export trade coexisted with heavy taxation and poverty; prosperous merchants were only part of the island’s population.

passages.title: Words, money and changing rulers
passages.text: Buying things could become confusing when coins of different weights and metal contents circulated together. From 1511 to 1518, Venetian authorities countermarked circulating money to fix its recognized value. A central stamp marked value, with four edge stamps intended to discourage clipping metal away. The coin was practically wearing its own inspection stickers.

passages.title: Words, money and changing rulers
passages.text: Later history extends beyond the map’s 1530 cutoff. In 1567, Venice began rebuilding Nicosia’s defences to face artillery, using eleven heart-shaped bastions and three gates. Those famous walls belong to the late Venetian emergency, not to every century shown here. Nicosia fell to Ottoman forces in 1570, followed by Famagusta in 1571.

Cyprus did not cease to exist in 1530. Venetian government continued until the Ottoman conquest of 1570 and 1571. This ended Venetian sovereignty, while Cypriot communities and religious traditions continued; some people fled to Venice. The island’s earlier Byzantine and Lusignan institutions had already undergone their own transformations.

sectionTitles: A republic, a division and two British bases
Names, schools and life across a ceasefire line
Clinics, clever water and a prehistoric village

passages.text: This card covers the atlas's modern Republic of Cyprus record, not British rule, medieval cyprus or the separate northern-cyprus record. Its 1960 feature spans much of the island but does not model post-1974 control. The 1994-2020 feature shrinks to a southwest fragment, omitting Nicosia and the east. The modern file splits off northern-cyprus, yet the main polygon includes test points inside both British Sovereign Base Areas. These are classroom shapes, not legal or effective-control boundaries.

passages.title: A republic, a division and two British bases
passages.text: The Republic of Cyprus was established on 16 August 1960 as British colonial rule ended. The founding treaty excluded Akrotiri and Dhekelia from the new republic and kept them under United Kingdom sovereignty as Sovereign Base Areas. That is why a map of the Republic should not quietly absorb the bases. The atlas's post-2020 Cyprus polygon does so at the tested points, making it a useful locator but a poor legal diagram.

passages.title: A republic, a division and two British bases
passages.text: The 1960 Constitution tried to make partnership structural: the president was to be Greek, the vice-president Turkish, and separate community rules shaped elections and public offices. The design recognized two constitutionally named communities, but everyday identities were and are more varied. The arrangement did not keep operating as drafted after the 1963 crisis, so the constitutional plan must not be mistaken for a description of every later government.

passages.title: A republic, a division and two British bases
passages.text: Intercommunal violence erupted in December 1963. Security Council Resolution 186 created UNFICYP in March 1964 to help prevent renewed fighting, support law and order and encourage a return to normal conditions. This was already a serious fracture ten years before the island's better-known 1974 division. UN peacekeepers reduced danger; they did not solve the constitutional dispute or make separated neighbourhoods whole again.

passages.title: A republic, a division and two British bases
passages.text: In July 1974 a coup backed by Greece's military rulers sought union with Greece. The UN account records the Turkish military intervention that followed and Turkish forces establishing control in the north. A de facto ceasefire took effect on 16 August, leaving opposing lines and a UN-patrolled buffer zone. These dates describe military control and division; they do not convert the atlas's later southwest fragment into an accepted frontier.

passages.title: A republic, a division and two British bases
passages.text: On 18 November 1983 the Security Council treated the northern authorities' declaration of an independent state as legally invalid and called on countries not to recognize any Cypriot state except the Republic of Cyprus. The atlas still has a separate northern-cyprus record. That separate record can help show a de facto administration, but it must not be read as United Nations recognition or as a second internationally accepted sovereignty.

passages.title: A republic, a division and two British bases
passages.text: The European Court of Human Rights has held that Turkey's armed forces exercised effective overall control of northern Cyprus and that Turkey's Convention responsibility extended to acts of the subordinate local administration there. This is a judicial test of responsibility, not recognition of a new sovereign border. It also explains why legal sovereignty, international recognition, a local administration and day-to-day military control cannot be collapsed into one map colour.

passages.title: A republic, a division and two British bases
passages.text: Cyprus joined the European Union on 1 May 2004. EU law treats the whole island as EU territory, but Protocol No. 10 suspends the acquis where the Republic's government does not exercise effective control. That carefully worded compromise is both an achievement and a limitation: membership joined Cyprus to EU institutions while leaving the island's core territorial settlement unresolved.

passages.title: Names, schools and life across a ceasefire line
passages.text: The Republic entered the United Nations on 20 September 1960, only five weeks after its establishment. That gave the young state a seat in an international organization; it did not guarantee that its internal power-sharing machinery would work. Keeping the dates separate helps: independence was 16 August, UN admission was 20 September, intercommunal violence began in 1963 and the present de facto division dates from 1974.

passages.title: Names, schools and life across a ceasefire line
passages.text: A modern written sample is Κυπριακή Δημοκρατία in Greek and Kıbrıs Cumhuriyeti in Turkish: both mean “Republic of Cyprus.” The first uses the Greek alphabet; an editorial transliteration is Kypriakí Dimokratía. The second uses the Turkish Latin alphabet. These are current official state names, not samples of ancient Cypriot syllabic writing and not proof that every islander uses the same language at home.

passages.title: Names, schools and life across a ceasefire line
passages.text: The education ministry's State Institutes run afternoon and evening classes around the government-controlled area. Since 2003 they have offered Greek without charge to Turkish Cypriots and Turkish without charge to Greek Cypriots. A language class cannot settle a territorial dispute, but it can let neighbours speak without outsourcing every sentence to an interpreter. Published enrolment and institute totals are snapshots, not a count of all education on the island.

passages.title: Names, schools and life across a ceasefire line
passages.text: The buffer zone runs about 180 kilometres and varies from only a few metres to several kilometres wide. Since 2003, crossing points have let more people move between the two sides. In Pyla, Greek Cypriot and Turkish Cypriot residents live in the same village under special UN arrangements. Elsewhere, barriers still separate homes, fields and relatives. So “divided island” describes a political reality, not two sealed boxes with no shared lives.

passages.title: Lace, rhyme and family knowledge
passages.text: In Lefkara and Kato Drys, lace makers traditionally sit together in streets and courtyards, talking while they work. Mothers and grandmothers have taught girls four main elements of Lefkaritika, combining counted patterns, cut work, satin-stitch fillings and edging. The craft can support income and social ties. It is a living practice among particular communities, not evidence that every Cypriot grandmother carries emergency lace in her handbag.

passages.title: Lace, rhyme and family knowledge
passages.text: Tsiattista turns conversation into a friendly verbal duel. Performers improvise rhyming couplets in the Greek Cypriot dialect, often with violin or lute at weddings, fairs and festivals. The trick is to answer quickly while keeping the metre and making the crowd laugh. It is closer to a centuries-old freestyle battle than a memorized recital, although UNESCO warns that skilled improvisers have become fewer and transmission needs support.

passages.title: Clinics, clever water and a prehistoric village
passages.text: Cyprus introduced the GeSY health system in 2019 and reached near-universal coverage through a single-payer framework using public and private providers. The reform reduced households' direct spending and widened access. Its homework is less glamorous but important: financial sustainability, staffing, quality monitoring and better health data. A health card opens doors; it does not by itself create enough nurses, appointments or reliable measurement.

passages.title: Clinics, clever water and a prehistoric village
passages.text: Wastewater from homes can get a second career. Cyprus's Water Development Department sends municipal sewage through tertiary treatment, then reuses much of the cleaned water for irrigation and some groundwater recharge under operating rules. Kid translation: yesterday's toilet water does not go straight onto somebody's salad; it passes through serious treatment and controlled reuse. The system saves scarce fresh water, but safe operation and separate networks still matter.

passages.title: Clinics, clever water and a prehistoric village
passages.text: Choirokoitia preserves a Neolithic settlement from the seventh to fifth millennia BCE. People built circular stone and mud-brick houses around shared spaces, cooked at hearths, used basins and buried relatives beneath house floors. Archaeologists recovered stone vessels, flint and bone tools. This is deep human heritage located in modern Cyprus, not a project of the republic founded in 1960 and not proof that its inhabitants were modern Greeks or Turks.

The Republic of Cyprus continues as the internationally recognized state, while a separate administration operates in the north under Turkish effective control and without the recognition requested by its 1983 declaration. EU law remains suspended there, and the UN buffer zone still marks the unresolved 1974 division. The atlas's open interval means continuity in the dataset, not a forecast that borders, bases or peace arrangements can never change.
