sectionTitles: Read the label and the border with care
How archaeologists know, and what they cannot know
Clothing, skilled work and moments of sound
Health, medicine, water and the toilet question

passages.text: “Dravidians” is the atlas’s label, not the name of one prehistoric nation, race, kingdom or culture. Dravidian properly names a diverse language family, and its reconstructed ancestor is a scholarly model, not a recorded speaker introducing themself. The map begins with a small southern polygon in 4000 BCE, expands it across most of South Asia at 1500 BCE, contracts it at 700 BCE and deletes it at 500 BCE. Those dramatic border changes are editorial; no matching conquest or migration is known. Archaeology gives a richer, local story. At Sanganakallu to Kupgal, Brahmagiri, Hallur, Maski and other named sites, communities herded cattle, sheep and goats; raised hardy millets and pulses; shaped pots and stone axes; built modest homes; exchanged materials; and later experimented with iron. Their practices varied by valley, hill and century. One delightfully messy clue is the ashmound: enormous deposits made largely from repeatedly burned cattle dung, so ancient cow pats became archaeological detective files. Pots, genes and graves still cannot tell us everyone’s language. The Indus signs remain undeciphered, while readable Tamil and other Dravidian writing comes after this card ends. No later text is borrowed as a prehistoric voice.

passages.title: Read the label and the border with care
passages.text: The live index calls the record “Dravidians,” marks it as a culture and assigns approximate dates of 4000 to 500 BCE. Its imported text instead counts modern language communities. This card preserves the exact id for the app while replacing that time-traveling summary with evidence appropriate to prehistory.

passages.title: Read the label and the border with care
passages.text: Dravidian is a language family of roughly eighty documented varieties, not a biological race or one culture. Comparative linguists group languages through recurring sound correspondences, shared grammar and inherited vocabulary. Present-day Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Gondi and smaller languages cannot simply be projected unchanged into 3000 BCE.

passages.title: Read the label and the border with care
passages.text: One statistical language-tree study places its median root around 4000 to 4500 years ago, but its broad credible range reaches roughly 3000 to 6500 years. That is a probability model calibrated partly with later written languages, not a radiocarbon date for a person, village or border.

passages.title: Read the label and the border with care
passages.text: South Asian languages have borrowed words and structures through long contact. A crop name shared across families might record exchange, bilingual neighbors or an older inheritance; it is not an ethnic name tag. Linguistic reconstruction and archaeology can test each other, but one cannot automatically label the other.

passages.title: Read the label and the border with care
passages.text: At 1500 BCE the atlas polygon expands from a small southern shape to most of South Asia and contains a hole around several northern points owned by “Vedic Aryans.” No excavation discovered that border. The geometry visualizes an editorial theory and must never be narrated as a continent-wide Dravidian state.

passages.title: How archaeologists know, and what they cannot know
passages.text: Radiocarbon dates measure once-living material, while stratigraphy checks which deposits lie above or below others. Bayesian models can combine dates with sequence information. At southern sites this work shortened some old culture chronologies and revealed overlapping villages, ashmounds and later traditions rather than tidy textbook blocks.

passages.title: How archaeologists know, and what they cannot know
passages.text: Flotation lets tiny charred seeds rise from excavated soil; specialists then compare their shape with modern reference collections. Animal bones record species, age and butchery. Together these methods show crops and herds at particular sites, but preservation and sampling mean “not found” does not always mean “never used.”

passages.title: How archaeologists know, and what they cannot know
passages.text: Surveyors at Sanganakallu to Kupgal walked measured transects, mapped surface scatters and linked quarries, workshops, shelters, settlements and monuments across the hills. This landscape view catches activities missed by a single trench and also shows why “one site, one people” is too simple.

passages.title: How archaeologists know, and what they cannot know
passages.text: Electrical resistance tomography recently detected buried burned-dung layers at Brahmagiri. Drone maps, exposed drainage cuts and electrical contrasts revealed at least nine possible ashmound features that older excavators had overlooked. Even a famous site can change when researchers ask new questions with less destructive tools.

passages.title: How archaeologists know, and what they cannot know
passages.text: Ancient DNA measures biological relationships and mixture, not spoken language or cultural loyalty. South Asian studies model several changing ancestry gradients and alternative routes of mixture. Tropical preservation is so difficult that Rakhigarhi yielded one usable genome after screening many remains; one person cannot represent a civilization.

passages.title: Hills, monsoons, water and movement
passages.text: Southern Deccan communities lived among granite hills, seasonal streams, dry savannah and patches of woodland. Rain arrived unevenly with the monsoon. Hilltops offered stone, visibility and defensible or memorable places; nearby plains offered soils and grazing. Each combination encouraged a different balance of crops, herds and movement.

passages.title: Hills, monsoons, water and movement
passages.text: Sanganakallu grew before about 1200 BCE and then was largely abandoned while some neighboring Tungabhadra and Krishna basin sites continued. Researchers connect that contrast partly to access to stable water during a weakening, fluctuating monsoon. Climate shaped choices, but it did not press one automatic “collapse” button.

passages.title: Hills, monsoons, water and movement
passages.text: Ashmound camps with little habitation refuse differ from villages rich in grinding stones and crop-processing debris. A useful model links them within networks: people and cattle could move between grazing or gathering places and more permanent farming settlements. The exact routes and membership of each group remain uncertain.

passages.title: Hills, monsoons, water and movement
passages.text: The atlas’s 1500 BCE shape stretches from arid northwest zones to humid eastern plains and tropical coasts. Those environments demand radically different water and food strategies. Treating every point as one subsistence culture would erase the ecological knowledge that made local communities successful.

passages.title: Hills, monsoons, water and movement
passages.text: Wells, tanks and irrigation works must be dated site by site. Published southern Neolithic evidence supports streams, seasonal runoff, stored water and landscape choice more securely than a category-wide hydraulic system. Later reservoirs or modern village routines are useful questions, never ready-made answers for 2000 BCE.

passages.title: Millet, beans, herds and dinner
passages.text: Charred remains from southern villages include browntop millet, bristly foxtail, mung bean and horsegram. These hardy foods fit short rainy seasons better than thirsty field systems. A meal might combine grain and pulses, but exact porridges, breads, spices and serving customs require residues or texts that rarely survive.

passages.title: Millet, beans, herds and dinner
passages.text: Horsegram is a drought-tough pulse useful to people and animals, yet its domestication history cannot be read from one seed. Researchers compare measurements, wild ranges, dates and find contexts across many sites. Its humble reputation today should not be projected backward onto ancient diners.

passages.title: Millet, beans, herds and dinner
passages.text: Cattle dominate the most dramatic ritual landscape because dung built the ashmounds and cattle images cover some rocks. Sheep and goats also mattered, especially as village life changed. Herds could supply meat, milk, hides, fiber, traction and manure, but each product needs its own direct evidence.

passages.title: Millet, beans, herds and dinner
passages.text: Later phases added wheat and barley unevenly to local millets and pulses. Crops traveled through exchange and adoption rather than arriving as one sealed “civilization package.” Their different growing seasons gave households more choices, but also increased work in sowing, weeding, harvesting, threshing and storage.

passages.title: Millet, beans, herds and dinner
passages.text: Rice became more important in parts of Iron Age and Early Historic South India, especially near and after 500 BCE, but the pattern was neither instant nor universal. Dryland millet-pulse farming remained valuable. A bowl of modern rice should not be treated as the timeless ancient southern menu.

passages.title: Homes, tools, pots and exchange
passages.text: Excavated southern Neolithic settlements include small circular houses built with posts, woven branches and clay daub. Hearths, floors and nearby work areas show practical household space rather than palaces. Roof materials seldom survive, so grass or thatch is plausible only where impressions and local evidence support it.

passages.title: Homes, tools, pots and exchange
passages.text: Potters formed mostly handmade vessels, then smoothed, burnished, fired and sometimes colored them. Pots cooked food, carried water and served gatherings; broken sherds now date layers and connect sites. Similar pottery can spread by trade or imitation, so it is not a dependable language detector.

passages.title: Homes, tools, pots and exchange
passages.text: Hiregudda became a busy dolerite axe-production place. Tens of thousands of flakes record roughing, thinning, reshaping and skilled choices from quarry to finished edge. Many completed axes left the workshop, showing exchange; their journeys do not reveal the buyers’ language or ethnicity.

passages.title: Homes, tools, pots and exchange
passages.text: Grinding hollows worn directly into granite and portable querns record the repetitive labor of turning seeds into usable food. Beads of carnelian or steatite and nonlocal stone point toward exchange. These networks could link households over distance without requiring merchants, money or a central government.

passages.title: Homes, tools, pots and exchange
passages.text: By the late second and first millennia BCE, smiths produced iron tools, weapons and fittings. Slag suggests smelting at fewer places while smithing was wider, so blooms or bars moved between communities. Copper, bronze and gold remained favored for some ornaments, giving metals several social meanings.

passages.title: Families, women, children and learning
passages.text: No census lists prehistoric households, marriages or inheritance rules. Houses, shared work areas and graves show cooperation, but a cluster of rooms is not automatically one modern-style nuclear family. Kin, neighbors, visitors and workers may all have shared food, tasks and care.

passages.title: Families, women, children and learning
passages.text: Women certainly lived, worked, learned and made decisions in these communities, but pots and spindle whorls do not carry the maker’s sex. Assigning all weaving, farming or herding to women or men would import later expectations. Skeletons, tool wear and work contexts must be combined before proposing gendered labor.

passages.title: Families, women, children and learning
passages.text: Child urn burials at Brahmagiri and several other sites make children archaeologically visible, though funerals represent decisions by survivors. Different treatment can reflect age, circumstance, belonging or ritual. It does not prove that children held less affection, status or personhood while alive.

passages.title: Families, women, children and learning
passages.text: Children probably learned by watching and helping: recognizing ripe millet, calming cattle, carrying water, shaping clay and safely striking stone. That is a reasonable inference from household production. There is no evidence for alphabet lessons or a formal school inside this exact prehistoric category.

passages.title: Families, women, children and learning
passages.text: Maski’s radiocarbon-dated cemetery shows grave practices diversifying gradually, with pottery, coffins, metals and stone architecture combined in different ways. Those choices may have negotiated kin, locality or cooperative ties. They do not disclose surnames, castes or one rule of descent.

passages.title: Clothing, skilled work and moments of sound
passages.text: Spindle whorls plus charred cotton and flax at Hallur around 1000 to 900 BCE show fiber preparation and spinning. Finished garments almost never survive in this climate. Cloth could be wrapped, tied or stitched, while hides and plant fibers may also have been used, but no universal costume is recoverable.

passages.title: Clothing, skilled work and moments of sound
passages.text: Stone-axe production was skilled work, not mindless rock smashing. Knappers selected dolerite, controlled flakes, ground edges and repaired tools. Apprentices likely learned through repeated practice because failed blanks and changing techniques remain at workshops, although no artifact records a master’s name or lesson plan.

passages.title: Clothing, skilled work and moments of sound
passages.text: Some Kupgal boulders ring like bells when struck, and pecked percussion marks occur near cattle images. Researchers measured the acoustics and mapped the art. Ancient people may have combined sound and image, but the tune, audience and occasion are unknown, so call it a possibility, not a prehistoric concert recording.

passages.title: Clothing, skilled work and moments of sound
passages.text: Engraved stone objects show deliberate pattern-making and portable visual communication. A repeated design might have marked memory, ownership, identity or beauty. Without a decipherment and longer patterned sequences, these marks are art or signs of uncertain meaning, not a readable Proto-Dravidian sentence.

passages.title: Clothing, skilled work and moments of sound
passages.text: Daily labor included tending animals, clearing and sowing fields, weeding, harvesting, threshing, grinding, cooking, fetching water, building, potting and tool repair. Tasks changed by season and household. Archaeology sees their debris far better than jokes, songs, games or rest, so silence is not evidence of joyless lives.

passages.title: Health, medicine, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Smoke, cuts, burns, animal kicks, parasites, childbirth, infection and food shortage were possible hazards, but this category has no medical manual. Healed bone can show survival and care after injury; teeth can reveal diet or stress. Neither identifies the healer, herb, prayer or treatment without supporting evidence.

passages.title: Health, medicine, water and the toilet question
passages.text: A skeleton from Balathal, outside the southern site group, was diagnosed with leprosy through a particular pattern of facial and limb changes. It demonstrates palaeopathology’s power and its limits: one carefully studied person documents disease there, not among everyone colored “Dravidian” on this map.

passages.title: Health, medicine, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Millets and pulses supplied carbohydrates and protein; animal foods could broaden diets. Harvest failure, contaminated water and crowded animal pens still created risk. Seed and bone totals describe what survived at a site, not equal portions for every woman, man or child or reliable meals in every season.

passages.title: Health, medicine, water and the toilet question
passages.text: No category-wide sewer, latrine or toilet has been securely identified for the exact southern Neolithic and Iron Age communities discussed here. People surely managed bodily waste, ash, broken pots and animal dung, but many routines leave faint traces. Inventing either indoor plumbing or one universal outdoor custom would be dishonest.

passages.title: Health, medicine, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Mohenjo-daro had wells, baths, drains and sewage disposal, but it belongs to the separately named Indus civilization and its language remains unknown. Those impressive toilets cannot be borrowed for this atlas umbrella merely because one hypothesis connects the Indus language with Proto-Dravidian.

passages.title: Belief, death, status and violence
passages.text: Burned cattle-dung ashmounds were built in repeated episodes and sometimes became focal places before villages expanded nearby. Feasting, seasonal gathering, purification or memorial practice are debated interpretations. The burned material and sequence are measurable; the spoken beliefs and exact ritual rules are not.

passages.title: Belief, death, status and violence
passages.text: Huge piles of ancient cow dung sound silly, but they are serious archives. Fibers, ash layers, animal remains and surrounding activity record penning and repeated burning. The fun fact is scientifically solid: a four-thousand-year-old cow pat can reveal more daily life than a king list.

passages.title: Belief, death, status and violence
passages.text: Neolithic and Iron Age burials include pits, urns, stone settings, coffins and varied grave goods. “Megalithic” describes monuments, not one ethnicity. Mortuary change could express memory, affiliation and difference; it does not prove a new race invaded whenever burial architecture changed.

passages.title: Belief, death, status and violence
passages.text: Iron swords, daggers and projectile points occur especially in some mortuary contexts, while tools appear in homes and graves. Weapons could enact violence or symbolize rank and group ties. They do not establish a standing army, named war or continent-wide political hierarchy.

passages.title: Belief, death, status and violence
passages.text: Unequal access to rare metals, elaborate graves or specialized production may indicate growing social differences. Coercion, captivity and forced labor are possible in human societies, but no source here securely documents a “Dravidian” slave system. Power should be described where evidence exists, not filled with dramatic guesses.

passages.title: Achievements, writing and what continued
passages.text: The great achievement was thousands of local decisions: domesticating and tending drought-resistant crops, coordinating herds, storing food, shaping stone and clay, and linking hills and plains. These solutions made life possible through variable monsoons without requiring one capital, emperor or unified “Dravidian civilization.”

passages.title: Achievements, writing and what continued
passages.text: Craft communities turned a dolerite ridge into an organized production landscape and later moved iron blooms between specialized and local smiths. Such networks reveal planning, teaching and trust. Exchange connected distinct communities; it did not erase their languages, identities or unequal access to valuable materials.

passages.title: Achievements, writing and what continued
passages.text: Contemporaneous written-language sample: none is securely attributable to this exact atlas record between 4000 and 500 BCE. Proto-Dravidian is reconstructed, not written. Indus signs remain undeciphered, and pottery graffiti are not readable sentences; supplying either as an original-script quotation would pretend certainty we do not have.

passages.title: Achievements, writing and what continued
passages.text: Readable Brahmi at Anuradhapura is argued from the early fourth century BCE, and Tamil-Brahmi attestation used by linguistic models is later still. Both fall after this card’s 500 BCE endpoint. A Tamil sample, transliteration and translation would therefore borrow a later daughter language as the umbrella’s voice.

passages.title: Achievements, writing and what continued
passages.text: At 500 BCE the atlas replaces this id with several political and cultural labels across different locations. That is not one fall or ethnic disappearance. Farms, herds, ironworking, exchange and Dravidian language histories continued through many named societies whose records must be studied on their own terms.

The exact atlas id disappears at 500 BCE. Tested points then belong to many other map labels, including Iron Age megalithic traditions, Hindu kingdoms, Magadha, Achaemenid territory and smaller northern polities. This patchwork is an editorial seam, not evidence that one prehistoric people was conquered or vanished in a single year. Local settlements, agriculture, herding, craft, exchange and language communities continued changing. Readable southern inscriptions and historically named Tamil, Chera, Chola, Pandya and other societies belong to later evidence and should receive their own cards rather than being declared automatic successors to an invented umbrella state.

sectionTitles: A changing government, a continuing city

passages.text: Benevento was a Lombard duchy and later a principality, but this imported record runs from 1000 to 1279, across the end of its ruling dynasty in 1077 and into papal government. Its later outline wrongly includes Sicily and greatly exaggerates Benevento’s territory. This card follows the city’s final Lombard rulers and its medieval life afterward; it does not describe a Beneventan state ruling that entire polygon.

passages.title: A changing government, a continuing city
passages.text: Benevento’s inhabitants accepted papal authority in 1051 after expelling their princes. The rulers returned in 1055, but their authority was increasingly subordinate to the pope. This uneven transition explains why 1077, the death of the last Lombard prince Landulf VI, is a dynastic endpoint rather than the first moment anyone considered papal government.

passages.title: A changing government, a continuing city
passages.text: Under the popes, Benevento developed local institutions as well as papal administration. The oldest surviving version of its city statutes dates to 1202. Consuls exercised local jurisdiction, although their powers changed and were contested. Medieval government could involve argument among citizens, officeholders and distant rulers, rather than one person making every decision.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work
passages.text: Some houses connected across streets by raised passages called pontili. Permission from the ruler was required, and the street underneath had to remain public. A family might gain a convenient route between properties while everybody else still needed room to pass below.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work
passages.text: A will dated December 1092 records a house with a fireplace. Other homes had upper floors reached by outside masonry stairs. These details distinguish particular buildings from a fantasy of identical medieval cottages. Comfort and construction varied from household to household.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work
passages.text: Benevento’s documented crafts included pottery, shoemaking, tailoring, carpentry, stoneworking and metalwork. Mills operated along the rivers, especially a channel diverted from the Sabato. These activities connected the city to farms and waterpower: a prince’s court needed a much larger working community around it.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work
passages.text: At Sant’Ilario a Port’Aurea, archaeologists studied a rubbish deposit in a chamber probably first used as an ossuary. Its pottery dates from the thirteenth to fifteenth centuries, after Lombard rule and partly after this map interval. Bowls, jugs, cooking pots and large storage vessels preserve the equipment of meals and provisions.

passages.title: Homes and skilled work
passages.text: Laboratory analysis of glazed pottery from two medieval sites in Benevento identified a group likely made locally. Some dark fragments may have been overfired rejects. The thirteenth- to fifteenth-century pottery tradition therefore preserves mistakes as well as attractive dishes. A pot that went wrong in the kiln can tell researchers how its successful neighbors were made.

passages.title: Buildings that kept older memories
passages.text: The cathedral expanded during the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, removing an older burial area in front of the church. Excavations beneath today’s floor distinguish those medieval changes from earlier churches and from modern rebuilding. A familiar place could be repeatedly reorganized as the community’s needs and ambitions changed.

passages.title: Buildings that kept older memories
passages.text: Funerary inscriptions for ninth-century Lombard princes were reused in the cathedral’s later facade. Their words outlived the tomb arrangement for which they had been carved. The stones are now museum evidence of both the earlier dynasty and the practical medieval habit of reusing valuable building material.

passages.title: Buildings that kept older memories
passages.text: A 2024 study brought scattered cathedral sculpture fragments back into conversation with one another. Its author proposed an earlier twelfth-century date for parts of the rebuilding and bronze door than some previous accounts had used. Reassembling fragments can change a building’s history; dates printed in older guides are not automatically the last word.

passages.title: Buildings that kept older memories
passages.text: Santa Sofia’s twelfth-century cloister includes carvings of seasonal agricultural work, with months from June to December surviving. Other capitals display fantastic creatures. The sculptors placed familiar labor beside imaginative beasts, giving a person walking around the courtyard much more to look at than a row of plain supports.

passages.title: Written and sung words
passages.text: An inscription in Santa Sofia’s cloister honors Abbot John IV, who governed from 1142 to 1176. Its Latin words “stat Quarti fama Iohannis” mean “the fame of John the Fourth endures.” This modern transcription comes from a carved capital and belongs to papal-era Benevento, after the Lombard dynasty had ended.

passages.title: Written and sung words
passages.text: Beneventan was also the name of a distinctive handwriting style used across southern Italy. A regional example is the Montecassino Exultet roll of about 1075 to 1080, now British Library Add. 30337. It contains Latin for an Easter ceremony, with red musical signs above the words. Script, language and tune did different jobs on the same parchment.

passages.title: Written and sung words
passages.text: On an Exultet roll, pictures faced the opposite direction from the words. As the reader let the scroll descend from the reading platform, listeners could see the images the right way up. This southern Italian format considered two audiences at once: the person singing the text and the people watching below.

passages.title: Written and sung words
passages.text: The battle near Benevento on 26 February 1266 ended with Charles of Anjou defeating Manfred, king of Sicily. It belongs to the city’s later medieval setting, nearly two centuries after the Lombard dynasty ended. The battle’s famous name should not be mistaken for the fall of an independent Lombard duchy in 1266.

Landulf VI’s death in 1077 ended the Lombard dynasty. Benevento continued as a papal city, with later occupations and local institutions. The imported 1279 endpoint is not the principality’s historical fall date.

sectionTitles: A household on a windy headland
Dinner travelled, and jars stayed useful
A window ledge with homework potential

passages.text: Dumnonia was an early medieval British kingdom in the south-western peninsula, associated with Devon and Cornwall. Its rulers probably used several centres, including Tintagel. This card follows the map’s 600 to 800 window but also uses earlier evidence from Tintagel’s prosperous fifth to seventh centuries. Those finds illuminate an exceptional coastal settlement, not every household across the kingdom.

passages.title: A household on a windy headland
passages.text: Tintagel offered steep cliffs, a narrow approach and broad sea views, but it also had fresh water. Some small rectangular buildings contained hearths. The settlement combined an unusually defensible position with the everyday necessities of warmth, cooking and drinking.

passages.title: A household on a windy headland
passages.text: Excavators uncovered stone walls, paving and steps on the southern terraces. A thick wall farther east could have supported a building or held back a terrace. Finding a wall is straightforward; deciding exactly what its builders needed it to do takes more work.

passages.title: A household on a windy headland
passages.text: Surveys identified roughly a hundred buildings across the headland. Their uses are not all settled: homes, stores and workshops remain possibilities. An impressive settlement plan cannot by itself tell us which room held somebody’s bed or where children spent their days.

passages.title: Dinner travelled, and jars stayed useful
passages.text: Fifth- or sixth-century amphora fragments from Tintagel came from Greece. These vessels carried wine and olive oil. Broken jars therefore record journeys across seas as well as the food and drink that wealthy occupants could obtain.

passages.title: Dinner travelled, and jars stayed useful
passages.text: Local slate discs probably closed reused amphorae with the help of beeswax. An imported container could begin another useful life after its original contents were gone. Keeping a good jar was sensible long before anyone had a kitchen cupboard full of them.

passages.title: Dinner travelled, and jars stayed useful
passages.text: A rotary quern from the northern ruins probably belongs to the post-Roman settlement. It ground grain into flour. Fragments of bowls, a stemmed glass and a flask, probably from southern France, reveal a very different part of meals: rare vessels that displayed the occupants’ status.

passages.title: Tiny scraps from the kitchen
passages.text: The 2016 excavation recovered barley, wheat and some oats from post-Roman rubbish deposits. The grains survived because they were charred. Rubbish can be an excellent historical archive, although most people making dinner were probably not thinking about future archaeologists.

passages.title: Tiny scraps from the kitchen
passages.text: Few weed seeds and little chaff accompanied those cereals. Researchers suggested that grain arrived already threshed and cleaned, probably from the surrounding countryside. Preparing food linked the coastal settlement to work on nearby farms.

passages.title: Tiny scraps from the kitchen
passages.text: Some barley had sprouted. That might represent preparation for beer, but the researchers also considered spoiled grain burned for disposal. The same tiny find can fit two different kitchen stories; it cannot settle the menu on its own.

passages.title: A window ledge with homework potential
passages.text: A seventh-century slate reused as a window ledge carries the Latin words “viri duo”, meaning “two men”, in English Heritage’s transcription. It also has names, Greek letters and Christian symbols. This is a surviving piece of local writing, not a reconstructed sentence invented for the map.

passages.title: A window ledge with homework potential
passages.text: The lettering combines styles associated with ordinary documents and decorated Gospel books. Specialists interpret it as possible writing practice by someone with scribal training. It supports literacy in a privileged Christian setting, not the claim that every child attended school.

passages.title: Letters, beliefs and later stories
passages.text: Aldhelm wrote to King Geraint and Dumnonia’s bishops about disagreements over calculating Easter and other church practices. The letter, probably from around the opening of the eighth century, shows a kingdom participating in literate religious debate. A calendar disagreement could reach the king’s desk.

passages.title: Letters, beliefs and later stories
passages.text: Tintagel’s famous connection with Arthur first appears in Geoffrey of Monmouth’s twelfth-century account, centuries after the early settlement. Archaeological evidence for wealthy occupants does not establish that the legendary king lived there. The real jars, buildings and writing are interesting without a royal autograph.

Dumnonia lost territory through West Saxon expansion rather than one securely dated final event. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records war with Geraint in 710 but does not give its outcome; a later writer adds that he fled. Devon became part of Wessex, while a British kingdom continued in Cornwall. The imported 800 cutoff is map coverage, not the disappearance of the region’s people.

passages.text: Dutch Brazil was a West India Company colony in northeastern Brazil, established by conquest in 1630 and lost in 1654. Sugar production, slavery, religious communities and ambitious scientific collecting shaped its short history. The imported map’s 1650 to 1715 range must not be mistaken for the colony’s actual lifespan.

passages.title: Work, faith and excavated homes
passages.text: Johan Maurits provided loans for Portuguese operators to reopen abandoned sugar mills. Dutch officials depended on people already familiar with the industry. Taking control of a colony did not instantly supply the practical knowledge needed to run its machinery and plantations.

passages.title: Work, faith and excavated homes
passages.text: Plantation labor was coerced. Enslaved African men, women and children were transported to Dutch Brazil, and the governor personally owned and traded enslaved people. His support for painting and science cannot be separated from the violence that supported colonial wealth.

passages.title: Work, faith and excavated homes
passages.text: Drawings associated with Zacharias Wagener record a Recife slave market and a woman branded with Johan Maurits’s initials. These are rare visual witnesses to an experience that polished colonial landscapes often concealed. They depict real systems of ownership and dehumanization.

passages.title: Work, faith and excavated homes
passages.text: Two religious schools, Talmud Torah and Etz Hayim, operated beside the Kahal Zur Israel synagogue. Rabbi Isaac Aboab da Fonseca arrived in Recife in 1642 at the community’s invitation. Worship, study and migration linked this neighborhood to Jewish communities across the Atlantic.

passages.title: Work, faith and excavated homes
passages.text: Excavation at the synagogue site revealed eight floor levels, fragments of Dutch pipes, glazed pottery and a ceramic piece with a menorah. These finds show how a building accumulated changes and everyday objects. The furniture now displayed there was reconstructed through research, not found intact.

passages.title: Work, faith and excavated homes
passages.text: The site also preserves a mikveh, a bath for religious purification. This gives a concrete glimpse of ritual life involving water. It should not be treated as evidence that every Recife household had the same bathing arrangements.

passages.title: Pictures, plants and written words
passages.text: Frans Post’s Brazilian Landscape with a House under Construction presents European, Indigenous and African figures in an apparently harmonious setting. The museum cautions that this idealized scene hides slavery’s harsh realities. A painting can preserve useful details while also giving a misleading impression of society.

passages.title: Pictures, plants and written words
passages.text: Post made the painting after returning to the Netherlands. His Brazilian scenes therefore combine remembered experience with later artistic choices. They are valuable historical evidence, but not snapshots taken while the events unfolded.

passages.title: Pictures, plants and written words
passages.text: Collectors did not work alone: Indigenous Brazilians, enslaved Africans and Portuguese residents brought specimens to naturalists. Research tracing the surviving botanical images emphasizes these often uncredited contributions. The knowledge printed under European authors’ names depended on many other people.

passages.title: Pictures, plants and written words
passages.text: A surviving plant specimen, an oil painting and a printed woodcut can be compared for Spigelia anthelmia, recorded as a remedy for intestinal worms. That chain shows how plant knowledge entered books. It documents historical medicine, not a recommendation to use the plant today.

passages.title: Pictures, plants and written words
passages.text: The same research follows Cleome gynandra, an African leafy vegetable eaten by enslaved Africans in Brazil. Editor Johannes de Laet grew seeds in the Netherlands in 1646, but the plant died as the weather turned cold. Food plants traveled with people, even across climates where they struggled.

passages.title: Pictures, plants and written words
passages.text: “Historia naturalis Brasiliae” means “Natural history of Brazil.” This Latin title appears on the 1648 book preserved in the John Carter Brown Library. It is an authentic printed sample of scholarly writing connected with the colony, rather than a reconstruction of ordinary conversation.

Dutch forces surrendered in January 1654, returning the occupied region to Portuguese rule. This ended the colonial government, not the lives or histories of its diverse inhabitants. The imported 1715 endpoint is incorrect for Dutch Brazil and remains a map-data issue to correct.

passages.text: This record follows Dutch colonial power from the VOC trading company into nineteenth-century state government. Its 1650 to 1878 dates are map coverage, not the colony’s lifespan. The imported outline has serious errors: before 1815 it suggests uniform control across much of the archipelago; from 1815 it wrongly includes southern Africa and retains only a small Asian fragment around Bangka. Read the history below independently of those shapes. Indonesian kingdoms and communities had their own rulers, languages and histories.

passages.title: A commercial company with armies
passages.text: The VOC’s charter allowed it to build forts, employ soldiers, negotiate treaties and appoint judges. Its power overseas therefore extended far beyond buying and selling. Some relationships with Asian rulers involved negotiation, while others rested on conquest or agreements extracted by force.

passages.title: A commercial company with armies
passages.text: The spice monopoly had violent foundations. In 1621, before this map interval begins, Jan Pieterszoon Coen’s forces killed and expelled inhabitants of Banda after they traded with competing buyers. Fortified nutmeg plantations followed. The later wealth associated with nutmeg and mace cannot be separated from this dispossession.

passages.title: A commercial company with armies
passages.text: Batavia also needed ordinary food. A painting of VOC establishments made around 1662 to 1663 recalls supplies bought at Lawec in Cambodia: rice, butter, pork and lard. Ships carried ingredients for meals alongside valuable spices. This describes company provisioning, not one menu shared by all residents.

passages.title: Family rooms and children’s futures
passages.text: Jan Brandes’s 1784 drawing shows his son Jantje holding a book while Flora, an enslaved woman, sits at a spinning wheel. Furniture, a carpet and pets fill the room. A domestic picture can preserve both a child’s access to books and the unequal labour that supported a comfortable colonial household.

passages.title: Family rooms and children’s futures
passages.text: Batavia’s Weeskamer managed inventories, guardianship of minors and inheritances until children reached adulthood. Founded in 1624, it left many records from the eighteenth century. Company employees and free citizens ran it. These papers let historians investigate family property and children’s circumstances, alongside the better-known records of ships and wars.

passages.title: Family rooms and children’s futures
passages.text: “Jantje met een boek in de hand” means “Jantje with a book in his hand.” These Dutch words are transcribed from Brandes’s caption on the 1784 drawing. They appear here in modern type, with a literal English translation. This is one colonial household’s written language, not a sample of every language spoken across the islands.

passages.title: Plants, learning and preserving knowledge
passages.text: On Ambon, Georg Everhard Rumphius compiled a large illustrated herbal recording plants and their uses. Names appear in Malay, Ambonese, Dutch and Latin, with other languages also represented. The surviving manuscripts connect natural history with local knowledge of useful plants; they preserve evidence for historians of medicine as well as botany.

passages.title: Plants, learning and preserving knowledge
passages.text: After Rumphius became blind in 1670, his wife Susanna and son Paul August helped him continue his studies. Later, a manuscript shipment sank in 1692, but a copy made before departure preserved that work. Copying a book by hand could be an extremely effective backup plan.

passages.title: Plants, learning and preserving knowledge
passages.text: Diponegoro’s education followed a different path. His chronicle describes growing up with his great-grandmother at Tegalreja, mixing with farming communities and learning from Muslim religious scholars. This is evidence for one Javanese prince’s upbringing, including family guidance and religious learning beyond European colonial schools.

passages.title: Plants, learning and preserving knowledge
passages.text: In exile in 1831 to 1832, Diponegoro composed his autobiographical chronicle in Javanese verse. The principal surviving copy was made in 1865 to 1866, using Pegon, Javanese written in Arabic characters. Its preservation gives readers a substantial Javanese account of events that Dutch officials also described from their own perspective.

passages.title: Colonial power, farming and health
passages.text: Diponegoro led the Java War from 1825 to 1830. Despite a promise of safe conduct, he was arrested during peace negotiations. A later painting commissioned by the Dutch commander De Kock presents the event as submission. Knowing who paid for a historical picture helps us ask whose version it tells.

passages.title: Colonial power, farming and health
passages.text: The cultivation system introduced in 1830 compelled Javanese farmers to grow crops for European markets and deliver them to the government at fixed prices. The Netherlands Trading Society shipped the goods for sale. Colonial revenue depended directly on decisions imposed on farming households and the use of their land.

passages.title: Colonial power, farming and health
passages.text: A medical school opened at the military hospital in Weltevreden, Batavia, in January 1851. Its first class comprised twelve Javanese young men. Instruction included anatomy, zoology and chemistry, taught in Malay. The school trained local practitioners within a colonial system in which access to education and care remained restricted.

passages.title: Colonial power, farming and health
passages.text: The 1849 plan for this training required applicants to read and write Malay and Javanese and agree to government service after study. Smallpox vaccination was a central task. Admission therefore depended on existing literacy, and medical learning was tied to the government’s staffing needs rather than offered to every child.

passages.title: Colonial power, farming and health
passages.text: Batavia began developing an artesian-well and hydrant system in 1873. The first public hydrant received a ceremonial opening in 1876. Early installations favoured the wealthier Weltevreden district. Getting cleaner water involved engineering, but its distribution also reflected the unequal geography of the colonial city.

passages.title: Colonial power, farming and health
passages.text: Residents pressed for better access. In 1876, representatives of Batavia’s Arab community formally requested hydrants for their neighbourhood. Water was a practical concern that brought people into negotiations with government. The request also shows that communities actively shaped demands for urban services.

The imported 1878 endpoint is not the end of Dutch colonial rule. Much later, after Japanese occupation during the Second World War, Sukarno and Hatta declared Indonesian independence on 17 August 1945. War and negotiations followed; the Netherlands transferred sovereignty on 27 December 1949. Indonesian communities and their histories continued through these changes of government.

sectionTitles: How to read this many-island map
Meals, clothes, homes and a little fun
Water, washing and the all-important toilet question
Science, preservation, music and written voices

passages.text: This record maps the late Dutch East Indies, a vast colonial state governed from Batavia and inhabited by many peoples with different languages, religions, family systems and local authorities. The years 1920 to 1938 belong to the atlas record, not to the colony’s full lifespan: its 1938 outline is silently reassigned to another Dutch id and colonial rule continued until Japan’s 1942 conquest. During these years schools, medicine, engineering, astronomy, archaeology, cities and nationalist organizations expanded, but access and power were deeply unequal. Children built new ways to learn, workers and families survived plantations and depression, and activists imagined Indonesia. The outline is a broad locator. It cannot prove uniform Dutch control, one culture, or one daily routine across thousands of islands.

passages.title: How to read this many-island map
passages.text: The exact atlas id appears only from 1920 to 1938. Its two snapshots use the same MultiPolygon: 15 separate outer rings and 908 coordinate positions. That tells us the importer reused a coarse outline for navigation. It does not tell us where authority was strong, negotiated or resisted on the ground.

passages.title: How to read this many-island map
passages.text: In 1938 the identical archipelago outline continues with the label “Dutch East Indies” but the civ id changes to netherlands-1878. Nothing constitutional happened to the colony that year. This is a database handoff hiding in plain sight, so the card will not invent a 1938 fall.

passages.title: How to read this many-island map
passages.text: The broad geometry reaches from northern Sumatra to western New Guinea and excludes Portuguese Timor around Dili. Yet coastal point tests can miss cities because the coast is simplified, and fifteen rings cannot inventory thousands of islands. Think “where to look,” not “perfect border tracing.”

passages.title: How to read this many-island map
passages.text: “Dutch East Indies” names a colonial state, not one civilization. Javanese, Sundanese, Minangkabau, Acehnese, Balinese, Chinese Indonesian, Indo-European, Papuan, Moluccan and many other communities lived within or across its claimed boundaries. A fact about one town or people is labelled that way below.

passages.title: Government, unequal law and resistance
passages.text: A governor-general and colonial administration held decisive power. The Volksraad, opened in 1918, contained appointed as well as elected members and began with advisory authority. Indonesians could debate and petition there, but it was never an equal parliament chosen freely by the whole population.

passages.title: Government, unequal law and resistance
passages.text: Colonial law sorted people into Europeans, the Indigenous population and “Foreign Orientals,” each connected to different bureaucracies, courts, procedures and taxes. Real lives did not fit tidy boxes, but paperwork could make a legal category shape schooling, work, travel, property and punishment.

passages.title: Government, unequal law and resistance
passages.text: The 1920 income tax was announced as one progressive scheme for residents aged fifteen and older above an income threshold. Actual taxation still varied by place and depended on local officials, village leaders and negotiation. A rule printed in Batavia was not automatically a uniform experience on every island.

passages.title: Government, unequal law and resistance
passages.text: After the 1926 to 1927 revolts, the government sent political prisoners to Boven Digoel in New Guinea. The remote camp isolated them from families and political networks under surveillance. Newspapers helped make the place a warning, while censorship shaped what readers could know.

passages.title: Government, unequal law and resistance
passages.text: The PNI, founded in 1927, sought Indonesian independence without cooperation with colonial rule. Authorities prosecuted and exiled leading nationalists. Repression could reach family life too: arrest or distant exile removed a wage earner, parent, child or sibling as well as a political organizer.

passages.title: Government, unequal law and resistance
passages.text: When public meetings were banned in 1933, New PNI members met secretly in small groups and reorganized underground. Cadre education helped the movement survive, even as police monitored, searched and arrested leaders. A “classroom” for politics might now be someone’s crowded front room with everyone listening for footsteps.

passages.title: Government, unequal law and resistance
passages.text: The 1936 Soetardjo petition asked for a conference to plan greater self-government within the Dutch kingdom, not immediate separation. The government waited until 1938 and rejected it. That refusal frustrated moderate nationalists who had tried the colony’s own official channel.

passages.title: Families, status and social life
passages.text: There was no single “Indies family.” Households and social life differed sharply by community, religion, place and wealth. Colonial legal status added another layer: officials tried to rank people by racial categories even when ancestry and daily cooperation did not fit their filing boxes.

passages.title: Families, status and social life
passages.text: A surviving Minangkabau example shows why local detail matters. At Nagari Sijunjung, descent and inherited property follow women’s lines, married couples are matrilocal, and a rumah gadang can house an extended clan. Male maternal relatives and elected penghulu also hold defined leadership roles.

passages.title: Families, status and social life
passages.text: The same Sijunjung record places houses beside rice fields, plantations, markets, mosques, a madrasah, graves and a customary hall. Children could learn clan knowledge in the rumah gadang as well as religion in a school. This is an enduring Minangkabau setting, not a model for Java, Bali or New Guinea.

passages.title: Families, status and social life
passages.text: The First Indonesian Women’s Congress met in Yogyakarta in December 1928. Seven groups initiated it, thirty organizations attended, and the official heritage account estimates about 700 participants. They did not all share one program, but coordination itself made women visible as national political actors.

passages.title: Families, status and social life
passages.text: Photographs record moments, not average lives. A 1925 album shows a front gallery, dining room and carpets in a Tjimahi home belonging to a Dutch family. It is useful evidence for one comparatively comfortable European household, and terrible evidence for what most Indigenous families owned.

passages.title: Children, schools and growing up
passages.text: By the 1930s, fewer than one quarter of Indigenous children were enrolled in primary school. Villages often carried much of the cost, while government spending favored schools for children with European legal status and ethnic Chinese children. Many children learned through family, religion, apprenticeship and work instead.

passages.title: Children, schools and growing up
passages.text: Bandung’s technical college opened in 1920 with one faculty and one major: road and water engineering. Its first class had 28 students, only two of them Indonesian. Four Indonesian students were among those who graduated as engineers in 1926. Higher education grew, but the doorway stayed very narrow.

passages.title: Children, schools and growing up
passages.text: Taman Siswa, founded in 1922, offered a different idea of school. Its Among system rejected forcing children and described the teacher as a pamong, a guide who supports development. It also argued that education should not belong only to society’s upper layers.

passages.title: Children, schools and growing up
passages.text: School and work often overlapped. Colonial policymakers debated limits on women’s and children’s labor, but employers defended cheap labor and described work as “natural” for Indonesians. The problem was not that children never learned; it was that the state invested little in giving most of them a real choice.

passages.title: Children, schools and growing up
passages.text: Youth organizations from Java, Sumatra, Sulawesi, Batak and Betawi communities joined student groups at the 1928 congress. Their resolution named a shared Indonesian homeland, nation and language. A tiny, privileged school population could still produce ideas that travelled far beyond campus gates.

passages.title: Work, farms and the Depression
passages.text: Most daily work never appeared in a famous speech. Census categories recorded agriculture, food and textile production, retail and domestic service, while much subsistence and communal farm work went uncounted. The mix changed by place, gender and class; there was no responsible “average Indonesian job.”

passages.title: Work, farms and the Depression
passages.text: The 1930 census of Java and Madura registered an occupation for nearly 30 percent of married women, especially in farming, food or textile production and retail. Yet it excluded much subsistence and communal agricultural work. The official number was large, and still managed to miss work.

passages.title: Work, farms and the Depression
passages.text: On Sumatran tobacco and rubber estates, many workers had been recruited from China and Java. Contracts backed by penal sanctions restricted movement, and desertion remained common. Oil palm was becoming an estate crop by the 1930s. “Modern plantation” could mean modern export profits and very old-fashioned coercion.

passages.title: Work, farms and the Depression
passages.text: The worldwide Depression devastated export-crop earnings. In Java’s towns, some workers endured wage cuts and worse conditions; others lost jobs, took casual work or returned to their home villages, where relatives supported them. A family network could function like unemployment insurance, without forms, offices or enough money.

passages.title: Work, farms and the Depression
passages.text: Colonial “development” mixed help with extraction. Ethical Policy irrigation could aid rice cultivation, but it also served sugar production; schooling supplied clerks and workers; resettlement policy also aimed to prevent protest. An impressive canal or classroom does not answer the crucial question: who chose it and who benefited?

passages.title: Meals, clothes, homes and a little fun
passages.text: A Java stereograph dated broadly 1900 to 1935 shows a warung with food displayed on a table. That is evidence of a small prepared-food business, not a menu: the catalogue cannot tell us whether the day’s star dish was rice, noodles, vegetables, sweets or something else. History sometimes leaves us hungry for labels.

passages.title: Meals, clothes, homes and a little fun
passages.text: Different islands, communities, religions and household budgets did not produce one colonial menu. The catalogue does not identify even the foods on this table, and the photograph belongs to inland Java. It cannot responsibly stand in for the entire archipelago, or even every Javanese dinner.

passages.title: Meals, clothes, homes and a little fun
passages.text: A cotton shoulder cloth from central Java shows indigo-and-white geometric batik. Historically, some patterns signaled rank, and court “forbidden patterns” were once restricted to nobility, though rules loosened. Clothes could keep sun off your shoulders and quietly announce where you stood in society, multitasking fabric!

passages.title: Meals, clothes, homes and a little fun
passages.text: The neat Tjimahi dining room and the Minangkabau rumah gadang are both real homes, yet they differ in community, household form, status and purpose. Placing them side by side shows why neither can serve as an all-purpose “Indies house.” Materials and floor plans followed local needs and resources.

passages.title: Meals, clothes, homes and a little fun
passages.text: Photographs were usually taken by people who could afford cameras, and catalogues often preserve the collector better than the cook, vendor, carpenter or child in view. Whenever a picture looks effortlessly “typical,” ask who pointed the lens, who supplied the caption and who never got named.

passages.title: Medicine, mosquitoes and unequal care
passages.text: People sought help from family knowledge, midwives, herbal specialists, religious healers, Indigenous physicians, pharmacies, clinics and hospitals. These systems overlapped. Colonial medical-school records illuminate trained doctors especially well, so silence about another healer must never be mistaken for proof that the healer did not exist.

passages.title: Medicine, mosquitoes and unequal care
passages.text: STOVIA in Batavia and NIAS in Surabaya trained Indies physicians. The civil service became the Public Health Service in 1925, and a university-equivalent Batavia Medical School opened in 1927 beside a hospital and laboratory. These were major institutions, but they produced only a small number of highly qualified doctors.

passages.title: Medicine, mosquitoes and unequal care
passages.text: Some students received bursaries for books, food and other expenses, then owed ten years of relatively low-paid colonial medical service. Indonesian physicians treated patients and built careers while facing lower status and discrimination from European colleagues. A white coat did not erase the colony’s color line.

passages.title: Medicine, mosquitoes and unequal care
passages.text: In the 1920s, malaria teams developed “species sanitation”: identify the breeding habitat of the local Anopheles mosquito species, then change that habitat. It was clever ecology, not one magic swamp-draining recipe. A historical review says it worked only in a few local situations with the right technical and social conditions.

passages.title: Medicine, mosquitoes and unequal care
passages.text: Mosquito control, clinics and medical schools were achievements; access remained uneven by race, class, employer and location. A plantation laboratory or Batavia teaching hospital could not make a doctor appear on a distant island. “The colony had modern medicine” and “this child could reach it” are different claims.

passages.title: Water, washing and the all-important toilet question
passages.text: Batavia’s water network was spectacularly unequal. In 1929, 6,926 kampong households received a combined 24 litres per second while 10,392 European households received 84. The chapter calculates that Europeans were about 7 percent of residents yet consumed 78 percent of residential piped water.

passages.title: Water, washing and the all-important toilet question
passages.text: Many kampong residents collected water from public hydrants or vendors rather than a tap at home. Free network water was curtailed by a 1926 paid-delivery rule, and demand dropped sharply. Pipes existed, but price and connection rules determined whether clean water actually reached a cooking pot.

passages.title: Water, washing and the all-important toilet question
passages.text: Colonial reformers often described kampongs as lacking pipes, drains, washing places and water closets. Their reports reveal real infrastructure gaps and also their prejudice: some writers blamed residents and used contemptuous language while protecting an unequal city. The source must be read for plumbing and power at the same time.

passages.title: Water, washing and the all-important toilet question
passages.text: Toilets were not one archipelago-wide technology. The urban chapter records planners complaining about missing water closets and sanitation, but it cannot tell us what share of families used a private, shared or non-piped facility. Evidence is strongest for city projects, weakest for a trustworthy “typical toilet.” No honest historian can flush that uncertainty away.

passages.title: Water, washing and the all-important toilet question
passages.text: Water history includes household use and the work of collecting it, not just pipes. Official plans count infrastructure more easily than the time and sore arms needed to bring vendor or hydrant water home. A network map therefore captures only part of daily labor.

passages.title: Science, preservation, music and written voices
passages.text: Bosscha Observatory was inaugurated in 1923 after an astronomy society formed in Bandung and donors funded instruments. It became a lasting research and teaching institution and passed to the Indonesian government in 1951. The telescope outlived the colonial state, and kept looking much farther than any empire ever reached.

passages.title: Science, preservation, music and written voices
passages.text: The colonial Archaeological Service began full restoration at Candi Panataran in 1918. Director Bosch brought Javanese dignitaries onto an advisory committee and shared results with students and teachers; the Depression then stopped most reconstruction. Calling this “discovery” would erase the communities who already knew the monuments.

passages.title: Science, preservation, music and written voices
passages.text: At Ngandong in the early 1930s, Geological Survey work uncovered ancient human braincases in a Solo River bone bed. A 1932 report used the name Homo soloensis; later researchers classify the finds as Homo erectus and have revised their age. Discovery is a process: the fossils stayed still while scientific labels moved around them.

passages.title: Science, preservation, music and written voices
passages.text: Authentic 1928 writing sample: “KAMI POETRA DAN POETRI INDONESIA” means “WE, THE SONS AND DAUGHTERS OF INDONESIA.” It uses period Malay/Indonesian spelling in Latin letters. It is one line from a political resolution, not a sample of Javanese, Balinese or the archipelago’s many other written languages.

passages.title: Science, preservation, music and written voices
passages.text: The same decision pledged one homeland, one nation and a unifying language, Bahasa Indonesia. That was a political choice made by youth organizations amid enormous linguistic diversity. A shared public language could connect islands without making home languages disappear.

passages.title: Science, preservation, music and written voices
passages.text: At the Second Youth Congress, journalist-musician W. R. Soepratman played Indonesia Raya without lyrics to reduce the danger of colonial repression. Imagine a room hearing a future national anthem while authorities still ruled the country it imagined. Sometimes a violin can make a very political noise.

The exact map id stops in 1938 because its unchanged geometry is reassigned, not because the Dutch East Indies ended. Japanese forces conquered the colony in 1942. Sukarno and Hatta proclaimed Indonesian independence on 17 August 1945; the Netherlands refused and fought to restore control before transferring sovereignty on 27 December 1949. Western New Guinea initially remained under Dutch administration and disputed. Dutch colonial government ended through conquest, revolution, war and negotiation; peoples, families, languages and local histories continued.

sectionTitles: Discoveries: a cookhouse and its contents
Food tools with stories to tell
Homes, clothes and travelling by river

passages.text: Suriname’s history includes Indigenous and Maroon communities, colonial settlements and migration across oceans. Cooking tools, carved gifts, writing and family records offer different views of everyday knowledge. The examples identify particular places and communities.

passages.title: Discoveries: a cookhouse and its contents
passages.text: At Jodensavanne, excavations of House de Meza in 2020 to 2022 recovered pottery identified as Indigenous and Maroon alongside colonial objects. Work at a nearby cookhouse in 2023 and 2024 found Indigenous pottery in the same layer as colonial artifacts, plus a stone mortar. These finds support research into shared materials and cooking practices. They do not identify the maker or user of every pot, or prove equal relationships in a society shaped by slavery.

passages.title: Discoveries: a cookhouse and its contents
passages.text: The Jodensavanne Foundation’s 2023 cookhouse record includes a nearly complete porcelain plate, part of a stoneware jug and an incomplete iron cauldron undergoing conservation. Different materials brought different qualities to serving, storing and cooking. Even fragments help reconstruct a working household. A recovered jug does not, by itself, reveal what someone drank from it on a particular day.

passages.title: Food tools with stories to tell
passages.text: A basket sifter from Pikin Saron, a Kalina village, has a square wooden frame and loosely woven palm fibres. The Lam Museum’s 2022 account explains how such sifters remove lumps from cassava flour and make its texture more even. Weaving knowledge becomes useful kitchen equipment. Lumpy flour has met its match, without a plug or a battery in sight.

passages.title: Food tools with stories to tell
passages.text: In 2018, visiting Matawai community members explained a decorated calabash spoon in the Smithsonian’s collection. They described this small spoon as a personal utensil for eating rice, with larger examples used for soup. Its bowl was cut from a hard-shelled gourd and decorated with incised designs. Community knowledge helps a museum understand how an object fits into meals and daily life.

passages.title: Food tools with stories to tell
passages.text: A Ndyuka wooden food stirrer in Milwaukee’s collection carries carved personal messages. The museum describes carved utensils given as expressions of affection, with some stirrers used for cooking and more delicate examples kept for their beauty. A practical object can also hold a relationship’s meaning. The caption does not translate this particular message, so its exact words remain unstated here.

passages.title: Homes, clothes and travelling by river
passages.text: The Surinaams Museum preserves a mahogany four-poster bed made in 1829 by the furniture maker Podekowitz on Paramaribo’s Wagenwegstraat. It belongs to a collection rich in furniture associated with the colonial elite. This was substantial, carefully made furniture, rather than a picture of how everyone slept. A single grand bed cannot represent all the country’s bedrooms.

passages.title: Homes, clothes and travelling by river
passages.text: Needlework samplers in the same museum record how young European women practised embroidery and mending in the late nineteenth century. Surviving stitches make learning visible: someone had to repeat a movement, control the thread and improve. The collection also preserves early-twentieth-century baby clothes. These are particular surviving objects, rather than evidence that every family dressed or taught its children alike.

passages.title: Homes, clothes and travelling by river
passages.text: Gerrit Schouten’s 1817 miniature scene shows a riverboat with six enslaved rowers, a steersman and a covered passenger compartment. The shelter has windows with shutters propped open by sticks. The model records both ingenuity and inequality: passengers could travel out of the sun and rain while others did the rowing. It is an artist’s carefully constructed view, not a photograph of a named journey.

passages.title: Writing, families and learning together
passages.text: In the early twentieth century, Afáka Atumisi developed a writing system for Ndyuka. Its signs represent syllables. A 2012 study explains that the sign for tu, meaning two, uses two strokes, while fo, meaning four, uses four. A little counting can help a reading lesson. The system is a distinctive achievement in making spoken language visible, though some signs can represent more than one sound.

passages.title: Writing, families and learning together
passages.text: Immigration registers for indentured workers arriving from British India between 1873 and 1916 can record parents, siblings and other relatives. Officials later added marriages, children and sometimes grandchildren born in Suriname. These documents help descendants reconnect family stories across oceans. Some registers were lost or badly damaged, and spelling varies, so an unsuccessful name search does not show that a person never existed.

passages.title: Writing, families and learning together
passages.text: In September 2024, nineteen volunteers aged 12 to 70 joined a supervised archaeology project at Jodensavanne. Four young participants came from neighbouring Redi Doti, an Indigenous village. The work included excavation, maintenance and conservation; a caption records young volunteers sifting earth for artifacts. Learning about the past can involve patient observation and teamwork as well as books.

passages.title: Writing, families and learning together
passages.text: Jodensavanne’s heritage is cared for through cooperation with Redi Doti. UNESCO describes the Indigenous village and the Jodensavanne Foundation sharing responsibility for preservation and agreeing together on changes to the management plan. This recognises living communities as participants in caring for history. A historic site is also part of someone’s present-day neighbourhood.

Suriname gained internal autonomy in 1954 and became an independent republic in 1975. These changes ended colonial government, not the histories of its communities. Crafts, languages and family knowledge continue through living people, with traditions changing as they are shared.

sectionTitles: An unusual republic with a wide reach

passages.text: The Dutch Republic was a seven-province confederation formed in 1588 during revolt against Spain. Provinces kept substantial independence while the States General handled war, diplomacy and shared costs. Seventeenth-century shipping, art and print helped some households prosper, but the VOC and WIC also used violence, conquest and slavery overseas. A look inside homes finds working women, schoolchildren, board games, laundry, potty chairs and tiny surprises in archaeological cesspits. Spain recognized the republic in 1648; French troops and Dutch Patriots ended its old political order in 1795. The imported map’s 1600 to 1783 dates are only snapshots.

passages.title: An unusual republic with a wide reach
passages.text: After renouncing Philip II in 1581, the northern provinces eventually chose to govern without a new monarch. From 1588 seven provinces formed a confederation; the States General handled shared defense and diplomacy, but local provinces kept much authority.

passages.title: An unusual republic with a wide reach
passages.text: The States General founded the VOC in 1602 and let it make treaties, build forts, hire soldiers and wage war in Asian waters. Calling it only a spice shop hides the company’s armed and political power.

passages.title: An unusual republic with a wide reach
passages.text: The WIC carried enslaved Africans to the Americas and fought for colonial footholds. The VOC used violence and slave labor around the Indian Ocean too. Dutch prosperity was connected to harms borne by people far beyond the republic’s European outline.

passages.title: An unusual republic with a wide reach
passages.text: Spain recognized the republic as independent in the 1648 Peace of Münster. The treaty also addressed overseas possessions and religious practice, reminding us that freedom for a state did not mean equal freedom for everyone under its influence.

passages.title: An unusual republic with a wide reach
passages.text: French troops and Dutch Patriots ended the old republic in January 1795 and proclaimed a Batavian Republic. Dutch families, towns and languages continued even though the seven-province political system changed.

passages.title: Pictures, lessons and written words
passages.text: Rembrandt, Vermeer, Frans Hals and Jan Steen made work during a remarkable Dutch painting market. Their art is a major achievement, but a painted rich interior is not a census of every kitchen.

passages.title: Pictures, lessons and written words
passages.text: A Rijksmuseum schoolroom painting shows a master, girl and boy pupils, writing papers and an hourglass on the desk. It is a glimpse of teaching tools, not proof that all children could attend school for the same length of time.

passages.title: Pictures, lessons and written words
passages.text: Printed maps and newspapers let readers follow battles such as the 1629 siege of Den Bosch. Families who could access news had a way to talk about distant war over a table at home.

passages.title: Pictures, lessons and written words
passages.text: An engraved glass dated 1600 bears “Concordia res parvae crescunt,” Latin for “Through unity small things grow.” That short written motto spoke to the provinces’ union; Latin appeared on an object used in Dutch life, alongside Dutch as the common language.

passages.title: Laundry, children and the loo
passages.text: Rijksmuseum objects suggest many seventeenth-century homes had open doors, with children or neighbors dropping in. Privacy worked differently, and household life depended heavily on women’s organization and labor.

passages.title: Laundry, children and the loo
passages.text: Many women earned money as well as running kitchens and caring for children. Remember that when a painting seems to show a woman merely standing inside: a household was also a workplace.

passages.title: Laundry, children and the loo
passages.text: A “kakstoel” was a small child’s chair with a hole and a pot underneath: a potty with furniture ambitions. A physician warned against leaving children on it too long. This is a museum object, not evidence that every child used one.

passages.title: Laundry, children and the loo
passages.text: Petronella Oortman’s splendid dolls’ house had two kitchens, a laundry room and even running water in the miniature show kitchen. It displayed adult wealth, not a typical home or a children’s toy.

passages.title: Laundry, children and the loo
passages.text: The contents of two Jordaan cesspits reveal everyday cooking and drinking vessels in modest Amsterdam households, with an occasional piece of Chinese porcelain. Archaeology can tell us about dinner and waste when written diaries cannot.

passages.title: Laundry, children and the loo
passages.text: People did not always wash their bodies often with water; clean linen could signal cleanliness instead. Pregnant women faced real danger in childbirth, and friends visited mothers in lying-in rooms afterward. These customs varied by class and household.

passages.title: Laundry, children and the loo
passages.text: Board games like Goose Game could involve money rather than being only children’s play. The same household might hear neighborhood chatter, handle laundry and discuss war news while children learned their letters.

The old Dutch Republic ended in 1795 when a French-backed revolution created the Batavian Republic. Dutch people, communities and language continued. The imported 1783 endpoint is a map-data limit, not the republic’s historical end.
