sectionTitles: First decode the atlas, and notice the misplaced polygon
From a protection treaty to a caliphal frontier government
Rebellion, fire, rebuilding and the clues stamped on silver
Neighbors squeeze the emirate, then citizens take the wheel
A river crossroads of markets, mints and workshops
Mosques, churches and communities sharing one city
Households, ranks, women and children behind the official record
Learning networks, and Arabic written right on a Tbilisi coin
Pine houses, bright bowls, food, clothing and uncertain play
Medicine, hot baths, water, waste, and the honest toilet gap

passages.text: Imagine a river city of pine houses, stone walls, hot sulfur baths and silver coins, where church bells and the call to prayer crossed the Mtkvari air. Arab armies first secured Tbilisi by treaty in the seventh century; from the 730s, caliphs governed eastern Georgia through an emir there. Local emirs later rebelled, survived the terrible burning of 853, made their office hereditary and stamped their own names beside the caliph's. Georgian kings steadily closed in. By the 1080s the emir dynasty was gone and wealthy city elders governed; David IV captured Tbilisi in 1122 and made it the Georgian capital. Markets, crafts, Muslim worship and learning continued under new rule. The atlas is doubly tricky: it shows the id only from 1100 to 1200, and its lone polygon does not even contain modern Tbilisi. Read that shape as a flawed locator, while coins, chronicles, archaeology and careful source limits tell the city's richer story.

passages.title: First decode the atlas, and notice the misplaced polygon
passages.text: The exact indexed id is emirate-of-tiflis, labeled “Emirate of Tiflis” and marked circa 1100 to 1200. Coverage records one border file and no card or completed review. Its imported summary itself says emirs ruled effectively only to about 1080 and the city fell in 1122, so the database dates are map coverage, not a dynasty's lifetime.

passages.title: First decode the atlas, and notice the misplaced polygon
passages.text: At the 1000 snapshot the target id is absent, even though Jaffarid emirs historically still ruled in Tbilisi. The broad imported `georgia` polygon owns every audited eastern Georgian city point. This predecessor seam proves that absence from one atlas layer cannot be read as proof that a polity did not exist.

passages.title: First decode the atlas, and notice the misplaced polygon
passages.text: At 1100 the target appears once as an unlabeled Polygon: one part, one ring and only seven positions. Its bounds are 44.8906° to 45.8339° east and 41.0977° to 41.7087° north; its coordinate-array SHA-256 is `0b1e8ea8b03040ea69734d51090a11e799fe1fc89177811132b93263f53c24b1`. Those are exact digital facts, not reconstructed medieval frontiers.

passages.title: First decode the atlas, and notice the misplaced polygon
passages.text: The strangest result is geographic: the exact modern Tbilisi coordinate lies outside the emirate polygon and inside the separate Georgia polygon. Every named audit point misses the target. Raw topology shows shared boundary arcs only with `georgia` and `kakheti-hereti`. The tiny shape sits southeast of its supposed capital, so it should be treated as displaced imported geometry.

passages.title: First decode the atlas, and notice the misplaced polygon
passages.text: At 1200 the emirate id vanishes and Georgia owns Tbilisi, Mtskheta, Rustavi, Gori, Dmanisi, Telavi and Kutaisi; it remains absent at 1279. Historically, city elders had replaced the emirs by the 1080s and David IV captured city and citadel in 1122. The atlas therefore starts late and ends seventy-eight years after conquest.

passages.title: From a protection treaty to a caliphal frontier government
passages.text: Arab forces first secured Tbilisi by a peace-and-security agreement around 654 to 655. The transmitted terms protected lives and worship while demanding payment by household. Modern scholarship warns that early treaty texts passed through later writers, so the agreement is evidence for submission and taxation, not a perfectly preserved form signed at a medieval desk before us.

passages.title: From a protection treaty to a caliphal frontier government
passages.text: The emirate took shape after the great Arab campaigns of the 730s. Its emir was originally a caliph-appointed official subordinate to a provincial governor, not automatically an independent king. From Tbilisi, early administrators claimed wide authority in eastern Georgia, while local nobles, churches and mountain communities continued to exercise power of their own.

passages.title: From a protection treaty to a caliphal frontier government
passages.text: A Kufic Arabic inscription from Tiflis dated Sha'ban AH 147, or 764 to 765 CE, and early mint evidence show Arabic as an official written language in the city. That does not mean everyone spoke Arabic at home: inscriptions reveal the language chosen by administrators and moneyers much more clearly than the speech of every Georgian, Armenian or other resident.

passages.title: From a protection treaty to a caliphal frontier government
passages.text: Abo's near-contemporary story gives a human-scale window into the eighth-century city. He was a young Arab skilled at mixing myrrh preparations who traveled with the Georgian ruler Nerse, learned among Christians and eventually died for refusing to abandon Christianity. Because the text is a martyr tale, its theology is central and its scenes are not neutral census notes.

passages.title: From a protection treaty to a caliphal frontier government
passages.text: Tbilisi sat in a steep Mtkvari valley with a fortress commanding crossings and routes. Government depended on more than a city wall: tribute collectors, soldiers, messengers and negotiations linked the capital to subordinate towns and countryside. Claims of control shrank over time, reminding us that an emir's title and his day-to-day reach were not always identical.

passages.title: Rebellion, fire, rebuilding and the clues stamped on silver
passages.text: By the early ninth century the Shuabid emirs were turning an appointment into local family power. Ishaq ibn Ismail became strong enough to challenge Baghdad. Caliph al-Mutawakkil responded with Bugha al-Kabir's 853 expedition, showing the emirate's central puzzle: it belonged to the Abbasid political world yet repeatedly tried to act on its own.

passages.title: Rebellion, fire, rebuilding and the clues stamped on silver
passages.text: Bugha's forces crossed the Mtkvari, took Tbilisi, burned the city and executed Ishaq. Medieval writers give enormous army and death totals; these are reported figures, not modern demographic measurements. The safest conclusion is still grim: the assault was catastrophic, involved regional allies on both sides and failed to create lasting, tight caliphal control.

passages.title: Rebellion, fire, rebuilding and the clues stamped on silver
passages.text: Nine or ten years after the burning, Tbilisi was striking Abbasid silver again. Six known dirhams dated AH 248, or 862 to 63, name the mint and caliph al-Musta'in. A coin cannot tell us how every street recovered, but minting requires skilled dies, metal, standards and officials. That is small, round evidence that urban institutions had resumed.

passages.title: Rebellion, fire, rebuilding and the clues stamped on silver
passages.text: From about the 880s the Jaffarids made emir rule hereditary for roughly two centuries. Coin sequences identify Mansur ibn Ja'far, Ja'far ibn Mansur and Ali ibn Ja'far, some barely visible in narrative sources. Numismatics supplies names and dates, while gaps and disputed readings warn against pretending we own a complete ruler-by-ruler diary.

passages.title: Rebellion, fire, rebuilding and the clues stamped on silver
passages.text: A dirham of Ja'far ibn Mansur dated AH 374, or 984 to 85, adds one exact point to the dynasty's story. Later issues carried a local emir's name beside the caliph's, expressing political independence without discarding the caliph's religious prestige. Medieval money was payment, official announcement and pocket-sized family tree all at once.

passages.title: Neighbors squeeze the emirate, then citizens take the wheel
passages.text: The emirate never lived alone inside a neat border. Around 900, Muhammad ibn Abi'l-Saj campaigned across Armenia and Caucasian Albania and occupied Tiflis after fighting King Smbat. His intervention connects the city to caliphal appointments, Azerbaijan and Armenian politics; it did not erase the longer Jaffarid line that resumed local rule.

passages.title: Neighbors squeeze the emirate, then citizens take the wheel
passages.text: By the eleventh century the united Georgian monarchy pressed hard around Tbilisi. Bagrat IV entered its citadel in 1045 after city elders invited him, yet shifting factions and negotiations prevented a simple permanent takeover. Medieval allegiance could change through invitation, hostage-taking, siege, tribute or bargain, not only through one decisive flag-raising moment.

passages.title: Neighbors squeeze the emirate, then citizens take the wheel
passages.text: Seljuk expansion changed the balance again. Alp Arslan and allies devastated Tbilisi and Kartli in 1068 and assigned Tbilisi and Rustavi to the ruler of Ganja; Bagrat then fought and arranged tribute with local heirs. These rapid switches explain why one colored polygon cannot capture overlordship, city government and military occupation simultaneously.

passages.title: Neighbors squeeze the emirate, then citizens take the wheel
passages.text: After the Jaffarid line ended in the 1080s, Tbilisi's ‘elders’ became full rulers. The Academy entry describes them as representatives chosen from wealthy citizens; al-Fariqi says leading people rotated authority month by month. That sounds almost like a city council, but it represented an upper urban group rather than every craft worker, widow or child.

passages.title: Neighbors squeeze the emirate, then citizens take the wheel
passages.text: Tbilisi, Dmanisi and Ganja appealed for outside help as David IV's campaigns tightened around them. A Muslim coalition met his army at Didgori in 1121 and lost; the following year David secured Tbilisi. The Academy source is clear about the strategic sequence, while spectacular medieval army totals remain too disputed for this children's card.

passages.title: A river crossroads of markets, mints and workshops
passages.text: Arabic geographers describe Tbilisi on both banks of the Mtkvari, defended by walls and gates and connected across the river. Roads led toward Armenia, Iran, the Caspian and mountain passes. A merchant's day depended on bridges, pack animals, interpreters, tolls and safety; ‘crossroads’ meant hard logistical work, not goods magically sliding along a map line.

passages.title: A river crossroads of markets, mints and workshops
passages.text: Geographers praise fertile surroundings, fruit and crops and list honey, wool, felt and silk textiles among products or traded goods. Such lists show availability and commercial reputation, not what every poor household owned. Silk could be an expensive bolt in a merchant's store while a felt item or wool cloth served a very different budget.

passages.title: A river crossroads of markets, mints and workshops
passages.text: The mint linked politics to market life. The AH 248 dirham was silver, roughly 26 millimetres across in listed specimens, and carried long formulas around a tiny field. Moneyers had to fit legible script onto metal smaller than many cookies, an accurate bit of medieval design pressure, with no need to imagine coins as modern pocket change.

passages.title: A river crossroads of markets, mints and workshops
passages.text: Ninth- through thirteenth-century eastern Georgian workshops made red- and light-clay bowls and dishes with slips, colored glazes and plant, animal or human motifs. Finds include a medieval Tbilisi pottery workshop. The date range crosses 1122, so these objects document urban craft continuity, not a perfectly labeled ‘emirate-only’ cupboard.

passages.title: A river crossroads of markets, mints and workshops
passages.text: Dmanisi, once tied to the emirate's wider urban network, preserves houses, storerooms, workshops, glass and pottery production, walls, a bath and a long water-access tunnel. It helps show what a regional city could require, but it lies about eighty kilometres away and many remains are later; it cannot become a substitute floor plan for Tbilisi.

passages.title: Mosques, churches and communities sharing one city
passages.text: Muslims governed the city, but Christians remained visible. Written sources imagine a soundscape where Islamic prayer and Christian worship occupied the same city. Coexistence did not mean modern equality or never fighting; Abo's execution and the earlier protection agreement show both pressure and negotiated space.

passages.title: Mosques, churches and communities sharing one city
passages.text: A congregational mosque, its preacher or khatib, and a qadi who judged Muslim cases were key institutions. In 1122 a khatib and qadi reportedly negotiated for the city. Later rebuilding makes the exact emirate-era mosque difficult to identify archaeologically, so the card names documented offices without drawing an invented perfect building.

passages.title: Mosques, churches and communities sharing one city
passages.text: Christian writing did not vanish under Muslim rulers. Ioane Sabanisdze composed Abo's martyrdom in Georgian near the event, framing the city through scripture and resistance. It proves skilled Georgian literary production and a Christian audience; because hagiography aims to inspire belief, its speeches and wonders demand a different reading from a tax record or coin.

passages.title: Mosques, churches and communities sharing one city
passages.text: Dmanisi's medieval cemetery contains Georgian, Armenian and Arabic inscriptions and Muslim and Christian sectors. That multi-confessional record belongs to another emirate-linked city and extends beyond 1122, yet it provides material evidence that people of several languages and religions lived, died and remembered relatives in the same regional urban world.

passages.title: Mosques, churches and communities sharing one city
passages.text: Biographical sources connect Tbilisi with Sunni, Shi'i and later Sufi scholars, but Djaparidze stresses how scant the evidence is: no local Muslim city chronicle survived, and distant biographers favored people who became famous elsewhere. Religious variety is supported; precise percentages, neighborhood maps and a year-by-year conversion graph are not.

passages.title: Households, ranks, women and children behind the official record
passages.text: The seventh-century agreement assessed a levy per household, so families were units through which government counted responsibility. It never supplies a standard household size or says every home contained the same relatives. A ‘family’ might include several generations, dependents or workers, but those possibilities must remain questions rather than manufactured statistics.

passages.title: Households, ranks, women and children behind the official record
passages.text: At the social top stood emirs, military commanders, landholding nobles and wealthy citizens; after the 1080s the elders represented the upper urban layer. Below that record-rich ceiling were merchants, craftspeople, servants, carriers and agricultural workers. Surviving texts name officeholders far more readily than the people hauling water, sweeping shops or tending ovens.

passages.title: Households, ranks, women and children behind the official record
passages.text: The al-Tiflisi biographies include jurists, poets, physicians, merchants, craftspeople and statesmen. A name ending in al-Tiflisi signals association with Tbilisi, not automatically ethnicity, birthplace or lifelong residence. This caution matters in a mixed city: scholars cannot turn every bearer into an Arab settler, converted Georgian or permanent resident without more evidence.

passages.title: Households, ranks, women and children behind the official record
passages.text: Broader Georgian legal evidence places dowry and some women's property interests as early as the ninth century, but emirate-specific documents rarely name ordinary women. That regional evidence suggests women participated in household property; it cannot establish equal inheritance, a typical dowry or the daily authority of a Tbilisi mother, widow or craftswoman.

passages.title: Households, ranks, women and children behind the official record
passages.text: Abo was about seventeen or eighteen when he reached this world and was already skilled at mixing fragrant or medicinal substances. His case shows a young person could learn a specialized craft and languages, but it is one exceptional hagiographic life. It does not give a normal school age, apprenticeship contract or chores chart for Tbilisi children.

passages.title: Learning networks, and Arabic written right on a Tbilisi coin
passages.text: Djaparidze found fifty-two people bearing the al-Tiflisi nisba in eighth- through fourteenth-century Arabic and Persian sources. Some traveled to Baghdad, Damascus and other study centers; several stayed abroad. This reveals a far-reaching learning network while also showing why fame overseas can distort our view of who taught children inside Tbilisi itself.

passages.title: Learning networks, and Arabic written right on a Tbilisi coin
passages.text: Al-Hasan ibn Bundar al-Tiflisi studied Arabic poetry and grammar around the tenth and early eleventh centuries and dedicated a work to Emir Ali ibn Ja'far. His lost books show a learned circle connected to the court. Loss matters: a title and later biography cannot reconstruct a classroom, library shelves or what his pupils, if any, actually read.

passages.title: Learning networks, and Arabic written right on a Tbilisi coin
passages.text: The physician and Syriac-to-Arabic translator Isa al-Raqqi al-Tiflisi served Sayf al-Dawla's court in Aleppo. A later Tiflis-born scholar, Hubaysh, wrote on medicine and astronomy after migrating west. Both lives demonstrate intellectual mobility, not a documented city hospital back home; court biographies reveal fame far better than ordinary healthcare access.

passages.title: Learning networks, and Arabic written right on a Tbilisi coin
passages.text: Christian learning in eleventh- and twelfth-century Georgia centered strongly on churches and monasteries, while advanced students sometimes traveled abroad and new academies emerged around David IV's age. This is regional context, not evidence that every Tbilisi child attended class. Most practical learning likely happened through households and work, though attendance figures do not survive.

passages.title: Learning networks, and Arabic written right on a Tbilisi coin
passages.text: Written-language sample, official Arabic mint legend, Tbilisi, AH 248 / 862 to 63: `بسم الله ضرب هذا الدرهم بتفليس سنة ثمان و اربعين و مائتين`. Transliteration: `bismi llāh ḍuriba hādhā al-dirham bi-Tiflīs sanat thamān wa-arbaʿīn wa-miʾatayn`. Translation: “In the name of God, this dirham was struck at Tbilisi in the year 248.” This is formal coin Arabic, not everyday conversation.

passages.title: Pine houses, bright bowls, food, clothing and uncertain play
passages.text: An Arabic source remarked that Tbilisi houses were built largely of pine, while walls and fortress works used more durable materials. Timber burns and rots, so surviving stone exaggerates elite and defensive architecture. We can picture a wooden city around its citadel, but no checked source supplies a universal room count, roof plan or furniture set.

passages.title: Pine houses, bright bowls, food, clothing and uncertain play
passages.text: Wool, felt and silk textiles appear in geographic descriptions of Tbilisi's products and trade. They prove textile work and exchange, not one citywide costume. Wealth, occupation, faith, season and origin all affected dress; the responsible card cannot put every child into a silk robe simply because silk passed through the market.

passages.title: Pine houses, bright bowls, food, clothing and uncertain play
passages.text: The city's fertile surroundings supplied crops and fruit, and geographers mention honey and watermills. Those clues support bread or grain foods, fruit and sweetening within the food system, but they do not preserve a weekly menu or portion sizes. Modern dishes are not pushed backward nine centuries merely because they taste wonderfully Georgian today.

passages.title: Pine houses, bright bowls, food, clothing and uncertain play
passages.text: Excavations in medieval Tbilisi found kilns and many vessel forms, including bowls, jugs, pots, oil lamps, salt holders, inkpots and lids, along with defective workshop pieces. Some layers are twelfth to thirteenth century or later, so they illuminate continuity across conquest. A cracked bowl in a waste pit is still evidence of making, using and discarding things.

passages.title: Pine houses, bright bowls, food, clothing and uncertain play
passages.text: No checked emirate-specific source preserves children's game rules, toys securely dated to this polity or a street-song melody. Bells, calls to prayer and recited sacred texts certainly made sound, and decorated bowls could delight the eye. Yet a coin can reveal an emir's name much more readily than whether children played tag after chores.

passages.title: Medicine, hot baths, water, waste, and the honest toilet gap
passages.text: Abo's skill mixing myrrh preparations and Isa al-Tiflisi's later fame as physician and translator show specialized knowledge of substances and healing. Neither source describes a public Tbilisi clinic, childbirth routine or care available to poor families. One craft-trained youth plus one migrant court doctor cannot become a complete healthcare system by wishful arithmetic.

passages.title: Medicine, hot baths, water, waste, and the honest toilet gap
passages.text: The eleventh-century Georgian Ustsoro Karabadini is a medical handbook drawing on regional and classical traditions and discussing remedies, including medicinal uses of wine. It proves written medicine in the broader Georgian world during the emirate's later centuries. It does not prove that a Tbilisi practitioner owned this exact book or followed every recipe.

passages.title: Medicine, hot baths, water, waste, and the honest toilet gap
passages.text: Tbilisi's naturally hot sulfur water made baths famous to medieval geographers; hot water did not need a wood fire before entering the bathing system. Baths offered washing and social space, but the checked sources do not give an emirate-era timetable, price list, gender schedule or exact number. Even naturally hot plumbing leaves cold historical questions.

passages.title: Medicine, hot baths, water, waste, and the honest toilet gap
passages.text: Water could come from the Mtkvari, wells and ceramic pipes from nearby ravines. A modern study traces that long tradition but explicitly says exposed pipe lines cannot be securely dated without more archaeology. Fetching and carrying water therefore remained crucial work; which house had direct supply in 900 is not something the evidence settles.

passages.title: Medicine, hot baths, water, waste, and the honest toilet gap
passages.text: The archaeological report identifies reservoirs and clay tubes and says broken pottery was sometimes buried or thrown into the Mtkvari. It does not securely identify an emirate-period household toilet, latrine network, sewer or wiping material. We know where some smashed pots went; the hoped-for medieval bathroom tour remains stubbornly unavailable.

David IV captured Tbilisi and its citadel in 1122, ending the post-Jaffarid elders' sovereignty and absorbing the city into the Kingdom of Georgia. Tbilisi became the Georgian capital, while Muslim residents retained worship, legal and scholarly institutions under negotiated privileges. The atlas endpoint of 1200 is a delayed geometry handoff, seventy-eight years after conquest.

passages.text: Alexander ruled Macedonia from 336 to 323 BCE and conquered an empire reaching from the eastern Mediterranean through Egypt and Iran to the Indus region. The imported map’s single outline runs from 323 to 300 BCE, beginning in Alexander’s death year. It sketches the conquests, not a united empire he continued to rule.

passages.title: Conquest and government
passages.text: Alexander crossed into Asia in 334 BCE. Victories over Darius III at Issus and Gaugamela opened the way to Babylon, Susa and the Persian royal heartland. Existing provincial structures often remained useful to the new ruler. Even so, a conquered region’s colour on a map can conceal places where resistance continued or effective royal control was limited.

passages.title: Conquest and government
passages.text: Conquest also destroyed lives and places. Tyre resisted a prolonged siege and was devastated; Alexander’s forces later reached Persepolis, where the royal buildings burned in 330 BCE. These losses belong beside the stories of victories and cultural exchange. The empire’s growth was not experienced as a triumph by everyone within it.

passages.title: Conquest and government
passages.text: A letter to Chios from 332 BCE ordered the return of exiles and the restoration of democracy. It also required the island to supply twenty warships with crews at its own expense and support a royal garrison until reconciliation. Local self-government therefore came with substantial military obligations and royal supervision.

passages.title: Families, food and practical paperwork
passages.text: At Tegea, regulations connected with Alexander’s recall of exiles in 324 BCE tried to settle a very practical problem: who owned a returning family’s home? The text discusses inherited property, women’s claims and gardens beside houses. It also sets deadlines for lawsuits. Coming home after political exile could mean complicated negotiations with the people already living there.

passages.title: Families, food and practical paperwork
passages.text: A contemporary inscription records Cyrene supplying grain during a shortage in Greece, around 330 to 326 BCE. Recipients included Athens and many other cities, as well as Alexander’s mother Olympias and his sister Cleopatra. This is evidence of food distribution and the royal women’s connections; it does not mean those enormous deliveries were simply their personal dinner supplies.

passages.title: Families, food and practical paperwork
passages.text: A supplies account from Bactria survives on leather nearly half a metre wide. It begins in June 324 BCE and continues for three months, dating its entries by Alexander’s reign while using Aramaic. The lower part is badly damaged, but the object still shows scribes doing the everyday work of recording supplies after conquest changed the name of the ruler.

passages.title: Families, food and practical paperwork
passages.text: At Susa in 324 BCE, Alexander arranged marriages linking Macedonian officers with Iranian noble families. Arrian describes bridegrooms seated for a banquet, brides being brought in, and the king providing dowries. Family relationships were being used to build political alliances. This is a later historian’s account of a royal event, rather than a description of everybody’s wedding.

passages.title: Families, food and practical paperwork
passages.text: Arrian also says Alexander offered to pay his soldiers’ debts. Some men were suspicious: writing down what they owed might reveal that they had overspent their pay. The king then allowed creditors to receive payment without the soldiers having to register their names. Even in a conquering army, money worries could follow people from one camp to the next.

passages.title: Learning, money and surviving words
passages.text: Before he became king, Alexander studied with Aristotle at Mieza alongside other aristocratic youngsters. Archaeologists have uncovered a large gymnasium there with a courtyard, colonnades and rooms interpreted as dining halls. Its identification as the school is a modern scholarly proposal; the nearby caves once widely presented as Aristotle’s classroom are no longer the only candidate.

passages.title: Learning, money and surviving words
passages.text: Plutarch says Alexander loved reading, requested books when they were hard to obtain on campaign, and kept a copy of the Iliad near his pillow. He also credits Alexander with an interest in medicine and advising sick friends about treatment. These are accounts written centuries afterward, useful for understanding his remembered interests without treating every anecdote as a contemporary medical record.

passages.title: Learning, money and surviving words
passages.text: A silver tetradrachm in the British Museum, dated to Alexander’s reign, weighs 17.21 grams. One side shows Herakles; the other has Zeus seated with an eagle and sceptre. These were images of gods and heroes that users could recognize on a small object. The catalogue leaves this particular coin’s mint uncertain, so its precise place of manufacture should remain open.

passages.title: Learning, money and surviving words
passages.text: Babylonian scholars kept watching the sky and recording earthly matters during Alexander’s rule. A diary for his final month includes commodity prices as well as planetary observations; missing pieces interrupt the entries. It puts the king’s death beside the work of measuring, observing and keeping accounts. A surviving related fragment in the British Museum is only six centimetres high.

passages.title: Learning, money and surviving words
passages.text: An inscription from Athena’s temple at Priene reads “ΒΑΣΙΛΕΥΣ ΑΛΕΞΑΝΔΡΟΣ ΑΝΕΘΗΚΕ ΤΟΝ ΝΑΟΝ ΑΘΗΝΑΙΗΙ ΠΟΛΙΑΔΙ”: “King Alexander dedicated the temple to Athena Polias.” The Greek comes from a surviving stone dedication of his reign. Spaces have been added to the capital-letter transcription for reading. The short message connects the king with a city’s goddess without proving that he personally designed or built the whole temple.

Alexander died in Babylon in June 323 BCE. His death began a struggle over the kingship and territories, rather than an orderly handover to three ready-made countries. Over the following decades, successor dynasties established kingdoms including the Ptolemies, Seleucids and Antigonids. Communities, trade and scholarship continued through these political upheavals; the later Hellenistic world grew from both older regional traditions and the connections intensified by conquest.

passages.text: The medieval Soninke empire of Ghana prospered through trans-Saharan exchange. Its power rested on commercial connections and political centers such as Kumbi Saleh, rather than a fixed border enclosing one people.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Gold moved north while salt moved south. Taxing imports and exports helped support imperial rule.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Camel caravans made long desert journeys possible; traders connected different ecological regions rather than transporting goods within a single uniform landscape.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Savanna agriculture and livestock breeding supported the societies through which the trade routes passed.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Al-Bakri described gold-adorned court equipment and clothing. Such written testimony records royal display, not the possessions of every household.

passages.title: Political change
passages.text: By the late twelfth century Ghana had lost its dominant position in the western Sudan gold trade as routes shifted. Its decline was a process, not a securely dated disappearance of Soninke society.

passages.text: England between 1000 and 1200 experienced Danish kingship, the Norman Conquest and the rise of the Angevin rulers. Its story also belongs to farmers, craftspeople, scholars, religious communities and families whose work supported royal power. Domesday Book records land and resources, Oxford reveals expanding teaching, and surviving buildings show impressive construction and water management. A London writer even described people skating on polished animal bones. This card covers the map’s two centuries; neither 1000 nor 1200 marks the birth or disappearance of England.

passages.title: Power, land and achievement
passages.text: Cnut ruled England from 1016 to 1035 and Denmark from 1018. For a time, the North Sea linked territories under the same king. England’s history was already connected to neighbors across the water.

passages.title: Power, land and achievement
passages.text: William of Normandy defeated Harold at Hastings in October 1066. Conquest changed the ruling elite and control of land, with consequences for the people who worked it. A new king’s victory did not mean a new beginning for every village.

passages.title: Power, land and achievement
passages.text: The 1086 Domesday survey asked who held land and what it could produce. Plough teams, mills, fisheries, meadows and woodland mattered to government. It was a remarkable administrative undertaking, but not a census naming every resident.

passages.title: Power, land and achievement
passages.text: At Castle Acre, masons built an elaborate priory church over decades. It was consecrated in 1146-1148, and the west end was finished in the 1160s. The stonework is evidence of skilled labor, planning and patrons able to command substantial resources.

passages.title: Families, work and winter fun
passages.text: A plough team in the Domesday teaching sources consisted of eight oxen. Farming demanded animals, equipment and coordinated labor. Picture steering that team before imagining a medieval farmer working alone with a little garden shovel.

passages.title: Families, work and winter fun
passages.text: Domesday distinguishes freemen, villagers, smallholders and enslaved people. These categories reveal unequal rights and obligations. A landowner’s household and a family bound to agricultural service did not experience the kingdom in the same way.

passages.title: Families, work and winter fun
passages.text: Queen Edith sponsored a book about her husband, Edward the Confessor. Family ties, property and patronage gave some elite women political influence. Queens are much easier to find in written records than most working women, so their lives cannot stand for everyone’s.

passages.title: Families, work and winter fun
passages.text: In 1173 William FitzStephen described Londoners skating on frozen Moorfields marshes. They tied polished animal bones to their feet and pushed with iron-tipped poles. Winter sport, medieval equipment: the wheels were definitely optional.

passages.title: Learning and a little Latin
passages.text: Teaching existed at Oxford by 1096, but the university has no known exact founding date. It grew rapidly after 1167, and by about 1190 a student from Friesland appears in its story. Learning crossed borders as well as generations.

passages.title: Learning and a little Latin
passages.text: The Bayeux embroidery tells the story of the conquest through pictures and Latin captions. One reads “ISTI PORTANT ARMAS AD NAVES”: “These men carry arms to the ships.” The cited catalogue preserves this wording in an 1821 copy of the medieval work. Latin here is a written narrative language, not a claim about what every family spoke at home.

passages.title: Medicine, water and toilets
passages.text: Castle Acre’s monks had an infirmary and used herbs within a medical tradition concerned with balancing bodily humors. The herb garden displayed there today is a reconstruction. Such evidence tells us about monastic care, not equal access to treatment across England.

passages.title: Medicine, water and toilets
passages.text: Castle Acre’s communal latrine was built over a water channel, with an upper level accessible from the dormitory. Its design carried waste away using flowing water. Even a monastery devoted to spiritual life needed to solve the very earthly problem of where the poo went.

England did not fall in 1200. John had become king in 1199, and the kingdom continued through later political and religious changes. The endpoint here belongs to the imported map coverage, while learning, settlement and household life continued beyond it.

sectionTitles: Schools, books and a writing sample

passages.text: This map period shows England under Henry VII and the early reign of Henry VIII, from 1492 to 1530. The Tudor dynasty had begun in 1485 and would last far beyond this interval. Royal marriage and court service shaped power, while farm leases, brewing, printed books and schooling shaped other lives. Bristol voyages reached North America, physicians obtained a charter to regulate their profession, and a printed fishing manual offered practical advice still easy to understand. The religious break with Rome came after this map period, not at England’s supposed disappearance in 1530.

passages.title: A kingdom looking outward
passages.text: Henry VII founded the Tudor dynasty after his victory in 1485; his son Henry VIII succeeded in 1509. The year 1492 is simply where this map record starts. It should not be mistaken for the founding of England or the Tudor family’s arrival.

passages.title: A kingdom looking outward
passages.text: John Cabot sailed from Bristol to North America in the Matthew in 1497. Research has also uncovered Italian financing for his ventures and Henry VII’s royal patent. These were voyages from England with international support; reaching a coast did not establish English rule over it.

passages.title: A kingdom looking outward
passages.text: Katherine of Aragon governed as regent in 1513 while Henry VIII campaigned in France. Her role during the Scottish invasion shows that a queen could exercise direct authority. Royal women’s work was more than producing heirs and appearing in portraits.

passages.title: Homes, families and social life
passages.text: Bayleaf farmhouse in Kent had six rooms around a hall, with part of the building added in the early sixteenth century. Its tenants held a substantial farm on a long lease. This surviving house gives us a specific farming household to investigate, not a model for every rich or poor family.

passages.title: Homes, families and social life
passages.text: Records name successive Bayleaf tenants around 1500-1540, including Thomas Wells, Edward Wells and Richard Scoriar. Their exact family relationships are uncertain. A shared surname is a clue, not permission to invent a family tree.

passages.title: Homes, families and social life
passages.text: Brewing was household work as well as a trade. A museum reconstruction based on sources reaching back to 1502 uses grain, water and hops, which were becoming more popular in England. Heating, stirring and storing a batch took work long before anyone could lift a cup.

passages.title: Homes, families and social life
passages.text: At court, family connections helped people find positions and marriage partners. Women served in the queen’s household, while powerful families sought advantageous alliances. These elite opportunities came with dependence on royal favor; they were not the normal life of a farm family.

passages.title: Homes, families and social life
passages.text: The Eltham Ordinances of 1526 set rules for the royal household. Rank affected food, lodgings and access to the monarch. Court life could be glamorous, but it also came with a rulebook and a lot of people deciding which door you could enter.

passages.title: Schools, books and a writing sample
passages.text: John Colet founded St Paul’s School in 1509 and entrusted its governance to London’s Mercers. Erasmus helped with planning and textbooks, and the statutes provided for 153 scholars. This was one influential school, not a system of schooling for every child.

passages.title: Schools, books and a writing sample
passages.text: Wynkyn de Worde printed a fishing treatise in 1496, part of the second edition of the Book of St Albans. Its traditional attribution to Juliana Berners is uncertain. Practical knowledge about tackle and fishing could circulate in print alongside religious and scholarly books.

passages.title: Schools, books and a writing sample
passages.text: A small sample of its English: “behynde a bushe that the fyshe se you not,” meaning “behind a bush so the fish cannot see you.” The advice is to keep out of sight and avoid casting a shadow over the water. Apparently the fish did not need to meet the angler before dinner.

passages.title: Medicine and the unglamorous palace
passages.text: In 1518 Henry VIII chartered the College of Physicians after an initiative by Thomas Linacre and five colleagues. It could license qualified practitioners and prosecute malpractice. This was a step in professional regulation, not the arrival of modern medicine or universal medical care.

passages.title: Medicine and the unglamorous palace
passages.text: Excavations at Hampton Court revealed toilet turrets from the manor that preceded Wolsey’s palace. Their waste emptied into the moat. One was incorporated into a building of the 1520s. A moat could be impressive scenery and a very poor place to go splashing.

passages.title: Medicine and the unglamorous palace
passages.text: Wolsey bought Hampton Court’s manor in 1514, and Henry VIII took over in 1529. Palace comfort depended on rank: important visitors received fine rooms, while servants found sleeping space around the kitchens. A palace’s luxury rested on other people’s labor.

England continued after the map record ends in 1530. In 1534, Parliament’s Act of Supremacy declared Henry VIII head of the Church of England, breaking ecclesiastical ties with Rome. That later transformation changed religious and political life; it was not the extinction of the kingdom or its communities.

passages.text: This chapter looks at scientific institutions in seventeenth-century England within the map's combined England-and-Ireland record. It also marks the later union of England and Scotland, which did not merge Ireland into Great Britain.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: The Royal Society's first meeting followed Christopher Wren's astronomy lecture in London in 1660. Its members gathered observations, performed experiments and discussed results.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Henry Oldenburg began Philosophical Transactions in 1665. The same year, Robert Hooke published the close observations collected in Micrographia.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The early Royal Society drew members from professional and aristocratic circles and admitted only men. Its meeting rooms represented a restricted part of society.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The English and Scottish Acts of Union created Great Britain on 1 May 1707. The new parliament first met that October.

passages.text: The atlas calls this layer “English territory” from 1279 to 1492. Its polygon combines much of England, sampled Welsh areas, almost all Ireland, and Gascony around Bordeaux and Bayonne. The shape repeats in 1279, 1300, and 1400. It is a modern editorial layer, not a contemporary country name or surveyed border. It excludes Tintagel, Conwy, and Calais while including Dublin, Cork, Bordeaux, and Bayonne. The Irish component especially needs caution: late-medieval English authority was concentrated in particular lordships, towns, and the Pale rather than evenly covering the island. The 1492 map removes this exact id. Its sampled English and Welsh locations plus Dublin and Cork become “england-1492,” while Bordeaux and Bayonne become France; the assignments persist in 1500. The boundary therefore changes both label and territorial story at a software seam. This card treats the shape as a navigation aid, then localizes evidence to named places, institutions, and communities. Its chapters follow political change, families, childhood, work, trade, medicine, sanitation, writing, faith, craft, and continuity without pretending that one color created one shared daily life.

passages.title: Read this atlas shape before trusting its color
passages.text: The exact index supplies one generated id, “english-territory,” with the display name “English territory” and approximate dates 1279 to 1492. It is absent in 1200 and has no imported summary, accepted override, or indexed card. Those are software facts, not proof that medieval people used this phrase as a country name.

passages.title: Read this atlas shape before trusting its color
passages.text: The 1279 feature is a MultiPolygon with three components: much of England and sampled Welsh areas, almost all Ireland, and southwest France around Bordeaux and Bayonne. London, York, Cardiff, Dublin, Cork, Bordeaux, and Bayonne fall inside; sampled Tintagel, Conwy, Edinburgh, Calais, Jersey, and the Isle of Man do not.

passages.title: Read this atlas shape before trusting its color
passages.text: The decoded 1279 and 1300 geometries are exactly identical. The 1400 file keeps the same 235 positions and sampled membership, but small coordinate-conversion drift changes its hash. That is technical encoding noise, not evidence that the coastlines and frontiers historically moved together.

passages.title: Read this atlas shape before trusting its color
passages.text: The Irish polygon is especially misleading. Richard II had to negotiate submissions from many Gaelic lords through interpreters in 1394 and 1395, and the settlement soon unraveled. A solid color covering nearly all Ireland therefore cannot mean one uniform law, tax system, language, or everyday allegiance.

passages.title: Read this atlas shape before trusting its color
passages.text: At the 1492 seam, sampled English and Welsh points plus the atlas’s Irish probes switch to “england-1492,” while Bordeaux and Bayonne switch to France. The kingdom did not reboot when a JSON file changed ids. Henry VII had already ruled since 1485, so this is a labeling seam under the same king.

passages.title: See how power worked through kings, assemblies, courts, and exclusion
passages.text: Edward I summoned assemblies to obtain advice, hear petitions, and secure taxation. The 1295 Parliament included knights and burgesses as well as magnates and clergy. It was not modern democracy, but bargaining over money helped make representatives and recorded consent increasingly important to royal government.

passages.title: See how power worked through kings, assemblies, courts, and exclusion
passages.text: Official chronology places eleven kings inside this interval, from Edward I to Henry VII. Some inherited as children, some were deposed, and some died violently. Those reign dates anchor political change, but royal sequence is not an everyday-life timeline; people planted, traded, raised families, and worshipped through several crowns.

passages.title: See how power worked through kings, assemblies, courts, and exclusion
passages.text: Manorial courts recorded land transfers, local customs, debts, damaged crops, stray animals, inheritance, and obligations. Their rolls can bring ordinary disputes unusually close, yet each manor had its own practices and record survival. One grumpy pig in one roll cannot represent every medieval neighborhood.

passages.title: See how power worked through kings, assemblies, courts, and exclusion
passages.text: People petitioned Chancery when they said ordinary legal remedies had failed. Surviving suits concern inheritance, marriage settlements, apprenticeships, debts, property, and trade. These stories reveal conflict and strategy, but plaintiffs shaped them to win help, so a petition is evidence with a purpose, not a secret recording.

passages.title: See how power worked through kings, assemblies, courts, and exclusion
passages.text: In 1290 the crown ordered Jews out of England after decades of discriminatory law, badges, taxation, and violence. Roughly three thousand people faced dangerous journeys while houses and property passed to the crown. This was state persecution and dispossession, not a footnote to a king’s castle-building résumé.

passages.title: Cross Wales, Ireland, Gascony, and the atlas’s missing places
passages.text: After Llywelyn ap Gruffudd’s death and the conquest of Gwynedd in 1282 and 1283, Edward I built castles and walled towns to control north Wales. Welsh resistance, law, language, worship, farming, and kinship did not vanish behind stone walls or beneath this atlas’s English-colored polygon.

passages.title: Cross Wales, Ireland, Gascony, and the atlas’s missing places
passages.text: Beaumaris Castle began in 1295 only after the crown cleared the nearby Welsh settlement of Llanfaes and forced residents to move. That makes the castle both an engineering achievement and evidence of coercion. A postcard-perfect wall can still have somebody’s demolished home underneath its origin story.

passages.title: Cross Wales, Ireland, Gascony, and the atlas’s missing places
passages.text: Gascon Rolls record English royal administration in Aquitaine from the thirteenth through fifteenth centuries: appointments, orders, disputes, privileges, finance, and petitions. They reveal government through paperwork and local negotiation. They do not turn every Gascon speaker, vineyard worker, merchant, or town into an English cultural copy.

passages.title: Cross Wales, Ireland, Gascony, and the atlas’s missing places
passages.text: Richard II’s Irish expedition used interpreters and formal submissions from more than eighty lords, yet peace soon fractured. English authority was strongest around particular towns and lordships and much weaker elsewhere. The map’s nearly island-wide component radically overstates direct, continuous control.

passages.title: Cross Wales, Ireland, Gascony, and the atlas’s missing places
passages.text: The target polygon also omits Calais, even though it became England’s sole remaining French bridgehead after Bordeaux fell in 1453. Meanwhile the map keeps Gascony colored English for another thirty-nine years. One boundary can therefore leave out a possession and preserve a lost one at the same time.

passages.title: Meet families, women, workers, widows, and unequal choices
passages.text: Most surviving law treated married women’s legal independence differently from widows’ or single women’s, but practice varied with place, status, property, custom, and circumstance. Women farmed, brewed, traded, served, managed homes, entered religious life, defended claims, and sometimes ran businesses. “No rights” is too simple to teach.

passages.title: Meet families, women, workers, widows, and unequal choices
passages.text: Widowhood could bring control of property or a business, yet also debt, lawsuits, poverty, family pressure, and danger. Records preserve energetic women because they entered transactions and disputes, but many lives remain faint. Evidence of agency should not be mistaken for equal power or easy choices.

passages.title: Meet families, women, workers, widows, and unequal choices
passages.text: A 1341 will left forty shillings each to a son and a daughter for apprenticeships. That does not prove equal training everywhere, but it shows one family planning skilled futures for both children. Education could be money, a contract, a workshop, and years beside a craftsperson rather than a classroom.

passages.title: Meet families, women, workers, widows, and unequal choices
passages.text: Margaret Brotherton, born into the royal family, married at about fifteen, had four children, controlled great estates, and pursued political and marital goals. Her unusual wealth makes her a useful named life, not an average woman. Elite biographies illuminate possibilities while loudly displaying their own social bias.

passages.title: Meet families, women, workers, widows, and unequal choices
passages.text: Family historians face a basic gap: England had no nationwide civil register of births, marriages, and deaths in this period. Wills, courts, taxes, guilds, and land records favor people with property or official contact. A quiet family can be historically real while leaving almost no named paperwork.

passages.title: Follow children through chores, learning, toys, and written language
passages.text: Children learned by watching, helping, practicing, attending school where available, and entering service or apprenticeships. Archaeology finds children’s fingerprints on pottery, while documents place some boys and girls in training. Age, wealth, location, health, and family need shaped who learned what and when.

passages.title: Follow children through chores, learning, toys, and written language
passages.text: A tiny lead-alloy jug dated broadly from the mid-thirteenth to early-fourteenth century overlaps this atlas interval only at its later end. It may have been a child’s toy for pretend household play. Fun fact: medieval children may have owned dollhouse crockery, although no child left a review saying “five stars, excellent tiny pouring.”

passages.title: Follow children through chores, learning, toys, and written language
passages.text: Girls as well as boys could enter apprenticeships, and some girls received schooling, especially in towns, elite households, or religious settings. Access was uneven. Learning also happened through food preparation, textile work, farming, worship, errands, storytelling, and care, none of which required a bell to announce class.

passages.title: Follow children through chores, learning, toys, and written language
passages.text: Written-language sample, late-fourteenth-century London English: “Whan that Aprill with his shoures soote.” Normalized reading: “When that April with his showers sweet.” Meaning: “When April with its sweet showers.” This is Chaucer’s Middle English, securely period-appropriate, but not the speech of every English, Welsh, Irish, or Gascon community.

passages.title: Follow children through chores, learning, toys, and written language
passages.text: A fifteenth-century manuscript writes the same opening with spellings such as “schowres swoote.” Medieval spelling was not standardized, and Margery Kempe composed her book through dictation to scribes. Together, these witnesses show both written variation and collaborative bookmaking. The Chaucer line remains one documented literary sample, not a universal voice.

passages.title: Enter homes, kitchens, villages, wardrobes, and working days
passages.text: At West Cotton, archaeology identifies house plots, crofts, yards, paddocks, a manor, streets, and a church. Such layouts joined home, storage, animals, gardening, and work. They show one excavated settlement changing through time, not a ready-made floor plan for London, Dublin, Bordeaux, or every village.

passages.title: Enter homes, kitchens, villages, wardrobes, and working days
passages.text: Wharram Percy preserves houses, a mill, fishponds, church, manor, lanes, and a latrine pit. Its evidence lets families explore an actual village landscape, yet the settlement changed over centuries. Archaeology is strongest when “people lived like this” becomes “people at this named place left these traces.”

passages.title: Enter homes, kitchens, villages, wardrobes, and working days
passages.text: Goodrich Castle accounts show a large household of relatives, guests, officials, and servants consuming food and organizing repairs. One account lists eighty-one pigs, which is less a cute petting zoo than a serious meat supply. Elite abundance should not be projected onto neighboring cottages.

passages.title: Enter homes, kitchens, villages, wardrobes, and working days
passages.text: Castle kitchens handled bread, meat, fish, drink, fuel, storage, serving, and mountains of washing-up. Bread quality marked rank, while cooks and servants worked long hours. A feast looked glamorous from the high table because somebody else had already met the onions, smoke, grease, and dishwater.

passages.title: Enter homes, kitchens, villages, wardrobes, and working days
passages.text: Long-toed poulaines became fashionable in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. Surviving shoes and criticism show both craft and social anxiety around dress. Pointy toes could signal style, but they did not make walking through mud magically dignified. Clothing evidence is strongest in particular finds and texts.

passages.title: Move wool, wine, people, money, and disputes
passages.text: Wool was England’s leading medieval export, while cloth, wine, and many other goods passed through ports. Customs accounts name merchants, cargoes, ships, origins, destinations, and payments. They document taxable trade especially well; smuggling, tiny exchanges, unpaid household labor, and goods that escaped the clerk remain harder to count.

passages.title: Move wool, wine, people, money, and disputes
passages.text: Records from 1330 to 1550 contain tens of thousands of immigrant names from many places and occupations. Some newcomers formed households, married, served, crafted, traded, or studied. “Foreign” was a legal and fiscal category, not a complete personality, and one tax list cannot capture every migrant.

passages.title: Move wool, wine, people, money, and disputes
passages.text: Manorial accounts connect fields, mills, rents, harvest labor, livestock, officials, and markets. Court rolls show neighbors enforcing custom and disputing land or debts. They can make a village look paperwork-heavy, but most conversations, favors, jokes, recipes, and acts of care never reached the roll.

passages.title: Move wool, wine, people, money, and disputes
passages.text: Chancery petitions expose broken deals among merchants, apprentices, spouses, heirs, lenders, and partners. Because petitioners emphasized unfairness, historians compare claims with replies and other records. Medieval people understood strategic storytelling perfectly well; adding “most wronged person in England” to a complaint was not a neutral survey response.

passages.title: Move wool, wine, people, money, and disputes
passages.text: Wills identify selected possessions, gifts, debts, relatives, charities, executors, and burial wishes. They illuminate material and social ties but survive unevenly, especially favoring wealthier people and southern jurisdictions. An object omitted from a will was not necessarily absent from a home, unloved, or unimportant.

passages.title: Treat sickness, live with disability, and investigate plague
passages.text: Medieval hospitals might offer shelter, food, nursing, prayer, and long-term support rather than modern diagnosis and emergency surgery. Some separated men and women; some served particular groups. Care mixed physical, social, and spiritual aims, and disability did not produce one universal institution or life path.

passages.title: Treat sickness, live with disability, and investigate plague
passages.text: The After the Plague project studies skeletons from the cemetery of Cambridge’s Hospital of St John to investigate diet, disease, injury, migration, and poverty. These people provide direct biological evidence, but each body belongs to one person and one institution, not a medical average for the entire atlas.

passages.title: Treat sickness, live with disability, and investigate plague
passages.text: John of Arderne wrote an illustrated surgical work in the fourteenth century and described treating anal fistula. The manuscript shows observation, instruments, recipes, and professional self-presentation. It also answers a timeless question: yes, medieval surgeons wrote seriously about bottoms, because painful problems do not become less real when history books feel embarrassed.

passages.title: Treat sickness, live with disability, and investigate plague
passages.text: During the Black Death, physicians explained illness through humors, environment, astrology, or corrupted air and might use bloodletting or herbal remedies. Many people could not afford a physician. Their theories differed from germ theory, but care, fear, observation, prayer, and practical nursing were not the same as doing nothing.

passages.title: Treat sickness, live with disability, and investigate plague
passages.text: Chemical testing of vessels from the infirmary at Spitalfields found residues including lead and mercury. The report is technical and preliminary, so residues do not automatically reveal one prescription, dose, or patient. Laboratory evidence can narrow possibilities while still requiring context, chronology, and healthy caution about poisonous ingredients.

passages.title: Answer the water, waste, bathing, and toilet questions honestly
passages.text: Castles used garderobes whose seats opened into shafts, pits, moats, or outside walls. Location, cleaning, water, and status varied. A grand castle could have impressive masonry and an extremely direct relationship with gravity. “Medieval toilet” therefore names several arrangements, not one universal porcelain-free design.

passages.title: Answer the water, waste, bathing, and toilet questions honestly
passages.text: Waste pits and garderobes needed emptying, and specialized workers sometimes removed accumulated filth. The job could be dangerous, smelly, and essential. Calling the workers “gong farmers” may delight children, but the useful lesson is urban infrastructure: somebody always has to make the sanitation system continue working.

passages.title: Answer the water, waste, bathing, and toilet questions honestly
passages.text: A 1328 London dispute described waste leaking from one household’s cesspit into a neighbor’s cellar. That single case proves neither universal filth nor effective sewerage. It does show household sanitation, property rights, smell, damage, and neighborly fury colliding in a record vivid enough to survive.

passages.title: Answer the water, waste, bathing, and toilet questions honestly
passages.text: London authorities also confronted blocked gutters and waste in streets. Rules and complaints show that people cared about drainage and nuisance even when enforcement failed. The city was not cheerfully swimming in muck; it was repeatedly arguing about who must move the muck, where, and at whose expense.

passages.title: Answer the water, waste, bathing, and toilet questions honestly
passages.text: London Museum records a medieval three-seat wooden toilet, while castles could also have multi-seat privies. Several users might sit side by side, so toilet privacy depended on place, building, and rank. The funniest safe fact is architectural: some medieval bathrooms treated “personal space” as an optional upgrade.

passages.title: Make books and glass, practice faith, count achievements, and continue
passages.text: Paper manuscripts circulated in England before printing, although paper was imported and parchment remained important. Scribes, parchmenters, papermakers abroad, merchants, binders, illuminators, readers, and libraries formed a knowledge supply chain. A book was an intellectual object and also an engineered stack of costly materials and labor.

passages.title: Make books and glass, practice faith, count achievements, and continue
passages.text: William Caxton brought printing to Westminster in 1476 and worked as printer, publisher, translator, and bookseller. Westminster Abbey says he published a hundred books between 1473 and his death. His press was a major achievement built from movable type, ink, paper, finance, language choices, skilled labor, and customers.

passages.title: Make books and glass, practice faith, count achievements, and continue
passages.text: York Minster’s Great East Window was commissioned from John Thornton in 1405 and made in about three years. Its scale celebrates design, glass painting, stonework, scaffolding, organization, and teams of workers. Naming the master matters, but so do the many hands that made a wall of pictures stand and shine.

passages.title: Make books and glass, practice faith, count achievements, and continue
passages.text: Parish churches organized worship, calendars, gatherings, charity, memory, and local status, while pilgrimage connected people and places. Criticism also grew, including Lollard challenges to church authority. Medieval religion was neither one unchanging belief nor mere superstition; it structured communities and also generated disagreement, exclusion, and reform.

passages.title: Make books and glass, practice faith, count achievements, and continue
passages.text: Bosworth in 1485 ended Richard III’s reign and began Henry VII’s, but dynastic victory did not end England, Wales, Ireland, or Gascony as lived places. Achievements in government, craft, care, trade, writing, farming, and art belonged to many people, including those absent from royal stories.

The atlas removes “english-territory” at 1492. Sampled English and Welsh points, Dublin, and Cork switch to “england-1492,” while Bordeaux and Bayonne switch to France; the same assignments remain in 1500. Henry VII’s kingdom continued, as did Welsh, Irish, French, and Gascon communities and their distinct histories. Bosworth had changed the ruling dynasty in 1485, not erased the population. This ending records an atlas relabeling and a long-delayed territorial correction, not a civilization’s fall.

sectionTitles: A question, a sculpture and a classroom

passages.text: Equatorial Guinea became independent from Spain on 12 October 1968. The atlas record begins in 1914, during colonial rule, and connects mainland Río Muni with Bioko. Its early polygon omits distant Annobón, so the outline is incomplete. This is a history of a changing colonial territory and republic, not one culture shared identically by all its communities.

passages.title: Power, labour and independence
passages.text: Cocoa plantations on Fernando Po, now Bioko, needed large workforces. Enrique Martino’s archival research traces coercive recruitment from Río Muni and eastern Nigeria between 1926 and 1945. Recruiters, transport networks and colonial officials shaped workers’ lives. A plantation’s output cannot be separated from the conditions under which people were made to produce it.

passages.title: Power, labour and independence
passages.text: Spain’s rule ended on 12 October 1968. The diplomatic record subsequently refers to Santa Isabel, the city later called Malabo, as the location of an embassy. Independence created new international relationships, but mainland and island communities retained different histories rather than suddenly becoming culturally interchangeable.

passages.title: Power, labour and independence
passages.text: Under Francisco Macías Nguema, political opponents suffered imprisonment and killing. The International Commission of Jurists documented that repression and the military coup of 3 August 1979, led by Teodoro Obiang Nguema. Its trial observer also criticized aspects of the proceedings against Macías. A ruler’s removal did not erase the need for justice.

passages.title: Power, labour and independence
passages.text: Oil discoveries in the 1990s brought rapid economic growth. The World Bank’s March 2025 assessment also describes declining oil revenues and inadequate investment in health and education. National income and family well-being are different measures: expensive infrastructure alone does not ensure a good classroom or dependable care.

passages.title: A question, a sculpture and a classroom
passages.text: “Yù gò lan mi Pichi?” means “Would you teach me Pichi?” Linguist Kofi Yakpo records this question, including its tone marks, in a study of Pichi. It is a useful first sentence for a visitor who wants to listen and learn, rather than assume that Spanish is everyone’s only language.

passages.title: A question, a sculpture and a classroom
passages.text: Pichi developed from Krio brought to Bioko by African settlers from Freetown in the nineteenth century. Yakpo’s survey describes it as a language of everyday communication across the island, shaped by further migration and contact with Spanish. Its history connects Equatorial Guinea with Sierra Leone and wider coastal networks.

passages.title: A question, a sculpture and a classroom
passages.text: A nineteenth-century Okak-Fang guardian figure in the Met was made from wood, copper alloy and palm oil. Its precise origin is catalogued as Gabon or Equatorial Guinea. Such sculptures stood above bark containers holding ancestors’ relics; the carved figure belonged to a family’s relationship with the dead, not simply to decoration.

passages.title: A question, a sculpture and a classroom
passages.text: During COVID school closures, the programme La Escuela en mi Casa, “School in My Home,” provided distance learning. UNICEF’s 2023 programme document reports that it reached 135,849 students. That is a record of the programme’s reported reach, while a smaller 2022 student survey examined participation and usefulness.

passages.title: Health and practical research
passages.text: School sanitation remained a serious problem. The same 2023 UNICEF document reported that only 9 percent of schools had handwashing facilities, citing preliminary research that year. A place to wash hands is part of the learning environment, alongside desks, teachers and books; the figure describes that study rather than every later school year.

passages.title: Health and practical research
passages.text: In October 2025, health and education authorities launched a school-health programme in Bata. Its stated targets included nutrition, mental health, infectious disease and violence affecting pupils. The announcement described a vitamin A pilot in Litoral among initial actions. It was a launch with planned work, not proof that all schools already had those services.

passages.title: Health and practical research
passages.text: Bioko has also contributed original malaria research. A study published in 2025 compared different levels of indoor insecticide spraying during 2021 and 2022, checking infections with rapid tests in annual household surveys. The researchers asked how to protect communities effectively with limited resources, testing an operational question rather than assuming more spraying always answers it.

passages.title: Health and practical research
passages.text: In 2018 the Bioko Marine Turtle Program attached satellite transmitters to six green turtles to study their journeys and feeding grounds. Local field assistants also worked at nesting-season camps. Following a turtle after it leaves the beach helps researchers understand why protection must extend beyond the patch of sand where its eggs were laid.

Spanish rule ended in 1968, and the 1979 coup replaced a government rather than ending the republic. Equatorial Guinea continues, with distinct island and mainland communities and ongoing questions about public services and the distribution of resource wealth.

sectionTitles: A regional people and their neighbors
Survival, teaching and the limits of the written record

passages.text: The Erie were an Iroquoian-speaking people south and east of Lake Erie. This map stretches their outline too far across Ohio and keeps the label until 1783, long after the wars of the 1650s dispersed their independent communities. Archaeologists debate which sites belong to Erie history; the shape cannot settle those questions.

passages.title: A regional people and their neighbors
passages.text: French records often call the Erie the Cat Nation. Scholars have questioned exactly which animal that name meant: William Engelbrecht discusses an interpretation involving raccoons. Another proposed derivation of the Iroquoian name refers to cherry trees. Neither explanation gives us a securely recorded Erie sentence.

passages.title: A regional people and their neighbors
passages.text: The Erie received Huron-Wendat refugees after the destruction of their homeland. A French missionary report from 1653 to 1654 describes these newcomers joining Erie communities. The information came through the Erie’s opponents, so it records a changing regional alliance without letting us hear the refugees directly.

passages.title: A regional people and their neighbors
passages.text: In 1654, Erie forces struck both Seneca and Onondaga enemies. The Onondaga leader Annenraes was captured and killed; a council later that year included mourning for him. These events show that the Erie were a serious military power before their own defeat, rather than passive spectators to regional war.

passages.title: Households traced through archaeology
passages.text: Simmons, near modern Elma in western New York, belongs to a village sequence often associated with Erie ancestors. Marian White traced movement between nearby settlements as communities sought fresh soil and firewood. Relocation involved rebuilding a neighborhood, not simply carrying a tent to the next campsite.

passages.title: Households traced through archaeology
passages.text: Four excavated Simmons longhouses ranged from 50 to 100 feet long and were about 22 feet wide. Builders adjusted their alignment to the level ground. A swamp, ravine and steep slopes helped protect the village, with a wooden palisade reinforcing its defenses.

passages.title: Households traced through archaeology
passages.text: Rubbish from Simmons contained brass-kettle scraps and iron fragments, probably from axes, that residents had reshaped into other objects. New imported metal became raw material for local makers. The same deposits held both patterned pottery and plain vessels: not every useful pot needed its best party clothes.

passages.title: Households traced through archaeology
passages.text: Bone combs illustrated from Simmons include small carved figures. Engelbrecht compared some of these with examples from Susquehannock country in Pennsylvania. A grooming tool could carry skilled decoration and connections worth investigating far beyond its owner’s home.

passages.title: Households traced through archaeology
passages.text: Similar pottery at Ripley and Newton-Hopper, about 68 miles apart, led Engelbrecht to investigate possible movements of people or close connections between settlements. Patterns on a pot can therefore contribute to a much larger question: how did communities move and stay connected?

passages.title: Households traced through archaeology
passages.text: Ripley once appeared in books as a straightforward Erie village. Later excavators challenged that account and suggested that it might instead have served as a ceremonial center, possibly as early as the 1300s. This unresolved site cannot supply a ready-made picture of every seventeenth-century Erie household.

passages.title: Survival, teaching and the limits of the written record
passages.text: Linguist Charles Julian found no recorded Erie vocabulary, though several personal and place names might preserve Erie forms. Without secure words and meanings, a translated Erie greeting cannot responsibly be supplied here. These limits concern the surviving record, not whether Erie people possessed a rich spoken language.

passages.title: Survival, teaching and the limits of the written record
passages.text: Gandeacteua and her mother survived the 1650s conflict as captives taken to an Oneida community. She later married François-Xavier Tonsahoten, a Huron-Wendat man who had also become part of an Iroquois community. Her life joins Erie history to families formed after displacement.

passages.title: Survival, teaching and the limits of the written record
passages.text: In 1667, Gandeacteua taught an Iroquoian language to the Jesuit Jacques Bruyas while learning about Christianity from him. An Indigenous woman was the language teacher in this exchange. The biography does not identify those lessons as a surviving vocabulary of her Erie mother tongue.

passages.title: Survival, teaching and the limits of the written record
passages.text: In spring 1669, Gandeacteua and other women planted corn at La Prairie, near Montreal. Their harvest prospered, and more families joined the settlement. This was a new, mixed mission community built after war; farming and family life continued beyond the loss of the Erie’s former political independence.

Haudenosaunee warfare defeated Erie political communities in the mid-1650s. Survivors entered other communities, so conquest must not be mistaken for the death of every Erie person. The imported 1783 cutoff is not a historical end date for their independent polity.
