passages.text: Griqualand West connects an older Griqua homeland with the diamond fields around Kimberley. Britain proclaimed a territory here in 1871; it was annexed to the Cape Colony in 1880. The map’s 1878 to 1914 window therefore includes decades when this was a region within a larger colony, not a separate state. The imported outline also excludes Kimberley, although the historical territory included the town. Its history includes Griqua communities, African migrant workers and colonial settlers.

passages.title: Communities before the diamond rush
passages.text: Griqua communities formed through the histories of Khoisan people, people of European descent and people whose ancestors had been enslaved. The Kok and Berends families drew followers north through Namaqualand and along the Orange River. These communities existed well before Britain created a colony bearing their name.

passages.title: Communities before the diamond rush
passages.text: Earlier settlements such as Klaarwater, later Griquatown, combined herding, hunting and trade; wheat was also grown around mission settlements. Horses and wagons connected households to distant markets. Missionary John Campbell described five languages being spoken at one settlement: an unusually busy place for anyone trying to follow every conversation.

passages.title: Communities before the diamond rush
passages.text: Captain Nicholas Waterboer was awarded the disputed diamond fields in the 1871 arbitration. That award did not preserve independent Griqua control: British colonial rule followed. The territory’s name can otherwise make this abrupt transfer of power easy to miss.

passages.title: Work, water and healthcare
passages.text: Under the 1871 digging rules, a claim measured 30 feet by 30 feet, about nine metres on each side. Inspectors marked boundaries with pegs and kept registers. Digging for diamonds meant both moving earth and keeping up with licences, payments and paperwork.

passages.title: Work, water and healthcare
passages.text: Doctor J. W. Matthews recalled that early diggers paid as much as a shilling for a bucket of water brought from springs four miles away. Writing in 1887, he described a later company supply from the Vaal River, about twenty miles away, serving mines and private homes. Water infrastructure mattered as much to daily life as shiny stones.

passages.title: Work, water and healthcare
passages.text: Matthews’s 1873 complaint about a jail hospital described a leaking tent where patients lay on a dusty floor without beds. His later account recorded hospital expansion and an isolation ward in 1882. The contrast shows the difficult work of building healthcare in a fast-growing mining settlement.

passages.title: Work, water and healthcare
passages.text: In 2003, a storm-water trench accidentally cut into unmarked graves near Kimberley’s Gladstone Cemetery. Researchers examined 107 skeletons, thought mostly to be migrant mine workers who died between 1897 and 1900. Their study brings people often missing from grand diamond-industry stories back into view.

passages.title: Work, water and healthcare
passages.text: The Gladstone study found fractures and changes associated with heavy physical work, alongside evidence of infectious disease. Researchers interpreted these together with records of dangerous mining and crowded living conditions. Diamond wealth and a worker’s health could follow very different paths.

passages.title: Learning, newspapers and written words
passages.text: Matthews also described Catholic mission education in the 1880s, including a school attended by about 200 people from the Indian community. His account places migration and schooling beside the better-known mining story: Kimberley’s classrooms drew on a much wider world.

passages.title: Learning, newspapers and written words
passages.text: Sol Plaatje edited Tsala ea Becoana from Kimberley in the early 1910s. Its four pages carried both Setswana and English. At first, the printing press was in King William’s Town, hundreds of miles from the editorial office: getting a newspaper made involved a remarkable amount of travel for the words.

passages.title: Learning, newspapers and written words
passages.text: The newspaper enterprise drew support from a network including Barolong landowners at Thaba Nchu, Thomas Mapikela and the publisher John Tengo Jabavu. This was a collaboration across towns, giving African readers and writers a public forum during an era of racial exclusion.

passages.title: Learning, newspapers and written words
passages.text: Written language sample: “Tsala ea Becoana” means “Friend of the Bechuana,” the historical English title recorded by the archive. A surviving issue is dated 25 February 1911 and catalogued as chiefly Setswana with some English, published in Kimberley. This is a local newspaper from the later regional phase.

Griqualand West’s separate colonial administration ended with Cape annexation in 1880, not with the map’s 1914 endpoint. Its towns and communities continued. The later hospital, cemetery and newspaper evidence belongs to that continuing regional history.

sectionTitles: Buffalo and the work of restoration
Games, written words and new community work

passages.text: The Aaniiih, also called Gros Ventre, are an Algonquian-speaking northern Plains people. The map’s Aaniiih record from 1530 to 1650 and Gros Ventre record from 1650 to 1783 use the same outline in northern Montana and southern Canada. These are coverage intervals, not separate peoples or lifetimes. At Fort Belknap, Aaniiih people share government with the distinct Nakoda nation.

passages.title: Earlier northern Plains connections
passages.text: An encounter recorded around 1754 placed Aaniiih people near the Saskatchewan River’s forks. Later alliances connected them with the Blackfeet: their history extends across today’s national border.

passages.title: Earlier northern Plains connections
passages.text: In 1876, Aaniiih people refused an agency move toward hostile neighbors, sacrificing annuities. Fort Belknap reopened in 1878. Refusal was a way to resist federal relocation.

passages.title: Food, shelter and skilled making
passages.text: The community’s history describes buffalo as a source of food, clothing and tipi coverings. Following herds required knowledge of animal movement and the skills to preserve meat and work hides for several different purposes.

passages.title: Food, shelter and skilled making
passages.text: In testimony gathered in 1901, women described slicing meat thinly and drying it on racks. Dried meat could be stored in rawhide containers or pounded with berries. Preservation supported households beyond the immediate hunt.

passages.title: Food, shelter and skilled making
passages.text: Tent making could be cooperative: a woman with enough prepared hides invited skilled makers to a feast. An expert fitted the pieces before others sewed them together, combining hospitality with specialised work.

passages.title: Food, shelter and skilled making
passages.text: Kroeber described a child’s robe, museum number 50-1751, decorated with coloured quillwork, tin and dyed horsehair pendants. The object records several materials and techniques used together in clothing.

passages.title: Food, shelter and skilled making
passages.text: A soft-hide bag, museum number 50-1738, appears in the same report. Such bags carried clothing and small household articles, with quillwork and beadwork adding decoration to a practical container.

passages.title: Knowledge in community institutions
passages.text: Aaniiih Nakoda College was designed to make further education available near home and reflect the lifeways of both Nations. Its programmes connect cultural study with fields such as ecology, nursing, computing and trades. The name adopted in 2011 explicitly recognises both peoples.

passages.title: Knowledge in community institutions
passages.text: In 2014, educator Clarena Brockie described White Clay Immersion School’s use of community projects, field learning and teaching between generations. Language was the means of learning across subjects, giving children sustained opportunities to use it.

passages.title: Knowledge in community institutions
passages.text: A reference grammar published in 2024 grew from work by Andrew Cowell, Terry Brockie and tribal members to retranscribe archival language records. It explains both earlier and modern forms, supporting community decisions about what to teach and how.

passages.title: Knowledge in community institutions
passages.text: The grammar also treats place names, personal names, greetings and traditional narrative. Preserving language involves how people address one another and describe their world, alongside its sounds and word structures.

passages.title: Buffalo and the work of restoration
passages.text: In August 2013, Yellowstone-origin bison arrived from Fort Peck to establish a new cultural herd at Fort Belknap. The project linked conservation with food and ceremonial uses. This was a specific restoration programme within an already living community.

passages.title: Buffalo and the work of restoration
passages.text: A project funded in 2024 planned wildlife-friendly fencing and a livestock water system to bring more pasture into the buffalo grazing system. Managing a herd also involves water, land access, infrastructure and consultation about cultural resources.

passages.title: Games, written words and new community work
passages.text: A Montana teaching resource reproduces a historic Gros Ventre shinny ball and curved stick. The ball’s buckskin covering was sewn around buffalo-hair stuffing. It is a useful reminder that a ball does not have to come from a factory: players and makers could turn available materials into sporting equipment.

passages.title: Games, written words and new community work
passages.text: In 1999, Aaniiih artist Chandler Good Strike made a model parfleche case now in the National Museum of the American Indian. He folded, painted and tied rawhide, adding felt and synthetic fabric. This documented modern work carries a container-making tradition forward through the materials and choices of an individual artist.

passages.title: Games, written words and new community work
passages.text: A short written sample is “báyaaah,” translated “house, home” in the 2012 Gros Ventre/White Clay Student Dictionary. Andrew Cowell compiled it with Terry Brockie and John Stiff Arm, drawing on earlier work with speakers. This is an attested modern teaching spelling, not a reconstructed inscription from 1650.

passages.title: Games, written words and new community work
passages.text: A 2012 library grant proposed putting Aaniiih and Nakoda translations into popular children’s books. After requesting publishers’ permission, staff would print translations on transparent labels and attach them to the pages. Familiar pictures could then accompany community languages during reading sessions and at local libraries.

passages.title: Games, written words and new community work
passages.text: A 2021 account describes college students trapping mosquitoes and testing them for West Nile virus. Samples also went to another laboratory for quality checks. This is a modern form of community health work in which students investigate the insects around their own homes and help provide information for public alerts.

passages.title: Games, written words and new community work
passages.text: The same college account describes a long-term study of organisms in the Milk River, a local drinking-water source. Studying the river’s living community adds evidence about water conditions. Classroom science becomes closely connected to an everyday question: what is happening in the water people depend on?

passages.title: Games, written words and new community work
passages.text: Fort Belknap began returning buffalo in the late 1970s, according to its buffalo program’s contribution to a 2022 Smithsonian research announcement. The shared community program connects ecological restoration with food and cultural relationships. Buffalo therefore belong in this story’s future as well as in its account of historic hunting.

Reservation confinement and assimilation policies reduced Aaniiih autonomy and disrupted language transmission. Aaniiih people continue, sharing the Fort Belknap government with Nakoda neighbours and building institutions for education and cultural renewal. The decline of fluent speakers did not mean the disappearance of the people or an end to language learning.

passages.text: These map labels cover the Indigenous Canary Islands, whose settlers came from North Africa. Strictly, Guanches names the people of Tenerife. Other islands developed distinct communities. The imported spans, 1500 BCE to 500 CE and 800 to 1878, are not reliable settlement or independence dates.

passages.title: Islands and authority
passages.text: A 2024 study assembled reliable radiocarbon dates to distinguish earlier Roman activity from permanent North African settlement. Its results place Indigenous colonization in the first centuries CE. The map’s 1500 BCE starting point cannot be treated as an established Guanche founding date.

passages.title: Islands and authority
passages.text: Late preconquest Tenerife had nine territories. Leaders described in historical accounts as menceyes mediated disputes over pasture, watering places and herds. A ruler’s working day could involve deciding whose goats belonged at the water source, as well as negotiating alliances.

passages.title: Homes, tools and clothing
passages.text: At Los Cabezazos in Tegueste, a cave used from the sixth century CE offered shelter near water and pasture. Tenerife also had stone huts: the circular or oval examples at Ifara used dry stone walls without mortar.

passages.title: Homes, tools and clothing
passages.text: Obsidian, a shiny volcanic glass, supplied sharp flakes called tabonas. Craftspeople could cut with these tools without metal blades. Basalt and other stone also served everyday work, including grinding grain and processing animal products.

passages.title: Homes, tools and clothing
passages.text: Goat leg bones became pointed awls, needles and spatulas for working skins, plant fibres and pottery. A herd therefore supplied materials for a household tool kit as well as milk and meat.

passages.title: Homes, tools and clothing
passages.text: Leather preserved mainly in funerary caves includes decorated pieces and repairs. Those patches show that useful material was worth mending. Even an archaeological museum can contain evidence of someone deciding that an old piece still had life in it.

passages.title: Food and a mountain landscape
passages.text: Archaeobotanists have identified barley, durum wheat, lentils, broad beans, peas and figs across the archipelago’s early farming evidence. These crops did not remain equally common everywhere: each island’s food history needs its own evidence.

passages.title: Food and a mountain landscape
passages.text: On Gran Canaria, dried figs survived in cave granaries, while tiny fig seeds also lodged in ancient dental cavities. Teeth can preserve an unexpectedly personal trace of a meal, although tooth decay itself was no treat.

passages.title: Food and a mountain landscape
passages.text: Gran Canaria’s Risco Caído mountain landscape contains cave homes, granaries and cisterns. These spaces linked shelter, stored food and water within a difficult landscape of cliffs and ravines; a cave could be useful far beyond simply keeping the rain off.

passages.title: Food and a mountain landscape
passages.text: The same landscape preserves sanctuaries, rock art and Libyco-Berber inscriptions. They are material evidence of religious and written traditions. They should not be collapsed into the political history of Tenerife simply because the map uses one broad label.

passages.title: Families and a written voice
passages.text: In his 1510 will, Juan Azanos named two sons as heirs. One had been taken captive and converted; his father knew his earlier name, Gualçitca, but not his new one. The document makes the separation of a family painfully concrete.

passages.title: Families and a written voice
passages.text: A written sample is “yo, Juan Azanos, guanche”: “I, Juan Azanos, a Guanche.” It opens his will of 18 November 1510, preserved in a modern scholarly transcription. This is Spanish notarial writing; the document names interpreters who understood his language, rather than claiming that he wrote Spanish himself.

Tenerife’s independent territories ended with the Castilian conquest in 1496, but Guanche people did not simply disappear. Records document survivors, families, land allocations and continuing place names. The imported 1878 endpoint is not the date of conquest or of an Indigenous people’s extinction.

passages.text: The modern Republic of Guatemala was proclaimed in 1847, before this map interval. Living Maya textile traditions, community kite-making and universities reveal creative work across different communities. The twentieth-century armed conflict and the 1996 peace agreements form another essential part of that history.

passages.title: Cloth, kites and community knowledge
passages.text: Museo Ixchel preserves a ceremonial huipil from Sacapulas, Quiché, dated to 1930. Its three cloth panels were joined by hand. The garment is a specific surviving example of skilled textile work, not a costume representing every Maya community.

passages.title: Cloth, kites and community knowledge
passages.text: Older women recognized the huipil as local, while younger interviewees did not recognize that former style. This comparison helped the museum study change. Clothing traditions can evolve within a living community; unfamiliarity with one garment does not mean the people vanished.

passages.title: Cloth, kites and community knowledge
passages.text: Giant kites in Santiago Sacatepéquez and Sumpango are made over several months for the days honoring saints and the dead. UNESCO traces this particular tradition to the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. Their makers associate them with communication with ancestors.

passages.title: Cloth, kites and community knowledge
passages.text: Making a kite involves designing and decorating its face with colored tissue paper, adding a reverse lining, and assembling fringes and tail. The huge finished object begins with many small tasks. It is patient collaborative craft, not just a large sheet thrown into the wind.

passages.title: Cloth, kites and community knowledge
passages.text: Kite designs can address environmental protection, violence and human rights. People learn by joining the work, and committees organize exhibitions and prizes. A commemorative tradition can also speak directly about the community’s present concerns.

passages.title: Education, public words and memory
passages.text: The University of San Carlos formed new student associations and expanded university outreach in 1920. The Huelga de Dolores returned in 1921 with satire and music. Student life included collective expression as well as classroom study.

passages.title: Education, public words and memory
passages.text: The earthquakes of 1917 to 1918 severely damaged university buildings. A new School of Natural Sciences and Pharmacy opened in 1928. Its construction is concrete evidence of rebuilding the physical spaces needed for education after disaster.

passages.title: Education, public words and memory
passages.text: A university laboratory established at Hospital San Juan de Dios in 2000 expanded capacity to investigate tuberculosis and fungal infections. It also trained personnel in diagnostic methods and biosafety for use elsewhere. Medical achievement includes building and sharing reliable laboratory skills.

passages.title: Education, public words and memory
passages.text: An 1847 printed manifesto explains the decree proclaiming Guatemala an independent republic. The Library of Congress preserves the publication, issued by Imprenta de la Paz. It witnesses a particular political claim rather than the beginning of Guatemala’s much older peoples.

passages.title: Education, public words and memory
passages.text: The manifesto’s Spanish title includes “erigiendo dicho estado en republica independiente”: “establishing that state as an independent republic.” This short passage comes from the attested 1847 printed title. Its spelling is preserved; the English wording is a translation.

passages.title: Education, public words and memory
passages.text: The government and URNG signed the Agreement on a Firm and Lasting Peace on 29 December 1996. UN work included verifying commitments and supporting institutions. Ending armed conflict required practical changes beyond announcing that the war was over.

passages.title: Education, public words and memory
passages.text: The Commission for Historical Clarification published Memory of Silence in 1999. Its findings showed that most victims were Indigenous Maya. Documenting those losses is essential to the country’s history, while recognizing the continued lives and agency of Maya communities.

Guatemala continues as a republic. The 1996 agreement ended the internal armed conflict, not the country or its Indigenous peoples. The 1847 republican proclamation predates the imported 1878 start, which is a map-coverage date rather than a cultural beginning.

sectionTitles: Sovereignty and the people who live with it

passages.text: Guinea became independent from France in 1958. This record represents the country centered on Conakry, with its own political history, linguistic creativity and living musical traditions.

passages.title: Sovereignty and the people who live with it
passages.text: Guinea’s National Assembly proclaimed independence on 2 October 1958. The country is sometimes called Guinea-Conakry to distinguish it from Guinea-Bissau and Equatorial Guinea. Its modern republic should not be confused with the much wider historical geographical expression Guinea.

passages.title: Sovereignty and the people who live with it
passages.text: Sékou Touré helped lead the break with French rule, then governed until 1984 through a one-party dictatorship. His government persecuted real and suspected opponents. Independence and freedom from repression are different historical questions, both important to families living under a new state.

passages.title: Sovereignty and the people who live with it
passages.text: Guinea completed a presidential election process in 2010, experienced another military coup in September 2021 and held a presidential election in December 2025. In January 2026, the African Union lifted its suspension. These changes concern government; the country and its people continued throughout.

passages.title: Writing, family teaching and performance
passages.text: Here is an attested original-script sample: “ߒߞߏ”, N’Ko, meaning “I say”. Written from right to left, it names a script used for Manding languages, including by Maninka speakers in Guinea. A short name can carry a powerful declaration that one’s language belongs on the page.

passages.title: Writing, family teaching and performance
passages.text: Solomana Kanté devised N’Ko in 1949, before Guinea’s independence. Its letters and added marks represent vowels and tones as well as consonants. This is a modern African invention with a continuing literary life, rather than an undeciphered ancient alphabet.

passages.title: Writing, family teaching and performance
passages.text: At Niagassola, the Dökala family safeguards the Sosso-Bala, a sacred balafon associated with Manding epic history. It has twenty wooden slats with gourds beneath. Its guardians preserve an instrument and a responsibility passed between generations.

passages.title: Writing, family teaching and performance
passages.text: The Balatigui, the family patriarch and instrument’s guardian, also teaches children balafon from around age seven. UNESCO notes that migration away from villages can reduce the number of pupils. Keeping a musical tradition alive requires future players, not just a safe storage room.

passages.title: Writing, family teaching and performance
passages.text: Baga D’mba headdresses express an ideal of motherhood and community well-being. A historical wooden example in the Met is almost 1.2 meters tall and was worn with raffia and cloth. This inherited performance art turns sculpture into something that moves among people.

passages.title: Research, classrooms and practical care
passages.text: Guinean health workers and participants helped test an Ebola vaccine during the 2015 epidemic. WHO, Guinea’s health ministry and international partners organized the research. The country contributed knowledge that could help future outbreaks elsewhere, while coping with devastating losses at home.

passages.title: Research, classrooms and practical care
passages.text: The study used rings of people connected to a diagnosed patient, including contacts of contacts. Researchers compared vaccination timing and tracked later illness. The 2016 final report found strong protection in that trial, a carefully measured result rather than a promise that every vaccine always prevents every case.

passages.title: Research, classrooms and practical care
passages.text: Danéné primary school in N’zérékoré had a broken borehole and badly deteriorated toilets. In 2021, UNICEF restored the water source and a four-cubicle latrine block. For a school of more than a thousand pupils, working facilities were an urgent part of keeping lessons going.

passages.title: Research, classrooms and practical care
passages.text: Parents’ association president Gabriel Sagno welcomed the repairs but asked for help with the remaining latrines. His account shows parents taking part in school life and evaluating what still needed work. A ribbon-cutting ceremony does not do the cleaning or fix every toilet.
Guinea remains a country. The African Union’s January 2026 decision to restore its participation followed a new election; questions of accountable government remain part of an ongoing history.

passages.text: The atlas begins this record in 1920, during Portuguese colonial rule. Guinea-Bissau proclaimed independence on 24 September 1973; Portugal formally recognized it the following year. The card follows that transition and the continuing country, whose mainland communities and Bijagós islands have distinct languages, farming knowledge and artistic traditions.

passages.title: From colony to republic
passages.text: Two dates matter in the independence story. The People’s National Assembly proclaimed the state on 24 September 1973. Portugal’s president signed recognition on 10 September 1974, after negotiations. Calling 1920 the country’s independence year would confuse an atlas snapshot with the end of colonial government.

passages.title: From colony to republic
passages.text: Independence did not end political conflict. The US diplomatic history records the suspension of its Bissau embassy operations on 14 June 1998 because of civil war. That was a disruption to government and ordinary lives within the republic, rather than the disappearance of Guinea-Bissau as a country.

passages.title: From colony to republic
passages.text: Before becoming a liberation leader, Amílcar Cabral worked as an agricultural scientist. From November 1953 to April 1954, his survey team included fellow agronomist Maria Helena Rodrigues, his wife. They investigated 2,248 family holdings in 356 villages, using sampling rather than pretending they could inspect every farm.

passages.title: From colony to republic
passages.text: Cabral’s published graph compared cultivated, burned and fallow land. It distinguished rice-growing and peanut-growing systems and questioned colonial enthusiasm for cash crops. A chart about soil could carry a political argument: farmers’ knowledge and the future of their land belonged at the centre of discussions about development.

passages.title: Books, speech and island knowledge
passages.text: A December 1964 PAIGC circular announced “Nosso Primeiro Livro de Leitura,” meaning “Our First Reading Book.” The document survives in the Amílcar Cabral archive. Publishing a beginner’s reader during the liberation struggle shows education as practical organizing work: a political movement also needed children and adults who could read.

passages.title: Books, speech and island knowledge
passages.text: Here is a short Kriyol sentence recorded by linguists: “N tene kaneta.” It means “I have a pen.” The 2013 APiCS language survey prints this as example 9 in its explanation of verbs. It is an attested modern teaching example, written in the Latin alphabet.

passages.title: Books, speech and island knowledge
passages.text: Kriyol connects speakers of different home languages in markets, public services and everyday conversation. The same linguistic survey describes experiments using it in bilingual education. Portuguese has a different formal role, while local African languages remain important: a child’s home, street and classroom need not sound exactly alike.

passages.title: Books, speech and island knowledge
passages.text: The Bijagós coastal and marine ecosystems entered the World Heritage List in 2025. Mangroves, mudflats and shallow channels shelter fish, turtles and migrating birds. Poilão is especially important for green-turtle nesting. The protected property covers selected high-value ecosystems, rather than turning every island into one undifferentiated nature reserve.

passages.title: Books, speech and island knowledge
passages.text: UNESCO credits local communities’ customary management alongside government conservation work. Marine protected areas created in 2000 and 2005 include the Urok Islands community area. Protecting the archipelago therefore involves people deciding how places and resources are used, as well as scientists counting animals.

passages.title: Water and the work of healthier homes
passages.text: In Quinara, sanitation meetings often took place under a mango tree. UNICEF’s 2019 account describes facilitators helping residents map where waste went and how flies, rainwater and hands could carry it home. The discussion was memorable because it connected an uncomfortable subject to the places families knew.

passages.title: Water and the work of healthier homes
passages.text: Families then built toilets with local materials. Quinara received open-defecation-free recognition in 2018, and follow-up visits checked continued use and hygiene practices. Soap and handwashing were part of the achievement. The useful invention here was also organizational: neighbours worked together to keep their surroundings cleaner.

passages.title: Water and the work of healthier homes
passages.text: A smartphone could help find a broken pump. UNICEF reports that mWATER mapping, begun in 2016 and continued in 2018, visited nearly 5,250 water points. Recording whether a pump actually worked made the map useful for repairs; a dot labelled “water” is not much help when the handle produces nothing.

Portuguese colonial rule ended through the 1973 proclamation and 1974 recognition. Guinea-Bissau continues as a republic; later conflict and changes of government did not end the country or its communities.

passages.text: This Gujarat is the western Indian sultanate, shown during Mahmud Begada’s reign. Its ports connected prosperous workshops and inland capitals with the Indian Ocean. The imported 1492 to 1500 outline is a short map window, not the dynasty’s lifetime or a map of the modern state.

passages.title: Capitals, ports and skilled hands
passages.text: Ahmad Shah founded Ahmedabad in 1411. Its Islamic monuments drew on the skills of local builders and on regional Hindu and Jain architectural traditions. Pillars, carved screens and open courtyards give the city’s mosques a distinct local character: new royal patrons hired people who already knew how to build beautifully.

passages.title: Capitals, ports and skilled hands
passages.text: After taking the fortified hill of Pavagadh in 1484, Mahmud Begada built a capital at Champaner below it. The resulting landscape combines an older sacred hill, defensive works, palace remains and monumental mosques. A change of ruler did not wipe the ground clean before the next city appeared.

passages.title: Capitals, ports and skilled hands
passages.text: The early sixteenth-century traveler Duarte Barbosa described exports including cotton cloth, silk, dyes, grain and pulses. Horses and pearls came in through overseas trade. Gujarat’s importance rested on busy production and exchange as well as armies: merchants needed useful cargo, not just impressive royal titles.

passages.title: Capitals, ports and skilled hands
passages.text: A cotton fragment made in Gujarat in the fifteenth or sixteenth century was found at Fustat in Egypt. Its printed pattern survives after the cloth itself traveled far from its workshop. This small museum object supplies physical evidence for the overseas reach of Gujarati textiles.

passages.title: Capitals, ports and skilled hands
passages.text: Another cotton fragment, probably from Ahmedabad, used wax to keep parts of the fabric from absorbing indigo dye. Removing the resist revealed the pattern. Flowers and geometric shapes emerged from a carefully planned sequence of covering and coloring, a little like drawing a picture that only appears after its bath.

passages.title: Homes, errands and the work of water
passages.text: Excavations at Champaner distinguish spacious compounds with gardens, animal areas and servants’ quarters from modest houses with one to three rooms. Some smaller homes shared protective compound walls. The capital contained different household budgets, not a city full of miniature palaces.

passages.title: Homes, errands and the work of water
passages.text: Shops stood along roads and at junctions; many occupied a single room, while larger ones could have underground storage. Archaeologists also recorded gravel road surfaces and stone paving on slopes. Shopping, storing goods and moving animals helped shape the city’s everyday layout.

passages.title: Homes, errands and the work of water
passages.text: The capital used a landscape of rainwater catchments, embankments, tanks, channels, wells and cisterns, including older works on the hill. Collecting seasonal rain required people to understand slopes and runoff. A tank’s water supply began well beyond the tank itself.

passages.title: Homes, errands and the work of water
passages.text: Some tanks serving mosques and wealthy houses had waterproof plaster and drains placed low enough to empty them for cleaning. Even an elegant water tank needed maintenance. Its practical plumbing mattered alongside the carved architecture around it.

passages.title: Homes, errands and the work of water
passages.text: In 1499, Rudabai funded the Adalaj stepwell from her own treasury. Women could be substantial architectural patrons, commissioning structures that joined access to water with elaborate stonework. The surviving work has firmer historical footing than romantic stories later told about its patron.

passages.title: Homes, errands and the work of water
passages.text: Bai Harir, a senior woman in the royal household, sponsored another remarkable well near Ahmedabad. Its Sanskrit inscription dates to 1499 and presents water as a benefit for living beings, including people, animals and plants. Public usefulness could be part of a patron’s claim to lasting remembrance.

passages.title: Homes, errands and the work of water
passages.text: The stepwell exhibition’s historians describe water collection as women’s work and wells as places for meeting and conversation. Their account spans a long history rather than one recorded day. Descending into a cooler space could bring a social pause into a demanding household chore.

passages.title: Words, learning and discoveries
passages.text: Bai Harir’s well carries the Sanskrit invocation नमामि विश्वकर्माणं, literally “I bow to Vishvakarman.” The words address the divine craftsman. This is a short passage in Nagari script from a real dedicatory inscription, rather than a reconstructed conversation between ordinary residents.

passages.title: Words, learning and discoveries
passages.text: Two illustrated Jain Kalpasutra leaves from Gujarat, dated about 1450, use costly blue pigment and gold. Donating such manuscripts to monastic libraries earned religious merit and supported learning. Beautiful books were valuable possessions that donors deliberately placed in a community’s care.

passages.title: Words, learning and discoveries
passages.text: The Kalpasutra’s wider religious life includes teaching monks and lay followers, recitation and ritual processions during Paryushan. The Walters manuscript account helps explain why a book might be listened to, carried and honored as well as read. These practices belong to the Shvetambara Jain tradition described by the museum.

passages.title: Words, learning and discoveries
passages.text: Modern conservators have used X-rays and infrared imaging to investigate drawings beneath Jain manuscript paintings. One studied leaf comes from Gujarat around the late fifteenth or early sixteenth century. Scientific imaging can uncover stages of an artist’s work without peeling away the finished picture.

passages.title: Later changes and surviving places
passages.text: Champaner ceased to be the capital and was abandoned as a royal city in 1536. Its later history still included village life and pilgrimage on Pavagadh. Palace ruins record a political departure; they do not mean that every person left the surrounding landscape forever.

passages.title: Later changes and surviving places
passages.text: A Mughal painting made around 1590 to 1595 celebrates Akbar’s Gujarat campaign and the 1573 victory at Surat. It was produced after the events for an imperial history. Its dramatic scene tells us about how the victors wanted their conquest remembered.

Akbar conquered the sultanate in 1572 and 1573. Muzaffar III later renewed resistance, including in 1583, but Gujarat became a Mughal province. Trade and skilled production continued through the political transition. The map’s 1500 endpoint falls decades before that conquest.

sectionTitles: Cloth, memory and learning to write

passages.text: Gunadule, also called Guna, Kuna or Tule, communities live in Colombia and Panama. This imported outline lies around Colombian Urabá and Darién, rather than covering the whole people or a later Panamanian comarca. Its 1492-1500 dates are map coverage. The relationship between early colonial populations and today’s Gunadule requires more care than a single colored polygon can convey.

passages.title: History, households and collective decisions
passages.text: ICANH traces Gunadule names in Spanish chronicles to around 1610, including Tunacunas, Cunacunas and Darienes. Communities defended their independence and sometimes allied with English and French privateers against Spanish power. Such alliances were part of regional politics, rather than evidence that everyone followed one distant ruler.

passages.title: History, households and collective decisions
passages.text: At the Darién museum, Gunadule and Emberá voices describe sacred histories carried by community authorities and passed to children. Their accounts connect living communities to the landscape. ICANH also notes uncertainty about the identity of earlier inhabitants, presenting distinct kinds of evidence side by side.

passages.title: History, households and collective decisions
passages.text: Colombian Gunadule communities include Caimán Nuevo in Antioquia and Arquía in Chocó. Panamanian communities have different regional arrangements. These places belong to a connected people, but their local authorities and territorial histories should not be flattened into one modern province.

passages.title: History, households and collective decisions
passages.text: The Colombian self-assessment describes extended households in which married daughters could remain with their parents while husbands joined their wives’ families. It also records riverside houses with palm roofs, cane or bamboo walls and earth floors. This describes a particular documented household pattern, not every family’s home.

passages.title: History, households and collective decisions
passages.text: The same study describes the community congress as a central place for decisions. Chiefs, spokespeople, community officers and specialists in plants and therapeutic songs had recognized roles. Public discussion linked practical government with the knowledge held by different members of the community.

passages.title: History, households and collective decisions
passages.text: Artesanías de Colombia describes farming and fishing as historical foundations of Gunadule subsistence. Textile work also earns money for households in Caimán Nuevo and Arquía. Making a beautiful blouse can therefore connect artistic knowledge with buying the other things a family needs.

passages.title: Cloth, memory and learning to write
passages.text: The Gold Museum collection includes a recent Gunadule blouse decorated with a geometric mola, catalogue A00660. Its recorded dimensions are 31.5 by 41 centimeters. The design is made from layers of cloth joined with needle and thread, a compact object holding a great deal of patient work.

passages.title: Cloth, memory and learning to write
passages.text: Mola makers use both geometric and recognizable figurative designs. Artesanías de Colombia identifies these as different categories of work. The precision comes from applying cloth to cloth: a vivid pattern depends on tiny stitches as much as on bold colors.

passages.title: Cloth, memory and learning to write
passages.text: In the 2016 study of protective molas, participants connect designs with caring for girls, women, the community and the Earth. These are spiritual meanings explained by the people who preserve them. A pattern may carry responsibilities and stories as well as decoration.

passages.title: Cloth, memory and learning to write
passages.text: The study describes a sagla, a community authority, drawing protective mola designs with a notebook, pencil and ruler. Designs remembered through teaching become new drawings. This documented visual practice is distinct from writing spoken sentences with an alphabet.

passages.title: Cloth, memory and learning to write
passages.text: A short alphabetic sample appears as a heading in the 2016 article: “Anmala gunadulemala bia daniggi”, translated alongside it as “Where do we Gunadule come from?” It is a modern published witness to the language, separate from the patterned visual language of molas.

passages.title: Cloth, memory and learning to write
passages.text: The museum’s learning activity explains that Guna girls in Colombian Urabá and Panama’s Caribbean communities learn to sew mola designs for their blouses. Lessons can take place through watching and practicing. The cloth becomes something to wear and something through which skill passes between generations.

passages.title: Cloth, memory and learning to write
passages.text: The 2009 Colombian language assessment found that families were the main setting for learning Tule. It also discussed a curriculum designed with community authorities and knowledgeable elders, alongside parents’ desire for Spanish and mathematics. Education involved choosing how several kinds of knowledge could fit together.

The map cutoff is not the end of the Gunadule. Communities persist in Colombia and Panama, with their own authorities, language teaching and artistic knowledge. This Colombian outline is not a substitute for the separate histories of Panamanian comarcas.

passages.text: Gunditjmara people maintain a living relationship with Country in south-western Victoria. At Budj Bim, generations shaped waterways into an aquaculture landscape. The map's imported date range describes its snapshots, not the beginning or end of Gunditjmara society.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Builders used volcanic stone to redirect water through channels, weirs and dams. These connected structures trapped, held and harvested kooyang, the short-finned eel.

passages.title: Science and environment
passages.text: Aquaculture depended on knowledge of seasonal eel movement, water flow and wetland ecology. Water management and food production were linked practices.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Kurtonitj preserves stone house sites alongside eel traps, channels and trees used for smoking eels. Settlement and food processing belong in the same landscape.

passages.title: Arts and knowledge
passages.text: Storytelling, dance and basket weaving transmit knowledge across generations. Fibre baskets also belong to the practical technology of eel harvesting.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: A cultural weir restored traditional flows into Tae Rak after earlier drainage. Gunditjmara customary responsibilities and cultural connections continue today.

passages.text: The Guptas ruled a large part of northern India during a period of influential mathematics, Sanskrit learning and religious art. Surviving temples, inscriptions and metalwork reveal the skills of craftspeople and the ambitions of patrons. These achievements belonged to a wider South Asian world: a work described as Gupta-period was not necessarily commissioned by a Gupta emperor.

passages.title: Mathematics and astronomy
passages.text: Aryabhata completed the Aryabhatiya at Kusumapura, usually associated with Pataliputra. It brings together mathematical rules and astronomical calculation, including a sine table and an approximation of pi equal to 3.1416.

passages.title: Mathematics and astronomy
passages.text: His method called kuttaka reduces problems about whole-number solutions to smaller steps. Such mathematics helped address astronomical questions about recurring planetary periods.

passages.title: Mathematics and astronomy
passages.text: Aryabhata used an alphabetic system to express numbers. Historians infer familiarity with place value, but that is different from a securely dated claim that he or the Gupta court invented the written zero.

passages.title: Metalworking and its surviving evidence
passages.text: The iron pillar now at Delhi's Qutb complex is associated with Chandragupta II. Its survival offers material evidence of skilled ironworking; its present location alone does not identify its original setting.

passages.title: Metalworking and its surviving evidence
passages.text: Analysis of the pillar's rust identified a protective layer containing iron phosphate. The study connects its unusual corrosion resistance to phosphorus in the iron and repeated wetting and drying, rather than to iron that never rusts.

passages.title: Art, architecture and belief
passages.text: A sandstone seated Buddha from Uttar Pradesh, now at the Metropolitan Museum, is dated to the first quarter of the fifth century. It is a specific surviving example of Gupta-period sculpture; the collection record does not establish an excavated findspot.

passages.title: Art, architecture and belief
passages.text: At Bhitargaon, builders used brick for a temple with a tall spire and terracotta panels of deities. India's heritage nomination dates it to the middle of the fifth century on stylistic grounds and leaves its dedication to Vishnu or Shiva unresolved.

passages.title: Art, architecture and belief
passages.text: The early sixth-century temple at Deogarh preserves elaborate stone carving and part of its tower. Alongside Bhitargaon, it shows that builders developed temple forms in different materials, rather than following a single construction technique.

passages.title: Art, architecture and belief
passages.text: Ajanta's later Buddhist caves belong to the same broad cultural period, but their patrons were Vakataka rulers and their feudatories. Their paintings should not be presented as a commission of the Gupta imperial court.

passages.title: Daily life, work and exchange
passages.text: The Mandsaur silk-weavers' inscription describes craftspeople moving from Lata to Dashapura with children and relatives. It preserves a community's account of migration and skilled work, although its praise of the city is commemorative poetry, not a household survey.

passages.title: Daily life, work and exchange
passages.text: The guild commemorated repairs to a Sun temple it had financed from its craft earnings. The inscription recalls the original foundation in 437 to 438 CE, showing artisans pooling resources for worship and maintenance across generations.

passages.title: Daily life, work and exchange
passages.text: Provincial and district officials governed alongside village institutions. Inscriptions also record trade guilds, while control of western ports connected the empire with overseas commerce. These institutions help explain the world beyond the royal court.

passages.title: Traditions beyond the dynasty
passages.text: Gupta-period sculptors developed Buddha images that influenced later Buddhist art across Asia. An artistic tradition could travel beyond the empire and outlast its rulers; the political endpoint of a dynasty is not the end of its cultural influence.

Gupta imperial rule broke apart through regional independence and repeated invasions, rather than one conquest by a single successor. Maitraka and Maukhari rulers were among the powers that emerged. Around 550 marks the conventional end of the imperial dynasty; communities and artistic traditions continued under changing governments.

sectionTitles: A large kingdom made from many local relationships
Fields, water, lamps and a useful zero
An educated household, poetry lessons and a written word

passages.text: The Gurjara-Pratiharas became a major north Indian power, moving their political center from western India to Kannauj. Their imperial history extends from the late eighth into the early eleventh century. The map’s 800 to 1000 dates cover only part of that history; its sweeping outline cannot show changing alliances or uneven control over individual districts.

passages.title: A large kingdom made from many local relationships
passages.text: Bhoja and Mahendrapala presided over the dynasty’s greatest power. Expansion brought conflict with the Palas in the east and the Rashtrakutas farther south and west. Holding such a large realm meant retaining the cooperation of powerful regional families as well as winning battles. Those subordinate rulers later became some of the kingdom’s strongest competitors.

passages.title: A large kingdom made from many local relationships
passages.text: Kings supported Brahmana recipients with grants of land, while their subordinate rulers were especially prominent temple patrons. These gifts helped turn religious relationships into political support. A temple inscription can therefore introduce several levels of power at once: the king, the local officer who commissioned a building, and the people supplying its daily needs.

passages.title: A large kingdom made from many local relationships
passages.text: At Pehowa, an inscription associated with Bhojadeva and dated 882 records a voluntary contribution from traders to maintain temples there and elsewhere. Commerce and worship met in an organized collection system. The record gives merchants a visible role in supporting public religious institutions, rather than leaving the entire story to kings and their armies.

passages.title: Fields, water, lamps and a useful zero
passages.text: Gwalior’s 876 endowment names cultivators Dallaka and Memmaka. Their two fields were described by the quantity of barley seed needed to sow them, with boundaries including rocks, another field and a water channel. This is wonderfully practical paperwork: a grand religious gift still needed someone to say exactly which patch of farmland was meant.

passages.title: Fields, water, lamps and a useful zero
passages.text: The same Gwalior record lists oil workers and guild leaders from several towns. They promised a measured amount of oil from each press every month to keep temple lamps burning. Religious lighting depended on repeated work, contributions and deliveries. The gift was an ongoing supply arrangement, not simply one impressive ceremonial donation.

passages.title: Fields, water, lamps and a useful zero
passages.text: A famous zero survives in this 876 Gwalior inscription. It describes a flower garden measuring 270 by 187 royal hastas and a daily supply of 50 garlands. Small circular zeros appear in 270 and 50. Here a mathematical notation helped record land and flowers: a memorable reminder that numbers had useful jobs outside a classroom.

passages.title: Fields, water, lamps and a useful zero
passages.text: A rock inscription at Rakhetra, dated around 942 to 943, records irrigation works on the river Urvasi, now called the Urra, provided by Vinayakapaladeva. It also preserves the writer’s name, Bhailadaman, son of Krishnaraja. Water management required construction, but its public record also needed somebody skilled at composing or writing the text.

passages.title: Carving buildings and telling stories
passages.text: At Gwalior, the Caturbhuj temple was excavated directly from rock. Its lintel inscription identifies Alla, an officer of Mihira Bhoja, as the commissioner. Making a building this way meant removing stone to create the space inside it. The surviving inscription connects that striking structure to a named official rather than an anonymous royal order.

passages.title: Carving buildings and telling stories
passages.text: Archaeological clearance at Vishvamitra Ka Tila in Pehowa uncovered stone sculptures showing episodes from the Ramayana and Mahabharata, as well as a baked-brick temple plinth. The official heritage account dates the site to around the ninth century. The finds show epic storytelling taking material form through the work of sculptors at a religious site.

passages.title: Carving buildings and telling stories
passages.text: A tenth-century sculpture from central India probably represents the goddess Gauri. A surviving hand holds a lotus bearing the elephant-headed Ganesha, while an iguana-like creature appears at her feet. Small women beside the goddess are interpreted as donors. The sculpture brings divine family imagery and human worshippers into one carefully carved object.

passages.title: An educated household, poetry lessons and a written word
passages.text: The court poet Rajashekhara served Mahendrapala at Kannauj. His wife Avantisundari was educated in literary criticism, and he quoted her opinions in his Kavyamimamsa. This particular household preserves a woman’s intellectual contribution through her husband’s surviving work. It offers a glimpse of learned family life without telling us how schooling worked in every home.

passages.title: An educated household, poetry lessons and a written word
passages.text: Rajashekhara’s Kavyamimamsa offered aspiring poets much more than advice about finding a rhyme. It discussed learning, talent, borrowing ideas without sliding into plagiarism, and describing the right plants, birds and seasons. He also recognized women’s poetic ability. Good writing demanded observation and study as well as imagination; even a court poet had homework.

passages.title: An educated household, poetry lessons and a written word
passages.text: His proposed daily routine for a poet included morning worship, reading, writing, a poetry discussion after lunch, evening socializing and sleep. This was advice for an ideal literary life, rather than a diary of everybody’s day. A gathering where people debated poems was part of the work, not merely time off from it.

passages.title: An educated household, poetry lessons and a written word
passages.text: The Sanskrit word “विष्णवे” (viṣṇave), meaning “to Vishnu,” appears in the opening invocation of Gwalior’s 876 endowment. This is a normalized Devanagari transcription of the word; the stone uses the older Siddhamatrika script. Its religious opening leads into very concrete records of land, lamp oil and flowers.

During the tenth century, regional lords gained independence and the empire contracted. Pratihara rule at Kannauj continued into the early eleventh century, beyond this map record’s endpoint. Its political fragmentation created space for other dynasties; it did not mean that farmers, merchants, temples or literary traditions suddenly disappeared in 1000.

sectionTitles: Discoveries: food and tools at Siriki
Homes that respond to family and climate
Building communities and places to learn

passages.text: Guyana’s everyday history joins practical skills with family and community life. Homes, public institutions, migration records and living craft traditions reveal different experiences of making a place to live, learn and gather.

passages.title: Discoveries: food and tools at Siriki
passages.text: At Siriki, a shell mound in northwestern Guyana, excavation found quantities of striped-snail shells alongside fish and mammal remains. A sample near its base dates broadly to the third millennium BCE. These food remains suggest a varied diet, rather than people living on shellfish alone.

passages.title: Discoveries: food and tools at Siriki
passages.text: Siriki also yielded quartz cores, worked flakes, bifaces and scrapers. The cores suggest tools were being made or reshaped there. Researchers could not determine exactly what the flakes cut. An archaeologist’s toolbox includes uncertainty: a sharp edge does not come with a label saying what was for dinner.

passages.title: Homes that respond to family and climate
passages.text: After emancipation, some African-descended families built modest cottages that expanded as their resources and households grew. The National Trust describes dividing a main room to give a new couple separate sleeping space. Cooking and toilet facilities initially occupied yard outbuildings. These arrangements changed over time, rather than following one permanent household plan.

passages.title: Homes that respond to family and climate
passages.text: The Demerara window combines a sash window with an angled, louvred outer shutter. It admits breezes while providing shade and shelter from rain. The National Trust describes a ledge where ice could be placed to cool incoming air. This ingenious arrangement does not mean every household could obtain or afford ice.

passages.title: Homes that respond to family and climate
passages.text: Ornamental iron cresting on some historic roofs did more than look impressive. The National Trust explains that it discouraged birds from roosting and fouling rainwater collected for household use. It was a decorative version of a do-not-perch sign, with a practical connection to the water supply.

passages.title: Homes that respond to family and climate
passages.text: Camp Street Koker in Georgetown is thought to date from the nineteenth century, when it served irrigation at Plantation Thomas. Around 1938, it received concrete support posts and improved lifting gear. This working structure preserves a history of managing water for cultivated land. Repairs and altered machinery can be part of a monument’s story, alongside its original construction.

passages.title: Building communities and places to learn
passages.text: In 1839, eighty-three formerly enslaved men and women pooled resources to buy Northbrook plantation on the East Coast of Demerara. It became the village of Victoria. A title document completed in 1841 included the original proprietors’ names. The purchase shows people working together to gain land and establish community life beyond plantation control.

passages.title: Building communities and places to learn
passages.text: Georgetown’s Public Free Library opened in 1909 in a building designed by Leonard Percival Hodge. An upper floor added in 1935 accommodated parts of the British Guiana Museum until it moved in 1951. Books and museum collections thus shared a building for a time, bringing different kinds of learning under one roof.

passages.title: Building communities and places to learn
passages.text: At a craft demonstration in Sophia in June 2019, older Indigenous craftspeople showed students skills including Macushi hammock weaving and basketry. Students from schools and the university attended. Such demonstrations make expertise visible through movements and materials. Knowing a language and knowing every craft are different skills, and young people can keep learning from those with more experience.

passages.title: Care, sanitation and family memories
passages.text: After 1894, Georgetown hospital’s maternity ward moved away from laundry fumes into a brighter, larger space. A 1908 account described mosquito nets on the children’s ward’s thirty cots. These details reveal attention to the surroundings of care. They do not establish that every family could reach the hospital or that childbirth there was safe.

passages.title: Care, sanitation and family memories
passages.text: Revised Demerara dairy rules published in 1912 barred using a dairy as a sleeping room and required separation from toilets and cesspools. A milk supply involved buildings, water, containers and people, as well as cows. The rules reveal what officials wanted to change; protests and enforcement problems show that a regulation was not the same as everyday reality.

passages.title: Care, sanitation and family memories
passages.text: Guyana’s National Archives preserves records of Indian indentured labour covering 1838 to 1917. These official documents contain personal information that can help descendants research ancestors and migration. They also record a system of colonial control. Reading them alongside family memories can recover individual stories without mistaking an official’s categories for a person’s whole identity.

passages.title: Care, sanitation and family memories
passages.text: A March 2025 account of Phagwah, also called Holi, describes gatherings with coloured powder, music and sweets such as sweet rice and peera. Families, friends and neighbours join the celebrations. The festival has Hindu religious meaning as well as a lively social life. In the midst of all that colour, remembering the original shade of your shirt might take concentration.

British colonial government ended with independence in 1966. Guyana became a republic in 1970, and its constitutional institutions changed again in 1980. The country and its communities continue, sharing craft knowledge, family memories and celebrations across generations.

sectionTitles: A home that was also a print shop

passages.text: This map label begins when the Habsburgs ruled much of the Low Countries, but it spans a great political split. Charles V yielded authority to Philip II in 1555. Religious persecution, demands for local rights and revolt led northern provinces to renounce Philip in 1581 and form a republic in 1588. Antwerp and much of the south remained under Habsburg government; war and a 1609 truce divided families and trade routes. The Plantin-Moretus house in Antwerp preserves a vivid example of family work, literacy, printing and illness, though it was a prosperous household, not everyone’s experience. In 1648 Spain recognized northern independence while retaining southern lands. The imported 1650 endpoint is map coverage, not the end of the southern Netherlands.

passages.title: One label, several political stories
passages.text: Charles V’s Habsburg lands included the Low Countries; in 1555 he passed rule to his son Philip II. Province, language and religion all mattered, so a single “Habsburg Netherlands” name can hide many loyalties.

passages.title: One label, several political stories
passages.text: Philip II’s religious policy and attempts to strengthen his authority provoked resistance. In 1581 rebellious provinces formally withdrew their obedience; the northern republic emerged in 1588. This did not make the southern provinces cease to be Habsburg lands.

passages.title: One label, several political stories
passages.text: Antwerp surrendered after a siege in 1585. Printer Christophe Plantin had worked in both Antwerp and Leiden during the conflict, then returned to Antwerp under Spanish rule. A map line could run through someone’s customers and relatives.

passages.title: One label, several political stories
passages.text: Archduke Albert and Isabella governed the southern Netherlands around 1600. The 1609 truce with the northern Republic allowed some movement and trade across the border; fighting resumed when it expired in 1621.

passages.title: One label, several political stories
passages.text: The Peace of Münster in 1648 made Spain recognize the northern Republic as independent. Spain and the Republic kept territories they then held, so the southern Habsburg Netherlands continued beyond this map record’s 1650 endpoint.

passages.title: A home that was also a print shop
passages.text: In Antwerp, the Plantin-Moretus workshop put type setters, press workers and proofreaders together. At its peak, more than sixty people worked there. Printing a book meant teamwork long before a copy could reach a reader.

passages.title: A home that was also a print shop
passages.text: Plantin’s daughters learned to read and write young and helped correct proofs. That is a striking example of girls’ education inside one skilled family business; most children did not grow up next to a printing press.

passages.title: A home that was also a print shop
passages.text: The print house held a family, apprentices, servants and maids as well as presses. Women helped run the business, and widows could keep it going. The boundary between “homework” and paid work was often a doorway.

passages.title: A home that was also a print shop
passages.text: A family member once worked, ate and slept with others in a room only about 3.5 by 4.5 meters. The prosperous firm had grander rooms too, but crowded space was still a real part of its history.

passages.title: A home that was also a print shop
passages.text: A Rubens design for this workshop carried “Labore et Constantia,” Latin for “through work and steadfastness.” Those three written words were the printer’s motto, stamped into a world of books and ideas.

passages.title: Bodies, water and everyday worries
passages.text: A 1589 family letter about Plantin’s last illness mentions doctors, a painful swelling and fever. It shows care and medical explanation in one household; it cannot tell us how every sick person was treated.

passages.title: Bodies, water and everyday worries
passages.text: Antwerp pharmacist Pieter Coudenberg grew plants for medicine and wrote a dispensatory. His remedies and botanical work show the period’s interest in healing, even when medicine could not stop many deadly infections.

passages.title: Bodies, water and everyday worries
passages.text: Seventeenth-century household digs in northern Amsterdam have found water cisterns and cesspits, with broken pots and dishes inside. A household’s toilet pit can become an archaeologist’s treasure chest, but this northern example is not a survey of every southern home.

passages.title: Bodies, water and everyday worries
passages.text: War, religious policy and migration changed where families could live and what they could publish. Plantin’s move between Leiden and Antwerp is one documented example of choices made under pressure, not just a tale of kings and armies.

The unified Habsburg Low Countries broke apart during the revolt. By 1648 the northern Republic had recognized independence, while Spain kept southern lands. The imported map label ends in 1650; the Habsburg southern provinces, Dutch Republic and their peoples continued beyond it.

sectionTitles: Incense, shipping and a working port
Building upward and working with local materials
A written place name and a metalworker’s correction

passages.text: Ancient Hadramawt was a South Arabian kingdom centred on Shabwa, connected with oasis farming and Arabian trade. Its recorded history begins before the map’s 323 BCE start, and independence ended around 300 CE, before the imported 500 cutoff. The outline is seriously incomplete: it includes eastern territory toward Dhofar but omits Shabwa and the port of Qana to the west. This card concerns the ancient kingdom and its communities, not the separate medieval “Hadramaut” record.

passages.title: Incense, shipping and a working port
passages.text: Frankincense is aromatic tree resin, rather than a flower or a manufactured perfume. Eastern communities collected it in Hadramawt and Dhofar, and merchants carried it toward the Mediterranean and other markets. People burned it in worship and used aromatic materials in perfumes and preparations. Its value linked rural producers with rulers, temples, traders and distant customers.

passages.title: Incense, shipping and a working port
passages.text: The coastal outpost of Sumhuram, at Khor Rori in today’s Oman, gathered incense for shipping toward Qana. From there, cargo could enter wider networks reaching the Mediterranean. Sea transport developed alongside older land routes; the kingdom’s commercial story was more complicated than one uninterrupted camel caravan crossing Arabia.

passages.title: Incense, shipping and a working port
passages.text: At Qana, excavators uncovered houses and a storeroom, together with hundreds of bronze coins and pottery from Africa and the Mediterranean. These finds help reconstruct a functioning port where people lived, stored goods and made transactions. Imported pots demonstrate connections, but they do not identify the nationality of every person who used them.

passages.title: Farms, kitchens and seasonal water
passages.text: Not everyone lived in an imposing tower house. Two homes excavated beside an oasis canal near Shabwa had mudbrick walls joined with pink mortar, sometimes finished with red plaster. Their ground floors contained storage rooms and kitchens. Coins from the second and third centuries CE help place these households within the ancient kingdom’s later history.

passages.title: Farms, kitchens and seasonal water
passages.text: Those canal-side kitchens yielded cooking pots, jars, bowls, grinding stones and mortars. These are practical traces of preparing and keeping food. Their inhabitants needed space for work and supplies as well as shelter. A jar full of provisions could matter more to supper than all the splendid decoration in the royal palace.

passages.title: Farms, kitchens and seasonal water
passages.text: Around Shabwa, old field boundaries and waterworks survive across areas now largely uncultivated. Pierre Gentelle’s survey combined aerial photographs with walking the ground, mapping features and collecting pottery and other finds. This joined landscape evidence with objects: an abandoned channel could help explain a city just as much as a carved inscription.

passages.title: Farms, kitchens and seasonal water
passages.text: Farmers diverted seasonal floodwater into channels and distributed it among prepared fields. The water also deposited fertile silt, slowly raising ground levels and complicating irrigation. Early in the third century CE, King Ili’azz Yalut commissioned a sluice at a new canal’s head. Keeping water useful required repeated adjustments, not simply building a dam once.

passages.title: Building upward and working with local materials
passages.text: Shabwa’s substantial houses stood on stone platforms, with upper storeys built using timber frames and mudbrick. Some rubble-filled foundation compartments were once mistaken for tombs or storage rooms. Examining how the walls fitted together changed the interpretation: a solid compartment supporting a building is not necessarily a room anyone could enter.

passages.title: Building upward and working with local materials
passages.text: Staircases linked the upper floors. In the royal palace, surviving mudbrick steps and traces of timber-supported flights help archaeologists reconstruct movement through the building. Building 72 had an unusual stone staircase. Upper rooms and household arrangements are partly reconstructed; the remains do not tell us that ancient men and women always occupied separate floors.

passages.title: Building upward and working with local materials
passages.text: Roof water needed a way down without soaking the walls. Excavators found gutters with bull-head spouts at Shabwa. Their decoration gave an animal face to a useful building part. Ancient architecture included such small practical decisions as well as monumental entrances and impressive heights.

passages.title: Building upward and working with local materials
passages.text: Shabwa also stood on a salt dome that was mined in antiquity. Salt supplied a local resource and a source of income alongside the city’s trade connections. The capital’s economy therefore involved extraction and work in its immediate surroundings, as well as luxury goods arriving from far away.

passages.title: Worship and skilled crafts
passages.text: A calcite incense burner associated with Shabwa shows a rider seated in front of a camel’s hump. The museum dates it tentatively to the third century CE. It stands 32 centimetres high, yet its shallow top holds only about 30 millilitres. The grand-looking carving had a surprisingly small working bowl.

passages.title: Worship and skilled crafts
passages.text: At Sumhuram, the temple dedicated to Sin included an altar, basins interpreted as places for ritual washing, and a kitchen for preparing ritual meals. Worship could involve water, food and shared activity as well as incense. These installations belong to a sanctuary; they are not evidence of bathrooms or healthcare in every home.

passages.title: Worship and skilled crafts
passages.text: Sumhuram’s furnaces, crucibles and ironworking waste show that the port also contained workshops. Archaeologists recovered many stone and bronze tools. Cargo did not simply pass through an empty warehouse beside the sea: residents made and repaired things in a settlement with its own working life.

passages.title: A written place name and a metalworker’s correction
passages.text: A bronze plaque from Sumhuram preserves “𐩨𐩪𐩣𐩠𐩧𐩣”, b-S¹mhrm, meaning “at Sumhuram”. These are modern typeset Old South Arabian letters for a Hadramitic phrase in line 3 of inscription KR 11. Excavated in 2013, the dedication is provisionally dated to the first century CE from its floor context and letter forms.

passages.title: A written place name and a metalworker’s correction
passages.text: That plaque was made by lost-wax casting and had already been repaired in antiquity. The maker also misjudged the space for its inscription: the last two letters of the donor’s name were added at the text’s end. Even an expensive bronze dedication could need the ancient equivalent of squeezing in a forgotten word.

passages.title: War, rebuilding and continuing settlement
passages.text: A sack of Shabwa around 225 to 230 CE badly damaged the royal palace. Hadramawt’s rulers subsequently returned and rebuilt above surviving foundations. The kingdom survived this interruption. Fourth-century Himyarite occupation belongs to a later political phase.

passages.title: War, rebuilding and continuing settlement
passages.text: At Qana, painted and inscribed Greek fragments date to the fourth century CE, after the kingdom had lost independence. Excavation also shows that the port lasted until the beginning of the Islamic era. A political border could change while buildings, shipping connections and the daily work of a coastal community continued.

Hadramawt lost its independence to Himyar around 300 CE, following regional warfare. This occurred before the map’s 500 endpoint. Its communities did not vanish together: Qana continued into the beginning of the Islamic era. The later medieval Hadramaut record concerns a different political setting, not an uninterrupted continuation of this ancient kingdom.
