passages.text: The atlas calls this layer “Hadramaut” and marks it as a state from about 1000 to 1715. Its own borders tell a messier story. The 1000 polygon joins Wadi Hadramawt to Mahra and Dhofar; by 1492 it reaches deep into southern Oman; in 1530 it suddenly contracts to a Hadramawt core. Real history contained ports, valley towns, tribes, learned families and changing local dynasties, sometimes under wider Ayyubid or Rasulid claims. The ancient Kingdom of Hadramawt had ended centuries earlier, so it is not this state reborn. Sharma’s excavated warehouses held pottery and goods arriving from China, India, the Gulf and East Africa. Al-Shihr exported fish, incense and ambergris. Farmers directed rare floodwater across fields, while builders repeatedly repaired tall mudbrick homes. Shibam’s famous sanitation was clever: house shafts separated waste, and dried material helped fertilize gardens, an entire city partly organized around toilets! Families, merchants, craftspeople, herders, scholars and enslaved people did not share equal power. Tarim became a center of Arabic learning, but surviving chronicles favor prominent men and genealogies, so ordinary women and children are harder to see. The map’s 1715 disappearance records an atlas category change, not the end of Hadramawt or its people.

passages.title: First, read the map cautiously
passages.text: The indexed record says “Hadramaut,” state, circa 1000 to 1715, but its twelve border files do not trace one verifiable government. The coverage is continuous as map data; political unity is not. This card therefore treats the id as an editorial territorial umbrella whose contents change.

passages.title: First, read the map cautiously
passages.text: The imported paragraph stretches Hadramawt across modern Hadramawt, Shabwah, Mahra, Dhofar and beyond. A scholarly regional reference instead distinguishes a stricter wadi-centered meaning from broad geographical usage. A modern administrative list cannot be projected backward as a medieval border or government.

passages.title: First, read the map cautiously
passages.text: Ancient Hadramawt was a kingdom centered on Shabwa and connected to Qana, but it ended around the third century CE. Medieval Arabic writers later used Hadramawt geographically. Calling the atlas’s 1000 layer that ancient kingdom revived would skip roughly seven centuries and invent continuity.

passages.title: First, read the map cautiously
passages.text: At 1492 the polygon includes Hadramawt cities, Dhofar, Mahra and tested points as far east as Mahout in Oman. In 1530 those eastern places split among Mahra, Gharra and Oman layers. That crisp switch exposes cartographic classification, not a surveyed frontier changing overnight.

passages.title: First, read the map cautiously
passages.text: Historians face another warning: medieval Hadrami documentation is scarce, and surviving accounts can promote genealogy or clan honor. Archaeology, architecture and archives help check chronicles, but none makes ordinary lives fully visible. Uncertainty here is historical honesty, not an empty space to fill with legend.

passages.title: Wadis, coast, desert and precious water
passages.text: Hadramawt combines a deeply cut inland wadi system, high limestone plateaus, desert margins and an Arabian Sea coast. Communities at Tarim or Shibam faced different water, travel and work from fishers at al-Shihr. The atlas color hides those ecological differences inside one shape.

passages.title: Wadis, coast, desert and precious water
passages.text: Rain could be rare yet violent. Farmers guided short-lived floodwater with banks, dikes and channels, gaining water and fresh sediment while risking fields and houses. “Spate irrigation” means catching a rush, not turning the wadi into a permanently flowing river.

passages.title: Wadis, coast, desert and precious water
passages.text: Water management was also social. Studies of Wadi Sana connect runoff and landforms with water rights, territory and cooperation. A channel reveals engineering, but its repair required decisions about labor and shares. Environmental need alone cannot tell us who controlled the gate or received water first.

passages.title: Wadis, coast, desert and precious water
passages.text: A historical study records a 1348 flood that destroyed palms and about twenty mosques around Tarim. Floods could nourish agriculture and suddenly wreck it, so resilient settlement required rebuilding. Dates in chronicles are valuable, though one recorded disaster cannot stand for every valley or century.

passages.title: Wadis, coast, desert and precious water
passages.text: The early atlas border absorbs monsoon-influenced Dhofar, but al-Balid’s archaeology shows its own rulers and commercial history. Mahra surveys likewise identify separate ports east of al-Shihr. Geography connected these regions; it did not make their political histories, communities or economies interchangeable.

passages.title: Towns, rulers and negotiated power
passages.text: Tarim, Shibam, al-Shihr, Sayun and Mukalla were not five offices of one timeless capital. Sources name different ruling families and phases, including Rashidids, Ayyubid intervention, Rasulid claims, Tahirid competition and Kathiri expansion. Control could mean tribute, a governor, a garrison or temporary submission.

passages.title: Towns, rulers and negotiated power
passages.text: Rasulid rule linked Hadramawt to a larger Yemeni sultanate from the thirteenth through fifteenth centuries, yet local families sometimes governed on its behalf. Even Rasulid origin stories were reworked to claim South Arabian legitimacy. A dynasty’s genealogy was political argument as well as family history.

passages.title: Towns, rulers and negotiated power
passages.text: Mukalla offers a useful local timeline: a small port is recorded in 1035, al-Muzaffar fortified it in 1271, and an al-Kassadi emirate began in 1703. Those dates show urban and political change without making Mukalla the capital of the entire atlas polygon throughout.

passages.title: Towns, rulers and negotiated power
passages.text: Sayun Palace became Badr Abu Tuwayriq’s residence in 1519. Its ventilation shaft, rainwater drainage, mudbrick, timber and lime record craft as clearly as rulership. Later additions mean the present seven-story building cannot be treated as an unchanged photograph of the palace in 1519.

passages.title: Towns, rulers and negotiated power
passages.text: The 1715 map does not hand Mukalla, Shibam, Tarim, Sayun or al-Shihr to a single successor id. Hadramawt’s places and institutions continued, including separate local powers. The atlas endpoint is therefore a deletion in this dataset, not a documented state-wide surrender or cultural ending.

passages.title: Ports, crafts and an ocean of exchange
passages.text: Sharma was a specialized, fortified entrepôt active roughly 980 to 1180. Excavators found warehouses and goods moving through an Indian Ocean web; about seventy percent of pottery was imported from regions stretching from China to East Africa. A busy cargo stop was not necessarily a large family city.

passages.title: Ports, crafts and an ocean of exchange
passages.text: Al-Shihr’s evidence mixes texts with a carefully excavated tell. Sources describe dried and large fish, incense, ambergris and fine camels; Indian pots held or cooked foods and liquids. Because excavation covered only part of the oldest quarter, absence elsewhere is not proof a craft or food was missing.

passages.title: Ports, crafts and an ocean of exchange
passages.text: Surveyors recorded 174 sites along the Hadramawt to Mahra coast and identified several active ports of about the ninth to twelfth centuries. That distribution replaces the idea of one lonely harbor. Coastal communities could compete, specialize, decline or continue on different schedules.

passages.title: Ports, crafts and an ocean of exchange
passages.text: Mukalla’s seaside buildings later combined residence and storage for merchants and fishers linked with Africa and India. The nomination also describes much later Indian-influenced architecture, which this card does not back-project. Trade contact was old; every visible palace façade is not medieval.

passages.title: Ports, crafts and an ocean of exchange
passages.text: Merchants and scholars traveled through Aden, the Hejaz, Dhofar, India and farther shores, but “Hadrami network” did not mean every resident went overseas. Farmers, builders, herders, servants and children made local lives possible while a smaller number of travelers connected distant households and markets.

passages.title: Food came from fields, herds, sea and trade
passages.text: Spate-water fields and palms supported valley settlements, while sheep and camels used drier country. Medieval Yemen-wide agricultural writings discuss wheat, sorghum, dates, grapes, cotton and many other plants, but a Rasulid handbook is not a Hadramawt grocery receipt. Local proof must remain local.

passages.title: Food came from fields, herds, sea and trade
passages.text: Fish mattered especially on the coast. Al-Shihr redistributed large and dried fish toward Oman, Aden and Basra; some dried catch even fed animals. Inland households had different access, so the port’s famous products should not become a single daily menu for every Wadi family.

passages.title: Food came from fields, herds, sea and trade
passages.text: Archaeologists found imported cooking and storage pots associated with water, milk and foods at al-Shihr. Those ceramics came through ocean trade. Pots prove containers and connections more securely than recipes; nobody can reconstruct one “Hadrami dinner” from a shard alone.

passages.title: Food came from fields, herds, sea and trade
passages.text: Rasulid court records show lavish redistribution and food allotments to royal women and enslaved people. That is evidence of hierarchy and palace supply, not ordinary abundance. A ruler’s kitchen could display imported wealth while rural or urban workers faced very different portions and seasonal risks.

passages.title: Food came from fields, herds, sea and trade
passages.text: Wadi Daw’an is renowned today for honey, palms, farming and herding, and UNESCO presents these as long-lived traditions. Medieval beekeeping is plausible within that continuity, but the detailed modern landscape is later comparison. The safest fun fact remains that honey connects flowers, skilled hive care and trade.

passages.title: Mud homes, clothing, work and moments of fun
passages.text: Shibam’s dense tower houses used sun-dried mudbrick and rose above a floodplain inside defensive walls. The surviving urban ensemble is chiefly sixteenth century, with older mosque and castle elements. Families repeatedly replastered earthen walls, so maintenance was skilled work, not a sign that mud was primitive.

passages.title: Mud homes, clothing, work and moments of fun
passages.text: Wadi Daw’an builders mixed mud, straw and palm material and used stone, palm trunks and sidr wood. Villages perched on slopes or outcrops above cultivated ground. UNESCO describes living continuity; individual medieval houses still require dating rather than assuming every traditional technique stayed unchanged.

passages.title: Mud homes, clothing, work and moments of fun
passages.text: House plans organized storage, privacy, ventilation, work and waste vertically. Sayun Palace’s central shaft moved light and air, while Shibam’s towers reduced exposed ground area. Architecture gives clues to movement through rooms, yet it rarely tells which child slept where or who told bedtime jokes.

passages.title: Mud homes, clothing, work and moments of fun
passages.text: Textiles, leather and metal were promoted in Rasulid Yemen, and port trade moved cloth and other goods, but this record lacks a securely dated Hadramawt wardrobe. Clothing varied by wealth, work, gender and town. Illustrated later dress should not become a medieval uniform for everyone in the polygon.

passages.title: Mud homes, clothing, work and moments of fun
passages.text: We know people gathered for worship, markets, weddings, visits and seasonal work, but surviving sources preserve elite genealogies and disputes better than games or humor. A kid-readable card can admit that laughter surely happened while refusing to invent a favorite toy, punch line or festival rule.

passages.title: Families, women, children and social rank
passages.text: Kin groups and family reputation could shape protection, marriage, office, property and conflict. Shibam’s dense defenses partly answered rivalry among prominent families. That evidence does not make every household a feuding clan: neighbors also had to cooperate on walls, water, streets and fields.

passages.title: Families, women, children and social rank
passages.text: Chronicles often foreground sada lineages, scholars and rulers, which makes genealogy look like all of society. Knysh shows those pedigrees can carry agendas. Craftspeople, fishers, farmers, herders, servants and enslaved people remain less individually named, though their labor supported towns and elite institutions.

passages.title: Families, women, children and social rank
passages.text: Women appear in court allotments, kin histories and later Hadrami ethnography, but direct 1000 to 1715 evidence for ordinary women is uneven. It would be reckless to assign all weaving, farming or childcare to one gender. Tasks changed with place, status, wealth, age and household need.

passages.title: Families, women, children and social rank
passages.text: Children learned language, prayer, manners and practical skills within households and workplaces; some studied reading and religious texts with teachers. Tarim’s scholarly reputation documents institutions more clearly than enrollment. We cannot assume every boy attended or that girls never learned from literate relatives.

passages.title: Families, women, children and social rank
passages.text: Slavery was part of medieval Yemeni society, with enslaved people recorded as soldiers, cooks, concubines, quarry workers, merchandise, salary recipients and even officials. Those different lives shared legal unfreedom, not one experience. Evidence for Hadramawt specifically is scattered, so regional examples are labeled as such.

passages.title: Learning, belief, books and a local Arabic sample
passages.text: Hadramawt became strongly associated with Shafi‘i law and Sufi teaching, but neither spread in one simple wave. Historians must compare biographies, genealogies and institutional claims because later writers could magnify a founder or lineage. Religious history was lived locally and remembered competitively.

passages.title: Learning, belief, books and a local Arabic sample
passages.text: Tarim’s mosques, retreats and learning centers made it an important scholarly town. The famous al-Mihdar Mosque originated in the fifteenth century, though its striking present minaret and many palace influences are later. Buildings can preserve long learning traditions while changing form repeatedly.

passages.title: Learning, belief, books and a local Arabic sample
passages.text: Libraries in Tarim, Aynat and Mukalla preserve Arabic historical, legal, religious and medical manuscripts. Catalogs reveal what survived, not what every family read. Copy dates can be later than composition, damaged volumes lose context, and private collections make the surviving sample selective.

passages.title: Learning, belief, books and a local Arabic sample
passages.text: A Kathiri document archive begins in 1622, offering firmer evidence for administration, transactions and named actors near the end of this card. Paper archives are major achievements of record keeping, yet survival favors institutions and property disputes more than children’s conversations or workers’ jokes.

passages.title: Learning, belief, books and a local Arabic sample
passages.text: Local written-language sample: رسالة المعاونة والمظاهرة والمؤازرة, Risālat al-muʿāwanah wa-l-muẓāharah wa-l-muʾāzarah, “The Treatise of Assistance, Support, and Aid.” Tarim scholar ʿAbdallāh al-Ḥaddād composed this Arabic work in 1069 AH, or 1658 to 59 CE, securely inside the mapped interval. One author’s title does not speak for everyone.

passages.title: Health, healing, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Fifteenth-century scholar Baḥraq al-Hadrami wrote a didactic work on Galenic medicine. His career shows medical knowledge could circulate through scholars even where trained physicians were scarce. A learned text records recommended ideas; it cannot prove how every sick villager was diagnosed or treated.

passages.title: Health, healing, water and the toilet question
passages.text: A fourteenth-century Rasulid travel guide advised on thirst, hunger, fatigue, weather, illness, foods and medicinal plants. It illuminates knowledge available in Yemen’s learned world, especially to travelers, but it is not a field notebook from every Hadramawt household or proof each remedy worked.

passages.title: Health, healing, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Care also happened without formal doctors: relatives could bring water, food, rest and company, while religious teachers encouraged visiting sick people. These acts are historically plausible and partly textually visible, but archaeology rarely preserves a bowl beside a patient with a label saying who cared.

passages.title: Health, healing, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Shibam’s heritage system separated liquid and solid waste through house shafts and outlets. Dried solids could fertilize nearby gardens, linking toilets, agriculture and mudbrick production. The funny truth is technically serious: town planning partly followed poo. Dating each installation still requires building-level study.

passages.title: Health, healing, water and the toilet question
passages.text: No single toilet arrangement is proven for every town or all seven centuries. Water installations, flood channels, wells and waste paths needed maintenance, while contaminated water and crowding could spread illness even without germ theory. The evidence is strongest at Shibam and must stay there.

passages.title: Conflict, coercion, achievements and continuity
passages.text: Walls, hilltop villages, towers and forts reveal insecurity as well as prestige. Shibam’s compact houses offered refuge during family rivalry, while Sayun Palace began as a defensive fortress. Fortification never guarantees constant war; it records preparation, authority and the value placed on protected homes and stores.

passages.title: Conflict, coercion, achievements and continuity
passages.text: Portuguese expansion brought armed coercion to the Indian Ocean and violence at al-Shihr in the early sixteenth century. Hadrami chronicles are crucial but must be read beside other records. A raid affected sailors, merchants and families; it was not merely a colorful meeting of cultures.

passages.title: Conflict, coercion, achievements and continuity
passages.text: Local rulers, tribal forces, townspeople, religious mediators and outside dynasties bargained, fought and collected revenue. Wider states could claim tribute without managing every alley or field. Treating power as layered better explains why the atlas border can coexist with several named political actors.

passages.title: Conflict, coercion, achievements and continuity
passages.text: Major achievements were cooperative and cumulative: directing floods, maintaining fields, building and replastering tall earthen homes, operating ports, navigating sea routes, copying books and sustaining teaching networks. None belongs to one dynasty alone, and much depended on workers whose names the chronicles omitted.

passages.title: Conflict, coercion, achievements and continuity
passages.text: At 1715 the exact map layer ends, but Hadramawt does not. Local institutions, valley towns, scholarship, farming and maritime connections continued in changing forms. The honest ending is political and cartographic continuity: no invented fall, extinction, successor state or frozen modern border.

The exact atlas id disappears in 1715, but the border snapshot assigns no single successor to audited Mukalla, Shibam, Tarim, Sayun or al-Shihr points. Hadramawt’s towns, local powers, farms, ports, archives and scholarly communities continued through new political arrangements. Because the layer had already merged and then separated Hadramawt, Mahra, Dhofar and southern Oman, its disappearance is best read as a taxonomy change rather than one state’s conquest, a people’s migration or a cultural ending.

passages.text: Under Hafsid rule, Tunis was a wealthy center of the western Islamic world. Its urban history joins markets, religious institutions and residential neighborhoods. The surviving medina contains work from several dynasties, so individual buildings require their own dates and patronage histories.

passages.title: Technology and towns
passages.text: Northern and southern suburbs developed in the thirteenth century around the older central medina. Tunis was an expanding urban settlement, not only a palace city.

passages.title: Arts and exchange
passages.text: Tunis connected the Maghreb, southern Europe and lands to the east. These links encouraged exchanges in architecture and the arts.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Souqs, residential quarters and gates formed an interconnected townscape. Their survival helps historians study urban organization alongside individual monuments.

passages.title: Learning and beliefs
passages.text: Mosques and madrasas belonged to the city's institutional landscape. Surviving examples span both the Hafsid era and later periods.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Subsequent rulers added new palaces, residences and religious buildings. The medina records continuity and change across political transitions.

sectionTitles: A village, a forest and the sea

passages.text: Haida Gwaii is the island homeland of a continuing Haida nation, not a vanished kingdom. The imported outline omits the southern archipelago and extends north toward Alaska; it is not a reliable boundary of Haida Gwaii. Examples below identify their own places and dates.

passages.title: A village, a forest and the sea
passages.text: At SG̱ang Gwaay, south of this map’s incomplete outline, remains of large wooden houses stand beside memorial and mortuary poles. These are traces of a nineteenth-century village. The carved figures record family histories and responsibilities, not simply decoration for an empty landscape.

passages.title: A village, a forest and the sea
passages.text: Deep deposits of discarded shells at the same site record a much longer history of eating and living there. Salmon and shellfish were important foods; red cedar supplied houses, canoes and carved poles. Different traces connect meals, transport and public monuments.

passages.title: A village, a forest and the sea
passages.text: A bentwood box begins with carefully cut grooves in a single plank. Steam softens the wood so its sides can turn at the corners. The technique combines precise measurement and knowledge of wood, four walls do not necessarily require four separate boards.

passages.title: A village, a forest and the sea
passages.text: Museum box VII-B-560, made by 1901 or earlier, stored eulachon oil. The catalogue notes that its wood remains saturated with the oil. This is unusually direct evidence of use: a beautiful carved container also preserves traces of an important food and trade product.

passages.title: Learning skilled hands
passages.text: The crest carved on that box refers to inherited rights and its owner’s identity. Haida designs are not a collection of interchangeable public logos. An object’s appearance can carry information about relationships and authority as well as the maker’s artistic skill.

passages.title: Learning skilled hands
passages.text: A spruce-root hat in the Canadian Museum of History, VII-B-892, dates to 1884 or earlier. Its maker used different twining methods on crown and brim. The fine root strands and consistent pattern reveal substantial preparation and patient, controlled handwork.

passages.title: Learning skilled hands
passages.text: The museum describes women learning weaving from mothers, aunts and grandmothers. Experienced weavers can recognize individual habits in the way a hat is finished. A family skill can carry knowledge too subtle to fit into a short written instruction.

passages.title: Learning skilled hands
passages.text: Haida weaver Ariane Xay Kuyaas explains choosing straight spruce roots of suitable, consistent sizes, then preparing them before weaving. Planning starts in the forest, not at the first stitch. Running short of matching material halfway through would be a frustrating kind of homework.

passages.title: Words, care and political change
passages.text: The Haida Gwaii Museum’s 2021 catalogue prints “Haawa, haw’aa” alongside “thank you” in its acknowledgements. These are attested contemporary written forms, reproduced from a specific publication. Haida has regional dialects; a modern written expression is distinct from the visual language of a carved crest.

passages.title: Words, care and political change
passages.text: The Haida Gwaii Watchmen programme began in 1981 with volunteers protecting old village sites. Watchmen stay at sites and share knowledge with visitors. Caring for places includes explaining why houses and poles remain connected to families whose ancestors lived there.

passages.title: Words, care and political change
passages.text: In April 2024, the Haida Nation and British Columbia signed the Rising Tide agreement recognizing Haida Aboriginal title. Implementation was arranged in stages. Recognition within Canadian law is a development in an ongoing relationship, not the first moment Haida people possessed a homeland.

passages.title: Words, care and political change
passages.text: A separate agreement with Canada, signed in December 2024 and publicly announced in February 2025, recognized Haida title to lands including the intertidal area. Its terms preserve private-property interests and public services while jurisdictions are reconciled through a transition period.

Epidemics and colonial policies disrupted villages and families, but Haida nationhood continued. Recent title agreements and community stewardship demonstrate ongoing authority and responsibility. The 1500 endpoint is only a map interval; it is not an ending for Haida people.

passages.text: The atlas paints Hainan as one separate “state” from about 700 to 1492. Its neat island outline barely changes, even while the nearby mainland switches from Tang to Song, Yuan and Ming. Real history was less tidy. Imperial governments created counties, registered households, collected taxes, sent officials and exiled famous critics, but their reach varied sharply between ports, farming districts and the forested central mountains. Communities now grouped under names such as Li or Hlai were diverse; the modern ethnic label, language map and Latin-based writing system cannot simply be carried backward. Sediment cores record intensified land use and migration, while chronicles, gazetteers, archaeology and living traditions each reveal different slices of life. Families farmed rice and yams, fished, gathered forest products, wove cotton, traded incense and maintained waterworks. Women’s textile knowledge became famous, although individual medieval makers are rarely named. Children learned at home and work; some entered schools that spread unevenly. Storms, malaria-like fevers, exile, taxation and warfare made island life difficult. A 1489 canal shows impressive cooperation. Toilets are harder: no securely excavated island-wide medieval latrine lets us describe everybody’s bathroom. The target vanishes in 1492 because the atlas changes categories; Hainan’s peoples and Ming administration continued.

passages.title: Read the map before believing its color
passages.text: The live record is a generated state layer called Hainan, covering nine consecutive intervals from 700 to 1492. It currently has only an imported modern summary. That is an editorial object to investigate, not proof that one island kingdom, ethnicity or government lasted unchanged for nearly eight centuries.

passages.title: Read the map before believing its color
passages.text: Every target snapshot uses one 26-position Polygon around the island. Three component hashes differ only through minute coordinate drift, not meaningful expansion. A few shoreline test points fall outside the simplified coast while nearby inland points remain inside, demonstrating cartographic simplification rather than historical exclusion.

passages.title: Read the map before believing its color
passages.text: Xuwen and Beihai across the strait belong to Tang, then Song, then Yuan; in 1400 both Yuan and Ming layers claim them. Hainan nonetheless keeps its separate target color. This seam exposes the atlas taxonomy: neighboring dynasties change while the island is artificially held apart.

passages.title: Read the map before believing its color
passages.text: Chronicles and gazetteers name officials, exiles, taxes, schools and revolts; archaeology and sediment cores reveal objects and land use; later traditions preserve skills. Each source has blind spots. Famous men dominate texts, cores blur individual events, and a living practice cannot be assigned an eighth-century birthday without proof.

passages.title: Read the map before believing its color
passages.text: “Li,” “Hlai,” Han migrant and islander are not interchangeable timeless boxes. Modern ethnography and state classification helped stabilize today’s Li category; Hlai varieties also differ. Population genetics can model ancestry among sampled people, but it cannot label a medieval pot, household or rebel by itself.

passages.title: Mountains, rivers, forests and stormy coasts
passages.text: Hainan rises toward a mountainous center, and major rivers flow outward toward different coasts. That terrain created many local travel and farming worlds rather than one flat island landscape. River valleys could support fields and movement, while steep forested country complicated official journeys and military control.

passages.title: Mountains, rivers, forests and stormy coasts
passages.text: A tropical monsoon brings heavy rain, but not evenly: eastern slopes receive more, western districts can be drier, and typhoons, droughts or unusual cold can damage crops. People needed flexible planting, storage and repair routines; a green island was never automatically an easy pantry.

passages.title: Mountains, rivers, forests and stormy coasts
passages.text: Offshore sediment cores preserve pollen, chemical indicators and erosion signals. Researchers connect stronger human impacts with migration in the Sui to Tang and especially Song periods. Core dates and source areas have uncertainties, so the evidence supports broad land-use intensification rather than a headcount for any one village.

passages.title: Mountains, rivers, forests and stormy coasts
passages.text: At Shuangchi Maar, pollen, charcoal and radiocarbon dates reveal long environmental histories. Such archives help distinguish climate shifts, burning and vegetation change, but they do not identify who lit a fire or why. Environmental science adds scale while written and archaeological evidence supply more local context.

passages.title: Mountains, rivers, forests and stormy coasts
passages.text: Central rainforest supported plants, animals, gathering, hunting and settlement while also sheltering communities beyond easy county supervision. UNESCO’s nomination links ecology with long Li continuity, but its modern heritage boundaries and ethnic language cannot simply be laid over every medieval century.

passages.title: Officials, counties and power that faded with distance
passages.text: Tang rulers established or reorganized counties but often worked through the influential Feng-Xian family and other local intermediaries. Scholarship describes elements of loose or indirect administration and episodes of resistance. A county name on paper did not guarantee an official could command every mountain settlement.

passages.title: Officials, counties and power that faded with distance
passages.text: The 900 to 1000 interval is unusually deceptive: the map leaves the Tang seam and island polygon unchanged while regimes around the region fractured and Southern Han power arose. The responsible card marks this as a source-and-map mismatch instead of inventing an independent Hainan dynasty to fill the color.

passages.title: Officials, counties and power that faded with distance
passages.text: Song government expanded administrative divisions and special arrangements for interior communities, while migration and commerce increased. Research on central Hainan still finds sharp differences in reach and interaction. Governance was negotiated through county seats, markets and local leaders rather than broadcast equally across the island.

passages.title: Officials, counties and power that faded with distance
passages.text: Yuan authorities pursued household registration, taxes and corvée, but Hainan remained divided among institutions and control was unstable. Registration itself could provoke evasion or resistance. A tax roll reveals what officials sought to count; it never captures everybody who moved, hid or lived beyond routine collection.

passages.title: Officials, counties and power that faded with distance
passages.text: Ming Qiongzhou Prefecture dates from 1369 in the museum chronology. Officials promoted farming and schools while expanding registration, yet repeated resistance and suppression show the coercive side of state-building. Development language in official sources must be read beside the people whose labor and land were being reorganized.

passages.title: Movement, exile, belief and many kinds of neighbor
passages.text: The Buddhist monk Jianzhen landed near Yazhou in 748 after a failed Japan voyage and stayed before continuing. His story places Hainan inside sea routes and religious networks. Later memorial sites celebrate him, so historians separate the voyage tradition from buildings or ceremonies created much later.

passages.title: Movement, exile, belief and many kinds of neighbor
passages.text: Exile was forced movement, not an adventurous holiday. Tang legal history describes long journeys, labor, loss of status and uncertain return. Hainan’s distance made it useful to governments as punishment. Families, servants and local hosts could bear costs that an exiled official’s elegant poem rarely records.

passages.title: Movement, exile, belief and many kinds of neighbor
passages.text: Su Shi’s 1097 to 1100 Danzhou exile is exceptionally well documented. He wrote, taught and managed illness while depending on local relationships. His voice helps animate one place and three years, but its survival reflects male elite literacy; thousands of neighbors left no comparable diary or collected works.

passages.title: Movement, exile, belief and many kinds of neighbor
passages.text: Migration increased cultivated land, markets and cultural contact, particularly in the Song period. Newcomers did not arrive on an empty island, and “migration” covers officials, soldiers, farmers, merchants, family members and forced travelers. Contact could bring exchange, marriage, competition, disease and conflict in different combinations.

passages.title: Movement, exile, belief and many kinds of neighbor
passages.text: Ports connected Buddhists, merchants, sailors and other travelers with mainland China and the wider sea. Evidence for particular Muslim communities or foreign traders is uneven and later traditions may compress centuries. It is safer to describe documented maritime diversity than assign every visiting cargo a permanent neighborhood.

passages.title: Rice, yams, fish, forest foods and shared water
passages.text: Farmers grew crops suited to wet lowlands and drier or sloping ground. Rice mattered, while local historical synthesis also finds yams in Song and Yuan writing. Diet still varied by ecology, season and wealth; one list of crops cannot tell us the contents of every family bowl.

passages.title: Rice, yams, fish, forest foods and shared water
passages.text: Fishing linked shore, estuary and river communities, while gathering and hunting used forest knowledge. Later records describe organized Li hunts, but projecting their exact rules backward would be unsafe. Archaeological bones, tools and settlement context are needed to identify which species were eaten at a particular site.

passages.title: Rice, yams, fish, forest foods and shared water
passages.text: Betel nut became a valued social and medicinal product in southern China. Historical medical research traces changing claims about its effects, including Song discussion. Chewing, trading and prescribing are different activities, and old medical authority does not prove that every remedy was effective or harmless.

passages.title: Rice, yams, fish, forest foods and shared water
passages.text: Forest products, especially aromatic goods such as incense, entered exchange networks connecting interior collectors, local brokers and ports. Those chains created opportunity and inequality. A fragrant object in an elite market could begin with difficult, poorly recorded labor far from the official who described its price.

passages.title: Rice, yams, fish, forest foods and shared water
passages.text: Waterworks required surveying, digging, gates, cleaning and agreements about turns. A local synthesis records Song works and a canal built in 1489. That late-Ming project is a real achievement inside the interval: less flashy than a palace, but potentially more useful when children, fields and animals needed water.

passages.title: Cotton, tools, markets and sea-spanning exchange
passages.text: Song and Yuan texts record Hainan cotton and mixed-fiber textiles. Production joined plant cultivation, cleaning, spinning, dyeing, weaving and finishing, often across several hands. A finished bolt embodies practiced knowledge and time; it should not be reduced to a single “invention moment” in a famous biography.

passages.title: Cotton, tools, markets and sea-spanning exchange
passages.text: Traditions connect Huang Daopo, a late-Song woman, with learning cotton techniques from Li communities before transforming production near Shanghai. Scholars debate details and later embellishment. The responsible lesson is cross-cultural technical exchange and women’s expertise, not a fairy tale in which one genius invents weaving alone.

passages.title: Cotton, tools, markets and sea-spanning exchange
passages.text: UNESCO’s living-heritage record documents spinning, plant dyeing, weaving and embroidery taught especially from mothers to daughters. This is valuable continuity evidence and a clue to embodied learning. It does not make every modern pattern, tool or gender arrangement a securely dated feature of 700 to 1492.

passages.title: Cotton, tools, markets and sea-spanning exchange
passages.text: Hainan functioned as a stopping and exchange zone on regional sea routes, especially under the Song. Cargo studies show official, merchant and small-scale networks could coexist. Most islanders were not ocean captains, yet farmers, packers, porters, boat repairers and food sellers helped make voyages possible.

passages.title: Cotton, tools, markets and sea-spanning exchange
passages.text: Coins and ceramics recovered offshore can date traffic and commercial connections, but findspots near reefs may lie outside this exact island polygon and shipwreck cargoes may have been merely passing. Maritime archaeology is powerful precisely when location, deposition, corrosion and route alternatives remain explicit.

passages.title: Homes, clothes, work, music and play
passages.text: County towns such as Yazhou developed walls, streets, offices, temples, markets and homes over many rebuilding phases. The surviving townscape mixes Song beginnings with later Ming and modern fabric. A present wall is evidence for urban memory, not an untouched backdrop for an eleventh-century street scene.

passages.title: Homes, clothes, work, music and play
passages.text: Boat-shaped houses in some Hainan communities used forms adapted to climate and available materials, but surviving examples and recent architectural studies are later. They offer comparative questions about ventilation, rain and shared space; they do not justify placing every medieval Hlai-speaking family in an identical house.

passages.title: Homes, clothes, work, music and play
passages.text: Clothing could use cotton and other fibers, shaped by work, climate, status and local fashion. Living Li textile traditions preserve extraordinary color and pattern knowledge, while medieval texts emphasize goods more often than wardrobes. The card therefore shows craft without inventing one island costume for eight centuries.

passages.title: Homes, clothes, work, music and play
passages.text: Daily labor included farming, water repair, fishing, gathering, childcare, cooking, weaving, carrying goods, sailing, clerical work and military service. Who performed a task varied by place, age, gender, wealth and compulsion. Official histories rarely count the sore backs behind a canal or cargo list.

passages.title: Homes, clothes, work, music and play
passages.text: Museum exhibits and today’s Yazhou song tradition preserve instruments, games, dance and oral performance, giving children an honest reminder that work was not the whole day. Exact medieval tunes and rules are not securely recoverable. We can say people made music and jokes without writing fake lyrics for them.

passages.title: Families, women, children and unequal chances to learn
passages.text: Households could include couples, children, elders, other kin, servants or dependents, but composition differed by community and status. Migration and exile separated some families and joined others. Genealogies preserve prominent lines far better than ordinary households, so no single “Hainan family” fits the interval.

passages.title: Families, women, children and unequal chances to learn
passages.text: Women’s textile knowledge is visible through both historical traditions and living practice, yet medieval women are seldom named individually. Huang Daopo’s exceptional fame should direct attention toward many teachers and makers, not erase them. Women also farmed, traded, managed homes and cared for people in varied arrangements.

passages.title: Families, women, children and unequal chances to learn
passages.text: Children learned speech, manners, food gathering, craft and work by watching, helping and practicing with relatives and neighbors. Mother-to-daughter textile teaching is documented in living heritage, not directly for every medieval village. Archaeology rarely records the patient corrections, teasing and repeated mistakes of apprenticeship.

passages.title: Families, women, children and unequal chances to learn
passages.text: Song officials and local advocates expanded schools, examinations and ritual education, but provision and access were uneven. Formal study favored families with time, connections and literacy; mountain distance mattered. A school’s existence does not mean every boy attended, and absence from rosters does not mean girls learned nothing.

passages.title: Families, women, children and unequal chances to learn
passages.text: Su Shi is remembered as a teacher in Danzhou, offering a vivid example of learned exchange during exile. He represents Classical Chinese literary culture, not all island childhood. Children in fishing, farming, craft and forest communities learned valuable knowledge that official examination records were not designed to recognize.

passages.title: Illness, care, drinking water and the toilet evidence gap
passages.text: Hainan’s heat, rain, insects, storms and difficult travel shaped health risks. Older writers often portrayed the far south as dangerously unhealthy, sometimes exaggerating to dramatize exile. Illness was real, but hostile literary stereotypes are not clinical surveys and should not make island residents seem naturally sickly.

passages.title: Illness, care, drinking water and the toilet evidence gap
passages.text: Historical research dates stronger Chinese medical institutions on Hainan to the Song and records Ming medical offices. Wider Song government medicine included texts, pharmacies and official programs, but island access was uneven. Most care still began with household food, rest, observation and locally known plants.

passages.title: Illness, care, drinking water and the toilet evidence gap
passages.text: Su Shi’s writings describe diet, rest and strategies for enduring illness during exile. They make self-care unusually personal, yet he was a literate official with distinctive resources and beliefs. His regimen should appear as one documented case rather than “what Hainan people did” when sick.

passages.title: Illness, care, drinking water and the toilet evidence gap
passages.text: Rivers, springs, wells, rain storage and canals could supply households and fields, but water had to be carried and protected from contamination. The sources document waterways and irrigation better than drinking practices. Children likely helped with water work, though exact chores require local household evidence.

passages.title: Illness, care, drinking water and the toilet evidence gap
passages.text: No cited excavation securely supplies an island-wide medieval toilet design for 700 to 1492. People certainly managed urine, feces, wash water and rubbish, but arrangements varied by town, village and field. The scientifically honest bathroom fact is the gap itself: never turn a later house drain into everybody’s toilet.

passages.title: Conflict, achievements, one written voice and continuity
passages.text: Resistance labeled “Li rebellions” in Ming records arose from taxation, registration, land pressure, abuses and local political struggles, followed by military suppression. Official labels can flatten different communities and motives. Violence affected food, homes and families, not merely the careers of commanders listed in chronicles.

passages.title: Conflict, achievements, one written voice and continuity
passages.text: Exile, taxation and corvée were also forms of coercion. A road, field or office might look like administrative progress while demanding forced travel or labor from particular people. Reading achievements honestly means asking who chose, who paid, who benefited and whose objections survived only as “disorder.”

passages.title: Conflict, achievements, one written voice and continuity
passages.text: Island achievements accumulated across communities: irrigation and canals, cotton skill, ports and navigation, schools, local ecological knowledge, farming, music and rebuilding after storms. The best history does not award them all to a dynasty or modern ethnicity; cooperation and exchange often outlasted official regimes.

passages.title: Conflict, achievements, one written voice and continuity
passages.text: Localized written sample, June 1100: 九死南荒吾不恨，茲遊奇絕冠平生。 Jiǔ sǐ nánhuāng wú bù hèn; zī yóu qíjué guàn píngshēng. “Even nine deaths in the southern wilds would bring no regret; this wondrous journey surpasses all my life.” It is Su Shi’s Classical Chinese voice after Danzhou exile, not a Hlai or island-wide voice.

passages.title: Conflict, achievements, one written voice and continuity
passages.text: No in-period Hlai text is securely attributable: the current Latin-based orthography dates to 1957, so borrowing it would fake a medieval sample. At 1492 the atlas id simply disappears and leaves tested island points unowned. Ming administration, Hlai-speaking communities and other island lives continued beyond the map category.

The exact Hainan target disappears at 1492, and audited points at Danzhou, Wuzhishan, Sanya and elsewhere gain no automatic successor owner in that snapshot. This is an atlas taxonomy boundary rather than a conquest, migration or extinction. Hainan remained under Ming institutions of uneven reach, while Hlai-speaking communities, migrant families, ports, farms, crafts and island exchange continued and changed beyond this card.

sectionTitles: Social life, freedom and practical engineering
Learning, medicine and what happens after flushing

passages.text: Across the region now called Haiti, household objects and living traditions reveal food, work and creativity: Taíno cloth stamps, colonial kitchen pottery, family soup-making and metal sculpture. These examples belong to different communities and centuries.

passages.title: Discoveries: food, clothes and play
passages.text: At En Bas Saline, archaeologists recovered fishing weights, cooking griddles, shell and bone tools, beads and stamps used to put patterns on cotton cloth. These objects come from a Taíno town occupied in the centuries around European contact. A patterned shirt has a history too: people cared about useful equipment and how things looked, long before machine-printed fabric.

passages.title: Discoveries: food, clothes and play
passages.text: Fish and shellfish supplied much of En Bas Saline’s animal food. Researchers found larger fish and a wider variety of animal remains in the central mound area than around the town’s edges. They interpret this as evidence that higher-status residents, probably chiefs, ate differently. Ancient dinner scraps can reveal inequalities that grand buildings alone cannot explain.

passages.title: Discoveries: food, clothes and play
passages.text: Excavations at sixteenth-century Puerto Real found kitchen vessels made in Indigenous and African traditions, alongside imported European goods. A clay griddle was used for manioc bread. The kitchens show how colonial food depended on knowledge from different communities, many of whose members worked under coercion. The people preparing a meal shaped its history as much as those owning the dining table.

passages.title: Discoveries: food, clothes and play
passages.text: Puerto Real’s household finds include gaming pieces, children’s toys, a jaw harp, needlework equipment and decorated book fasteners. These are unusually personal traces of leisure and learning. They mostly illuminate the better-documented Spanish households, however. A toy found in one home cannot tell us what every child owned, and the lives of poorer and enslaved residents are less visible in these excavations.

passages.title: Social life, freedom and practical engineering
passages.text: In 1772, officials in Port-au-Prince prohibited nighttime dances called Kalendas by enslaved and free people of colour. The regulation reveals attempts to control social gathering as well as work. It records what authorities wanted to stop, rather than proving that people stopped dancing.

passages.title: Social life, freedom and practical engineering
passages.text: Haitian independence in 1804 was a victory over French colonial rule and slavery. Freedom still had to be defended in everyday work: the John Carter Brown Library’s exhibition explains that Louverture and several early Haitian governments imposed forced plantation labour. Ending legal slavery did not immediately give everyone the right to choose their work.

passages.title: Social life, freedom and practical engineering
passages.text: The early nineteenth-century Citadelle Henry needed more than cannon and thick walls. Its builders included channels and cisterns to supply and store water. The fortress was intended to protect the new country, and its water system helped support people inside it. Even a mountain stronghold needs the practical equivalent of remembering everyone’s water bottle.

passages.title: Family food and creative work
passages.text: Joumou soup brings pumpkin, vegetables and other ingredients into a dish shared on January 1, Haiti’s Independence Day, and at Sunday breakfast. UNESCO’s 2021 heritage account describes women organizing preparation and children helping with ingredients, alongside farmers and utensil-makers. The meal connects a household to a much wider circle of work and celebration. Families can have their own versions.

passages.title: Family food and creative work
passages.text: In a 2023 report from Port-au-Prince, Marie France Damas cooked soup while her husband took restaurant orders and her daughter chopped vegetables. The business helped pay for her children’s schooling. This is one family’s documented experience, showing how a cherished meal could support both household income and education.

passages.title: Family food and creative work
passages.text: Smithsonian’s 2022 account follows metalworker Josnel Bruno turning a discarded steel oil drum into a vase. He flattens the metal, draws his design, then cuts it with a chisel called a burin. Flowers, birds and fruit inspire his work in Croix-des-Bouquets. The old container gains a dramatically different job description: from industrial storage to handmade art.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and what happens after flushing
passages.text: In October 2013, fourteen Haitian doctors began the first medical residencies at University Hospital in Mirebalais. Their training covered children’s medicine, internal medicine and surgery, with an hour of dedicated teaching each day alongside supervised clinical work. A teaching hospital is also a workplace where already-qualified doctors continue learning from more experienced colleagues.

passages.title: Learning, medicine and what happens after flushing
passages.text: A 2013 engineering report describes where that hospital’s toilet, sink and laundry water went: a treatment system using bacteria to break down organic waste, followed by chlorine disinfection. Flushing was only the start of the journey. The less glamorous parts of a hospital require skilled design too, even if the pipes rarely get a thank-you card.

French colonial rule ended with Haitian independence in 1804. The map’s earlier 1783 endpoint is not that event. Later political changes did not end Haitian cultural life: family food traditions and creative work continue.

sectionTitles: Family work and an awkward toilet question
Clothes with colour and clever patterns

passages.text: Hallstatt names an archaeological culture of the Early Iron Age, conventionally about 800 to 450 BCE, rather than one kingdom. The map’s 400 to 323 BCE label and enormous outline are misleading. These examples focus on the Austrian salt-mining community and its wider connections.

passages.title: Salt preserved more than dinner
passages.text: The salty, air-poor conditions inside Hallstatt’s mines preserved wood, leather, wool, food scraps and even human waste. Most archaeological sites lose much of this material to decay. Here, a worn shoe or torn piece of cloth can survive beside the more glamorous metal objects.

passages.title: Salt preserved more than dinner
passages.text: The surviving collection is still incomplete. Archaeologists mainly find things miners lost, discarded or reused underground, rather than everything a family owned. A mine is a wonderful time capsule, but it is not a neatly packed suitcase containing someone’s whole life.

passages.title: Dinner below ground
passages.text: Food remains include barley, millet and broad beans, along with animal bones. Researchers suggest a hearty mixture resembling Ritschert, a stew still known in the eastern Alps. The comparison is useful, but no ancient recipe book supplies the exact quantities or cooking instructions.

passages.title: Dinner below ground
passages.text: Hazelnut shells, fruit pips and small bentwood boxes add variety to the picture. Some boxes probably held cheese. Wooden utensils and pottery indicate food preparation underground, so the mine was a place for eating as well as extracting salt.

passages.title: Dinner below ground
passages.text: A 2021 study found fungal DNA in one Iron Age sample of preserved poop that points to blue cheese and beer. The fungi include Penicillium roqueforti and Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Archaeology sometimes discovers an impressive food tradition by examining something nobody intended to save.

passages.title: Dinner below ground
passages.text: These scientific results came from a small number of samples, not a survey of every household. Another Iron Age sample contained evidence of intestinal worms. The findings reveal both skilled food processing and uncomfortable health problems, without telling us which treatments the miners knew.

passages.title: Family work and an awkward toilet question
passages.text: Children’s skeletons show signs of heavy physical work. A small cap and small shoes also connect children with the mining world, although a shoe could belong to a small adult. Researchers suggest young children may have tended burning wood splints that supplied light; their exact jobs remain uncertain.

passages.title: Family work and an awkward toilet question
passages.text: Wear on women’s skeletons suggests repeated carrying of heavy loads on one shoulder. A strap carried by one person or a pole shared by two are possible explanations. The evidence shows demanding work, but does not reveal one universal household division of chores.

passages.title: Family work and an awkward toilet question
passages.text: Human waste occurs across the Iron Age workings, suggesting miners did not have one designated underground toilet area. Preserved clothing also contains lice-egg shells. These are unusually direct clues about hygiene: the archaeological record can be fascinating and rather itchy at the same time.

passages.title: Clothes with colour and clever patterns
passages.text: Some Hallstatt-period fabrics used threads only about 0.1 to 0.2 millimetres thick, with roughly 20 to 30 threads per centimetre. Weavers made stripes, checks and varied twill patterns. Fine cloth required patient skill; prehistoric clothing was not automatically a shapeless brown sack.

passages.title: Clothes with colour and clever patterns
passages.text: Weavers could create patterns even without changing the colour. Threads spun in opposite directions reflected light differently when arranged together. Blue, yellow and red dyes offered other possibilities. The results combine knowledge of materials with close attention to how a finished surface would look.

passages.title: Clothes with colour and clever patterns
passages.text: Yarn was spun with hand spindles, and hanging weights kept loom threads under tension. Small tablets could be turned to weave patterned narrow bands. The surviving work demonstrates complex learned skills, although it does not tell us the names of teachers or describe formal schools.

passages.title: Trade, memory and missing voices
passages.text: Salt connected the mining community with people who supplied food, tools and clothing. Routes followed Alpine valleys, and salt travelled beyond the mountains. Its uses included seasoning, preserving food and processing hides. A successful mine therefore depended on many workers who never entered a tunnel.

passages.title: Trade, memory and missing voices
passages.text: The cemetery contains both cremations and burials of whole bodies, with vessels, jewellery and weapons reflecting distant connections. These offerings show how people marked death and status. They cannot simply be treated as a complete inventory of what everyone used in daily life.

passages.title: Trade, memory and missing voices
passages.text: For these miners, this card cannot offer a securely identified written sentence in their own language. The evidence here comes from material remains. Designs on cloth demonstrate skilled communication through patterns, but they are not a deciphered alphabet that we can turn into a greeting.

Hallstatt is an archaeological period, not a state with one fall date. At the Austrian mining site, a debris flow in the middle of the fourth century BCE buried workings and parts of the valley. Mining continued in a different area around Dammwiese; the disaster did not erase the wider population.

sectionTitles: A city governed by citizens, but which citizens?
A small home with a shared courtyard
Fire, water and the problem of clean streets

passages.text: Hamburg was a self-governing trading city on the Elbe, with a powerful merchant elite and a much larger population of working families. This entry follows its eighteenth- and nineteenth-century free-city history. The map’s 1715 to 1878 span is only a display interval: French rule interrupted its autonomy, and Hamburg continued after 1878.

passages.title: A city governed by citizens, but which citizens?
passages.text: After French rule, Hamburg regained its place as a free city and became a founding member of the German Confederation in 1815. Much of the earlier governing order returned. Officials even abandoned the French civil registers in favor of church records again, showing that restoration reached into how families’ births and marriages were recorded.

passages.title: A city governed by citizens, but which citizens?
passages.text: Writing sample: Article 6 of the 1860 constitution says, “Die höchste Staatsgewalt steht dem Senate und der Bürgerschaft gemeinschaftlich zu.” This means, “The highest state authority belongs jointly to the Senate and the citizens’ assembly.” The German wording survives in the constitutional text, reproduced in a scholarly edition with its historical spelling.

passages.title: A city governed by citizens, but which citizens?
passages.text: The new constitution did not give every adult an equal vote. One group of representatives was elected by qualifying male citizens who paid tax; other seats involved property owners and selected bodies. Women were excluded. The elaborate rules help explain how merchant and established civic interests retained influence even after reform.

passages.title: A small home with a shared courtyard
passages.text: The grocers’ guild built homes for twenty members’ widows in 1676, before this map interval, and the houses remained in use through the nineteenth century. Support for older women also freed shop premises for new guild members. This was organized retirement housing for a particular occupational community, rather than help available to everyone.

passages.title: A small home with a shared courtyard
passages.text: Each widow’s narrow home had rooms on two levels. The cramped kitchen received daylight through an internal window, while the upstairs living room included an enclosed sleeping alcove. Today’s museum furniture comes from other nineteenth-century Hamburg grocers’ households, so it illustrates that living environment rather than preserving one resident’s untouched possessions.

passages.title: A small home with a shared courtyard
passages.text: The widows shared a toilet at the end of the courtyard and used two water pumps until pipes arrived late in the nineteenth century. Wood and peat could be brought through a loft opening. Getting water, fuel and a little privacy all required more movement around the courtyard than turning a modern tap.

passages.title: Fire, water and the problem of clean streets
passages.text: From 5 to 8 May 1842, fire spread through central Hamburg. Inadequate supplies of firefighting water helped turn a blaze into a disaster. Rebuilding became an opportunity to change streets and infrastructure, while engineer William Lindley helped design a more coordinated system for supplying the city with water.

passages.title: Fire, water and the problem of clean streets
passages.text: Hamburg’s first modern sewer, locally called a Siel, went into service in 1843. Lindley planned drainage that flowed downhill under gravity, together with water supply and hydrants for firefighters. The Rothenburgsort waterworks began supplying water in 1848. These were connected pieces of infrastructure, not simply a taller public fountain.

passages.title: Fire, water and the problem of clean streets
passages.text: Piped water did not automatically mean safely filtered water. Hamburg’s centralized supply began in 1848, but the Kaltehofe sand-filtration works did not provide filtered drinking water until 1893, after this entry’s map interval. That gap is a useful reminder that delivering water and cleaning it are separate engineering jobs.

passages.title: Learning, work and getting around
passages.text: Charlotte Paulsen’s association created childcare institutions for working mothers and a school for poor girls. The children were meant to receive education and encouragement, not merely supervision. In 1866 these efforts came together in the Paulsenstift, which also offered training for girls leaving school.

passages.title: Learning, work and getting around
passages.text: Johanna Goldschmidt founded Hamburg’s Fröbel association in 1860 to train kindergarten teachers professionally. Education became a field in which women organized institutions and pursued skilled work. The same movement had to overcome expectations that a girl’s future marriage made serious vocational education unnecessary.

passages.title: Learning, work and getting around
passages.text: The Sandtorhafen, developed in the mid-1860s, brought quays, storage sheds and railway access together at a new harbor basin. Cranes and specialized teams changed loading and unloading. A cargo’s journey increasingly linked ship, quay, warehouse and train, although difficult manual work remained part of port life.

passages.title: Learning, work and getting around
passages.text: Even after the old fortifications were dismantled, gates and barriers controlled movement into Hamburg. Tolls helped collect city duties and limit outside goods. These restrictions lasted until the turn of 1860 to 1861. Street names associated with old barriers preserve traces of a city where an evening journey could involve a gate and a fee.

passages.title: Learning, work and getting around
passages.text: A municipal report published in 1887 looks back on the arrival of gas street lighting. An 1845 trial was interrupted when storm flooding damaged the gasworks; regular service began in September 1846. By that year’s end, the account lists 2,020 gas lamps. Lighting streets required pipes, fuel and maintenance behind every flame.

Hamburg became a constituent state of the German Empire in 1871. Its trading city and civic institutions continued beyond the imported map’s 1878 endpoint, although wider German political changes repeatedly altered their powers. The endpoint does not represent a conquest or the abandonment of the city.

passages.text: The Han ruled China for four centuries, with a brief interruption, and set the pattern that later dynasties followed: an emperor advised by scholar-officials trained in the Confucian classics, a census-taking bureaucracy, and a capital laid out on a grid. Paper, the seismoscope and the first great history of China were made under the Han, and the Silk Road opened during their reign. The Chinese still call their majority people the Han.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Cai Lun presents the court with paper made from bark, hemp and rags. Paper travels west along the Silk Road and reaches Europe a thousand years later.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Zhang Heng builds a seismoscope: a bronze vessel that dropped a ball into one of eight dragon mouths to show the direction of a distant earthquake.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: The wheelbarrow, the crank handle and the stern-mounted rudder are all first attested in Han China.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: The Taichu calendar reform sets the civil year, with its intercalary months, on the footing that Chinese calendars follow in principle to this day.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: The Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art: systems of linear equations solved by a method equivalent to Gaussian elimination, rules for negative numbers, and an approximation of pi.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Zhang Heng's water-driven armillary sphere turns with the heavens, and he catalogues about 2,500 stars.

passages.title: Science
passages.text: Xu Shen's Shuowen Jiezi, the first dictionary to analyse Chinese characters by their components, is presented to the throne.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Du Shi harnesses a water wheel to the bellows of a blast furnace. Cast iron becomes cheap enough for ploughshares and hoes.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Brine wells drilled hundreds of meters deep with bamboo derricks in Sichuan, and natural gas piped through bamboo to boil the brine for salt.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Silk woven on multi-shaft treadle looms. Han silks have been found in Roman-era graves at Palmyra in Syria.

passages.title: Arts and letters
passages.text: The tombs at Mawangdui are sealed, preserving silk paintings, a silk map, and the earliest complete copies of the Daodejing.

passages.title: Arts and letters
passages.text: Sima Qian completes the Records of the Grand Historian, 130 chapters covering two thousand years and the model for every later Chinese dynastic history.

passages.title: Arts and letters
passages.text: The fu rhapsodies of Sima Xiangru, the folk songs collected by the Music Bureau, and lacquerware from Sichuan workshops exported across Asia.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Emperor Wu makes the Confucian classics the basis of official learning; the Imperial Academy follows in 124 BCE.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The White Horse Temple at Luoyang, by tradition China's first Buddhist temple, marks the arrival of Buddhism along the Silk Road.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Wang Chong's Lunheng argues that thunder is not the anger of heaven and that the dead have no consciousness.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Zhang Daoling founds the Way of the Celestial Masters in Sichuan, the first organized Daoist religion.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Zhang Qian sets out for the west. His reports of Ferghana horses, Parthia and India open what is now called the Silk Road.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The Protectorate of the Western Regions is set up in the Tarim Basin, securing the route to Central Asia.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: An embassy claiming to come from the Roman emperor Andun (Marcus Aurelius Antoninus) reaches the Han court by sea, according to the Book of Later Han.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The census counts 57,671,400 people, most of them farming households of about five on small plots of millet, wheat and rice, taxed in grain, cloth and labour.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Chang'an, the Western Han capital, sits inside about 25 km of walls with nine markets, and is one of the two largest cities in the world alongside Rome.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Games of liubo and cuju kickball, and the clay tomb figures of dancers, farmyards and watchtowers that show the Han world in miniature.

Weakened by court factions and the Yellow Turban rebellion of 184, the dynasty ended when Cao Pi accepted the abdication of Emperor Xian in 220. China split into the Three Kingdoms of Wei, Shu and Wu.

sectionTitles: A new state in a divided north

passages.text: Han-Zhao was a Southern Xiongnu-led state of northern China, historically dated 304-329. Its later phase is called Former Zhao. It was separate from the earlier Han dynasty and from rival Later Zhao. The imported map spans 300-400 and places a simplified outline well north of Chang’an and Luoyang, cities crucial to this story. It is not a reliable picture of the state’s full territory or lifetime.

passages.title: A new state in a divided north
passages.text: The Southern Xiongnu had already lived under Jin authority before Liu Yuan’s revolt. During the Jin princes’ civil wars, his aristocratic supporters built a government of their own. Their rise belonged to a world of settled communities, armies and competing courts, rather than a sudden arrival from outside China.

passages.title: A new state in a divided north
passages.text: Calling the state Han was a political choice. Liu Yuan invoked an admired earlier dynasty; the later name Zhao recalled another prestigious historical name. Historian Wu Honglin studies these names as statements about rulers’ identities and claims to authority. A familiar name did not make this the old Han empire reborn.

passages.title: A new state in a divided north
passages.text: Han-Zhao’s victories reshaped China. Its forces captured Luoyang in 311 and Chang’an in 316, taking Jin emperors prisoner. These were destructive conquests: the siege of Chang’an caused severe hunger. Winning a capital could make a ruler powerful while making the lives of the city’s families much harder.

passages.title: A new state in a divided north
passages.text: Liu Yao had been orphaned and raised by Liu Yuan. This family relationship mattered politically as well as personally. Hu Hong emphasizes adoption when explaining Liu Yao’s position within the ruling house; uncertain details of distant ancestry should not obscure the practical importance of being brought up in that household.

passages.title: A new state in a divided north
passages.text: After turmoil in 318, Liu Yao established his court at Chang’an and adopted the name Zhao in 319. Shi Le, formerly part of the same military coalition, established a rival Zhao regime. Historians distinguish Former Zhao from Later Zhao: the two governments eventually became enemies.

passages.title: A new state in a divided north
passages.text: Ruling meant more than commanding cavalry. Han-Zhao established official posts and supported agriculture. Its rulers adopted Chinese governmental and literary practices while retaining connections to Xiongnu leadership. Fields and administrators helped sustain the court and its soldiers.

passages.title: Households, food and care
passages.text: At Xiangjisi village near Xi’an, archaeologists excavated a tomb called M7 containing a pottery stove, well, mill, dishes and a spoon. It dates broadly from late Western Jin through Former or Later Zhao. These objects offer a nearby household comparison; its exact ruling dynasty remains uncertain.

passages.title: Households, food and care
passages.text: The same tomb included pottery chickens, a pig, a dog and a male attendant. Cooking, animals and service were important enough to represent in burial. A miniature kitchen can be an archaeological treasure, even without a miniature chef. The objects express burial choices, rather than proving every home looked alike.

passages.title: Households, food and care
passages.text: Chemical clues in bones can reveal meals that vanished long ago. A study of 25 people buried in the wider Guanzhong region during the Sixteen Kingdoms period found a diet dominated by millet, with some other plant foods or animals fed on them. This broader regional sample cannot provide a separate menu for Han-Zhao alone.

passages.title: Households, food and care
passages.text: The Book of Jin reports strict rules under Liu Yao: embroidered silk clothing depended on official rank, drinking was permitted after late-autumn farm work, and cattle slaughter was restricted to certain sacrifices. These were royal commands, with harsh penalties, rather than a diary of what everyone actually did.

passages.title: Households, food and care
passages.text: When Liu Yao was wounded and captured, his enemy assigned a doctor named Li Yong to treat him. The history identifies Li as a specialist in wounds and says he accompanied the injured ruler in a carriage. This records care for one important prisoner, not a general hospital system.

passages.title: Learning, stories and written words
passages.text: Liu Yao established schools near Chang’an’s palaces. The historical account describes selecting 1,500 students aged 13 to 25 and recruiting learned teachers. Successful students could receive court appointments. These were selective institutions preparing people for service, not schools attended by every child.

passages.title: Learning, stories and written words
passages.text: Liu Cong was remembered as a writer as well as a ruler, with more than a hundred poems and dozens of other compositions. Those works are now lost. A royal author could have plenty of readers in his lifetime and still leave no surviving collection for today’s children to open.

passages.title: Learning, stories and written words
passages.text: A song praised the defeated commander Chen An for caring for his soldiers. According to the transmitted history, Liu Yao admired it and ordered his court musicians to perform it, even though Chen An had been an opponent. Music could preserve affection for someone whom the victorious government had fought.

passages.title: Learning, stories and written words
passages.text: A reported discovery in 321 became a political argument: a piece of white jade supposedly carried a prophecy. Courtiers debated whether it promised victory or warned of danger. Historian Dong Gang examines the wordplay and political purposes of the story. This is a report in historical texts, not a surviving excavated message authenticated here.

passages.title: Learning, stories and written words
passages.text: A later history preserves Liu Yao’s message to his heir after his capture in 329: 勿以吾易意也, modern Mandarin wù yǐ wú yì yì yě, translated here as “Do not change your resolve on my account.” This is Chinese in modern type from the seventh-century Book of Jin. It is not his surviving original letter or an example of a separate Xiongnu script.

passages.title: Learning, stories and written words
passages.text: Much of this state’s history reached us through later compilations. Cui Hong’s early history of the Sixteen Kingdoms was used by subsequent historians, but its original text was eventually lost. Scholars compare surviving quotations and reconstructions, which helps explain why an apparently detailed story can still require careful checking.
Later Zhao conquered the remaining Han-Zhao regime in 329 after capturing Liu Yao. Its rulers’ defeat did not erase the region’s communities. The map’s 400 endpoint is only imported coverage.
