passages.text: Hanover was a German electorate whose ruler also became king of Great Britain in 1714. The territories remained separate states. Hanover became a kingdom in 1814 and was annexed by Prussia in 1866, so the imported map’s later endpoint does not represent continued Hanoverian independence.

passages.title: Gardens, machines and knowledge
passages.text: Herrenhausen’s great fountain required a waterworks, not just an impressive stone basin. Engineers used the River Leine to drive machinery that forced water toward the garden. By 1720 the jet reached roughly thirty-five metres: royal spectacle depended on practical engineering.

passages.title: Gardens, machines and knowledge
passages.text: The garden’s water system also needed extensive digging. Soldiers worked on the canal surrounding the Great Garden, while the machinery building stood on piles. Behind the elegant view were earthworks, structural supports and a great deal of labor.

passages.title: Gardens, machines and knowledge
passages.text: The Herrenhausen orangery was built in 1723 as winter shelter for plants grown in pots. Gardening therefore included moving and protecting living collections season by season. An orangery was a serious piece of plant-care infrastructure, not simply a decorative room with a citrus name.

passages.title: Gardens, machines and knowledge
passages.text: Göttingen’s university opened in 1737 and became an important center of research and teaching. Its history later included mathematician Carl Friedrich Gauss. The institution gives this small German kingdom a place in the history of science beyond the royal family.

passages.title: Gardens, machines and knowledge
passages.text: In May 1833 Gauss and Wilhelm Weber successfully tested an electromagnetic telegraph in Göttingen. A wire more than a kilometre long linked the physics collection with the observatory, crossing the town’s roofs and towers. Electricity could now carry signals between working scientists.

passages.title: Gardens, machines and knowledge
passages.text: Their apparatus was an early working telegraph, not the internet in miniature. Its importance lay in turning electrical effects into a usable signaling experiment over a real distance. Later systems developed the idea further; several inventors contributed to telegraphy.

passages.title: Birth, borders and political courage
passages.text: Göttingen’s maternity institution offered lodging, food and care to women who were often unmarried. Directors’ diaries from the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries preserve their experiences. This is unusually direct evidence for pregnancy and birth among people largely absent from royal portraits.

passages.title: Birth, borders and political courage
passages.text: The arrangement came with obligations: patients performed light work such as spinning or weaving and became subjects for clinical instruction. Assistance and unequal power existed together. Describing the institution simply as free healthcare would hide the demands placed on women and their babies.

passages.title: Birth, borders and political courage
passages.text: The 1824 boundary treaty with the Netherlands dealt with markers, ditches and drainage as well as lines on a map. One surviving archival map records the arrangements around the Twist area. Borders could alter the management of shared land and water used by rural communities.

passages.title: Birth, borders and political courage
passages.text: In 1837 King Ernst August rejected Hanover’s 1833 constitution. Seven Göttingen professors protested, including Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm, better known for collecting stories. Their stand cost all seven their jobs; three were also ordered out of the kingdom.

passages.title: Birth, borders and political courage
passages.text: The protest was about an oath and the limits of royal authority, not just a disagreement between a king and some famous authors. University teaching existed inside a political system that could dismiss its scholars. The episode made academic independence a very practical problem.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: German, Hanover’s constitution of 26 September 1833, section 3: “Die Regierungsform des Königreiches ist die erblich-monarchische.” Translation: “The kingdom’s form of government is hereditary monarchy.” The same constitution prescribed limits and obligations; four years later its revocation provoked the Göttingen professors’ protest.

Prussia annexed Hanover in 1866, ending its independent kingdom. Its territory became a Prussian province, while towns, universities and local communities continued. The map’s coverage extending to 1878 must not be read as a surviving sovereign Hanoverian state.

sectionTitles: Gardens, books and a written sample

passages.text: Egypt occupied the trading and scholarly city of Harar from 1875 until May 1885. Its officials sought revenue and control over routes toward the Somali coast, meeting substantial resistance. The map’s “Harer (Egypt)” label runs from 1878 to 1914, long beyond the occupation. Its broad outline across northern Somali territories must not be read as continuous Egyptian control.

passages.title: Conquest and its physical traces
passages.text: Egyptian officials made maps while reorganizing taxation, roads and government. A street plan or survey helped administrators see what they wanted to govern. These drawings are therefore evidence of both geographical knowledge and imperial ambition; a line on a map did not make resistance disappear.

passages.title: Conquest and its physical traces
passages.text: Occupation brought coercion as well as new institutions. Egyptian campaigns disrupted Oromo political arrangements and pressed communities to settle under closer supervision and adopt Islam. Somali resistance also limited authority along the routes to the coast. The city and its hinterland did not experience occupation in the same way.

passages.title: Conquest and its physical traces
passages.text: Aw Ansar, remembered as the Mosque of the Egyptians, was built during the occupation. The World Heritage nomination singles out its richly decorated outer façade as unusual within Harar. A surviving wall can preserve a political episode long after its officials have departed.

passages.title: Conquest and its physical traces
passages.text: An institutional history records a hospital among the stone buildings erected by the Egyptian administration. It also describes strengthened city walls and a new fort to the northwest. Medical facilities and military defenses appeared together in a programme designed to make occupation durable.

passages.title: Households and working lives
passages.text: Egyptian officer Muhammad Mukhtar described women helping sustain their households through productive work and manual crafts. His account gives women an active economic role, although it remains an outsider’s observation. Reading it alongside family documents offers a fuller picture than a list of governors alone.

passages.title: Households and working lives
passages.text: Records from Egyptian-administered Harar include marriage contracts, divorces and manumissions, documents releasing enslaved people. These reveal families negotiating legal relationships and people seeking freedom. Historian Adam Nieuważny studies the documents’ language and spelling as well as their contents: even everyday paperwork can become a historical discovery.

passages.title: Households and working lives
passages.text: Harari homes recorded in the 2004 heritage nomination have masonry seating platforms, wall niches, and displays of baskets and plates. Furniture, architecture and decoration work together. These surviving interiors show a domestic tradition continuing after Egyptian rule; they are not a dated inventory of every nineteenth-century house.

passages.title: Households and working lives
passages.text: The same 2004 survey describes Harari women making baskets at home, while women from nearby villages brought their own baskets into the city to sell. A basket could be useful equipment and wall decoration. The kitchen cupboard and the art gallery did not always need separate rooms.

passages.title: Gardens, books and a written sample
passages.text: Harar’s heritage survey distinguishes irrigated garden land, called masnu, from rain-fed bukhra. Fruit trees, coffee and other demanding crops grew nearer the walls; less thirsty crops occupied outer land. The description explains a landscape organized around water and the possibility of walking out to work and returning home.

passages.title: Gardens, books and a written sample
passages.text: Harar already had a sophisticated book culture before the occupation. A late-eighteenth-century Qur’an now at Princeton uses Italian paper and generous margins for scholarly notes. Colored divisions guide the reader through the page. The book is evidence of artisans connecting local scholarship with materials circulating across the Indian Ocean.

passages.title: Gardens, books and a written sample
passages.text: Bookbinding was a skilled local trade: Egyptian Major Mohammed Moktar remarked on Harar’s binders in 1875. Surviving manuscripts can even preserve separate dates for copying and binding. A book could acquire its protective cover years after its words were written, much as a well-used favorite gets a new jacket.

passages.title: Gardens, books and a written sample
passages.text: A short written sample is “al-Fātiḥa,” meaning “The Opening,” the Arabic chapter name identified by scholar Sana Mirza in the late-eighteenth-century Harari Qur’an at Princeton. This is her scholarly transliteration in Latin letters. The manuscript predates Egyptian rule and illustrates the city’s established Islamic learning.

Egyptian withdrawal in May 1885 restored Emir Abdallahi’s rule briefly. Menelik’s forces conquered Harar in January 1887. Governments changed, while the city’s households, crafts and religious scholarship continued.

sectionTitles: Through the gate and into the market

passages.text: The Hausa states were a group of kingdoms and cities, not one empire with a single ruler. Kano offers unusually rich surviving walls, palace buildings, markets and manuscripts. This card uses named Kano evidence without treating it as a description of every Hausa household or town.

passages.title: Through the gate and into the market
passages.text: Kano’s earthen defenses developed in stages. Nigeria’s heritage nomination describes earlier foundations, medieval building and a further extension in the 1500s. Surviving earthworks are evidence of repeated urban investment, not a wall built all at once.

passages.title: Through the gate and into the market
passages.text: Kano’s gates controlled passage through its walls. The nomination links gateways, palace and market as parts of the historical city.

passages.title: Through the gate and into the market
passages.text: Kurmi market was arranged in lanes specializing in different goods, including leatherwork, textiles, metalwork and spices. A shopper could head toward the right craft instead of searching one enormous jumble. The nomination also records the market’s continuing activity.

passages.title: Through the gate and into the market
passages.text: Rumfa, who ruled Kano from 1463 to 1499, is credited with the palace. The complex separates administration, family space and service areas. Its present layout records a living institution with a long building history, not a frozen fifteenth-century family photograph.

passages.title: Learning, government and written words
passages.text: In the 1490s, the scholar Muhammad al-Maghili visited Kano and Katsina. He wrote advice for Kano’s ruler Muhammad Rumfa. Political power involved arguments about justice and obligations as well as armies and walls.

passages.title: Learning, government and written words
passages.text: A manuscript of one of those works survives in Morocco’s national library. Its preservation there shows that the written connections of Hausa courts reached beyond today’s national borders. A surviving copy is not necessarily the author’s own handwriting.

passages.title: Learning, government and written words
passages.text: “تاج الدين فيما يجب على الملوك” is an Arabic title catalogued by Kano Archives: “The crown of religion concerning what is required of kings.” It belongs to the advice-to-rulers tradition associated with al-Maghili and Rumfa. The archive’s copy is not precisely dated here.

passages.title: Learning, government and written words
passages.text: Language and script are different things. Kano’s archive preserves Arabic histories alongside the Hausa Song of Bagauda in Ajami, meaning Hausa written with adapted Arabic letters. A page in Arabic-looking script is not automatically in the Arabic language.

passages.title: Learning, government and written words
passages.text: The archive’s digitization account describes locating manuscripts with community librarians and copyists, then photographing them on site. Preservation depends on families and local scholars as well as large institutions.

passages.title: People across changing states
passages.text: Hausa identity developed through language, social relationships, migration and intermarriage. The scholarly summary on Hausaness specifically includes people of Fulani, Arab, Tuareg and Nupe backgrounds. A colored political area cannot contain all the ways people identified themselves.

passages.title: People across changing states
passages.text: The political change beginning in 1804 created Sokoto’s emirates in much of Hausaland. It did not empty markets or make Hausa speech vanish. The atlas’s 1815 boundary marks a mapping transition, rather than the date every Hausa kingdom ended.

passages.title: People across changing states
passages.text: Kano’s continuing market and preserved manuscripts show continuity. Altered buildings and recopied texts still require careful dating.

The Sokoto revolution beginning in 1804 changed rulership across much of Hausaland. Hausa communities and language continued through emirate and later colonial rule. There is no single extinction date for a people or uniform fall date for all these states.

passages.text: The Heian period was the high age of the Japanese court. With the Fujiwara regents running politics from Heian-kyo, the aristocracy turned to poetry, calligraphy and romance, and its women wrote the first great works of Japanese prose.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Murasaki Shikibu wrote The Tale of Genji, often called the world's first novel.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Sei Shonagon finished The Pillow Book, her lists and observations of court life.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The kana syllabaries took shape, so that Japanese could be written without Chinese.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Phoenix Hall of Byodoin at Uji was built for the Fujiwara, with its Amida by the sculptor Jocho.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Saicho founded Tendai on Mount Hiei and Kukai brought Shingon from China, the esoteric schools of the court.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Genshin's Essentials of Rebirth spread devotion to Amida Buddha and the Pure Land.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The sensibility of mono no aware, the pathos of passing things, ran through court writing.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Aristocratic life turned on poetry contests, music, calligraphy, incense and love affairs conducted by letter.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Court women, writing in kana, produced the diaries and tales that define the age.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Tale of Genji remains at the center of Japanese literature.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The kana syllabaries are still the core of Japanese writing.
The Minamoto destroyed the Taira in the Genpei War, ending at Dan-no-ura in 1185; Minamoto no Yoritomo ruled from Kamakura and was named shogun in 1192.

sectionTitles: Public words and a short political life

passages.text: The Helvetic Republic was the centralized Swiss state established in 1798 under French influence and replaced in 1803. The atlas’s 1800 to 1815 interval extends into a different constitutional era. Its outline is a snapshot of changing borders, rather than a picture of today’s Switzerland or a republic that lasted until 1815.

passages.title: Reorganizing a country
passages.text: Representatives adopted the first Helvetic constitution at Aarau on 12 April 1798. A printed brochure survives in the Federal Archives. The new system created national ministries and reduced cantons to parts of a central administration, a sharp change from their earlier sovereignty.

passages.title: Reorganizing a country
passages.text: A map printed in August 1798 warned that its canton boundaries were provisional. Its maker advertised movable-type map printing that could quickly show revisions. There had been 22 cantons in April and 18 only weeks later: mapmakers had unusually fast-moving homework.

passages.title: Reorganizing a country
passages.text: Construction workers at Mümliswil found 173 silver coins in 1987, mostly French and Bernese. The latest was a Helvetic 40-batzen coin dated 1798. This gives the earliest possible burial date; the mixture shows that a new republic did not make older money vanish overnight.

passages.title: Reorganizing a country
passages.text: The republic tried to organize money around a franc divided into ten batzen and one hundred rappen. Its early coins used an armed Swiss figure with a liberty flag. A coin combined a practical unit for payments with a miniature statement about the new state.

passages.title: Children, teachers and care
passages.text: Minister Philipp Albert Stapfer’s 1799 survey asked teachers what they taught, which books they used, and how long the school day lasted. It also asked whether children attended in summer or winter. A questionnaire preserves the practical questions behind an ambitious education reform.

passages.title: Children, teachers and care
passages.text: Other questions asked about teachers’ families and children, second jobs, pay in grain or wood, and whether the school building was falling apart. Education depended on household livelihoods and buildings as well as lessons. The paperwork gets surprisingly close to ordinary family life.

passages.title: Children, teachers and care
passages.text: Stapfer proposed lessons in French, drawing and singing alongside reading, writing and arithmetic, with improved teacher pay. His full bill failed in Parliament. Some educational councils nevertheless used the circulated plan as a guide, so rejected legislation could still influence classrooms.

passages.title: Children, teachers and care
passages.text: Pestalozzi accepted work with children orphaned by the fighting at Stans. That institution closed in 1799 after about six months when its rooms were requisitioned. In 1800 he taught at Burgdorf and developed a boarding school, teacher training and an orphanage there.

passages.title: Children, teachers and care
passages.text: Poor relief remained largely a local responsibility, and many communities lacked enough resources. The republic supported some needy people and charitable societies. Cantonal health commissions also struggled without effective common rules for medical practice: new offices could have much less power than their titles suggested.

passages.title: Public words and a short political life
passages.text: At Beromünster’s oath ceremony on 22 August 1798, a procession, musicians and girls singing patriotic songs accompanied the constitutional oath taken by 1,525 men. The official account describes two boys representing the French and Helvetic republics exchanging an embrace. Children helped stage an adult political message.

passages.title: Public words and a short political life
passages.text: A wooden liberty-tree board from Bauma in 1798 proclaimed “Alle haben gleiche Rechte”: “Everyone has equal rights.” The German words survive in a specific public inscription. They express the revolution’s ideal; the ceremony’s male oath-takers and the period’s conflicts remind us that its application was contested.

passages.title: Public words and a short political life
passages.text: The constitution promised press freedom, and publications reported parliamentary debates. Critics used the same opening. In November 1798 the government introduced censorship against opposition newspapers. Readers could encounter both the promise of public debate and attempts to restrict it within the republic’s first year.

Civil war in 1802 exposed the central government’s weakness. Napoleon’s Act of Mediation of 19 February 1803 ended the Helvetic Republic and restored a more federal structure, while retaining changes such as the status of former subject territories as cantons. Switzerland’s communities continued through this constitutional transformation.

sectionTitles: A highland kingdom linked to distant worlds
Saving water and preparing everyday food
Belief, care and a changing political world

passages.text: Himyar grew from Yemen’s highlands into the leading power of late ancient South Arabia, with its capital at Zafar. Its rulers absorbed neighbouring kingdoms and extended influence farther north. The atlas’s approximate 1 BCE to 600 CE span combines different political phases; its broad repeated shapes cannot show each conquest. Independent Himyar and the later Ethiopian-backed rulers must be distinguished.

passages.title: A highland kingdom linked to distant worlds
passages.text: Himyar’s power rested in Yemen’s highlands, where centres such as Zafar grew alongside agricultural terraces and dams. Its rivals included Saba to the north and Hadramawt to the east. Their changing alliances and wars eventually gave way to Himyarite annexation around the late third and early fourth centuries.

passages.title: A highland kingdom linked to distant worlds
passages.text: Makhawan, associated with modern al-Makha or Mocha, was a port serving Himyar. Maritime routes brought luxury goods from India and the Mediterranean into South Arabia. Inland rulers therefore belonged to a seaborne trading world as well as a mountain landscape of fields, roads and fortified settlements.

passages.title: A highland kingdom linked to distant worlds
passages.text: Himyar later extended its influence into central Arabia. The tribe of Kinda acted as an intermediary in administering northern territories. This was more complicated than colouring a single solid block on a map: rulers could work through other political groups rather than directly governing every settlement themselves.

passages.title: Saving water and preparing everyday food
passages.text: Terraces helped farmers retain soil and rainwater on slopes. Large stone walls across valleys also held these resources in place. Near Zafar, the al-Shaʿbani reservoir preserves Himyarite-style masonry within a system altered through long use. Catching water before it ran downhill was a major practical achievement.

passages.title: Saving water and preparing everyday food
passages.text: At the non-elite settlement of al-Adlaʿ, studied alongside Zafar, most pottery consisted of plain storage jars, cooking pots, platters and large bowls. A small proportion was more finely finished. Archaeology brings the kingdom down to kitchen scale: people needed somewhere to store ingredients, cook and serve food.

passages.title: Saving water and preparing everyday food
passages.text: Excavators at Zafar recovered charred barley and several kinds of wheat, alongside oats. Some deposits appear to preserve grain prepared for consumption. Burnt seeds are tiny clues to a much larger farming system: researchers can identify crops even when the meals and the people who ate them are long gone.

passages.title: Saving water and preparing everyday food
passages.text: Other plant remains included lentils, peas, sesame, flax, grapes, dates and almonds. These finds reveal a varied supply of food and useful plants. They do not tell us one standard menu for every household, but they give a richer picture than imagining an entire kingdom surviving on a single grain.

passages.title: Saving water and preparing everyday food
passages.text: Zafar also yielded patterned glass, including an imported fragment with opaque green and translucent decoration. Such small finds show that attractive objects reached the capital through wider connections. A broken piece can preserve evidence of trade long after the complete vessel has vanished.

passages.title: Saving water and preparing everyday food
passages.text: Stone lamps and vessels were recorded during excavation and museum inventory. Some lamps had a hole for the wick, while a lid had a reclining lion-like figure for its grip. Practical equipment could also be playful: even a container lid might come with its own little animal.

passages.title: Letters, learning and family hopes
passages.text: People in ancient South Arabia wrote everyday documents on wooden sticks and palm-leaf stalks, using a pointed tool and a flowing cursive script. This older regional practice continued into Himyar’s time; a surviving example illustrated by specialist Peter Stein dates to the fifth century. A letter could literally be a piece of wood.

passages.title: Letters, learning and family hopes
passages.text: Documents recorded private and business correspondence, contracts and payments. Some carried signatures; settled agreements could be cancelled by scratching or breaking the wood. Writing exercises found among documents also reveal scribal training. Before anyone could handle important contracts, they had to learn their letters.

passages.title: Letters, learning and family hopes
passages.text: An inscription dated January 465 commemorates a sanctuary built at Dulaʿ, near Sana’a. Its patron asked that he, his wife and his children should live justly, and hoped for virtuous children. This elite family prayer offers a small, personal glimpse beyond royal titles and military victories.

passages.title: Letters, learning and family hopes
passages.text: A palace inscription associated with Yehuda Yakkuf, around 380 to 420, includes “mrʾ ḥyn w-mwtn”: “Lord of life and of death”. This is a scholarly transcription of its Sabaic wording into Roman letters. The original belongs to South Arabia’s own written tradition, not to the later Arabic script.

passages.title: Belief, care and a changing political world
passages.text: Around380 to 384, royal inscriptions stopped invoking the older gods and adopted language about one heavenly Lord. Jewish belief became important at court, while religious life remained diverse. The evidence does not let historians assign one identical faith or set of practices to every family in the kingdom.

passages.title: Belief, care and a changing political world
passages.text: For an earlier regional example of concern for well-being, a bronze hand from second- or third-century South Arabia carries Wahab Ta’lab’s dedication to his patron deity. Its named Zafar may differ from Himyar’s capital. The object records a personal religious offering; it does not establish a medical treatment.

passages.title: Belief, care and a changing political world
passages.text: Researchers reported in 2022 that severe early-sixth-century drought probably added to Himyar’s troubles. They compared an Oman cave’s mineral layers with other climate evidence and historical records. Less rainfall could strain fields and water systems, but drought worked alongside war and political upheaval rather than explaining everything by itself.

passages.title: Belief, care and a changing political world
passages.text: King Yusuf’s persecution of Christians, including the killing of people at Najran, brought suffering within the kingdom and a response from Christian Aksum across the Red Sea. Ethiopian forces displaced him and installed another ruler. Religious conflict was also a struggle over political power and regional alliances.

passages.title: Belief, care and a changing political world
passages.text: Under the later ruler Abraha, repairs to the great Marib dam accompanied diplomacy. In 548 representatives of neighbouring powers met at Marib while local groups helped with the works. Maintaining inherited infrastructure remained essential even when the people at the top of the government had changed.

Aksumite conquest in the sixth century ended the independent dynasty, but later rulers continued to govern Himyar. Persian intervention then brought another change of power, with provincial government established around 575. These changes did not erase the region’s people or their accumulated skills. The map’s 600 endpoint is only a broad imported boundary.

sectionTitles: An excavated town beside the Vaigai
A king’s words and places of learning

passages.text: “Hindu kingdoms” is a broad imported map label, not the name of one ancient empire. Its outlines jump between northern, central and southern regions from 500 BCE to 800 CE. They neither locate every kingdom accurately nor identify everyone’s religion. Buddhist, Jain and diverse Brahmanical traditions shared these landscapes. The examples below concern particular places and periods; the atlas also has separate Maurya, Gupta, Pallava and Chalukya cards.

passages.title: Many states, many traditions
passages.text: Around the beginning of this map span, northern India contained powerful regional states often called mahajanapadas. Magadha became the core of the later Mauryan empire. Buddhism and Jainism developed alongside Brahmanical traditions. A label based on one modern religious category cannot adequately describe this political and intellectual variety.

passages.title: Many states, many traditions
passages.text: The Guptas consolidated much of northern India in the fourth century CE. Their era saw Sanskrit literature and religious sculpture flourish, including Buddhist images. In the south, maritime commerce connected communities with Rome and Southeast Asia. These overlapping histories belonged to different courts, ports and communities, rather than a single government directing the whole subcontinent.

passages.title: Many states, many traditions
passages.text: Harsha, who ruled in the seventh century, became a major northern king and a patron of Buddhist learning. His court belonged to a world of Sanskrit literature, diplomatic travel and competing regional powers. The Chalukyas were important rivals to the south; the map’s enormous shared outline should not be read as Harsha’s personal territory.

passages.title: Many states, many traditions
passages.text: Southern courts also supported distinctive literary cultures. Tamil devotional poets addressed Shiva and Vishnu in a regional language, while Pallava, Pandya and Chalukya rulers sponsored monuments and religious institutions. Their communities included Buddhists and Jains as well. Shared artistic ideas could travel between rival kingdoms without making their governments, languages or beliefs identical.

passages.title: An excavated town beside the Vaigai
passages.text: Keeladi, near Madurai in southern India, preserves an early historic town associated with the Sangam age. Excavators found ovens, pots, brick remains and grooved roof tiles. These objects bring the story down from royal courts to cooking, shelter and maintenance. The site’s evidence spans layers; every object should not be assigned the same year.

passages.title: An excavated town beside the Vaigai
passages.text: A terracotta well uncovered at Keeladi in 2021 had interlocking rings and raised rope-like decoration. One exposed ring measured 77 centimetres across. Its decorated upper part may once have been visible above ground. A working water installation could receive ornamental attention too, rather like making the useful corner of a home look nice.

passages.title: An excavated town beside the Vaigai
passages.text: Spindle whorls, beads, bangles, dice and gaming pieces were among the Keeladi finds. They point to textile work, adornment and recreation within the same settlement. A spindle whorl helped turn fibre into thread; the small game pieces remind us that ancient life contained play as well as chores. The finds do not identify each player’s age.

passages.title: A king’s words and places of learning
passages.text: A copperplate grant from Banskhera bears a striking royal formula. In scholarly Roman transliteration, its Sanskrit begins “svahasto mama”, meaning “my own hand”, followed by Harsha’s royal titles and name. The inscription dates to his year 22, approximately 628 CE. This is one northern royal document, not a sample of every language spoken across the map.

passages.title: A king’s words and places of learning
passages.text: The Banskhera plate also names an engraver, Isvara, and two beneficiaries of the grant. The royal formula appears in enlarged, ornamental letters. Thus the surviving record brings together a king’s authority, a craftsperson’s work and named recipients. The words claiming the king’s own hand should not be confused with a claim that he personally cut every letter into copper.

passages.title: A king’s words and places of learning
passages.text: Nalanda in Bihar became a major Buddhist residential and teaching institution from the fifth century CE onward. Its monasteries combined places to live with places to study and worship. This is an important reminder that the areas gathered under the map’s “Hindu kingdoms” label also contained influential Buddhist communities and centres of learning.

passages.title: A king’s words and places of learning
passages.text: Nalanda’s visible ruins contain many generations of construction, including eleven monasteries and fourteen temples within the protected property. Archaeologists excavated and conserved the site in the early twentieth century. Some modern repair bricks carry discreet dates. Looking closely means separating ancient building, later additions and the work that keeps fragile ruins standing today.

passages.title: Teeth, children, water and medicine
passages.text: The late-seventh-century Chinese monk Yijing described chewing a small piece of wood to clean the teeth. He reported that even children around three years old were taught the habit. His account mixes observations with advice for Buddhist readers; it preserves a memorable family routine without proving that every household followed it in exactly the same way.

passages.title: Teeth, children, water and medicine
passages.text: Yijing also described checking water for tiny creatures and straining it through cloth. Monks were supposed to return trapped insects safely to water. The stated aim was to avoid harming living beings. A filter here belonged to religious discipline, so it should not be mistaken for evidence that people understood modern germ theory.

passages.title: Teeth, children, water and medicine
passages.text: In Yijing’s account, images of Hariti, a protective mother figure, received offerings of food in monasteries. She was shown with a baby and other children, and people who wanted children approached her. Such practices connected religious institutions with family hopes. The story’s promises of answered prayers are beliefs recorded by the traveller, not medical evidence.

passages.title: Teeth, children, water and medicine
passages.text: Medical knowledge travelled beyond these kingdoms. The Bower manuscript, written on birch bark and dated broadly to the fourth through sixth centuries, preserves Sanskrit medical material related to Indian traditions. It was found near Kucha in Central Asia, outside this map’s footprint. Its survival shows the movement of texts and healing knowledge, rather than the services available in every Indian village.

passages.title: Building skills that outlasted dynasties
passages.text: At Pattadakal, Queen Lokamahadevi commissioned the Virupaksha temple around 740 to commemorate her husband’s southern victories. The monuments bring together architectural forms associated with northern and southern India. A queen’s patronage and the work of designers, stonecutters and sculptors became visible in a building that survived the court that commissioned it.

passages.title: Building skills that outlasted dynasties
passages.text: At Ellora, the Kailasa temple was cut from living rock rather than assembled entirely from separate blocks. Its carvings include Ravana trying to lift Shiva’s mountain. Rashtrakuta patronage supported this eighth-century achievement. The wider cave group also contains Buddhist monuments and later Jain caves, so everything visible at Ellora does not belong to one dynasty or to years before 800.

The imported label stops at 800 CE, but there was no common fall of “the Hindu kingdoms”. Rashtrakuta, Pala and Gurjara-Pratihara power continued into later centuries, and religious communities, languages and institutions kept changing. Individual dynasties had their own endings; this umbrella record should not replace those histories or imply that a population disappeared.

sectionTitles: A giant building site left unfinished
A town of crops, crafts and worshippers
What continued after the atlas label

passages.text: The atlas alternates two broad labels: “Rajput kingdoms” in 1000 to 1100 and 1200 to 1279, and “Hindu kingdoms” in 1100 to 1200. This shared page covers regional ruling networks, not one empire or everyone’s religion. The middle outline covers the northwest; the later one misleadingly reaches southern India. These are unreliable borders. Examples complement separate dynasty cards; Bhojpur and Chandravati lie outside the middle-century outline.

passages.title: Power, families and political relationships
passages.text: Forts anchored control over surrounding farmland as well as military defence. IGNOU’s historical survey connects regional strongholds with rural property and landed authority. A king needed food and people behind the walls, and connections beyond them.

passages.title: Power, families and political relationships
passages.text: Marriage between ruling clans helped create political alliances and social standing. Rajput identity developed through changing relationships among families, warriors and landholders; it was not a single unchanged ancestry shared by everyone living in these territories.

passages.title: Power, families and political relationships
passages.text: At Kiradu in 1161, Somesvara’s praise inscription placed a local Paramara ruler within the power of the Chaulukya king Kumarapala. Such records reveal layered authority: an ambitious regional lord could advertise victories while acknowledging a more powerful king.

passages.title: Power, families and political relationships
passages.text: An early twelfth-century Jalor inscription credits Queen Melaradevi, wife of Visala, with furnishing a Shiva temple with a golden cupola. Royal women could commission highly visible religious gifts in their own names. This is one queen’s documented patronage, not a description of every woman’s opportunities.

passages.title: A giant building site left unfinished
passages.text: At Bhojpur, the eleventh-century Paramara king Bhoja is associated with an enormous Shiva temple that was never completed. Its surviving hall has four columns about 12 metres tall. The unfinished structure lets researchers investigate decisions that a completed building might have hidden.

passages.title: A giant building site left unfinished
passages.text: Builders scratched architectural drawings onto the surrounding rock: plans, pillars, doorways, capitals and measurements for spacing columns. These were working aids at the construction site. Imagine doing your geometry homework on the ground, then using the answer to position a giant stone pillar.

passages.title: A giant building site left unfinished
passages.text: Carved blocks still lie around Bhojpur, and surviving earthen ramps help explain how heavy building materials could be raised. Nearby dam remains show that the project also reshaped the Betwa river landscape. ASI excavations in 1950 investigated the temple area, adding excavation evidence to the visible ruins.

passages.title: A town of crops, crafts and worshippers
passages.text: Excavations at Chandravati from 2013 to 2016 uncovered remains of a town with substantial religious buildings. Researchers describe temple platforms built in brick and the use of marble from the Ambaji area. Stone arriving from a quarry had to pass through the hands of transport workers, builders and sculptors.

passages.title: A town of crops, crafts and worshippers
passages.text: A Chandravati panel dated to the twelfth or thirteenth century shows worshippers queued before a Jain image. The excavators interpret objects in their hands as possible water pots for ritual bathing of the image. Even a carved medieval crowd seems familiar: everyone waiting for a turn.

passages.title: A town of crops, crafts and worshippers
passages.text: Another sculpture of the same broad period shows a woman adjusting her anklet. Religious art could include recognizable gestures of dressing and adornment. This little action gives a more personal glimpse than a list of royal victories, although an idealized sculpture is not a household photograph.

passages.title: A town of crops, crafts and worshippers
passages.text: Charred crop remains from Chandravati’s roughly 800 to 1300 phase include barley and rice; the researchers also illustrate wheat from that phase. Winter and summer crops both appear. These are actual traces of the plant economy, though surviving seeds cannot tell us precisely what every family ate for dinner.

passages.title: A town of crops, crafts and worshippers
passages.text: Researchers dated charred grain, seeds and wood, then compared the town’s evidence with pollen from nearby Mandovari Lake. They interpret the diverse medieval crops alongside relatively favourable monsoon conditions. Burnt food can be a disaster for a cook and a useful clue for an archaeologist.

passages.title: Learning and words that survive
passages.text: A twelfth-century Sarasvati from Pallu, now in the National Museum, stands about 77 centimetres high and carries symbols including a book and rosary. The museum identifies her as the Jain goddess of learning. Books mattered in this religious imagery, but the statue cannot tell us how many children attended lessons.

passages.title: Learning and words that survive
passages.text: Kiradu’s Sanskrit inscription says “प्रशस्तिमकरोदेतां”, here rendered in modern Devanagari from the scholarly transcription praśastim akarod etāṃ: “composed this eulogy”. The next words name Narasimha acting at the king’s order. These are words from a specific 1161 court monument, not a sample of everyone’s everyday speech.

passages.title: Learning and words that survive
passages.text: The Kiradu record survives on a temple pillar and has been studied through impressions and successive editions. Some letters have been lost or damaged. The modern edition marks restored passages with brackets; the short sample above avoids those restorations.

passages.title: What continued after the atlas label
passages.text: Later Rajasthan forts enclosed temples, homes, markets and palaces, with water-harvesting systems that helped sustain these communities. Jaisalmer remains inhabited. These buildings developed over many centuries, so its present-day streets and reservoirs should not all be assigned to the map’s 1000 to 1279 interval.

passages.title: What continued after the atlas label
passages.text: Chandravati’s excavations show occupation continuing into the late seventeenth century. Its eventual decline was much later than this atlas cutoff. The study considers environmental stress alongside historical and institutional changes, rather than giving every settlement in the region one shared disaster story.

There was no collective collapse in 1200 or 1279, the endpoints of these imported labels. Regional dynasties faced different wars, successions and changing alliances, while Rajput courts and communities continued for centuries. Rajasthan’s surviving fort traditions extend into the eighteenth century and include later interactions with Sultanate and Mughal architecture.

sectionTitles: Several courts, several kinds of power
Roads, shopping and pictures on the walls

passages.text: This is the atlas’s broad label for several southern Indian states in 1700-1783, especially around Madurai, Thanjavur and Ramnad. It is not one Hindu empire. The 1700 outline also reaches Mysore and the far southwest; the 1715 outline contracts eastward. Neither boundary tracks every changing ruler. This card follows distinct southern courts, their subjects and their dealings with Mughal, Carnatic and European powers.

passages.title: Several courts, several kinds of power
passages.text: Thanjavur’s Maratha kingdom began under Ekoji in the 1670s. Its rulers later paid tribute within the Mughal governor’s southern political order and clashed with Arcot’s nawab. Their southern court should not simply be treated as another name for the whole Maratha Empire.

passages.title: Several courts, several kinds of power
passages.text: Madurai’s Queen Mangammal governed as regent for her young grandson. She accepted Mughal tribute demands while negotiating with neighboring powers. The university history records her 1701 land gift to a Muslim dargah. The map’s religious label can hide the practical alliances and varied religious communities of these kingdoms.

passages.title: Several courts, several kinds of power
passages.text: A Tamil copper grant dated 1733 names two villages, Suriyan Kuttam and Sembikuttam, and their recipient Anand Iyengar, son of Narayana Iyengar. The grantor’s connection to the Ramnad royal family is also spelled out. Government survives here as named land, named families and a durable legal record.

passages.title: Several courts, several kinds of power
passages.text: Ramnad’s Ramalinga Vilasam palace contained both an audience hall and royal living quarters. Built during Kizhavan Sethupathi’s reign, 1674-1710, it brought political ceremony and an elite household into the same complex. Its surviving rooms show a ruler’s residence, not the typical size or comfort of ordinary homes.

passages.title: Roads, shopping and pictures on the walls
passages.text: Mangammal’s public works included improved roads toward Rameswaram, tree planting and irrigation. These could matter to travelers and farming households as much as palaces did. The same regional history records severe droughts in 1710 and 1720, a reminder that a ruler’s building projects did not remove dependence on rain.

passages.title: Roads, shopping and pictures on the walls
passages.text: A 1760 copper plate from Tiruchendur records traders’ monthly expenses for cotton, tobacco and trousers, alongside support for worship at a monastery. The merchants came from several named places, including Sivakasi. Trousers have made it into the historical record: accounting could preserve details that a royal battle story would leave out.

passages.title: Roads, shopping and pictures on the walls
passages.text: The same plate places this support in Avani, a month of the Tamil calendar, and decorates the record with Murugan and his consorts, Ganesha and a peacock. Religious gatherings, merchant contributions and crafted legal documents intersected. Its copper sheet is roughly 37 centimeters tall, a fairly substantial receipt to put in your pocket.

passages.title: Roads, shopping and pictures on the walls
passages.text: Ramnad’s palace paintings depict battles with Thanjavur’s Marathas and contacts with Europeans. They also include Ramayana scenes and water sports, with descriptions in colloquial language. Walls could present stories as well as royal prestige. These are courtly representations; a painted activity does not prove that every household enjoyed it.

passages.title: Money, learning and healing
passages.text: A copper coin catalogued as an eighteenth-century Madurai Nayak issue weighs 2.1 grams and measures only 1.2 centimeters across. Its reverse gives the Tamil city name Madurai in two lines. The museum does not know where this particular coin was found or assign it to a named king, so its date remains broad.

passages.title: Money, learning and healing
passages.text: The Saraswathi Mahal Library grew from a Nayak court collection and received support from Thanjavur’s Maratha rulers. Manuscripts made earlier scholarship available to later readers. The especially famous collecting of Serfoji II belongs mainly after 1798, beyond this map interval; it should not be quietly moved back into 1700.

passages.title: Money, learning and healing
passages.text: Tulaja I, also called Tukkoji, was a royal author whose medical works survive in the Thanjavur manuscript tradition. Scholar V. Raghavan identified Dhanvantarivilasa as a work written at the request of Tulaja’s son Ekoji. This is a concrete family connection in the production of learned medicine.

passages.title: Money, learning and healing
passages.text: Raghavan also described a compilation attributed to Tulaja containing medical formulas and lists of Sanskrit herb names with Tamil equivalents. Naming a plant in more than one language helped connect kinds of learned knowledge. These learned compilations do not tell us how widely treatment was available.

passages.title: A musical voice that survived
passages.text: Shahaji’s early eighteenth-century Telugu opera Pallaki Seva Prabandha draws on ritual at Tiruvarur. Parvati’s companions try to approach Shiva, who eventually travels to her in a palanquin. Songs, spoken narrative links and verse carry the story. The imagined divine court even makes room for the poet-king’s own work.

passages.title: A musical voice that survived
passages.text: A short Telugu sample, in the Music Academy’s modern Roman transliteration, is kadalimpakurōyi pallaki: “Don’t swing the pallaki so.” A pallaki is a palanquin. In the song’s playful religious imagery, careful bearers must avoid disturbing the worlds within the god. This presents a transmitted period text, not the handwriting of Shahaji.

passages.title: A musical voice that survived
passages.text: The opera survived through both manuscripts and performers. In the twentieth century P. Sambhamoorthy located its songs in the singing of Veerammal and wrote down their music. His 1955 edition printed Telugu lyrics and Tamil-script notation. Spoken language and the script used to record music need not be the same thing.

No single kingdom fell in 1783. Madurai’s Nayak rule ended with Chanda Sahib’s conquest in 1736, while Thanjavur’s Maratha court continued. Thanjavur transferred administration to the British in 1799 and retained a smaller royal establishment until 1855. The atlas cutoff is not the disappearance of southern communities, their languages or their cultural traditions.

sectionTitles: A writer’s name and surviving voices

passages.text: This atlas label covers parts of western India and the Deccan in 323-200 BCE, not one empire or one religion. A northwestern outline disappears at 300 BCE; the Deccan outline remains. It includes places where Ashoka later left imperial edicts, so it cannot show uninterrupted independence. Local communities, assemblies, kingdoms and expanding imperial authority need separate histories.

passages.title: What the umbrella label conceals
passages.text: Some early states called ganas or sanghas shared power among groups of men, often styled rajas. Historians describe these as oligarchies. The label “republic” does not establish universal voting rights, and evidence for northern assemblies cannot identify the government of every Deccan settlement.

passages.title: What the umbrella label conceals
passages.text: At Brahmagiri, Ashoka’s message passes through the prince and senior officers at Suvarnagiri to officials at Isila. An inscription therefore preserves an administrative chain, not just a king’s slogan. This third-century BCE evidence sits inside the atlas’s supposed kingdoms-and-republics outline.

passages.title: What the umbrella label conceals
passages.text: Maski’s inscription became especially important because it names Ashoka himself. Mining engineer C. Beadon encountered it in 1915 while prospecting for gold. A search for one kind of treasure helped recover another: a named ruler’s message cut into a boulder.

passages.title: Settlements, fields and skilled work
passages.text: Surveyors at Maski found a change from several smaller Iron Age settlements to a large Early Historic settlement covering about 15 hectares. This broader phase begins around 300 BCE and lasts well beyond the card’s end. The pattern suggests people concentrated into fewer, larger communities; it is not an exact census for 250 BCE.

passages.title: Settlements, fields and skilled work
passages.text: Near Maski, rock surfaces used to process gold ore contain grinding hollows and deeper collection receptacles. Ashoka’s edict stands near a route toward this working area. Researchers suggest imperial interest in the gold, but proximity alone cannot prove that the emperor owned the mine or managed every worker.

passages.title: Settlements, fields and skilled work
passages.text: Studies of the interior Deccan describe farming cereals and pulses alongside keeping cattle, sheep and goats. Fields and herds supported one another in these regional economies. This is the long-term background to the early historic settlements, rather than evidence for one standard meal served in every home.

passages.title: Settlements, fields and skilled work
passages.text: Scattered artifacts across clay-rich fields around Maski have been interpreted as evidence for manuring in the Iron Age or Early Historic period. Household refuse carried out to fields can leave tiny traces over a wide area. Archaeologists therefore look beyond impressive monuments to understand farming and the reuse of everyday waste.

passages.title: Settlements, fields and skilled work
passages.text: Stone-built memorials also formed part of these landscapes. Their shapes varied, and building them continued across several archaeological periods. Researchers argue that making monuments and gathering around them helped establish community ties. Their interpretation concerns shared labor and remembrance, rather than treating every large grave as a clearly identified king’s tomb.

passages.title: Water and family contributions
passages.text: At Girnar, later inscriptions remember a reservoir made under Chandragupta’s governor Pushyagupta and improved under Ashoka. This western place lies in the atlas’s first outline. The account shows how later rulers linked water management with earlier royal service; it is retrospective testimony, not a building receipt surviving from Chandragupta’s lifetime.

passages.title: Water and family contributions
passages.text: Bhattiprolu’s Buddhist relic-casket inscriptions name a ruler, Kubhiraka, alongside organized groups. ASI dates them broadly to the third or second century BCE, possibly beyond this card’s endpoint. Their language is Prakrit in a southern form of Brahmi. A distinctive script does not make the language Telugu.

passages.title: Water and family contributions
passages.text: One Bhattiprolu casket record brings a family into view: Kura and his parents contributed to containers for Buddhist relics. Stone receptacles protected smaller precious containers. Remembering donors in writing connected family resources, specialist craft and a religious community. The record does not reveal the family’s full wealth or everyday household arrangements.

passages.title: A writer’s name and surviving voices
passages.text: At Brahmagiri, the Prakrit words Chapaḍena likhite mean “written by Chapada.” This is a modern scholarly transliteration of a third-century BCE Brahmi inscription. The accompanying word for the scribe uses Kharoshthi. Two scripts appear in one record; they do not establish that every resident spoke two languages.

passages.title: A writer’s name and surviving voices
passages.text: A modern experiment copied Ashokan lettering with different chisels, then compared its marks with Karnataka inscriptions. Tool wear and sharpening changed the widths of lines. Writing a message on rock required physical craft as well as words: unlike a page, the boulder offered no easy eraser. The experiment tests possibilities, not one proven ancient toolkit.

passages.title: A writer’s name and surviving voices
passages.text: Ashoka’s Brahmagiri message urges respect for parents and elders, truthfulness and compassion toward animals. These instructions bring family conduct into a public inscription. They tell us what the ruler wanted people to do; they cannot measure how kindly every household actually behaved.

passages.title: A writer’s name and surviving voices
passages.text: Later Buddhist communities at Kanaganahalli near Sannati carved limestone stories and royal figures, including a labeled Ashoka. The surviving reliefs date from the first century BCE to the third century CE. They show his later remembrance, not a portrait carved during his reign. Buddhism and regional patronage continued after this map label stopped.
The 200 BCE cutoff marks no collective fall. Mauryan involvement preceded it; later Satavahana patronage shaped Kanaganahalli. Regional communities and their varied traditions continued.
