sectionTitles: First, test the map against the kingdom
A name, a takeover and rulers reconstructed from scraps
Jayapala faces Ghazni, and the line survives the map seam
Kings, local patrons, alliances and a wall of watchtowers
Roads, harvests, markets and money with a bull
Temples that mixed building traditions and living religions
A stone voice, a coin label and lessons for princes
Families, ranks and what childhood sources forgot
Homes, bowls, jewelry, work and a handful of game pieces
Health, water, bathrooms, toilets and what continued

passages.text: Picture a kingdom as a chain of guarded mountain gates: Kabul behind high passes, fertile Swat beyond watchtowers, and Hund beside the rushing Indus. The rulers now called Hindu Shahis inherited this crossroads around 822 CE and gradually shifted east as Saffarid and Ghaznavid power squeezed their western lands. In the atlas, however, hindu-shahis exists only from 900 to 1000, misses Kabul, Peshawar, Hund and Swat, and floats across part of the Punjab. The historical story is bigger. Lalliya, Kamalavarman, Bhima Deva and Jayapala ruled through forts, alliances, inscriptions, temples and widely circulating coins. Jayapala fought Sebüktegin and Mahmud; Anandapala, Trilocanapala and Bhimapala continued after the atlas erased their id. By about 1026 or 1027 the dynasty ended under Ghaznavid conquest. Archaeology recovers straight streets, kitchens, bathrooms, drains, wells, dice and tiny beads, while honest gaps remain about ordinary children, healers and household toilets.

passages.title: First, test the map against the kingdom
passages.text: The exact imported record is id “hindu-shahis,” name “Hindu Shahis,” circa 900 to 1000. It was missing a card and researched override. Kingdom of Kapisa, Kingdom of Kashmir, Saffarids, Samanids and Ghaznavids are separate records, so this card cannot quietly absorb or overwrite them.

passages.title: First, test the map against the kingdom
passages.text: At 900 the target is one Polygon with one ring and 14 positions. Its bounds are 71.700° to 79.149° east and 28.336° to 33.346° north; coordinate SHA-256 is 5be7f04275d2d1f39b061cb9ececf79104c5691ab986e7badae71f9b3afc9b12. Nandana, Katas, Lahore and Sialkot test inside.

passages.title: First, test the map against the kingdom
passages.text: The same polygon excludes Kabul, Kapisa, Ghazni, Laghman, Peshawar, Hund, Taxila, Barikot, Udegram, Swat, Bilot, Bannu, Chitral, Srinagar and Multan. Missing Hund and Barikot is especially serious because inscriptions, archaeology and texts directly connect those places to Late Shahi rulers.

passages.title: First, test the map against the kingdom
passages.text: At 900 the atlas assigns every tested secure center from Kabul through Hund and Swat to samanid-empire, while hindu-shahis occupies a southern Punjab shape. This is not a small fuzzy-edge problem. The two layers place the dynasty outside much of its best-attested political and archaeological landscape.

passages.title: First, test the map against the kingdom
passages.text: The target is absent at 700, 800, 1000, 1100 and 1200. Kingdom of Kapisa covers the Kabul and Swat tests in 700; a broad Abbasid layer covers them in 800; Ghaznavids cover Kabul by 1000. Premodern power followed forts, roads and alliances, so these abrupt atlas blocks are illustrations, not surveyed borders.

passages.title: A name, a takeover and rulers reconstructed from scraps
passages.text: “Hindu Shahis” is a modern standard label built largely from al-Biruni’s phrase for the later “Shahis of al-Hind.” Recent scholarship often says Late Shahis because religion did not flip like a switch and the realm contained Hindu, Buddhist and Muslim communities. The atlas id stays exact even while the card explains that history.

passages.title: A name, a takeover and rulers reconstructed from scraps
passages.text: Al-Biruni says Kallara was a Brahmin minister who imprisoned Lagaturman and took the kingship after finding treasure and gaining power. He wrote about two centuries later and shaped the event as a moral tale. Archaeologists cautiously place the transition around 822, rather than treating every detail as eyewitness reporting.

passages.title: A name, a takeover and rulers reconstructed from scraps
passages.text: Lalliya, probably ruling from about 870 to 902, is associated by the Rajatarangini with Udabhanda beside the Indus. The name may connect with Samanta Deva coin issues, but titles on coins do not map neatly onto personal names in chronicles. Matching them is a scholarly hypothesis, not a solved name tag.

passages.title: A name, a takeover and rulers reconstructed from scraps
passages.text: Kamalavarman appears under several names: Kamalu in al-Biruni, Kamaluka or Toramana in the Kashmiri chronicle, and Kamalavarman in the Dewai inscription. Different languages and literary purposes preserved different forms. Historians align them by sequence and family connections while admitting that the chronology remains putative.

passages.title: A name, a takeover and rulers reconstructed from scraps
passages.text: Bhima Deva, approximately 921 to 964, receives a mountain of titles on the Dewai stone: great king over kings, supreme lord and Shahi. Such language tells us how a court wanted power to sound. It does not prove that Bhima personally controlled every place where later maps draw a solid color.

passages.title: Jayapala faces Ghazni, and the line survives the map seam
passages.text: Jayapala saw the new power at Ghazni as a threat and fought Sebüktegin in the 980s. Sebüktegin moved through Laghman toward Peshawar and defeated him twice. Later narratives supply speeches, storms and moral lessons; the safer history is repeated war, frontier loss and a shifting balance west of the Indus.

passages.title: Jayapala faces Ghazni, and the line survives the map seam
passages.text: Mahmud defeated Jayapala in 1001, just after the atlas removes the Shahi layer. Older accounts say Jayapala abdicated and died by fire from shame. Because those motives come through courtly historical traditions, the card labels the reported self-immolation instead of entering the king’s mind as if a camera were present.

passages.title: Jayapala faces Ghazni, and the line survives the map seam
passages.text: Anandapala succeeded and helped assemble a broad coalition against Mahmud. The coalition lost near Peshawar or Waihind in 1008. A famous story blames panic after Anandapala’s elephant bolted, but battle tales often compress chaos into one dramatic animal; alliances, terrain and organization mattered too.

passages.title: Jayapala faces Ghazni, and the line survives the map seam
passages.text: Trilocanapala ruled after about 1010 and sought Kashmiri military help. Kalhana’s later chronicle praises his courage while criticizing allied commanders. This shows active diplomacy and fighting after the atlas endpoint, but it is also a literary account written for Kashmir, not a neutral battlefield report.

passages.title: Jayapala faces Ghazni, and the line survives the map seam
passages.text: Al-Biruni lists Trilocanapala’s death in 1021 or 1022 and Bhimapala five years later. Iranica dates the final ending to 1026. The bundle uses circa 1027 to reflect the conversion and source uncertainty, then links the territorial conquest to ghaznavid-emirate without claiming every community changed overnight.

passages.title: Kings, local patrons, alliances and a wall of watchtowers
passages.text: Royal inscriptions display elaborate hierarchy, but administration below the king is only patchily visible. At Barikot, a fragment names Jayapala and three people who patronized reconstruction of a devakula, a religious building. Local action and royal time appear together without proving the project was ordered or paid for by the king.

passages.title: Kings, local patrons, alliances and a wall of watchtowers
passages.text: Udabhanda, now Hund, stood at an Indus crossing and is repeatedly called the town or capital of Gandhara in early medieval sources. Its location made it useful for courts, travelers and armies. “Capital” still should not be imagined as one permanent modern ministry building governing every mountain valley by paperwork.

passages.title: Kings, local patrons, alliances and a wall of watchtowers
passages.text: In Swat, archaeologists trace a planned defensive system of hilltop fortresses, smaller garrison forts and watchtowers along roads and passes. These guarded fertile land, water and movement. A tower could warn a valley faster than a distant palace, making geography part of government rather than scenery behind it.

passages.title: Kings, local patrons, alliances and a wall of watchtowers
passages.text: Castle cities such as Udegram and Barikot squeezed dense settlement onto defended slopes, often with a hilltop citadel and a Brahmanical temple. Springs and wells helped people endure inside. Archaeologists use “palace” or “castle” cautiously because ruined walls rarely arrive with room labels.

passages.title: Kings, local patrons, alliances and a wall of watchtowers
passages.text: Marriage linked Shahi and Kashmiri elites. Bhima Deva’s granddaughter Didda married the Kashmiri king Kshemagupta, and the kingdoms exchanged military aid. This is evidence for dynastic family strategy at the top. It cannot be stretched into a rule for how farmers, artisans or servants chose partners.

passages.title: Roads, harvests, markets and money with a bull
passages.text: Routes ran east from Kabul along the Kabul River and through the Khyber approaches, while alternatives crossed the Kurram and Tochi valleys toward the Indus. None was an effortless highway. Narrow passes, snow, mud, river crossings and raiders shaped the cost and season of moving armies, letters, pilgrims and goods.

passages.title: Roads, harvests, markets and money with a bull
passages.text: Swat’s well-watered loess soils supported reliable double cropping compared with drier plains that depended more heavily on the monsoon. Forts concentrated around this productive landscape. The evidence supports valuable harvests and storage, but it does not turn the entire Shahi realm into one identical green farm.

passages.title: Roads, harvests, markets and money with a bull
passages.text: Late Shahi silver coins usually show Shiva’s bull Nandi beneath a Proto-Sharada legend and a spear-holding horseman on the other face. Copper series could show an elephant and lion. The designs joined religious and military signals in pocket-sized objects, though users did not need to read every letter to recognize the type.

passages.title: Roads, harvests, markets and money with a bull
passages.text: The earliest Late Shahi silver issues weighed about four grams, later settling near three to 3.1 grams. XRF tests show changing silver and intentionally added copper, but metal percentages do not identify one mine with certainty. A coin can reveal policy and resources without confessing exactly where its ore began.

passages.title: Roads, harvests, markets and money with a bull
passages.text: Coin finds cluster in Kabulistan, Uddiyana and Gandhara, with especially strong archaeological evidence from places such as Barikot and Udegram. Their spread marks payment and movement, not a perfectly outlined empire. Wider early medieval markets also exchanged grain, cloth, animals, salt and craft goods through routes and towns.

passages.title: Temples that mixed building traditions and living religions
passages.text: Salt Range temples combined northern Indian Nagara forms with older Gandharan habits and Iranian-related true arches, domes and vaults. Builders cut porous kanjur into regular courses, used mortar, then covered walls with lime plaster and color. The result was local invention from several traditions, not a copied architecture kit.

passages.title: Temples that mixed building traditions and living religions
passages.text: At Barikot, a Shahi temple stood high above a steep stair and probably rose more than twelve meters from its floor. Its rubble core, retaining walls, cut stone and plaster required planners, quarry workers, carriers and masons. Monumental height also controlled the visitor’s first view like careful stage scenery.

passages.title: Temples that mixed building traditions and living religions
passages.text: Hindu worship became prominent, with temples dedicated to Shiva, Vishnu and other deities, but Buddhist objects and institutions did not instantly vanish. Kabul and Gandhara also included Muslim communities. A dynastic nickname cannot make every subject share one belief, and religious change unfolded differently from place to place.

passages.title: Temples that mixed building traditions and living religions
passages.text: Shahi-period sculptors made sacred figures in marble, stucco, copper alloys and clay. Red-clay artists built a core around a wooden peg, pressed faces in molds, modeled hair by hand and attached tiny ornaments. What looks magically lifelike began with recipes, armatures, fingers and many chances for the nose to go crooked.

passages.title: Temples that mixed building traditions and living religions
passages.text: Copper-alloy images used varied alloys, casting choices and surface treatments. Researchers cannot yet assign every statue to a workshop from chemistry alone because makers remelted metal and selected mixtures for color, hardness or easier casting. Technical skill is real; a neat factory label would be less real.

passages.title: A stone voice, a coin label and lessons for princes
passages.text: Most Late Shahi inscriptions use Sanskrit in Proto-Sharada, with Sharada emerging around the eleventh century. Scripts traveled beyond dynastic borders and served royal praise, donations, land records, religious formulas and even graffiti. Writing culture was varied, so one inscription style cannot be called everybody’s handwriting.

passages.title: A stone voice, a coin label and lessons for princes
passages.text: Authentic sample from the damaged Dewai inscription, in readable modern Devanagari normalization: “परमभट्टारक-महाराजाधिराज-परमेश्वर-शाहि-श्री-भीमदेवः”. The original is tenth-century Sanskrit in Proto-Sharada characters. This display supplies letters restored by editors and changes scripts for readability; it is not a tracing of the stone.

passages.title: A stone voice, a coin label and lessons for princes
passages.text: Transliteration: “paramabhaṭṭāraka-mahārājādhirāja-parameśvara-śāhi-śrī-bhīmadevaḥ”. Translation: “the supreme venerable great king over kings, supreme lord, Shahi, illustrious Bhima Deva.” This is formal royal titulature, not a greeting heard in an ordinary kitchen, and each grand title describes a claim to rank rather than measured territory.

passages.title: A stone voice, a coin label and lessons for princes
passages.text: Coin legends offered shorter writing. One common series reads “śrī sāmanta deva,” normalized as “श्री सामन्तदेव,” meaning “Illustrious Samanta Deva.” Scholars increasingly treat Samanta Deva as a title shared across issues rather than one securely identified king. A British Museum example is only ten millimeters wide.

passages.title: A stone voice, a coin label and lessons for princes
passages.text: Al-Biruni says grammarian Ugrabhuti taught Prince Anandapala and sent his completed book to Kashmir. Anandapala supported its learned reception with gifts. This is unusually direct evidence for an elite teacher, pupil and manuscript network. It says nothing certain about whether a potter’s daughter attended a formal school.

passages.title: Families, ranks and what childhood sources forgot
passages.text: Royal genealogy makes some elite women visible: Didda was Bhima Deva’s granddaughter and became queen in Kashmir. Her marriage connected ruling houses, but the sources name her because she mattered to dynastic politics. They rarely preserve a shepherd mother’s choices, a craftswoman’s authority or a grandmother’s stories.

passages.title: Families, ranks and what childhood sources forgot
passages.text: Early medieval society used Brahmanical varna ideals alongside many local jatis, occupations and negotiated ranks. Court service, land, craft, gender and religious status shaped opportunity. These categories were not a tidy four-row classroom chart, and evidence written by elites reveals hierarchy more readily than ordinary people speaking for themselves.

passages.title: Families, ranks and what childhood sources forgot
passages.text: At Hund, gates opened from houses onto streets laid at right angles, suggesting households lived within an organized neighborhood. Rooms, halls, ovens and repeated floors show activity through time. Archaeology finds spaces and objects, though it cannot tell whether each room held a nuclear family, relatives, servants, tenants or several combinations.

passages.title: Families, ranks and what childhood sources forgot
passages.text: Children are almost invisible in written Shahi records. Miniature pots, terracotta animals, ivory dice and pendants were excavated at Hund, but context and purpose vary: some might relate to play, ritual, teaching or adult use. Calling every small object a toy would make a charming museum label and weak archaeology.

passages.title: Families, ranks and what childhood sources forgot
passages.text: Most learning probably happened through participation: speaking local languages, helping with animals or food, observing craft steps and memorizing religious or family knowledge. That is a careful inference from household and occupational life, not a surviving Shahi timetable. Formal Sanskrit study is securely visible mainly among princes, scribes and learned specialists.

passages.title: Homes, bowls, jewelry, work and a handful of game pieces
passages.text: Hund’s excavators found rooms and halls built in stone masonry, often with pebble or slab floors. Its pottery included bowls, cups, pitchers, jars, lamps, cooking pots, storage vessels and plates. That gives a sturdy household toolkit, although one excavation area cannot furnish every mountain village in exactly the same style.

passages.title: Homes, bowls, jewelry, work and a handful of game pieces
passages.text: Cooking pots, ovens, storage jars, sickle fragments and millstones connect meals to harvesting, storing, grinding and heating. Swat’s double-crop fields could feed towns and travelers. The evidence does not preserve a Late Shahi cookbook, so the card stops at grain foods and varied local produce instead of inventing tonight’s stew.

passages.title: Homes, bowls, jewelry, work and a handful of game pieces
passages.text: Gold earrings, hundreds of beads, bangles, rings, antimony rods and pendants show adornment at Hund. Beads used carnelian, lapis, agate, glass, clay, bone and ivory. Textiles rarely survived there, so clothing is reconstructed cautiously from sculptures showing tunics, shawls and jewelry, not as one uniform for everyone.

passages.title: Homes, bowls, jewelry, work and a handful of game pieces
passages.text: Work left sharper clues: sickles for harvesting, knives and axes for cutting, nails and bars for building, arrowheads for weapons, and weight cubes or cowries for exchange. Wider early medieval production relied on skilled practice and unequal labor. A tool names a task more readily than the worker’s age, pay or legal status.

passages.title: Homes, bowls, jewelry, work and a handful of game pieces
passages.text: Barikot’s later medieval fill contained clay dice and dozens of board-game tokens cut from pottery or stone, while Hund produced ivory dice. Some deposits were dumped during the Ghaznavid phase, so the pieces show regional play around the Shahi transition rather than a game securely owned by one Shahi child. The rules are lost.

passages.title: Health, water, bathrooms, toilets and what continued
passages.text: The wider Susruta tradition discusses anatomy, surgery, remedies and learning from a teacher, but its textual layers and dates are debated. It supplies South Asian medical background, not a patient chart from Hund. Direct evidence for Shahi physicians, midwives, household caregivers and access to treatment remains frustratingly sparse.

passages.title: Health, water, bathrooms, toilets and what continued
passages.text: Antimony rods from Hund may have served eye cosmetic or medicinal preparation, yet the object alone cannot choose between beauty, health or both. Knives are equally unsafe to relabel as surgical tools without context. Archaeology rewards careful verbs: an implement was found; its exact user and purpose may remain unknown.

passages.title: Health, water, bathrooms, toilets and what continued
passages.text: Water systems were serious infrastructure. Hund had a stone-ringed well; Swat forts enclosed springs and masonry wells; Barikot raised water from a deep couloir to a cistern; another fortified center had three springs, a large well and a stepped tank. Drinking, cooking, ritual, washing and defense could all depend on maintenance.

passages.title: Health, water, bathrooms, toilets and what continued
passages.text: Hund’s pre-Muslim buildings included bathrooms paved with long watertight slabs. Drains carried water into the main street, sometimes into large sewerage pots beneath the outlets. This is unusually direct sanitation evidence, though the report groups several pre-Muslim phases and does not identify an ordinary household latrine or a flushing toilet.

passages.title: Health, water, bathrooms, toilets and what continued
passages.text: Ghaznavid conquest ended the Shahi ruling line around 1026 or 1027, but people, fields, roads, coin habits, temples and craft knowledge continued. At 1000 the atlas had already erased the exact id; by 1100 it redraws the region again. A dynasty can end while a potter still opens the workshop next morning.

After Jayapala, Anandapala and Trilocanapala fought a long defensive struggle, al-Biruni places Bhimapala’s death five years after 1021 or 1022. Modern syntheses therefore end the Late Shahi line around 1026 or 1027. Ghaznavid rule took the main territorial core, especially the western Punjab, but Kashmir ties, religious communities, fortified settlements, farms, waterworks, coin designs and craft practices did not vanish in one year. This card records conquest at circa 1027 and names ghaznavid-emirate as the political successor, while keeping the atlas’s premature 1000 disappearance visible as a separate data problem.

materialEvidence.question: Does a concrete finding have an identifiable context, date, interpretation and evidence limit?

dailyLife.question: Does the account explain ordinary practices with evidence rather than only rulers?

artsScienceTechnology.question: Are achievements concrete and correctly attributed to this polity and period?

chronologicalPhases.question: Are source-supported phases distinguished from map snapshot dates?

endingContinuity.question: Does the narrative identify what ended or continued, with dates, mechanism and uncertainty?

uncertainty.question: Are uncertainties attached to particular claims rather than a blanket disclaimer?

sectionTitles: Families, fields and learning in Vengi
Crafts, different faiths and surviving words

passages.text: “Hindu states” is a changing atlas label for parts of India between 700 and 1000, not one kingdom. Its outlines jump from the northeast to western and peninsular regions, then shrink to a tiny northern fragment. These examples belong to distinct communities and dynasties, not a uniform religious population.

passages.title: Reading the changing map
passages.text: The 700 outline covers parts of Bengal and Assam. In 800 the label instead covers disconnected western and eastern peninsular areas; by 900 it is a small fragment in northern Uttar Pradesh. Abhaneri, discussed here for regional comparison, falls outside the sampled outlines. None of these boundaries establishes a shared religion or government.

passages.title: Reading the changing map
passages.text: Vengi inscriptions describe enemies, relatives and rival claimants rather than a united religious bloc. Amma I’s Ederu charter praises him for overcoming hostile kinsmen and winning his father’s troops. These are a court’s claims about a particular succession struggle; the neighbouring Rashtrakutas and other dynasties require their own histories.

passages.title: Northeastern towns and river work
passages.text: Ambari, in present-day Guwahati, was rediscovered during foundation digging for a Reserve Bank building in 1969. ASI distinguishes an occupation phase from roughly the seventh to twelfth centuries. A modern construction project opened a window onto a much older settlement; its later remains must be separated from that medieval phase.

passages.title: Northeastern towns and river work
passages.text: Ambari also yielded Chinese celadon dated to the tenth to twelfth centuries. Some therefore belongs after this map window. Such pottery points to connections beyond the Brahmaputra valley, although a traded bowl alone cannot identify who carried it or who ate from it.

passages.title: Northeastern towns and river work
passages.text: At Tezpur, a boulder beside the Brahmaputra carries a decree of Harjjaravarman dated 829 to 830. ASI describes a warning to fishermen about crossing a marked fishing area. River resources required rules as well as boats. This belongs to later Kamarupa history, after the atlas label has shifted away from Assam.

passages.title: Northeastern towns and river work
passages.text: Scholars also read references to boatmen in state service in the Tezpur inscription. River work linked food gathering, transport and royal administration. Fishing communities were participants in the region’s economy, not just background figures in stories about kings. The article’s descriptions of modern Majuli life cannot simply be assigned to the ninth century.

passages.title: Fetching water and gathering together
passages.text: Chand Baori at Abhaneri descends approximately 19.5 metres, with repeated flights of steps on three sides. Official accounts place its early construction around the eighth or ninth century. The changing water level could be approached down the staircase: getting water involved a rather longer walk than turning a tap.

passages.title: Fetching water and gathering together
passages.text: Rajasthan Tourism describes Chand Baori as both a water-conserving structure and a gathering place offering relief from the heat. Water infrastructure could create social space. Its spectacular surviving galleries belong to a monument with a building history, so every visible feature should not be dated to the first construction campaign.

passages.title: Fetching water and gathering together
passages.text: In Vengi, the museum history credits Vijayaditya II, an early ninth-century ruler, with feeding houses, shelters offering drinking water to travellers, and irrigation tanks. These activities supported movement and cultivation as well as religious patronage. A water station was a practical kindness on a hot journey.

passages.title: Families, fields and learning in Vengi
passages.text: The Cevuru charter of Amma I, from the early tenth century, links a favour to the soldier Vemaraja with Prince Vijayaditya’s first rice-feeding ceremony. A royal child’s milestone became an occasion for public generosity. This is one documented court celebration, not a rule for every family.

passages.title: Families, fields and learning in Vengi
passages.text: The same charter locates fields using a marshy pool, a stream, neighbouring land and the king’s field. Telugu landscape words appear inside its formal Sanskrit framework. A legal document needed landmarks people could recognize: grand royal titles did not replace knowing which stream bordered the field.

passages.title: Families, fields and learning in Vengi
passages.text: A grant of Vijayaditya II in Pishtapura district names a recipient’s father and grandfather and praises the family’s Vedic learning. Land patronage supported specialist scholarship across generations. This is evidence for a learned Brahman family, rather than a census of children attending school.

passages.title: Families, fields and learning in Vengi
passages.text: That grant was made at Trikotishvara during a lunar eclipse and confirmed by pouring water. It then lists neighbouring villages to define the property. Ceremony and practical geography belonged together: the water marked a formal gift, while the boundaries specified what was actually being given.

passages.title: Families, fields and learning in Vengi
passages.text: Amma I’s Ederu charter awarded Gonturu and twelve hamlets to a military retainer, with a tax exemption. Such grants show how rulers rewarded service through local resources. The document publicly addressed householders in the district, reminding us that a royal gift affected people already living and working there.

passages.title: Families, fields and learning in Vengi
passages.text: The Ederu charter praises Chalukya Bhima I for supporting distressed and helpless people alongside dancers and singers. It presents generosity as an attribute of good kingship. The wording records a royal ideal and a claim of patronage; it does not identify a hospital or establish the reach of medical care.

passages.title: Crafts, different faiths and surviving words
passages.text: Copper charters were substantial handmade objects. An Indian Museum set from Chandavallu consists of three plates, a ring and an inscribed seal associated with Vijayaditya II. The plates measure only about fourteen by five centimetres. Important royal information could be packed into a small, durable metal bundle.

passages.title: Crafts, different faiths and surviving words
passages.text: A later Vengi grant, from Amma II’s reign in the mid-tenth century, gave land to two Jain temples at Vijayavatika, now Vijayawada. It is a useful check on the atlas shorthand. A dynasty associated with Hindu royal language could also support Jain institutions; religious life was not neatly contained by a map colour.

passages.title: Crafts, different faiths and surviving words
passages.text: One authentic word is “स्वस्ति” (svasti), “Greetings,” opening Amma I’s Cevuru charter. The Sanskrit appears here in modern Devanagari, not the original southern letterforms. The charter also uses Telugu “koḍu,” “stream,” shown in scholarly Roman transcription. Both belong to this early tenth-century Vengi document, not a language shared by everyone under the atlas label.

passages.title: Crafts, different faiths and surviving words
passages.text: The Cevuru plates were found around 1928 when Polavarapu Ankayya cleared debris from a collapsed mud house. Chhabra later borrowed them for study. An ordinary repair or clearing job could recover a royal document that had long outlived its original owners.

The atlas endpoint of 1000 is not a common fall date. Vengi’s struggles continued, including Chola-backed intervention around 1000, while regional communities and religious institutions endured. This shifting umbrella ends as a map label; the named kingdoms have separate political histories.

sectionTitles: Read the atlas shape before treating it as history
See colonial government, courts, cities, and their limits
Keep Taíno people, survival, and agency in the story
Follow African lives through slavery, freedom, and resistance
Meet families, children, learners, and unequal classrooms
Enter homes, kitchens, wardrobes, and working days
Move sugar, hides, ceramics, people, and contraband
Treat illness, survive epidemics, and preserve healing knowledge
Ask where water, drains, waste, and toilets actually went
Hear language, faith, creativity, and the 1715 continuation

passages.text: The atlas calls this layer “Hispaniola (Spain)” from 1530 to 1715, but its geometry is not simply Hispaniola. In 1530 and 1600 one feature combines Jamaica, Puerto Rico, and Hispaniola. In 1650 and 1700 Jamaica disappears while Puerto Rico stays attached. Coastal cities fall outside the simplified shores. At 1715 eastern Hispaniola becomes “spain,” labeled Santo Domingo (Spain), western points become the anachronistic atlas id “haiti,” and San Juan receives an erroneous Danish Virgin Islands label. The map also lags politics. Spanish rule centered on Santo Domingo and named settlements, then contracted after forced depopulation in 1605 and 1606 opened space for western interlopers. French settlement expanded before the 1697 Treaty of Ryswick recognized France in the west; a precise border still did not appear at once. The layer therefore groups separate islands, simplifies shorelines, overstates uniform authority, and delays partition by eighteen years. This card treats it as an editorial aid. Its chapters use archives and excavated places to follow Taíno survival, African agency, slavery, government, family, childhood, work, food, health, water, waste, writing, faith, craft, trade, resistance, and continuity.

passages.title: Read the atlas shape before treating it as history
passages.text: The index contains one generated record named “Hispaniola (Spain),” dated approximately 1530 to 1715. It is absent from the 1500 map and has a modern-island imported summary, but no card or researched override. Those database facts do not establish that every resident, port, mountain settlement, or neighboring island shared one Spanish identity or government.

passages.title: Read the atlas shape before treating it as history
passages.text: In 1530 and 1600 the target is a three-component MultiPolygon. Its decoded pieces cover coarse versions of Jamaica, Puerto Rico, and Hispaniola. Santiago, Higüey, Hinche, Cap-Haïtien, Port-au-Prince, Léogâne, and San Juan fall inside, although several coastal city coordinates miss the simplified shore. This is an imperial grouping, not one island outline.

passages.title: Read the atlas shape before treating it as history
passages.text: The 1650 and 1700 versions drop the Jamaica component but retain Puerto Rico and Hispaniola as one label. Both use the same two-component decoded geometry. A reader therefore cannot interpret a color change as a surveyed border, a demographic census, or evidence that control was equally strong across hundreds of kilometers.

passages.title: Read the atlas shape before treating it as history
passages.text: Santo Domingo, Puerto Plata, Azua, Les Cayes, Tortuga, Saona, and Gonâve all fall outside the target under this atlas point test, despite their relevance to the history being told. Coarse shorelines can miss real coastal places. The card uses named evidence rather than making the polygon decide who existed.

passages.title: Read the atlas shape before treating it as history
passages.text: At 1715 the exact id disappears. Sampled eastern points become “spain,” labeled Santo Domingo (Spain); western points become the anachronistic atlas id “haiti”; and San Juan becomes the unrelated “virgin-islands-danemark.” Ryswick had recognized France in the west in 1697. The lag and Puerto Rico error reveal an editorial seam, not new states appearing together.

passages.title: See colonial government, courts, cities, and their limits
passages.text: Santo Domingo concentrated a governor, cabildo or town council, Real Audiencia, chancery, customs house, cathedral, monasteries, and other institutions. These offices made the city a major center of Spanish imperial administration. Their surviving masonry demonstrates organized power, but an impressive courthouse could issue orders much farther than officials could reliably enforce them.

passages.title: See colonial government, courts, cities, and their limits
passages.text: The city's plaza-centered grid, rebuilt on the west bank of the Ozama after 1502, influenced later Spanish American town planning. Straight streets organized government, worship, commerce, and elite property. They did not make the colony socially tidy: enslaved workers, servants, craftspeople, traders, children, migrants, and prisoners filled the planned blocks with unequal lives.

passages.title: See colonial government, courts, cities, and their limits
passages.text: A 1545 royal letter discussed about one hundred enslaved and free residents of Moorish or Berber background, including skilled masons and carpenters who were married and had children. The episode shows imperial sorting by religion, ancestry, status, and usefulness, while residents and city officials argued for locally valuable families to remain.

passages.title: See colonial government, courts, cities, and their limits
passages.text: Contraband spread because official fleets and legal imports did not meet local needs. Residents traded with foreign Protestant merchants despite royal bans, linking survival to disobedience. The practice crossed social levels, so “Spanish colony” describes a jurisdictional claim without proving that every transaction followed Spain's commercial rules or every inhabitant shared imperial loyalties.

passages.title: See colonial government, courts, cities, and their limits
passages.text: Drake's force captured Santo Domingo in 1586, looted it, and demanded ransom. A Spanish royal letter treated the attack as part of the Anglo-Spanish conflict and ordered a response. The raid damaged a symbolic capital, but the colony continued. Stone walls, titles, and paperwork were real achievements without being invulnerability spells.

passages.title: Keep Taíno people, survival, and agency in the story
passages.text: Spanish conquest, forced gold labor, food seizure, violence, and introduced disease caused catastrophic Taíno death. The scale is debated, and older claims of complete extinction erase survivors. Indigenous people joined new households, moved, resisted, and transmitted knowledge. A demographic disaster can be both devastating and followed by living continuity.

passages.title: Keep Taíno people, survival, and agency in the story
passages.text: Surviving Indigenous communities maintained traditions in agriculture, pottery, weaving, food, music, and healing. These practices changed as people navigated coercion and new African and European neighbors. Continuity does not mean an untouched pre-1492 world; it means people carried skills, words, memories, kinship, and choices through colonial disruption.

passages.title: Keep Taíno people, survival, and agency in the story
passages.text: Enriquillo's long resistance forced negotiation in the early 1530s and secured an autonomous Indigenous settlement. Other Taíno people escaped, fought, or built rural communities. Calling the settlement a simple Spanish gift reverses the evidence: it emerged because Indigenous organizing made conquest expensive and incomplete.

passages.title: Keep Taíno people, survival, and agency in the story
passages.text: At El Cabo in eastern Hispaniola, archaeology follows a Taíno household landscape occupied for centuries into the first decades of European contact. House remains and objects make domestic life visible without supplying every person's name. One excavated community can challenge disappearance stories, but it cannot stand for the entire island after 1530.

passages.title: Keep Taíno people, survival, and agency in the story
passages.text: A 1558 Santo Domingo prison inventory lists Antonio as “yndio,” while a 1549 report described Indigenous maroons operating with a Black leader near La Vega. Both records come through colonial officials and coercive institutions. Even so, they directly refute the idea that Indigenous presence or political action had ended before this card begins.

passages.title: Follow African lives through slavery, freedom, and resistance
passages.text: Early sugar investment joined machinery, skilled technicians, and coerced labor. A 1518 license authorized technicians plus fifteen enslaved Black men and two enslaved Black women for a mill. The document records a business plan from above; it does not tell us the workers' names, consent, families, knowledge, or strategies for surviving the work.

passages.title: Follow African lives through slavery, freedom, and resistance
passages.text: By the mid-sixteenth century, Africans outnumbered Spaniards in some estimates and powered sugar, ranching, transport, construction, domestic service, and craft. Maroons created settlements, grew varied crops, managed feral livestock, freed people from slavery, and defended territory. Those communities made Spanish conquest partial rather than completed.

passages.title: Follow African lives through slavery, freedom, and resistance
passages.text: A confiscated Portuguese ship led to a 1555 to 1556 Santo Domingo auction of enslaved people. Records describe women, men, and a small girl through color, illness, branding, price, and purchaser. The detail is evidence of commodification and bodily harm, never permission to treat the people themselves as collectible curiosities.

passages.title: Follow African lives through slavery, freedom, and resistance
passages.text: Catalina Fernández, a free Black woman, obtained permission to sail from Seville to Santo Domingo in 1539 with her daughter Francisca de Castilla. Their license shows voluntary Black migration and a family moving together across the Atlantic. It also shows how freedom still required documents that officials could demand and inspect.

passages.title: Follow African lives through slavery, freedom, and resistance
passages.text: María de Cota was born in Santo Domingo, enslaved in a household that moved to Seville, manumitted through a will, and later traveled with her young daughter. Her record preserves mobility, motherhood, legal strategy, and attachment to birthplace. It cannot tell us whether every hoped-for opportunity became real.

passages.title: Meet families, children, learners, and unequal classrooms
passages.text: Just before this layer begins, a 1527 crown order sought more enslaved Black women and promoted marriage among Black residents because officials feared rebellion by a male-majority population. That was population management, not family welfare. People still formed relationships and pursued kin under conditions that let owners and officials buy, sell, move, or separate them.

passages.title: Meet families, children, learners, and unequal classrooms
passages.text: The 1545 correspondence about Moorish and Berber residents described men and women, marriages, children, masons, carpenters, enslavement, and freedom in the same dispute. Family life crossed legal categories, while authorities judged households by ancestry, religion, labor, and supposed danger. The archive reveals families, but mostly when government wanted to classify them.

passages.title: Meet families, children, learners, and unequal classrooms
passages.text: Puerto Real archaeology places non-European servants and possible family members inside households; less privileged European residents might have an Indigenous wife or mother. These observations make mixed households visible while warning us how badly elite inventories and masonry excavations undercount laborers, informal kin, and families living in humbler buildings.

passages.title: Meet families, children, learners, and unequal classrooms
passages.text: Santo Domingo housed an early university, while book hardware appears in better-off excavated Puerto Real households. Together they show organized higher study and some household literacy. Neither source provides an enrollment list or proves broad access, so the card cannot say which children, women, workers, or rural families studied there.

passages.title: Meet families, children, learners, and unequal classrooms
passages.text: Excavated Puerto Real homes yielded gaming pieces, children's toys, a jaw harp, needlework evidence, and book hardware. These finds place play, sound, handiwork, and reading beside labor. Fun fact: someone could finish chores, lose a game piece, and make music without leaving a diary about any of it.

passages.title: Enter homes, kitchens, wardrobes, and working days
passages.text: Puerto Real's better-off households used walled compounds, several rooms, tiled floors, patios, drains, imported ceramics, glass, wood furniture, and horses. Archaeologists also expect many humbler wood-and-thatch buildings that left fainter traces. A masonry house is easier to find centuries later, which can make wealth look more normal than it was.

passages.title: Enter homes, kitchens, wardrobes, and working days
passages.text: Cooking in Spanish households often used Indigenous- or African-made pottery. Cooks combined manioc, turkey, turtle, and local resources with Iberian preferences for mammal meat. The result was neither purely Spanish nor a timeless “island diet.” Enslaved and Indigenous expertise shaped what appeared on colonial tables, although owners often claimed the household's prestige.

passages.title: Enter homes, kitchens, wardrobes, and working days
passages.text: Sugar complexes joined cane fields, animal or hydraulic mills, boiling and purging spaces, warehouses, roads, rivers, forest fuel, technical knowledge, and forced labor. Their surviving machinery is an engineering achievement and a landscape of exploitation at once. Admiring how gears and water moved must include asking whose bodies kept the system moving.

passages.title: Enter homes, kitchens, wardrobes, and working days
passages.text: As sugar weakened, ranching, hides, and ginger grew more important. Enslaved workers herded cattle, processed hides, farmed, transported goods, and maintained estates, while maroons also managed livestock outside Spanish control. “Cowboy” is too cheerful a shortcut here: similar skills operated under radically different conditions of bondage, freedom, and flight.

passages.title: Enter homes, kitchens, wardrobes, and working days
passages.text: A Nuremberg thimble, imported goods, locally made pottery, and a 1558 list naming a Black shoemaker show craft work without reconstructing one universal outfit. Clothes could display rank, but making or repairing them did not guarantee freedom, wealth, or comfort. One thimble also cannot tell us who held it.

passages.title: Move sugar, hides, ceramics, people, and contraband
passages.text: Spain's licensed trade system routed legal commerce through approved ships and officials, but fewer vessels called as richer mainland colonies drew attention away. Settlers sought alternatives. Smuggling supplied manufactured goods and enslaved people while joining Catholic residents to Dutch, English, French, and Portuguese traders whom imperial law called enemies or intruders.

passages.title: Move sugar, hides, ceramics, people, and contraband
passages.text: Puerto Real exported cattle hides through illegal rescate with foreign ships. The crown ordered the town abandoned and destroyed in 1579, yet residents continued trading from Bayahá until authorities destroyed that settlement in 1605. Burning a marketplace could move commerce and families; it did not burn away demand, skill, or maritime routes.

passages.title: Move sugar, hides, ceramics, people, and contraband
passages.text: On the eve of this atlas layer, officials worried that settlers left for places where they could exploit larger Indigenous workforces. Wealthy colonists proposed tax-free imports of equipment and enslaved Africans instead. The 1528 plan treated coerced labor as a remedy for depopulation, exposing how “development” tied investment, settlement, and bondage together.

passages.title: Move sugar, hides, ceramics, people, and contraband
passages.text: A royal license from 1518 allowed four enslaved Black Christians to travel with a Santo Domingo notary. That year, treasury officers also requested broader access to enslaved labor. Legal paperwork connected the colony to the coercive Atlantic system. A stamped permit changed an importer's legal risk, not the enslaved person's lack of consent.

passages.title: Move sugar, hides, ceramics, people, and contraband
passages.text: Puerto Real households used pottery and glass from Spain and Italy, later joined by German stoneware, Chinese goods, and items linked to French, English, or Portuguese trade. Objects crossed political borders more easily than atlas colors suggest. Archaeology identifies connections, but a shard cannot by itself reveal whether it arrived by gift, purchase, theft, or contraband.

passages.title: Treat illness, survive epidemics, and preserve healing knowledge
passages.text: A late-seventeenth-century archival memory credited an unnamed Black woman with sheltering and treating sick people in her bohío around 1497 to 1501, before the formal San Nicolás hospital. The memory does not securely establish her legal status or methods. It does preserve a Black caregiver at the origin of colonial institutional medicine.

passages.title: Treat illness, survive epidemics, and preserve healing knowledge
passages.text: Santo Domingo's San Nicolás de Bari became an early formal hospital, alongside the cathedral, customs house, university, and court. “Hospital” did not mean a modern emergency department with antibiotics. It joined shelter, nursing, food, worship, administration, and unequal access in a society where labor status and ancestry shaped treatment.

passages.title: Treat illness, survive epidemics, and preserve healing knowledge
passages.text: Taíno survivors maintained healing traditions as well as agriculture, weaving, pottery, food, and music. African and European knowledge also entered households and institutions. The record supports medical exchange, but it rarely lets us assign every remedy to one origin or decide whether a particular patient trusted a healer, friar, midwife, relative, or several.

passages.title: Treat illness, survive epidemics, and preserve healing knowledge
passages.text: Introduced diseases helped drive catastrophic Indigenous mortality, and a 1586 smallpox epidemic also reduced the enslaved population. Hunger, overwork, violence, displacement, and poor shelter could magnify illness. Exact totals remain debated, so the safest lesson is causal and human: epidemics struck societies already made more vulnerable by colonial coercion.

passages.title: Treat illness, survive epidemics, and preserve healing knowledge
passages.text: The 1555 to 1556 auction described a small enslaved girl with visible skin disease and a brand before a tailor bought her. The record documents inspection for sale, not a diagnosis or care plan. Her illness should direct attention to bodily harm, childhood vulnerability, and the archive's cold commercial gaze.

passages.title: Ask where water, drains, waste, and toilets actually went
passages.text: Archaeology in Santo Domingo has identified a sixteenth-century system carrying water from a noria near San Francisco toward the main plaza, plus springs, household wells, and small lifting devices. Some household norias were operated by enslaved people. Urban water engineering therefore joined public infrastructure to coerced daily labor.

passages.title: Ask where water, drains, waste, and toilets actually went
passages.text: Santo Domingo's sixteenth-century conduit moved lifted water toward the main plaza, while household wells and smaller norias served other users. This was infrastructure, but it was not a universal tap network or sewer. A pipe beneath a street can be impressive without secretly becoming modern indoor plumbing for every home.

passages.title: Ask where water, drains, waste, and toilets actually went
passages.text: No water wells have been located in the excavated Puerto Real areas described by the Florida Museum. That absence does not prove residents lacked wells or safe water; unexcavated zones, rivers, containers, rain collection, and perishable equipment remain possibilities. “Not found” is an archaeological result, not permission to invent a convenient answer.

passages.title: Ask where water, drains, waste, and toilets actually went
passages.text: Sugar mills stood near rivers and forests because production needed water, transport, and large amounts of fuel wood. Industrial water use therefore affected where people worked and how landscapes changed. The channels served machinery first; they should not be mistaken for equal household access to clean drinking water or effortless washing.

passages.title: Ask where water, drains, waste, and toilets actually went
passages.text: The published Puerto Real synthesis identifies drains, patios, boundaries, corrals, and gardens but no securely interpreted privy or toilet. People obviously produced waste; the fixture and disposal route are the missing evidence. Fun fact withheld by archaeology: no excavated sign says “colonial bathroom, please form an orderly line.”

passages.title: Hear language, faith, creativity, and the 1715 continuation
passages.text: Written-language sample from a 1558 Spanish prison list: “El negro de gonçalo garçia çapatero con grillos.” CUNY DSI supplies the translation, “Gonçalo Garçia, Black, shoemaker, with shackles.” This is a clerk's terse administrative Spanish, with period spelling and an ambiguous “de”; it records confinement and work, not the prisoner's own voice.

passages.title: Hear language, faith, creativity, and the 1715 continuation
passages.text: That Spanish sentence cannot stand for Taíno languages or the many African languages carried to Hispaniola. Colonial clerks favored the language of government and often compressed people into racial and legal labels. Taíno words and knowledge survived in Caribbean speech and practice even where alphabetic records failed to preserve full Indigenous voices.

passages.title: Hear language, faith, creativity, and the 1715 continuation
passages.text: Santo Domingo's cathedral, monasteries, hospital, university, customs house, fortress, and grid influenced later cities. These are architectural and institutional achievements, built through Indigenous, African, and European skill within conquest and slavery. Naming coercion does not erase craft; admiring craft does not absolve the system that commanded and benefited from it.

passages.title: Hear language, faith, creativity, and the 1715 continuation
passages.text: At Puerto Real, locally made pottery, cooking, medicine, music, dance, religion, art, architecture, and language show Afro-Indigenous-European cultural formation. Archaeologists stress women's central role in domestic exchange. “Mixture” must not sound frictionless: creativity happened amid unequal power, forced migration, survival, intimacy, resistance, and ordinary family decisions.

passages.title: Hear language, faith, creativity, and the 1715 continuation
passages.text: The atlas ends this id in 1715, eighteen years after Ryswick recognized a French western possession. Eastern Spanish Santo Domingo, western Saint-Domingue, Taíno descendants, African communities, mixed families, towns, farms, churches, maroons, and trade all continued. The endpoint corrects a belated map label; it does not describe a people's extinction or a colony vanishing.

At the 1715 atlas seam, “hispaniola-spain” disappears. Sampled eastern points move to “spain,” labeled Santo Domingo (Spain), and western points move to the anachronistic atlas id “haiti”; Puerto Rico is misassigned to a Danish Virgin Islands layer. Ryswick had recognized French possession in the west in 1697, while no precise border was fixed then. People, families, farms, maroon communities, institutions, and trade continued on both sides. This is a delayed, flawed relabeling, not a fall or extinction.

dailyLife.question: Does the account explain ordinary practices with evidence rather than only rulers?

artsScienceTechnology.question: Are achievements concrete and correctly attributed to this polity and period?

chronologicalPhases.question: Are source-supported phases distinguished from map snapshot dates?

endingContinuity.question: Does the narrative identify what ended or continued, with dates, mechanism and uncertainty?

uncertainty.question: Are uncertainties attached to particular claims rather than a blanket disclaimer?

sectionTitles: A capital and an international power
Belief, writing and the empire's end

passages.text: The Hittite kingdom ruled from central Anatolia and became a major power in Syria during roughly 1650 to 1200 BCE. Hattusha was its capital. The map starts before this kingdom and repeats a large outline long after its collapse: its 2000 to 500 BCE span must not be read as one continuously surviving empire.

passages.title: A capital and an international power
passages.text: Hittite armies reached far beyond the Anatolian plateau. Murshili I raided Aleppo and Babylon, but was assassinated after returning home. Later kings rebuilt imperial strength. Control depended on changing campaigns, royal centers and agreements with neighboring rulers; the repeated map outline cannot show those shifting relationships.

passages.title: A capital and an international power
passages.text: At Hattusha, the defensive circuit stretched for more than eight kilometers. The Upper City had a double wall with over a hundred towers. Carved lions guarded one entrance, while a stone tunnel passed beneath the great artificial bastion at the Sphinx Gate. Arriving at the capital involved some impressive architecture.

passages.title: A capital and an international power
passages.text: The archive preserves a peace agreement between the Hittites and Egypt, usually called the Qadesh treaty. Alongside diplomacy, its clay tablets recorded laws, commerce, religion and stories. A government could need both an agreement with a rival king and instructions for a festival, and both could end up on clay.

passages.title: A capital and an international power
passages.text: Royal women also participated in diplomacy. Queen Puduhepa had an official seal, and a surviving Akkadian letter was sent to her by the Egyptian queen Naptera. Their correspondence gives us named women communicating across the same international world as their royal husbands.

passages.title: Water, work and family life
passages.text: Keeping a capital supplied required storage as well as walls. Excavation has revealed buried granaries and artificial ponds. In the densely occupied Lower City, people lived close to the Great Temple; religious buildings, homes and practical installations all belonged to the same working city.

passages.title: Water, work and family life
passages.text: A low depression behind broad earth banks in Hattusha was once even proposed as a royal burial place. Coring in 2002 instead supported its interpretation as a water reservoir. Archaeologists still have to work out how separate installations supplied the city; this evidence does not establish running taps in every house.

passages.title: Water, work and family life
passages.text: Hittite law clause 10 required someone who injured another person to arrange care and supply a replacement worker during recovery. The offender also owed six shekels of silver and the doctor's fee. An injury could disrupt a household's livelihood, so the rule addressed both healing and unfinished work.

passages.title: Water, work and family life
passages.text: Marriage involved families and transfers of wealth. Clause 28 discusses a promised marriage, a competing match and who should repay the earlier bride payment. Both father and mother appear in the rule. Such texts reveal parental authority and economic obligations, while telling us much less about the daughter's own wishes.

passages.title: Water, work and family life
passages.text: Farm animals could produce very ordinary disputes. Clause 66 allowed owners to reclaim livestock that had wandered into somebody else's enclosure without treating the neighbor as a thief. The law even considered a pig getting into a field or grain heap. Keeping dinner away from somebody else's dinner was evidently a practical problem.

passages.title: Water, work and family life
passages.text: Children could learn a craft within their family, while outside training could cost money. A legal rule listed six shekels of silver for teaching trades such as carpentry, weaving or metalworking. Midwifery also belonged among skills passed through practical instruction. Education often meant learning how to do a job.

passages.title: Water, work and family life
passages.text: Scribal training demanded a different toolkit: hundreds of signs and the ability to compose official documents. One scribal family can be followed through four generations in the thirteenth century BCE. Learning began with simpler signs and small tablets before longer compositions. A family business might involve clay paperwork rather than a shop.

passages.title: Water, work and family life
passages.text: Chariot horses had carefully planned care. The Kikkuli training text describes exercise, feeding, watering, rest and treatments such as blankets or massages. Its surviving thirteenth-century BCE copy preserves an older training tradition associated with a specialist from Mitanni. These animals had a timetable, and someone had to follow it from early morning until late at night.

passages.title: Belief, writing and the empire's end
passages.text: A silver drinking vessel from the fourteenth or thirteenth century BCE ends in the head and forelegs of a stag. Its maker attached the antlers and handle separately. Around the rim, people approach deities with offerings. The imagery suggests ceremonial use, making the cup both skilled metalwork and a miniature religious scene.

passages.title: Belief, writing and the empire's end
passages.text: Hittite scribes adapted cuneiform from the Akkadian tradition. They combined syllable signs with signs representing whole words, and used the script for several languages, including Hittite, Luwian, Hurrian and Akkadian. A single archive therefore preserves several linguistic worlds. The language of a tablet cannot be identified merely by its wedge-shaped marks.

passages.title: Belief, writing and the empire's end
passages.text: During an epidemic, King Mursili II appealed to the gods and said that people had been dying for twenty years. His prayers considered broken oaths and divine anger, while seeking relief for the country. The testimony preserves fear and a religious explanation; it does not identify the infection in modern medical terms.

passages.title: Belief, writing and the empire's end
passages.text: A short Hittite writing sample from that prayer is “ki-i-ma ku-it i-ya-at-ten”, translated “What is this that you have done?” This is a scholarly transcription of cuneiform from KUB XIV 10 with KUB XXVI 86, not the original wedge shapes. The question addresses the gods: even a powerful king could sound bewildered.

passages.title: Belief, writing and the empire's end
passages.text: Tree rings from central Anatolia indicate an unusually severe run of dry years around 1198 to 1196 BCE. Repeated crop failures could overwhelm stored supplies. Researchers connect this climatic stress with the era of imperial collapse, while emphasizing political pressures and uneven local outcomes. Drought is a possible contributor, not a complete explanation.

The central Hittite state disintegrated around 1200 BCE. Evidence suggests Hattusha was emptied by its administration before later fires, rather than simply destroyed in one known invasion. Smaller successor kingdoms, especially toward northern Syria, preserved parts of Hittite political and cultural traditions. The map's 500 BCE endpoint is not the date this empire fell.

sectionTitles: Family work, food and sacred places

passages.text: Otomí communities have a long history across central Mexico, with several languages and regional names, including Hñähñu. They did not form one unchanged kingdom. The broad 1492 to 1500 map label and the smaller 1530 to 1650 “Otomies” outline describe different areas and periods; this narrative also follows colonial communities around Guanajuato and Querétaro. Neither outline marks the full territory of today’s Otomí peoples.

passages.title: Cities, records and political choices
passages.text: Huamango overlooks the Acambay valley from the San Miguel plateau. Builders levelled difficult ground and made broad terraces for temples and residential platforms. INAH identifies it as an Otomian settlement: a specific archaeological example, rather than the capital of every Otomí community.

passages.title: Cities, records and political choices
passages.text: Huamango’s pottery helps trace connections. Excavators provisionally distinguished an earlier phase with incense burners, braziers and burial vessels resembling material at Tula, and a later phase with comparisons to Teotenango and Calixtlahuaca. Similar objects point toward relationships; they do not by themselves identify a conquering army.

passages.title: Cities, records and political choices
passages.text: The sixteenth-century Huamantla Codex was painted on bark paper. It recounts a group’s migration from Chiapan toward Tlaxcala, encounters and battles, and later Spanish arrival and a church. Images preserve an Otomí account of place and history within the colonial period.

passages.title: Cities, records and political choices
passages.text: Conservators studying the Huamantla Codex identified cochineal red in sampled paint. Looking through a microscope at tiny pigment traces helps explain how artists made the manuscript, alongside historical readings of its pictures. Material analysis supplies evidence that a modern photograph alone cannot provide.

passages.title: Cities, records and political choices
passages.text: Otomí communities made different political choices during Spanish invasion. At Tecoac in 1519, Otomí defenders guarded a Tlaxcalan frontier and fought Cortés’s force. Elsewhere some communities allied with Spaniards against Mexica power. One ethnic label cannot stand for a single decision made by everyone.

passages.title: Cities, records and political choices
passages.text: The later map’s northern outline belongs in the history of a mixed colonial frontier. Crespo and Cervantes examine Otomí-speaking settlement in Guanajuato and Querétaro, including the Sierra Gorda foothills. Some Otomí leaders participated in conquest and settlement, creating communities within a changing colonial political landscape.

passages.title: Family work, food and sacred places
passages.text: INPI emphasizes that households differ between regions: some are nuclear families, while others include extended relatives. Planting and harvest bring family members into shared work. Godparent relationships also create valued ties beyond a household, connecting families through religious and social responsibilities.

passages.title: Family work, food and sacred places
passages.text: In the Mezquital valley, agave supported more than one craft. Its fibres supplied textiles, while its sap could be fermented into pulque. Fournier connects these activities with pottery for holding and processing sap, showing how a plant crop, containers and household work belonged to the same economy.

passages.title: Family work, food and sacred places
passages.text: Working with scattered maguey plants also shaped where people lived. Fournier argues that their continuing care helped support permanent but dispersed settlements in the Mezquital. This is an interpretation of an economic landscape: a house did not need to stand in a dense city to belong to an organized farming community.

passages.title: Family work, food and sacred places
passages.text: In the Tolimán area of Querétaro, Otomí-Chichimeca families maintain chapels devoted to ancestors. UNESCO describes annual journeys to sacred hills and Bernal rock, with ceremonies asking for water in a dry landscape. These are living local traditions with their own community setting.

passages.title: Family work, food and sacred places
passages.text: Tolimán celebrations also involve chimales, large temporary structures made from reeds and leafy coverings. Their construction brings people together around an offering. A structure can be important even when its makers intend it to stand only for a celebration rather than for centuries.

passages.title: Writing and continued life
passages.text: “Ki hats'i” means “Good morning”. INALI prints it as a common greeting in Hñähñu of the Valle del Mezquital and credits Nicandro González Peña for the recorded voice. This is a modern, regionally identified language sample; other Otomí varieties can use different forms.

passages.title: Writing and continued life
passages.text: Otomí writing standards were developed with community representatives, teachers, activists, the Academy of Hñähñu Language and Culture, researchers and INALI. The participants came from several states. Agreeing how to write sounds can help people share teaching materials while recognizing regional diversity.

Spanish colonial rule changed political relationships, settlement and landholding, without bringing all Otomí communities to one common ending. Languages, families and local institutions continue. The map cutoffs of 1500 and 1650 are coverage dates, not the disappearance of a people.

passages.text: The Haudenosaunee are a continuing confederacy of nations. The Onondaga Nation's own accounts describe government, food, ceremonies and wampum as living practices connecting community responsibilities with historical memory.

passages.title: Government
passages.text: Clan Mothers select the Hoyane who represent their clans in council. They can remove a leader who fails to represent the clan, after warnings.

passages.title: Technology and memory
passages.text: Wampum makers cut, round, sand and drill shell beads. Woven strings and belts support the remembrance of agreements and their histories.

passages.title: Diplomacy
passages.text: Wampum strings can carry invitations to council meetings. They also identify leadership titles and give weight to a speaker's words.

passages.title: Food and daily life
passages.text: Corn, beans and squash are the Three Sisters. Onondaga food traditions also include fishing, hunting, gathering and sharing food within the community.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Thanksgiving Address opens gatherings by acknowledging people, the natural world and their interdependence. Speakers express it in their own words.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: Clan Mothers help sustain ceremonies and teach younger generations. These are present-day responsibilities, not customs of a vanished society.

sectionTitles: Water had to arrive at the right speed
Buildings large enough to bring people together
A lizard waiting for its chemical bath
What can be read, and what continues

passages.text: Hohokam is an archaeological label for related material traditions of ancestral Sonoran Desert communities, not the known name of a single ancient nation. The map’s 1492 to 1500 interval is misleading: the large settlement pattern described here had changed by about 1450. This card explains the earlier canal-building communities and their continuing descendants, rather than placing an unchanged state in that late outline.

passages.title: Water had to arrive at the right speed
passages.text: Farmers built canals to bring river water to villages and fields. At S’edav Va’aki beside the Salt River, local bedrock helped direct water toward canal entrances. Choosing an intake location was an engineering decision tied to the landscape, before the long labour of digging even began.

passages.title: Water had to arrive at the right speed
passages.text: A canal that slopes too steeply sends water racing against its banks; one too level lets silt settle and obstruct the flow. The builders had to find a workable gradient and keep maintaining it. Making water travel gently across a dry landscape was a lasting technical achievement.

passages.title: Homes opened toward shared space
passages.text: Excavated pithouses leave postholes and hard, smooth floors, sometimes with caliche plaster. At Pueblo Grande, archaeologists also found pits where builders prepared caliche. Burned pieces of wall daub can preserve impressions of grass and wood, allowing vanished walls to leave surprisingly detailed clues.

passages.title: Homes opened toward shared space
passages.text: Groups of houses faced shared courtyards. Archaeologists interpret these clusters as settings for cooperation among related households, including food preparation, weaving and child care. The layout is observable; the precise family relationships are an interpretation. A courtyard could be a workplace and a place to keep children nearby.

passages.title: Homes opened toward shared space
passages.text: Manos and metates, handstones and larger grinding surfaces, reveal food preparation near homes. Plant residues can sometimes identify what was ground. Other finds, such as prepared clay, help locate pottery work. Cooking equipment and craft materials let researchers reconstruct activities on a household scale.

passages.title: Fields and gathering grounds
passages.text: Cultivated foods included maize, beans and squash, while cotton supplied fibre. People also gathered cactus foods, mesquite pods and agave, and took fish and other animals. Irrigation did not make the surrounding desert irrelevant: families combined several sources of food and useful materials.

passages.title: Fields and gathering grounds
passages.text: Pueblo Grande’s residents accumulated rubbish in mounds near their homes. Some surfaces appear to have been burned and covered with fresh soil, perhaps to control smells and pests. Ancient rubbish management also created a useful archive: yesterday’s discarded fragments can become today’s evidence for everyday life.

passages.title: Buildings large enough to bring people together
passages.text: Oval depressions surrounded by earth banks are commonly called ballcourts. At S’edav Va’aki, the museum dates their wider importance to about 750 to 1200 and notes associations with exchange. Their exact activities remain uncertain; we cannot confidently supply teams, rules or a score for an ancient match.

passages.title: Buildings large enough to bring people together
passages.text: The Great House at Casa Grande was built in the fourteenth century. Builders mixed local calcium-rich caliche with water and piled it into thick walls. Horizontal joins still mark successive courses left to dry before more material was added. The building preserves the rhythm of its construction.

passages.title: Buildings large enough to bring people together
passages.text: The Great House also required wooden supports. The National Park Service describes timbers brought from forests as far as sixty miles away, with smaller saguaro ribs placed across supporting beams. A monument made from local earth still depended on planning, transport and materials from beyond the immediate settlement.

passages.title: A lizard waiting for its chemical bath
passages.text: At Snaketown, excavators found a shell ornament with a horned-lizard design still protected by a resistant coating. It had not yet passed through the etching stage. This unfinished object helps explain how makers shielded parts of a surface while an acid removed the exposed shell around the design.

passages.title: A lizard waiting for its chemical bath
passages.text: Shell specialist Chris Lange identifies fermented saguaro juice as a plausible weak acid for this process. Most dated etched-shell examples belong to about 950 to 1150. The objects show chemical craft knowledge, while the exact liquid used on an individual piece remains a proposed reconstruction.

passages.title: What can be read, and what continues
passages.text: Casa Grande’s builders left no securely readable written language in the evidence presented by the National Park Service. Its written visitor history begins with Eusebio Kino in 1694, centuries later. There is no translated ancient sentence to show here; descendant communities’ oral histories and the archaeological record remain distinct sources of knowledge.

Large settlements and canal networks changed during the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries; this is not evidence that their people vanished. S’edav Va’aki’s museum describes movement into smaller villages after 1400 and identifies continuing Akimel O’odham descendants. The 1500 map endpoint supplies neither a conqueror nor a single cause for these changes.
