sectionTitles: Art and institutions across political change

passages.text: The medieval Kingdom of Hungary connected monasteries, towns, farms and royal courts across a territory larger than modern Hungary. Surviving textiles, vessels, tiles and books reveal imported skills alongside local production. Ottoman expansion and rival claims to the crown divided political authority in the sixteenth century, while communities and institutions continued under different governments.

passages.title: Building, devotion and skilled metalwork
passages.text: Benedictine monks settled at Pannonhalma in 996, before the kingdom conventionally dated from 1000. Its churches were rebuilt repeatedly. The church begun in 1224 contains earlier remains, making the complex evidence of successive communities rather than one untouched medieval building.

passages.title: Building, devotion and skilled metalwork
passages.text: Pannonhalma's red-marble Porta Speciosa leads into a cloister built in 1486. Later alterations changed doors and windows. Traces of an earlier cloister and refectory entrance show how prayer, movement and communal meals shaped the monastery's built environment.

passages.title: Building, devotion and skilled metalwork
passages.text: A centaur-shaped bronze hand-washing vessel in the Hungarian National Museum was made at Hildesheim in the 1220s. Its arrival in Hungary may reflect court connections. The object demonstrates imported metalworking and elite washing practices, not a Hungarian invention of the form.

passages.title: Building, devotion and skilled metalwork
passages.text: The gilded-silver vessel from Beszterec, dated to the later eleventh century, carries a Greek inscription and animal ornament. Its partly reconstructed supports matter when reading its present appearance. Byzantine manufacture and religious use connected the kingdom with another artistic world.

passages.title: Building, devotion and skilled metalwork
passages.text: Stephen and Gisela donated the textile now called the Coronation Mantle to the Szekesfehervar basilica in 1031. It began as a priestly vestment and later entered coronation ritual. A surviving object could acquire new political meaning long after its first use.

passages.title: Building, devotion and skilled metalwork
passages.text: A STEPHANO REGE ET GISLA REGINA means ‘by King Stephen and Queen Gisela.’ These Latin words are embroidered in the dedication on the vestment donated in 1031 and later converted into Hungary’s coronation mantle. This is an earlier surviving inscription, not a new text made during the late-medieval map interval.

passages.title: Comfort, sight and making books
passages.text: Late-fifteenth-century tiles from the Bothar workshop at Besztercebanya, now Banska Bystrica, include glazed images of saints. Unfinished and spoiled pieces survived as well. They reveal production behind the decorated stoves that changed domestic heating, rather than only finished luxury objects.

passages.title: Comfort, sight and making books
passages.text: A leather spectacle frame dated before 1470 was found behind an altar panel at Liptoszentandras, now Liptovsky Ondrej. It is direct evidence of an aid to sight. Its hiding place does not identify its wearer or establish how many people owned spectacles.

passages.title: Comfort, sight and making books
passages.text: Fifteenth-century printed missals left blank spaces for initials and pictures to be painted by hand. Printing therefore worked alongside skilled manual decoration. The finished pages preserve cooperation between old and new methods of making books.

passages.title: Comfort, sight and making books
passages.text: Matthias's Corvina library commissioned decorated manuscripts at Buda as well as obtaining Italian books. Study of the codex containing Pietro Ranzano's history of Hungary reassigned its production from Naples to Buda, showing why an Italian-looking style does not prove an Italian workshop.

passages.title: Comfort, sight and making books
passages.text: The library's surviving bindings and illumination help reconstruct an organised late-fifteenth-century workshop. High-ranking church patrons also ordered its books. These manuscripts record collaborative specialist labour and patronage, as well as the writings preserved on their pages.

passages.title: Art and institutions across political change
passages.text: The Nyirbator choir stalls name their Bathory patrons and the year 1511; another panel carries the maker's mark F. Marone. Inlaid cupboards display books and kitchen utensils. The furniture brings images of familiar possessions into an elaborate setting for worship.

passages.title: Art and institutions across political change
passages.text: The division of Hungary left several settings for skilled work. The museum documents mining and guild production in Royal Hungary, while Hutterite communities moving there and later to Transylvania practised tin-glazed pottery. Political boundaries did not halt the movement of craftspeople.

The defeat of 1526 and Ottoman occupation of Buda in 1541 unfolded in stages. Rival kingship, Ottoman conquest and the emergence of Transylvania divided the medieval kingdom. Habsburg rulers retained the Hungarian crown in Royal Hungary. Neither the earlier Hungary record’s 1492 endpoint nor the late-phase record’s 1530 endpoint marks the disappearance of Hungarian society.

sectionTitles: At school, at home and out in town
Keeping well and reading the written record

passages.text: This map's Imperial Japan record covers 1878 to 1914: late Meiji and the first years of Taishō. The imperial state had begun with the Meiji Restoration in 1868 and continued well beyond the last mapped year. Its railways, schools, factories and parliament changed many lives, but political rights were limited and overseas expansion brought conquest and colonial rule. A single map color cannot show those differences within Japan, Taiwan and Korea.

passages.title: Power, industry and their costs
passages.text: The 1889 constitution created an Imperial Diet, but it also preserved strong imperial authority. In the first lower-house election in 1890, voting was limited to men meeting a tax requirement; only about one percent of the population could vote. A schoolchild hearing about a 'new parliament' should know that almost every adult around them still lacked a ballot.

passages.title: Power, industry and their costs
passages.text: Japan's industrial exhibitions were workshops of ideas as much as displays: visitors could see looms, pumps, printing presses and even an ice-making machine. One 1877 show listed 211 machinery exhibits. Some clever devices were too expensive to spread widely, so seeing a machine at a fair did not mean it had arrived in every village.

passages.title: Power, industry and their costs
passages.text: At Tomioka, imported French machines, silkworm farming, technical teaching and cool storage for silkworm eggs formed a connected silk-making system. Raw silk became a major export. Behind the impressive machines lay careful work with tiny living larvae and delicate thread, as well as workers whose experiences varied between mills.

passages.title: Power, industry and their costs
passages.text: Victory in the 1894 to 95 war with Qing China brought Taiwan under Japanese colonial control. People on the island resisted the takeover with armed force; the new rulers installed a governor-general. War and empire were not simply a story of machines, flags and treaties: they changed who could govern homes and communities.

passages.title: Power, industry and their costs
passages.text: Japan's 1904 to 05 war with Russia increased its regional power. In 1910 it annexed Korea and assumed its government and administration. The surviving annexation treaty explains the colonial state's claims, but cannot stand in for the wishes of the people whose sovereignty was removed.

passages.title: At school, at home and out in town
passages.text: A child in the early 1900s might spend more years in elementary school than a child a generation earlier. Public elementary fees were abolished in principle in 1900, when compulsory education was set at four years; in 1907 the requirement became six years. Opportunities grew, although school experiences and access still depended on place, family and gender.

passages.title: At school, at home and out in town
passages.text: A 1902 bribery scandal over approved schoolbooks helped bring state-produced textbooks from 1903. Surviving 1909 to 10 examples cover reading, arithmetic, science, geography, history and even brush and pencil drawing. Imagine opening a drawing book while the grown-ups argued over who got to choose it.

passages.title: At school, at home and out in town
passages.text: An 1887 print shows well-off women working with a sewing machine, an exciting new device in its day. The museum notes that expensive Western-style clothes were then within reach of only upper classes. The picture tells us what an artist chose to show, not how every Japanese mother, tailor or seamstress dressed.

passages.title: At school, at home and out in town
passages.text: Trains changed social outings as well as trade. A line from Shimbashi to Yokohama opened in 1872, before this map's starting date. Later guidebooks followed new rail routes, and trains made visits to Kawasaki Daishi temple easier for city families. A timetable could now help plan a holiday that once required a long walk.

passages.title: At school, at home and out in town
passages.text: Around 1910, magazines for girls and women sat alongside newspapers and illustrated humor. Artist Takehisa Yumeji's drawings appeared in roughly 45 periodicals by that year, including a magazine called Tokyo Puck. The printed page was a way to meet fashions, stories and jokes without going to a theater.

passages.title: Keeping well and reading the written record
passages.text: An 1880 government cholera booklet offered a very practical warning: don't dig a well beside a toilet. It also warned against muddy water and spoiled food. Some of its explanations of infection predated modern germ science, but the advice shows that water, waste and disease were urgent everyday worries, not just matters for doctors.

passages.title: Keeping well and reading the written record
passages.text: The original 1889 constitution bears the Japanese title '大日本帝国憲法' (Dai-Nippon Teikoku Kenpō), meaning 'Constitution of the Empire of Japan.' These are the document's own characters, not invented period flavor. The same text formally promised speech and association within limits set by law: written rights and who could actually exercise power were different questions.

passages.title: Keeping well and reading the written record
passages.text: The map stops at 1914, two years after the Meiji emperor's death and the start of the Taishō era. It does not show the full later story of the empire. Treat each year on the slider as a view of the map data, not a date when all these schools, freedoms or colonial borders appeared at once.

1914 ends this imported map record, not Imperial Japan. The Taishō government continued after the Meiji era, and Japanese imperial rule extended into the Shōwa period before ending in 1945. Japan, its people and their language continued; the empire's end should never be confused with their disappearance.

passages.text: Tawantinsuyu joined diverse Andean regions through roads, administration and local labor. Its infrastructure drew on earlier Andean traditions and adapted construction to mountains, valleys and coastal environments.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Road builders used bridges, stairs, paving and drainage suited to different terrain. The network linked centers of production, government and worship.

passages.title: Food and farming
passages.text: Communities built and maintained terraces that created level planting areas while resisting erosion. Water conduits also protected roads from damaging runoff.

passages.title: Water engineering
passages.text: Stone channels and storage facilities managed rainfall and snowmelt for resources shared among families.

passages.title: Storage
passages.text: Colcas were storehouses whose siting and construction kept supplies cool and dry. Their contents included potatoes, maize, quinoa, clothing and tools.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The road system moved goods including textiles, feathers, food and shell. It incorporated earlier routes and knowledge from Andean communities.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: Andean languages and traditions continued under Spanish rule. Weavers combined established textile techniques and designs with new imagery.
Pizarro captured Atahualpa in 1532 and had him killed in 1533. Spanish conquest dismantled imperial government, while Andean peoples continued and adapted their traditions.

passages.text: The atlas labels one east-coast and highland polygon “India” from 1783 to 1800. It is not the modern country, the whole subcontinent, or even one historical state. The same outline becomes “Circars” in 1800. It covers places around Ganjam, Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam, Rajahmundry, Masulipatnam, Jeypore and Bastar, mixing Company-controlled coastal districts with powerful estates and inland communities whose authority remained layered. Elsewhere the Mughal emperor still reigned with limited reach; Maratha rulers and chiefs, Mysore, Hyderabad, Sikh misls, Rajput courts and many smaller powers pursued their own futures. Families in this footprint farmed rice and millets, wove cotton, traded, carried water, repaired tanks, learned languages and crafts, and sought care from varied healers. Children could learn at home, in workshops, schools, courts or religious settings; opportunity depended on place, wealth, caste, gender and patronage. Company revenue pressure and warfare made ordinary competence harder, and famine struck the Northern Circars in 1791 to 1792. At Padmanabham in 1794, Company troops killed Vizianagaram’s raja during a dispute over payment and arms. A growling wooden tiger organ from neighboring Mysore supplies one unforgettable fun fact. The map’s 1800 rename records editorial shorthand, not the birth or disappearance of a people.

passages.title: First, shrink the label to what the map actually draws
passages.text: The live row says “India,” approximately 1783 to 1800, and the coverage ledger calls it a state. Yet its one 37-position polygon spans only part of today’s Andhra Pradesh, Odisha and Chhattisgarh. Database type and national-looking name do not prove one government, people or border.

passages.title: First, shrink the label to what the map actually draws
passages.text: Audited interior points include Ganjam, Berhampur, Vizianagaram, Padmanabham, Visakhapatnam, Samalkot, Rajahmundry, Masulipatnam, Vijayawada, Jeypore, Koraput and Bastar. Nearby Puri, Cuttack, Sambalpur, Raipur and Kanker fall in the atlas’s Maratha layer; Warangal falls under its anachronistic Golconda label. These are database assignments, not surveyed frontiers.

passages.title: First, shrink the label to what the map actually draws
passages.text: The shape resembles a broadened Northern Circars corridor, but it reaches into Jeypore and Bastar and omits part of the historical Circars. Company coastal claims, zamindari estates, tributary relations and highland authority overlapped. The card therefore calls it an editorial regional layer, not a legal frontier.

passages.title: First, shrink the label to what the map actually draws
passages.text: At 1715 the atlas drops nearly all audited points into one Mughal Empire polygon. By 1783 it splits Bengal, Maratha, Mysore, Carnatic, Madras, Hyderabad-like and other layers. That dramatic change mainly exposes shifting editorial categories and political fragmentation, not crisp sovereignty suddenly appearing.

passages.title: First, shrink the label to what the map actually draws
passages.text: The imported paragraph discusses first human settlement and the Indus civilization thousands of years earlier. Those are major histories, but they cannot explain an eighteenth-century coastal revenue district. Replacing it prevents children from mistaking every era and region of South Asia for a single story.

passages.title: Evidence: records, surveys, landscapes and missing voices
passages.text: Company revenue papers record assessments, debts, leases and orders because officials wanted income. They can illuminate administration while making a village look like a number. Reading them beside regional histories helps recover negotiation and resistance, though many farmers, laborers and children remain unnamed.

passages.title: Evidence: records, surveys, landscapes and missing voices
passages.text: The Mackenzie Collection preserves maps, road notes, drawings, inscriptions and surveys from southern India, including the Circars and Deccan. Surveyors gathered local knowledge, then reorganized it for colonial use. A measured road is evidence of travel and state interest, not automatic proof of control beside it.

passages.title: Evidence: records, surveys, landscapes and missing voices
passages.text: Koraput’s plateaus, valleys, rivers, monsoon rainfall and forest differ sharply from coastal deltas. A modern district survey helps locate those physical contrasts, but present boundaries and environmental measurements cannot be copied backward as an exact 1790 landscape. Climate, land use and names changed.

passages.title: Evidence: records, surveys, landscapes and missing voices
passages.text: Scholarship on highland Odisha and Bastar rejects the cartoon of sealed “tribes” outside history. Courts, ritual centers, cultivators, forest users, traders and mobile specialists interacted through plural authority. Evidence is uneven, so one should neither erase highland politics nor invent uniform institutions across the polygon.

passages.title: Evidence: records, surveys, landscapes and missing voices
passages.text: Vizianagaram loan files show that money linked local rulers and the Company before open battle. The Padmanabham record then reveals coercion and succession. Historians triangulate such papers with gazetteers, family traditions and geography because every archive preserves interests as well as facts.

passages.title: Many powers, Company coercion and the Padmanabham crisis
passages.text: The Mughal emperor Shah Alam II still supplied titles and legitimacy but commanded limited territory. Maratha chiefs, Mysore, Hyderabad, Rajput courts, Sikh misls and many smaller rulers pursued separate interests. “India” names the atlas card; it does not name a united eighteenth-century nation-state or army.

passages.title: Many powers, Company coercion and the Padmanabham crisis
passages.text: The East India Company was a chartered corporation with armies, revenue collectors and diplomatic agents. Pitt’s India Act added a government Board of Control while leaving Company directors in place. Children can picture the oddity: a business with forts and soldiers, watched by politicians across an ocean.

passages.title: Many powers, Company coercion and the Padmanabham crisis
passages.text: Northern Circar control grew through a Mughal farman in 1765, agreements with the Nizam in 1766 and 1768, revenue experiments, local leases and military pressure. Guntur followed in 1788. This layered sequence is more accurate than coloring the coast British after one imagined conquest.

passages.title: Many powers, Company coercion and the Padmanabham crisis
passages.text: At Padmanabham in 1794, Company forces defeated Vizianagaram’s raja after demands involving payment and the reduction of armed retainers. The battle killed the raja and others. Calling it merely “law enforcement” accepts the conqueror’s view; calling it national liberation invents a later nation.

passages.title: Many powers, Company coercion and the Padmanabham crisis
passages.text: The minor heir escaped into hill country, received protection and eventually returned under a negotiated settlement. That story shows families, retainers and highland connections shaping politics after battlefield defeat. Colonial power expanded, yet it still needed intermediaries, agreements and people who could refuse cooperation.

passages.title: Fields, food, famine and the labor behind every meal
passages.text: Coastal plains supported wet-rice cultivation where rainfall, rivers, tanks and labor allowed; drier uplands supported millets, pulses and mixed crops. Modern crop studies confirm extraordinary regional diversity but cannot provide a household menu for 1783. Soil, status, season and market access mattered.

passages.title: Fields, food, famine and the labor behind every meal
passages.text: Rice on a plate concealed many jobs: preparing fields, transplanting or sowing, weeding, guarding, harvesting, threshing, storing, pounding and cooking. Families divided work by age, gender, skill and circumstance, but no single rule covered every caste, community, estate or ecological zone inside the polygon.

passages.title: Fields, food, famine and the labor behind every meal
passages.text: Millets can thrive with less standing water than paddy and helped diversify risk in uplands. That does not make them “poor people’s leftovers.” Later Odisha research documents crop knowledge and taste, while historical evidence is too patchy to attach one grain, recipe or social meaning to every 1790 family.

passages.title: Fields, food, famine and the labor behind every meal
passages.text: In 1791 to 1792, crop failures in the Northern Circars met wartime movement, demand for supplies, labor disruption and revenue pressure. Hungry people ate grain before it ripened. Famine was therefore not just bad weather; political economy influenced who had reserves, wages, transport and relief.

passages.title: Fields, food, famine and the labor behind every meal
passages.text: Food crossed social boundaries through markets, temple and court kitchens, military supply, wages, gifts and household hospitality. Yet caste hierarchy and poverty shaped who cooked, served and ate with whom. A colorful bazaar should not hide hunger, debt or the compulsory labor behind elite abundance.

passages.title: Cotton, craft, trade and a garden full of science
passages.text: Coromandel cotton required growers, cleaners, spinners, weavers, washers, dyers, painters, merchants, packers and sailors. The Met’s surviving long cloth is beautiful evidence of coordinated skill. Company contracts connected artisans to world markets while also pressing prices, schedules and access to buyers.

passages.title: Cotton, craft, trade and a garden full of science
passages.text: Indian cottons traveled around the Indian Ocean and Atlantic, influencing clothing and design far beyond this coast. “Interwoven” is literal and historical: fibers and colors crossed oceans, while knowledge remained rooted in expert hands. Global fame did not guarantee fair payment to the maker.

passages.title: Cotton, craft, trade and a garden full of science
passages.text: A loom could stand near domestic life, so paid production, childcare, cooking and preparation overlapped. Comparative textile history helps historians ask whose labor vanished from merchant accounts, especially women’s spinning and family assistance. Exact task divisions still varied by community, caste, contract and household need.

passages.title: Cotton, craft, trade and a garden full of science
passages.text: At Samalkot, Company botanist William Roxburgh developed a garden and worked with Indian collectors and artists before publishing Plants of the Coast of Coromandel from 1795. The pictures joined careful local observation to imperial networks; catalogues often preserved the European director more clearly than collaborators.

passages.title: Cotton, craft, trade and a garden full of science
passages.text: A fun science challenge hides in those plant paintings: before photography, an illustrator had to show veins, roots, flowers and fruit accurately enough for comparison. The image is both art and data. It also asks an ethical question, whose plant knowledge guided what the artist chose to show?

passages.title: Homes, clothing, work, travel and play
passages.text: Homes ranged from dense coastal settlements and estate centers to villages and dispersed upland dwellings. Materials could include earth, timber, thatch, tile or masonry according to resources and status. The polygon offers no standard house plan, and surviving elite buildings overrepresent wealthy lives.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, work, travel and play
passages.text: Cotton cloth could be practical clothing, trade good, tax-paying commodity, marker of rank and gift. Cut, drape, color and ornament varied by region, community, work and wealth. A museum textile proves technique and circulation, not what every child or laborer wore on an ordinary day.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, work, travel and play
passages.text: People walked, rode, used pack animals, carts, river craft and coastal boats. Mackenzie road surveys reveal routes that officials considered useful, while travelers still depended on weather, ferries, guides, rest places and local permission. A line on a survey was never a frictionless highway.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, work, travel and play
passages.text: Daily work included farming, herding, fishing, weaving, dyeing, pottery, metalwork, building, carrying, cooking, cleaning, accounting, guarding, soldiering and care. Occupation could be shaped by caste and dependency, yet people negotiated, combined and changed work rather than living as labels in a rigid chart.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, work, travel and play
passages.text: Children surely joked, raced, sang and improvised games, but archives rarely record their exact toys in this footprint. Rather than invent one, imagine the universal temptation of a puddle after monsoon rain, and then ask what archaeological object, image or written account would turn imagination into evidence.

passages.title: Family, women, children, school and practical learning
passages.text: Households could include relatives, dependents, servants, apprentices and laborers, with composition changing through marriage, migration, debt, death and employment. Bengal port studies reveal paid and coerced household work, but they are comparison, not a template for every Telugu-, Odia- or highland-speaking home.

passages.title: Family, women, children, school and practical learning
passages.text: Women’s work could include cultivation, processing grain, spinning, textile preparation, vending, domestic management and care, but status and tasks varied enormously. Merchant and revenue papers often hide this labor. Historians must avoid both claiming universal equality and portraying women as passive everywhere.

passages.title: Family, women, children, school and practical learning
passages.text: Children learned by watching, helping and practicing: recognizing seed, controlling thread tension, counting goods, carrying messages, remembering kin and observing ritual. Age and opportunity depended on wealth, caste, gender, patronage and locality. “Education” should include this demanding expertise rather than only classrooms.

passages.title: Family, women, children, school and practical learning
passages.text: Schools and scholarly communities used several languages and scripts, with teachers supported through fees, gifts, institutions or patrons. Access was unequal, and surviving nineteenth-century surveys cannot be pasted unchanged onto 1783. Still, they challenge the myth that learning began only when British officials arrived.

passages.title: Family, women, children, school and practical learning
passages.text: Telugu and Odia were distinct major languages across different parts of the polygon; other languages flourished in highlands and mobile communities. Persian and English served some courts and administrations, while Sanskrit and learned vernaculars had specialized roles. Multilingual life defeats the idea of one “Indian language.”

passages.title: Healing, medicine, belief and unequal chances to recover
passages.text: Families sought care in a plural medical world: learned Ayurvedic or Unani practitioners, locally respected healers, midwives, specialists, household knowledge and Company surgeons could coexist. Training and explanation differed. “Traditional medicine” is too broad if it turns changing expertise into one unchanging box.

passages.title: Healing, medicine, belief and unequal chances to recover
passages.text: Company services employed Indian dressers and medical workers who translated instructions, prepared treatments and cared for soldiers and patients. Their labor complicates a simple European-versus-Indian story. Employment did not erase unequal pay, command or the military purposes of colonial medicine.

passages.title: Healing, medicine, belief and unequal chances to recover
passages.text: Healing could involve food, rest, bathing, massage, plant or mineral preparations, surgery, prayer, vows and protective rites, chosen in combinations that made sense to patients. Evidence for a named remedy does not prove safety or effectiveness, and practice varied across language, religion, caste and region.

passages.title: Healing, medicine, belief and unequal chances to recover
passages.text: War, famine and displacement made illness harder to survive by weakening nutrition, crowding travelers and consuming labor and supplies. A soldier’s account and the Northern Circars famine history show that disease and hunger accompanied campaigns. Health depended on power and provisioning, not medicine alone.

passages.title: Healing, medicine, belief and unequal chances to recover
passages.text: Belief was equally varied: Hindu, Muslim, Christian, Indigenous and locally specific practices could shape calendars, healing, food, kin duties and patronage. The Met’s multi-court chronology displays artistic diversity, while highland scholarship warns against forcing every shrine or ritual into a single civilizational system.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets and what the evidence cannot promise
passages.text: Tanks, wells, ponds, rivers and household vessels supplied water, with access shaped by season, maintenance, status and settlement. South Asian water architecture joined engineering to ritual and social rules. A structure could store water brilliantly while access remained unequal or water quality still changed.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets and what the evidence cannot promise
passages.text: Irrigation tanks needed repeated desilting, bank repair, sluice care and agreements over flows. Later South Indian history shows colonial revenue priorities changing maintenance, but it should be used as comparison for trends, not proof that every tank inside the 1783 polygon failed in one identical way.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets and what the evidence cannot promise
passages.text: Households handled ash, sweepings, food scraps, animal dung, wastewater and broken objects every day. Some waste became fuel, fertilizer or reusable material; some accumulated. Written officials noticed filth selectively, often using it to rank colonized people, so their disgust must be read as evidence and prejudice together.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets and what the evidence cannot promise
passages.text: No source here establishes one standard toilet for this entire polygon in 1783 to 1800. People used varied household facilities, outdoor places or containers, but claiming a universal pit, drain, wiping material or caste rule would exceed the evidence. The honest bathroom fact is local records are thin.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets and what the evidence cannot promise
passages.text: Water carrying, vessel cleaning, drainage and caring for sick people consumed time that official maps ignore. Children and adults learned which sources tasted safe and when floods or stagnant water brought danger. Good sanitation was practical labor, even when archaeology cannot preserve its daily instructions.

passages.title: War, writing, remarkable objects and the 1800 rename
passages.text: The Mysore wars affected the wider south through requisitions, marching armies, displaced families, hunger and disease. Tipu Sultan was ruler of Mysore, not ruler of this whole polygon or every South Asian. Hyderabad, Maratha chiefs and the Company formed shifting alliances for their own reasons.

passages.title: War, writing, remarkable objects and the 1800 rename
passages.text: After Seringapatam fell in 1799, soldiers and officials seized Tipu’s court objects. Museum provenance research now exposes looting that older victory stories celebrated. Asking how an object reached London is part of history; admiration for craftsmanship need not excuse the violence of acquisition.

passages.title: War, writing, remarkable objects and the 1800 rename
passages.text: Fun fact from neighboring Mysore: Tipu’s Tiger is a nearly life-sized wooden automaton with an organ. Turning its handle made a tiger growl and a European victim moan. It belongs to Tipu’s court, not a generic “Indian toy,” and reached Britain after the 1799 looting.

passages.title: War, writing, remarkable objects and the 1800 rename
passages.text: Localized written sample, from Tipu’s Persian court manuscript dated 1793 to 1798: “احکامنامه”, Aḥkāmnāmah, “Book of ordinances.” Persian was one court language in Mysore. This title is contemporaneous regional evidence, not the language of every Telugu, Odia, highland or other family in the target.

passages.title: War, writing, remarkable objects and the 1800 rename
passages.text: At 1800 the atlas reuses the exact same coordinate component under “circars”; by 1815 a broader East India Company layer owns every audited core point. These are cartographic taxonomy changes. Communities, households, languages and regional powers continued while colonial territorial control grew unevenly.

At 1800 the atlas assigns the identical 37-position polygon and geometry hash to the id circars. No boundary moves. By 1815 the broader British East India Company layer covers the audited core. This is an editorial rename followed by a later atlas consolidation, while Telugu-, Odia- and highland-speaking communities, estates and regional institutions continued under increasingly coercive Company power.

materialEvidence.question: Does a concrete finding have an identifiable context, date, interpretation and evidence limit?

dailyLife.question: Does the account explain ordinary practices with evidence rather than only rulers?

artsScienceTechnology.question: Are achievements concrete and correctly attributed to this polity and period?

chronologicalPhases.question: Are source-supported phases distinguished from map snapshot dates?

endingContinuity.question: Does the narrative identify what ended or continued, with dates, mechanism and uncertainty?

uncertainty.question: Are uncertainties attached to particular claims rather than a blanket disclaimer?

sectionTitles: First read the label, government, census, and writing honestly
Follow farms, monsoons, famine, food, and drinking water
Enter homes, clothing, toilets, and uneven sanitation
Meet families, kin, women, and unequal social worlds
Watch children learn in homes, schools, workshops, and play
Work, weave, print, travel, and exchange across distance
Face plague, medicine, childbirth, injury, and care
See politics, resistance, repression, and competing futures
Speak many languages, practice beliefs, read, sing, and imagine
Celebrate achievements and close with change, not disappearance

passages.text: This card follows the atlas label “India” from 1900 to 1914, but the colored feature is broken: its only exact polygon is two small pieces in today’s Iran-Pakistan Baluchistan borderland. Delhi, Kolkata, Mumbai, Lahore, Dhaka, Hyderabad and every other tested subcontinental city fall outside it; a separate British Raj layer covers them. So the card explains the wider history requested by the label while refusing to call that sliver a national border. British India’s provinces were ruled directly by colonial officials, while hundreds of princely states kept rulers under British paramountcy. Burma lay within the Raj’s administration; Ceylon, Nepal, Bhutan, Portuguese Goa and French enclaves had different statuses. Families spoke many languages, followed many religions, and lived in farms, towns, ports, courts and forest communities. Famine and plague shaped the opening years. Railways, schools, laboratories, newspapers, textiles and early cinema changed daily life unevenly. Congress, the Muslim League, Swadeshi organizers, workers, peasants, women writers and many others pursued different futures. In 1911 the capital moved toward Delhi and Bengal’s partition was reversed. The atlas endpoint is a redraw, not independence, which came amid Partition in 1947.

passages.title: First read the label, government, census, and writing honestly
passages.text: The exact 1900 feature is not a map of India. It has two tiny components between about 60.8 and 63.3 degrees east, shares arcs with Persia and the British Raj, and contains none of the tested South Asian cities. A separate British Raj layer covers them. Treat this as a malformed border fragment.

passages.title: First read the label, government, census, and writing honestly
passages.text: Historical Baluchistan was not one unit. Baloch- and Brahui-speaking communities, Makran networks, the Kalat khanate, British agencies and Qajar Iranian authorities related differently. Frontier correspondence records officials negotiating lines around 1900. The atlas sliver crosses that zone; it cannot be assigned one ethnicity, language, economy or polity.

passages.title: First read the label, government, census, and writing honestly
passages.text: The 1901 and 1911 censuses asked about language, religion, caste or tribe, occupation, sex, marriage and literacy. Those answers provide precious evidence, but officials designed the categories and sometimes treated fluid identities as fixed ranks. A census table is a source made by people, not society frozen in glass.

passages.title: First read the label, government, census, and writing honestly
passages.text: Contemporaneous written-language sample, localized to Bengali literature: “আমার সোনার বাংলা, আমি তোমায় ভালোবাসি।” (Amar sonar Bangla, ami tomay bhalobashi), “My golden Bengal, I love you.” Tagore composed the song in 1905. This is one author's Bengali line, not speech for every person or the Baluchistan sliver.

passages.title: First read the label, government, census, and writing honestly
passages.text: The broader label must distinguish Crown-run provinces from princely states under British paramountcy, and Burma from separately governed Ceylon, Nepal, Bhutan, Portuguese Goa and French Pondicherry. The modern Republic described by the imported summary did not yet exist. Historical “India” needs dates, jurisdiction and local names, especially on a children's map.

passages.title: Follow farms, monsoons, famine, food, and drinking water
passages.text: Most people depended directly or indirectly on agriculture, but rice deltas, wheat plains, millet country, tea gardens, pastoral zones and forest livelihoods demanded different calendars. Rainfall failure could crush crops and wages together. Land revenue, credit, tenancy and market access shaped who had grain after a bad harvest.

passages.title: Follow farms, monsoons, famine, food, and drinking water
passages.text: The western famine of 1899 to 1902 crossed this card's opening years. Relief works, camps and codes existed, yet access and conditions were contested, and hunger traveled with disease. Children should not picture one empty pantry: scarcity struck households differently according to land, wages, caste, gender, location and official choices.

passages.title: Follow farms, monsoons, famine, food, and drinking water
passages.text: There was no single “Indian meal.” Rice, wheat breads, millets, pulses, vegetables, fish, meat, milk products, oils and spices varied by ecology, income, community and religious practice. Colonial gazetteers list local crops and markets, but their authors' judgments must not be mistaken for a family's own recipe book.

passages.title: Follow farms, monsoons, famine, food, and drinking water
passages.text: Families drew water from wells, tanks, rivers, stepwells, municipal taps and household storage, depending on place. Access could be restricted by caste, class, gender and neighborhood. Piped systems expanded in some cities, while many villages received little investment. Clean water infrastructure was social power as well as engineering.

passages.title: Follow farms, monsoons, famine, food, and drinking water
passages.text: Women and children often carried water, processed grain, tended animals or helped with seasonal tasks, but work patterns were never identical across regions. A brass or earthen water pot could be everyday technology: shaped for carrying, cooling and pouring. Fun fact: evaporation through porous clay can cool its contents without electricity.

passages.title: Enter homes, clothing, toilets, and uneven sanitation
passages.text: Homes ranged from courtyard houses and apartment-like urban chawls to bamboo, timber, mud-brick, stone, thatch or tile structures. Climate, land, occupation and wealth mattered. “Traditional Indian house” is therefore too vague to be useful. Domestic spaces also changed as reformers debated privacy, respectability and family roles.

passages.title: Enter homes, clothing, toilets, and uneven sanitation
passages.text: Clothing showed region, occupation, wealth and choice: saris had many draping styles; dhotis, lungis, pajamas, tunics, shawls, turbans, caps, coats and uniforms appeared in different settings. Hand spinning, weaving, dyeing and embroidery employed skilled workers, while factory cloth and swadeshi politics changed what fabric could mean.

passages.title: Enter homes, clothing, toilets, and uneven sanitation
passages.text: Some city houses had private latrines, many residents depended on shared or public facilities, and many settlements used outdoor places. Municipal Bombay debated public toilets, placement and maintenance, but provision was unequal. A plan on paper did not guarantee water, privacy, safety, cleaning or access for women and poorer neighborhoods.

passages.title: Enter homes, clothing, toilets, and uneven sanitation
passages.text: Human waste removal frequently relied on workers forced into stigmatized, dangerous manual cleaning through caste hierarchy and municipal practice. Telling sanitation history only as pipes and porcelain erases those people. Cleaner cities for some could mean degrading labor and health risks for others, a system with long afterlives.

passages.title: Enter homes, clothing, toilets, and uneven sanitation
passages.text: Railway cars and migrant ships made water and toilets especially urgent. Crowding, inadequate facilities and poor cleaning could turn a long trip into misery. Regulations reveal concern about disease, yet enforcement varied. Fun fact with no romance attached: rapid transport also created impressively rapid new arguments about who should clean the bathroom.

passages.title: Meet families, kin, women, and unequal social worlds
passages.text: A household might include a nuclear family, several generations, widowed relatives, servants, apprentices or seasonal migrants. Residence and inheritance differed across regions and communities. Colonial officials often assumed a male household head, while women's paid, farm and domestic work could disappear inside the category “dependent.”

passages.title: Meet families, kin, women, and unequal social worlds
passages.text: Marriage age, widowhood, remarriage and property rules varied by community and law. Reform debates were real, but elite writing did not describe every household. Census figures can trace patterns while hiding negotiation, affection, conflict or care. Children should not confuse an average age with the story of one girl's life.

passages.title: Meet families, kin, women, and unequal social worlds
passages.text: Women worked in cultivation, food processing, craft, domestic service, markets, factories, teaching and writing. Their visibility in records depended on what an enumerator counted as work. Regional census tables and women's histories together correct the false picture of all women staying inside identical homes.

passages.title: Meet families, kin, women, and unequal social worlds
passages.text: Act VI of 1901 in Bengal sought to regulate women migrants and unsettled neat colonial ideas of a fixed household. Travel for labor could involve opportunity, coercion, surveillance and family strategy at once. A woman's movement across a district boundary cannot be read automatically as freedom or victimhood.

passages.title: Meet families, kin, women, and unequal social worlds
passages.text: Religion shaped festivals, food, schools, marriage and charity for many people, but Hindu, Muslim, Sikh, Buddhist, Jain, Christian, Jewish, Parsi, Adivasi and other lives were internally diverse. Neighbors cooperated and quarreled for local reasons. Neither census columns nor political organizations owned every believer's opinion.

passages.title: Watch children learn in homes, schools, workshops, and play
passages.text: Children learned languages, manners, beliefs, songs, chores and trades from relatives and neighbors long before or alongside formal school. Apprenticeship, religious instruction and observation mattered. School enrollment records reveal access, not all learning, and absence from a classroom does not mean an empty mind.

passages.title: Watch children learn in homes, schools, workshops, and play
passages.text: Access to school differed sharply by sex, caste, class, region and religion. Fees, distance, household labor and distrust of institutions could keep children away. Mission, government, community and privately supported schools pursued different goals. Girls' enrollment grew from a low base, with determined local advocates facing resistance.

passages.title: Watch children learn in homes, schools, workshops, and play
passages.text: Baroda's ruler introduced compulsory primary education in parts of the princely state before extending it more widely. A 1908 parliamentary exchange shows British observers discussing that experiment. It is a useful reminder that a princely government could innovate independently rather than simply wait for a policy from Calcutta.

passages.title: Watch children learn in homes, schools, workshops, and play
passages.text: Begum Rokeya wrote “Sultana's Dream” in 1905 and established a girls' school in Calcutta in 1911 after earlier work in Bhagalpur. Her playful reversed world used science and satire to question gender restrictions. It shows that education history includes imagination, humor and institution-building together.

passages.title: Watch children learn in homes, schools, workshops, and play
passages.text: Children played with locally made dolls, balls, tops, kites, board games, riddles and improvised objects, though the evidence is scattered and class-biased. A museum toy proves that one object existed, not that every child owned it. Fun fact: a scrap of paper and wind can outperform a fancy toy.

passages.title: Work, weave, print, travel, and exchange across distance
passages.text: Agriculture supported the largest share of livelihoods, alongside artisans, herders, fishers, miners, domestic workers, merchants, clerks, soldiers and professionals. Census occupations compress seasonal combinations into tidy boxes. Someone could cultivate in one season, carry goods in another and repair tools without fitting one permanent label.

passages.title: Work, weave, print, travel, and exchange across distance
passages.text: Indian textile workers mastered cotton, silk, wool, resist dyeing, block printing, embroidery and many regional specialities. Industrial imports damaged some livelihoods, while mills expanded in Bombay and Ahmedabad. Swadeshi campaigns turned buying cloth into politics, although handmade fabric remained work, income and clothing before it became a symbol.

passages.title: Work, weave, print, travel, and exchange across distance
passages.text: Railways connected pilgrimage centers, ports, markets, workplaces and relatives, but passengers experienced different classes and crowded third-class conditions. Faster travel could lower trade costs and widen information, yet benefits remained uneven. Tracks did not automatically erase famine, discrimination or the long walk from a village to a station.

passages.title: Work, weave, print, travel, and exchange across distance
passages.text: Ports linked Bombay, Calcutta, Madras, Karachi and Rangoon with the Indian Ocean and global markets. Sailors, dockworkers, brokers and migrants moved goods and news. Colonial trade rules favored imperial priorities, while Indian merchants and workers made their own calculations within unequal systems. Exchange was active participation, not passive “opening.”

passages.title: Work, weave, print, travel, and exchange across distance
passages.text: The railway network required surveyors, engineers, plate layers, signal staff, station workers, guards and huge maintenance crews. It was an engineering achievement built through Indian labor and financed within a colonial economy. A train timetable could reorganize clocks, markets and missed connections, proving that modern frustration also has history.

passages.title: Face plague, medicine, childbirth, injury, and care
passages.text: Bubonic plague struck Bombay from 1896 and spread elsewhere. Colonial measures included inspections, segregation and forced entry that provoked fear and resistance, especially when officials violated homes and women's privacy. Public health was never just germs and laboratories; trust, coercion, housing and livelihoods shaped whether people cooperated.

passages.title: Face plague, medicine, childbirth, injury, and care
passages.text: Waldemar Haffkine developed and tested a plague vaccine in India, and laboratories expanded production. Vaccination could protect people, but delivery, consent, confidence and cold storage mattered. The scientific achievement should be taught beside the unequal colonial setting and the risks borne by Indian subjects and staff.

passages.title: Face plague, medicine, childbirth, injury, and care
passages.text: People sought care from family members, midwives, vaidyas, hakims, religious specialists, charitable dispensaries, hospitals and newly trained medical professionals. Systems overlapped instead of forming two sealed boxes called “traditional” and “Western.” Remedies and authority varied by locality, and one source cannot inventory medicine for the whole subcontinent.

passages.title: Face plague, medicine, childbirth, injury, and care
passages.text: Pregnancy and childbirth usually unfolded at home with female relatives or attendants, while maternity hospitals and trained midwifery expanded unevenly. Maternal and infant danger was high, but official records often heard institutions more clearly than households. Care could combine experienced hands, ritual, practical knowledge and new medical advice.

passages.title: Face plague, medicine, childbirth, injury, and care
passages.text: Health also meant food, clean water, ventilation, rest and safe work. Plague camps, crowded housing and famine relief exposed how policy could separate disease from its social causes. No honest card can promise one miracle remedy. Sometimes the best medicine would have been wages, grain, a clean drain and officials people trusted.

passages.title: See politics, resistance, repression, and competing futures
passages.text: The Indian National Congress included moderates seeking constitutional reform and activists demanding sharper pressure; their 1907 Surat meeting split amid procedural and strategic conflict. “Nationalist” did not mean one plan. Provincial leaders, students, workers, peasants and businesspeople entered politics through different issues and organizations.

passages.title: See politics, resistance, repression, and competing futures
passages.text: The 1905 partition of Bengal triggered petitions, boycotts, public meetings, songs, volunteer activity and national education projects. Participation varied, and communal and class tensions complicated the movement. Reversal in 1911 was a major political result, yet the new province arrangement still came from imperial authority.

passages.title: See politics, resistance, repression, and competing futures
passages.text: The Muslim League formed in 1906 amid debates over representation, education, security and relations with colonial power. Muslim politics were never one bloc, just as Congress did not speak for every Hindu or every Indian. Separate electorates in 1909 institutionalized communal political categories with long consequences.

passages.title: See politics, resistance, repression, and competing futures
passages.text: The Indian Councils Act enlarged legislative councils and permitted more discussion, but executives kept decisive authority. Voting was narrow and indirect. Separate Muslim electorates addressed demands for representation while also hardening political classification. Children should not mistake a council seat for universal democracy or complete self-government.

passages.title: See politics, resistance, repression, and competing futures
passages.text: The Press Act 1910 let authorities demand securities and seize publications considered dangerous. Official catalogues of proscribed works reveal censorship across languages and genres. Printers, editors and readers still circulated arguments. Coercion used police and law as well as soldiers, while resistance could happen through a poem, pamphlet or purchase.

passages.title: Speak many languages, practice beliefs, read, sing, and imagine
passages.text: The 1901 census attempted to classify a bewildering range of languages and dialects. Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Austroasiatic, Tibeto-Burman and other language families crossed political borders. Multilingual people switched speech by home, market, school or office, so a census “mother tongue” column cannot capture every daily conversation.

passages.title: Speak many languages, practice beliefs, read, sing, and imagine
passages.text: Writing appeared in Bengali, Devanagari, Perso-Arabic, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Gurmukhi, Malayalam, Kannada, Odia and many other scripts, as well as English. Printing connected readers unevenly because literacy, price and distribution mattered. No one script can stand as “Indian writing” for this enormous, multilingual history.

passages.title: Speak many languages, practice beliefs, read, sing, and imagine
passages.text: Temples, mosques, shrines, gurdwaras, churches, monasteries, fire temples and household practices organized time and community in different places. Reform movements debated authority and custom from within religious traditions. Belief was lived through meals, calendars, music, charity and family duties, not merely a box enumerated every ten years.

passages.title: Speak many languages, practice beliefs, read, sing, and imagine
passages.text: Tagore's songs, poems and educational experiments joined Bengali forms with wide humanist conversations. His 1913 Nobel Prize brought unprecedented international attention, but it did not make him the only Indian writer or the spokesman for every community. Literature can be celebrated without turning one laureate into a continent.

passages.title: Speak many languages, practice beliefs, read, sing, and imagine
passages.text: Early Indian cinema drew on theater, photography, music and entrepreneurial experiment. Dadasaheb Phalke's “Raja Harishchandra” appeared in 1913, though preservation is incomplete and filmmaking developed in several centers. Fun fact: silent films were rarely truly silent, because live musicians and explainers could make a screening wonderfully noisy.

passages.title: Celebrate achievements and close with change, not disappearance
passages.text: The Indian Institute of Science emerged through an unusual partnership involving Jamsetji Tata's philanthropy, Mysore state support and colonial approval; students entered in 1911. Its history shows that science was built by institutions, technicians, teachers, donors and governments, not a lone genius suddenly discovering a laboratory.

passages.title: Celebrate achievements and close with change, not disappearance
passages.text: In 1913 Srinivasa Ramanujan sent mathematical results to G. H. Hardy at Cambridge, beginning a famous collaboration. His path included self-directed study and insecure employment, so the story is more than effortless genius. An achievement can be astonishing while still depending on paper, postage, readers and someone willing to reply.

passages.title: Celebrate achievements and close with change, not disappearance
passages.text: Craft workers, printers, railway crews, teachers, nurses, vaccinators, writers and organizers made less famous discoveries every day: how to fix a loom, schedule trains, teach a class or keep vaccine usable. History should celebrate those distributed achievements alongside prizes, especially when archives preserve elite names more readily than workers' voices.

passages.title: Celebrate achievements and close with change, not disappearance
passages.text: The 1911 capital announcement and Bengal reunification changed administration without ending colonial rule. When war began in 1914, Indian soldiers, taxpayers, workers and families would be drawn into a global conflict under British authority. The exact atlas feature had already disappeared, demonstrating that its endpoint is a data seam rather than independence.

passages.title: Celebrate achievements and close with change, not disappearance
passages.text: The target never returns in the atlas snapshots checked through 1960. British rule continued until 1947; independence came with the violent Partition creating India and Pakistan, while later borders and states changed again. This card assigns no automatic successor to a malformed sliver. People, languages, institutions and political struggles continued far beyond 1914.

The exact atlas id vanishes at the 1914 snapshot, but neither the peoples of the subcontinent nor British colonial rule ended then. The two-component Baluchistan fragment reverts to Persia on the map and later to Iran; the separate British Raj layer continues. World War I opened a new phase, followed by mass movements, constitutional struggles, independence and the violent 1947 Partition. Because the exact feature is malformed and has no honest single heir, this packet records continuity, leaves fell null, and invents no successor chain.

sectionTitles: A written voice and continuing history

passages.text: This map record crosses major changes: colonial rule in 1938, an independent Dominion from 15 August 1947, and the republic from 26 January 1950. Its first polygon is misplaced near the Strait of Hormuz. Later outlines are coarse snapshots, not reliable guides to Partition or disputed borders. The stories below follow independent India while keeping those boundaries between phases clear.

passages.title: Independence and making a republic
passages.text: Independence changed who could govern. The 1947 Independence Act created the Dominions of India and Pakistan from 15 August. India’s independent Dominion phase therefore belongs between colonial government and the republic, rather than being folded into either one.

passages.title: Independence and making a republic
passages.text: Partition also broke up homes and communities. The Partition Museum preserves Jogen Chowdhury’s 1958 ink drawing of refugees at Sealdah railway station. He made it at nineteen after observing the station: the consequences of a boundary could still be visible in people’s daily lives years later.

passages.title: Independence and making a republic
passages.text: Building the new union meant integrating hundreds of princely states as well as former British provinces. Patel’s negotiations were central, but accessions were not uniformly peaceful. Hyderabad’s incorporation involved Indian military action in 1948.

passages.title: Independence and making a republic
passages.text: Language helped reshape the internal map. The 1956 reorganisation created fourteen states and six union territories. Further changes followed: Maharashtra and Gujarat emerged in 1960, showing that the republic’s internal boundaries continued to develop.

passages.title: Independence and making a republic
passages.text: In the first general elections of 1951 to 1952, each candidate had a separate ballot box bearing a symbol. Voters dropped their paper into their chosen candidate’s box. Pictures made the choice accessible to people who could not read names: an enormous democratic exercise depended on a very practical design.

passages.title: Independence and making a republic
passages.text: The Emergency declared in June 1975 brought arrests and press censorship. Some newspapers protested with blank editorial spaces. The 1977 election defeated Congress and brought the Janata Party to power, a decisive change achieved through voting.

passages.title: Independence and making a republic
passages.text: The Constitution prohibits caste-based discrimination and abolishes untouchability. These are legal commitments, not evidence that discrimination instantly disappeared. Their practical reach includes access to public wells, roads and restaurants.

passages.title: Independence and making a republic
passages.text: India’s Constitution describes a union of states. A council of ministers headed by the prime minister advises the president and is collectively responsible to the elected House of the People. Government therefore depends on institutions beyond a single leader.

passages.title: Food, livelihoods and social life
passages.text: Operation Flood, launched in 1970, linked village milk producers with town and city customers through dairy cooperatives and a National Milk Grid. Milk collection was part of a larger system involving transport, animal feed and veterinary care: breakfast in a city could depend on a farmer far away.

passages.title: Food, livelihoods and social life
passages.text: Dairy cooperatives also offered members education and services for their animals. The programme’s later expansion included more women members and women’s dairy societies. Family livelihoods therefore involved organisation and access to services as well as the daily job of milking.

passages.title: Food, livelihoods and social life
passages.text: Kolkata’s Durga Puja turns craft workshops into part of a vast public celebration. Artisans make unfired clay images, with the eyes painted on Mahalaya. Temporary pavilions become places for art and gathering; at the festival’s close, the images are immersed in water. This is one regional Hindu tradition within India’s varied social life.

passages.title: Food, livelihoods and social life
passages.text: The rupee’s relationship with other currencies changed during reforms of the early 1990s. After adjustments in 1991 and a dual-rate system in 1992, India moved to a unified market-determined exchange rate in 1993. Such rules affected the money calculations behind buying and selling across borders.

passages.title: Learning, lunch and school toilets
passages.text: School meals connect learning with the ordinary need for lunch. Akshaya Patra describes its work serving primary and upper-primary children in government and government-aided schools under PM POSHAN. The kitchens, delivery routes and school dining arrangements are part of the support that helps a school day function.

passages.title: Learning, lunch and school toilets
passages.text: In 2002 Akshaya Patra introduced a machine that could make 10,000 rotis in an hour for wheat-based menus. Its central kitchens also use large cauldrons and rice chutes. Feeding children on this scale requires some serious kitchen engineering: the rolling pin has industrial competition.

passages.title: Learning, lunch and school toilets
passages.text: At Adarsh Ramanand Middle School in Bihar, UNICEF reported in March 2025 on a Saheli Kaksh, or friendly corner, with menstrual products, a resting bed and spare uniforms. One mother, Sita Devi, described how her daughter could attend more regularly. Privacy and basic supplies can matter as much as a textbook.

passages.title: Learning, lunch and school toilets
passages.text: The same Bihar school expanded its girls’ toilets and installed group handwashing facilities. Drinking-water drums stood outside classrooms. Students also helped separate rubbish: wet waste became compost for the garden, while dry waste went for collection. A school can teach useful science through its taps and compost heap.

passages.title: Learning, lunch and school toilets
passages.text: Water work could open a route into public leadership. In UNICEF’s June 2025 account, Sita Sardar of Ulidih in Jharkhand organised a village water committee and worked on water testing and wastewater management. After serving as a Jal Sahiya, a community water worker, she became an elected village head in 2022.

passages.title: Health and scientific discoveries
passages.text: In 1976, after retirement, eye surgeon G. Venkataswamy founded an eleven-bed hospital in Madurai. Aravind developed a system combining paying patients with subsidised or free treatment. The story of medical innovation here includes how to organise care so that more people can reach it.

passages.title: Health and scientific discoveries
passages.text: Aravind’s nonprofit Aurolab began in 1992 to manufacture affordable supplies, including the tiny artificial lenses used in cataract surgery. Making an essential component locally helped reduce a barrier to treatment. A medical breakthrough can be a small manufactured object as well as a new discovery in a laboratory.

passages.title: Health and scientific discoveries
passages.text: India’s polio effort took vaccination beyond clinics. Health workers reached children at homes, schools and transit points, while community and religious leaders helped address doubts. The campaign needed repeated visits and patient explanations, not simply a vaccine sitting on a shelf.

passages.title: Health and scientific discoveries
passages.text: On 13 January 2026, WHO marked fifteen years since the region’s last wild-poliovirus case, recorded in Howrah in 2011. Continued vaccination and surveillance still mattered. This milestone concerned wild poliovirus; it did not mean that all forms of polio had disappeared everywhere.

passages.title: Health and scientific discoveries
passages.text: Chandrayaan-3 landed on the Moon on 23 August 2023. Its Pragyan rover travelled about 101 metres across the southern high-latitude surface while instruments investigated the surroundings. A short walk by human standards became an unusually valuable journey for a robot on another world.

passages.title: Health and scientific discoveries
passages.text: The rover’s laser instrument identified sulphur in lunar surface material, while other measurements examined additional elements. ISRO released mission science data in 2024 for researchers. The achievement was not only landing safely: it was returning measurements that other scientists could investigate.

passages.title: A written voice and continuing history
passages.text: The 2024 official Hindi Constitution begins “हम, भारत के लोग” (ham, Bhārat ke log), meaning “We, the people of India.” This is a modern printed witness to the constitutional language, not a claim to reproduce the handwriting of 1949. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949.

India continues as a republic. This record has no historical fall date: its open map range joins colonial and independent phases, while examples from 2025 and 2026 are dated reports, not descriptions of every household. The flawed imported outline cannot settle current territorial disputes.

sectionTitles: Building a republic and changing governments
Practical cooperation, heritage and written words

passages.text: Modern Indonesia emerged from an anti-colonial struggle across a diverse archipelago. Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta proclaimed independence on 17 August 1945; war and negotiations continued before the Dutch sovereignty transfer in December 1949. This card follows the republic through changing governments, rather than treating earlier island kingdoms as the same state. Its imported outlines are coarse snapshots, not exact annual borders.

passages.title: Building a republic and changing governments
passages.text: The proclamation did not end colonial rule overnight. The Netherlands tried to regain control, and a destructive war followed. The 1949 settlement created a federal United States of Indonesia; a united republic replaced it in 1950. Independence Day commemorates the 1945 declaration, rather than the later diplomatic transfer.

passages.title: Building a republic and changing governments
passages.text: Indonesia helped convene the Asian-African Conference at Bandung in April 1955. Delegates from twenty-nine countries discussed peace, cooperation and freedom from colonial domination. Photographs, films and documents preserve a moment when recently independent states sought a larger voice in world affairs.

passages.title: Building a republic and changing governments
passages.text: Political life changed sharply under Sukarno and then Suharto. Parliamentary democracy gave way to Guided Democracy in 1959. Suharto’s later New Order promoted economic growth while restricting political opposition; corruption and repression were part of the system as well as roads, factories and rising output.

passages.title: Building a republic and changing governments
passages.text: In 1965 and 1966, the army and allied militias killed large numbers of people accused of supporting the Communist Party. Many others were imprisoned. Declassified embassy records document the campaign. Its victims and their families belong in this history alongside the leaders who gained power.

passages.title: Building a republic and changing governments
passages.text: The Asian financial crisis devastated livelihoods in 1997 and 1998, and Suharto left office amid mass protest. Reformasi, the reform era, brought political openings. Decentralization laws taking effect in 2001 moved substantial responsibility for services to local governments, changing where citizens sought decisions about schools and health care.

passages.title: Building a republic and changing governments
passages.text: The map’s 1960 snapshot already includes western New Guinea, although the United Nations transferred its administration to Indonesia on 1 May 1963. That is a dating mismatch in the imported geometry. Administrative transfer should not be confused with evidence that every resident agreed with the political settlement.

passages.title: Building a republic and changing governments
passages.text: East Timor has its own history. The 1999 consultation rejected the proposed autonomy arrangement within Indonesia; violence and a United Nations administration followed. Timor-Leste became independent in May 2002. A changing outline must not turn this separate country into an eternal part of Indonesia.

passages.title: Families, crafts and learning together
passages.text: Batik makers draw dots and lines of hot wax on cloth so that selected areas resist dye. They can remove the wax and repeat the process for further colours. The design depends on planning what the dye will leave untouched: some of the artistry happens by keeping colour out.

passages.title: Families, crafts and learning together
passages.text: Batik can accompany family milestones as well as everyday clothing. UNESCO’s documentation describes patterned cloth used to carry babies and in marriage ceremonies. Patterns and uses vary: this is a living textile tradition carried through families and workshops, not a uniform worn by everyone in the archipelago.

passages.title: Families, crafts and learning together
passages.text: In an angklung ensemble, players shake bamboo instruments to sound their assigned tones. A melody can be shared across several people, making careful listening essential. Smithsonian research describes its use in music education and cultural diplomacy. Even someone responsible for one note has to arrive at exactly the right moment.

passages.title: Families, crafts and learning together
passages.text: Jamu preparation links plant knowledge, work and social trust. UNESCO’s 2023 account describes makers, mostly adult women, growing herbs and spices and passing skills among relatives and neighbours. Customers discuss their needs with practitioners. This documents a medicinal tradition and its relationships, rather than proving every preparation effective.

passages.title: Families, crafts and learning together
passages.text: A 2020 UNICEF profile follows Marlina in Sabang, Aceh, whose cake-making and laundry income fell during the pandemic while her injured husband could not fish. A local child-support programme helped her buy eggs, fish and vegetables. Family wellbeing depended on paid work, caregiving and public support together.

passages.title: Families, crafts and learning together
passages.text: The same programme connected families with posyandu, community health posts offering growth monitoring and feeding and parenting advice. The health visit and the household food budget were linked. This was a particular Sabang programme described in 2020, rather than a promise that every family received identical assistance.

passages.title: Schools, water and medical discoveries
passages.text: At Sinar Hungku early-childhood centre in the Arfak Mountains, a 2025 report shows teacher Bertha welcoming children with high-fives. Lessons and play also faced practical obstacles: severe weather, too few teachers, and children accompanying parents to the fields. A classroom’s success depended on the surrounding community as well as teaching materials.

passages.title: Schools, water and medical discoveries
passages.text: Good toilets can change whether someone seeks health care. In a February 2024 report, eighteen-year-old Nur Annisa described avoiding her local clinic because of poor facilities. Renovations at Puskesmas Mancobalang in South Sulawesi added secure, accessible, gender-separated toilets, menstrual supplies and mirrors.

passages.title: Schools, water and medical discoveries
passages.text: That clinic also installed water towers and solar panels to maintain water supplies through difficult conditions. Reliable sanitation needed more than a new toilet bowl: it needed water and power. The project addressed droughts and outages that had made daily hygiene difficult for patients and staff.

passages.title: Schools, water and medical discoveries
passages.text: Researchers in Yogyakarta tested a striking dengue-control idea: releasing mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria. The trial involved Gadjah Mada University, Monash’s World Mosquito Program and the Tahija Foundation. Results published in 2021 found about 77 percent less dengue in treated areas compared with control areas, and 86 percent fewer dengue hospitalizations.

passages.title: Schools, water and medical discoveries
passages.text: The dengue experiment divided the study area into twenty-four clusters, randomly choosing twelve for mosquito releases while routine control continued in both groups. People attending local clinics with fever were tested. Careful comparison made it possible to assess the intervention rather than simply noticing that one season had fewer illnesses.

passages.title: Practical cooperation, heritage and written words
passages.text: Community planning became one route to improving village life. A World Bank account from 2014 describes PNPM Mandiri, launched in 2007, which supported local discussions, employment and small infrastructure projects. Decisions about shared needs were part of the work, alongside the physical construction.

passages.title: Practical cooperation, heritage and written words
passages.text: On Simeulue, smong stories passed down memories of earlier tsunamis and the need to escape to higher ground. A 2024 United Nations field report describes how that knowledge helped save lives in 2004 and entered school teaching. Grandparents’ stories could carry information as consequential as anything in a textbook.

passages.title: Practical cooperation, heritage and written words
passages.text: Modern Indonesians also preserved much older achievements. The major restoration of Borobudur in 1973 to 1983 reused original stone while improving stability and drainage. The temple was built in the eighth and ninth centuries; this later achievement was conservation, including the unglamorous but essential job of giving rainwater a way out.

passages.title: Practical cooperation, heritage and written words
passages.text: The National Archives reproduces the proclamation’s opening in modern spelling: “Kami bangsa Indonesia dengan ini menyatakan kemerdekaan Indonesia”, meaning “We, the Indonesian people, hereby declare Indonesia’s independence.” This is Indonesian in Latin script, from the declaration of 17 August 1945. The spelling shown follows the archive’s 2013 transcription, not a claim to reproduce the original typed letterforms.

Indonesia continues as a republic; the fall of Suharto’s government in 1998 was a political transition, not the end of the country. Later accounts here are dated. Regional identities and arguments over rights, representation and territorial history remain part of its continuing story.
