sectionTitles: Homes, music, food and shared skills

passages.text: This record follows modern Iraq, whose monarchy ended in 1958 and whose Ba’ath government emerged a decade later. It does not combine the ancient Mesopotamian kingdoms or Abbasid Caliphate into one uninterrupted state. The imported span begins in 1945; five broad outlines run only to 2020. They do not show changing wartime control or internal regional government, and their last year is not Iraq’s disappearance.

passages.title: Governments, oil and conflict
passages.text: Iraq’s British mandate status ended in 1932, before this map record begins. A monarchy remained until the coup in Baghdad on 14 July 1958. That upheaval also ended Iraq’s short-lived union with Jordan. The political institution changed sharply, while cities, families and working communities continued through the transition.

passages.title: Governments, oil and conflict
passages.text: The Ba’ath Party seized power in 1968. Saddam Hussein became president in 1979, concentrating authority at the top of the state. Iraq fought Iran from 1980 to 1988, while military production expanded. A country with major industrial ambitions also committed enormous resources to a prolonged and destructive war.

passages.title: Governments, oil and conflict
passages.text: In the 1988 Anfal campaign, Saddam Hussein’s government attacked Kurdish communities, destroyed villages and made civilians disappear into detention and killing operations. Human Rights Watch reconstructed the campaign from captured government documents and interviews with survivors. This was organized persecution, not a natural disappearance of villages or a change that can be explained by a map colour.

passages.title: Governments, oil and conflict
passages.text: Iraq’s invasion of Kuwait in 1990 brought international sanctions and the 1991 Gulf War. Ordinary households faced severe shortages and damaged services. The United Nations created Oil-for-Food in 1995, allowing supervised oil sales to finance food, medicine and other humanitarian needs. It was an emergency arrangement within sanctions, rather than ordinary unrestricted trade.

passages.title: Governments, oil and conflict
passages.text: A coalition led by the United States and Britain invaded Iraq in March 2003 and captured Baghdad in April. Saddam’s government fell, and the Coalition Provisional Authority administered the occupation. Power passed to an Iraqi interim government in June 2004 amid insurgency and civil unrest. Removing the regime did not end the violence or erase the Iraqi state.

passages.title: Governments, oil and conflict
passages.text: Baghdad hosted the conference that founded OPEC in September 1960. Iraq joined Iran, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela as the five original members. Their representatives met in Al-Shaab Hall to coordinate oil-producing countries’ interests. Decisions made around a conference table connected Iraqi resources with the wider world’s demand for fuel.

passages.title: Governments, oil and conflict
passages.text: The 2005 constitution describes Iraq as a federal parliamentary republic. It recognizes Arabic and Kurdish as official languages and the Kurdistan region as a federal region. These provisions acknowledge a country containing different communities and institutions. Constitutional promises describe the intended legal order; they do not by themselves prove equal treatment in everyday life.

passages.title: Homes, music, food and shared skills
passages.text: In the southern marshes, a mudhif is a large gathering building made from reeds and papyrus. Bundles form sweeping arches, and woven mats furnish the interior. Skilled builders lead the work, but neighbours help collect materials and maintain the space. A community building can begin with plants gathered from the landscape around it.

passages.title: Homes, music, food and shared skills
passages.text: A mudhif welcomes visitors and provides space for weddings, storytelling, discussion and the settlement of disagreements. Children and young people learn customs and craft skills through participation. UNESCO describes management by tribal sheikhs alongside community involvement. The same room may host serious conversation one day and a celebration the next.

passages.title: Homes, music, food and shared skills
passages.text: Iraqi maqam brings Arabic poetry together with a singer and instrumental ensemble. The singer improvises while instruments such as the santur, jawzah fiddle and hand drums accompany the performance. UNESCO records gatherings in homes, coffeehouses and theatres. Listening is a social occasion as well as a musical one, with room for an experienced singer to surprise the audience.

passages.title: Homes, music, food and shared skills
passages.text: Older Iraqi houses can have shanasheel, projecting windows with carved wooden latticework. A UNESCO architectural account explains how these features admit moving air while reducing direct sunlight. This is an inherited building tradition shared with neighbouring regions, not something invented by the modern state. A handsome window can also be hard-working shade.

passages.title: Homes, music, food and shared skills
passages.text: In a 2021 FAO interview, Nineveh dairy farmer Dhuhaa Najm Shith recalled feeding her buffalo and milking them before sunrise. Her household sold raw milk and made qimar, a thick cream, for city markets. Work at home connected animal care, food processing and family income. Preparing breakfast ingredients could begin while customers were still asleep.

passages.title: Homes, music, food and shared skills
passages.text: Marshland food production depends on sufficient water for people, reeds and buffalo. During a July 2022 visit, FAO reported low water, poor animal health and declining milk production. Some families were moving their herds to other places with water. This dated account shows why the future of a familiar food can depend on river management and climate.

passages.title: Learning, health, discoveries and rebuilding
passages.text: At Mujahid al-Arabi Primary School in al-Karma, Anbar, children had studied in crowded temporary rooms after wartime damage. A 2023 UNDP account describes the rebuilt school’s library, clean toilets and drinking water, alongside football and friendships. Twelve-year-old Saif especially enjoyed maths. Rebuilding a school meant restoring ordinary routines as well as walls.

passages.title: Learning, health, discoveries and rebuilding
passages.text: ISIL occupied Mosul in 2014 and destroyed al-Nouri Mosque during its retreat in 2017. Restoration teams first removed explosives and hazardous material, then sorted rubble for fragments that could be reused. Iraqi heritage specialists and international partners worked together. Rebuilding required patient recording and conservation, not simply clearing everything away and starting over.

passages.title: Learning, health, discoveries and rebuilding
passages.text: Excavations near al-Nouri’s prayer hall began in August 2021 and uncovered four rooms dating to the twelfth century. Coins of the Atabeg period helped date them; jars, pottery and carved stone also appeared. Archaeologists think the rooms were probably used for ritual washing. The modern rebuilding project unexpectedly opened a window into an older building’s daily use.

passages.title: Learning, health, discoveries and rebuilding
passages.text: Two children in Baghdad developed paralytic polio in 2014 after a long absence of the disease. Iraqi health authorities, WHO, UNICEF and other partners responded with vaccination campaigns coordinated across the region. WHO’s account describes transmission being interrupted within ten months. The achievement depended on reaching children repeatedly, including families displaced by conflict.

passages.title: Learning, health, discoveries and rebuilding
passages.text: Floods in November 2018 damaged toilets, showers and water supplies in Jeddah and Airstrip camps near Qayyarah. UNICEF’s report describes workers clearing waste from sanitation systems while others restored drinking water and delivered soap and hygiene supplies. For displaced families, a working toilet also depended on drains, maintenance and safe water beyond the cubicle.

passages.title: Learning, health, discoveries and rebuilding
passages.text: A 2015 WHO report describes a health clinic assembled from six caravans in a displaced-person camp on the Najaf road in Kerbala. It included a laboratory, pharmacy, wound-dressing rooms and maternal and child health services. Movable buildings brought several kinds of care together while families were living away from home.

passages.title: Learning, health, discoveries and rebuilding
passages.text: Article 11 of the 2005 constitution reads “بغداد عاصمة جمهورية العراق”: “Baghdad is the capital of the Republic of Iraq.” A Latin transliteration is “Baghdād ʿāṣimat Jumhūriyyat al-ʿIrāq.” The Arabic sample comes from Parliament’s modern digital text, checked against the English constitutional translation. It is one official language’s writing, not a claim that every Iraqi speaks Arabic.

Iraq continues as a state with federal constitutional institutions. The monarchy ended in 1958 and Ba’ath rule ended in 2003; neither event meant that Iraq’s peoples and communities disappeared. The dataset’s last polygon ends in 2020, but this is a limit of the imported maps, not a historical fall date.

sectionTitles: An Irish writer and an imaginary traveller

passages.text: This atlas record concerns the eighteenth-century Kingdom of Ireland, not medieval Gaelic kingdoms or today's Irish state. Its parliament and social institutions existed within a monarchy shared with Britain. The map continues the label to 1815, although the separate Irish parliament ended when the union took effect in 1801.

passages.title: Government and public institutions
passages.text: The Irish Volunteers, formed in 1778, pressed for changes to restrictions on Irish commerce. In 1782 British ministers accepted major legislative changes. These developments concerned political and commercial power, not equal voting rights for every resident.

passages.title: Government and public institutions
passages.text: The 1800 union legislation was debated and approved before it came into force on 1 January 1801. Keeping the law's passage and implementation separate helps explain why sources give both years.

passages.title: Government and public institutions
passages.text: Marsh's Library opened under an Act of 1707 to give readers a place to study. Its first librarian, Élie Bouhéreau, was a Huguenot refugee from France. A Dublin institution preserved books and expertise carried across borders.

passages.title: Government and public institutions
passages.text: By the mid 1760s, more than 1000 books had disappeared from Marsh's. Readers were then supervised at a table or locked into reading cages. The librarian's solution to book theft was considerably more dramatic than a reminder email.

passages.title: Birth, learning and practical work
passages.text: Bartholomew Mosse founded Dublin's lying-in hospital in 1745 to provide maternity care and training. It moved to the present Rotunda site in 1757. These buildings document an organized response to childbirth needs, not proof that every mother could obtain safe care.

passages.title: Birth, learning and practical work
passages.text: Plays, performances of Handel's music and lotteries raised money for the new maternity hospital. Entertainment and philanthropy were connected: an evening out could help pay for wards and equipment.

passages.title: Birth, learning and practical work
passages.text: Lisburn's weavers brought cloth to the market house before a separate brown-linen market was built around 1750. Making cloth and finding buyers were linked stages of work. A successful textile industry still depended on many individual households and workers.

passages.title: Birth, learning and practical work
passages.text: The Royal Dublin Society, founded in 1731, offered premiums for tree planting from 1742. Awards were one way to encourage agricultural and economic experiments. They show what an institution promoted, not that every landowner followed its advice.

passages.title: Birth, learning and practical work
passages.text: The Society established its drawing school in 1750, teaching figure, landscape and ornamental work; architectural drawing followed in the 1760s. Art education could support useful design and building skills as well as pictures for display.

passages.title: Birth, learning and practical work
passages.text: In the early 1800s, Lisburn's market-house assembly room hosted dinners, dances, concerts and speakers. This example belongs after the 1801 union, within the atlas's later years. Changes in parliamentary government did not stop local social life.

passages.title: An Irish writer and an imaginary traveller
passages.text: Jonathan Swift published the book usually called Gulliver's Travels in 1726. Its invented voyages let him criticize human behaviour and institutions. It is an achievement of imaginative writing, not evidence that tiny islanders or giant people actually existed.

passages.title: An Irish writer and an imaginary traveller
passages.text: Travels into Several Remote Nations of the World is part of the book's original English title. Here remote means far away. This short written sample comes from a specific 1726 work; it does not imply that English was everyone's home language in Ireland.

The separate Irish parliament ended under the union that took effect on 1 January 1801. Irish communities and institutions continued within the United Kingdom. The map's 1815 endpoint is a later coverage boundary, not the date Ireland lost its people or the year the parliamentary union began.

passages.text: This is the modern Irish state, not a Kingdom of Ireland. Its constitutional development began before the first 1938 map snapshot: the Irish Free State dates to 1922, followed by the 1937 Constitution. Electricity, schooling, water supplies and community sport show how public changes reached ordinary households.

passages.title: A state, a name and public decisions
passages.text: The 1922 Constitution Committee left records of its work on the Irish Free State's institutions. Constitutions are written through discussion and choices, not simply discovered ready-made. This founding phase predates the atlas's 1938 beginning.

passages.title: A state, a name and public decisions
passages.text: The Republic of Ireland Act came into operation on 18 April 1949. The enactment and its commencement are different dates. This is a constitutional milestone in an already existing state, not the sudden appearance of Irish people or culture.

passages.title: A state, a name and public decisions
passages.text: Éire is ainm don Stát means “The name of the State is Éire.” It comes from Article 4 of the Constitution in the official online Irish text, which uses modern standardized spelling. Irish language and Latin script should not be confused with each other.

passages.title: Electricity and the work of a home
passages.text: The Rural Electrification Scheme began in 1946; its first pole was erected at Kilsallaghan, County Dublin, on 5 November. Bringing power to scattered homes required surveying, poles, wires and crews. A switch on the wall was the visible end of a much larger job.

passages.title: Electricity and the work of a home
passages.text: The 1957 ESB film More Power to the Farmer shows hand washing, butter churning and carrying water in buckets. Its demonstrations promoted electrical alternatives. This was a persuasive company film, so its scenes are evidence of an argument for change, not a neutral picture of every farm.

passages.title: Electricity and the work of a home
passages.text: The film also shows customers asking about charges and deciding whether to sign up. A new machine could promise less work while still raising questions about cost. Household modernization depended on decisions as well as technology.

passages.title: Electricity and the work of a home
passages.text: The 1961 census counted 301,774 farm dwellings; 237,904 obtained water from a well, fountain, pump or other source rather than a piped supply. These figures concern farm dwellings specifically. They show why fetching water remained a major practical issue.

passages.title: Electricity and the work of a home
passages.text: In that same farm-dwelling table, only 30,943 had use of a fixed bath and 31,500 a hot-water tap. A house with electrical light did not automatically have a modern bathroom. Different improvements reached families at different times.

passages.title: Getting to school and playing together
passages.text: A 1967 Department of Education circular set out free post-primary education. Removing tuition costs changed the possibilities facing families, although educational access involves more than the price of lessons.

passages.title: Getting to school and playing together
passages.text: The 1967-68 public accounts record free school transport from 1 April 1967. For a pupil living far from school, a practical way to get there mattered alongside classroom policy. A bus route could be part of an educational achievement.

passages.title: Getting to school and playing together
passages.text: Hurling and camogie connect playing skills with clubs, families and local communities. UNESCO's 2018 description emphasizes learning through practice and coaching. It records a living tradition, not one frozen version played identically in every century.

passages.title: Getting to school and playing together
passages.text: The same tradition depends on volunteers who coach, organize teams and help clubs operate. Social life includes the work surrounding a match, as well as the players on the field. The final score is only part of what a community makes together.

Ireland continues as a sovereign state. Constitutional milestones in 1922, 1937 and 1949 describe changes in its institutions, while membership of the European Communities began in 1973. Its people, languages, public institutions and everyday traditions continue to develop.

passages.text: Irlanda is this atlas's label for early medieval Ireland, here shown in 800-1000. It includes Gaelic kingdoms and monastic communities in a landscape increasingly connected with Scandinavian settlements. It is not the eighteenth-century Kingdom of Ireland or the modern Irish state. Books and excavated objects reveal overlapping cultural worlds.

passages.title: Making objects worth keeping
passages.text: The eighth-century Ardagh Chalice combined silver with elaborate decorative work in other materials. Its many separately made elements had to be fitted together. An impressive church vessel was also the result of a highly organized craft process.

passages.title: Making objects worth keeping
passages.text: Gold filigree, glass and enamel decorate the chalice. The names of apostles appear around its bowl. Ornament and writing worked together in a Christian ceremonial object, rather than serving as a guide to the drinking cups in ordinary homes.

passages.title: Making objects worth keeping
passages.text: The chalice came to light in 1868 when a boy digging potatoes in Ardagh ringfort disturbed a flagstone. A smaller cup and four brooches were also found. A spectacular accidental discovery does not preserve every detail that a modern excavation would record.

passages.title: The work behind a book
passages.text: The Book of Kells was made around 800, but scholars cannot securely divide its production between Iona and Kells. The monasteries were connected. Its modern home in Dublin does not establish exactly where each medieval page was written.

passages.title: The work behind a book
passages.text: The book contains 340 parchment leaves made from calfskin. Specialists distinguish four major scribes and several artists. Writing, preparing pages and designing ornament were skilled tasks; “made by monks” leaves much of the actual work unexplained.

passages.title: The work behind a book
passages.text: Scientific study revised an attractive old story: the blue pigment probably did not come from expensive lapis lazuli. Indigo or woad provided blue. Testing the material can change the story told about an object's trade connections.

passages.title: Towns, grooming and ordinary things
passages.text: Dublin excavations recovered more than 2,000 combs, including a small group identified as Scandinavian. Such personal objects reveal grooming and skilled manufacture; they are not merely decorations beside swords in a Viking display.

passages.title: Towns, grooming and ordinary things
passages.text: Researchers examine the combs’ materials, manufacturing techniques and wear. Wear can help indicate how much an object was used before being discarded. A personal grooming tool carries evidence of both its maker’s skill and its owner’s repeated actions.

passages.title: Towns, grooming and ordinary things
passages.text: The National Museum's Viking Ireland gallery uses excavated evidence to model a Dublin house. A reconstruction helps visitors imagine built space, but its finished appearance includes interpretation where wooden buildings no longer survive intact.

passages.title: Towns, grooming and ordinary things
passages.text: The same exhibition brings together evidence for craftworking and trade. A town required people who made and repaired ordinary things as well as merchants. This urban example should not be projected unchanged onto every farm or monastery in Ireland.

passages.title: A writer and his cat
passages.text: Messe ocus Pangur Bán means “I and white Pangur.” These Old Irish words begin a ninth-century poem preserved in a manuscript on the European continent. They are evidence of Irish-language learning abroad, not an inscription excavated in an Irish house.

passages.title: A writer and his cat
passages.text: The poem compares a scholar's search for understanding with his cat's hunting. Its memorable pairing makes quiet study feel human. It describes one literary household, not proof that every Irish monastery kept a named cat.

The atlas changes this label at 1000, but Irish kingdoms, monasteries and Scandinavian-linked towns continued. The National Museum challenges the familiar tale that Clontarf in 1014 simply drove all Vikings out. Political change and cultural contact continued; neither date marks the disappearance of Ireland's people.

passages.text: The Haudenosaunee are a continuing alliance of Native nations whose heartlands include present-day New York. “Iroquois” is the imported map label. Its early outline extends far into New England and should not be mistaken for a precise boundary of the confederacy.

passages.title: An alliance built through relationships
passages.text: Onondaga’s account of the Great Peace tells how the Peacemaker and Hiawatha helped bring formerly warring nations together. The longhouse became a political image: different nations could share responsibilities while retaining their own places within the alliance.

passages.title: An alliance built through relationships
passages.text: At Onondaga, clan membership passes through mothers. People of the same clan in another Haudenosaunee nation are also treated as relatives. That connection could make a journey feel less like arriving among strangers and more like visiting extended family.

passages.title: An alliance built through relationships
passages.text: Clan Mothers select the spokesmen who represent their clans in council. They also have authority to remove a leader after warnings if he fails his responsibilities. Leadership is a relationship with the community, not simply a powerful man’s personal possession.

passages.title: An alliance built through relationships
passages.text: The same account describes Clan Mothers naming babies and teaching younger and older people. Political responsibility, family life and education are closely connected. A child’s name belongs within a continuing community, with names available for later generations.

passages.title: Longhouses, pottery and games
passages.text: A traditional Onondaga longhouse held related families of a clan. A newly married husband moved into his wife’s family longhouse. Aunts and grandparents helped raise children, so home life extended beyond the parents and children of one small household.

passages.title: Longhouses, pottery and games
passages.text: At the Mohawk village of Garoga, archaeologists found thirteen longhouses within a palisade. Radiocarbon evidence places this settlement around 1550 to 1582. The remains give a particular village and period behind the general image of a Haudenosaunee longhouse.

passages.title: Longhouses, pottery and games
passages.text: Garoga also yielded thousands of pottery fragments and 43 lumps of unfired clay, probably prepared for making vessels. Pots with carefully shaped collars and incised patterns served cooking and storage. An unfinished lump can reveal the workshop behind a finished bowl.

passages.title: Longhouses, pottery and games
passages.text: Onondaga’s account of lacrosse describes handmade hickory sticks and teams formed by clans or by younger and older men. The game has ceremonial importance as well as athletic skill. Its meaning reaches beyond the score at the end.

passages.title: Memory, words and endurance
passages.text: Wampum beads require cutting, rounding, smoothing and drilling shell. Speakers use the woven strings and belts to remember agreements and histories. The Onondaga Nation describes them as living records whose meaning is carried through knowledgeable people and repeated telling.

passages.title: Memory, words and endurance
passages.text: An invitation to council could combine wampum with a notched wooden stick. Removing a notch each day counted down to the meeting. It was a calendar reminder with no battery to charge, carried together with the reason everyone needed to gather.

passages.title: Memory, words and endurance
passages.text: A modern written Onondaga sample is “Oñgwehoñwe’”, translated by the Nation as “the Real People”. Its language page connects the term with songs and identity. This is today’s Latin-script presentation; wampum itself is not an alphabet spelling out these words.

passages.title: Memory, words and endurance
passages.text: The 1779 American campaign burned villages and food supplies, causing displacement and hardship. Onondaga families later rebuilt in smaller houses while maintaining kinship and government. Their history continues beyond warfare and beyond the map’s 1783 endpoint.

War and dispossession greatly reduced Haudenosaunee lands, but the confederacy and its nations did not end in 1783. Member communities continue their governments, languages and ceremonies; Onondaga maintains its council and longhouse on part of its ancestral territory.

passages.text: “Islamic and Hindu states” is a changing atlas umbrella across parts of South Asia, not one empire or a complete description of its communities. The 1530 and 1600 main outlines include Ahmedabad, Gaur and much of central India; a small coastal patch also appears in 1530. The 1650 outline contracts to east-central India, including Jabalpur, Ramnagar, Nagpur, Raipur and Bastar. These snapshots can preserve outdated political boundaries. Named sultanates, Gond kingdoms, the Mughal Empire and other regional states retain their own histories. Religion alone did not determine a person’s language, occupation or political allegiance.

passages.title: Several states, several political stories
passages.text: At the western end of the early outline, Gujarat’s sultanate came under Mughal rule in 1573. Ahmedabad’s inclusion in the 1600 umbrella should therefore not be read as proof that the same independent sultanate survived. A map snapshot can lag behind a major political change.

passages.title: Several states, several political stories
passages.text: Bengal followed a different sequence. The Husain Shahi dynasty fell in 1538, followed by Afghan rulers and Mughal intervention. In 1576 Mughal forces defeated Daud Karrani at Rajmahal. That battle changed the ruling order, but regional resistance and the work of establishing control did not simply disappear in one afternoon.

passages.title: Several states, several political stories
passages.text: Central Indian Gond kingdoms developed their own systems of authority. Garha-Katanga was organized through clan-controlled garhs and smaller village groupings. Trapping and exporting elephants brought wealth: a powerful animal could be a diplomatic asset as well as expensive cargo. Several Gond states coexisted; they were not one interchangeable kingdom.

passages.title: Several states, several political stories
passages.text: Royal family life could become government. After Dalpat Shah’s death, Durgavati governed Garha-Katanga for her young son, assisted by ministers. She resisted a Mughal invasion and died in 1564. Remembering her only as somebody’s wife or mother misses her own political and military authority.

passages.title: Households, roads and water
passages.text: Food moved with families. The seventeenth-century traveler Peter Mundy described Banjara caravans carrying wheat and rice, in which wives and children traveled alongside traders and their oxen. They bought grain where it cost less and sold it elsewhere. His account gives a glimpse of mobile households that helped connect settled towns and armies to supplies.

passages.title: Households, roads and water
passages.text: Near Garha, a chain of tanks used the slope of the land: overflow from Maharaj Tal fed lower tanks, eventually draining toward the river system. Geologist K.G.Vyas describes five linked tanks that still survive. The landscape did part of the carrying, with gravity supplying the muscle. Individual construction dates are not established for every tank.

passages.title: Households, roads and water
passages.text: Step-wells in the Jabalpur area made water reachable by stairs. Vyas describes stone lining in upper soil layers while sound water-bearing rock below could remain unlined, allowing groundwater to enter. He interprets some nearby tanks without canals as serving drinking and household needs. This is evidence about collecting water, not proof of universal piped supplies or toilets.

passages.title: Households, roads and water
passages.text: At Ramnagar’s Moti Mahal, the royal kitchen, bedrooms, halls and stables belonged to a carefully arranged palace complex. A stepped water feature occupied the central courtyard. Its drainage directed stormwater toward the Narmada. Keeping rain moving away from rooms was an architectural achievement; the surviving description does not establish a citywide sewage system.

passages.title: Households, roads and water
passages.text: The residence of the king’s minister at Ramnagar offered practical comfort as well as status. A high entrance wall screened the interior and blocked strong sunlight. Rooms were arranged around a courtyard, with lower roofs along its inner edge. Privacy and shade mattered in designing a home, even when the resident was an important official.

passages.title: Craft, learning and written voices
passages.text: A sixteenth-century bridal casket associated with Gujarat and Goa or Lisbon combines teak, silver and shimmering mother-of-pearl. Its decorative technique is Indian, while its form follows European models. Objects like this served Portuguese clients, especially in Asia. It is a record of skilled cross-cultural production, not a model of every local wedding gift.

passages.title: Craft, learning and written voices
passages.text: An early seventeenth-century Gujarat pen box carries Persian verses about calligraphy. Shell pieces and a lacquer-like substance decorate a container for writing tools. Such objects were made for local use and export. Learning to form beautiful letters could be celebrated on the very box that held the tools, although an expensive example tells us about patrons rather than universal literacy.

passages.title: Craft, learning and written voices
passages.text: Ramnagar’s 1667 Sanskrit inscription praises Queen Sundari Devi for gardens, ponds and donations and commemorates her temple. Its words present an ideal of generous rulership; they are royal praise, not an independent survey of everyone’s welfare. Archaeologists can compare that written claim with the surviving buildings rather than treating either source as the whole story.

passages.title: Craft, learning and written voices
passages.text: A short phrase from that inscription reads “abhavatsundarī devī rānī tasya mahīpateḥ,” translated “That king had a beautiful queen, Sundari Devi.” This is the published scholarly transliteration of Sanskrit originally carved in Devanagari at Ramnagar in 1667. The modern letters shown here reproduce an edited reading of damaged stone, not its original appearance or everyday Gondi speech.

passages.title: Craft, learning and written voices
passages.text: The inscription also makes skilled people visible. It names the scholar Jayagovinda and associates his family with learned debate and poetic meter; it names Simhasahi, Dayarama and Bhagiratha as the temple’s expert builders. A royal monument required more than a ruler with an idea: scholars and craftspeople supplied specialized knowledge.

The 1700 cutoff ends this atlas category, not all its communities or states. Gond royal building at Ramnagar belongs to a continuing regional history. The broad religious label gives way to more specific political stories; families, languages and practical skills outlast changes in map colors.

passages.text: This imported label covers East African coastal towns, especially the Swahili trading world, rather than every Islamic city or one united empire. African settlements developed into connected centres with distinct rulers and communities. The map’s 1000 to 1650 window is a broad regional selection; individual towns began and changed at different times.

passages.title: Ports, power and architecture
passages.text: These towns belonged to a sailing network. Medieval Yemeni records describe ships travelling from Mogadishu to Arabian ports, while a vessel from Kilwa reached Aden with rice in 1336. Merchants moved food, cloth, ivory and other goods; the same routes also carried enslaved people.

passages.title: Ports, power and architecture
passages.text: At Kilwa, gold and ivory from the African interior could be exchanged for Persian ceramics, Chinese porcelain, silver and perfumes. Coastal prosperity therefore depended on inland producers and routes as well as ships arriving over the horizon.

passages.title: Ports, power and architecture
passages.text: Kilwa’s Great Mosque combined coral stone and lime mortar with domes and vaults. Some vaults contained imported Chinese porcelain as decoration: an overseas bowl could become part of a building rather than remain on a dinner table.

passages.title: Ports, power and architecture
passages.text: Husuni Kubwa, built around 1310 to 1333, included a large eight-sided bathing pool. The surviving palace makes elite comfort unusually visible, although a ruler’s pool tells us much more about wealthy residents than ordinary household washing.

passages.title: Meals, work and neighbours
passages.text: At Songo Mnara, charred seeds reveal a varied pantry: pearl millet, finger millet, sorghum, rice, beans, coconut and fruits such as baobab. Studying the tiny burnt leftovers helps recover meals that disappeared centuries before anyone could write down their recipes.

passages.title: Meals, work and neighbours
passages.text: Fish bones are plentiful at Songo Mnara, but they are not a simple menu chart. Chemical analysis of seven people’s bones suggested that certain grains and cattle or chicken contributed more to their diets than marine foods. Archaeologists compare different clues because a heap of bones can be misleading.

passages.title: Meals, work and neighbours
passages.text: House 44 doubled as a workplace. Spindle whorls, the small weights used when spinning thread, occurred in every room, showing that cotton production was woven into household life. Cooking and manufacturing shared space: no separate office commute required.

passages.title: Meals, work and neighbours
passages.text: Stone houses were only part of the town. Excavations at Songo Mnara also uncovered earth-and-daub homes whose residents used imported pottery, ornaments and coins. A building’s material alone cannot tell us whether its occupants were poor.

passages.title: Meals, work and neighbours
passages.text: In Songo Mnara’s houses, mangrove beams supported roofs, and small wall recesses held oil lamps. Bright white walls once carried fabric hangings. The building commonly labelled the Palace is interpreted by the community research project as a particularly grand merchant’s home.

passages.title: Meals, work and neighbours
passages.text: Benches beside doorways provided places for relatives and friends to sit and talk. That small architectural detail gives the ruined streets a social soundtrack: conversation belonged at the threshold between a home and the wider town.

passages.title: Water, inequality and written words
passages.text: Gedi stood about 6.5 kilometres inland, yet participated in ocean trade. Its two enclosing walls separated a monumental centre from more modest houses used by most residents. Imported luxury objects reveal connections and wealth, but its commerce also included the export of enslaved people.

passages.title: Water, inequality and written words
passages.text: Gedi’s builders provided wells, stone water conduits, storage jars and tanks. Surviving houses include bathrooms and toilets, while sumps drained rainwater from courtyards and streets. Keeping a crowded town supplied and drained required practical engineering as well as impressive monuments.

passages.title: Water, inequality and written words
passages.text: A copper coin issued at Kilwa around 1320 to 1335 preserves the Arabic words يثق بالواحد المنان, translated by the Ashmolean Museum as “Trust in the One (God), the Bountiful.” Its other side names al-Hasan ibn Sulayman. This is an Arabic coin inscription, not a specimen of written Swahili.

There was no single fall of these towns in 1650. Gedi was eventually abandoned, while coastal communities continued. Songo Mnara remains a lived-in island whose residents help interpret and care for its heritage.

passages.text: This 1500 to 1530 atlas label groups disconnected parts of Sind and Makran, Gujarat, and the Deccan. It is regional shorthand, not one empire or religious population. Thatta’s Samma court and neighbouring Mandu had distinct histories. Named sultanates retain their own cards; Mandu and Bidar appear below only as comparisons.

passages.title: Reading the map and its different courts
passages.text: The three outlines include Thatta, Ahmedabad, Champaner and Burhanpur, but exclude Mandu, Bidar and Golconda at the sampled 1500 snapshot. Those boundaries cannot describe every Muslim-ruled territory, still less everyone’s religion. The examples below name their locations because courts, craftspeople and books belonged to overlapping regional worlds.

passages.title: Reading the map and its different courts
passages.text: Thatta stood near the Indus delta and became the capital of successive Samma, Arghun and Tarkhan dynasties. Its surviving stone and brick monuments preserve several centuries of patronage. A later tomb beside an earlier one is therefore evidence of changing rulers, not a single royal family reigning throughout.

passages.title: Reading the map and its different courts
passages.text: Jam Nizamuddin’s tomb at Makli makes stone look almost embroidered: lotus bands, sunflower panels, geese, miniature spires and Arabic calligraphy share its walls. Sindh’s conservation department compares the workmanship with Gujarat. Craftsmen could combine an extensive visual vocabulary within one ruler’s memorial.

passages.title: Reading the map and its different courts
passages.text: At Mubarak Khan’s enclosure in Makli, inscriptions name patrons and preserve a royal genealogy, while several graves share the walled space. One entrance records construction in 1490, just before this map window. The monuments make family remembrance visible, although later completion and some relationships remain debated.

passages.title: Women, skilled work and long-distance cloth
passages.text: In Ahmedabad, Bai Harir Sultani held responsibility in Sultan Mahmud Begada’s royal household and sponsored a mosque, tomb and stepwell complex. ASI dates the mosque to 1500 from its central prayer-niche inscription. A woman’s administrative position and building patronage can therefore be traced in a surviving place.

passages.title: Women, skilled work and long-distance cloth
passages.text: Bai Harir’s mosque has five domed bays, with the central dome raised above the others at a clerestory level. Carved columns and smaller domes also frame her tomb’s veranda. Builders arranged light, height and ornament together; the structure was more than a decorated flat room.

passages.title: Women, skilled work and long-distance cloth
passages.text: The nearby well also had a planted setting. Burgess’s archaeological survey translates its Arabic inscription as mentioning fruit-bearing trees beside the ornamented building. He distinguishes the Sanskrit inscription’s 1499 dating from the Arabic inscription’s 1500 date. The paired records show why a monument need not have one simple birthday.

passages.title: Women, skilled work and long-distance cloth
passages.text: A cotton cloth probably made in Gujarat during the 1500s shows twelve women playing stringed instruments, each with a parrot perched on one hand. Their skirts and blouses alternate red and blue. Block printing, resist dyeing and painting worked together: pattern, colour and a small musical parade on fabric.

passages.title: Women, skilled work and long-distance cloth
passages.text: That cloth is just over five metres long and was found on Sulawesi in Indonesia. Its old darns, newer patches and lasting fold mark reveal a life beyond manufacture. A valuable textile could cross seas and keep being repaired. Its exact travel route and arrival date are not recorded.

passages.title: Women, skilled work and long-distance cloth
passages.text: At Burhanpur, the National Monuments Authority credits Begum Rokeya with completing Bibi Sahib’s mosque after work began under Adil Khan III. Its broad dating, 1520 to 1540, crosses the map’s endpoint. The building extends the story of women as patrons into a different royal court.

passages.title: Women, skilled work and long-distance cloth
passages.text: The same Burhanpur mosque preserves two Persian inscriptions on pillars and an Arabic religious inscription over the gate. Its architectural style also reflects Gujarat. Languages and building ideas could travel without making the two courts one state. Here, the stones retain more than one kind of written voice.

passages.title: A neighbouring court’s kitchens and classrooms
passages.text: Mandu lies outside these outlines, but its books offer unusually close evidence for a neighbouring sultanate around 1500. The Book of Delights began under Ghiyas al-Din and appears to have continued under Nasir Shah. One samosa recipe combines minced meat, onion, ginger and aubergine before frying the filled pastry in ghee.

passages.title: A neighbouring court’s kitchens and classrooms
passages.text: Another Mandu recipe turns leftover rice-cooking water into broth with mung pulses, seasoning and mint. The manuscript illustrates preparing the rice water. Even an elaborate royal recipe collection found a use for something a hurried cook might pour away: rice-cooking liquid could have another job.

passages.title: A neighbouring court’s kitchens and classrooms
passages.text: The Book of Delights gathers remedies and perfumes alongside food. It shows courtly interest in bodily care as well as taste and fragrance. Such recipes document historical practice; they do not establish that a treatment worked, or tell us what medical care an ordinary family could obtain.

passages.title: A neighbouring court’s kitchens and classrooms
passages.text: Mandu’s illustrated Key of the Learned was a learning tool for moving between languages. Its text was composed in 1468 to 1469 and the surviving illustrated copy is dated around 1490, before this map window. Persian entries acquire Arabic and Hindavi equivalents, while pictures help explain objects and words.

passages.title: A neighbouring court’s kitchens and classrooms
passages.text: That dictionary includes a hobbyhorse: its Hindavi name, ḍanḍā-mūhī, means “stick-face.” The scribe added dots to a Perso-Arabic letter to represent a local sound. Children’s toys entered a serious language manual. Even a pretend horse could give an adult scholar a spelling problem.

passages.title: Machines, careful reading and water
passages.text: Mandu’s Wonders of Mechanics adapted al-Jazari’s Arabic engineering book into Persian for Nasir Shah. Its earliest known copy dates to 1508. Technical diagrams and local vocabulary helped readers understand mechanical devices across languages. A book explaining a machine is evidence of technical learning, not proof that every illustrated device was built there.

passages.title: Machines, careful reading and water
passages.text: A Persian note in that Mandu manuscript reads, in scholarly transcription, “ṣaḥīḥ ast ghalaṭ nīst”: “It is correct; it is not incorrect.” The book was copied in 1508 and verified the following year; the note is associated with that checking by handwriting. A delightfully emphatic proofreader, preserved on paper.

passages.title: Machines, careful reading and water
passages.text: Nearby Bidar, also outside this particular outline, preserves a fifteenth-century underground water system. Gently sloping tunnels carried groundwater, with vertical shafts giving access from above. Builders adapted a technique associated with Iranian migrants to local water-bearing rock: the slope, rather than an electric pump, moved the water.

passages.title: Machines, careful reading and water
passages.text: Keeping those tunnels useful requires care above ground too. Modern conservation, whose planning phase ran from 2016 to 2018, addressed solid waste with filters and household rubbish collection. That is a present-day conservation lesson, not a claim about medieval toilets. Water infrastructure depends on maintenance as well as clever construction.

There was no collective collapse of “Islamic states” in 1530. The atlas simply ends this label. Thatta later passed through Arghun and Tarkhan rule and came under Mughal government in 1592; Burhanpur’s building work continued beyond the window. Particular dynasties changed, while cities, craft traditions and multilingual communities continued.

sectionTitles: A state, its neighbours and a misleading outline
Care, discovery and the journey after a flush
Conflict and civilian lives, with dated evidence

passages.text: Modern Israel was proclaimed on 14 May 1948. This atlas starts its label in 1938, during British Mandatory Palestine, and repeatedly includes Gaza and the whole West Bank. That outline is not a map of recognized Israeli sovereignty, pre-1967 borders or present control. The last geometry ends in 2020; the state continues. This card distinguishes Israeli institutions and communities from Palestinians living under occupation, while following their connected histories through sources available on 23 September 2026.

passages.title: A state, its neighbours and a misleading outline
passages.text: In 1947 the United Nations proposed partition into Jewish and Arab states, with a special international arrangement for Jerusalem. Israel’s establishment in 1948 came amid war. Many Palestinian Arabs fled or were expelled from their homes. Independence for Israelis and dispossession for Palestinians are connected parts of this history; the atlas’s single colour cannot express them.

passages.title: A state, its neighbours and a misleading outline
passages.text: For Jewish survivors of the Holocaust, reaching a new home often followed years of waiting in displaced-persons camps. The United States Holocaust Memorial Museum records that around 140,000 survivors entered Israel in the years after its founding. These were people rebuilding lives and families after persecution, not simply numbers added to a national population.

passages.title: A state, its neighbours and a misleading outline
passages.text: Israel occupied Gaza and the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, in the 1967 war. In its advisory opinion of 19 July 2024, the International Court of Justice treated these as occupied Palestinian territory and found Israel’s continued presence unlawful. The imported polygon should therefore never be read as proof that these territories belong to Israel.

passages.title: A state, its neighbours and a misleading outline
passages.text: Israel removed its settlements and permanent military presence from Gaza in 2005. The ICJ explained in 2024 that this had not entirely ended its occupation-related obligations: those remained linked to its effective control. Troop locations alone do not settle the legal question.

passages.title: A state, its neighbours and a misleading outline
passages.text: Jerusalem needs its own qualification. Israel’s 1980 Basic Law designates it the capital and the seat of the Knesset, government and Supreme Court. The ICJ’s 2024 opinion treats East Jerusalem as occupied territory and rejects acquisition of territory through annexation. The location of government offices and international recognition of territorial claims are different questions.

passages.title: A state, its neighbours and a misleading outline
passages.text: The Knesset has 120 members, elected through national proportional elections. Seats are shared among party lists rather than assigned to 120 separate local constituencies. Basic Laws set out central institutions and rights. Looking at an election result therefore means asking how several parties might work together, as well as which party won the most seats.

passages.title: A state, its neighbours and a misleading outline
passages.text: A governing coalition is an agreement among parties willing to support a government. Partners negotiate policies and ministerial responsibilities; other parties form the opposition. Coalition bargaining helps explain why a small party can matter greatly when a government needs its votes. This describes how the system works, not whether any particular bargain is fair.

passages.title: A state, its neighbours and a misleading outline
passages.text: Diplomacy changed relationships that had once been defined by war. Egypt and Israel signed their peace treaty on 26 March 1979 after the 1978 Camp David negotiations. The negotiations also attempted a framework for Palestinian self-government, but that question was not resolved by the Egyptian-Israeli treaty.

passages.title: A state, its neighbours and a misleading outline
passages.text: The Oslo process brought mutual recognition between Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization in 1993 and arrangements for limited Palestinian self-government. Further agreements divided responsibilities in the West Bank; they did not create a final peace settlement. Israel’s separate treaty with Jordan in October 1994 ended the state of war between those neighbours.

passages.title: Families, books and something sweet
passages.text: Mimouna, celebrated by many Moroccan and other North African Jewish families after Passover, brings friends and neighbours through open doors for sweet food. The National Library describes mufleta pancakes, singing and the next day’s picnics. Its undated photograph includes adults and children clapping and playing a tambourine. One useful party skill: leave enough room for both music and pancakes.

passages.title: Families, books and something sweet
passages.text: The National Library’s Mimouna account also describes migration from Morocco and settlement in development towns and villages. Families brought practices with them and adapted them in new settings. A festival can preserve memories of another country while becoming part of neighbourhood life in Israel; it does not mean every Israeli family has the same background or customs.

passages.title: Families, books and something sweet
passages.text: Ten families started a bilingual preschool in Haifa in 2012. According to the Hand in Hand school network, parents later petitioned the municipality to keep their children learning together. The programme moved through Arab and Jewish host schools and reached 271 pupils in the 2021/22 school year. Shared education here grew through persistent family organizing, including the very ordinary challenge of finding enough classrooms.

passages.title: Families, books and something sweet
passages.text: At Hand in Hand’s Jaffa school, an annual book week celebrates Hebrew and Arabic literature, with parents taking part in activities. Children can encounter the same neighbourhood through more than one language. This is a particular school community’s practice, not a claim that every school in Israel teaches in both languages.

passages.title: Families, books and something sweet
passages.text: A short Hebrew writing sample comes from the declaration of 14 May 1948: מדינת ישראל, transliterated Medinat Yisra’el, means “State of Israel.” These words appear in the Knesset’s official transcription of the founding document. This is a modern Hebrew witness with a known date, not an ancient inscription or a sample representing every language spoken by the country’s communities.

passages.title: Care, discovery and the journey after a flush
passages.text: The European Observatory’s 2024 health-system account describes four nationwide health plans operating under National Health Insurance. They cannot reject enrollees, and resident coverage does not depend on whether contributions have been paid. Families obtain care through an organized system of plans and providers, rather than having to build a separate arrangement from scratch whenever a child gets sick.

passages.title: Care, discovery and the journey after a flush
passages.text: Coverage still has important limits. The same 2024 study says foreign workers need private insurance, while adult refugees, asylum-seekers and undocumented migrants are outside National Health Insurance. Their children’s coverage depends on a parental contribution. A description of Israeli resident healthcare should not be stretched across everyone inside this atlas’s especially misleading outline.

passages.title: Care, discovery and the journey after a flush
passages.text: Tipat Halav family health centres offer free preventive services for children from birth to six. Nurses check growth and development, help parents with questions and provide vaccinations and screening. A baby’s appointment can therefore include measuring, listening and conversation as well as a needle. The service is meant to help families notice needs early, before a problem becomes an emergency.

passages.title: Care, discovery and the journey after a flush
passages.text: The water leaving a toilet has another journey ahead. The Central Bureau of Statistics describes Shafdan, the Dan Region wastewater project, as collecting and treating sewage, recharging treated water into groundwater and recovering it for reuse. Its agricultural tables record irrigation with treated effluent. Cleaning and reusing water requires infrastructure; this is not permission to put untreated sewage on crops.

passages.title: Care, discovery and the journey after a flush
passages.text: Ada Yonath of the Weizmann Institute shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry with Venkatraman Ramakrishnan and Thomas Steitz for explaining ribosome structure and function. Ribosomes are the cell’s protein-making machinery. The researchers used X-ray crystallography to reveal their shapes in great detail. Their work also helped explain how some antibiotics interfere with bacterial ribosomes: a tiny machine can matter enormously to medicine.

passages.title: Conflict and civilian lives, with dated evidence
passages.text: On 7 October 2023, Hamas and other Palestinian armed groups attacked Israel, killing civilians and taking hostages. A UN Commission of Inquiry reported in June 2024 that these actions included war crimes. Its separate investigation of Israeli operations in Gaza through December 2023 also found war crimes, including attacks on civilians and starvation as a method of warfare. These were the commission’s investigative findings, not criminal convictions of every person involved.

passages.title: Conflict and civilian lives, with dated evidence
passages.text: On 16 September 2025, the same independent UN commission concluded that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. Its analysis covered conduct from October 2023 through July 2025 and examined killings, destruction of living conditions and evidence of intent. This serious conclusion belongs to a UN fact-finding body; it should not be mislabeled a final judgment by the International Court of Justice.

passages.title: Conflict and civilian lives, with dated evidence
passages.text: A ceasefire announcement does not instantly rebuild homes or hospitals. OCHA’s report dated 18 September 2026, published on 21 September, described continuing danger in Gaza despite the October 2025 ceasefire. Damaged housing, restrictions on essential supplies and shortages affecting health services continued to harm civilians. This dated account is evidence about occupied Palestinian territory, not a description of normal conditions for every household in Israel.

passages.title: Conflict and civilian lives, with dated evidence
passages.text: The same September 2026 report describes risks to water wells, wastewater workers and rubbish collection in Gaza, including temporary dumping sites that had run out of space. Sanitation depends on safe workers, fuel, equipment and access as well as pipes and toilets. Losing these services makes everyday tasks dangerous for families and adds public-health risks to the direct harm of fighting.

Israel continues as a state; the atlas’s 2020 geometry cutoff is not a national ending. Evidence checked through 23 September 2026 describes continuing occupation and severe civilian suffering. Israeli and Palestinian communities retain distinct identities and histories despite this misleading outline.

passages.text: Italy united as a kingdom in 1861 and made Rome part of the state in 1870. Many people still worked rural land or emigrated, and many could not read. Fascist rule from 1922 brought dictatorship, colonial war, antisemitic laws and World War II. Resistance and a 1946 popular referendum opened the republic, whose constitution protected rights and public health. Schooling, migration and appliances transformed family life, though homes and regions changed at different speeds. Italy continues; the imported map begins in 1878, after unification.

passages.title: From kingdom to republic
passages.text: The first Italian parliament met in 1861, and Rome was taken in 1870. The map’s 1878 beginning comes later than both events. “Italy” on a map does not mean every village immediately shared the same speech, schooling or comforts.

passages.title: From kingdom to republic
passages.text: In 1871 about 68.8% of people counted by Italian statistics could not read. That meant a posted law or newspaper was not useful to many families without someone to read it aloud. Education grew over generations rather than appearing overnight at unification.

passages.title: From kingdom to republic
passages.text: Many Italians left poor rural areas for work abroad between unification and the postwar period. A departure could separate a family for years; later, migration from the south to northern factories reshaped households inside Italy too.

passages.title: From kingdom to republic
passages.text: Fascists came to power in 1922, then dismantled political freedoms. Mussolini’s government invaded Ethiopia in 1935. The colonial war was part of the dictatorship’s history, not an achievement for the people attacked.

passages.title: From kingdom to republic
passages.text: In 1938 the Fascist state imposed antisemitic laws: Jewish teachers and pupils were driven from public schools, jobs were lost, and mixed marriages were banned. After German occupation began in 1943, Jews in Italy faced deportation and murder.

passages.title: From kingdom to republic
passages.text: Italian partisans and other anti-fascists resisted the regime and Nazi occupation. In 1946 voters chose a republic after dictatorship and war. A government change did not erase bereavement or rebuild a home by itself.

passages.title: Children, kitchens and bathrooms
passages.text: At unification most people could not read; by 1951, 90% of people aged six and older had at most primary school completion, according to ISTAT. Night and adult classes later helped people missed by childhood schooling. A child’s opportunities varied by place, class and gender.

passages.title: Children, kitchens and bathrooms
passages.text: From 1960 to 1968 the broadcaster RAI taught basic literacy on television in “Non è mai troppo tardi,” or “It is never too late.” That is both a show title and a good family-life fact: a grandparent could become a student while sitting by the TV.

passages.title: Children, kitchens and bathrooms
passages.text: After World War II, factories drew people from farms and southern regions to northern cities. By 1966 about 60% of families had a television and refrigerator, but only 32% had a washing machine. New appliances changed chores without making laundry vanish.

passages.title: Children, kitchens and bathrooms
passages.text: The 1951 census asked separately whether a dwelling had piped drinking water, a latrine, a bath, electricity, gas and heat. Those were not automatic parts of a “home.” Later decades saw a marked rise in internal toilets and bathing facilities, with uneven regional progress.

passages.title: Children, kitchens and bathrooms
passages.text: A bathroom statistic can hide a family’s daily puzzle: an inside toilet, running water and a warm shower are three different comforts. ISTAT tracks them separately, so one old house could have one but not the others.

passages.title: Children, kitchens and bathrooms
passages.text: In 1946 women voted in the republic referendum and 21 women entered the constituent assembly. A mother or grandmother could now shape national law with a ballot, though work and family expectations still differed.

passages.title: Health, words and continued life
passages.text: The constitution, effective in 1948, says “La Repubblica tutela la salute come fondamentale diritto dell’individuo,” or “The Republic protects health as a fundamental right of the individual.” This is a short sample of written Italian from Article 32.

passages.title: Health, words and continued life
passages.text: In 1978 Italy created its public National Health Service, designed for universal access rather than care tied only to a particular job. It turned the constitution’s health principle into a wider system, though services still required funding and local organization.

passages.title: Health, words and continued life
passages.text: The 1978 mental-health reform shifted care away from the old asylum system and toward community-based approaches. Someone with a mental illness was a person to care for, not a life to hide away. Implementation and local conditions mattered.

passages.title: Health, words and continued life
passages.text: Italy was one of six countries that signed the 1957 Treaty of Rome establishing the European Economic Community. Trade and cooperation became part of the republic’s story, alongside the much smaller stories of homes and schools.

passages.title: Health, words and continued life
passages.text: Italian is the language of the constitutional line shown here, but some communities also maintain historical minority languages. The Italian state reports school and local efforts to keep those languages in use. One written sample cannot represent every voice.

passages.title: Health, words and continued life
passages.text: Italy continues as a republic. The 1861 kingdom, Fascist dictatorship and 1946 republican vote mark major state changes, but families, regional communities and languages carried their histories through them. The imported polygon does not certify each border or lived identity.

Italy continues as a republic chosen in 1946. The kingdom formed in 1861, while its people and regional communities have longer histories; Fascist rule and war did not end them. The map’s 1878 starting border is later than unification and is not a certificate of every border or language.

sectionTitles: An elephant helps with the weaving
Two dates on a piece of mail

passages.text: This 1878 to 1914 map entry concerns coastal trading settlements and the expansion of French rule in what became Côte d’Ivoire. The colony was formally created on 10 March 1893, after the map’s opening date. Its people belonged to different communities with their own histories; a colonial name and outline cannot turn them into one timeless culture.

passages.title: A port with many neighbours
passages.text: Grand-Bassam became the first colonial capital and an important port and trading centre. Its built landscape included a N’zima fishing village alongside districts assigned to administration, commerce and different populations. The town was both a place of everyday work and a physical expression of unequal colonial power.

passages.title: A port with many neighbours
passages.text: Galleries, verandas and gardens helped adapt buildings to the tropical setting. African, European and Middle Eastern residents brought different experiences to the town. UNESCO describes both coexistence and conflict: the surviving streets should not be mistaken for a postcard of everyone living on equal terms.

passages.title: An elephant helps with the weaving
passages.text: Baule and neighbouring Guro weavers were known for indigo-and-white cotton cloth. On a narrow-band loom, heddle pulleys helped lift and separate threads so a shuttle could pass between them. This small moving part made repeated work easier, while the weaver supplied the skill and rhythm.

passages.title: An elephant helps with the weaving
passages.text: One surviving Baule pulley has an elephant’s head. The museum dates it broadly from the nineteenth to the mid-twentieth century, so it cannot be assigned to a single map year. Carvers decorated tools used in public view: even a working loom could have a little elephant looking down.

passages.title: An elephant helps with the weaving
passages.text: A Baule comb from central Côte d’Ivoire carries a rooster above its teeth. Made from ivory and metal and dated to the nineteenth or twentieth century, it shows the care given to personal objects. Its owner is unknown; we should not invent a hairstyle, wedding or family story for it.

passages.title: Markets before the colonial boundary
passages.text: Gold-working traditions long preceded French rule. An older Akan brass weight, dated to the sixteenth or seventeenth century and attributed to Ghana or Côte d’Ivoire, belongs to a regional system for weighing gold. Such objects were cast by replacing a wax model with molten metal inside a mould.

passages.title: Markets before the colonial boundary
passages.text: The decree creating the colony did not itself establish peaceful control over every settlement. Historian Christophe Wondji’s study of Bingerville describes opposition from local Ebrié residents and an uprising in 1903. Building a new administrative centre meant taking decisions over places where people already lived.

passages.title: When disease interrupted the port
passages.text: A 1911 medical report described repeated yellow-fever outbreaks on the Ivory Coast between 1899 and 1905. It reported that steamers avoided the port for four months in 1903. Illness affected travel, commerce and livelihoods as well as the patients themselves; a harbour could be busy one season and isolated the next.

passages.title: When disease interrupted the port
passages.text: The report described a change toward drainage and mosquito-control measures, replacing earlier practices that included burning houses. This is evidence of changing public-health ideas at the time. It is not a complete account of every household’s sanitation, and it cannot tell us which toilets an ordinary family used.

passages.title: Two dates on a piece of mail
passages.text: A postcard caption describes loading mahogany onto the steamer Colonia at Grand-Bassam in September 1905. A message on its reverse is dated August 1906. These different dates distinguish the event represented from the later use of the card, an easy detail to miss when reading an old picture.

passages.title: Two dates on a piece of mail
passages.text: Another card carries “Embarquement des billes d’acajou”, meaning “Shipment of mahogany timber”. Its postmark reads 23 September 1907. This short French sample survives through the Smithsonian’s catalogue transcription. It records colonial printed language, not a greeting in one of the region’s African languages.

passages.title: Whose idea of a capital?
passages.text: Wondji’s research shows that colonial planners argued over the relationship between an administrative capital and a commercial port. Merchants and officials wanted towns to serve the collection and export of products. That helps explain the competition among Grand-Bassam, Bingerville and Abidjan, beyond simply comparing their buildings.

The 1914 map endpoint did not end French colonial rule. Côte d’Ivoire became independent on 7 August 1960. Grand-Bassam’s communities and crafts also continued beyond the colonial capital’s decline; political administration and the lives of a town do not share one ending date.

passages.text: This record follows independent Côte d’Ivoire, also called Ivory Coast in English, from 1960. Independence ended French sovereignty; it did not begin the histories of the many communities living within the new state.

passages.title: Making and remaking the republic
passages.text: On 7 August 1960, the country gained independence from France. That same day, an American recognition letter went to Félix Houphouët-Boigny and the US consulate in Abidjan became an embassy: diplomatic paperwork provides a dated trail of the new republic entering international relations.

passages.title: Making and remaking the republic
passages.text: Here is a short writing sample from Article 1 of the November 1960 constitution: “Union, Discipline, Travail.” In English, this French motto means “Unity, Discipline, Work.” The document also named French as the official language; this state text does not represent all the languages spoken at home.

passages.title: Making and remaking the republic
passages.text: Peacekeeping was part of a difficult political recovery. The UN created UNOCI in 2004 to help implement a peace agreement. After the disputed 2010 presidential election, violence escalated when Laurent Gbagbo refused to leave office following the UN-certified victory of Alassane Ouattara; Ouattara was inaugurated in May 2011.

passages.title: Cassava, crafts and community
passages.text: Attiéké begins as cassava rather than wheat. Producers grind the tubers, mix them with fermented cassava, turn the mixture into small grains and steam it. The cooled food can be packed in baskets lined with cassava leaves: a whole sequence of skilled work sits behind a seemingly simple plate.

passages.title: Cassava, crafts and community
passages.text: UNESCO’s account describes women preparing, preserving and selling attiéké, while men contribute to cultivation, harvesting, transport and grinding. Knowledge passes through watching, doing and spoken instruction within families. Learning to make dinner can also mean learning a business.

passages.title: Cassava, crafts and community
passages.text: Attiéké connects ordinary meals with public occasions. It appears at home, in restaurants, at weddings and other gatherings. Its affordability helps explain its wide use, while production and sales provide income, especially for women.

passages.title: Cassava, crafts and community
passages.text: Among Guro communities around Bouaflé and Zuénoula, a Zaouli performance joins several arts: a carved mask, woven costume, music, singing and fast-moving dance. The dancer is the most visible participant, but sculptors, textile workers and musicians help make the performance possible.

passages.title: Cassava, crafts and community
passages.text: Zaouli is learned through people as well as objects. Experienced performers teach younger participants during lessons and performances, while festivals and dance competitions bring communities together. UNESCO’s account identifies seven mask types, each associated with a legend: a mask carries a story as well as a face.

passages.title: Classrooms and everyday infrastructure
passages.text: In UNICEF’s account of a 2018 Gonzagueville pilot, Adja, a mother of three, earned money collecting discarded plastic. Unpredictable prices sometimes left her storing sacks at home. Recycling therefore involved family income and working conditions, as well as getting rubbish out of streets.

passages.title: Classrooms and everyday infrastructure
passages.text: That pilot classroom used interlocking recycled-plastic bricks developed by the Colombian enterprise Conceptos Plasticos. The imported bricks were assembled in five days with a hammer, rather like an enormous construction toy. The report expected forty kindergarten pupils when term began; wider local production was still a future plan.

passages.title: Classrooms and everyday infrastructure
passages.text: In 2024, UNICEF reported replacing worn-out hand-powered pumps in nineteen Bounkani villages, improving drinking-water access for roughly 7,600 people. A functioning pump is an unglamorous achievement with a very practical audience: everyone carrying the next bucket.

passages.title: Classrooms and everyday infrastructure
passages.text: School hygiene needs maintenance as much as construction. The same 2024 report describes training 148 school principals and supervisors in Bouna and Ferkessedougou. Activities covered handwashing, wastewater, rubbish and toilet upkeep. A toilet is only useful if someone keeps it usable.

The republic did not end with its civil conflicts. UNOCI closed on 30 June 2017 after completing its mandate, while state institutions and community life continued. The mission’s departure marks a change in international support, not the disappearance of Côte d’Ivoire.
