sectionTitles: Discoveries: wood, clay and a sunken kitchen
Home life, including the toilet question

passages.text: Jamaica’s history is full of skilled makers and memorable voices. A carved wooden spirit figure, a kitchen recovered from the sea and locally made clay pots offer different windows into the past. Maroon traditions, Miss Lou’s performances and reggae show people creating, preserving and sharing knowledge across generations.

passages.title: Discoveries: wood, clay and a sunken kitchen
passages.text: A Taíno wooden figure known as the Birdman was reported found in a Jamaican cave in 1792. Its beak and wings combine bird and human features, with surviving shell inlay. Scientific study places its wood around 1000 to 1150 CE. Carved from hard guaiacum, it preserves extraordinary woodworking skill, although its precise original ritual setting is unknown.

passages.title: Discoveries: wood, clay and a sunken kitchen
passages.text: In Port Royal’s submerged Building 4, archaeologists found iron cooking pots, copper pails, a wooden bucket, pewter spoons and ceramic bowls on a brick kitchen floor. These objects survived the city’s 1692 earthquake. Together they reveal equipment for preparing and serving food; they do not identify the cooks or tell us exactly what was on the menu.

passages.title: Discoveries: wood, clay and a sunken kitchen
passages.text: Excavations at New Street in Port Royal recovered fragments of locally made cooking and storage vessels from the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. DAACS researchers compare clay, firing traces and shaping marks to distinguish different ways of making pottery. Enslaved Jamaicans produced and traded these wares: the objects record craft and exchange within a system that denied their makers freedom.

passages.title: Discoveries: wood, clay and a sunken kitchen
passages.text: A small handmade clay whistle also came from the New Street excavations. Researchers think it was probably made in eighteenth-century Jamaica by an enslaved person. Its maker and user remain unidentified. We can recognise an object designed to make sound without deciding that it was definitely a child’s toy or inventing the tune someone played.

passages.title: Home life, including the toilet question
passages.text: Late seventeenth-century Port Royal inventories describe parlors used for both entertaining and sleeping. Some beds could fold away during the day. A room might have to be ready for visitors after being somebody’s bedroom. These lists record possessions after property owners died, so they show particular households rather than how every Jamaican lived.

passages.title: Home life, including the toilet question
passages.text: One Port Royal parlor inventory includes a “close stoole chaire”: a toilet chair of a type that held a chamber pot beneath the seat. Furniture could have a surprisingly practical second job. The inventory records the chair, but says nothing about who emptied its pot. That missing task matters when imagining the household’s daily work.

passages.title: Community, care and learning
passages.text: At Moore Town in eastern Jamaica, Maroon heritage includes the abeng, a horn blown through an opening in its side and used for communication over distance. Descendants of communities that escaped enslavement preserve this knowledge alongside their own institutions and communally held land. Passing on a tradition can mean learning how to listen as well as how to make a sound.

passages.title: Community, care and learning
passages.text: Moore Town’s Kromanti ceremonies bring together singing, dancing and distinctive drumming to invoke ancestral spirits. They draw on African traditions reshaped within the Maroon community. These are religious practices with meaning for participants, not simply a stage performance. UNESCO also records missionary opposition and migration as pressures on their transmission.

passages.title: Community, care and learning
passages.text: As a girl in early nineteenth-century Kingston, Mary Seacole learned to care for patients by watching her mother at work. Her mother ran a lodging house where army officers and their families also received care. Seacole later helped with patients herself. In this household, learning a caring profession began through observation and participation, before her better-known work overseas.

passages.title: Community, care and learning
passages.text: Louise Bennett-Coverley, known as Miss Lou, welcomed children into stories, folk songs, dance and poetry through her television programme Ring Ding. She championed Jamaican Creole as a language worthy of performance and literature. Children could hear familiar speech celebrated in public and participate in cultural life themselves. Their voices belonged in the show.

passages.title: Music and independence
passages.text: Reggae grew from Jamaican musical creativity, especially in Western Kingston, drawing on earlier local styles and sounds circulating around the Caribbean and beyond. Its songs could address injustice and resistance as well as love and spiritual life. Listening to music can therefore open a conversation about society, not just provide a beat for dancing.

passages.title: Music and independence
passages.text: In a 2017 letter, Edna Manley College described courses exploring reggae’s history and development, alongside a folk collection assembled by Olive Lewin. The college’s arts schools had come together in 1976. Learning about music could involve both performing it and studying how earlier generations made it: instruments and archives both had a place.

passages.title: Music and independence
passages.text: Jamaica became independent on August 6, 1962, with Alexander Bustamante as its first prime minister. Responsibility shifted from British colonial control to Jamaica’s elected government. The change concerned who governed the country; its people’s languages, family knowledge and cultural creativity had histories reaching far beyond that constitutional date.

British colonial rule ended with independence in 1962. Jamaica continues as an independent country, while communities sustain and reshape their own cultural traditions. Political independence is a change in sovereignty, not the beginning or ending of the island’s people.

sectionTitles: What this map shape means, and what it does not
Ports, money, mines and long-distance exchange
Work, food, houses and what people wore
Families, women, children and time together
Learning, art and a real line of writing
Objects, neighbours and what continued after 1530

passages.text: This atlas record is best read as a window onto Japan during the late Muromachi period, after the Onin War and amid the early Sengoku age. It was not a unified empire: Ashikaga shoguns remained important in Kyoto, but regional daimyo, military brokers, religious institutions, towns, villages and the imperial court all exercised power. Trade, craft, farming, scholarship and art continued through recurrent conflict. The 1492 start and 1530 end are map-library choices, not the birth or collapse of Japan; the Ashikaga shogunate itself lasted until 1573.

passages.title: What this map shape means, and what it does not
passages.text: The indexed record is exactly japan, circa 1492 to 1530, with two observed map intervals. Its generated aliases “Empire of Japan” and “Japanese Empire” belong to a much later age and are not used here. The content audit marks this exact record as missing before integration.

passages.title: What this map shape means, and what it does not
passages.text: Both target maps are broad four-part MultiPolygons covering Kyushu, Shikoku, Honshu and Hokkaido. The 1492 version has 324 positions; the 1500 version has 329. These coast-scale shapes do not draw daimyo domains, temple lands, estates, town jurisdictions or front lines.

passages.title: What this map shape means, and what it does not
passages.text: Hokkaido is the clearest atlas glitch. In 1400 it lies in the separate Ainu feature; in 1492 and 1500 the same broad island is moved into japan; in 1530 it returns to ainu-1530. Museum history instead shows Ainu societies, trade, Wajin settlements in the south and conflict, not Ashikaga control of the whole island.

passages.title: What this map shape means, and what it does not
passages.text: Okinawa and Shuri fall outside every target polygon. That matches an essential political distinction: the independent Ryukyu Kingdom, unified in 1429 and ruled by the Second Sho dynasty from 1469, was pursuing its own diplomacy, trade and building under King Sho Shin. It must not be folded into this card’s “Japan.”

passages.title: What this map shape means, and what it does not
passages.text: Kyoto, Sakai, Ashikaga School and the future Iwami mine all test inside the imported outline, but point-in-polygon only answers where the atlas drew them. It does not prove that the shogun governed each place in the same way. Political authority was negotiated among court, shogun, daimyo, temples, towns and local communities.

passages.title: Power after the Onin War
passages.text: The 1467-1477 Onin War ended before this card but shaped everything that followed. Kyoto had been devastated and Ashikaga power badly weakened. Provincial daimyo retained substantial power, so a single colored outline should be read as a chronological label, not proof of a unified chain of command.

passages.title: Power after the Onin War
passages.text: In 1493, shogun Yoshitane left Kyoto to intervene in a succession conflict in Kawachi. A coup led by Hosokawa Masamoto deposed him. The event shows how the shogun’s title mattered while military brokers could decide who held it; “Japan” was not a modern centralized nation-state.

passages.title: Power after the Onin War
passages.text: Kyoto City records fighting at Funaokayama in 1511, near an approach from Tamba. Battles around the capital affected more than famous warriors: fires, disrupted roads and armed compounds touched the same urban landscape where households, markets, workshops and religious institutions continued to function.

passages.title: Power after the Onin War
passages.text: Farmers and other villagers were political actors too. The National Museum’s medieval gallery explains that communities made demands and sometimes fought warriors, while regional daimyo tried to consolidate rule. “Warring States” therefore involved negotiation, collective action and local organization as well as battles between lords.

passages.title: Power after the Onin War
passages.text: From 1527, an Ashikaga claimant, Hosokawa Harumoto and Miyoshi Motonaga operated from Sakai while Yoshiharu’s camp was displaced. One historian calls this a “Sakai bakufu,” but the NDL reference page labels that name a hypothesis. The safest picture is overlapping rival centres, not a clean nationwide transfer.

passages.title: Ports, money, mines and long-distance exchange
passages.text: Licensed trade with Ming China worked through tallies and tributary diplomacy. The shogunate used the title “king of Japan” to fit Ming rules, while actual ship management involved daimyo, temples, shrines and merchants. Diplomatic language, commercial profit and decentralized power travelled on the same ships.

passages.title: Ports, money, mines and long-distance exchange
passages.text: A wind-driven crossing to China took at least a month, and waiting for winds plus overland travel could stretch a round trip across years. Japan exported sulfur, swords and fans and imported silk and copper coins. There was no standard Japanese-minted currency, so money itself was an import.

passages.title: Ports, money, mines and long-distance exchange
passages.text: The Hosokawa and Ouchi competed over rights to Ming missions, and their rivalry led to the Ningbo incident in 1523. Modern scholarship cautions against turning the aftermath into a simple story of one family’s monopoly. Foreign trade was valuable, political and sometimes violent.

passages.title: Ports, money, mines and long-distance exchange
passages.text: Sakai grew as a trading and self-governing city; merchant councillors appear in records by 1484. Archaeology also records repeated disaster: large fires in 1494, 1508 and 1526. A prosperous port could be connected, wealthy and politically assertive while rebuilding over and over.

passages.title: Ports, money, mines and long-distance exchange
passages.text: Iwami Ginzan’s documented discovery and early development begin in 1526, near this card’s end. Ore first went by land to Tomogaura and then by sea to Hakata. The famous cupellation technique arrived in 1533, so the mine’s huge later production must not be pulled backward into 1492-1530.

passages.title: Work, food, houses and what people wore
passages.text: The National Museum’s child-focused gallery shows women from Katsura selling ayu fish in Kyoto, large saws derived from China making lengthwise timber cutting easier, and water wheels lifting water into paddies. These examples make “technology” concrete: baskets, blades and water power changed ordinary work.

passages.title: Work, food, houses and what people wore
passages.text: At Ichijodani, excavators found sea-bream bones with knife marks, shells, seeds and charred rice. Knives, iron pots and grinding bowls survived too. This one castle town joined fields, forests and the Japan Sea in its diet; it is evidence for a place, not a menu eaten by everyone.

passages.title: Work, food, houses and what people wore
passages.text: A chopping board at Ichijodani had once been a serving tray, and inexpensive lacquer bowls were mass produced for everyday meals. Medieval recycling could be extremely practical: when a tray retired from table duty, it apparently applied for a second career under the kitchen knife.

passages.title: Work, food, houses and what people wore
passages.text: Sakai excavations reveal narrow, deep homes for ordinary merchants and craftspeople, along with pots, pans, chopsticks, buckets and both local and imported ceramics. Some wealthy merchants had large compounds and storehouses. Urban housing therefore ranged widely, and the excavated layers extend beyond this exact card.

passages.title: Work, food, houses and what people wore
passages.text: The 1525 Kyoto-screen database catalogues 1,426 painted figures by age group, occupation, clothing, headgear, hairstyle, object and activity. It records kosode, hats, veils, tied and shaved hair among many choices. The classifications help us inspect social difference, but a painted crowd is not a population survey.

passages.title: Families, women, children and time together
passages.text: Family authority did not follow one simple rule. A museum study finds men increasingly represented households in later fifteenth-century property documents, yet sixteenth-century pictures often show widow nuns leading women or whole families. Class, region, life stage and the survival of records all shape what historians can see.

passages.title: Families, women, children and time together
passages.text: The 1525 screen shows an aristocratic residence with a woman interpreted as the householder’s wife and a girl wearing her hair in two buns. They watch a bird-song contest beside flowering plum. This is a lovely glimpse of elite family sociability, with the museum’s “probably” labels kept intact.

passages.title: Families, women, children and time together
passages.text: Elsewhere on the same screen, women in kazuki veils walk along Shinmachi Street while children lead dogs. That does not prove every child had a pet. It does prove the artist considered children, dogs and street life worth painting, which may be history’s oldest surviving Kyoto dog-walk cameo.

passages.title: Families, women, children and time together
passages.text: Elite warrior boys often went through genpuku between about eleven and seventeen, receiving an adult name and hearing stories of martial achievement. Some lower-ranking warriors marked adulthood by shaving the front and crown of the head. Medieval graduation could involve more haircut and renaming than homework.

passages.title: Families, women, children and time together
passages.text: A painted Kanze Noh stage has men and women standing around its open sides as two actors cross the bridgeway. Kyoto townspeople also revived the Gion festival in 1500 after wartime interruption. Performance and festival offered shared time, though access and experience differed by wealth and status.

passages.title: Learning, art and a real line of writing
passages.text: Ashikaga School students studied Confucian learning, divination and later military strategy. There was no modern timetable: students copied classical Chinese books and largely studied on their own. Rules required clerical status. This specialized institution is evidence of advanced learning, not proof that most children attended school.

passages.title: Learning, art and a real line of writing
passages.text: The renga poet Socho visited Ashikaga School in 1509. Its lecture and study halls then burned sometime between 1528 and 1531, a date range that crosses this card’s endpoint. Books and institutions could connect distant scholars, yet fire and war made learning spaces physically fragile.

passages.title: Learning, art and a real line of writing
passages.text: Written-language sample: くはうさま. Letter by letter this is ku-hau-sama; the museum glosses it 公方様, conventionally read kubō-sama, “the lord” or here “the shogun.” It is hiragana on the 1525 Kyoto screen, using historical spelling and usually unmarked voicing. Hiragana is a Japanese syllabary developed from cursive forms of Chinese characters.

passages.title: Learning, art and a real line of writing
passages.text: Sesshu’s 1495 Splashed-Ink Landscape suggests mountains with a few rough brushstrokes. Around 1513, Kano Motonobu adapted Chinese-derived ink conventions with Japanese decorative methods. These famous surviving works show artistic experimentation and patronage; they tell us much less about what hung in an ordinary home.

passages.title: Learning, art and a real line of writing
passages.text: The 1525 Kyoto screen turns an entire city into its subject, including commoners and elites in daily movement. Its 1,426 catalogued figures are an extraordinary achievement of observation and later research. The artist still selected, arranged and stylized the view, so absence from the screen is not absence from history.

passages.title: Medicine, water, drains and toilets
passages.text: A 1468 work called Enju Ruiyo treated nutrition and health care, showing that learned medicine joined food and the body in written study. The listed surviving object is a 1793 transcription. One copied medical book cannot tell us who obtained treatment, how practitioners worked locally or whether a remedy helped.

passages.title: Medicine, water, drains and toilets
passages.text: Later medical historians read a Kyoto physician’s text as describing a syphilis outbreak in 1512 and a Kanto temple record as describing another in 1513. This is serious evidence of a new epidemic, but the diagnosis, transmission route and “first arrival” date are retrospective scholarly interpretations rather than modern laboratory results.

passages.title: Medicine, water, drains and toilets
passages.text: Tea sat between medicine, sociability and display. It still carried a medicinal reputation, but people also played tea-origin guessing games, and sixteenth-century samurai and merchants ordered specialist kettles for ceremonies. A warm drink could be treatment, competition and hospitality, depending on the cup and company.

passages.title: Medicine, water, drains and toilets
passages.text: Sakai archaeology finds packed-earth roads with rain drains, tile- or pottery-lined wells and unglazed jars buried as latrine tanks beside streets, probably so waste could be collected for fertilizer. This is excellent toilet evidence for one city across layered dates. It does not establish islandwide sewers, equal clean-water access or modern sanitation.

passages.title: Medicine, water, drains and toilets
passages.text: Water systems were local labor, not invisible magic. Rural water-lifting wheels moved irrigation water from lower ground into paddies. Surviving evidence is uneven, so the honest answer for many villages and households is simply that their detailed water and waste arrangements are not yet known.

passages.title: Objects, neighbours and what continued after 1530
passages.text: A wheel-thrown Seto- or Mino-ware tea bowl dated 1510-1530 combined features admired in different Chinese ceramics. It is a small technological and artistic achievement: potters transformed imported models into locally made wares. Its glittering lacquer repairs are later, so they are not evidence for this card’s own years.

passages.title: Objects, neighbours and what continued after 1530
passages.text: Muromachi achievements were not only military. Commercial and transport networks expanded while patrons supported linked verse, Noh, tea, gardens and ink painting. Many celebrated objects come from elites or temples, however, so “cultural flourishing” should not erase hunger, forced service, fire, epidemic or the destruction caused by war.

passages.title: Objects, neighbours and what continued after 1530
passages.text: The 1525 screen is crowded with seasons, ceremonies, trades, homes and streets. It is tempting to call it a photograph, but it is better treated as a brilliantly organized argument about a city. Historians can compare its details with documents and excavation without assuming every painted gesture happened at one moment.

passages.title: Objects, neighbours and what continued after 1530
passages.text: Ainu people did not enter history only when an atlas moved a polygon, and they did not disappear when it moved back. The National Ainu Museum presents Ainu language, life, history, work and exchange from Ainu perspectives into the present. The Hokkaido geometry problem is therefore both cartographic and human.

passages.title: Objects, neighbours and what continued after 1530
passages.text: In 1530 the atlas relabels the three main islands japan-warring-states and returns Hokkaido to an Ainu feature. No state ended that year. Conflict was already under way, the Ashikaga shogunate continued until 1573, and the existing later card takes over from this artificial cutoff. People, towns, farms, arts and institutions continued.

The map changes labels in 1530, but neither Japan nor the Ashikaga political world ended then. The successor polygon is nearly the same across Kyushu, Shikoku and Honshu, while Hokkaido is reassigned to an Ainu feature. Conflict continued, and the Ashikaga shogunate remained until 1573. This card hands the atlas chronology to japan-warring-states without pretending that one country vanished or a new people appeared at midnight on 1 January 1530.

sectionTitles: Children, schools and a written voice
New ways to count days and cross distances

passages.text: This map record follows Japan from 1783 to 1878, crossing a major political break. Tokugawa shoguns governed alongside regional domain lords until the Meiji Restoration of 1868. The new imperial government centralized power while schools, medicine and communications changed. Neither boundary of this map interval marks the beginning or disappearance of Japan.

passages.title: Government, borders and belonging
passages.text: The Restoration was followed by fighting, not an instant peaceful handover. The Boshin War continued into 1869. In 1871 the government abolished the domains and replaced them with prefectures whose governors it appointed. A regional lord’s territory was becoming part of a centrally administered state.

passages.title: Government, borders and belonging
passages.text: Family rules changed too. In 1871 decrees permitted marriages across the former divisions between samurai, aristocrats and commoners. The same year’s Emancipation Edict abolished official outcaste status. These were changes to legal categories; issuing an edict alone could not erase people’s prejudices.

passages.title: Government, borders and belonging
passages.text: The map holds one northern outline for 1815 to 1878, but borders changed during that span. In the 1875 treaty with Russia, Japan surrendered its rights in Sakhalin in exchange for eighteen Russian-held Kuril islands. The outline should not be read as a precise treaty map for every selected year.

passages.title: Food, families and neighborhood life
passages.text: The Tenmei famine devastated Tsugaru in northern Honshu in 1783 to 1784, driving people away in search of survival. Later memorials preserve a community response: twelve of the monuments studied by historian Sekine Tatsuhito were erected jointly by groups of two to ten villages to remember the dead.

passages.title: Food, families and neighborhood life
passages.text: An 1854 print helps document year-end preparations for mochi, pounded rice cakes. The National Diet Library explains that ordinary customers ordered from sweet shops while samurai and wealthy merchant households pounded their own. Buying a festive treat and making it at home were both part of the story.

passages.title: Food, families and neighborhood life
passages.text: Some late Edo mochi sellers also supplied the entertainment. Morisada manko describes a performer chanting while swinging his mallet and tossing round pieces into a dish from a distance. Snack preparation could come with an acrobatic show. The Library also preserves an 1861 theatre print of mochi-pounding vendors.

passages.title: Food, families and neighborhood life
passages.text: Public bathing became a target of new rules. Tokyo prohibited mixed bathing in 1869, but the order had to be issued repeatedly because people did not consistently obey. Even the bathhouse reveals how a government’s preferred version of daily life could differ from actual habits.

passages.title: Illness, care and medical learning
passages.text: In 1858 doctors trained in Dutch medicine pooled money to establish a vaccination center in Edo. A fire destroyed its building that same year, but work continued at other locations, including physician Ito Genboku’s residence. Medical care depended on people and cooperation as well as a permanent hospital building.

passages.title: Illness, care and medical learning
passages.text: That vaccination institution became part of the shogunate’s administration in 1860 and taught Western medicine, anatomy through autopsy, and vaccination by 1861. After further reorganizations it became the University of Tokyo’s medical faculty in 1877. Its history connects late Tokugawa medical learning with early Meiji university education.

passages.title: Illness, care and medical learning
passages.text: During the 1858 cholera epidemic, physician Ogata Koan translated foreign accounts and assembled a book about the disease. The outbreak spread through port cities and reached Edo. Translating knowledge was urgent practical work for doctors confronting an illness that frightened families across the country.

passages.title: Illness, care and medical learning
passages.text: A print responding to cholera in the 1850s stages a battle between vegetables and fish, with the vegetables winning. The Library relates this to an Edo market panic in which fish sales collapsed and vegetable prices rose. The picture records people’s beliefs and anxieties, rather than a reliable rule for preventing disease.

passages.title: Children, schools and a written voice
passages.text: National school reform did not immediately put every child behind a desk. In 1873 the recorded primary-school enrollment rate was 39.9 percent for boys and 15.1 percent for girls. These figures count children enrolled, not how often they attended, and show a large gap between the promise of schooling and access.

passages.title: Children, schools and a written voice
passages.text: Kyoto’s prefectural school opened in 1872 to teach girls English, sewing and handicrafts. In 1875 it added abacus work, arithmetic and calligraphy. Its changing timetable placed practical textile skills beside language and calculation: a school day could include both a needle and an abacus.

passages.title: Children, schools and a written voice
passages.text: A different experiment in Tokyo illustrates how small and fragile new opportunities could be. The government girls’ school recorded only 38 pupils in 1873 and was discontinued in 1877. Girls’ education developed through multiple local and private efforts, rather than one uninterrupted expansion of a single school.

passages.title: Children, schools and a written voice
passages.text: Here is an attested Japanese book title: 学問のすゝめ, Gakumon no susume, meaning “An Encouragement of Learning.” Keio University reproduces this spelling for Fukuzawa Yukichi’s work, first issued in 1872 and expanded to seventeen pamphlets by 1876. The first installment addressed people establishing a school in his hometown of Nakatsu.

passages.title: New ways to count days and cross distances
passages.text: Japan’s calendar reform made for an exceptionally short December. After the old calendar’s December 2 came January 1, 1873, under the Gregorian system. The abrupt change caused confusion, and Fukuzawa published explanations. Nobody skipped a day of living, but people suddenly needed new labels for their appointments.

passages.title: New ways to count days and cross distances
passages.text: Modern postal routes linked Tokyo with Kyoto and Osaka in 1871. A nationwide network followed in 1872, then flat-rate postage and postcards in 1873. A brief family message could use a standard postal service instead of depending entirely on the arrangements available along a particular journey.

passages.title: New ways to count days and cross distances
passages.text: Post offices soon handled more than words. Postal money orders and savings services began in 1875, alongside international mail. Sending money and setting some aside became part of the institution’s work too: the post office was becoming a place for household finances as well as letters.

passages.title: New ways to count days and cross distances
passages.text: The railway between Shimbashi and Yokohama opened in October 1872. Artists made woodblock prints of stations and trains around the opening, giving this new machinery a place in an established visual art. A steam train could therefore travel across a printed sheet as well as along its tracks.

The shogunate ended in the 1868 Restoration, while Japan’s people and many institutions continued through the upheaval. The imperial government survived subsequent rebellions, including the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877. The map’s 1878 cutoff is a change of atlas record, not the end of the Meiji state.

sectionTitles: Connections, local histories and living memory

passages.text: This atlas record joins imperial Japan before 1945 to postwar Japan from 1960 onward. The intervening occupation has a separate map record; Japan itself did not disappear. Imperial colonies and occupied societies had their own histories. The 1938 snapshot assigns Cambodia and Cochin China to Japan prematurely, while later outlines omit Okinawa. These shapes are not reliable year-by-year borders. This card follows political transformation and selected everyday experiences, without treating twentieth-century Japan as one unchanged empire.

passages.title: Power, participation and war
passages.text: In January 1915, Japan presented China with twenty-one demands, seeking privileges in Shandong, Manchuria and elsewhere. China accepted a revised ultimatum in May after most of the final group of demands had been removed. Diplomatic pressure accompanied Japan’s expanding power.

passages.title: Power, participation and war
passages.text: The 1925 voting reform removed the tax qualification for male voters, but excluded people receiving public or private assistance. Women still could not vote. The same political bargain produced the anti-communist Peace Preservation Law: wider participation coexisted with stronger repression.

passages.title: Power, participation and war
passages.text: Japan’s expanding war in China included the mass killing of civilians at Nanjing in 1937. The December 1941 attack on Pearl Harbor widened the Pacific war. Military expansion brought occupation and suffering to neighboring societies, not simply a larger colored area on a map.

passages.title: Power, participation and war
passages.text: The atlas’s 1938 outline already includes features labeled Cambodia and Cochin China under Japan. Diplomatic records instead place Japanese demands for bases in southern Indochina in July 1941. A coarse snapshot can slide later events backward, so this map should not establish who controlled a particular town in 1938.

passages.title: Power, participation and war
passages.text: American atomic bombs devastated Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945. On 2 September, Japanese representatives signed the surrender aboard USS Missouri in Tokyo Bay. The surviving document records an enormous political break, while survivors and displaced families faced the work of rebuilding.

passages.title: Rebuilding government and family rights
passages.text: The U.S.-led Allied occupation ran from 1945 to 1952, although the map’s occupation label lasts until 1960. Occupation reforms redistributed agricultural land toward tenant farmers and reduced large landlords’ power. Political change could therefore alter who owned the field a family worked.

passages.title: Rebuilding government and family rights
passages.text: Women voted in the general election of 10 April 1946, and thirty-nine women won seats in the Diet. The National Diet Library preserves a campaign poster carrying words by writer Ikuta Hanayo encouraging women to vote. Political participation became visible in both polling places and printed messages.

passages.title: Rebuilding government and family rights
passages.text: The new constitution took effect on 3 May 1947. It located sovereignty in the people, made the emperor a symbol without governing powers, and renounced war as a means of settling international disputes. These provisions distinguish postwar institutions from the earlier imperial order.

passages.title: Rebuilding government and family rights
passages.text: A short Japanese sample is “個人の尊厳” (kojin no songen), “individual dignity.” It appears in Article 24 of the constitution promulgated in 1946, in the rules for laws on marriage and family. This is the library’s transcription; the romanized reading is supplied here. The article also specifies spouses’ equal rights.

passages.title: Rooms, bathwater and growing up
passages.text: The preserved Okawa house in Tokyo’s Den’enchofu suburb was built in 1925. Bedrooms, a dining room and a study surrounded the living room. Its entirely Western-style rooms were unusual at the time. One house reveals a family’s architectural choices without turning them into everybody’s standard home.

passages.title: Rooms, bathwater and growing up
passages.text: Kodakara-yu, a Tokyo public bathhouse built in 1929, had a grand curved gable, carvings of seven lucky gods and a decorative dressing-room ceiling. The preserved building makes a splendid reminder that washing could involve shared neighborhood spaces. Even a bathhouse could dress up for company.

passages.title: Rooms, bathwater and growing up
passages.text: Japan’s 1954 School Lunch Law established a national framework for meals, financing and support. Preparation standards covered kitchen equipment and nutritional content, and the program expanded to lower secondary schools in 1956. Feeding pupils required cooks, supplies and budgets as well as lunchboxes.

passages.title: Rooms, bathwater and growing up
passages.text: School health was another part of childhood. The 1958 School Health Law specified school physicians, dentists and pharmacists and their professional roles. A school could become a place for health checks as well as lessons, although the law alone does not prove identical services at every school.

passages.title: Health, food and useful inventions
passages.text: About thirty million people still lacked medical insurance in 1956, according to the health ministry’s historical account. In 1961, expanded National Health Insurance brought farmers and self-employed people into universal coverage. It helped families manage medical bills; insurance coverage did not make every treatment free.

passages.title: Health, food and useful inventions
passages.text: The same account describes a coordinated campaign against tuberculosis: antibiotics entered insurance coverage in 1950, followed by screening, BCG vaccination and visits from public-health nurses. Hospitals mattered, but schools, workplaces and homes also became places where disease prevention happened.

passages.title: Health, food and useful inventions
passages.text: In 1958, Momofuku Ando developed Chicken Ramen in a small shed behind his home in Ikeda. Adding hot water turned the dried product into a quick meal. It is a kitchen invention with a pleasantly modest workshop: the famous noodles began without a grand laboratory.

passages.title: Health, food and useful inventions
passages.text: UNESCO’s 2013 description of washoku highlights New Year preparations: pounding rice cakes, arranging symbolic foods and sharing dishes with relatives or neighbors. Special tableware and skills passed between generations make a meal a social occasion. These are documented traditions, not a menu followed identically by every family.

passages.title: Health, food and useful inventions
passages.text: Toilets acquired their own engineering story. TOTO introduced its WASHLET warm-water cleansing seat in 1980, then a self-cleaning spray wand in 1983. A bathroom fitting could have moving parts and a design history! These are product milestones, not evidence that every household immediately owned one.

passages.title: Connections, local histories and living memory
passages.text: The Tokaido Shinkansen opened on 1 October 1964, creating a high-speed rail connection on Japan’s main transport corridor. The operator’s 2024 report also stresses ordinary regional trains used for work and school. Famous express trains and everyday commuting belong to the same transport story.

passages.title: Connections, local histories and living memory
passages.text: Okinawa’s experience followed a different timetable. After the devastating 1945 battle, it remained under U.S. administration until 15 May 1972. Local history and Ryukyuan cultural traditions continued through these political changes. The later atlas outline’s omission of Okinawa must not erase the islands or their residents.

passages.title: Connections, local histories and living memory
passages.text: On 11 March 2011, the earthquake off northeastern Japan generated a devastating tsunami. Japan’s meteorological agency records that some observation stations stopped reporting because of tsunami damage, broken networks and power failures. Preserved measurements and accounts help explain both the disaster and the limits of instruments during it.

Japan continued after the empire’s defeat, with transformed institutions under the postwar constitution. The atlas’s 1960 return to this label and its last stored 2020 boundary are mapping seams, not founding or disappearance dates.

Homes, food, clothing, transport, and neighborhood life
Work, farms, factories, labor, and economic recovery
Families, women, marriage, migration, and belonging
Children, play, care, meals, and unequal childhoods

Water, toilets, waste, insects, and environmental sanitation
Power, censorship, minorities, bases, and contested democracy
Culture, technology, achievements, surprises, and the 1960 seam

passages.text: The atlas calls this layer “Japan (USA),” but Japan did not become part of the United States. The name compresses the U.S.-led Allied occupation, which began after surrender in 1945 and ended when the peace treaty took effect in 1952. Japan remained a country whose government operated under the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers. After 1952 it was sovereign while linked to the United States through bases and security agreements. The atlas keeps this id until its 1960 snapshot. Its four-part polygon covers Hokkaido, Honshu, Shikoku, Kyushu and islands represented by coarse coastlines; it omits Okinawa, Amami and Ogasawara. This geometry is not a jurisdictional inventory: several coastal city-center probes also fall outside its shorelines. The time span fuses two phases that require separate reading. Occupation authority shaped government and reconstruction through 1952; afterward, sovereign Japan negotiated its American security relationship. The 1960 endpoint marks an atlas switch back to japan-1914, not collapse, annexation, independence or succession. This card separates map label, state, occupation chain of command, base presence, and daily life, and never invents a “Japan-USA” polity.

passages.title: Read the atlas label, government, islands, and writing carefully
passages.text: The exact live id is japan-usa, labeled “Japan (USA)” for 1945 to 1960. It has one observed border feature and a missing deep card. Its imported summary describes modern Japan generally, so it cannot explain occupation government, the exact geometry, or this deliberately bounded postwar interval.

passages.title: Read the atlas label, government, islands, and writing carefully
passages.text: The 1945 feature is one MultiPolygon with four components, four rings, 324 positions, and a bounding box from about 129.34 to 145.45 degrees east and 30.89 to 45.43 degrees north. It has no direct shared arcs. Long-range snapshots confirm that this hybrid id exists only here, between japan-1914 regimes.

passages.title: Read the atlas label, government, islands, and writing carefully
passages.text: The surrender instrument placed the authority of the emperor and Japanese government under the Supreme Commander, while the peace treaty took effect in 1952. Together these documents define occupation and its legal endpoint; neither records annexation to the United States, a changed citizenship, or a sovereign “Japan-USA” polity.

passages.title: Read the atlas label, government, islands, and writing carefully
passages.text: Okinawa, Amami, and Ogasawara lie outside the exact polygon. Okinawan archives document U.S. institutions continuing after 1952 and a different administrative path. These island histories belong as explicit comparisons, not evidence that occupation of the four main islands lasted fifteen years or that all excluded islands shared one timetable.

passages.title: Read the atlas label, government, islands, and writing carefully
passages.text: Contemporaneous written sample, from Constitution Article 24: 「婚姻は、両性の合意のみに基いて成立し」 (Kon'in wa, ryōsei no gōi no mi ni motozuite seiritsu shi), “Marriage shall be based only on the mutual consent of both sexes.” This securely dated formal Japanese legal text is not a sample of every person’s speech.

passages.title: Homes, food, clothing, transport, and neighborhood life
passages.text: Air raids left severe housing shortages in many cities. Families doubled up, adapted damaged buildings, built makeshift rooms, or searched regulated rental markets while timber, land, and capital remained constrained. Reconstruction varied by city and tenure, so photographs of barracks or new estates cannot define every household.

passages.title: Homes, food, clothing, transport, and neighborhood life
passages.text: Ration cards did not guarantee enough food. People queued, substituted unfamiliar ingredients, traded possessions, cultivated small plots, and used black markets at legal and personal risk. The National Showa Memorial Museum preserves objects and images of these shortages; a major synthesis connects them to defeat without making Tokyo universal.

passages.title: Homes, food, clothing, transport, and neighborhood life
passages.text: Rural livelihood-improvement groups, often organized around women, identified household problems and tested changes with limited local resources. Documented projects included improved kamado stoves, nutrition, and sanitation. They show practical local experimentation and women’s organizing, not instant nationwide modernization or proof that every participating household changed alike.

passages.title: Homes, food, clothing, transport, and neighborhood life
passages.text: Clothes and bedding were valuable household resources. Families patched garments, remade adult clothing for children, shared bedding, and conserved fuel before later consumer recovery widened choices. Museum displays can make such practices tangible, but their reconstructed rooms represent selected experiences rather than one standard postwar Japanese home.

passages.title: Homes, food, clothing, transport, and neighborhood life
passages.text: By 1958 to 1960, a studied Tokyo suburban white-collar community organized days around commuting, school, neighborhood obligations, shopping, and a wage-earner household ideal. That close fieldwork illuminates emerging middle-class rhythms while remaining one pseudonymous suburb, not a template for farmers, miners, Ainu villages, or crowded lodgers.

passages.title: Work, farms, factories, labor, and economic recovery
passages.text: Millions returned from former imperial territories, but “repatriate” covered unequal routes from Manchuria, Korea, Taiwan, Sakhalin, the Pacific, and elsewhere. Returnees searched for relatives, housing, ration registration, schooling, and work while bringing different losses and skills. Reintegration helped redefine who counted within postwar Japan.

passages.title: Work, farms, factories, labor, and economic recovery
passages.text: The Constitution protected workers’ rights to organize, bargain, and act collectively, yet legal language did not settle workplace power. The drafting record establishes a negotiated guarantee, not actual wages, hazards, job security, union strength, or voice in factories, mines, offices, farms, and casual employment.

passages.title: Work, farms, factories, labor, and economic recovery
passages.text: Land reform transferred much tenanted farmland to cultivators and altered village power, while everyday gains still depended on yields, prices, credit, family labor, and local administration. Rural livelihood programs added household, nutrition, and sanitation projects. Neither reform erased small plots, gendered work, or regional inequality.

passages.title: Work, farms, factories, labor, and economic recovery
passages.text: Economic stabilization checked inflation through tight budgets, credit restraint, and a fixed 360-yen exchange rate. Those policies improved planning conditions but also forced closures, layoffs, and household adjustment. A macroeconomic turning point should be read beside rationing, housing, and labor evidence, since national recovery never arrived evenly.

passages.title: Work, farms, factories, labor, and economic recovery
passages.text: Korean War procurement accelerated orders for Japanese factories, shipping, repair, and services. It helped convert fragile stabilization into faster recovery, but prosperity was neither automatic nor morally simple: a nearby war generated demand, and benefits differed by industry, firm, region, employment status, and household responsibilities.

passages.title: Families, women, marriage, migration, and belonging
passages.text: Article 24 grounded marriage in mutual consent and equal spousal rights, challenging the prewar household system in law. Revised family rules changed marriage, divorce, inheritance, and household authority, but constitutional equality did not remove unpaid labor, employment barriers, domestic conflict, or the pressure to perform respectable family roles.

passages.title: Families, women, marriage, migration, and belonging
passages.text: The election law was revised in December 1945, and women cast ballots in the April 1946 general election. Enfranchisement opened formal political participation and brought women into the Diet, yet it did not guarantee equal power within parties, workplaces, homes, unions, or local institutions.

passages.title: Families, women, marriage, migration, and belonging
passages.text: Births surged after the war, then birth rates fell through the 1950s as mortality also changed. Official vital statistics let readers trace births, deaths, natural increase, and infant mortality, but national aggregates conceal sharp differences by income, city and countryside, region, pollution exposure, and access to care.

passages.title: Families, women, marriage, migration, and belonging
passages.text: Zainichi Korean families faced a post-imperial shift from colonial-subject status toward foreign registration and legal insecurity. A politically contested program to North Korea began in 1959. It should not be reduced to simple homecoming: family division, information, discrimination, politics, and individual motives differed.

passages.title: Families, women, marriage, migration, and belonging
passages.text: Late-1950s salaryman households became a powerful ideal, with paid work centered on the husband and home management associated with the wife. Fieldwork in one Tokyo suburb shows aspirations, budgeting, schooling, and neighborhood ties, while its narrow setting warns against calling this the timeless or universal Japanese family.

passages.title: Children, play, care, meals, and unequal childhoods
passages.text: Children experienced bereavement, missing relatives, damaged homes, hunger, street work, institutional care, and abrupt adult responsibilities. Others retained family support and returned to school quickly. Museum sections devoted to children preserve photographs, school objects, toys, and ration-era materials without turning one display into a universal childhood.

passages.title: Children, play, care, meals, and unequal childhoods
passages.text: The postwar baby boom enlarged young cohorts while infant mortality fell substantially across the following years. Those trends reflect food, infection control, maternal care, household conditions, and wider recovery, but a national series cannot show each child’s survival chances or isolate one program as the cause.

passages.title: Children, play, care, meals, and unequal childhoods
passages.text: School lunches resumed as emergency nutrition and gradually expanded, making eating part of the school day as well as household life. Menus and coverage varied, so not every pupil received the same meal. Lunch programs connected imported supplies, local kitchens, health checks, attendance, and lessons about nutrition.

passages.title: Children, play, care, meals, and unequal childhoods
passages.text: Play survived scarcity through handmade balls, stilts, paper games, songs, improvised toys, and neighborhood space, while organized sport also returned. The postwar National Athletic Meet began in 1946. Objects and government histories reveal possibilities, but children’s leisure depended on work duties, safety, disability, gender, and local resources.

passages.title: Children, play, care, meals, and unequal childhoods
passages.text: Ainu children in Hokkaido inherited living languages, stories, foodways, games, craft, and kin ties while facing assimilation and discrimination. Postwar cultural preservation could support transmission yet also reshape practice for schools, tourism, or display. Evidence must remain community-specific rather than presenting one frozen Ainu tradition.

passages.title: Education, classrooms, curriculum, and opportunity
passages.text: The 1947 School Education Law established six years of elementary school, three of lower secondary, three of upper secondary, and four of university, with nine compulsory years. The structure widened a common route on paper, while buildings, fees beyond compulsory school, entrance competition, disability access, and family resources shaped attendance.

passages.title: Education, classrooms, curriculum, and opportunity
passages.text: Tentative 1947 courses of study replaced militarized schooling with new subjects and methods, including social studies, homemaking, and freer study periods. Teachers had to interpret changing guidance with uneven textbooks, materials, training, and classroom space. A national curriculum therefore describes an intention, not identical lessons everywhere.

passages.title: Education, classrooms, curriculum, and opportunity
passages.text: Education reform expanded local boards, coeducation, new textbooks, and democratic language while occupation review influenced acceptable content. Japanese officials, educators, parents, students, and occupation staff all participated with unequal power. Later policy also emphasized science and technical training as reconstruction moved toward industrial growth.

passages.title: Education, classrooms, curriculum, and opportunity
passages.text: Bomb damage, teacher shortages, overcrowding, and lack of books made reform materially difficult. Communities reused rooms, ran shifts, shared supplies, and rebuilt while pupils also needed food and clothing. Institutional expansion was real, but judging it only by laws or enrollment hides what teaching required each day.

passages.title: Education, classrooms, curriculum, and opportunity
passages.text: Constitution Article 26 recognized an equal right to education and required guardians to ensure compulsory education without tuition. Legal equality mattered, yet progression beyond compulsory school still reflected household income, location, gender expectations, examination systems, health, and the uneven availability of upper-secondary and university places.

passages.title: Medicine, nutrition, disease, disability, and care
passages.text: Postwar public-health administration rebuilt health centers and prioritized tuberculosis, enteric and other infectious diseases, maternal and child care, sanitation, and health education. Clinics, hospitals, pharmacies, midwives, doctors, nurses, and household caregivers formed an uneven system; institutional design cannot prove equal treatment in every prefecture.

passages.title: Medicine, nutrition, disease, disability, and care
passages.text: A nationwide nutrition survey began amid 1945 scarcity, measuring diet and physical condition to guide relief and policy. Such surveys made malnutrition visible in standardized categories, yet sampling and measurement cannot reproduce every meal, black-market purchase, rural harvest, institutional ration, or unequal household distribution.

passages.title: Medicine, nutrition, disease, disability, and care
passages.text: Rural health improved through interacting changes in food, maternal and child services, tuberculosis control, agriculture, household environments, social education, and local organization. The evidence supports a multicausal story, not a single medical miracle. Mountain villages, fishing communities, and peri-urban settlements followed different routes.

passages.title: Medicine, nutrition, disease, disability, and care
passages.text: Occupation censorship restricted public circulation of some Hiroshima and Nagasaki images until 1952. Later survivor drawings and testimony became vital evidence of remembered destruction. Their creation dates and retrospective character must remain visible; this visual-history source documents representation and censorship, not a complete medical history of atomic-bomb survivors.

passages.title: Medicine, nutrition, disease, disability, and care
passages.text: Minamata disease was officially reported in 1956 after residents developed severe neurological illness linked to contaminated seafood and industrial mercury. Recognition and effective response lagged behind suffering. The case exposes how rapid growth could transfer corporate and regulatory costs onto fishing families, children, disabled people, and polluted ecosystems.

passages.title: Water, toilets, waste, insects, and environmental sanitation
passages.text: Toilets ranged from older privies to improved designs, and campaigns connected excreta management with parasites and disease. Reform did not produce one national fixture: building type, water access, municipal service, farm use of night soil, cost, and local enforcement shaped what households actually used.

passages.title: Water, toilets, waste, insects, and environmental sanitation
passages.text: Neighborhood movements against mosquitoes and flies targeted standing water, exposed waste, drains, breeding sites, and household practices. Their history shows sanitation as repeated collective labor, not only pipes or expert orders. Participation and results varied, so “eradication” language would overstate what local campaigns achieved.

passages.title: Water, toilets, waste, insects, and environmental sanitation
passages.text: Reorganized health centers joined infectious-disease surveillance, maternal and child care, sanitation, and health teaching within local administration. Services and access differed by region and population. The institutional history establishes responsibilities and priorities, not equal staffing, trust, transport, treatment, or results in every community.

passages.title: Water, toilets, waste, insects, and environmental sanitation
passages.text: Livelihood-improvement groups addressed smoke, stove efficiency, kitchen work, food preparation, drainage, and household cleanliness with locally available materials. These practical changes could reduce drudgery and health risks, yet programs relied heavily on women’s labor and could turn structural shortages into private household responsibility.

passages.title: Water, toilets, waste, insects, and environmental sanitation
passages.text: Industrial recovery intensified water pollution before regulation caught up. The 1958 water-quality laws covered limited waters and did not prevent disasters already unfolding, including Minamata. Sanitation history must therefore include both household waste control and the much larger effluent decisions of factories and government.

passages.title: Power, censorship, minorities, bases, and contested democracy
passages.text: The surrender instrument subordinated Japanese governing authority to the Supreme Commander, while constitutional drafting records show negotiation over equality and social rights. Democratic reform therefore occurred under unequal occupation power and Japanese participation. These documents establish formal authority and debate, not identical implementation in every institution or locality.

passages.title: Power, censorship, minorities, bases, and contested democracy
passages.text: Occupation censors monitored mail, telephones, newspapers, broadcasting, books, and film from 1945 into 1949. The survival of censor marks makes that control concrete. New freedoms and secret review coexisted, so a story of uncomplicated democratization would miss a central contradiction of the period.

passages.title: Power, censorship, minorities, bases, and contested democracy
passages.text: Debate over Hiroshima and Nagasaki, imperial violence, war responsibility, the emperor, and victimhood unfolded under censorship and later Cold War priorities. Visual evidence resurfacing in 1952 altered public memory. Careful history distinguishes Japanese civilian suffering from crimes committed across Asia and the Pacific.

passages.title: Power, censorship, minorities, bases, and contested democracy
passages.text: Hokkaido was and remains an Ainu homeland. The 1899 assimilation regime and discrimination continued to shape postwar language, land, work, schooling, and cultural transmission. Ainu people were citizens within the polygon, not a vanished preface to Japanese history, and communities made different choices about preservation and public performance.

passages.title: Power, censorship, minorities, bases, and contested democracy
passages.text: Okinawans outside this polygon endured displacement, refugee camps, prolonged U.S. rule, and expanding bases. Archives document coercive land acquisition and island-wide protest. This separate history corrects the atlas label: American military power lasted beyond 1952, but its legal form and local burden were not identical across Japan.

passages.title: Culture, technology, achievements, surprises, and the 1960 seam
passages.text: Sony introduced the TR-55 transistor radio in 1955 after pursuing transistor licensing and development. The exact model offers a concrete engineering milestone and a portable form of listening. A corporate history is reliable for product chronology, but it cannot prove immediate ownership or shared listening habits nationwide.

passages.title: Culture, technology, achievements, surprises, and the 1960 seam
passages.text: Refrigerators, washing machines, and vacuum cleaners became symbols of changing domestic life, though early models were expensive and diffusion was uneven. Mechanical heritage records preserve actual machines and dates. Their labor-saving promise also raises questions about who performed housework and who could afford electricity and space.

passages.title: Culture, technology, achievements, surprises, and the 1960 seam
passages.text: Toyota’s first-generation Crown appeared in 1955 as a tangible marker of domestic automobile engineering and industrial recovery. It did not mean that most families owned cars. Roads, public transport, company fleets, taxis, prices, and worker conditions belong beside the celebrated model in any account of mobility.

passages.title: Culture, technology, achievements, surprises, and the 1960 seam
passages.text: Fun fact: Chicken Ramen went on sale on August 25, 1958. The product made quick preparation and food-processing technology visible in an ordinary meal, but a company origin story cannot show instant universal adoption. Rice, noodles, fish, vegetables, regional dishes, ration memories, and household budgets still shaped diets.

passages.title: Culture, technology, achievements, surprises, and the 1960 seam
passages.text: From 1955, Tokyo artists combined photography, graphic design, performance, film, sound, and protest as commerce and politics accelerated. Their work makes cultural experimentation part of high growth, while remaining city-centered. At 1960 the atlas changes ids; Japanese people, institutions, arguments, and creativity continue across that seam.

At the 1960 snapshot, the exact japan-usa id disappears and the atlas resumes japan-1914 over the same four main-island components. This is a label correction, not a fall, annexation, independence, or new country: the Allied occupation had already ended in 1952. The revised U.S.-Japan security treaty preserved American facilities, while Okinawa remained under separate U.S. administration outside this polygon. The Japanese state continues across the atlas seam. The packet therefore records continuity, leaves fell null, and creates no successor polity.

What a town’s rubbish can tell us
Families and tea behind the castle walls
Books and a ruler’s written mark

passages.text: This record follows Japan’s competing regional lords, the campaigns of Nobunaga and Hideyoshi, and the establishment of Tokugawa government. The atlas span, 1530 to 1650, starts after the civil wars began and continues well into the early Edo period. Its broad outline groups Honshu, Shikoku and Kyushu together without showing rival domains; it does not mean a single government controlled them throughout. Hokkaido lies outside this imported outline.

passages.title: Unification changed government and people’s work
passages.text: Regional military lords, known as daimyo, competed for territory while Ashikaga authority weakened. Nobunaga and Hideyoshi assembled much larger concentrations of power, and Ieyasu established the durable Tokugawa order. Their patronage also reshaped art: richly decorated castles announced the resources and ambitions of their owners.

passages.title: Unification changed government and people’s work
passages.text: Hideyoshi’s 1588 sword-collection order demanded that farmers surrender weapons, including firearms. It connected disarmament with reliable rent collection and preventing uprisings, while promising that farmers would prosper through cultivation. The decree reveals an effort to control rural society; it does not prove that every weapon was successfully collected.

passages.title: Unification changed government and people’s work
passages.text: Portuguese visitors brought matchlock firearms in 1543, and Japanese craftspeople soon produced guns themselves. Armourers also adapted European-style plate armour. These encounters changed workshops and military equipment, linking local skill to objects arriving by sea.

passages.title: Unification changed government and people’s work
passages.text: Unification at home did not end warfare abroad. Hideyoshi launched two devastating invasions of Korea, aiming ultimately at China. Trade and travel with neighbouring countries existed alongside these campaigns. The period’s celebrated castles and art belong to a history that also caused severe suffering beyond Japan.

passages.title: What a town’s rubbish can tell us
passages.text: Excavations at Ichijodani recovered fish bones, shells, seeds and charred rice. Red sea bream bones retain knife marks from preparation. Food came from the sea, cultivated fields and wooded surroundings. Even after the meal was forgotten, a small cut on a bone could tell archaeologists that someone had been cooking.

passages.title: What a town’s rubbish can tell us
passages.text: One Ichijodani chopping board had previously been a wooden serving tray. The museum also displays ordinary lacquer bowls made with simpler, cheaper techniques than luxury pieces. Everyday cooking involved reused objects and affordable utensils, alongside the handsome vessels that usually attract attention in museums.

passages.title: What a town’s rubbish can tell us
passages.text: At the port town of Sakai, excavators found roads built from repeated layers of packed earth, with side drains for rainwater. Wells lined with specially made tiles appear from the sixteenth century. The lining helped prevent the sandy ground around the well from collapsing into the water supply.

passages.title: What a town’s rubbish can tell us
passages.text: Sakai’s excavated toilets often used unglazed jars buried with their mouths exposed. They stood beside streets, which the city’s archaeologists suggest made waste easier to collect for fertilizer. Even the least glamorous household container could have a second job helping crops grow.

passages.title: What a town’s rubbish can tell us
passages.text: Fire layers beneath Sakai preserve former streets and house plots. The city burned during the Osaka summer campaign of 1615, after which the Tokugawa laid out a larger town. Archaeologists distinguish this rebuilt area from the smaller trading community that had flourished before the destruction.

passages.title: Families and tea behind the castle walls
passages.text: In a letter written from his headquarters in 1593, Hideyoshi told his wife One about diplomacy and military orders, then added that he had caught a cold. He also addressed Yodo-dono’s pregnancy with concern for One’s feelings. Affairs of state, illness and complicated family relationships could share a single sheet of paper.

passages.title: Families and tea behind the castle walls
passages.text: The private upper enclosure of Hideyoshi’s Osaka Castle housed members of his family, including One, Yodo-dono and his son Hideyori. Its original stone walls were later buried during Tokugawa rebuilding; part was discovered in 1984. The later castle concealed an earlier household’s fortified setting below ground.

passages.title: Families and tea behind the castle walls
passages.text: Himeji’s surviving early seventeenth-century castle combines timber buildings, white-plastered earthen walls, gates and interconnected defensive structures. Its elegant rooflines belonged to a working military headquarters. The white appearance earned it the name White Heron Castle, a peaceful-sounding nickname for a carefully defended place.

passages.title: Families and tea behind the castle walls
passages.text: An early seventeenth-century black Raku tea bowl in the Metropolitan Museum was moulded by hand rather than shaped on a potter’s wheel. Such lightweight earthenware could be fired in small indoor kilns. Tea enthusiasts valued the rough, understated surface: impressive hospitality did not always require the shiniest cup.

passages.title: Books and a ruler’s written mark
passages.text: In early seventeenth-century Kyoto, Saga editions gave older literature carefully designed covers, paper and illustrations. Their wooden printing type sometimes joined two to four characters in one piece, preserving the flowing effect of handwriting. Printing could multiply a book while still making its pages look elegantly written.

passages.title: Books and a ruler’s written mark
passages.text: A 1608 printed Tales of Ise used a text descended from a copy Fujiwara Teika had made for his granddaughter in 1234. The National Archives preserves this illustrated edition. A family manuscript could help carry an older story into a new age of publishing, long after its first readers were gone.

passages.title: Books and a ruler’s written mark
passages.text: A 1568 letter from Nobunaga confirms a man named Tohachi’s possession of rice fields. The museum cannot identify Tohachi more precisely. This small document shows another side of military authority: people needed written confirmation of the land on which wealth and livelihoods depended.

passages.title: Books and a ruler’s written mark
passages.text: The letter bears 天下布武, read tenka fubu, in Nobunaga’s red seal. The museum renders it as “establishing military presence in the territory.” The characters here use modern type, not the seal’s carved lettering. Scholars debate how widely its word tenka extended: the slogan does not by itself prove a claim to rule the whole world.

Tokugawa rule emerged before the atlas’s 1650 cutoff. Osaka Castle fell in 1615, ending the Toyotomi military challenge, and the Tokugawa rebuilt it from 1620. Japan’s regional societies, workshops and literary traditions continued under a new political order; the map’s old label outlasts the conflicts it describes.

passages.text: The Jin dynasty briefly reunified China after the Three Kingdoms, but internal weakness and uprisings by the peoples of the north led to the loss of the north in 316. The Eastern Jin survived in the south as a center of Chinese culture.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Wang Xizhi writes the Preface to the Orchid Pavilion, the most admired piece of Chinese calligraphy, at a spring gathering of poets.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Landscape painting begins to emerge as an independent art form; Gu Kaizhi paints the Admonitions scroll.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Huiyuan founds a Buddhist community on Mount Lu; translation projects and monasteries multiply.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The monk Faxian sets out for India to collect Buddhist texts, and returns by sea fifteen years later.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove, of the Wei to Jin transition, exemplify literati withdrawal and philosophical debate.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Eastern Jin preserved Chinese high culture in the south while the north underwent ethnic mixing.
The last Eastern Jin emperor abdicated to Liu Yu, a powerful general who founded the Liu Song dynasty.

A painter's words and what survived

passages.text: The Jurchen-led Jin dynasty ruled northern China from 1115 to 1234, after overthrowing the Liao. This is a different dynasty from the earlier Jin of late antiquity. The index dates of 1200 to 1279 are misleading: an existing map overlay represents 1115 to 1234, using a coarse outline to correct a base map that confines Jin mainly to the northeast.

passages.title: Ruling a northern empire
passages.text: Wanyan Aguda founded the dynasty in 1115 in the region of modern Harbin. His successors moved their main court south: Beijing became the central capital in 1153, and Kaifeng became the refuge of the court in 1214. Those moves trace both expansion into northern China and the later pressure of Mongol invasion.

passages.title: Ruling a northern empire
passages.text: The conquest of 1127 displaced the Northern Song court, but diplomacy continued between the northern Jin and southern Song. A silk handscroll attributed to Yang Bangji may depict a Song delegation meeting its Jin hosts. Its exact subject is uncertain, yet its continued Northern Song painting style is part of the cultural story.

passages.title: Ruling a northern empire
passages.text: Jin government belonged to a longer history of institutions as well as conquest. Historian Tao Jing-shen examined how it inherited features of Northern Song government and passed institutions to later conquering dynasties. A change in the ruling house could alter who held power while retaining and reshaping ways of administering a large country.

passages.title: Ruling a northern empire
passages.text: Schooling could happen in Jurchen as well as Chinese. Emperor Shizong ordered translations of Chinese classics in 1164. A Song envoy traveling in 1169 or 1170 noticed a roadside sign in Baozhou advertising Jurchen studies. The detail makes the language visible beyond the palace: someone was offering lessons near an ordinary street.

passages.title: Ruling a northern empire
passages.text: The first Jurchen-language civil examinations were held in 1173. Candidates answered a policy question in at least500 characters. Preparing required translated books, teachers and practice in composition. This was an effort to build a literary culture in Jurchen, alongside examinations conducted in Chinese, rather than simply abandoning one language for another.

passages.title: Sleeping, making things and enjoying a performance
passages.text: A tiger-shaped ceramic pillow in the University of Michigan collection was made during the Jin dynasty. It is a hard neck rest, a type that could keep carefully arranged hair above the bed. The tiger supplies the decoration rather than the softness. Henan and Shanxi kilns specialized in such Cizhou wares.

passages.title: Sleeping, making things and enjoying a performance
passages.text: Another pillow, now in Montreal, carries a bird perched on bamboo and a maker's stamp naming the Zhang family. Its potters covered gray stoneware with white slip, painted in iron black and added a transparent glaze. A familiar household object can preserve both a workshop's name and the steps of its craft.

passages.title: Sleeping, making things and enjoying a performance
passages.text: Luxury clothing could advertise a favorite elite activity. A surviving Jin silk brocade shows a falcon attacking a swan, woven with gilded strips against green silk. Historical descriptions connect this pattern with robes worn by Jurchen noblemen at the annual spring hunt. Fashion could tell a hunting story before its wearer said a word.

passages.title: Sleeping, making things and enjoying a performance
passages.text: At Houma in Shanxi, the Jin tomb of Dong Ming contained a brick stage with five actor figures. Another Jin tomb at Ershui preserved written fragments of three story-singing pieces. Performance mattered enough to enter the imagined afterlife. These finds supply evidence for entertainment beyond the official histories of emperors and wars.

passages.title: Sleeping, making things and enjoying a performance
passages.text: Money was more complicated than a dynasty inventing a banknote. Research on the period before the 1190s describes continued use of Northern Song copper coins and uneven supplies of cash. It interprets early Jin jiaochao as deposit certificates used to transfer funds. A paper claim on money and everyday cash did different jobs.

passages.title: Sleeping, making things and enjoying a performance
passages.text: Medical learning produced arguments as well as remedies. The later History of Jin describes physician Liu Wansu writing several books and favoring medicines classified as cooling. He explained illness through the medical theories of his time. The biography preserves an influential approach to treatment, rather than evidence that every household used it.

passages.title: A painter's words and what survived
passages.text: The late-twelfth-century painting Wind and Snow in the Fir Pines survives with the signature of Li Shan. It also accumulated inscriptions from later admirers, including a Qing emperor. A scroll can therefore have several historical layers: the Jin painting and its maker's signature belong to a different time from later collectors' comments.

passages.title: A painter's words and what survived
passages.text: The painter's original Chinese signature reads “平陽李山製”, translated by the Smithsonian as “Made by Li Shan of Pingyang.” It is a short, securely identified written sample from the Jin period. Chinese was one of the languages used in this Jurchen-ruled state; these characters are not a sample of the separate Jurchen script.

passages.title: A painter's words and what survived
passages.text: The Mongol conquest brought severe destruction between 1211 and 1234. Stone inscriptions studied by historian Jinping Wang also show how people rebuilt social relationships afterward in Shanxi. Buddhist monks, Daoist priests and women appear as participants in that changing society. The dynasty's defeat did not end the lives or history of its communities.

Mongol and Southern Song forces defeated the last Jin court at Caizhou in 1234. This ended the dynasty, not the peoples of northern China or their cultural traditions. The index's 1279 cutoff belongs to the imported record and must not be treated as a second Jin fall.
