passages.text: Picture a hill capital where drums rolled past the Temple of the Tooth, rice terraces stepped down wet valleys, and guards watched narrow forest passes. This was the Kingdom of Kandy, also called Senkadagala, Sri Lanka's last independent royal state. Its best-documented capital era began in the 1590s, about sixty years before the atlas first colors `kandy` in 1650. Kandyan rulers defeated Portuguese invasions, invited Dutch help and then resisted Dutch coastal power, while chiefs, monks, farmers and artisans held together an unequal service-based state. Monks crossed the ocean to Siam; royal workshops made carved guns, ivory panels and jeweled blades; household life revolved around land, kin, rice and water. British troops entered Kandy in 1803 but failed to hold it. In 1815, British invasion, court divisions and the Kandyan Convention ended the kingdom exactly where the atlas polygon stops. Rebellion in 1817 to 1818 continued resistance under colonial rule, not the monarchy. The map is a useful inland locator, but its broad northern reach and missing Sabaragamuwa areas are not a measured border.

passages.title: First decode the atlas label, shape and date seams
passages.text: The exact indexed id is `kandy`, displayed simply as “Kandy,” circa 1650 to 1815. There is no alias or authored link. Coverage calls it a state with five border files and five observed intervals, but the imported summary switches between city and kingdom and says the monarchy lasted to 1818. This card keeps the database id while correcting the polity and its 1815 ending.

passages.title: First decode the atlas label, shape and date seams
passages.text: At 1600 the exact target is absent; one sweeping imported `saylan` feature owns the inland audit points even though Kandy was already a royal capital. At 1650 `kandy` appears as one unlabeled Polygon with one ring and fifteen positions. Its bounds are 80.03420034200343° to 81.39501395013951° east and 6.473453302778211° to 8.86864347057223° north.

passages.title: First decode the atlas label, shape and date seams
passages.text: The 1650 coordinate-array SHA-256 is `8b64cda6d8a63220de0678596bee707fe2601a72c341f8f2be1b5054809f57b3`; 1700 has exactly the same decoded shape. Their raw arcs differ, `[[659,-659]]` and `[[698,-698]]`, because topology files encode shared lines independently. Both touch features called `ceylon` and `ceylon-dutch`, showing a digital inland/coastal seam rather than a surveyed treaty frontier.

passages.title: First decode the atlas label, shape and date seams
passages.text: The 1715 layer unexpectedly splits Kandy into two exact features: a main seventeen-position polygon with hash `9173f390e8cb00c01398edc1ea6ba2647a53d6dbacd364ab62dc721f4dac53f1`, plus a four-position northwestern sliver with hash `8ed3c680f28e1d76cedf9089a25763ac110a005ce8ae8fe8f8662c36e2a4ebf2`. None of the twenty named audit points lands in that tiny fragment, so it should not be spun into a historical enclave without evidence.

passages.title: First decode the atlas label, shape and date seams
passages.text: At 1783 and 1800 the target returns to one fifteen-position polygon, with bounds 80.03420034200343,6.472753338276618 to 81.39501395013951,8.868633898640546 and hash `ccb3a56e28ae27d146190ababfdc054d296157c4749fdf9a9208daf573633ff7`. It vanishes at 1815 and stays absent in 1878, when Ceylon successor features cover the highlands.

passages.title: Read the colored area as a locator, then meet the kingdom
passages.text: Across all five exact layers, the main polygon contains Kandy, Matale, Dambulla, Nuwara Eliya, Badulla, Mahiyangana, Kurunegala, Anuradhapura and Polonnaruwa. It excludes every coastal test point, which captures the inland-versus-littoral story in broad strokes. Yet it also excludes Ratnapura and Kegalle, historically important Kandyan zones, while stretching far north and east beyond equally secure administration.

passages.title: Read the colored area as a locator, then meet the kingdom
passages.text: Senkadagalapura, the city now called Kandy, became the capital in the 1590s under Vimaladharmasuriya I. His marriage to Dona Catarina reinforced a royal claim, and victory over Portugal at Danture in 1594 helped consolidate power. The atlas start of 1650 therefore misses roughly six decades of the best-documented independent highland kingdom.

passages.title: Read the colored area as a locator, then meet the kingdom
passages.text: Kandyan defense used narrow approaches, watched passes, forests and deception. At Danture, troops let an invading Portuguese force enter, disrupted its support and struck in difficult country. Terrain mattered because people knew how to use it; mountains were not magic walls. The city was entered or captured more than once, including by Dutch troops in 1765 and British troops in 1803.

passages.title: Read the colored area as a locator, then meet the kingdom
passages.text: The kingdom was never isolated from the sea. Monks and envoys sailed between Kandy and Siam carrying letters, texts and ritual knowledge, while intermediaries crossed several political jurisdictions. Coastal forts could restrict routes, but the court still used gifts, religious ties and foreign partners to seek room for action in a connected Indian Ocean world.

passages.title: Read the colored area as a locator, then meet the kingdom
passages.text: The historical endpoint really is 1815. British forces occupied the capital, Sri Vikrama Rajasinha was deposed, and chiefs signed a Convention on 2 March that transferred sovereignty. The Uva-Wellassa uprising began in 1817 under colonial rule. Calling that rebellion a kingdom lasting to 1818 confuses resistance in Kandy's name with continued sovereign monarchy.

passages.title: A king ruled through chiefs, land records and required service
passages.text: The king stood at the center of court and sacred authority, but government worked through powerful officials. Two leading adigars advised, judged and commanded; disavas managed outer provinces; rate mahatmayas headed districts nearer the capital; village headmen and scribes handled local business. Offices created ladders of access, obligation and rivalry, not a modern ministry with identical desks everywhere.

passages.title: A king ruled through chiefs, land records and required service
passages.text: Land and labor were tied together through rajakariya, literally royal work. Depending on status and tenure, people owed public labor, military service, specialized craft work, produce or payments to crown, chiefs or temples. Roads, bridges and campaigns did not build themselves. The system also fixed unequal caste duties, so a glittering palace rested on compulsory work that children should not mistake for volunteering.

passages.title: A king ruled through chiefs, land records and required service
passages.text: Palm-leaf `lēkam miti` registers tracked land, taxes and services at court, while village scribes cut deeds for property and inheritance onto prepared ola leaves. Local chiefs authenticated documents. This paper trail was literally leafy: useful enough that Portuguese and Dutch administrators adapted it, even while trying to make people accept colonial paper records.

passages.title: A king ruled through chiefs, land records and required service
passages.text: Provincial chiefs possessed influence, followers and revenue, yet their authority depended on royal appointment, local networks and their ability to deliver services. Kings balanced noble families; nobles could bargain, obstruct or rebel. The fall of 1815 grew from this political structure and British intervention, so “the people suddenly chose Britain” is much too simple for a divided court and many communities.

passages.title: A king ruled through chiefs, land records and required service
passages.text: Caste and rank shaped occupations, marriage, service and even privileges such as clothing or architecture. Yet the official hierarchy was not a frozen diagram: rulers depended on chiefs, headmen, farmers, monks, artisans and soldiers across distant provinces. D'Oyly recorded offices after conquest for a British audience, so his tidy constitutional ladder reveals structure more clearly than local bargaining or low-status voices.

passages.title: Fight, bargain, trade, and watch allies become rivals
passages.text: Rajasinghe II's 1638 treaty invited the VOC to attack Portuguese positions. Kandy expected recovered strongholds; the Dutch expected repayment and commercial privilege. After Portugal was expelled, the Company kept coastal forts and lucrative routes. The deal solved one danger while creating another, a useful lesson that allies can agree on an enemy without agreeing on the world afterward.

passages.title: Fight, bargain, trade, and watch allies become rivals
passages.text: Cinnamon connected highland politics with coastal labor and global commerce. VOC officials wanted access to cinnamon lands and feared that peelers might flee toward Kandy. The court could influence people in contested zones and use that leverage in diplomacy. Pepper, areca, elephants, textiles, salt and other goods also moved, but exact cargoes and royal income changed over time.

passages.title: Fight, bargain, trade, and watch allies become rivals
passages.text: In 1765 Dutch troops captured the city and looted palaces and temples. A gold sabre, silver sabre, dagger, two wall guns and Lewke's cannon became war booty. Their survival proves a sack, not permanent Dutch rule over the highlands: troops withdrew, Kandy continued as a kingdom, and a new settlement reshaped the coastal boundary in 1766.

passages.title: Fight, bargain, trade, and watch allies become rivals
passages.text: When Britain took the Dutch coast in 1796, Governor North first sought a subsidiary alliance that would have limited Kandyan freedom. Court figures pursued competing strategies, and historians warn that calling one minister simply a traitor flattens uncertain evidence. Diplomacy failed; the British marched into Kandy in 1803, then lost control of the capital and much of the expedition.

passages.title: Fight, bargain, trade, and watch allies become rivals
passages.text: Kandyan resistance depended on information as much as ambushes: routes, river crossings, food supplies, village obligations and remembered boundaries. British officers tried to turn that knowledge into surveys and administrative geography after 1803. A mountain pass on a map is only a line; to soldiers carrying equipment in rain, watched by local forces, it could decide whether an army ate, moved or escaped.

passages.title: The Tooth Relic, ocean-crossing monks and brilliant craft
passages.text: The palace and Temple of the Tooth stood side by side because custody of the Buddha's tooth relic strengthened royal legitimacy. The first Kandyan shrine was built around 1603, destroyed in 1637 and rebuilt in 1697; major surviving work belongs to Kirti Sri Rajasinha's eighteenth-century rebuilding. Granite, limestone, wood, terracotta, metal and ivory carried painted and carved decoration.

passages.title: The Tooth Relic, ocean-crossing monks and brilliant craft
passages.text: Kandyan monks sought a valid higher-ordination lineage overseas. After dangerous negotiations and voyages, Siamese monks led by Upali arrived and ordinations were restored in 1753. This religious project was also diplomacy: Kandy, Ayutthaya and the VOC each had goals, and ships carrying monks, books and ritual objects could become channels for friendship, dependence and political spying.

passages.title: The Tooth Relic, ocean-crossing monks and brilliant craft
passages.text: A 1756 palm-leaf letter connected Kandy and Siam in Pali, Sinhala and Southeast Asian manuscript worlds. Its surviving formulas discuss refuge and ordination pronunciation, while catalogues record related Sinhala accounts. Learning lived in performed sound as well as writing: getting a syllable right mattered because communities believed the validity of ordination depended on correct recitation.

passages.title: The Tooth Relic, ocean-crossing monks and brilliant craft
passages.text: An eighteenth-century ivory panel from the Kandy region shows a female temple dancer in a carefully posed movement, framed by carved plantlike and diamond patterns. It proves skilled carving and a dance image in sacred architecture. It does not identify the model or prove that every village performed the same steps, costume or music.

passages.title: The Tooth Relic, ocean-crossing monks and brilliant craft
passages.text: Royal workshops made or finished prestige objects with iron, wood, silver, gold, ivory and gems. Wall guns combined defense with carved and engraved ornament; a small Kandyan-type knife survives in ivory and silver. Such costly objects reveal specialists and court display, but an aristocrat's blade is poor evidence for the tools or clothing of a rice-farming household.

passages.title: Families could arrange residence, property and work in several ways
passages.text: Kandyan customary law distinguished `diga` marriage, in which a woman generally joined her husband's household, from `binna` marriage, in which a husband joined the wife's home or `mulgedera`. Residence affected inheritance and family land. These were legal-social patterns with exceptions and arguments, not two buttons that automatically determined every couple's happiness or power.

passages.title: Families could arrange residence, property and work in several ways
passages.text: Fraternal polyandry, brothers sharing a wife, was documented in some Kandyan households and could keep land and labor together. It was neither universal nor uniquely Kandyan, and colonial writers often treated unfamiliar families as scandalous curiosities. The careful question is where and why a household used the arrangement, not whether all people inside the atlas polygon lived that way.

passages.title: Families could arrange residence, property and work in several ways
passages.text: Marriage form affected a woman's ties to her natal home and her claims within family property: diga and binna arrangements carried different expectations, while actual cases produced exceptions and arguments. Legal records make property rules visible far more often than women's own explanations of work, affection, conflict or ambition, so a rule book cannot stand in for every life.

passages.title: Families could arrange residence, property and work in several ways
passages.text: A seventeenth-century outsider observed children learning songs at bedtime, visiting neighboring houses to sleep when homes were crowded, practicing formal errands and sometimes splashing in a bowl while being washed. Robert Knox watched Kandyan life for years but wrote through captivity and European prejudice, so these vivid scenes are clues, not a census of every childhood.

passages.title: Families could arrange residence, property and work in several ways
passages.text: House layout could organize family life. A central court and veranda provided light, air, cooking, work and social space; darker rooms stored cloth and sometimes sheltered childbirth or sleeping. Rice bins advertised household security. The architectural study mostly reconstructs free farmers, sub-elites and elites, so the poorest laborers' shelters and enslaved people's spaces remain less visible.

passages.title: Learning moved through voices, sand, leaves and specialists
passages.text: Children likely learned farming, cooking, craft and etiquette within households and work groups, although direct childhood records are scarce. Specialized literacy belonged to scribes, monks, officials and some families. Palm-leaf deeds and court registers prove trained writers worked at village and royal levels; they do not supply a school census or literacy percentage for girls, boys or castes.

passages.title: Learning moved through voices, sand, leaves and specialists
passages.text: Monasteries and court circles sustained Pali and Sinhala textual learning, religious recitation and copying. The 1750s missions required envoys, interpreters, monks and people able to compare formulas across languages and scripts. Weliwita Saranankara's reform world was scholarly and political, but there was no universal classroom system reaching children of every gender, caste and province.

passages.title: Learning moved through voices, sand, leaves and specialists
passages.text: Palm-leaf documents were made objects, not loose notebook paper. Leaves were dried and cut, letters incised, pigment rubbed in, and boards or cord protected a bundle. Village scribes recorded property while court registers tracked dues. Reading and writing therefore joined craft skill, memory and authority: a small mark could affect land or labor for a family.

passages.title: Learning moved through voices, sand, leaves and specialists
passages.text: Medical knowledge also traveled orally and on ola manuscripts. Surviving collections preserve herbal remedies, diagnostic ideas and treatment instructions, but most catalogued leaves are not securely dated to one Kandyan reign. They show a durable tradition of recording care; they cannot name the healer in a particular 1700 village or prove every remedy worked.

passages.title: Learning moved through voices, sand, leaves and specialists
passages.text: Education included performance. Temple images preserve dancers; monastic ritual required exact recitation; court and festival processions used drums and movement. A modern University of Peradeniya study records Kandyan healing lineages joining song, drumming, dance, astrology and medicine. That is evidence of continuity, not permission to project every modern step unchanged back to 1650.

passages.title: Rice terraces, jackfruit, workshops and market journeys
passages.text: Rice fields climbed hills in level steps that shared water from springs, channels and ponds. Communities coordinated planting and harvest; women transplanted and weeded in Knox's account. Meals centered on rice with greens, pepper, citrus, coconut, roots or jackfruit, while fish or meat varied by wealth and place. Betel chewing turned visits and news-sharing into a very long snack break.

passages.title: Rice terraces, jackfruit, workshops and market journeys
passages.text: Rajakariya organized more than royal pageantry. Cultivators supplied produce and labor; craftspeople owed specialized service; people repaired routes or served in wartime according to tenure and status. Household work also remained essential. Calling the economy merely “self-sufficient farming” misses redistribution, compulsory service, temple lands, provincial officials and goods moving across political borders.

passages.title: Rice terraces, jackfruit, workshops and market journeys
passages.text: Ordinary and sub-elite houses used nearby timber, clay, straw and plant fibers. Wattle-and-daub walls and thatched roofs needed repair; rice bins, mortars, cooking areas and work space mattered more than decorative symmetry. Better houses might add carved timbers, tiles, limewash, extra courts, kitchens, granaries, stables and cattle sheds, but some features required royal privilege.

passages.title: Rice terraces, jackfruit, workshops and market journeys
passages.text: Metalworkers and woodcarvers could turn a weapon into both tool and artwork. The two heavy wall guns seized in 1765 had carved wood and engraved symbols; Lewke's cannon carried gold, silver, gems and Kandyan motifs. These objects also expose unequal resources: court workshops concentrated materials and labor that most families could never wear or display.

passages.title: Rice terraces, jackfruit, workshops and market journeys
passages.text: The 1638 bargain itself shows why access to coastal forts, ships and overseas commerce mattered to Kandy. The court exchanged trading advantages for Dutch military help against Portugal, but the partners later disputed control of captured ports. Records illuminate valuable routes and official privileges far better than the small loads carried by unnamed market traders.

passages.title: Homes, medicine, water and an honest toilet report
passages.text: Most dwellings were low, single-storey and built of timber, clay and thatch; elite manor houses repeated courtyard units and gained tiled roofs, limewash, carving or extra buildings. Surviving grand houses create a preservation trap: durable status architecture is easier to study than a poor family's repaired walls, smoky cooking corner or temporary shelter.

passages.title: Homes, medicine, water and an honest toilet report
passages.text: Healing mixed household plant knowledge, specialist traditions, Buddhist or deity ritual and written medical recipes. Knox said people used leaves and bark for purging, wounds and eyes; modern manuscript collections preserve broader indigenous systems. His claim that everyone was their own physician is an outsider's exaggeration, and neither source proves equal access or safe results.

passages.title: Homes, medicine, water and an honest toilet report
passages.text: The city complex included ponds, channels and a royal bathing house, while Sri Vikrama Rajasinha created the artificial lake between 1803 and 1807. Rural rice cultivation demanded careful control of spring, rain and channel water. Royal waterworks could impress visitors, but they do not prove piped household supply, and diverting labor or water could burden cultivators.

passages.title: Homes, medicine, water and an honest toilet report
passages.text: Knox reports frequent body washing, hand and mouth washing around meals, and using water after defecation. That is useful seventeenth-century practice evidence. Checked sources do not supply a kingdom-wide map of latrines, drains or sewage disposal. We have a bathing house and washing habits, not a royal toilet census, an amusing gap, but one that must stay a gap.

passages.title: Homes, medicine, water and an honest toilet report
passages.text: The palace-temple ensemble used granite bases, timber, stone, terracotta, metal and ivory, with painted ceilings and carved dancers, acrobats and animals. Construction demanded quarrying, carpentry, transport and maintenance as well as artists. The monument tells us what royal and sacred patronage could assemble; it should never be used as the standard bedroom of a farmer.

passages.title: Read the ending in Sinhala, then trace what continued
passages.text: The written sample comes from Article 5 of the Sinhala Kandyan Convention, signed at Kandy on 2 March 1815. Original script: `බුද්ධ ශාසනයද දෙවාගමද කඩකල නොහැකිව පවත්වන්ඩ ඕනෑවා`. Transliteration: `buddha śāsanayada dēvāgamada kaḍakala nohækiva pavatvanḍa ōnǣvā`. Translation: “The Buddha's dispensation and worship of the gods must be maintained inviolate.” This is formal legal Sinhala from a bilingual annexation instrument, not ordinary conversation.

passages.title: Read the ending in Sinhala, then trace what continued
passages.text: In 1803 British troops occupied the capital but could not secure the countryside or sustain their position. That failure revealed the difference between entering Kandy and controlling the kingdom. Twelve years later Britain combined larger forces, local alliances and accumulated geographic knowledge. The ending was therefore neither an inevitable stroll through hills nor a single battle won by superior weapons.

passages.title: Read the ending in Sinhala, then trace what continued
passages.text: John D'Oyly learned Sinhala, consulted monks and writers, built networks and worked as an intelligence agent who encouraged division between king and nobles. He also drafted the Convention. Language learning can create understanding and trust, but in this case it served imperial conquest too, a sharp example of knowledge carrying political power.

passages.title: Read the ending in Sinhala, then trace what continued
passages.text: Sovereign Kandy ended in 1815, exactly where the atlas polygon disappears. The Convention deposed Sri Vikrama Rajasinha, transferred authority to the British Crown and promised protection for Buddhism. The direct map successor is `ceylon-1815`; that database arrow describes annexation, not an instant erasure of Kandyan communities, law or memory.

passages.title: Read the ending in Sinhala, then trace what continued
passages.text: Rebellion began in 1817 across former Kandyan regions, after annexation. Colonial forces defeated it, but royal ceremonies, legal concepts and claims to kingship were later reworked in petitions and resistance. Dating the kingdom to 1818 confuses post-conquest struggle with monarchy; continuity means people adapting older institutions and symbols under new rule.

British forces occupied Kandy, deposed Sri Vikrama Rajasinha and secured the Kandyan chiefs' Convention on 2 March 1815, transferring sovereignty to the British Crown. The 1817 to 1818 uprising was resistance after annexation, not evidence that the kingdom survived to 1818. Kandyan religious, legal, artistic and political traditions continued under new rule.

passages.text: Kanem, east of Lake Chad, was the earlier heartland of Sayfawa power. Its beginnings remain uncertain; excavated settlements illuminate elite buildings and working materials.

passages.title: Building and working materials
passages.text: At Tié Kalaté S2, discarded bricks lie in a depression where clay was extracted and fired. Nearby residences stood on dunes.

passages.title: Building and working materials
passages.text: Tié’s substantial enclosure is a candidate for Njimi, the royal capital. The identification remains argued rather than confirmed by a naming inscription.

passages.title: Building and working materials
passages.text: A study of excavated iron nails distinguishes four main forms used in twelfth- to fourteenth-century Kanem. These ordinary fasteners preserve metalworking choices that monumental buildings alone cannot show. Their precise use must be established from archaeological context.

passages.title: Adornment and long-distance exchange
passages.text: At Tié, glass dominates the recovered beads, alongside smaller numbers made from ostrich eggshell, metal and stone. Bone pendants and cowries also served as ornaments. This assemblage describes personal adornment at the excavated site, not everyone’s dress.

passages.title: Adornment and long-distance exchange
passages.text: Many glass beads are tiny cylinders or rounded forms. Makers cut drawn glass and often reheated it to soften sharp edges. Red-brown and yellow shades were common in the recovered collection.

passages.title: Adornment and long-distance exchange
passages.text: Chemical analysis links a few beads with the glass industry around Ile-Ife in present-day Nigeria. Much of the remaining glass has affinities farther east. The results support African exchange connections, while the exact routes and intermediaries remain uncertain.

passages.title: Writing, travel and unequal exchange
passages.text: The Arabic Diwan preserves a royal succession record. Historians compare its chronology with other texts and archaeological dates.

passages.title: Writing, travel and unequal exchange
passages.text: Saharan exchange included enslaved people, horses and cloth. The court’s connections rested partly on coercion as well as commerce.

passages.title: Writing, travel and unequal exchange
passages.text: Cairo was an important meeting point for pilgrims from Kanem and later Borno travelling toward Mecca. Dewière’s study treats pilgrimage as religious practice that also carried people, goods and ideas between African regions.
In the late fourteenth century, the Sayfawa court left Kanem for Borno under pressure from Bulala rivals. Kanem continued under other rulers while the dynasty rebuilt its power west of the lake.

passages.text: Borno developed west of Lake Chad as a centre of Sayfawa government and scholarship. Its history includes scholarly communities, farming settlements and changing dynasties, as well as royal capitals.

passages.title: Farming, fishing and exchange
passages.text: At Garumele, a settlement associated with Borno’s history, excavators found abundant fish remains together with sheep, goat and cattle bones. Oral traditions connect it with royalty, but its precise occupation dates and capital status remain debated.

passages.title: Farming, fishing and exchange
passages.text: The range and quantity of fish at Garumele suggest specialist fishing. Researchers propose that some fish arrived already processed, while herders supplied livestock. These are interpretations of bone distributions, not proof of a known market organisation or preservation recipe.

passages.title: Farming, fishing and exchange
passages.text: Nineteenth-century Borno depended on agriculture. Many people combined farming with seasonal crafts or trade. Kyari Mohammed stresses the importance of regional commerce alongside Saharan routes, challenging a picture of an economy sustained only by distant caravans.

passages.title: Learning and manuscript arts
passages.text: Some scholarly villages combined study with farming and enjoyed royal exemptions. Students advanced from Quran memorisation to Arabic grammar, Old Kanembu translation and interpretation. Education rested on organised communities as well as individual teachers.

passages.title: Learning and manuscript arts
passages.text: The Konduga Quran survives as loose leaves kept in a leather folder and satchel. Italian watermarks identify imported paper. Different hands added Arabic commentary and Old Kanembu glosses around the main text, preserving several readers’ work.

passages.title: Learning and manuscript arts
passages.text: A later copy of the Konduga manuscript’s final page preserved its annotations as well as its Quranic text. The copy used a different page layout. This unusual duplication protected a record of teaching, not only the main scriptural passage.

passages.title: Learning and manuscript arts
passages.text: Owners patched the Konduga Quran with paper strips and stitches after moisture damaged its lower margins. Repeated repairs show care across generations. A surviving manuscript can record maintenance and reuse alongside the original scribe’s achievement.

passages.title: Learning and manuscript arts
passages.text: Extensive written annotations became less common during nineteenth-century upheaval, but handwritten Qurans and oral translation continued. Bondarev proposes links with political and educational changes; he does not establish one decree that ended the practice.

passages.title: Power and its human costs
passages.text: Rabih’s administration demanded produce and other revenues through local authorities under military supervision. Mohammed’s research describes confiscation and punishment as tools of rule. These burdens make the occupation a history of households and livelihoods as well as battles.

Rabih conquered Borno in 1893. French forces and African allies defeated him in 1900; colonial partition followed. Royal institutions and regional communities continued under altered authority, while the independent state’s political order ended through successive conquests rather than a single timeless “fall.”

sectionTitles: Skilled work, from baskets to steel

passages.text: The Kanien’kehá:ka, or Mohawk, are a continuing nation within the Haudenosaunee Confederacy. Their communities have distinct local histories. This imported outline broadly follows the Mohawk Valley and St. Lawrence region; it does not mark one fixed border or imply that the nation ended in 1500.

passages.title: Villages, families and food
passages.text: Mohawk clan identity traditionally passes from mother to child. The nation’s three clans are Bear, Wolf and Turtle, although Akwesasne also includes people from other Haudenosaunee clans. These relationships link families to responsibilities that extend beyond a single household.

passages.title: Villages, families and food
passages.text: At Otsungo, a Mohawk archaeological site not disturbed by plowing, a magnetometer detected buried hearths arranged in rows. Their pattern helped researchers identify longhouses even where wooden walls had vanished. The places people warmed themselves and cooked can outlast the house itself.

passages.title: Villages, families and food
passages.text: The New York State Museum explains longhouse construction using sturdy posts, bent rafters and sheets of bark. Bark lashings tightened as they dried. Building depended on choosing the right trees and harvesting materials at suitable seasons: the forest supplied both walls and fasteners.

passages.title: Villages, families and food
passages.text: The museum’s Mohawk Valley village reconstruction places corn, beans and squash fields near fortified homes. Archaeological interpretation joins buildings with the land needed to feed their occupants. A village was more than the houses inside its palisade; its food-growing landscape mattered too.

passages.title: Skilled work, from baskets to steel
passages.text: Akwesasne cornwashing baskets have a zigzag weave that helps remove the outer hulls from boiled corn during rinsing. Other baskets use an open weave to sift cornmeal, leaving large pieces for further grinding. A kitchen tool’s pattern can be beautiful and useful at the same time.

passages.title: Skilled work, from baskets to steel
passages.text: Black ash supplies strong, thin splints for basketry, but the trees face environmental threats. Akwesasne’s environmental task force collects seeds, records where they grew, dries them and stores them for planting. Protecting a craft can begin with caring for a tree decades before it becomes a basket.

passages.title: Skilled work, from baskets to steel
passages.text: For more than a century, many Kahnawà:ke men worked as ironworkers, often in the United States. The community’s account links this work to language change, as English became increasingly useful. Journeys for work connected life in Kahnawà:ke with distant construction sites.

passages.title: Skilled work, from baskets to steel
passages.text: Kahnawà:ke also maintains its own hospital, schools, social services, police service and media. These institutions are part of contemporary Mohawk life. A history card that stops at longhouses would miss children going to school, patients receiving care and a community managing everyday needs.

passages.title: Displacement, words and continuity
passages.text: The 1784 Haldimand agreement provided land along the Grand River for Mohawk and other Six Nations people after losses during their British alliance in the American Revolution. Its provision extended six miles on each side of the river. This history belongs to particular relocated communities, not to every Mohawk family.

passages.title: Displacement, words and continuity
passages.text: Akwesasne now crosses the Canada to United States border and the boundaries of Ontario, Quebec and New York. It has related but distinct traditional and elected governing bodies. The border divides jurisdictions, while family ties and community identity continue across it.

passages.title: Displacement, words and continuity
passages.text: The Akwesasne Child Care Program greets families with “She:kon/Hello!” Its exact written Mohawk greeting means “Hello!” This is a contemporary language sample from a working community service, not an invented phrase assigned to the map’s 1492 date.

passages.title: Displacement, words and continuity
passages.text: Kahnawà:ke’s language and cultural center began its adult immersion programme in 2002. The two-year course combines instruction with practical exercises and activities outside class. Adults study so that Mohawk can take a fuller place in conversations, families and community life.

War, displacement and colonial policies changed Mohawk communities without ending the nation. Kahnawà:ke, Akwesasne and other communities continue their own political and cultural work. The 1500 map endpoint is a display interval, not an event in which Mohawk people disappeared.

passages.text: The Kansa, Kanza or Kaw are a distinct Dhegiha-speaking people whose river villages and hunting grounds made them influential across Kansas. Their descendants continue as the Kaw Nation. The imported Kansas-region outlines and their 1492 or 1530 start dates are approximate map coverage, not proof of fixed borders or settlements that early; the Nation’s history describes migration toward the Plains over several centuries.

passages.title: Villages, food and useful skills
passages.text: By the middle of the eighteenth century, Kanza influence extended across much of northern and eastern present-day Kansas, with hunting grounds farther west. The state’s name preserves theirs. River valleys supported settlements and movement, while relations with neighboring peoples shaped access to resources and trade.

passages.title: Villages, food and useful skills
passages.text: In the early nineteenth century, households at Fool Chief’s Village lived in bark-covered houses with a central fire and sleeping bunks around the walls. Four to eight large posts supported a lodge, and a roof opening let smoke escape. A blanket or hide served as the door.

passages.title: Villages, food and useful skills
passages.text: The yearly schedule combined farming and travel. Families planted in spring, went on a summer bison hunt, returned for the autumn harvest and hunted again in winter. A village could look quiet because its residents were away doing another essential part of their work.

passages.title: Villages, food and useful skills
passages.text: Bison hides also connected Kanza households to distant markets. The historical society describes readily available manufactured trade goods in their villages. Hunting supplied both household needs and things to exchange, so changes in demand could reach far beyond the place where a hide was prepared.

passages.title: Villages, food and useful skills
passages.text: The flood of 1844 devastated gardens on the Kansas River bottomlands, where Kanza women raised corn, beans, melons and other vegetables. Water swept away crops, houses and fences; another flood followed in 1845. Food security depended on weather and river behavior as well as diplomacy.

passages.title: Villages, food and useful skills
passages.text: Kaw Mission opened classes in 1851 in a two-story stone building at Council Grove. About thirty Kanza boys lived in four upstairs dormitory rooms and studied reading, writing, spelling and arithmetic. Missionaries also sought to teach Christianity and reshape family life; this was far more than a new school building.

passages.title: Villages, food and useful skills
passages.text: Families were selective about that mission: the historical society reports that only orphaned or dependent boys attended, and girls did not. The school closed in 1854 because of its costs. Kanza children’s education cannot be reduced to this short-lived institution or its missionaries’ ambitions.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: The 1825 treaty cut Kanza-controlled land to a narrow reservation west of the future city of Topeka. The Nation describes roughly twenty million acres reduced to about two million. Promised annual payments did not undo the loss of hunting territory or prevent further demands for land.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: The 1846 treaty required another major cession and a move toward Council Grove. Its promises included education, farming support and money for a replacement mill. Federal delays in defining the new reservation left people struggling through relocation, while treaty language offered protections that did not last.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: In 1873, the United States forced the Kanza from Kansas to Indian Territory, now Oklahoma. Congressional action in 1872 had authorized the disposal of their remaining Kansas lands. Distinguishing those two years matters: a law could order removal before families were actually compelled to leave.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: Oklahoma did not bring a permanent end to displacement. Kaw Reservoir later covered land associated with Washunga. The tribal council house, residents and cemetery had to be relocated. Places holding government business, homes and family memory were all affected by the reservoir project.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: Under Chairwoman Wanda Stone and the Executive Council, the Nation entered federal self-governance arrangements with the Indian Health Service in 1995 and the Bureau of Indian Affairs in 1996. These arrangements gave tribal administrators more control over adapting funded services to community needs.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: A small modern writing sample is “Nompéaⁿhi.”, translated in the Kaw Nation’s family language workbook as “I’m hungry.” The raised n marks part of the spelling. It is a useful household sentence from a teaching publication, not a reconstructed inscription from the map’s earliest year.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: The same workbook teaches that a fuller sentence can say whether someone is sitting, standing or moving. Learners practice matching these words to the person they mean. Kanza grammar can keep track of posture while an English speaker is still deciding whether to say “fine” or “tired”.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: In 2025, language students made a film about the forced removal, acting in Kaá’nze with guidance from elders including Little Carol Clark, Lynn Williams and Lavina Spotted Bear. Kaw filmmaker Dylan Bellmard directed it. Children were learning language while helping tell a difficult part of their own history.

passages.title: Land, government and living language
passages.text: The Nation also offers language lessons built around family camping. At its museum, an exhibition combines audio stories with photographs, treaty reproductions and a clan book. These are practical ways to connect speaking, listening and looking at evidence across generations.

The imported map cutoffs do not mark the end of the Kanza people. Forced removal, allotment and reservoir construction transformed their homelands, but the Kaw Nation continues as a self-governing community with elected institutions, language teaching and services for its citizens.

sectionTitles: A capital built for politics and ordinary meals
Family records, weaving and a language still used

passages.text: Kaqchikel communities belong to Guatemala’s Maya world. Before Spanish invasion, Iximche headed a powerful western confederation, while eastern Chajoma’ communities retained substantial independence. The imported 1492-1500 outline is a broad cultural approximation, not proof that Iximche governed every place inside it. This account follows the capital’s archaeology and later Kaqchikel writing, family life and learning.

passages.title: A capital built for politics and ordinary meals
passages.text: Iximche was founded between 1463 and 1470 after a break with K’iche’ power. Its ruling alliance included the Xajil and Sotz’il groups. A rebellion by the Tuquche’ in 1493 reveals sharp disagreements within the confederation, rather than a single harmonious royal household.

passages.title: A capital built for politics and ordinary meals
passages.text: The capital occupied a defensible ridge with steep ravines. Yet archaeological discussion also places settlement beyond its fortified core. Looking only at the surviving plazas would leave much of the lived-in town outside the picture.

passages.title: A capital built for politics and ordinary meals
passages.text: Excavators found built-in benches and sunken hearths in the Great Palace. Grinding stones, obsidian knives, tortilla griddles and kitchen vessels lay among its remains. Even an impressive palace needed equipment for the unglamorous daily business of making dinner.

passages.title: A capital built for politics and ordinary meals
passages.text: The builders levelled plazas on sloping ground and installed cement-lined gutters to carry rainwater away. Managing a downpour was part of urban engineering. These excavated channels document drainage; the report does not identify them as toilets.

passages.title: A capital built for politics and ordinary meals
passages.text: Structure 8 was a ballcourt with a playing area about 100 feet long and 23 feet wide. Two coats of plaster preserved evidence of renovation. Keeping a public playing surface usable was a recurring construction job.

passages.title: A capital built for politics and ordinary meals
passages.text: Temple 2 once had painted decoration in red, yellow and blue. Fine incised outlines helped guide the painted figures. The surviving fragments remind us that buildings now seen as subdued ruins could originally carry vivid color.

passages.title: A capital built for politics and ordinary meals
passages.text: Spanish forces initially entered Iximche as allies in 1524. Abusive tribute demands helped turn alliance into resistance, and Kaqchikel leaders abandoned the city. The struggle continued beyond the capital’s evacuation, with resistance documented at least through 1535.

passages.title: Family records, weaving and a language still used
passages.text: A manuscript now at Penn Libraries includes births, baptisms, marriages, disputes and community contributions dated between 1586 and 1619. Its family record was also a civic record: remembering who married or contributed could matter alongside remembering rulers and wars.

passages.title: Family records, weaving and a language still used
passages.text: The surviving manuscript was probably copied between 1619 and 1650 and contains 50 paper leaves, written in indigo ink. Several Xahila-family writers contributed to its history. Its present form is a colonial-era witness carrying memories of earlier generations.

passages.title: Family records, weaving and a language still used
passages.text: A short written sample is “Haok ki xoh pax pa tinamit vae.” Brinton’s 1885 edition translates its heading as “How We went forth from the City.” It introduces the account of leaving Iximche. This preserves that edition’s spelling, rather than modern standardized Kaqchikel.

passages.title: Family records, weaving and a language still used
passages.text: For a 2008 exhibition, Spurlock Museum displayed three Kaqchikel women’s blouses, or po’t, made on backstrap looms. Their designs represented particular towns. Magda Silvia Sotz Mux served as cultural consultant and guest artist, helping visitors understand clothing through a maker’s knowledge.

passages.title: Family records, weaving and a language still used
passages.text: A health project reported in 2020 worked with midwives to improve a newborn-care phone application. Pictograms and Kaqchikel audio prompts reduced dependence on typed text. Midwives tested changes with the developers, contributing practical expertise about how the tool would work during actual visits.

passages.title: Family records, weaving and a language still used
passages.text: Oxlajuj Aj, Tulane’s Kaqchikel language program in Guatemala, began in 1987. Expert local instructors combine spoken practice with grammar and writing, while local leaders and scholars give presentations. Students learn by using the language, including structured practice that avoids translating every sentence through Spanish or English.

The map’s 1500 cutoff is not an ending. Iximche lost its role during Spanish invasion, but Kaqchikel communities continued recording history and family affairs; Kaqchikel remains a language of teaching and daily expertise.

sectionTitles: Belief, learning and a written message

passages.text: The Qara Khitai built a Central Asian empire after Khitan leaders moved west from the collapsing Liao world. Its history runs from 1124 to the Mongol conquest in 1218, with a change of ruling dynasty in 1211. This imported map starts only in 1200 and ends in 1279; its oversized outline extends far into the northern steppe. Treat it as a rough regional marker, not an exact frontier or survival date.

passages.title: Power, rulers and neighbors
passages.text: Khitan refugees from the Jin conquest of Liao established the new ruling group. Their empire eventually reached from the Oxus region toward the Altai, including much of Xinjiang. Calling it Western Liao preserves its eastern dynastic connection, although its political center now lay in Central Asia.

passages.title: Power, rulers and neighbors
passages.text: The victory over the Seljuks in 1141 had an extraordinary afterlife: news of it helped inspire the European legend of Prester John. A real Central Asian military success became material for a distant imagined Christian ruler. The Qara Khitai rulers themselves were Buddhist.

passages.title: Power, rulers and neighbors
passages.text: Most subordinate rulers kept their own titles and armies. The Qara Khitai directly administered the region around their capital, Balasaghun, but generally did not station permanent troops throughout their vassal states. Governing this empire involved working through other governments.

passages.title: Power, rulers and neighbors
passages.text: Women could exercise supreme political authority. After Yelü Dashi died in 1143, his widow Tabuyan governed while their son was young. Later, Pusuwan, the sister of Yelü Yilie, took power when his sons were still children. These were consequential rulers making military and diplomatic decisions, not merely names beside a king.

passages.title: Power, rulers and neighbors
passages.text: Royal family relationships shaped politics. The Yelü ruling family maintained marriage links with the Xiao family: Tabuyan came from Xiao, and Pusuwan married Xiao Duolubu. Such connections helped organize authority and military leadership. This evidence concerns elite families; it does not describe every household in the empire.

passages.title: Cities, journeys and everyday things
passages.text: The ruling court moved between seasonal pastures. Its route linked winter grazing around Balasaghun with summer areas near the Tian Shan and Issyk Kul. Kochkor lay on this travel corridor. For these mobile elites, changing the season could mean changing the address.

passages.title: Cities, journeys and everyday things
passages.text: Balasaghun was an established town before the Qara Khitai arrived. Its baked-brick minaret, with a spiral staircase inside, dates to the late tenth or early eleventh century. Archaeologists have also found houses, market areas, pottery and jewelry across the town’s long occupation. The new rulers inherited a working urban landscape.

passages.title: Cities, journeys and everyday things
passages.text: Merchants connected places on both sides of the empire. Biran’s study identifies goods from Jin and Song China at Balasaghun and Samarkand, and Muslim merchants from Balasaghun visiting Jin markets. Much eastern commerce appears to have passed through the Tangut state. A journey to market could cross several governments.

passages.title: Cities, journeys and everyday things
passages.text: Fine robes associated with the Khitai were prized at Seljuk and Khwarazmian courts, while Qara Khitai wine reached Jin markets. These exchanges carried fashions and tastes as well as money. They also depended on travelers who could negotiate unfamiliar places and political boundaries.

passages.title: Cities, journeys and everyday things
passages.text: At Kök-Tash in Kyrgyzstan, researchers argue that an underground, house-like brick mausoleum belonged to Qara Khitai elites. It combined features comparable to Liao tombs with local building materials. Its disturbed history makes the attribution a careful archaeological argument, rather than a name conveniently written above the door.

passages.title: Cities, journeys and everyday things
passages.text: Fragments from that mausoleum allowed archaeologists to reconstruct a blue-glazed ceramic table only 21 centimeters high, standing on four legs. Bronze mirrors and jade plates were also found. These are glimpses of elite funerary equipment, not a shopping list for an ordinary family’s kitchen.

passages.title: Belief, learning and a written message
passages.text: Buddhist rulers governed a population that was largely Muslim and settled. Their generally tolerant policies allowed different religious communities to persist under the same imperial roof. The arrangement depended heavily on local institutions and rulers, rather than making every subject adopt the court’s religion.

passages.title: Belief, learning and a written message
passages.text: Learning continued in the subordinate Qarakhanid cities. In Bukhara in 1200, al-Faryabi wrote a work on morality and piety, drawing on earlier books and providing a bibliography. Even medieval authors had to keep track of their reading! This is evidence for learned book culture, not universal school attendance.

passages.title: Belief, learning and a written message
passages.text: A tiny writing sample survives on coins: 續興, read Xuxing, means roughly “Continued prosperity.” It is the era-name portion of the Chinese legend 續興元寳. Numismatists attribute these coins to Yelü Yilie in the mid-twelfth century. The sample is Chinese used by the ruling state, not a translation of Khitan.

passages.title: Belief, learning and a written message
passages.text: The round coins have square central holes. Examples reported from several sites in the Chu valley helped researchers correct an earlier misreading of the inscription and reconsider the emperor’s recorded era name. A small object can make historians reopen a large book, though the reported findspots are not sealed archaeological deposits.

Kuchlug seized power in 1211; the last Khitan Gürkhan died in 1213. Mongol forces eliminated Kuchlug in 1218, ending the polity. The imported 1279 cutoff therefore does not mark its historical fall. Its people and their skills continued under new rulers.

sectionTitles: Read the map before reading the culture
Build a chronology without inventing a nation
Settle between mountains, rivers and grasslands
Cast bronze, shape clay and solve practical problems
Move ideas, foods and objects across wide networks
Bury the dead, remember kin and display differences
Reconstruct families, childhood and learning carefully
Eat, dress, live and work without a fantasy village
Ask what bodies, water and waste can really tell us
Watch traditions change and archaeology improve

passages.text: Stand in the Minusinsk Basin about 3,000 years ago and you might hear livestock, hammering bronze and grain being ground beside a warm hearth. Archaeologists call many of the graves, houses, pots and metal objects here “Karasuk,” after a local river. That is a modern research label, not the name of a kingdom or a people recorded in writing. Communities differed across southern Siberia and neighboring steppes. Some kept cattle, sheep, goats and horses; some added millet to meals; skilled founders cast curved knives, daggers, ornaments and tools. Families built large timber-framed or partly sunken houses, while stone-lined graves preserve food vessels, jewelry and weapons better than ordinary clutter. This uneven survival makes cemeteries look louder than daily life. Radiocarbon dating, isotope chemistry, X-rays, dental study and ancient DNA now reveal overlapping traditions, mobility and mixed ancestry rather than one marching nation. The atlas draws an enormous Karasuk zone from 1500 to 500 BCE. Evidence fits the Minusinsk core best, and most chronologies place its transition toward Tagar and other Early Iron Age traditions around the ninth or eighth century BCE.

passages.title: Read the map before reading the culture
passages.text: The exact target is id “karasuk-culture,” label “Karasuk culture,” kind “culture,” marked circa 1500 to 500 BCE and generated from historical basemaps. It has three border intervals, no live card and no researched override. The imported summary's huge range is a research lead, not proof of a single bounded society.

passages.title: Read the map before reading the culture
passages.text: At 1500 BCE the feature is one polygon with one ring and 46 coordinate positions. Its bounds are 50.506705° to 100.025200° east and 41.314711° to 57.601645° north; the coordinate array hashes to c0948a536114f0baf0c9246d281bee5380591c0ceeb7f85615ad7c40990127b5. This is a reproducible display object, not an excavated frontier.

passages.title: Read the map before reading the culture
passages.text: At 1000 BCE the atlas repeats the 1500 BCE coordinates exactly: one polygon, 46 positions, identical bounds and the same c0948a... coordinate hash. Tested points from the Minusinsk Basin through Altai, central Kazakhstan, the Aral's northeast and the northern Tian Shan all remain inside. A five-century frozen border is strong evidence of basemap reuse.

passages.title: Read the map before reading the culture
passages.text: At 700 BCE the polygon gains one coordinate position and hashes to 0e32fc8397dd530a2cf0bc607e13bb0bef0dc6e87c91f758d1ef16e8af7e18cf, yet its bounds and all nineteen test-point results remain unchanged. Dzungaria, western Mongolia, Baikal, Transbaikal and northern Tarim remain outside. The tiny edit does not repair the enormous historical generalization.

passages.title: Read the map before reading the culture
passages.text: At 2000 BCE, Minusinsk and Altai test points overlap atlas labels for Andronovo and Afanasevo, while central Kazakhstan and the Aral-side steppe are Andronovo. At 500 BCE Karasuk vanishes, but most core and steppe test points are simply blank. These are predecessor and disappearance seams in one dataset, not proven ethnic replacements.

passages.title: Build a chronology without inventing a nation
passages.text: “Karasuk” is an archaeological classification built from recurring burial forms, pottery and metalwork. Yale's comparative description calls the wider tradition a social field of independent, interacting groups without political integration. No king list, capital, tax system or army is known, so the atlas culture layer must never be narrated like an empire.

passages.title: Build a chronology without inventing a nation
passages.text: Researchers traditionally divided the sequence into Classic Karasuk and Kamenniy Log, sometimes called Late Karasuk or Lugavskaya. Human-bone dates put much Classic material in the fourteenth to tenth centuries BCE and Kamenniy Log material in the twelfth to ninth. Because the ranges overlap, they may be partly coexisting traditions rather than neat successive chapters.

passages.title: Build a chronology without inventing a nation
passages.text: A modern chronology review stresses that the Minusinsk Late Bronze Age was long bundled under the Karasuk concept and that absolute dating remains difficult. That warning matters: a label created for ordering finds can hide local sequences, mixed cemeteries and different research traditions. Dates in this card are ranges with uncertainty, not birthdays for a people.

passages.title: Build a chronology without inventing a nation
passages.text: The Poperechnaya-1 burial in the Aley Steppe has a 1500 to 1200 BCE radiocarbon range, a shallow grave, Karasuk-like posture, pottery, meat remains and a curved ring-pommel knife. Its authors interpret mobility beyond Minusinsk. It demonstrates a person's or community's connections, not a political border reaching every point on the atlas polygon.

passages.title: Build a chronology without inventing a nation
passages.text: Cranial measurements and genome-wide comparisons both show variation among people buried with Karasuk-associated material. Classic and Kamenniy Log samples differ, and sampled genomes are highly heterogeneous. Biology cannot supply the missing self-name or language, and neither skull shape nor DNA turns an archaeological assemblage into one ethnicity.

passages.title: Settle between mountains, rivers and grasslands
passages.text: The strongest Karasuk evidence comes from the Khakass-Minusinsk Basin, an intermontane trough ringed by the Western and Eastern Sayan, Abakan Range and Kuznetsk Alatau. The Yenisei and tributaries cross steppe and foothill zones. This compact, resource-rich setting is not equivalent to the atlas's enormous Aral-to-upper-Yenisei shape.

passages.title: Settle between mountains, rivers and grasslands
passages.text: Southern Siberian archaeology long favored visible stone monuments and burial mounds. Systematic survey shows settlements are harder to find and researchers can suffer “monumental myopia.” A cemetery-rich record therefore exaggerates funerals and metal grave gifts while muting herding camps, cooking debris, repairs and the ordinary places where children actually grew up.

passages.title: Settle between mountains, rivers and grasslands
passages.text: At Torgazhaks, excavators found large rectangular, post-framed buildings joined by passages; the regional museum describes some as more than 250 square meters and probably warm-season structures without heating fires. Other partly sunken houses had clay-coated floors, posts, wall benches, hearths and storage pits. These examples are impressive but not a universal floor plan.

passages.title: Settle between mountains, rivers and grasslands
passages.text: Livestock keeping was central, with cattle, sheep, goats and horses represented in the broader synthesis. Later-phase assemblages show a rising sheep-and-goat share, while sickles, mattocks and quernstones point to plant processing. “Pastoral” did not mean wandering every day, and agriculture did not mean every household farmed the same field.

passages.title: Settle between mountains, rivers and grasslands
passages.text: Rivers supplied water and perhaps some fish, but isotope scientists found modern fish can carry a radiocarbon reservoir offset while paired ancient human and land-animal dates mostly do not. That result questions how much freshwater fish contributed to sampled diets. It also shows why archaeologists test water chemistry before turning a bone date into a calendar fact.

passages.title: Cast bronze, shape clay and solve practical problems
passages.text: Curved bronze knives and daggers are famous Karasuk markers. Craftspeople cast them in stone or clay molds and sometimes finished handles with rings, knobs, mushrooms or animal heads. A memorable pommel helps archaeologists compare workshops, but a similar knife hundreds of kilometers away can reflect exchange, imitation or travel instead of one conquering population.

passages.title: Cast bronze, shape clay and solve practical problems
passages.text: Chemical and trace-element work distinguishes the movement of primary copper from the circulation of alloys and finished objects around Minusinsk. Founders still had to control heat, molds and recipes, then finish or recycle metal. That chain of decisions was a major achievement, while individual specialists' names and social standing remain unknown.

passages.title: Cast bronze, shape clay and solve practical problems
passages.text: X-ray fluorescence found tin in the Poperechnaya-1 ring-pommel knife, an alloy pattern uncommon in local Irmen metal. One tested blade cannot define all “Karasuk bronze”: ores, recipes and recycling varied across space. Chemical analysis works best beside shape, burial context and radiocarbon evidence, which is exactly why the study combined all four.

passages.title: Cast bronze, shape clay and solve practical problems
passages.text: Hand-built vessels could have rounded or flat bases, fine slip or burnished surfaces. Potters arranged zigzags, rhombs, triangles, chevrons and meanders, sometimes filling patterns with white paste against a dark surface. Decoration shows learned choices and social signaling; it does not decode into a lost alphabet, and plain pots mattered just as much for daily work.

passages.title: Cast bronze, shape clay and solve practical problems
passages.text: Weapons include daggers and spearheads, while later contexts contain simple bridle pieces. These objects show that people could fight and manage horses; they do not reveal a standing army, casualty count or named war. Burial display can make weapons seem commoner than they were at home, so conflict must remain a possibility rather than the card's main plot.

passages.title: Move ideas, foods and objects across wide networks
passages.text: Bronze mirrors and related technologies crossed Central Asia and northern China through complicated networks. Modern network analysis warns against treating every matching object as a migrating tribe. Raw metal, finished gifts, traveling founders, copied molds and local experiments can all spread a form. The atlas's smooth polygon hides those branching paths.

passages.title: Move ideas, foods and objects across wide networks
passages.text: The Aley burial's authors connect increased mobility with craft and trade centers near ore sources in the Ob-Irtysh steppe and central Kazakhstan. “Probably” matters: a knife's alloy and a grave's parallels support contact, but cannot identify the traveler's route, language or motive. Trade here is an archaeological model built from converging clues.

passages.title: Move ideas, foods and objects across wide networks
passages.text: Stable carbon isotopes place regular millet consumption in southern Siberia during the Late Bronze Age, after earlier claimed examples were redated. Sickles, querns and mattocks fit cereal work, and contact with northern China is plausible. Yet bone chemistry records foods eaten over years, not a seed's farm, recipe or merchant, so the exact route stays open.

passages.title: Move ideas, foods and objects across wide networks
passages.text: A Karasuk-like knife or burial outside Minusinsk is most useful when compared with local material. At Pyatiletka-1, four radiocarbon dates, birch timbers, nearby clay and an unusual rite were studied together before migration was proposed. This method respects the neighboring Irmen, Korchazhka and Yelovka traditions instead of erasing them under one big name.

passages.title: Move ideas, foods and objects across wide networks
passages.text: The atlas includes central Kazakhstan, the Aral-side steppe and northern Tian Shan but excludes Dzungaria and western Mongolia, a crisp division no excavation synthesis supports. Comparative scholarship instead pictures independent communities sharing selected technologies. Use the polygon to find a topic; use dated sites to decide what actually belongs in a historical claim.

passages.title: Bury the dead, remember kin and display differences
passages.text: Many graves were pits or stone cists within square or rectangular stone enclosures, sometimes covered by low mounds. Bodies and containers followed recurring orientations and placements, but practices changed by phase and locality. The durable stone makes death unusually visible; wooden household objects and soft furnishings rarely receive the same archaeological spotlight.

passages.title: Bury the dead, remember kin and display differences
passages.text: Some graves held one or two bowls near the head and meat near the feet. These were funeral offerings, not a complete menu for the deceased's lifetime. They show that food and containers mattered in burial ritual, while isotope chemistry and settlement debris are needed before telling children that everyone ate the same ceremonial portion each day.

passages.title: Bury the dead, remember kin and display differences
passages.text: Many graves had few objects or none, while others included beads, vessels, bronze tools or weapons. That contrast may reflect status, age, gender, ritual choice, disturbance or unequal survival. It supports cautious discussion of social inequality, but not a made-up pyramid of kings, nobles and peasants for which Karasuk evidence does not exist.

passages.title: Bury the dead, remember kin and display differences
passages.text: Analysis of roughly four hundred anthropologically sexed tombs found small cemetery clusters interpreted as family groups, with adults central and younger people arranged around them. This is valuable evidence for kinship in mortuary organization. A burial cluster still cannot tell us exactly who shared a house, inherited livestock or made everyday family decisions.

passages.title: Bury the dead, remember kin and display differences
passages.text: Engraved river pebbles from Torgazhaks show faces, figures and geometric designs; some have been interpreted in fertility or birth rituals. Rock-art specialists also warn that style-based dates can blur Karasuk, transitional and later Scythian images. Pictures provide evidence for visual practice, but their meanings are hypotheses, not captions left by the artists.

passages.title: Reconstruct families, childhood and learning carefully
passages.text: Kin-group cemetery clusters make family an evidence-based part of the story, yet “family” may have included relatives, marriage partners, fostered children and dependents in arrangements we cannot name. Archaeology sees chosen burial relationships, not every affectionate, tense or practical relationship at home. Household reconstructions should therefore stay plural and modest.

passages.title: Reconstruct families, childhood and learning carefully
passages.text: Women's graves in the analyzed sample often contained more jewelry and clothing ornaments, while some high-status burials included awls, beads and shell imitations. These patterns show that gender shaped funeral display. They cannot prove that every woman sewed, lacked political influence or held the same rank in life as a nearby man.

passages.title: Reconstruct families, childhood and learning carefully
passages.text: Children and infants appear in family cemetery layouts, often toward cluster edges, so they were included in acts of remembrance rather than absent from society. Grave placement can reveal age categories, but it does not preserve games, chores, affection or discipline. A quiet child's grave should not become a complete biography.

passages.title: Reconstruct families, childhood and learning carefully
passages.text: No school building, alphabet lesson or named teacher is securely known. Children probably learned herding, pottery, food preparation, building and metalwork by watching and practicing with older people, but that is an inference from skilled traditions, not a surviving timetable. Apprenticeship is a careful model; a Karasuk classroom would be an invention.

passages.title: Reconstruct families, childhood and learning carefully
passages.text: No securely identified Karasuk toy, board game or children's song appears in the cited excavation syntheses. Decorated pebbles and miniature-looking objects may tempt playful guesses, but ritual, tool and ornament interpretations also exist. The evidence-safe answer is that children surely played, while the rules, words and favorite objects have not survived clearly.

passages.title: Eat, dress, live and work without a fantasy village
passages.text: Food evidence combines livestock bones, grain-processing tools, residues, burial offerings and human isotopes. Cattle, sheep, goats, horses, millet and probably other gathered or cultivated foods did not appear in identical proportions everywhere. A recent review estimates meaningful millet intake in sampled Karasuk people but warns that dental differences cannot simply be blamed on one crop.

passages.title: Eat, dress, live and work without a fantasy village
passages.text: Beads, plaques, buttons and bronze clothing ornaments show that garments could carry visible decoration, especially in burial. Fibers, hides and ordinary work clothes preserve poorly, so exact cuts, colors and seasonal wardrobes remain uncertain. Jewelry can tell us where something was placed on a body more confidently than what every living person wore.

passages.title: Eat, dress, live and work without a fantasy village
passages.text: Some houses were partly dug into the ground for insulation; later rectangular examples reached roughly 150 to 160 square meters and held hearths in rows. Large space may have sheltered extended households or shared work, but floor area does not count residents automatically. Even a Bronze Age house could feel crowded without supplying archaeologists a guest list.

passages.title: Eat, dress, live and work without a fantasy village
passages.text: Quernstones, mattocks, awls, molds, knives and animal gear reveal jobs: tending herds, cutting plants, grinding grain, sewing, casting metal and repairs. Grave context rarely tells who performed each task. Assigning every tool to men or women would paste modern expectations onto incomplete evidence.

passages.title: Eat, dress, live and work without a fantasy village
passages.text: Hearths warmed rooms and cooked food, while handmade pots carried, stored or served it. A line of hearths in a large house might look like an ancient catering operation, but its actual scheduling is unknown. Soot, broken pottery and floor features reveal repeated work more reliably than a specific stew or household recipe.

passages.title: Ask what bodies, water and waste can really tell us
passages.text: A dental study compared 214 people from five Minusinsk cultural horizons. Karasuk-associated teeth contributed evidence for calculus, caries, enamel hypoplasia, tooth loss and age-related decline. These markers reveal diet and physiological stress only imperfectly; they are not patient charts, and apparent differences can reflect age, sampling and preservation.

passages.title: Ask what bodies, water and waste can really tell us
passages.text: No medical recipe, named healer, surgical manual or securely identified Karasuk medicine kit survives. One peripheral, culturally debated burial contained an adult who survived a cranial opening, showing skilled intervention without proving a general medical system. Skeletal and dental lesions reveal stress more readily than herbs, splints, anesthesia or a healer's title.

passages.title: Ask what bodies, water and waste can really tell us
passages.text: Settlements in the core basin lay within a landscape crossed by the Yenisei, Abakan, Oya, Tuba and smaller waterways. People could fetch water, but no Karasuk aqueduct, piped network or standardized well system is established by the cited sources. River access is geographic evidence; the pot, path and person carrying each drink are mostly missing.

passages.title: Ask what bodies, water and waste can really tell us
passages.text: No securely published Karasuk toilet, latrine, sewer or purpose-built waste drain appears in these sources. Settlement archaeology is much thinner than cemetery archaeology, so absence of a found toilet is not proof that people ignored cleanliness. It means we should not draw a Bronze Age bathroom where excavation has not identified one.

passages.title: Ask what bodies, water and waste can really tell us
passages.text: Hearth ash, storage pits, animal remains and broken pots can enter occupation layers through cooking, dumping, cleaning, reuse, trampling and later disturbance. Without a sealed waste feature, archaeologists cannot label every dirty patch a rubbish heap. Karasuk sanitation probably relied on household routines, but their frequency and rules are unknown.

passages.title: Watch traditions change and archaeology improve
passages.text: Radiocarbon work places the transition from Kamenniy Log-associated Karasuk material to the earliest Tagar culture around the ninth century BCE. “Transition” fits better than “fall”: pottery, metal skills, households and populations could continue while burial styles and classifications changed. The atlas's 500 BCE endpoint is therefore not a defensible destruction date.

passages.title: Watch traditions change and archaeology improve
passages.text: The culture was named after finds near the Karasuk River and organized as an archaeological category through early twentieth-century work. Older knife typologies helped build the sequence, but later radiocarbon science revised it. Jettmar's 1950 study is valuable as history of research, not a final ethnic map or modern chronology.

passages.title: Watch traditions change and archaeology improve
passages.text: Direct human-bone dates reduce dependence on matching object shapes, but samples still bring problems. Old timber or charcoal can predate a grave; intrusive later burials can look too young; mixed cemeteries can combine periods. Researchers test context and material instead of accepting a machine-generated date without archaeological review.

passages.title: Watch traditions change and archaeology improve
passages.text: Modern investigation combines radiocarbon dating, X-ray fluorescence, clay and wood identification, dental pathology, isotopes, ancient DNA and Raman spectroscopy. At Boyary I, pigment chemistry is precise while a Karasuk date remains stylistic and tentative. Better instruments sharpen a measurement; they do not automatically settle which cultural label belongs on an image.

passages.title: Watch traditions change and archaeology improve
passages.text: Written-language sample: none securely known. Original script: not applicable. Transliteration: not applicable. Translation: not applicable. Date and context: Karasuk-associated communities of the late second to early first millennium BCE are reconstructed from objects, graves, houses and bodies. Geometric pot designs, engraved pebbles and petroglyphs are visual evidence, not demonstrated writing, so inventing readable words would be false.

By roughly the ninth or eighth century BCE, assemblages in the Minusinsk Basin are usually classified within emerging Tagar and other Early Iron Age traditions. That change involved continuity as well as new burial forms, horse use, metalwork and regional networks. The atlas keeps “Karasuk culture” until 500 BCE, then deletes the polygon without filling most tested core points. No evidence supports a single conquest, collapse or vanished people at that seam.
