sectionTitles: A dynasty across cities and caravan routes
A dictionary and a small sample of writing

passages.text: The Qarakhanids linked Central Asian cities, mountain routes and Turkic ruling families. Their eastern and western branches followed different political paths. This map’s 1100 to 1200 span and oversized single outline are approximate coverage, not the dynasty’s lifetime or a frontier. Earlier foundations and later conquests appear below as context.

passages.title: A dynasty across cities and caravan routes
passages.text: The ruling family treated the realm as a collective inheritance, distributing territories among its members. Around 1040 it divided into western and eastern khanates, associated with Samarkand and with Balasaghun and Kashgar. Several royal relatives could exercise power at once, making a single list of kings misleading.

passages.title: A dynasty across cities and caravan routes
passages.text: The Qara Khitai took Balasaghun in 1134 and defeated the Seljuk-led alliance at Qatwan in 1141. Qarakhanid princes still ruled locally under the new overlords. A familiar dynasty could remain on coins even after its freedom to decide policy had shrunk.

passages.title: A dynasty across cities and caravan routes
passages.text: Travel to Song China involved paperwork and limits as well as camels. In 1078 the Chinese court restricted a Qarakhanid delegation to fifty people. Duturaeva’s study also identifies an earlier mission lodged at a postal station in Kaifeng, whose delegation included diplomatic and military officers.

passages.title: A dynasty across cities and caravan routes
passages.text: Meng Yuanlao’s account of New Year audiences in Kaifeng describes envoys from Khotan arriving with wives and sons. He noticed patterned felt hats, belted robes and camels carrying bags and bronze bells. This specific court scene puts families into the history of long-distance travel; the caravan certainly did not arrive silently.

passages.title: Streets, baths and meals
passages.text: Excavations at Taraz have exposed residential and commercial buildings, a main street, a water-supply system and caravanserais where travellers could stop. The remains connect the city’s famous trading role with the practical work of maintaining streets, buildings and water. The excavations of 2011 to 2016 added substantially to this picture.

passages.title: Streets, baths and meals
passages.text: Two bathhouses beneath the area of Taraz’s modern central market were dated to the tenth through twelfth centuries. One uncovered in the 1960s had four rooms, a clay seat and troughs or bathing basins. Bathing required a purpose-built place with fittings, not merely a convenient stretch of river.

passages.title: Streets, baths and meals
passages.text: Another Taraz bathhouse, excavated in 1938, had richly decorated walls: yellow six- and eight-pointed stars stood against a reddish-brown ground, with stems and leaves nearby. The museum interprets its layout as separate male and female sections. A washing trip could also put a bather in a room full of patterns.

passages.title: Streets, baths and meals
passages.text: For earlier regional food history, the mountain town of Tashbulak in present-day Uzbekistan offers something better than a guessed menu: ancient food remains. Its ninth- to eleventh-century deposits included peach and grape remains, melon seeds, and walnut and pistachio shells. These finds record foods handled at this particular town.

passages.title: Streets, baths and meals
passages.text: Tashbulak stood roughly 2,200 metres above sea level, too high for many of the fruit trees represented in its refuse. Researchers infer that lower-elevation communities supplied some of these foods. Mountain-town life depended on connections with farming districts; a peach could have travelled uphill before someone ate it.

passages.title: Streets, baths and meals
passages.text: The food study sampled a rubbish deposit beside an area interpreted as a bazaar. Researchers used flotation to recover small plant remains from soil, then identified seeds and fragments. A discarded fruit stone can become evidence of trade centuries later. Archaeology sometimes gives the rubbish heap the last word.

passages.title: Care, learning and skilled work
passages.text: A document from 1066, before this map’s century, established an endowment for a hospital serving poor people at Samarkand. It placed the institution south of the main bazaar. This is concrete evidence for organized medical care in the Qarakhanid city, although the document does not supply a complete guide to its treatments.

passages.title: Care, learning and skilled work
passages.text: A second 1066 document supported a madrasa, an institution of learning. The endowments described income-producing properties, many of them caravanserais near the bazaar. Education and care were therefore tied to the city’s commercial property. The college’s precise identification among excavated ruins remains disputed.

passages.title: Care, learning and skilled work
passages.text: Excavated palace pavilions at Samarkand preserve another side of eleventh- and twelfth-century life. Fallen wall paintings included birds, dancers, hunting dogs and guards presenting royal symbols. These were elite settings, but the fragments preserve the work of painters and decorators whose names the royal chronicles rarely celebrate.

passages.title: Care, learning and skilled work
passages.text: At Uzgen, archaeologists uncovered a pottery workshop with four rectangular furnaces dated to the late twelfth century. Firing vessels required a workshop, fuel and careful control of heat. These remains make the craft workers behind city life visible alongside the more conspicuous monuments of their rulers.

passages.title: Care, learning and skilled work
passages.text: Uzgen’s attached brick mausoleums carried carved plaster, terracotta ornament and bands of writing. Their inscriptions include dates in 1152, 1186 and 1187, connecting architecture with the dynasty’s later generations and commanders. The lettering was part of the building’s decoration as well as a way of remembering the dead.

passages.title: Care, learning and skilled work
passages.text: Bukhara’s Kalyan minaret preserves a more personal building record: terracotta inscriptions date construction to 1127 under Arslan Khan and name its builder, Bako. A steep spiral stair runs inside the tower. Its survival gives the medieval skyline a named craftsperson as well as a royal patron.

passages.title: A dictionary and a small sample of writing
passages.text: Mahmud of Kashgar completed his compendium of Turkic language in Baghdad in 1074, intending to teach Turkic to Arabic speakers. Its only known surviving manuscript is a later copy completed in 1266, now in Istanbul’s Millet Manuscript Library. The distinction matters: an eleventh-century work can survive in a book copied almost two centuries afterward.

passages.title: A dictionary and a small sample of writing
passages.text: A Qarakhanid copper coin in the Ashmolean bears the Arabic words محمد رسول الله, meaning “Muḥammad is the messenger of God.” The museum dates it to before 1178 and attributes it to Sulayman Tafghaj Khan. This is Arabic religious writing on a dynasty’s coin, not a sample of Turkic speech; the short excerpt joins the inscription’s line breaks.

The map stops in 1200, before the final dynastic losses. The eastern restoration attempt failed in 1211; Khwarazmian expansion extinguished western and Ferghana rule in 1212-13. These political endings did not erase the region’s towns, communities or Turkic literary traditions.

passages.text: Picture a confederation moving between cold mountain pastures and busy Silk Roads towns. The Karluks were never one frozen tribe or a tidy modern country. In the early 700s, their leaders served and fought larger Türk empires; then Karluks joined the revolt that broke the Second Türk empire, lost a struggle with the Uyghurs and moved west. They helped the Abbasid side win at Talas in 751 and by 766 controlled Suyab and Talas under a ruler called yabghu. Herds, irrigated fields, workshops, caravans and several religions met in their realm. After 840, some rulers claimed higher prestige, but the later Qarakhanid dynasty cannot safely be called simply “the Karluks.” Islam spread gradually, especially after Samanid forces captured Talas in 893, while named Karluk groups continued for centuries. The atlas adds two giant caution signs: its 700 polygon lies far east of the later heartland, and the target vanishes at 800 and 1000 despite being indexed continuously. Treat its shapes as snapshots from an imported historical dataset, not hoofprint-perfect borders.

passages.title: Begin with the atlas, including its missing centuries
passages.text: The exact target is karluks, labelled “Karluks” and indexed circa 700 to 1000. Initial coverage called it an approximate state with two mapped intervals, 700 to 800 and 900 to 1000, and no card. Those ranges describe atlas files, not three centuries of one fixed border or government.

passages.title: Begin with the atlas, including its missing centuries
passages.text: At 700 the target is one Polygon with one ring and 16 coordinate positions, a small eastern outline rather than a continent-wide claim. Its bounds are [84.55944559445595, 39.71380489249975, 101.05121051210511, 46.205906017734634], and its coordinate SHA-256 is f9cf29d6bbd20652b1d201baa40210f20ff4e830c86a984173b3f79ad3d93f6d. Those figures come from decoded coordinates.

passages.title: Begin with the atlas, including its missing centuries
passages.text: That 700 shape contains Beshbalik/Jimsar but misses Suyab, Balasagun, Taraz, Talas, Issyk-Kul and Ili. A separate Western Turk feature covers several western points, while Göktürk and Tibetan features cover other tested places. The map shows an eastern snapshot, not the later Karluk heartland.

passages.title: Begin with the atlas, including its missing centuries
passages.text: The target disappears entirely at 800, although this is the best-documented century of the Karluk yabghu around Suyab and Talas. At 900 it returns as a much larger, west-shifted 138-position Polygon, bounds [64.94644946449466, 39.68339044940879, 91.33471334713346, 46.682859784388384], hash 1020a34a849e86cad0216d704c81a64a35f26250a877e53415a3fda167c592bd. The change is geometrically dramatic.

passages.title: Begin with the atlas, including its missing centuries
passages.text: The 900 shape includes Suyab, Balasagun, Taraz, Talas, Issyk-Kul, Ili, Beshbalik, Tashkent and Otrar, but misses Kashgar, Fergana, Samarkand and Bukhara. Karluks vanish again at 1000; the separately indexed karkhanids appear only at 1100. These are atlas seams, not proof of mass disappearance.

passages.title: A mobile federation emerged between rival Türk powers
passages.text: Early Karluks were a federation rather than a single bloodline or nation-state. One eighth-century inscription presents three component groups, while a later geographical work counts seven. The different numbers probably reflect changing coalitions and labels, so neither should be frozen into an eternal tribal checklist.

passages.title: A mobile federation emerged between rival Türk powers
passages.text: Chinese accounts place Karluk groups around the upper Irtysh and northern Tien Shan under Western Türk authority in the mid-seventh century. Their economy was strongly pastoral. Subordination did not erase their own leaders, followers or ability to change alliances when imperial power weakened.

passages.title: A mobile federation emerged between rival Türk powers
passages.text: Eastern Türk rulers extended control over them in the early eighth century, but Karluks rebelled during 711 to 714. That conflict belongs before the atlas polygon’s later westward story: it helps explain why a group seen east of the Tien Shan could become a major actor farther west.

passages.title: A mobile federation emerged between rival Türk powers
passages.text: Karluks joined Basmils and Uyghurs against the Second Türk empire in 742 to 745. Victory did not create a Karluk empire: Uyghur leaders won the contest among the allies, defeated Karluk forces and pushed many west. Confederation politics could turn yesterday’s teammate into tomorrow’s pursuer.

passages.title: A mobile federation emerged between rival Türk powers
passages.text: The atlas has separate gokturk, western-gokturk-khaganate and uyghurs ids; no independent Türgesh id was found in the audited index. Those data choices must stay distinct from history: Karluks served, fought and succeeded parts of these coalitions without becoming aliases for every Türk-speaking neighbor.

passages.title: War and diplomacy carried them toward Suyab and Talas
passages.text: Tang forces captured Suyab in 748, and an Abbasid army with Karluk support defeated the Tang near Talas in 751. The sources agree Karluks mattered in the battle; accounts differ over timing and motives, so the familiar tale of one perfectly timed battlefield betrayal deserves caution.

passages.title: War and diplomacy carried them toward Suyab and Talas
passages.text: Talas did not make Karluks the inventors of paper. Papermaking already existed in China and paper reached western markets before 751; the story of captive artisans founding the first Samarkand mill may be partly legend. A dramatic battle is memorable, but technology travels through longer networks.

passages.title: War and diplomacy carried them toward Suyab and Talas
passages.text: By 766 Karluk leaders had taken Suyab and Talas and eliminated competing Türgesh khagans after prolonged factional war. Their ruler used yabghu, a prestigious title below khagan. This was a new regional balance built from migration, alliance and seizure, not an empty land awaiting arrival.

passages.title: War and diplomacy carried them toward Suyab and Talas
passages.text: Suyab itself had been founded and developed largely by Sogdians before Karluk rule. Its roads, craft quarters and shrines connected Chinese, Sogdian, Turkic and other communities. Capturing a city meant governing inherited people and infrastructure, not replacing everyone behind its walls overnight.

passages.title: War and diplomacy carried them toward Suyab and Talas
passages.text: Muslim geographers later placed the Karluk to Oghuz frontier near Isfijab on the middle Syr Darya and Karluk settlement south of Issyk-Kul. Some Karluk groups reached upper Oxus country. These reports describe a broad, shifting human landscape; they do not outline a surveyed sovereign border.

passages.title: A yabghu governed people, routes and negotiated loyalties
passages.text: The early paramount leader was called elteber under Türk overlords; later the western confederation’s ruler was a yabghu. Neither title automatically meant an all-powerful khagan. Authority depended on component groups, military followers, pastures, towns and deals with neighboring courts, and could weaken when alliances shifted.

passages.title: A yabghu governed people, routes and negotiated loyalties
passages.text: A Karluk yabghu joined Sogdian and Tibetan interests in supporting the rebel Rafi ibn Layth against Caliph Harun al-Rashid. That episode shows Karluk diplomacy working across language and religion. It also warns against drawing clean civilizational teams on a frontier full of temporary partnerships.

passages.title: A yabghu governed people, routes and negotiated loyalties
passages.text: The Uyghur empire’s collapse in 840 changed steppe prestige, and later traditions associate Karluk rulers with claims to the title khagan. Evidence for the exact moment and succession is thin. A higher title could announce ambition without proving a centralized replacement empire appeared on schedule.

passages.title: A yabghu governed people, routes and negotiated loyalties
passages.text: Qarakhanid origins remain debated because early internal narratives are lost and coins do much of the historical work. Karluk, Chigil, Yaghma and Uyghur explanations have all been proposed. The safest wording is that Karluks were an important component, not that every Qarakhanid was simply a renamed Karluk.

passages.title: A yabghu governed people, routes and negotiated loyalties
passages.text: Satuk Bughra Khan’s conversion near Kashgar, his death around 955, the reported mass conversion around 960 and the conquests of Bukhara in 992 and 999 belong to Qarakhanid history. They explain transformation near the atlas endpoint without turning the whole 700 to 1000 card into one dynasty.

passages.title: Herds, fields, workshops and caravans shared the landscape
passages.text: Pastoral families managed sheep, horses, cattle, camels and goats, while towns and foothill oases supported grain and garden agriculture. Mobile people needed manufactured goods and settled food; towns needed animals, transport and wool. The Karluk economy worked through those connections, not a herder-versus-farmer wall.

passages.title: Herds, fields, workshops and caravans shared the landscape
passages.text: Irrigation sustained much Central Asian cultivation, especially around older Sogdian settlements. Karluk rule inherited canals, fields and skilled communities rather than inventing them. Exact eighth-century yields around Suyab are unknown, so the card does not turn regional agricultural patterns into a fake harvest spreadsheet.

passages.title: Herds, fields, workshops and caravans shared the landscape
passages.text: Sogdian merchants had dominated many overland routes under earlier Türk protection. Their networks weakened after Tang withdrawal, partly revived under Uyghurs and changed again under Samanids. Karluk territory sat within this moving system of caravans, tolls, diplomacy and multilingual brokerage.

passages.title: Herds, fields, workshops and caravans shared the landscape
passages.text: Silk, musk, silverwork, amber, medicinal plants, perfumes, precious metals and enslaved people appear among long-distance goods. A caravan catalogue reveals regional exchange and exploitation; it does not mean each Karluk household owned exotic perfume or that every traveller crossed the whole route.

passages.title: Herds, fields, workshops and caravans shared the landscape
passages.text: Coins show changing public languages. Earlier Western Türk issues in Semirechye carry Sogdian inscriptions; ninth- and tenth-century “proto-Qarakhanid” issues increasingly use Arabic Kufic. Numismatists do not label every coin Karluk, but the sequence reveals institutions that outlived a single ruling coalition.

passages.title: Belief changed by town, camp and century
passages.text: The 732 Kül Tigin inscription invokes the sky god Tengri and a sacred Türk political world, useful context for early Karluk rivals and allies. It is an external elite monument, not a Karluk creed. The reviewed sources do not preserve one statement of belief spoken for every Karluk group.

passages.title: Belief changed by town, camp and century
passages.text: Suyab’s archaeology includes Buddhist sanctuaries, a Zoroastrian cemetery and Nestorian Christian churches. Their dates and users vary, but together they show that Karluk rulers inherited a religiously mixed city. A shrine inside their realm did not automatically convert every herding family outside it.

passages.title: Belief changed by town, camp and century
passages.text: Contact with Muslim merchants, towns and courts began before mass conversion. The Samanid ruler Ismail ibn Ahmad attacked and captured Talas in 893, and tenth-century geographers noted mosques in towns east of Talas. Islamization was a process with uneven local timing, not one day’s switch.

passages.title: Belief changed by town, camp and century
passages.text: Ak-Beshim also produced crosses, Christian objects, Turkic-Sogdian inscriptions and a later manuscript codex. Several finds come from tenth- or early eleventh-century contexts. They illuminate the city’s long transition, while their presence cannot identify the religion or literacy of an unnamed Karluk household.

passages.title: Belief changed by town, camp and century
passages.text: UNESCO describes Ak-Beshim and Burana as Silk Roads towns where Indian, Chinese, Sogdian and Turkic traditions met. That broad heritage framing is useful, but its tentative-list boundaries and later monuments should not be mistaken for the exact Karluk polygon or a single-period settlement plan.

passages.title: Families and children are visible mostly around the edges
passages.text: A confederation joined named groups under leaders and followers, so kinship and political loyalty mattered, but the sources reviewed do not give an ordinary Karluk family size, marriage age or household rulebook. Royal titles tell us about rank more readily than affection, adoption or daily care.

passages.title: Families and children are visible mostly around the edges
passages.text: Society included mobile pastoral households, warriors and chiefs, along with farmers, merchants, artisans and religious specialists in towns. These categories overlapped and were unequal. Sources spotlight male rulers, while women’s herding, textile, food and family work is plausible but seldom individually documented for Karluks.

passages.title: Families and children are visible mostly around the edges
passages.text: No surviving Karluk school register or child’s exercise survives from 700 to 1000 in the reviewed evidence. A Chinese account says Sogdian boys in Kang began book and commercial study at five; that is useful urban comparison, not permission to assign the same classroom to every Karluk child.

passages.title: Families and children are visible mostly around the edges
passages.text: Pastoral children probably learned animal care, routes, tools and weather through household work, an inference from the economy rather than a Karluk lesson plan. Children in multilingual towns could encounter Sogdian, Turkic, Chinese and later Arabic writing, but access depended on family, occupation and status.

passages.title: Families and children are visible mostly around the edges
passages.text: Archaeologists at Ak-Beshim combine excavation, ground-penetrating radar, animal-bone study, plant remains and radiocarbon dating. That teamwork can reconstruct activities rulers ignored. Even so, identifying a small object as a child’s possession is difficult because adults also spun thread, played games and lost things.

passages.title: Homes, clothes, food, work and play changed across the centuries
passages.text: Mobile pastoralists used portable shelters and felt-working traditions, while towns had mud-brick buildings. No excavated structure can be securely labelled a standard eighth-century “Karluk tent.” The honest picture allows tents, camps and city houses without pretending one floor plan served everyone.

passages.title: Homes, clothes, food, work and play changed across the centuries
passages.text: Late tenth-century Ak-Beshim houses had two-room plans, wall benches, ovens and domestic pottery; tools included knives, awls, beads and spindle whorls. These are valuable atlas-end, early Qarakhanid-transition clues. They cannot be copied backward unchanged into a Karluk camp of 720.

passages.title: Homes, clothes, food, work and play changed across the centuries
passages.text: Felt, rugs, leather footwear, horse equipment and jewelry belonged to regional pastoral manufacture and exchange. Directly dated Karluk wardrobes are scarce, so bright costume reconstructions should be labelled artistic. Clothes had to handle riding and weather, but no source supplies one mandatory Karluk outfit.

passages.title: Homes, clothes, food, work and play changed across the centuries
passages.text: Late tenth- to early eleventh-century Ak-Beshim deposits contain sheep and goat most often, then cattle and some horse, plus barley, wheat, millet, lentil, grapes, melons, apples, pear and pomegranate. This is an urban transition menu and waste record, not three centuries of identical Karluk dinners.

passages.title: Homes, clothes, food, work and play changed across the centuries
passages.text: A worn, perforated sheep ankle bone was catalogued as a chuko game piece, and excavators noted a possible ceramic bell. Both come from the late occupation horizon; player age and the bell’s use remain uncertain. Archaeology gives us a game clue, not a complete tournament bracket or concert programme.

passages.title: Medicine, water and toilets require unusually careful labels
passages.text: A modern study of Tibetan medical histories finds a notice connecting the physician Harina with Garlok, interpreted as Qarluq. This is a later textual tradition, not a surviving Karluk medical manual or excavated clinic. It hints at knowledge exchange but cannot reconstruct everyday diagnosis, herbs or surgery.

passages.title: Medicine, water and toilets require unusually careful labels
passages.text: Medicinal plants travelled in Central Asian trade, but a commodity list is not a prescription. Families surely cared for injury, childbirth and illness, yet the reviewed sources do not securely identify a Karluk healer’s kit or treatment recipe. The card therefore keeps practical medicine largely unknown.

passages.title: Medicine, water and toilets require unusually careful labels
passages.text: Water supported animals, irrigated fields and dense towns. At Ak-Beshim, one late pit may have been a well or toilet, but excavators found no clear water-flow trace and later refuse filled it. Ambiguity is the result: one hole cannot confidently be both plumbing diagram and privy.

passages.title: Medicine, water and toilets require unusually careful labels
passages.text: Another deep pit was cautiously called a presumed toilet because of its contents and stratigraphy. Both sanitation candidates date around the late tenth or early eleventh century, near or just beyond the atlas endpoint. Neither proves that eighth-century Karluk camps or towns used the same arrangement.

passages.title: Medicine, water and toilets require unusually careful labels
passages.text: Excavated streets had gravel and slag surfaces, but the studied section produced no confirmed ditch for rainwater or sewage. Burana preserves later bathhouse and water-main evidence from Qarakhanid urban life. No secure 700 to 900 Karluk latrine, sewer or hygiene rule survives in the reviewed record.

passages.title: One stone sentence names the Karluks, but from outside
passages.text: The Kül Tigin memorial was erected in 732 for an elite of the Second Türk empire. Its Turkic sides use the right-to-left Old Turkic runiform script, while another face carries Chinese. It is contemporary evidence about Karluks from a rival court, not a Karluk-authored national monument.

passages.title: One stone sentence names the Karluks, but from outside
passages.text: Original script, Kül Tigin North 1: “𐰚𐰇𐰠𐱅𐰃𐰏𐰤 : 𐰘𐰃𐱅𐰃𐰆𐱃𐰔 : 𐰖𐱁𐰃𐰭𐰀 : 𐰴𐰺𐰞𐰸 : 𐰉𐰆𐰑𐰣 : 𐰼𐰇𐰼 : 𐰉𐰺𐰆𐰺 : 𐰼𐰚𐰠𐰃 : 𐰖𐰍𐰃 : 𐰉𐰆𐰡𐰃”. It is a complete carved sentence on the memorial monument, and the visible qarluq bodun words mean “Karluk people” in its own political context.

passages.title: One stone sentence names the Karluks, but from outside
passages.text: Transliteration: “Kül Tigin yiti otuz yašïna qarluq bodun ärür barur ärklï yaγï boltï.” Translation: “When Prince Kül was twenty-seven years old, the Karluk people became an enemy who began to act freely and independently.” Punctuation and spelling follow a modern scholarly edition.

passages.title: One stone sentence names the Karluks, but from outside
passages.text: The sentence reports conflict from the victors’ memorial voice. It proves that the name Qarluq/Karluk was politically meaningful in 732 and records an independence claim. It does not prove every Karluk spoke exactly the monument’s prestige dialect or could read its script.

passages.title: One stone sentence names the Karluks, but from outside
passages.text: After the Karluk yabghu polity transformed, named Karluk groups remained under Qarakhanid and later rulers. Towns, herding networks and families also continued while titles and faiths changed. Continuity of people and practices is real; it should not be rewritten as one uninterrupted state lasting forever.

There was no single day when all Karluks vanished. A conventional political transition around the mid-tenth century marks the rise of Qarakhanid rulers, but their tribal origins remain disputed and their Islamization unfolded over time. Qarakhanids captured Bukhara permanently in 999, while Karluk-named groups, pastoral work, towns and trade continued under new governments. The atlas carries karluks to 1000 but has no exact feature in that snapshot, then draws a separate misspelled karkhanids id at 1100. This bundle therefore treats about 940 as a cautious transformation marker, not a conquest that erased a people.

passages.text: The atlas id “kashmir-and-ladakh” spans 1279 to 1492, but its huge polygon is an editorial basket, not one kingdom. It covers tested Srinagar, Jammu, Leh, Kargil, Skardu, Muzaffarabad, Rawalpindi, and Manali while missing Gilgit and Hunza. Inside it, Kashmir passed from late Sanskrit-court rule to the independent Shah Mir Sultanate in 1339. Ladakh followed separate Tibetan Buddhist dynasties and local chiefs; Baltistan, Jammu, and other hill societies had still other histories. Kashmir's chronicles illuminate courts, conflict, learning, irrigation, and crafts. Ladakh's temples, inscriptions, murals, and archaeology illuminate patrons, workshops, routes, and religious networks, but ordinary households appear only in flashes. Even the evidence travels unevenly: royal poetry survives where a shepherd's shopping list usually does not. This card therefore treats farming, herding, families, children, medicine, sanitation, and schooling with local limits instead of inventing one regional routine. At 1492 the atlas splits the footprint among Delhi Sultanate, Tibet, Chagatai, and Punjab labels. That is a software seam. Kashmir remained independent, Ladakhi rule continued, and mountain communities did not simultaneously vanish, move house, or receive four differently colored memos.

passages.title: First, unbundle the map
passages.text: The live index gives the exact id “kashmir-and-ladakh,” display name “Kashmir and Ladakh,” and approximate coverage from 1279 to 1492. The preceding 1200 layer has no exact feature, while the coverage registry finds it in three later snapshots. Those database facts identify a drawing, not a contemporary country's official name.

passages.title: First, unbundle the map
passages.text: The 1279 and 1300 target rings share the same coarse bounds, roughly 72.79 to 81.79 degrees east and 29.98 to 35.50 north. Srinagar, Jammu, Leh, Kargil, Skardu, Muzaffarabad, Rawalpindi, and Manali test inside, an implausibly broad footprint for one securely documented government.

passages.title: First, unbundle the map
passages.text: The 1400 ring changes by only two coordinate positions and adds a shared atlas edge with the Timurid Empire. This is useful for reading the graphic, not evidence for a surveyed border. The files encode no treaty, garrison, tax list, or testimony from people along that line.

passages.title: First, unbundle the map
passages.text: Gilgit and Baltit-Hunza test outside the target while nearby Skardu tests inside. The southern shape reaches Rawalpindi and Manali. That uneven selection warns against treating the label as a cultural area, ethnic map, watershed, or union of everything modern readers might call Kashmir and Ladakh.

passages.title: First, unbundle the map
passages.text: The imported summary speaks broadly about Kashmir and Ladakh as regions, but it cannot repair the medieval identity problem. This card instead names Valley sultans, Ladakhi chiefs, Balti and Jammu contexts when sources permit. A shared mountain backdrop is scenery, not a constitutional document.

passages.title: Courts, chronicles, and political change
passages.text: Jonaraja's Sanskrit chronicle covers Kashmir from 1148 to 1459 and was commissioned by Zain al-Abidin. Its critical editor distinguishes the retrospective account of pre-1339 rule from the author's nearer and sometimes eyewitness material. Court access supplied detail, but patronage also shaped what received praise or blame.

passages.title: Courts, chronicles, and political change
passages.text: The 1339 accession of Shah Mir marks a real dynastic transition in Kashmir. It does not establish a unified “Kashmir and Ladakh” kingdom. Histories of the Sultanate center the Valley, while Ladakh's own sequence is reconstructed chiefly from much later chronicles and monument evidence.

passages.title: Courts, chronicles, and political change
passages.text: Ladakh's royal chronicle is nearly the only narrative source for its political story before the fifteenth century, and it was compiled later. Historians therefore cannot simply line up every ruler and date beside Kashmir's better-attested court sequence. A neat chart can be tidier than the surviving evidence.

passages.title: Courts, chronicles, and political change
passages.text: Srivara served four Kashmir sultans and described events he personally experienced through 1486. His writing confirms that independent court politics continued close to the atlas endpoint. It also remains elite literary history, better at named rulers and crises than at counting farmers, servants, or displaced children.

passages.title: Courts, chronicles, and political change
passages.text: The Sultanate did not end in 1492. Later struggles eventually brought Chak rule and Mughal annexation in 1586, well outside this card. Leaving the override's fell field null prevents a software color change from becoming a fabricated death date for either Kashmir or Ladakh.

passages.title: Work, food, fields, herds, and roads
passages.text: A social-economic synthesis describes medieval Ladakh as combining agriculture, pastoralism, and trade. Monasteries held land, while household organization related to taxation and ownership. The article ranges broadly across the medieval period, so it supports structural possibilities rather than a claim about every family in 1317.

passages.title: Work, food, fields, herds, and roads
passages.text: The same study describes social rank expressed in forms of address and even seating order at gatherings. That is a wonderfully human detail: where one sat could speak before one did. Yet the evidence cannot supply a universal floor plan or prove identical etiquette in every Valley, Balti, or Ladakhi settlement.

passages.title: Work, food, fields, herds, and roads
passages.text: Archaeological route studies document paths, rock art, forts, and nodes across Ladakh. Routes moved travelers, ideas, and goods, but many tracks were reused for centuries. A route on the ground rarely carries a little date stamp, so period use must be argued rather than assumed from visibility alone.

passages.title: Work, food, fields, herds, and roads
passages.text: Kashmir's agrarian history centers rice and also records saffron as a valuable crop. Court sources discuss policy and famine more readily than sowing calendars, women's field labor, tenant rights, or children's chores. The crop list is useful; a complete peasant diary has not survived with it.

passages.title: Work, food, fields, herds, and roads
passages.text: Accounts of Zain al-Abidin credit him with supporting cultivation, commerce, and multiple crafts. These measures required surveyors, diggers, carriers, cultivators, artisans, and traders whose names seldom enter royal narratives. “The king built it” is historical shorthand, not a claim that he personally wielded every shovel.

passages.title: Families, women, children, and social worlds
passages.text: Wanla's foundation program sought merit for chief Bhak Darskya, his parents, and all beings; murals also show family members and monks performing ritual. This is unusually vivid evidence for an elite donor family. It does not reveal ordinary marriage ages, inheritance shares, sleeping arrangements, or village childcare.

passages.title: Families, women, children, and social worlds
passages.text: A Cambridge history notes that Muslim princesses became brides of Buddhist Ladakhi princes as Baltistan Islamized, sometimes acting as dowager queens and patrons of both mosques and monasteries. These royal alliances show women's political agency, not a template for the marriages or choices of non-elite women.

passages.title: Families, women, children, and social worlds
passages.text: The specialist study of Himalayan Muslim queens treats marriage as diplomacy between Buddhist and Muslim ruling houses. Princess-brides could preserve religious identity while shaping patronage. Their visibility is exceptional precisely because most women's voices, domestic work, pregnancies, widowhood, and property arrangements remain far less securely documented.

passages.title: Families, women, children, and social worlds
passages.text: No reviewed source supplies a secure 1279 to 1492 household census for this whole polygon, and none establishes one family form across Kashmir, Ladakh, Baltistan, Jammu, and the hill country. Families certainly existed; the honest gap concerns their size, composition, authority, and variation.

passages.title: Families, women, children, and social worlds
passages.text: Children appear indirectly as descendants, students, novice monks, heirs, and members of families, but the sources do not give a representative child's schedule, games, discipline, diet, or workload. Royal sons are unusually visible because succession mattered to chroniclers; that is a very biased class register.

passages.title: Learning, languages, and the written sample
passages.text: Sultanate education histories describe madrasas teaching Quranic studies, law, language, literature, philosophy, mathematics, logic, and metaphysics under named teachers. These institutions demonstrate advanced learning, but they do not prove mass enrollment. Schools leave famous graduates more readily than lists of children who never entered them.

passages.title: Learning, languages, and the written sample
passages.text: Zain al-Abidin's court is associated with libraries, imported books, and a translation bureau working among Sanskrit, Persian, Arabic, and other languages. Such patronage brought specialists together. It cannot tell us the literacy rate, whether girls attended, or what most farmers could read.

passages.title: Learning, languages, and the written sample
passages.text: Nund Rishi's remembered Kashmiri shruks matter because they locate religious expression in a regional spoken language, while Persian and Sanskrit carried other courtly and learned work. The surviving tradition has complex transmission; a later-recorded verse should not be silently presented as his autograph.

passages.title: Learning, languages, and the written sample
passages.text: Written-language sample, normalized Arabic: السلطان الأعظم زين العابدين. Transliteration: al-sulṭān al-aʿẓam Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn. Translation: “the greatest sultan, Zayn al-Abidin.” It is a ruler's copper coin legend from his 1420 to 1470 reign, not a sample of household conversation or every local language.

passages.title: Learning, languages, and the written sample
passages.text: The museum describes the coin as a 5.99 gram copper kaserah, partly worn, with a diamond-shaped knot, part of “zarb Kashmir,” and a date in Arabic words on the reverse. The display normalizes the obverse rather than pretending to reproduce every worn die mark.

passages.title: Belief, ritual, and changing communities
passages.text: Wanla's first-half-of-the-fourteenth-century temple contains clay sculpture, manuscript-paper figures, and murals arranged around tantric Buddhist teachings. Its inscriptions connect a local chief's patronage with Drigung transmission. This documents one powerful religious network, not the beliefs of everyone inside the atlas shape.

passages.title: Belief, ritual, and changing communities
passages.text: Researchers identify at least ten painters at Wanla, including masters and apprentices, although an inscription names three artists in a family workshop. Style moved away from earlier Kashmiri models toward Central Tibetan-derived forms. Artistic change here was a workshop history, not proof that people suddenly changed identity.

passages.title: Belief, ritual, and changing communities
passages.text: Epigraphy, art history, and radiocarbon evidence place the Wanla group across several fourteenth-century decades. Related temples and gateway stupas spread through a patron network. That combination is stronger than dating by visual resemblance alone, yet individual building phases still carry ranges rather than exact opening days.

passages.title: Belief, ritual, and changing communities
passages.text: Nund Rishi's late-fourteenth- and early-fifteenth-century setting reflects a Kashmir where Islam was growing but not instantly uniform. Rishi and Sufi traditions interacted with older practices. Conversion unfolded through people, institutions, persuasion, patronage, and pressure, not through a single light switch in 1339.

passages.title: Belief, ritual, and changing communities
passages.text: Wooden mosque forms linked Kashmir with Baltistan, Gilgit, and Hunza through shared building knowledge: log walls, doors, windows, roofs, pyramidal profiles, and tall finials. Attribution and surviving fabric require special care because fire, repair, and rebuilding repeatedly changed famous monuments over later centuries.

passages.title: Medicine, illness, hunger, and care
passages.text: The reviewed sources do not provide a secure patient casebook, physician's kit, prescription, childbirth record, or hospital register for ordinary people across this 1279 to 1492 region. Absence of those records is not absence of care; it limits what kinds of care we can responsibly describe.

passages.title: Medicine, illness, hunger, and care
passages.text: Kashmir's chronicles record famine, epidemic, war, and political violence, correcting the romantic picture of an eternally happy valley. Such narratives show collective danger but rarely separate outcomes for women, children, servants, craftspeople, migrants, or disabled people. A disaster story is not a modern health survey.

passages.title: Medicine, illness, hunger, and care
passages.text: The early-fourteenth-century invasion crisis is associated with hunger and social breakdown in Kashmir's historical tradition. Chroniclers foreground rulers and moral causes more than practical nursing, wound care, food distribution, or burial labor. Readers should see both the catastrophe and the ordinary helpers whom the text leaves unnamed.

passages.title: Medicine, illness, hunger, and care
passages.text: Agrarian histories report sharp food-price crises in periods of disruption. Prices reveal scarcity, but they do not supply household ration sizes, nutrition, infant mortality, or equal access to grain. A court that intervened in markets could still leave remote or poor families hardest hit.

passages.title: Medicine, illness, hunger, and care
passages.text: Waterworks and cultivated landscapes could support health indirectly by moving water and food, but no source here tests water quality, diagnoses pathogens, or measures life expectancy. Medieval people understood illness through learned, local, religious, and practical frameworks that these particular records do not map household by household.

passages.title: Water, washing, waste, and toilets
passages.text: UNESCO's landscape account attributes canals, embankments, gardens at Naushehar and Andurkot, and the island garden Zani Lank to Zain al-Abidin. Many surviving features are later Mughal fabric, so the source supports earlier attributions and water planning, not an untouched fifteenth-century garden tour.

passages.title: Water, washing, waste, and toilets
passages.text: The island and canal projects required surveying, earthmoving, transport, maintenance, and control of water. Court language assigns achievement to the sultan, while the workforce largely disappears. Even a royal garden had somebody doing the muddy jobs; history simply misplaced most of their name tags.

passages.title: Water, washing, waste, and toilets
passages.text: No reviewed source securely identifies a household toilet, latrine seat, cesspit, chamber pot, sewer, or human-waste rule for Kashmir or Ladakh between 1279 and 1492. Water channels and drains must not be promoted automatically into toilets. Medieval plumbing deserves evidence, not wishful porcelain.

passages.title: Water, washing, waste, and toilets
passages.text: Architectural records emphasize timber, masonry, reused foundations, roof forms, courtyards, and religious spaces rather than bathing schedules or rubbish removal. Fires and rebuilding also complicate the fabric. The sanitation answer is therefore a documented gap, not a claim that residents ignored cleanliness.

passages.title: Water, washing, waste, and toilets
passages.text: Wanla's temple used stone masonry, earthen materials, timber, plaster, pigments, clay, manuscript paper, and gold. Its study does not identify a contemporary latrine or village waste system. A spectacular painted sanctuary can survive while the less glamorous bathroom archaeology refuses to pose for posterity.

passages.title: Craft, building, and discoveries
passages.text: The new Ladakh survey documents 114 ruined and intact temples within analysis of 2,100 heritage sites. It compares plans, orientation, construction materials, topography, geography, and chronology. Ruins count as evidence too: an unroofed wall may preserve regional patterns that a repeatedly restored showpiece obscures.

passages.title: Craft, building, and discoveries
passages.text: Wanla's three-story temple grew in phases rather than arriving as one finished master plan. Murals progressed from ground floor toward gallery and lantern, and multiple workshops participated. Achievement here means sustained coordination among patrons, builders, sculptors, painters, ritual experts, and material suppliers.

passages.title: Craft, building, and discoveries
passages.text: Wood analysis identifies Himalayan blue pine in Wanla pillars and willow in beams, while conservation study distinguishes original pieces from repairs. Species identification turns “wooden temple” into a supply story involving selection, felling, transport, shaping, joinery, and replacement in a high-altitude environment.

passages.title: Craft, building, and discoveries
passages.text: Kashmir's coin catalogue records silver and copper issues of independent sultans with Arabic and Persian legends, mint information, and ruler titles. Coins joined authority to everyday exchange, but a catalogued coin does not reveal wages, market frequency, or whether remote households used cash for every transaction.

passages.title: Craft, building, and discoveries
passages.text: Sultanate mosques adapted regional materials and building forms rather than simply copying a distant template. Scholarship identifies wooden construction and local roof profiles, while surviving buildings have undergone major repairs. Architecture shows skilled synthesis, but present appearance cannot be read as a frozen photograph of 1402.

passages.title: Conflict, endings, and what continued
passages.text: Fortified Wanla joined settlement, palace, temple, and outpost on a defended hill. Its inscription celebrates Bhak Darskya's conquests of strategic sites, the view of a patron's success. It cannot by itself count casualties, name displaced families, or establish how every neighboring community understood those campaigns.

passages.title: Conflict, endings, and what continued
passages.text: Political and religious violence in Kashmir affected sanctuaries and communities before and during Sultanate rule. Source criticism matters because chronicles interpret destruction morally and politically. A careful account acknowledges victims and coercion without turning every reign, Muslim subject, Hindu subject, or Buddhist neighbor into one undifferentiated camp.

passages.title: Conflict, endings, and what continued
passages.text: The 1492 atlas assigns Srinagar, Anantnag, Jammu, and Kargil to Delhi Sultanate, Leh to Tibet, Skardu to Chagatai, and Muzaffarabad and Rawalpindi to Punjab. That four-way split is explicit in the data, but no historical event field explains or justifies the sudden simultaneous changes.

passages.title: Conflict, endings, and what continued
passages.text: In 1500 the editorial owners change again at some probes, further demonstrating that atlas colors are not a narrative of synchronized conquest. Kashmir's Sultanate, Ladakhi rulers, Balti communities, religious institutions, routes, farms, workshops, and families continued on their own timelines through the 1492 display seam.

passages.title: Conflict, endings, and what continued
passages.text: The responsible ending is continuity: no fell year, no single predecessor, and no single successor. Separate polities later changed through succession, conflict, alliance, and conquest, but this combined id merely stops. The people did not disappear when the polygon did, which is fortunate because maps are terrible landlords.

At 1492 the exact “kashmir-and-ladakh” feature disappears. The atlas reassigns Srinagar, Anantnag, Jammu, and Kargil to Delhi Sultanate; Leh to Tibet; Skardu to Chagatai; and Muzaffarabad and Rawalpindi to Punjab. Those colors encode no shared conquest, royal death, migration, or social rupture. Kashmir's independent Sultanate continued, Ladakhi rule continued, and Balti, Jammu, and hill communities followed distinct histories. The override therefore leaves fell null and names no single successor. Courts changed while households, fields, herds, routes, workshops, languages, and religious institutions continued through the editorial seam.

materialEvidence.question: Does a concrete finding have an identifiable context, date, interpretation and evidence limit?

dailyLife.question: Does the account explain ordinary practices with evidence rather than only rulers?

artsScienceTechnology.question: Are achievements concrete and correctly attributed to this polity and period?

chronologicalPhases.question: Are source-supported phases distinguished from map snapshot dates?

endingContinuity.question: Does the narrative identify what ended or continued, with dates, mechanism and uncertainty?

uncertainty.question: Are uncertainties attached to particular claims rather than a blanket disclaimer?

sectionTitles: Family gatherings, food and a dancing goat
Learning, care and the practical business of water

passages.text: This is the modern Republic of Kazakhstan, independent since 16 December 1991, not the earlier Kazakh Khanate or every steppe community. The atlas begins in 1994 and supplies three border snapshots ending in 2020, while leaving the country’s lifetime open. Its simplified Caspian coast even leaves the city of Aktau outside the outline. The map is not a legal boundary survey. Soviet-era examples below are clearly labeled inherited history; modern family practices vary across this diverse country.

passages.title: Independence and political change
passages.text: Kazakhstan declared independence on 16 December 1991, before this atlas record starts. The new state inherited institutions and infrastructure from a Soviet republic while creating its own national government. Independence did not mean that the people or their cultures suddenly began in 1991; it changed sovereignty and the framework within which they lived.

passages.title: Independence and political change
passages.text: The Constitution adopted in 1995 shaped a long period under President Nursultan Nazarbayev. He resigned on 19 March 2019, and Kassym-Jomart Tokayev addressed Parliament as president the next day. The official speech is evidence for the transfer, while its praise of the outgoing leader is the government’s own political presentation.

passages.title: Independence and political change
passages.text: January 2022 brought unrest and deadly violence. Constitutional amendments followed that June, including the replacement of the Constitutional Council with a Constitutional Court and removal of the death penalty from the Constitution. OSCE observers nevertheless found that the November presidential election lacked genuine competition. Changing legal rules and changing how political power operates are related but different processes.

passages.title: Independence and political change
passages.text: A new Constitution adopted at the March 2026 referendum entered into force on 1 July, replacing the 1995 text. Elections to the new Kurultai legislature followed on 23 August. In their preliminary assessment, international observers described technically prepared elections but limited political alternatives and concerns about vote counting. The new framework should therefore be described alongside evidence about its implementation.

passages.title: Independence and political change
passages.text: A short Kazakh writing sample is Қазақстан Республикасының Конституциясы, “Constitution of the Republic of Kazakhstan.” An editorial Latin rendering is Qazaqstan Respublikasynyñ Konstitutsiyasy. These Cyrillic words head the official Kazakh text of the Constitution effective from July 2026. They demonstrate a specific modern written form, not the script of medieval steppe inscriptions or a claim that everyone in the country uses only one language.

passages.title: Legacies, livelihoods and large projects
passages.text: The famine of 1930 to 1933 happened under Soviet rule, decades before independence. Historian Sarah Cameron’s research links the catastrophe to state campaigns that forced rural people into collective farms and factories and confiscated livestock; she estimates more than 1.5 million deaths. Russian- and Kazakh-language sources help recover this history. Remembering it today does not make the modern republic the government that caused it.

passages.title: Legacies, livelihoods and large projects
passages.text: The Soviet Union conducted more than 450 nuclear tests at Semipalatinsk between 1949 and 1989. The test site closed on 29 August 1991, before Kazakhstan’s December independence. The country subsequently renounced the nuclear arsenal left on its territory. Kazakhstan also promoted the International Day Against Nuclear Tests on the closure anniversary. This is a history of stopping testing, not of an independent Kazakh nuclear-testing programme.

passages.title: Legacies, livelihoods and large projects
passages.text: Diversion of rivers for irrigation helped shrink the Aral Sea during the Soviet era and afterwards. The 13-kilometre Kok-Aral Dike, completed in August 2005, helped retain water in the northern part. The World Bank’s 2008 account reported falling salinity and a fish harvest rising from about 50 tonnes in 2004 to about 2,000 in 2007. This was an important local recovery, not restoration of the entire sea.

passages.title: Legacies, livelihoods and large projects
passages.text: Oil remains economically important, but national growth does not describe every household’s experience. The World Bank’s February 2026 update linked strong 2025 output growth partly to higher oil production, while noting falling real incomes and consumption supported by borrowing. A busier economy and a family struggling with prices can exist at the same time.

passages.title: Legacies, livelihoods and large projects
passages.text: Baikonur connects several political eras. The Soviet launch centre sent up Sputnik in 1957 and Yuri Gagarin in 1961. After the Soviet Union dissolved, Russia leased the site from independent Kazakhstan. Those famous early flights were Soviet achievements on this territory; they should not be relabeled inventions of a state founded thirty years later.

passages.title: Legacies, livelihoods and large projects
passages.text: On 2 September 2015, Kazakh cosmonaut Aidyn Aimbetov launched from Baikonur with Sergey Volkov of Russia’s space agency and Andreas Mogensen of the European Space Agency on a mission to the International Space Station. NASA confirmed that all three reached orbit. Just before liftoff, the station itself had passed over Kazakhstan: the destination was already racing overhead while the crew prepared to chase it.

passages.title: Family gatherings, food and a dancing goat
passages.text: UNESCO’s 2024 account of betashar describes a wedding welcome built around song and the unveiling of the bride. A singer names relatives, the bride and her sisters-in-law greet them with bows, and the groom’s mother welcomes her into the family. Relatives shower the newlyweds with sweets and coins. Elders pass on the practice; it is one documented Kazakh tradition, not a rule followed by every household.

passages.title: Family gatherings, food and a dancing goat
passages.text: In orteke, a musician plays a two-string dombyra while strings from their fingers move a wooden mountain-goat puppet. The goat taps and hops on a drum surface in time with the music. Some experts manage three or more puppets. That is a concert and a tiny goat dance party run by the same pair of hands. UNESCO inscribed this performing art in 2022.

passages.title: Family gatherings, food and a dancing goat
passages.text: A cooking competition at the Kokshetau cultural centre brought ten local enterprises together to make Nauryz kozhe, a festive dish associated with the spring celebration. The regional account describes a seven-ingredient version with water, meat, barley, kefir, kurt, salt and herbs. Judges considered presentation as well as taste. The accompanying display included quilting, weaving and felt work: plenty to look at between spoonfuls.

passages.title: Family gatherings, food and a dancing goat
passages.text: UNESCO describes orteke as a way for adults and children to communicate as well as entertain each other. Skills pass through communities and apprenticeships, with festivals and competitions helping performers learn from neighbours. Musical education can happen through watching hands, listening carefully and trying again, as well as through written lessons.

passages.title: Learning, care and the practical business of water
passages.text: In 2022, seventeen-year-old Amina Pusurmanova joined the UniSat programme in Almaty. Participants designed cases, saw their designs printed in 3D, assembled devices and learned from teammates across Central Asia. Amina described Uzbek participants helping her use circuit-design software. The devices flew into the stratosphere that March, not into orbit. Learning science also meant asking a new friend for help.

passages.title: Learning, care and the practical business of water
passages.text: A 2023 UNICEF report follows home-visiting nurse Aizharkyn in Zhetysay. Her work includes looking at a baby’s feeding and development, the family’s living conditions and possible dangers, then referring children to specialists when needed. She also attended emergency-preparedness training. Care here travels to the household and considers how a child lives, rather than stopping at a clinic doorway.

passages.title: Learning, care and the practical business of water
passages.text: Astana hosted the Global Conference on Primary Health Care in October 2018. Its declaration renewed an international commitment to accessible community-based care and recalled the 1978 Alma-Ata declaration, made when Kazakhstan was a Soviet republic. Hosting an agreement is a diplomatic and public-health contribution; it does not by itself prove that every family can obtain the care it needs.

passages.title: Learning, care and the practical business of water
passages.text: School toilets became a public issue, not just a caretaker’s problem. WHO’s 2024 account describes an assessment of 153 schools and collaboration between campaigners, ministries and specialists. A national standard effective that January set requirements linked to pupil numbers and included children with additional needs. A toilet must be usable by the children actually attending the school; adopting a standard is only one step towards that result.

Kazakhstan remains a continuing state. The atlas’s last border interval ends in 2020 because of data coverage, not national collapse. The 2026 Constitution and parliamentary election mark institutional change within the same republic; observers’ concerns about political competition show why legal changes require continuing scrutiny. Communities, family practices and public services have their own histories within that ongoing political story.

sectionTitles: A capital and a royal family
Food, work and things people used

passages.text: The Kazan Khanate arose in the Middle Volga and Kama region as the Golden Horde fragmented, conventionally dated to 1438 or 1445. Its inhabitants included Turkic and Finno-Ugric communities. The imported 1530 to 1600 outline is seriously misplaced: it excludes Kazan itself and extends towards western Siberia. It should not be treated as the territory of this khanate. The historical state ended in 1552, before the map interval closes.

passages.title: A capital and a royal family
passages.text: Kazan’s citadel stood at the centre of the khanate’s political, military and commercial life. Archaeological remains are essential for understanding that capital: much of the Kremlin visible today belongs to construction after the Russian conquest. Its surviving ensemble combines buildings from the sixteenth to nineteenth centuries with evidence of earlier occupation, rather than preserving the khans’ city intact.

passages.title: A capital and a royal family
passages.text: When Khan Safa Giray died in 1549, his young son Utyamysh Giray inherited power and his mother Suyumbike became regent. She governed amid rival aristocratic groups and conflict with Moscow. Her government was overthrown in 1551, and mother and son were sent to Moscow. A royal childhood could become a matter of dangerous international politics.

passages.title: Food, work and things people used
passages.text: A regional synthesis covering the thirteenth to mid-sixteenth centuries lists rye, oats, barley, millet and buckwheat among farmers’ crops. Different ploughs suited different soils, while harrows broke up the ground and scythes cut vegetation. This was a landscape of cultivated fields as well as rivers and towns; the list describes the broader period rather than the contents of one excavated pantry.

passages.title: Food, work and things people used
passages.text: Village households also worked leather and wood, producing goods that included wooden utensils and the timber frames of buildings. Women spun thread and wove cloth; specialist smiths and potters supplied neighbours and markets. Keeping a household going involved a long chain of skilled tasks, well before anyone could sit down to a meal.

passages.title: Food, work and things people used
passages.text: Excavations at the Kazan Kremlin and Iske Kazan have recovered wheel-made pottery, including jars, jugs, bowls, plates and inkwells. Some vessels were glazed or decorated with incised patterns. Finds also include pouring vessels with animal-shaped details, such as ram or horse heads. Even a practical container could have a little personality.

passages.title: Food, work and things people used
passages.text: Leather shoes could carry embossed patterns or embroidery in silk thread. Archaeologists also found carved alabaster panels with scrolling plant ornament used in buildings. These surviving pieces show makers decorating both things worn on the body and the spaces around them. The evidence records skilled work, although it cannot tell us what every family could afford.

passages.title: Food, work and things people used
passages.text: A surviving brass wine pitcher shaped like a waterbird preserves a craftsman’s name: Nasyr, identified as Emin Khan’s coppersmith. It belongs to the late fifteenth or early sixteenth century. A named maker is a welcome change from anonymous objects: we can connect metalworking skill with a particular person, while recognising that this elaborate vessel belonged to a privileged setting.

passages.title: Rules, writing and learning
passages.text: A charter issued by Sahib Giray in 1523 protected a named family’s privileges. It exempted its beneficiaries from demands such as certain taxes, providing lodgings, and supplying food or fodder. These exemptions reveal the kinds of obligations other people could face. They were special privileges, rather than a promise that every household could turn away officials.

passages.title: Rules, writing and learning
passages.text: The seal on that 1523 charter includes the Arabic words “السلطان الاعظم”, meaning “The greatest sovereign”. This sample follows the scholarly transcription and translation published by I. A. Mustakimov on page 43 of his edition. It is Arabic in the seal of a Turkic-language document, shown here in modern type rather than as a picture of the original lettering.

passages.title: Rules, writing and learning
passages.text: The poet Muhammadyar explored what a good society should look like. His Gift to Men, written in 1539 to 1540, praised justice, honesty and peaceful life. Light of Hearts followed in 1542, discussing virtues that rulers and others should practise. These were arguments about how people ought to behave, not a report that everyone already behaved beautifully.

passages.title: Rules, writing and learning
passages.text: The medrese, or school, attached to Kazan’s principal mosque had a substantial manuscript collection. Across the Tatar khanates, such libraries gathered works in Arabic, Persian and Turkic literary traditions. Books connected religious study with a wider written culture. A school library tells us that organised learning existed, without establishing that every child attended school.

passages.title: An unexpected survival
passages.text: The 1523 charter resurfaced in 1912, long after the khanate had ended. Scholar Saeed Vakhidi found it with a farmer, Rakhmatulla Akhmarov, who kept it as a healing talisman. It entered a museum collection after Vakhidi acquired it in 1920. This later belief helped preserve an important document; it is not evidence that the charter could cure illness.

Ivan IV’s forces captured Kazan in October 1552 and ended the independent khanate. Resistance in its former lands continued until 1557. Russian administration replaced the khans’ government, while Tatar language, religious life and cultural traditions continued through major disruption. The imported map endpoint of 1600 does not mark a later fall of this state.

sectionTitles: A kingdom rooted in a valley

passages.text: Kazembe was an eastern Lunda kingdom centred on the lower Luapula valley, in today’s Zambia and Democratic Republic of the Congo. Tribute, trade, fishing and cultivation supported it. The imported polygon is displaced south and east of that heartland.

passages.title: A kingdom rooted in a valley
passages.text: Kazembe’s heartland was the lower Luapula valley. Its influence extended beyond that core through flexible institutions and symbols of authority. This helps explain why the kingdom should not be imagined simply as a modern country with a uniformly administered border.

passages.title: A kingdom rooted in a valley
passages.text: The town council’s historical tradition recalls royal emblems including a knife, staff, belt, beads and a cutting of a mutaba tree. The living tree belongs beside portable regalia in that account: planting could connect a new royal seat with an older political inheritance.

passages.title: A kingdom rooted in a valley
passages.text: Lake Mweru and the Mofwe Lagoon supplied fisheries, while access to Katanga’s copper linked the valley to wider exchange. The council’s account places food resources alongside minerals in the kingdom’s prosperity. Fish mattered long before anyone made a modern economic chart.

passages.title: At the court in 1867
passages.text: Livingstone recorded that a new ruler established his court in a new place. In November 1867 he described a reed enclosure with the queen’s house behind the chief’s, and cassava and cotton growing inside. A court included productive plants as well as royal rooms.

passages.title: At the court in 1867
passages.text: At a royal appearance he noted decorated headgear and imported cloth, including material from Manchester. Those details connect a Luapula court to distant workshops. Imported fabric was incorporated into local displays of authority rather than simply replacing them.

passages.title: At the court in 1867
passages.text: December entries list gifts of dried fish, beer and baskets of cassava. These particular exchanges show food moving through hospitality and royal relationships. They give us a more concrete picture than a general statement that people “lived by agriculture”.

passages.title: At the court in 1867
passages.text: On New Year’s Day 1868 Livingstone described broad iron hoes and recorded buying them with cloth. A tool could cultivate soil and also be a valuable exchange object. Cloth, metal and food connected work in the field with a much wider trading world.

passages.title: Memory, performance and writing
passages.text: Historian David Gordon traces how shrines and natural features became associated with ancestors and conquests. Remembering history through the landscape supported both Lunda migrant identities and Shila identities rooted in the valley. Different communities could remember the same political expansion differently.

passages.title: Memory, performance and writing
passages.text: The Umutomboko ceremony’s modern public form developed under changing political conditions. University of Zambia research identifies government support in 1971 as an important step in popularizing it. A living tradition can grow and reorganize while drawing on older royal practices.

passages.title: Memory, performance and writing
passages.text: The town council describes a ceremony presided over by Mwata Kazembe and attended by people from Zambia and the neighboring Congo. Such gatherings make the continued royal institution visible across a border that now divides parts of its historical social world.

passages.title: Memory, performance and writing
passages.text: In a Lunda tale recorded by Robert Cancel, the trickster Kalulu asks his in-laws for farmland and plants an enormous garden. The story brings marriage, cultivation and cleverness together. It is a modern recorded performance, not a literal report of events at the old court.

passages.title: Memory, performance and writing
passages.text: A short written trace from an outsider’s record is the Portuguese title “O Muata Cazembe”, meaning “The Mwata Kazembe”. Gamito’s expedition account survives in later editions. This title records the royal office in a visitor’s language; it is not claimed as indigenous court writing.

After defeat in 1899, Mwata Kazembe negotiated a settlement under colonial rule. The royal institution survived in altered form, rather than the people or their traditions vanishing. The map’s 1878 cutoff is earlier than that change.
