passages.text: Imagine a royal message cut into stone in 1135: “Panjalu is victorious.” Beyond it lie Brantas River rice fields, brick sanctuaries, markets, scribes, poets and a court at Daha. This is the historical Kediri kingdom, also called Panjalu. It grew from Airlangga's divided realm around 1042 and lasted until Kertajaya was defeated by Ken Angrok in 1222. Under Jayabhaya, poets completed the Bhāratayuddha, remaking an Indian epic in Old Javanese rather than merely copying it. Farmers and water managers inherited dams and channels built to tame the flood-prone Brantas. Traders connected Java to sea routes, while inscriptions recorded tax privileges, officials, craftspeople and healers. Yet evidence is lopsided: stone orders and court poems survive better than children's lessons, wooden homes or toilets. The atlas creates a second puzzle. Its exact “Kediri” layer begins in 1279, fifty-seven years after the kingdom ended, continues through the Majapahit age to 1492, and stretches from Java into southern Borneo and eastern Sumbawa. That is not historical Kediri. This card tells the historical story while marking the imported dates and shape as a serious data error.

passages.title: Audit the broken atlas identity
passages.text: The exact indexed record is id “kediri,” label “Kediri,” circa 1279 to 1492, generated from historical basemaps. It has three border intervals and had no card or override at audit time. Its own imported summary describes the older Panjalu kingdom, exposing a date-content contradiction inside the dataset.

passages.title: Audit the broken atlas identity
passages.text: Historical Kediri or Panjalu belongs roughly to the mid-eleventh century through 1222. The atlas starts its feature in 1279, fifty-seven years after Ken Angrok defeated Kertajaya, and continues it through the Majapahit age. The displayed interval therefore cannot be used as the kingdom's historical lifespan.

passages.title: Audit the broken atlas identity
passages.text: The 1279 feature is a MultiPolygon with four parts, four rings and 152 positions. Its bounds are 109.115° to 118.983° east and 9.177° south to 1.369° south. Its coordinate SHA-256 is f83aa5c5eb3c6adf43527c2983265bfb6144715d713e14afd20eb7f9db0c1753. Those numbers audit a display object, not royal control.

passages.title: Audit the broken atlas identity
passages.text: Point tests place Daha, Kelud, Trowulan, Singhasari, Yogyakarta and Semarang inside, but also Banjarmasin in southern Borneo and Bima in eastern Sumbawa. Meanwhile the Brantas delta, Janggala or Sidoarjo, Surabaya and Tuban fall outside. This is far too broad and strangely selective for historical Panjalu.

passages.title: Audit the broken atlas identity
passages.text: The 1300 geometry is byte-for-byte identical to 1279. At 1400 it keeps four parts and 152 positions with only tiny coordinate changes, producing SHA-256 17651100a0500fdc3fe8dcd9fb6a7b1819d9311c21f42695b3dbcf85fd429642. The same footprint persisted for more than a century. Repetition across seams makes the error durable; it does not make it historical.

passages.title: Separate Kediri from neighboring identities
passages.text: At 1200, during the real Kediri period, the atlas uses the generic id “east-java” with almost the same giant geometry. That feature cannot be silently renamed Kediri because East Java also contained Janggala and, after 1222, Singhasari. A regional bucket is not a tested political alias.

passages.title: Separate Kediri from neighboring identities
passages.text: Singhasari begins with Ken Angrok's victory in 1222 and belongs to much of the century that the atlas assigns to “east-java” and then “kediri.” No exact singhasari id exists in the imported index. Its absence is a catalog problem, not evidence that Kediri survived under another label.

passages.title: Separate Kediri from neighboring identities
passages.text: Majapahit began in 1293 and has a separate coverage record and card even though it lacks an imported border feature. The atlas “kediri” polygon overlaps Majapahit's entire era. It must never become an alias for Majapahit merely because the broad shape resembles later Javanese power.

passages.title: Separate Kediri from neighboring identities
passages.text: Daha or Kediri remained an important place-name after 1222, and later rulers could claim Kediri connections. Those later political identities, including fifteenth-century Daha or Girindrawardhana contexts, are not automatically the eleventh- to thirteenth-century Panjalu kingdom. A familiar place can outlive several states.

passages.title: Separate Kediri from neighboring identities
passages.text: At 1492 the exact target vanishes and the atlas assigns all tested Java, Borneo and Bima points to “malaysian-islamic-states.” That seam is historically impossible and supplies no conqueror. The override therefore records no fall or successor, while the card gives the actual Kediri ending in 1222.

passages.title: Follow rulers, conflict and diplomacy carefully
passages.text: Airlangga's 1041 Pucangan inscription and his retirement around 1042 anchor the background. Tradition describes a split between Janggala and Panjalu, perhaps to manage succession. The names are useful, but historians debate the exact mechanics and borders, so no ruler drew the atlas shape shown here.

passages.title: Follow rulers, conflict and diplomacy carefully
passages.text: Bameswara appears in dated Kediri inscriptions from 1117. A 1120 order connected with Panumbangan granted sima status, meaning specified fiscal privileges and duties. It shows a king rewarding or reorganizing a locality through a formal document, not abolishing every other levy across the realm.

passages.title: Follow rulers, conflict and diplomacy carefully
passages.text: Jayabhaya's 1135 Hantang inscription celebrates Panjalu victory. The enemy and full campaign are harder to reconstruct than the slogan, so the card does not manufacture a battle map. A victory formula proves royal commemoration; it cannot tell us how many fought or what every village experienced.

passages.title: Follow rulers, conflict and diplomacy carefully
passages.text: Inscriptions name a succession of rulers after Jayabhaya, but their reign boundaries are not a continuous official calendar. Archaeological surveys use dated charters and regnal titles to build a sequence while leaving gaps visible. Uncertainty is evidence about survival, not permission to invent palace drama.

passages.title: Follow rulers, conflict and diplomacy carefully
passages.text: Sources remember Kertajaya, also connected with the name Śrṅga, in conflict with Ken Angrok. The decisive defeat came in 1222 and shifted the political center toward Singhasari. Later chronicles add memorable scenes; historians compare them with inscriptions instead of treating every episode as eyewitness reporting.

passages.title: See government beyond the palace
passages.text: Royal inscriptions were official acts, commonly cut on stone or copper and sometimes known on palm leaf. They could establish privileges, obligations, boundaries, witnesses and curses. Because rulers chose what deserved durable recording, inscriptions illuminate administration while favoring exceptional grants over ordinary days.

passages.title: See government beyond the palace
passages.text: Sima land was relieved from specified burdens and assigned duties, often supporting a sanctuary or rewarding service. Charters list royal officials, gifts, taxes, witnesses and oath ceremonies. “Tax-free” is too simple: residents might exchange one set of payments for another lasting obligation.

passages.title: See government beyond the palace
passages.text: Specialist citralekha prepared inscriptions. They needed command of Old Javanese language and script, royal formulae and bureaucratic order. Their work joins education to government: a crooked letter was not merely untidy when it helped define land, dues and a king's command.

passages.title: See government beyond the palace
passages.text: Chinese reports describe ministers, hundreds of lower officials, treasuries and granaries in “Java.” This can suggest organized court government near the Kediri era, but the report compresses information from different times and places. It should corroborate broad capacity, not supply a precise Kediri civil-service chart.

passages.title: See government beyond the palace
passages.text: The title taṇḍa appears for elite guards or warriors in Old Javanese literary and epigraphic records from Kediri onward. Comparing poem and inscription helps identify a real office without assuming every flamboyant literary duel happened exactly as sung. Court security, military status and storytelling overlapped but were not identical.

passages.title: Work with the Brantas and wider trade
passages.text: Kediri's heartland lay along the Brantas basin near Daha. Rice farming benefited from fertile volcanic soils but also faced Kelud eruptions and a river that could flood or change course. Geography offered food and movement only when communities maintained fields, banks, crossings and channels.

passages.title: Work with the Brantas and wider trade
passages.text: In 1037, just before the partition, Airlangga's government and local communities built the Wringin Sapta dam to control Brantas flooding that disrupted fields and boats. Kediri inherited this engineered landscape. The dam is close background, not an invention that should be credited to Jayabhaya.

passages.title: Work with the Brantas and wider trade
passages.text: Old Javanese inscriptions use terms for dams, dikes, reservoirs, tunnels and channels, and name water-related officials. Such systems required repeated clearing and repair; one royal inauguration could not stop mud, roots or monsoon damage forever. Irrigation was organized labor as much as a clever structure.

passages.title: Work with the Brantas and wider trade
passages.text: A Chinese compilation near the end of the Kediri age describes Java growing rice, millet, beans, sugarcane, bananas and taro, ploughing with buffaloes and collecting a rice-related rent. It is regional outsider evidence, not a menu or tax receipt from every village around Daha.

passages.title: Work with the Brantas and wider trade
passages.text: The same account lists foreign merchants, metals, silks, ceramics, aromatics and pepper exchange. River routes connected interior production with ports, but the atlas strangely excludes much of the Brantas delta. Trade goods reveal networks; they do not prove Panjalu ruled every place where a jar or coin traveled.

passages.title: Read poems, religion and learning
passages.text: The Bhāratayuddha was completed in 1157 by Mpu Sedah and Mpu Panuluh under Jayabhaya's patronage. It retold the Mahābhārata war in Old Javanese kakawin form. Adaptation required mastery of language, meter and court culture; this was creative scholarship, not ancient copy-and-paste.

passages.title: Read poems, religion and learning
passages.text: Other kakawin associated with Kediri courts include Hariwangsa, Ghaṭotkacāśraya and Smaradahana. Patron and date assignments differ in confidence. Lists of titles show a lively literary world, but they cannot tell how many listeners understood every Sanskrit allusion or owned a manuscript.

passages.title: Read poems, religion and learning
passages.text: The 1157 composition survives through later manuscript traditions, especially in Bali. A copied palm-leaf page may be centuries younger than the poem it carries, and scribes could adapt wording. Historians separate original court context, later recopying and modern printed edition instead of assigning one date to all three.

passages.title: Read poems, religion and learning
passages.text: Śaiva, Buddhist and other Indic traditions appear in texts, inscriptions and sculpture. Tondowongso finds include Brahma, Candra, Surya, Nandi and a yoni. That group illuminates a sacred complex; it does not prove every Kediri subject followed one identical ritual practice.

passages.title: Read poems, religion and learning
passages.text: Learning likely happened through court and religious specialists, scribal apprenticeship, memorization and household practice. The technical skill of poets and citralekha is secure; an ordinary-child school schedule is not. The evidence supports trained learners without supplying enrollment rates, classrooms or universal literacy.

passages.title: Inspect crafts, buildings and archaeology
passages.text: Tondowongso preserves a brick sanctuary complex with sculpture and an eleventh- to thirteenth-century horizon. Excavation connects it to the broad Airlangga-Kediri age, yet dating individual construction phases remains difficult. A religious compound is excellent craft evidence and a poor blueprint for an ordinary home.

passages.title: Inspect crafts, buildings and archaeology
passages.text: At Besole, archaeologists studied brick remains and a gateway in a landscape connected with Kediri-period inscriptions. Attribution is cautious because buildings can be repaired, reused or rebuilt. A brick that sits in Kediri country is not automatically stamped with one ruler's name.

passages.title: Inspect crafts, buildings and archaeology
passages.text: The Palah inscription of 1197 records devotion under King Śrṅga at the place later called Panataran. Most impressive monuments visible in the surviving complex belong to Majapahit centuries, however. The early inscription proves sacred continuity, not that Kertajaya commissioned every tower tourists see.

passages.title: Inspect crafts, buildings and archaeology
passages.text: Brahma, Candra, Surya, Nandi and yoni finds show quarrying, stone selection, iconographic planning and skilled carving. Some objects were unfinished or displaced, and research continues. Archaeologists compare style, material and context rather than sorting every statue by the nearest famous king.

passages.title: Inspect crafts, buildings and archaeology
passages.text: Very little stone sculpture can be assigned securely to Kediri. The huge Boro Gaṇeśa is debated around the Kediri-Singhasari transition, and its carved textile patterns invite comparison with traded cloth. The honest achievement story includes masterpieces, disputed dates and a large missing record.

passages.title: Meet families, ranks, women and children
passages.text: Court poems describe marriages, longing, kin and ceremony, but their heroes are not a census. Research across Old Javanese kakawin finds arranged marriage, elopement or abduction themes and cousin marriage, while warning that one later poem cannot simply be backdated into every Kediri household.

passages.title: Meet families, ranks, women and children
passages.text: Society included royal families, high officials, religious specialists, guards, scribes, village authorities, farmers, traders, artisans, performers and dependent laborers. Rank shaped obligations and rewards. Inscriptions reveal named categories better than personal feelings, so a tax list cannot explain how every family negotiated status.

passages.title: Meet families, ranks, women and children
passages.text: Women appear in literary marriage stories and in the work of textile production, exchange and household life, but direct Kediri biographies are rare. Elite heroines cannot stand for all women, and silence in a royal inscription does not mean women were absent from farms, markets or ritual.

passages.title: Meet families, ranks, women and children
passages.text: Children probably learned by watching work, memorizing stories and prayers, practicing crafts or letters when their household had access. Specialist poets and inscription writers prove advanced teaching existed. No consulted source provides a typical Kediri child's timetable, school age or literacy percentage, so none is invented.

passages.title: Meet families, ranks, women and children
passages.text: Kakawin were made for skilled performance and listening as well as reading. Music, recitation and dramatic movement could carry stories beyond the small group able to write difficult meters. Even so, audience size and access varied; “court culture” should not be stretched into universal entertainment.

passages.title: Eat, dress, live, work and play
passages.text: Near-contemporary Chinese reporting lists rice, millet, beans, gourds, coconut, banana, sugarcane, taro, fish, fowl, ducks and goats for Java. It also mentions salt boiled from seawater. This is a regional abundance list, not proof that every inland child ate meat, sugar or imported spice daily.

passages.title: Eat, dress, live, work and play
passages.text: Textiles moved as valuable goods, payments and signs of status. Old Javanese writing names cloth in gifts and ceremony, while sculpture preserves carved patterns. Fiber, weave and decoration depended on wealth and setting; a jeweled court garment would have been wildly impractical in a muddy rice field.

passages.title: Eat, dress, live, work and play
passages.text: Wood, bamboo, thatch and earth likely made many homes, which helps explain why temples and inscriptions dominate archaeology. A Chinese account praises painted dwellings and merchant lodges, but it describes “Java” through outsider reports. No secure standard Kediri house plan survives to furnish room by room.

passages.title: Eat, dress, live, work and play
passages.text: Work joined farmers and buffalo teams, water managers, boat crews, traders, builders, stone carvers, textile makers, performers, guards and scribes. Inscriptions name specialized service categories, but occupation could overlap with household and seasonal labor. One title does not freeze a person into a modern job description.

passages.title: Eat, dress, live, work and play
passages.text: A Chinese report mentions boat outings, hill trips, flutes, drums, castanets, mime, cockfighting and pig fighting in Java. These vivid details may reflect elite spectacle, regional custom or recycled information. They are evidence for reported amusements, not permission to schedule every Kediri child for a pig match.

passages.title: Test medicine, sanitation, writing and continuity
passages.text: The 1194 Kĕmulan inscription includes walyan, interpreted as a healer, among named specialists. That direct local term is strong evidence that healers existed, but the charter names a category rather than a remedy. It reveals neither treatment recipes, success rates nor access for an ordinary family.

passages.title: Test medicine, sanitation, writing and continuity
passages.text: Brantas dams, channels and reservoirs supported fields, transport and flood control. Sacred water structures served ritual purposes. None of those automatically supplied safe drinking water: irrigation, bathing and household water are different systems, and consulted Kediri sources do not describe routine boiling, wells or water quality.

passages.title: Test medicine, sanitation, writing and continuity
passages.text: No consulted authoritative source securely identifies an ordinary Kediri household toilet, sewer network, garbage collection schedule or handwashing rule. Organic structures rarely survive, and temple drains are not toilets. The safest reconstruction is an explicit gap, not a suspiciously modern bathroom built from silence.

passages.title: Test medicine, sanitation, writing and continuity
passages.text: Authentic sample, 1135 CE Hantang inscription, National Museum D 9: scholarly transliteration “pañjalu jayati”; translation, “Panjalu is victorious.” It is a short Sanskrit victory formula inside an Old Javanese inscription cut in Kediri quadrate script. Original glyphs are not reproduced because Unicode text would not be a facsimile of the carved forms.

passages.title: Test medicine, sanitation, writing and continuity
passages.text: The kingdom ended politically with Kertajaya's defeat in 1222, but Daha, fields, temples, language and stories continued under new rulers. Panji tales later spread through many regions and versions. That cultural afterlife is continuity, not proof that the same Kediri state ruled until the atlas endpoint of 1492.

Ken Angrok defeated Kertajaya in 1222, ending Kediri or Panjalu as the dominant independent kingdom and opening Singhasari rule. The successor has no exact imported id, so no invented link is added. Daha and its communities remained important, Old Javanese works continued through later copies and adaptation, and Panji traditions traveled far beyond East Java. The atlas feature's 1279 start and 1492 disappearance are data seams, not the kingdom's birth and fall.

passages.text: Cantia is a Latin name used by Bede for Kent. This card serves both imported labels, but the map’s Cantia outline spreads far beyond the south-eastern kingdom and must not be treated as its verified territory. The Cantia interval of 600 to 800 and Kent interval of 800 to 1000 are map coverage, not the lives of two separate kingdoms. The named sites below are in historical Kent; several institutions continued after royal independence ended.

passages.title: Written law and religious learning
passages.text: Queen Bertha worshipped at St Martin's before Augustine's arrival in 597. Aethelberht welcomed the mission and gave it land outside Canterbury. Conversion therefore developed through existing relationships, royal decisions and new institutions.

passages.title: Written law and religious learning
passages.text: The abbey probably founded in 598 combined churches and a cemetery with gardens, orchards and vineyards. Its school drew monks from far away, connecting learning with the practical support of a resident community.

passages.title: Written law and religious learning
passages.text: Textus Roffensis preserves early Kentish laws in a manuscript compiled in the early 1120s. Its survival makes older legal writing accessible, but the date of this copy must be distinguished from the seventh-century rules it transmits.

passages.title: Written law and religious learning
passages.text: Aethelberht's law code sets compensation for injuries and property offences, with distinctions among rulers, clergy, free people and enslaved people. It reveals ranked legal categories; it does not prove that every prescribed payment was enforced.

passages.title: Written law and religious learning
passages.text: An Old English sample from Aethelberht’s laws reads “Gif feaxfang geweorð ·L· sceatta to bote.” In Christopher Monk’s translation, grabbing someone by the hair calls for compensation of fifty sceattas. The wording survives in a twelfth-century copy of a much earlier code. Hair-pulling even had its own entry in the legal price list.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: At Lyminge, a gaming piece was made from a hollow bone cylinder with turned end caps and a bronze rivet. Found in a royal hall setting, it gives tangible evidence of skilled manufacture and play, though the game's exact rules remain unknown.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: Broken luxury drinking glass and animal bones accompanied Lyminge's late-sixth- and seventh-century royal complex. Together with the halls and gaming piece, these finds support an interpretation of gatherings organised around feasting and display.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: Lyminge's eighth- and ninth-century deposits contain more large marine fish bones, including cod and whiting, than its earlier occupation. The study identifies increasing consumption while warning that recovery methods and different deposits affect comparisons.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: Sheep became more prominent in later Lyminge animal remains, while pigs declined. Loomweights, bone needles, pin-beaters and spindle whorls also occur. The researchers suggest increased wool production, but reserve judgment pending fuller analysis of the flocks.

passages.title: Food, textiles and entertainment
passages.text: A 741 grant records a fishery on the River Lympne for Lyminge. Written landholding evidence helps explain how an inland religious community could obtain coastal foods; fish bones alone cannot establish a particular fasting rule.

passages.title: Survival and institutional change
passages.text: After a raid in 804, Lyminge's community received refuge in Canterbury. Coins, building activity and dated butchered bones show subsequent occupation at Lyminge, challenging the assumption that one recorded attack immediately destroyed the monastery.

passages.title: Survival and institutional change
passages.text: By the late ninth century the Lyminge monastery appears to have been abandoned. Sustained military pressure is the researcher's likely explanation. Tenth-century settlement returned under Canterbury's archbishops, showing that the place's history outlasted that institution.

passages.title: Survival and institutional change
passages.text: At Canterbury, tenth-century monastic reform organised prayer, reading and manual work. In 978 the abbey's dedication was extended to include Augustine. This later institutional history should not be mistaken for continued Kentish royal independence.

Kent entered a subordinate West Saxon kingdom around 825; separate kingship ended in 860. Communities and religious institutions continued, as Canterbury's later reforms and Lyminge's renewed settlement demonstrate.

sectionTitles: A house, a family and a school
A newspaper sample and money in circulation

passages.text: This entry covers Kenya under British colonial rule, especially the 1920s and 1930s. The colony and the coastal protectorate had different legal arrangements. Railways, towns and schools changed opportunities, but racial restrictions on land, movement and political power made those changes deeply unequal.

passages.title: Railways, work and controlled movement
passages.text: The railway reached Nairobi in 1899 and the lakeside terminus later named Kisumu in 1901. Transport infrastructure helped towns grow along the line. These dates describe the network inherited by people living in the 1920s, not new construction in the selected year.

passages.title: Railways, work and controlled movement
passages.text: Indian workers and African labourers helped construct the railway, and some Indian workers also opened small shops. Rail history therefore includes migration, commerce and difficult labour, alongside engineering plans drawn by British officials.

passages.title: Railways, work and controlled movement
passages.text: The Smithsonian preserves a thin tin kipande case made in the 1920s, with loops for a neck chain. It once held folded employment papers dated 1925. An object small enough to wear could carry a government’s authority into a worker’s daily movements.

passages.title: Railways, work and controlled movement
passages.text: The papers in a kipande recorded an African owner’s name and work history and rules restricting movement. This specimen was collected much later, in 1986. Its museum arrival is not the date when the colonial identification system was used.

passages.title: A house, a family and a school
passages.text: Colonial authorities restricted African ownership of urban land. Some employers provided only bachelor rooms for workers, making it difficult for families to settle together. Housing policy shaped who could live in a town, not merely how buildings looked.

passages.title: A house, a family and a school
passages.text: Asian residents also faced restrictions on property ownership and representation, while some Nairobi neighbourhoods were demolished under public-health justifications. Historians describe African and Asian resistance to these policies; residents were not passive recipients of town planning.

passages.title: A house, a family and a school
passages.text: Alliance School opened near Nairobi in 1926 under Protestant missions. By 1928 it offered a four-year secondary course and the Cambridge School Certificate. Schooling could become a route toward professional work, although access remained highly limited and unequal.

passages.title: A house, a family and a school
passages.text: Earlier, Maseno pupils had demanded more than gardening, carpentry and hygiene instruction. A 1910 strike helped secure teaching in English, mathematics and geography. This background shows pupils themselves pressing to change what colonial-era education allowed them to learn.

passages.title: A house, a family and a school
passages.text: During the 1930s, Kikuyu independent schools drew on donated land, elected committees and community fundraising. Families helped create institutions when existing education did not meet their aspirations. Choosing a school could also express a position in religious and political debates.

passages.title: A newspaper sample and money in circulation
passages.text: “Muigwithania”, meaning “The Reconciler”, is the Kikuyu title of the newspaper associated with the Kikuyu Central Association and Jomo Kenyatta. Surviving 1928 and 1929 issues preserve the language in the Latin alphabet. This sample follows the catalogue’s spelling.

passages.title: A newspaper sample and money in circulation
passages.text: The same newspaper collection includes English translations and correspondence between colonial officials. Those documents preserve African arguments against colonial rule, but they also show how the state watched the press. An archive can record both a voice and the surveillance directed at it.

passages.title: A newspaper sample and money in circulation
passages.text: Regional money changed from rupees through an intermediate florin to shillings and cents. The currency transition linked everyday purchases to decisions made by the East African Currency Board. Older and newer names for money could coexist while people adjusted.

British rule ended when Kenya became independent on 12 December 1963; it became a republic the following year. The 1938 map endpoint does not mark independence. Colonial institutions changed, while the people who had lived, worked and organized under them continued building their country.

sectionTitles: Institutions, money and a Swahili sample

passages.text: Kenya became independent in 1963 and a republic in 1964; the map’s 1960 start still falls within colonial rule. Its later history includes new public institutions, environmental organizing and mobile communication, alongside persistent inequalities. Daily experience differs between communities, towns and rural households.

passages.title: Institutions, money and a Swahili sample
passages.text: Kenya’s first independent government operated within the Commonwealth with a governor-general representing the monarch. In 1964 it became a republic. These were distinct constitutional steps, rather than a single moment when every inherited institution changed at once.

passages.title: Institutions, money and a Swahili sample
passages.text: The 2010 constitution reintroduced the Senate alongside the National Assembly. This restored a national institution that had disappeared earlier in independent Kenya’s history.

passages.title: Institutions, money and a Swahili sample
passages.text: The first national banknotes carried “Banki Kuu ya Kenya”, meaning “Central Bank of Kenya”, alongside the English name. This short Swahili sample is attested on the initial notes issued in 1966; official writing could appear in more than one language on a familiar everyday object.

passages.title: Institutions, money and a Swahili sample
passages.text: Those notes combined Jomo Kenyatta’s portrait with scenes of economic activity. Currency served as a means of payment and a portable statement about the new state. The paper in a pocket could carry both a price and a national story.

passages.title: Trees, telephones and practical achievements
passages.text: Wangari Maathai founded the Green Belt Movement in 1977 after rural women reported drying streams, insecure food supplies and longer walks for firewood. Planting trees addressed everyday work and resources as well as the appearance of a landscape.

passages.title: Trees, telephones and practical achievements
passages.text: The movement connected environmental work with community education and public participation. Maathai received the 2004 Nobel Peace Prize for work linking sustainable development, democracy and peace. The achievement involved organized groups of women, not just one celebrated individual planting alone.

passages.title: Trees, telephones and practical achievements
passages.text: M-PESA launched in Kenya in 2007. Safaricom’s retrospective describes trial users sending money to one another when the original pilot had focused on loan repayments. Users helped reveal a different purpose for the technology: getting money to another person without carrying it there.

passages.title: Trees, telephones and practical achievements
passages.text: The system connected phone accounts with ordinary cash: people could deposit money, send balances and redeem them. The innovation depended on a practical network around the phone, not only a clever screen menu.

passages.title: School toilets and community knowledge
passages.text: UNICEF’s 2025 account of St. Marks Makutano school in Kitui describes cleaner toilets, running water, private spaces for girls and accessible cubicles. A school building is more usable when its toilets support privacy and different physical needs as well as classroom attendance.

passages.title: School toilets and community knowledge
passages.text: The same school’s health club tended a garden and made soap to help pay for cleaning supplies. Pupils took part in looking after facilities and explaining hygiene. Toilets may not win a school talent show, but keeping them usable takes organization and skill.

passages.title: School toilets and community knowledge
passages.text: Among coastal Mijikenda communities, Kaya forest traditions connect naming, marriage, reconciliation and remembrance with particular places. Councils of elders act as custodians. These are living community practices with local histories, not ceremonies shared identically by every Kenyan.

passages.title: School toilets and community knowledge
passages.text: Traditional rules governing Kaya resources have contributed to conserving biodiversity. UNESCO also records pressure from land demand and urbanization. Protecting a forest can therefore involve knowledge, relationships and community authority as well as preventing trees from being cut down.

Kenya continues as an independent republic. Colonial rule ended in 1963, while later constitutional reforms changed its institutions. Its communities, languages and social movements remain part of an ongoing history, with achievements and unresolved inequalities rather than a single ending.

passages.text: Kerma was the capital of a Nubian kingdom on the Nile in present-day Sudan. Its prosperity rested on herding, cultivation and exchange between African interiors and Egypt. This page follows the kingdom, its earlier background and what archaeology reveals about its people.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Excavators mapped houses with courtyards containing kitchens and grain silos. These remains show how households organized cooking and storage around shared outdoor space.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Temple workshops and storerooms clustered around the Western Deffufa. A palace contained a large circular building interpreted as a royal audience hall, revealing distinct religious and political spaces.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: At Middle Kerma grave 253, researchers recorded 4,899 cattle skulls. They interpret the association between large tombs and numerous skulls as a display of the deceased person's wealth and power.

passages.title: What excavations reveal
passages.text: Some cattle horns had been deliberately reshaped; cut marks and altered growth preserve evidence of the practice. Researchers suggest specially valued animals were distinguished this way, while warning against copying modern herders' beliefs directly onto ancient Kerma.

passages.title: Arts and technology
passages.text: Kerma potters shaped exceptionally thin cups by hand, then polished their red surfaces. Controlled firing produced black rims and interiors, evidence of skilled handling of both clay and the firing atmosphere.

passages.title: Arts and technology
passages.text: A tulip-shaped beaker in Manchester Museum was excavated at Kerma in 1913. Its smooth, shining finish was made by burnishing the clay before firing; the form was achieved without a potter's wheel.

passages.title: Arts and technology
passages.text: Cattle also appeared in small figurines found in the city and in paintings in a funerary chapel. Their presence in art as well as graves suggests a significance extending beyond food and exchange.

passages.title: Daily life and food
passages.text: Animal bones from the capital show that domestic livestock supplied most of the meat evidence. Cattle, sheep and goats dominated; the researchers observed a later increase in sheep and goats relative to cattle.

passages.title: Daily life and food
passages.text: Fine beakers existed alongside heavier storage jars, sometimes stamped around the rim. Stone implements remained in use beside metal technology, preserving evidence of practical choices in everyday tools.

passages.title: Burial, belief and social rank
passages.text: Graves preserve wooden beds, personal ornaments, sandals and containers for oils or ointments. Larger, richer tombs show growing inequality; some also contained accompanying people interpreted as victims of funerary killing.

passages.title: Trade and cultural connections
passages.text: A Kerma-style beaker now at the Metropolitan Museum was excavated at Abydos in Egypt. Such finds demonstrate connections across the Nile Valley, but the museum cautions that pottery alone cannot establish whether the people buried with it were Nubian traders.

passages.title: What continued after conquest
passages.text: Survey finds include Egyptian pottery together with Nubian pottery. Stuart Tyson Smith interprets the settlement pattern as evidence that some local elites retained cultural and political latitude under Egyptian rule; conquest did not erase Nubian society.

passages.title: What remains uncertain
passages.text: The relationship between the earlier Pre-Kerma settlement and the royal city is not fully demonstrated. Excavated buildings and objects reveal much, but their locations do not establish precise kingdom borders.

Egyptian New Kingdom campaigns ended Kerma's independence. The excavation mission places the capital's destruction around 1450 BCE, after a longer conquest associated with Thutmose I and Thutmose III; this is an approximate endpoint, not a known single day of collapse.

sectionTitles: Making a home and a living

passages.text: Sibir was a western Siberian khanate connecting forest, river and steppe communities. This atlas shows 1492 to 1600, not its complete political lifetime. Its nearly unchanged outline cannot track shifting tribute relationships, expansion or conquest. Turkic-speaking Tatars, Khanty and Mansi belonged to different communities within its changing reach.

passages.title: Rulers, rivers and power
passages.text: The khanate emerged from the breakup of the Golden Horde. Chimgi-Tura, at present-day Tyumen, was an earlier seat. In the 1490s the Taybugid dynasty shifted its center to Isker, also called Sibir. Kuchum, from a rival Shaybanid line claiming descent from Chinggis Khan, seized power in 1563.

passages.title: Rulers, rivers and power
passages.text: Local life depended on fishing, hunting, livestock, cultivation and skilled metalworking. Trade brought textiles, carpets, ornaments and medicines from Central Asia, while furs and hunting birds traveled outward. Siberian households participated in networks reaching Kazan, the Nogai steppe and Russia.

passages.title: Rulers, rivers and power
passages.text: A message could be an object. Chronicles describe Kuchum summoning followers by sending gilded arrows. Tataurov compares this account with large decorated arrowheads from Isker and proposes a signaling function. The connection is an interpretation: a fancy arrowhead does not come with its original delivery instructions.

passages.title: Rulers, rivers and power
passages.text: Seals helped make authority visible. Large signet rings found at western Siberian sites carry designs including tamgas, faces or mounted warriors. A Russian rendering of Kuchum’s 1571 oath says he attached his seal. An official could authenticate a promise with an object small enough to wear.

passages.title: Making a home and a living
passages.text: At Isker, keys and chest handles survive among objects assigned to the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. Researchers connect the chests with safekeeping important possessions. We cannot open them to discover a family’s treasures, but the hardware preserves the familiar business of putting something away and locking it up.

passages.title: Making a home and a living
passages.text: The same collections include bone awls, unfinished bone objects and a spoon handle. These small pieces bring cutting, piercing and making utensils into the picture beside all the weapons. Bone could become a useful tool or part of a meal’s equipment, rather than simply being thrown away.

passages.title: Making a home and a living
passages.text: Regional potters mixed crushed old pottery into clay and pressed rows of dents or comb-like impressions over their vessels. Many pots had rounded bottoms. At Tunus, a sixteenth-century layer contains several ceramic traditions together: even a collection of broken dinnerware can preserve evidence of neighbors with different habits.

passages.title: Making a home and a living
passages.text: Isker’s objects also include Chinese bronze mirrors, beads, jewelry and painted porcelain fragments. These imports suggest access to valued goods through long-distance exchange. Some people could look into a metal mirror and use dishes that had traveled much farther than they had; those luxuries were not every household’s possessions.

passages.title: Making a home and a living
passages.text: Adamov’s 2021 study identifies evidence for blacksmiths, metal casters, jewelers, tailors and leatherworkers at Isker. Silver and copper coins also occur. A royal center needed people repairing clothing, working hides and making everyday objects as well as warriors and rulers; the author argues for a substantial resident community.

passages.title: Children, health and written words
passages.text: Some royal children and grandchildren had tutors called atalyks. These men also performed diplomatic missions and collected tribute. The same person might look after a prince’s upbringing and then leave on government business. This is evidence about the ruling household, not a school system available to every child.

passages.title: Children, health and written words
passages.text: During negotiations in 1597, Kuchum requested medicines seized with a Bukhara caravan. He wanted their return as a test of Russian promises. The account reveals remedies moving along trade routes, but does not identify their ingredients or demonstrate whether they worked.

passages.title: Children, health and written words
passages.text: A real voice survives through translation. Kuchum’s 1597 letter says, in the preserved Russian wording: “а Сибирь не яз отдал, сами естя взяли”. Transliterated: a Sibir ne yaz otdal, sami estya vzyali. It means “I did not give up Siberia; you took it yourselves.” This is an archaic Russian rendering quoted by historians, not the khan’s original Tatar script or a sample of everybody’s speech.

passages.title: Children, health and written words
passages.text: How did letters cross languages? A March 1570 official report records a letter from Kuchum written in Tatar and separately mentions sending its translation to Ivan IV. Couriers, readers and translators made diplomacy possible. The source itself reminds us that the language preserved in an archive may differ from the language first written.

passages.title: Discoveries and difficult evidence
passages.text: The Irtysh has eroded Isker, and early souvenir collecting scattered finds and destroyed their contexts. Tataurov and Tataurov questioned whether it was a permanent capital. Adamov’s later study argues for a resident town using its substantial deposits, fortifications and craft evidence. Archaeologists disagree over the settlement’s scale and character.

passages.title: Discoveries and difficult evidence
passages.text: Adamov reports that the late-fifteenth-century settlement covered at least 2.6 hectares and had a complex system of defenses. Large bricks found in 2019 suggest masonry buildings, although that is a proposal rather than a recovered palace plan. A small surviving site can conceal a much larger landscape lost to a river.

passages.title: Discoveries and difficult evidence
passages.text: Not everything found at Isker belonged to the khans. Adamov’s 2020 study identified at least twenty vessel rims, a clay spindle whorl and three bronze fittings that may belong to the sixth- to ninth-century Potchevash culture. A spindle whorl helps turn fibers into thread. These objects illuminate earlier inhabitants, centuries before Kuchum.

passages.title: Conquest and what continued
passages.text: An official list dated 4 September 1598 names members of Kuchum’s captured household, including children aged five and six. The military defeat reached families as well as soldiers. Such lists record people through their captors’ administration; the young prisoners were real children, not just entries in a victory report.

passages.title: Conquest and what continued
passages.text: Siberian Tatar communities continued after the khanate’s loss of independence and live in western Siberia today.
Muscovite conquest continued after Isker’s capture. Kuchum was defeated in 1598 but remained free afterward. The atlas’s 1600 seam does not mark a single surrender by every community.

sectionTitles: Homes, meals and family influence in the 1330s
Learning and a small writing sample

passages.text: The Golden Horde grew from the western conquests of the Mongol Empire and became a major power connecting the Eurasian steppe, Rus principalities and trading cities. Its history includes skilled metalwork, multilingual books, mobile households and ambitious urban building. The later Great Horde appears under the map’s 1492 label. The dated examples below distinguish fourteenth-century daily life from the politics of the late fifteenth century.

passages.title: Power, cities and craftsmanship
passages.text: Batu’s forces conquered the steppes north of the Black and Caspian Seas in 1236-1240. His dynasty descended from Jochi. The map’s first appearance in 1279 therefore comes decades after its rise.

passages.title: Power, cities and craftsmanship
passages.text: Berke was Muslim, and all khans from Öz Beg onward followed Islam. An alliance with Egypt’s Mamluk rulers in 1262-1263 also shows how diplomacy reached far beyond the steppe.

passages.title: Power, cities and craftsmanship
passages.text: Bolgar preserves a mosque, minaret, mausoleums, baths and palace remains. These buildings make urban life visible alongside the better-known horse-riding armies. Its history also joins nomadic communities to settled craft and trading centers.

passages.title: Power, cities and craftsmanship
passages.text: At Kitsivka 1 in present-day Ukraine, archaeologists found pottery, metal vessels, tools and clothing fittings from the Golden Horde period. The settlement stood near a river crossing. Such finds reveal everyday work and connections, rather than just the names of rulers.

passages.title: Power, cities and craftsmanship
passages.text: A steel helmet decorated with silver may bear Jani Beg’s name. The Metropolitan Museum treats that reading as a possibility, not a certainty. The object still shows skilled metalworking and the use of inscriptions on prestigious equipment.

passages.title: Power, cities and craftsmanship
passages.text: A silver half-dirham of Tokhtamysh in Oxford is only 18 millimeters across. Its mint name, royal titles and religious words fit on that small surface. Coins could carry both money value and a ruler’s public message.

passages.title: Homes, meals and family influence in the 1330s
passages.text: Ibn Battuta described felt-covered homes carried on wagons, with horses, oxen or camels pulling them. Moving house could mean taking the house along. His account describes travelers and a royal camp, not every household.

passages.title: Homes, meals and family influence in the 1330s
passages.text: He recorded millet porridge with mare’s milk, meat and pasta cooked with milk. These are a visitor’s observations, not a menu shared by everyone across an enormous territory.

passages.title: Homes, meals and family influence in the 1330s
passages.text: Elite wives and princesses could control property and exercise authority. Court households also depended on servants and enslaved people. A queen’s influence tells us little about the freedoms of the women serving her.

passages.title: Homes, meals and family influence in the 1330s
passages.text: Black Sea markets traded grain, furs, wax and honey, alongside goods arriving from farther east. They also sold enslaved people. Commercial connections created wealth, but could bring captivity and family separation.

passages.title: Learning and a small writing sample
passages.text: The fourteenth-century Codex Cumanicus contains vocabulary in Latin, Persian and Cuman, a Turkic language. Preserved in Venice, it shows people assembling tools for communication across languages. A word list is a practical achievement: conversations do not translate themselves.

passages.title: Learning and a small writing sample
passages.text: Bolgar’s nomination dossier describes madrasahs, institutions for education, among its fourteenth-century urban developments. These references show organized learning, but do not tell us that every child attended school or had the same opportunities.

passages.title: Learning and a small writing sample
passages.text: An Arabic sample from Tokhtamysh’s late-fourteenth-century coin reads “السلطان الاعظم” (al-sultan al-aʿzam), meaning “the supreme sultan.” It is a royal title, not evidence that all residents spoke Arabic at home. This inscription belongs to the earlier Golden Horde, before the Great Horde’s final decades.

passages.title: Baths, water and medical care
passages.text: An archaeological study published in 2002 counted 25 excavated Golden Horde bathhouses: 14 communal and 11 private. That was the evidence known to its author then. Baths were substantial urban buildings, with washing also important in Muslim religious life.

passages.title: Baths, water and medical care
passages.text: Bolgar’s fourteenth-century development included water supply and drainage, according to its heritage dossier. These systems required planning and maintenance. The evidence cited here does not establish what sort of toilet every household used; bathhouses and drains are not proof of a flush toilet in every home.

passages.title: Baths, water and medical care
passages.text: Medieval writers mention a hospital, or bimaristan, at Urgench. A modern study uses those reports to investigate care in the Golden Horde. Details reconstructed by comparison with other hospitals remain proposals, and the evidence does not establish a hospital in every town.

passages.title: Baths, water and medical care
passages.text: A study of medieval accounts describes hot and mineral springs used as treatments, as well as bathing. This tells us what people tried when ill. It does not show that those treatments worked by modern medical standards.

passages.title: Fragmentation and the Great Horde
passages.text: Civil war followed Berdibeg’s death in 1359. Tokhtamysh later reunited much of the Jochid realm, but conflict with Timur weakened his position. The larger Golden Horde eventually divided into several states.

passages.title: Fragmentation and the Great Horde
passages.text: By the 1430s, the Great Horde claimed to be the senior continuation of the old realm. Other khanates pursued their own authority.

passages.title: Fragmentation and the Great Horde
passages.text: Ahmed Khan withdrew from the Ugra confrontation in 1480. This weakened his claim over Muscovy, but the Great Horde continued afterward.

passages.title: Fragmentation and the Great Horde
passages.text: In 1501-1502, harsh winter conditions, shortages and desertions undermined Shaikh Ahmed. Politics depended on feeding people and animals as well as winning alliances.

passages.title: Fragmentation and the Great Horde
passages.text: Crimea’s Mengli Giray defeated Shaikh Ahmed in 1502. Shaikh Ahmed survived. The often-repeated story that Sarai was destroyed that year is disputed.

passages.title: Fragmentation and the Great Horde
passages.text: Successor khanates inherited political and literary traditions of the Golden Horde. Its legacy reached across Crimea, Central Asia and Siberia. A political breakup did not make languages, skills or communities disappear.

The Great Horde lost power to the Crimean khan in 1502. This was a political defeat within a wider succession of states, not the disappearance of the Golden Horde’s peoples. Jochid political and literary traditions continued in successor khanates.

passages.text: The Khazar confederation linked the Black Sea, Caucasus and lower Volga from the mid-600s to the late 900s. Turkic rulers governed a population with many languages, livelihoods and religions. Its influence depended on trade and diplomacy as well as armies.

passages.title: A ruler describes everyday work
passages.text: Writing around 960, King Joseph described leaving his winter city in spring for vineyards, fields and seasonal work. This is a ruler's account of his own world, but it reminds us that Khazar life included cultivation as well as herding.

passages.title: A ruler describes everyday work
passages.text: Joseph described Jews, Christians and Muslims sharing an urban settlement. His account also mentions enslaved people. Religious variety and commercial connections did not make this an equal society.

passages.title: A ruler describes everyday work
passages.text: Hasdai's letter reports ships carrying fish, skins and other merchandise from Khazaria to Byzantium. River and sea connections helped link northern resources with larger markets.

passages.title: A ruler describes everyday work
passages.text: Joseph credited the earlier ruler Obadiah with supporting synagogues, schools and visiting Jewish scholars. This is evidence of how the court presented its religious learning, not proof that all children attended school.

passages.title: Objects and buildings
passages.text: The British Museum displays iron stirrups and a bridle-bit from near Bielowodsk in the Perm region, dated to the 800s-900s. The possible grave context is uncertain; the objects are associated with the Khazars and their contacts.

passages.title: Objects and buildings
passages.text: Silver sheet decorates the bridle-bit with vines and flowers. The museum connects these motifs with Byzantine and Slavic art. Even horse equipment could carry designs across cultural boundaries.

passages.title: Objects and buildings
passages.text: Sarkel on the lower Don was built with fired brick and had towers, a moat and several internal sectors. These are excavated architectural features, more informative than merely calling the fortress powerful.

passages.title: Objects and buildings
passages.text: At nearby Semikarakorsk, builders combined mud-brick defenses with fired-brick structures in the citadel. The different materials show local construction choices; fired brick was already used there before the Byzantine mission associated with Sarkel.

passages.title: Objects and buildings
passages.text: Workshops adjoined walls at Semikarakorsk and the Tsimliansk Right-bank fortress. These places supported work and administration as well as soldiers. Archaeologist Valery Flyorov warns that the biggest wall circuit need not have been the most defensible.

passages.title: Families, beliefs and written words
passages.text: The Schechter letter credits a woman named Serah with encouraging a ruler's turn toward Judaism. It is a religious story preserved in a later copy, not a contemporary diary; nevertheless, its author gives a woman an active role in the court's remembered history.

passages.title: Families, beliefs and written words
passages.text: The same letter describes a marriage between Joseph and an Alan king's daughter after conflict between their fathers. Its narrative presents marriage as a way of making political peace, rather than a model for all households.

passages.title: Families, beliefs and written words
passages.text: A small Hebrew sample is בארץ קזריא, meaning “in the land of Khazaria.” It appears in the Schechter letter, recto left, line 7. The surviving Cambridge manuscript is a later copy of a text about tenth-century Khazaria, not the ruler's original handwriting.

passages.title: Families, beliefs and written words
passages.text: The famous Kyivan letter should not simply be called Khazar handwriting. A 2026 re-examination finds a mainly Slavic setting and treats a Khazar connection as possible rather than established. Different Hebrew documents need their own histories.

Rus and Turkic attacks broke Khazar power during the 960s. The traditional date 965 and Ibn Hawqal's account dated 968-969 cannot be neatly combined into one certain fall day. Refugees returned and communities continued; the map's 1100 endpoint is not an imperial lifetime.

A later adventure in melon growing

passages.text: The Khiva Khanate grew from Uzbek Arabshahid rule in Khorezm, established in 1511. Its oasis towns and irrigated fields lay around the lower Amu Darya. The map shows 1530 to 1783, not the state’s full lifetime. Its broad, nearly unchanged outline should not be read as proof of constant control across deserts and steppe. Later buildings and documents below are dated separately.

passages.title: Water, work and unequal power
passages.text: In the seventeenth century, Abul Ghazi and other rulers developed canals and distributed newly irrigated land among Uzbek groups. Waterworks helped turn political promises into farms. Crown land could be leased or cultivated by enslaved workers, so expansion also depended on deeply unequal control of land and labor.

passages.title: Water, work and unequal power
passages.text: Keeping water moving required regular digging. In Khiva, government-organized compulsory work was called bigar; its crucial canal-building and repair duty was qazu. Workers maintained major channels and dams that supported agriculture. This was an obligation imposed on people, not a cheerful volunteer gardening club.

passages.title: Water, work and unequal power
passages.text: Smaller channels had a different organization. Local communities arranged work on sub-canals, which was not counted as the government’s bigar. A farm could therefore depend on both neighborhood cooperation and state demands. The distinction helps explain why irrigation involved social organization as well as engineering.

passages.title: Water, work and unequal power
passages.text: Captivity was part of the khanate’s economy. Enslaved people included Persians captured in raids and Russians seized on frontier routes; they worked in households and fields. Nader freed captives in 1740, but slavery returned and survived until its abolition after the Russian conquest of 1873.

passages.title: Homes and shared spaces
passages.text: Surviving traditional Khivan houses enclose a courtyard, with reception space under a portico supported by carved wooden posts and more private rooms beyond. UNESCO identifies eighteenth- and twentieth-century variants. These homes show how builders arranged privacy, hospitality and outdoor space within a closely packed town.

passages.title: Homes and shared spaces
passages.text: A clever feature of traditional Khivan homes is the tall ulu-aivan, an open porch facing a lower porch across the courtyard. Builders aligned it to catch the wind and guide air inward. Architecture supplied some of the cooling: an impressive trick before anyone could reach for an electric fan.

passages.title: Homes and shared spaces
passages.text: Djuma Mosque was rebuilt in 1788 to 1789, just after this map record ends. Its roofed prayer hall incorporated elements from older buildings. Reuse preserved earlier craftsmanship inside a later structure: the age of a carved support need not be the age of the building surrounding it.

passages.title: Homes and shared spaces
passages.text: A later school shows how education fitted into a working city. Alla-Kuli’s madrasa, built in 1835, occupied a difficult site beside the eastern gate and above the market entrance. Its builders had to accommodate existing streets and structures. Monumental learning institutions were neighbors of everyday commerce.

passages.title: Historians, handwriting and an original title
passages.text: Abul Ghazi was both ruler and historian. During ten years in Isfahan after 1629, he studied Persian and Arabic histories alongside traditions remembered from home. His later historical works were written in Chaghatay Turkic. Knowledge moved across languages, courts and personal journeys, not only through conquest.

passages.title: Historians, handwriting and an original title
passages.text: شجرۂ تراكمه, Shajara-yi Tarakima, means “Genealogy of the Turkmen.” Abul Ghazi wrote this Chaghatay Turkic work in 1659 to 1660. The sample uses the title’s modern scholarly Arabic-script typography; it is not a facsimile of his handwriting. Its family histories drew on earlier books and traditions.

passages.title: Historians, handwriting and an original title
passages.text: Another history, the Shajara-yi Turk, outlived its first author. Anusha Khan commissioned the scholar Mulla Mahmudi to continue his father’s work. Mahmudi had also taught Anusha. Research on manuscript 851 in Tashkent suggests it may preserve the continuator’s own hand, although that remains a scholarly argument.

passages.title: Historians, handwriting and an original title
passages.text: That manuscript contains inserted leaves and writing squeezed into margins. Toshov identifies an added account of China on folios 84 to 86, with nearby text moved into a margin. Handwritten history could be revised and expanded. Before “insert paragraph,” a writer sometimes had to insert actual paper.

passages.title: Historians, handwriting and an original title
passages.text: Writing also handled practical government business. Around eleven thousand texts seized by Russian forces in 1873 form the collection called the Archive of the Khans of Khiva. Records in Chaghatay concern taxes, property, military affairs and diplomacy: the paperwork behind royal power survives alongside literary books.

passages.title: A later adventure in melon growing
passages.text: In 1875, long after the map’s endpoint, Hungarian grower Bertalan Ónody visited Khiva to investigate farming. Muhammad Rahim II permitted his travels and supplied a guide familiar with local agriculture. The visitor needed local expertise: arriving with an enthusiasm for melons was only the beginning of learning how they grew.

passages.title: A later adventure in melon growing
passages.text: Ónody took seeds home and published accounts of Khivan crops and melon cultivation in 1877. His attempt to turn the imported seeds into a profitable business failed. The episode captures both the appeal of the region’s produce and the difficulty of moving an agricultural success from one setting to another.

The map’s 1783 endpoint was not a collapse. A reduced khanate survived Russia’s invasion of 1873 as a protectorate. Bolshevik conquest ended the last khan’s rule in February 1920. The monarchy disappeared, while Khorezm’s communities and cultural traditions continued.

sectionTitles: Healthcare, learning and a written voice

passages.text: The Khmer Empire made Angkor a major centre of power, art and water engineering in mainland Southeast Asia. Its successive capitals flourished from the ninth century onward in what is now Cambodia. The atlas’s broad outlines extend into neighbouring regions; its 900 to 1492 interval is map coverage, not precise founding and fall dates. A temple city also contained families, gardens, cooks and craftspeople.

passages.title: Kings, capitals and public life
passages.text: The political centre did not always remain at Angkor. Jayavarman IV established Koh Ker in 921, first as a rival capital and then, from 928 to 944, as the empire’s sole capital. Its builders worked with enormous single blocks of stone. Royal competition helped produce striking new architecture before the court moved back to Angkor.

passages.title: Kings, capitals and public life
passages.text: Suryavarman II commissioned Angkor Wat in the early twelfth century as a royal temple dedicated to Vishnu. Its galleries and towers gave religious ideas monumental form. During the sixteenth century it became an important Buddhist pilgrimage destination, drawing visitors from beyond Cambodia. The same building could acquire new sacred purposes while remaining deeply meaningful.

passages.title: Kings, capitals and public life
passages.text: Jayavarman VII’s late-twelfth-century Bayon temple placed a Buddha protected by a Naga at its centre. Inscriptions in its chapels also identify gods brought together from different provinces. The temple linked royal authority with a wider sacred landscape. Its famous tower faces remain debated rather than securely identified portraits of one person.

passages.title: Kings, capitals and public life
passages.text: The Elephant Terrace was a platform for royal pavilions, about 300 metres long. Large postholes help reveal wooden buildings that have disappeared. The Chinese visitor Zhou Daguan reported that the king appeared at a golden window to hear complaints and give judgments in the late thirteenth century. Government could be a very public performance.

passages.title: Homes, meals and useful discoveries
passages.text: Excavations inside Angkor Wat’s enclosure found traces of twelfth-century households: postholes, flat stones, pottery and cooking features. The archaeologists could not reconstruct a complete house, but these remains show people living around the sacred monument. Families left a quieter archaeological record than kings, sometimes just a cooking place and broken dishes.

passages.title: Homes, meals and useful discoveries
passages.text: Cooking in the temple enclosure used both portable ceramic stoves and hearths built at ground level. Rice husks and the bases of rice grains show processing on site. Plants associated with domestic gardening included bananas, palms and pepper. Preparing supper involved growing, cleaning and processing ingredients before anything reached the pot.

passages.title: Homes, meals and useful discoveries
passages.text: Charred cotton seeds from the Angkor Wat households probably relate to textile production. Residents may have grown cotton for exchange or processed it at home. This is a useful reminder that household work could produce clothing materials as well as meals. The seeds survive because some were burned, accidentally preserving a trace of an ordinary industry.

passages.title: Homes, meals and useful discoveries
passages.text: Bayon’s carved scenes include small market stalls, workers laying out a road and women preparing fish on skewers. These are artistic images, but their specific tasks bring working people into view alongside rulers and gods. Even a magnificent capital needed somebody to prepare dinner; the stone fish, unfortunately, are no longer accepting orders.

passages.title: Homes, meals and useful discoveries
passages.text: Angkor’s canals, catchments and embankments formed a connected water system built up over centuries. A modern network study showed how long drought followed by unusually wet years could destabilize it. Water engineering was a major achievement, but keeping old channels working required maintenance. Researchers still debate how environmental stress and political changes interacted.

passages.title: Healthcare, learning and a written voice
passages.text: The Say Fong hospital inscription of 1186 describes two physicians and other staff. Its instructions assign cooks duties involving water, fuel and cleaning the temple, while women pound rice. Healthcare depended on feeding people and maintaining the institution as well as the work of doctors.

passages.title: Healthcare, learning and a written voice
passages.text: The same hospital text lists rice for patients and supplies such as honey, sesame, ginger and cardamom. It promises treatment across the four social categories named in the inscription and asks future rulers to protect the foundation. These are royal provisions and aspirations, not proof that every patient received the same care or that every remedy worked.

passages.title: Healthcare, learning and a written voice
passages.text: Queen Indradevi composed a Sanskrit poem carved on the great stele of Phimeanakas around 1190 to 1200. It honoured her deceased sister Jayarajadevi and their husband, Jayavarman VII. Its final verses celebrate learning and her own composition. A woman at court could be an accomplished author and patron; this does not tell us how widely ordinary girls attended school.

passages.title: Healthcare, learning and a written voice
passages.text: A hospital stele east of Ta Keo, dated 1108 in the Saka calendar, or 1186 CE, opens “namo vuddhāya”, meaning “Homage to the Buddha”. This is the editor’s Roman-letter transcription of Sanskrit originally carved in Khmer script. The brief greeting belongs to a Buddhist hospital foundation, linking written royal patronage with concern for illness.

passages.title: What changed and what continued
passages.text: Mud from Angkor Thom’s moat preserves a history of its surroundings. Researchers found less evidence of burning, erosion and forest disturbance from the early fourteenth century. By that century’s end, floating vegetation suggests the moat was no longer maintained. This supports a gradual reduction of activity in the administrative centre, long before the familiar 1431 collapse story.

passages.title: What changed and what continued
passages.text: Angkor is still an inhabited landscape. UNESCO describes villages, rice farming, weaving, palm-sugar production and ceremonies at temple sites. These are living Khmer communities, not actors filling an empty ruin. Modern practices need their own dates and histories, but their presence makes clear that the disappearance of imperial power did not mean the disappearance of Khmer people.

Angkor’s role as an imperial centre diminished through a long transformation involving changing settlement, water management and regional conflict. The traditional 1431 Ayutthayan attack does not explain all the archaeological changes. Angkor Wat later flourished as a Buddhist pilgrimage site, and Khmer communities continued. The atlas endpoint of 1492 is not a documented moment when this people or its culture ended.

sectionTitles: Named people, family memories and written words

passages.text: “Khoisan” is an umbrella label for diverse Khoe and San peoples, not one kingdom or one established language family. The map’s vast outline and 4000 BCE to 1530 CE interval cannot define a single people’s territory or lifespan. The examples below identify particular communities and distinguish archaeological evidence from later recorded lives.

passages.title: Many peoples and changing livelihoods
passages.text: Linguists distinguish Kx’a, Tuu and Khoe-Kwadi among the language families grouped under the southern African Khoisan label. Shared click sounds do not make them one language. Khoe-Kwadi itself includes communities with different histories of herding and gathering; a language name is not a job description.

passages.title: Many peoples and changing livelihoods
passages.text: A small toe bone from Spoegrivier Cave in Namaqualand helps date a major change. Researchers tested ancient proteins to distinguish sheep from similar wild animals, confirming a domestic sheep about two thousand years old. Herding arrived in a region where people already had deep knowledge of wild foods and animals.

passages.title: Many peoples and changing livelihoods
passages.text: An ostrich egg could become a water container. A Peabody Museum object collected in 1958 is catalogued as a possible San water carrier, perforated at one end. The Origins Centre describes plugged eggshell containers used to save scarce water: a remarkably practical use for something that began as an egg.

passages.title: Many peoples and changing livelihoods
passages.text: Food gathering also called for tools. The Origins Centre explains how San and Khoe women used pointed digging sticks to reach roots and bulbs, sometimes adding a stone weight with a hole through it. Its displayed example is dated 1970, documenting a later practice rather than fixing the invention’s date.

passages.title: Many peoples and changing livelihoods
passages.text: The same museum shows the engineering of a composite hunting arrow: connected sections and an attached tip that could separate after striking. Hunters also made adhesives to fasten components. These were carefully designed tools, requiring knowledge of materials, animal behavior and tracking.

passages.title: Homes, landscape and art
passages.text: Among Nama pastoralists in the Richtersveld, a house can travel with its owners. Domed homes use woven rush mats that can be taken apart when families move between grazing places. UNESCO’s account describes a living tradition: moving house can mean bringing the actual house along.

passages.title: Homes, landscape and art
passages.text: Richtersveld grazing is organized across communally managed land and seasonal stockposts. Pastoralists also gather useful and medicinal plants and preserve stories connected to places. Knowledge of when to move animals and where to find plants is part of caring for both a household and a landscape.

passages.title: Homes, landscape and art
passages.text: Tsodilo in Botswana preserves more than 4,500 rock paintings. Its hills and waterholes remain sacred to San and Hambukushu communities. The paintings span different periods and are not all securely dated; the site is a record of many visitors and inhabitants, not an illustrated diary of one timeless population.

passages.title: Named people, family memories and written words
passages.text: The |Xam storyteller ||kabbo helped teach Wilhelm Bleek and Lucy Lloyd his language after being released from a Cape Town convict station. Their recordings from the 1870s and 1880s eventually supplied the 1911 book Specimens of Bushman folklore. Remembering the speakers’ names restores people to an archive often known mainly by its collectors.

passages.title: Named people, family memories and written words
passages.text: A later childhood remembered in the archive belongs to |uma, who arrived in Cape Town in 1880 after abduction and separation from his family. He recalled his mother building their grass sleeping hut and gathering fruit and kernels. His affection for the fruit of the |kui tree preserves one child’s taste of home.

passages.title: Named people, family memories and written words
passages.text: |uma, Da, Tamme and !nanni made hundreds of drawings and watercolors showing remembered plants, animals, foods and routes. At Mowbray they also built grass huts for play, including one for other children in the household. Their pictures preserve detailed environmental knowledge alongside the ordinary wish to play and remember home.

passages.title: Named people, family memories and written words
passages.text: A modern written example of |Xam appears in South Africa’s coat of arms, introduced in 2000: “!ke e: /xarra //ke,” officially translated as “diverse people unite.” The special marks represent speech sounds. This is a modern commemorative use of the language, not a prehistoric inscription.

passages.title: Named people, family memories and written words
passages.text: In 2017, South African San representatives set out their own research ethics code. It asks researchers to explain projects clearly, respect privacy, acknowledge knowledge and share benefits fairly. Communities were defining how outsiders should work with them, including protections for children and family life.

The map stops in 1530, but these peoples’ histories do not. Later records document displacement and violence as well as family knowledge and creativity. Living Nama traditions and the San research code show communities maintaining culture and asserting rights in the present.
