sectionTitles: An empire and its ruling family
A busy city, water and skilled hands
A written sample and lives beyond conquest

passages.text: The Anushteginid Khwarazmshahs rose from governors in Khwarazm, south of the Aral Sea, to rulers of a large empire across Central Asia and Iran. Their hereditary line ruled from 1097 to 1231. This imported record is misleading: its southern Afghanistan and Pakistan outline omits Khwarazm and most of the empire, while its 1279 endpoint extends decades beyond the dynasty.

passages.title: An empire and its ruling family
passages.text: Qutb al-Din Muhammad became governor of Khwarazm in 1097, and his descendants made the office hereditary. His son Atsiz repeatedly challenged Seljuk authority but also submitted when circumstances required it. Independence emerged through campaigns, negotiations and changing alliances. The family’s early position was quite different from the enormous empire later ruled by Muhammad II.

passages.title: An empire and its ruling family
passages.text: Tekesh defeated the last Great Seljuk sultan, Toghril III, in 1194 and extended Khwarazmian power into western Iran. Winning territory did not guarantee a welcome for his soldiers. Resistance and attacks on Khwarazmian troops after his death reveal how fragile distant control could be, even when a ruler’s title and victories looked impressive.

passages.title: An empire and its ruling family
passages.text: Terken Khatun, Tekesh’s wife and Muhammad II’s mother, was an important political figure. Her marriage helped connect the dynasty with northern steppe military allies. After her son became ruler in 1200, she retained a powerful following and influence over decisions. Royal family relationships could shape armies and government, as well as life inside the palace.

passages.title: A busy city, water and skilled hands
passages.text: At medieval Dehistan, archaeologists have identified water-supply works, bathhouses, sewage infrastructure and brick-paved surfaces. These are useful traces of washing, moving water and keeping a busy settlement functioning. The official heritage report describes the medieval city broadly, so every drain cannot be assigned to one Khwarazmian ruler. Sewage remains alone do not establish modern flushing toilets.

passages.title: A busy city, water and skilled hands
passages.text: Dehistan also had workshops making bricks, bronze vessels and lamps, glazed ceramics and glass. Caravanserai remains mark places connected with travelers and trade. A pot or lamp involved specialist labor before it reached a household. The archaeological picture includes the makers and merchants who kept city life going alongside the more visible rulers and monumental buildings.

passages.title: A busy city, water and skilled hands
passages.text: The mosque associated with Muhammad II is one of Dehistan’s major Khwarazmian monuments. Its surviving portal and nearby minaret belong to a city whose important buildings accumulated over centuries. Another minaret dates to 1004 or 1005, before this dynasty. Looking at a ruined skyline therefore requires sorting buildings by age, rather than giving every tower to the same king.

passages.title: A busy city, water and skilled hands
passages.text: At Kunya-Urgench, the mausoleum attributed to Tekesh has a conical roof rising above a tall, many-sided drum. Brick patterns and surviving turquoise tiles decorate it, while the entrance has small projecting forms often compared to stalactites. The ICOMOS evaluation gives its date cautiously as around 1195. Its striking shape depended on skilled brickworkers and careful construction.

passages.title: Children, medicine and learning
passages.text: Jorjani arrived in Khwarazm in 1110 and wrote a Persian medical encyclopedia for Qutb al-Din Muhammad. Its ten books organized topics from anatomy and hygiene to fevers, surgery, skin problems and medicines. A reader could turn to a particular area of the body or kind of illness. This was a substantial working arrangement of medical knowledge, including ideas inherited from Avicenna.

passages.title: Children, medicine and learning
passages.text: Children’s teeth had a place in Jorjani’s medical writing. He discussed baby teeth, their replacement and teething, as well as the structure of adult teeth. Oral hygiene and toothpicks also received attention. These passages reveal practical concerns familiar to families: growing teeth, sore mouths and keeping teeth clean, even though medieval explanations and treatments differed from those used today.

passages.title: Children, medicine and learning
passages.text: Jorjani explained that completing his medical encyclopedia was difficult while he was also treating patients and directing the court pharmacy. He wanted to travel, collect plants and consult experts about medicines, but lacked the time. He therefore limited part of his discussion to familiar substances. Even a royal author could have too much work and too little time.

passages.title: Children, medicine and learning
passages.text: Zamakhshari compiled an Arabic-Persian dictionary for the ruler Atsiz. It grouped material under nouns, verbs and other grammatical categories, and also arranged words by meaning and rhyme. One surviving manuscript includes explanations in Chorasmian instead of Persian. Such books helped readers navigate a multilingual learned world; they do not by themselves tell us how many ordinary children attended school.

passages.title: A written sample and lives beyond conquest
passages.text: “ذخيره خوارزمشاهى” means “The Treasure of Khvarazm’Shah”, the title of Jorjani’s Persian medical encyclopedia. This is the National Library of Medicine catalogue’s typeset transcription, linked to manuscript P5, folio 1b, line 11. That surviving copy is seventeenth-century; the work itself was composed for the Khwarazmian court after 1110. The later manuscript preserves a much older book.

passages.title: A written sample and lives beyond conquest
passages.text: The Mongol army destroyed Urgench in 1221, but the city was rebuilt and remained important afterward. Much later monuments in today’s archaeological park belong to those subsequent centuries. A dynasty’s defeat was a political ending, not a single final date for every street or family. The ruined city preserves several different periods of destruction, rebuilding and eventual abandonment.

Mongol invasion shattered the empire. Jalal al-Din continued fighting after victories and defeats, fled across the Indus in 1221 and later campaigned in Iran and neighboring regions. He never recovered Khwarazm and was killed near Mayyafariqin in August 1231 while escaping renewed Mongol pressure. His death ended the ruling line’s struggle for an empire, although displaced troops and the region’s communities continued their histories.

sectionTitles: Learning, letters and a real writing sample
Bathing, illness and what the evidence can tell us

passages.text: Kyivan Rus was a changing network of rulers, towns and rural communities centered on Kyiv. Its builders made monumental churches, its craftspeople worked precious metals, and some residents sent wonderfully ordinary messages on birch bark. Its cultural inheritance reaches across present-day Ukraine, Belarus and Russia. These two map intervals cover different political phases: especially after the early twelfth century, a broad Rus label includes increasingly independent regional powers.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and unequal lives
passages.text: Princes governed networks of towns and dependent villages rather than neat modern provinces. Harvard’s cultural mapping project stresses that both internal and external boundaries changed. A colored outline is therefore a rough guide to a complicated political world.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and unequal lives
passages.text: Households depended on grain, livestock, fishing and hunting. Forests supplied materials and fuel.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and unequal lives
passages.text: The Ruskaia Pravda collected rules about injury, property, debts and witnesses during the eleventh and twelfth centuries. Surviving manuscripts are later copies, and scholars disagree about the dates of individual versions. This was a developing legal tradition, not one untouched book handed down from a single ruler.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and unequal lives
passages.text: Legal compensation differed with social rank. Enslaved people and people bound by debt lived alongside free householders and powerful elites. The beautiful objects in museums cannot tell us that everyone shared the same wealth or freedom.

passages.title: Rulers, towns and unequal lives
passages.text: Inheritance rules distinguished commoners, nobles and widows. Family relationships shaped who could receive property; wills could be spoken before relatives. Sorting out who got the family possessions was already serious business. These rules describe legal expectations, not every family’s actual behavior.

passages.title: Buildings, jewelry and discoveries
passages.text: Saint Sophia in Kyiv preserves eleventh-century mosaics and frescoes, including the Virgin Orans with raised arms. Byzantine masters and local builders contributed to the cathedral under Yaroslav. The art makes religious teaching visible through images as well as words.

passages.title: Buildings, jewelry and discoveries
passages.text: The cathedral’s surrounding complex includes much later baroque buildings. A visitor can therefore see several historical periods at once. The eleventh-century mosaics and the later additions should not all be assigned to Yaroslav’s lifetime.

passages.title: Buildings, jewelry and discoveries
passages.text: A finger ring attributed to Kyiv and dated 1000-1200 combines silver, gilded silver and dark niello decoration. The Metropolitan Museum interprets its crosses as signs of Christian faith. This small object connects skilled metalwork with the beliefs of a particular wearer, whose name is unknown.

passages.title: Buildings, jewelry and discoveries
passages.text: Gold and enamel jewelry now in the Metropolitan Museum came from Kyiv hoards discovered in 1842 and 1906. The 1842 find lay in the old apse of the Church of the Tithes. These objects reveal elaborate ornament, but their later sale and dispersal complicate efforts to reconstruct the original groups.

passages.title: Buildings, jewelry and discoveries
passages.text: Pekarska’s research followed old reports and collections to reconnect scattered treasures. Some pieces had disappeared or been melted down. Knowing where an object was found can matter as much as knowing how brightly it shines.

passages.title: Learning, letters and a real writing sample
passages.text: Birchbark document 591 from Novgorod’s Nutny excavation is an alphabet dated approximately 1025-1050. Its opening letters are “а б в г д е ж”. Someone was practicing the building blocks of writing. The surviving exercise does not identify the learner’s age or prove that every child attended school.

passages.title: Learning, letters and a real writing sample
passages.text: Evidence for women’s schooling is fragmentary. An encyclopedia account associates Anna Vsevolodivna with a girls’ school at Saint Andrew’s convent in late-eleventh-century Kyiv. It is evidence of a particular institution, not universal access to education.

passages.title: Learning, letters and a real writing sample
passages.text: Manuscripts, inscriptions and birchbark documents preserve different parts of literate life. Monastic copying helped transmit books, while private letters preserve business and personal concerns. Many surviving manuscripts cannot be dated to a single year.

passages.title: Learning, letters and a real writing sample
passages.text: In letter 246, dated roughly 1025-1050 with a possible later shift, Zhirovit complains to Stoyan that a debt has gone unpaid for nine years. The whole letter survived in Novgorod’s Nerevsky excavation. Chasing an overdue payment clearly predates email.

passages.title: Learning, letters and a real writing sample
passages.text: Letter 752, from Novgorod around 1100, complains about an unanswered invitation and asks for a reply. Its broken passages admit more than one reading, and its precise date is debated. Even with those gaps, the disappointment sounds familiar: messages had feelings attached long before phones did.

passages.title: Learning, letters and a real writing sample
passages.text: A later Novgorod letter, number 227, addresses the writer’s mother and discusses payments and property. It dates to about 1160-1180, after Novgorod had gained political autonomy. It illustrates family dealings in the wider Rus cultural world, not continuing government from Kyiv.

passages.title: Learning, letters and a real writing sample
passages.text: Here is a short Old East Slavic sample in Cyrillic from that actual birchbark letter: “водае семоу :в: гривьне”, meaning “give this person two grivnas.” The letter в between marks represents the number two. The words come from document 227, not a modern phrase translated backward into medieval spelling.

passages.title: Bathing, illness and what the evidence can tell us
passages.text: Archaeologists have found eleventh-century wooden bathhouses in Novgorod. A specialist history also records late-eleventh-century masonry baths in Kyiv and Pereyaslavl, following Byzantine traditions. Warm washing places required fuel, water and labor as well as a building.

passages.title: Bathing, illness and what the evidence can tell us
passages.text: Bathhouses tell us about washing, but the sources used here do not establish the toilet arrangements of a typical Rus home. A bath is not automatically a bathroom with a flushing toilet. Household sanitation deserves its own evidence.

passages.title: Bathing, illness and what the evidence can tell us
passages.text: Orthodox tradition remembers Agapitus of Kyiv’s Cave Monastery as a healer using vegetables and prayer in the eleventh century. The church’s retelling is a saint’s life, with miraculous events. It shows how healing and holiness were linked in religious memory; it does not demonstrate that a remedy cured a particular illness.

passages.title: Bathing, illness and what the evidence can tell us
passages.text: Stories about the Cave Monastery also require careful dating. The first Kyivan Cave Patericon collection arose between 1215 and 1230, drawing on earlier traditions; surviving versions are later still. A story about an eleventh-century monk is not necessarily an eyewitness record written in his lifetime.

passages.title: Fragmentation and later history
passages.text: After Mstyslav’s death in 1132, regional rulers increasingly pursued their own interests. Kyiv remained important, but shared dynastic ancestry did not mean constant political unity.

passages.title: Fragmentation and later history
passages.text: Novgorod’s revolt in 1136 increased its autonomy. Its assembly and elected officials mattered, although wealthy families exercised great influence. Calling it a republic does not mean everyone had equal political power.

passages.title: Fragmentation and later history
passages.text: Kyiv was sacked in 1169 during conflict among Rus princes. Fragmentation involved destructive warfare as well as shifting political loyalties.

passages.title: Fragmentation and later history
passages.text: After these map intervals, the 1240 siege devastated Kyiv and the Church of the Tithes was destroyed. Surviving art, manuscripts and later traditions nevertheless show cultural continuities. Political defeat and destruction did not erase the people or everything they knew.

Rus political unity weakened gradually as regional principalities grew more independent. The map cutoffs at 1100 and 1200 are coverage boundaries, not extinction dates. Kyiv suffered Mongol conquest in 1240, while communities and cultural traditions continued across the region.

sectionTitles: Building and dividing a steppe power
Archaeological discoveries and a recorded word

passages.text: The Kimek-Kipchak khaganate was an eastern steppe political formation, distinct from the later western Cuman-Kipchak groupings. This atlas displays it only from 1000 to 1100 across an enormous outline extending from western Kazakhstan toward the Altai and western Mongolia. The polygon simplifies mobile communities and shifting authority; its far eastern edge is not proof that one ruler continuously controlled every valley. The earlier Kimek confederation and its eleventh-century transformation require more than a single map snapshot.

passages.title: Building and dividing a steppe power
passages.text: The confederation brought several groups into a political alliance around the Irtysh. It gained strength after the collapse of the Uyghur khaganate in 840, when some displaced groups joined it. Kimek and Kipchak were related names within this history, but they should not be treated as two spellings for every member of a single people.

passages.title: Building and dividing a steppe power
passages.text: The khagan appointed regional leaders, while ruling offices and possessions could pass within families. This gave local dynasties durable power, sometimes enough to challenge the center. Relations with Oghuz, Karluk, Kyrgyz and Qarakhanid neighbors included alliances and campaigns. Governing a wide steppe required negotiating with other powerful households.

passages.title: Building and dividing a steppe power
passages.text: A foundation legend preserved by the Persian historian Gardizi connects a founding figure with water. Historian V. V. Tishin treats the account as evidence to investigate names and the union’s diversity, not a literal birth certificate for a nation. Even the proposed equivalence of Kimak and Yemak remains debated among specialists.

passages.title: Food, homes and useful hands
passages.text: Herds included sheep, horses and cattle, and movement followed available pasture. Some households used felt-covered wooden dwellings transported on ox-drawn carts. Moving house could involve taking the house along. The pattern varied: sources also describe groups who stayed longer in one place and cultivated crops.

passages.title: Food, homes and useful hands
passages.text: Gardizi, writing around 1050, describes summer horse milk and meat preserved for winter among the Kimek. He names sheep, horse and cattle meat. This outside account suggests a seasonal food strategy: milk when it was available, and preserved food for colder months. It does not provide a complete menu for every household.

passages.title: Food, homes and useful hands
passages.text: Wool and hides became far more than clothing. The scholarly synthesis describes felt-making, woven textiles and rugs, leather containers, footwear and covers for bows. Such work turned animal products into shelter and portable equipment. It required practiced hands and material knowledge, even where no classroom or school building survives.

passages.title: Food, homes and useful hands
passages.text: The Pavlodar museum reports fire-making steels and knives in both male and female Kimek-period graves. These modest tools belong beside the more eye-catching weapons and jewelry in our picture of the past. Burial offerings suggest their significance; they cannot tell us precisely how every family divided its daily chores.

passages.title: Food, homes and useful hands
passages.text: At mound sites along the Pavlodar Irtysh, archaeologists found animal bones and pieces of pottery, interpreted as remains of commemorative feasts. Potters mixed crushed stone into clay, and vessels often had a row of impressions around the neck. A broken pot can preserve the gestures of the person who decorated it.

passages.title: Archaeological discoveries and a recorded word
passages.text: At Semiyarka 2, researchers studied a medieval burial exposed among dunes near a much older settlement. The dagger, arrowheads and other objects support a proposed date in the later ninth to earlier tenth century, before this atlas window. Keeping those layers apart matters: older settlement pottery does not automatically belong to the buried person.

passages.title: Archaeological discoveries and a recorded word
passages.text: Objects near the Semiyarka burial included belt or harness fittings. One metal plaque preserved impressions of textile in its corrosion. Other fittings had silvered surfaces and small attachment pins. Scientists compared metal composition as well as shape, showing how a tiny decoration can preserve clues to both clothing and manufacturing.

passages.title: Archaeological discoveries and a recorded word
passages.text: Reexamining excavated Kimek metalwork, researcher L. Turganbayeva identified recurring geometric and plant designs, including trefoils, palmettes and heart-shaped forms. Buckles and earrings were practical objects with carefully planned decoration. These patterns connect individual artifacts with wider craft traditions without making every similar object evidence of the same ethnicity.

passages.title: Archaeological discoveries and a recorded word
passages.text: Studies of Upper Irtysh cemeteries also ask how gender and status affected burial. Differences appear in grave placement, food offerings and accompanying objects. Archaeologist F. Kh. Arslanova drew attention to the standing of some women. These findings open questions about social roles; a richly furnished grave alone cannot reconstruct an entire family’s life.

passages.title: Archaeological discoveries and a recorded word
passages.text: A short recorded word is قمز, rendered qımız by scholar Helga Anetshofer and meaning fermented mare’s milk. Gardizi’s Persian history, composed around 1050, attributes the term to the Kimek. The Arabic-script spelling shown here follows a modern publication of that transmitted text. It is an external written witness to a Turkic word, not a surviving Kimek autograph or proof of everyone’s literacy.

The khaganate weakened as regional rulers gained independence and neighboring movements altered the steppe balance. By the mid-eleventh century, Kipchak groupings had become dominant farther west. The atlas’s 1100 endpoint is not a documented common conquest date, and political fragmentation did not mean that its communities vanished.

sectionTitles: What happened when a king planned to move a city?
Homes and water in an Ionian city
A written promise, a remembered victory and an ending

passages.text: This record is best understood as the Asian realm of Antigonus I, a powerful successor of Alexander the Great. Its broad eastern Mediterranean outline fits that setting better than the later Antigonid kingdom in Macedonia. However, the imported 300 to 200 BCE interval begins just after Antigonus died at Ipsus in 301 BCE. His power developed during the struggles after Alexander’s death in 323 BCE; the map cannot represent his kingdom surviving for another century.

passages.title: Building a successor kingdom
passages.text: Antigonus had served Alexander before becoming a formidable rival to other successor generals. Appointed governor of Phrygia in 333 BCE, he already possessed an important base when Alexander died. His later kingdom grew from military command and competition among the successors.

passages.title: Building a successor kingdom
passages.text: Skepsis honored Antigonus after the peace of 311 BCE, planning sacrifices, a festival and citizens’ garlands. His sons received honors too: a public celebration could also advertise a political relationship.

passages.title: Building a successor kingdom
passages.text: After Demetrius’s naval victory in 306 BCE, Antigonus and his son adopted royal titles. Plutarch describes Antigonus sending Demetrius a diadem and a letter addressing him as king. Victory and family partnership helped turn commanders into a royal house.

passages.title: Building a successor kingdom
passages.text: Building naval power required many kinds of work. Diodorus describes Antigonus assembling woodcutters, sawyers and shipwrights in the mid-310s BCE, then bringing timber from Lebanon to the coast. Long before a sailor could pull an oar, someone had to fell, move and shape a tree.

passages.title: Building a successor kingdom
passages.text: The same account names shipyards at Tripolis, Byblos and Sidon, with another in Cilicia using timber from the Taurus mountains. Rhodes also agreed to build ships with imported wood. The fleet depended on a network of ports and supplies rather than one enormous royal workshop.

passages.title: What happened when a king planned to move a city?
passages.text: Around 303 BCE, Antigonus proposed merging Lebedos with Teos. His letter required replacement building plots and temporary housing without rent while new homes were built. These were plans and instructions; the inscription does not prove that every household actually moved.

passages.title: What happened when a king planned to move a city?
passages.text: The envoys also worried about feeding a larger population. They requested a fund that traders could borrow against security to import grain. Antigonus initially preferred supplies from nearby royal land, but his letter ultimately allowed the proposed grain fund.

passages.title: What happened when a king planned to move a city?
passages.text: Combining cities meant combining rules. Teos and Lebedos agreed to borrow the laws of Kos temporarily, and Antigonus directed envoys to copy them and bring back a sealed version. Running the new community required paperwork as well as construction.

passages.title: What happened when a king planned to move a city?
passages.text: The letter even required a burial place for the people of Lebedos. A relocation plan had to make room for remembering relatives, not simply for streets and houses. This is a small but telling detail of civic and family life.

passages.title: Homes and water in an Ionian city
passages.text: Priene offers a nearby archaeological comparison. Its town was laid out in the mid-fourth century BCE, before Antigonus’s royal title. A common house design arranged rooms around a courtyard, including a main living room and a room for entertaining. Family activities shared space with social visits.

passages.title: Homes and water in an Ionian city
passages.text: Modern research at Priene challenges the idea that identical plots produced identical households. Even the earliest houses did not always follow the same plan, and property boundaries changed later. A tidy street grid was no guarantee that every family had the same space or resources.

passages.title: Homes and water in an Ionian city
passages.text: Priene drew water from springs above the town through clay pipes, while channels along its streets carried wastewater away. These features belong to the city’s broader late-Classical and Hellenistic infrastructure. The hillside provided a useful water source, but keeping a town supplied still required pipes and maintenance.

passages.title: Homes and water in an Ionian city
passages.text: Excavators at Priene carefully record objects room by room to understand how homes were used. Much surviving household material comes from a destruction around 140 to 130 BCE, long after Antigonus. Those later finds help reconstruct the city’s continuing life, but cannot simply be assigned to his reign.

passages.title: A written promise, a remembered victory and an ending
passages.text: The Greek words “τοῖς Λεβεδίοις ἀμισθί”, transliterated tois Lebediois amisthi, mean “to the Lebedians without charge”. They come from the housing clause in Antigonus’s letter, around 303 BCE. This modern scholarly transcription preserves a practical promise of free accommodation.

passages.title: A written promise, a remembered victory and an ending
passages.text: A silver coin of Demetrius, dated 300 to 294 BCE, shows Nike, the goddess of victory, on a ship’s prow and Poseidon with his trident. Minted at Salamis on Cyprus, it recalls the naval victory of 306. The coin is later than Antigonus’s death: his son continued advertising the family’s achievements.

passages.title: A written promise, a remembered victory and an ending
passages.text: At Ipsus in 301 BCE, Antigonus faced an alliance of rival rulers. Plutarch describes Demetrius’s cavalry pursuing opponents too far and enemy elephants blocking its return. Antigonus was killed, and his Asian dominion broke apart. The account explains a military defeat, not the disappearance of its inhabitants.

Antigonus died at Ipsus in 301 BCE and the victors divided his Asian realm. Demetrius survived and later ruled Macedonia; the family continued there in later generations. The imported 200 BCE endpoint is not Antigonus I’s fall, and his kingdom must be distinguished from later Antigonid Macedonia.

sectionTitles: A famous story and a difficult historical question
Cooking, trade and very busy bees
Later Judah: writing, people and health

passages.text: The biblical books of Samuel and Kings describe David and Solomon ruling from Jerusalem. The scale, political organization and archaeological traces of a united monarchy in the tenth century BCE remain debated. The imported map’s 1500-500 BCE span and enormous fixed outline are not evidence for that kingdom’s lifespan or borders. This card separates the biblical narrative, dated regional discoveries and clearly labelled evidence from the later kingdoms of Israel and Judah.

passages.title: A famous story and a difficult historical question
passages.text: In 2 Samuel 5, representatives of Israel meet David at Hebron, acknowledge him as king and enter an agreement with him. The story then makes Jerusalem his royal centre. It presents kingship through relationships with elders, warfare and divine support. This is the biblical account, not a surviving tenth-century government record.

passages.title: A famous story and a difficult historical question
passages.text: First Kings describes Solomon building a temple in Jerusalem, with cedar panelling, carved decoration and gold. It even pictures stones prepared before reaching the building site. These details shaped later religious memory and architectural imagination; quoting the description does not establish that an excavated building is Solomon’s temple.

passages.title: A famous story and a difficult historical question
passages.text: Archaeologist Kyle Keimer warns that modern labels such as empire can smuggle modern expectations into ancient evidence. He asks how rulers controlled territory and persuaded communities to recognize their authority. Researchers therefore debate both the size of the proposed kingdom and what political unity would actually have meant.

passages.title: A famous story and a difficult historical question
passages.text: A later discovery provides a different kind of clue. Ninth-century BCE fragments of the Tel Dan stele carry an Aramaic reference to the House of David. Found in 1993 and 1994, they attest that dynastic name outside the Bible. They do not draw David’s borders or establish the scale of his government.

passages.title: Olive pits, walls and administration
passages.text: A 2024 Jerusalem study assembled 103 radiocarbon measurements from five excavation areas. Some charred remains dated to the twelfth through tenth centuries BCE. The authors identify early occupation whose character remains uncertain. Tiny organic fragments can establish human presence without telling us whether a particular king ordered a particular wall.

passages.title: Olive pits, walls and administration
passages.text: At Khirbet Qeiyafa, researchers dated 17 burnt olive pits found together inside a jar in a destruction layer. Four were divided between two laboratories as a check. The results placed them around 1000 BCE. An olive pit becomes a clock because the carbon it absorbed while growing changes predictably after death.

passages.title: Olive pits, walls and administration
passages.text: Qeiyafa’s excavators interpret its fortifications and public buildings as evidence for early Judahite organization. Alexander Fantalkin and Israel Finkelstein instead emphasize northern connections in its material culture. The town is real; its political affiliation and precise chronology remain disputed. A dated town cannot, by itself, settle every argument about a united kingdom.

passages.title: Olive pits, walls and administration
passages.text: A large Qeiyafa building occupied the summit, with walls thicker than those of ordinary houses. Excavators call it a probable administrative building. Another building beside the city wall contained rows of stone columns and was interpreted as a storehouse. Organizing storage and substantial construction required coordinated work, whoever held political authority.

passages.title: Olive pits, walls and administration
passages.text: Qeiyafa also yielded hundreds of storage jars, with fingerprints pressed into handles. Their clay was locally sourced according to material analysis. Such repeated marks helped archaeologists investigate organized production and storage. Ancient fingerprints are a wonderfully direct trace of hands at work, although they do not identify the individual potters.

passages.title: Cooking, trade and very busy bees
passages.text: The excavated Qeiyafa houses included courtyards, several rooms and spaces built into the double city wall. Clay cooking ovens found in courtyards place some food preparation outdoors. A household’s working space could extend into what looks, on a plan, like military architecture: the city wall also helped form people’s back rooms.

passages.title: Cooking, trade and very busy bees
passages.text: Grinding equipment at Qeiyafa came from different landscapes. Some stones were made from coastal beach rock, while basalt tools connected the settlement with other source areas. Cypriot juglets and Egyptian objects add evidence of wider exchange. Even preparing food could depend on materials brought from beyond the immediate neighbourhood.

passages.title: Cooking, trade and very busy bees
passages.text: At Tel Rehov in the Jordan Valley, clay cylinders from the tenth to early ninth centuries BCE proved to be beehives. Researchers found actual bee remains inside them, including immature bees. This is regional evidence for specialist food production around the debated period, without demonstrating that David or Solomon controlled the apiary.

passages.title: Cooking, trade and very busy bees
passages.text: The Tel Rehov bees resembled an Anatolian subspecies rather than the local one. Researchers proposed two possibilities: bee populations once had different ranges, or beekeepers imported suitable colonies. Either way, managing hives inside a town took skill. Honey production involved rather more planning than finding something sweet and hoping it would not sting.

passages.title: Cooking, trade and very busy bees
passages.text: Qeiyafa’s ritual rooms contained special objects, including small shrine models. A carved stone example reproduces elaborate doorways and roof details. These models offer rare evidence for how people represented sacred buildings. Archaeologists compare them with later architectural traditions and biblical descriptions, while keeping the models distinct from the Jerusalem temple itself.

passages.title: Later Judah: writing, people and health
passages.text: A securely identified later Hebrew sample appears on royal jar handles from Jerusalem around 700 BCE: l-m-l-k, meaning “belonging to the king”. This is the museum’s Latin-letter transcription of Hebrew letters, not an imitation of their ancient shapes. These administrative stamps belong to later Judah, roughly three centuries after the traditional setting of Solomon.

passages.title: Later Judah: writing, people and health
passages.text: A jasper seal from Lachish, dated 750-700 BCE, combines a winged sphinx with a Hebrew inscription naming Hannah as its owner. The Ashmolean notes that surviving women’s seals from this period are rare. This later object brings a named woman into view, although it cannot tell us how every family divided property or work.

passages.title: Later Judah: writing, people and health
passages.text: Later Jerusalem even preserves evidence from the toilet. A study of two latrines, dated to the seventh and early sixth centuries BCE, detected Giardia parasite antigens in both. The result reveals an intestinal-health problem in these households. These are centuries-later Judahite finds, so they cannot diagnose people living in David’s time.

passages.title: Later Judah: writing, people and health
passages.text: First Kings explains the kingdom’s division through a dispute over heavy labour: Rehoboam refuses demands for relief, and northern Israelites choose Jeroboam. That is the text’s account of political rupture after Solomon. Much later, Babylonian records document Judean families rebuilding livelihoods abroad through farming, contracts and business, showing lives continuing after royal institutions ended.

The biblical account describes division after Solomon. Later Israel lost independence to Assyria in the late eighth century BCE, and Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BCE. Judean communities continued under subsequent empires. Neither conquest matches the imported map’s 500 BCE endpoint.

sectionTitles: A royal family in a wider war

passages.text: Gala, also called Gaia, ruled the Massyles of eastern Numidia and was the father of Massinissa. This map record is badly mistimed: its 200 to 100 BCE window begins after Gala’s death, around 206 BCE. The outline lies in northeastern Algeria. The story below distinguishes his third-century kingdom from earlier monuments and the later Numidian life visible in that region.

passages.title: A royal family in a wider war
passages.text: Livy tells a vivid story about Gala’s grandson Massiva: orphaned, he was brought up by his grandfather, then accompanied his uncle Massinissa to Spain. Captured after joining a battle against orders, he was returned by Scipio. This is a later Roman account of a royal childhood, shaped partly to praise Scipio.

passages.title: A royal family in a wider war
passages.text: When Gala died, the crown did not pass straight to his son. Livy describes succession through Gala’s brother Oesalces and then Capusa, followed by a violent struggle involving Mezetulus and the young Lacumaces. Massinissa returned from Spain and recovered his father’s realm. Royal family trees could become battlefield maps.

passages.title: A royal family in a wider war
passages.text: In the following decades, Massinissa’s ambitions reached well beyond his father’s kingdom. He expanded at the expense of both western Numidian rivals and Carthage. Scholars caution that the western conquest sequence is poorly documented; the enormous later kingdom should not be projected backward onto Gala.

passages.title: Builders, houses and city life
passages.text: An earlier landmark near Batna is the Medracen, a monumental circular tomb with a stepped roof, Doric-style columns and Egyptian-inspired details. Gabriel Camps placed its construction in the later fourth or early third century BCE. It shows the resources and architectural connections of earlier Numidian rulers; the name of its occupant remains uncertain.

passages.title: Builders, houses and city life
passages.text: Inside the Medracen, an eleven-step stair leads into a long passage. In 1969, Camps examined cedar beams in its roof, including fire-marked timbers; earlier writers had mistaken the construction. Radiocarbon tests on the wood helped investigate the monument’s age. Even a royal tomb depended on skilled carpentry as well as stonework.

passages.title: Builders, houses and city life
passages.text: Later Numidian Cirta, today Constantine, occupied a rocky plateau protected by the deep Rhummel gorge on two sides and steep ground on another. An approach from the southwest linked it to the Koudiat hill. The landscape helped make the city defensible while shaping how people reached its streets.

passages.title: Builders, houses and city life
passages.text: A dwelling identified toward Sidi M’cid, beyond Cirta’s main plateau, contained Campanian pottery that dated occupation to at least the first century BCE. A household’s broken dishes can therefore help date a neighborhood. This house belongs after Gala’s lifetime, just after the map’s imported period.

passages.title: Builders, houses and city life
passages.text: At El Hofra outside Cirta, inscriptions in Punic, Neo-Punic, Greek and Latin preserve traces of a sanctuary and its changing community of worshippers. These finds help recover a city whose ancient remains were heavily damaged by later rebuilding. Different written languages survive where much of the architecture does not.

passages.title: Food, offerings and written names
passages.text: A small offering stone in the Louvre names Hannibaal, son of Bodmelqart, dedicating a vow to Baal Hammon in thanks for being heard and blessed. The museum dates it between 225 and 50 BCE and tentatively associates it with El Hofra. Here a father’s name helps identify a person otherwise almost lost to history.

passages.title: Food, offerings and written names
passages.text: The same stone fragment has a carved rudder above a double-moulded panel holding the inscription. Someone planned both the image and the words before cutting the stone. Its careful layout makes a personal act of worship into a surviving example of craft and design.

passages.title: Food, offerings and written names
passages.text: Under Massinissa in the early second century BCE, Numidian grain surpluses supplied Roman armies overseas. Archaeologists Papi and Martorella calculate more than 2.2 million Roman modii in recorded deliveries during the century’s first thirty years. Behind those royal shipments stood the recurring work of sowing, harvesting, storing and transporting cereal crops.

passages.title: Food, offerings and written names
passages.text: Written language sample: GYY is the scholarly transliteration of Gala’s name in the Punic text of a bilingual dedication from Dougga, about 138 BCE. It means the personal name Gaia or Gala. This later memorial to his son Massinissa preserves the family relationship; Dougga lies east of this imported outline.

Gala’s rule ended with his death around 206 BCE. The ensuing succession struggle eventually brought his son Massinissa back to power; eastern Numidia became part of a larger kingdom. The map’s 100 BCE endpoint marks neither Gala’s death nor the disappearance of Numidian communities.

sectionTitles: Arts, education and the royal court

passages.text: The Hawaiian Kingdom joined islands with much older political and cultural traditions. Its people developed newspapers, constitutional institutions and international connections while maintaining knowledge of land, water and the arts. This card follows the monarchy from Kamehameha I's consolidation in 1795 to its overthrow in 1893; unification of the principal islands was completed in 1810.

passages.title: Food and environmental engineering
passages.text: At Heeia, parallel basalt walls packed mainly with coral slowed the movement of water. Sluice gates controlled freshwater and seawater flows, maintaining brackish conditions in which algae could feed herbivorous fish. This engineering tradition long predates the unified kingdom.

passages.title: Food and environmental engineering
passages.text: Fishponds helped maintain a food supply when rough seas interrupted ocean fishing. Heeia remained part of the kingdom's lived landscape: Abner Paki received much of the surrounding land during the Mahele of 1848.

passages.title: Discoveries in surviving newspapers
passages.text: Ka Lama Hawaii began publication at Lahainaluna Seminary on Maui in 1834. Surviving issues preserve Hawaiian-language writing from the kingdom itself, giving readers access to contemporary voices alongside later histories.

passages.title: Discoveries in surviving newspapers
passages.text: A letter from Hanalei printed in Ka Hae Hawaii on 14 January 1857 set out Hawaiian month names and day counts. Its author, J. W. Q. Kaia, worried that younger readers no longer knew them. The museum cautions that month names varied between islands.

passages.title: Discoveries in surviving newspapers
passages.text: A surviving Ka Nupepa Kuokoa issue displays the Hawaiian flag in color on 1 January 1862. The original held at Hamilton Library is evidence of printing and national expression that can be lost in poor reproductions; conservation and digitization make such details easier to study.

passages.title: Work, government and public life
passages.text: The Kuhina Nui shared governing authority with the monarch, including land distribution, treaties and justice. Women of high chiefly rank held the office first. Calling it simply a prime ministership understates the authority of these early co-regents.

passages.title: Work, government and public life
passages.text: The constitution of 1840 provided for a council of nobles and a representative body chosen by the people. Early legislative rules developed over time; a written constitution did not immediately create equal political power for everyone.

passages.title: Work, government and public life
passages.text: Lahaina linked local households with visiting whaling ships, trade and, later, sugar plantations. From the 1850s Chinese immigrants worked under plantation contracts, and some settled on Maui after those contracts ended. The kingdom's economic history includes these workers as well as its rulers.

passages.title: Arts, education and the royal court
passages.text: Completed in 1882, Iolani Palace combined a royal home with rooms for official receptions and visiting dignitaries. Hula performances and grand balls formed part of its public and ceremonial life.

passages.title: Arts, education and the royal court
passages.text: Liliuokalani composed Aloha Oe in 1878, before becoming queen. Her work as a composer forms part of a larger musical legacy remembered alongside her political life.

passages.title: Arts, education and the royal court
passages.text: In 1886 Liliuokalani founded an educational society to support schooling for Hawaiian girls with limited means. Her public work connected royal patronage with access to education beyond the court.

passages.title: Arts, education and the royal court
passages.text: The Highways Act of 1892 protected public trails and rights of access. Its continuing importance to Hawaiian trail preservation shows how a kingdom-era law can shape the landscape after a change of government.

passages.title: After the overthrow
passages.text: A royalist attempt to restore Liliuokalani in 1895 failed. She was tried in the palace throne room and confined in an upstairs room, turning the royal residence into a place of imprisonment.

passages.title: After the overthrow
passages.text: Hawaiians organized petitions against annexation in 1897, and Liliuokalani continued to protest. These records preserve organized political opposition after the monarchy had been overthrown.

passages.title: After the overthrow
passages.text: Congress passed its annexation resolution on 7 July 1898. This later US action must be distinguished from the overthrow of the monarchy in 1893.

On 17 January 1893, the Committee of Safety overthrew Liliuokalani with support from the US minister and US Marines, establishing a Provisional Government. A republic followed in 1894. The removal of the monarchy did not end Hawaiian people, culture or opposition to annexation.

sectionTitles: A kingdom at the mountain crossings
Clothes, crops and the changing seasons
A king’s name in your hand

passages.text: The atlas’s Kingdom of Kapisa covers 700 to 800, within the era of the early, often called Turk, Shahis. Their power connected the Kabul basin with Gandhara on routes between Central Asia and the Indus country. The broad polygon is a simplified political outline, not a surveyed frontier. Earlier Kushan and Hephthalite history and the later Hindu Shahi dynasty belong to different phases.

passages.title: A kingdom at the mountain crossings
passages.text: Kapisa occupied the northern end of the Kabul basin, near routes up the Panjshir and Ghorband valleys. These led toward passes through the Hindu Kush. Water and fertile land made the basin a valuable stopping place on journeys between Central Asia and the Indus country.

passages.title: A kingdom at the mountain crossings
passages.text: The political balance gradually shifted from Kapisa toward Kabul, whose position was easier to defend. The shift does not mean that all older inhabitants moved away. Nor should Begram’s famous Kushan-era treasures be presented as goods made for this eighth-century dynasty.

passages.title: A kingdom at the mountain crossings
passages.text: Chinese records document royal missions and succession. Around 738 or 739, Tegin Khurasan Shah was succeeded by his son Frum Kesar, also known as Fromo Kesaro. Bofuzhun followed in 745. The differently recorded names show why historians compare chronicles with coins. These rulers supported Buddhist institutions alongside Hindu cults; a dynastic label does not describe every subject’s religion.

passages.title: Clothes, crops and the changing seasons
passages.text: In the 720s, the Korean pilgrim Hyecho described the ruler spending summers in cool Kapisa and winters in warmer Gandhara. Snow made the highland winter uncomfortable. Even a king could find that the sensible response to freezing weather was to change his address with the season.

passages.title: Clothes, crops and the changing seasons
passages.text: Hyecho says both men and women in Kapisa wore shirts, trousers and boots, with broadly similar clothing. His travel account gives a practical glimpse of dress in this mountain country. It does not preserve a complete wardrobe for every occupation or social class.

passages.title: Clothes, crops and the changing seasons
passages.text: His list of Kapisa’s products includes grapes, wheat, barley and saffron, alongside horses, sheep, cattle, donkeys and camels. Grain fields, fruit growing and livestock all contributed to livelihoods. This is a traveler’s inventory of resources, not a surviving recipe for the royal dinner.

passages.title: Clothes, crops and the changing seasons
passages.text: Hyecho also describes local families supporting monasteries and people making daily offerings at the Shahi monastery’s relic shrine. Religious life involved ordinary donors as well as rulers. His account lets us see repeated community activities, rather than only a procession of kings.

passages.title: Communal spaces and craft knowledge
passages.text: Tepe Narenj near Kabul contained a circular chapel with sixteen bodhisattva figures standing on a circular bench. Excavator Zafar Paiman dates the illustrated chapel to the eighth century. The assembled figures gave worshippers a shared setting for encountering Buddhist sacred imagery, rather than a single isolated statue.

passages.title: Communal spaces and craft knowledge
passages.text: At Tepe Narenj and nearby Qol-e Tut, large clay figures were built over wooden skeletons, using successive modeling layers and sometimes a thin gypsum finish. The sites span the fifth through eleventh centuries. Their makers combined carpentry, careful mixing and surface finishing; a giant figure began with very practical craft skills.

passages.title: Communal spaces and craft knowledge
passages.text: Modern analysis found lapis-lazuli blue and iron-rich hematite red on a Qol-e Tut wall-painting fragment. A sculpture fragment carried pink made with hematite in a gypsum-based coating. These tiny remains recover part of a once colorful environment, even where whole painted scenes have disappeared.

passages.title: Communal spaces and craft knowledge
passages.text: One analyzed fragment was a sculpted toe only about four centimetres across. Researchers avoided cutting it into a thin section because they wanted to preserve it. Studying the past can mean learning as much as possible from a tiny piece while leaving it available for future questions.

passages.title: Clay figures and small clues
passages.text: At Fondukistan in the Ghorband valley, excavators uncovered a courtyard with a small central stupa and niches filled with sculpture and paintings. A seventh-century clay divinity, now in the Musée Guimet, comes from this setting. It introduces the artistic world immediately before this map window.

passages.title: Clay figures and small clues
passages.text: The figure’s sculptor shaped tiny curls, necklaces and delicate folds in clay. It originally pointed toward a Buddha and faced a matching figure, now lost. Viewers encountered a carefully arranged scene. Planning the whole niche mattered as much as making one beautiful statue.

passages.title: Clay figures and small clues
passages.text: Coins beneath Fondukistan’s royal-couple sculptures help refine the site’s chronology. An older Sasanian coin carried later stamps, including one dated around 689. The deposit therefore cannot be earlier than that mark. A tiny stamped detail can correct the apparent age of an entire setting.

passages.title: Clay figures and small clues
passages.text: At Qol-e Tut near Kabul, excavated coins illuminate seventh-century exchange before this map window. Researchers distinguish local-market coins from higher-silver Sasanian and Arab issues suited to wider transactions. A coin accepted nearby was not necessarily equally useful when its owner crossed into another region.

passages.title: A king’s name in your hand
passages.text: A Tegin coin in Vienna’s Kunsthistorisches Museum is only 13.9 millimetres across and weighs 0.73 grams. Its portrait wears a crown with a large crescent. Dated approximately 680 to 740, it compresses royal imagery into an object small enough to vanish between your fingers.

passages.title: A king’s name in your hand
passages.text: Its Bactrian legend is read as tagino šauo, “Tegin, the king.” This is a Latin transliteration of the museum’s reading, not a reconstruction of every letter on the coin. The catalogue marks the legend as irregular. Written royal titles could travel wherever the money circulated.

The atlas’s year 800 is not a recorded fall. The early Shahi dynasty gave way to Kallara’s later Shahi line around 822, with the precise accession date debated. Changing rulers did not instantly replace the region’s people or religions; local institutions and religious traditions continued through further political change.

sectionTitles: Kings, buildings and historical detective work

passages.text: This map record covers Kashmir around 700 to 800 CE, during the Karkota dynasty. Its rulers supported temples, monasteries and learned communities. The imported outline is approximate, not a surveyed frontier or a statement about modern sovereignty. The dynasty continued beyond the map’s endpoint.

passages.title: Kings, buildings and historical detective work
passages.text: Much of the royal story comes from Kalhana, writing around 1149 to 1150. His chronicle preserves earlier dynastic information, but he lived centuries after the Karkotas. Historians compare its chronology with outside records instead of treating every royal story as an eyewitness report.

passages.title: Kings, buildings and historical detective work
passages.text: Kalhana associates Lalitaditya’s religious foundations with grants of villages to Brahmins. Royal patronage connected temples with landed resources, making control of the countryside part of the story too.

passages.title: Kings, buildings and historical detective work
passages.text: Parihasapura, founded by Lalitaditya in the eighth century, contained Buddhist and Hindu monuments. Surviving remains include a stupa, a monastery and Vishnu temples. Its builders worked with enormous stone blocks: creating a royal religious center required organized labor as well as impressive royal ambitions.

passages.title: Kings, buildings and historical detective work
passages.text: Excavation at Parihasapura in 1914 exposed buildings beneath the ruined site. Archaeology lets a visitor compare the physical remains with written accounts: platforms, blocks and building plans survive even when the original roofs and many images have disappeared.

passages.title: Kings, buildings and historical detective work
passages.text: Martand was a sanctuary of Surya, the sun god. Its surviving courtyard and carved stonework still make the building’s scale visible. Looking at a temple means looking at the work of people who quarried, shaped and fitted the stone, as well as the deity honored there.

passages.title: Kings, buildings and historical detective work
passages.text: Even coins can be historical puzzles. Numismatist John Deyell questioned the traditional attribution of some gold-alloy coins to Kashmir’s Karkota rulers: their find locations and several royal names do not fit comfortably. A familiar museum label can be a research question rather than the final answer.

passages.title: Households, winter and words
passages.text: The Nilamata Purana preserves rituals associated with Kashmir. Its editor Ved Kumari Ghai dates the core broadly to the sixth through eighth centuries, with later additions. Its festival instructions reveal household ideals, rather than proving that every family celebrated identically.

passages.title: Households, winter and words
passages.text: For snowfall celebrations, the Nilamata recommends substantial cloaks, special food and gathering on the snow with children, relatives, friends and servants. Music accompanies the meal. Apparently a winter picnic required both a good guest list and very warm clothes.

passages.title: Households, winter and words
passages.text: Another celebration calls for lamps at houses, shops, crossroads and rivers, with cloth decorating the shops. Friends, relatives and servants share a meal after sunset. The same text exempts children and sick people from that day’s fasting requirement.

passages.title: Households, winter and words
passages.text: Written-language sample: नमस्ते नागराजेन्द्र means “Salutation to you, sovereign-king of the Nagas.” This Sanskrit greeting opens a hymn to Nila, the serpent king. It is shown in modern Devanagari transcription of the transmitted text, not copied from an eighth-century inscription.

passages.title: Makers, donors and miniature worlds
passages.text: A Kashmir Buddha figure dated around 800 stands only 14.6 centimeters high. Its maker combined brass with silver and copper inlays; a forehead setting once held a gemstone. The sculpture represents the infant Buddha with several adult attributes, including curled hair and elongated earlobes.

passages.title: Makers, donors and miniature worlds
passages.text: The same figure carries a donor’s message in Kashmir’s Sharada script. The museum translates its opening as “This is the pious gift of Shrideva,” but the donor’s following description is uncertain. That small inscription preserves a person’s name and an act of generosity across twelve centuries.

passages.title: Makers, donors and miniature worlds
passages.text: An eighth-century ivory carving from Kashmir fits a dancer and two musicians into a piece about 4.5 centimeters wide. One musician plays a drum hanging from his shoulders; the other holds what the curator tentatively identifies as a tambourine. Tiny does not mean simple.

passages.title: Makers, donors and miniature worlds
passages.text: Traces of color remain on that ivory. The curator suggests it belonged to a portable shrine and may portray a Buddhist story involving Mara’s daughter. Its music-making figures are therefore evidence of artistic imagination and familiar instruments, rather than a labeled photograph of an ordinary party.

passages.title: Makers, donors and miniature worlds
passages.text: Another eighth-century Kashmir ivory shows the Buddha descending three steps after teaching his mother in heaven. At just 6.4 centimeters high, it turns a story about a son and his mother into something small enough to carry. Attendants hold ceremonial accessories beside him.

passages.title: Makers, donors and miniature worlds
passages.text: A late eighth-century stone Vishnu has four faces: a human face, a lion, a boar, and a fierce face carved behind the halo. You have to look around the sculpture to discover the fourth. This form was especially important in Kashmir’s religious art.

passages.title: Makers, donors and miniature worlds
passages.text: The Vishnu sculpture also turns equipment into characters. Its original attendants personified the god’s discus and mace; the mace figure is now missing. The earth goddess appears between his legs. The sculptor packed divine relationships into a single stone image about a meter tall.

The map ends at 800, but the Karkota dynasty did not. Utpala rulers succeeded it around the middle of the ninth century. Kashmir’s religious, literary and artistic communities continued through that political change.

passages.text: Cassander, also spelled Kassander, took control of Macedonia after Alexander the Great’s empire fragmented. He was master of Macedon from 316 BCE and adopted the royal title around 305 BCE. The imported map record runs from 300 to 200 BCE, but he died in 297 BCE: most of that displayed interval belongs to later rulers, not his kingdom.

passages.title: A ruler after Alexander
passages.text: Cassander married Alexander’s half-sister Thessalonike and rebuilt Thebes, but his consolidation of power was also violent. He had the young Alexander IV killed around 310 BCE, removing Alexander the Great’s son from the struggle for the throne.

passages.title: A ruler after Alexander
passages.text: He established two major cities in strategic coastal positions: Cassandreia took his own name, while Thessaloniki took his wife’s. A city’s name could advertise a royal family almost as effectively as a coin.

passages.title: A ruler after Alexander
passages.text: Thessaloniki’s foundation in 316/5 BCE brought together inhabitants from 26 surrounding townships. Building a new royal city meant moving people as well as laying out streets. The city’s later importance grew from this deliberate concentration of population around the Thermaic Gulf.

passages.title: A growing capital
passages.text: Pella expanded northward in Cassander’s time. Its Hellenistic plan arranged buildings in regular blocks between straight streets, with a broad route through the centre. Planning a capital meant organising movement between the harbour, market and palace.

passages.title: A growing capital
passages.text: The Hellenistic city had clay water pipes and large masonry drains with openings for cleaning. Water had to arrive, and wastewater had to leave. Those maintenance openings are a reminder that ancient plumbing needed somebody willing to do the unpleasant jobs.

passages.title: A growing capital
passages.text: Pella’s houses commonly centred on courtyards, sometimes surrounded by colonnades. Rich households decorated dining rooms with mosaics; smaller houses might have just one broad porch. Surviving grand residences should not be mistaken for everybody’s address.

passages.title: A growing capital
passages.text: The House of Dionysus has pebble mosaics dated 325 to 300 BCE, including Dionysus riding a panther and a lion hunt. These floors belong to the generation of Cassander’s rise. Dinner guests had dramatic scenes beneath their feet.

passages.title: A growing capital
passages.text: At the palace, a swimming pool, dressing room and adjoining bath were built near the end of the fourth century BCE. Excavated pottery and coins help establish the date. The researchers identify this bathing suite as royal: the king’s swimming arrangements were not a public pool for the whole city.

passages.title: A growing capital
passages.text: A small terracotta figure of sleeping Eros came from a child’s burial in Pella’s eastern cemetery and is dated 325 to 300 BCE. This quiet object brings a child into a history so often dominated by adult rulers and battles. Its burial context is known; the child’s personal story is not.

passages.title: Coins and family property
passages.text: A bronze coin dated about 305 to 297 BCE carries the Greek words ΚΑΣΣΑΝΔΡΟΥ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩΣ, “of King Cassander”. This is the museum’s transcription of the ancient inscription, not a phrase invented for the card. Even a small coin could announce who claimed to rule.

passages.title: Coins and family property
passages.text: The same coin shows Heracles wearing a lion skin on one side and a young rider on the other. Cassander placed his own name beside familiar heroic and equestrian imagery. Royal messages travelled on objects people could hold in one hand.

passages.title: Coins and family property
passages.text: A recorded inscription from Cassandreia confirms land for Perdikkas, son of Koinos, including property previously allotted to his father and grandfather. The grant made ownership hereditary and allowed descendants to exchange or sell it. Family advantage could be written into royal decisions.

passages.title: Coins and family property
passages.text: That grant also exempted Perdikkas and his descendants from taxes on imports and exports connected with the property. It is a glimpse of unequal economic privilege: one favoured household received written advantages that should not be assumed for every farmer.

Cassander died in 297 BCE. Quarrels among his heirs soon destabilised Macedonia, which continued under other rulers. His personal kingdom therefore ended long before the imported map’s 200 BCE endpoint, while his new cities outlasted the dynasty.

sectionTitles: A king’s name and another king’s face

passages.text: Lysimachus built one of the kingdoms that emerged after Alexander the Great’s death. His power began in Thrace and later extended into western Anatolia and Macedonia. The imported map shows mainly Thrace from 300 to 200 BCE. That outline misses much of his later kingdom, and its dates continue long after his death in 281 BCE.

passages.title: Power around the straits
passages.text: After the battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE, Lysimachus gained extensive lands in Asia Minor. He later shared and then took control of Macedonia. His kingdom changed substantially within one lifetime, so a single Thracian outline cannot represent its maximum reach.

passages.title: Power around the straits
passages.text: Lysimacheia, founded in 309 BCE, bore the king’s name and stood in a strategic position near the Hellespont. After his death, other rulers repeatedly competed for it. A new city could outlast its founder while remaining caught between larger powers.

passages.title: Building cities and moving households
passages.text: Across the water in Anatolia, Lysimachus refounded Ephesos around 300 BCE. The project gathered people from nearby smaller settlements into a planned city. The Austrian Archaeological Institute describes the resettlement as forced: a king’s impressive urban project could mean an unwanted move for a household.

passages.title: Building cities and moving households
passages.text: Ephesos’s Hellenistic plan included a regular street grid and a fortification circuit about nine kilometres long along the hills. Those surviving walls help identify this early city beneath later building phases. Many famous monuments visible at Ephesos today were rebuilt or added under Rome.

passages.title: Building cities and moving households
passages.text: Strabo, writing centuries later, tells an unsettling story about the move: Lysimachus allegedly blocked drains during heavy rain to flood the old settlement and make residents leave. This is an ancient author’s account, not an event established by excavated plumbing. It shows how coercive the king’s reputation could be.

passages.title: Fields, families and food
passages.text: A marble land grant from Cassandreia, dated 285/4 BCE, lists wooded estates and a vineyard given to Limnaios, son of Harpalos. It identifies neighbours as well as areas. Royal property was described through usable resources and local boundaries, not just lines on a grand map.

passages.title: Fields, families and food
passages.text: The same grant allowed Limnaios and his descendants to keep, sell, exchange or give away the estates. This is unusually direct evidence for inherited family wealth under Lysimachus. Such royal favour tells us about a privileged household rather than all rural families.

passages.title: Fields, families and food
passages.text: An Athenian decree credits the poet Philippides with persuading Lysimachus to send 10,000 Attic medimnoi of wheat, distributed to Athenians in 299/8 BCE. A poet at court could do practical diplomatic work. In this case his useful words helped bring grain.

passages.title: Fields, families and food
passages.text: After the battle of Ipsus, Philippides also secured the release of Athenian prisoners. Those who wanted to leave received clothing and travel money from him; others chose further military service. The decree counts more than 300 people helped. It preserves individual choices within a much larger war.

passages.title: Fields, families and food
passages.text: Athens later rewarded Philippides with a bronze statue in the theatre, public dining privileges and a front-row seat at civic competitions. These honours reveal a social world in which poetry, festivals, generosity and royal connections could reinforce one another.

passages.title: A king’s name and another king’s face
passages.text: An Otago Museum silver coin minted at Colophon about 299 to 296 BCE reads ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩ[Σ] ΛΥΣΙΜΑΧΟΥ, “of King Lysimachus”. The brackets mark a restored letter in the catalogue’s transcription. This small Greek inscription comes from the Anatolian side of his kingdom, beyond most of the imported outline.

passages.title: A king’s name and another king’s face
passages.text: Lysimachus also issued coins showing Alexander with the ram’s horn of the god Amun, while Athena appeared on the reverse. The face was Alexander’s, although the money named Lysimachus. The British Museum explains this as a claim to inherit the conqueror’s prestige.

Lysimachus was killed fighting Seleucus at Corupedium in 281 BCE. His Asian lands passed to the Seleucids, while Macedonia entered another struggle for power. His kingdom did not survive intact until the map’s 200 BCE endpoint, although its cities and communities continued.

sectionTitles: A kingdom and the stories told about it
Belief, small money and surviving writing
Conquest did not mean everyone disappeared

passages.text: This record best fits the kingdom of Sind ruled by Dahir before the Arab conquest. Its broad outline includes neighboring frontier regions and should not be read as a precise border. The imported 700 to 800 interval crosses a major change: Dahir was defeated and killed in 712, and Arab provincial rule followed. It does not represent one Hindu kingdom surviving unchanged until 800.

passages.title: A kingdom and the stories told about it
passages.text: The later Chachnama preserves a tradition about earlier rulers at Aror and the rise of the Brahman Chach, whose family ruled before the conquest. Its account combines royal succession with questions of caste, loyalty and legitimacy. Historians must distinguish that remembered dynasty from every dramatic detail told about its members.

passages.title: A kingdom and the stories told about it
passages.text: The surviving Persian Chachnama was produced in the thirteenth century, long after Dahir. Historian Manan Ahmed reads it as a work about political authority, legitimacy and the responsibilities of rulers, rather than a straightforward translation of an earlier conquest record. Other scholars allow more inherited material. Its stories require careful interpretation.

passages.title: A kingdom and the stories told about it
passages.text: In the Chachnama’s story, Chach first succeeds as a scribe, and a queen helps him reach the throne. Advice, writing skills and family alliances matter alongside soldiers. These are themes of a later political narrative; they do not give us a school timetable or establish how every household lived.

passages.title: Food, workshops and everyday objects
passages.text: Xuanzang describes wheat, millet, livestock and small, one-humped camels. He also reports differently colored salts used medicinally. His seventh-century account records historical remedies, not proof that they worked.

passages.title: Food, workshops and everyday objects
passages.text: Banbhore stood beside the Gharo creek in the Indus delta region, where remains from several periods include a fortified center, harbor installations, workshops and urban quarters. Its position connected river-country communities to sea routes. Identifying it with the famous port of Debal is plausible but remains debated.

passages.title: Food, workshops and everyday objects
passages.text: Excavations at Banbhore have produced glass, ivory and worked shells from both pre-Islamic and Islamic phases. Such materials preserve the work of people who shaped useful and decorative objects. The port’s history includes makers and customers, as well as rulers and visiting ships.

passages.title: Food, workshops and everyday objects
passages.text: The Banbhore museum separates painted pottery dating before the conquest from eighth-century storage jars and white-paste pottery. These ordinary containers help show change across the political transition. A big jar is evidence of storage, but its original contents need separate evidence: an empty pot does not come with a surviving grocery label.

passages.title: Food, workshops and everyday objects
passages.text: Researchers at Banbhore found clay moulds with repeated cells, nicknamed honeycomb moulds. They relate these to metalworking and coin production during the site’s long history. Studying an unfinished object or a workshop tool can reveal a manufacturing process that a finished treasure conceals.

passages.title: Food, workshops and everyday objects
passages.text: A water tank discovered beneath later Banbhore buildings is tentatively linked to ninth-century urban changes. It belongs after Dahir’s kingdom, showing that residents continued investing in water infrastructure. The discovery cannot establish that seventh-century homes had the same system, still less private flushing toilets.

passages.title: Belief, small money and surviving writing
passages.text: At Tharro, archaeologist N. G. Majumdar reported over a hundred small Buddhist tablets inside a mass of unbaked clay. Some showed a seated Buddha, others a row of shrines. Their inscriptions were assigned to the seventh or eighth century. These modest offerings show religious expression through clay and writing, beyond royal monuments.

passages.title: Belief, small money and surviving writing
passages.text: A study of small silver pieces reportedly found near the Sindh-Baluchistan border examined 254 specimens. Most weighed about 1.15 to 1.25 grams, and their average diameter was around 16 millimeters. Their ruler and exact place of issue remain uncertain; dealer-reported findspots cannot substitute for a recorded excavation.

passages.title: Belief, small money and surviving writing
passages.text: The same study reads one Brahmi inscription as ha-ma-va, a scholarly transliteration of three letter-units. Its meaning is unknown: it might be an abbreviation or control mark. Even the function of these unusual pieces has been debated. We can show the reading without inventing a translation or calling it Dahir’s motto.

passages.title: Belief, small money and surviving writing
passages.text: Xuanzang calls Sind “信度國” (Xìndù guó), “country of Sind”. This seventh-century Chinese witness, shown in modern type and pinyin, records an outsider’s name rather than local speech.

passages.title: Conquest did not mean everyone disappeared
passages.text: Al-Baladhuri’s ninth-century history describes both violent fighting and negotiated submission. At Alor, it reports an agreement to spare inhabitants and leave temples standing, while imposing tribute. This was a change of political power with different local outcomes, not one identical experience for every town.

Dahir’s defeat and death in 712 ended his kingship. Conquest and resistance continued afterward, while towns and religious communities faced new rulers and tributary obligations. The atlas endpoint of 800 is a map cutoff, not the date when Sind’s people or culture vanished.
