sectionTitles: A surviving voice and its discovery

passages.text: This record refers to Sukhothai, a Tai kingdom in what is now Thailand, conventionally dated from 1238 to incorporation into Ayutthaya in 1438. The imported 1100 to 1200 map interval is too early for that kingdom. Its enormous outline also extends far beyond Sukhothai’s central Thai heartland and is not a dependable historical border. The evidence below concerns the later kingdom and the continuing life of its towns, rather than a Sukhothai empire in 1100.

passages.title: Towns and water
passages.text: Sukhothai belonged to a network of important towns. Si Satchanalai combined monasteries with a major pottery industry, while Kamphaeng Phet guarded southern approaches and trade routes. Looking at all three changes the picture from one royal capital to a connected landscape of worship, work, transport and defense.

passages.title: Towns and water
passages.text: Dams, reservoirs, ponds and canals helped manage seasonal water. Their purposes included agriculture, ordinary water supply, communication and ritual, while moats also protected urban spaces. Keeping a town working required more than building temples: people had to guide water to useful places and cope with flooding. Surviving earthworks reveal that practical engineering beneath the famous monuments.

passages.title: Potters, workshops and journeys
passages.text: Excavations at Ban Ko Noi and Ban Pa Yang, beside the Yom River near Si Satchanalai, revealed successive types of pottery kilns. The Thai Ceramic Archaeology Project investigated them intensively during the 1980s. Comparing underground and later surface kilns showed that workshop technology changed over time. Researchers still use approximate and sometimes differing dates for the earliest production phases.

passages.title: Potters, workshops and journeys
passages.text: A small stoneware tube in the Asian Civilisations Museum was a useful workshop tool. Supports of this kind helped potters fire vessels of different sizes with less risk of pieces sticking together. Circular marks on vessel bases can record where the supports touched them. A mark that looks like a blemish can therefore explain how a whole kiln load was stacked.

passages.title: Potters, workshops and journeys
passages.text: Not every firing worked. A fifteenth-century Sukhothai bowl fragment in the British Museum is still attached to its circular kiln support. Its fish decoration survives, but the bowl failed to separate cleanly from its equipment. This workshop reject preserves a small manufacturing mishap. The museum records it as a field-collected fragment, rather than a precisely excavated household object.

passages.title: Potters, workshops and journeys
passages.text: Pottery recovered from the Ko Khram shipwreck helped overturn an older story that Sukhothai’s kilns had finished working before Si Satchanalai’s industry developed. Both centers operated during part of the same period, including the fifteenth century. Sukhothai ceramics also reached places in Indonesia, the Philippines and Japan. Their journeys continued across changes of political ruler.

passages.title: Families, festivals and sacred art
passages.text: The Ram Khamhaeng inscription describes inheritance through a household’s land, rice stores, animals and dependents. Its list includes wives and children within a father’s estate. That wording reveals a hierarchical family world, quite different from modern equal individual rights. This is a royal text’s description of order, not a survey proving that every family lived alike.

passages.title: Families, festivals and sacred art
passages.text: The same inscription describes a Kathina festival with gifts to monks, flowers, cushions and pillows, followed by a procession with music and singing. It presents religious giving as a social occasion as well as a sacred duty. Because the text praises its ruler and its dating is debated, this lively account should be read as its portrayal of the city.

passages.title: Families, festivals and sacred art
passages.text: Artists made the Buddha appear in motion as well as seated in meditation. A bronze Walking Buddha now in Saint Louis dates to the fourteenth or fifteenth century and stands about 38 centimeters high. Such a surviving object brings the artistic tradition down from monumental scale to something a child can measure with a ruler. Its museum date spans the kingdom’s later history.

passages.title: Families, festivals and sacred art
passages.text: At Wat Si Chum, slate panels combine carved pictures with short Thai captions about the Buddha’s previous lives. Panel 27 shows a teaching ascetic, a king and another ascetic lying down; its story compares a renouncer’s happiness with a king’s. These were illustrated lessons in a temple passage. Scholars debate their precise dates, placing them within the late medieval Sukhothai tradition.

passages.title: A surviving voice and its discovery
passages.text: “ในน้ำมีปลา” means “there is fish in the water”. This is a modern Thai transcription of words on face 1, lines 18 to 19, of the Ram Khamhaeng inscription, traditionally dated 1292. The original letter shapes differ. Its authorship and date have been debated, so the famous phrase is a sample from a specific surviving text, not independent proof that everyone had enough food.

passages.title: A surviving voice and its discovery
passages.text: Prince Mongkut, then a Buddhist monk and later King Rama IV, found the inscription at old Sukhothai in 1833, according to the National Archives’ account. Writing covers four faces of the stone, now held in Bangkok’s National Museum. Its rediscovery made an old royal account available to later readers, who have continued to argue about how best to interpret it.

Sukhothai was incorporated into Ayutthaya in 1438. That political ending did not erase its communities or artistic traditions. Pottery production and exchange continued under later rulers. The imported map endpoint of 1200 is therefore neither the kingdom’s actual end nor an abandonment date for its towns.

sectionTitles: Traces of work and everyday surroundings
A king’s image and a written name

passages.text: Syphax ruled the Masaesyles in western and central North Africa during the late third century BCE. His reign ended in 203 BCE, before this record’s imported 200 to 100 BCE map interval. The outline cannot establish his kingdom’s dates or precise borders.

passages.title: Power between Rome and Carthage
passages.text: Siga in the west and Cirta farther east were royal centers. Syphax’s expanding kingdom brought different communities under one ruler, but its southern boundary remains uncertain.

passages.title: Power between Rome and Carthage
passages.text: Livy describes Syphax asking a Roman envoy to remain as an infantry instructor. Training meant organizing recruits and teaching them to keep formation: an army needed practice as well as horses and weapons.

passages.title: Power between Rome and Carthage
passages.text: In Appian’s account, Syphax hosted the rival commanders Scipio and Hasdrubal at a banquet, where they shared a dining couch. That is one way to make awkward dinner guests sit together. The story reflects the king’s importance to both powers.

passages.title: Power between Rome and Carthage
passages.text: Syphax married Sophonisba, daughter of the Carthaginian commander Hasdrubal, as their alliance strengthened. Royal family relationships and territorial competition were intertwined with the war.

passages.title: Traces of work and everyday surroundings
passages.text: Excavations beside the Tafna at Siga found successive buildings and thick layers of broken pottery. The excavator placed this occupation broadly across the Hellenistic centuries, beginning before Syphax. His capital had an existing urban past.

passages.title: Traces of work and everyday surroundings
passages.text: The Siga deposits included Campanian pottery and several amphora forms. These durable fragments give archaeologists evidence of containers and connections that survive when the people who handled them left no personal diary.

passages.title: Traces of work and everyday surroundings
passages.text: Builders at Siga strengthened walls with dressed stone. Vuillemot suggested that one room had a sloping earthen roof waterproofed with lime, but could not decide whether these large rooms were homes or storerooms. Archaeology sometimes leaves the room labels blank.

passages.title: Traces of work and everyday surroundings
passages.text: The nearby Beni Rhénane royal mausoleum illustrates regional building skill, although its date and royal owner are disputed. Craftspeople used stone from a nearby quarry and mortar incorporating local volcanic material and gypsum from the surrounding district.

passages.title: Traces of work and everyday surroundings
passages.text: At Beni Rhénane, underground chambers followed the monument’s curved and straight sides. Stone barriers closed entrances. These remains reveal specialized stoneworking and careful planning in the region’s royal funerary tradition.

passages.title: A king’s image and a written name
passages.text: A surviving copper coin cataloged as Syphax’s measures 25 millimeters across and weighs 7.38 grams. The small object carries a bearded royal portrait on one side and a galloping rider on the other.

passages.title: A king’s image and a written name
passages.text: The rider’s cloak streams behind him and he holds a scepter; the king’s portrait wears a diadem. Those carefully chosen details turn a small piece of money into a portable statement of royal authority.

passages.title: A king’s image and a written name
passages.text: The coin’s Punic writing includes “SPQ”, the consonants of the name Syphax in scholarly transliteration. The longer legend adds a royal title. This is a written sample from his coinage, shown in Latin letters rather than a reconstruction of the original engraved shapes.

Syphax lost his kingdom in 203 BCE and died in captivity in Italy. His son Vermina retained a reduced kingdom for a time, while Massinissa gained the eastern conquests. Numidian communities continued under new rulers.

sectionTitles: Political limits and a written voice

passages.text: The Kingdom of the Two Sicilies formally united Naples and Sicily in 1816. This map label starts earlier, so the card also explains achievements under the preceding Bourbon crowns and the separate Napoleonic government on the mainland. The unified kingdom combined major scientific and industrial projects with political repression and repeated revolutions.

passages.title: Silk, schooling and domestic life
passages.text: At San Leucio near Caserta, silk machinery was installed in the 1780s with help from foreign specialists. The royal industrial settlement predates the formal 1816 kingdom. It linked imported expertise with the daily work of spinning and weaving luxurious cloth.

passages.title: Silk, schooling and domestic life
passages.text: The settlement’s 1789 code required education and regulated work and pay. It also abolished dowries within the community and prescribed uniform clothing. These were rules for a particular royal colony, not evidence that every woman and child across southern Italy enjoyed the same conditions.

passages.title: Silk, schooling and domestic life
passages.text: San Leucio’s rules included mutual assistance for elderly people and those unable to work. The planned expansion into Ferdinandopoli, however, was never completed as intended. Reforming a small community on paper and transforming an entire society were very different scales of ambition.

passages.title: Silk, schooling and domestic life
passages.text: The silk works depended on a branch of the Carolino aqueduct. After driving production, water returned to the Peschiera basin. The same royal landscape joined useful machinery and ornamental water: a beautiful fountain view could be connected to a working industrial system.

passages.title: Silk, schooling and domestic life
passages.text: Maria Carolina’s rooms at Caserta preserve a bidet, dressing table and bathtub among the furnishings studied by the museum. These objects make royal washing arrangements tangible. They are evidence for an elite interior, not a census of ordinary families’ plumbing.

passages.title: Plants, planets and steam
passages.text: Palermo’s larger botanical garden was established from 1789 and inaugurated in 1795. Bernardino da Ucria arranged its collections using Linnaeus’s classification. Plants were being organized as teaching material, while the garden’s buildings provided spaces for study and cultivation.

passages.title: Plants, planets and steam
passages.text: On 1 January 1801, Giuseppe Piazzi observed the object now called Ceres from Palermo. Further observations showed its movement, and Gauss later helped calculate its orbit. Now classified as a dwarf planet, Ceres connects Sicilian observation with an international mathematical effort.

passages.title: Plants, planets and steam
passages.text: Naples’s Capodimonte observatory began under Joachim Murat in 1812 and was completed under Ferdinand I in 1819. The project crossed a change of regime. Its history is a useful reminder that an institution’s achievements cannot always be assigned neatly to one dynasty.

passages.title: Plants, planets and steam
passages.text: The Naples to Portici railway opened on 3 October 1839. Its roughly 7.4-kilometre inaugural journey took about eleven minutes. It was a short route, but a real change in transport; the engineering drew on British locomotive designs and the work of Armand Bayard.

passages.title: Plants, planets and steam
passages.text: In 1840 the crown began acquiring land for the Pietrarsa works. The surviving factory halls housed specialized stages of production and now contain railway collections. A steam railway required a continuing workforce and repair capacity, not just a ceremonial first ride.

passages.title: Political limits and a written voice
passages.text: Revolutions in 1820 and 1848 forced concessions before royal power reasserted itself. Sicilian demands for independence also conflicted with control from Naples. These struggles explain why scientific projects and royal factories could coexist with fierce opposition to the monarchy.

passages.title: Political limits and a written voice
passages.text: Italian, Giuseppe Piazzi’s words reproduced by INAF from his historical record: “non vi essendo Cielo più bello del Partenopeo”. Translation: “there being no sky more beautiful than Naples’s.” The phrase belongs to his discussion of Naples and its observatory. The exhibition does not date this individual quotation, so an exact year would be misleading.

Garibaldi’s campaign and Piedmontese intervention brought annexation in 1860. The Bourbon court’s last major stand at Gaeta ended on 13 February 1861, and the territory entered the new Kingdom of Italy. Resistance and social conflict continued afterward; this was the end of a state, not of southern Italian communities.

sectionTitles: A frontier court with distant connections
A sanctuary that needed skilled hands
Later conquests and an uncertain archaeological ending

passages.text: The Zunbils, also called Rutbils, ruled Zabulistan in southern Afghanistan, separate from but connected to Kabul’s rulers. Independence emerged after about 680. Earlier accounts describe a shrine to Zun alongside Buddhist institutions. This map’s 700 to 800 interval is only an eighth-century snapshot. Its outline includes Kandahar and part of Zamindawar but omits Ghazni, an important royal center, and Bost, sometimes within the realm. Kabul lies outside it. The boundary is therefore an incomplete approximation, not a surveyed frontier.

passages.title: A frontier court with distant connections
passages.text: Zabul’s rulers sought recognition far beyond Afghanistan. Tang records describe investitures in 720 and 738, and an embassy to China in 753. These diplomatic ties existed alongside recurring warfare and tribute demands on the western frontier.

passages.title: A frontier court with distant connections
passages.text: In the 720s, the Korean pilgrim Hyecho described Zabul’s king as the Kabul king’s nephew, ruling independently. He distinguished Turkic rulers and soldiers from other inhabitants. His account reveals a politically connected but culturally diverse country, rather than one uniform ethnic kingdom.

passages.title: A frontier court with distant connections
passages.text: Royal silver coins combined several languages; copper issues commonly used Middle Persian. Their designs borrowed from Sasanian and Arab-Sasanian money. A coin could carry an Iranian-looking royal portrait and several written traditions together. Its date is not always convertible securely into our calendar.

passages.title: Clothes, crops, families and generosity
passages.text: Hyecho compared Zabul’s products and clothing with neighboring Kapisi, where he listed grapes, barley, wheat, pack animals and fine-wool garments. Men and women there wore shirts, trousers and boots. This regional comparison offers useful clues to daily life, although it is not an excavated Zabul household inventory.

passages.title: Clothes, crops, families and generosity
passages.text: The same traveler reported brothers sharing a wife in Zabul and several neighboring countries, associating this arrangement with preserving a household’s livelihood. This is his broad description of family organization, not proof that every local family followed one marriage pattern.

passages.title: Clothes, crops, families and generosity
passages.text: Hyecho found Buddhist monasteries and described the chief Satakgan giving gold and silver in quantities reportedly exceeding the king’s gifts. Religious generosity could make a powerful public statement. A chief might outshine his ruler without needing a bigger crown.

passages.title: A sanctuary that needed skilled hands
passages.text: Tapa Sardar near Ghazni was much older than the mapped kingdom. After a seventh-century fire, builders reconstructed its chapels around the late seventh or early eighth century. Its ruins preserve a major religious center, although the imported polygon leaves the Ghazni area outside its edge.

passages.title: A sanctuary that needed skilled hands
passages.text: In Chapel 63, artists made a reclining Buddha about 15 meters long, representing his final passing into nirvana. Clay, paint and gilding produced an enormous religious image. This was sculpture on a scale that made even a grown-up visitor look very small.

passages.title: A sanctuary that needed skilled hands
passages.text: How did sculptors keep everything together? At Tapa Sardar, they built yellow-clay cores mixed with straw, added red-clay surfaces, and used wooden sticks to attach heads and limbs or fasten images to walls. Seventh- and eighth-century masterpieces depended on practical knowledge of humble materials.

passages.title: A sanctuary that needed skilled hands
passages.text: Fire sometimes baked these clay decorations into harder terracotta, helping fragments survive while destroying their painted finish. A dark fragment today can therefore conceal a much brighter original appearance. Damage and preservation can be parts of the same object’s story.

passages.title: A sanctuary that needed skilled hands
passages.text: A surviving head of Durga from Chapel 23 is approximately 64 centimeters high. Finding this goddess within a Buddhist sanctuary is a reminder that its religious imagery drew on interconnected traditions. The head belongs to the site’s later sculptural production, broadly the seventh or eighth century.

passages.title: A sanctuary that needed skilled hands
passages.text: A late-period pottery fragment from Tapa Sardar’s second terrace shows two running goats pressed into its red-clay surface. The vessel was wheel-turned and stamped. At only 9.1 centimeters across, the surviving piece preserves both a potter’s technique and a tiny animal scene.

passages.title: Reading and rediscovering the evidence
passages.text: Molded decoration on Tapa Sardar’s late-period thrones and small stupas imitated jewelry and uncut gemstones. Giulia Forgione interprets some unusual gem shapes as symbols of purity. These were clay representations of precious things, demonstrating how artists could communicate wealth and religious ideas without covering every surface in actual jewels.

passages.title: Reading and rediscovering the evidence
passages.text: On a Zabulistan coin, Harmatta and Litvinsky transcribe the short Brahmi-script legend as “šrī vākhudevah” and translate it “His Highness the Majestic Lord.” This is their scholarly Roman-letter transcription of an eighth-century royal formula, not a reproduction of the original letter shapes. Their exact ruler identification and calendar conversion are less secure than this broad attribution; the sample should not stand for everybody’s everyday speech.

passages.title: Reading and rediscovering the evidence
passages.text: Italian archaeologists investigated Tapa Sardar in the 1960s and 1970s and resumed work in 2003. Fragile clay required strengthening during excavation and careful laboratory treatment. Measurements, photographs and find locations let researchers reconstruct relationships among pieces even when the original sculptures are badly broken.

passages.title: Later conquests and an uncertain archaeological ending
passages.text: After the map’s cutoff, Yaqub ibn Layth’s Saffarid armies transformed the region. A Zunbil was killed around 864 to 865, but his son Firuz recovered territory before renewed campaigns. Accounts place further fighting in the late 860s and early 870s. This was a sequence of defeats and recoveries, not an instantaneous disappearance.

passages.title: Later conquests and an uncertain archaeological ending
passages.text: Tapa Sardar’s final abandonment is a separate question. Scholars debate whether a recorded temple destruction in 795 refers to this site, while its art also has connections pointing toward the ninth century. Neither the map ending in 800 nor a convenient conquest date settles when its last worshippers left.

Saffarid campaigns in the later ninth century broke Zunbil power in stages; sources describe Firuz’s capture in 873 after earlier recovery. The atlas stops in 800, well before these events. The political defeat concerns a ruling house, not the disappearance of southern Afghanistan’s inhabitants.

sectionTitles: Land loss, community art and language

passages.text: The Kiowa became a major southern Plains power through migration, horse-centered life and alliances. Earlier traditions place them much farther north. Both imported outlines, dated 1492 and 1530, show southern territory associated with later history; neither proves that early southern boundary. Kiowa people and their tribal government continue today.

passages.title: Movement, families and remembering events
passages.text: Kiowa origin traditions place ancestors near the Missouri and Yellowstone headwaters. Later histories describe movement toward the Black Hills before the southern Plains. The remote sequence is uncertain, so tracing migration requires more care than coloring one large area and treating it as a timeless homeland.

passages.title: Movement, families and remembering events
passages.text: Around 1790, Kiowa and Comanche leaders turned former hostility into an enduring alliance. Kansas Historical Society recounts Guikate spending a year with the Comanche before returning with a favorable report. The relationship strengthened their influence over hunting grounds, trade and military affairs across the southern Plains.

passages.title: Movement, families and remembering events
passages.text: In the horse-centered Plains period, bison hunting, gathered foods and portable homes helped Kiowa families move across large distances. Horses supported hunting and warfare, while hides supplied shelter. This way of life belongs to a changing historical period; horses should not be inserted into a scene dated 1492.

passages.title: Movement, families and remembering events
passages.text: Tipi designs could belong to particular people and families. A Smithsonian model made by Tsakai between 1897 and 1904 preserves his father Bellowing Elk’s Black Star design, with white circles representing stars. It is a small model documenting an older design, not the family’s full-size home.

passages.title: Movement, families and remembering events
passages.text: A Kiowa cradleboard from about 1895 combines carved wood, hide, cloth, beadwork, ribbon and metal tacks. Museum cataloguers identify it as a baby carrier. Such an object brings childcare into the historical picture: families invested skilled work and decoration in something made for a very small passenger.

passages.title: Movement, families and remembering events
passages.text: A pictorial calendar records the spectacular meteor shower of 1833. In the entry reproduced by James Mooney, stars appear above a small child representing calendar keeper Set-t’an in his first winter. The drawing helps recall a named event and its story; it is not an alphabetic sentence.

passages.title: Land loss, community art and language
passages.text: At Medicine Lodge Creek in 1867, Kiowa, Comanche and Plains Apache representatives negotiated with United States commissioners. The resulting agreements involved a reservation in present-day Oklahoma and the surrender of extensive lands. A treaty was supposed to establish obligations between governments; it did not make the signers’ peoples disappear.

passages.title: Land loss, community art and language
passages.text: On September 28, 1874, United States troops attacked camps in Palo Duro Canyon occupied by Kiowa, Comanche and Cheyenne families. Soldiers burned homes and winter supplies and killed most captured horses. Destroying transport and stored food made it much harder for survivors to remain outside the reservation.

passages.title: Land loss, community art and language
passages.text: Lone Wolf challenged the federal government’s division and sale of reservation land. The Supreme Court ruled against him and the tribes in 1903. The National Archives preserves the case alongside the treaty record: legal documents reveal both Native efforts to defend agreements and the government’s power to override them.

passages.title: Land loss, community art and language
passages.text: Kiowa photographer Horace Poolaw recorded relatives and neighbors at weddings, parades, ball games and everyday outings from the 1920s onward. One surviving photograph shows his children Robert and Linda dressed up for their father’s camera around 1947. His pictures preserve community life from a family member’s viewpoint.

passages.title: Land loss, community art and language
passages.text: In a Kiowa handgame described by anthropologist William Meadows, one team hides marked pieces while another guesses their location. Drumming and singing add distraction. Wooden sticks keep score; in the Kiowa version he describes, the team with fewer sticks wins. A calm face can be part of the strategy.

passages.title: Land loss, community art and language
passages.text: A short modern writing sample is “Hàyá èm bánmà?”, meaning “Where are you going?” The Kiowa Tribe’s language page prints the phrase with a pronunciation guide and linked lesson. The accents are part of the teaching spelling, and the sample is contemporary rather than an inscription from the map’s early dates.

passages.title: Land loss, community art and language
passages.text: Language preservation also means preparing new teachers. The department advertised a credentialed teacher-training program for 2025 to 2026 and explicitly recognizes different Kiowa orthographies. Its work links speakers, learners and community organizations so that written resources can lead back to people speaking together.

The imported map cutoffs precede much Kiowa southern Plains history. Military defeat and allotment transformed landholding and daily life, but Kiowa communities continued. Language teaching and community art remain part of that ongoing history.

sectionTitles: Read the atlas before reading a kingdom
Chiefs, land, and competing political worlds
Farming, food, fishponds, and environmental skill
Family, social life, gender, and celebration
Children, education, oral knowledge, and writing
Homes, clothing, tools, crafts, and work
Medicine, health, care, and honest limits
Religion, arts, games, achievements, and continuity

passages.text: This exact atlas layer lasts only from 1492 to 1500, and its name is misleading. Kō Hawaiʻi Paeʻāina did not yet mean the unified nineteenth-century Hawaiian Kingdom. The map draws three coarse components around parts of Hawaiʻi Island, Maui, and Oʻahu, while omitting Kauaʻi, Niʻihau, Molokaʻi, Lānaʻi, Kahoʻolawe, and even tested places such as Hilo, Hāna, and Oʻahu's North Shore. The same three shapes simultaneously belong to the atlas's “Polynesians” layer. Archaeology instead reveals local households, expanding fields, fishpond engineering, specialist crafts, sacred places, and increasingly powerful but competing island polities. Scholars debate when those political systems crossed any threshold from chiefdoms to states; no neat 1492 foundation event survives. Evidence also varies sharply by district and date, so a practice documented at Kohala, Kona, Kahikinui, or Kīpahulu cannot automatically describe every family on three islands. Knowledge traveled through observation, apprenticeship, chant, genealogy, story, dance, and ceremony. No secure Hawaiian writing sample survives from 1492 to 1500; alphabetic Hawaiian print began in 1822. At the 1500 software seam this duplicate label vanishes, while the underlying Polynesians shapes remain. Communities, farms, languages, and political histories continued.

passages.title: Read the atlas before reading a kingdom
passages.text: The exact id appears once, in the 1492 border file, as one MultiPolygon with three components, three rings, and forty-eight decoded positions. Its bounding box surrounds parts of Hawaiʻi Island, Maui, and Oʻahu. A display polygon is not a surveyed frontier, land deed, census, or declaration of political unity.

passages.title: Read the atlas before reading a kingdom
passages.text: Tested Kailua-Kona, Waimea, Kealakekua, Lāhainā, Honolulu, and Waiʻanae fall inside. Tested Hilo, Hāna, northern Oʻahu, Molokaʻi, Lānaʻi, Kahoʻolawe, Kauaʻi, and Niʻihau fall outside. Those exclusions describe this coarse artwork, not the historical limits of Hawaiian settlement, culture, travel, or kinship.

passages.title: Read the atlas before reading a kingdom
passages.text: The three target rings exactly match a simultaneous three-component Polynesians feature after ring direction and starting vertices are normalized. Rapa Nui sits in a separate Polynesians polygon. The duplicated Hawaiian footprint exposes a labeling problem: the map stored the same island artwork twice under identities with very different meanings.

passages.title: Read the atlas before reading a kingdom
passages.text: There are no directly shared topology arcs between the duplicate features because the same outlines were encoded independently. Yet all six tested inside points have both owners in 1492. The lack of shared arc identifiers does not cancel the spatial duplication; normalized coordinates and identical point membership demonstrate it.

passages.title: Read the atlas before reading a kingdom
passages.text: The target is absent in 1400, present in 1492, and absent again in 1500 and 1600. The Polynesians owner persists through both seams. The much later kingdom-of-hawaii layer starts on this footprint only by 1815, so later monarchy geometry cannot be smuggled backward by two hundred years.

passages.title: Chiefs, land, and competing political worlds
passages.text: The Ancient Hawaiian State examines a long transformation from chiefs whose authority was strongly symbolic toward warrior rulers and more centralized island governments. Its scope reaches across centuries and later evidence. It supports a process of political change, not a single “Hawaiian Kingdom” founded in 1492 or one ruler over all islands.

passages.title: Chiefs, land, and competing political worlds
passages.text: Archaeologists describe Hawaiian society as a classic chiefdom case that may have crossed into archaic state complexity before 1778. Evidence includes population, intensive agriculture, royal centers, heiau, and divine kingship. “May have crossed” matters: scholarly categories are analytical tools, and the threshold is debated rather than stamped onto one year.

passages.title: Chiefs, land, and competing political worlds
passages.text: Temple archaeology traces changing strategies of authority from fifteenth-century agricultural shrines toward later systems serving broader political economies. It supports gradual transformation in ritual organization. It does not show that every heiau answered to one court in 1492, or that identical worship and obligations operated on Hawaiʻi, Maui, and Oʻahu.

passages.title: Chiefs, land, and competing political worlds
passages.text: Dated offerings in Kona gardens begin with farming around 1400, while the archaeological and oral evidence for four powerful archipelago-wide kingdoms belongs around 1600. That sequence makes later consolidation visible without dragging it backward. A garden offering can connect farming and religion; it cannot identify a universal king for this card.

passages.title: Chiefs, land, and competing political worlds
passages.text: Aliʻi, ritual and technical specialists called kahuna, cultivating and fishing makaʻāinana, and people held in the lowest social category occupied unequal positions in later descriptions of traditional society. The source supplies a broad model rather than a 1490s census. Roles, rank, rights, and burdens varied by place and changed over time.

passages.title: Settlements, movement, exchange, and discovery
passages.text: Polynesian navigators reached Hawaiʻi in voyaging canoes and brought useful plants and animals. By the card's interval, centuries of settlement had produced distinct Hawaiian lifeways, and long-distance contact with other Polynesian islands had diminished. This background explains origins and adaptation; it does not make every canoe in 1492 an ocean-crossing vessel.

passages.title: Settlements, movement, exchange, and discovery
passages.text: At Kahuku in Kaʻū, archaeology places early settlement centuries before the card and indicates intensively managed mid-elevation fields by about the mid-1400s. The evidence shows people changing a demanding volcanic landscape through accumulated labor. It is local Hawaiʻi Island history, not proof that Oʻahu and Maui followed the same schedule.

passages.title: Settlements, movement, exchange, and discovery
passages.text: Nuʻu on Maui contains more than sixteen hundred recorded features grouped into seventy-six archaeological sites, including agricultural terraces, residential enclosures, shrines, toolmaking remains, and burials. Dating indicates use by the broad 1400s to 1600s range. Discovery here means careful survey of a lived landscape, not a sudden invention in 1492.

passages.title: Settlements, movement, exchange, and discovery
passages.text: Haleakalā preserves stone shelters, trails, and quarry sites rather than permanent summit towns. Temporary enclosures protected travelers from cold, fog, wind, and rain while people visited for ceremony, observation, or stone. That contrast reminds readers that “settlement” includes seasonal movement and specialist work as well as houses occupied year-round.

passages.title: Settlements, movement, exchange, and discovery
passages.text: Kalaupapa archaeology records house sites, taro fields, irrigation, walls, temples, fresh-water use, forest harvesting, fishing, salt gathering, and coastal collecting. These linked activities moved materials from uplands to sea. The evidence is from Molokaʻi, which this polygon omits, so it is a comparator for Hawaiian practice rather than target geometry.

passages.title: Farming, food, fishponds, and environmental skill
passages.text: Hawaiʻi Volcanoes archaeology finds early agricultural walls dating to the 1400s and 1500s, with sweet potato suited to dry landscapes. Farmers built stone alignments, modified soils, and worked around rainfall and lava. These achievements accumulated through ordinary labor; the source cannot assign one wall to one named 1490s household.

passages.title: Farming, food, fishponds, and environmental skill
passages.text: In Leeward Kohala, forty-eight radiocarbon dates from forty-three residential features show household numbers and locations expanding with the field system between 1400 and 1800. Probable household fission accompanied subdivision into smaller socioeconomic units. This is unusually detailed local evidence, but it remains a long trend rather than an annual population count.

passages.title: Farming, food, fishponds, and environmental skill
passages.text: Farmers grew wet taro in irrigated pondfields where water allowed, while dryland systems supported crops such as sweet potato, yam, banana, breadfruit, and sugar cane in different settings. Fishing remained fundamental. A shared crop list does not create one island-wide menu; season, rainfall, coast, rank, and household access shaped meals.

passages.title: Farming, food, fishponds, and environmental skill
passages.text: Huilua Fishpond on Oʻahu used a five-hundred-foot rock seawall to enclose seven acres near Kahana Stream. Hawaiian ponds admitted water and managed fish in sheltered environments, though Huilua's exact building date is unknown. Think “careful fish traffic engineering,” with the joke aimed at gates, not at the people maintaining them.

passages.title: Farming, food, fishponds, and environmental skill
passages.text: At Kaloko and ʻAimakapā, walls, channels, porous lava, and mākāhā sluice gates managed exchange between ocean and pond. The huge dry-stacked wall diffused wave energy while water still circulated. This was sophisticated marine engineering maintained over generations; a surviving structure does not reveal an exact 1492 keeper, harvest, or ownership rule.

passages.title: Family, social life, gender, and celebration
passages.text: ʻOhana names a family structure rooted in connection and regeneration, with collective responsibilities extending beyond a narrow modern household. Native Hawaiian scholarship describes children learning within networks of parents, grandparents, relatives, and knowledgeable community members. Much detail survives in later records, so the card presents continuity carefully rather than freezing every practice in 1492.

passages.title: Family, social life, gender, and celebration
passages.text: Family education could begin very early and combine affection, responsibility, correction, observation, work, story, and spiritual relationship. Children were participants in ʻohana life, not empty containers waiting for a classroom. The evidence preserves cultural principles; it cannot supply one universal age schedule, adoption pattern, bedtime, or division of care.

passages.title: Family, social life, gender, and celebration
passages.text: Excavated kauhale at Kahikinui reveal grouped household buildings and routines in which men and women used separate earth ovens for some foods yet ate together in a hale noa with women and children. These findings localize daily life on Maui. They do not authorize one floor plan or gender routine for every island.

passages.title: Family, social life, gender, and celebration
passages.text: Broad traditional accounts describe women beating wauke bark into kapa while men pounded cooked taro into poi, alongside fishing, collecting seaweed and shellfish, tending animals, farming, worship, song, chant, and dance. Such accounts illuminate coordinated work and social life, but real households could vary with skill, rank, environment, and need.

passages.title: Family, social life, gender, and celebration
passages.text: Makahiki was a seasonal religious and social time associated with Lono, offerings, rest, feasting, dance, and games, yet each island observed it differently and most written description comes from Hawaiʻi Island in later centuries. The source is valuable precisely when its uneven geography and retrospective evidence remain visible.

passages.title: Children, education, oral knowledge, and writing
passages.text: Aʻo describes learning through attentive listening, close observation, imitation, repeated practice, work, and relationships with people who held specialized knowledge. These methods could operate in family life, craft, farming, navigation, ceremony, and healing. The source does not turn every gathering place into a school or claim equal access across rank and gender.

passages.title: Children, education, oral knowledge, and writing
passages.text: Kūpuna and other ʻohana members could guide children through genealogy, values, place knowledge, language, story, responsibility, and skilled action. Native Hawaiian scholarship treats learning as relational and lived. Because many accounts were written after contact, this card does not pretend to reconstruct a typical 1490s lesson word for word.

passages.title: Children, education, oral knowledge, and writing
passages.text: Stone tools, shelters, quarry remains, trails, and unfinished work show that technical knowledge had to be practiced. An adze maker selected dense basalt and transformed it through a laborious sequence; users then hafted cutting edges to work wood. The displayed modern replica illustrates a method, not an excavated object dated exactly to 1498.

passages.title: Children, education, oral knowledge, and writing
passages.text: Written-language sample status: absent. No secure written Hawaiian sample survives from 1492 to 1500. Hawaiian history, genealogy, and knowledge flourished through oral forms, while missionaries and Hawaiian collaborators developed alphabetic spelling in the 1820s. Printing the first Hawaiian primer in 1822 is more than three centuries too late for this card.

passages.title: Children, education, oral knowledge, and writing
passages.text: The archive identifies the first page of the first Hawaiian book printed by Elisha Loomis in January 1822. That dated object is the safe comparison point. Displaying a modern phrase, nineteenth-century newspaper line, or present-day diacritics as a surviving 1490s manuscript would manufacture evidence, so this card provides no original, transliteration, or translation.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, tools, crafts, and work
passages.text: Kahikinui excavations examined nineteen kauhale clusters, meaning groups of houses, most dating broadly before European contact. Separate buildings and hearths organized cooking, sleeping, family interaction, storage, prayer, and work. The archaeology opens an intimate window but cannot pin every cluster to 1492 or make rural Maui a universal Hawaiian housing blueprint.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, tools, crafts, and work
passages.text: At Kīpahulu, pā hale foundations belonged to larger household compounds, while walls could mark living areas, animal enclosures, irrigated taro terraces, sacred places, or land divisions. Many walls were reused in several eras. A rectangle of stone therefore needs context before anyone confidently labels it a bedroom, barn, temple, or fifteenth-century boundary.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, tools, crafts, and work
passages.text: Kapa makers soaked and pounded plant fibers until thin, then used grooved wooden beaters to texture and watermark cloth. Kapa became clothing, bedding, and ceremonial material. Traditionally women made cloth while men carved beaters. The rhythmic work might sound like household percussion, but producing durable fabric demanded patience and technical control.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, tools, crafts, and work
passages.text: Basalt adzes supported woodworking for houses, tools, and canoes, while archaeological game boards and stones preserve kōnane and ʻulu maika. Surfing and sledding also belonged to recreation. Material culture shows that daily life mixed hard work with strategy and play; it does not tell us who won a particular family match.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, tools, crafts, and work
passages.text: Modern kapa practitioners preserve and revive fermentation, watermarking, natural pigment, beating, and ceremonial knowledge. Their work helps explain material possibilities and living continuity. It is not a reenactment video from 1492, so personal reflections recorded today are identified as present-day relationships with ancestors rather than quoted as medieval testimony.

passages.title: Medicine, health, care, and honest limits
passages.text: Polynesian voyagers brought plants that served food, fiber, dye, light, and medicinal purposes. Noni, for example, is documented in later Hawaiian practice for wounds, boils, fractures, and sore muscles, while kukui supplied lamp fuel. This institutional plant guide preserves use knowledge but cannot prove one remedy's recipe or frequency in 1492.

passages.title: Medicine, health, care, and honest limits
passages.text: Healing involved knowledgeable specialists as well as household care, plants, diet, touch, chant, prayer, and relationships among body, community, and sacred life. The surviving traditions deserve respect without pretending they were one standardized clinic. The plant evidence does not reveal dosage, diagnosis, survival rate, or equal access among islands and ranks.

passages.title: Medicine, health, care, and honest limits
passages.text: A modern Native Hawaiian medicine garden at the University of Hawaiʻi preserves plants and teaching relationships in consultation with cultural practitioners. It demonstrates living knowledge and continuity, not an exact fifteenth-century pharmacy inventory. The card therefore avoids assigning every currently documented medicinal plant, preparation, or Hawaiian name to this eight-year interval.

passages.title: Medicine, health, care, and honest limits
passages.text: Specialists learned demanding knowledge by long observation, practice, correction, memory, and responsibility. Those educational patterns make skilled healing plausible without supplying a 1490s medical chart. No reviewed source provides a named patient, fever count, childbirth register, surgical case, disability census, life expectancy, or island-wide public-health authority for this target.

passages.title: Medicine, health, care, and honest limits
passages.text: The atlas index, missing-card registry, and border geometry encode no disease, injury, pregnancy, infant care, elder care, epidemic, diet deficiency, or treatment outcome. Those files establish identity and scope only. Silence is not proof that illness or care was absent; it is a boundary against invented statistics and modern medical labels.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets, and sanitation
passages.text: University of Hawaiʻi research emphasizes that water meaning and management varied within and between islands because windward rainfall, leeward dryness, geology, springs, and streams differed. Irrigation contributed to production and political change, but no single water regime fits this polygon. Local knowledge linked practical management with relationships to deities, land, and community.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets, and sanitation
passages.text: Where water permitted, farmers diverted streams through dams, ditches, canals, and terraced pondfields so flow moved from higher to lower plots. Elsewhere people relied more on dryland crops. These systems required construction, clearing, repair, coordination, and erosion control. They were infrastructure, although they were not modern municipal water networks.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets, and sanitation
passages.text: Fishpond channels and porous stone walls circulated seawater while sluice gates managed fish movement and harvesting. This was food and water engineering at the coast, not drinking-water treatment. A beautifully working mākāhā tells us about tides, masonry, maintenance, and fish; it does not secretly double as a household tap or sewer outlet.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets, and sanitation
passages.text: Kahikinui household archaeology identifies house groups, hearths, ovens, activity areas, and eating arrangements, but the reviewed abstract reports no securely dated 1492 latrine or flush toilet. Absence from this source is not proof that one disposal practice covered Maui. It means the card cannot responsibly draw a medieval bathroom plan.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets, and sanitation
passages.text: Kīpahulu archaeology documents walls, houses, fields, and fishing gear across layered occupations, yet it does not establish an island-wide sewer, waste collector, rubbish schedule, bathing rule, or household toilet for 1492 to 1500. Waste practices are archaeologically difficult and locally variable. “We do not know” is better plumbing than an invented flush.

passages.title: Religion, arts, games, achievements, and continuity
passages.text: Makahiki joined seasonal observation, offerings, ceremony, feasting, dance, and athletic play. Games included wrestling, boxing, sledding, spear throwing, surfing, canoe races, and ʻulu maika. The festival's later documented forms varied by island, so the list illuminates a tradition without scheduling an identical tournament on every shore in 1492.

passages.title: Religion, arts, games, achievements, and continuity
passages.text: Archaeological kōnane boards and ʻulu maika stones show strategy and sport in material form, while surfing and hōlua sledding required practiced bodies and specialized places or equipment. These are achievements of leisure, design, and learning. They also remind children that historical people did not spend every waking minute farming solemnly.

passages.title: Religion, arts, games, achievements, and continuity
passages.text: Fifteenth-century shrines associated with agriculture formed part of a longer transformation in sacred architecture and political authority. Later temple systems became more centralized, but the sequence developed over centuries. The achievement lies in coordinated building, ritual knowledge, and landscape design; its chronology resists a tidy “kingdom begins here” marker.

passages.title: Religion, arts, games, achievements, and continuity
passages.text: Haleakalā archaeology includes places for ceremony, star knowledge, travel, shelter, and basalt quarrying. Earlier collectors sometimes disturbed burials; repatriation returned ancestral remains and burial objects to Native Hawaiian care. Discovery is therefore not just finding artifacts. Ethical stewardship, community knowledge, and recognizing harm are part of how the past is studied.

passages.title: Religion, arts, games, achievements, and continuity
passages.text: The 1500 seam removes the misleading target while keeping identical Polynesians coverage. The later researched Hawaiian Kingdom card begins in 1795 and ends in 1893, a distinct historical monarchy. Between those facts lies centuries of island political change. This card ends with continuity, not an imaginary fall or an early coronation for Kamehameha.

At 1500 the exact target disappears, but every tested point it covered remains inside the atlas's Polynesians layer with the same three island components. Nothing in the seam records conquest, collapse, migration, or cultural disappearance. The successor is a technical atlas identity: Hawaiian households, farms, sacred places, languages, crafts, and competing political histories continued beyond it.

passages.text: Kong became a major Dyula commercial and political center in what is now northern Côte d’Ivoire, connected with communities far into present-day Burkina Faso. Its rulers and allied warrior houses did not govern every place within a tidy border. The imported 1783 to 1914 interval is a map window, extending beyond the destruction of the old capital.

passages.title: Power and households
passages.text: Seku Wattara’s seizure of power early in the eighteenth century made Kong a force beyond its immediate surroundings. Its armies reached toward the Niger and fought Asante. Yet Launay emphasizes that nearby chiefdoms could trace connections to Kong without being directly governed by it.

passages.title: Power and households
passages.text: Watara warrior houses joined relatives with many dependants who farmed, traded or fought. Historian Mahir Şaul describes them as enduring social and economic units. Their power also rested on enslavement: captives could become household labourers or be sold through long-distance networks.

passages.title: Work, water and learning in 1888
passages.text: Binger counted about 150 indigo dye pits in two parts of Kong. Their walls were waterproofed with material made from heated earth. Weaving spaces filled openings between houses: cloth production shaped the streets, and dyeing gave some corners a distinctly noticeable smell.

passages.title: Work, water and learning in 1888
passages.text: Among requests recorded by Binger were help against Guinea worm and a way to drill through granite to obtain well water. These were practical concerns about health and water supply, voiced by the residents he met, rather than luxuries requested for a royal palace.

passages.title: Work, water and learning in 1888
passages.text: The religious leader Sitafa supervised roughly twenty Arabic schools, according to Binger, and also taught adults and elders. Learning did not stop at childhood. The visitor describes senior townspeople attending discussions of religious books several times a week.

passages.title: Work, water and learning in 1888
passages.text: An Arabic safe-conduct given to Binger in March 1888 begins “الحمد لله”, meaning “Praise be to God”. This is a normalized transcription of the surviving manuscript facsimile. Arabic served written diplomacy here; the sample is not written Jula.

passages.title: Buildings made to be maintained
passages.text: Kong’s small mosque has radiocarbon evidence reaching the seventeenth or eighteenth century. Oral tradition specifically credits Imam Barro with bringing plans from Djenné in 1729. The two kinds of evidence offer different levels of precision and should be read together.

passages.title: Buildings made to be maintained
passages.text: The region’s earthen mosques use rounded earth bricks and protective plaster. Timber poles projecting from walls help support the buildings and provide footholds for maintenance. The apparent sticks poking out are useful equipment: repairing a wall begins with somewhere to stand.

passages.title: Buildings made to be maintained
passages.text: Compared with Djenné’s architecture, these southern mosques often have stouter, tapering buttresses. ICOMOS connects the differences with wetter conditions and local building traditions. Builders adapted a shared architectural language to the weather and skills of their own communities.

passages.title: Writing and continuing knowledge
passages.text: In fieldwork conducted in Burkina Faso in 2012, Coleman Donaldson documented Jula written in adapted Arabic script, including medicinal notebooks and texts composed for his research. This later evidence shows a living literacy associated with the former Kong region; it is not a surviving royal archive.

passages.title: Writing and continuing knowledge
passages.text: Donaldson prints “Kpón ká jùlakán”, translated “Kong’s Jula”. This is his modern Latin transcription of a name speakers used for a prestigious language form. His participants had not grown up in Kong, showing how the town’s linguistic reputation could travel beyond its streets.

passages.title: Writing and continuing knowledge
passages.text: Kong’s great mosque was destroyed during Samory’s campaign in 1897 and rebuilt by its community. Its continued maintenance is part of a living religious landscape. UNESCO’s 2021 inscription recognizes both the buildings and the knowledge needed to keep earthen architecture standing.

The destruction of Kong in 1897 broke the old capital’s position; the imported 1914 endpoint is not its conquest date. Colonial rule reshaped the region, while Kong’s residents rebuilt, worshipped and maintained their architectural traditions. The town and its communities did not disappear with the earlier political order.

sectionTitles: A divided peninsula and a changing state
Food, songs and words shared across generations

passages.text: North Korea, officially the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, was established in 1948. This atlas record begins only in 1960; its four border snapshots end in 2020 although the index remains open. The coarse outline leaves Chongjin outside North Korea and places Dandong, a city in China, inside. It is unsuitable for legal borders or military control. This modern-state card uses dated local and institutional evidence, rather than describing all Korean history.

passages.title: A divided peninsula and a changing state
passages.text: The DPRK was proclaimed on 9 September 1948, with Pyongyang as its capital. Its founding preceded this map record by twelve years. Political division produced two Korean states; it did not turn their shared earlier histories into histories belonging exclusively to one government.

passages.title: A divided peninsula and a changing state
passages.text: North Korean forces attacked South Korea on 25 June 1950. The war involved a United Nations command and Chinese forces, among others. The agreement signed on 27 July 1953 ordered opposing forces back two kilometres each from a military demarcation line, creating a buffer zone. It was an armistice, not a peace treaty.

passages.title: A divided peninsula and a changing state
passages.text: Postwar plans rebuilt steelworks, chemical plants, electric power and machinery production. Heavy industry received priority over consumer goods. The official emphasis on self-reliance coexisted with substantial Soviet and Chinese assistance. Factories and power stations mattered enormously, but official production targets cannot simply be read as measurements of what families could buy.

passages.title: A divided peninsula and a changing state
passages.text: Political power stayed within one family. Kim Il Sung ruled until his death in 1994; Kim Jong Il succeeded him and died in December 2011; Kim Jong Un then took power. The Workers’ Party, security institutions and military form part of this highly centralized system. This is a history of succession, not competitive elections.

passages.title: A divided peninsula and a changing state
passages.text: A devastating famine developed during the 1990s. The loss of former Soviet support, failures of the planned economy, shortages of fuel and agricultural inputs, and floods compounded the crisis. A single bad harvest does not explain it. Families faced shortages while the systems for producing and distributing food broke down.

passages.title: A divided peninsula and a changing state
passages.text: On 17 September 1991, the UN General Assembly admitted both the DPRK and the Republic of Korea. The resolution dealt with two separate applications. Membership gave both states a place at the United Nations; it did not reunify the peninsula or settle the military confrontation.

passages.title: Weapons, observation and human rights
passages.text: The CTBTO monitoring organization records six declared North Korean nuclear tests between 2006 and 2017. After the first, instruments detected both seismic signals and radioactive xenon at a station in Canada. These traces helped identify an underground explosion across a vast distance. They are evidence from monitoring, not a census of the country’s weapons.

passages.title: Weapons, observation and human rights
passages.text: UN sanctions include restrictions on arms and designated financial assets. Humanitarian assistance has exceptions and exemption procedures: the Security Council says the measures are not intended to harm the civilian population. The rules governing a shipment and the practical ability to reach families are separate questions; an exemption is not proof that supplies arrived.

passages.title: Weapons, observation and human rights
passages.text: A UN Commission of Inquiry reported systematic and widespread human-rights violations in 2014, including political imprisonment and severe restrictions on information. The government denied the commission entry. Investigators used public testimony, confidential interviews and other evidence. These are attributed findings of a UN inquiry, whose access limitations matter, rather than a claim that researchers could freely visit every institution.

passages.title: Weapons, observation and human rights
passages.text: The same inquiry described songbun, a state classification linked to family background and perceived loyalty. It could affect housing, work, education and marriage. The report also noted that money and market activity complicated this hierarchy. A child’s opportunities could therefore depend on decisions about relatives as well as on the child’s own abilities.

passages.title: Food, songs and words shared across generations
passages.text: WFP describes families supplementing public rations through relatives in the countryside, kitchen gardens and markets. Food access depends on more than whether crops exist: transport, money, agricultural supplies and the ability to obtain a share all matter. These household strategies help explain everyday effort without treating every family as equally secure or equally hungry.

passages.title: Food, songs and words shared across generations
passages.text: Pyongyang raengmyon is cold buckwheat noodles traditionally served in a brass bowl, with broth and garnishes such as meat, vegetables or kimchi. UNESCO’s 2022 account describes families and neighbours sharing it at celebrations. Long noodles can express wishes for long life. Grandmothers and mothers pass on skills, while cooks also learn at work and in schools. A bowl can carry a family lesson.

passages.title: Food, songs and words shared across generations
passages.text: Arirang is a family of songs with many local forms, rather than one tune sung identically everywhere. UNESCO’s 2014 account describes children learning from parents, neighbours and schools, and people singing with family or friends. Different versions can express separation, reunion, sadness or joy. A familiar melody can travel between generations without everyone singing exactly the same words.

passages.title: Food, songs and words shared across generations
passages.text: A dated Hangul sample is 판문점 선언, romanized here as Panmunjeom seoneon, meaning “Panmunjom Declaration.” It appears in the title of the joint declaration signed by Kim Jong Un and Moon Jae-in on 27 April 2018. The witness is a South Korean government transcription of their joint document, not a North Korean-only publication. Its promises record an agreement at that moment, not proof that lasting peace followed.

passages.title: Learning, treatment, water and toilets
passages.text: A 2025 UN Special Rapporteur statement describes a legal commitment to twelve years of compulsory schooling. It notes high literacy and near-universal school completion as of 2017, alongside reports of school contributions that poorer families struggled to meet and barriers for children with disabilities. An education law, a dated survey and a family’s actual access answer different questions.

passages.title: Learning, treatment, water and toilets
passages.text: The same statement describes a network of hospitals and clinics and a legal promise of free care. It also reports shortages of medicines, equipment, trained staff, water and electricity. Patients could have to bring supplies or buy medicines themselves. Having a clinic building nearby did not guarantee that it had everything needed for treatment.

passages.title: Learning, treatment, water and toilets
passages.text: A toilet needs a safe destination for its waste as well as somewhere to sit or squat. UNICEF’s account of the 2017 survey found widespread unsafe waste handling among households using improved pit latrines or septic tanks. Some waste reached fields, open pits or water. “Improved” describes the facility type; it does not automatically mean the whole sanitation chain is safely managed.

passages.title: Learning, treatment, water and toilets
passages.text: In Myonggan County, UNICEF reported in 2019 that a gravity-fed water system served 16,000 people, eight nurseries and kindergartens, six schools and two health facilities. Gravity does the pushing, reducing dependence on electrically powered pumps. The report also describes children practising handwashing. A useful school improvement can be as ordinary as water arriving when someone turns a tap.

passages.title: Learning, treatment, water and toilets
passages.text: WHO’s account of a March 2023 catch-up vaccination campaign describes local clinics and nurseries arranging waiting, registration, vaccination and observation spaces. The campaign addressed doses missed in 2021 and 2022. The sequence matters: healthcare includes finding the child’s record and checking them afterwards, as well as giving an injection.

passages.title: Learning, treatment, water and toilets
passages.text: A September 2024 UNICEF campaign announcement aimed to reach more than 800,000 children and 120,000 pregnant women. Cold boxes, refrigerators, freezers and temperature loggers helped protect vaccine supplies. The target counts describe a plan, not independently verified completed vaccinations for every recipient. Keeping medicine cold can be an important part of getting it safely to a family.

The DPRK continues as a state; the atlas’s 2020 border-data cutoff is not a political ending. In a 30 April 2026 UN briefing, its nuclear and missile programmes remained a major concern. Korean communities, family practices and hopes cannot be reduced to weapons or government policy. This is dated historical context, not a live assessment of the border or a forecast of reunification.

sectionTitles: A republic within a divided peninsula
Homes, food and skills passed between generations
School, health and the unglamorous plumbing
Engineering and a sample of Korean writing

passages.text: The Republic of Korea was founded in 1948 in the southern part of a divided peninsula. Its history joins war and reconstruction, authoritarian government, industrial growth and a hard-won democratic transition. This map record begins in 1960, twelve years after the republic was established.

passages.title: A republic within a divided peninsula
passages.text: Japanese colonial rule ended in 1945. The Republic of Korea was established on 15 August 1948, followed by a separate northern government that September. The modern southern state is therefore distinct from earlier Korean kingdoms and from North Korea; shared language and history did not produce a single postwar government.

passages.title: A republic within a divided peninsula
passages.text: North Korean forces invaded the south on 25 June 1950. Fighting drew in United Nations forces and Chinese troops. The agreement of 27 July 1953 halted open hostilities and created a demilitarized zone four kilometers wide, but it was an armistice rather than a permanent peace treaty.

passages.title: A republic within a divided peninsula
passages.text: The map’s southern outline is a simplified snapshot, not a picture of all Korean cultural communities or every sovereignty claim. Article 3 of the republic’s constitution claims the peninsula and adjacent islands, while Article 4 directs the state to pursue peaceful unification. Those constitutional claims should not be confused with the area actually drawn here.

passages.title: A republic within a divided peninsula
passages.text: Student-led opposition helped drive Syngman Rhee from power in 1960. Park Chung-hee’s military coup followed in 1961. Rapid economic growth under military-backed governments accompanied restrictions on political freedom; major demonstrations in 1987 helped force the move to democratic elections.

passages.title: Power, work and public memory
passages.text: Gwangju’s uprising lasted from 18 to 27 May 1980. The surviving archive includes documents and photographs concerning resistance to military rule, subsequent efforts to punish perpetrators and compensation for victims. Its preservation makes civic history something researchers can examine through evidence, including records created by people caught in the events.

passages.title: Power, work and public memory
passages.text: Industrial expansion involved deliberate policy choices. A World Bank historical study identifies the early 1960s as a turning point from replacing imported goods with domestic production toward manufacturing for export. It examines incentives facing government and business leaders, reminding us that factories grew within institutions and political bargains, not by magic.

passages.title: Power, work and public memory
passages.text: The 1997 financial crisis exposed serious economic vulnerabilities. On 4 December the IMF approved a three-year credit arrangement worth about US$21 billion, with only part immediately available and later disbursements tied to reviews. This was an emergency financing program with conditions, not a gift of the entire sum on one day.

passages.title: Power, work and public memory
passages.text: The 1987 constitution provides for direct presidential election and a single five-year term. It also recognizes equal educational opportunity and bases marriage and family life on individual dignity and equality between the sexes. These are legal commitments whose practical realization must be judged through people’s experiences.

passages.title: Power, work and public memory
passages.text: Democratic institutions faced another severe test after President Yoon Suk-yeol declared martial law on 3 December 2024. On 4 April 2025 the Constitutional Court removed him from office, finding constitutional and statutory violations, including military and police interference with the National Assembly. The ruling concerned impeachment and removal, not a criminal sentence.

passages.title: Homes, food and skills passed between generations
passages.text: Seoul’s apartment landscape developed rapidly in the 1960s and 1970s. The Seoul Museum of History identifies the Mapo complex of 1962 and the apartment-district system introduced in 1976 as important steps. New housing in Gangnam changed the city’s scale and the setting of household life, although apartments never represented every family’s experience.

passages.title: Homes, food and skills passed between generations
passages.text: One family’s home became a historical source. A father, mother, daughter and son lived in Seocho Samho Apartment Building 9 for about thirty years from 1981. They kept much of its interior unchanged. Before the complex’s 2014 demolition, museum staff collected interior materials; the family also donated furniture and household objects.

passages.title: Homes, food and skills passed between generations
passages.text: The museum recreated that apartment using original fittings, but added some objects and adjusted its floor plan for the gallery. Visitors can investigate recent family life through ordinary furnishings. A museum treasure need not be a king’s crown: sometimes the useful evidence is what a family kept at home.

passages.title: Homes, food and skills passed between generations
passages.text: Kimjang means making and sharing kimchi, preserved vegetables prepared with seasonings and fermented ingredients. UNESCO’s 2013 account describes a yearly rhythm: seafood preparation in spring, obtaining salt in summer, drying peppers later, then communal work in late autumn. Preparing food for winter can turn a kitchen into a seasonal workshop.

passages.title: Homes, food and skills passed between generations
passages.text: Kimjang also carries family knowledge. Recipes and practical skills pass between generations, while households exchange food and cooperate over large batches. The social gathering matters alongside the finished vegetables: sharing the work and the results helps maintain relationships with relatives and neighbors.

passages.title: Homes, food and skills passed between generations
passages.text: On Jeju Island, haenyeo women harvest sea foods such as abalone and sea urchins by diving without oxygen equipment. UNESCO describes dives to ten meters and an experience-based hierarchy in which skilled seniors guide others. This is demanding ecological and bodily knowledge acquired through training, observation and long practice.

passages.title: Homes, food and skills passed between generations
passages.text: Contemporary haenyeo schools combine one-to-one mentoring with lessons in safety and marine ecology. Museum activities let children learn through miniature tools and stories from retired divers. The lesson is not simply how to gather a catch: it is also how a community teaches respect for the sea and keeps knowledge alive.

passages.title: School, health and the unglamorous plumbing
passages.text: PISA’s 2022 survey assessed 6,454 fifteen-year-olds in 186 Korean schools. Students performed above the OECD average in mathematics, reading and science. These results concern particular skills and a particular age group; they do not describe every talent a child may have, from friendship to music or practical craftsmanship.

passages.title: School, health and the unglamorous plumbing
passages.text: The same survey asked about school life. An estimated 78 percent of students said they made friends easily and 79 percent felt they belonged at school. Yet 22 percent reported low satisfaction with life. Looking at friendship and well-being alongside test scores gives a fuller picture of education.

passages.title: School, health and the unglamorous plumbing
passages.text: Universal health coverage was achieved in 1989, twelve years after social health insurance began. A WHO review describes further reforms in the early 2000s: insurance societies were merged into a single insurer and medicine prescribing was separated from dispensing. Organizational changes could matter to ordinary patients as much as new equipment.

passages.title: School, health and the unglamorous plumbing
passages.text: Insurance did not mean that every treatment became free. The same review, published in the 2010s, explains that private providers delivered much care and households still faced co-payments and charges for services outside the benefits package. It identifies protecting patients from high personal costs as an important continuing problem.

passages.title: School, health and the unglamorous plumbing
passages.text: Seoul’s growth also produced dirty water. The city’s Sewerage Science Museum describes pollution of Cheonggyecheon and the Han River and the construction of the Cheonggyecheon sewage treatment plant in 1976. Processing urban wastewater was a major piece of public infrastructure, even if pipes and treatment tanks rarely receive the applause given to skyscrapers.

passages.title: School, health and the unglamorous plumbing
passages.text: Suwon has a museum with an unusually honest shape: a giant toilet. Sim Jae-duck commissioned the toilet-shaped Haewoojae house, completed in 2007 to mark the founding of the World Toilet Association. His family later donated it to the city. Children’s activities now use this memorable building to teach toilet etiquette and sanitation culture.

passages.title: Engineering and a sample of Korean writing
passages.text: On 21 June 2022, the second launch of the domestically developed Nuri rocket successfully placed its performance-verification satellite in the target orbit. Signals from the satellite confirmed communication with the ground. The achievement joined propulsion, guidance, construction and tracking: spaceflight requires many separate systems to cooperate.

passages.title: Engineering and a sample of Korean writing
passages.text: One Nuri engineering challenge was a large propellant tank about 3.5 meters across with walls only two to three millimeters thick. KARI describes overcoming difficult design and manufacturing problems to build it. Large does not necessarily mean thick: reducing unnecessary mass is crucial when an engine must lift the whole vehicle.

passages.title: Engineering and a sample of Korean writing
passages.text: Here is a securely dated Korean writing sample: 채식주의자, romanized Chaesikjuuija, meaning “The Vegetarian.” This is the title of Han Kang’s Korean novel published in 2007, recorded in the Nobel Prize bibliography; its English translation appeared in 2015. The script shown is Hangul, reproduced from the modern printed title.

passages.title: Engineering and a sample of Korean writing
passages.text: Han Kang received the 2024 Nobel Prize in Literature for prose exploring historical trauma and human vulnerability. Her work demonstrates another kind of achievement: literature can examine how public violence and private lives connect. The award recognizes a writer’s work, rather than making a novel a factual account of every Korean household.

The Republic of Korea continues; there is no historical fall date to assign to this map record. Changes of president and the 2025 impeachment ruling concern the government within a continuing state. Its democratic institutions and the peninsula’s division remain distinct parts of its history.

Occupation rule, Korean political projects, and the 1948 transfer
Founding, land, repression, elections, and democratic protest
War, displacement, family separation, and the armistice
Households, women, children, shelter, and daily adaptation
Schools, textbooks, tent classrooms, and student voices
