sectionTitles: An imperial court with a powerful neighbour
Food, family visits and the government’s demands
Rooms, objects and hopes preserved underground

passages.text: Later Jin was the northern Chinese dynasty founded by Shi Jingtang in 936 and conquered by the Khitan in 947. Its court ruled from Kaifeng during the turbulent Five Dynasties era. This is a separate state from ancient Jin and the later Jurchen Jin. The atlas dates fit its historical lifespan, but its polygon is a coarse illustration of the northern realm, not a precise record of changing control.

passages.title: An imperial court with a powerful neighbour
passages.text: Shi Jingtang had commanded a frontier region for Later Tang. Khitan military help enabled him to found Later Jin, but the alliance had a heavy price: he ceded sixteen northern prefectures. His new dynasty therefore began with a powerful neighbour controlling territory that earlier northern Chinese courts had held.

passages.title: An imperial court with a powerful neighbour
passages.text: The border bargain outlived Later Jin. Song emperors later tried repeatedly to recover the lost prefectures without lasting success. A decision made to secure one ruler’s throne shaped the strategic problems of later dynasties. The atlas excludes these prefectures in its approximate Later Jin outline.

passages.title: An imperial court with a powerful neighbour
passages.text: Shi Chonggui was Shi Jingtang’s nephew and adopted son. The later New History describes officials placing him on the throne when the founder died in 942. Succession was a family matter with enormous public consequences: a child’s position in the imperial household could affect who commanded armies and appointed officials.

passages.title: Food, family visits and the government’s demands
passages.text: In 940, the court ordered public and private debts outstanding through the end of 938 to be cancelled. The Old History preserves the decree. It reveals a government trying to relieve old obligations, although the order alone cannot tell us how successfully each household obtained relief.

passages.title: Food, family visits and the government’s demands
passages.text: Officials visiting their parents received gifts of tea and medicines under an order of 940. The court explicitly followed an earlier precedent. Family duties and official employment overlapped: a trip home could come with useful supplies for the visit.

passages.title: Food, family visits and the government’s demands
passages.text: The same year, Shi Jingtang stopped deliveries of garden melons and fruit from Luoyang and Jingzhao. The stated reason was concern for the people doing the work. A ruler’s fruit bowl had a transport bill, paid partly in other people’s labour.

passages.title: Food, family visits and the government’s demands
passages.text: Locusts threatened food supplies in 943. The New History records soldiers being sent to catch them and civilians offered grain for collecting them. Fighting a harvest-eating swarm required hands as well as orders; the same annals also describe coercive grain requisitions during this difficult year.

passages.title: Printing, history and small change
passages.text: Shi Jingtang enjoyed explanations of the Daodejing by the Daoist Zhang Jianming. In 940 he ordered its two parts carved onto printing blocks, with a new preface by He Ning, for distribution. A conversation at court could lead to a much larger copying project.

passages.title: Printing, history and small change
passages.text: The work now called the Old Book of Tang was completed in 945 under Later Jin. Its 200 chapters drew on records available relatively soon after Tang’s fall. Preserving the previous dynasty’s history became one of this short-lived court’s most durable achievements: later readers could study events far beyond their own memories.

passages.title: Printing, history and small change
passages.text: The National Museum of China preserves a Later Jin Tianfu Yuanbao coin measuring 2.2 centimetres across. Its description explains that new dynastic coins circulated alongside older Tang money. A change of emperor did not mean everyone immediately emptied their purse and replaced every coin.

passages.title: Rooms, objects and hopes preserved underground
passages.text: A tomb excavated at Jinci in 2005 belonged to Lady Wang and dates to 937. Its brick chamber imitates a timber building, with painted pillars, doors and windows. Craftspeople created an architectural setting underground, leaving details of construction and decoration that real wooden rooms often lose.

passages.title: Rooms, objects and hopes preserved underground
passages.text: Lady Wang’s grave contained ceramic vessels, a bronze mirror, hairpins, thirteen Kaiyuan coins and an iron ploughshare. The surprising mix brings grooming, containers, money and farming tools together in a burial. The official Guo Zhimi arranged it, but the inscription does not identify his relationship to her.

passages.title: Rooms, objects and hopes preserved underground
passages.text: The 937 epitaph includes 子孫興盛，諸災永息, rendered here in modern traditional type. Modern Mandarin reads zǐ sūn xīng shèng, zhū zāi yǒng xī: “May descendants flourish; may all calamities cease.” This translated wish comes from a burial invocation. The carved text is contemporary, while the typeface and pronunciation guide are modern.

passages.title: Rooms, objects and hopes preserved underground
passages.text: Dayunyuan monastery at Pingshun was founded in 938, initially under another name. Its surviving Amitabha hall belongs to the Five Dynasties period, while much of the complex is later. Inside are period murals with richly coloured lines and raised gilded details. Worshippers encountered skilled woodworking and painting together; the surviving hall preserves a rare part of that setting.

passages.title: A royal family after conquest
passages.text: After the conquest, the captive imperial family was sent north. The New History lists a physician, seven cooks and tea-and-wine attendants among its reduced household, yet later describes hardship and gathering wild plants for food. These are the experiences of a displaced royal group, whose former rank no longer guaranteed comfort.

The Khitan destroyed Later Jin after its field army surrendered and Kaifeng fell in early 947. Shi Chonggui survived as a captive. This ended the dynasty, not the lives of its population or the circulation of its books and coins.

passages.text: Later Liang was the first of the Five Dynasties that ruled northern China between the Tang and Song. Founded by Zhu Wen, a former rebel who deposed the last Tang emperor, it controlled only part of northern China and faced constant military threats.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Kaifeng developed as the capital, though smaller and less cosmopolitan than Tang Chang'an.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Five Dynasties period saw the rise of military strongmen who dominated politics.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Printing technology continued to develop during this unstable period.
Li Cunxu of Later Tang conquered Later Liang and captured its capital Kaifeng in 923.

sectionTitles: A new dynasty using an old name
A tomb that preserves a furnished world

passages.text: Later Tang was a short-lived northern Chinese dynasty founded by Li Cunxu in 923. Its Shatuo-led ruling network claimed the prestige of the earlier Tang, but was a separate regime. The map’s 923-937 interval and coarse outline simplify changing control, military governorships and rival states; they do not describe a reunited China.

passages.title: A new dynasty using an old name
passages.text: Li Cunxu’s power grew from the northern military world of his father, Li Keyong. Shatuo leaders worked with people of several backgrounds, including Sogdian, Uighur and Chinese connections. The family’s granted Li surname helped its claim to carry on the earlier Tang’s authority.

passages.title: A new dynasty using an old name
passages.text: Li Cunxu conquered Later Liang in 923, ruled from Luoyang and sent an army that captured Chengdu in 925. Disgruntled soldiers brought his reign to a violent end in 926. Winning battles and keeping troops supplied, paid and loyal were different jobs. His successor Li Siyuan became Emperor Mingzong.

passages.title: A new dynasty using an old name
passages.text: Mingzong cultivated cooperation with civilian advisers and military commanders, reduced waste and directed revenue toward the public treasury. Historian Richard Davis presents his reign as a period of relative stability, while also noting its harsh punishments. Effective management did not mean gentle government.

passages.title: Families, fields and food
passages.text: Military families could be made through adoption as well as birth. Li Keyong recruited skilled fighters as surrogate sons, and Mingzong himself entered his household as an adopted youth. Such relationships helped build armies, but disputes between sons and brothers also made succession dangerous.

passages.title: Families, fields and food
passages.text: Women in the ruling household could advise and teach. Before Later Tang’s founding, Li Keyong’s wife Lady Liu trained household women in riding and archery. Under Mingzong, Empress Cao and Consort Wang supported one another at court. These are particular elite lives, not a rule for every woman.

passages.title: Families, fields and food
passages.text: A 929 edict preserved in a later institutional compilation required farming households to report their planted acreage, with groups of five households guaranteeing the declarations. Local officials were forbidden to send inspectors to remeasure it. Fields were both a family livelihood and a subject of government paperwork.

passages.title: Families, fields and food
passages.text: The same compilation records a 931 order that military farms should recruit unattached migrants and cultivate ownerless wasteland, rather than draw registered taxpayers away from their home counties. Rival demands for workers could reach straight into village life.

passages.title: Families, fields and food
passages.text: An early Song collection tells of Mingzong sharing a drink made with poppy seeds with commanders during a supply shortage. A modern historian examines it as food history. This later anecdote offers a glimpse of making do during campaigning, not an everyday menu for the whole population.

passages.title: Families, fields and food
passages.text: After the change of ruler in 926, the imperial kitchen staff was cut to fifty. Even the reduced royal kitchen was a substantial workplace! The recorded cut shows how court luxury depended on many workers, and why palace expenses became a political issue.

passages.title: A tomb that preserves a furnished world
passages.text: Wang Chuzhi’s tomb at Quyang in Hebei, dated to 924, preserves an elite world formed before Later Tang. Its carved and painted decoration and buried epitaph survived despite robbery. Wang’s career crossed the earlier Tang and Five Dynasties transition; the tomb is not an emperor’s palace.

passages.title: A tomb that preserves a furnished world
passages.text: A relief from the tomb depicts fifteen figures, including musicians, a conductor and dancers. Excavated in 1995, it gives researchers an unusually detailed picture of performance. The stone cannot play the tune, but the performers’ instruments and arrangement preserve clues to how an ensemble worked.

passages.title: A tomb that preserves a furnished world
passages.text: Painted furnishings include tall folding screens, a three-part screen, an almost square screen and low horizontal ones. Art historian Jonathan Hay uses these images to study room decoration. A screen could be furniture and a place for pictures at once, bringing painted scenery into an elite interior.

passages.title: A tomb that preserves a furnished world
passages.text: The tomb’s epitaph and later official biographies do not agree about the family position of Wang Du, Wang Chuzhi’s successor. Comparing them reveals how families and historians shaped reputations. An inscription is valuable evidence, but praising the deceased was part of its job.

passages.title: Money, writing and learning
passages.text: Shanghai Museum holds a cast copper Tiancheng yuanbao coin from Mingzong’s Tiancheng reign. It is just 23.66 millimetres across and carries regular-script characters. The museum records it as a donation by Sun Ding, so its catalogue does not establish an excavated household context.

passages.title: Money, writing and learning
passages.text: The coin’s legend is 天成元寶, read in modern Mandarin as tiānchéng yuánbǎo: literally, “original treasure of the Tiancheng era,” a currency title. These are modern printed forms of the attested Chinese characters, not a reproduction of the casting; the pronunciation is modern, too.

passages.title: Money, writing and learning
passages.text: A change of ruler did not empty everyone’s purse. The Bank of Japan’s Currency Museum explains that earlier Tang Kaiyuan coins continued circulating under the northern Five Dynasties, whose own minting was often limited. Old coins could outlast the government that issued them.

passages.title: Money, writing and learning
passages.text: Under Later Tang, Feng Dao promoted a government project to print the Confucian Classics with carved wooden blocks. The Directorate of Education used earlier Tang stone inscriptions as models. The achievement was organized editing and reproduction of authoritative texts; private woodblock printing already existed.

passages.title: Money, writing and learning
passages.text: Those Five Dynasties editions have been lost, according to the National Palace Museum. Surviving later books help trace their influence, but the museum’s illustrated Mencius volume is a Southern Song edition. A photograph of an old book is not automatically a photograph of the first edition!

Shi Jingtang rebelled with Khitan assistance in 936, and Later Tang collapsed as Later Jin took power. The last emperor’s reign ended in January 937, explaining the map’s endpoint. The ruling house lost the throne; communities, officials, books and earlier monetary traditions continued under new political arrangements.

sectionTitles: A short dynasty with lasting institutions
Books and the work of scholars

passages.text: Later Zhou ruled from Kaifeng between 951 and 960, the last of northern China’s Five Dynasties. Its rulers strengthened central armies and government before the Song took power. This was a separate medieval dynasty, not the ancient Zhou. The map’s coarse outline simplifies changing control and neighboring independent states.

passages.title: A short dynasty with lasting institutions
passages.text: Guo Wei came to power in 951 after turning his army back toward Kaifeng and ending Later Han rule. Historian Peter Lorge treats the story of soldiers demanding that their commander become emperor as political theater. The same pattern appeared again when Later Zhou itself lost power.

passages.title: A short dynasty with lasting institutions
passages.text: The succession in 954 depended on family ties and military promises. Chai Rong was Guo Wei’s adopted son. Before dying, Guo required senior generals to swear loyalty to him. An adoption could shape an empire’s future, but an oath still needed powerful people willing to keep it.

passages.title: A short dynasty with lasting institutions
passages.text: The new ruler immediately faced an invasion by Northern Han, supported by Khitan cavalry. Chai Rong gathered troops and marched to meet them near Gaoping in 954. Rival rulers controlled substantial armies and territory: the emperor at Kaifeng could claim supreme authority without possessing all of China.

passages.title: A short dynasty with lasting institutions
passages.text: Chai Rong strengthened the Metropolitan and Palace Commands, the principal central armies. Regular civil officials also helped rebuild government. Bringing military power closer to the throne reduced dependence on regional military governors, although the central army’s own commander would eventually replace the ruling house.

passages.title: Fields, households and service
passages.text: A 952 edict transferred certain state estates to their existing tenants, including houses, mulberry land, carts and oxen. Households were to register their holdings; poorer households received three years’ relief from labor duties. These were orders intended to stabilize farming families after upheaval.

passages.title: Fields, households and service
passages.text: Returning refugees could face another family already farming their land. Rules issued in 955 divided some recovered property between returnees and tenants. Houses, trees and gardens newly created by tenants were protected from return. Rebuilding a home was also a legal problem.

passages.title: Fields, households and service
passages.text: Feng Hui’s large tomb in Shaanxi had a corridor, an antechamber and a burial chamber with side rooms. Its painted brick walls pictured people, including musicians and dancers. This was an elite vision of a well-served household carried into burial, rather than a plan of every family’s home.

passages.title: Fields, households and service
passages.text: In paintings from this tomb, dated to 958, female attendants carry a towel, a spittoon and a cushion. Even grand households needed someone to manage the small comforts of sitting down and keeping tidy. These are depicted service objects, not evidence of a universal public sanitation system.

passages.title: Fields, households and service
passages.text: An epitaph supplied the name of the tomb’s occupant, Feng Hui, who died in 952. Its formal Chinese writing lets researchers connect the decorated rooms with an identifiable person. Archaeology can sometimes recover both a room full of entertainment and the name on the guest list.

passages.title: Metalworkers, money and readable writing
passages.text: Cangzhou’s huge iron lion was cast in 953 and stands more than five metres high. A lotus seat rests on its back. Art historians connect it with a vanished Buddhist temple and a lost bodhisattva figure. This was a metalworking project on a scale far beyond a household cooking pot.

passages.title: Metalworkers, money and readable writing
passages.text: The lion’s grid of seams preserves clues to its manufacture. Craftspeople assembled a mould from clay pieces, then poured iron in stages. Iron pegs helped connect the cooling layers. Those lines are traces of a giant mould and a difficult casting job, not a lion assembled from little iron tiles.

passages.title: Metalworkers, money and readable writing
passages.text: A copper coin in the Fitzwilliam Museum is only 23.67 millimetres across and weighs 2.75 grams. Its reverse has a crescent above the central hole. The museum dates this one-cash coin to 955-960, giving us a small surviving object from the dynasty’s final years.

passages.title: Metalworkers, money and readable writing
passages.text: The coin reads 周元通寶, which the museum translates as “Zhou First Currency.” Modern Mandarin pinyin is zhōuyuán tōngbǎo. The Chinese shown here is modern typesetting of an attested period inscription, and the pronunciation is modern; neither reproduces the original casting or tenth-century speech.

passages.title: Books and the work of scholars
passages.text: The great government project to carve printing blocks for the Confucian Classics was completed in 953. It had begun under Later Tang and continued through several governments. Scholars and craftspeople could finish a long job even when the name of the dynasty changed around them.

passages.title: Books and the work of scholars
passages.text: In 956, the court asked scholars to review ritual vessels and ceremonial jades. Nie Chongyi and his critics even disputed whether a jade disk’s hole should be round or square. To them, the shape helped express correct ritual and authority. A surprisingly serious argument about a small hole!

passages.title: Books and the work of scholars
passages.text: Nie submitted fifty-three designs in 957: ten jades and forty-three vessels. The Ministry of Works sent the designs into production, and the implements were ready by 959. Learning involved texts, pictures and workshops working together to furnish ceremonies for imperial ancestors and Heaven and Earth.

passages.title: Books and the work of scholars
passages.text: The project outlived Later Zhou. Nie presented his expanded illustrated ritual book to the new Song emperor in 961. Its history makes the transition visible: a court could lose its throne while its scholars continued writing and arguing over the same designs.

Chai Rong died in 959. In 960, the Palace Command’s leader Zhao Kuangyin displaced the final Later Zhou ruler and founded Song. The dynasty ended, but its concentration of military and administrative power helped equip the new government.

passages.text: Latvia declared independence in 1918. Its interwar republic redistributed farmland and built universities, factories and public markets. Parliamentary democracy ended in the 1934 coup. Occupation in 1940 destroyed practical independence, although the Latvian state continued to exist in international law.

passages.title: Public life and new possibilities
passages.text: The 1922 constitution gave voting rights to qualifying Latvian citizens of both sexes over 21. The first Saeima election drew more than 800,000 voters. Voting was a new way to shape the country, although the 1934 coup later closed parliament.

passages.title: Public life and new possibilities
passages.text: Land reform between 1920 and 1937 broke up large holdings. Land entered a State Land Fund and was redistributed to other residents as private property. For families receiving land, the republic’s decisions changed who controlled the fields and the future of a farm.

passages.title: Public life and new possibilities
passages.text: The University of Latvia began in 1919 with nine faculties, including medicine, engineering, chemistry, agriculture and architecture. Veterinary medicine joined in 1920. Training people to design buildings, treat patients and care for farm animals belonged to the same effort to build a new state.

passages.title: Public life and new possibilities
passages.text: In 1920, Riga’s new medical faculty received a former Orthodox seminary building. It became the Anatomikum, later housing anatomy, physiology, hygiene, microbiology and other departments. Students also learned in city hospitals, including the children’s hospital. Medical education needed laboratories and real clinical practice.

passages.title: Public life and new possibilities
passages.text: Riga’s radio service officially opened on 1 November 1925 with a transmission of Puccini’s opera Madame Butterfly. Experimental broadcasts had begun in October. A performance in the opera house could now reach listeners through a radio receiver, giving live music a new route into people’s homes.

passages.title: Public life and new possibilities
passages.text: VEF in Riga began industrial production of Walter Zapp’s Minox camera in 1938, following his Tallinn prototype. Tallinn’s Photography Museum preserves an early Riga-made example with serial number 118 and its leather case. Making a tiny camera reliably was a factory achievement as well as an inventor’s idea.

passages.title: Public life and new possibilities
passages.text: Riga’s Freedom Monument was unveiled on 18 November 1935. Residents’ donations financed Kārlis Zāle’s monument to independence and those who had died fighting for it. Granite and copper turned a public fundraising effort into a lasting landmark.

passages.title: Food, health and leisure
passages.text: Riga’s new Central Market opened in 1930 under roof structures reused from German Zeppelin hangars. Engineers used only their upper sections and built lower brick and concrete supports. Keeping the enormous original height would have made indoor temperatures difficult to manage. Even a market roof had to think about the groceries.

passages.title: Food, health and leisure
passages.text: The market combined electric lighting and central heating with an extensive basement network. Passages below the pavilions helped move and store goods away from the bustle above. Shopping depended on a less visible working world beneath the stalls.

passages.title: Food, health and leisure
passages.text: Ķemeri’s state-funded hotel opened in 1936 with hydrotherapy rooms on its ground floor, allowing the resort to offer treatments throughout the year. Museum postcards show mud being collected and baths being prepared. These were historical treatment practices; the hotel’s architecture and equipment reveal the investment behind them.

passages.title: Food, health and leisure
passages.text: Ķemeri also hosted major chess tournaments in 1937 and 1939 to attract visitors. A health resort could sell peaceful surroundings, social life and the excitement of a match. The spectators’ hearts may have raced even when the players remained firmly seated.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: Latvian, article 1 of the constitution adopted in 1922: “Latvija ir neatkarīga demokrātiska republika.” Translation: “Latvia is an independent democratic republic.” The sample follows the official 1993 republication of the earlier constitutional text.

The USSR occupied and illegally annexed Latvia in 1940. Nazi occupation followed, then Soviet rule returned during the war. Latvia retained legal state continuity and restored full independence in 1991. The map’s 1945 endpoint is not the date independence was first lost.

passages.text: Latvia restored full independence in 1991 after decades of occupation. The renewed parliamentary republic joined the European Union in 2004 and adopted the euro in 2014. Its recent history includes new public institutions, converted scientific equipment and communities keeping local traditions alive.

passages.title: Books, science and practical inventions
passages.text: On 18 January 2014, thousands of people formed a human chain to pass books from Latvia’s old National Library building to its new home. The ceremonial move made readers part of the opening celebrations. A book could cross the city with a remarkable number of helping hands.

passages.title: Books, science and practical inventions
passages.text: The library’s People’s Bookshelf invited readers to donate a book with a personal note on its title page. Donated volumes were displayed in a glass wall rising through several floors. The collection preserves people’s attachments to books as well as the books themselves.

passages.title: Books, science and practical inventions
passages.text: At Irbene, former Soviet military intelligence antennas gained a scientific future after Russian troops withdrew in 1994. Researchers established a radio astronomy centre using dishes 32 and 16 metres across. Equipment once associated with secrecy became part of international efforts to study the universe.

passages.title: Books, science and practical inventions
passages.text: Irbene’s later telescope upgrades included extremely cold radio receivers to help measure faint signals. A research paper reports one part operating at 14 kelvin, close to absolute zero. From October 2015 the upgraded 32-metre telescope took part in joint international observing sessions.

passages.title: Books, science and practical inventions
passages.text: MikroTik was registered in Latvia in 1996 and develops networking products including routers, switches and wireless systems. These devices help move information between computers. Latvia’s modern technical work therefore includes the ordinary-looking boxes that let other people’s computers talk to each other.

passages.title: Daily life, sanitation and community
passages.text: Riga’s Daugavgrīva wastewater plant began operating in 1991. Sewage passes through mechanical cleaning before biological treatment using activated sludge, and a laboratory checks the treated water. Flushing a toilet starts a journey that needs pipes, pumps and a great deal of organized work.

passages.title: Daily life, sanitation and community
passages.text: Daugavgrīva’s equipment was upgraded in 1999, including aeration, screens and grit traps. Further biological treatment improvements followed in 2014. A functioning modern city depends on repeated investment in this hidden infrastructure, even when its residents rarely think about what happens after the flush.

passages.title: Daily life, sanitation and community
passages.text: The Suiti community in western Latvia combines Catholic religious traditions with older local customs and modern life. Its cultural identity includes distinctive dress, food, celebrations and women’s drone singing, in which a sustained vocal sound accompanies the melody.

passages.title: Daily life, sanitation and community
passages.text: The Suiti Cultural Heritage Foundation, established in 2013, organizes informal learning for ages ranging from preschool children to seniors. Its work connects handicrafts, music, local speech and seasonal celebrations. Keeping a tradition alive involves opportunities to practise it together, rather than only storing it in an archive.

passages.title: Daily life, sanitation and community
passages.text: Latvia’s Song and Dance Celebration grows from rehearsals in local groups and community centres. Most participants are amateurs, guided by conductors and instructors. The large festival is the visible result of many smaller evenings spent practising with neighbours, friends and fellow singers.

passages.title: Daily life, sanitation and community
passages.text: In 1998 Latvia added a fundamental-rights chapter to its constitution. It includes protection for minority communities’ languages and cultural identities. These rights matter in schools, cultural associations and family life in a country whose residents have several linguistic and cultural backgrounds.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: Latvian, article 112 of the constitution’s modern rights chapter: “Ikvienam ir tiesības uz izglītību.” Translation: “Everyone has the right to education.” The quotation follows the Saeima’s Latvian consolidated text. This chapter was added in 1998, long after the original 1922 constitution.

Latvia continues as an independent republic. Its 1991 restoration renewed the state established in 1918; the map’s 1994 label marks later coverage. Membership in the European Union is a subsequent chapter in that continuing history.

passages.text: This card follows the Lebanese Republic through the atlas's circa-1945-to-present display record. Lebanon ended the French mandate in 1943, the United States recognized it in 1944 and French forces left in 1946, so the map's opening year is a convenient layer date rather than a founding moment. Its repeated historical outlines and later modern polygon are approximate coverage, not a border-by-border account of wars or control.

passages.title: Independence, institutions and repeated shocks
passages.text: Lebanese leaders declared the French mandate ended in November 1943. US recognition followed in September 1944, diplomatic relations in November 1944 and the remaining French forces left in 1946. Those dates answer different questions: who claimed independence, who recognized it and when foreign soldiers withdrew. The atlas's 1945 start sits between them and should not be mistaken for the birthday of Lebanon.

passages.title: Independence, institutions and repeated shocks
passages.text: Lebanon's constitution describes a parliamentary republic and protects religious communities' schools. Parliamentary seats are divided equally between Christians and Muslims, then proportionally among confessional groups and regions until a non-confessional electoral law is adopted. This arrangement was designed to share power in a diverse country, but a constitutional formula cannot by itself remove inequality, patronage or disagreement.

passages.title: Independence, institutions and repeated shocks
passages.text: The republic's early decades mixed commerce and cultural life with serious fault lines. Refugees arrived after the 1948 Arab-Israeli war, and in 1958 armed conflict broke out among Lebanese factions amid wider regional rivalry. The crisis ended, but tensions over political representation, inequality and Palestinian armed organizations continued. By April 1975, one violent incident triggered a much larger breakdown that years of mistrust had prepared.

passages.title: Independence, institutions and repeated shocks
passages.text: The civil war was not one two-sided contest. Alliances shifted among Lebanese militias and parties, Palestinian organizations and foreign states. Israel's 1982 invasion forced the PLO evacuation from Beirut. After Israeli forces entered West Beirut, Maronite militiamen massacred Palestinian civilians in Sabra and Shatila. Naming the perpetrators matters, and the crime must not be assigned to an entire religious community.

passages.title: Independence, institutions and repeated shocks
passages.text: Lebanon's government sent the United Nations a July 1990 programme for implementing the Taif Charter. It called for constitutional reform, reconciliation, the restoration of state authority and the surrender of militia weapons. The programme helped move the country out of open civil war, but it was a plan to be carried out, not a magical switch. Institutions, neighborhoods and families still had to rebuild after fifteen years of violence.

passages.title: Independence, institutions and repeated shocks
passages.text: Syrian forces and intelligence remained powerful in postwar Lebanon. A UN investigation records that Syrian forces withdrew in May 2005 after Security Council action, while also describing the earlier pervasive influence of Syrian military intelligence. Withdrawal changed the political landscape; it did not end domestic division, outside influence or armed conflict. A date on a troop movement is a milestone, not an instant cure.

passages.title: Independence, institutions and repeated shocks
passages.text: Lebanon's financial crisis began in 2019, followed by the port explosions, pandemic pressures and wars. The World Bank estimated that the economy grew in 2025 after years of contraction, then projected a 6.4 percent contraction for 2026 after renewed fighting began in March. That August 2026 forecast is a dated snapshot. It shows how damaged housing, displacement, interrupted tourism and weakened banks reach ordinary household budgets.

passages.title: Archaeology, preservation and a very social breakfast
passages.text: At Baalbek, enormous stone structures preserve layers of religious history. Phoenician traditions were joined to Hellenistic and Roman forms, and the Roman sanctuary rose over earlier remains. One terrace monolith weighs more than 800 tons, while columns of the Temple of Jupiter reached about 20 metres. These ancient feats belong to earlier societies; modern Lebanon's achievement is studying and caring for what survived.

passages.title: Archaeology, preservation and a very social breakfast
passages.text: UNESCO listed Baalbek in 1984. Lebanon's Directorate General of Antiquities has consolidated and restored monuments, while conservation plans try to protect the ruins from urban pressure and conflict damage. Archaeological discovery is not always a shiny object popping out of the ground; often it is patient comparison of walls, inscriptions and building layers, followed by the less glamorous superhero work of stopping stone from cracking.

passages.title: Archaeology, preservation and a very social breakfast
passages.text: After the 2020 port explosions, Li Beirut linked the repair of schools, museums, historic buildings and cultural livelihoods. By 2025, UNESCO reported training young heritage specialists, restoring major cultural sites and helping the Directorate General of Antiquities with storage and digitization equipment. Later teams also assessed conflict damage at Tyre and Baalbek. Preservation became both skilled employment and emergency response.

passages.title: Archaeology, preservation and a very social breakfast
passages.text: A familiar morning food is al-man'ouché: thin dough spread with mixtures that can include thyme, sumac, toasted sesame, salt and olive oil, then baked. People may add tomatoes, cucumbers, olives, mint, labneh or other cheeses and drink tea with it. It is breakfast with enough possible toppings to run a tiny election, although the most important vote may be whether anyone gets the last piece.

passages.title: Archaeology, preservation and a very social breakfast
passages.text: UNESCO describes parents teaching children how to prepare man'ouché and apprentices learning in small bakeries, many of them family-run. The morning trip to a neighborhood oven can become a social visit, and the food appears in homes and community gatherings across religious backgrounds. Daily life here is not just what people eat; it is who mixes the dough, who learns by watching and who chats while breakfast bakes.

passages.title: Archaeology, preservation and a very social breakfast
passages.text: The port explosions also brought a youth-led civic response. UNICEF and partners involved more than 1,900 young people in debris removal, small repairs, meal distribution and mask production; some had construction training through vocational courses. Their work did not erase the disaster or replace public responsibility. It does show teenagers and young adults turning practical skills into help for neighbors when streets, homes and services were damaged.

passages.title: Writing, classrooms and medicine
passages.text: The constitution's Article 1 begins, “لبنان دولة مستقلة ذات وحدة لا تتجزأ وسيادة تامة”, officially rendered as “Lebanon is an independent, indivisible, and sovereign state.” Arabic is read from right to left, and Article 11 names it the national official language. This is a modern typed constitutional sample from an article amended in 1943, not an ancient inscription and not proof that every constitutional promise is always fulfilled.

passages.title: Writing, classrooms and medicine
passages.text: Lebanon's constitution protects freedom of education and the right of religious communities to establish schools under general state rules. In practice, schooling has repeatedly been interrupted by financial crisis, displacement and fighting. A constitutional right supplies a legal foundation, while safe buildings, paid teachers, transport, electricity and family income determine whether a child can actually reach a desk and keep learning.

passages.title: Writing, classrooms and medicine
passages.text: The 2020 port explosions damaged education across Beirut. UNESCO and partners completed rehabilitation of 280 educational institutions within eighteen months, including direct work on schools, vocational centres, university buildings and eleven school libraries. Reopening meant more than replacing windows: teams supplied furniture and equipment, restored libraries and trained teachers and librarians. A repaired classroom is infrastructure, but it is also a place where routines can return.

passages.title: Writing, classrooms and medicine
passages.text: War damaged schools again in 2026. A September assessment by the Ministry of Education and UNICEF covered 1,089 facilities and found 436 damaged and 37 destroyed after hostilities that began in March. Education teams used in-person, distance and blended arrangements while planning repairs, learning recovery and psychosocial support. These figures are dated to that survey; they are not a permanent total in a changing emergency.

passages.title: Writing, classrooms and medicine
passages.text: Beirut has trained physicians for generations. The medical school that became AUB's Faculty of Medicine opened in 1867, and its first doctors graduated in 1871. During the Second World War its bacteriology department produced vaccines used by local government. That is a chain from classroom to laboratory to public service, built long before the modern atlas layer and carried into the republic rather than invented overnight in 1945.

passages.title: Writing, classrooms and medicine
passages.text: AUB's medical center kept treating casualties during the 1975-1990 civil war even as conflict damaged education and drove staff away. In a later era, Lebanon's Ministry of Public Health and WHO set 2026-2029 priorities that include primary care, hospitals, digital health, medicine management, workforce investment and emergency preparedness. Medical achievement includes discoveries and machines, but also keeping trained people and supplies working through a crisis.

passages.title: Water, toilets and the quiet machinery of daily life
passages.text: Since the financial crisis began, many public water systems have struggled to power pumps, treat water and perform repairs. Some households have depended on costly private water trucks, while many wastewater plants have been non-functional or far below capacity. That means a kitchen tap and a toilet are connected to electricity, public finance and engineering. Plumbing may hide in the wall, but the systems behind it are enormous.

passages.title: Water, toilets and the quiet machinery of daily life
passages.text: The same UNICEF programme records more than 500 repairs to water systems in 2024 and support for rehabilitating sixteen wastewater facilities by 2025. Repairs are a public-health achievement because treated water and safely handled sewage interrupt routes by which disease spreads. A wastewater plant will probably never win a beauty contest, but when it works, everyone downstream has a better day.

passages.title: Water, toilets and the quiet machinery of daily life
passages.text: Displacement makes ordinary bathroom privacy much harder. During the 2024 emergency, UNICEF reports that work at 187 displacement sites installed 713 showers and 413 toilets. These were emergency facilities, not a measure of toilets in Lebanon as a whole. Still, the numbers reveal a basic truth children understand immediately: a shelter needs safe places to wash and go to the bathroom, not just mattresses and a roof.

passages.title: Water, toilets and the quiet machinery of daily life
passages.text: After the Beirut port explosions, UNICEF and partners reported safe sanitation access for more than 197,000 people and public-water reconnections for more than 23,000. Other teams supplied hygiene kits, repaired schools and health facilities and supported families. A working toilet or water pipe may be less photogenic than a famous temple, yet it can decide whether a family can remain safely at home while a neighborhood recovers.

Lebanon continues as a republic; this atlas record has no historical end date. Its 2100 geometry cutoff is a display horizon, not a forecast. As of September 2026, renewed conflict and damaged schools made continuity painfully practical: keeping government, family life, education, medicine, water and culture operating. Civil war, withdrawal, financial collapse and explosions changed institutions and daily routines, but none marks the disappearance of Lebanon or its people.

sectionTitles: History and the evidence people leave
Skilled hands, shared celebrations and everyday care

passages.text: Lenca history spans communities in Honduras and eastern El Salvador, with varied local traditions and language records. The imported 1492-1500 outline is not a single kingdom’s measured border. This account distinguishes Honduran evidence from Salvadoran Potón heritage, and later documented practices from the much earlier centuries represented on the map.

passages.title: History and the evidence people leave
passages.text: Lempira became a central figure in memories of resistance to Spanish conquest in 1537. Accounts of his death disagree. In a 1558 petition, Rodrigo Ruiz claimed credit and requested a reward; historian Blanca Moreno’s study questions contradictions in that testimony. A reward application deserves careful reading.

passages.title: History and the evidence people leave
passages.text: In the Tencoa district, colonial missions grew among existing Lenca population centers. Archaeologists investigated sites including Viejo Celilac, Viejo Jalapa, Yamala, Gualala and Macholoa. These locations help researchers connect earlier settlement patterns with the places named in colonial records.

passages.title: History and the evidence people leave
passages.text: Tencoa-area registers from 1807 and 1809 record individual names, ages, marital status and tribute status. Such lists can reveal families and obligations that are nearly invisible in stories focused on famous commanders. They also show communities continuing long after the conquest.

passages.title: History and the evidence people leave
passages.text: Much older regional archaeology at Yarumela includes grinding stones, mortars, obsidian tools and evidence of wattle-and-daub houses. The excavation report interprets maize farming as fundamental, with cassava less certain. These finds illuminate the region’s past without proving the language spoken by every ancient household.

passages.title: History and the evidence people leave
passages.text: Penn Libraries preserves Berendt’s transcription of Squier’s vocabularies from four Honduran villages. The lists contain 84 words and numbers up to 70. Squier collected the Guajiquiro material in June 1853. Keeping the village names attached matters because local forms were not all identical.

passages.title: History and the evidence people leave
passages.text: A written sample from Hernández and Pinart’s 1897 Guajiquiro vocabulary is “cuy gailainá”, translated as “It is raining.” The printed Spanish gloss is “Está lloviendo.” This is a nineteenth-century record of speech in one Honduran community, not a newly invented ancient sentence.

passages.title: Skilled hands, shared celebrations and everyday care
passages.text: A Honduran Lenca vessel made in 2012, now in the National Museum of the American Indian, was built by hand using coils and finished with clay slip. At 30 centimeters tall, it provides a documented modern example of pottery skill. Its catalogue records a gallery purchase, not an archaeological excavation.

passages.title: Skilled hands, shared celebrations and everyday care
passages.text: In Guatajiagua, El Salvador, a 2024 field account shows a potter shaping a comal, a cooking griddle, then scraping it with a tool made from a dried gourd. Handles are added and a smooth stone polishes the surface. Useful workshop equipment can begin as a fruit.

passages.title: Skilled hands, shared celebrations and everyday care
passages.text: The same account documents pottery fired in an adobe kiln and dipped while still hot into a dark plant dye made from nacascol. Timing helps the color adhere. The familiar black finish comes from a sequence of skilled decisions, not simply finding black clay in the ground.

passages.title: Skilled hands, shared celebrations and everyday care
passages.text: José Gabino Manuelles of Yamaranguila described Guancasco celebrations that bring neighboring communities together with their sacred images, dancers and musicians. His account names drums, flute, maraca and masks, and describes invitations to teach young people. A celebration can also be a lesson in maintaining relationships.

passages.title: Skilled hands, shared celebrations and everyday care
passages.text: In its 2008 account, COPINH described a Lenca teacher-training school organized with Honduras’s Ministry of Education. The program aimed to strengthen community education, language and culture, including access for remote villages. Teachers were being prepared to connect schoolwork with local knowledge.

passages.title: Skilled hands, shared celebrations and everyday care
passages.text: A COPINH publication records eight women’s gatherings between January and August 2018 focused on health and ancestral knowledge. Participants shared experiences, questions, reflections and creative work. The record shows women learning together and documenting their concerns, without establishing that every recorded remedy is effective.

passages.title: Skilled hands, shared celebrations and everyday care
passages.text: After pandemic disruption and hurricane damage, COPINH supported community gardens in places including Pueblo Viejo and Montaña Verde. Its 2023 report describes a year of learning about organic fertilizer and caring for soil. Adding vegetables and fruit aimed to broaden diets beyond the main crops.

passages.title: Skilled hands, shared celebrations and everyday care
passages.text: Salvadoran language work also produced teaching books. Vásquez’s study identifies Potón Piau, developed by Consuelo Roque and Salvador Hernández and first printed in 2000. Recording and teaching Potón concerns a distinct local heritage; a Guajiquiro word list cannot simply replace it.

Spanish conquest transformed local authority, but the Lenca people did not disappear in 1500 or with Lempira’s death. Family records, living pottery traditions and community-led education document continuity through major changes in language, government and daily life.

passages.text: León was a medieval Iberian monarchy with cities, monasteries and institutions of learning. Royal women shaped its buildings and books. Although the atlas keeps León separate until 1279, its crown was permanently united with Castile under Ferdinand III in 1230.

passages.title: Government and learning
passages.text: In 1188, Alfonso IX’s royal assembly included representatives of towns alongside nobles and church leaders. UNESCO recognizes the Decreta as an exceptionally early documentary witness to European parliamentary practice. This was medieval representation, not voting rights for every adult.

passages.title: Government and learning
passages.text: The Decreta emphasized procedures for accusations, witnesses and legal disputes. Instead of settling every quarrel through private force, the king promised routes through recognized courts. Rules tell us what authorities wanted people to do, not that every dispute was handled fairly.

passages.title: Government and learning
passages.text: Sealed summons were part of the documented legal system. A seal helped turn a written order into an identifiable act of authority. The surviving Decreta tradition includes later copies as well as original documents, so not every manuscript was physically written in 1188.

passages.title: Government and learning
passages.text: Alfonso IX founded Salamanca’s schools in 1218. This was an institution for advanced study, not a compulsory school for every Leonese child. It continued after the union with Castile, showing how a political boundary can change while a school survives.

passages.title: Government and learning
passages.text: The 1047 Beatus manuscript commissioned by Ferdinand and Sancha has 98 vivid miniatures. Its pictures illustrate a commentary on Revelation, including fantastic creatures. It is a later copy of a much earlier work, not the lost original written by Beatus.

passages.title: Government and learning
passages.text: Making that book required 317 parchment leaves, two columns of writing and coordinated illumination. The library cautiously associates its production with Facundus and perhaps San Isidoro. Those qualifications matter: a beautiful manuscript does not automatically reveal a securely identified workshop.

passages.title: Royal households and everyday evidence
passages.text: Ferdinand and Sancha built a palace beside San Isidoro in the mid-eleventh century. Two rooms survive. In the twelfth century, Infanta Sancha Raimúndez adapted the former royal gallery as her own chamber and oratory, a concrete example of a royal woman shaping domestic and devotional space.

passages.title: Royal households and everyday evidence
passages.text: The same room later became a scriptorium used by the canons. Its visible sixteenth-century wall paintings belong to another phase. A room’s latest decoration should not be used to reconstruct what a twelfth-century resident saw.

passages.title: Royal households and everyday evidence
passages.text: The ivory crucifix donated by Ferdinand and Sancha in 1063 had a cavity behind Christ intended for a relic of the True Cross. It could be carried or mounted for display. Its carving connects skilled material work with public religious practice.

passages.title: Royal households and everyday evidence
passages.text: On the crucifix, Latin names and titles read “FREDINANDVS REX / SANCIA REGINA”: “Ferdinand the king / Sancha the queen.” The inscription identifies a royal couple. It gives Sancha an explicit written presence in the gift rather than leaving the queen invisible.

passages.title: Royal households and everyday evidence
passages.text: The royal burial chapel’s fresco of the announcement to the shepherds depicts pastoral life in a biblical scene. It is useful evidence for how medieval artists pictured herding, but it is not a photograph of a particular Leonese farm.

passages.title: Royal households and everyday evidence
passages.text: San Isidoro’s defensive tower reused part of León’s Roman wall and later became a bell tower. In one structure, we can see military fabric being adapted for a religious community. Reuse carried older urban materials into the routines of medieval life.

Ferdinand III united León and Castile permanently in 1230. León’s separate royal succession ended, but its institutions, settlements and regional identity continued within the larger crown. The atlas’s 1279 endpoint is later than this political union and must not be interpreted as a separate conquest.

sectionTitles: A mountain in history and memory
Homes that are works of art
Music at work, at home and in healing

passages.text: Lesotho’s national story took shape around Moshoeshoe I’s mountain stronghold at Thaba Bosiu. Clay sculptures of parents, children and musicians bring everyday lives into this history alongside rulers and political events.

passages.title: A mountain in history and memory
passages.text: Thaba Bosiu became Moshoeshoe I’s political centre in 1824. Lesotho’s heritage account describes stone walls, gateways and lookout posts strengthening the plateau’s natural defences. It also records an oral tradition that the mountain grew taller at night. That story belongs to how the place was remembered and understood; it is not a measurement of a mountain changing height.

passages.title: Homes that are works of art
passages.text: Writing in 2020, artist ‘Matsooana Sekokotoana explains how Basotho women decorated homes with litema. Designs were worked into damp earth plaster, sometimes with coloured stones making a mosaic. Cow dung helped bind the mud. The wall was a surface for skilled pattern-making as well as shelter. Her account describes a practice that has become less common as building methods change.

passages.title: Homes that are works of art
passages.text: Sekokotoana also describes a ceramic plate she made using two litema designs: boliba, associated with deep water, and lihlaba, with hills or mountains. She arranged them to evoke Lesotho’s landscape. She recalls her father encouraging patience, a lesson she connected with the careful painting. Family advice and the patterns of home found another life on a plate.

passages.title: Getting dressed for the mountains
passages.text: A blanket made around 2012 and held by the British Museum combines black and turquoise with four red vertical stripes. Its feather design belongs to the Victoria England range. The catalogue identifies wool and cotton, and manufacture at Aranda’s mill in Randfontein, South Africa. An object associated with Basotho dress can also reveal production and trade across the border.

passages.title: Getting dressed for the mountains
passages.text: The museum explains that wearing blankets are wrapped around the body and secured at the shoulders, providing warmth in Lesotho’s cold mountain conditions. The familiar stripes usually run vertically when worn. A blanket can be part of getting dressed as well as going to bed. The catalogue describes a living clothing tradition with different designs, rather than one outfit worn by everyone.

passages.title: Little sculptures, everyday people
passages.text: Samuele Makoanyane, who lived from 1909 to 1944, made small clay figures of people around him. Iziko’s collection includes a woman feeding a baby and another rolling a sleeping mat. These are an artist’s representations, not photographs of every household. Their subjects put childcare and ordinary work into a museum collection alongside portraits of kings and warriors.

passages.title: Little sculptures, everyday people
passages.text: In 1935, collector Percival Kirby commissioned Makoanyane to model musicians and their instruments. Seven figures were completed, including a herdboy playing the lesiba and a woman with a drum. The exhibition lets viewers examine these fragile sculptures as digital models. Close attention to the tiny players helps preserve evidence of performance as well as the sculptor’s individual skill.

passages.title: Music at work, at home and in healing
passages.text: A lesiba combines a stick, a stretched string and a quill. Pusetso Nyabela’s 2022 museum report describes players using their breath to make the quill vibrate, rather than simply plucking a tune. Associated with shepherds, the instrument also supplied a familiar sound before Radio Lesotho’s news. Small materials can make a very distinctive voice.

passages.title: Music at work, at home and in healing
passages.text: A revival project in 2007 and 2008 found older women in Leribe who still played the lekope, with instruments hanging on their house walls. The report describes a string stretched along a reed and a player’s mouth shaping the sound. Skills that seemed to be disappearing were still present in particular homes.

passages.title: Music at work, at home and in healing
passages.text: Recordings from the late 1950s and early 1960s documented the lekope in hlophe, a ritual healing dance. Nyabela discusses music, singing, clapping and beliefs about ancestral help. These recordings preserve accounts of healing and performance; they do not test the medical effectiveness of a treatment.

passages.title: Reading, learning and remembering families
passages.text: Morija’s archives preserve Leselinyana, a newspaper first published in 1863, alongside church registers, letters, government reports and Sesotho hymnals. French, Sesotho and English all appear in the collections. Such records let researchers follow reading, music and public debate through time. A newspaper’s small notices can open questions quite different from those answered by a royal portrait.

passages.title: Reading, learning and remembering families
passages.text: The Hub at Morija opened in 2015 as a place for digital creativity. The museum describes internet access and training in photography, film, writing and information technology. It connects a town known for historical collections with new ways of making and sharing stories. Learning about the past can happen in the same community as learning to use a camera or computer.

passages.title: Reading, learning and remembering families
passages.text: David-Frédéric Ellenberger collected oral histories and genealogies from 1866 to 1905. His interview notes, letters and maps survive at Morija, and a British Library project digitised the archive. The notes offer evidence about families and remembered events, but they also reflect what a missionary asked and chose to record. Preserving a source includes understanding the viewpoint through which it was made.

passages.title: Paintings older than the kingdom
passages.text: A 2013 heritage evaluation describes Sehlabathebe’s rock paintings in shelters and overhangs: human figures, animals including eland, and colours from earthy yellow to dark red and white. These works belong to San histories that extend beyond the later story of the Basotho kingdom. Interpreting their spiritual meanings takes research; a painted animal is not automatically a literal record of a hunting trip.

British rule ended on 4 October 1966. Lesotho continues as an independent kingdom, with later changes of government forming part of its history. The map’s Basutoland and Lesotho records do not represent the extinction and replacement of three separate peoples.

passages.text: Lesotho’s national story took shape around Moshoeshoe I’s mountain stronghold at Thaba Bosiu. Clay sculptures of parents, children and musicians bring everyday lives into this history alongside rulers and political events.

passages.title: A mountain in history and memory
passages.text: Thaba Bosiu became Moshoeshoe I’s political centre in 1824. Lesotho’s heritage account describes stone walls, gateways and lookout posts strengthening the plateau’s natural defences. It also records an oral tradition that the mountain grew taller at night. That story belongs to how the place was remembered and understood; it is not a measurement of a mountain changing height.

passages.title: Homes that are works of art
passages.text: Writing in 2020, artist ‘Matsooana Sekokotoana explains how Basotho women decorated homes with litema. Designs were worked into damp earth plaster, sometimes with coloured stones making a mosaic. Cow dung helped bind the mud. The wall was a surface for skilled pattern-making as well as shelter. Her account describes a practice that has become less common as building methods change.

passages.title: Homes that are works of art
passages.text: Sekokotoana also describes a ceramic plate she made using two litema designs: boliba, associated with deep water, and lihlaba, with hills or mountains. She arranged them to evoke Lesotho’s landscape. She recalls her father encouraging patience, a lesson she connected with the careful painting. Family advice and the patterns of home found another life on a plate.

passages.title: Getting dressed for the mountains
passages.text: A blanket made around 2012 and held by the British Museum combines black and turquoise with four red vertical stripes. Its feather design belongs to the Victoria England range. The catalogue identifies wool and cotton, and manufacture at Aranda’s mill in Randfontein, South Africa. An object associated with Basotho dress can also reveal production and trade across the border.

passages.title: Getting dressed for the mountains
passages.text: The museum explains that wearing blankets are wrapped around the body and secured at the shoulders, providing warmth in Lesotho’s cold mountain conditions. The familiar stripes usually run vertically when worn. A blanket can be part of getting dressed as well as going to bed. The catalogue describes a living clothing tradition with different designs, rather than one outfit worn by everyone.

passages.title: Little sculptures, everyday people
passages.text: Samuele Makoanyane, who lived from 1909 to 1944, made small clay figures of people around him. Iziko’s collection includes a woman feeding a baby and another rolling a sleeping mat. These are an artist’s representations, not photographs of every household. Their subjects put childcare and ordinary work into a museum collection alongside portraits of kings and warriors.

passages.title: Little sculptures, everyday people
passages.text: In 1935, collector Percival Kirby commissioned Makoanyane to model musicians and their instruments. Seven figures were completed, including a herdboy playing the lesiba and a woman with a drum. The exhibition lets viewers examine these fragile sculptures as digital models. Close attention to the tiny players helps preserve evidence of performance as well as the sculptor’s individual skill.

passages.title: Music at work, at home and in healing
passages.text: A lesiba combines a stick, a stretched string and a quill. Pusetso Nyabela’s 2022 museum report describes players using their breath to make the quill vibrate, rather than simply plucking a tune. Associated with shepherds, the instrument also supplied a familiar sound before Radio Lesotho’s news. Small materials can make a very distinctive voice.

passages.title: Music at work, at home and in healing
passages.text: A revival project in 2007 and 2008 found older women in Leribe who still played the lekope, with instruments hanging on their house walls. The report describes a string stretched along a reed and a player’s mouth shaping the sound. Skills that seemed to be disappearing were still present in particular homes.

passages.title: Music at work, at home and in healing
passages.text: Recordings from the late 1950s and early 1960s documented the lekope in hlophe, a ritual healing dance. Nyabela discusses music, singing, clapping and beliefs about ancestral help. These recordings preserve accounts of healing and performance; they do not test the medical effectiveness of a treatment.

passages.title: Reading, learning and remembering families
passages.text: Morija’s archives preserve Leselinyana, a newspaper first published in 1863, alongside church registers, letters, government reports and Sesotho hymnals. French, Sesotho and English all appear in the collections. Such records let researchers follow reading, music and public debate through time. A newspaper’s small notices can open questions quite different from those answered by a royal portrait.

passages.title: Reading, learning and remembering families
passages.text: The Hub at Morija opened in 2015 as a place for digital creativity. The museum describes internet access and training in photography, film, writing and information technology. It connects a town known for historical collections with new ways of making and sharing stories. Learning about the past can happen in the same community as learning to use a camera or computer.

passages.title: Reading, learning and remembering families
passages.text: David-Frédéric Ellenberger collected oral histories and genealogies from 1866 to 1905. His interview notes, letters and maps survive at Morija, and a British Library project digitised the archive. The notes offer evidence about families and remembered events, but they also reflect what a missionary asked and chose to record. Preserving a source includes understanding the viewpoint through which it was made.

passages.title: Paintings older than the kingdom
passages.text: A 2013 heritage evaluation describes Sehlabathebe’s rock paintings in shelters and overhangs: human figures, animals including eland, and colours from earthy yellow to dark red and white. These works belong to San histories that extend beyond the later story of the Basotho kingdom. Interpreting their spiritual meanings takes research; a painted animal is not automatically a literal record of a hunting trip.

British rule ended on 4 October 1966. Lesotho continues as an independent kingdom, with later changes of government forming part of its history. The map’s Basutoland and Lesotho records do not represent the extinction and replacement of three separate peoples.

sectionTitles: An emperor, religion and the state
City streets and objects people handled

passages.text: Southern Liang ruled from 502 to 557, during China’s division into rival northern and southern states. Jiankang, today’s Nanjing, was its principal political and cultural center. This is distinct from the much later Liang dynasty of the 900s. The imported outline stretches far north and south and remains unchanged throughout the period; it overstates what can be treated as secure, continuous Liang control.

passages.title: An emperor, religion and the state
passages.text: Xiao Yan began as an officer under Southern Qi, rose as a general, and founded Liang in 502. Remembered as Emperor Wu, he became a major Buddhist patron. His later autobiography presents his victory as a reluctant rescue of the people. That is a ruler explaining why he deserved power, and historians must read it as an argument as well as a record.

passages.title: An emperor, religion and the state
passages.text: A royal effort to stop monks eating meat provoked real debate. Some monastic traditions permitted certain meat received as alms, while other Buddhist texts condemned eating it. Emperor Wu favored the stricter rule. This mattered to the contents of a monastery’s cooking pot, but it does not mean every Liang family was vegetarian or that all Buddhists had always agreed about food.

passages.title: An emperor, religion and the state
passages.text: Emperor Wu recalled receiving lavish foods from distant places, then losing his appetite because his dead parents could no longer share his good fortune. He said he stopped eating fish and meat, including at banquets with officials. This personal account joins dining to filial duty: even an emperor could describe the dinner table as a place to remember his parents.

passages.title: City streets and objects people handled
passages.text: Modern construction in Nanjing has exposed streets, bridges, wells and brick drains from ancient Jiankang. Excavations around the Daxing Palace area found drains at street level and beneath roads. The remains belong to several successive Six Dynasties periods, including the Southern Dynasties. They reveal the city infrastructure Liang inherited and altered, although each uncovered drain cannot be assigned specifically to Liang.

passages.title: City streets and objects people handled
passages.text: A little stoneware tea bowl and its stand in the Metropolitan Museum have lotus decoration beneath a celadon glaze. The bowl is about 10 centimeters across. The museum assigns the set to Liang or the following Chen dynasty, so its exact date is uncertain. It gives a tangible sense of refined tableware without proving that ordinary households all drank from equally elegant cups.

passages.title: City streets and objects people handled
passages.text: One surviving Liang coin is a cast copper-alloy wuzhu piece weighing just under two grams. It has a central hole and a dot above and below it. Such modest objects belong beside palaces in a history of government: issuing money required metal, molds and skilled production. This single museum specimen tells us its material and form, rather than the price of anyone’s groceries.

passages.title: Learning, paper and family help
passages.text: Researchers examining Dunhuang manuscripts distinguish a group of paper associated with the Liang and Chen south. Made with hemp or ramie fibers, it has particularly fine screen impressions, about eight or nine lines per centimeter. The pages preserve the work of papermakers as well as scribes. A beautiful written text began with people preparing fibers and making a usable sheet.

passages.title: Learning, paper and family help
passages.text: The Liang scholar Huang Kan wrote explanations of Confucius’s Analects. A manuscript now held by Keio University was copied around the sixth century, only decades after his work was composed. Copies preserved in Japan helped the text survive after it was lost in China. Learning depended on people copying and keeping books, sometimes far from the place where a teacher first worked.

passages.title: Learning, paper and family help
passages.text: Zhou Xingsi of Liang composed the Thousand Character Classic in 250 phrases of four characters each, without repeating a character. The pattern made an enormous stock of written words into an organized text. Later calligraphers copied the text in their own handwriting. A thousand different characters is quite a writing assignment, especially when copying them neatly by hand.

passages.title: Learning, paper and family help
passages.text: Yan Zhitui remembered losing his father as a child during Liang times. An older brother and a cousin helped raise him and continue his studies. Family support could therefore mean relatives taking over both care and teaching when a parent died. His later writing records one educated family’s experience, rather than a school system available to every child.

passages.title: Medicine and a written sample
passages.text: Tao Hongjing’s pharmaceutical commentary, composed around 500 just before Liang began, remained part of this era’s learned medicine. A surviving manuscript preserves discussion of gathering, preparing and classifying medicinal substances. Later copies carried this knowledge onward. These instructions reveal historical medical thinking and the practical work of collecting ingredients; they do not establish that the remedies were effective.

passages.title: Medicine and a written sample
passages.text: “天地玄黃” can be translated literally as “Heaven is dark; earth is yellow.” These are the opening four characters of the Thousand Character Classic associated with Zhou Xingsi. The National Palace Museum records them on a much later Song-period calligraphy scroll attributed to Huang Tingjian. This is a surviving later witness to a Liang text, not Zhou’s original handwriting; the printed characters here normalize its brush forms.

passages.title: War, lost books and survival
passages.text: After Hou Jing’s rebellion was defeated in 552, Yan Zhitui worked for Emperor Yuan at Jiangling, comparing copies of books to identify the best texts. The work lasted about two years. Western Wei’s attack in late 554 destroyed much of the collection, and Yan became a captive again. War damaged the practical machinery of learning: shelves, manuscripts and the people who knew how to use them.

In 557, Chen Baxian deposed the Liang emperor and founded Chen, ruling a smaller southern territory. This ended the main Liang dynasty after years of warfare, rather than ending life or culture in southern China. Jiankang continued as a political, religious and artistic center under its new rulers.
