passages.text: This 1783 to 1800 atlas record highlights northern Maratha power around Ujjain, Gwalior and the approaches to Delhi. Its broad outline excludes Pune, Dhar and Maheshwar and cannot represent every local ruler’s authority. It is a regional view of several Maratha states and their neighbors, separate from the wider Maratha Confederacy card.

passages.title: Power, paperwork and changing borders
passages.text: Ujjain was the Scindias’ chief town during this map interval. A court needed residences, artisans and merchants as well as soldiers. The later move to a new capital at Gwalior in 1810 helps explain why the dynasty is so often associated with Gwalior today.

passages.title: Power, paperwork and changing borders
passages.text: Mahadji Scindia strengthened his armies by employing the European officer Benoit de Boigne. Training and military organization helped turn a northern Maratha ruling house into a formidable power. Mahadji’s death in 1794 brought Daulat Rao to the throne, rather than ending the state.

passages.title: Power, paperwork and changing borders
passages.text: Diplomacy generated a mountain of paper. The British Library catalogues hundreds of pages of correspondence between the Bengal government and David Anderson, its agent with Scindia, in 1782 and 1783. These surviving records let historians examine negotiation alongside the much more visible battles.

passages.title: Power, paperwork and changing borders
passages.text: A small Gwalior rupee complicates a single-color map: a 1781 example carries both a flower and a pistol mark. Numismatic research attributes it to the neighboring Rana of Gohad’s occupation, not Scindia. Tiny symbols can expose changes of government that broad outlines conceal.

passages.title: Homes, curiosity and health in 1792
passages.text: Visiting Ujjain in 1792, William Hunter described timber house frames filled with brick, under tiled or terraced roofs. On the paved main bazaar, shops occupied the lower storey and owners lived above. For some shopkeepers, the journey home was simply upstairs.

passages.title: Homes, curiosity and health in 1792
passages.text: At Barua Sagar in 1792, Jhansi’s governor Raghunath Hari showed Hunter English books, including an encyclopedia whose illustrations local artists had copied. He wanted a language teacher and received a dictionary. This was an adult ruler’s personal study, not a public school system.

passages.title: Homes, curiosity and health in 1792
passages.text: The same governor demonstrated an electrical machine made by a member of his staff. It charged a jar and startled spectators with shocks; he asked how it worked. Hunter’s account catches a small court workshop experimenting with science, not merely collecting impressive objects.

passages.title: Homes, curiosity and health in 1792
passages.text: Hunter says Raghunath Hari had visited Kanpur for medical help. At Barua Sagar he offered guests cabbages, lettuce and celery from his garden. One patient’s journey had also become a route for exchanging tastes and plants.

passages.title: Art, water and neighboring courts
passages.text: Ujjain’s Maratha-period buildings preserved a lively craft world: woodworkers carved balconies and galleries, while temple paintings brought together artistic influences from Pune, Kangra and Malwa. A decorated balcony was both part of a house and a public display of its makers’ skill.

passages.title: Art, water and neighboring courts
passages.text: Ujjain inherited an observatory established earlier by Jai Singh of Jaipur. Its Nadi Valay instrument uses a shadow to tell time, with different faces lit in different seasons. The surviving complex was restored later: scientific heritage accumulated across rulers rather than starting afresh with each dynasty.

passages.title: Art, water and neighboring courts
passages.text: Nearby Maheshwar lies outside this atlas outline, but its Holkar court belongs in the regional story. Ahilyabai took power with the Peshwa’s permission in 1767. Her patronage welcomed poets, scholars and craftspeople, and her public audiences provided a place to bring grievances.

passages.title: Art, water and neighboring courts
passages.text: Ahilyabai’s projects included wells, tanks, river steps and rest houses along pilgrimage routes. These buildings addressed practical needs as well as religious ones: travelers needed water, places to stop and access to the river. This is evidence of public provision, not of universal household plumbing.

passages.title: A mango dispute, writing and living skills
passages.text: A 1787 document from Dhar, just outside the mapped region, concerns a dispute over mango trees in Sahib Rai’s orchard. Anwar Beg and Sayyid Azam withdrew their claim before a judge and local officials. Even an orchard could leave a paper trail lasting centuries.

passages.title: A mango dispute, writing and living skills
passages.text: The Dhar writing sample is fārigh-khaṭṭī, a Persian documentary term used here for a release from a claim. This is the historian’s Roman transcription of the 1787 document, not a reconstruction of its handwritten letters. Its witnesses used both Perso-Arabic and Nagri scripts.

passages.title: A mango dispute, writing and living skills
passages.text: Dhar’s archive also preserves Hindi administrative orders under Maratha rulers, with vocabulary inherited from Persian administration. Government did not operate in only one language. Families guarding property documents could carry records across changes of dynasty, keeping old claims relevant to new officials.

passages.title: A mango dispute, writing and living skills
passages.text: Much later, in a 2020 account from Maheshwar, REHWA described teaching women to weave and running the Ahilya School for weavers’ children. A designer discussed seasonal colors and exchanging ideas with artisans over lunch. This is a modern continuation of regional textile work, not an eighteenth-century classroom.

passages.title: After the map stops
passages.text: The year 1800 is an atlas boundary, not the disappearance of the northern states. Wars followed in 1803 to 1805 and 1817 to 1818. At Mahidpur in December 1817, the East India Company’s forces defeated Indore’s army, illustrating how military defeat reshaped regional power.

Maratha states continued after this map’s 1800 endpoint. Subsequent Anglo-Maratha wars transformed their independence and relationships with the East India Company. Cities, households, crafts and records outlasted these political changes.

passages.text: The Maitrakas ruled from Valabhi in western India from roughly the fifth to the eighth century. Their kingdom supported trade, religious institutions and celebrated learning. The map’s 700 to 800 span selects its late phase; its broad western Indian polygon is an approximate outline, not proof of a fixed frontier.

passages.title: Kings, fields and connections
passages.text: A sixth-century charter remembers Bhatakka and Dharasena as generals, then Dronasimha as a maharaja, or great king. The family’s own account connected military service with growing royal rank. Its extravagant battle praise is also a reminder that rulers helped write their reputations.

passages.title: Kings, fields and connections
passages.text: Dhruvasena I’s order addressed officials, watch-station officers, soldiers and other people responsible for administration. A grant needed more than a king’s announcement: the people collecting dues and enforcing authority also had to recognize it.

passages.title: Kings, fields and connections
passages.text: That grant names village holdings and irrigation works, gives land to two Brahmins, and provides for their descendants. It invokes merit for the king’s parents. Family remembrance, religious practice and the control of productive land meet in one legal document.

passages.title: Kings, fields and connections
passages.text: Xuanzang described Valabhi as a place where rare goods arrived from distant regions and some families possessed enormous wealth. He also connected the subordinate region of Suratta with sea commerce. These are a seventh-century traveler’s impressions of prosperous commercial connections.

passages.title: Food, care, water and repairs
passages.text: A grant of 609 provided for monks’ clothing, meals, beds or seats, and medicines for sick members of the community. Care had an economic foundation: endowments were intended to keep supplies coming. The document does not identify a particular treatment or describe a public hospital.

passages.title: Food, care, water and repairs
passages.text: In 605, Shiladitya I supported the Dudda monastery with a village, three fields, two irrigation cisterns and four wells with flower gardens. The wells and gardens lay within Valabhi’s territory. Water helped sustain both productive land and the flowers used in worship.

passages.title: Food, care, water and repairs
passages.text: The 609 grant also budgeted for repairing cracked or damaged monastery buildings and supplying flowers, incense and lamp oil for worship. A religious establishment needed a maintenance plan. Even a grand sacred building could develop an unglamorous crack.

passages.title: Food, care, water and repairs
passages.text: Shiladitya I’s official religious title expressed devotion to Shiva, yet he funded Buddhist communities. His successors continued such grants. Personal worship and royal patronage could reach different religious groups, making the kingdom’s institutional life more varied than a single royal title suggests.

passages.title: Food, care, water and repairs
passages.text: Xuanzang reported an annual seven-day royal assembly at which monks received food, robes and medicine. Public giving joined royal display with practical provision. His account is a witness to court-supported religious hospitality, rather than a menu for every family in Valabhi.

passages.title: Women, teachers and workshops
passages.text: The noblewoman Dudda founded a monastery for monks. Merchants, learned monks and senior officials also established Buddhist institutions. Royal grants often maintained foundations created by somebody else: the king was not the only person who could organize a lasting institution.

passages.title: Women, teachers and workshops
passages.text: Valabhi also contained nunneries with their own economic resources. Copper plates preserve royal support for these women’s communities. Such records add organized female religious life to a historical picture that would otherwise be dominated by kings and male travelers.

passages.title: Women, teachers and workshops
passages.text: Xuanzang associated a monastery near the city with Gunamati and Sthiramati, scholars who composed widely circulated works. Valabhi’s importance rested partly on ideas that could travel beyond its walls. His description concerns advanced religious scholarship, not universal elementary schooling.

passages.title: Women, teachers and workshops
passages.text: A grooved shell-bangle fragment from Vallabhipur, catalogued as Maitraka, was carefully cut and polished. It is a small surviving piece of personal adornment. Someone valued a smooth finish even on an object far less grand than a royal monument.

passages.title: Women, teachers and workshops
passages.text: Another excavated ornament is a pale stone bead, smoothed on the outside and pierced through the centre. The tiny hole allowed it to be threaded. This modest object preserves the patient shaping and drilling that lay behind a finished piece of jewellery.

passages.title: Discoveries and words on copper
passages.text: Excavations reported in 2026 exposed burnt-brick walls at Darbargarh and mud-brick as well as fired-brick remains near Mafat Nagar. ASI officials provisionally placed recovered material within the fifth to eighth centuries. These discoveries are gradually adding actual buildings to the city known from documents.

passages.title: Discoveries and words on copper
passages.text: The same excavation season recovered gaming pieces alongside coins, seals and ornaments. Games belong in the picture of this busy settlement too. The preliminary report does not identify the rules, so we cannot yet challenge a Maitraka player to a properly reconstructed match.

passages.title: Discoveries and words on copper
passages.text: Most complete Maitraka charters consist of two copper plates, held together by rings. A seal showing a bull helped authenticate the document. These durable title deeds were designed to preserve rights: important paperwork could be distinctly heavier than a sheet of paper.

passages.title: Discoveries and words on copper
passages.text: Written Sanskrit: “स्वस्ति वलभीतः” (svasti valabhītaḥ), “Hail! From Valabhī.” This greeting opens Dhruvasena I’s Palitana plates, dated Valabhi year 206 in the sixth century. The words are shown in modern Devanagari type, not the original engraved letter shapes; this witness predates the map’s 700 start.

Maitraka grants continued into 765 or 766. Invasions in the later eighth century probably ended the dynasty, but the sequence and date of Valabhi’s destruction are uncertain. The imported 800 endpoint should not be read as an exact fall date or the disappearance of the region’s inhabitants.

passages.text: Majapahit, founded in eastern Java in 1293, was the last great Hindu-Buddhist kingdom of the archipelago. Under Hayam Wuruk and his minister Gajah Mada it claimed overlordship from Sumatra to the Moluccas and set the pattern that Indonesia's founders looked back to.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Nagarakretagama, a poem by Mpu Prapanca finished in 1365, describes the court, the royal progress and the lands that sent tribute.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Red brick temples and gateways at Trowulan, and terracotta figures and piggy banks from the capital.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Wayang shadow plays and gamelan are named in Majapahit texts and carved on its reliefs.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Javanese rice bought the cloves, nutmeg and mace of the Moluccas, which Majapahit ships carried west.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Chinese cash coins were the currency; missions went to the Ming court, and Chinese and Muslim traders lived in the ports.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Shiva and the Buddha were worshipped together; the court poem Sutasoma's line Bhinneka Tunggal Ika, unity in diversity, is Indonesia's motto.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The realm was a mandala of vassals around a divine king, held by ritual and tribute more than by garrisons.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Indonesia's founders invoked Majapahit's reach when they drew the nation's borders.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Its Hindu-Javanese culture lives on in Bali, where nobles and priests moved as Islam spread in Java.
The kingdom shrank after Hayam Wuruk's death in 1389 and a civil war; the Muslim sultanate of Demak took the last Majapahit capital around 1527.

sectionTitles: Learning, writing and keeping track of things
Buildings that changed purpose, and discoveries today

passages.text: Makkura is the map’s name for Makuria. Its capital, Dongola, grew around a fortified centre beside the Nile. Houses, churches and workshops reveal a city of builders and makers as well as rulers.

passages.title: At home, including the bathroom
passages.text: House A at Old Dongola had a bathroom with heated water and painted walls, plus a toilet upstairs. These excavated features show that some residents devoted considerable effort to comfort and sanitation. An upstairs toilet belongs in the history of medieval engineering too. This particular house does not tell us that every family enjoyed the same facilities.

passages.title: At home, including the bathroom
passages.text: A study of four Dongola house compounds, spanning the fourteenth to seventeenth centuries, examined chemical traces in floors. Comparisons with reference samples helped locate activities, especially food preparation, where few visible objects remained. A swept floor can still hold clues. The researchers found that similar-looking homes could be used in different ways as residents’ needs changed.

passages.title: At home, including the bathroom
passages.text: From the fourteenth century onward, many Dongola dwellings grouped small residential buildings around a shared courtyard. Rooms included benches and storage spaces for vessels and equipment. Archaeologists examine how shared and separate working areas shaped household relationships. A floor plan can suggest how people met and worked together, but it cannot establish every resident’s family tree.

passages.title: Learning, writing and keeping track of things
passages.text: A rubbish deposit beside Dongola’s monastery church contained pottery fragments used for writing exercises. Examples include a Coptic alphabet and archangels’ names written in an unpractised hand. Other pieces carry Greek grammar exercises. Broken pottery could serve as a writing surface. These finds show learning, although they do not reveal every pupil’s age or how many children attended lessons.

passages.title: Learning, writing and keeping track of things
passages.text: A monastery room yielded two groups of dishes bearing the names of religious leaders Lazaros and Stephanos. Each group included roughly ten pots. Writing could identify belongings as well as record prayers. These names connect ordinary tableware with particular people, though the finds do not prove whether each leader ate alone or shared meals with others.

passages.title: Learning, writing and keeping track of things
passages.text: Some Dongola inscriptions switch between Greek and Old Nubian. Other texts present psalms in both languages, sometimes alternating the language from verse to verse. This makes multilingual religious life visible on the walls. The texts preserve written choices, but they do not tell us that every resident spoke both languages fluently.

passages.title: Families, land and neighbours
passages.text: A land-sale document from Qasr Ibrim names a woman, Kapopi, selling property inherited from her mother to Neuesi, an official’s daughter, and Anenikoli. A 2019 reanalysis dates it to November 1, 1191, while noting an older discussion using 1190. This northern Nubian record preserves a woman acting in a property transaction, without proving that every woman had identical rights or wealth.

passages.title: Families, land and neighbours
passages.text: Old Nubian land sales often described a plot by naming neighbouring owners and the land upstream and downstream along the Nile. The 2019 study argues that descriptions normally proceed from south to north. Finding your field depended on relationships between people and places: the neighbours were part of the address. Some readings and exact locations remain uncertain.

passages.title: Small objects and skilled making
passages.text: A pot beneath the pavement of the church on Kom D at Dongola contained a necklace of about one hundred beads. Materials included coloured glass, faience, shell, bone and stone. Researchers interpreted it as a seventh-century foundation deposit. The necklace shows materials brought together in an unusual setting; its placement does not tell us who previously wore it, or whether anyone did.

passages.title: Small objects and skilled making
passages.text: Dongola ornaments included marine shells altered for suspension. Some cowrie shells had their upper surfaces removed or pierced; larger cone shells had their tips cut off. One pierced shell still had a leather thong. These objects connect inland adornment with marine materials and skilled preparation, while the route taken by each shell remains unknown.

passages.title: Buildings that changed purpose, and discoveries today
passages.text: Dongola’s Mosque Building preserves an Arabic foundation inscription dated 1317. Architectural study shows the earlier monumental hall being adapted for worship, including a prayer niche and new plaster over painted walls. Its earlier role as a royal audience hall is an interpretation of its plan and decoration. One building’s conversion did not mean that every resident changed religion that year.

passages.title: Buildings that changed purpose, and discoveries today
passages.text: In a discovery announced in 2023, archaeologists investigating a later house found an opening into a small painted chamber below its floor. One scene shows a Nubian ruler with Christ and Archangel Michael. Preliminary reading of a difficult inscription mentions a King David and protection for a city. The identification and historical occasion were still being investigated: a dramatic painting is not a photograph of a known event.

Makuria fragmented during the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. The court left Dongola in the 1360s, but the city continued under a smaller kingdom and later within the Funj sphere. Changes of government and religion unfolded over time. The map’s 1492 endpoint does not establish a single conquest or the disappearance of Nubian communities.

passages.text: Malacca, founded about 1400 by Parameswara, a prince from Palembang, became within a century the greatest port of Asia, where the monsoons met. Its sultans made Islam and Malay the faith and language of the archipelago's trade.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Ships from China, Gujarat, Bengal, Arabia, Java and the Spice Islands met at Malacca to exchange cloth, spices, tin, gold and porcelain.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Tomé Pires, writing just after the conquest, counted 84 languages spoken in the city and wrote that whoever was lord of Malacca had his hand on the throat of Venice.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Zheng He's fleets called at Malacca from 1405, and the sultanate sent missions to the Ming court.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The ruler adopted Islam around 1414, taking the name Iskandar Shah; Malacca became a center from which Islam spread to Java and the islands.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Undang-Undang Melaka, the laws of Malacca, and the Malay Annals were written in Malay in the Arabic script.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Malay spread as the lingua franca of maritime Southeast Asia and became Malaysian and Indonesian.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Malacca's laws and court customs set the model for the Malay sultanates.
Afonso de Albuquerque took the city in August 1511 after a month's fighting; the sultan fled and his heirs founded Johor.

sectionTitles: A cooking pot with its own feet
A game with room for the pieces
Family gatherings with words worth practising
Many family histories, more than one kind of evidence

passages.text: Malagasy history brings together varied communities and long-distance connections. Research into ancestry finds both African and Asian contributions, with regional differences. No single family custom, craft or royal dynasty represents everybody on the island.

passages.title: A cooking pot with its own feet
passages.text: Northern Madagascar’s stone-vessel industry flourished during the centuries around 800 to 1500. Tripod pots from Vohémar have three feet that could hold the bowl over a fire. Soot and burnt residues show heating, while finds in settlements support everyday use alongside burial uses. The residues have not established exactly what every pot contained.

passages.title: A cooking pot with its own feet
passages.text: Broken stone pots were sometimes repaired instead of discarded. At Vohémar, two surviving examples were held together with iron bands and mortar. Other fragments have drilled holes for joining pieces with metal clamps. Repairs show the value placed on keeping a vessel useful. A cracked pot could get another chance, though a repaired pot was not necessarily watertight.

passages.title: Books made from local materials
passages.text: The Bibliothèque nationale de France describes manuscripts from southeastern Madagascar written in Arabic characters to record Malagasy. Several are on locally made Antaimoro paper. Writing systems can travel and be adapted to a different language: using Arabic letters does not mean that the words on every page are Arabic. These manuscripts preserve a regional tradition of keeping knowledge in writing.

passages.title: Books made from local materials
passages.text: One volume, catalogued as Malayo-polynésien 285, combines Antaimoro paper with a binding of zebu hide. The record identifies both the writing surface and the cover. A book is also a made object, requiring materials and practical skills as well as words. This particular binding does not tell us how every Malagasy book was produced.

passages.title: Wooden houses and family patterns
passages.text: Zafimaniry builders in Madagascar’s southeastern highlands use wooden joints in which a shaped end fits into a matching opening. UNESCO describes houses and tombs assembled without metal nails or hinges. Different tree species suit different jobs. Good building depends on knowing the material as well as making the pieces fit; this tradition has a great deal of knowledge tucked into its joints.

passages.title: Wooden houses and family patterns
passages.text: Carving appears on Zafimaniry walls, window frames, stools, chests and tools. Some patterns have named meanings: UNESCO describes a spider’s-web motif associated with family ties and a honeycomb with community life. The decoration can therefore carry ideas about relationships as well as display skill. These meanings belong to this tradition, rather than being a dictionary for every pattern across Madagascar.

passages.title: A game with room for the pieces
passages.text: A fanorona board in Islington’s educational handling collection is made from light wood, with black lines and little side drawers for the playing pieces. Two players move along the board’s lines and try to capture their opponent’s pieces. This collected example uses plastic pieces, so it illustrates a continuing game rather than an ancient excavated set. Even a strategy game benefits from somewhere to put everything away.

passages.title: A game with room for the pieces
passages.text: The same collection tells a story about Prince Andriantompokoindrindra, who was so absorbed in fanorona that he failed to return to his father and lost the chance to become king. It is presented here as a traditional story, not a verified explanation of a royal succession. It certainly gives the familiar request to stop playing a game unusually high stakes.

passages.title: Family gatherings with words worth practising
passages.text: Kabary is an art of public speaking using proverbs, carefully arranged phrases and wordplay. It commonly involves two speakers addressing a gathering, and some performances last hours. Skill lies in choosing and arranging words for the occasion. A speech can be something people come together to enjoy, rather than merely an announcement before the interesting part.

passages.title: Family gatherings with words worth practising
passages.text: Kabary also belongs at family gatherings where several generations take part. UNESCO describes growing participation by women and younger people in an art formerly associated especially with older elite men. A tradition can continue while the people who perform it change. Listening, joining in and learning how to speak are part of its social life.

passages.title: Many family histories, more than one kind of evidence
passages.text: A 2017 genetic study sampled 2,704 people in 257 Malagasy villages. Its results supported ancestry connected with both eastern Africa and Southeast Asia, with differences across the island. Such research can help investigate population history, but it does not identify the family who owned an excavated pot or decide somebody’s cultural identity. Archaeology, languages and community histories ask related questions using different evidence.

Malagasy peoples continue today, with local traditions, shared connections and changing ways of life. Living practices such as kabary show participation across generations. The map’s endpoint in 1000 is not an extinction date, nor the end of Malagasy culture.

sectionTitles: Paintings are evidence, not a code we can simply crack
Dinner takes more knowledge than a recipe
The dance with kitchen utensils in the pack
A university begins in a former school
Pupils who asked for better toilets

passages.text: Malawi’s regional history includes rock paintings, shared meals and skills learned through practice. Evidence comes from archaeological sites and from living communities whose traditions differ across the country.

passages.title: Paintings are evidence, not a code we can simply crack
passages.text: At Chongoni, red rock paintings include circles, radiating lines and other geometric patterns made with red oxide pigment. Researchers associate this earlier tradition with hunter-gatherers. Suggested links with rainmaking are interpretations, rather than translations of a known written code. A circle on a rock does not come with its original caption.

passages.title: Paintings are evidence, not a code we can simply crack
passages.text: Later Chongoni paintings used white clay for animal-like and other figures. Many are linked with Chewa women’s ceremonies, and painting continued into the twentieth century. Excavations also recovered hunted-animal bones around two thousand years old. Researchers warn that these finds are difficult to connect with particular paintings: dating a meal’s remains does not automatically date the art nearby.

passages.title: Dinner takes more knowledge than a recipe
passages.text: Nsima is a thick porridge made with maize flour, and its name also refers to a wider culinary tradition. UNESCO’s account follows the work from growing and storing maize through pounding, preparing accompaniments and serving. The finished bowl is only the last stage of a much longer chain of skills.

passages.title: Dinner takes more knowledge than a recipe
passages.text: Sharing nsima provides an occasion for families to spend time together. Children learn food skills from adults through practice, while recipes, schoolbooks and festivals offer other ways to pass on the tradition. Learning dinner can involve both a book and watching someone who already knows what to do.

passages.title: The dance with kitchen utensils in the pack
passages.text: In Tchopa, a Lhomwe performance from southern Malawi, dancers move in a circle and cross one another’s paths to drums of three sizes. Some carry packs containing farming tools, animal skins, puppets or old kitchen utensils. The equipment links performance with work and everyday objects. Getting ready for this dance can involve more than finding your shoes.

passages.title: The dance with kitchen utensils in the pack
passages.text: Tchopa knowledge passes through rehearsals and performances, with children increasingly joining older practitioners. The group also has roles for costume makers, drum makers and musicians. UNESCO describes members helping one another during bereavement or illness and sharing farm labour when someone is overburdened. The relationships continue after the dancing stops.

passages.title: Care as a community gathering
passages.text: Vimbuza is a healing tradition associated with Tumbuka communities in northern Malawi. UNESCO describes people staying in a healer’s village house, with singing, drumming and dance forming part of their care. Women and children gather around the person receiving the ritual. This account records cultural understandings of illness and spiritual help, and shows care involving a wider community. It does not establish that the ritual cures an illness.

passages.title: A university begins in a former school
passages.text: The University of Malawi began teaching on 29 September 1965 with ninety students in Blantyre, using a former secondary-school campus. Its institutional establishment had come in 1964. The small first intake helps make a large institution’s beginning easier to picture: a university can start with a group of learners before it develops several campuses and colleges.

passages.title: A university begins in a former school
passages.text: The university’s history records Kamuzu College of Nursing joining as a constituent college in September 1979, followed by a College of Medicine in Blantyre in 1991. These institutions made training nurses and doctors part of the university’s work. The dates describe that institutional history, rather than when Malawians first practised healing or cared for sick relatives.

passages.title: Pupils who asked for better toilets
passages.text: A 2024 UNICEF report describes the water, sanitation and hygiene club at Mbande Primary School in Karonga. Its student chairperson, Gladson Kaunda, said members met on Mondays and pressed the school committee for more toilets and spaces for adolescent girls. They received supplies including buckets and soap. Pupils were helping shape their school environment as well as learning in it.

passages.title: Pupils who asked for better toilets
passages.text: At Mkazomba Primary School in Lilongwe, a 2024 UNICEF report describes a solar-powered water system with storage tanks, taps and handwashing facilities. Pupils had previously walked to a village well to fetch water. Water nearer their classrooms also helped with cleaning toilets, and local community members received maintenance training. Keeping a school running involves pipes and practical skills as well as lessons.

British rule ended when Nyasaland became independent Malawi on 6 July 1964. The country became a republic in 1966 and continued through the change from Banda’s rule to multiparty government in 1994. The map’s earlier start date does not make Malawi independent in 1920, and changes of government did not end its communities.

sectionTitles: First, decode a very strange map label
Tin, rubber, rails and the people who made them move
Homes, families, clothes, food and time together
North Borneo was its own world, not an extra peninsula
Classrooms, newspapers and a real Malay phrase
Medicine, mosquitoes, water and the toilet evidence
What changed, what endured, and what 1920 did not end

passages.text: The atlas's “Malaya” record is an umbrella for a connected region, not one country that ruled unchanged from 1650 to 1920. Its fixed two-part polygon covers much of the western Malay Peninsula and a slice of North Borneo, excludes Singapore and much of the peninsula's east coast, and quietly joins territories that never shared one government. The real story moves from Johor-Riau maritime power and Malayo-Bugis rule through Dutch and British treaty-making, distinct Malay sultanates, Straits Settlements, protected and federated states, and the separately chartered British North Borneo Company. Trade in tin and rubber linked ports, mines, plantations, farms, railways and migrant workers while concentrating wealth and danger unevenly. Families lived in kampongs, towns, estates, longhouses and port neighborhoods; children might study, help at home or sell food; medicine ranged from community midwives to new laboratories; toilets ranged from detached rural structures to urban cesspits and night-soil buckets. Malay, Jawi, Chinese, Tamil, English and Indigenous languages shared this world. The 1920 endpoint is only an atlas handoff: independent Malaya came in 1957 and Malaysia in 1963.

passages.title: First, decode a very strange map label
passages.text: The exact atlas record is “malaya,” approximately 1650-1920, with ten continuous map intervals. “Malaya” is useful as a regional label here, but it was not one state lasting 270 years. Johor-Riau, Malay sultanates, Dutch and British colonies, protected states and company-ruled North Borneo all had different governments.

passages.title: First, decode a very strange map label
passages.text: Every one of the ten imported intervals repeats the same two-part outline. The western part contains tested Malacca, Johor Bahru, Kuala Lumpur and Penang points, yet excludes Kota Bharu, Kuala Terengganu and Singapore. A static shape cannot record the period's wars, treaties or changing administrations.

passages.title: First, decode a very strange map label
passages.text: The eastern piece contains the tested Kota Kinabalu point but excludes Kuching and Bandar Seri Begawan. It therefore pulls part of North Borneo into “Malaya” even though British North Borneo had its own chartered-company government and Indigenous societies. The two colored pieces never formed one 1650-1920 polity.

passages.title: First, decode a very strange map label
passages.text: Singapore is outside the polygon, but its port, treaties, schools, newspapers, hospitals, rail links and markets were deeply entangled with the peninsula. Singapore examples appear only when they illuminate that connected Straits world, and each one is labeled so children do not mistake an island case for everybody's life.

passages.title: First, decode a very strange map label
passages.text: At 1920 the database changes this footprint to a card called “Malaysia.” History did not. The Federation of Malaya became independent in 1957, and Malaysia formed in 1963 with Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore. The atlas is about forty-three years early, which is impressively early even for a map with a time machine.

passages.title: Courts, companies and colonial bargains
passages.text: Johor helped the Dutch East India Company dislodge the Portuguese from Melaka in 1641 and received special trade and political privileges. In the later seventeenth century its rulers, officials, Orang Laut allies and merchants shaped traffic through the straits. Dutch partnership did not make Johor a Dutch colony.

passages.title: Courts, companies and colonial bargains
passages.text: When Sultan Mahmud II was killed in 1699 without a direct heir, rival claims shook the kingdom. Bugis leaders later helped the Bendahara dynasty and held the office of Yang Dipertuan Muda, or viceroy. Malay royal legitimacy and Bugis military-commercial power worked together, sometimes uneasily.

passages.title: Courts, companies and colonial bargains
passages.text: Riau became a prosperous eighteenth-century port until war with the Dutch ended in defeat in 1784. Johor's political center had moved among rivers, islands and courts, so a modern peninsula-only mental picture misses the maritime realm. Boats, sea lanes and island communities were part of how authority worked.

passages.title: Courts, companies and colonial bargains
passages.text: After Sultan Mahmud III died, rival heirs gained Dutch and British backing. Britain recognized Hussein in exchange for the 1819 Singapore arrangement; the 1824 Anglo-Dutch treaty then partitioned an older connected realm into European spheres. A treaty line changed states, but it did not stop relatives, traders or languages at sea.

passages.title: Courts, companies and colonial bargains
passages.text: From the 1870s, British treaties installed advisers in Malay states while rulers retained formal authority, especially over Islam and custom. The four Federated Malay States joined administratively in 1896, but five other states remained outside it, and all nine were constitutionally distinct from Penang and Melaka. “British Malaya” was a patchwork, not one ordinary colony.

passages.title: Tin, rubber, rails and the people who made them move
passages.text: Melaka and George Town grew through centuries of exchange among the Malay Archipelago, China, India, the Middle East and Europe. Warehouses, religious buildings, shophouses, townhouses, foods and languages accumulated rather than arriving in one tidy “multicultural” package. Trade created opportunity, hierarchy and conflict together.

passages.title: Tin, rubber, rails and the people who made them move
passages.text: Near 1900, Malaya produced close to half the world's rubber and more than thirty percent of its tin. Those striking shares came from mines, plantations, ports, credit and labor, not from rubber trees politely shipping themselves. Profits and hardships were distributed very unevenly.

passages.title: Tin, rubber, rails and the people who made them move
passages.text: Colonial employers recruited large numbers of Chinese and Indian workers for tin and rubber. Indentured labor survived until 1914, with immigration law making workers easier to discipline and deport. Malay farming households supplied food, while colonial writing often treated domestic and subsistence work as idleness instead of labor.

passages.title: Tin, rubber, rails and the people who made them move
passages.text: Railways first linked Taiping to Port Weld in 1885 and Kuala Lumpur to Klang in 1886. By 1909 public transport could carry a traveler between Penang and Singapore through trains and a ferry. Tamil workers operated and maintained sections of line, and Hindu shrines marked some work communities along the route.

passages.title: Tin, rubber, rails and the people who made them move
passages.text: Causeway construction began in 1919 after train-ferries struggled with growing traffic. Its April 1920 foundation ceremony sits exactly at this card's endpoint, but the road-and-rail link opened later, in 1923-24. Even heroic engineering projects have construction schedules, budget arguments and a stubborn refusal to finish on the map's preferred date.

passages.title: Homes, families, clothes, food and time together
passages.text: Traditional Malay houses varied by coast, river, wealth and region. A modern museum architectural account describes raised timber structures that encouraged airflow and reduced flood risk, with a main room for family meals, rest and guests, a sleeping section and a linked kitchen. Modular additions could grow with a household.

passages.title: Homes, families, clothes, food and time together
passages.text: The same account places bathroom and latrine structures away from the main dwelling. That arrangement made sense in a hot, wet environment without household sewer pipes, but it is a tradition-level description, not proof that every village used one plan. Homes built of organic materials also survive poorly, making ordinary architecture harder to count.

passages.title: Homes, families, clothes, food and time together
passages.text: A late nineteenth- to early twentieth-century Terengganu sarong combines tied-and-dyed weft threads with gold songket weaving. Its decorated front panel was described for women. One beautiful museum object shows skill, trade and taste; it cannot outfit every Malay, Chinese, Indian or Indigenous person in the atlas shape.

passages.title: Homes, families, clothes, food and time together
passages.text: In connected Singapore streets, hawkers sold satay, noodles, vadai, roasted nuts, fruit, cloth and household goods. Some children sold cakes or banana fritters to help family income, while ice-ball sellers became favorites near schools. This is lively city evidence, not a peninsula-wide lunch menu, and child work was necessity rather than a cute game.

passages.title: Homes, families, clothes, food and time together
passages.text: Malay village pastimes included carved spinning tops, boat races and kite flying; coastal foodways drew on fish, sago and rice according to ecology and means. A Lingga historian documents these as living traditions with older roots, so the safest claim is continuity and adaptation, not that every child in 1700 followed today's tournament rules.

passages.title: North Borneo was its own world, not an extra peninsula
passages.text: The British North Borneo Company received a royal charter in 1881 and claimed governmental powers over territory now in Sabah. A British charter explains the company's legal machinery; it does not prove that dozens of Indigenous communities surrendered authority, understood the document alike or experienced company rule in the same way.

passages.title: North Borneo was its own world, not an extra peninsula
passages.text: Sabah's official overview names Kadazan-Dusun, Murut, Bajau and many other communities. It connects livelihoods with wet and upland rice, fishing, hunting, diving, horses, rivers and communal longhouses. These broad traditions varied by place and changed over time, so they are starting points, not character costumes.

passages.title: North Borneo was its own world, not an extra peninsula
passages.text: A company settlement at Gaya Bay stood near an existing Bajau community. Mat Salleh's followers destroyed it in 1897, after which the company shifted to mainland Api-Api, later Jesselton, and developed a port and railway stop. Calling this simply “city founding” would hide both prior residents and armed resistance.

passages.title: North Borneo was its own world, not an extra peninsula
passages.text: The company government opened a press at Kudat in 1883 for the North Borneo Herald and Official Gazette, moved it to Sandakan in 1885 and to Jesselton in 1918. Printing helped an administration issue information and rules; the existence of a press does not tell us how many children could read its language or afford its pages.

passages.title: North Borneo was its own world, not an extra peninsula
passages.text: A woman's rattan-and-brass girdle collected in Sabah and dated broadly to the 1850s-1910 was once catalogued as Murut, then corrected to Dusun after Sabah Museum advice. The correction is a useful museum lesson: labels can improve when curators listen to local expertise, and a brass belt deserves better than being filed under “close enough.”

passages.title: Classrooms, newspapers and a real Malay phrase
passages.text: School access was sharply unequal. In the Straits Settlements in 1901, about 22 percent of Malay boys aged fifteen and under attended Malay vernacular boys' schools, compared with no more than 2 percent of Malay girls in girls' schools. These figures cover Singapore, Penang and Melaka, not every state or community.

passages.title: Classrooms, newspapers and a real Malay phrase
passages.text: The Government Malay Press began in 1885, and Singapore printers supplied schoolbooks to the Straits Settlements, Malay states, Johor, Muar, Borneo and Sarawak. Newspapers sometimes filled the shortage of readers. A printed textbook could travel farther than a pupil who still had work, fees or distance blocking the classroom door.

passages.title: Classrooms, newspapers and a real Malay phrase
passages.text: Jawi Peranakkan ran from 1876 to 1895 in Malay written with Jawi, an Arabic-derived script. It carried news, advertisements, government notices, poetry and discussion of health and schooling. Circulation was limited and centered on literate urban readers, so a surviving newspaper is evidence of a public conversation, not universal literacy.

passages.title: Classrooms, newspapers and a real Malay phrase
passages.text: Written-language sample: “Bahawa ini surat,” meaning “This is a letter.” It opens an 1857 Malay diplomatic letter from Johor's Temenggung Ibrahim to Napoleon III. The original was written in Jawi; the words shown here are the British Library catalogue's Latin transliteration because its digital manuscript image is unavailable, not a pretend facsimile.

passages.title: Classrooms, newspapers and a real Malay phrase
passages.text: The full letter paired elaborate respect with gifts of a keris and cloth and was written on European laid paper in gold ink. It shows Malay courtly composition, Jawi literacy and global diplomacy meeting on one folio. It tells us about an elite chancery, not how a market vendor wrote a shopping list.

passages.title: Medicine, mosquitoes, water and the toilet evidence
passages.text: Care began long before modern hospitals. In Singapore, Malay bidan learned birth knowledge from experienced women and usually attended home births. Colonial hospitals initially served soldiers and officials far better than Indigenous and migrant residents; trained nursing expanded slowly after nuns entered the General Hospital in 1885.

passages.title: Medicine, mosquitoes, water and the toilet evidence
passages.text: By 1910 Singapore offered a course for Asian midwives, and infant-health nurses made home visits from 1911; a 1915 ordinance required midwife registration in the Straits Settlements. These programs could provide knowledge and referral, while also imposing colonial definitions of certification on older community practice.

passages.title: Medicine, mosquitoes, water and the toilet evidence
passages.text: Kuala Lumpur's Institute for Medical Research opened in 1901 to investigate malaria, beri-beri, dysentery and other diseases. Researchers studied mosquitoes and later linked beri-beri with nutrient loss from heavily milled rice. Medical research was a major institutional achievement, but laboratories did not make treatment equally reachable.

passages.title: Medicine, mosquitoes, water and the toilet evidence
passages.text: At Klang, Malcolm Watson used drainage and other environmental changes against malaria from 1900. Cases fell sharply in particular projects, and port work could resume. The result depended on mosquito ecology and organized labor; it was not a universal cure, and colonial programs often protected commercially valuable places first.

passages.title: Medicine, mosquitoes, water and the toilet evidence
passages.text: Toilets differed drastically. A vernacular-house account places latrines away from the main room. In Singapore in 1889, many toilets emptied into earth or cesspits, while paid workers carried bucketed “night soil”; cholera pushed water, drainage and public-latrine reforms. Neither example proves a regional sewer system. The honest answer is many arrangements, unequal service and plenty still unknown.

passages.title: What changed, what endured, and what 1920 did not end
passages.text: The era produced striking achievements without belonging to one government: multilingual ports, court diplomacy, ship and river networks, timber architecture, weaving, newspapers, schools, tropical-disease research and rail engineering. Each rested on named communities and workers, so “Malaya achieved” is shorthand that should never erase who did the work.

passages.title: What changed, what endured, and what 1920 did not end
passages.text: Colonial growth also brought coercion and unequal risk. Indentured labor, racialized job systems, dangerous mines and plantations, limited schooling for girls, uneven hospitals and sanitation all sat beside export statistics. A chart that says “rubber boom” cannot show the tired hands tapping trees before breakfast.

passages.title: What changed, what endured, and what 1920 did not end
passages.text: Johor-Riau's political unity broke in 1824, yet Malay court traditions, family links, maritime travel, religion, poetry and trade crossed the new boundary. In North Borneo, Indigenous communities remained while company offices and rail stops expanded around them. State change and cultural continuity happened at the same time.

passages.title: What changed, what endured, and what 1920 did not end
passages.text: Nothing historically collapsed in 1920 to justify removing the malaya id. Construction crews were still building the Causeway, sultans and colonial governments still operated, North Borneo remained company-ruled, and families kept working and learning. Only the atlas label changes, prematurely, to “Malaysia.”

passages.title: What changed, what endured, and what 1920 did not end
passages.text: Later milestones belong after this card: independent Malaya in 1957 and Malaysia in 1963. Those states inherited connected economies and institutions but were not simply the 1650 shape waking up with a flag. People, languages and memories continued across every administrative rename.

No single Malayan state ended in 1920, because no single state matched this card in the first place. The database merely changes its label to “Malaysia,” while Malay sultanates, British colonial administrations, the Federated and Unfederated Malay States, the Straits Settlements and British North Borneo continued under distinct arrangements. The Federation of Malaya became independent in 1957; Malaysia formed in 1963. Political names and borders changed, while families, communities, languages, trade routes, craft, faith and social ties continued and adapted.

Breakfast, gold thread and four-line diplomacy
Writing, classrooms and healthcare on wheels
Water, toilets and dignity in ordinary life

passages.text: This card follows the territories that became modern Malaysia, but the atlas starts in 1920, thirty-seven years before independent Malaya and forty-three years before Malaysia formed. Its repeated outline gives an approximately present-day peninsula-and-Borneo shape to earlier colonial periods, has no Malaysia feature for 1938 to 1945, excludes Singapore even for 1963 to 1965, and leaves Kuching outside its simplified Sarawak edge. Brunei has a separate record. Treat this as display coverage, not a legal or historical border survey. Earlier Malays, the Malacca Sultanate and the broad imported ‘Malaysian Islamic states’ record have separate cards.

passages.title: From colonies to a federation
passages.text: The atlas label ‘Malaysia’ in 1920 is a shortcut, not an early founding date. The imported shape combines the Malay Peninsula with Sabah and Sarawak long before those territories joined one federation. It also repeats modern exclusions backward: Singapore is outside every Malaysia outline, including the years when it was actually a member. The 1938-1945 polygon gap is a data gap, not evidence that the people or territories disappeared.

passages.title: From colonies to a federation
passages.text: Japanese troops advanced into Malaya in December 1941 and occupied it until 1945. British military administration returned after the war, followed by the Malayan Union in April 1946. Opposition to that scheme helped reshape postwar politics. In June 1948, the colonial government declared an Emergency amid communist armed revolt. These events belong to colonial Malaya and Borneo's wartime experience, not to a sovereign Malaysian government that did not yet exist.

passages.title: From colonies to a federation
passages.text: The Federation of Malaya declared independence on 31 August 1957. Its Constitution established parliamentary government and a constitutional monarch selected from the Malay rulers. The first bicameral Parliament, consisting of the King, Senate and elected House of Representatives, opened in 1959. Independence created a new sovereign state, but it still did not include Sabah, Sarawak or Singapore.

passages.title: From colonies to a federation
passages.text: Malaysia was declared on 16 September 1963 after agreements involving Malaya, Britain, Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore. Brunei did not join. The federation therefore linked territories across the South China Sea rather than simply renaming Malaya. The atlas's uninterrupted modern-looking shape hides both the negotiations that created this arrangement and the different political histories of Sabah and Sarawak.

passages.title: From colonies to a federation
passages.text: Singapore's membership lasted less than two years. The separation agreement was signed in Kuala Lumpur on 7 August 1965 and entered into force on 9 August, making Singapore an independent and sovereign state. Malaysia continued without it. A changing membership is not the same as the end of the federation, which is why this card continues after 1965.

passages.title: From colonies to a federation
passages.text: The official planning record describes the 1969 racial violence as a crisis that prompted the Rukun Negara principles and the New Economic Policy. The policy sought national unity, poverty reduction and economic restructuring. Those were government goals, not a magic switch that made unequal lives equal. Later debate over distribution and opportunity is part of the history too, so policy aims should be distinguished from measured results.

passages.title: Factories, finance and a very old cave archive
passages.text: Since independence, Malaysia shifted from an economy dominated by agriculture and commodities toward manufacturing and services. Electrical parts and appliances became major exports, while life expectancy and education rose. The same World Bank overview warns that inequality, weak reading outcomes and shortages of high-skill jobs remain. Economic success can be real without landing evenly in every household.

passages.title: Factories, finance and a very old cave archive
passages.text: Malaysia's electrical and electronics industry began with eight component manufacturers operating in the 1970s and grew into a network making semiconductor devices and consumer and industrial electronics. Local companies work beside multinational firms, so the achievement is an industrial ecosystem rather than one lone inventor. A chip packaged or tested in Malaysia may end up inside an object used thousands of kilometres away.

passages.title: Factories, finance and a very old cave archive
passages.text: Malaysia also helped develop sustainable Islamic finance. In 2017, a RM250 million issuance became the world's first green sukuk, a bond-like instrument designed to finance environmentally beneficial work while following Islamic-finance rules. By 2023, the World Bank counted more than forty Malaysian green sukuk issues. ‘Green’ describes what the financing supports; the certificates are not printed on spinach.

passages.title: Factories, finance and a very old cave archive
passages.text: Niah National Park's caves in Sarawak preserve at least 50,000 years of human interaction with rainforest environments. Archaeologists study deep deposits, prehistoric rock paintings and boat-shaped burials. Local communities still follow molong, ‘take only what you need’, when gathering guano and edible birds' nests. This ancient record long predates Malaysia, while protecting and studying it is part of life in the modern country. One cave can be archive, workplace and ecosystem at once.

passages.title: Factories, finance and a very old cave archive
passages.text: The Thirteenth Malaysia Plan covers 2026 to 2030. It proposes reform of the local semiconductor industry, stronger research and innovation, education and health reform, better regional balance, and environmental protection. These headings reveal current priorities, not achievements already completed. A five-year plan is a national to-do list with a budget and bureaucracy attached; historians must return later to ask what actually happened.

passages.title: Breakfast, gold thread and four-line diplomacy
passages.text: UNESCO describes Malaysian breakfast culture as time spent together over foods such as nasi lemak and roti canai and the drink teh tarik. Homes, markets and eateries bring together cooks and diners from Malay, Chinese, Indian and other communities. Skills pass through families and teaching. The hardest morning quiz may be rice, flatbread or both, but the larger habit is sharing affordable food and conversation.

passages.title: Breakfast, gold thread and four-line diplomacy
passages.text: Songket weavers insert extra gold or silver threads so patterns seem to float over a coloured cloth. Expert women work at a two-pedal loom called a kek, sometimes for months; men also contribute by making weaving equipment. Once limited to royalty, songket now appears at weddings, births, festivals and state ceremonies. Months of work make it a spectacularly poor choice for homework started the night before.

passages.title: Breakfast, gold thread and four-line diplomacy
passages.text: A pantun commonly has four lines with an a-b-a-b rhyme pattern. Verses can speak about romantic love, family, community or nature and appear at weddings, ceremonies, schools and workshops. Because a pantun can approach a difficult idea indirectly and politely, it has even served in diplomacy and conflict resolution. Children can try the form themselves: four lines, alternating rhymes, and preferably no diplomatic incident before lunch.

passages.title: Writing, classrooms and healthcare on wheels
passages.text: Article 152 begins, ‘Bahasa kebangsaan ialah bahasa Melayu’, meaning ‘The national language shall be the Malay language’. This official Malay sample uses the Roman alphabet and reads left to right. The same constitutional passage says people may use, teach and learn other languages outside official purposes. A national language rule therefore does not mean that Malaysia has only one spoken or written language.

passages.title: Writing, classrooms and healthcare on wheels
passages.text: On an island near Sandakan, Sabah, stateless children studied in a wooden school on stilts after families sought a teacher and the community helped create a learning centre. Other centres taught reading, counting, music and practical skills. One teacher celebrated when pupils could finally text friends instead of sending voice notes. Mothers also taught sewing, helping teenagers make bags and shirts. These centres fill a gap but do not grant the recognized schooling every child deserves.

passages.title: Writing, classrooms and healthcare on wheels
passages.text: Education access differs sharply. UNICEF identifies missing birth documents, disability exclusion, distance, cost and language as barriers. Some Orang Asli and other Indigenous children live far from schools or meet a national classroom in an unfamiliar language. Work with local groups has supported mother-tongue education and alternative learning. Enrollment figures alone cannot tell whether a child can reach class, understand the lesson or feel included.

passages.title: Writing, classrooms and healthcare on wheels
passages.text: Malaysia's rural maternal and child health network expanded under a three-tier system from 1956. Midwife clinics linked families to small and large health centres for referral, while outpatient and dental care were added. Later reforms integrated school health, family planning, nutrition and primary care; mobile bus and boat clinics joined the system in 2010. Medicine here was also an organizational invention: bringing care closer before an emergency began.

passages.title: Writing, classrooms and healthcare on wheels
passages.text: Distance still matters. In March 2023, a Sabah Health Department-led convoy brought doctors, nurses and dentists by four-wheel-drive vehicles to three Kemabong villages. Some residents otherwise faced more than five hours of walking to the nearest clinic. Children received medical and dental checks, while staff joined plant games and exercise to know the community. Nearby teenagers climbed about 100 metres up a hill for phone service, a very steep password to the internet.

passages.title: Water, toilets and dignity in ordinary life
passages.text: A 2021 UNICEF and university report used dated estimates showing 93% of Malaysia's population with safely managed drinking water and 87% with safely managed sanitation in 2017, while 88% of household wastewater was safely treated in 2020. Those high national figures can hide people in informal settlements, undocumented families and some Indigenous communities who were missing from statistics or still lacked reliable service. A toilet average cannot flush away an inequality.

passages.title: Water, toilets and dignity in ordinary life
passages.text: A children's activity centre in Kota Kinabalu opened to citizen and non-citizen children aged seven to fifteen. It paired reading, writing and counting lessons with food, showers, play and rest, and included ramps and accessible toilets for children with disabilities. A ramp that ends at an unusable bathroom would be a cruel joke; including both shows why sanitation and accessibility belong in the same plan as education.

passages.title: Water, toilets and dignity in ordinary life
passages.text: Floods can turn normal water and toilet systems into emergencies. In Rantau Panjang, a mother described evacuating with her children to a school shelter that had no water or electricity. Crowding and dirty floodwater increase sanitation and disease risks. Her son learned to move schoolbooks to a high shelf before the water rose. That practical family routine is climate adaptation at child height: save people first, then keep tomorrow's lessons dry.

Malaysia continues as a federal constitutional monarchy and parliamentary state; this atlas record has no historical end date, and its 2100 display horizon is not a prediction. Singapore's 1965 separation changed the federation without ending it. The official 2026-2030 plan sets future goals for education, health, higher-value industry, regional balance and environmental care, but goals remain to be tested against results. Families, languages and cultural practices also continue to change within the living country.

sectionTitles: Water, food and a line of writing

passages.text: This atlas label is an umbrella for parts of the Southeast Asian archipelago between 1492 and 1650, not modern Malaysia or a single Islamic empire. Its very broad outlines include Demak in Java and Gowa in Sulawesi, reach Timor and initially extend into New Guinea. They exclude several famous capitals, including Malacca, Johor Lama, Brunei, Banda Aceh and Banten. Neither common government nor uniform religious affiliation can be read from that shape. The examples below focus on Java and Sulawesi, with neighboring comparisons identified separately; named sultanates retain their own histories.

passages.title: Different courts and busy ports
passages.text: Demak’s Great Mosque has a three-tiered roof, four principal support posts and an open veranda. Its architecture gave Muslim worship a recognizably Javanese setting. Local accounts connect the building with Raden Fatah and the Wali Songo religious teachers, and interpret a turtle emblem as the year 1479. Those foundation traditions should be distinguished from dates of later repairs and surviving timber.

passages.title: Different courts and busy ports
passages.text: In 1975, archaeologists surveyed Tridonorejo, Moro Demak and Wonosalam. They found roof tiles, bowls, water vessels called kendi, beads and pieces of Chinese and Vietnamese ceramics dated to the fourteenth through sixteenth centuries. These modest fragments bring homes and exchange into view alongside royal stories. Excavation at Tridonorejo also uncovered settlement remains, including building fragments and shells.

passages.title: Different courts and busy ports
passages.text: Gowa’s growth involved deliberate building. The ruler Tumaparisi Kallonna moved its center from Tamalate to Somba Opu, developed a wharf and ordered an earthen wall around the palace in 1525. A defended coastal capital brought royal authority closer to ships and cargo. The Indonesian archaeological service identifies this port as an important meeting place for traders from different parts of the archipelago.

passages.title: Different courts and busy ports
passages.text: Gowa and neighboring Talloq had separate ruling houses and a close political partnership. Together they headed a wider federation extending beyond southern Sulawesi. Their power depended on armed forces, fortifications and diplomacy as well as commerce. Historian Tristan Mostert stresses that Makassar was a seat of regional government, not simply a market where ships happened to stop.

passages.title: Different courts and busy ports
passages.text: Commercial rivalry could turn violent. The Dutch East India Company, or VOC, sought control of the spice trade, while Gowa-Talloq pursued its own regional ambitions. In 1615, departing Dutch traders tried to seize Gowan dignitaries as hostages, killing some people and taking others captive. Local political rivalries and European alliances helped shape the conflict.

passages.title: Families, faith and learning
passages.text: In 1605, the rulers of Talloq and Gowa adopted Islam, taking the names Sultan Abdullah Awalul Islam and Sultan Alauddin. This was a change at particular courts, not the simultaneous conversion of everyone across the islands. Gowa’s early harbor-building and political expansion had already begun before its ruler became Muslim.

passages.title: Families, faith and learning
passages.text: Makassar’s court annals recorded marriages, births and deaths as matters of public importance. An entry in 1631 names I Taniq, a daughter born to a wife of Daeng Kalula. Such notices reveal family connections around the court, although ordinary households rarely received comparable attention in this record.

passages.title: Families, faith and learning
passages.text: A royal hall built in 1631 was named Macciniqdanggang, or “Watching Trade.” The ruler stayed there, linking court life with commercial activity. The same year’s annals also recorded a ban on paying interest on debts: buying, borrowing and religious rules could meet in everyday transactions.

passages.title: Families, faith and learning
passages.text: Gowa-Talloq’s intellectual curiosity could generate an enormous shopping request. In 1644, its statesman Pattingalloang ordered geographical and scientific equipment through the VOC, intending to pay for it. His requested globe would have been more than 1.3 meters across, roughly twice the diameter of the largest standard Blaeu globes then made in the Netherlands. Finding desk space might have been a challenge.

passages.title: Families, faith and learning
passages.text: Part of that order was sent to Makassar in February 1648: a world map described in Spanish, a four-volume Latin atlas, a burning glass and two telescopes. These objects offered ways to study distant places and optics. They document an unusually well-connected court’s interests, rather than a standard school curriculum for children throughout the islands.

passages.title: Water, food and a line of writing
passages.text: Banten, west of this record’s outline, offers a useful neighboring comparison. Its Tasikardi lake was built under Maulana Yusuf, who ruled from 1570 to 1580, to help supply fields and the palace. An island initially served as a retreat for his mother and later as a royal family recreation place. The same landscape could support crops, contemplation and an outing.

passages.title: Water, food and a line of writing
passages.text: The Banten water system also included terracotta pipes and three stations where water settled and passed through sand and palm fiber before reaching the palace. Archaeologists can trace practical efforts to improve water clarity. The surviving system accumulated over time, so every filter cannot be assigned to the lake’s sixteenth-century foundation, nor does clearer water prove modern standards of safety.

passages.title: Water, food and a line of writing
passages.text: Later archaeology at Banten connects cooking with cultural exchange. In deposits studied across the seventeenth to early nineteenth centuries, Dutch residents used locally made cooking pots and lids; archival records also show a shift from bread toward rice. Hired cooks and local women preparing household meals helped transmit techniques. Much of this evidence extends beyond 1650, but it shows how political encounters continued around the stove.

passages.title: Water, food and a line of writing
passages.text: For a Makassarese language sample, Cummings prints “naniaq bosi kontu banning,” translated “there was rain like thread,” under 2 May 1631. This is modern Roman transliteration, not a picture of the script. His principal manuscript, VT 25, is dated 1874 and uses Arabic-derived serang writing; it preserves earlier annals. Another copy says stones instead of thread, a reminder that copied words can change.

passages.title: Water, food and a line of writing
passages.text: Malacca and Johor must also stay distinct. In neighboring territory beyond this polygon, the Portuguese conquest of Malacca in 1511 displaced its court, whose rulers rebuilt their authority along the Johor River. A dynasty could continue after losing a capital. Aceh and Brunei likewise have separate atlas records; this plural label is not a reason to merge their courts or populations.

There was no single fall of these “states” in 1650: that is an atlas cutoff. Gowa’s control of Makassar was broken later, in the war of 1666 to 1669, by the VOC and local allies led by Arung Palakka. Other courts and communities followed different paths, which this regional label cannot reduce to one conquest.

sectionTitles: A modern country and its written voices
People who keep buildings and books alive

passages.text: The modern Republic of Mali emerged from decolonization in 1960. It is a separate state from the medieval Mali Empire, although its communities preserve and reinterpret much older histories.

passages.title: A modern country and its written voices
passages.text: This map record represents the modern republic. In 1960, the former French Sudan separated from the short-lived federation with Senegal and became the Republic of Mali. It was not the medieval empire surviving unchanged.

passages.title: A modern country and its written voices
passages.text: Mali’s recent political history includes a 2012 rebellion and coup, followed by military takeovers in 2020 and 2021. These changes disrupted government without ending the country. Families’ experiences of conflict, displacement and rebuilding belong beside the stories of presidents and soldiers.

passages.title: A modern country and its written voices
passages.text: A 2016 Bamanankan writing sample is the published title “taamacogo yɛlɛma : mun na hadamaden bɛ jͻ ka taama”, paired with “The Upright Revolution: Or Why Humans Walk Upright”. Malian writer Ismaila Samba Traoré translated Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o’s story. The Latin-based spelling preserves sounds beyond ordinary English letters.

passages.title: People who keep buildings and books alive
passages.text: Djenné’s Great Mosque receives new earthen plaster before the rains. In 2025, communal work took place on 25 May and 12 June. The current building dates to 1907, while the town’s Islamic architectural history is much older.

passages.title: People who keep buildings and books alive
passages.text: The plaster called banco mixes earth and water with natural additives, including rice bran, baobab powder and shea butter. The Barey-Ton association of masons organizes the work. A magnificent building needs recipes and regular maintenance, as well as an architect’s original idea.

passages.title: People who keep buildings and books alive
passages.text: Men, women, children and visitors join the annual event, which also passes knowledge to younger generations. Conservation becomes a public occasion. Keeping a landmark standing can mean getting together and getting muddy.

passages.title: People who keep buildings and books alive
passages.text: During the 2012 occupation of Timbuktu, residents and the heritage organization SAVAMA-DCI rescued most of the city’s ancient manuscripts. Many moved to Bamako. These were family and institutional collections, protected through local effort at considerable risk.

passages.title: People who keep buildings and books alive
passages.text: A 2015 conference identified suitable storage boxes and digitization as urgent needs for the rescued manuscripts. Saving a book from destruction is only the beginning: paper also needs careful handling, suitable storage and people who can help future readers use it.

passages.title: Performance, learning and family health
passages.text: At Markala, Bambara, Bozo, Marka and Somono communities hold festivities with masks, puppets, drums and dancing. Animal figures express social virtues. The celebrations follow harvest rites and lead into a period of fishing, connecting performance with the working year.

passages.title: Performance, learning and family health
passages.text: Markala’s festivities also create opportunities to discuss quarrels between families and communities. Older people teach young initiates ritual skills. A puppet performance can therefore be entertainment, education and a setting for repairing relationships.

passages.title: Performance, learning and family health
passages.text: Senufo balafons have wooden keys above gourd resonators. In the form described by UNESCO, delicate membranes made from spider egg-sac material cover holes in the gourds and change the sound. Ingenious musical engineering does not always involve electricity.

passages.title: Performance, learning and family health
passages.text: Children begin learning on smaller balafons before moving to full-sized instruments with a teacher. Music accompanies work, celebrations and funerals. These Senufo traditions cross borders into neighboring countries, illustrating why a cultural map never fits perfectly inside a political one.

passages.title: Performance, learning and family health
passages.text: In 2019, Fatoumata Barry taught displaced families in Sévaré through puzzles and playful demonstrations. Ada Diagayété helped compare washing with and without soap. Their stadium shelter had gained sixteen latrines, six showers and six taps: teaching and practical facilities worked together.

Mali continues as a country despite prolonged conflict and political upheaval. Its communities maintain social life, education and heritage through these disruptions; a coup is not the disappearance of a people.

passages.text: Mali connected West African gold-producing regions with a wider commercial and intellectual world. Mansa Musa became internationally famous through his pilgrimage, while architecture and oral performance preserved different forms of cultural memory.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Gold and salt served long-distance commerce; cowrie shells also entered local exchange during the fourteenth century.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Mansa Musa passed through Cairo during his pilgrimage in 1324 to 1325. His distribution of gold made a strong impression on contemporaries.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Timbuktu's Djingareyber Mosque traces its initial construction to Musa's return from pilgrimage. Later rebuilding means the surviving fabric represents multiple periods.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Mande jeliw transmit historical epics through skilled performance. Musical accompaniment helps structure and pace narratives.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Mosque architecture and scholarship connected Timbuktu to Islamic networks while local building practices remained central.
