sectionTitles: Family, learning and a roof with a history

passages.text: This late Mali entry concerns smaller Manding powers in the Upper Niger region. Kangaba’s rulers claimed Mali’s inheritance and defended access to goldfields. It should not be read as Mansa Musa’s much earlier empire surviving with unchanged institutions.

passages.title: Power, landscape and historical memory
passages.text: Historian Jan Jansen argues that refuges and fortified places formed coordinated groups along Kangaba’s northern frontier. His reconstruction uses geography, buildings and genealogies together, and is an interpretation of a poorly documented political landscape.

passages.title: Power, landscape and historical memory
passages.text: The Niger and western escarpment limited cavalry movements. Defenders adapted their forces to this terrain: a river, a cliff and a flat corridor posed very different problems for a mounted army.

passages.title: Power, landscape and historical memory
passages.text: Gold and the trade in enslaved people helped sustain the ruling elite. The wealth behind political survival therefore also depended on coercion and on people whose lives were disrupted by warfare.

passages.title: Power, landscape and historical memory
passages.text: Kangaba’s later importance does not prove it was the medieval empire’s capital. Historians have questioned how that identification entered colonial accounts. A community can inherit an important political tradition without every remembered location being securely established.

passages.title: Family, learning and a roof with a history
passages.text: Kangaba’s circular Kamablon, which UNESCO’s nomination dates to 1653, shelters objects important to the community and serves as a meeting place. Its thatched roof is renewed every seven years in a ceremony that continues today.

passages.title: Family, learning and a roof with a history
passages.text: In the documented modern ceremony, young people about twenty or twenty-one remove the old roof and build its replacement under elders’ supervision. Practical construction skills and explanations of the building’s meaning are learned together: roofing is also a history lesson.

passages.title: Family, learning and a roof with a history
passages.text: Keita clan members and Diabate griots organize the ceremony, while griots from Kela recount Manden history. Gathering also provides opportunities to strengthen relationships and settle disagreements. This is a living practice, not proof that every detail was identical in 1653.

passages.title: Family, learning and a roof with a history
passages.text: Stories about marriages between Muslim scholars and warrior families helped explain political legitimacy in the wider western Sudan. Jansen’s study examines how a child’s success in such stories connected ancestry to the right to rule.

passages.title: Family, learning and a roof with a history
passages.text: Those accounts sometimes emphasize descent through women and sometimes through men. They reveal arguments about inheritance and authority among elites; they cannot tell us the marriage arrangements of every family in Kangaba.

passages.title: Spoken heritage and written history
passages.text: The Manden Charter survives as an oral heritage associated with the region. Its living presentations discuss peace, education, food security and respect for people. Recognizing its cultural importance is different from claiming that an original medieval written constitution survives.

passages.title: Spoken heritage and written history
passages.text: UNESCO describes the Charter’s teaching as passing between generations through local gatherings and ceremonies. Speech, performance and memory are therefore historical evidence too, though scholars must ask when particular versions were recorded and how they changed.

passages.title: Spoken heritage and written history
passages.text: A contemporary regional written tradition appears in al-Saʿdi’s seventeenth-century Arabic chronicle, whose title is “تاريخ السودان”: “History of the Sudan”. Here Sudan means the broad West African region. This is an external regional comparison, not a surviving Kangaba court text; the spelling is attested in its published Arabic edition.
The map stops in 1783, but Kangaba’s authority continued. Nineteenth-century warfare and new alliances reshaped the region; its peoples and traditions did not vanish with an imperial label.

sectionTitles: Read the atlas shape before turning it into a country
Two Malla communities appear more clearly than one neat state
Assembly politics was collective, organized and unequal
Neighbors, roads and Magadha shaped the political horizon
Fields, crafts and travel kept the republics alive
Families and ranks appear at the edges of elite stories
Learning was mostly oral; the only safe local inscription is later
Homes, cloth, music and play leave uneven clues
Food, illness, water and toilets need extra-honest labels
Death made Kusinara famous, while archaeology complicates the memory

passages.text: Imagine a small republic where powerful families meet in an assembly hall while farmers, craftspeople, traders and children keep two connected towns alive. Ancient texts place the Mallas around Kusinara and Pava in the eastern Ganga plain. They had no single hereditary king like neighboring monarchies, yet ‘republic’ did not mean everyone voted: elite lineage heads probably held power. The Mallas became famous because Buddhist tradition says the Buddha died near Kusinara. Families gathered, music sounded, chiefs organized the funeral and the Pava branch demanded its own share of the relics. Those vivid stories were transmitted later, so archaeology must check them, and Kushinagar's surviving monuments are mostly later still. The atlas adds another puzzle: its one tiny 500 to 400 BCE polygon includes Kushinagar and a Pava candidate but turns into a generic region at 400, long before a securely dated conquest is known. By the later fourth century BCE the area falls inside Magadha and then Maurya. Malla rule faded; its roads, settlements and sacred memory did not.

passages.title: Read the atlas shape before turning it into a country
passages.text: The exact indexed identity is id “malla,” display name “Malla,” with an approximate 500 to 400 BCE lifetime generated from historical basemaps. It remains a missing, unreviewed state card with one observed border interval. The imported Wikipedia summary is only a research lead; this card replaces it with mapped claims and explicit uncertainty.

passages.title: Read the atlas shape before turning it into a country
passages.text: At 500 BCE the target is one Polygon with one ring and twelve coordinate positions. Its bounding box is 83.5910359103591 to 84.88344883448838°E and 25.857261115193694 to 26.910706825889818°N. The feature properties contain no label field. Kushinagar, the Fazilnagar Pava candidate and Deoria test inside; nearby Padrauna and Gorakhpur do not.

passages.title: Read the atlas shape before turning it into a country
passages.text: The imported topology uses arcs [[−325, −332, 335, −305]]. After canonicalizing reversed arc numbers, it shares arc 304 with hindu-kingdoms, 324 with Kasi and 331 with Kosala. These are reproducible file seams, not surveyed ancient frontiers: rivers moved, ancient boundary stones are missing and the broad neighbor label hides several peoples.

passages.title: Read the atlas shape before turning it into a country
passages.text: The drawn patch places Varanasi in Kasi and Kaushambi in Vatsa while assigning Vaishali and Rajgir to a generic hindu-kingdoms feature. Lumbini and Kapilavastu fall in Kosala; Shravasti and Ayodhya oddly fall in Pancala. This proves the atlas is an approximate display mosaic, so its point ownership cannot settle historical overlordship or travel routes.

passages.title: Read the atlas shape before turning it into a country
passages.text: There is no malla feature at 700, 400, 323, 300 or 200 BCE. Before it, every tested point is swallowed by vedic-aryans; after it, Kushinagar first becomes hindu-kingdoms, then Magadha by 323 and Maurya by 300. Unrelated Himalayan and Thai labels hit other probes later, exposing imported seam errors rather than migrations.

passages.title: Two Malla communities appear more clearly than one neat state
passages.text: Official teaching lists Malla among sixteen mahajanapadas and locates its capital at Kusinara in the Deoria area of eastern Uttar Pradesh. Mahajanapada means a large territorial polity, but the list compresses different political forms into one chart. Malla was not simply a miniature hereditary kingdom matching every modern district boundary.

passages.title: Two Malla communities appear more clearly than one neat state
passages.text: University syntheses describe several Malla branches, especially communities centered at Kusinara and Pava. Kusinara is widely linked with modern Kasia or Kushinagar; Pava's location has drawn disagreement, including Padrauna and other candidates. The district promotes Fazilnagar as Pava, so this card labels it a candidate rather than an archaeological certainty.

passages.title: Two Malla communities appear more clearly than one neat state
passages.text: Gana-sangha is variously translated as republic, oligarchy or clan polity. Historians warn that calling it a modern democracy smuggles in elections, citizenship and equal votes that the evidence does not show. Malla's governing participants were likely elite lineage heads; an assembly could restrain one ruler while still excluding most residents.

passages.title: Two Malla communities appear more clearly than one neat state
passages.text: No contemporary Malla constitution, tax roll, family archive or stone decree survives from 500 to 400 BCE. Political reconstruction depends heavily on Buddhist and Jain works transmitted orally and written down later, checked against archaeology and comparison. That evidence can reveal institutions and memories, but it cannot recover meeting minutes word for word.

passages.title: Two Malla communities appear more clearly than one neat state
passages.text: The ancient Ganga-plain Mallas must be kept separate from Nepal's Malla dynasty, which the Metropolitan Museum dates from about 1200 to 1768 to 1769. A shared name across roughly seventeen centuries does not prove one state, dynasty or bloodline. Later Mallas elsewhere, modern surnames and the ordinary Sanskrit word associated with wrestlers are not atlas aliases.

passages.title: Assembly politics was collective, organized and unequal
passages.text: DN 16 says the Mallas of Kusinara were gathered in a sandhagara, an assembly or town hall, ‘on business’ when Ananda brought news of the Buddha's approaching death. The scene makes collective deliberation imaginable and names a political building. It is transmitted religious literature, not an excavated council chamber or contemporary stenographic record.

passages.title: Assembly politics was collective, organized and unequal
passages.text: University syntheses describe gana-sanghas as councils of important clan and family heads working with a selected chief, with ordinary people outside the ruling body. That is a useful model for Malla if held loosely. The texts do not identify every office, voting rule, term length or which households counted as ‘important.’

passages.title: Assembly politics was collective, organized and unequal
passages.text: The Kusinara and Pava Mallas act as separate bodies in the relic story. After the cremation, the Mallas of Pava send their own envoy to Kusinara and demand a share because they too are aristocrats. A negotiated division follows. This is stronger evidence for two political communities than for one centralized Malla capital commanding both.

passages.title: Assembly politics was collective, organized and unequal
passages.text: The Pali text calls the Kusinara group kosinaraka malla and addresses them as Vasetthas, lineage language suited to aristocratic self-identity. Later traditions count hundreds of chiefs, but exact totals are not administrative statistics. The safest portrait is a small ruling stratum acting through assemblies over a larger population whose voices survive poorly.

passages.title: Assembly politics was collective, organized and unequal
passages.text: Coordinating messengers, a guarded assembly hall, a long public rite and bargaining with outside claimants shows impressive collective capacity in the narrative. It does not establish ministries or a standing civil service. Malla's political achievement was durable cooperation among elite houses, even when that cooperation was narrower than citizenship in a modern republic.

passages.title: Neighbors, roads and Magadha shaped the political horizon
passages.text: Textual geography places Malla east or southeast of the Sakyas and near the Vajji-Licchavi world. The two Malla centers sat among many small clan polities rather than in an empty buffer zone. Ancient neighbor relations could mix kinship, travel, alliance and conflict; a shared atlas arc cannot choose among those relationships.

passages.title: Neighbors, roads and Magadha shaped the political horizon
passages.text: NIOS reconstructs a major route from Shravasti through Kapilavastu and Kusinara toward Vaishali. That line could carry merchants, renouncers, messengers and news across political borders. It supports Kusinara's connected location, not a paved Malla highway with measured milestones, inns or a state postal schedule.

passages.title: Neighbors, roads and Magadha shaped the political horizon
passages.text: University studies group Malla and Vajji among eastern gana-sanghas, but a shared political category does not prove one federation. Their institutions and alliances come through later literary traditions. The atlas draws no Vajji id here and instead uses a generic hindu-kingdoms neighbor, another reason to separate texts from topology.

passages.title: Neighbors, roads and Magadha shaped the political horizon
passages.text: The wider struggle among mahajanapadas ended with Magadha becoming paramount. University synthesis treats monarchies and republics as parts of that changing political field, while the atlas places former Malla probes in Magadha only at 323 BCE. Malla probably lost autonomy during this expansion, but no source used here names its last chief or final battle.

passages.title: Neighbors, roads and Magadha shaped the political horizon
passages.text: The 400 BCE disappearance is therefore an atlas endpoint, not a documented surrender date. At 400 the core probes become a broad hindu-kingdoms feature; at 323 they become Magadha; at 300 they become Maurya. The honest ending is gradual or poorly recorded absorption into larger eastern states, with no single successor link pretending to be exact.

passages.title: Fields, crafts and travel kept the republics alive
passages.text: Across the middle Ganga plain, wetter land, iron tools and expanding cultivation helped support larger settlements and political institutions. Iron objects do not automatically prove state control, and the evidence is regional rather than a Malla farm ledger. Still, food surplus and clearing labor formed the material base beneath assemblies and traveling teachers.

passages.title: Fields, crafts and travel kept the republics alive
passages.text: Early urbanization was uneven: towns depended on villages, cultivators, herders and craft workers around them. Potters, textile workers, metalworkers, builders and traders supplied objects that survive better than their names. Kusinara and Pava belonged to this networked world, but no complete fifth-century BCE street plan or market register survives for either.

passages.title: Fields, crafts and travel kept the republics alive
passages.text: A canonical scene calls Cunda of Pava a kammara, often translated smith or metalworker, and makes his household prosperous enough to host a large meal. It gives a rare named worker and patron, though scholars debate both the occupational nuance and narrative date. Cunda cannot stand for every artisan or prove a guild system.

passages.title: Fields, crafts and travel kept the republics alive
passages.text: DN 16 depicts Pukkusa, identified as a Malla, traveling on the Pava to Kusinara road while carts pass and dust rises; he offers two fine golden-colored cloths. The episode evokes roads, wheeled transport, elite textiles and mobile religious exchange. As a crafted teaching story, it is vivid evidence of remembered possibilities rather than traffic counts.

passages.title: Fields, crafts and travel kept the republics alive
passages.text: Early excavators at Kasia recovered pottery, bricks, seals, coins and Buddhist monuments from many centuries. Their own reports debated the identification and layers; spectacular later finds cannot all be moved backward into Malla government. Archaeology confirms a long-lived place, while the 500 to 400 BCE town's size, walls, workshops and population remain poorly resolved.

passages.title: Families and ranks appear at the edges of elite stories
passages.text: When news reaches the Kusinara assembly, DN 16 says the Mallas, their sons, daughters-in-law and wives go family by family to pay respects. This is valuable kinship vocabulary and includes women and children in public mourning. It does not reveal household size, marriage age, inheritance rules or whether daughters joined political decisions.

passages.title: Families and ranks appear at the edges of elite stories
passages.text: Households joined food production, care, craft knowledge, property and ritual. Learned classifications describe ranked varnas and many occupations, but prescriptive categories do not map every home neatly. Elite lineage status clearly mattered in Malla politics; cultivators, servants and laborers supported society while remaining far less visible in the surviving religious narratives.

passages.title: Families and ranks appear at the edges of elite stories
passages.text: Women appear as wives and daughters-in-law in the Kusinara narrative, and wider early Buddhist traditions preserve women donors and renouncers. Nothing reviewed proves that Malla women sat in the political assembly, nor that all were excluded in identical ways. The card therefore reports presence, labor and grief without inventing constitutional rights.

passages.title: Families and ranks appear at the edges of elite stories
passages.text: Children in farming and craft households likely learned by watching, carrying, tending, pounding, sorting and gradually taking harder tasks. That is a bounded inference from regional subsistence, not a recovered Malla chore list. Wealth, gender, age, season and status would have changed work, and affection or play rarely leaves plant remains.

passages.title: Families and ranks appear at the edges of elite stories
passages.text: Textbooks describe the enormous shared labor needed to build fortifications, cultivate fields and supply early states, including work by men, women and children. Malla's elite council did not erase such unequal effort. Taxes, dues or service probably varied locally, but no reviewed Malla tablet tells us the rate, collector or penalty.

passages.title: Learning was mostly oral; the only safe local inscription is later
passages.text: Formal Vedic learning preserved words through listening, memorizing, exact pronunciation and multiple recitation patterns under a teacher. Such training was specialized and unequal, while most children learned speech, work, ritual and manners at home or beside experienced adults. No evidence supports universal Malla schools, classrooms, exams or widespread fifth-century BCE literacy.

passages.title: Learning was mostly oral; the only safe local inscription is later
passages.text: Buddhist, Jain, Ajivika and Brahmanical teachers moved through a crowded religious landscape and addressed householders as well as renouncers. Malla's connection to the Buddha's last journey made Kusinara especially memorable in Buddhist texts, but that does not make every resident Buddhist or erase older and competing practices.

passages.title: Learning was mostly oral; the only safe local inscription is later
passages.text: No defensible inscription issued by the Malla republics during 500 to 400 BCE was found in the reviewed archaeological and epigraphic sources. Canonical Pali is authentic to a later transmitted tradition, not a surviving contemporary Malla manuscript. The card therefore refuses to manufacture a royal motto, alphabet or vernacular sentence for the atlas period.

passages.title: Learning was mostly oral; the only safe local inscription is later
passages.text: A transparent later local sample is “deya-dharmo yaṁ mahā-vihāra-svāmino haribalasya.” Modern Devanagari normalization: “देयधर्मोऽयं महाविहारस्वामिनो हरिबलस्य”. Transliteration: “deya-dharmo ’yaṃ mahā-vihāra-svāmino haribalasya.” Translation: “This is the meritorious religious gift of Haribala, master of the great monastery.” It is a Kushinagar donor line, not Malla-state speech.

passages.title: Learning was mostly oral; the only safe local inscription is later
passages.text: The words are Sanskrit carved on the pedestal of the reclining Buddha image at Kasia. The undated inscription is assigned paleographically to about the end of the fifth century CE, roughly nine centuries after the atlas card. Devanagari above is only a readable normalization; the original northern Brahmi-derived letter shapes must be studied on the stone or plate.

passages.title: Homes, cloth, music and play leave uneven clues
passages.text: Early historic settlement across northern India mixed earthen floors, timber, reeds, thatch and increasing brick use, but materials and plans varied by place and wealth. Later brick monasteries at Kushinagar cannot serve as ordinary Malla houses. Archaeology preserves walls and pots more readily than sleeping arrangements, privacy, quarrels or bedtime stories.

passages.title: Homes, cloth, music and play leave uneven clues
passages.text: The funeral route in DN 16 carries the Buddha's body north of Kusinara, through a northern gate, across the center and out an eastern gate. It offers a literary image of gates, streets and a shrine called Coronation. Without matching fifth-century walls, it is not a surveyed city map and should not guide a reconstruction brick by brick.

passages.title: Homes, cloth, music and play leave uneven clues
passages.text: The Mallas are said to wrap the body in hundreds of paired cloth layers and prepare awnings and pavilions. This shows textiles as valuable ceremonial material and implies skilled spinning, weaving and handling. The number belongs to an extraordinary royal-style funeral, so it cannot tell us how many garments ordinary children owned or what daily colors they wore.

passages.title: Homes, cloth, music and play leave uneven clues
passages.text: Dance, song, instrumental music, garlands and fragrances accompany the public rites. The scene proves that performers and sensory display made ceremonies memorable in the transmitted tradition. It does not provide a children's songbook, instrument inventory or weekly entertainment schedule; those delightful details vanish faster than brick and stone.

passages.title: Homes, cloth, music and play leave uneven clues
passages.text: No securely dated Malla-period toy, game board or playground from Kusinara or Pava was identified in the reviewed reports. Children almost certainly played, imitated adults and invented games with perishable or ordinary objects, but those are humane inferences. A pot sherd is not automatically a toy just because it fits a small hand.

passages.title: Food, illness, water and toilets need extra-honest labels
passages.text: Ganga-plain archaeobotany records changing mixtures of rice, barley, wheats, millets, pulses, oilseeds and useful fruits across sites and centuries. That supports a varied regional pantry and seasonal farming rather than a single ‘Malla menu.’ It cannot prove every listed crop grew inside the tiny polygon or reached every household bowl.

passages.title: Food, illness, water and toilets need extra-honest labels
passages.text: Cunda's famous final meal includes the Pali term sukaramaddava. Scholars have proposed different foods, and the evidence does not securely decide between pork, mushroom and other explanations. A kid-readable card should call it an uncertain special dish, not solve a centuries-old philological puzzle with a confident dinner label.

passages.title: Food, illness, water and toilets need extra-honest labels
passages.text: Ancient care could combine diet, plants, washing, touch, observation, ritual and spoken formulas. Surviving Charaka and Sushruta collections took shape through later compilation, so their mature medical systems cannot simply be pasted into a Malla clinic. DN 16's illness stories show concern and vulnerability, not prescriptions or proof of professional doctors in every town.

passages.title: Food, illness, water and toilets need extra-honest labels
passages.text: DN 16 mentions drinking and bathing at the Kakuttha stream and other nearby waters, while travelers and households carried water in vessels. This supplies a literary waterscape, not a municipal pipe plan. No reviewed fifth-century Malla well, filter or drain can securely be assigned to the republic, and water quality is unknowable.

passages.title: Food, illness, water and toilets need extra-honest labels
passages.text: A Vinaya procedure elsewhere in the Kosala region distinguishes drinking water, foot-washing water and water for rinsing after defecation, and orders communal spaces swept. It proves practical sanitation rules in a regulated monastic tradition, not Malla household plumbing. No secure Malla latrine, toilet seat, sewer or poop pit is documented, ancient bottoms remain archaeologically uncooperative.

passages.title: Death made Kusinara famous, while archaeology complicates the memory
passages.text: DN 16 remembers Kusinara as the place of the Buddha's final nirvana. Malla families gather, chiefs wash and dress ceremonially, music and garlands accompany the body, and guards protect the relics before division. These details make Malla collective action visible, while their sacred narrative setting prevents us from treating every number as civic paperwork.

passages.title: Death made Kusinara famous, while archaeology complicates the memory
passages.text: The present Mahaparinirvana complex includes a 6.1-meter reclining image and monuments excavated from the nineteenth century onward. Ramabhar's stupa phases are difficult to date, and much surviving fabric is centuries later than the republic. The monuments preserve pilgrimage memory; they do not by themselves prove an intact 500 BCE Malla building.

passages.title: Death made Kusinara famous, while archaeology complicates the memory
passages.text: Excavation history identifies modern Kushinagar with ancient Kusinara through work by Cunningham, Carlleyle, Vogel and later investigators. Early ASI work also recorded uncertainty before inscriptions and accumulated evidence strengthened the identification. Archaeological identification is an argument built over time, not a place-name magic trick that turns every mound into the text's city.

passages.title: Death made Kusinara famous, while archaeology complicates the memory
passages.text: Jain tradition links Mahavira's death with a Pava, but surviving texts and chronologies are later and the place is often associated with Pawapuri in Bihar. That cannot automatically be merged with the Malla Pava candidate near Kushinagar. Similar names and sacred memories require comparison, not a shortcut that gives one town every famous death.

passages.title: Death made Kusinara famous, while archaeology complicates the memory
passages.text: Malla autonomy disappears without a securely dated final scene, yet the core enters Magadha and Maurya in later atlas layers, while Kushinagar's monuments became a major pilgrimage center. The polygon ends; people, routes and sacred memory continue. That continuity belongs to the place and its communities, not to an imaginary unbroken Malla republic or the medieval Nepal dynasty.

The atlas removes malla at its approximate 400 BCE seam, but no consulted source records a last chief, siege, treaty or surrender in that exact year. The core becomes a generic hindu-kingdoms feature at 400, Magadha by 323 and Maurya by 300. Historical syntheses place the small gana-sanghas within Magadha's expanding political horizon. Malla's separate autonomy was absorbed or dissolved, while Kusinara, Pava traditions, roads and religious memory continued. The ending is therefore marked uncertain and no single successor link is asserted as an instantaneous, fully documented transfer.

passages.text: This layer shows Malta and Gozo during part of British colonial rule, from 1878 to 1920. The islands were a Mediterranean imperial stronghold as well as homes, workplaces and farming communities. The map dates mark selected coverage: they are neither the beginning nor the end of British rule. This card concentrates on colonial daily life and the movement towards self-government.

passages.title: School, clothing and getting around
passages.text: Many government schools around 1880 occupied rented houses. Rooms designed for families could become overcrowded classrooms with poor ventilation. Historian Conrad Thake describes the difficulty of adapting these buildings: adding pupils did not magically add fresh air or elbow room.

passages.title: School, clothing and getting around
passages.text: School toilets also drew fierce criticism. Keenan complained about offensive smells at schools including Cospicua and Senglea, and many schoolhouses lacked playgrounds. A child’s school day could therefore involve both cramped lessons and very little proper space for running about afterwards.

passages.title: School, clothing and getting around
passages.text: In his report published in 1880, Patrick Keenan said primary schools reached fewer than two-fifths of children aged five to ten. He also reported that most pupils of those ages were still learning letters or a primer. These are the inspector’s findings, showing how uneven access to schooling remained.

passages.title: School, clothing and getting around
passages.text: A surviving lace skirt from the late nineteenth or early twentieth century was made in separate pieces by several skilled workers. Differences in its stitches help reveal that teamwork. Its thirty-two panels were sewn together by hand: this was an elaborate project, not a garment that appeared at the push of a button.

passages.title: School, clothing and getting around
passages.text: The same skirt has evidence that someone was once sewn into it for an occasion. Getting undressed meant cutting the fastening threads. Lace-makers worked with bobbins on a pillow or roller, controlling threads with great care. The surviving luxury garment reveals both fashionable display and the labour behind it.

passages.title: School, clothing and getting around
passages.text: Malta’s railway began in 1883 and its tram system in 1905. The systems linked Valletta with places including Mdina and the Three Cities, carrying people and goods more quickly than traditional horse carriages. Steam whistles became part of island life before growing motor traffic helped displace the rail services.

passages.title: Health, money and political change
passages.text: Themistocles Zammit investigated goats during the search for the cause of Malta fever. His 1905 Royal Society paper reported experiments on their susceptibility to the infection. A familiar farm animal had become a scientific clue in understanding an illness that troubled the islands.

passages.title: Health, money and political change
passages.text: Research connected infected goats’ milk with the transmission of brucellosis, also called Malta fever. British military establishments replaced goats’ milk with tinned or condensed milk, greatly reducing their problem. Civilian acceptance was slower and disputed. Finding a cause and persuading a whole society to change its habits were different jobs.

passages.title: Health, money and political change
passages.text: In August 1914, the outbreak of the First World War prompted Malta’s first official local currency notes. There were five denominations in shillings and pounds. They were a temporary precaution and were withdrawn the following year, after which the islands again depended on currency imported from Britain.

passages.title: Health, money and political change
passages.text: After the war, bread and other essential foods were scarce and expensive. Dockyard dismissals, new taxes and unequal treatment of Maltese and British workers added to public anger. For many households, arguments about colonial government were closely connected with the practical question of affording dinner.

passages.title: Health, money and political change
passages.text: University students protested, newspapers faced censorship and activists demanded more political rights. These tensions contributed to the revolt of 7 June 1919, remembered as Sette Giugno. Heritage Malta’s exhibition places the event within wider demands for self-government after the First World War.

passages.title: Health, money and political change
passages.text: A new constitution in 1921, just after this map layer ends, gave the Maltese a greater role in running their country. It remained a step within colonial rule. Independence came in 1964, and Malta became a republic in 1974, after further political struggles and constitutional changes.

passages.title: A newspaper in Maltese
passages.text: The newspaper of 25 April 1912 carries the title “IL HABIB”, meaning “The Friend”. This preserves its printed spelling rather than silently replacing it with modern “Il-Ħabib”. Its front page lists a postal subscription costing three shillings a year in Malta and Gozo. Written Maltese carried news, arguments and everyday information into readers’ homes.

The 1920 endpoint is a map cutoff. Colonial government continued after the 1921 constitution. Malta gained independence in 1964 and became a republic in 1974; the people and islands continued through those changes.

sectionTitles: Government and a changing pocketful of coins

passages.text: This layer shows the Republic of Malta during the map’s 1994 to 2020 coverage. The republic was already established: independence came in 1964 and republican government in 1974. Malta, Gozo and the smaller islands form a Mediterranean archipelago whose households combine local language and traditions with close international connections. Neither endpoint marks the creation or disappearance of the country.

passages.title: Government and a changing pocketful of coins
passages.text: Malta’s route into the European Union was debated rather than automatic. Its application was paused in 1996 and reactivated after the 1998 election. Negotiations began in 2000, and a referendum in 2003 supported joining. Malta became a member on 1 May 2004.

passages.title: Government and a changing pocketful of coins
passages.text: The euro replaced the Maltese lira on 1 January 2008. To prepare, banks received new notes and coins before the changeover, and the public could buy small starter kits from 10 December 2007. People could examine their new coins before using them for ordinary shopping.

passages.title: Government and a changing pocketful of coins
passages.text: For January 2008, payments could be made in either euros or Maltese lira notes and coins. The overlap ended on 31 January. This short transition gave households and shops time to adjust, rather than requiring everyone to empty every old coin from every drawer overnight.

passages.title: Government and a changing pocketful of coins
passages.text: Malta is a parliamentary republic with one chamber of parliament. The prime minister heads the government, while the president’s role is largely ceremonial. Distinguishing these jobs helps explain why a national ceremony and the day-to-day work of governing can involve different people.

passages.title: Bread, family and learning
passages.text: Ftira is a flattened sourdough bread with a firm crust and an airy inside. A split loaf can hold olive oil, tomato, tuna, capers or olives. UNESCO added its associated knowledge and customs to its heritage list in 2020. Here a much-loved lunch also carries a history of skilled work.

passages.title: Bread, family and learning
passages.text: Ftira still needs skilled hands to shape it, even where other bread-making jobs use machines. Apprentices learn by watching and doing. At home, people pass on ideas for fillings, while cooking blogs and social media also share variations. A recipe can travel between generations and between screens.

passages.title: Bread, family and learning
passages.text: A 2018 European research report describes grandparents as important carers for many Maltese children under three. It also notes expanding childcare provision and more mothers of young children in paid work. Family care could involve several generations as well as services outside the home.

passages.title: Bread, family and learning
passages.text: The same report describes football, ballet and clubs among children’s activities after school. In the Maltese families studied, digital reading coexisted with valued printed books, and many parents worried about internet safety. The findings concern a research sample, giving a glimpse of family life rather than a rule for every home.

passages.title: Public health and community work
passages.text: Three new wastewater plants changed what happened after toilets were flushed. Plants in Gozo and northern Malta began operating in 2007 and 2008; Ta’ Barkat followed in June 2011. The environment authority describes this programme as a way to stop raw sewage being discharged into the sea.

passages.title: Public health and community work
passages.text: Moving into Mater Dei Hospital in November 2007 required a carefully coordinated transfer from St Luke’s. The official report records 411 acute patients and nine babies moved during the process. Some non-acute patients stayed behind. Opening a hospital meant moving people safely as well as unlocking a new building.

passages.title: Public health and community work
passages.text: Blood donation also went out into the community. The transfusion service records 206 blood drives in 2008, including visits to clinics and factories, collecting 3,124 units. A refurbished mobile unit was inaugurated in 2009. Ordinary volunteers helped provide something that hospitals could not simply manufacture.

passages.title: Public health and community work
passages.text: Village festas bring volunteers, bands, bells and street food together. UNESCO’s later 2023 account explains that preparation continues through the year and that some parishes hold children’s processions with a smaller statue. These continuing celebrations give children ways to participate, rather than only watching the grown-ups.

passages.title: A sentence in Maltese
passages.text: Article 5 of the Maltese constitution reads: “L-ilsien Nazzjonali ta’ Malta huwa l-ilsien Malti.” It means “The National language of Malta is the Maltese language.” This quotation follows the government’s 2019 printed text. The following paragraph also identifies Maltese and English as official languages, showing how language is part of public life as well as family conversation.

The map stops at 2020, but the Republic of Malta continues. It remains a parliamentary republic and a member of the European Union. Its later history belongs to continuing communities rather than an ending civilisation.

sectionTitles: Crafts that carry names and meanings

passages.text: The Mamluk sultanate centred on Cairo and governed Egypt and much of Syria. Rulers drawn from military households supported institutions and specialised crafts. Surviving buildings and objects illuminate urban services, skilled labour, trade and the public display of authority.

passages.title: Institutions and exchange
passages.text: Military recruits entered the ruling system through enslavement, education and training, followed by manumission and service. Advancement was not solely hereditary. This path to elite office depended on coercive recruitment and should not be confused with freedom from social hierarchy.

passages.title: Institutions and exchange
passages.text: Trade in silks and spices helped finance patronage. Textiles and carpets also circulated internationally. Skilled production connected merchants and workshops with wealthy buyers well beyond the sultanate.

passages.title: Water, teaching and care
passages.text: Qalawun’s complex on Cairo’s al-Mu’izz Street joined a school, mosque, tomb and hospital. The arrangement brought teaching and care into an architectural foundation that also preserved the ruler’s memory. The building’s functions were broader than royal burial alone.

passages.title: Water, teaching and care
passages.text: Shaykhu’s sabil, established in 1354, supplied water to passers-by. Its rock-cut rooms have openings to cisterns below, and jars were used in distribution. The surviving structure shows how storage and service worked together in a city street.

passages.title: Water, teaching and care
passages.text: Qayitbay’s fifteenth-century complex combined a madrasa, a public water facility and a kuttab for Qur’anic teaching to poor Muslims. A courtyard and surrounding halls organised the school. Education, water supply and commemoration shared one foundation.

passages.title: Water, teaching and care
passages.text: Wooden furnishings at Qayitbay’s madrasa include a pulpit and a Qur’an reciter’s chair inlaid with ivory. Their construction demonstrates skilled joinery and ornament in objects used for teaching and worship, alongside the stonework of the building.

passages.title: Crafts that carry names and meanings
passages.text: A glass lamp made for Amir Qawsun around 1329 to 1335 combines a blown body and applied foot with enamel and gilding. Its inscription identifies the patron. The museum regards a mosque or tomb-hospice as its probable destination, rather than a proven findspot.

passages.title: Crafts that carry names and meanings
passages.text: A fourteenth-century tray stand bears a cup emblem and an inscription naming Husain, son of Qawsun. Brass was worked and inlaid with contrasting metals. Stands of this kind held trays of fruit and other food, connecting elite dining with symbols of court office.

passages.title: Crafts that carry names and meanings
passages.text: The Five Medallion Carpet, dated around 1500, uses wool for its foundation threads and knotted surface. Repeated geometric forms organise the long design. Its attribution to Egypt, probably Cairo, remains an attribution, not a documented excavation location.

passages.title: Crafts that carry names and meanings
passages.text: A fifteenth-century engraved brass box names Muhammad al-Hamawi, the timekeeper at Damascus’s Umayyad Mosque. His office supervised prayer times and announcements concerning Ramadan. The box probably held food; it documents a specialist’s role without itself being a timekeeping instrument.

Ottoman conquest ended the Egyptian sultanate in 1517. Tuman Bey was captured and executed in Cairo after resisting the invasion. Mamluk elites retained influence under Ottoman rule, so the loss of the sultanate did not immediately eliminate its military households or social power.

sectionTitles: How to read a region that keeps changing rulers
Warlord power, invasion and a state built under occupation
Resistance, total war and the violent 1945 break
Railways, soybeans, factories and who paid for growth
Homes, meals, clothes and a little entertainment
School days, printed words and culture under supervision
Doctors, nurses, plague control and medical crimes

passages.text: This card follows Northeast China through forty years in which the map’s single word, “Manchuria,” conceals repeated upheaval. Zhang Zuolin and Zhang Xueliang built regional power around armies and railways; Japan’s 1931 invasion created the dependent state of Manchukuo; planned factories, schools, films and clinics grew beside dispossession, censorship, forced mobilization and Unit 731’s crimes. Chinese, Manchu, Korean, Mongol, Japanese and Russian families did not live one interchangeable life: they farmed soy and sorghum, slept on heated kangs, queued for scarce rooms and food, studied under unequal systems, listened to radio and argued with propaganda. Soviet invasion ended the colonial regime in 1945, civil war followed, and the People’s Republic turned the Northeast into a heavy-industry center while mass health campaigns tackled water, waste and disease. The atlas ends this regional id in 1960, during the Great Leap famine; Northeast China and its peoples continued.

passages.title: How to read a region that keeps changing rulers
passages.text: The exact id manchuria is an atlas umbrella from 1920 to 1960, not the name of one continuous state. In 1914 the same core sits inside the badly dated qing-dynasty record; later it covers a warlord base, Japanese-occupied Manchukuo, a Soviet invasion zone and PRC provinces. One color is doing the work of several governments.

passages.title: How to read a region that keeps changing rulers
passages.text: The 1920 and 1930 target polygons are byte-for-byte identical after TopoJSON decoding: one outer ring, 187 positions and the same bounding box. Armies, administrations and railway power changed during those eighteen years; the frozen outline does not. It is a locator, not a year-by-year border survey.

passages.title: How to read a region that keeps changing rulers
passages.text: The id disappears from the 1938 snapshot. Shenyang, Harbin, Changchun and Hailar are then swallowed into japan-1914, and manchuria returns in 1945. That bookkeeping choice must never be read as popular union with Japan. The card keeps Manchukuo’s colonial dependence and Chinese resistance explicit.

passages.title: How to read a region that keeps changing rulers
passages.text: Dalian fails every target point test even though its port and the South Manchuria Railway were central to the region’s history. Simplified coastal geometry clipped it away. When a map says a famous railway port is apparently swimming just outside its own story, trust the documented history rather than the pixel.

passages.title: How to read a region that keeps changing rulers
passages.text: At the 1960 seam, the same core cities pass into the china polygon. Northeast China did not vanish, and people did not wake up with different grandparents because a JSON id changed. “Manchuria” can also carry imperial and outsider meanings, so the card uses “Northeast China” for the postwar region where useful.

passages.title: Warlord power, invasion and a state built under occupation
passages.text: Zhang Zuolin’s Fengtian clique ruled from Shenyang with an army funded by taxes, trade and access to a resource-rich region. Japanese railway and military interests both supported and constrained him. Calling this simply “independent Manchuria” would hide the Republic of China, local coercion and the foreign concessions crisscrossing its politics.

passages.title: Warlord power, invasion and a state built under occupation
passages.text: In 1928 Japanese officers bombed Zhang Zuolin’s train, hoping his death would help expand their control. His son Zhang Xueliang instead declared allegiance to the Nationalist government. A family succession therefore produced an outcome the plotters had not wanted: a stronger public claim that the Northeast belonged within China.

passages.title: Warlord power, invasion and a state built under occupation
passages.text: On 18 September 1931 a small explosion damaged South Manchuria Railway track near Mukden. Japanese army officers blamed Chinese forces and used it as the pretext for a sweeping operation. Contemporary reports show major cities taken within days. The speed and scale make “protecting one bit of track” a very unconvincing job description.

passages.title: Warlord power, invasion and a state built under occupation
passages.text: The 1932 Lytton Commission did not treat Manchukuo as the product of a genuine, spontaneous independence movement. It recognized China’s sovereignty while proposing a negotiated autonomous arrangement. The League could investigate and condemn, but it could not force the Kwantung Army to leave; Japan later withdrew from the organization.

passages.title: Warlord power, invasion and a state built under occupation
passages.text: Puyi supplied imperial ceremony, while Japanese military and bureaucratic networks held decisive power. Manchukuo advertised harmony among peoples and a modern developmental state. That language mattered because officials, teachers and filmmakers repeated it; it did not make unequal rule equal, or conquest consensual.

passages.title: Resistance, total war and the violent 1945 break
passages.text: Armed resistance did not end when the new flag went up. Chinese volunteer armies, Communist guerrillas and other local forces fought Japanese and Manchukuo troops, while civilians faced reprisals, policing and demands for supplies. “Bandit” in an official file might describe a robber, a guerrilla or simply someone the state wanted discredited.

passages.title: Resistance, total war and the violent 1945 break
passages.text: From 1937, Manchukuo became a deeper rear base for Japan’s war in China. State agencies pushed production, youth organizations and political ritual toward total mobilization. Some residents collaborated, some resisted, many adapted to survive, and the same person could make different choices as danger, hunger and family duties changed.

passages.title: Resistance, total war and the violent 1945 break
passages.text: Japanese settlement was presented as peaceful pioneering, yet land acquisition and armed protection placed settlers inside a coercive colonial project. Settler families also endured harsh climates, debt and later abandonment. Recognizing their suffering does not erase the greater power that placed them on land taken from Chinese communities.

passages.title: Resistance, total war and the violent 1945 break
passages.text: In August 1945 the Soviet offensive shattered the regime. Soviet statements describe disarming Japanese forces and removing prisoners to the USSR; refugee research records confusion, flight, separation and death among civilians. Official military verbs such as “disarmed” fit neatly in a telegram. A lost child did not experience 1945 so neatly.

passages.title: Resistance, total war and the violent 1945 break
passages.text: The end of Manchukuo did not create peace. Nationalist and Communist forces raced for railways, cities, weapons and factories. Contemporary U.S. reporting was full of claims about Soviet help and Communist organization that observers themselves could not always verify. The Northeast became a central theater of renewed Chinese civil war.

passages.title: Railways, soybeans, factories and who paid for growth
passages.text: Railways did far more than carry passengers. Different gauges and competing lines channeled soybeans from station districts toward Dalian, shaped which market a village used and gave railway companies economic and political power. A soybean could become oil, animal feed or fertilizer after a journey organized by timetables, warehouses and empire.

passages.title: Railways, soybeans, factories and who paid for growth
passages.text: Manchukuo’s planners built mines, steelworks, chemicals, dams and machine plants through a controlled economy dominated by Japanese military and corporate interests. These were substantial industrial achievements by engineers and workers. Calling them proof of benevolent rule would ignore expropriation, coercion and the war those factories supplied.

passages.title: Railways, soybeans, factories and who paid for growth
passages.text: Rural families often combined farming with migration, tenancy and side work. Research on southern villages finds high burdens from landlords, security charges and protection rackets, with households moving when survival became impossible. A model village on a poster could have straight roads while the family budget underneath it was thoroughly crooked.

passages.title: Railways, soybeans, factories and who paid for growth
passages.text: Korean “collective farms” supplied the Kwantung Army and Japanese markets. By 1944 they held about 24,000 immigrant families inside settlements designed for surveillance and control. Families hoped leased land might become theirs after debts were paid, but the same arrangement tied work, residence and policing tightly together.

passages.title: Railways, soybeans, factories and who paid for growth
passages.text: After 1949 the PRC repaired and expanded inherited industry. Soviet-aid projects enlarged Anshan steel and built giant machinery works in Shenyang and Harbin. Workers gained technical skills and produced nationally important goods, while heavy-industry priority also directed housing, food and investment toward strategic cities rather than evenly across the countryside.

passages.title: Families, migration and social rank
passages.text: No single “Manchurian family” existed. Han Chinese migrants, Manchu communities, Mongols, Koreans, Japanese settlers, Russians and others used different languages, religions and kinship customs. Class, city or village, gender and legal status often mattered as much as an ethnic label. The state’s harmony posters simplified households that were busy being complicated.

passages.title: Families, migration and social rank
passages.text: Paperwork could split neighbors into different political boxes. Japanese koseki, Manchukuo minseki and residence records overlapped awkwardly for Japanese, Korean and Taiwanese subjects. Registration affected who belonged where, while the regime never solved one clear nationality law. Even an empire can discover that families refuse to fit tidy filing drawers.

passages.title: Families, migration and social rank
passages.text: Japanese emigration campaigns recruited rural households and unmarried young men, then sought wives for settlement. Propaganda praised brave pioneer families; memory studies show hardship, abandoned women and children, and the unequal land system around them. Family was both a source of care and a tool through which the empire tried to plant permanence.

passages.title: Families, migration and social rank
passages.text: Korean migrants were not merely an ethnic stripe on a poster. Many were farming families living under Japanese colonial subjecthood, company leases and anti-guerrilla surveillance. Some pursued land and stability; others met debt and exploitation. Their position differed from Japanese settlers and Chinese villagers, even when all worked the same cold soil.

passages.title: Families, migration and social rank
passages.text: Housing shortages and homelessness made official talk of modern cities feel remote to many urban residents. People shared rooms, moved repeatedly, relied on relatives or improvised shelter. The surviving study draws on later recollections and newspapers, so it cannot reconstruct every household; it does recover the constant work of finding somewhere to sleep.

passages.title: Homes, meals, clothes and a little entertainment
passages.text: Northeast winters could last for months, making the heated kang platform the warm heart of many traditional Manchu homes. People could eat, welcome visitors, talk and sleep on it. A kang was part bed, part bench and part radiator, excellent engineering, though anyone claiming the warmest spot probably inspired a family argument.

passages.title: Homes, meals, clothes and a little entertainment
passages.text: Food depended on place and purse. Sorghum, called gaoliang, appears in accounts of rural and school meals; soybeans were a major cash crop, while wheat, millet, maize and vegetables also mattered. Wartime rationing made staples and fuel harder to obtain. A railway full of export soy did not guarantee a full family bowl.

passages.title: Homes, meals, clothes and a little entertainment
passages.text: A girls’ school report described students and Japanese teachers eating gaoliang, living in mud houses and sleeping on kangs. The article came through a colonial newspaper eager to praise devotion, so its cozy details require caution. Students really did clean rooms and repair heating; propaganda decided what moral readers should extract from the chores.

passages.title: Homes, meals, clothes and a little entertainment
passages.text: Clothing changed with weather, work, fashion, income and politics. Visual research tracks representations of Manchu women’s hair and dress across Chinese, Japanese, Manchu and Western sources into the 1940s. That evidence warns against dressing everyone in one timeless costume. Padded winter layers were practical; identity was never stitched from one pattern.

passages.title: Homes, meals, clothes and a little entertainment
passages.text: Radio and film offered entertainment, jobs and propaganda at once. Listeners could hear more than one language; Chinese filmmakers made dialogue features for Chinese audiences while negotiating censorship and commercial taste. Viewers sometimes wanted a good story more than a lecture. Empires, like parents, can discover that a captive audience is still a critic.

passages.title: School days, printed words and culture under supervision
passages.text: School access was unequal by location, ethnicity, gender and family income. Colonial officials expanded institutions while also using classrooms to teach loyalty. Some Japanese educators promoted child-centered language lessons rooted in ordinary life; military orthodoxy kept pressing harder. A textbook about breakfast could still be part of an argument about empire.

passages.title: School days, printed words and culture under supervision
passages.text: Girls’ secondary schooling mixed literacy and vocational training with lessons about domestic service, motherhood and sacrifice to the state. Mongol pupils were asked to clean, mend screens and repair kangs; teachers offered Japanese dances. The girls learned real skills, but the curriculum imagined their education flowing onward to husbands, fathers and children.

passages.title: School days, printed words and culture under supervision
passages.text: Authentic written sample: “創立滿洲國” (modern Mandarin pinyin: chuànglì Mǎnzhōuguó) means “establish the State of Manchuria.” It appears in the 1 March 1932 founding proclamation in traditional Chinese characters. This is the regime speaking in an official document, not proof that thirty million residents agreed with what the document claimed.

passages.title: School days, printed words and culture under supervision
passages.text: The Manchuria Film Association employed Chinese actors, writers, directors and technicians to make Chinese-language entertainment. They worked inside a Japanese-financed propaganda institution but still argued over stories, dialogue and technique. Skills and professional networks survived the regime; some workers continued in postwar socialist cinema after the studio changed political owners.

passages.title: School days, printed words and culture under supervision
passages.text: Radio planners hoped dual-language broadcasting would make a new “Manchurian” identity, yet reception and participation fell short of official ambition. A family might hear music, news, advertising and orders from the same box. The technology widened a public sphere while giving the state another voice at the dinner table.

passages.title: Doctors, nurses, plague control and medical crimes
passages.text: Pneumonic plague began in the region in late 1920 and lasted into 1921. The historical study counts more than 9,300 deaths, over half in Harbin. Russian and Chinese districts had separate authorities, so disease control also became a struggle over jurisdiction, movement and whose neighborhood received which rules.

passages.title: Doctors, nurses, plague control and medical crimes
passages.text: Manchukuo Red Cross hospitals offered mobile clinics, ambulances, home nursing, maternity and child care; nurses also served primary schools. Those services helped real patients. The organization simultaneously supported the Kwantung Army’s nation-building and later wartime mobilization, so a bandage and a propaganda poster could share an institution.

passages.title: Doctors, nurses, plague control and medical crimes
passages.text: Colonial medical colleges trained practitioners and produced research, but power shaped whose body counted as protected. Scholarship documents unethical experimentation and dissections involving Chinese people before Unit 731’s worst crimes. “Modern medicine” is not automatically humane; methods, consent and the value assigned to a patient’s life matter.

passages.title: Doctors, nurses, plague control and medical crimes
passages.text: Unit 731 near Harbin deliberately infected prisoners and civilians, conducted lethal experiments and developed biological weapons. Victims included Chinese people and others held without consent; accurate totals may never be known because evidence and prisoners were destroyed in 1945. This was organized atrocity, not an unfortunate medical mistake.

passages.title: Doctors, nurses, plague control and medical crimes
passages.text: After the war, U.S. officials traded protection from prosecution for data from Japanese biological-warfare researchers. That decision denied justice and helped bury victims’ stories. A scientific notebook produced through torture does not become ethical because another government wants its results; the cover-up belongs inside the history of medicine too.

passages.title: Water, toilets, cleanliness and postwar campaigns
passages.text: Manchukuo promoted modern avenues and showcase buildings, but ordinary accounts describe housing shortages, dirty water, waste and inadequate sanitation. Infrastructure differed sharply between planned districts and poorer neighborhoods. A grand boulevard is easy to photograph; the queue at a shared pump or latrine is where urban modernity receives its less glamorous exam.

passages.title: Water, toilets, cleanliness and postwar campaigns
passages.text: The early PRC made “water improvement” part of Patriotic Health Campaigns: protect household supplies, improve wells, spread hygiene information and reduce waterborne disease. The national review cannot prove identical implementation in every Northeast village, but it identifies the program residents encountered and the practical problem officials meant to solve.

passages.title: Water, toilets, cleanliness and postwar campaigns
passages.text: Campaigns also targeted rubbish, flies, rats, mosquitoes and toilets. Some communities built latrines and composted night soil before using it as fertilizer, reducing parasite exposure when done properly. That is not a glamorous discovery, but preventing feces from delivering yesterday’s dinner guests a fresh crop of worms is a serious public-health achievement.

passages.title: Water, toilets, cleanliness and postwar campaigns
passages.text: Posters taught families to clean homes and kitchens, stop spitting, vaccinate and recognize disease. Pictures could communicate where literacy was limited. Campaigns expanded prevention, yet politics and mass pressure shaped participation, and services remained uneven. Sweeping a lane helped; it could not substitute for trained staff, medicine or safe pipes.

passages.title: Water, toilets, cleanliness and postwar campaigns
passages.text: In 1958 the Great Leap pulled labor toward crash industrial and collective projects as food production and distribution deteriorated. The Northeast’s recorded famine mortality was generally below the worst-hit provinces, partly because strategic urban and industrial populations had stronger claims on grain. “Less catastrophic” remains a grim comparison, not a fun fact.

Nothing called “Manchuria” fell in 1960. The atlas merely merges this regional polygon into china. By then Liaoning, Jilin, Heilongjiang and adjoining areas were governed within the People’s Republic, families and factories continued, and the Great Leap famine was still unfolding. The earlier political ending came in 1945, when Soviet invasion destroyed Manchukuo; even that did not end the region’s communities or settle control, because civil war followed. Treat 1960 as a database handoff and 1945 as a regime collapse, not as the disappearance of a place or a people.

passages.text: Mandan communities built farming villages along the Missouri River and became important partners in Plains exchange. The imported outline lies near their historic village country in present-day North Dakota, but its dates describe map coverage. Mandan people remain a distinct people within today’s Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation.

passages.title: Farming, homes and village discoveries
passages.text: Double Ditch, north of present-day Bismarck, preserves a Mandan village occupied for roughly three centuries, from around 1490 to 1785. Its name is misleadingly modest: researchers have identified four successive defensive ditches. The settlement’s changing boundaries record a community repeatedly rebuilding its surroundings.

passages.title: Farming, homes and village discoveries
passages.text: Geophysical instruments revealed buried hearths, storage pits and two previously unrecognized fortifications at Double Ditch. Archaeologists then checked the signals through excavation. The combination uncovered parts of village life that a walk across the grassy surface could easily miss.

passages.title: Farming, homes and village discoveries
passages.text: Mandan farmers raised corn, beans, squash, sunflowers and tobacco. Stored harvests supported village life and exchange with other Plains communities, while hunting supplied bison and other animals. A farming village could therefore be a trading destination as well as a place to grow dinner.

passages.title: Farming, homes and village discoveries
passages.text: Community-authored teaching materials describe women owning and building earthlodges, with men helping move heavy logs. Wood, branches, grass and earth formed substantial homes. Mandan builders used clay in their coverings, and strong roofs could become places to sit and watch village activity.

passages.title: Farming, homes and village discoveries
passages.text: Relatives often placed their lodges near one another. Children could play close to family while adults visited and worked. The same teaching account describes cottonwood collected after spring ice had knocked trees down, then left to dry: housebuilding began well before the house appeared.

passages.title: Farming, homes and village discoveries
passages.text: Harvest preservation required practical defenses against hungry animals. Raised drying platforms helped keep food away from dogs. Women dried crops for later use, turning a short growing season into meals that could last through much colder weather.

passages.title: Farming, homes and village discoveries
passages.text: Underground food caches were lined with grasses and sticks, reached by a ladder and carefully covered. Some were inside lodges, others outside. Concealing the lid protected an important family store: the pantry could be beneath your feet.

passages.title: Farming, homes and village discoveries
passages.text: In the game called tchung-kee, Mandan and Hidatsa players rolled a small stone ring and threw long poles, trying to send a pole through the moving opening. The challenge joined timing, aim and competition. A little ring could demand a surprisingly large amount of skill.

passages.title: Trade, disruption and living language
passages.text: The American Fur Company built Fort Clark beside a Mandan village in 1830 to 1831. In 1832, the steamboat Yellow Stone delivered goods and carried beaver pelts and bison robes back toward St. Louis. Village trade now connected households to a much longer commercial river route.

passages.title: Trade, disruption and living language
passages.text: In 1837, the steamboat St. Peters arrived carrying people infected with smallpox. A devastating epidemic swept through the Mandan village at Fort Clark. Survivors left to join Hidatsa communities near the Knife River. These were catastrophic human losses, followed by survival and rebuilding rather than the end of Mandan people.

passages.title: Trade, disruption and living language
passages.text: Commissioned in 1905, Sitting Rabbit’s remarkable map stretched along a canvas more than 23 feet long. It recorded Missouri River places and older villages through Mandan knowledge and pictorial detail. The river’s bends were adapted to the long format, creating a historical landscape that could be unrolled.

passages.title: Trade, disruption and living language
passages.text: The Garrison Dam project displaced families from fertile Missouri bottomlands in the twentieth century. MHA Nation’s history describes lost farms and communities and relocation onto less productive uplands. A change in the river’s level could therefore alter food production, neighboring relationships and the places where family memories lived.

passages.title: Trade, disruption and living language
passages.text: A modern Mandan writing sample is “Ráátinitak shí’sh.” The MHA Nation website translates it as “It is good that you all arrived”. The site prints distinct Hidatsa and Arikara welcomes beside it, making clear that the three affiliated peoples have different languages.

passages.title: Trade, disruption and living language
passages.text: A Mandan alphabet coloring book published in 2016 invites children to trace letters and words and use a color key. Its exercises make literacy something a child can practice with a pencil.

passages.title: Trade, disruption and living language
passages.text: MHA Nation’s language programs maintain separate work for Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara. Mentor-and-apprentice learning connects experienced speakers with learners who can become future teachers. Modern classes and children’s resources belong to the continuing history of these communities.

The imported endpoint of 1783 is not an ending for the Mandan people. Epidemics, relocation and later flooding of river-bottom lands transformed community life. Mandan identity and language work continue within the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation.

Edwin Ko, Amanda Foster and Robert Rugh: Mandan ABC Coloring Book, 2016

sectionTitles: Many communities and an early urban world
Households, skilled hands and material clues
Music, teaching and a modern written sample

passages.text: “Mandes” is a broad map label for diverse Mande-speaking peoples, not one kingdom. Its enormous 900 to 1000 polygon should not be read as a precise language frontier. Regional archaeology and clearly dated later examples reveal distinct communities, occupations and artistic traditions; they do not give every enclosed settlement one identity.

passages.title: Many communities and an early urban world
passages.text: Mande is a language family with dozens of members, divided into major Western and South-Eastern branches. Sharing linguistic relationships does not make their speakers one dynasty, religion or occupation. The map’s short label covers a far more varied human story.

passages.title: Many communities and an early urban world
passages.text: At Jenné-jeno in Mali, excavators traced a city that had grown to roughly thirty-three hectares by about 600 to 800 CE. Its substantial mud-brick enclosure and neighboring settlement mounds show urban life before the Mali Empire. This is regional evidence, not a census of its residents’ languages.

passages.title: Many communities and an early urban world
passages.text: The 1977 excavations at Jenné-jeno recovered evidence of African rice, fish and cattle. These linked floodplain farming, fishing and herding in an economy that supported permanent settlement. A city’s history can begin with reliable meals as well as famous rulers.

passages.title: Many communities and an early urban world
passages.text: Sandstone grinding equipment and volcanic stone ornaments found in the delta had to come from beyond the local floodplain. The excavators also identified distant copper and gold connections during the first millennium CE. Everyday food preparation and personal decoration both depended on exchange.

passages.title: Households, skilled hands and material clues
passages.text: Later excavations at Jenné-jeno found relatively little variation between sampled areas in quantities of imported copper, stone and other goods. That complicates an easy picture of one fabulously rich quarter. The researchers caution that vanished materials, including textiles, could once have displayed differences that no longer survive.

passages.title: Households, skilled hands and material clues
passages.text: At nearby Djenné, a different, later excavation uncovered a well lined with stacked pots whose bottoms were open. Lower occupation deposits were provisionally dated to the fifteenth to seventeenth centuries. Ceramic vessels could serve underground engineering as well as kitchens.

passages.title: Households, skilled hands and material clues
passages.text: A photograph taken in Sissingué in 1992 records potter Fatoumata Kouyaté beginning a vessel with a cylinder of clay. She presses and hollows it by hand, then draws the sides upward. This named craftswoman’s method makes the shaping process visible, before firing turns soft clay into a useful container.

passages.title: Households, skilled hands and material clues
passages.text: A Malinke hunter’s shirt in the Carlos Museum, made in the late nineteenth or early twentieth century, carries leather packets, shells, claws and horns on cloth. Its attachments expressed accumulated knowledge and protective beliefs. The garment could become a changing record of its wearer’s experience.

passages.title: Music, teaching and a modern written sample
passages.text: At Nyagassola in Guinea, the Dökala family safeguards the Sosso-Bala, a balafon associated with Manding epic traditions. Its twenty wooden slats have calabashes beneath them. UNESCO’s account describes a living musical responsibility passed within a family, not simply an old object in storage.

passages.title: Music, teaching and a modern written sample
passages.text: The Balatigui, the instrument’s guardian, also teaches balafon to children from about seven years old. UNESCO identified the departure of young people from the village as a threat to transmission. An instrument’s future depends on someone learning how to play it.

passages.title: Music, teaching and a modern written sample
passages.text: A 2004 N’Ko encoding proposal prints “ߕߐ߮”, transliterated tô and translated “name”. It explains that related Manding varieties can share this spelling while pronouncing it differently. This is an attested modern written example; N’Ko was devised in 1949, long after the map’s medieval interval.

passages.title: Music, teaching and a modern written sample
passages.text: N’Ko records vowels and tone with letters and added marks. Its decorative sign “߷”, called gbakurunen, represents the three stones that hold a cooking pot over a fire and marks major text divisions. A familiar household arrangement thus has a place on the written page.

The map’s endpoint in 1000 is not the fall of the Mande-speaking peoples. Different communities subsequently joined or formed states, changed livelihoods and developed new forms of writing and art. Their shared language relationships never gave them one founding date or a single ending.

Turn a wild plant into a dependable crop
