sectionTitles: Read the map before believing its giant label
Cross dry valleys, wet forests, estuaries and cold highlands
Follow domestication without inventing one first farmer
Turn plants, fish and game into actual meals
Choose between moving camp, returning to shelters and building villages
Make stone edges, hot pots, fiber gear and exchange routes
Grow up inside households, networks and changing social ranks
Face sore teeth, unsafe food, scarce water and the toilet question
Ask about belief, rank, conflict and play without filling gaps
Celebrate real achievements and let the false ending dissolve

passages.text: The atlas gives one enormous color the name “Mesoamerican hunter-gatherers and maize farmers” from 2000 to 1500 BCE. The decoded polygon is stranger than that label: it runs from northwestern Mexico and the lower Rio Grande through Central America and Colombia, then follows parts of the Andes to Cuzco and Lake Titicaca. It excludes several nearby coasts and cities. Nobody called this whole shape home, shared one language, or followed one economy. Archaeology instead reveals local worlds. Some families moved among seasonal camps, caves, fishing places and fields. Others lived in villages, stored harvests, fired pottery, exchanged volcanic glass, or tended maize, squash, avocado, chili, tubers and many wild plants. In the Titicaca highlands, households combined quinoa, potatoes and camelids; on tropical coasts and wetlands, fish, shellfish, roots and tree fruits mattered. Tiny starch grains, phytoliths, charred seeds, bones, residues, isotopes, ancient DNA, house floors and radiocarbon dates supply different clues, each with limits. At 1500 BCE the atlas replaces the color with several new labels. That is a cartographic edit, not the fall of one civilization.

passages.title: Read the map before believing its giant label
passages.text: The indexed record preserves the exact id, the accented display name “Mesoamerican hunter-gatherers and maïze farmers,” circa dates from 2000 to 1500 BCE, and kind “culture.” Coverage records exactly one border interval and no earlier card or summary. Those are database facts, not proof of one ancient culture, ancestry, language or government.

passages.title: Read the map before believing its giant label
passages.text: At 2000 BCE the target is one Polygon with 504 positions and bounds from about 113 degrees west to 65 degrees west, and from 25 degrees south to 32 degrees north. Sampled points inside include Hermosillo, Mexico City, Tikal, Panama City, Bogota, Cuzco and La Paz. Tucson, Merida, Belize City, Quito and Lima fall outside.

passages.title: Read the map before believing its giant label
passages.text: At 1500 BCE the target vanishes. Hermosillo and Chihuahua become “desert hunter-gatherers,” much of Mexico and Central America becomes “maize farmers,” Villahermosa becomes “Olmec,” and Cartagena, Bogota, Cuzco and La Paz become “manioc farmers.” The 1000 BCE file repeats those categories. That seam describes atlas editing, not a continent-wide takeover.

passages.title: Read the map before believing its giant label
passages.text: Contemporaneous written-language sample: none is securely known for this exact umbrella and interval. Original script: unavailable. Transliteration: unavailable. Translation: unavailable. The debated Cascajal signs date around 900 BCE, roughly six centuries after this card ends, and belong to a specific Gulf Coast context. Borrowing them, Maya glyphs or a modern language would fabricate evidence.

passages.title: Read the map before believing its giant label
passages.text: A seed can be directly dated, starch may be identified on a tool, and bone chemistry can estimate long-term diet. A story about who planted, taught or ruled is an inference. Modern farming or craft practice can suggest possibilities only as labeled comparison. This card keeps those three levels separate and never treats an atlas border as an excavation result.

passages.title: Cross dry valleys, wet forests, estuaries and cold highlands
passages.text: The Central Balsas is a seasonal tropical forest, not a dusty “desert cradle.” Lake sediments, pollen, phytoliths and charcoal show changing vegetation and human activity. Lakes and stream edges offered water and workable soils. A microscopic maize trace records cultivation nearby, but it does not reveal a fenced field, its owner or how many meals depended on it.

passages.title: Cross dry valleys, wet forests, estuaries and cold highlands
passages.text: Tehuacan-Cuicatlan combines arid and semiarid valleys, cactus forests, agaves, oaks and sharp elevation changes. UNESCO records a twelve-thousand-year sequence of adaptation, domestication and water management. The landscape rewarded detailed knowledge of springs, seasonal rain and useful plants. Particular canals or dams still need their own dates before being assigned to 2000 BCE.

passages.title: Cross dry valleys, wet forests, estuaries and cold highlands
passages.text: Central Panama preserves a different story. Pollen, phytoliths and charcoal indicate long-running forest disturbance, burning and cultivation. Forest farming was not simply “destroy the jungle and plant corn.” People used patches, edges, tree foods, seed crops and roots. Lake cores capture broad vegetation change, while excavated tools identify what was processed at particular places.

passages.title: Cross dry valleys, wet forests, estuaries and cold highlands
passages.text: Soconusco households lived beside a Pacific plain threaded with rivers, lagoons and rich estuaries. Earlier mobile groups collected marsh clams; around 1900 BCE permanent villages appeared, yet inland and estuary sites used different vessel shapes and resources. The wetland was a food pantry and travel route, not empty ground waiting for farmers.

passages.title: Cross dry valleys, wet forests, estuaries and cold highlands
passages.text: At nearly 3,900 meters in the Titicaca Basin, frost, thin air and changing lake levels shaped another mapped world. Local evidence tracks mixed cultivation, herding, hunting and gathering rather than maize farming alone. Climate studies help reconstruct water levels, but researchers warn against turning every environmental shift into an automatic migration or political collapse.

passages.title: Follow domestication without inventing one first farmer
passages.text: At Xihuatoxtla in the Central Balsas, maize starch and cob phytoliths occur on grinding tools and in deposits dated to about 8,700 years ago. The investigators tested whether people used teosinte ears or maize stalk sugar and found evidence favoring maize kernels and cobs. That is strong local evidence, not the name of an inventor or village.

passages.title: Follow domestication without inventing one first farmer
passages.text: Guila Naquitz Cave produced directly dated small maize cobs as well as much older domesticated squash. The maize already differed from wild teosinte, yet domestication continued after its first appearance. Selection happened through countless choices about seeds, planting places and harvests. It was a long relationship among people, plants and environments, not a single lightning-bolt discovery.

passages.title: Follow domestication without inventing one first farmer
passages.text: Coxcatlan Cave once seemed to provide a perfectly stacked crop timeline. Direct AMS dating later showed that some organic remains had moved vertically in parts of the deposit. Squash, bottle gourd and maize dates had to be reassessed. This correction is an achievement: good archaeology checks old collections instead of protecting a famous story from new measurements.

passages.title: Follow domestication without inventing one first farmer
passages.text: Maize, chili and common bean did not necessarily originate in the same Mexican valley. A study combining genetics, archaeology, plant distributions and historical linguistics points to different likely origin regions. Even that model carries uncertainty. A useful “food package” could form gradually as crops traveled, without a committee deciding that every household must plant the same garden.

passages.title: Follow domestication without inventing one first farmer
passages.text: The polygon also reaches the Titicaca highlands, where maize is the wrong default. Jiskairumoko tools preserve potato starch, and nearby research finds quinoa, other tubers and camelid foods through the Terminal Archaic and Early Formative. These communities developed a separate high-altitude food system. Their inclusion proves how misleading the atlas label can be.

passages.title: Turn plants, fish and game into actual meals
passages.text: Human bone chemistry from Belize shows maize becoming important unevenly. Some individuals ate substantial maize between about 4700 and 4000 years ago, and after 4000 years ago it became a persistent staple in that sample. At Western Lagoon, fish canals instead reveal an intensive aquatic strategy around this era. Neighboring communities could build very different meals from the same broad landscape.

passages.title: Turn plants, fish and game into actual meals
passages.text: El Gigante rockshelter in Honduras preserves avocado, ciruela, squash, maize and later beans. Hundreds of direct plant dates reveal long gaps between visits and a stronger shift toward field crops after 4000 years ago. During this card's interval, productive maize was present, but tree fruits remained important. Farming and orchard-like tending could share the same food world.

passages.title: Turn plants, fish and game into actual meals
passages.text: Early Soconusco village deposits contain charred maize, beans and avocado, while estuaries supplied clams, fish and shrimp. Cacao residues occur in vessels at specific Pacific and Gulf Coast sites, including San Lorenzo contexts beginning near 1800 BCE. Residue proves a cacao product touched a pot; it cannot tell us that everyone drank chocolate or used one recipe.

passages.title: Turn plants, fish and game into actual meals
passages.text: Panamanian tools carry starch from maize, yams, arrowroot, Calathea, Zamia and, around 1650 BCE, manioc. Some Zamia and cassava foods contain natural toxins and require careful processing. Modern chemistry shows why crushing, soaking, fermenting or roasting can help, but one starch grain cannot reveal the ancient recipe, cassava variety or exact safety sequence.

passages.title: Turn plants, fish and game into actual meals
passages.text: Grinding stones directly show kernels being crushed. Alkaline cooking called nixtamalization later made maize softer and improved nutrition, but the earliest direct vessel evidence currently cited for the Maya area is many centuries after this interval. So this card does not serve 1800 BCE tortillas as fact. Ancient cooks boiled, ground and mixed foods, while exact recipes remain uncertain.

passages.title: Choose between moving camp, returning to shelters and building villages
passages.text: Xihuatoxtla was a boulder shelter used repeatedly by small groups. Stone tools, hearth-related charcoal and plant residues suggest seasonal movement combined with cultivation near water. Growing maize did not instantly bolt people to one permanent house. Families could tend plots, collect wild foods, hunt and revisit protected places on a yearly round.

passages.title: Choose between moving camp, returning to shelters and building villages
passages.text: Systematic survey in the Cuauhtemoc region finds some of Soconusco's earliest pottery-using villages around 1900 BCE. Settlements ranged in size rather than appearing as one sudden city. Survey sees distributions of artifacts across space; excavation adds floors, pits and refuse. Together they show village growth without proving that every mapped household became sedentary at once.

passages.title: Choose between moving camp, returning to shelters and building villages
passages.text: Monagrillo communities in Panama made pottery from about 3520 to 1300 calibrated BCE. At the coastal type site, shell growth studies suggest much dry-season use, while other places lay inland or in foothills. People could maintain recurring coastal work camps and more permanent bases elsewhere. “Pottery user” therefore does not automatically mean “full-time village farmer.”

passages.title: Choose between moving camp, returning to shelters and building villages
passages.text: El Gigante is a huge dry rockshelter, yet its crop sequence contains occupation gaps lasting centuries. Deep valley-bottom soils below offered better farming than the steep surrounding slopes. A shelter can preserve thousands of cobs while still being only one stop in a broader landscape. Archaeological abundance is not always the same thing as year-round residence.

passages.title: Choose between moving camp, returning to shelters and building villages
passages.text: By about 2300 BCE, Jiskairumoko had five pithouses arranged in a circle, each with storage alcoves. Repairs, cleaning and patterned refuse support long residence. This is direct evidence for a settled highland hamlet. It does not identify a mayor, property deeds or a universal Andean house plan, and it shares no necessary identity with Mexican villages.

passages.title: Make stone edges, hot pots, fiber gear and exchange routes
passages.text: Xihuatoxtla people reduced local stone cores into flakes used as knives, scrapers, borers and other working edges. Grinding bases and handstones handled plant foods. Later levels include obsidian blades, but the early toolkit was mostly local. “Simple flake” describes manufacture, not intelligence; choosing a quick sharp edge can be excellent engineering.

passages.title: Make stone edges, hot pots, fiber gear and exchange routes
passages.text: San Jacinto 1 in northern Colombia shows that mobile gatherers could also be expert potters. They mixed plant fiber into clay, decorated vessels and gathered seasonally to process wild plants. Researchers infer serving, feasting or short storage more strongly than cooking. Pottery did not wait for intensive farming, and decoration did not require a state workshop.

passages.title: Make stone edges, hot pots, fiber gear and exchange routes
passages.text: Monagrillo potters layered clay slabs, finished rims in varied ways and achieved estimated firing temperatures above 800 degrees Celsius, surprisingly high for open firing. Chemical and mineral study identifies more than one clay source. Fun fact: a plain-looking sherd can preserve a whole engineering problem about clay, air, fuel, heat and timing.

passages.title: Make stone edges, hot pots, fiber gear and exchange routes
passages.text: At San Lorenzo, geochemical tests trace obsidian cutting tools to distant volcanic sources. In the Titicaca Basin, nonlocal obsidian reached lake islands, with watercraft exchange securely visible by about 1600 BCE. These are separate networks thousands of kilometers apart. Similar shiny stone never proves one transcontinental trade league or shared leadership.

passages.title: Make stone edges, hot pots, fiber gear and exchange routes
passages.text: Dry Tehuacan contexts preserve ixtle cord along with stone tools, cobs and seeds. Cord implies twisting fibers for carrying, tying, netting or other tasks, but it does not reconstruct a wardrobe. Most cloth, wood and basketry decay, especially in tropical soil. Ancient people were surrounded by “soft technology” that museum cases often fail to show.

passages.title: Grow up inside households, networks and changing social ranks
passages.text: Village floors, hearths and trash clusters identify repeated domestic activity, not a modern nuclear-family diagram. A house could include partners, children, elders, other kin, visitors or dependents. Soconusco settlement differences show that households were becoming more varied, but archaeology cannot assign one marriage rule or descent system to everyone inside the atlas polygon.

passages.title: Grow up inside households, networks and changing social ranks
passages.text: Belize rockshelters contain adults, juveniles and infants buried across a long span. Isotopes reveal diets, while ancient DNA detects population movement and mixture. Neither method turns every nearby burial into a biological family. The evidence makes children visible and shows changing connections, but spoken identities and household membership require more than bones placed in one shelter.

passages.title: Grow up inside households, networks and changing social ranks
passages.text: An earlier Coxcatlan burial belongs to a woman who had severe tooth loss, abscesses, an old injury and skeletal changes consistent with long-distance carrying. She survived for years, suggesting assistance with food and work. This is a moving local comparison, not permission to assign all farming, carrying or healing in 2000 BCE to women.

passages.title: Grow up inside households, networks and changing social ranks
passages.text: Children had to learn when seeds were ready, how clay should feel, where fish moved and how a cutting edge was struck. No exact-period schoolhouse or lesson text survives. Later pottery ethnoarchaeology shows children learning beside relatives through observation and practice, a useful possibility rather than direct proof for every ancient household.

passages.title: Grow up inside households, networks and changing social ranks
passages.text: Plant knowledge included gathering, tending favored wild stands, planting, protecting useful trees and selecting seed. Modern Mesoamerican studies show a continuum rather than a clean wild-versus-farm switch. Such expertise was transmitted socially, but the archaeological record rarely names the teacher. Women, men, elders and children must remain possible participants unless local evidence narrows the answer.

passages.title: Face sore teeth, unsafe food, scarce water and the toilet question
passages.text: The Coxcatlan woman had worn teeth, cavities, abscesses, arthritis and a healed injury. Her case shows how skeletons can record chronic pain, diet and workload. It predates this card and represents one person, so it cannot supply a regional health score. Evidence of survival suggests care, but it does not identify a healer or treatment.

passages.title: Face sore teeth, unsafe food, scarce water and the toilet question
passages.text: Stable carbon and nitrogen isotopes estimate major long-term food inputs, not vitamin levels, recipes or every hungry season. Belize results show maize increasing while forest foods remained. Researchers correct infant nitrogen values for nursing effects, a reminder that age matters. A diet can be reconstructed statistically without telling us whether a particular child liked dinner.

passages.title: Face sore teeth, unsafe food, scarce water and the toilet question
passages.text: People surely treated cuts, fever, pain and childbirth, but no securely identified 2000 to 1500 BCE medical kit or prescription belongs to this umbrella. Useful plants are not automatically medicines, and red pigment in a burial is not a drug. The honest card records care and botanical knowledge while leaving diagnosis, healer roles and dosage unknown.

passages.title: Face sore teeth, unsafe food, scarce water and the toilet question
passages.text: Water shaped where people camped and settled. Tehuacan-Cuicatlan later developed canals, wells, aqueducts and dams, while Titicaca pithouses clustered near river terraces as lake conditions changed. These landscapes show water knowledge over long spans. Exact structures need direct dates, so the card does not hand every 1800 BCE household an irrigation canal.

passages.title: Face sore teeth, unsafe food, scarce water and the toilet question
passages.text: No standard toilet, sewer or latrine is securely documented for this enormous category. People probably used outdoor places, pits or refuse zones, but soil, water and later occupation can erase them. Coprolites and parasite eggs sometimes preserve diet and infection; identifying the human or animal producer is difficult. “No toilet found” is evidence uncertainty, not proof of careless hygiene.

passages.title: Ask about belief, rank, conflict and play without filling gaps
passages.text: At Jiskairumoko, a burial dating about 2155 to 1936 BCE included cold-hammered native-gold beads. The necklace suggests display and emerging difference, but gold did not require a king or full-time metalworkers. Burial treatment can express memory, affection, identity or status. It cannot reveal one Andean religion, much less beliefs across the entire polygon.

passages.title: Ask about belief, rank, conflict and play without filling gaps
passages.text: San Jacinto's elaborate fiber-tempered vessels were probably used for serving, feasting or short storage rather than everyday cooking. That interpretation joins vessel form, decoration, wear and site context. A gathering may have mixed food, stories and social display, yet no surviving song, prayer or party invitation tells archaeologists exactly what participants believed.

passages.title: Ask about belief, rank, conflict and play without filling gaps
passages.text: By about 1650 BCE, Soconusco settlement sizes, buildings and valued goods suggest emerging privilege. Scholars debate how leadership worked and whether some large structures were elite residences or communal spaces. Inequality can begin before a palace appears, but “some people had more” does not prove taxes, slavery, police or a coercive state spanning Mesoamerica.

passages.title: Ask about belief, rank, conflict and play without filling gaps
passages.text: Points, blades and projectiles could hunt animals, cut plants, defend people or hurt human opponents. Context and skeletal trauma are needed before calling an artifact a war weapon. None of the reviewed evidence supports one army, conquest or warfare system across the atlas layer. Conflict was possible locally; a continent-sized battlefield is an unsupported story.

passages.title: Ask about belief, rank, conflict and play without filling gaps
passages.text: Direct evidence for games and jokes in this interval is scarce. Children could play while learning, and gatherings surely included emotion, but archaeology has not preserved a rulebook or punch line. A safer fun fact comes from pottery science: Monagrillo firing sometimes exceeded 800 degrees Celsius, so ancient potters managed a tiny outdoor heat laboratory without a thermometer.

passages.title: Celebrate real achievements and let the false ending dissolve
passages.text: Crop domestication was experimental biology stretched across generations. People noticed variation, saved seed, moved plants, altered habitats and kept foods worth the work. Squash could become softer-rinded, and maize cobs held kernels instead of scattering them. The achievement belongs to many Indigenous cultivators, including mobile communities, rather than one named genius or royal farm ministry.

passages.title: Celebrate real achievements and let the false ending dissolve
passages.text: Ancient DNA from people in Belize records south-to-north movement before intensive maize farming, while maize genomes reveal later gene flow from South America into Central America. Plants and people both moved, but not always together or once. Genetic ancestry is not a language label, and crop ancestry is not proof that one migrating “maize people” replaced everyone else.

passages.title: Celebrate real achievements and let the false ending dissolve
passages.text: Cold-hammering native gold at Jiskairumoko and moving obsidian across Lake Titicaca show experimentation and connection at high altitude. Neither needed a large state. Storage, pithouse repair, lake travel and fine metalwork are achievements too, even if they leave smaller monuments than later civilizations. The atlas's maize-centered title should not hide these Andean accomplishments.

passages.title: Celebrate real achievements and let the false ending dissolve
passages.text: The endpoint is a redraw. “Maize farmers” covers most sampled Mexican and Central American places, “Olmec” appears around Villahermosa, “desert hunter-gatherers” covers the northwest, and “manioc farmers” receives Andean and Colombian points. San Lorenzo's earliest INAH phase begins at about 1500 BCE, exactly the seam, so it cannot be projected backward across the old polygon.

passages.title: Celebrate real achievements and let the false ending dissolve
passages.text: Communities continued after 1500 BCE, and people still cultivate diverse maize today. UNESCO records eight Indigenous groups in Tehuacan-Cuicatlan; FAO documents seed saving, selection and exchange in Chiapas. Those living practices demonstrate continuing knowledge, not a simple family tree from every excavated seed. The card ends with continuity because only the atlas umbrella disappears.

At 1500 BCE the atlas retires one huge, inaccurate umbrella and replaces it with several other broad labels. No common polity fell, and no shared people disappeared. Local families, villages, camps, crops, fishing places, exchange routes and languages continued along different paths. The endpoint records a legend seam, with no invented predecessor or successor chain.

passages.text: Mexico became independent in 1821, after centuries of Indigenous histories and Spanish colonial rule. The republic, restored after a brief second empire, entered an era of rail construction and the long presidency of Porfirio Díaz. Revolution began in 1910, and a 1917 constitution reshaped land, work and education claims. Children’s schools, tortilla-making kitchens and access to doctors or toilets tell a less uniform story than the border. Mexico continues with many Indigenous languages and communities; the imported map begins only in 1878.

passages.title: A state that changed shape
passages.text: After a long war, Mexico achieved independence in 1821. The 1824 constitution made it a representative federal republic. The 1878 date in this map is only the first imported border view, not the country’s birthday.

passages.title: A state that changed shape
passages.text: Mexico later endured foreign intervention and a second empire. The republic was restored in 1867. Its governments changed, while Indigenous peoples and local communities continued their own lives through these state transitions.

passages.title: A state that changed shape
passages.text: During the long Díaz era, railways connected mines, farms and cities, often with foreign capital. Trains could move goods faster, but a new line did not make land, wages or political influence equal for everyone.

passages.title: A state that changed shape
passages.text: Revolution broke out in 1910 as several movements fought over power and land. It was not one army or one neatly finished day. The 1917 constitution was a major result, including claims about education, land and labor.

passages.title: A state that changed shape
passages.text: Women organized against Díaz, wrote, carried supplies, nursed wounded people and sometimes fought. Carmen Serdán also helped organize military nurses. The word “soldadera” hides many different jobs, risks and political choices.

passages.title: A state that changed shape
passages.text: The revolution’s constitution made workers’ claims part of the national legal framework, alongside land and education. A right written in 1917 still had to be fought for at a particular farm, mine or factory.

passages.title: A state that changed shape
passages.text: Article 27 placed land and water questions at the center of the new constitutional order. In 1938 President Lázaro Cárdenas expropriated the oil industry after a conflict between workers and companies, invoking national resource rights.

passages.title: School, home and food
passages.text: A 1925 plan for rural schools asked teachers to connect lessons with daily village life and avoid rigid classroom routines. A child might learn through local work and community problems, though schools differed widely and did not reach every child.

passages.title: School, home and food
passages.text: The original 1917 constitution opened Article 3 with “La enseñanza es libre” or “Teaching is free.” That is a brief sample of written Spanish from the period; the education article has been amended since, and many Mexican children also speak Indigenous languages.

passages.title: School, home and food
passages.text: A tortilla begins before the frying pan: maize is simmered with food-grade limewater, rested, milled into dough and cooked. This ancient nixtamal process makes everyday food more nourishing. In Náhuatl, a tortilla is called “tlaxcalli.”

passages.title: School, home and food
passages.text: A warm tortilla can also be an edible wrapper for beans, vegetables or meat. Families and regions prepare maize in many ways, including tamales and atole; the tortilla is a continuing tradition, not proof that every household eats the same dinner.

passages.title: School, home and food
passages.text: Toilet history is less glamorous but just as revealing. Mexico’s census tracks toilets, piped water and drainage separately, because a flush toilet, a latrine and a sewer connection are different things. Whether your home had one depended on place and resources.

passages.title: School, home and food
passages.text: Mexico’s many Indigenous languages remain living home and community languages. A 2020 census count used by INPI found over seven million speakers. Spanish on a constitution page cannot stand in for what every grandparent, child or neighbor speaks.

passages.title: Care, rights and political change
passages.text: Mexico founded the IMSS in 1943 to combine health care and social protection for covered workers and their families. A workplace card could help when someone got sick, but many people outside formal employment needed different routes to care.

passages.title: Care, rights and political change
passages.text: From the 1970s, IMSS programs extended some services to poorer communities without ordinary payroll coverage. That later expansion is a clue that earlier worker insurance had not reached everyone.

passages.title: Care, rights and political change
passages.text: The 2000 presidential election brought a party change after decades of dominance by one party. The electoral institute describes this as an alternation built on earlier reforms; it did not mean all problems were solved in one vote.

passages.title: Care, rights and political change
passages.text: Mexico continues as a federal republic. Its 1821 independence, 1867 restoration, 1917 constitution and 2000 electoral change mark different transformations of a continuing country; none is the first day of its Indigenous peoples.

Mexico continues as a federal republic. Independence came in 1821, the republic was restored in 1867, and the 1917 constitution still frames state history. Indigenous peoples and languages continue across all those dates; the imported 1878 border snapshot does not verify their territories or every historic boundary.

materialEvidence.question: Does a concrete finding have an identifiable context, date, interpretation and evidence limit?

dailyLife.question: Does the account explain ordinary practices with evidence rather than only rulers?

artsScienceTechnology.question: Are achievements concrete and correctly attributed to this polity and period?

chronologicalPhases.question: Are source-supported phases distinguished from map snapshot dates?

endingContinuity.question: Does the narrative identify what ended or continued, with dates, mechanism and uncertainty?

uncertainty.question: Are uncertainties attached to particular claims rather than a blanket disclaimer?

sectionTitles: Read the atlas identity and polygon honestly
The 1490s joined war, diplomacy and trade
A lake city was an engineering project
Chinampas, markets and kitchens fed millions of errands
Families, ranks, women and children shaped each neighborhood
Religion, calendars and writing joined memory to power
Cloth, houses, crafts, music and games filled ordinary time
Healing, water, baths and toilets need careful evidence
The empire ended; Nahua peoples did not

passages.text: Imagine paddling toward Tenochtitlan in 1495. Canoes crowd canals beside white-plastered houses; traders unload maize, cacao, cotton cloth, feathers and obsidian; two aqueducts bring spring water toward a city built in a lake. At the center, bright temples rise above markets, schools, workshops and neighborhoods. This power was not one simple “Aztec nation.” Tenochtitlan’s Mexica rulers worked with Texcoco and Tlacopan in the Triple Alliance, while hundreds of altepetl, local city-states, kept their own leaders, rivalries and traditions. Armies and tribute tied the patchwork empire together, often harshly, but unconquered Tlaxcala and the Purépecha state resisted it. The atlas shows only 1492 to 1500 and calls the feature “Mexihcah.” Historically, the alliance began around 1428, continued past 1500 under the separate atlas id aztec-empire, and was broken in 1521 by a huge Indigenous-Spanish coalition, siege, hunger and epidemic disease. Colonial manuscripts preserve Nahuatl voices, pictures and memories, but they were made after invasion and must be read beside archaeology. Mexica imperial rule ended; Nahua peoples, languages, arts and communities did not.

passages.title: Read the atlas identity and polygon honestly
passages.text: The exact indexed id is mexihcah-triple-alliance, displayed “Mexihcah (Triple Alliance),” circa 1492 to 1500. The coverage ledger classifies it as a state with one border file, one observed interval, no researched card, no review, and no override. This packet fills that exact missing record.

passages.title: Read the atlas identity and polygon honestly
passages.text: A separate indexed id, aztec-empire, already claims the historical Triple Alliance from 1428 to 1521 and has a short researched card. The two ids are not successive countries: they are overlapping database identities for the same imperial system. “Mexihcah” most directly names the Mexica of Tenochtitlan, not every allied or tributary people.

passages.title: Read the atlas identity and polygon honestly
passages.text: At 1492 the target is one Polygon with one part, one ring and 109 coordinate positions. Its bounds are [-101.94761947619476,16.34168785177978,-94.8159481594816,21.885411342450965]. The raw-coordinate SHA-256 is dbc0cc19bd3c57b16d53c1deead14005d9cba135a368feb9f7390789ff3f517d; its rotation-and-direction-independent canonical hash is c6dcd8c3548ba39e982307c627ff0292c909544c7a6ea83ac913f7b9ec83c392. Those decimals measure encoding, not political certainty.

passages.title: Read the atlas identity and polygon honestly
passages.text: Point tests put Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, Tlacopan, Cempoala, Oaxaca, and wrongly unconquered Tlaxcala, inside the ring. It excludes the Purépecha capital Tzintzuntzan, Tehuantepec, Tapachula and independent Tututepec. It also overlaps Nahua, Cholulteca, Otomí, Totonac and Binnizá display polygons. That is imported map layering, not proof those peoples became Mexica.

passages.title: Read the atlas identity and polygon honestly
passages.text: Neither alliance id appears at 1400. At 1500, mexihcah-triple-alliance disappears and aztec-empire appears as a 49-position polygon with bounds [-105.5080550805508,16.172741995985177,-93.74313743137431,22.895904517527384], raw hash 116fcd553f02270465c02f0690d8dec426c2fe9da9c88dc9129d2bfca1a1a8d8 and canonical hash e5678e9b2d0575027ac720f102b6761881aee6b2e82cd112d3b3f1d389259d2f. By 1530 every tested point is mapped as New Spain.

passages.title: Three capitals shared power unequally
passages.text: The alliance emerged from a war that overthrew Azcapotzalco around 1428. Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan brought different dynasties, armies and claims into the partnership. Later sources disagree about the exact moment and original bargain, so historians reconstruct formation from traditions rather than reading a surviving treaty signed by all three rulers.

passages.title: Three capitals shared power unequally
passages.text: The core partners were not one ethnic unit: Mexica ruled Tenochtitlan, Acolhua ruled Texcoco, and Tepaneca ruled Tlacopan. Each capital had its own tlatoani, or speaker-ruler. A royal serpent labret from the wider region connects powerful speech, mouth ornaments and office, but one elite jewel cannot describe ordinary government.

passages.title: Three capitals shared power unequally
passages.text: Tenochtitlan became the dominant partner, yet “emperor” can hide negotiated rule. Many subjected altepetl kept local dynasties and laws if they delivered tribute and military help. Garrisons or governors appeared in some strategic places, while other districts were linked through clients, roads or fear. The empire was powerful because it was flexible, and vulnerable for the same reason.

passages.title: Three capitals shared power unequally
passages.text: An altepetl was a local political community tied to land, water, patron deities and a ruling house. The Triple Alliance usually ruled through these communities rather than replacing every council. Tribute collectors, judges and local nobles stood between households and distant capitals, so a farmer in Oaxaca did not receive daily orders straight from Tenochtitlan.

passages.title: Three capitals shared power unequally
passages.text: Colonial tribute manuscripts picture cotton cloth, warrior suits, feathers, cacao, rubber, gold and other deliveries from named provinces. They are invaluable, but the Codex Mendoza was commissioned around 1541 to 1542 under Spanish government. It recalls an earlier system through Indigenous painting and colonial annotations; it is not an untouched 1495 treasury spreadsheet.

passages.title: The 1490s joined war, diplomacy and trade
passages.text: The entire atlas window lies inside Ahuítzotl’s reign, 1486 to 1502. Archaeology assigns Templo Mayor phase VI, the House of the Eagles and flood-repair floors to this era. The king enlarged institutions already built by predecessors; 1492 did not start his government, the alliance, Tenochtitlan or Mexica history.

passages.title: The 1490s joined war, diplomacy and trade
passages.text: Ahuítzotl’s forces campaigned against Huaxyacac in 1494 and toward Tehuantepec in 1497, while long-distance merchants and frontier politics reached Soconusco. Control remained thin and contested in the far south. A tribute list or garrison can show pressure without proving continuous occupation of every mile between the capital and coast.

passages.title: The 1490s joined war, diplomacy and trade
passages.text: Tlaxcala resisted conquest and endured a long Mexica economic blockade. Its city falls inside the atlas polygon anyway, making the ring historically wrong at a crucial point. Tlaxcalan leaders later chose alliance with Cortés for their own political reasons; calling them merely Spanish helpers erases an independent state and its strategic choices.

passages.title: The 1490s joined war, diplomacy and trade
passages.text: The Purépecha or Tarascan state defeated a major Mexica invasion and defended a fortified western frontier. Tzintzuntzan correctly falls outside the target point test, but a smooth polygon still cannot show contested marches, empty buffer zones, raids or shifting client towns. Imperial strength had a hard western limit.

passages.title: The 1490s joined war, diplomacy and trade
passages.text: Pochteca merchants organized long journeys from central Mexican cities and moved feathers, stones, cloth and other costly goods through linked markets. Their routes also created diplomatic knowledge and danger, but not every merchant was a state spy. The Florentine account is a later Nahua history of merchant institutions, not a trip diary from 1495.

passages.title: A lake city was an engineering project
passages.text: Tenochtitlan grew on islands and reclaimed shallows. Straight causeways joined it to shore, canals carried canoes through the city, and neighborhood streets connected houses, workshops and shrines. This was not a city that merely “floated”: builders drove stakes, moved fill, laid stone, repaired embankments and continually negotiated soft lake mud.

passages.title: A lake city was an engineering project
passages.text: Chapultepec springs fed connected cisterns and channels, then aqueducts carried fresh water toward the capital. Sacred meanings and practical engineering met in the same system. Archaeological and historical work also shows unequal delivery: elite districts and palaces had better conduits, while many commoner households depended on water carriers.

passages.title: A lake city was an engineering project
passages.text: Waterworks could fail spectacularly. Sources blame Ahuítzotl’s Acuecuexco project for a devastating flood, and excavated temple precinct floors show repeated raising against subsidence and inundation. Engineers managed risk; they did not conquer it. The lake gave transport, food and fertile mud while constantly threatening foundations and drinking supplies.

passages.title: A lake city was an engineering project
passages.text: At the Templo Mayor, paired stairways led to shrines of Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc, connecting war, rain, food and Mexica state ceremony. Rulers repeatedly enclosed earlier stages inside larger ones. Modern excavation therefore reads a layered building, not one frozen pyramid; many colonial structures now sit above the buried precinct.

passages.title: A lake city was an engineering project
passages.text: Stoneworkers quarried, hauled, pecked, ground and polished volcanic and other stones using stone or hardwood tools, fiber cords, water and sand. Sculpture could be brightly painted, so today’s gray museum surfaces are incomplete. Monumental carving demonstrates skilled teams and supply chains, not metal saws, secret lasers or effortless royal magic.

passages.title: Chinampas, markets and kitchens fed millions of errands
passages.text: Chinampas were long constructed plots raised from shallow lake beds with mud, vegetation and retaining edges; calling them “floating gardens” is catchy but physically misleading. Canals gave access and moisture. Archaeologists have uncovered a canal-and-field complex under modern Mexico City, while Xochimilco preserves a living descendant landscape.

passages.title: Chinampas, markets and kitchens fed millions of errands
passages.text: Xochimilco became a major tributary and food supplier after conquest by Tenochtitlan. Its farmers and boat crews retained local identities and interests; in 1521 some lake towns changed sides under pressure. A cabbage-shaped green patch on a map cannot show who owned a plot, rowed a canoe or decided which army to feed.

passages.title: Chinampas, markets and kitchens fed millions of errands
passages.text: Tlatelolco’s market served the paired island cities and offered regional food, cloth and luxury goods. Specialized sellers and officials organized exchange, while smaller towns held their own markets. Tribute entered storehouses through political obligation; market trade involved negotiated exchange. Mixing them together makes every cacao bean look confiscated, which the evidence does not support.

passages.title: Chinampas, markets and kitchens fed millions of errands
passages.text: Palace stores held dried maize, beans, chia, amaranth, salt, chile and squash seeds, supervised by stewards and tribute gatherers. These records reveal institutional reserves, not the exact pantry of every family. Common meals centered on maize foods with beans, squash, chiles and local greens; access to cacao, meat and luxury foods varied sharply.

passages.title: Chinampas, markets and kitchens fed millions of errands
passages.text: Long-distance goods could move by human carriers and canoes because Mesoamerica had no draft animals or wheeled freight system. That limitation encouraged dense route knowledge, relay labor and valuable lightweight cargo. Obsidian blades, salt, pottery and food moved alongside feathers, gold and greenstone; ordinary necessities mattered even when museums display jewels.

passages.title: Families, ranks, women and children shaped each neighborhood
passages.text: Nahua society distinguished nobles, commoners, merchants, priests, warriors, dependent laborers and enslaved people, but these were not modern race boxes. Rank affected land, clothing, schooling, courts and tribute. Military achievement could bring status to some men, while debt or punishment could create dependency; local practice differed across the empire.

passages.title: Families, ranks, women and children shaped each neighborhood
passages.text: A calli meant both a house and a household world; relatives, spouses, children and dependents shared work and ritual. Neighborhood communities often organized land and service. Colonial household records are richer after 1521 than before it, so historians should not turn one ideal family picture into a universal rule for residence or marriage.

passages.title: Families, ranks, women and children shaped each neighborhood
passages.text: Women ground nixtamal, cooked, spun and wove; many also traded in markets, served temples, managed property or worked in specialist households. Men dominated high imperial offices and warfare. These were strong gender expectations, not proof every woman or man did identical work, and colonial writers often squeezed complex lives into moral examples.

passages.title: Families, ranks, women and children shaped each neighborhood
passages.text: Codex Mendoza scenes show boys carrying loads or fishing and girls grinding maize or weaving, with dots marking ages. The pictures make household teaching vivid, but Indigenous artists made the manuscript around 1541 to 1542 for a colonial patron. They describe remembered norms and stages, not surveillance footage of every child before 1500.

passages.title: Families, ranks, women and children shaped each neighborhood
passages.text: Young people learned first through household work and oral instruction. Later accounts describe telpochcalli linked to commoner neighborhoods, calmecac for elite and priestly learning, and institutions for girls. Curricula joined discipline, song, ritual, rhetoric, calendrics, public labor and warfare. Attendance, ages and access varied; “universal school” is too confident.

passages.title: Religion, calendars and writing joined memory to power
passages.text: The Templo Mayor joined Huitzilopochtli, Mexica patron of war and solar power, with Tlaloc, an older rain and fertility deity worshiped across Mesoamerica. That pairing linked conquest to agriculture. Subject communities kept many local gods and rites, so “Aztec religion” should not flatten hundreds of altepetl into one identical belief system.

passages.title: Religion, calendars and writing joined memory to power
passages.text: Mexica specialists coordinated a 260-day ritual count with a 365-day seasonal count; their combinations repeated over a 52-year cycle. The festival year included eighteen twenty-day periods plus additional days. Colonial correlations to European dates remain debated, and a calendar organized farming and ritual without functioning like a modern weather app.

passages.title: Religion, calendars and writing joined memory to power
passages.text: Human sacrifice was real, public and politically meaningful. Excavation of the Huei Tzompantli found postholes and a circular skull-built element, with studied remains including men, women and children from phases 1486 to 1521. Archaeology confirms killing and display; it does not automatically confirm every huge total reported by later writers.

passages.title: Religion, calendars and writing joined memory to power
passages.text: Authentic colonial Nahuatl sample from the 1577 Florentine Codex, Book 9: diplomatic transcription “Izcatqui in iuh tlamanca in ie uecauh.” Normalized spelling: “Izcatqui in iuh tlamanca in ye huecauh.” Translation: “Here follows the way in which things were long ago.” It introduces a Nahua account of merchant history.

passages.title: Religion, calendars and writing joined memory to power
passages.text: The sample is alphabetic Nahuatl written after invasion by Indigenous collaborators in a Franciscan project; it is not a preconquest codex line. “Normalized” means modern editors regularized colonial spelling, not that the sound is certain. Preconquest tlacuiloque also used pictorial and name/place signs, which plain Unicode letters cannot reproduce.

passages.title: Cloth, houses, crafts, music and games filled ordinary time
passages.text: Cotton mantles, featherwork, greenstone, gold ornaments and warrior costumes arrived as tribute or trade and signaled rank. Maguey fiber served more ordinary cloth and cordage. Surviving luxury objects exaggerate elite life because damp soil destroyed most textiles; a gold ornament cannot stand in for everyone’s daily wardrobe.

passages.title: Cloth, houses, crafts, music and games filled ordinary time
passages.text: Men commonly wore a loincloth and mantle; women wore a skirt and blouse-like huipil, with fabric quality, decoration and permitted styles shaped by rank. Dress also varied by region and occasion. Later illustrated manuscripts preserve valuable details, but conquerors’ labels and idealized figures require comparison with fragments, tools and sculpture.

passages.title: Cloth, houses, crafts, music and games filled ordinary time
passages.text: Most commoner houses used adobe, reeds, timber and plaster around work or courtyard space; nobles occupied larger compounds. Neighborhoods included temples, schools, workshops and canal landings. Organic building materials and the colonial city erased much evidence, so the preserved sacred precinct should not become the floor plan of every home.

passages.title: Cloth, houses, crafts, music and games filled ordinary time
passages.text: Farmers, fishers, canoe operators, porters, builders, potters, weavers, featherworkers, stonecutters, merchants, healers, priests and scribes kept the metropolis working. Palace storehouses also employed stewards and tribute officials. Many people combined seasonal tasks; a title in a manuscript may name an office without describing the holder’s entire day.

passages.title: Cloth, houses, crafts, music and games filled ordinary time
passages.text: A carved teponaztli slit drum could sound at weddings, royal processions, agricultural dances or ballgames, and one example continued in use after conquest. Patolli and the ballgame mixed play, ritual and wagering. Nobody recorded every rule for us, so declaring a fifteenth-century “final score” would be magnificent nonsense.

passages.title: Healing, water, baths and toilets need careful evidence
passages.text: Nahua healers used plant preparations, massage, setting, steam, diet, prayer and divination in combinations that do not fit a simple modern split between medicine and religion. The 1552 Badianus Manuscript illustrates 185 medicinal plants, but it was composed and translated after conquest in a colonial college and cannot prove every 1490 treatment.

passages.title: Healing, water, baths and toilets need careful evidence
passages.text: The Florentine Codex records named plants, drinks, washes and other remedies for particular complaints. Those recipes preserve Nahua knowledge and colonial-era practice; they are not medical advice, clinical trials or evidence that every treatment worked. Some ingredients may be pharmacologically active, while other explanations belong to a different theory of bodies and illness.

passages.title: Healing, water, baths and toilets need careful evidence
passages.text: Midwives advised pregnant people, delivered babies, spoke ritual counsel and recommended steam-bath care in later Nahua accounts. The temazcal could support washing, warmth, recovery and ceremony. Book 6 was compiled after conquest, so its richly detailed speeches may be edited literary forms as well as evidence for practice.

passages.title: Healing, water, baths and toilets need careful evidence
passages.text: Fresh water came from springs and aqueducts, yet access was unequal and many households relied on carriers. Bathing and steam baths were valued, but clean bodies did not make lake water germ-free. Canals mixed transport, agriculture and wastewater, and the city had no modern pressurized household network or universal treatment plant.

passages.title: Healing, water, baths and toilets need careful evidence
passages.text: A scholarly sanitation study reports privies in public places and many houses, with excrement collected by canoe, while finding no citywide drainage system; organic wastes could be reused on chinampas. Much detail comes from early colonial descriptions rather than preserved toilet seats. Waste recycling reduced some pollution but carried health risks, history need not smell like a superhero story.

passages.title: The empire ended; Nahua peoples did not
passages.text: The invasion beginning in 1519 was not a duel between Cortés and Motecuhzoma. Tlaxcalan, Texcocan, Huexotzincan and many other Indigenous forces supplied the great majority of coalition fighters and pursued their own goals. Internal rivalries, tributary resentment and succession politics made the alliance network fracture under pressure.

passages.title: The empire ended; Nahua peoples did not
passages.text: Smallpox killed Cuitlahuac and many others; blockade severed food and water; brigantines challenged Mexica canoes; fighting devastated Tenochtitlan and Tlatelolco. Cuauhtemoc’s capture in August 1521 ended organized imperial defense. Disease mattered enormously, but it was one force within diplomacy, civil conflict, siege and mass Indigenous warfare.

passages.title: The empire ended; Nahua peoples did not
passages.text: Most detailed descriptions were written after conquest. The Florentine Codex joins Nahua testimony and art to a Franciscan program; the Codex Mendoza answers a Spanish viceroy’s questions; Spanish soldiers defended their deeds. Reading accounts against archaeology and one another reveals knowledge and bias instead of choosing one “perfect eyewitness.”

passages.title: The empire ended; Nahua peoples did not
passages.text: In 1531, Huexotzinco communities used eight painted amatl panels as testimony in a lawsuit over excessive colonial taxation. The document proves Indigenous scribes and plaintiffs adapted older pictorial accounting to a new court. It also warns against calling every Nahua opponent of Tenochtitlan a permanent friend of Spanish rule.

passages.title: The empire ended; Nahua peoples did not
passages.text: Imperial institutions were broken, temples destroyed and communities devastated, yet Nahua history continued through towns, families, land claims, manuscripts, worship, art and language. Mexico’s INPI today recognizes diverse Nahua peoples across many states and many language varieties. Living Nahuas are contemporary communities, not museum leftovers from an “extinct Aztec race.”

The target feature ends at the 1500 atlas seam, but the historical Triple Alliance did not. The same polity immediately appears under the separate aztec-empire id and continued until the 1519 to 1521 invasion, Indigenous coalition, epidemic and siege broke its imperial government. Colonial rule then reordered land, labor, religion and political authority with terrible demographic consequences. Even that conquest was not cultural extinction: Nahua towns, language varieties, manuscripts, families, arts and political action continued. Because the 1500 endpoint is a database identity swap rather than a fall, this card records fell: null and creates no false successor state.

sectionTitles: River villages, skilled work and recreation

passages.text: The Miami, or Myaamia, are a Great Lakes people whose farming villages and river connections supported wide regional influence. The broad Myaamia and narrower Miami outlines are approximations. A separate Oklahoma outline dated 1492 is anachronistic: Miami settlement there followed nineteenth-century removals. Miami communities continue in Oklahoma, Indiana and beyond.

passages.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation
passages.text: Miami villages stood near rivers that connected settlements through canoe travel. The Indiana community’s history places their homeland across parts of present-day Indiana, Ohio, Illinois and Michigan. Hunting, fishing and cultivation worked together in a landscape where water routes could link relatives and trading partners.

passages.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation
passages.text: Miami white flour corn drew an early eighteenth-century observer’s attention for its fine husks and pale flour. Historian Cameron Shriver follows this crop through later sources, including twentieth-century Miami farmers. Corn was both a lasting food tradition and an agricultural achievement maintained through enormous political change.

passages.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation
passages.text: In a 2023 account, weaver Jared Nally describes harvesting inner bark from trees such as basswood and gathering other plant fibers later in the year. Separating usable fibers and rolling or spinning thread could take as long as weaving itself. A finished textile contains a great deal of work that is easy not to see.

passages.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation
passages.text: The winter game snowsnake sends a length of wood sliding through snow. Players try to make it travel farther and straighter than an opponent’s throw. Myaamia community programs have been reviving the game: snow becomes a playing surface, and the snake is reassuringly wooden.

passages.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation
passages.text: Lacrosse remains an opportunity to meet relatives and neighbors as well as compete. A 2022 community account describes an annual Myaamia game with Seneca-Cayuga participants, including youth camps. It also distinguishes older games from newer adaptations that introduce Myaamia language into familiar card games.

passages.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation
passages.text: In 2024, Myaamia sugar camps operated in Ohio, Indiana and Oklahoma. Sap was boiled down into syrup or sugar; a typical maple yield required about 40 gallons of sap for one gallon of syrup. Oklahoma participants also tapped black walnut because local sugar maples were scarce. Breakfast sweetness required buckets of effort.

passages.title: Resistance, removal and rebuilding
passages.text: Miami leader Little Turtle helped lead a Native coalition that defeated United States forces in 1790 and 1791. Before the Battle of Fallen Timbers in 1794, he urged peace. These changing decisions belonged to a wider struggle over homelands involving several allied peoples, rather than one isolated Miami army.

passages.title: Resistance, removal and rebuilding
passages.text: The Treaty of Greenville in 1795 required extensive land cessions. Further treaties narrowed Miami control over their homeland, and an 1840 agreement called for removal beyond the Mississippi. Treaty dates mark government decisions; the forced journey itself came later.

passages.title: Resistance, removal and rebuilding
passages.text: On October 11, 1846, five canal boats carrying Miami people reached Cincinnati. There they were forced aboard the steamboat Colorado to continue west along the Ohio River. A university archival exhibit places this transfer within the removal journey, revealing how ordinary transport networks became instruments of forced displacement.

passages.title: Resistance, removal and rebuilding
passages.text: Other Miami families secured permission to stay in Indiana. Their descendants form the Miami Nation of Indiana, with continuing government, cultural programs and relationships to western Miami relatives. Its own history distinguishes that community’s existence from its lack of federal recognition as a sovereign tribal nation today.

passages.title: Resistance, removal and rebuilding
passages.text: The western Miami faced another move after an 1867 treaty, with migration from Kansas into present-day Oklahoma in the late 1860s and 1870s. The Miami Tribe of Oklahoma established its government there. That sequence explains why an Oklahoma polygon cannot accurately represent Miami territory in 1492.

passages.title: Children, archives and speaking again
passages.text: Language revitalization draws on documents spanning the late 1600s through the 1960s. A Myaamia Center report explains how researchers analyze old records, compare forms and develop resources for present-day use. The work connects archival scholarship with families learning words together; it is a gradual effort across generations.

passages.title: Children, archives and speaking again
passages.text: A short modern writing sample is “Tipeewe neeyolaani”, translated as “It is good to see you.” Miami University’s tribal-relations page prints both forms in its Myaamia teaching list. The greeting follows contemporary community teaching spelling.

passages.title: Children, archives and speaking again
passages.text: During 2023 summer programs, children made miniature lodges with coverings that represented elm bark and cattail mats. They also practiced kinship words on family trees, while older participants made films and mentored younger learners. Model building helped connect household history, language and living family relationships.

The imported map cutoffs are not the end of Miami history. Removal created separated communities without ending Miami identity. The Oklahoma Tribe and Indiana community continue, while research and family learning help carry Myaamia language into daily life.

passages.text: These entries follow Milan through Spanish and Austrian government, with the last Sforza years at the beginning of the earlier map interval. They are phases of a changing territorial state, not two unrelated civilizations. Its surviving hospital, theatre, libraries and printed books show care, work and argument alongside imperial rule.

passages.title: Hospitals, water and work
passages.text: Milan’s great hospital, the Ca’ Granda, had been founded in 1456, before these map intervals. Its foundation ceremony included small vessels of oil, wine, milk, honey and water and a lead book. These were symbolic deposits, not a recipe for treating patients.

passages.title: Hospitals, water and work
passages.text: The Ca’ Granda’s buildings grew over roughly three centuries, helped by citizens’ gifts and bequests. The recurring Festa del Perdono raised support. Hospital care depended on lasting institutions and donors, not simply on a duke paying for one impressive building and walking away.

passages.title: Hospitals, water and work
passages.text: The hospital placed latrines in corridors beside the wards. Channels supplied with rainwater helped carry waste away. Convenient toilets were part of the architectural plan centuries before modern hospital plumbing; surviving remains have also been altered, so today’s building is not an untouched fifteenth-century snapshot.

passages.title: Hospitals, water and work
passages.text: Wastewater from the hospital passed under the Naviglio canal and toward agricultural land used for irrigation and fertilizing. That is evidence of engineered drainage and reuse, not proof of modern sewage treatment or protection from infection. The unglamorous pipes deserve a place beside the grand courtyards.

passages.title: Hospitals, water and work
passages.text: A courtyard originally associated with baths was used for servants and nurses by the early seventeenth century. Such changing uses remind us that a hospital needed workers and service spaces as well as beds. The elegant architecture was also somebody’s workplace.

passages.title: Hospitals, water and work
passages.text: A new assessment of Milanese taxable wealth was completed in 1560. Officials sought to distribute costs, but urban and rural interests and existing privileges complicated the process. A government’s demand for money reached farms and households, even when its records speak in the language of institutions.

passages.title: Learning, music and printed arguments
passages.text: The Sforza Castle became a barracks during foreign rule. Its changing function is a reminder that a former prince’s residence could become a military workplace. Spanish, Austrian and French rulers reused the same formidable building rather than rebuilding Milan from scratch after every conquest.

passages.title: Learning, music and printed arguments
passages.text: Brera’s art collection began in 1776 in connection with the academy, giving students examples to study. Its formal museum opened in 1809, after this Austrian phase. Many later additions came from suppressed religious houses: a museum’s collection can preserve the effects of political upheaval.

passages.title: Learning, music and printed arguments
passages.text: After the Jesuit establishment passed to the state in 1773, Brera gathered learning institutions in one complex, including an observatory, botanical garden and library. The Braidense library opened to the public in 1786. Books, plants and the sky became neighboring subjects of investigation.

passages.title: Learning, music and printed arguments
passages.text: La Scala opened in 1778 with Salieri’s Europa riconosciuta, replacing a theatre destroyed by fire. Maria Theresa authorized the new building, designed by Giuseppe Piermarini. Its name preserves the church formerly on the site; the audience was entering a newly constructed theatre, not an ancient Roman one.

passages.title: Learning, music and printed arguments
passages.text: La Scala’s boxes had owners whose names can be traced in archival records beginning in 1778. An evening at the theatre was also a social occasion shaped by property and status. The records illuminate the people who held boxes, not a representative sample of every Milanese family.

passages.title: Learning, music and printed arguments
passages.text: The Italian title “Dei delitti e delle pene” means “On Crimes and Punishments.” A surviving 1764 edition preserves these words from Cesare Beccaria’s famous argument about criminal justice. The Milanese author published in Livorno; a book could travel across political borders faster than a government changed its laws.

French conquest in 1796 ended this phase of Austrian government and brought new political arrangements. Milan remained inhabited and important. Neither the 1715 endpoint of the first map entry nor the 1800 endpoint of the later one is a reliable single date for the city’s “fall.”

sectionTitles: Books and the study of nature

passages.text: Zhu Yuanzhang founded the Ming dynasty in 1368 after rebellion against Mongol Yuan rule. Its history includes enormous building projects, skilled workshops and a flourishing world of books and trade. The conventional endpoint, 1644, marks the loss of Beijing; Ming loyalist courts continued afterward. Imported borders are coarse snapshots: the later northeastern outline is especially broad and must not be read as proof of uniform direct administration everywhere inside it.

passages.title: Imperial projects and distant connections
passages.text: The Forbidden City in Beijing was constructed between 1406 and 1420 for the Yongle emperor, Zhu Di. Its halls, courtyards and gates organised the business and ceremonies of the imperial court. Later Qing rulers also used the complex, and repairs changed it over time. A palace visitor today sees many layers of history beyond its original Ming construction.

passages.title: Imperial projects and distant connections
passages.text: Ming builders added substantial masonry defences to a much older history of frontier walls. The Great Wall was a system of towers, shelters, forts and passes as well as long stretches of wall. Routes along it allowed movement between defensive positions. Its immense construction required sustained work and maintenance; it was never simply one wall completed by one emperor.

passages.title: Imperial projects and distant connections
passages.text: Between 1405 and 1433, seven imperial maritime expeditions associated with Zheng He travelled through established Indian Ocean networks. The fleets visited Southeast Asia and India, with missions reaching the Persian Gulf and East Africa. They carried diplomacy, goods and demonstrations of imperial power. Sailors were entering busy trading worlds whose merchants had connected these coasts long before.

passages.title: Imperial projects and distant connections
passages.text: A blue-and-white porcelain canteen made at Jingdezhen around 1402 to 1424 borrowed its shape from Islamic metal vessels. Its blue decoration came from cobalt. Although shaped like something carried on a shoulder strap, this surviving example seems too heavy for practical use. Smithsonian curators suggest it was ornamental: a water-carrier shape that may have stayed comfortably at home.

passages.title: Money, school and play
passages.text: Ming paper money pictured what it was worth: a one-guan note showed a string of 1,000 copper coins. Notes were first issued in 1375, although paper currency already had a long Chinese history. The system faced counterfeiting and other problems, while silver increasingly served as money by weight. Carrying a picture of coins was easier than carrying all the coins themselves.

passages.title: Money, school and play
passages.text: A copper-alloy ritual cup dated 1520 names a county magistrate and academy instructors. Its inscription ends “大明正德庚辰年造”: “Made in the gengchen year of the Zhengde reign of the Great Ming”, equivalent to 1520. The museum transcribes the Chinese in standard script. This surviving object connects writing, local officials and an academy’s ceremonial life; it is not an ordinary pupil’s drinking cup.

passages.title: Money, school and play
passages.text: The painting Bird peddler, from the late fifteenth or early sixteenth century, shows six boys fascinated by birds, crickets and two white rabbits. Cages, perches and feeding dishes fill the display. The museum identifies this as an idealised aristocratic scene, with a servant playing the seller. It records an elite fantasy of happy childhood, complete with a very tempting pet shop.

passages.title: Homes and a water supply
passages.text: At Hongcun in Anhui, a channel dug around 1405 brought water from a nearby stream into the village. Roughly two centuries later, the South Lake enlarged the system. Watercourses linked houses and ponds, and streets followed their course. Planning a neighbourhood meant thinking about where water would flow, alongside where people would walk and build.

passages.title: Homes and a water supply
passages.text: Nearby Xidi grew as members of the Hu family developed merchant careers from the fifteenth century. Surviving houses, built and altered across the Ming and Qing periods, commonly combine timber frames, brick walls and a courtyard. Small outer windows helped with security. Wealth from business could return home as buildings, bridges and spaces used by extended families.

passages.title: Books and the study of nature
passages.text: Late Ming readers could buy illustrated drama, poetry and art books. The Huntington’s exhibition includes a 1617 edition of The Peony Pavilion with woodblock pictures carved by members of the Huang family. Such publications required collaboration between writers, artists, carvers, printers and publishers. A printed picture was the product of skilled hands as well as a good story.

passages.title: Books and the study of nature
passages.text: The Yongle Encyclopedia, compiled from 1403 to 1408, gathered material on subjects ranging from history and geography to religion and science. It was a manuscript compilation, not a printed set for every household. Surviving volumes come from a later copy made in 1562 to 1567. Some preserve passages from earlier books that have since disappeared, making the encyclopedia a refuge for otherwise lost knowledge.

passages.title: Books and the study of nature
passages.text: Li Shizhen spent decades assembling the Compendium of Materia Medica; its first draft was completed in 1578. It described plants, animals and minerals thought to have medicinal properties, while revisiting earlier accounts and correcting mistakes. The book records a major effort to organise knowledge about nature and healing. Its historical importance does not establish that every remedy it contains is effective.

Li Zicheng’s rebels captured Beijing in April 1644, and the Chongzhen emperor died by suicide. Qing forces entered the city in June after defeating Li with allied troops. Ming loyalist governments then resisted in southern China for years. Thus 1644 marks the loss of the main Ming court, not an overnight replacement of every government, community or cultural tradition.

passages.text: Minoan is the modern name for Bronze Age Cretan culture, with several palatial centers rather than one securely documented island-wide kingdom. Its crafts, exchange networks and administrative writing linked Crete to the wider Mediterranean.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Palaces at Knossos, Phaistos, Mallia and Zakros grouped rooms around central courts. Lighting, ventilation and sanitary facilities formed part of their design.

passages.title: Writing
passages.text: Cretan hieroglyphic writing and Linear A appear on administrative tablets and ritual objects. Palace record keeping helped organize economic activity.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Wall paintings show rituals and the natural world. Jewelers worked with filigree and granulation, while engravers carved seal stones.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: A small agate gem in the Met depicts a griffin and is dated approximately 1450 to 1400 BCE. Objects preserve artistic continuity beyond a single palace destruction.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Crete exported timber, textiles, food and luxury crafts, while importing metals and other raw materials.

passages.title: Change and continuity
passages.text: Widespread destruction around 1450 BCE accompanied growing Mycenaean influence. Linear B administration and mixed pottery styles followed; neither the destruction nor cultural change has a securely identified single cause.
