passages.text: Between 1300 and 1492 this atlas label covers parts of Borneo and southwestern Sulawesi. It is regional shorthand, not one kingdom or a reliable description of everyone’s religion. In South Sulawesi, growing rice production and overseas exchange helped local ruling communities develop into larger kingdoms. Their histories belong beside, rather than inside, the story of any single distant empire.

passages.title: Several societies under one label
passages.text: The decoded outlines include Soppeng, Gowa, Bantaeng and the Mahakam region around Kutai Lama. They exclude Java, Bali and western Sarawak. The similarly named earlier states record mostly covers Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula, while another minor-kingdoms label includes India. None is a substitute for these island communities’ own history.

passages.title: Several societies under one label
passages.text: Kutai Lama stood beside the Mahakam River in eastern Borneo. Later Kutai tradition places a royal centre there around 1300. That traditional starting date should not be confused with a securely dated foundation inscription, or with the much earlier Muara Kaman inscriptions upstream. Different places and periods lie behind the familiar name Kutai.

passages.title: Several societies under one label
passages.text: Researchers interpreting Sewo in Soppeng describe a shift from hill settlements toward gentler lowlands suited to rice fields. Their explanation links systematic cultivation and food surpluses with the joining of farming villages into a kingdom during the fourteenth century. Political change was also a change in where people worked and lived.

passages.title: Food, water and skilled hands
passages.text: At Allangkanangnge, a former Bugis palace site, researchers recovered microscopic silica traces from rice husks. These phytoliths survive after the plant has gone. Combined with ceramics, they provide direct evidence for rice in the development of agrarian kingdoms. A rice plant can leave a clue much smaller than a grain.

passages.title: Food, water and skilled hands
passages.text: From around 1300, clearing forest, directing water and building embanked rice fields demanded coordinated labour in South Sulawesi. Farmers also faced insects, rodents and hungry birds. More rice could support more people and trade, but harvests did not become automatic just because a ruler wanted a surplus.

passages.title: Food, water and skilled hands
passages.text: River and lake communities could obtain fish, salt and edible plants as well as grain. Rivers such as the Saddang and Jeneberrang served as routes between settlements. This environmental setting helps explain why fields, fishing places and waterways mattered together, instead of reducing every family’s food to a bowl of rice.

passages.title: Food, water and skilled hands
passages.text: Just outside the atlas’s southern Borneo outline, Patih Muhur offers a useful building comparison. Archaeologists found shaped ironwood posts with square holes for crosspieces; supporting logs and smaller wooden braces helped stop them sinking into wet ground. Keeping a heavy structure upright in soft soil required more than simply planting a tree trunk.

passages.title: Food, water and skilled hands
passages.text: One Patih Muhur wood test was reported as a broad medieval age, but its relationship to later historical accounts is unresolved. The excavator called for more samples and improved analysis. The braced timbers are real; their precise date and identification with a named kingdom’s port remain questions.

passages.title: Families, power and protection
passages.text: South Sulawesi kingdoms drew authority from descent groups that recognized both parental lines. Some joined several such groups in alliances. Kinship could therefore shape who ruled and who supported a ruler. This describes political organization; it does not tell us that every household had the same size or daily routine.

passages.title: Families, power and protection
passages.text: A later Soppeng genealogy remembers Wé Tékéwanua as a woman ruler and links her family’s marriages with neighbouring lands. It also credits her with encouraging rice planting. Historian Stephen Druce warns that the earliest generations rely on oral tradition. The account reveals how later people remembered women and family alliances in royal history.

passages.title: Families, power and protection
passages.text: Bulu Matanre in Soppeng had stone defenses protecting a mountain pass. Archaeologists place its occupation broadly between the fourteenth and seventeenth centuries. Not every nearby hill settlement was fortified. Controlling a route offers a practical explanation for this wall without making every fortress the result of the same drought or war.

passages.title: Families, power and protection
passages.text: At Kutai, rivers linked several successive centres rather than one unchanging capital. Archaeological collections contain ceramics, beads, coins, sculpture and animal remains from different periods. These objects reveal many kinds of activity, but a museum display assembled today is not a photograph of a single medieval family’s belongings.

passages.title: Writing, memory and learning
passages.text: A later Bugis historical text opens, in scholarly Roman transcription, Iana sureq poadaqadaqéngngi tanaé ri Soppéng: “This is the writing that tells of the land of Soppéng.” Ian Caldwell records this wording in manuscript versions studied for his 1988 thesis. The text appeared in Bugis script in Matthes’s 1864 collection; this is a later written witness, not a surviving page from 1300.

passages.title: Writing, memory and learning
passages.text: The Soppeng history was probably first written down in the eighteenth century. Its remembered place names nevertheless helped researchers investigate older settlements. Written tradition and archaeology can ask questions of each other: a story suggests where to look, while pottery can test how old occupation there actually was.

passages.title: Writing, memory and learning
passages.text: Later Bugis manuscripts preserved calendars, diaries, genealogies and religious or historical works as well as poetry. Surviving collections often contain copies commissioned in the nineteenth century. Copying and comparing texts preserved knowledge, but the date of a surviving book must be distinguished from the age of the events it describes.

passages.title: Writing, memory and learning
passages.text: For a clearly later example of literary skill, Colliq Pujie, Queen Mother of Tanete, copied a major Bugis La Galigo manuscript in the nineteenth century. Leiden preserves its twelve volumes. A woman’s sustained scholarly work helped transmit an enormous epic; the physical books are centuries later than this map interval.

1492 is an atlas stopping point, not a shared conquest. South Sulawesi’s kingdoms continued; Goa and Talloq became major powers in the sixteenth century, and Islam spread among Bugis and Makasar communities around 1600. Borneo’s centres followed other histories. Political and religious change did not erase their communities or languages.

sectionTitles: Building, learning and caring for places
A written witness and a nearby meal

passages.text: This atlas label groups changing parts of Sumatra, the Malay Peninsula and, in some snapshots, Borneo between 800 and 1279. It does not identify one kingdom or a population sharing one religion. Archaeology reveals ports, craft settlements and religious centres with different histories. Ancient Kedah comprised several settlements.

passages.title: Reading a changing map
passages.text: The 800 outline includes Barus and Kedah; the 1000 outline combines northern Sumatra and Borneo. Kedah returns in 1100 but lies south of the 1200 outline. These are atlas categories, not an empire’s expansion. Barus examples after 900 continue its local history beyond the drawn boundary.

passages.title: Reading a changing map
passages.text: Barus, on Sumatra’s western coast, exported camphor and appears in accounts from far beyond the island. Its archaeological goods include ceramics and glass connected with several Asian regions. A port’s importance could rest on forest products and shipping contacts, not simply on the size of a palace.

passages.title: Merchants, objects and everyday work
passages.text: At Lobu Tua near Barus, excavators found an earthen fort with a surrounding ditch. Ceramics place the settlement broadly from the later ninth century to the end of the eleventh. A defended trading settlement needed shared space and collective effort as well as people arriving with cargo.

passages.title: Merchants, objects and everyday work
passages.text: The Lobu Tua stone, now Museum Nasional object D.42, records a Tamil merchant guild in 1088. Its tax arrangements show traders acting together and writing down obligations. International commerce involved meetings and rules as well as adventurous voyages: somebody still had to sort out the bill.

passages.title: Merchants, objects and everyday work
passages.text: Sungai Mas in Kedah made its own glass beads. A study tested 22 beads and raw-material samples rather than assuming every attractive bead came from India. Its results support local manufacture from the sixth through thirteenth centuries, a reminder that port communities were producers as well as customers.

passages.title: Merchants, objects and everyday work
passages.text: Glassmakers’ choices affected both colour and whether a bead was transparent or opaque. Researchers examined major and trace elements associated with these properties at Sungai Mas. Small ornaments preserve evidence of considerable material knowledge; an ancient workshop was doing sophisticated things on a very tiny scale.

passages.title: Merchants, objects and everyday work
passages.text: Barus finds include small round stone boxes with lids and an object compared with an eyebrow pencil. These may reveal personal grooming and cosmetics, although their exact uses remain uncertain. Archaeology sometimes gets surprisingly close to someone’s dressing table without recovering the person’s name.

passages.title: Building, learning and caring for places
passages.text: At Bukit Choras, researchers announced two life-sized stucco statues in 2023, associated with a Buddhist temple dated to the eighth or ninth century. The surviving walls and stairs help reconstruct how people approached a sacred building. Similarities with objects in Sumatra and West Java reveal artistic connections, not a proven shared ruler.

passages.title: Building, learning and caring for places
passages.text: A further Buddha found beside the north wall in 2024 was made of stucco, a mixture of lime, water and sand. This is a useful correction to the idea that ancient sculpture always meant carving solid rock: builders could shape a prepared mixture into a human-sized figure.

passages.title: Building, learning and caring for places
passages.text: Bukit Choras studies also record two ancient water tanks, laterite-brick remains and iron nails. Water storage mattered to the site, but the available study summary does not establish the tanks’ exact dates or a toilet system. These are traces of infrastructure, not a complete account of household hygiene.

passages.title: Building, learning and caring for places
passages.text: Researchers used contour maps, magnetism, electrical resistivity and ground-penetrating radar around Bukit Choras. Such methods look for buried structures before digging. Learning about the past can begin by measuring the ground rather than turning it into a giant hole.

passages.title: Building, learning and caring for places
passages.text: The 2024 Bukit Choras statue was moved temporarily to a university laboratory for conservation and further study. Preserving an excavation is skilled work in its own right. A spectacular discovery needs careful handling before it can safely become something families learn from.

passages.title: A written witness and a nearby meal
passages.text: A tiny bottle-green glass seal found at Lobu Tua in 1997 bears Arabic writing. Its second line can be represented in normalized modern letters as محمد, transliterated Muḥammad: the personal name Muhammad. Scholar Ludvik Kalus tentatively dated the object to the tenth or eleventh century. It was found outside a secure archaeological layer and was probably imported.

passages.title: A written witness and a nearby meal
passages.text: The seal measures only about 15 by 13 millimetres. Its letters were engraved backwards for making an impression; Kalus suggested it might also have served as a personal talisman. This individual object shows why the map’s Hindu-and-Buddhist label must not erase other beliefs or visitors.

passages.title: A written witness and a nearby meal
passages.text: Kota Cina near modern Medan lies outside these exact polygons, but offers a useful neighbouring comparison for northern Sumatran life. Layers dated broadly to the eleventh through thirteenth centuries contain wooden post sections and palm-fibre cord. Perishable building materials can survive when the ground preserves them, although these pieces do not reveal a whole family’s floor plan.

passages.title: A written witness and a nearby meal
passages.text: At the same nearby Kota Cina site, dense heaps of discarded shells are interpreted as food remains. Cockles and clams help put ordinary meals back into a story often dominated by imported luxuries. Dinner left evidence too, even when the plates, conversations and people have disappeared.

There was no single collapse in 1279. Kedah settlements continued into the fourteenth century. Nearby Kota Cina was abandoned in the early 1300s; researchers suggest silting waterways may have impeded seagoing vessels. That is one local environmental explanation, not an ending for every port or community under this atlas label.

sectionTitles: Builders, water and stories in stone
Learning, health and an authentic written word

passages.text: The atlas label “Minor Hindu Kingdoms” is not the name of a state. Its 1279 outline combines parts of India with Borneo and Sulawesi; its 1300 outline covers India alone. This card uses named Indian examples, especially Hoysala and Kakatiya communities. Their importance was not “minor,” and the label cannot establish everyone’s religion. The island fragments belong to a different regional history.

passages.title: Rulers, grants and changing power
passages.text: At Somanathapura in Karnataka, an inscription dates the village and Keshava temple to 1268, eleven years before this map interval. Somanatha, a senior military officer serving Narasimha III, founded the settlement. Major building projects connected rulers, officers and the agricultural economy.

passages.title: Rulers, grants and changing power
passages.text: The Malkapuram record, catalogued as 1261, connects a grant promised by Ganapatideva with the formal gift made by his daughter Rudramadevi. A religious teacher organized its endowments. This earlier Kakatiya example comes from near Guntur, outside the imported outline: women could be central actors in royal patronage.

passages.title: Rulers, grants and changing power
passages.text: In 1323, a Delhi Sultanate army captured Warangal and took the Kakatiya ruler Prataparudra prisoner. This was a particular dynasty’s defeat. It did not end every regional community or create a single replacement state across the entire map label.

passages.title: Builders, water and stories in stone
passages.text: At Palampet, Ramappa temple construction began in 1213, before this map interval. Builders used porous, lightweight bricks in the tower above heavier stonework. The nickname “floating bricks” describes a clever choice of material to reduce roof weight. The tower was not trying to sail away.

passages.title: Builders, water and stories in stone
passages.text: Ramappa’s setting includes a Kakatiya reservoir, irrigation works and cultivated fields. Water storage linked farming with the temple landscape. Cultivation and ceremonies shared a carefully arranged landscape: reservoir, channels, fields and buildings belonged in the same picture.

passages.title: Builders, water and stories in stone
passages.text: At Halebidu, older temple carvings remained part of the region’s cultural landscape. One scene shows Krishna sheltering a community beneath a mountain: cattle, herders and musicians huddle below, while monkeys and birds occupy the heights. It is a sacred story with remarkably busy details, not a literal weather report.

passages.title: Work, worship and shared meals
passages.text: Somanathapura’s foundation record earmarked revenue for decoration, dancing and daily or seasonal festivals. Behind a celebration stood an endowment and people doing paid or supported work. A beautifully carved temple also required an ongoing operating budget.

passages.title: Work, worship and shared meals
passages.text: Halebidu inscriptions from the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries record donations by both men and women from different occupations and social backgrounds. Offerings included flowers, food, scented water and lamp light. Religious life involved many contributors beyond the royal family.

passages.title: Work, worship and shared meals
passages.text: As a nearby comparison outside the atlas outline, Malkapuram’s endowed community included more than sixty Brahmin families, teachers, cooks, artisans and a physician. Supporting learning and ritual required numerous practical jobs. This is a record of one organized settlement, not a census of all medieval families.

passages.title: Work, worship and shared meals
passages.text: The same Malkapuram endowment included a feeding house whose provision was described as serving people regardless of caste or creed. Land revenue was assigned to maintain it. Shared meals were a concrete charitable purpose, even in a society with pronounced social divisions.

passages.title: Learning, health and an authentic written word
passages.text: An inscription dated 1300 describes Somanathapura as a settlement of learned Brahmins. Earlier foundations and later grants show how a place could combine worship with scholarly residence. This documents a particular learned community, not schooling for every child.

passages.title: Learning, health and an authentic written word
passages.text: In the nearby Malkapuram comparison, the thirteenth-century inscription names medical institutions. Scholar Dominik Wujastyk transcribes ārogyaśālā, meaning “hospital,” and prasūtiśāla, “birthing house.” These are Sanskrit words in modern scholarly Roman transcription. The source establishes named facilities, rather than their treatment success or a surviving modern-style ward.

passages.title: Learning, health and an authentic written word
passages.text: At that Malkapuram foundation, land was divided to support the temple, students and monastery, and charitable institutions including maternity and general medical care. The record allotted shares to a physician and an administrative worker. Care depended on a financial arrangement, not only on a generous promise.

passages.title: Learning, health and an authentic written word
passages.text: A separate comparison at Palakol, outside this outline, comes from 1300. An inscription names Vasudeva as skilled in treating horses and identifies his father Anantapandita as a horse physician too. It gives a small glimpse of medical expertise within a family, although it does not describe their lessons or remedies.

passages.title: How historians recover the details
passages.text: Malkapuram’s evidence is physically substantial: its pillar carries about 200 lines across three sides. Sanskrit verse forms most of the text, while Telugu supplies details such as village boundaries. A monument can preserve practical administration alongside praise of its patrons.

passages.title: How historians recover the details
passages.text: An earlier coastal comparison is Motupalli’s edict of 1244 to 1245, outside this atlas outline. It promised foreign merchants that shipwrecked cargo would face ordinary customs duties rather than wholesale seizure. A royal inscription could address the alarming practical question: what happens to your goods when your ship wrecks?

There was no collective collapse in 1400. Kakatiya rule ended in 1323, while Hoysala power ended in the 1340s. At Somanathapura, later Vijayanagara and Nayaka patrons supported repairs and grants. Communities and institutions continued under changing authorities; the atlas endpoint is a mapping limit.

passages.text: The atlas label “minor states” covers parts of Anatolia and the Armenian highlands from 200 to 1 BCE. It is a catch-all for a region of distinct kingdoms and communities, not the name of a single people or a judgment that their histories were unimportant. Its broad shape includes Gordion, Amaseia, Mazaka and Artaxata, but excludes tested points at Pergamon, Sinope and Nemrut. Galatian communities, Cappadocia, Pontus and Armenian rulers therefore need their own local histories; this card offers examples within the region while keeping named-polity cards separate.

passages.title: Kingdoms, routes and authority
passages.text: Cappadocia was ruled through royal and noble estates, fortified places and districts headed by important nobles. Temples also held land and influence. A map colored for one king can conceal several layers of authority between a court, a village and the people who cultivated its fields.

passages.title: Kingdoms, routes and authority
passages.text: Royal marriages connected Cappadocia with larger neighbors. Ariarathes IV married a Seleucid princess, and his daughter later married the king of Pergamon. Such family relationships could support alliances, but kinship did not stop wars or rival claims to the throne.

passages.title: Kingdoms, routes and authority
passages.text: At the eastern end of the outline, Artaxias established Artaxata beside the Araxes as a fortified royal city. It became a long-lived Armenian capital. The story that Hannibal designed it is doubted by the scholarly source; the city’s importance does not depend on giving a famous visitor all the credit.

passages.title: Kingdoms, routes and authority
passages.text: One small object carried a king’s image much farther than a palace wall. A silver drachm attributed to Ariarathes VII, dated approximately 116 to 101 BCE and minted at Mazaka, shows his diademed head and Athena holding the victory figure Nike. It weighs just over four grams: portable royal imagery in a pocket-sized piece of metal.

passages.title: Homes, food and practical skills
passages.text: At Galatian-period Gordion, excavators found jars and cooking pots on house floors and courtyard surfaces, along with small containers for oils or cosmetics, loom weights and Mediterranean shells. These objects place cooking, grooming, textile work and distant connections in the same lived spaces. An imported shell demonstrates movement of objects, not the birthplace of its owner.

passages.title: Homes, food and practical skills
passages.text: Some Gordion houses used stone foundations with slots for wooden posts and walls of organic material covered in mud plaster. The plant material decayed, leaving distinctive traces for excavators. These were engineered buildings made from several materials; the bits that survive best are not a complete picture of the original home.

passages.title: Homes, food and practical skills
passages.text: Changes in hearths, ovens, food-processing tools and textile equipment led archaeologist Mary Voigt to argue that the Galatian migrants included families, not only hired soldiers. A workshop for potters and figurine makers and a nearby metalworking area add a picture of specialized crafts. The family conclusion is an interpretation of several kinds of evidence together.

passages.title: Homes, food and practical skills
passages.text: Late Hellenistic households at Gordion often owned mismatched pottery: gray and brown vessels, painted and plain, combining different traditions. Almost no house contained two identical examples. Anyone worried about a perfectly matching dinner set would have found plenty to rearrange. The actual dishes show that several styles could share the same table.

passages.title: Homes, food and practical skills
passages.text: The surviving plans show Gordion houses with courtyards; some also had upper stories. Excavators have inventoried roughly 1,500 complete Hellenistic vessels, as well as glass containers, figurines, coins and tools. The evidence is unusually rich because some buildings were abandoned with belongings still inside, not because every resident was wealthy.

passages.title: Homes, food and practical skills
passages.text: Cappadocia’s resources included wheat, fruit, livestock and minerals. Horses mattered to defense as well as wealth. Greek education also formed part of royal family life, and some princes trained at Athens. These reports describe resources and elites; they do not establish universal schooling.

passages.title: Writing and what changed
passages.text: Artaxias’s second-century BCE boundary stones offer a short written witness: MLK RWNDKN, translated “Orontid king.” This is scholarly transliteration of Aramaic, with an alternative reading recorded by James Russell. It advertised dynastic legitimacy on land markers; it is not Armenian script or a phrase spoken by everyone inside the atlas outline.

passages.title: Writing and what changed
passages.text: Gordion’s settlement history was not one uninterrupted decline. The excavation project distinguishes three Galatian phases and a reoccupation around 150 to 100 BCE, after the Roman campaign of 189 BCE. Distinctive iron brooches help identify that later phase. An abandoned house can mark one local disruption while a community’s broader history continues.

The atlas ends this umbrella at 1 BCE, without a common conquest. Cappadocia’s monarchy continued until Roman annexation in 17 CE. Political institutions changed at different times; the broad label’s disappearance should not be mistaken for all the region’s communities vanishing together.

sectionTitles: A garden, households and practical craft
Temples, water and a written word

passages.text: This atlas label groups parts of the Malay Peninsula, Sumatra and Java between 600 and 800. “Under Indian influence” describes cultural connections, not rule by an Indian government or a single local state. The polygons include tested points at Kedah, Palembang, Kota Kapur and Dieng, while clipping other important places such as Borobudur and Batujaya. Ports, rulers and religious communities used ideas and scripts from South Asia in their own settings. Srivijaya, early Javanese courts and Kedah remain distinct histories; the later regional umbrella beginning in 800 has a different outline and its own card.

passages.title: Routes, rulers and obligations
passages.text: The Chinese monk Yijing sailed from Guangzhou in 671 on a Persian ship and visited Srivijaya before continuing toward India. His route included Kacha, usually identified with Kedah, where he used a merchant vessel. Religious travel depended on commercial shipping: a pilgrimage could require negotiating the same winds and ports as a cargo voyage.

passages.title: Routes, rulers and obligations
passages.text: The Kedukan Bukit stone near Palembang records a 682 expedition associated with Dapunta Hyang. Its account combines river travel, people walking, supplies and the making of a wanua, or settlement. The precise route and some readings remain debated. It shows organized movement and political ambition, rather than proving that the entire atlas polygon belonged to Srivijaya.

passages.title: Routes, rulers and obligations
passages.text: A 686 inscription at Kota Kapur on Bangka threatens those who betray Srivijaya’s ruler or his appointed authorities. It mentions a military expedition against Bhumi Jawa. The wording records an intention and an assertion of power; it is not a complete campaign diary establishing the conquest of every part of Java.

passages.title: Routes, rulers and obligations
passages.text: The Kota Kapur text is arranged in ten lines on a tall stone. To read its lines from left to right in their normal orientation, a reader would lay the stone with its pointed end to the left. Inscriptions need careful looking as well as language knowledge: even deciding which way is up can matter.

passages.title: A garden, households and practical craft
passages.text: The Talang Tuwo inscription, dated 684, describes a garden established by Sri Jayanasa near Palembang. Its plants included coconut, areca, sugar palm, sago and bamboo, with other gardens, dams and ponds also mentioned. The text wishes that travelers find food and drinking water. This is a royal dedication and statement of intent, not a measured report of every person’s diet.

passages.title: A garden, households and practical craft
passages.text: That dedication also wishes for thriving fields, livestock, trustworthy friends and faithful spouses, and freedom from illness and disturbed sleep. Its hopes reveal everyday anxieties alongside Buddhist aspirations. Enslaved people appear among possessions expected to prosper, exposing the unequal society behind royal benevolence. Wishes for health do not establish a hospital or prove that disease had been prevented.

passages.title: A garden, households and practical craft
passages.text: At Sungai Mas in Kedah, researchers compared the material in ancient bricks with clay from the Muda River basin. The similarities support local manufacture. Temple building drew on regional skills and raw materials, even while religious ideas traveled widely. An imported idea did not require importing every brick needed to put it into practice.

passages.title: A garden, households and practical craft
passages.text: A large granite jar found beside the sanctuary steps at Sungai Mas has been interpreted as a water container for visitors to wash their feet. It belonged to a complex with additions over several centuries; the associated makara is dated broadly to the seventh through ninth centuries. This is a site-specific interpretation of ritual cleanliness, not evidence for toilets in every home.

passages.title: A garden, households and practical craft
passages.text: Glass lumps and finished beads at Sungai Mas point to manufacture as well as trade. Compositional studies compare the glass with material from other regions rather than declaring every bead an import. Producing these small ornaments required control of materials and technique. Their size can hide the amount of skilled work involved.

passages.title: Temples, water and a written word
passages.text: Dieng’s temples stand on a volcanic plateau about 2,000 meters above sea level. Heritage researchers place early construction in the late seventh and early eighth centuries, with further work continuing later in the eighth. Sacred buildings here belonged to a Javanese setting far from the coastal ports. The plural map label should not flatten these different landscapes into one capital.

passages.title: Temples, water and a written word
passages.text: Ancient channels are part of Dieng’s archaeological landscape. Much later, nineteenth-century investigators encountered temples standing in water, and recovery involved drainage and excavation. These traces make water management part of the site’s story, but they do not prove that all channels were built at the same time or carried household sewage.

passages.title: Temples, water and a written word
passages.text: A small Old Malay word from Talang Tuwo is niyur, meaning “coconut palm.” Cœdès prints it in his transcription of line 2 among the garden’s trees. These Latin letters are a scholarly transliteration of the 684 inscription’s South Indian-derived writing, not the original letterforms. A familiar plant connects the royal text with practical food-growing concerns.

There was no common fall in 800. Sungai Mas continued as a port beyond the eighth century, and the regions followed different political and religious paths. Later atlas labels and named states must be read as new scopes, not the disappearance of these communities.

passages.text: This combined map label covers separate powers in western Tanzania: Mirambo’s Urambo, neighbouring Unyanyembe, and Nyungu-ya-Mawe’s state in Ukimbu. Their alliances and rivalries changed. The outline is not evidence that Mirambo ruled all three, or that his state survived until the imported endpoint of 1914.

passages.title: States beside the caravan road
passages.text: Unyanyembe’s royal centre at Itetemia stood beside the growing commercial town of Tabora. Its links to long-distance trade made it influential in its own right. It was a competitor of Mirambo’s Urambo, not simply a district in his empire.

passages.title: States beside the caravan road
passages.text: Nyungu-ya-Mawe appointed military governors, called vatwale, to supervise provinces in Ukimbu and channel resources toward his centre. He and Mirambo were once allies, but control of caravan routes strained their relationship by 1880. One map colour hides considerable political disagreement.

passages.title: States beside the caravan road
passages.text: Mirambo often kept chiefs who submitted to him, while replacing others with local headmen after conquest. Communities supplied fighters and provisions. His military success therefore depended on village labour as well as battlefield leadership, and imposed heavy demands on conquered people.

passages.title: Work, families and practical knowledge
passages.text: Mid-nineteenth-century observers described Nyamwezi women growing and processing grain, making meals and brewing grain beer. Some women travelled with caravans, sometimes with babies. Their work helped keep both households and long journeys going; experiences differed sharply between free and enslaved women.

passages.title: Work, families and practical knowledge
passages.text: Local specialists exchanged baskets, pottery, stools, bark boxes, mortars and pestles between villages. Smiths and medical practitioners also supplied skills that a household might seek from outside. Everyday equipment had makers, repairers and trading routes of its own.

passages.title: Work, families and practical knowledge
passages.text: Many Nyamwezi caravan porters were skilled wage workers. They could stop a march to demand better terms. Cloth and beads served as pay and bought provisions along the road: your wages could arrive as fabric rather than coins.

passages.title: Work, families and practical knowledge
passages.text: A caravan guide needed languages as well as a good sense of direction. The kirangozi located paths, food and water and negotiated payments to chiefs. Getting everyone safely to the next meal was part of the job description.

passages.title: Work, families and practical knowledge
passages.text: Contact with coastal traders also carried ideas about healing into inland communities. Pallaver traces the gradual borrowing of practices without assuming that everyone immediately converted to Islam. Towns such as Tabora were meeting places for knowledge as well as merchandise.

passages.title: Food security and surviving words
passages.text: Farmers in Unyanyembe adjusted crop choices to rainfall. Millet and sorghum tolerated drought better than rice and maize; stored harvests helped bridge bad seasons. A well-stocked granary could matter as much as a well-stocked armoury.

passages.title: Food security and surviving words
passages.text: Warfare encouraged people to gather inside large stockaded settlements. Abandoned land returned to bush, creating conditions favourable to tsetse flies and threatening cattle. Defensive walls solved one danger while changing the landscape around them.

passages.title: Food security and surviving words
passages.text: Drought and warfare fed each other in Mirambo’s final years. Raids seized food and people for agricultural labour, while fighting destroyed fields. Famine weakened his system before tributaries rebelled after his death in December 1884.

passages.title: Food security and surviving words
passages.text: Written Swahili survives in a list apparently naming people captured by Mirambo: “hao kila mtu kwa watu wake”, translated as “each is there for his men.” Shown here is the editor’s Roman transcription of Arabic-script Swahili. The document’s precise date and origin are unknown; it is not Mirambo’s autograph.

Mirambo’s state fragmented after his death in 1884. Unyanyembe fell under German conquest from 1893; Nyungu’s political system in Ukimbu was dismantled in 1895. These were separate endings, not a shared collapse in 1914. Nyamwezi and Kimbu communities continued under changing rule.

sectionTitles: Power, trade and changing political borders

passages.text: Miskito communities live along the Caribbean coast and rivers of Honduras and Nicaragua. Their history includes influential regional leaders, British alliances and persistent village authority. The imported 1492-1500 polygon is an approximate cultural outline: the better-documented Miskito kings belong to much later centuries. A single royal border cannot capture all communities or settle historians’ disagreements about how centralized their government was.

passages.title: Power, trade and changing political borders
passages.text: How much power did a Miskito king possess? Historian Mary Helms emphasizes village elders and regional leaders as well as English connections. In the accounts she examines, a visiting king could encourage people to follow their own local elders. Royal titles did not automatically erase village authority.

passages.title: Power, trade and changing political borders
passages.text: British settlers supplied firearms and sometimes joined Miskito allies in attacks on Spanish positions. Trade also changed everyday possessions, including cloth and metal cooking pots. Some Miskito traders sold captives into slavery, so this expanding coastal power carried severe costs for neighboring peoples.

passages.title: Power, trade and changing political borders
passages.text: The 1860 Treaty of Managua ended Britain’s protectorate and recognized Nicaraguan sovereignty. It also promised Miskito self-government according to local customs, within limits compatible with that sovereignty. That uneasy compromise created a reserve rather than simply handing every village an identical new government.

passages.title: Power, trade and changing political borders
passages.text: Nicaraguan authorities incorporated the reserve in 1894. This ended its separate political arrangement, but not Miskito identity. Later conflict again disrupted families: the Inter-American Commission documented the relocation of thousands from the Coco River region in early 1982.

passages.title: Power, trade and changing political borders
passages.text: Nicaragua’s 1987 autonomy statute established a new regional framework, and regional councils began work in 1990. These institutions served a coast shared by several peoples. Regional autonomy and the survival of Miskito communities should not be confused with restoration of the old royal system.

passages.title: River skills, households and learning
passages.text: A small carved wooden paddle in the National Museum of the American Indian was collected along the Coco River in 1924. The catalogue identifies it as Miskito and as a model or miniature. It preserves the shape of river equipment without proving who carved it or whether it was a child’s toy.

passages.title: River skills, households and learning
passages.text: Conzemius’s 1932 account describes a turtle-hunting harpoon with a strong cord attached to the canoe’s bow, rather than a floating marker. Its wooden shaft and metal point worked together. This historical technique depended on careful handling of both boat and line.

passages.title: River skills, households and learning
passages.text: In interviews reported from 2010, Miskito women described territory through everyday needs: cassava, plantains, beans, house timber and animals. Family graves and nearby relatives mattered too. A homeland could be a food cupboard, a building supply and a family history all at once.

passages.title: River skills, households and learning
passages.text: Moravian missionaries established themselves at Bluefields in 1849 and later opened posts among Miskito communities. Their gatherings included bread, coffee, prayers and hymns. They also pressed families to alter houses and marriage practices, changes that prompted resistance as well as conversion.

passages.title: River skills, households and learning
passages.text: Neighbors and relatives helped clear garden plots and build houses. In nineteenth-century mission accounts discussed by von Oertzen, cassava beer accompanied such work parties. Missionary bans on the drink could therefore disrupt cooperation between households, not just change what appeared in a cup.

passages.title: River skills, households and learning
passages.text: A modern written sample is “wina”, meaning “meat” or “body”; the 2007 URACCAN study distinguishes “winá”, meaning “from”. These spellings follow the authors’ proposed accent marks. The tiny mark helps readers notice a difference that their discussion links to spoken stress.

passages.title: River skills, households and learning
passages.text: The same researchers listened to elders, radio programs, religious gatherings and community assemblies when studying pronunciation. Pictures and real objects helped include people who did not read. Their work treated community speech as evidence for better bilingual teaching materials.

passages.title: River skills, households and learning
passages.text: UNICEF’s 2023 community-protection booklet was offered in Spanish and Miskito. It directed families toward trusted relatives, friends, elders, health workers and women’s organizations when someone needed help. Written Miskito thus also belongs to practical efforts to care for people today.

Neither the map’s 1500 cutoff nor the reserve’s annexation in 1894 ended the Miskito people. Later regional institutions, language research and family-support materials document continuing communities, whose experiences extend across both Nicaragua and Honduras.

passages.text: Mixtec rulers governed several competing kingdoms in southern Mexico, linked by marriages, warfare and trade. The imported “empire” outline is misplaced west of much of the Mixtec heartland; it should not be read as their territorial boundary.

passages.title: Kingdoms, families and books
passages.text: Lord Eight Deer Jaguar Claw joined Tilantongo, Teozacoalco and Tututepec under his rule. His story was exceptional within a landscape of competing kingdoms. A powerful ruler could unite several courts without creating one permanent empire for every Mixtec community.

passages.title: Kingdoms, families and books
passages.text: The Tonindeye Codex unfolds like a concertina. Its 47 painted deerskin leaves carry a prepared pale surface and vivid pigments. Fully extended, the book is more than eleven metres long: this family history would not fit across an ordinary kitchen table.

passages.title: Kingdoms, families and books
passages.text: One codex scene shows Lady Five Flint giving birth to an heir, with the child still connected by the umbilical cord. Births and marriages mattered because claims to land and rule depended on relationships between families.

passages.title: Kingdoms, families and books
passages.text: A short reading supplied by the museum is “Iya Nacuaa”, meaning “Lord 8 Deer”. This is a scholarly Latin-script rendering of the ruler’s name represented in the pictorial manuscript, dated 1200 to 1521; its painted signs are not alphabetic letters.

passages.title: Kingdoms, families and books
passages.text: Calendar names linked a person to a day in a 260-day cycle. Animal signs and other images helped identify those days. In 2021, Mixtec researchers used the surviving books together with Indigenous knowledge to reinterpret their communities’ histories.

passages.title: Homes, materials and skilled work
passages.text: Excavations at Yucundaa uncovered a palace with patios and rooms reserved for rulers and nobles. Architecture suggests that these spaces combined residence, ritual and formal meetings. For the court, home and workplace could be parts of the same complex.

passages.title: Homes, materials and skilled work
passages.text: At that palace, investigators compare doorways, room plans, renovations and refuse from an associated rubbish deposit. Even royal rubbish has something to say: discarded material helps test ideas suggested by impressive walls and painted histories.

passages.title: Homes, materials and skilled work
passages.text: Cotton moved between different environments. A historical study describes the inland kingdom of Teozacoalco obtaining it from the coast near Tututepec. A cloth’s story could therefore begin in warm coastal fields and continue in workshops far inland.

passages.title: Homes, materials and skilled work
passages.text: A Mixtec gold necklace in the Met has beads shaped like jaguar teeth. Its delicate loops were modeled in wax and cast in metal, a technique called false filigree. What looks like tiny bent wires could begin as a carefully shaped wax model.

passages.title: Homes, materials and skilled work
passages.text: The museum compares this necklace with objects excavated in Monte Albán’s Tomb 7. That tomb contained mixed remains of men, women and children, suggesting reuse or secondary burial. Its riches cannot securely identify one famous king as the principal occupant.

passages.title: Colonial upheaval and continuing communities
passages.text: Spanish conquest in Oaxaca involved rival local alliances as well as armed expeditions. Some Zapotec rulers sought help against Tututepec; other communities resisted. These choices had local purposes, even as Spanish rule brought new forms of domination.

passages.title: Colonial upheaval and continuing communities
passages.text: Ancient DNA from ten people buried at Teposcolula-Yucundaa identified Salmonella Paratyphi C. Researchers propose it as a strong candidate behind the local 1545 epidemic. Teeth preserved evidence that could help investigate a catastrophe centuries after the people died.

Spanish rule and colonial tribute transformed Mixtec kingdoms during the sixteenth century; the imported 1530 cutoff is not one empire’s fall. Mixtec peoples, languages and historical traditions continue, and Indigenous scholars actively interpret the surviving books.

passages.text: Mixtec history connects distinct kingdoms and communities in Oaxaca. Painted books record ruling families whose interests sometimes conflicted. Archaeology adds the work of farmers, householders and craftspeople to histories often centred on dynasties.

passages.title: Farming and household life
passages.text: At Nicayuhu, archaeologists excavated Postclassic houses beside terraced fields. Stone foundations and repeatedly renewed floors show long use. Rooms around patios included hearths; sloping floors and heated annexes were interpreted cautiously as possible steam baths.

passages.title: Farming and household life
passages.text: Nicayuhu households used ordinary pottery and stone tools. Obsidian blades were scarce and sometimes reshaped to prolong their working life. The excavated assemblages reveal maintenance and economical reuse alongside the better-known luxury arts.

passages.title: Farming and household life
passages.text: Lama-bordo terraces trap soil carried by seasonal runoff behind barriers. Nicayuhu’s excavated layers suggest gradual construction and repair. Pérez Rodríguez argues that households could create these productive fields without a royal administration directing every stage.

passages.title: Farming and household life
passages.text: Pérez Rodríguez’s later interviews document farmers’ detailed knowledge of soils, weather, plants and pests. Households still built, maintained and farmed lama-bordos. Comparison with excavated terraces helps explain this durable farming practice without assuming that ancient labour arrangements were identical to modern ones.

passages.title: Books and historical knowledge
passages.text: Codex Bodley is a long painted deerskin strip folded into pages. A white preparation layer supported the images, while red bands organised the reading. Its format made relationships among people, places and events visible across successive panels.

passages.title: Books and historical knowledge
passages.text: Bodley includes genealogies of families that sometimes opposed each other. Pohl treats its selection and arrangement of stories as a historical problem, not a neutral list of kings. Its painting date remains unresolved after 1500 and may be early colonial.

passages.title: Metal, colour and sound
passages.text: A gold necklace at The Met combines jaguar-tooth-shaped beads with small bells. Artisans modelled delicate loops in wax before casting them in metal. This “false filigree” technique produced intricate links without attaching separate wires afterward.

passages.title: Metal, colour and sound
passages.text: The necklace’s bells lacked clappers but could strike one another as the wearer moved. Jaguar imagery associated the ornament with power. The Met compares it with an excavated Tomb 7 necklace; the museum’s object is not itself recorded as that tomb find.

passages.title: Metal, colour and sound
passages.text: Mixtec painters decorated ceramic vessels with animals, deities and geometric designs in several colours. Tripod vessels and cups with shaped supports show that the pot’s structure contributed to its effect as much as its painted surface.

passages.title: Metal, colour and sound
passages.text: Rattles, scrapers, conch instruments and drums occur in burial assemblages described by the Museo Chileno. Their presence suggests music’s ceremonial importance. These finds preserve instrument types, although they cannot recover a performance’s full sound or meaning.

passages.title: Communities across political change
passages.text: Spanish rule brought compulsory labour demands and introduced crops and livestock. Cochineal dye and cotton textiles became important colonial products. These changes affected what households made and owed, without replacing every older crop, skill or community relationship.

passages.title: Communities across political change
passages.text: INPI’s contemporary account describes migrants maintaining ties with their places of origin and taking part in communal responsibilities. This is evidence of continuing, changing Mixtec communities. It should not be used as a timeless description of every preconquest household.

Mexica expansion and then Spanish colonial conquest altered the kingdoms’ authority. Encomienda and other colonial demands reshaped work and landholding. Mixtec communities and cultural knowledge continued through these changes; there was no single event that ended the people’s history.

passages.text: Moche societies flourished along Peru's northern coastal valleys during the first through eighth centuries CE. Their ceramics preserve an unusually rich visual record of people, animals, plants and ritual activity.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Potters used molds to produce standardized vessel shapes while varying their painted and sculpted decoration.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Many vessels combine red and cream slip painting with modeled figures. Complex scenes could cover the surface of a stirrup-spout bottle.

passages.title: Portraiture
passages.text: Portrait bottles may depict recognizable individuals. Scholars debate how their social identities related to the vessels' eventual placement in burials.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Fine decorated pottery also occurs in residential compounds. Wear, repairs and excavated household contexts show that many vessels served the living before burial.

passages.title: Food and gatherings
passages.text: Decorated vessels participated in household rituals and feasts, including the sharing of food and corn beer.

passages.title: How we know
passages.text: Images include crops, animals, healers and supernatural beings. They are a visual source, but an image alone cannot tell us every detail of the activity it depicts.

What does your patient do for a living?
Schools, care and a garden with a purpose

passages.text: The Duchy of Modena and Reggio was an Este-ruled state in northern Italy, with Modena as its capital after the loss of Ferrara in 1598. This imported 1650 to 1815 record is only a rough guide: its outline extends too far north toward Mantua, and the continuous date range hides the interruption of ducal rule from 1796 to 1814. The restored duchy survived well beyond 1815, ending in 1859.

passages.title: A capital rebuilt around a court
passages.text: In 1598, before this map interval, the Este rulers lost Ferrara to the papacy and moved their capital to Modena. They retained Modena, Reggio and Garfagnana. The new capital inherited court collections, administrative traditions and a dynasty whose ambitions were larger than one city.

passages.title: A capital rebuilt around a court
passages.text: The restoration of 1814 did not simply switch an old government back on. Francesco IV issued a plan of government on 28 August, organizing centralized institutions under the ruler’s personal control. Records from these ministries survive, showing how a small duchy managed finance, education, diplomacy and internal affairs.

passages.title: Boats, washing and water
passages.text: Modena had an inland port. Francesco I’s Darsena began operating around the middle of the seventeenth century, and in 1667 sloping loading areas were added so carts could reach the water’s edge. Heavy goods could travel by boat before continuing their journey on wheels.

passages.title: Boats, washing and water
passages.text: Canals powered mills and machinery used for spinning and making paper. Washwomen cleaned clothes in spring-fed channels and spread them on meadows outside the walls. Water was a workplace as well as a route for travelers: the same city needed laundry, flour, cloth and transport.

passages.title: Boats, washing and water
passages.text: Wells supplied drinking water to homes, courtyards and public fountains. The city’s coat of arms even shows two crossed drilling tools, honoring the skill of reaching groundwater. A detailed city plan drawn by Giovanni Battista Boccabadati in 1684 records canals and underground drains, helping us reconstruct this watery landscape.

passages.title: What does your patient do for a living?
passages.text: Bernardino Ramazzini taught medicine in Modena from 1682 and published his study of workers’ illnesses in 1700. He treated occupation as a serious clue when investigating disease. The health of people who earned their living with their hands belonged in medical scholarship too.

passages.title: What does your patient do for a living?
passages.text: Writing sample: the Latin title of Ramazzini’s 1700 Modena book is “De morbis artificum diatriba,” meaning “A discussion of the diseases of workers.” The University of Iowa preserves and catalogs this edition, printed by Antonio Capponi. Latin let scholarly readers in different countries share a medical argument.

passages.title: What does your patient do for a living?
passages.text: In the expanded version of his treatise, published after he moved to Padua, Ramazzini connected stoneworkers’ dust with breathing problems and described irritation suffered by laundry workers. He considered both harmful substances and awkward bodily movements. These observations concern several occupations and places, not a survey proving that every Modenese worker had the same illness.

passages.title: Schools, care and a garden with a purpose
passages.text: University teaching was renewed in Modena in 1682 with subjects including philosophy, medicine, law and theology. Municipal resources and donations helped support it. In 1772, ducal reform placed the university under direct state control and funding, connecting advanced education more closely to government needs.

passages.title: Schools, care and a garden with a purpose
passages.text: Part of the new hospital opened on 30 November 1758. The duke commissioned medals to place in its foundations, turning the building itself into a message for the future. The surviving complex reminds us that eighteenth-century urban improvement included places intended for treating illness.

passages.title: Schools, care and a garden with a purpose
passages.text: The Albergo dei Poveri, built between 1764 and 1771, combined support for destitute people with work. In 1788 it became the Albergo delle Arti. These names describe an institution that joined charity, training and labor; they should not be mistaken for an ordinary hotel where guests booked a holiday.

passages.title: Schools, care and a garden with a purpose
passages.text: In 1758, the duke set aside part of his court garden for medicinal plants. A public botany chair followed, and the garden came under university administration in 1772. Beds of useful plants surrounded a central pool that supplied irrigation and held aquatic species. This garden was a living classroom.

The duke left Modena in June 1859, and provisional governments replaced the Austria-Este administration. The state archive preserves the assembly’s decrees ending the dynasty and seeking union with Sardinia. The duchy’s end belonged to Italian unification, not to the imported map cutoff of 1815.

sectionTitles: Clues left in a sheltered canyon
Making pots, painting animals and learning skills

passages.text: Mogollon is an archaeological name for varied farming communities of the American Southwest and adjoining northern Mexico, not one empire. This map’s outline is displaced far south into Mexico and does not reliably show that culture area. Its 800 to 1000 interval also covers only part of a much longer history. The named regional examples below extend beyond those dates.

passages.title: Building homes and finding water
passages.text: In the Tularosa Basin, the people archaeologists call Jornada Mogollon first built circular houses partly dug into the ground, framed with wooden beams. Later houses included square adobe buildings. These changing plans show families solving the problem of shelter in different ways over time.

passages.title: Building homes and finding water
passages.text: At Lake Lucero and the Huntington site, villages stood near places where rainwater flowed down from the San Andres Mountains. The surrounding landscape also supplied salt and gypsum. Archaeologists suggest some gypsum was processed into wall plaster, turning a local mineral into part of a home.

passages.title: Building homes and finding water
passages.text: Farming in the Tularosa Basin supplemented hunting and gathering. Deer, rabbits and birds remained important quarry, while pottery and bow-and-arrow technology appear in the archaeological record. A village’s food supply depended on several activities rather than a single dependable harvest.

passages.title: Building homes and finding water
passages.text: Gila’s Cave 1 has small storage rooms, a fire pit and a larger area interpreted as a once-enclosed living space. Places for supplies, cooking and family activity fitted within the natural shelter. The open ruin visitors see is missing walls and coverings that once shaped daily movement.

passages.title: Building homes and finding water
passages.text: Of 32 plant species identified in the Gila dwellings, 24 were wild. Grapes, berries, acorns and piñon nuts joined cultivated corn, beans and squash. That plant list records a much wider pantry than the label farmer might suggest.

passages.title: Clues left in a sheltered canyon
passages.text: The south-facing Gila caves offered shelter and useful seasonal temperature regulation, above a canyon with a year-round stream. Protected maize cobs survived for centuries inside. A dry, sheltered corner can preserve evidence of an ordinary meal far longer than an exposed field can.

passages.title: Clues left in a sheltered canyon
passages.text: Yucca sandals found at Gila show plant fibers becoming footwear. The park also describes yucca as a possible shampoo ingredient. Those are different kinds of evidence: excavated sandals are actual objects, while the washing use comes from knowledge of what the plant can do.

passages.title: Clues left in a sheltered canyon
passages.text: Original wooden roof beams remain in Gila’s Cave 3. Matching their tree-ring patterns helps archaeologists date the timber and place much of the room building in the 1280s. A tree’s cut date supplies a strong clue, though reused or stored wood need not mark construction day exactly.

passages.title: Clues left in a sheltered canyon
passages.text: Heavy soot on cave ceilings and artifacts from earlier cultural groups indicate temporary sheltering long before the masonry rooms were built. The cave therefore holds several histories at once. An older hunting tool found there need not have belonged to the later house builders.

passages.title: Making pots, painting animals and learning skills
passages.text: One Mimbres bowl in the Metropolitan Museum depicts two rounded rabbits and dates broadly from the mid-ninth to twelfth century. Rabbits were both familiar food animals and popular painted subjects. The vessel lets us see an artist’s choices without pretending the picture captions itself.

passages.title: Making pots, painting animals and learning skills
passages.text: Western New Mexico University’s museum includes miniature vessels and pots identified as children’s work among its Southwest collections. These objects widen the story beyond accomplished adult makers. Small hands and learners also belong in the history of a craft, even when their names are lost.

passages.title: Making pots, painting animals and learning skills
passages.text: Writing: no readable Mogollon-language sentence is supplied. The Gila park identifies its builders through archaeology and notes that they left oral history rather than a written language. Painted animals, geometric decoration and rock images are not a deciphered transcript that can be given an invented translation.

Mogollon settlements and material traditions changed along different regional paths, with many mountain communities relocating before about 1450. Their people did not simply vanish. Researchers connect their descendants with several later Southwestern communities, although the exact relationships remain debated. The map’s 1000 endpoint marks neither a conquest nor the end of this longer history.

passages.text: The Mohegan are a continuing Native nation centered on southeastern Connecticut and the Thames River. Their distinct seventeenth-century polity under Uncas emerged through a split from Pequot leadership. The imported regional outline and 1492 to 1500 dates predate that political development; they should not be read as the lifetime or precise borders of Uncas’s government.

passages.title: Politics and objects with histories
passages.text: Uncas rose within Pequot leadership before breaking with its sachems over relations with European newcomers. He led followers west of the Thames River and established a separate Mohegan political community. The tribe’s account preserves this leadership history alongside older origin traditions.

passages.title: Politics and objects with histories
passages.text: Mohegan forces allied with English colonists during the Pequot War, and Mohegan leaders participated in the 1638 Hartford treaty that distributed Pequot survivors. This alliance increased Mohegan influence while contributing to their neighbors’ dispossession. Shared language and ancestry did not prevent stark political conflict.

passages.title: Politics and objects with histories
passages.text: At seventeenth-century Fort Shantok, investigators recovered shell fragments, bead-making debris and sandstone polishing blocks. Researcher Margaret Bruchac examined an altered iron nail, item 10289, whose narrow end matched the hole in a shell bead. She interprets it as a reused drill bit, showing artisans adapting available metal to skilled work.

passages.title: Politics and objects with histories
passages.text: The Tantaquidgeon Museum identifies a shell-bead collar dated around 1638 with Uncas. Its description interprets two white triangles as marking the division between Mohegan and Pequot villages. Here a surviving object carries a community account of political relationships, rather than merely displaying an attractive pattern.

passages.title: Politics and objects with histories
passages.text: The Huntington holds an ash-splint basket made around 1880 by a Mohegan maker identified as J. H. S., accession 2016.25.50. Dyed strips decorate the woven container. The museum explains that soaking thin wood splints made them flexible enough to weave into useful carriers for household belongings.

passages.title: Food, gathering and everyday learning
passages.text: Yokeag is parched, ground corn. The tribe describes grinding it with a mortar and pestle as part of the Wigwam Festival, linking food preparation with earlier generations. Its contemporary account even mentions serving it on ice cream. Traditional ingredients can find very modern company in a bowl.

passages.title: Food, gathering and everyday learning
passages.text: Emma Baker revived the Wigwam Festival in 1860, connecting it with the Mohegan Church Ladies’ Sewing Society. Food, crafts and gathering helped sustain community ties while land was being divided. This later history gives the celebration a role in political survival as well as seasonal thanksgiving.

passages.title: Food, gathering and everyday learning
passages.text: The Mohegan educational guide describes storytelling as a cycle of listening, observing, remembering and sharing. Repeated stories can reveal different lessons as listeners grow. Elders’ knowledge is therefore part of education, alongside the skills learned in schools.

passages.title: Food, gathering and everyday learning
passages.text: A tribal library proposal submitted in 2020 describes story times, book clubs, cultural workshops and seasonal celebrations already serving different ages. It links library work with the Tantaquidgeon Museum and garden spaces. Modern education joins books with the practical knowledge carried by plants and people.

passages.title: Medicine, writing and teaching
passages.text: Gladys Tantaquidgeon learned herbal knowledge and spirituality from older Mohegan women, then studied anthropology at the University of Pennsylvania. Her research also involved Delaware, Nanticoke, Cayuga and Wampanoag communities. Her 1942 study of Delaware medicine records another people’s practices, so its remedies should not all be labeled Mohegan.

passages.title: Medicine, writing and teaching
passages.text: In 1931, Gladys, her brother Harold and their father John founded the Tantaquidgeon Museum in Uncasville. Teaching visitors about Native people was central to their work against prejudice. A family’s collections and knowledge became a public educational institution.

passages.title: Medicine, writing and teaching
passages.text: Fidelia Fielding spoke Mohegan with her grandmother Martha Uncas and kept diaries in the language. The tribe records that Cornell agreed to return the surviving diaries in 2020. Her everyday writing preserved language at a time when English dominated surrounding institutions.

passages.title: Medicine, writing and teaching
passages.text: In her May 30, 1904 diary entry, Fielding wrote “ner weger nower Jeets sug.” The published transcription gives the meaning “I love to see the birds.” This preserves her own spelling as transcribed by Stephanie Fielding; the document separately supplies phonetic notation and a modern respelling. It is a small, personal glimpse of language in daily life.

passages.title: Medicine, writing and teaching
passages.text: Mohegan minister Samson Occom raised money in Britain for Native education, then returned to find that the project had moved away from his hopes. He later helped establish Brothertown among the Oneida in New York. The tribe’s biography records Dartmouth’s 2022 agreement to return his papers, including letters, journals and early written Mohegan.

passages.title: Dispossession and continuity
passages.text: Nineteenth-century division and taxation of Mohegan land reduced the remaining reservation. The tribe’s historical guide describes people working in mills, whaling, military service and domestic employment. Continuing to belong to the community did not require every family to earn a living in the same way.

passages.title: Dispossession and continuity
passages.text: The United States acknowledged the Mohegan Tribe federally in 1994. Gladys Tantaquidgeon’s correspondence about births, marriages, graduations and deaths helped document the community’s persistence. Family news that might look ordinary in a box of papers became important evidence of a nation’s continuing life.

Land loss and colonial supervision transformed Mohegan sovereignty, but the nation continued and received federal acknowledgment in 1994. The imported 1500 endpoint neither marks a conquest nor the disappearance of Mohegan people; even Uncas’s separate polity belongs to later history.

sectionTitles: Homes with a decorated source of warmth
Money with a name and an animal

passages.text: The map’s medieval Moldova means the principality usually called Moldavia in English. It was not the modern Republic of Moldova. The imported outline is misleading: it omits Suceava and much of the principality’s historical western territory. Suceava’s fortress and town were major centres of princely government, craft production and household life during the fifteenth century.

passages.title: Homes with a decorated source of warmth
passages.text: Archaeologists at Suceava identified fifteenth-century houses built from wood covered with clay. Some stood on stone foundations, and some had cellars. Ordinary construction materials can leave clues even when the wooden building itself has disappeared.

passages.title: Homes with a decorated source of warmth
passages.text: Tile stoves were a recurring feature of the fifteenth-century town’s houses. Some tiles were simple, while others carried elaborate Gothic decoration. A source of indoor warmth could also be a large decorative feature, rather like furniture that happened to heat the room.

passages.title: Homes with a decorated source of warmth
passages.text: Workshops stood among homes rather than in a completely separate industrial district. Excavations identified jewellery-making, bronze-working and bone-working near residences. Richer houses and modest dwellings also occurred alongside one another, complicating a simple picture of separate rich and poor neighbourhoods.

passages.title: Money with a name and an animal
passages.text: Under Stephen the Great, who ruled from 1457 to 1504, the Suceava mint produced silver groși and half-groși. Coins excavated at Orheiul Vechi include his issues. Their designs combine the ruler’s name, a shield and an aurochs head with other heraldic symbols.

passages.title: Money with a name and an animal
passages.text: A typeI coin legend reads “MONETA MOLDAVIE”, Latin for “money of Moldavia”. The museum transcribes it beside the aurochs-head design. Scholars disagree about the exact issuing dates, but the proposed typeI ranges fall within Stephen’s early reign, between 1457 and 1476.

passages.title: Family paperwork survived too
passages.text: A charter dated 17 March 1492 confirmed villages held by Şteful and his sister Marina after they lost the document inherited from their grandfather. Even a medieval family could face the dreaded missing-paperwork problem. Here, a replacement record protected a brother’s and sister’s property claim.

passages.title: Family paperwork survived too
passages.text: Other surviving documents record gifts by the treasurer Iuga to Putna Monastery in 1476. Such records connect named officials, religious institutions and property. Donations were also transactions that people wanted written down and remembered.

passages.title: Family paperwork survived too
passages.text: A 2022 exhibition assembled forty-one documents issued by Stephen’s chancery between 1458 and 1503, plus Iuga’s three records. Most were issued at Suceava, with others at Vaslui, Iași or Bădeuți. Their dates and places let historians follow a government operating through several princely residences.

passages.title: Architecture, colour and sound
passages.text: Suceava’s late-fourteenth-century fortress remained a principal residence of Moldavian rulers for almost two hundred years. Surviving carved stonework records building methods and decoration, including Gothic themes prominent in the fifteenth century. Government required rooms and skilled builders as well as rulers.

passages.title: Architecture, colour and sound
passages.text: Late-fourteenth- and early-fifteenth-century Moldavian churches could be decorated with ceramic discs, cross-shaped floral pieces and bricks, some glazed. These elements formed coloured bands around windows and beneath roofs. Fired clay contributed to the appearance of important public buildings as well as domestic heating.

passages.title: Architecture, colour and sound
passages.text: Siret’s Holy Trinity Church preserves this kind of ceramic architectural decoration. Archaeological fragments also come from Suceava, Cetatea Albă, old monasteries and other settlements. Comparing intact buildings with excavated pieces helps researchers reconstruct decorative traditions that no longer survive everywhere.

passages.title: Architecture, colour and sound
passages.text: The oldest surviving bells assigned to the medieval Moldavian state date from Stephen the Great’s reign. Bells can preserve inscriptions, decorations and coats of arms as well as producing sound. They are material records of the people and institutions that commissioned them.
Moldavia did not disappear in 1492. Much later, the 1859 election of Alexandru Ioan Cuza in both Moldavia and Wallachia began their union, leading toward the modern Romanian state.

sectionTitles: A woven wall could tell a family story
Writing and living with political change

passages.text: The Republic of Moldova declared independence in 1991 and adopted its constitution in 1994. This is the modern state, not the medieval principality of Moldavia. The outline includes territory beyond the central government’s effective control in Transnistria, so it must not be read as a map of uniform political control.

passages.title: A woven wall could tell a family story
passages.text: Wall carpets in Moldova and neighbouring Romania traditionally helped insulate and decorate houses. Patterns could identify a weaver’s community. Their makers combined practical household use with complex colour and design, turning a warm wall covering into something worth displaying.

passages.title: A woven wall could tell a family story
passages.text: Carpets also formed part of brides’ dowries and accompanied important family ceremonies. In funeral customs they could symbolise passage to the afterlife. These are documented cultural meanings attached to textiles, rather than properties of the wool itself.

passages.title: A woven wall could tell a family story
passages.text: Weavers work on vertical or horizontal looms, building the design through repeated thread work. Skills have passed through families and also through classes, workshops and museums. The craft links patient hand movements with memories of particular people and places.

passages.title: Welcoming spring with two colours
passages.text: Mărțișor customs celebrate the beginning of spring with red-and-white threads that people make, give and wear. The shared regional tradition includes untying the thread when a flowering tree, swallow or stork signals spring’s arrival. Weather watching becomes part of a personal ornament.

passages.title: Welcoming spring with two colours
passages.text: Older women, teachers, craftspeople and museum workshops teach thread-making skills. UNESCO records the practice in Moldova, Romania, Bulgaria and North Macedonia. People attach protective meanings to the colours and objects, while children learn a small craft that can be given to someone else.

passages.title: The school toilet matters
passages.text: A school assessment conducted in 2023 and 2024 covered 968 institutions in Moldova. At that time, pupils in 88 schools had access only to outdoor toilets. This is a concrete reminder that school life includes warmth, privacy and a place to wash hands as well as textbooks.

passages.title: The school toilet matters
passages.text: At Baimaclia’s Mihai Eminescu Gymnasium, staff described the difficulty of children going outside to use toilets in cold weather. Hard water affected pipes and fixtures, and there was no central sewerage connection. Improving a bathroom could therefore involve both plumbing and wider village infrastructure.

passages.title: The school toilet matters
passages.text: A 2026 workshop taught school staff how to inspect and maintain sanitation facilities, spot faults and keep supplies available. A new tap is useful only while water comes out of it. The programme treated everyday cleaning and repairs as part of protecting children’s learning environment.

passages.title: Schooldays during a pandemic
passages.text: In August 2020, national ministries and international partners produced Romanian-language handbooks for pupils returning to education during COVID-19. The guides addressed the journey to school, classrooms, libraries, canteens and toilets. They also included advice about emotional well-being.

passages.title: Schooldays during a pandemic
passages.text: A My Schedule section helped students record opening times, lesson starts, canteen access and digital learning tools. Separate materials served primary, secondary and vocational education. These surviving guides show how an international emergency rearranged the ordinary timetable of a child’s day.

passages.title: Writing and living with political change
passages.text: The 1991 independence declaration describes Moldova as “SUVERAN, INDEPENDENT ŞI DEMOCRATIC”, meaning “sovereign, independent and democratic”. This Romanian wording appears in the Constitutional Court’s 2022 printed edition, page 11. It is a documented modern text using Latin letters, not a medieval inscription.

passages.title: Writing and living with political change
passages.text: Armed conflict in 1992 divided control around the Dniester, also called the Nistru. Later negotiations included practical confidence-building between the sides. The OSCE’s 2014 account emphasised solutions that could improve daily contacts while the larger political dispute remained unresolved.
The modern republic continues; the unresolved Transnistrian conflict complicates effective control within its internationally recognised borders.
