passages.text: This record begins while Montenegro was still joined with Serbia. A referendum in 2006 led to a separate independent republic. The modern outline therefore crosses a major change in sovereignty; it should not imply that Montenegro was already independent in 1994. Its families, coastal associations and northern farming communities continued through that change.

passages.title: A maritime association comes ashore
passages.text: The Boka Navy of Kotor preserves seafaring traditions through a voluntary cultural association. Membership is open to men, women and children. Its modern work commemorates maritime life and brings generations together, rather than functioning as a present-day combat navy.

passages.title: A maritime association comes ashore
passages.text: At formal celebrations, members wear colourful traditional uniforms, carry historic weapons and perform the kolo circle dance. The coordinated steps make a public ceremony out of inherited movement and dress. Historic objects become part of a performance in the town’s shared spaces.

passages.title: A maritime association comes ashore
passages.text: The association transmits knowledge of maritime history, customs and traditional skills. Younger participants learn through involvement with older members. Its heritage includes people remembering and practising together, alongside the uniforms and objects that can be displayed in a museum.

passages.title: Inviting more children to preschool
passages.text: The Preschool for All campaign began in March 2015 in five northern municipalities with particularly low attendance. UNICEF and the education ministry worked with local preschools and communities. Some places had available classroom capacity but needed stronger connections with families.

passages.title: Inviting more children to preschool
passages.text: Arts and educational events invited parents and young children to experience preschool activities. Partners included drama, music and ballet institutions, as well as teacher educators. Learning through songs, movement and play could help families picture what a preschool day offered.

passages.title: Inviting more children to preschool
passages.text: The campaign expanded to six more northern municipalities in 2016. Its posters show children painting, shaping clay, reading picture books and playing. These surviving campaign materials document the everyday activities used to explain early learning to the public.

passages.title: Cheese is also a livelihood
passages.text: At the 2017 Days of Pljevlja Cheese, producers presented cheeses and cream for judging, tasting and sale. Around a hundred producers submitted 172 samples. The event connected household and farm production with customers beyond an individual village.

passages.title: Cheese is also a livelihood
passages.text: Pljevlja cheese received national protection of its origin in 2017. The event included producers from the wider cross-border Drina-Tara region as well as Montenegro. A named local food could support both a sense of place and practical cooperation between farming communities.

passages.title: Words establishing a republic
passages.text: Article 1 of the constitution begins “Crna Gora je nezavisna i suverena država”, meaning “Montenegro is an independent and sovereign state”. This attested Montenegrin sentence uses Latin letters. The constitution was adopted in October 2007, after the independence referendum.

passages.title: Words establishing a republic
passages.text: The constitution gives Cyrillic and Latin scripts equal status and identifies several languages in official use. A country’s written life can therefore use more than one alphabet. These provisions concern public institutions, alongside the languages used within individual households.

passages.title: Words establishing a republic
passages.text: The 2007 constitution also describes the state as ecological and committed to social justice. Such language sets out constitutional goals. It records how lawmakers defined the republic, rather than proving that every environmental or social problem had been solved.

passages.title: A close and consequential vote
passages.text: In the May 2006 referendum, 55.5 percent of valid votes supported independence. The result led to the June declaration. The vote also shows that citizens held different views about their state’s future, even as the new republic’s institutions took shape.
The union with Serbia ended for Montenegro in 2006, and the independent republic continued. This was a change in sovereignty, not an ending of the country’s communities or cultural life.

sectionTitles: Discoveries: beads, sugar and household drainage
A volcano, scientific work and a continuing community

passages.text: Montserrat’s history includes Indigenous beadmaking, plantation labour, community schooling and music. Volcanic eruptions forced major changes after 1995, but the island’s society continued. This card connects discoveries and everyday life across the two map records for the same island.

passages.title: Discoveries: beads, sugar and household drainage
passages.text: At precolonial Trants, stone and shell beads survive alongside evidence of unfinished production. David Watters’s research identified manufacturing stages showing that island craftspeople worked imported raw materials. Other beads may have arrived already finished. A necklace can therefore reveal both skilled local work and connections across the sea; it does not by itself identify the wearer’s rank.

passages.title: Discoveries: beads, sugar and household drainage
passages.text: At Little Bay’s eighteenth-century cattle mill, archaeologists exposed a masonry channel in 2006. It carried pressed cane juice through the mill wall toward the boiling house, where the juice became sugar. This surviving connection helps reconstruct the sequence of plantation work. The archive also reports missing field records, so later sediment and pottery cannot simply be treated as the mill’s original floor.

passages.title: Discoveries: beads, sugar and household drainage
passages.text: In Area 2 of Little Bay’s workers’ village, a ditch cut around a house platform appears to have diverted rainwater from the home. Stone alignments also suggested steps and supports. These modest traces illuminate household care under slavery. Erosion and later land use damaged the site, making a complete reconstruction of each home impossible.

passages.title: Discoveries: beads, sugar and household drainage
passages.text: The workers’ village also yielded fragments of handmade earthenware associated with cooking, eating and storing water. Some vessel identifications remain tentative because the pieces are small. Imported ceramics and bottle glass occur too. A broken pot is useful evidence, but it cannot tell us every ingredient in the family’s supper.

passages.title: Schools, food and music
passages.text: After apprenticeship ended, emancipated Montserratians founded primary schools for their children. Brown University’s project chronology records seventeen schools in 1840, compared with one in 1838. Archaeologists excavated a schoolhouse on Potato Hill, where toys were among the finds. Education became part of building life after slavery.

passages.title: Schools, food and music
passages.text: In July 2012, seven Montserrat Secondary School pupils aged thirteen to sixteen joined a three-week archaeology programme. They excavated, washed and labelled finds, and then led public tours. Lessons included reading old documents critically. Here, learning history meant doing some of the investigating and explaining it to the adults.

passages.text: Goat water belongs in a dinner bowl: despite the name, it is a meat stew. The tourism authority describes it as a communal dish at weddings, christenings, parties and funerals, and a favourite Friday lunch. Cooking over a wood fire contributes flavour. The shared meal brings people together at very different moments in family life.

passages.title: Schools, food and music
passages.text: AIR Montserrat opened in 1979 and brought recording technology and musicians to the island. Its studio history lists work by local artist Arrow as well as Dire Straits, the Police and other visiting performers. Hurricane Hugo damaged the building and equipment in 1989, ending this studio’s operation years before the volcano crisis.

passages.title: A volcano, scientific work and a continuing community
passages.text: The eruption that began on 18 July 1995 changed where people could live and work. Plymouth was evacuated repeatedly before the final evacuation in April 1996. Pyroclastic currents, fast-moving mixtures of volcanic material and gas, reached the town in 1997. Losing a capital and homes was a human disaster, not a disappearance of Montserratian people or identity.

passages.title: A volcano, scientific work and a continuing community
passages.text: Even the scientists had to move. The observatory began in temporary premises in Plymouth, relocated as evacuation zones expanded, and eventually operated from Mongo Hill, where staff could not actually see the volcano. A purpose-built facility followed in 2003. Monitoring depended on instruments and teamwork as well as watching the mountain.

passages.title: A volcano, scientific work and a continuing community
passages.text: Volcano monitoring combines several kinds of clues. Instruments record earthquakes, ground movement and gas emissions; solar-powered remote stations can send measurements back to the observatory. These observations help scientists assess changing conditions. Montserrat’s scientific achievement includes sustained measurement and communication, rather than a machine that predicts an eruption with certainty.

passages.title: A volcano, scientific work and a continuing community
passages.text: At the National Museum in Little Bay, visitors can learn about precolonial life and more recent history, and try playable musical instruments. Preserving culture can involve making a sound yourself as well as looking at an old object. The museum represents continuing community work in the island’s north.

Montserrat continues as a British Overseas Territory. Plymouth’s evacuation and destruction changed where people lived, while cultural and scientific institutions continued elsewhere. The constitution introduced in 2011 did not grant independence. The map’s endpoints are not the end of Montserratian society.

sectionTitles: Discoveries: beads, sugar and household drainage
A volcano, scientific work and a continuing community

passages.text: Montserrat’s history includes Indigenous beadmaking, plantation labour, community schooling and music. Volcanic eruptions forced major changes after 1995, but the island’s society continued. This card connects discoveries and everyday life across the two map records for the same island.

passages.title: Discoveries: beads, sugar and household drainage
passages.text: At precolonial Trants, stone and shell beads survive alongside evidence of unfinished production. David Watters’s research identified manufacturing stages showing that island craftspeople worked imported raw materials. Other beads may have arrived already finished. A necklace can therefore reveal both skilled local work and connections across the sea; it does not by itself identify the wearer’s rank.

passages.title: Discoveries: beads, sugar and household drainage
passages.text: At Little Bay’s eighteenth-century cattle mill, archaeologists exposed a masonry channel in 2006. It carried pressed cane juice through the mill wall toward the boiling house, where the juice became sugar. This surviving connection helps reconstruct the sequence of plantation work. The archive also reports missing field records, so later sediment and pottery cannot simply be treated as the mill’s original floor.

passages.title: Discoveries: beads, sugar and household drainage
passages.text: In Area 2 of Little Bay’s workers’ village, a ditch cut around a house platform appears to have diverted rainwater from the home. Stone alignments also suggested steps and supports. These modest traces illuminate household care under slavery. Erosion and later land use damaged the site, making a complete reconstruction of each home impossible.

passages.title: Discoveries: beads, sugar and household drainage
passages.text: The workers’ village also yielded fragments of handmade earthenware associated with cooking, eating and storing water. Some vessel identifications remain tentative because the pieces are small. Imported ceramics and bottle glass occur too. A broken pot is useful evidence, but it cannot tell us every ingredient in the family’s supper.

passages.title: Schools, food and music
passages.text: After apprenticeship ended, emancipated Montserratians founded primary schools for their children. Brown University’s project chronology records seventeen schools in 1840, compared with one in 1838. Archaeologists excavated a schoolhouse on Potato Hill, where toys were among the finds. Education became part of building life after slavery.

passages.title: Schools, food and music
passages.text: In July 2012, seven Montserrat Secondary School pupils aged thirteen to sixteen joined a three-week archaeology programme. They excavated, washed and labelled finds, and then led public tours. Lessons included reading old documents critically. Here, learning history meant doing some of the investigating and explaining it to the adults.

sectionTitles: Children, writing and the limits of evidence

passages.text: Here “Moravians” marks communities in and around Moravia during 700 to 800. It is earlier than the ninth-century polity called Great Moravia and is not its full territory or lifetime. Archaeology reveals growing centres and skilled crafts, while the imported outline should be treated as a broad regional approximation.

passages.title: Settlements before the great churches
passages.text: Eighth-century Mikulčice occupied raised ground among branches of the Morava river. Slightly higher, sandy surfaces offered drier places to live than the lowest ground. The landscape itself helped determine where people established homes.

passages.title: Settlements before the great churches
passages.text: Hooked spurs and Avar-period bronze objects from eighth-century Mikulčice indicate people with riding equipment and connections beyond the settlement. These finds helped archaeologists recognise an important centre before its better-known ninth-century churches and palace.

passages.title: Settlements before the great churches
passages.text: At Pohansko near Břeclav, the Forest Nursery excavation area contained houses and pottery from settlement phases preceding Great Moravia. Some abandoned houses were partly covered by the later fortification. That physical overlap establishes a sequence: the homes came before the defensive wall.

passages.title: Settlements before the great churches
passages.text: Pottery from those early Pohansko settlements can be compared with urns from the cremation cemetery. Matching forms help researchers relate places where people lived to places where the dead were buried. These comparisons provide dates and connections where written household records have not survived.

passages.title: Making clothes, tools and iron
passages.text: Before the ninth-century expansion, craftspeople at Mikulčice worked bone and antler. Waste, partly shaped material and unfinished needle cases are evidence of production, even where the actual workshop building has not been identified. A half-finished case can be more revealing than a perfect finished one.

passages.title: Making clothes, tools and iron
passages.text: Spindle whorls, weaving weights, awls and needle cases connect the earlier Moravian settlements with making and repairing clothing. Finds from Mikulčice and Olomouc-Povel preserve different steps in the work. Much textile production could happen at household level, rather than requiring a separate specialist shop.

passages.title: Making clothes, tools and iron
passages.text: Woodworking tools from pre-Great Moravian hoards include drills, saws and drawknives alongside axes and chisels. Builders needed woodworking skills for homes, fortifications and everyday equipment. The tool kit shows that timber was shaped with more varied methods than simply chopping a tree down.

passages.title: Making clothes, tools and iron
passages.text: At Dolní Sukolom, three iron-smelting furnaces are dated by comparison with nearby Želechovice to around the transition from the eighth to the ninth century. Their construction included recessed hearths and long tunnels. The date is an archaeological comparison, not a year written on the furnaces.

passages.title: Making clothes, tools and iron
passages.text: Researchers analysed slag and ore from the Uničov region to investigate where the metalworkers obtained their raw materials. Similarities linked the furnaces with local magnetite-hematite ore sources. The discarded lumps left by smelting help reconstruct a supply network for making iron.

passages.title: Children, writing and the limits of evidence
passages.text: One early feature at Pohansko’s northeastern outer settlement contained the burial of a newborn child, dated to the seventh or eighth century. The child was included in a modern ancient-DNA study. This small grave brings a very young person into the record, but does not reveal their name or the circumstances of their death.

passages.title: Children, writing and the limits of evidence
passages.text: An earlier discovery shows that writing was encountered in the region before this map period. A cattle rib from Břeclav-Lány, dated around 600, carries Germanic runes and came from a settlement associated with early Slavs. The identity and spoken language of the person who carved it remain uncertain.

passages.title: Children, writing and the limits of evidence
passages.text: Four intact signs near the end of the Lány inscription are “ᛖᛗᛞᛟ”, transliterated “e m d o”. They belong to an alphabet sequence, so there is no sentence to translate. Uneven forms and omitted letters support the interpretation of a writing exercise, rather than a message about daily events.

passages.title: Children, writing and the limits of evidence
passages.text: Glagolitic writing belongs to the later ninth-century story of Great Moravia. It provided letters suited to Slavic religious texts and teaching. The earlier rune fragment is not evidence that eighth-century Moravian villages already used this later alphabet, or that ordinary people were generally literate.

The year 800 ends this imported label, not the local population. Existing settlements changed and expanded into the ninth-century centres of Great Moravia. The earlier communities therefore have a history of transformation, rather than a documented collective fall in 800.

sectionTitles: A capital for rulers and students

passages.text: This entry covers Morocco from 1300 to 1492, chiefly the later Marinid era and the transition to Wattasid rule. Fez was a centre of government, learning and skilled production. The regional label spans political change rather than one uninterrupted dynasty.

passages.title: A capital for rulers and students
passages.text: The Marinids built Fez Jdid in 1276, before this entry’s first map year. It provided a new royal and military quarter beside the older city. A medieval capital could grow by adding a government town rather than by demolishing its existing neighbourhoods.

passages.title: A capital for rulers and students
passages.text: Marinid expansion reached Tunis in 1347, but the Black Death in 1348 and subsequent rebellions helped undermine this wider ambition. The dynasty’s cultural monuments outlasted its ability to hold a large North African empire together.

passages.title: A capital for rulers and students
passages.text: Buinaniya Madrasa in Fez was built in the 1350s. Its plan includes two facing classrooms and a prayer hall. A school building brought teaching, worship and the movement of students into one carefully arranged space.

passages.title: A capital for rulers and students
passages.text: Water crossed the madrasa’s southern side in a channel from the Wadi Lamtiyyin; two small bridges gave access to the prayer hall. A courtyard basin and an associated ablution building remind us that water supply and washing were practical parts of institutional life.

passages.title: A capital for rulers and students
passages.text: A hydraulic clock stood opposite Buinaniya. Water, architecture and the scheduling of communal life were connected here. The madrasa’s surviving fabric also includes later repairs, so a present-day view cannot be treated as an untouched photograph of the 1350s.

passages.title: A capital for rulers and students
passages.text: A Quran volume now in the Bavarian State Library was associated with the Marinid ruler Abu Yaqub Yusuf, who reigned from 1286 to 1307. It is the last part of a twelve-volume set, written on parchment in Maghribi script: a substantial book project rather than a pocket paperback.

passages.title: Homes, hands and letters
passages.text: A fourteenth-century door from a ruined Fez house survives in the Batha Museum. Its wood and wrought iron preserve a large main door with a smaller gate inside. Domestic craftsmanship deserves attention alongside the palace and mosque.

passages.title: Homes, hands and letters
passages.text: That door has two knockers of different sizes. The museum explains that the higher, larger one allowed a visitor riding a mule to knock without dismounting. Medieval convenience: the doorbell was adapted to the transport!

passages.title: Homes, hands and letters
passages.text: A ceiling fragment from the al-Misbahiya madrasa, built in 1346 to 1347, combines carved cedar pieces into stars and other geometric shapes. Traces of red, white, green and blue show that this wooden surface was once much more colourful than plain brown timber.

passages.title: Homes, hands and letters
passages.text: A tile panel from Buinaniya was made by removing parts of the glazed surface so that script stood out against the exposed background. The Batha fragment was recovered during modern restoration. It records both medieval craft and the later work of conserving it.

passages.title: Homes, hands and letters
passages.text: A silver half dirham struck at Azammur under Abd al-Haqq II names its ruler and mint. It weighs about 0.65 grams. Such a small object can locate an otherwise poorly documented mint within the political history of the fifteenth century.

passages.title: Homes, hands and letters
passages.text: The coin’s reverse includes امير المسلمين, “commander of the Muslims.” This Arabic title is shown in modern type from the published transcription. The coin belongs to Abd al-Haqq II’s reign, 1420 to 1465, rather than to every period labelled Morocco.

The Marinid dynasty ended when Abd al-Haqq II was killed during the Fez rebellion of 1465. The Wattasids subsequently established their own government, securing Fez in 1472. Fez’s households, schools and workshops continued across the political transition, which falls inside this map entry’s dates.

sectionTitles: Cities and the people who sustained them
Light, food and words at home

passages.text: This map window spans the later Saadian era, the rise of Alaouite rule in the seventeenth century, and the protectorates established in 1912. Its 1650 to 1938 dates are mapping limits, not Morocco’s lifetime.

passages.title: Cities and the people who sustained them
passages.text: Moulay Ismail, who reigned from 1672 to 1727, made Meknes his capital. The palace city and older medina were distinct ensembles divided by walls. Their different spaces preserve a ruler’s administrative ambitions alongside an existing urban community.

passages.title: Cities and the people who sustained them
passages.text: Meknes’s surviving heritage includes hammams, merchant inns, private houses and large granaries as well as palaces. These buildings span several periods. They make washing, storage, commerce and shelter visible beside royal display; they should not all be assigned to one sultan.

passages.title: Cities and the people who sustained them
passages.text: The royal state also relied on coercion. Historian Chouki El Hamel studied registers used under Moulay Ismail to justify enslaving Black Moroccans, including people who had been free. The policy provoked opposition among Muslim scholars; official paperwork could manufacture a claim to ownership rather than prove a just right.

passages.title: Cities and the people who sustained them
passages.text: Sultan Sidi Mohamed ben Abdallah, ruling from 1757 to 1790, developed Essaouira as a royal Atlantic port. Its planned fortifications drew on European military design within a Moroccan urban setting. Goods could pass between inland African routes, the coast and European shipping.

passages.title: Cities and the people who sustained them
passages.text: Essaouira’s population included Muslim, Jewish and Christian communities and people of different backgrounds. Its port was a meeting place as well as a defensive project. The surviving town preserves the settings of exchange without implying that every resident experienced identical opportunities.

passages.title: Cities and the people who sustained them
passages.text: A treaty concluded in 1786 formalised relations with the United States. In 1821, Sultan Moulay Suleiman gave the Americans a building in Tangier for their diplomatic mission. The surviving institutional history shows diplomacy expressed through both written agreements and a very tangible house.

passages.title: Light, food and words at home
passages.text: A nineteenth-century batta jug in the Batha Museum held lamp oil. It has a rounded body, narrow neck and pouring lip, and stands only 14 centimetres high. Before an electric light switch, keeping a lamp supplied required small, purpose-made containers like this.

passages.title: Light, food and words at home
passages.text: Fez and Meknes potters made these jugs for different markets. Green examples went particularly to southern oasis regions, while urban buyers could obtain more elaborate multicoloured decoration. One familiar vessel shape could be adapted to several customers.

passages.title: Light, food and words at home
passages.text: A shallow Fez dish from the first half of the nineteenth century is 40 centimetres across. Dishes of this type served bastila, a filled pie, but this especially symbolic example may have been primarily decorative. A beautiful plate is not proof of the exact meal once eaten from it.

passages.title: Light, food and words at home
passages.text: Its blue decoration was painted with cobalt oxide and its yellow with an iron-based pigment. A mosque-like arch frames a word arranged as a mirror image. The dish shows potters combining material knowledge, architectural references and writing on a domestic form.

passages.title: Light, food and words at home
passages.text: The dish’s Arabic word is الملك, al-mulk, “sovereignty” or “power,” interpreted by the museum as divine power. It is printed here in ordinary letters; the original is highly stylised, mirrored Kufic. This is an attested object inscription, not a phrase invented for the card.

passages.title: Light, food and words at home
passages.text: Later in this entry’s period, the French Protectorate developed a planned capital at Rabat, especially from 1912 to 1930, alongside older urban layers. Its government buildings and neighbourhoods record colonial intervention as well as architectural exchange.
The 1912 protectorates limited Moroccan sovereignty without abolishing the monarchy. Independence returned in 1956. The map’s break at 1938 is not a conquest date or the disappearance of Morocco.

sectionTitles: Institutions, writing and a changing capital

passages.text: Modern Morocco regained independence in 1956, before this map entry begins. Its Arabic- and Amazigh-speaking society includes varied urban and rural communities. The examples below describe specific institutions and practices, not every household.

passages.title: Institutions, writing and a changing capital
passages.text: The 2011 constitution describes Morocco as a constitutional monarchy. A constitutional text tells us how institutions are formally defined; it should not be mistaken for proof that every declared right or principle is fully realised in everyday life.

passages.title: Institutions, writing and a changing capital
passages.text: A short Arabic writing sample appears in Article 4: الله، الوطن، الملك, “God, Homeland, King.” These are the words of the state motto in a specific published document, presented here in normal Arabic type.

passages.title: Institutions, writing and a changing capital
passages.text: Article 5 recognises Amazigh alongside Arabic as an official language. That provision matters for a country whose heritage cannot be reduced to one language. A written constitution records a legal commitment, while the practical history of language use is more varied.

passages.title: Institutions, writing and a changing capital
passages.text: Rabat’s protected urban landscape includes an early twentieth-century planned capital alongside much older quarters and monuments. Its buildings make different periods visible in the same city. Modern residents use and conserve a place inherited from both precolonial and colonial histories.

passages.title: Institutions, writing and a changing capital
passages.text: Some imported modern outlines include Western Sahara. Its sovereignty is disputed, and the United Nations lists it as a Non-Self-Governing Territory. A map polygon is not evidence that this dispute is settled.

passages.title: Family knowledge, food and music
passages.text: Couscous preparation is shared heritage across Morocco, Algeria, Mauritania and Tunisia. UNESCO’s 2020 record describes forming and steaming cereal grains and combining them with ingredients that vary with season and place. There is no single recipe that represents every household.

passages.title: Family knowledge, food and music
passages.text: Learning to make couscous often happens through watching and helping within families and communities. The meal brings people together, while the equipment connects cooks with potters and makers of wooden utensils. A bowl of food has quite a workforce behind it.

passages.title: Family knowledge, food and music
passages.text: In southwest Morocco, producing argan oil involves harvesting and drying fruit, removing pulp, cracking the hard shells, sorting kernels, grinding and kneading. UNESCO documents a chain of skilled tasks rather than one magical squeeze of a tree.

passages.title: Family knowledge, food and music
passages.text: Argan knowledge has often passed between women, including mothers and daughters, through practice. Artisans make the hand mills and other equipment. Precise handling during processing is part of the skill, not simply a list of ingredients.

passages.title: Family knowledge, food and music
passages.text: Argan oil also appears in social life: UNESCO records its use as a wedding gift and in special dishes. These are documented practices of particular communities. They should not be projected automatically onto every Moroccan wedding or earlier century.

passages.title: Family knowledge, food and music
passages.text: Gnawa music and ritual carry memories of communities shaped by slavery and its aftermath. UNESCO’s record describes stringed instruments and metal castanets in urban traditions, with different instrumental combinations elsewhere. Music preserves histories that a political timeline can easily overlook.

passages.title: Family knowledge, food and music
passages.text: Gnawa gatherings may include extended ritual performance, and practitioners transmit their knowledge through associations and festivals as well as community life. Healing is part of participants’ religious understanding; describing that belief is different from recommending a medical treatment.

passages.title: Family knowledge, food and music
passages.text: Noor I, near Ouarzazate, began operating in February 2016 with 160 megawatts of solar generating capacity. The project brief distinguishes this completed plant from later phases then being developed. It is a concrete example of Morocco building modern energy infrastructure, alongside its better-known historic monuments.

Morocco continues as a state and a living society. Independence in 1956 and constitutional change in 2011 mark transformations rather than a final fall. An open-ended map entry does not predict an unchanging future.

passages.text: Mossi political history includes several kingdoms in present-day Burkina Faso. Their populations developed through conquest, migration and incorporation of existing communities. Ouagadougou was influential, but it was not an ancient capital governing every Mossi kingdom.

passages.title: Communities, trade and authority
passages.text: Duperray’s research describes kingdoms formed through encounters between incoming ruling lineages and established populations. Political incorporation did not erase differences of origin. This helps explain why a single map label covers multiple communities and centres of authority.

passages.title: Communities, trade and authority
passages.text: Yarse communities included Muslim merchants. Oral traditions link many lineages with Mande origins, while others became Yarse through local relationships. Duperray’s interviews reveal changing identities rather than a merchant population with one uniform ancestry.

passages.title: Communities, trade and authority
passages.text: The protectorate treaty of January 1897 helped France claim a wider territory. Beucher argues that officials enlarged the apparent authority of Ouagadougou’s ruler, the Moogo Naaba, to justify colonial control. The resulting hierarchy cannot simply be projected backward.

passages.title: Making useful and valued things
passages.text: A Smithsonian Mossi vessel, made in the middle or late twentieth century, carries impressed patterns below and incised zigzags above. The museum describes pottery used for water, grain, cooking and brewing beer, placing decorated ceramics within ordinary household work.

passages.title: Making useful and valued things
passages.text: The Smithsonian’s technique account describes shaping clay over a mould, then adding coils to build the upper vessel. Drying, decoration and firing followed. Millet stalks, wood and manure supplied fuel. Both men and women participated in these pottery traditions.

passages.title: Making useful and valued things
passages.text: A late twentieth-century Mossi shawl in the British Museum consists of thirteen narrow cotton strips sewn together. Handspun thread, indigo dye and additional patterned weft at the ends show several kinds of work within one textile.

passages.title: Making useful and valued things
passages.text: The museum suggests this cloth may be a diisa prestige shawl, given by a mother to a son on marriage and later used as a burial shroud. That social interpretation is qualified; it is not a securely documented biography of this particular textile.

passages.title: Sculpture, performance and evidence
passages.text: The High Museum’s karan-wemba figure represents an honoured older woman. Its ridged coiffure and geometric bodily marks connect sculpture with appearance and social status. Patt relates the work to Yatenga traditions while stressing differences among Mossi artistic communities.

passages.title: Sculpture, performance and evidence
passages.text: Radiocarbon analysis placed the High Museum figure’s wood around the sixteenth century. Wood age does not establish when an artist carved it. Patt considers the possibility of a much later sculpture made from old timber, so an exact early creation date remains unproven.

passages.title: Sculpture, performance and evidence
passages.text: The PLU collection account describes carving masks from green wood with an adze and knife, then smoothing them with rough leaves. A mask’s performance required further work: fibre fittings, clothing and rattles connected the carved object with a moving, sounding costume.

passages.title: Sculpture, performance and evidence
passages.text: The same account places cooking, grinding and grain storage within household compounds. These workspaces connect the material arts with food preparation and farming. They describe recorded Mossi settings, not a single house plan shared by every kingdom or historical century.

French forces occupied Ouagadougou in September 1896, followed by the 1897 protectorate. Other kingdoms had their own encounters with colonial rule. Royal authority was constrained and reshaped; this political change did not mark the disappearance of Mossi people or their artistic traditions.

sectionTitles: What a ship’s jars can tell us
A fort that had to save the rain
Grandparents and children in the orchestra

passages.text: Mozambique’s Indian Ocean coast connected local communities with distant trading worlds. Its history also lives in musical skills shared across generations and in the cloths through which women remember their lives. These stories follow particular places and communities within a diverse country.

passages.title: What a ship’s jars can tell us
passages.text: The wreck identified as Nossa Senhora da Consolação, lost near Mozambique Island in 1608, yielded containers known as olive jars. A 2023 study compares their thick walls and rounded shapes with other shipwreck finds. Such jars could carry oil, wine or foodstuffs, and their forms helped them fit within a curved hull. The name does not prove that every recovered jar still contained olives.

passages.title: What a ship’s jars can tell us
passages.text: Two pots from the same collection were identified with the local Lumbo pottery tradition. They raised a puzzle: was that tradition used later than some land excavations suggested, or did hurried recovery mix material from different wrecks? Mahumane and Simbine leave both possibilities open. A pot can be an exciting discovery partly because it creates a better question, not because it instantly settles one.

passages.title: A fort that had to save the rain
passages.text: São Sebastião Fortress collected rain from its roofs into cisterns. UNESCO’s history explains how stored water helped people withstand a Dutch siege in 1607 and also supplied visiting ships. Its construction had drawn on stonemasons from Goa, local residents and enslaved labourers. The surviving building preserves engineering achievements within a history of unequal power and coerced work.

passages.title: A fort that had to save the rain
passages.text: A 2009 restoration report describes repairing channels, pipes and cisterns, then sending water to a new cistern outside the fort for island residents. A roof could work as part of a water supply as well as keep rain off a room. Looking after an old building could therefore help maintain something people needed every day.

passages.title: A fort that had to save the rain
passages.text: Junior architect Mohammad Cassimo told the restoration team that he had grown up on the island and wanted to help restore it. He joined surveys and daily supervision of the work. His account links learning a profession with caring for a place remembered from childhood.

passages.title: Homes, toilets and a hospital
passages.text: Mozambique Island includes stone-and-lime buildings in the north and a southern neighbourhood called macuti, after its palm-leaf roofs. UNESCO describes different building traditions shaped by African, Swahili, Arab and European connections. The island is a lived-in town as well as a heritage site, with homes forming an important part of what survives.

passages.title: Homes, toilets and a hospital
passages.text: A 2014 conservation report explains that macuti roofing was becoming harder to obtain and some residents preferred metal roofs. It also records efforts to repair houses and discuss conservation in schools. Keeping an architectural tradition alive involves residents’ costs and choices, as well as the appearance of a roof. A home has to be somewhere people can actually live.

passages.title: Homes, toilets and a hospital
passages.text: The same report includes a photograph of a public toilet built in 2012 and describes residents and the municipality cleaning living areas. It also records work on water supplies and damaged cisterns. Toilets belong in the history of a town just as much as palaces do: people need practical services while living among historic buildings.

passages.title: Homes, toilets and a hospital
passages.text: The island’s old hospital dates to 1877. In 2015, the health ministry began conservation work that included cleaning, surveying the structure and investigating drainage and cisterns. This record shows how caring for a healthcare building also meant caring for the systems behind its walls. It does not establish which treatments every patient received there.

passages.title: Grandparents and children in the orchestra
passages.text: Chopi timbila ensembles in southern Inhambane bring together wooden xylophones of different sizes. Calabashes beneath the wooden bars act as resonators, with beeswax helping seal them. UNESCO’s account describes children playing alongside their grandfathers. Learning means listening and practising within an ensemble, where a young player can hear an experienced musician right beside them.

passages.title: Grandparents and children in the orchestra
passages.text: These performances are also a way to comment on community life. New pieces accompany weddings and other gatherings; the m’zeno song can use humour and sarcasm to address current events. A musician’s hands may play different rhythms at the same time. The music can ask both the audience and the player to pay close attention.

passages.title: Cloth can hold a memory
passages.text: A capulana bought in Maputo’s Elephant market in September 2003 has printed circles showing Mozambique’s provinces, surrounded by spears and shields. The British Museum records it as cotton and says cloths of this type are worn by women. The catalogue tentatively places its manufacture in India. Something bought for wearing can also reveal the movement of designs and goods across borders.

passages.title: Cloth can hold a memory
passages.text: In 2019 and 2020, the WITH Coastal Style project worked with women in Katembe’s fishing communities across Maputo Bay. Researchers collected stories connected with capulanas, including cloths preserved and passed between generations. The project brought these memories into museum and community exhibitions. Keeping a piece of cloth can help a family keep a story, too.

passages.title: Masks, voices and growing up
passages.text: UNESCO’s 2023 account of Makonde mapiko describes masked dancers representing people or animals, with drums and a choir. Performances accompany rites of passage and also other occasions. Singers may challenge the masked dancers with provocative songs. Learning the dance helps pass on community values while young people navigate growing up; it is one particular tradition within Mozambique’s many communities.

passages.title: Whose work, and whose memories?
passages.text: A UN report from 1966 preserved testimony about the effects of colonial labour systems. Speakers described workers compelled into jobs or crop production and men leaving to seek wages abroad, separating families. The record shows why accounts of ports and plantations must also ask who did the work and what choices they had. It records testimony and arguments presented to the committee, rather than a census of every household.

passages.title: Whose work, and whose memories?
passages.text: The island’s Slave Memory Garden commemorates slavery along the Indian Ocean coast. A 2015 government report records restoration work there and describes the memorial as a joint Mozambique and Réunion initiative. The garden makes remembrance part of the present-day town, asking visitors to consider the people whose forced journeys also shaped its maritime history.

Portuguese colonial sovereignty ended when Mozambique became independent on 25 June 1975. The country continued through civil war, the 1992 peace agreement and the 1994 multiparty elections. Those political transitions did not erase its communities or the local histories carried in buildings, objects and living practices.

sectionTitles: Objects and words to look for

passages.text: Babur founded the Mughal dynasty in 1526. His successors built a major South Asian empire through warfare, alliances and administration, ruling peoples with many languages and religions. The map’s 1526 to 1857 record uses only a few broad outlines from 1530 to 1783; these cannot show every contested frontier, the interruption under the Sur rulers, or later regional independence.

passages.title: Building an empire
passages.text: Akbar’s conquests included Gujarat, whose trading cities gave the empire access to the Arabian Sea. His power rested on a strong administrative system as well as armies. Ports and commercial routes helped connect the inland court with distant markets.

passages.title: Building an empire
passages.text: Akbar invited scholars of several religions to court discussions, including Muslims, Hindus, Jains, Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians. These meetings belonged to a particular ruler’s intellectual and political program; Mughal religious policies changed across reigns.

passages.title: Building an empire
passages.text: The court could travel as a vast tented settlement containing royal women, nobles, servants and followers. Under Jahangir, two sets of tents allowed the next stopping place to be prepared before the travelers arrived. Moving house could mean moving a whole temporary neighborhood.

passages.title: Fields, families and town life
passages.text: Agriculture supplied most imperial revenue. Village cultivators faced assessors, collectors and record keepers seeking the state’s share, while crops grown for sale connected villages to towns. Palaces depended on work far beyond their walls.

passages.title: Fields, families and town life
passages.text: Babur described irrigation near Lahore and Dipalpur: a bullock turned geared wheels that lifted a circulating chain of pitchers from a well. The pitchers emptied into a trough carrying water onward. This was a machine he observed in use, not an invention credited to the emperor.

passages.title: Fields, families and town life
passages.text: Rural women worked in fields and crafts: sowing, weeding, processing harvested grain, spinning and preparing clay for pottery. Household production drew on the labor of women and men. The seclusion associated with elite royal women cannot describe all families across the empire.

passages.title: Fields, families and town life
passages.text: Documents from Rajasthan, Gujarat and Maharashtra preserve women’s complaints to village councils about husbands neglecting wives and children. The records often omit the petitioner’s own name, identifying her through a male relative. Family disputes survive, but the archive does not give everyone an equal voice.

passages.title: Fields, families and town life
passages.text: Gulbadan Begum, Babur’s daughter and Akbar’s aunt, wrote a Persian prose chronicle that recorded women’s experiences and family relationships. She also led royal women on a pilgrimage to Arabia and stayed there for years. The household included travelers, advisers and authors, not simply people waiting silently behind palace walls.

passages.title: Fields, families and town life
passages.text: Lahore’s Shahi Hammam, built in 1634, was a public bathhouse. Excavators uncovered furnaces, drainage and a heating network: hot air and smoke warmed the floors while heated water reached the bathing rooms. A comfortable bath required fuel, maintenance and some serious work underneath the floor.

passages.title: Fields, families and town life
passages.text: Nearby, the Wazir Khan Mosque complex built in 1634 to 1635 included entrance shops intended for calligraphers and bookbinders. Worship, skilled work and the city’s book trade occupied adjoining spaces. Making a manuscript involved more people than the person whose words appeared on its pages.

passages.title: Learning, care and close observation
passages.text: A painting made at Lahore around 1595 shows boys reading in a school courtyard. A teacher works with a pupil on a carpeted platform while other students read alone or with tutors. Ascribed to Khem Karan, it illustrates a treatise on ethics: a carefully composed view of education rather than a classroom photograph.

passages.title: Learning, care and close observation
passages.text: After becoming emperor in 1605, Jahangir recorded an order calling for free hospitals and the appointment of physicians in the empire’s major cities. It expresses a royal commitment to care, but an order alone cannot establish how fully services reached patients. His memoir records what the ruler wanted to proclaim.

passages.title: Learning, care and close observation
passages.text: Mansur’s painting of two vultures, made around 1615 to 1620, distinguishes the birds through their forms and finely shaded feathers. The Met describes them as ornithologically accurate, while identifying the rocky setting as imagined. Close observation and artistic arrangement could share the same page.

passages.title: Learning, care and close observation
passages.text: The royal book workshops brought together calligraphers, painters and bookbinders. In the Akbarnama manuscript now at the V&A, small inscriptions identify different hands: one artist designed a picture and another applied its colors, sometimes with a specialist adding portraits. A celebrated page could be a team project.

passages.title: Objects and words to look for
passages.text: The Taj Mahal at Agra commemorates Mumtaz Mahal, Shah Jahan’s wife. Work began in 1632; the mausoleum was completed in 1648 and the wider complex by 1653. Craftspeople combined white marble, carved ornament and colored stone inlay. Its garden, riverfront position and carefully arranged buildings work together as a designed landscape.

passages.title: Objects and words to look for
passages.text: A red sandstone window screen at the Met dates to the later sixteenth century. Its pierced geometry cast moving patterns across a room as daylight changed. Weathering on one side suggests an exterior window. Stone could make a surprisingly delicate filter for light.

passages.title: Objects and words to look for
passages.text: Jahangir’s inkpot, dated 1618 to 1619, was made from nephrite jade and gold. Its broad, heavy form made it difficult to knock over. Even luxurious writing equipment had a practical job: keeping the ink inside the pot was a useful beginning.

passages.title: Objects and words to look for
passages.text: A Persian inscription on a portrait of Jahangir holding his father Akbar’s picture includes “عمل نادر الزمان,” meaning “painted by Nadir al-Zaman.” The Louvre dates the painting to 1600 to 1615 and identifies that artist as Abu al-Hasan. This short sample follows the museum’s transcription of the words on Akbar’s green globe.

passages.title: Objects and words to look for
passages.text: As imperial workshops contracted, painters sought patrons in other courts, including Bikaner, Bundi, Lucknow and Murshidabad. After Nadir Shah’s devastating raid on Delhi in 1739, dispersal intensified. Political weakening could uproot skilled people while helping artistic practices develop in new regional settings.

British forces captured Delhi in 1857 and dismantled the last Mughal court. Bahadur Shah Zafar was tried and exiled to Burma in 1858, when Crown rule replaced Company government. The dynasty’s end did not end South Asian communities or Mughal artistic traditions, which had already spread to regional patrons.

passages.text: Muisca communities lived in Colombia’s eastern highlands, farming, weaving, trading and making extraordinary metal offerings. They belonged to several interacting chiefdoms rather than one centrally ruled empire. The map’s eight-year window is only a snapshot of a much longer history.

passages.title: Leaders, fields and markets
passages.text: At the Spanish arrival in 1537, at least four large regional chiefdoms centred on Bogotá, Tunja, Duitama and Sogamoso. Each included smaller communities and local leaders. Their relationships were political and religious, but they were not all subjects of a single king.

passages.title: Leaders, fields and markets
passages.text: Maize was a staple alongside potatoes, beans, squashes and other crops. The Gold Museum’s educational account describes soups, tamales and arepas. A familiar-looking maize meal could connect modern visitors with ingredients cultivated in these highlands centuries ago.

passages.title: Leaders, fields and markets
passages.text: Households worked their own plots and also supplied labour for leaders’ fields. The museum links this tribute to ceremonies and large gatherings. Food production supported both family meals and the occasions that brought communities together.

passages.title: Leaders, fields and markets
passages.text: Salt from Zipaquirá and Nemocón could be exchanged for cloth, pottery and produce. Cotton arrived from warmer environments. Traders connected communities with different resources, so a highland household did not have to grow or make everything it used.

passages.title: Small objects with big stories
passages.text: In 1969 a farmer found the famous gold raft inside a ceramic container in a cave near Pasca. It did not come out of Lake Guatavita. Recording where an object was actually found matters, even when a more famous place dominates the story.

passages.title: Small objects with big stories
passages.text: The raft is interpreted as a ceremonial offering representing a leader and attendants. The museum relates it to accounts of chiefly installation and gifts placed in sacred water. It is a miniature ritual scene, rather than proof of a lost city made of gold.

passages.title: Small objects with big stories
passages.text: Its makers cast the raft in one piece using a lost-wax mould. The museum considers 1200 to 1500 a likely period, while emphasizing that an exact manufacture date cannot be established. A tiny object can preserve a remarkably complicated piece of metalworking.

passages.title: Small objects with big stories
passages.text: A different offering from Fusagasugá shows an arched-back feline with whiskers and protruding eyes. Only a few centimetres long, the flat metal animal nevertheless looks ready to spring. The museum dates this lost-wax casting broadly to 600 to 1600.

passages.title: Small objects with big stories
passages.text: Microscope-based research examined thirteen groups of Muisca offerings and distinguished the work of multiple makers. Details of wax modelling and casting let researchers investigate artists and apprentices, rather than treating every small gold figure as anonymous treasure.

passages.title: Words and lives after conquest
passages.text: A short Muisca sample in a seventeenth-century baptism sermon is “mue zemosqua”: “I bathe you”. Saravia’s edition prints this wording from an anonymous manuscript now in Colombia’s National Library. Its Latin-script religious text records language under colonial evangelization, not preconquest alphabetic writing.

passages.title: Words and lives after conquest
passages.text: The sermon describes a priest pouring water during baptism. The surviving manuscript connects the study of language with a concrete encounter between children, families and missionaries. Its religious purpose also shaped which words its compiler chose to preserve.

passages.title: Words and lives after conquest
passages.text: A colonial-period burial from Pisba preserved a woven cap, a headband and a two-colour cotton bag alongside other belongings. Such finds show that practices and craft knowledge continued after Spanish conquest, even as communities experienced deep political and religious pressure.

Spanish conquest beginning in 1537 broke apart the larger Muisca chiefdoms and imposed encomienda tribute. Local leadership and communities continued within those unequal colonial arrangements. The imported 1500 endpoint predates this upheaval and is not a historical collapse.

passages.text: The Ashikaga shoguns governed from Kyoto, but shared Japan’s political world with emperors, temples and powerful provincial lords. The indexed span is 1336 to 1573; its surviving map shapes instead run from 1333 to 1492. Neither outline nor label means uniform shogunal control over every community.

passages.title: Rulers, rivals and trade
passages.text: Ashikaga Takauji helped overthrow the Kamakura government, then broke with Emperor Go-Daigo. His new Kyoto administration emerged in 1336. The imperial split and his appointment as shogun in 1338 explain why museums use several starting dates for this complicated transition.

passages.title: Rulers, rivals and trade
passages.text: The shogunate was not an all-powerful national command centre. Provincial daimyo influenced both politics and culture. Rivalries helped produce the Onin War of 1467 to 1477, damaging Kyoto and weakening the government that was supposed to coordinate warrior rule.

passages.title: Rulers, rivals and trade
passages.text: Yoshimitsu sent an embassy to Ming China in 1401, beginning a new era of licensed official exchange. Japan received copper coins and silk thread, while sulfur, swords and folding fans travelled the other way. Imported money helped sustain Japanese commerce.

passages.title: Rulers, rivals and trade
passages.text: Trade licenses used a clever anti-forgery device: writing crossed the edge of a document onto a register. Officials matched the two halves of the characters. It was a paper puzzle with serious consequences for whether a ship could trade.

passages.title: Homes, work and health
passages.text: At sixteenth-century Ichijodani, a typical small house plot had a frontage of about six metres, a well and a backyard toilet. Other houses lacked their own facilities. Even a castle town needed everyday arrangements for water and waste.

passages.title: Homes, work and health
passages.text: Ichijodani bead makers left unfinished crystal prayer beads, pieces broken during drilling and polishing stones. These workshop failures are useful discoveries: a perfect bead shows the result, while a broken one can reveal how the craftsperson tried to make it.

passages.title: Homes, work and health
passages.text: Medicine-compounding tools and a fragment of the Chinese medical text Tangye bencao helped identify a probable doctor’s residence at Ichijodani. The museum also records scholars editing and printing medical books there. Medical learning travelled alongside merchants, monks and refugees from war.

passages.title: Homes, work and health
passages.text: A medical manuscript completed just after this period supplies a further window into earlier practice. Manase Dosan’s Keitekishu, presented to the emperor in 1574, assembled more than thirty years of treatment records. Its surviving autograph shows a physician organising experience into a substantial reference work.

passages.title: Homes, work and health
passages.text: The Hiroshima museum’s reconstruction of fourteenth-century Kusado Sengen separates a craft household’s earthen work floor from its wooden living floor. Its imagined family scenes illustrate archaeological and pictorial evidence; they are not records of one named family caught in a particular moment.

passages.title: Homes, work and health
passages.text: Kusado Sengen’s reconstructed market includes fish, shellfish, seaweed, salt, rice, beans and vegetables. Excavated canals help explain how supplies arrived by boat. It is a useful reminder that the history of warrior government also happened beside food stalls and loading places.

passages.title: Homes, work and health
passages.text: Women could participate in government through writing. At the imperial court, female attendants transmitted a sovereign’s wishes in letters known as nyobo hosho, which became frequent official documents during the Muromachi and Sengoku periods. Household service could involve political responsibility.

passages.title: Learning, art and social gatherings
passages.text: Sesshu’s ink landscape of 1495 served a surprisingly practical purpose: his pupil Josui Soen requested it as evidence that he had learned the master’s painting method. On the journey home, Soen collected poems from six Kyoto monks on the same scroll.

passages.title: Learning, art and social gatherings
passages.text: The painting’s inscription also records Sesshu’s study in China and his Japanese artistic predecessors. Its loose-looking ink still forms a carefully structured landscape. Artistic education involved travel, personal instruction and deliberate claims about who had taught whom.

passages.title: Learning, art and social gatherings
passages.text: At early shoin-style tea gatherings, Ashikaga collections needed specialist curators. They cared for artworks, arranged their display and prepared tea while the host sat with guests. An elegant afternoon depended on knowledgeable work behind the scenes.

passages.title: Learning, art and social gatherings
passages.text: Murata Shuko helped turn attention towards modest Japanese ceramics paired with Chinese utensils. Townspeople’s gatherings increasingly featured hosts making tea before their guests. A cup could become a reason to discuss taste, friendship and the pleasure of an imperfect object.

passages.title: Learning, art and social gatherings
passages.text: A surviving Seto tea jar from about 1500 is only 8.3 centimetres tall, with thick brown glaze and splashes around its neck and shoulder. Museum treasures can be small enough to fit in a hand; cultural importance does not require castle-sized packaging.

passages.title: Learning, art and social gatherings
passages.text: A tiny Japanese sample is “糸ざくら” (ito-zakura), “weeping cherry.” It appears in the museum’s transcription of Ashikaga Yoshiaki’s poem for a 1568 cherry-viewing gathering at Nanyo-ji. This is a transmitted poem in modern transcription, not a newly verified autograph.

passages.title: Destruction and discoveries
passages.text: Ichijodani belonged to the regional Asakura family. Nobunaga’s army burned the town in 1573, showing how the final years of Ashikaga rule could end violently far from Kyoto too. Its destruction must not be mistaken for the fate of every Japanese town.

passages.title: Destruction and discoveries
passages.text: Excavations at Ichijodani began in 1967. The museum reports more than 1.7 million recovered items, bringing streets, workshops and household routines back into view. Political chronicles name commanders; archaeology also lets us meet the people who filled containers, repaired tools and fetched water.

Oda Nobunaga forced the last Ashikaga shogun, Yoshiaki, out of Kyoto in 1573. The shogunate ended, but regional warfare and Japanese communities continued. Its artistic practices, institutions and memories survived the loss of the ruling government.

sectionTitles: Ships, workshops and a connected coast
Homes and meals at neighbouring Qalhat
Water, bathing and finding tiny clues
A written glimpse and changing powers

passages.text: The map’s Muscat label covers a broad Omani region from about 1000 to 1530, rather than one continuous kingdom ruled from the town. Inland Bahla and coastal Qalhat reveal different centres of power. Their archaeology helps explain the wider world of Muscat’s sailors, neighbours and trading partners.

passages.title: A region with several centres
passages.text: At inland Bahla, the Banu Nebhan made their capital and dominated central Oman from the twelfth to late fifteenth centuries. Their mud-brick fort stood on stone foundations beside an oasis. UNESCO places this political centre within Oman’s distinctive Ibadi Islamic setting.

passages.title: A region with several centres
passages.text: Ibn Battuta described Muscat on his 1347 return journey as a small town with abundant fish. He placed this chain of Omani ports under Hormuz. His account catches one traveller’s particular moment, rather than defining five centuries of government.

passages.title: A region with several centres
passages.text: Qalhat also had a woman in government: Bibi Maryam administered it during her husband Ayaz’s absences and continued after his death, remaining active at least until 1319. The great building associated with her name preserves a striking reminder of authority beyond kings alone.

passages.title: Ships, workshops and a connected coast
passages.text: Qalhat, a separate port near present-day Sur, traded across the Persian Gulf and Indian Ocean towards India and eastern Asia. Horses, dates, incense and pearls moved through its commercial networks. The coastline connected inland producers to customers far beyond Arabia.

passages.title: Ships, workshops and a connected coast
passages.text: An underwater survey in 1998 found more than twenty stone anchors off Qalhat. These heavy, practical objects give the vanished harbour a tangible presence: a busy trading port needed ways to stop its ships from drifting away.

passages.title: Ships, workshops and a connected coast
passages.text: Excavators uncovered a fourteenth-century pottery workshop at Qalhat. Chemical analysis helped separate locally made ceramics from imports. Some household containers therefore came from neighbourhood craftspeople, even in a port famous for distant connections.

passages.title: Ships, workshops and a connected coast
passages.text: Plant remains from workshop B39 include rice, finger millet, pulses and sesame. Researchers considered Indian and Yemeni connections, while leaving room for local cultivation. A seed can reveal a surprisingly international shopping list, but it does not carry its own shipping label.

passages.title: Homes and meals at neighbouring Qalhat
passages.text: Building B94 contained two adjoining houses without an internal doorway between them. Courtyards organised domestic space, and some Qalhat houses probably had upper floors. Archaeology reveals neighbours and shared building patterns more securely than it reveals who was related to whom.

passages.title: Homes and meals at neighbouring Qalhat
passages.text: A study of B94 combined animal bones, fish remains and plant material. Their distribution suggested where food was processed and other household activities took place. The researchers treated these room functions as interpretations assembled from small traces left behind.

passages.title: Homes and meals at neighbouring Qalhat
passages.text: Among identified terrestrial animal remains at B94, sheep and goats dominated. Food also linked the port to date-palm gardens and livestock in its surrounding oasis economy. The dinner table depended on both maritime connections and nearby land.

passages.title: Homes and meals at neighbouring Qalhat
passages.text: Fish remains indicate intensive exploitation of open-water fishing grounds. Qalhat’s seafood supply was therefore connected to work beyond the beach: fishermen had to reach the waters where these fish lived before anyone could bring a catch home.

passages.title: Homes and meals at neighbouring Qalhat
passages.text: In workshop B39, plant material in room E suggested food preparation and crop cleaning. Craft and kitchen activities could leave traces in the same building. Researchers recovered familiar staples including dates, wheat and lentils alongside the less local crop possibilities.

passages.title: Water, bathing and finding tiny clues
passages.text: Bahla’s oasis relied on wells and falaj channels that carried groundwater from distant sources. Keeping palms and people supplied required managing seasonal water as well. The surviving system illustrates the engineering and collective maintenance behind an apparently green patch in a dry landscape.

passages.title: Water, bathing and finding tiny clues
passages.text: At Qalhat, a large vaulted cistern near Bibi Maryam’s monument held more than 280 cubic metres of water. Its roof reduced evaporation. Stone and waterproof sarooj mortar helped residents store a precious supply instead of letting the sun drink it first.

passages.title: Water, bathing and finding tiny clues
passages.text: Qalhat’s partly excavated bathhouse had nine rooms, many with basins or tubs. Underground heating chambers, brick openings and pipes inside walls show how warmth circulated. Bathing here involved substantial plumbing and heating equipment, not simply carrying a bucket to the sea.

passages.title: Water, bathing and finding tiny clues
passages.text: Modern archaeologists used sieving and flotation to recover tiny plant and animal remains from Qalhat’s buildings. In flotation, light material can be separated with water. These patient techniques make burnt seeds and other easily missed scraps useful evidence for ordinary life.

passages.title: A written glimpse and changing powers
passages.text: A short Arabic witness is Ibn Battuta’s “فوصلت إلى مسقط”: “I arrived at Muscat.” This is a modern typeset transcription of his fourteenth-century travel account, not a local stone inscription or a surviving manuscript from the visit itself.

passages.title: A written glimpse and changing powers
passages.text: Qalhat’s decline is still being investigated. A geological study found displaced terrace deposits and altered stream courses along the Qalhat Fault, making earthquake activity a plausible contributor. This supports a possibility rather than a securely dated earthquake that explains everything.

passages.title: A written glimpse and changing powers
passages.text: Muscat’s harbour became a strategic Portuguese position after 1507. The occupation’s defensive system eventually included the paired forts Al Jalali and Al Mirani. Their later development must not be projected backwards onto every medieval scene shown by this map.

passages.title: A written glimpse and changing powers
passages.text: The later turning point came in 1650, when the Ya’aruba expelled the Portuguese from Muscat. This was part of a wider sequence of recoveries along the coast. Ports, residents and maritime skills continued through the change in political control.

The imported label ends in 1530, but Muscat did not disappear then. Portuguese rule continued until 1650, followed by Omani control. The map boundary is a change of record, not the end of the town or its communities.

passages.text: Muscogee histories connect southeastern ancestral places, a changing network of towns and continuing nations. Ocmulgee's surviving clay architecture, town councils and later government buildings show different forms of collective life. The later Creek Confederacy and the present Muscogee Nation must not be projected unchanged onto the map's fifteenth-century snapshot.

passages.title: Reading Ocmulgee's surviving floor
passages.text: Ocmulgee is an ancestral homeland of the Muscogee Nation. Its long occupation is evidence of successive communities at a place; it does not establish that the later Creek Confederacy existed throughout all those earlier centuries.

passages.title: Reading Ocmulgee's surviving floor
passages.text: The Earth Lodge preserves an original clay floor dating approximately to the early eleventh century. The enclosing walls and roof visitors see were reconstructed in the 1930s. Separating those elements helps distinguish surviving archaeology from a modern interpretation of the building.

passages.title: Reading Ocmulgee's surviving floor
passages.text: Seats, a central hearth and a raised bird effigy were formed into the floor. Their arrangement supports interpretation as a special gathering place. Differences in seating do not by themselves establish a complete social hierarchy, an interpretation the park's bulletin explicitly questions.

passages.title: Reading Ocmulgee's surviving floor
passages.text: The round lodge used internal roof supports, while nearby houses were usually smaller and rectangular. Different building forms reveal deliberate choices about public and domestic space. The exact meanings of the bird's imagery remain uncertain.

passages.title: Town life, relationships and exchange
passages.text: Historic towns placed council houses beside ceremonial plazas, with grounds for ball play and chunkey nearby. A meko worked with advisers. These spaces joined public decisions, gatherings and recreation within a town.

passages.title: Town life, relationships and exchange
passages.text: Maternal clans organized belonging, while people also maintained ties to particular towns. The confederacy included speakers of different languages. A shared political network did not erase those local relationships and differences.

passages.title: Town life, relationships and exchange
passages.text: During the eighteenth century, deerskin commerce displaced the earlier trade in enslaved people. Relations with colonial traders affected town alliances and livelihoods. Exchange offered opportunities while also drawing communities into violent external demands.

passages.title: Town life, relationships and exchange
passages.text: Before removal, Muscogee households included farmers and cattle owners, and some people enslaved others. This varied economy matters: forced migration uprooted established livelihoods and also carried the coercion of slavery into the new western setting.

passages.title: Government buildings and continuing authority
passages.text: From 1878 to Oklahoma statehood in 1907, the Council House at Okmulgee housed the Principal Chief, Supreme Court, education offices and National Council chambers. Its rooms show government as everyday administrative work as well as public ceremony.

passages.title: Government buildings and continuing authority
passages.text: The Nation was forced to leave the building at statehood and regained it in 2010. Restoration completed in 2018 recovered its historic room layout for interpretation. Regaining a building was an act of stewardship by an existing Nation, not the creation of a new people.

passages.title: Government buildings and continuing authority
passages.text: The constitution's election certificate records ratification on 6 October 1979. Its separate executive, legislative and judicial articles set out national institutions, while article II protects the organization of tribal towns. The document records both change and continuing local traditions.

passages.title: Removal and survival
passages.text: In 1836 and 1837, United States authorities forced large numbers of Muscogee people toward Indian Territory by land and water. Detention, inadequate supplies and dangerous travel caused profound suffering. Communities rebuilt afterward while maintaining ties to southeastern homelands.

Coerced land cessions and removal transformed Muscogee political geography in the nineteenth century. Later allotment and statehood imposed further losses, but the Muscogee Nation and its communities continue. The map's 1492 to 1500 interval is not a supported lifespan for the people or the later confederacy.
