passages.text: Mutapa was a Shona state of the northern Zimbabwe plateau and adjacent Zambezi lowlands, with connections extending into present-day Mozambique. It existed before the map’s 1492 start and continued after its 1650 endpoint. Older European maps often exaggerated the reach of its rulers.

passages.title: Towns, homes and manufacture
passages.text: Baranda, near Mount Fura and the gold-bearing Mukaradzi valley, is usually identified with the trading place Massapa. Sixteenth- and seventeenth-century remains include local pottery, imported ceramics and glass, revealing a substantial African settlement within an international trading world.

passages.title: Towns, homes and manufacture
passages.text: Soot on Baranda pots points to cooking, while burnishing tools support local manufacture of its polished graphite-coated pottery. Traders needed meals as well as merchandise; kitchens were part of this commercial settlement’s working life.

passages.title: Towns, homes and manufacture
passages.text: The published Baranda assemblage includes 9,006 sherds of locally made pottery. Most vessels served daily needs, but the researchers argue that some pottery also circulated in exchange. A broken cooking pot can therefore help tell both a household and a trading story.

passages.title: Towns, homes and manufacture
passages.text: Chemical analysis of Baranda’s glass beads identifies a south Asian origin for most of those studied. The beads were small, but their journeys connected inland African communities with production and exchange across the Indian Ocean.

passages.title: Towns, homes and manufacture
passages.text: Researchers combined bead shapes, excavated layers, X-ray fluorescence and Raman spectroscopy. These methods check the glass itself rather than assigning a date from colour alone; attractive objects can also be surprisingly informative scientific samples.

passages.title: Towns, homes and manufacture
passages.text: Baranda’s ironworking remains include furnace material, slag and air-pipe fragments. Study of these residues distinguishes smelting ore from later work on the metal, making skilled production visible even when a complete furnace no longer survives.

passages.title: Towns, homes and manufacture
passages.text: Comparing Baranda with the much earlier Swart Village suggested changes in ironworking practice. The authors explicitly challenge the idea that African metal production stayed unchanged for two thousand years; local technologies had histories of experimentation and adaptation.

passages.title: Family, government and evidence
passages.text: A Portuguese account quoted in the historical synthesis describes a royal compound with separate dwellings for the ruler, queen and attendants, surrounded by a wooden enclosure. This is evidence about a court household, not the floor plan of every family’s home.

passages.title: Family, government and evidence
passages.text: The same description places clay-covered wooden buildings beneath thatched roofs. Political importance did not require every palace to be built like Great Zimbabwe’s surviving stone walls; different building materials could house an important court.

passages.title: Family, government and evidence
passages.text: Diogo de Alcaçova’s early report drew on people at Sofala and focused on gold, rival rulers and possible alliances. Historian Ana Cristina Roque shows why these reports must be read as interested Portuguese accounts, not neutral surveys of the entire interior.

passages.title: Family, government and evidence
passages.text: The 1506 letter contains the Portuguese words “o nome de rey he Menamotapam”: “the title of the king is Menamotapam”. The spelling comes from the published original text. It records a foreign writer’s rendering of the royal title, not a Shona sentence written by the Mutapa court.

passages.title: Family, government and evidence
passages.text: Historians compare oral genealogies with contemporary documents because neither gives a perfectly straightforward succession list. David Beach’s study revised earlier reconstructions, illustrating how questioning a source can make the history more accurate rather than less valuable.

Mutapa power contracted and shifted through succession conflicts, Portuguese encroachment and the rise of Rozvi power. Smaller dynastic centres survived long after 1650. Colonial expansion eventually removed their independent power, while communities and some royal lineages continued.

sectionTitles: River villages, skilled work and recreation

passages.text: The Miami, or Myaamia, are a Great Lakes people whose farming villages and river connections supported wide regional influence. The broad Myaamia and narrower Miami outlines are approximations. A separate Oklahoma outline dated 1492 is anachronistic: Miami settlement there followed nineteenth-century removals. Miami communities continue in Oklahoma, Indiana and beyond.

passages.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation
passages.text: Miami villages stood near rivers that connected settlements through canoe travel. The Indiana community’s history places their homeland across parts of present-day Indiana, Ohio, Illinois and Michigan. Hunting, fishing and cultivation worked together in a landscape where water routes could link relatives and trading partners.

passages.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation
passages.text: Miami white flour corn drew an early eighteenth-century observer’s attention for its fine husks and pale flour. Historian Cameron Shriver follows this crop through later sources, including twentieth-century Miami farmers. Corn was both a lasting food tradition and an agricultural achievement maintained through enormous political change.

passages.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation
passages.text: In a 2023 account, weaver Jared Nally describes harvesting inner bark from trees such as basswood and gathering other plant fibers later in the year. Separating usable fibers and rolling or spinning thread could take as long as weaving itself. A finished textile contains a great deal of work that is easy not to see.

passages.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation
passages.text: The winter game snowsnake sends a length of wood sliding through snow. Players try to make it travel farther and straighter than an opponent’s throw. Myaamia community programs have been reviving the game: snow becomes a playing surface, and the snake is reassuringly wooden.

passages.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation
passages.text: Lacrosse remains an opportunity to meet relatives and neighbors as well as compete. A 2022 community account describes an annual Myaamia game with Seneca-Cayuga participants, including youth camps. It also distinguishes older games from newer adaptations that introduce Myaamia language into familiar card games.

passages.title: River villages, skilled work and recreation
passages.text: In 2024, Myaamia sugar camps operated in Ohio, Indiana and Oklahoma. Sap was boiled down into syrup or sugar; a typical maple yield required about 40 gallons of sap for one gallon of syrup. Oklahoma participants also tapped black walnut because local sugar maples were scarce. Breakfast sweetness required buckets of effort.

passages.title: Resistance, removal and rebuilding
passages.text: Miami leader Little Turtle helped lead a Native coalition that defeated United States forces in 1790 and 1791. Before the Battle of Fallen Timbers in 1794, he urged peace. These changing decisions belonged to a wider struggle over homelands involving several allied peoples, rather than one isolated Miami army.

passages.title: Resistance, removal and rebuilding
passages.text: The Treaty of Greenville in 1795 required extensive land cessions. Further treaties narrowed Miami control over their homeland, and an 1840 agreement called for removal beyond the Mississippi. Treaty dates mark government decisions; the forced journey itself came later.

passages.title: Resistance, removal and rebuilding
passages.text: On October 11, 1846, five canal boats carrying Miami people reached Cincinnati. There they were forced aboard the steamboat Colorado to continue west along the Ohio River. A university archival exhibit places this transfer within the removal journey, revealing how ordinary transport networks became instruments of forced displacement.

passages.title: Resistance, removal and rebuilding
passages.text: Other Miami families secured permission to stay in Indiana. Their descendants form the Miami Nation of Indiana, with continuing government, cultural programs and relationships to western Miami relatives. Its own history distinguishes that community’s existence from its lack of federal recognition as a sovereign tribal nation today.

passages.title: Resistance, removal and rebuilding
passages.text: The western Miami faced another move after an 1867 treaty, with migration from Kansas into present-day Oklahoma in the late 1860s and 1870s. The Miami Tribe of Oklahoma established its government there. That sequence explains why an Oklahoma polygon cannot accurately represent Miami territory in 1492.

passages.title: Children, archives and speaking again
passages.text: Language revitalization draws on documents spanning the late 1600s through the 1960s. A Myaamia Center report explains how researchers analyze old records, compare forms and develop resources for present-day use. The work connects archival scholarship with families learning words together; it is a gradual effort across generations.

passages.title: Children, archives and speaking again
passages.text: A short modern writing sample is “Tipeewe neeyolaani”, translated as “It is good to see you.” Miami University’s tribal-relations page prints both forms in its Myaamia teaching list. The greeting follows contemporary community teaching spelling.

passages.title: Children, archives and speaking again
passages.text: During 2023 summer programs, children made miniature lodges with coverings that represented elm bark and cattail mats. They also practiced kinship words on family trees, while older participants made films and mentored younger learners. Model building helped connect household history, language and living family relationships.

The imported map cutoffs are not the end of Miami history. Removal created separated communities without ending Miami identity. The Oklahoma Tribe and Indiana community continue, while research and family learning help carry Myaamia language into daily life.

sectionTitles: Power, diplomacy and a changing kingdom
Books, learning and a coin’s written voice

passages.text: Mysore was a major southern Indian power under Haidar Ali and Tipu Sultan, then a reduced Wodeyar kingdom under British supremacy. This map’s 1783 to 1815 coverage crosses the conquest of 1799. Its broad outlines do not accurately show the resulting territorial partition, and neither endpoint marks the kingdom’s founding or final disappearance.

passages.title: Power, diplomacy and a changing kingdom
passages.text: Haidar Ali rose through military leadership and took effective control of Mysore; his son Tipu ruled directly after him. Persian served as the court’s official language. The kingdom’s objects therefore speak in several ways: through royal images, Persian inscriptions and the Arabic religious phrases used on coins.

passages.title: Power, diplomacy and a changing kingdom
passages.text: Srirangapatna, often called Seringapatam in older English records, stood on an island in the Kaveri River. It combined a royal capital with a fortress. Monsoon rains, river crossings and mountain routes mattered to the armies approaching it, as much as the strength of its walls.

passages.title: Power, diplomacy and a changing kingdom
passages.text: After the 1792 war, two of Tipu’s sons were handed to Cornwallis as guarantees that the peace terms would be fulfilled. Robert Home painted the meeting. These royal children were drawn directly into diplomacy: a treaty could place members of a ruler’s family in an enemy’s custody.

passages.title: Power, diplomacy and a changing kingdom
passages.text: Three ambassadors from Mysore arrived in Paris in July 1788 carrying cotton robes and jewellery for the French royal couple. They sought a military alliance and French manufactured goods. Louis XVI welcomed commercial ties, but the embassy did not secure the formal military alliance Tipu wanted.

passages.title: Power, diplomacy and a changing kingdom
passages.text: The final attack on Srirangapatna on 4 May 1799 involved British armies and troops supplied by Hyderabad’s Nizam. Tipu was killed and his independent regime ended. The subsequent Mysore princely state preserved a dynasty and local government, but under a fundamentally different balance of power.

passages.title: Meals, markets and health
passages.text: In 1800, Buchanan described ragi being ground as needed in a handmill near Srirangapatna. Its flour became a thick cooked pudding and cakes fried in oil. Preparing a meal began with processing the grain, long before anyone could ask whether dinner was ready.

passages.title: Meals, markets and health
passages.text: Buchanan found firewood expensive around Srirangapatna. Women collected cattle dung, shaped it into cakes, dried them on walls and carried baskets into town to sell. Their work supplied cooking fires and a daily market. His account records practical recycling alongside the hard labour of gathering and carrying.

passages.title: Meals, markets and health
passages.text: A bridge across the Kaveri’s southern branch also carried an aqueduct into the town and island. Buchanan described granite supports, stone beams and a channel lined with brick and plaster beside the roadway. The same structure helped people cross the river and brought water across it.

passages.title: Meals, markets and health
passages.text: A portrait painted by Thomas Hickey around 1805 has been interpreted as showing Mysore royal women supporting smallpox vaccination. One woman presents her left upper arm. Historian Nigel Chancellor linked this gesture and the women’s jewellery with court encouragement of vaccination. The sitters’ identities and the picture’s purpose remain interpretations, rather than facts supplied by a caption on the canvas.

passages.title: Ingenious objects and skilled makers
passages.text: Mysore’s rockets used hammered iron casings attached to long bamboo poles or blades. The iron contained greater pressure than the paper-based casings common in contemporary European rockets. Metalworkers and military specialists helped develop a weapon that made a powerful impression on opposing armies.

passages.title: Ingenious objects and skilled makers
passages.text: Reports and captured rocket cases from India helped stimulate William Congreve’s experiments in Britain in the early nineteenth century. Mysore’s military defeat did not end its technical influence. A technology could travel into the workshops of a former opponent and be developed further there.

passages.title: Ingenious objects and skilled makers
passages.text: Tipu’s famous wooden tiger contains a small organ. Turning a handle made sounds and moved the arm of the European soldier represented beneath the animal. This elaborate palace object expressed hostility toward an enemy. Its surviving mechanism also preserves the work of instrument makers and woodworkers.

passages.title: Ingenious objects and skilled makers
passages.text: A surviving war turban combines a wicker frame, leather, quilted silk, velvet lining and muslin wrapping. Its steel face guard carries gold decoration and tiger forms. The National Army Museum traces this example from the spoils of 1799 through Cornwallis’s family, giving unusually clear evidence of its later journey.

passages.title: Ingenious objects and skilled makers
passages.text: At the Sèvres factory, Mysore’s ambassadors received a porcelain service made for Tipu and portrait busts as personal gifts. The busts were left unglazed, creating a marble-like surface. The surviving objects reveal diplomacy conducted through skilled manufacture as well as conversations and letters.

passages.title: Books, learning and a coin’s written voice
passages.text: One Quran owned by Tipu had been copied in 1613, long before his reign. Persian tables were added for his use, including information about the chapters and their order of revelation. The book’s changing pages show an older manuscript being adapted for a later reader.

passages.title: Books, learning and a coin’s written voice
passages.text: That manuscript’s leather binding has a triangular flap which tucks under the front cover to protect the page edges. It was stored flat. Gold-painted flowers decorate the margins. Protecting a valuable book could be a work of art in its own right.

passages.title: Books, learning and a coin’s written voice
passages.text: In 1800, the naturalist Francis Buchanan recovered his own old botanical notebook. A colleague had accidentally taken it overseas; Mysore troops later captured it, and it was preserved and rebound in Tipu’s library. After the British conquest, Major Ogg returned it. This study notebook had travelled through a surprisingly eventful chain of owners.

passages.title: Books, learning and a coin’s written voice
passages.text: Tipu issued coins in several metals and denominations through multiple mints. Henderson’s museum catalogue distinguishes large gold ahmadis from smaller pagodas and fanams, which fitted existing southern Indian currency traditions. New royal names and inscriptions therefore coexisted with familiar kinds of money.

passages.title: Books, learning and a coin’s written voice
passages.text: A gold ahmadi dated 1198 in the Islamic calendar opens its reverse inscription with هو السلطان, huwa al-sulṭān, meaning “He is the Sultan.” The museum catalogue prints the Arabic and translates it. This short royal formula is authentic writing from Tipu’s coinage; it is Arabic, rather than a sample of everyday Kannada speech.

The conquest of 1799 ended Tipu’s rule, but Mysore continued as a Wodeyar princely state under British supremacy. The map’s 1815 cutoff is not its fall. The kingdom survived into the twentieth century and became part of independent India in 1947; its communities and cultural traditions continued through these political changes.

sectionTitles: Games and writing you can inspect

passages.text: This Mysore record covers 1815 to 1878, after the Wodeyar dynasty’s restoration in 1799. Its coarse outline includes Mysuru and Bengaluru but cannot show their changing jurisdictions. Royal government gave way to British commissioners in 1831; the return of administration to the dynasty in 1881 lies beyond the map’s endpoint. The earlier Mysore card covers Tipu Sultan and the 1799 transition.

passages.title: A kingdom with divided authority
passages.text: British authorities justified taking over Mysore’s administration in 1831 by citing rebellion and alleged misgovernment. This was a transfer of effective power, not the disappearance of the royal family. Later histories dispute the colonial justification, so the change should not be described simply as a benevolent rescue.

passages.title: A kingdom with divided authority
passages.text: The restoration of administration in 1881 came after this card’s dates. Maharaja Chamarajendra received ruling powers on 25 March, with Rangacharlu as diwan. A Representative Assembly followed inOctober. These were important institutional changes, but an elite consultative assembly was not universal voting rights.

passages.title: Homes, food, messages and learning
passages.text: Rice’s 1877 gazetteer describes low earthen houses with inward-facing courtyards and verandahs. Wealthier homes could have paved, drained courts and carved wooden pillars; poorer roofs were often thatched. The courtyard brought daylight into homes with few outward-facing openings.

passages.title: Homes, food, messages and learning
passages.text: Ragi was a major staple. The gazetteer’s report for 1874 to 1875 notes that its price rose despite a good harvest, while rice and some pulses became cheaper. A family’s food budget could depend on which grain it relied upon.

passages.title: Homes, food, messages and learning
passages.text: The local Anche post relied on runners: in 1875 to 1876 its routes totaled 2,312 miles, linking 152 receiving offices. Private letters, newspapers and official dispatches traveled through a relay of runners.

passages.title: Homes, food, messages and learning
passages.text: The 1868 village-school scheme proposed night classes for people unable to attend during working hours. Pupils would pay for lighting. Learning after work meant finding both time and a lamp.

passages.title: Homes, food, messages and learning
passages.text: Maharaja’s College grew from a free school founded in 1833. The government took over the school in 1868, and college affiliation followed in 1879, after this map interval. Separating those dates avoids putting later university buildings and courses into an earlier classroom.

passages.title: Homes, food, messages and learning
passages.text: Bengaluru’s Literary and Scientific Institute began in 1868 on Museum Road. It later became the Bowring Institute. Its history is a reminder that adult learning also took place in associations; the institution’s familiar later building belongs to a different phase, beyond 1878.

passages.title: Hospitals, toilets and water
passages.text: Bowring Hospital began admitting patients in 1868. Rice describes a plan adapted from a Paris hospital, with space to separate disease categories and caste groups. Medical buildings could expand treatment while also reproducing social divisions; a hospital was not automatically an equal space.

passages.title: Hospitals, toilets and water
passages.text: Bengaluru’s military settlement and adjoining neighborhoods shared connected water systems. In the 1860s, investigators found that rainy-season overflow could wash sewage toward wells. A boundary between jurisdictions did not stop dirty water: drainage problems needed attention across the whole area.

passages.title: Hospitals, toilets and water
passages.text: Some slopes near horse-keepers’ and grass-cutters’ homes served as public latrines. Officials seeking healthier barracks proposed removing nearby homes. The history of sanitation therefore includes a hard question: who received protection, and who risked losing a place to live?

passages.title: Hospitals, toilets and water
passages.text: Water engineers tried different solutions. An 1865 proposal would have collected rain from barrack roofs in underground reservoirs, but officials chose another scheme. This was a proposed system, not a household service that everyone actually received.

passages.title: Hospitals, toilets and water
passages.text: The 1870s famine was also a water emergency. Families faced drying wells and tanks while some people resorted to ditches and puddles. Contemporary reporting contrasted water carted for troops and horses with inadequate help for residents. Hunger, disease and unequal access reinforced one another.

passages.title: Games and writing you can inspect
passages.text: Manuscripts associated with Krishnaraja Wadiyar III preserve a tiger game with two tiger pieces facing 25 people. The sides have different jobs: tigers jump to capture, while the people try to block them. Being outnumbered does not necessarily make the tiger the underdog!

passages.title: Games and writing you can inspect
passages.text: The game’s board combines a square grid with triangles attached to its sides. Players follow marked lines, and the people are placed before they can move. Surviving diagrams preserve a form of practical reasoning: planning space, anticipating an opponent and turning a drawing into play.

passages.title: Games and writing you can inspect
passages.text: A twenty-cash coin dated 1833 carries the Kannada name ಕೃಷ್ಣ, transcribed Kṛṣṇa, or Krishna. It names the ruler in the catalogue’s reading. The short sample is a modern Unicode rendering of an attested coin inscription, verified in the government museum’s 1889 catalogue.

passages.title: Games and writing you can inspect
passages.text: That small 1833 coin mixes Kannada, Persian and English lettering, including XX CASH for its value. Money moved among readers of different languages. A coin could advertise a ruler, identify a mint and state a denomination in very little space.

passages.title: How evidence survives
passages.text: Writing in 1908 about collecting in the 1890s, R. P. Jackson recalled villagers bringing him old coins and sometimes asking whether he was exchanging them officially for new money. Objects that now sit in collections once had owners, prices and uncertain futures outside museums.

passages.title: How evidence survives
passages.text: Karnataka’s archives preserve Mysore government proceedings from 1843 and gazettes from 1866, alongside commissioners’ files and manuscripts in several languages. These records allow historians to investigate government beyond palace portraits: decisions, correspondence and administration also left evidence.

The atlas ends in 1878 while British commissioners still governed. Administration returned to Chamarajendra in 1881, under continuing British paramountcy. Mysore’s institutions and communities continued beyond that transition; the map endpoint is not the kingdom’s extinction.

sectionTitles: Clothes, hair and a special drink
A seat, a family and a sound

passages.text: This map groups northern European Bronze Age communities under a very broad label. Its outline reaches far beyond Scandinavia into eastern Europe, so it cannot stand for one kingdom or shared way of life. The examples here focus on well-documented Danish and Scandinavian communities; Denmark’s Bronze Age is conventionally dated about 1700 to 500 BCE.

passages.title: A farmhouse full of clues
passages.text: At Bjerre Site 7 in northwestern Denmark, a ninth-century BCE longhouse was at least fifteen metres long. Fire pits, grains and food crusts show that much cooking happened at its eastern end. Thin-walled serving vessels concentrated farther west, suggesting different tasks in different parts of the house.

passages.title: A farmhouse full of clues
passages.text: Nearly 1,800 pieces of raw amber were recovered at Bjerre. Some lay in storage pots or compact clusters. Researchers suggest the household collected and stored amber for exchange, possibly obtaining metal in return. A farm could therefore be connected to distant places while producing much of its own food.

passages.title: A farmhouse full of clues
passages.text: Bjerre also produced evidence of flint tool making and small-scale metalworking, including crucible and mould fragments. Bronze Age does not mean people stopped using stone. Householders selected materials for particular jobs, and flint remained useful for cutting, scraping and other everyday work.

passages.title: Clothes, hair and a special drink
passages.text: A young woman buried at Egtved in 1370 BCE wore a short tunic and a skirt made from cords, with a spiral-decorated bronze belt plate. Her teeth suggest she was about sixteen to eighteen. Preserved clothing lets us see a real outfit rather than imagine everyone in generic animal skins.

passages.title: Clothes, hair and a special drink
passages.text: Her belongings included a horn comb, a small bark box with a bronze awl, and traces of a hair net. Such objects connect dress with work and grooming. The burial is unusually rich evidence, so it should not be treated as the standard wardrobe of every household.

passages.title: Clothes, hair and a special drink
passages.text: A bark bucket from the same grave retained residue from a fermented drink, probably beer sweetened with honey. Analysis also identified berry-related evidence, wheat and bog myrtle. Pollen can preserve clues to ingredients, although it does not supply an exact recipe or prove what everyone drank daily.

passages.title: A seat, a family and a sound
passages.text: At Guldhøj, a man buried in the later fifteenth century BCE had a folding chair placed at his feet. It was made from ash wood with dark pitch inlaid into carved decoration. The seat had been otter skin, of which only a fragment survives. Portable furniture has a very long history.

passages.title: A seat, a family and a sound
passages.text: Three oak-coffin burials at Borum Eshøj held an older woman, an older man and a younger man. Wood for at least two coffins was felled in 1351 BCE. They may have been related, but the attractive idea of a small family remains an interpretation rather than an established family tree.

passages.title: A seat, a family and a sound
passages.text: Curved bronze trumpets called lurs had a mouthpiece at one end and a decorated plate at the other. Modern players can produce a range of natural notes on surviving examples. We can hear the instruments, but we do not know the actual tunes people played at Bronze Age gatherings.

passages.title: Pictures of journeys
passages.text: The Trundholm Sun Chariot, made around 1400 BCE, places a horse and a decorated sun disc on wheels. The museum interprets it as the sun’s journey with a divine horse. It is a striking model of movement and belief, not an ordinary cart shrunk for archaeological convenience.

passages.title: Pictures of journeys
passages.text: A ship appears on a ceremonial sword from Rørby, with crew members drawn as short lines. Related ship images were carved into rock in Denmark, Sweden and Norway. The repeated motif links objects and landscapes across the sea without telling us the names of the people aboard.

passages.title: Pictures of journeys
passages.text: These ships, spirals and sun images offer a visual language, but the cited examples are not a deciphered alphabet. This card cannot provide an attested sentence spoken or written by their makers. Their pictures survive more clearly than their words.

Around 500 BCE, Danish communities increasingly worked iron from local deposits, marking the conventional beginning of the Iron Age. This was a change in technology and society, not the fall of one northern empire. The vast imported outline cannot give every community the same ending.

sectionTitles: A kingdom of routes, towns and families
Meals, crafts and words that survived

passages.text: The Nabataean kingdom linked Petra and Arabian oasis towns to long-distance caravan routes. Its people were merchants, farmers, builders and craftsworkers. This imported map spans 300 BCE to 200 CE and repeats broad outlines across several centuries; it does not show exact changing frontiers. Rome annexed the kingdom in 106 CE, well before the map cutoff, while its towns and communities continued.

passages.title: A kingdom of routes, towns and families
passages.text: Petra stood where routes from Arabia and the wider eastern trading world met routes toward the Mediterranean. During the first century BCE, King Aretas III briefly held Damascus. Pompey's Roman intervention checked that northern expansion. Political power and commerce were closely connected, and neither followed one unchanging border.

passages.title: A kingdom of routes, towns and families
passages.text: Hegra, in today's northwest Saudi Arabia, was another important Nabataean town. Its inhabited center covered about 50 hectares, with houses built mainly from mud bricks and streets that did not form a neat rectangular grid. Most residents lived in a working town, not inside the great rock-cut tombs visitors photograph today.

passages.title: A kingdom of routes, towns and families
passages.text: Hegra's tomb inscriptions record legal rights as well as remembrance. Many name owners from the same family, the stonecutter, and the reigning king's year. The dated inscriptions run from 1 to 75 CE. A grand facade could therefore carry something like a family property record, written where everyone approaching could see it.

passages.title: A kingdom of routes, towns and families
passages.text: One basalt memorial from Madaba commemorated the military commander Artobel. Its date names the 46th year of Aretas IV, corresponding to 37 CE. Now in the Vatican Museums, the stone makes a useful contrast with anonymous ruins: it preserves a particular person, a military office, and the kingdom's way of dating events.

passages.title: Growing food and managing water
passages.text: Hegra's oasis used more than 130 wells to reach underground water. Some were as much as 20 meters deep. These were major pieces of infrastructure, partly cut through sandstone. Keeping crops and households supplied required work beneath the ground as well as the impressive stonecarving visible above it.

passages.title: Growing food and managing water
passages.text: Plant remains from Hegra reveal gardens organized in layers: date palms above fruit trees and vines, with grains and smaller crops below. Archaeologists identified barley, wheat, lentils and other plants. It is a wonderfully compact arrangement: a garden with an upstairs, a middle floor and a ground floor.

passages.title: Growing food and managing water
passages.text: At Petra, channels, ceramic pipes, cisterns and diversion works moved and stored water. Leigh-Ann Bedal's research also emphasizes flood protection: builders redirected sudden torrents away from vulnerable structures. Desert engineering had to handle both scarcity and dangerous excess. Too little water and too much water were different problems for the same city.

passages.title: Growing food and managing water
passages.text: The space once called Petra's Lower Market turned out to contain an ornamental garden and monumental pool. Bedal's excavations changed its interpretation beginning in 1998. In the Nabataean and later Roman city, impressive water displays could express wealth and authority. A ruler able to maintain a lush garden was visibly demonstrating control over a precious resource.

passages.title: Growing food and managing water
passages.text: A drain under the Great Temple's western entry area was covered with stone slabs. The excavation team interprets it as a Nabataean wastewater channel that later also served Roman-period baths. Bringing clean water in was only half the practical challenge; used water needed a route out.

passages.title: Meals, crafts and words that survived
passages.text: A painted bowl excavated at Tawilan near Petra has a rounded bottom and a design divided into five leafy segments. It belongs to the thin pottery for which Nabataean workshops became known around the first centuries BCE and CE. The elaborate decoration rewarded a closer look at the table, not just at a palace wall.

passages.title: Meals, crafts and words that survived
passages.text: Food traces survive even in tombs. Jennifer Ramsay's analysis of samples from Petra's shaft tombs identified wheat, barley, lentils, grapes, figs and dates. These could represent food eaten during funerary gatherings or offerings for the dead. They tell us about particular rituals; they do not give a complete menu for every Nabataean household.

passages.title: Meals, crafts and words that survived
passages.text: Near a shrine at Little Petra, a short inscription says “šlm hbwls”, translated “Peace! Habōlos”. This is the published Roman-letter transcription of Nabataean Aramaic, not its ancient lettering. The same inscription writes the name in Greek as “Αβολος”. Its exact date is unknown. Two written forms of one name offer a small glimpse of a multilingual environment.

passages.title: Meals, crafts and words that survived
passages.text: Hegra preserves 111 monumental tombs,94 with decorated fronts. Their carvings combine forms associated with several neighboring artistic traditions. These were purposeful memorial buildings, with rooms cut into the sandstone behind the facades. The achievement involved design, stone selection and skilled labor, not merely finding a picturesque cliff.

passages.title: Meals, crafts and words that survived
passages.text: Petra's history continued after 106. The Great Temple excavation sequence places a bath complex in the Roman period, with later Roman and Byzantine alterations. Hot rooms stood above heating spaces, and cold bathing areas formed part of the complex. These discoveries illuminate the town's later life and should not all be credited to the independent Nabataean kings.

passages.title: Meals, crafts and words that survived
passages.text: The kingdom disappeared, but its roads remained useful. At Hegra, the long-distance route continued after the ancient city's abandonment and later served pilgrimage journeys toward Mecca. A change of rulers, an abandoned neighborhood and the end of a trade route are different events, sometimes separated by many generations.

Rome incorporated the Nabataean kingdom into the province of Arabia in 106 CE under Trajan. The monarchy ended; local communities and buildings continued under new government. The imported 200 CE endpoint is not a second conquest.

sectionTitles: Water for a city and a school

passages.text: This record begins while Namibia was still under South African rule. Independence came on 21 March 1990 after a long liberation struggle and international negotiations. Modern Namibia includes many languages and communities, with distinctive achievements in water engineering and living traditions of music, craft and shared celebration.

passages.title: Rule, resistance and independence
passages.text: Hosea Kutako’s appeals against South African rule reached the United Nations through Reverend Michael Scott from 1946. Decades of petitions, political organizing and international debate followed. Independence required Namibians’ sustained efforts, not merely a new name printed on a map.

passages.title: Rule, resistance and independence
passages.text: In 1959, resistance to forced removal from Windhoek’s Old Location ended in deadly violence. Apartheid planners moved Black residents toward Katutura. Museum documentation records doors marked with letters assigning different African groups to separate areas, making racial classification visible in the built environment.

passages.title: Rule, resistance and independence
passages.text: Preparing the 1989 election meant reaching rural voters as well as towns. UNTAG reports that mobile teams covered some 2,200 rural registration points. Elections and the constituent assembly then helped turn a negotiated settlement into institutions for an independent country.

passages.title: Water for a city and a school
passages.text: Windhoek began adding highly treated reclaimed wastewater to its drinking-water supply in 1968. In a dry region, engineers found a way to use water again. The achievement depends on treatment and checking water quality; simply reusing dirty water would be a completely different matter.

passages.title: Water for a city and a school
passages.text: The newer Goreangab reclamation plant, operating from 2002, uses multiple treatment barriers before its water is blended with other supplies. This is an important sanitation story: wastewater becomes a resource through carefully managed engineering, not through wishing very hard at a tap.

passages.title: Water for a city and a school
passages.text: At Onakatumbe Combined School in 2017, handwashing stations stood near classrooms and toilets. Children practiced washing before snacks and after toilet visits. Learning to use soap became part of the school day alongside reading and mathematics.

passages.title: Water for a city and a school
passages.text: A broken borehole at King Kauluma Combined School in late 2017 disrupted meals and closed flush toilets. UNICEF’s 2018 account describes pupils bringing small bottles from home until a tanker supplied the school. Water infrastructure mattered to eating, learning and using the loo at once.

passages.title: Gatherings, music and writing
passages.text: For northern Namibia’s Oshituthi shomagongo festival, men carve wooden cups and tools from cattle horns while women prepare baskets and clay pots. Fruit gathering and juice processing involve younger people too. A celebration begins long before anyone arrives to sing or dance.

passages.title: Gatherings, music and writing
passages.text: As women prepare the fermented marula drink, they also share songs, poems, family concerns and craft knowledge. Young people learn by watching and joining the work. The gathering links food preparation to conversation and education, rather than separating those parts of life.

passages.title: Gatherings, music and writing
passages.text: Nama and Damara ancestral music accompanies occasions such as weddings and celebrations welcoming rain. A UNESCO-supported documentation project in 2018 and 2019 worked with community knowledge. Musical skill survives through people teaching and performing it, as well as through recordings.

passages.title: Gatherings, music and writing
passages.text: A written Oshindonga example appears in a 2013 community consent letter: “Omukanda gwepitikilo”, translated there as “Certificate of Consent”. The document authorized a heritage nomination on behalf of northern traditional authorities. Communities were writing their own decision into the preservation process.

passages.title: Gatherings, music and writing
passages.text: The republic’s constitution supplies an English sample: “This Constitution shall be the Supreme Law of Namibia.” In plain language, the constitution is the highest legal authority. The sentence comes from Article 1, linking the written founding document to the new state established in 1990.

Namibia continues as an independent republic. The 1945 start of this map record belongs to the period of South African rule; it is not Namibia’s independence date. The decisive constitutional transformation occurred in 1990, while families and cultural communities span both periods.

passages.text: The atlas keeps the name “Nan Chao” on maps from 800 to 1279, but history refuses to fit that label. Nanzhao was a powerful kingdom centered around Erhai Lake and present-day Dali. Its rulers balanced Tang China and Tibet, fought far beyond their capital, sponsored Buddhism, moved books and crafts, and depended on farmers who shaped water into rice fields. Then the Nanzhao ruling house fell in 902. Short-lived regimes followed, and the different Dali kingdom began in 937. Mongol armies conquered Dali in 1253, yet the atlas still carries the older name for another twenty-six years. The map geometry has problems too: its 800 and 900 shapes miss the actual capital region and stretch far southeast; only the 1000 shape shifts back over Dali. This card follows the atlas interval while clearly changing political chapters. Along the way, inscriptions, excavated kilns, painted scrolls, family names and even music played on leaves reveal lives that no single kingdom label can hold.

passages.title: First, inspect the atlas label
passages.text: At 800 the exact id is one 20-position polygon, but Taihe, Dali and Weishan all test outside it. Kunming and faraway Luang Prabang test inside. The imported shape therefore misses Nanzhao’s Erhai capital core and reaches much too far southeast; it is a display error, not a historical frontier.

passages.title: First, inspect the atlas label
passages.text: The 900 layer repeats almost the same problem in 21 positions: Taihe and Weishan remain outside while Kunming and Luang Prabang remain inside. This snapshot stands only two years before Nanzhao’s historical end, so its misplaced outline cannot rescue the label by representing an earlier heartland.

passages.title: First, inspect the atlas label
passages.text: By 1000 the atlas shape jumps west. Its 12-position polygon now includes Dali, Weishan and Kunming but leaves Luang Prabang outside. The geography is closer to the political center, yet the name is now anachronistic: the Duan family’s Dali kingdom, founded in 937, ruled this core.

passages.title: First, inspect the atlas label
passages.text: The 1100 and 1200 polygons keep nearly the same west-shifted footprint, with 12 and 14 positions respectively. Both include Dali and Kunming. These layers can help locate successor-era history, but calling that history “Nan Chao” hides the Later Dali kingdom and its own rulers.

passages.title: First, inspect the atlas label
passages.text: The separate nan-zhao id appears at 700, while nan-chao begins at 800 and disappears at 1279. Those seams belong to the atlas database. This card does not alias the two ids, and 1279 cannot be a local fall date: Nanzhao ended in 902 and Dali fell in 1253.

passages.title: Diplomacy, war and hard choices
passages.text: Nanzhao’s kings maneuvered between Tang China and the Tibetan empire. Alliances changed when rulers judged that a neighbor had become dangerous or useful. That was statecraft in a crowded borderland, not proof that Nanzhao permanently belonged to either empire. Armies, marriage ties, titles and envoys all shaped the contest.

passages.title: Diplomacy, war and hard choices
passages.text: In 829 Nanzhao forces attacked Chengdu and carried off prisoners, including artisans and silk weavers. The raid expanded the kingdom’s access to valuable skills through violence. A beautiful textile made afterward might preserve technical knowledge while concealing the forced journey of the worker who knew how to weave it.

passages.title: Diplomacy, war and hard choices
passages.text: Nanzhao forces took Annan, centered in northern Vietnam, in 863 and held it until Tang armies recovered the region in 866. A garrison of about 20,000 shows the scale of occupation. The episode also warns against treating every place touched by an army as a permanent part of one kingdom.

passages.title: Diplomacy, war and hard choices
passages.text: Military success rested on more than mounted warriors. Officials collected supplies, craftspeople repaired equipment, farmers produced grain and routes carried messages through difficult terrain. The surviving sources celebrate rulers and campaigns far more often than these workers, so reconstructing war means noticing the labor that court narratives leave mostly unnamed.

passages.title: Diplomacy, war and hard choices
passages.text: The 766 Dehua Stele gives Nanzhao’s own court explanation for breaking with Tang and aligning with Tibet. Much of the stone later became difficult to read, while older written copies preserved more. It is a political argument from one side, valuable precisely because readers can compare its purpose with its information.

passages.title: One label, four political chapters
passages.text: Nanzhao’s ruling house was overthrown in 902. This is the card’s central chronology correction: almost four-fifths of the atlas interval comes after the historical kingdom had ended. Families, farms, workshops and temples did not vanish, but the state called Nanzhao no longer governed them.

passages.title: One label, four political chapters
passages.text: Changhe ruled from 903 to 927, followed by two more short regimes before Dali began in 937. Changhe rulers still used Buddhist ideas of kingship, showing continuity without turning them into Nanzhao kings. A successor may inherit ceremonies, scribes and sacred stories while remaining a different government.

passages.title: One label, four political chapters
passages.text: Duan Siping founded the Dali kingdom in 937. In 1094 Gao Shengtai replaced Duan rule with the brief Dazhong regime; Duan rule returned in 1096. Historians therefore distinguish Earlier and Later Dali. Even the successor state has a seam that the smooth atlas label does not show.

passages.title: One label, four political chapters
passages.text: Later Dali government joined Duan monarchs with powerful Gao, Yang and Dong families and with leaders on the kingdom’s edges. Some units were militarized and semi-autonomous. This was layered rule built through personal and clan alliances, so a map outline cannot tell us how tightly any distant community was controlled.

passages.title: One label, four political chapters
passages.text: Mongol armies defeated Dali in 1253. Yuan rulers then used local personnel and institutions rather than erasing them, while the atlas waits until 1279 to drop “nan-chao.” The later date matches a broad imperial milestone better than local succession. Conquest changed the framework of power and preserved selected pieces of it.

passages.title: Water, fields and food on the table
passages.text: Around Erhai, farmers expanded wet-rice cultivation with terraces, channels and embankments. Waterworks supported dense settlements and the capitals at Taihe and Yangjumie. They were achievements made by planners and many laborers, not magic gifts from kings, even when royal inscriptions claimed the credit.

passages.title: Water, fields and food on the table
passages.text: The 766 Dehua inscription praises flood control, rice, millet, orchards, household mulberry plots and grain stored for nine years. It predates this card by 34 years but belongs to the same Nanzhao court. Its sweeping abundance is royal rhetoric, not proof that every family always had enough food.

passages.title: Water, fields and food on the table
passages.text: Fan Chuo says paddy fields produced one rice harvest, then farmers sowed barley after the rice and harvested it in spring. The sequence is a valuable clue to intensive cropping. It describes particular fields in a ninth-century gazetteer, so it cannot be assumed for every elevation or community in Yunnan.

passages.title: Water, fields and food on the table
passages.text: Fan Chuo reports that an eleventh-lunar-month gathering involved brewing drink, preparing cattle and sheep, and entertaining relatives and neighbors. That is a vivid meal scene, but it comes from a ninth-century outsider and a special gathering. It cannot stand for breakfast, lunch and dinner in every household all year.

passages.title: Water, fields and food on the table
passages.text: Fan Chuo describes salt wells whose output supplied food and says officials controlled access to at least one especially valued well. Salt makes meals taste different and helps preserve food, but a gazetteer’s attention to production and taxation tells us little about how much each household could afford.

passages.title: Families, courtship and social rank
passages.text: Fan Chuo describes noblewomen in silk skirts and jackets with brocade, pearls, gold, shells and amber. He separately mentions female servants in skirts and felt coverings. The contrast reveals household rank more clearly than it reveals every woman’s routine, because an elite-focused outsider noticed display and difference.

passages.title: Families, courtship and social rank
passages.text: The same account says young men made evening music with gourd instruments or even leaves during courtship. A leaf could become a tiny instrument without a workshop. This charming report belongs to a selected ninth-century setting; it does not prove that every family approved the same matches or courtship rules.

passages.title: Families, courtship and social rank
passages.text: A later Dali Buddhist handscroll names married donors Chen Qing and his wife Lian. Their joint appearance shows a household sponsoring religious art, while the carefully recorded names let us glimpse real people behind the image. Patronage could express devotion, status, family memory or several of these at once.

passages.title: Families, courtship and social rank
passages.text: The same scroll links a father named Chen Qing with a son named Qingfu by repeating Qing. Museum documentation identifies this as a Yunnanese genealogical naming practice. One family’s names cannot define the whole population, but they preserve a small, unusually personal clue about kinship and remembrance.

passages.title: Families, courtship and social rank
passages.text: Fan Chuo’s feast passage brings relatives and neighbors together as guests, which shows that social life reached beyond one nuclear household. Yet a festival visit cannot tell us who normally shared a roof, how children divided work or how inheritance operated. Those family details remain largely unrecorded.

passages.title: Learning, books and an honest language sample
passages.text: Elite Nanzhao young men studied literacy and numeracy in Chengdu. This is evidence for selected male students crossing a political border, not a kingdom-wide school system. The sources reviewed do not establish universal childhood education, village classroom routines or a comparable curriculum for girls, so those gaps should stay visible.

passages.title: Learning, books and an honest language sample
passages.text: Dali obtained Sinitic books through the horse trade and used them to train officials. A 1173 list includes classics, histories, rhyming guides, Buddhist sutras and works on medicine. That collection shows what educated elites valued; it does not tell us how many copies existed or who beyond court circles could read them.

passages.title: Learning, books and an honest language sample
passages.text: The short sample 厄塞流潦 means “blocking the floodwaters.” It comes from the transmitted Chinese text of Nanzhao’s 766 Dehua inscription. The phrase is directly tied to the Nanzhao court, though it falls just before this card’s 800 opening and survives through copying as well as the weathered stone.

passages.title: Learning, books and an honest language sample
passages.text: This sample is Literary Chinese used for an official monument, an external prestige language for government writing. It is not a phonetic record of everyday speech and should not be presented as a sentence in modern Bai, Yi or another living language. The honest label matters more than pretending the missing voice survives.

passages.title: Learning, books and an honest language sample
passages.text: Dali manuscripts and paintings could combine Chinese writing with Sanskrit Buddhist formulas. Zhang Shengwen’s late twelfth-century scroll includes Chinese and Sanskrit pillars among hundreds of figures. This multilingual page-world reflects court religion and learned exchange, while leaving most people’s spoken words unrecorded.

passages.title: Temples, workshops and spectacular art
passages.text: At Wuzhishan near Taihe, excavators uncovered courtyards with main halls, side corridors and porches. Buddhist images and miniature pagodas helped identify a temple complex. The site turns court religion into a built place where stone foundations, roof tiles, movement paths and repeated repairs mattered every day.

passages.title: Temples, workshops and spectacular art
passages.text: Kilns east of the temple held firing supports, spacers, molds and imperfect glazed pottery. Rejects are archaeological treasure because they preserve production mistakes that finished objects hide. The evidence places practical manufacturing beside sacred buildings, where potters, carriers and builders contributed to an impressive religious landscape.

passages.title: Temples, workshops and spectacular art
passages.text: A tile from Building One bears the Chinese characters 官家舍利, interpreted as “royal relics.” Excavation director Zhu Zhonghua proposed that the hall may have enshrined relics linked with the ruling house. The interpretation is plausible but still a proposal; no named king was found neatly labelled inside.

passages.title: Temples, workshops and spectacular art
passages.text: The 899 Illustrated History of Nanzhao tells how Acuoye Guanyin introduced Buddhism and granted the first kings a sacred mandate. The story helped the late court explain why its dynasty deserved to rule. It is an achievement of political storytelling and religious art, not an eyewitness report from Nanzhao’s beginnings.

passages.title: Temples, workshops and spectacular art
passages.text: A Dali sculpture at the Metropolitan Museum gives Avalokiteshvara twenty-four arms holding objects such as the sun, moon, bell and vajra. Cast in gilt arsenical bronze in the eleventh or twelfth century, it joins technical skill with a protective tantric form. Each arm turns theology into visible design.

passages.title: Trade routes carried things and ideas
passages.text: Yunnan’s horse trade joined the region to neighboring courts and markets. Exchange was political as well as commercial: rulers wanted strong animals and dependable partners, while handlers needed fodder, tack and safe stages. A caravan’s success depended on practical knowledge that elite accounts rarely bother to name.

passages.title: Trade routes carried things and ideas
passages.text: Silver left Yunnan and cowries entered its monetary life, linking mountain communities with distant markets. These flows did not make everyone a wealthy merchant. Miners, pack-animal handlers, brokers, officials and customers met the same network from different positions, and surviving sources name some of them far less often than rulers.

passages.title: Trade routes carried things and ideas
passages.text: The artisans and silk weavers seized at Chengdu in 829 show the darkest route by which techniques moved. Forced migration could enlarge a victor’s workshops while breaking families elsewhere. Describing craft “exchange” without this episode would make war look cleaner than it was and erase the people made to carry knowledge.

passages.title: Trade routes carried things and ideas
passages.text: Zhang Shengwen’s Dali scroll, dated by its colophon to about 1172 to 1175, shows an emperor making offerings amid hundreds of Buddhist figures. Its styles connect Tang and Song China with Tibetan and Southeast Asian traditions. Court artists transformed wide networks into one carefully ordered visual world.

passages.title: Trade routes carried things and ideas
passages.text: The atlas polygons reach across routes, but a route is not a border. Horses, shells, silver, pilgrims, books and armies could cross places that no ruler controlled tightly. The 800 geometry’s reach toward Luang Prabang should therefore never be defended merely by saying that Nanzhao traded toward Southeast Asia.

passages.title: Health, medicine, clean water and missing toilets
passages.text: A Dali book list from 1173 included works on medicine. That proves medical knowledge circulated among literate collectors, but the title list does not reveal the remedies inside, the training of healers or ordinary access to care. No responsible card can turn a court library into a complete public-health system.

passages.title: Health, medicine, clean water and missing toilets
passages.text: Protective Buddhist images and formulas mattered to Nanzhao and Dali patrons, and people may have sought safety through ritual. The sources reviewed here do not let us equate spiritual protection with clinical treatment or name a standard household medicine kit. Religious care and bodily treatment can overlap without being identical.

passages.title: Health, medicine, clean water and missing toilets
passages.text: Channels, embankments and flood control helped fields and settlements manage water. They do not automatically prove safe drinking water, disease prevention or equal access. Agricultural engineering can improve food security while leaving household water questions unanswered, so the evidence supports water management more strongly than sanitation claims.

passages.title: Health, medicine, clean water and missing toilets
passages.text: Wuzhishan’s halls used stone foundations and drains around courtyards. Those drains show builders directing water away from structures, probably including rain and runoff. The excavation report does not identify them as sewage channels, and a temple’s drainage cannot be generalized into a citywide sewer system.

passages.title: Health, medicine, clean water and missing toilets
passages.text: No securely identified Nanzhao or Dali toilet, latrine, cesspit or household waste system appears in the archaeological reports reviewed for this card. That is a limit of the present evidence, not proof that people had no arrangements. We can discuss documented drains; we should leave toilet design unknown.

Historical Nanzhao ended when its ruling house was overthrown in 902. Dali began in 937, survived a brief dynastic interruption, and fell to Mongol armies in 1253. Yuan rulers then reused local elites, institutions and religious-political traditions. The atlas’s 1279 cutoff belongs to its imported timeline, not to the death of a people or the fall of “Nan Chao.” Communities around Erhai continued under new governments, carrying forward farms, crafts, kinship, trade and Buddhist institutions while political names and structures changed.

sectionTitles: Power and the evidence beneath Guangzhou
Food, clothing, health and small comforts
Water engineering, exchange and the kingdom’s ending

passages.text: Nanyue was a powerful kingdom founded by Zhao Tuo around 203 BCE, ruling across parts of today’s southern China and northern Vietnam. Its capital was Panyu, now Guangzhou. The atlas’s 200 to 1 BCE interval continues long after Han conquest in 111 BCE. Its outline also misses Guangzhou, just north of the drawn boundary, so the capital’s archaeological examples below sit outside this imperfect polygon.

passages.title: Power and the evidence beneath Guangzhou
passages.text: Zhao Tuo had served the Qin regime before establishing his own kingdom after its collapse. His realm linked areas now divided between China and Vietnam. Relations with the Han court changed over time: recognition, rivalry and negotiation all mattered. Modern national borders are a poor guide to this ancient political landscape.

passages.title: Power and the evidence beneath Guangzhou
passages.text: In 1983, construction workers at Xianggang in Guangzhou uncovered stone slabs above a royal tomb. Excavators found a seven-chamber burial with a gold seal identifying its occupant as Zhao Mo, Nanyue’s second ruler. The discovery let objects speak alongside the written histories.

passages.title: Power and the evidence beneath Guangzhou
passages.text: The tomb was a major building project beneath a hill. Its red sandstone blocks came from Lianhua Mountain outside Guangzhou rather than simply from the hole being dug. Transporters, stoneworkers and builders were essential to the royal monument, even though their own names do not survive in this account.

passages.title: Power and the evidence beneath Guangzhou
passages.text: Royal luxury had a grim human cost. Fifteen other people were buried as sacrificial victims in the king’s tomb. Their presence is evidence of coercion within this court, not a reason to imagine that every Nanyue family buried its dead in the same way.

passages.title: Food, clothing, health and small comforts
passages.text: One bronze roasting stove from the king’s tomb had four little wheels and could be pushed. Its rectangular body was about 61 centimetres long, with slightly raised corners. A movable cooking station was already a practical idea more than two thousand years ago: royal catering had wheels.

passages.title: Food, clothing, health and small comforts
passages.text: Rice, millet and fruit seeds recovered at the palace help reconstruct its food supply. These tiny plant remains complement the impressive serving vessels in the royal tomb. A menu written only from gold and jade would miss the grains and fruit that people actually needed to grow.

passages.title: Food, clothing, health and small comforts
passages.text: A wooden slip excavated at the palace in 2004 identifies “jujube tree No. 94”. This wonderfully ordinary label brings an orchard into the story of a royal court. Even fruit trees could acquire paperwork; keeping track of productive plants was part of managing the palace.

passages.title: Food, clothing, health and small comforts
passages.text: Two small bronze printing plates were found with evidence of matching patterns on silk from the tomb’s western side chamber. Researchers interpret the smaller plate as a guide for alignment and the larger as the main design. Patterned cloth required careful positioning as well as attractive shapes.

passages.title: Food, clothing, health and small comforts
passages.text: Bronze and iron pounding tools accompanied colored mineral substances interpreted as medicines in Zhao Mo’s tomb. The museum connects them with a royal search for longevity. They record attempts to preserve health and life; their burial with the king does not establish that the preparations worked.

passages.title: Food, clothing, health and small comforts
passages.text: The tomb also contained pouring vessels, basins and other water containers. Museum researchers connect these with elite hand-washing rituals shared with the Han court. Keeping hands clean could be part of formal etiquette, with specialized equipment making an everyday action into a ceremony.

passages.title: Food, clothing, health and small comforts
passages.text: A bronze incense burner combined four separate compartments beneath one lid, pierced with diamond-shaped openings. Traces of silk wrapping remained on it. The object shows how carefully designed furnishings could bring scent as well as visual decoration into elite surroundings.

passages.title: Craftspeople, households and written records
passages.text: The king’s jade burial suit contained 2,291 plaques, joined or attached using silk and cloth. Its hand and foot coverings used smooth pieces pierced for thread; much of the torso reused pieces cut from older jade or offcuts. Even a spectacular royal burial involved sorting materials and resourceful assembly.

passages.title: Craftspeople, households and written records
passages.text: Another gold seal names the Lady of the Right, a court title. Its handle is a small turtle with space underneath for a cord. Such an object preserves a woman’s formal rank within the royal household, although it tells us far less about her thoughts, relationships or daily responsibilities.

passages.title: Craftspeople, households and written records
passages.text: Eight bronze goudiao instruments from the tomb carry numbered inscriptions identifying manufacture by the Music Office in Emperor Wen’s ninth year, dated by the museum to 129 BCE. Their graded sizes and numbers connect music with organized workshops and court administration, as well as with performance.

passages.title: Craftspeople, households and written records
passages.text: More than 120 iron tools in the royal tomb relate to farming, fishing and handicrafts. Their presence draws attention to the productive work behind courtly wealth. The glittering objects survived beside reminders of people cultivating land, catching food and making things.

passages.title: Craftspeople, households and written records
passages.text: Wooden documents recovered from a palace well record official titles, administration, fruit cultivation and hide processing. They show literate workers organizing practical activities, alongside objects associated with ink and writing. This evidence establishes recordkeeping; it does not reveal how many children attended school.

passages.title: Craftspeople, households and written records
passages.text: Here is a royal writing sample: 文帝行玺, “Administrative Seal of Emperor Wen”. These are the museum’s modern Chinese character forms for the four characters cut in small seal script on Zhao Mo’s gold seal. The late-second-century BCE object was found on his chest; its dragon handle and imperial wording make authority visible.

passages.title: Water engineering, exchange and the kingdom’s ending
passages.text: The royal garden used a large stone-lined pond and an artificial stone brook. Their excavation revealed designed scenery rather than an untouched stream. At another Guangzhou site, a wooden watergate formed part of the city’s flood-control system: managing water served both pleasure and protection.

passages.title: Water engineering, exchange and the kingdom’s ending
passages.text: A silver box from the royal tomb has raised lobes hammered into its body, gilding and an added gilt-bronze foot. The museum relates its technique to West Asian metalworking. It is evidence for connections across long distances, while its exact workshop and journey remain less certain.

passages.title: Water engineering, exchange and the kingdom’s ending
passages.text: Han forces conquered Nanyue in 111 BCE, ending its ruling dynasty. In northern Vietnam, cultural traditions continued under the new imperial order: the national history museum points to bronze drums, pottery and bells with Dong Son features. Political defeat did not make the region’s communities vanish.

Han conquest in 111 BCE ended the Nanyue kingdom. The atlas continues its label to 1 BCE, which should be read as a mapping overhang rather than continued royal independence. Communities and local traditions endured within a changed political order.

sectionTitles: Builders, potters and a possible royal shrine
Later ninth-century glimpses of family and learning

passages.text: Nanzhao was a powerful kingdom centered on the Erhai Lake region of Yunnan, with capitals near present-day Dali. It united neighboring polities in the eighth century and continued into the early tenth. This map record covers only 700 to 800, and its imported outline is seriously misplaced: it lies mainly farther south and omits the Erhai capital region. It should not be read as a reliable boundary of Nanzhao.

passages.title: A kingdom between powerful neighbors
passages.text: Nanzhao developed from the Mengshe polity south of Erhai. Piluoge united neighboring rulers with Tang support, but his successors did not remain obedient clients. Geluofeng aligned with Tibet and defeated Tang armies; Yimouxun later broke with Tibet. These changing relationships helped a regional kingdom bargain with two much larger powers.

passages.title: A kingdom between powerful neighbors
passages.text: King Geluofeng erected the Dehua Stele in 766 to explain the break with the Tang court and the relationship with Tibet. It presents the king’s side of the dispute. Later weathering erased much of its lettering, but earlier written copies preserve more of the text. Reading the monument today therefore involves both stone and the history of copying it.

passages.title: A kingdom between powerful neighbors
passages.text: Later, in 829, Nanzhao forces raided Chengdu and carried off prisoners, including artisans and silk weavers. Skills could travel through violent displacement as well as peaceful exchange. The event helps explain why an account of fine cloth or craft techniques must also ask about the people compelled to leave their homes.

passages.title: Water, fields and royal promises
passages.text: The 766 Dehua inscription praises works that controlled flooding and opened land for rice and millet. It also describes draining reservoirs and creating orchards in wet ground. This is royal praise, rather than an excavated engineering plan, but it shows what the court considered a ruler’s achievement: making water support crops instead of ruining them.

passages.title: Water, fields and royal promises
passages.text: The same inscription boasts of households with mulberry plots and government stores sufficient for nine years. Mulberries evoke silk production, while the stores advertise security against shortages. Those sweeping claims cannot be treated as a survey proving every family was prosperous. They tell us what kinds of abundance the king wanted readers to associate with his reign.

passages.title: Water, fields and royal promises
passages.text: “厄塞流潦” means “blocking the floodwaters.” These Chinese characters come from the transmitted text of the 766 Dehua inscription, quoted in a modern scholarly edition. They provide a small sample of the court’s written Chinese, rather than a transcription of an everyday spoken language. Here royal writing celebrates a practical concern that every farming family would understand.

passages.title: Builders, potters and a possible royal shrine
passages.text: At Wuzhishan near the early capital Taihe, excavators found courtyard buildings with main halls, side corridors and entrance porches. Nanzhao-period Buddhist images and miniature pagodas helped identify the remains as a temple area. Both the buildings and the objects found inside mattered to understanding its purpose.

passages.title: Builders, potters and a possible royal shrine
passages.text: Wuzhishan’s eastern kilns contained firing supports, spacers, molds and imperfect glazed pottery. These workshop leftovers show production near the temples. Finished objects tell us what people wanted to make; rejects preserve evidence of work that went wrong. An impressive religious complex also had a practical manufacturing side.

passages.title: Builders, potters and a possible royal shrine
passages.text: Wuzhishan builders used stone foundations and provided courtyard drainage. One hall occupied two levels, with adjoining corridors and porches. The remains show attention to moving people and water through the site. These are architectural drains; the excavation account does not establish toilets or household sewers.

passages.title: Builders, potters and a possible royal shrine
passages.text: A tile from Wuzhishan’s Building One carries the characters “官家舍利,” interpreted as referring to royal relics. Excavation director Zhu Zhonghua suggested that the building may have enshrined relics connected with the ruling family. Miniature pagodas and pottery vessels strengthen the religious interpretation, but the royal identification remains a proposal, not a named royal burial discovered intact.

passages.title: Later ninth-century glimpses of family and learning
passages.text: The ninth-century writer Fan Chuo describes a major gathering beginning on the first day of the eleventh lunar month. People brewed drink, prepared cattle and sheep, and entertained relatives and neighbors. His account gives shared meals and visits a place in Nanzhao’s social life. The date belongs to a lunar calendar, not automatically to November on ours.

passages.title: Later ninth-century glimpses of family and learning
passages.text: Fan Chuo describes noblewomen wearing silk skirts and jackets, with a square of brocade draped above them. Pearls, gold, shells and amber decorated hair or ears. He also mentions female servants wearing skirts and felt coverings. The contrast is a useful glimpse of household status, though it comes from a Tang outsider’s description of selected people.

passages.title: Later ninth-century glimpses of family and learning
passages.text: He also describes young men making evening music with gourd instruments or even leaves, using the sounds in courtship. A leaf could become a musical instrument without a trip to a shop. This is a reported social custom from the ninth-century text; it does not prove that every community in the kingdom followed the same rules.

passages.title: Later ninth-century glimpses of family and learning
passages.text: Elite young men from Nanzhao studied literacy and numeracy in Chengdu. Historian Shao-yun Yang distinguishes them from Silla students who went to Chang’an and sat Tang examinations. Learning across the border could help Nanzhao’s own government and ambitions. Studying another court’s methods did not require accepting that court’s right to rule at home.

passages.title: Later ninth-century glimpses of family and learning
passages.text: The Illustrated History of Nanzhao, composed in 899, tells a Buddhist foundation story in which Acuoye Guanyin introduces the religion and gives the earliest kings a sacred mandate. It is evidence of how the later court imagined and justified its past. Its divine encounters should be read as religious storytelling, not as independently verified events in the first kings’ lives.

Nanzhao’s ruling house was overthrown by Zheng Maisi around 902 to 903, long after the map’s 800 cutoff. Several short-lived regimes followed before Duan Siping founded the Dali kingdom in 937. Political rule changed while settlements, farming and Buddhist traditions continued; Nanzhao’s ending was not the disappearance of the region’s people.
