sectionTitles: A palace well and a busy city
A written voice and its stories

passages.text: The Naples entry samples the southern mainland kingdom during Spanish viceregal rule. It is more than the city of Naples, and it should not be silently merged with Sicily. Spanish government lasted from 1503 to 1707, beyond the map’s 1530 to 1700 interval. Palace archaeology, banking records and music schools offer unusually concrete windows into life in its capital.

passages.title: A palace well and a busy city
passages.text: The Royal Palace begun in 1600 was designed by Domenico Fontana as a residence for the Spanish viceroys. A royal building did not mean the Spanish king personally lived there year-round: the viceroy governed on his behalf.

passages.title: A palace well and a busy city
passages.text: Excavations in 1999 to 2000 recovered around 5,000 objects and ceramic fragments from a well at the older palace. The well probably first supplied water and later received rubbish. Broken things can be wonderfully informative: an archaeologist’s useful evidence may once have been somebody else’s unwanted mess.

passages.title: A palace well and a busy city
passages.text: The palace-well finds include pottery from Naples and other Italian production centers, as well as Spanish wares from places such as Manises and Valencia. They reveal connections through objects used or discarded at this particular site. A palace deposit is not a random sample of every Neapolitan kitchen.

passages.title: A palace well and a busy city
passages.text: A blue-and-white Chinese porcelain bowl from the late sixteenth century appeared among the well’s finds. It shows that an object could reach Naples through long-distance exchange. One bowl does not establish who transported it, who ate from it or whether a Chinese community lived beside the palace.

passages.title: A palace well and a busy city
passages.text: Naples’ water administration left records of expenditure on the Carmignano aqueduct in 1629 and later water concessions. These documents show that moving and allocating water required money and rules. They cannot, by themselves, tell us what kind of toilet or wash space an individual family possessed.

passages.title: Credit, children and music
passages.text: The Monte della Pietà began in 1539 to make interest-free loans against pledged possessions for people in need. It later accepted deposits and received royal recognition as a bank in 1584. Charity and finance developed together rather than occupying entirely separate worlds.

passages.title: Credit, children and music
passages.text: Household belongings could become temporary security for a loan. The Pietà accepted linen, wool and silk as well as precious objects. The bank archive distinguishes limited interest-free lending from other loans that charged interest: “charitable bank” did not mean that every transaction was free.

passages.title: Credit, children and music
passages.text: The Annunziata bank, established in 1587, helped support an orphanage, hospital and girls’ school. Another bank founded in 1589 was connected with the Incurabili hospital. Financial records therefore preserve practical links between savings, credit and the care of vulnerable people.

passages.title: Credit, children and music
passages.text: The early Neapolitan conservatories cared for poor or abandoned children. Music formed part of their religious activities in the sixteenth century. The name later became strongly associated with professional musical training, but these institutions began with a wider charitable purpose.

passages.title: Credit, children and music
passages.text: During the seventeenth century, conservatory musicians increasingly performed for paying patrons, and musical training attracted outside pupils. Performance could support an institution as well as teach a trade. This does not mean all Neapolitan children learned music or that every child in care became a celebrated composer.

passages.title: A written voice and its stories
passages.text: Giambattista Basile’s Lo cunto de li cunti appeared after his death in installments from 1634 to 1636. Written in Neapolitan, its fifty tales reshaped storytelling traditions into elaborate literature. Stories can preserve language and imaginative worlds without being literal reports of daily events.

passages.title: A written voice and its stories
passages.text: The title “Lo Cunto de li Cunti” means “The Tale of Tales.” This short Neapolitan sample uses Latin letters and is attested in the original title transcribed in a later scholarly edition. Its repeated word cunto makes the title sound like an invitation to settle in for another story.

passages.title: A written voice and its stories
passages.text: Basile’s collection also includes verse interludes voiced by figures such as cooks, servants and household officials. Their presence brings work and social hierarchy into the literary performance. These are crafted voices, however, not interviews with real palace employees or a census of ordinary family life.

Spanish viceregal rule ended in 1707, rather than at the atlas’s 1700 cutoff. The Kingdom of Naples and its population continued under subsequent rulers. This entry’s ending therefore describes a change of government, not the destruction of Naples or the disappearance of its culture.

passages.text: The Nara period gave Japan its first permanent capital, Heijo-kyo, laid out on the grid of the Tang capital Chang'an. The court ran the country under the ritsuryo codes, made Buddhism a state religion and compiled its first histories and poetry.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Manyoshu, an anthology of 4,516 poems by emperors, courtiers and frontier guards, was compiled; its latest dated poem is from 759.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Kojiki, and in 720 the Nihon Shoki, recorded the myths and early history of the imperial line.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The Great Buddha of Todaiji, a bronze figure about 15 meters high, was dedicated in a ceremony attended by monks from India and China.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Emperor Shomu ordered a state temple and nunnery in every province.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The ritsuryo codes, the Taiho of 701 and the Yoro of 718, organized government, taxes and land on Tang models.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Confucian learning was taught at the state academy to train officials.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Chinese characters were used for all government records, and census and tax registers were kept on paper.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Trunk roads with post stations linked the capital to the provinces.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara were listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Manyoshu remains the foundation of Japanese poetry.
Emperor Kanmu moved the capital to Heian-kyo, today's Kyoto, in 794, the start of the Heian period.

sectionTitles: A homeland visible in material evidence

passages.text: The Narragansett are a continuing Native nation of the Rhode Island region, with coastal settlements, inland resources and important relationships with neighboring peoples. Their leaders were major participants in seventeenth-century New England politics. The imported 1492 to 1500 outline is a broad ancestral-area sketch, not a modern reservation boundary or the lifetime of the nation.

passages.title: A homeland visible in material evidence
passages.text: Salt Pond, archaeological site RI 110 at the head of Point Judith Pond, preserves a large coastal village dated by the state’s account to about 1100 to 1300 CE. Archaeologists found traces of houses, other structures, cooking places and food storage. These are clues to a working community, not simply isolated valuable objects.

passages.title: A homeland visible in material evidence
passages.text: Plant specialists found maize in five archaeological features at Salt Pond. Their 2008 study combines these remains with associated dating evidence to establish cultivation before European settlement. Charred food that survived underground can answer questions that a written visitor’s description never addressed.

passages.title: A homeland visible in material evidence
passages.text: A Narragansett basket dated to around 1675 survives in the Rhode Island Historical Society’s collection as 1842.2.1. Basswood splints and corn husk are combined with red wool. A later note describes a hurried gift, but the museum calls most of that story myth. The basket itself preserves evidence of careful weaving.

passages.title: A homeland visible in material evidence
passages.text: In 2013, Rhode Island’s transportation department purchased approximately 52 acres containing the Salt Pond site after a dispute over proposed housing. The Narragansett Tribal Historic Preservation Office participated in its protection. Archaeological knowledge here depended on decisions about roads, development and the survival of a culturally important place.

passages.title: Food, seasons and relationships
passages.text: Lorén Spears describes winter villages sheltered by inland woods and located near fresh water. Summer brought movement toward bays and salt ponds. Seasonal living joined access to food, building materials and protected places, rather than keeping every household in one location year-round.

passages.title: Food, seasons and relationships
passages.text: Fishing weirs guided fish into places where people could catch them. Women dried or smoked catches for later meals, while older children helped tend gardens. Seaweed and fish fertilized crops. Family food supplies depended on coordinated work on land and water.

passages.title: Food, seasons and relationships
passages.text: In 1636, Canonicus and Miantanomi permitted Roger Williams to settle at Providence. Spears explains the agreement as permission to use land under Narragansett authority. Colonists’ treatment of such agreements as outright purchases helped turn diplomatic arrangements into disputes over sovereignty.

passages.title: Food, seasons and relationships
passages.text: The December 1675 Great Swamp attack killed Narragansett civilians as well as fighters during the regional war. Colonists subsequently enslaved survivors, including people sent to the Caribbean. Remaining Narragansett joined with Niantic relatives and allies, rebuilding community amid devastating losses.

passages.title: Writing, teaching and community life
passages.text: The Narragansett Dawn, edited by Princess Redwing and Ernest Hazard in 1935 and 1936, carried language lessons, cultural and political discussion, and news of births and deaths. Copies preserved by the University of Rhode Island show a community describing itself in print, including the everyday milestones that larger histories can overlook.

passages.title: Writing, teaching and community life
passages.text: An attested modern written greeting is “Asco wequassinummis, neetompooag!” Lorén Spears translates it as “Hello my friends” at the start of her 2017 Tomaquag Museum account. This is a named Narragansett writer’s published language sample, rather than a phrase reconstructed for the map’s fifteenth-century setting.

passages.title: Writing, teaching and community life
passages.text: Spears’s 2017 account of Nikommo describes a gathering with a feast, social activities and gifts for people in need. Clothing, toys and handmade items could circulate through the giveaway. The occasion connected celebration with looking after other households: sharing was part of the event itself.

passages.title: Writing, teaching and community life
passages.text: A 2018 Tomaquag Museum article shows Skyla Jennings, identified as Narragansett, learning basket making in an arts-and-wellness class. Another photograph shows Lorén Spears teaching corn-husk doll making. These named examples document learning through hands and materials alongside classroom education in a modern community.

passages.title: Land loss and continuing government
passages.text: An 1882 auction broadside documents the sale of reservation land during Rhode Island’s attempt to dissolve Narragansett political status. Treating Native people as isolated individuals could make collectively held land easier to sell. The document is evidence of a state policy, not proof that the nation consented to disappear.

passages.title: Land loss and continuing government
passages.text: Narragansett people continued monthly meetings and their annual August gathering after the state’s attempted detribalization. They retained recognized leaders and raised money for land claims. These ordinary acts of meeting, contributing and choosing representatives helped sustain institutions when outsiders claimed the community had ended.

passages.title: Land loss and continuing government
passages.text: A land-claim settlement in 1978 restored approximately 1,800 acres, and federal acknowledgment followed in 1983. The tribal history also records a longhouse built in the early 1940s as a meeting place. A continuing nation needed spaces for practical government as well as ceremonies.

Narragansett sovereignty and landholding suffered severe losses through colonial war and later state policies, but the people and their institutions continued. The map’s 1500 endpoint is only an imported coverage cutoff; federal acknowledgment in 1983 recognized an enduring community.

sectionTitles: A spa town, a train and traveling water
A crowd demanded a different government

passages.text: The Duchy of Nassau was a small German state between the Rhine, Main, Lahn and Dill, existing from 1806 to 1866. Its rulers joined older territories into a new administration, while schools, spas and the mineral-water trade changed local life. This imported record runs from 1815 to 1878, but its later years are misleading: Nassau had lost independence to Prussia in 1866.

passages.title: Joining territories and changing rules
passages.text: Nassau-Usingen and Nassau-Weilburg joined to form the duchy in 1806. Their agreement of 5 September called for bringing their troops together under common administration. Even a small new state had practical problems to solve: soldiers and officials who had served different rulers now needed to work together.

passages.title: Joining territories and changing rules
passages.text: The government reorganized Nassau into twenty-eight administrative districts in 1816, each headed by an appointed official. Earlier reforms had abolished serfdom in 1808 and compulsory labor obligations in 1812. These changes altered what rulers and landlords could demand from inhabitants, while leaving strong authority in the state’s hands.

passages.title: Joining territories and changing rules
passages.text: Writing sample: the 1814 constitutional edict declares, “Wir haben keine Abgaben von Unsern Unterthanen erhoben, außer für Bedürfnisse des Staats,” meaning “We have levied no taxes on our subjects except for the needs of the state.” This German passage survives in an 1817 printed collection. It is the rulers’ account of their conduct, rather than proof that subjects agreed with every tax.

passages.title: Learning, farming and family care
passages.text: The school reform of 1817 required boys and girls to attend elementary school from six to fourteen, without distinctions of social rank or religion. It aimed to bring children into shared schools and applied throughout the year. The curriculum included language, numbers, measuring, religion and singing: more than memorizing a few prayers.

passages.title: Learning, farming and family care
passages.text: Teacher preparation mattered too. The reform drew on reports commissioned from all twenty-eight districts in 1809 and on the educational methods of Pestalozzi. Officials also regulated classrooms, furniture, teaching materials, salaries and inspection. A new school policy required desks and trained adults as well as a grand announcement.

passages.title: Learning, farming and family care
passages.text: An agricultural institute opened in Idstein in 1818 and later moved to Hof Geisberg near Wiesbaden. There, winter teaching allowed young farmers to study while remaining available for farm work during the growing season. The school also offered advice and helped develop new fruit-tree varieties. Education had to fit around crops that would not wait.

passages.title: Learning, farming and family care
passages.text: Nassau organized a network of doctors employed as public officials, aiming to make medical care available to poorer inhabitants as well as wealthy patients. Municipalities paid two thirds of their salaries. The reform connected local tax money with an everyday need: someone trained to help when a household faced illness.

passages.title: Learning, farming and family care
passages.text: An orphan fund established under the 1816 poor-relief edict supported the care and education of children who had lost their parents. A widows’ and orphans’ fund followed in 1820. These institutions show how family crises became a concern of public administration, although they were not the same as today’s universal welfare arrangements.

passages.title: A spa town, a train and traveling water
passages.text: Wiesbaden gained a Kursaal in 1810 as a place for social gatherings. Licensed gambling found a permanent home there that May. The spa town offered visitors sociability and entertainment alongside treatment; not every activity promising excitement was likely to improve a visitor’s wallet.

passages.title: A spa town, a train and traveling water
passages.text: A palace built between 1813 and 1820 for the hereditary prince took on a different role: it housed the museum, state library and government offices. Rooms intended for a royal household became places for collections, books and administrative work. Its later use preserves a small story of how public institutions grew.

passages.title: A spa town, a train and traveling water
passages.text: The first scheduled train left Wiesbaden for Kastel on 10 March 1840; the connection to Frankfurt opened on 13 April. Railways added a new way to reach the spa town and neighboring commercial centers. Trips that once depended on roads, horses or boats could now include a railway timetable.

passages.title: A spa town, a train and traveling water
passages.text: Niederselters shipped mineral water in pottery jugs across Europe. A jug recovered from a wreck in the Bay of Gdańsk was dated around 1820. Its stamp carries Selters and HN, short for Herzogtum Nassau, or Duchy of Nassau. A container lost with a ship became evidence of long-distance trade.

passages.title: A spa town, a train and traveling water
passages.text: The municipal account reports one to two million jugs filled annually between 1806 and 1830. Apothecaries, doctors, merchants and innkeepers sold the water, which customers valued as a supposed remedy. Filling and transporting all those vessels joined a local spring to potters, traders and consumers far beyond Nassau.

passages.title: A crowd demanded a different government
passages.text: In March 1848, reformers circulated nine demands through leaflets and word of mouth. On 4 March, Duke Adolph accepted them before a large crowd in Wiesbaden. Promises included press freedom and freedom of association and religion. News could travel on paper, but conversation helped carry it across the countryside.

Nassau sided with Austria in the war of 1866. After Austria’s defeat, Prussia annexed the duchy, ending its independence. The territory’s inhabitants and local communities continued under a different government; the map’s continuation to 1878 must not be read as another twelve years of ducal rule.

passages.text: Natal was a British colony on southern Africa’s Indian Ocean coast, with African communities, settler farms and towns, and Indian workers and traders. Plantation labour, schools and printing presses all shaped its history. It was distinct from the neighboring Zulu kingdom.

passages.title: Colony, migration and work
passages.text: The colony’s dates begin before this map record. Britain annexed Natal in 1843 and initially administered it from the Cape; Natal became a separate colony in 1856. The imported 1878 starting point is a surviving map snapshot, not the founding year.

passages.title: Colony, migration and work
passages.text: Natal was a British colony while the Zulu kingdom remained a separate African state. Britain’s 1878 ultimatum demanded changes that would destroy Zulu independence, and invasion followed in 1879. Their proximity on a map must not erase the distinction between colony and kingdom.

passages.title: Colony, migration and work
passages.text: The Truro arrived in November 1860 with Indian indentured workers. Their contracts supplied labour to colonial employers, especially plantations. Later Indian traders also came independently, so “Indian migrant” did not describe one occupation or one route into Natal.

passages.title: Colony, migration and work
passages.text: Historian Jo Beall documents women plucking tender tea leaves on Natal estates. Men and children also worked in estate production, with tasks divided by age and gender. Tea in a cup concealed a demanding sequence of picking, carrying and processing.

passages.title: Colony, migration and work
passages.text: Women’s work continued after paid estate tasks. Household duties and small garden plots helped feed children and adults. Beall’s research places this less visible labour beside employers’ records, showing why a wage or contract alone cannot describe a family’s working day.

passages.title: Colony, migration and work
passages.text: In 1861 Bauboo Naidoo opened a shop in Durban’s Field Street selling condiments and foods missing from workers’ rations. The tiny detail matters: migration carried tastes and cooking knowledge, and people sought familiar ingredients rather than simply accepting an employer’s menu.

passages.title: Schools, newspapers and gardens
passages.text: John and Nokutela Dube founded Ohlange in 1901 after gaining experience in the United States. The school connected education with African institution-building. Remembering both founders keeps Nokutela’s contribution visible beside the much more frequently named John Dube.

passages.title: Schools, newspapers and gardens
passages.text: A short isiZulu writing sample is “Ilanga lase Natal”, meaning “The Natal Sun”. The newspaper began under John Dube at Ohlange in 1903. A newspaper title could announce a public voice in a reader’s own language before they had read a single article.

passages.title: Schools, newspapers and gardens
passages.text: The surviving Ilanga collection allows readers to study an African newspaper as a sequence of issues, rather than only a famous editor’s biography. Its establishment at Ohlange links a school to the work of printing and distributing information.

passages.title: Schools, newspapers and gardens
passages.text: At Phoenix, a printing press became part of a communal settlement. Gandhi bought the land in 1904 and moved the press for Indian Opinion there from Durban. Producing a newspaper involved physical work as well as ideas: the entire press had to change address.

passages.title: Schools, newspapers and gardens
passages.text: Phoenix residents cultivated food gardens and experimented with communal self-sufficiency. The settlement also provided meals, accommodation and education for families of people involved in nonviolent protest campaigns. Political activity depended on ordinary tasks such as feeding children and keeping a place to sleep.

passages.title: Schools, newspapers and gardens
passages.text: Recruitment of Indian indentured labour for Natal ended in 1911 after decades of mistreatment and controversy. The workers and their descendants did not disappear when recruitment stopped; Indian South African communities continued building families, businesses, associations and public lives.

Natal joined the Union of South Africa on 31 May 1910 and became a province. Its communities continued through this change of government. The map record extends to 1914, but that endpoint is not the colony’s constitutional ending.

passages.text: Natchez communities farmed the lower Mississippi landscape and gathered at ceremonial mound centres. By the late seventeenth century, their settlement districts retained substantial autonomy. The Great Sun’s prominence did not make every local chief his obedient provincial governor.

passages.title: Farms, food and useful objects
passages.text: Natchez farmers grew maize, beans and squash while also hunting, fishing and gathering wild foods. Many families lived on dispersed farms and travelled to mound centres for gatherings, rather than residing permanently beside the ceremonial buildings.

passages.title: Farms, food and useful objects
passages.text: Grand Village excavations recovered charred maize, hickory nuts and black walnut shells. Common beans came from a context associated with French trench excavation. The remains support a varied food history, but mixed deposits cannot identify every meal’s date or maker.

passages.title: Farms, food and useful objects
passages.text: A clay pipe from Grand Village has incised chevrons around its bowl and a zigzag beneath it. Other pipe fragments retain interior charring. These small finds preserve both deliberate surface decoration and traces of use.

passages.title: Farms, food and useful objects
passages.text: Neitzel interpreted a carefully modelled clay fragment as an imitation of a European brass bell. Its incisions and suspension hole suggest a maker adapting an introduced form in another material. The surviving fragment does not prove how the complete object sounded.

passages.title: Collective building and social life
passages.text: Emerald Mound carries secondary mounds on a vast raised platform. Unlike centres arranged around a ground-level plaza, its ceremonial space occupied the platform’s summit. The surviving structure shows how earthmoving could create an entire elevated setting for public activity.

passages.title: Collective building and social life
passages.text: The monument required repeated movement and placement of soil. The National Park Service illustrates a possible basket-carrying process, but exact crew sizes and working schedules remain unknown. Its scale demonstrates collective achievement without supplying a documented construction diary.

passages.title: Collective building and social life
passages.text: Barnett describes matrilineal moieties, or paired social divisions, providing marriage partners and reciprocal services. Their competition included stickball. Such relationships linked kinship, obligations and recreation; European comparisons with their own class systems could obscure how they worked.

passages.title: Exchange and historical evidence
passages.text: In the early eighteenth century, Natchez people sought firearms, metal cooking pots and woollen cloth from French settlers. Havard’s research also describes settlers depending on Native hunting and healing knowledge. These relationships involved mutual exchange before open warfare devastated them.

passages.title: Exchange and historical evidence
passages.text: Natchez is generally classified as a language isolate: no close linguistic relatives are established. The Sam Noble Museum’s catalogue names Nancy Raven, Sam Watt and Peggy Leaf among the people whose knowledge contributed to Mary Haas’s field notebooks.

passages.title: Displacement and continuing knowledge
passages.text: Refuge among Creek and Cherokee communities did not end displacement. Many Natchez descendants later experienced forced removal to present-day Oklahoma. These nineteenth-century events followed the earlier French war and should not be compressed into one migration.

passages.title: Displacement and continuing knowledge
passages.text: The Natchez Nation compiled an English-to-Natchez wordlist, documented by UBC researchers in 2023. It drew on speakers and other resources and invited contributions for new terms. Language work makes continuity visible beyond accounts that end with the eighteenth-century war.

French military retaliation in the 1730s forced Natchez people from their homeland; some captives were enslaved in the Caribbean. Survivors joined other Native communities, and descendants continued their history through later removals. The destruction of those settlements was not the extinction of the people.

sectionTitles: Family introductions, learning and a living language

passages.text: The Navajo, or Diné, are a living Indigenous people whose homeland spans the American Southwest. Navajo Nation sources call it Diné Bikéyah. This shared card covers the map’s Navajo, Navaho and Diné Bikéyah labels. Their different outlines and 1492 to 1650 date windows are imported coverage, not reliable borders or the beginning and ending of a single state.

passages.title: Homes, sheep and skilled hands
passages.text: In northwestern New Mexico, Navajo builders made small masonry pueblitos during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Many stood on boulders or outcrops with wide views. They provided shelter and cooking space as well as refuge during conflict, so a defensible position also had to work as a home.

passages.title: Homes, sheep and skilled hands
passages.text: Pueblito remains include roofs, hooded fireplaces, nearby hogan foundations and small openings used to check a doorway. A family could cook, keep out weather and watch an entrance in the same compact building. These practical architectural details survive alongside the story of warfare.

passages.title: Homes, sheep and skilled hands
passages.text: Diné weavers adopted wool from introduced churra sheep and incorporated it into their textile traditions. The upright loom let makers build a cloth through the patient crossing of threads. Behind a finished blanket stood an entire chain of work, beginning with keeping the animals alive.

passages.title: Homes, sheep and skilled hands
passages.text: At Hubbell Trading Post, established in Ganado in 1878, Navajo customers exchanged blankets, wool, sheep and pelts for goods such as flour, coffee, tools and cloth. The post also supplied news and jobs. A shopping trip could therefore carry both household supplies and neighborhood information home.

passages.title: Homes, sheep and skilled hands
passages.text: The predominantly red geometric style called Ganado Red became associated with the trading post. Hubbell promoted particular designs for outside buyers, while Navajo weavers supplied the artistry and labor. Rugs linked skilled household production to a market whose tastes could influence what makers were asked to weave.

passages.title: Homes, sheep and skilled hands
passages.text: A 2016 Hubbell workshop offered hands-on dyeing, spinning and weaving, together with learning about Churro sheep. The program had begun in 2000 to share fiber skills and animal husbandry. Before anyone could weave a beautiful design, the wool still had to become usable yarn.

passages.title: Removal, return and political rebuilding
passages.text: In 1864, United States forces drove Navajo people from their homeland to Bosque Redondo in eastern New Mexico. In a 2018 anniversary message, Navajo leadership remembered four years of imprisonment and suffering there. The Long Walk was forced displacement, not a voluntary migration to find better farmland.

passages.title: Removal, return and political rebuilding
passages.text: The treaty concluded at Fort Sumner on June 1, 1868 allowed a return home. Its text also promised the purchase of 15,000 sheep and goats and support for the journey. Reading the document makes rebuilding tangible: families needed animals, food and transport as well as permission to leave.

passages.title: Removal, return and political rebuilding
passages.text: The first modern Navajo council was created in 1923, and reforms in 1989 reorganized national government through separated branches. These are changes in the institutions of a continuing people. They should not be mistaken for the invention of Navajo community life or its first traditions of leadership.

passages.title: Removal, return and political rebuilding
passages.text: The first group of 29 Navajo Marine recruits arrived for training in May 1942. They helped develop a military code with an initial vocabulary of 211 terms and a system for spelling English letters. The achievement combined language expertise, memorization and radio training; it was more than ordinary conversation overheard on a battlefield.

passages.title: Family introductions, learning and a living language
passages.text: Navajo scholar Shelly C. Lowe explains that her clan comes through her mother and passes to her children. Introducing clan relationships and home community helps people place one another within a network of relatives. An introduction can be a miniature family map rather than just a name.

passages.title: Family introductions, learning and a living language
passages.text: Remembering school in Ganado, Lowe describes designing rugs on craft paper, beadwork and other cultural arts in class. She also heard Navajo from school cooks and aides as well as relatives. Language and skills traveled through ordinary encounters, from the classroom to the people preparing lunch.

passages.title: Family introductions, learning and a living language
passages.text: Written language sample: yá’át’ééh, translated by Lowe as “It is good,” is a Navajo greeting printed in her 2022 interview. This is an attested modern spelling of a living language. It is not presented as an inscription surviving from the map’s sixteenth-century window.

The Diné endured forced removal and returned after the 1868 treaty. Their nation, families and language continue, with government institutions changing over time. None of the imported map endpoints should be read as the extinction of the Navajo people.

sectionTitles: A court with gardens and practical government
Travelers, friends and two languages on one sheet

passages.text: The kingdom of Pamplona, later called Navarre, linked communities on both sides of the Pyrenees. Royal government, pilgrimage routes and towns left a rich written record. Its atlas interval 1000 to 1530 spans both independent monarchy and the conquest beginning in 1512; the single outline cannot represent every later division between Upper and Lower Navarre.

passages.title: A court with gardens and practical government
passages.text: Charles III and Queen Eleanor transformed Olite’s palace during his 1387 to 1425 reign. Its irregular towers, rooms and gardens grew into a complex royal residence. This was exceptional courtly luxury, not a model of the typical Navarrese family home.

passages.title: A court with gardens and practical government
passages.text: The municipality names Martín Périz of Estella as a master of masonry and Lope “el Barbicano,” a Muslim craftsman from Tudela, for carpentry. Named workers make the palace more than an anonymous royal achievement; different skills and communities helped create it.

passages.title: A court with gardens and practical government
passages.text: Water from the Cidacos was raised with a bucket mechanism to the reservoir tower and distributed through lead pipes to gardens and fountains. The royal greenery depended on engineering and maintenance, not a naturally self-watering castle.

passages.title: A court with gardens and practical government
passages.text: Olite’s court kept a menagerie including lions, a camel and an ostrich, as well as birds and hunting animals. These creatures advertised wealth and connections. Their presence does not tell us how comfortably the animals lived.

passages.title: A court with gardens and practical government
passages.text: The Fuero General was compiled in the thirteenth century in Navarro-Aragonese. No author is securely identified, and it gained authority gradually through judicial use. A legal tradition could develop through repeated copying and practice rather than one dramatic founding decree.

passages.title: A court with gardens and practical government
passages.text: Codex A1, a fourteenth-century copy of the Fuero, uses black and red ink and includes Philip III’s 1330 amendment. This particular book makes change visible: law was revised, not simply frozen forever in a medieval manuscript.

passages.title: Travelers, friends and two languages on one sheet
passages.text: At Roncesvalles, the bishop of Pamplona organized a brotherhood of clergy and laypeople to care for pilgrims in 1127. The institution expanded during the 1130s. Hospitality at a mountain crossing meant dealing with travelers’ practical needs, not only maintaining a church.

passages.title: Travelers, friends and two languages on one sheet
passages.text: Kings, nobles, bishops and grateful pilgrims gave the Roncesvalles institution land and income. Those endowments supported assistance. A hospital needed continuing resources; an impressive founding story alone could not feed the next group of tired travelers.

passages.title: Travelers, friends and two languages on one sheet
passages.text: Surviving charters for Puente la Reina and Sangüesa from 1122, and San Saturnino in Pamplona from 1129, show how towns along the pilgrimage world were organized through written privileges. The archive also preserves an Irache charter concerning a pilgrims’ hospital.

passages.title: Travelers, friends and two languages on one sheet
passages.text: Two officials, Martín de San Martín and Machín de Zalba, exchanged short letters on the same sheet, probably in 1416. The first asks about a tax reduction and then about dinner plans. Medieval office correspondence could switch from money to supper surprisingly quickly.

passages.title: Travelers, friends and two languages on one sheet
passages.text: Zalba replied that he could not attend dinner because he had guests at home, then answered the tax question in Basque. The pair switched between Navarrese Romance and Basque. This proves these particular officials could use both, not that every inhabitant had the same language skills.

passages.title: Travelers, friends and two languages on one sheet
passages.text: San Martín’s Basque farewell reads “jaunatiçula egun hon”: “May God give you a good day.” The spelling is preserved in the archive’s transcription of the probably 1416 letter. Basque was written here in Latin letters, within a document otherwise using Romance.

Ferdinand’s invasion in 1512 began a prolonged conquest, not an instant disappearance of Navarre. Upper Navarre joined the Castilian crown in 1515 while retaining important institutions. Lower Navarre followed a separate path and was incorporated into the French monarchy in 1620. Communities and regional identities continued on both sides of the mountains.

sectionTitles: Making a living in a dry landscape

passages.text: Nasca, also spelled Nazca, describes related communities of Peru’s dry southern coast, famous for painted pottery and enormous ground drawings. Their history grew from Paracas traditions and continued into the eighth century CE. The imported 100 BCE to 600 CE span covers only part of this changing cultural tradition, not the lifespan of a single unified kingdom.

passages.title: Making a living in a dry landscape
passages.text: At Marcaya, households of both high and low status possessed colorful painted ceramics. Fine-looking pottery was therefore not reserved for the very richest. Excavating homes helps reveal who actually used the objects that later ended up in museum cases.

passages.title: Making a living in a dry landscape
passages.text: Certain vessel shapes at Marcaya were restricted to higher-status homes. Vaughn interprets these households as intermediaries between the village and gatherings at Cahuachi. Sharing a broad pottery tradition could coexist with differences in influence and special serving equipment.

passages.title: Making a living in a dry landscape
passages.text: An isotope study in the Las Trancas Valley found greater meat consumption among higher-status people, while access to maize was less sharply divided. Food choices can leave chemical traces in human remains, helping researchers study inequality beyond impressive buildings and rich graves.

passages.title: Making a living in a dry landscape
passages.text: Puquios collect groundwater through underground galleries for fields and household use. A major archaeological survey proposed their origins during middle or later Nasca times, rather than the earliest phase. Their construction dates remain a research question, so they should not all be assigned one birthday.

passages.title: Making a living in a dry landscape
passages.text: Nasca potters applied colored slips before firing, making decoration more durable than earlier post-fired paint. This allowed rich colors and intricate designs to become part of the pot’s surface. Even a beautiful bowl still had to survive its trip through the fire.

passages.title: Making a living in a dry landscape
passages.text: A bottle dated 1 to 400 CE shows hummingbirds feeding from flowers painted at the bases of its two spouts. Artists worked the vessel’s shape into the scene. Nasca pottery depicts many plants and animals, including more than twenty kinds of birds.

passages.title: Gatherings, giant drawings and change
passages.text: Pigments, brushes and polishing tools found at Cahuachi preserve traces of ceramic production. Elaborate bottles accompanied feasts, processions and offerings there. The artists’ skill helped make public gatherings visually memorable as well as socially important.

passages.title: Gatherings, giant drawings and change
passages.text: A Nasca vessel depicts a procession of finely dressed people playing panpipes, accompanied by dogs and carrying parrots. The scene offers a lively glimpse of performance and valued birds. It records an artistic representation, rather than the exact sound of a surviving song.

passages.title: Gatherings, giant drawings and change
passages.text: Geoglyph makers removed dark weathered stones to expose a lighter surface underneath. They created animal figures, spirals, rectangles and very long straight lines. The desert itself became the drawing surface, using straightforward techniques on an extraordinary scale.

passages.title: Gatherings, giant drawings and change
passages.text: The Nasca to Palpa drawings accumulated over many generations, including a Paracas phase before classic Nasca. Some broad tracks could accommodate groups of people. Archaeologists connect the landscape with ritual activity, while the precise purpose of every figure remains unresolved.

passages.title: Gatherings, giant drawings and change
passages.text: Plant evidence from the lower Ica Valley suggests that clearing huarango woodland for fields made irrigation and soils more vulnerable to major floods. The trees had supplied food, fuel and protection for the valley floor. This is a local environmental history, not a complete explanation for every Nasca community.

passages.title: Gatherings, giant drawings and change
passages.text: No securely readable Nasca inscription supplies an original-language sentence and translation. Painted beings and geoglyphs communicated ideas visually, but recognizing a hummingbird is different from reading words. Their spoken language cannot simply be recovered by treating each picture as an alphabet letter.

The decline of Cahuachi’s regional ceremonial influence brought reorganization rather than the disappearance of all Nasca people. Excavations at Late Nasca Cocahuischo reveal communities maintaining and changing their traditions. Wari influence later helped reshape the region. The map’s 600 CE cutoff is earlier than the end of the usual Late Nasca chronology, around 750 CE.

sectionTitles: Pots, cooking and things held in the hand
A prince’s letters and a changed world

passages.text: The Ndebele kingdom developed in what is now Zimbabwe under Mzilikazi and his successor Lobengula. It incorporated people of different origins into a powerful regional state. This record concerns northern Ndebele history, rather than every community elsewhere bearing the Ndebele name.

passages.title: A capital that moved
passages.text: Mzilikazi left Zululand in 1822 and built a new state through migration, warfare and incorporation of other communities. By about 1840 it was established in the Zimbabwe region. The kingdom’s population was therefore more varied than a single royal genealogy suggests.

passages.title: A capital that moved
passages.text: Lobengula founded Old Bulawayo in 1870, then left it in 1881 for a new capital near the present city. The old settlement was burned. The move means that an account simply saying “Bulawayo” needs a date before it can be placed accurately.

passages.title: A capital that moved
passages.text: The Old Bulawayo heritage site includes the Indaba tree, associated with public affairs, and the location of a Jesuit mission. These features put discussion and religious encounters beside royal residences in the landscape of a capital.

passages.title: A capital that moved
passages.text: A museum reconstruction made in 1998 included eight beehive-shaped houses, the king’s residence, a wagon shed, palisade and cattle enclosure. These were modern reconstructions of a historical settlement; a destructive fire in 2010 became another chapter in the site’s history.

passages.title: Pots, cooking and things held in the hand
passages.text: Research on Old Bulawayo pottery draws on comparison with Ndebele potters and household practice. Vessel shapes can suggest different jobs, but the comparison must be tested against excavated remains. A broken pot is useful evidence precisely because researchers ask how it was actually used.

passages.title: Pots, cooking and things held in the hand
passages.text: The comparative research describes imbiza vessels used in cooking porridge and preparing beer. Other vessels are associated with serving beer and ceremonies. A family’s pottery collection could therefore connect everyday food preparation with larger gatherings and ritual obligations.

passages.title: Pots, cooking and things held in the hand
passages.text: Soot can help investigators recognize cooking pots, but it can also hide decoration. Archaeologists must look past a vessel’s dirty surface to understand both use and design. The washing-up that nobody finished can become a clue centuries later.

passages.title: Pots, cooking and things held in the hand
passages.text: Aberdeen’s museum preserves a wooden straining spoon catalogued as Matabele. It is only 22.7 centimetres long, a kitchen-sized object rather than royal regalia. Its exact manufacture date is unrecorded, so it offers material context without being assigned to a particular year of Lobengula’s reign.

passages.title: A prince’s letters and a changed world
passages.text: After conquest, Lobengula’s son Njube was educated at Zonnebloem in Cape Town. Colonial authorities resisted his return because of his political significance. Schooling in this case also separated a young man from home and placed limits on his freedom to travel.

passages.title: A prince’s letters and a changed world
passages.text: Njube’s 1898 letters ask for money for books and mention debt from tram travel. These details show a student managing very ordinary expenses while living through extraordinary political upheaval. A royal family’s history can include a troublesome transport bill.

passages.title: A prince’s letters and a changed world
passages.text: His 14 October 1898 English letter includes: “Will you please let me go Home fore Holiday”. In modern spelling, he asks permission to go home for a holiday. This is his attested written voice, including “fore”; it is not offered as an isiNdebele-language sample.

passages.title: A prince’s letters and a changed world
passages.text: The British South Africa Company’s 1893 campaign was a war of conquest. Historian Paul Gundani examines how supporters used religious and moral arguments to justify it. Reading those arguments critically helps distinguish claims made by invaders from the consequences for the people they defeated.

The kingdom lost its independence in the British South Africa Company’s conquest of 1893. Ndebele people and language continued beyond that defeat. The imported map interval extending to 1914 should not be read as another twenty-one years of independent royal government.

sectionTitles: Conquest and lives beyond the court

passages.text: Ndongo was a kingdom in the Kimbundu-speaking region of present-day Angola. Its ruler, the Ngola, held authority through relationships with local polities. Its political history cannot be reduced to a fixed territory ruled uniformly from one capital.

passages.title: Work, markets and rivers
passages.text: The Kwanza corridor connected farming, pastoralism, iron production and salt supplies with trading settlements. Angola’s heritage account places this exchange before Portuguese conquest. Food and working materials circulated alongside the later expansion of captive trading.

passages.title: Work, markets and rivers
passages.text: Kabasa, also written Cabaça, was both a royal centre and an important market. Other fairs operated under royal officers. Markets supplied neighbouring communities and linked more distant places, making their regulation a practical part of government.

passages.title: Work, markets and rivers
passages.text: River navigation linked parts of the interior with coastal exchange. The Kwanza had both navigable stretches and obstacles; overland paths and scattered markets also mattered. The trading landscape was a network of different routes, not one uninterrupted river highway.

passages.title: Governing a varied kingdom
passages.text: Local sobas governed smaller polities that entered the king’s orbit through conquest or agreement. Thornton describes expansion as incorporation of these units. Their own rulers remained important, helping explain why alliances could shift during wars with the Portuguese.

passages.title: Governing a varied kingdom
passages.text: Jesuit accounts from the 1580s recorded hundreds of local political units. Thornton treats the unusually precise reported count as possible evidence of fiscal knowledge gained at court. It is testimony about administration, not a modern census independently confirmed for every settlement.

passages.title: Governing a varied kingdom
passages.text: Kijiko were unfree people who could hold revenue-collecting roles. Capturing them disrupted Ndongo’s administration. Fonseca stresses that Portuguese translations as “slaves” can conceal these particular functions.

passages.title: Resistance, knowledge and its costs
passages.text: At Kindonga, Njinga’s supporters stored food and weapons on Kwanza islands. Their knowledge of branching channels helped them avoid pursuing forces. Geography, provisioning and local experience worked together in resistance.

passages.title: Resistance, knowledge and its costs
passages.text: A lunga, a double metal bell, marked authority in a military camp. Fonseca describes a demand that Njinga surrender hers when seeking an ally’s protection, linking a tangible object with a political negotiation.

passages.title: Resistance, knowledge and its costs
passages.text: Njinga offered refuge to people escaping enslavement and recruited African soldiers trained in Portuguese service. This brought people with different experiences into her following. Protection and military organisation helped rebuild power after displacement.

passages.title: Resistance, knowledge and its costs
passages.text: Resistance to Portuguese conquest did not mean opposition to all enslavement. From Matamba, Njinga exchanged captives for Dutch support and firearms. Her alliances could protect followers while harming those captured as enemies.

passages.title: Conquest and lives beyond the court
passages.text: After Pungo Andongo fell in 1671, members of the royal family were deported to Brazil and later Portugal. Lara follows these exiles through Atlantic records. The kingdom’s defeat continued in the displacement of identifiable people, beyond the battlefield itself.

Portuguese forces captured Pungo Andongo in 1671 after a siege, killing its ruler and ending that royal centre’s resistance. Njinga had died in Matamba in 1663. These separate events should not be collapsed into one ruler’s defeat or the disappearance of Mbundu communities.

passages.text: The exact atlas id “nepal” covers 1200 to 1279. Its decoded ten-position polygon is a coarse western Himalayan shape, not modern Nepal. It includes tested Nuwakot, Pokhara, Jumla, Doti, and Lumbini, while excluding Kathmandu, Patan, Bhaktapur, and Simraungadh. Period sources usually call the Kathmandu Valley Nepal or Nepal Mandala, while a distinct Khasa kingdom grew around Sinja in the west. Early Valley Malla rulers survive mainly in dated Sanskrit manuscript colophons and later chronicles; western archaeology preserves settlements, pipes, monuments, and routes. These records illuminate courts, donors, monasteries, and ritual places more clearly than most households. Agriculture, craft production, manuscript copying, pilgrimage, and exchange across India and the Tibetan plateau connected communities without making them uniform. Workers, women, and children remain less visible than kings and donors, so daily-life claims are locally bounded and candid about gaps. At 1279 the feature vanishes: tested points become Tibet or Delhi Sultanate colors. This is an atlas seam, not proof of conquest, migration, or social collapse. Separate Nepal ids reappear in 1492 and 1650 as independent snapshots, not automatic successors.

passages.title: Read the map before trusting the label
passages.text: The live index contains one exact id, “nepal,” named “Nepal,” with approximate coverage from 1200 to 1279. One border file carries it, while the exact card, review, and researched override remain missing. The imported summary describes today's multilingual country and is not valid copy for a medieval feature.

passages.title: Read the map before trusting the label
passages.text: The 1200 feature is one Polygon, one ring, and ten decoded positions. Its bbox is 80.10260102601029, 27.27706261766734 to 85.86265862658627, 30.191319255656083; its decoded geometry SHA-256 is f4d85a7e28dba748287fe20d271edaa82f049f6a2a7ca68ed3b9308dc25d0a66. These are reproducible display-data facts, not surveyed medieval borders or sovereignty coordinates.

passages.title: Read the map before trusting the label
passages.text: Tested Nuwakot, Pokhara, Jumla, Doti, and Lumbini fall inside. Kathmandu, Patan, Bhaktapur, Kirtipur, Banepa, Lo Manthang, Nepalgunj, Simraungadh, Janakpur, Biratnagar, and the Khasa-Tatopani crossing do not. The shape therefore emphasizes western hills while excluding the Kathmandu Valley historical core discussed by most early Malla sources.

passages.title: Read the map before trusting the label
passages.text: At 1200 the target directly shares encoded arcs with the atlas's “tibet” and “delhi-sultanate” features. Kathmandu and its neighboring Valley cities lie in the Tibet color, while southern lowland probes lie in the Delhi Sultanate color. Shared arcs and fills describe this dataset, not actual tribute, occupation, language, or religion.

passages.title: Read the map before trusting the label
passages.text: The later ids “nepal-1492” and “nepal-1650” are separate indexed records, not automatic successors. The 1492 shape repeats the coarse western footprint; the 1650 shape changes its northern edge. Both again omit the tested Valley core. Reused coloring cannot turn three intermittent snapshots into one continuously bounded state.

passages.title: Courts, titles, and limited political reach
passages.text: Arimalla is the first ruler in this sequence regularly associated with the Malla title, but “Malla” meant a prestigious title rather than proof that every later namesake belonged to one family. Kathmandu Valley Mallas and western Khasa Mallas must remain separate. Their overlapping labels are a historian's trap with excellent branding.

passages.title: Courts, titles, and limited political reach
passages.text: The 1201 Sivadharma colophon gives Arimalladeva elaborate Shaiva royal titles and names Ranaka Haridharasimha as an official. Such formulae show how authority was announced through religion and local office. They do not reveal the actual reach of commands, tax collection, or control across the atlas's western polygon.

passages.title: Courts, titles, and limited political reach
passages.text: Critical chronology for 1200 to 1279 is assembled from manuscript dates, inscriptions, and chronicles copied later. Sources become substantially richer only after this card's interval. Exact regnal lists vary, so the card uses broad teaching phases and identifies uncertainty instead of pretending that a tidy modern timeline survived from every court.

passages.title: Courts, titles, and limited political reach
passages.text: Western Khasa rulers established seasonal centers around Sinja and Dullu during the thirteenth century. Archaeology and inscriptions frame a regional formation tied to pilgrimage and mountain routes. That history fits much of the drawn polygon better than Valley Malla history, yet it still cannot certify the atlas line as a Khasa frontier.

passages.title: Courts, titles, and limited political reach
passages.text: Sinja and Kathmandu were not interchangeable capitals. Nepal's Department of Archaeology describes Sinja as a western Khasa center, while the atlas audit places Kathmandu, Patan, and Bhaktapur outside this polygon. Political power, landscape, and surviving evidence differ; “Nepal” is an editorial doorway, not one palace speaking for everyone.

passages.title: Farms, routes, exchange, and mountain work
passages.text: A broad history links medieval Valley agriculture, craft work, and trade, but most of its economic evidence comes from later Malla centuries. It supplies questions about cultivators and artisans, not a measured 1200 harvest, crop list, household budget, or proof that the western hills followed the same pattern.

passages.title: Farms, routes, exchange, and mountain work
passages.text: Bhaktapur's long-lived water system linked canals, stone spouts, ponds, household supply, and cultivation. The study traces change and reuse across centuries, so continuity into 1200 to 1279 is context rather than a complete period map. It cannot name every working channel or each family responsible for maintenance.

passages.title: Farms, routes, exchange, and mountain work
passages.text: Sankhu lay on an old route from the Kathmandu Valley toward Tibet. Pack animals, porters, religious travelers, artisans, and merchants made such links work, although route studies rarely preserve their names or wages. A connected road did not erase different languages, authorities, or local risks along the journey.

passages.title: Farms, routes, exchange, and mountain work
passages.text: Aniko's later epitaph places the Valley-trained artisan in Tibet and at the Yuan court. Elite commissions moved skills across mountains, but his exceptional career cannot establish ordinary mobility or wages. One famous traveler did not make every craft worker an international commuter.

passages.title: Farms, routes, exchange, and mountain work
passages.text: The 1316 epitaph places Aniko in Tibet and at the Yuan court during this interval. His exceptional mobility shows elite commissions moving skills across mountains. It cannot represent an ordinary craft career, and modern national borders should not be inserted into his thirteenth-century journey.

passages.title: Homes, food, clothing, and ordinary work
passages.text: The 1255 chronicle says many houses and temples collapsed and survivors lived outside for weeks. It does not describe floor plans, roofing, ownership, or whether households shared courtyards. The disaster makes ordinary shelter briefly visible, but its silence prevents one “typical Nepali house” from being invented across western hills and the Valley.

passages.title: Homes, food, clothing, and ordinary work
passages.text: An architectural study shows how famous Valley buildings combine old traditions, rebuilding, and uncertain dates. Its careful separation of surviving fabric from legends is more useful than declaring every brick wall or carved timber medieval. It offers construction context, not a typical thirteenth-century floor plan or household inventory.

passages.title: Homes, food, clothing, and ordinary work
passages.text: At Sinja, excavators found building cells, thresholds, paths, pits, pottery, glass, and animal bone. One relevant radiocarbon range begins around 1270 but runs to 1420, and later occupation complicates the assemblage. These finds illuminate tasks and rooms near the seam without furnishing a household inventory for the whole 1200 to 1279 period.

passages.title: Homes, food, clothing, and ordinary work
passages.text: A broad history attributes cotton spinning, weaving, metalwork, woodwork, and trade to medieval Valley households and specialists. Most supporting detail comes from later Malla centuries. For this card, it shows enduring occupational traditions worth investigating, while clothing cuts, loom ownership, work hours, and gendered labor in 1200 remain insufficiently documented.

passages.title: Homes, food, clothing, and ordinary work
passages.text: Sinja excavations recovered pottery and animal bone, but mixed phases prevent a dependable 1200 to 1279 menu. The finds show food-related activity only broadly; they do not place modern dal bhat on every thirteenth-century plate. History should ask before raiding someone's lunchbox.

passages.title: Families, status, belief, and social life
passages.text: Somadeva's 1201 manuscript donation names benefits sought for mother, father, teachers, daughters, sons, and grandchildren. That makes kin and teaching relationships directly visible in a dated source. Because this is a learned donor's religious commission, it cannot define marriage, inheritance, household size, or affection for every social group.

passages.title: Families, status, belief, and social life
passages.text: The painted manuscript from Sri Lham Mahavihara names the monk Puspasena as its recipient and locates skilled work inside a religious institution. It reveals patronage and institutional relationships, not the monk's household, childhood, or daily timetable. Even a splendid book leaves most social life outside its covers.

passages.title: Families, status, belief, and social life
passages.text: Shaiva and Buddhist manuscript production overlapped rather than forming sealed populations. Arimalla's royal titles invoke Shiva and Pashupati, while Sri Lham Mahavihara produced a painted Buddhist book for monk Puspasena. Elite religious sources reveal plural patronage, but they leave household practice, local deities, and disagreement only partly visible.

passages.title: Families, status, belief, and social life
passages.text: Sankhu's nomination describes an old settlement on the Valley-to-Tibet route, but its prominent surviving Vajrayogini complex is largely seventeenth century. A sacred place could gather residents, pilgrims, workers, and traders without preserving their conversations. Long continuity must not turn later buildings into a 1200 street scene.

passages.title: Families, status, belief, and social life
passages.text: Early Malla histories favor rulers, titles, officials, and manuscript dates. Farmers, herders, porters, servants, women outside donor formulas, and lower-status workers rarely appear by name. Imbalance matters: silence in court-centered chronology is not absence from society or a population census.

passages.title: Children, education, languages, and one written sample
passages.text: No reviewed source preserves a typical child's timetable, games, chores, or age at apprenticeship between 1200 and 1279. Manuscripts demonstrate teachers, monks, scribes, and learned patrons; craft careers imply training. They do not establish universal schooling, literacy rates, or equal access for girls, rural children, and lower-status families.

passages.title: Children, education, languages, and one written sample
passages.text: A 1316 Chinese epitaph tells how the young Aniko studied texts, calligraphy, painting, modeling, and casting before traveling. The account concerns an exceptional artisan and was written after his death. It is delightful evidence for an idealized child prodigy, not proof that every seven-year-old had bronze repair homework.

passages.title: Children, education, languages, and one written sample
passages.text: The dated Valley manuscripts used here are Sanskrit, while Sinja's institutional nomination records thirteenth-century Devanagari-script evidence in the western center. Script, language, place, and genre must remain separate: a court colophon or inscription cannot establish what every porter, farmer, child, or craft worker spoke at home.

passages.title: Children, education, languages, and one written sample
passages.text: Written-language sample, Nepalese manuscript, 1 January 1216: “राज्ये ह्यरिमल्लदेवीये” (rājye hy arimalladevīye), “during the reign of Arimalladeva.” The source prints a normalized Devanagari transcription of a Sanskrit colophon, not a facsimile of the original hand. Its exact copying workshop or Valley locality is not identified.

passages.title: Children, education, languages, and one written sample
passages.text: A University of Pennsylvania leaf preserves Sanskrit from the Astasahasrika Prajnaparamita and is broadly dated 1200 to 1399; painted images were added over the writing later. That range is too wide to call the leaf a 1200 to 1279 product. It does show why text, painting, and object date must be separated.

passages.title: Medicine, health, bodies, and disaster
passages.text: A palm-leaf Susrutasamhita copied in Nepal in 878 preserves a major Sanskrit medical text. The institutional record establishes learned medical writing centuries before this card, but not which thirteenth-century healers read it, which treatments they used, or whether ordinary patients could reach a manuscript-trained practitioner.

passages.title: Medicine, health, bodies, and disaster
passages.text: The institutional record describes the 878 medical manuscript as covering surgery and diseases involving skin, heart, gynecology, and other fields. Those are topics in a learned text, not clinical outcomes from 1200 to 1279. Preserved knowledge and everyday practice must remain separate unless a securely dated local medical record connects them.

passages.title: Medicine, health, bodies, and disaster
passages.text: The 1255 earthquake account implies crush injuries, exposure, bereavement, disrupted water, and prolonged fear as aftershocks continued. Yet it names no hospital, physician, medicine, or organized relief. The honest health history therefore describes hazards and source silence rather than importing a fully documented emergency service into the medieval Valley.

passages.title: Medicine, health, bodies, and disaster
passages.text: The reviewed medical manuscript record supplies no securely dated 1200 to 1279 patient case, physician's kit, prescription, hospital register, or childbirth account. That is a survival problem, not evidence that care did not exist. Family help, ritual care, herbs, and specialists remain possible but unquantified.

passages.title: Medicine, health, bodies, and disaster
passages.text: Water infrastructure affected health even though its builders did not use germ theory. Channels, recharge ponds, tanks, and stone spouts helped move water toward fields and settlements, but the sources provide no thirteenth-century water-quality tests or equal-access survey. A beautiful spout could still demand cleaning, repair, and fair distribution.

passages.title: Water, waste, bathing, and the toilet question
passages.text: An architectural study of two Valley buildings separates documented water structures from legends and later rebuilding. That matters because spouts, tanks, shrines, and masonry changed across centuries. Surviving water architecture shows continuity, but not that every component worked unchanged in 1200 or reached every household equally.

passages.title: Water, waste, bathing, and the toilet question
passages.text: Bhaktapur research describes cascaded reuse: water moved among domestic supply, recharge, and cultivation rather than entering one modern sewer. That helps explain labor around collection and maintenance. The study examines a long-lived system, however, and cannot tell us the exact bucket route, cleaning roster, or neighborhood access in 1237.

passages.title: Water, waste, bathing, and the toilet question
passages.text: At Sinja, archaeological survey recorded an earthen pipe system among the capital's remains. Its elements are not all securely dated inside 1200 to 1279. The pipes demonstrate water engineering in the western center, but neither their full route nor a thirteenth-century maintenance organization is securely reconstructed.

passages.title: Water, waste, bathing, and the toilet question
passages.text: No reviewed source securely identifies a 1200 to 1279 latrine, toilet seat, cesspit, chamber pot, or rule for disposing of human waste in these communities. Drains and spouts managed water, but a drain is not automatically a toilet. Medieval plumbing deserves credit without receiving imaginary porcelain accessories.

passages.title: Water, waste, bathing, and the toilet question
passages.text: The reviewed water study describes channels, spouts, ponds, recharge, reuse, and maintenance, but it does not identify a thirteenth-century rubbish route, sewage service, cleaning roster, or neighborhood sanitation rule. Those absences matter: a sophisticated water network did not automatically provide every modern municipal service.

passages.title: Craft, buildings, books, and religious achievement
passages.text: A thirteenth-century Kathmandu Valley ritual-vessel handle is cast in copper alloy as five intertwined nagas with human torsos, snake hoods, jewels, crowns, and extended bodies. The object demonstrates sophisticated openwork metal craft and water symbolism. Its museum record does not identify the workshop, patron, wage, or user's household.

passages.title: Craft, buildings, books, and religious achievement
passages.text: A thirteenth-century Valley image of Lakshmi combines copper alloy with semiprecious-stone inlay. It is strong evidence for casting, finishing, stone setting, and religious patronage, but weak evidence for production volume or artisan status. A surviving masterpiece is the opposite of an average object; museums are excellent at keeping overachievers.

passages.title: Craft, buildings, books, and religious achievement
passages.text: Sri Lham Mahavihara produced an early thirteenth-century Sanskrit manuscript for the monk Puspasena with striking painted wooden covers. The colophon names the monastery as a great monastery of an auspicious great image. That joins calligraphy, painting, woodworking, religious donation, and institutional life in one securely period-bound object.

passages.title: Craft, buildings, books, and religious achievement
passages.text: The 1216 Harihara commentary survives with a dated post-colophon tied to Arimalladeva's reign. Producing a manuscript required prepared writing material, ink, a trained hand, exemplars, checking, and patronage. Copying was skilled labor as well as learning; a ruler's date formula should not make the scribe's material work disappear.

passages.title: Craft, buildings, books, and religious achievement
passages.text: Sankhu preserves a long settlement and pilgrimage history, but its nomination dates the prominent Vajrayogini temple complex chiefly to the seventeenth century. This card therefore gives priority to dated thirteenth-century manuscripts and objects. Famous later buildings illustrate continuity and rebuilding, not an unchanged photograph of 1200.

passages.title: Danger, affected communities, and the exact 1279 seam
passages.text: Sinja's ridge includes large ditches, ramparts, a monumental gateway approach, and defensive interpretations, but excavators repeatedly stress ambiguous dates and later building. Fortifications redirect paths, demand labor, and shelter some people while burdening others. They do not by themselves prove a particular battle inside 1200 to 1279.

passages.title: Danger, affected communities, and the exact 1279 seam
passages.text: Khasa expansion linked western hill centers, pilgrimage places, and routes, yet political growth could affect cultivators, carriers, ritual communities, and chiefs differently. Inscriptions usually praise rulers and donations rather than list displaced families. Warfare and negotiation must therefore be described as community pressures without inventing a casualty total or ethnic bloc.

passages.title: Danger, affected communities, and the exact 1279 seam
passages.text: The 1255 earthquake was not warfare, but it was the interval's clearest mass danger. Houses and temples fell, the king died, and survivors stayed outside while aftershocks continued. Women, children, servants, laborers, monks, and marginalized residents are not separately counted; the chronicle's collective suffering hides unequal exposure.

passages.title: Danger, affected communities, and the exact 1279 seam
passages.text: At the exact 1279 seam, “nepal” disappears. Nuwakot, Pokhara, and Jumla switch to the atlas's Tibet color, while Doti and Lumbini switch to Delhi Sultanate; the same ownership persists in 1300. These are software layers with no encoded conquest event, migration, royal death, or social rupture.

passages.title: Danger, affected communities, and the exact 1279 seam
passages.text: Later “nepal-1492” and “nepal-1650” records reappear after gaps of 213 and 150 years. They are not named as successors in this card because intermittent reuse of a label does not establish one continuous state. Farms, routes, workshops, water systems, families, languages, and religious communities continued through the 1279 display seam.

At 1279 the exact “nepal” feature disappears: tested member points are reassigned to the atlas's Tibet and Delhi Sultanate layers, with no encoded conquest or population break. The 1300 snapshot keeps those colors. Separate Nepal ids return for 1492 to 1500 and 1650 to 1700, after long gaps, and cannot be treated as automatic successors. The override therefore leaves fell null and names no single successor. Valley and western courts changed, while households, farming, routes, crafts, manuscripts, religious institutions, water systems, and languages continued through the editorial seam.
