passages.text: The exact atlas id “nepal-1492” lasts only from 1492 to 1500. Its eight-position polygon is a coarse western Himalayan display shape, not modern Nepal and not one Malla kingdom. Tested Nuwakot, Pokhara, Jumla, Doti, and Lumbini lie inside; Kathmandu, Patan, Bhaktapur, Kirtipur, Banepa, Lo Manthang, and the eastern and southern lowlands do not. The exclusion matters because much surviving late-fifteenth-century evidence describes the Kathmandu Valley. There, Yaksha Malla's former realm had already divided into competing courts at Bhaktapur, Kathmandu, and Patan. Communities inside the polygon belonged to distinct local political landscapes; the drawn shape does not make them one government or one everyday culture. Routes, manuscripts, religious traditions, and skilled craft connected particular places without erasing those differences. The eight annual teaching windows reflect the atlas interval, not eight securely documented yearly revolutions. Surviving evidence is uneven: courts and religious institutions speak louder than children, women, farmers, porters, or remote households. At 1500 the id vanishes; its tested points switch to broad Tibet and Delhi Sultanate labels. That is an atlas seam, not a conquest, national birth, or social collapse.

passages.title: Read the atlas before reading the history
passages.text: The live index has one exact “nepal-1492” record named “Nepal,” circa 1492 to 1500. Coverage records one border file, while the exact card and researched override are absent. Its imported summary describes the modern multilingual country, so this packet replaces that collision instead of quietly carrying it into the Middle Ages.

passages.title: Read the atlas before reading the history
passages.text: The 1492 target is one Polygon with one ring and eight decoded positions. Its bounding box runs from 80.10260102601029, 27.27706261766734 to 85.86265862658627, 30.191319255656083. The decoded geometry SHA-256 is b2cd2aec60caa3cae98828373a1f0adca6172108a10a7cef67bf17f1f67fd91a. Those are dataset facts, not surveyed medieval boundaries.

passages.title: Read the atlas before reading the history
passages.text: Tested Nuwakot, Pokhara, Jumla, Doti, and Lumbini are inside. Kathmandu, Patan, Bhaktapur, Kirtipur, Banepa, Lo Manthang, Nepalgunj, Simraungadh, Janakpur, Biratnagar, Khasa, Shigatse, and Varanasi are outside. The map therefore excludes the Kathmandu Valley communities that dominate the late Malla written record.

passages.title: Read the atlas before reading the history
passages.text: The target shares encoded arcs only with atlas features called “tibet” and “delhi-sultanate.” In both 1400 and 1492 the Kathmandu Valley probes fall under the Tibet color, while southern and eastern owners vary. These labels describe a generalized map, not uniform tribute, occupation, ethnicity, language, or belief.

passages.title: Read the atlas before reading the history
passages.text: Separate ids named “nepal,” “nepal-1492,” and “nepal-1650” appear in 1200, 1492, and 1650 snapshots, with absences at their endpoints. The first two reuse a coarse footprint; the third changes its northern edge. Intermittent colors do not prove one continuous state waiting politely between map files.

passages.title: Courts, principalities, and political limits
passages.text: Yaksha Malla's death preceded competing centers of rule, but surviving manuscripts and later chronicles do not support a perfectly clean three-son partition. Raya Malla is associated with Bhaktapur and Ratna Malla with Kathmandu; Patan and Banepa had their own powerful actors. “The three kingdoms” is useful shorthand, not a complete constitutional diagram.

passages.title: Courts, principalities, and political limits
passages.text: The atlas index begins this exact feature in 1492, but neither the index nor the border file records a foundation ceremony, ruler, or constitutional change in that year. The start date organizes display coverage. It cannot fill later annual gaps, and it should not be mistaken for the birth of a state.

passages.title: Courts, principalities, and political limits
passages.text: Raya Malla's 1493/94 grant was made with royal relatives present and announced before subjects, revealing a Bhaktapur court, religious patronage, and a public political act. It does not demonstrate command over Nuwakot, Jumla, Doti, Lumbini, or other places inside the map shape, none of which the document makes his uniform territory.

passages.title: Courts, principalities, and political limits
passages.text: Jumla and Doti test inside the polygon, while Kathmandu, Patan, and Bhaktapur test outside. That result alone defeats a Valley-centered reading of the whole feature. The label “Nepal” is atlas shorthand here; it does not make one named Malla ruler, law, tax system, or court govern every included place.

passages.title: Courts, principalities, and political limits
passages.text: Oxford's history presents the late Malla Valley as rival kingdoms with their own political structures and urban cultures. That frame matters here: neighboring courts could share temples, monasteries, artists, and languages without forming one state. Political vocabulary stays local because the atlas shape and modern Nepal's government did not define their authority.

passages.title: Towns, routes, trade, and regional variety
passages.text: Kathmandu, Patan, and Bhaktapur were important urban centers, but every one lies outside this exact polygon. Academic history treats them as rival Malla courts with distinct political structures. Their evidence supplies neighboring context, not permission to repaint the target as a Kathmandu-centered state or assume that every city followed identical rules.

passages.title: Towns, routes, trade, and regional variety
passages.text: The Kathmandu Valley's fertile soil and position across routes toward Tibet supported unusual urban specialization. Inscriptions and Newari place-names reveal long literacy and settlement histories. This describes the excluded Valley, while the hills and western basins inside the target had different densities, work patterns, and access to long-distance exchange.

passages.title: Towns, routes, trade, and regional variety
passages.text: Tucci describes Nepal as a cultural intermediary between India and Tibet, visible in manuscripts, inscriptions, religion, and art. “Intermediary” means people, objects, and ideas crossed particular routes; it does not mean all transit passed through one court. Porters, merchants, monks, and craftspeople remain less named than elite patrons in the evidence.

passages.title: Towns, routes, trade, and regional variety
passages.text: Lumbini's archaeological area preserves a long pilgrimage history, with monastic remains and stupas spanning many centuries. Because the tested point sits inside the target, it adds a lowland sacred landscape to the card. It does not prove Malla administration, shared taxation, or the everyday religion of western hill households.

passages.title: Towns, routes, trade, and regional variety
passages.text: The polygon stretches from far-western Doti through Jumla and Pokhara toward Nuwakot, while excluding Lo Manthang, Nepalgunj, and the Kathmandu Valley cities. Its span suggests very different terrain and access, but geometry is not a route map. It cannot supply a caravan timetable, customs post, travel time, or common market.

passages.title: Religion, literature, art, craft, and discovery
passages.text: The Met's survey of Nepalese painting follows Buddhist and Hindu commissions across manuscript illustrations, painted book covers, and cloth paintings. That evidence makes religious patronage and workshop skill visible in the Kathmandu Valley. It does not establish one ritual mix, temple plan, or devotional routine for every community inside the western polygon.

passages.title: Religion, literature, art, craft, and discovery
passages.text: Newar artists made manuscript illustrations, painted book covers, and cloth paintings for Buddhist and Hindu patrons. The Met identifies a distinctive fifteenth-century development in rich decoration and precise brushwork. That achievement belongs to skilled workshops and patrons in the Kathmandu Valley, outside the exact polygon, and cannot describe every western craft tradition.

passages.title: Religion, literature, art, craft, and discovery
passages.text: A sixteenth-century Malla-period Bhairava in copper alloy demonstrates the virtuosity for which Newari metalworkers became known across the Himalayas. The object postdates 1492 to 1500, so it serves as later craft context only. A shiny survivor is excellent evidence for technique, but a terrible population census.

passages.title: Religion, literature, art, craft, and discovery
passages.text: Architectural study describes Valley buildings made with earth in brick and tile together with timber, and it warns that famous structures have layered repairs and disputed dates. Materials can illuminate craft continuity. Assigning a photographed, rebuilt, or later palace unchanged to a 1490s household would still be architectural time travel.

passages.title: Religion, literature, art, craft, and discovery
passages.text: Modern discovery has shaped what can be told. Tucci's field study brought attention to Malla inscriptions and monuments, while manuscript cataloging recovered dated colophons that anchor rulers. Discovery here means scholars finding and interpreting surviving evidence, not medieval people suddenly inventing their own temples, books, or artistic skill.

passages.title: Farming, environment, food, and connected work
passages.text: Rolled palm-leaf deeds preserve land transactions, loans, property transfers, and other agreements across the Malla centuries. They reveal an economy in which households and institutions managed valuable rights in writing. Their long date range does not provide a precise 1492 crop yield, rent, or family field size across the polygon.

passages.title: Farming, environment, food, and connected work
passages.text: The Valley's exceptional fertility helped support dense towns and a division of labor among farmers, merchants, and craftspeople. That relationship explains neighboring Malla urbanism. The polygon itself stretches across western hills and the Terai, so Valley soil and market density cannot be copied across the shape like one giant agricultural recipe.

passages.title: Farming, environment, food, and connected work
passages.text: The decoded shape spans western hills and a narrow lowland edge, but its eight points contain no fields, terraces, herd counts, or harvest records. The map supports geographic caution, not an environmental reconstruction. Crops, livestock, household labor, and seasonal shortages in this short interval remain unevenly documented.

passages.title: Farming, environment, food, and connected work
passages.text: Neither the exact index nor the border file supplies a shared 1490s menu, and the reviewed period evidence does not repair that silence across the whole polygon. Modern dishes cannot simply be carried backward. History may be hungry for detail, but it still needs permission before raiding a medieval lunch basket.

passages.title: Farming, environment, food, and connected work
passages.text: Network studies make circulation visible through manuscript colophons, production places, patrons, and religious institutions. They reveal connected work without supplying a payroll. Porters, pack-animal handlers, road maintainers, and household laborers remain harder to identify, so the card does not invent wages, work hours, or equal access across the included principalities.

passages.title: Families, women, associations, and social life
passages.text: The 1493/94 Bhaktapur grant says Raya Malla acted with the royal family present. That is direct evidence for a courtly kin group participating in a public religious gift. It is not a model household: the document does not tell us how farmers divided childcare, how spouses negotiated property, or what most homes looked like.

passages.title: Families, women, associations, and social life
passages.text: Malla-period rolled palm-leaf deeds record land transactions, loans, property transfers, and other agreements. Those documents show that households and institutions managed valuable rights in writing. The collection spans the thirteenth to eighteenth centuries, so it proves a documentary tradition, not that every surviving deed or legal formula belonged to 1492.

passages.title: Families, women, associations, and social life
passages.text: Guthi associations could finance worship, festivals, funerals, roads, shelters, and charitable purposes through land and member obligations. An ethnohistorical synthesis also warns that their structure changed after the Malla era. The card therefore treats guthi as a durable institutional family of practices, not a frozen rulebook for every 1490s neighborhood.

passages.title: Families, women, associations, and social life
passages.text: Later descriptions say guthi membership could follow family and marriage ties, with rank and duties organized by seniority. Because these observations are not a 1490s household survey, they cannot establish one marriage pattern, women's experience, or children's role across the period. They instead show which questions surviving land and ritual institutions can help historians ask.

passages.title: Families, women, associations, and social life
passages.text: Preserved catalogs and manuscripts name texts, rulers, donors, scribes, and learned specialists more readily than ordinary households. Women, children, servants, cultivators, porters, and low-status workers appear less often. Documentary silence measures preservation and power as much as population; an unnamed life is not an absent life.

passages.title: Children, learning, manuscripts, and written language
passages.text: Modern manuscript scholarship examines medieval Nepalese book production, readers, editors, and scribal intervention. Those fields make advanced learned work visible without turning every religious institution into a modern school. The reviewed evidence does not establish age grades, classrooms, universal enrollment, or equal access for children across the polygon.

passages.title: Children, learning, manuscripts, and written language
passages.text: The Durbar Library catalog lists texts on religion, medicine, astronomy, drama, poetry, rhetoric, and politics. Such range suggests advanced specialist learning and copying. It does not show a curriculum for every child, a literacy rate, or equal access by gender and status; preserved libraries heavily favor learned and elite production.

passages.title: Children, learning, manuscripts, and written language
passages.text: Modern manuscript scholarship studies collections, codicology, readers, editors, scribal intervention, and the production of medieval Nepalese works. A surviving book was a material object and an edited text, not a transparent transcript. Palm leaf offered no convenient undo button, so corrections and layout choices became evidence for how people worked.

passages.title: Children, learning, manuscripts, and written language
passages.text: Written-language sample, shown in modern Devanagari normalization: “राज्ये श्री जय रायमल्ल नृपतेः.” Transliteration: “rājye Śrī Jaya Rāyamalla nṛpateḥ.” Meaning: “in the reign of King Śrī Jaya Rāyamalla.” It comes from a Gita Govinda colophon dated Nepal Samvat 616, 1495/96, in the Bhaktapur ruler's manuscript context.

passages.title: Children, learning, manuscripts, and written language
passages.text: The printed source gives the colophon in Roman transcription; the Devanagari above is a modern normalization, not a facsimile of the manuscript's original letterforms. It is learned Sanskrit, not a sample of everyone's speech. Palaeographic research also warns that scripts, hands, and dating must be compared across dated witnesses.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, crafts, and daily routines
passages.text: Architectural research describes Newar buildings from farmhouse to palace as using earth in brick and tile together with timber. Dense Valley towns packed houses along narrow streets. This is useful neighboring context, while the western polygon held different settlements. The evidence does not supply one universal floor plan, room count, or sleeping arrangement.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, crafts, and daily routines
passages.text: Rolled palm-leaf documents preserve property and credit agreements rather than room-by-room household descriptions. They show that durable records mattered to families and institutions, but they do not reveal a universal floor plan, sleeping arrangement, storage system, or guest room. Legal survival is not a complete tour of a home.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, crafts, and daily routines
passages.text: Manuscript scholarship reconstructs preparation, copying, correction, reading, and preservation as skilled material work. That supports bookmaking craft, not a complete clothing history. Exact 1490s garment cuts, children's dress, loom ownership, work hours, and the division of textile labor remain too thinly documented for confident reconstruction.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, crafts, and daily routines
passages.text: Newari urban life rested on a sophisticated division of labor supported by fertile land and trade. That social complexity does not make status equal: occupations, religious roles, and access to learning differed. Nor should Valley categories be stretched over Jumla, Doti, Lumbini, or other communities whose languages and institutions had distinct histories.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, crafts, and daily routines
passages.text: Painted manuscripts, wooden book covers, and devotional cloth paintings required prepared surfaces, pigments, brushes, precise hands, and practiced composition. Museum collections preserve the finished achievement more readily than the spilled pigment or sore fingers. The joke is gentle; Newar artists' skilled work for Buddhist and Hindu patrons was real.

passages.title: Medicine, health, healing, and evidence limits
passages.text: The Durbar Library catalog lists medicine among Nepal's preserved manuscript genres beside religion, astronomy, poetry, drama, and politics. That cataloged range makes learned medical texts visible, but not their use in 1492. A library list cannot prove that a village practitioner owned, read, or followed any particular work.

passages.title: Medicine, health, healing, and evidence limits
passages.text: An institutional manuscript record describes Sanskrit material on Ayurvedic diagnosis and treatment written in Nepalakshara script on birch bark. Its date is not secure. The object therefore demonstrates textual transmission, not a hospital register, and cannot reveal how often families saw healers, treated injuries, or paid for care.

passages.title: Medicine, health, healing, and evidence limits
passages.text: Neither the exact civilization index nor the polygon records illness, childbirth, injury, disability, epidemics, sanitation enforcement, bedside care, or oral remedies. Those repository files establish scope and geometry only. The card refuses to convert a mapped label into health statistics, named clinics, or equal access across western communities.

passages.title: Medicine, health, healing, and evidence limits
passages.text: An undated Nepalakshara manuscript on birch bark preserves Sanskrit material on Ayurvedic diagnosis and treatment. Because its date is not secure, it cannot be assigned to this eight-year window. It is included to show a manuscript tradition and the discipline required to say “we do not know” when chronology will not cooperate.

passages.title: Medicine, health, healing, and evidence limits
passages.text: Wellcome's “Ayurvedic Man” comes from eighteenth-century Kathmandu, roughly three centuries later. It shows how medical bodies could be diagrammed in a later manuscript, but it is not a picture of 1490s practice. No reviewed source supports exact rates of illness, named clinics, vaccination, or one uniform healing system across the polygon.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets, achievements, and the seam
passages.text: Kathmandu Valley water systems linked royal canals, ponds, tanks, recharge areas, and sunken stone spouts. Archaeology and inscriptions trace important elements earlier than this card. The network supported cultivation and domestic collection in the excluded Valley, but the evidence does not map every channel working in 1492 or every household carrying water.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets, achievements, and the seam
passages.text: A peer-reviewed review explains that hiti systems captured, conveyed, filtered, and publicly delivered water. That is a major engineering achievement, not automatic proof of modern plumbing. Water had to be collected, carried, stored, and kept usable, and access could vary by neighborhood, season, maintenance, and social arrangements.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets, achievements, and the seam
passages.text: UNESCO notes that public hiti fountains originated in the sixth century and remained communal water sources over generations. Its modern restoration case demonstrates living continuity, not an unchanged medieval routine. A public spout could be technically clever and socially important without piping drinking water into every fifteenth-century kitchen.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets, achievements, and the seam
passages.text: The reviewed water sources document channels, ponds, tanks, and public spouts, but no secure 1492 household toilet, sewer network, waste collector, or bathing schedule. A beautifully carved spout is not evidence of a flush toilet; archaeology refuses that upgrade, however convenient it would be.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets, achievements, and the seam
passages.text: At 1500 the exact id ends. Tested Nuwakot, Pokhara, and Jumla switch to the atlas's Tibet layer; Doti and Lumbini switch to Delhi Sultanate. People, farms, courts, shrines, manuscripts, and routes continued. The ending is continuity with technical successor labels, not conquest, extinction, or a modern national boundary appearing.

The exact “nepal-1492” feature disappears at the 1500 atlas seam. Nuwakot, Pokhara, and Jumla are relabeled “tibet,” while Doti and Lumbini are relabeled “delhi-sultanate.” Neither broad label proves uniform conquest or ownership. Valley Malla courts, western principalities, pilgrimage places, households, and trade routes continued beyond the software handoff.

materialEvidence.question: Does a concrete finding have an identifiable context, date, interpretation and evidence limit?

dailyLife.question: Does the account explain ordinary practices with evidence rather than only rulers?

artsScienceTechnology.question: Are achievements concrete and correctly attributed to this polity and period?

chronologicalPhases.question: Are source-supported phases distinguished from map snapshot dates?

endingContinuity.question: Does the narrative identify what ended or continued, with dates, mechanism and uncertainty?

uncertainty.question: Are uncertainties attached to particular claims rather than a blanket disclaimer?

passages.text: The exact atlas id “nepal-1650” covers 1650 to 1700, but its broad western hill polygon is not modern Nepal and is not one Malla kingdom. It includes tested Nuwakot, Pokhara, Lo Manthang, Jumla, Doti, and Lumbini while excluding Kathmandu, Patan, Bhaktapur, Kirtipur, and Banepa. Those excluded Valley cities were three rival kingdoms whose courts drew wealth from farming, crafts, coinage, and India-Tibet trade. Farther west, Gorkha and shifting Baisi and Chaubisi states had their own rulers, alliances, communities, and frontiers. Pratap Malla, Srinivasa Malla, Jagat Prakash Malla, Jitamitra Malla, and Bhupatindra Malla sponsored buildings, manuscripts, festivals, music, and performance while also bargaining, blockading, fighting, taxing, and commanding labor. Surviving records favor kings, priests, donors, and merchants. Farmers, porters, artisans, dependent workers, women, and children appear unevenly, so later customs cannot simply be projected backward. A 1670 multilingual pond inscription provides a rare secure writing sample. At 1700 the atlas erases the target and recolors every tested member point as Mughal Empire. That is a false political ending: neither the Valley kingdoms nor western hill states were annexed by the Mughals then.

passages.title: Read the atlas label as an aggregate, not a state
passages.text: The live index has one exact “nepal-1650” record named “Nepal,” approximately 1650 to 1700. One border file carries it, but the exact card, override, identity review, chronology review, and border review are missing. Its imported summary describes today's country and cannot serve as seventeenth-century copy.

passages.title: Read the atlas label as an aggregate, not a state
passages.text: The decoded target is one Polygon with one ring, 33 positions, and bbox 80.10260102601029, 27.27700303211668 to 85.87705877058772, 30.455210042300024. Its geometry hash is d204bc33ad743ae31db7e291ae08f40d66db1cbc0a92c6adb0168b242bc3d037. Coordinates audit the software feature, not a surveyed historical frontier, political census, or legal boundary.

passages.title: Read the atlas label as an aggregate, not a state
passages.text: Tested Nuwakot, Pokhara, Lo Manthang, Jumla, Doti, and Lumbini fall inside the target. Kathmandu, Patan, Bhaktapur, Kirtipur, Banepa, Nepalgunj, Simraungadh, Janakpur, Biratnagar, the Khasa crossing, Shigatse, and Varanasi do not. The shape therefore excludes the best-documented Malla urban core while gathering very different western places.

passages.title: Read the atlas label as an aggregate, not a state
passages.text: At 1600 most Valley and central probes carry the catch-all id “islamic-and-hindu-states,” while several western and lowland probes carry “mughal-empire.” At 1650 the new target takes only six tested points. These abrupt assignments reveal atlas generalization; they cannot establish sovereignty, ethnicity, language, or everyday law.

passages.title: Read the atlas label as an aggregate, not a state
passages.text: At 1700 and again in 1715, every tested target-member point is colored “mughal-empire.” In 1783 a separate “nepal-1783” shape includes all tested Nepal-related points, including the Valley capitals. The exact target is also distinct from “nepal” and “nepal-1492”; matching names never authorize merged cards, dates, or political stories.

passages.title: Meet three Valley kingdoms and many western states
passages.text: Kathmandu, Patan, and Bhaktapur were separate city kingdoms, not districts of one seventeenth-century nation. Their Malla courts competed for routes, ritual standing, and political advantage, yet shared a dense Valley world of Newar towns, agriculture, temples, markets, kinship, and craft production. Court borders did not seal daily connections.

passages.title: Meet three Valley kingdoms and many western states
passages.text: West of the Valley, “Baisi” and “Chaubisi” named shifting groupings rather than two tidy federal blocs. The far-western Karnali region included Jumla and other hill states; the Gandaki region included Gorkha, Lamjung, Kaski, Tanahun, and neighbors. Membership and power changed, so lists need dates and caution.

passages.title: Meet three Valley kingdoms and many western states
passages.text: Gorkha, founded as an independent Shah kingdom in 1559, was still one relatively small hill state in this card's period. Its official heritage history describes rivalry with Lamjung, farming as its economic base, forts toward the Trishuli, and relationships with Valley rulers. Later unification should not be read backward into 1650.

passages.title: Meet three Valley kingdoms and many western states
passages.text: Srinivasa's career illustrates divided authority inside a court: he received administrative responsibilities by 1640, shared rule from 1648, was crowned in 1661, and abdicated in 1685. Documenta Nepalica also names parents, spouses, and a son, but a royal genealogy cannot stand in for ordinary family organization.

passages.title: Meet three Valley kingdoms and many western states
passages.text: Jitamitra's 1673 to 1696 Bhaktapur reign and Bhupatindra's succession in 1696 belong to one city kingdom, not the whole polygon. Getty records both as architectural patrons. Buildings may bear royal names while embodying the planning, quarrying, carpentry, brickwork, metalwork, transport, and maintenance of many unnamed workers.

passages.title: Follow diplomacy, war, trade, coins, and revenue
passages.text: Around 1650 Kathmandu secured privileged access for its merchants in Lhasa and rights to mint Tibetan coinage from bullion supplied from Tibet. The agreement made commercial opportunity and royal seigniorage inseparable. “Nepal” in later summaries can hide that specific court advantage and the distinct interests of Patan and Bhaktapur.

passages.title: Follow diplomacy, war, trade, coins, and revenue
passages.text: A Nepal Rastra Bank history links Bhim Malla's mission with duty-free trade and silver coin circulation in Tibet. That account is useful for institutional memory but should not become a story of effortless prosperity. Caravans faced weather, altitude, animals, customs politics, credit risk, and long separation from families.

passages.title: Follow diplomacy, war, trade, coins, and revenue
passages.text: Kathmandu, Patan, and Bhaktapur produced contemporaneous Malla coinages. Coins carried authority and facilitated exchange, but metal content, acceptance, and access mattered. A royal right to mint did not mean every market transaction used silver: produce, labor, credit, and smaller-value media remained central to household economies.

passages.title: Follow diplomacy, war, trade, coins, and revenue
passages.text: The 1658 to 1660 fighting involved blocked roads, changing alliances, burned property, deaths, prisoners, tribute, and new political claims. Calling these episodes “minor quarrels,” as one older account does, risks minimizing residents' losses. Small wars can still be enormous to the household whose roof, crop, relative, or freedom disappears.

passages.title: Follow diplomacy, war, trade, coins, and revenue
passages.text: Rulers drew resources from agricultural dues, customs and tolls, land assignments, and labor obligations. Nepal's official customs history traces medieval trade collection, while legal scholarship records slavery and other unfree dependency. Categories and surviving documents vary, but dependent people must not disappear behind cheerful images of caravans and temple building.

passages.title: Work the land, market, road, and workshop
passages.text: Irrigated rice and other grains, vegetables, livestock, and seasonal tasks sustained Valley towns; hill ecologies supported different crop mixes and herding. Landholding, tenancy, ritual rank, slope, rainfall, and access to water shaped work. Court-centered sources rarely tell us how one poor harvest redistributed hunger within a family.

passages.title: Work the land, market, road, and workshop
passages.text: Later Newar fieldwork shows households combining farming with pottery, building labor, carrying, shopkeeping, ritual service, or other crafts. It cannot be copied unchanged into 1650. It does help historians ask better questions about seasonal multitasking, small plots, tenancy, and why a single caste label never equals one livelihood.

passages.title: Work the land, market, road, and workshop
passages.text: Kathmandu's Asan market and Uray merchant institutions preserve long commercial histories reaching back into Malla urban life. Merchants needed packers, porters, brokers, lenders, innkeepers, food sellers, translators, and animal handlers. Trade history becomes misleading when it names only kings who negotiated privileges and merchants whose records survived.

passages.title: Work the land, market, road, and workshop
passages.text: Fired brick, carved timber, stone, bronze, terracotta, pigment, cloth, paper, and metal coinage demanded specialized skill and supply chains. UNESCO's monuments demonstrate extraordinary craft, but surviving palaces and temples overweight elite commissions. Everyday pots, repairs, tools, baskets, and work clothes mattered more often to most residents.

passages.title: Work the land, market, road, and workshop
passages.text: Medieval prescriptions tied some occupations, dress, and residence to caste rank, but practice was more varied than a neat chart. Oxford's collaborative study finds distinct priests, patrons, artisans, farmers, merchants, and low castes while stressing internal variation. Treat prescriptive rules as claims about order, not a census of everyone's work.

passages.title: Enter homes, meals, clothes, streets, and social rank
passages.text: Malla-period urban blocks used closely built multistory brick-and-timber houses, courtyards, narrow lanes, squares, and monastery compounds. Location and housing reflected wealth, occupation, and caste hierarchy. A courtyard could be kitchen approach, workshop, play space, storage route, and neighborly meeting place, usually without the luxury of doing only one job.

passages.title: Enter homes, meals, clothes, streets, and social rank
passages.text: Most families ate from local agricultural cycles rather than palace menus. Rice and other grains mattered in the Valley, while pulses, vegetables, dairy, and meat varied by ecology, means, caste, and religious practice. Agricultural history supports the broad pattern, but any single “Newar diet” would flatten inequality and western communities inside the atlas polygon.

passages.title: Enter homes, meals, clothes, streets, and social rank
passages.text: Clothing could signal occupation, gender, status, community, and ritual occasion, yet textiles survive poorly compared with stone temples. Medieval caste rules prescribed dress for some groups, while surviving images show court finery. Neither tells us every child's patched garment or every laborer's weather protection, so ordinary wardrobes remain modestly reconstructed.

passages.title: Enter homes, meals, clothes, streets, and social rank
passages.text: Urban morphology linked streets, squares, palace space, temples, shops, and residential quarters, but surviving layouts must not become a perfect caste diagram. Movement through lanes and access to ritual or market centers could express hierarchy. The arrangement reflected social power and changing use, not merely charming traditional zoning.

passages.title: Enter homes, meals, clothes, streets, and social rank
passages.text: UNESCO's palace squares and temple ensembles preserve public architecture rather than an average home. Timber roofs, brick walls, carved openings, and courtyards show climatic and craft intelligence, but earthquakes, fire, repair, reuse, and later restoration complicate dating. A beautiful facade is evidence that must still be interrogated.

passages.title: See families, women, children, caste, and coercion
passages.text: Families organized care, inheritance, marriage, work, worship, and migration, but no reviewed source supplies one representative 1650 household. Later Newar research identifies joint families, patrilineal kinship, guthi ties, caste, residence, and Hindu-Buddhist coexistence; it is a comparison, not a license to project one pattern across every earlier hill, lowland, rural, or urban family.

passages.title: See families, women, children, caste, and coercion
passages.text: Later Newar life-cycle research records girls' ihi rites and considerable variation among communities. It cannot prove that every girl in 1650 followed the same sequence. Use it to explain a living tradition and an evidence limit, never to turn all women or children into timeless performers of one custom.

passages.title: See families, women, children, caste, and coercion
passages.text: Sati appears in late-century inscriptions, including reports of women dying after elite men. The documents do not establish free consent, and one research account explicitly considers coercion. These deaths were not a romantic loyalty test. Surviving queens, donors, workers, widows, and women outside courts also prevent one cruel practice from defining womanhood.

passages.title: See families, women, children, caste, and coercion
passages.text: Reviewed evidence for children is clearest in ritual scholarship and elite imagery, not daily schedules. Later study of girls' ihi rites cannot reconstruct a 1650 childhood. A painted royal elephant calf beside its mother is court imagery, not proof of schooling. Tiny elephants, sadly, left no homework.

passages.title: See families, women, children, caste, and coercion
passages.text: Caste, debt, slavery, compulsory labor, gender, and political rank constrained choice. Legal-historical evidence confirms unfree statuses without yielding a full population count. Human costs belonged to named and unnamed people who carried loads, worked land, served households, built monuments, or were bought, punished, captured, or displaced.

passages.title: Learn languages, manuscripts, education, and a written sample
passages.text: Learning happened in courts, Brahman households, Buddhist viharas, ritual lineages, workshops, and merchant families rather than a universal school system. Reading, recitation, account keeping, performance, craft instruction, and manuscript copying demanded different skills. Access depended on status, gender, community, patronage, money, and the purpose of study.

passages.title: Learn languages, manuscripts, education, and a written sample
passages.text: Sanskrit served learned and royal purposes; Newari carried rich local literary and administrative life; Middle Nepali also appears before Gorkha conquest. Maithili and other languages circulated through courts, migration, trade, and performance. The language history defeats any claim that one language uniformly defined this polygon or every resident.

passages.title: Learn languages, manuscripts, education, and a written sample
passages.text: Written-language sample, 1670, Rani Pokhari in Kathmandu: “असल पनाली माथी को देवल”. Transliteration: “asala panālī māthī ko devala.” Published translation: “the temple standing on the asala panālī.” It is a Middle Nepali phrase from a royal pond inscription, presented here in normalized modern Devanagari for readable display.

passages.title: Learn languages, manuscripts, education, and a written sample
passages.text: The sample is not a character-for-character facsimile. “Asala panālī” is a technical place or channel expression left untranslated by the philological source, and spellings vary across transcription. The larger inscription includes Sanskrit and Newari. A royal public text demonstrates multilingual writing, not everyone's spoken sentence.

passages.title: Learn languages, manuscripts, education, and a written sample
passages.text: Srinivasa's painted manuscript covers show patron, priest, sacred book, and deities, while viharas supported copying and learning. These objects required authors, scribes, painters, woodworkers, pigment makers, ritual specialists, and readers. Education history must credit this production network rather than imagining a solitary king writing every page.

passages.title: Join ritual, festival, music, theatre, art, and architecture
passages.text: Hindu and Buddhist traditions coexisted with Tantric and local practices across the Valley, often sharing craftsmen, spaces, images, and festivals without becoming identical. Changu Narayan contains Vaishnava, Shaiva, and Shakta significance. Religious plurality involved negotiation and rank as well as the harmonious fusion celebrated by heritage summaries.

passages.title: Join ritual, festival, music, theatre, art, and architecture
passages.text: Mahanī was embedded in the ritual fabric of distinct Malla city-states. Heidelberg research emphasizes that different royal houses used different specialists and ritual programs. Court worship of Durga supported kingship, but urban participants also made, carried, sang, watched, cleaned, cooked, and organized the festival beyond palace authorship.

passages.title: Join ritual, festival, music, theatre, art, and architecture
passages.text: Pratap Malla's Sanskrit praise poem on Taleju's golden doors demonstrates literary ambition and royal devotion. The text belongs to a specific court and temple setting. It cannot be generalized as the prayer of every farmer, Buddhist household, western hill community, or low-status worker inside the atlas outline.

passages.title: Join ritual, festival, music, theatre, art, and architecture
passages.text: Seventeenth-century Malla theatre used raised dabali platforms and could draw kings, courtiers, and wider audiences. Performance joined text, music, dance, costume, carpentry, and public space. Court sponsorship mattered, while actors, musicians, craftspeople, and spectators made the event real. Even royal entertainment required a very nonroyal amount of carrying.

passages.title: Join ritual, festival, music, theatre, art, and architecture
passages.text: Seventeenth-century terracotta goddesses and late-century Bhaktapur architecture show modeling, firing, carving, masonry, and metal ornament at high levels. Getty names royal patrons but not every maker. The achievement belongs to workshop communities and material knowledge, while restoration and uncertain attribution caution against assigning every surviving surface to one reign.

passages.title: Seek healers, medicines, bodies, and health limits
passages.text: People could seek household knowledge, ritual care, plant and mineral remedies, learned Ayurvedic treatment, or practical assistance from specialists, but records favor texts and patrons. Distance, cost, caste, gender, trust, ingredients, and the seriousness of illness shaped access. No source supports one medical system reaching every settlement.

passages.title: Seek healers, medicines, bodies, and health limits
passages.text: The old Nepalese Susrutasamhita manuscript preserves a learned medical tradition from long before this card's period. Its survival and study show that physicians and scribes could transmit specialized texts. It does not prove that a seventeenth-century child in Jumla could summon a manuscript-trained doctor when a stomachache arrived.

passages.title: Seek healers, medicines, bodies, and health limits
passages.text: An eighteenth-century Kathmandu manuscript associated with the Bhavaprakasha joined a physician's knowledge with Tibetan artists and calligraphers. It falls just after this card and therefore supplies continuity, not direct 1650 evidence. Its collaborative making nevertheless warns against treating medical knowledge as sealed inside one language or community.

passages.title: Seek healers, medicines, bodies, and health limits
passages.text: Health depended on food security, clean water, warmth, housing ventilation, workload, pregnancy and birth care, injury, and exposure to people and animals as much as on named remedies. The reviewed court chronicles do not quantify infant mortality, epidemics, disability, or life expectancy for 1650 to 1700. Honest absence beats invented precision.

passages.title: Seek healers, medicines, bodies, and health limits
passages.text: Manuscript learning and specialist lineages could transmit recipes and procedures, while practical knowledge also moved orally through families and occupations. Viharas and learned households were not public hospitals. A text's presence in the Valley establishes intellectual resources, not equal treatment, reliable dosage, or safe outcomes for every patient.

passages.title: Trace water, drains, waste, toilets, and continuity
passages.text: Kathmandu Valley water systems linked rajkulo canals, irrigated fields, ponds, settlement supply, and long-lived community management. The infrastructure predates this card and crossed ruler changes. Users still experienced water through carrying, cleaning, repair, seasonal flow, and negotiated access, not as an abstract engineering diagram.

passages.title: Trace water, drains, waste, toilets, and continuity
passages.text: The Rani Pokhari inscription says water came from numerous sacred sources, and the scholarly edition notes a canal from Sundarijal. The pond and central temple made hydraulic work part of ritual kingship. Sacred water was still moved by channels, vessels, builders, cleaners, and people with very practical muddy feet.

passages.title: Trace water, drains, waste, toilets, and continuity
passages.text: A Bhaktapur institutional case study describes rajkulo supply, stone-spout drainage, wastewater flow, ritual obligations, and guthi maintenance. It draws on later arrangements and cannot automatically date every channel or rule to 1650. The secure conclusion is a layered water tradition whose exact seventeenth-century operation varied by place and repair history.

passages.title: Trace water, drains, waste, toilets, and continuity
passages.text: Later documentation records house sinks, clay wastewater pipes, lanes, drains, and compost pits in Newar settlements. It does not securely inventory seventeenth-century toilets. Therefore this card will not assign one latrine design, wiping material, or waste occupation to all residents. “Evidence missing” is more accurate than a picturesque smell.

passages.title: Trace water, drains, waste, toilets, and continuity
passages.text: The atlas ends the target in 1700 and replaces its sampled footprint with Mughal Empire, but the three Valley kingdoms, Gorkha, Baisi and Chaubisi polities, households, farms, workshops, routes, rituals, and water systems continued. Bhupatindra's reign itself runs beyond the seam. The map changes; these societies do not vanish.

At the 1700 atlas seam, “nepal-1650” disappears and all six tested member points move to “mughal-empire,” a replacement that persists in 1715. This was no Mughal annexation or Nepalese collapse. The Valley's three Malla kingdoms and numerous western states continued; a much later and wider “nepal-1783” record reflects a different political era and atlas geometry.

sectionTitles: A kingdom, changing borders and governments
Discoveries, technology and a written sample

passages.text: This record follows Nepal from the expanding Shah kingdom through Rana rule, struggles over democracy and the republic. Its 1783 start is an atlas snapshot, not Nepal’s founding date. Earlier Kathmandu Valley kingdoms have separate histories, and the changing map outline needs particular care.

passages.title: A kingdom, changing borders and governments
passages.text: Prithvi Narayan Shah’s forces took Kathmandu in 1768 and defeated the three Malla kingdoms by 1769. Expansion joined previously separate states under the Gorkha dynasty. This was a process of conquest and political consolidation, not the beginning of the many communities and traditions living within Nepal.

passages.title: A kingdom, changing borders and governments
passages.text: The atlas draws Nepal far west into Garhwal already in 1783. That is premature: Gorkha dominion there followed the invasion of 1803. The repeated 1800 outline also compresses later expansion. Its contraction from 1815 broadly signals military defeat, but these snapshots do not establish precise yearly frontiers or resolve present boundary disputes.

passages.title: A kingdom, changing borders and governments
passages.text: War with the East India Company lasted from 1814 to 1816. British victory changed Nepal’s relationship with the growing colonial power in India. Recruitment of Nepalese soldiers into Company service began in 1815. Later Gurkha service is one strand of Nepal’s history; it should not make every Nepali person seem a soldier.

passages.title: A kingdom, changing borders and governments
passages.text: From 1846, the Rana family made the prime ministership hereditary and reduced Shah kings largely to ceremonial roles. Relatives controlled access to power. Rana government lasted until 1951, so a palace bearing a king’s name does not necessarily show who made the political decisions during this period.

passages.title: A kingdom, changing borders and governments
passages.text: After the democratic opening of 1951 and an elected government in 1959, King Mahendra took power in 1960. The 1962 constitution organized the partyless Panchayat system around royal authority. A popular movement restored multiparty democracy in 1990. Nepal’s political story repeatedly turned on who could participate and who could dismiss a government.

passages.title: A kingdom, changing borders and governments
passages.text: The Maoist insurgency began in 1996, and the ensuing war brought severe suffering and demands for social change. A peace agreement in 2006 opened another political transition. In May 2008 the monarchy was abolished. Ending a dynasty was a change in state institutions; Nepal’s people and country continued.

passages.title: Homes, work and family life
passages.text: During his 1802 to 1803 visit, Francis Buchanan Hamilton described Newar brick houses with tiled roofs and carved wooden window screens. Architectural notes he included describe upper-floor benches overlooking the street. A window could let in air and light while giving a household a sheltered place to watch neighborhood life. These are an outside observer’s Kathmandu Valley examples.

passages.title: Homes, work and family life
passages.text: Hamilton also described strong paper made at Bhaktapur from a shrub’s bark, useful for wrapping packages. He reported that local production did not meet demand and that paper and raw material also arrived from Tibet. Paper-making was part of a trading world, not an isolated craft locked inside one valley.

passages.title: Homes, work and family life
passages.text: In Patan and Bhaktapur, Hamilton recorded workshops making copper, brass and bell-metal vessels for export to Tibet. Pots, lamps and other worked metal carried local skills beyond the valley. This early-nineteenth-century description reminds us that international trade could involve practical household objects as well as royal luxuries.

passages.title: Homes, work and family life
passages.text: A familiar meal described by Nepal’s Tourism Board is dal, a lentil soup, with bhat, boiled rice, and tarkari, vegetables, often with achar or pickle. Other meals use roti or a thick cooked flour dish, and momos are popular dumplings. Regions and households vary: one plate cannot stand for everyone in the country.

passages.title: Homes, work and family life
passages.text: During the Hindu festival Dashain, many families visit elders for blessings and tika, a forehead mark made with rice, yogurt and red color. The Tourism Board also describes new clothes, feasts, kite flying and village swings. A family reunion can include looking up at a kite as well as looking across a crowded table.

passages.title: Homes, work and family life
passages.text: Tharu women interviewed in Lumbini in 2025 wove grasses into baskets for storing grain, carrying things and presenting wedding gifts. Panmati Tharuni recalled learning at twelve, leaving unfinished weaving to play and returning later. Her mother started the basket’s center for her. Learning a demanding craft could happen between ordinary childhood distractions.

passages.title: Learning, healthcare and everyday improvements
passages.text: In Mugu in 2019, community health volunteer Dev Laxmi Malla brought a handbook with pictures to a mothers’ group. Training helped her explain pregnancy and newborn services through discussion and role-play. Healthcare depended partly on trusted people making information understandable, not only on hospital buildings or equipment.

passages.title: Learning, healthcare and everyday improvements
passages.text: The same Mugu programme formed fathers’ groups to encourage men’s involvement in children’s wellbeing. It also collected expectant mothers’ phone numbers so information could arrive by text message. A family health system could connect a local meeting, a volunteer’s walk and a message on a phone.

passages.title: Learning, healthcare and everyday improvements
passages.text: Tilganga’s eye-care institute, inaugurated in 1994, became a WHO collaborating centre in 2019. Its work joined cataract treatment, specialist training, an eye bank and production of artificial lenses used inside the eye. Lenses made in Nepal were exported abroad. This was both medical care and precise manufacturing, with knowledge shared internationally.

passages.title: Learning, healthcare and everyday improvements
passages.text: UNICEF’s 2022 account of Bhanu Secondary School in Surkhet describes water storage and group handwashing facilities, five toilets each for girls and boys, and an accessible toilet. Students helped plan improvements. Sanitary pads and more suitable toilets reduced a practical worry for girls. The school had reached one star in its improvement scheme, with more work ahead.

passages.title: Learning, healthcare and everyday improvements
passages.text: Afsana Khatun returned to formal schooling after completing the nine-month SAGE programme in 2022. UNICEF’s 2024 story describes literacy and numeracy lessons using music, games and drama, alongside life skills. Facilitators helped her enroll at Shree Nepal Rashtriya Secondary School in Parsa. A second route into education mattered when her first route had broken down.

passages.title: Discoveries, technology and a written sample
passages.text: After the 2015 earthquakes, archaeologists used ground-penetrating radar and excavations before rebuilding monuments. At Patan’s Char Narayan Temple they found an earlier timber-and-clay platform. Kasthamandap’s foundations proved undamaged despite the building’s collapse. These findings helped distinguish what needed replacement from what could still support reconstruction; the older remains are not inventions of the Shah period.

passages.title: Discoveries, technology and a written sample
passages.text: On 17 June 2019, NepaliSat-1 was released from the International Space Station’s Kibo module. Nepal’s Academy of Science and Technology and Japan’s Kyushu Institute of Technology developed it together. The BIRDS-3 project used CubeSats only ten centimeters along each side. A spacecraft could be small enough to fit between two hands.

passages.title: Discoveries, technology and a written sample
passages.text: The 2015 constitution organized Nepal as a federal democratic republic, with federal, provincial and local government. It recognized the country’s many languages and communities. A constitutional promise sets rules and goals; it does not by itself prove that every person receives equal treatment or that political disputes are finished.

passages.title: Discoveries, technology and a written sample
passages.text: The Nepali title “नेपालको संविधान”, transliterated “Nepālko saṃvidhān”, means “Constitution of Nepal”. It appears in the Law Commission’s text of the constitution promulgated on 20 September 2015. The sample uses Devanagari script. It is a modern written witness from Nepal, not an inscription surviving from the eighteenth-century kingdom.

passages.title: Discoveries, technology and a written sample
passages.text: Nepal’s constitutional flag description has two triangular shapes, a moon and a sun. Schedule 1 supplies a surprisingly elaborate construction method using lines, arcs and measurements. A flag can become a geometry exercise: drawing its shape correctly takes more thought than coloring a rectangle.

passages.title: Discoveries, technology and a written sample
passages.text: Political rights remained contested after the republic’s creation. In a communication dated January 2026, UN experts raised allegations of killings, detention and excessive force during the youth-led protests of September 2025. These were concerns requiring investigation, not final court findings. Constitutional government and accountability have continued to be matters people struggle over.

Nepal continues as a country. The monarchy ended in 2008; the 2015 constitution set out a federal republic. Those political transformations did not end its communities, languages, household traditions or continuing debates about rights and representation.

sectionTitles: The map label crosses a revolution
Ocean trade, illness and the toilet question

passages.text: This “Netherlands” map label covers roughly 1715 to 1800, not a single unchanged state. The Dutch Republic governed the northern provinces until 1795. William IV became stadtholder in 1747, a war with Britain strained the republic after 1780, and Dutch Patriots aided by France established the Batavian Republic in 1795. Portraits, decorated homes, guild manuals and school scenes show some lives, while poor sanitation and smallpox show common risks. Dutch overseas companies and plantations brought goods and profits through conquest and enslaved labor. The 1800 endpoint belongs to this imported map record; the Netherlands did not vanish then.

passages.title: The map label crosses a revolution
passages.text: For most of this map’s 1715 to 1800 span, the northern Netherlands was a republic of provinces, not a modern unified kingdom. The States General handled shared matters while provincial power remained important.

passages.title: The map label crosses a revolution
passages.text: In 1747 William IV became stadtholder across the republic’s provinces. It was still called a republic, but the Orange family’s office grew more dynastic. Families could disagree strongly about whether that was good government.

passages.title: The map label crosses a revolution
passages.text: The war with Britain from 1780 to 1784 battered the Dutch navy, trade and finances. Patriots blamed the old leadership and pushed for more political voice; some were forced into exile before returning with French support.

passages.title: The map label crosses a revolution
passages.text: In January 1795 the old republic gave way to the Batavian Republic. A national assembly met in 1796; a constitution followed in 1798. This is the era’s main political break, not the map’s round-number endpoint in 1800.

passages.title: The map label crosses a revolution
passages.text: A 1798 draft constitution said “Alle menschen zijn, als menschen, aan elkander gelijk,” or “All people, as people, are equal to one another.” It is original Dutch writing, though its promised equality did not include women or enslaved people.

passages.title: Homes, learning and craft
passages.text: The Rijksmuseum’s eighteenth-century rooms show how wealthy families invested in decorated houses and portraits. A canal-house parlor could be dazzling, but it should not be mistaken for every Dutch child’s home.

passages.title: Homes, learning and craft
passages.text: An eighteenth-century schoolroom print shows a teacher checking a girl’s work while a boy writes, and the teacher holds a paddle. It shows that children could learn, and that classroom discipline might be less charming than the picture.

passages.title: Homes, learning and craft
passages.text: An Amsterdam silversmith printed a detailed how-to book in 1721 and sold it through his guild. Learning a craft could involve reading instructions as well as watching and practicing, though such access varied by trade and family.

passages.title: Homes, learning and craft
passages.text: Museum collections show musicians, shopkeepers and families as well as grand merchants. Portraits record a particular person’s resources and choices; they are clues to social life, not a fair survey of a whole population.

passages.title: Ocean trade, illness and the toilet question
passages.text: The VOC brought pepper, tea, coffee, textiles and porcelain from Asia, backed by soldiers and authority to wage war. A cup of tea in a Dutch home could connect to a much harsher story abroad.

passages.title: Ocean trade, illness and the toilet question
passages.text: Dutch plantations in Suriname produced sugar and other crops through the forced labor of enslaved Africans. People who escaped slavery formed Maroon communities and fought and negotiated for freedom. Profits in Europe hid those lives.

passages.title: Ocean trade, illness and the toilet question
passages.text: War and company debts brought the VOC close to collapse; its charter ended on 1 January 1800. The people and territories under Dutch rule did not gain freedom simply because the company’s paperwork ended.

passages.title: Ocean trade, illness and the toilet question
passages.text: Crowded Dutch towns struggled with waste and unsafe water. Some Amsterdam canal houses had cesspits; poorer households might use a bucket or tub as a toilet. Emptying it was a daily chore, and waste could end up in a canal.

passages.title: Ocean trade, illness and the toilet question
passages.text: Smallpox was a grave threat to Amsterdam children in the eighteenth century. Cowpox vaccination arrived in Amsterdam around 1800, at the edge of this map span, and uptake differed by class. Medicine offered hope but not an instant rescue for everyone.

The old Dutch Republic ended in 1795 and the Batavian Republic carried political reform into the next century. The imported Netherlands record stops at 1800, but the land, people and new state continued. Dutch colonial rule and enslavement continued beyond that map endpoint as well.

passages.text: In the early twentieth century, Dutch engineers and designers experimented with ways to manage water and domestic space. This chapter pairs a steam pumping station with an adaptable family home.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Wouda pumping station opened at Lemmer in 1920 to help prevent flooding in low-lying Friesland, using steam power to move water.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Wouda installation integrated a boiler house, chimney, fuel storage, drainage canal and sluices. Water management required an entire connected system.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Truus Schroder-Schrader commissioned the house designed by Gerrit Rietveld in Utrecht in 1924. Its design expressed ideas associated with De Stijl.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The Schroder House used a flexible internal arrangement so rooms could change with their functions. Furniture and interior space were treated as parts of one design.
