sectionTitles: Finding a kingdom beyond its outline
Herds, homes and education in a later account
Objects explained by a local museum
What colonial rule changed, and what survives

passages.text: Nkore was one of the Great Lakes kingdoms in what is now southwestern Uganda. The imported 1815 to 1878 interval is a map window, not its lifespan. The outline extends far west into today’s Democratic Republic of the Congo and misses much of the Nkore heartland; it is not a reliable political boundary. Later Ankole institutions and museum objects are identified below by their own dates.

passages.title: Finding a kingdom beyond its outline
passages.text: Nkore was smaller than Rwanda and Buganda but maintained political independence through repeated pressures and raids. Historian D. A. Low places its eventual submission to British domination between 1898 and 1901, after this map window closes. Its story is not a conquest dated to 1878.

passages.title: Finding a kingdom beyond its outline
passages.text: In 1987, Andrew Reid and Peter Robertshaw revisited former capital sites linked in oral traditions to particular Bagabe, or rulers. They assessed places with potential for excavation. Matching remembered royal locations with surviving earth and settlement traces is a research method, not a license to invent a palace plan.

passages.title: Herds, homes and education in a later account
passages.text: Writing in 1915, missionary John Roscoe described herders arranging temporary grass houses around a circle, with doors facing inward and thorn barriers between them. The enclosure kept cattle together at night. This later, partial outsider account records a practical settlement design, not every family’s house in 1815.

passages.title: Herds, homes and education in a later account
passages.text: Roscoe also described clay watering troughs where cattle could not reach the water directly. Some people drew water while others controlled crowding so each animal could drink. Managing a herd meant planning the queue as well as finding the grass.

passages.title: Herds, homes and education in a later account
passages.text: In Roscoe’s account, young princes were placed with responsible chiefs to learn cattle management and community customs. Royal training could include practical herding knowledge, not just ceremony. The account was published in 1915 and should not be treated as a school timetable for all children.

passages.title: Objects explained by a local museum
passages.text: Igongo’s 2012 catalogue documents a churning gourd and a small clay pot used to scent milk containers with smoke. The latter fitted beneath an inverted vessel while fragrant herbs burned inside. These objects record skilled milk preparation; the catalogue does not date them to the map’s nineteenth-century interval.

passages.title: Objects explained by a local museum
passages.text: A three-metre papyrus-and-reed stretcher, called engozi, is documented for carrying sick people, brides or the dead in Ankole and Kigezi. It shows how neighbours could transport someone without a wheeled vehicle: a practical piece of equipment with several very different community uses.

passages.title: Objects explained by a local museum
passages.text: The catalogue’s gourd trumpet was played by herders to relieve boredom, including by imitating birds and cattle. Looking after a herd could have a soundtrack. The explanation comes from museum staff in March 2012, rather than an assumed ancient invention date.

passages.title: Objects explained by a local museum
passages.text: “Enyungu y’amaizi” means “water pot” in the Runyankore label printed in that 2012 catalogue. Its clay vessel rests on a dry banana-fibre ring. This is attested modern writing in Latin script, paired with the museum’s English translation, rather than a surviving precolonial inscription.

passages.title: What colonial rule changed, and what survives
passages.text: Under British rule, Ankole became larger even as its ruler lost independent sovereignty. Low describes Mbaguta emerging as its principal chief after rivals were removed. Political survival therefore included negotiation and unequal power, while the boundaries of the colonial kingdom differed from those of older Nkore.

passages.title: What colonial rule changed, and what survives
passages.text: The 1901 agreement recognized Kahaya and named chiefs but allowed British authorities to depose them for breaching its terms. It imposed hut and gun taxes and placed major land and mineral claims under colonial government. A written agreement could preserve titles while sharply restricting what their holders controlled.

passages.title: What colonial rule changed, and what survives
passages.text: A 2021 Cambridge museum report describes work with Uganda’s museum on returning selected objects on loan, including material representing Ankole and Bahima communities. It acknowledges varied acquisition routes, including confiscation, theft, gifts and purchases. Studying an object also means asking how it left its owners.

The 1878 map endpoint did not end Nkore. Colonial rule changed its institutions around 1901, and Uganda abolished the monarchies in 1967 under Milton Obote. Abolishing a royal office did not erase Banyankore people, Runyankore or the knowledge preserved in families and museums. The older independent kingdom, colonial Ankole and living communities should remain distinct.

sectionTitles: Cloth in daily use and burial
People and their words in the later region
A familiar gesture, and paintings saved

passages.text: Nobatia, also called Nobadia, was a kingdom of Lower Nubia. Houses, royal burials and churches reveal different settings of life. Its later union with Makuria changed political institutions while regional communities and crafts continued.

passages.title: Houses and food storage
passages.text: Early Nobatian houses at Qasr Ibrim had substantial stone walls, internal divisions and storage pits beneath floors. Straight intersecting lanes organised the settlement. The pits preserve evidence of keeping provisions within buildings.

passages.title: Houses and food storage
passages.text: Later houses at Qasr Ibrim used smaller stones, mud-brick partitions and compacted-earth floors. Some retained sunken storage bins. Building techniques changed while household storage continued.

passages.title: A remarkable game set
passages.text: A wooden game board found beside Tomb 3 at Qustul had ivory playing squares and silver fittings. A leather bag underneath contained fifteen ivory counters, fifteen ebony counters and five ivory dice. Researchers identify the game as Duodecim scripta, a relative of later backgammon. This late-antique royal burial find shows a well-equipped player’s world, although it cannot tell us who won or how widely families played.

passages.title: A remarkable game set
passages.text: The same Qustul set included fragments of a wooden dice tower with silver fittings and carved dolphins beside its lower opening. The reconstructed object shows the care put into gaming equipment as well as the board itself. Even the dice had a grand entrance. The surviving pieces do not preserve a complete local rulebook.

passages.title: Royal display and its limits
passages.text: The great burial mounds at Qustul and Ballana cover elaborate underground tombs. Rich objects and the remains of sacrificed animals and people accompanied elite burials. They reveal concentrated power and coercion, rather than the living conditions of an average family.

passages.title: Royal display and its limits
passages.text: Greek texts identify the kingdom as Noubadia and name Silko among its rulers. This written evidence helps connect political names with an archaeological landscape. The older label “X-Group” describes a research classification, not the people’s own name.

passages.title: Cloth in daily use and burial
passages.text: At Qasr Ibrim, seams and hems allow researchers to distinguish some garments from otherwise unidentifiable scraps. Early medieval cotton also survives in cushions and reused rags used as mattress filling. Cloth could pass through several uses before entering the archaeological record.

passages.title: Cloth in daily use and burial
passages.text: Early Christian graves at Kulubnarti contain unusually open cotton fabrics interpreted as shrouds. Other funerary bindings combine light plant fibres with dark wool. These finds show choices in fibre, structure and colour, but burial cloth cannot stand for an entire everyday wardrobe.

passages.title: Faras: art across political change
passages.text: The early seventh-century church at Faras was followed by a later cathedral. Surviving wall paintings were applied in tempera to plaster. Most of the preserved paintings date from the eighth to fourteenth centuries, after independent Nobatia.

passages.title: Faras: art across political change
passages.text: Faras preserves epitaphs naming clergy and locally produced pottery alongside its painted walls. These are different kinds of evidence for a religious community: written remembrance, workshop production and decorated spaces used for worship.

passages.title: Faras: art across political change
passages.text: In later medieval Nubia, painters of luxury pottery adapted motifs also found in manuscripts and church decoration. Some broken bowls were drilled and stitched together again. These repairs reveal the value attached to decorated vessels and the work invested in extending their use.

passages.title: Faras: art across political change
passages.text: Medieval Nubian texts survive in Greek, Coptic and Old Nubian, sometimes combining languages. Religious fragments and commercial or legal documents preserve different uses of writing. This later record should not be projected unchanged into the earlier independent kingdom.

passages.title: People and their words in the later region
passages.text: Two foundation texts at Faras, in Greek and Coptic, commemorate Bishop Paulos’s cathedral in 707. They name King Mercurius, linking the building to a Makurian ruler governing the northern region. These carved records help historians trace political change; the date of a cathedral’s foundation does not by itself date the kingdoms’ union.

passages.title: People and their words in the later region
passages.text: A Faras visitor named Ogijino left a short invocation to Jesus with his name on a wall. His signature survives in the published record, but his occupation and reason for visiting are unknown. It preserves one person’s wish to be remembered in a religious place.

passages.title: People and their words in the later region
passages.text: A twelfth-century Old Nubian list of church properties was found at Qasr Ibrim in a jar beneath a house floor. Its paper had been folded along four horizontal and three vertical lines. The document connects landholding with careful record keeping in the later Nobadian region. A pottery jar could hold paperwork as well as provisions.

passages.title: People and their words in the later region
passages.text: A 2023 re-reading of a Faras church inscription identifies Iesousanya as a female deacon and the daughter of Marianos Osa. The text probably dates to the thirteenth or fourteenth century, long after independent Nobatia. The original plaster crumbled after excavation, so a tracing preserves the evidence. This interpretation recovers a woman’s religious role and family connection without establishing the duties or status of every woman.

passages.title: A familiar gesture, and paintings saved
passages.text: A Faras painting of Saint Anne shows a finger touching her lips. The museum dates it broadly from the eighth to early tenth century. Curator Bożena Mierzejewska discusses silence and prayer as possible meanings of the gesture. It may look like a familiar request to be quiet, but its religious meaning needs its own explanation. The surviving image is fragmentary, so Anne’s original full pose is uncertain.

passages.title: A familiar gesture, and paintings saved
passages.text: Faras’s cathedral was submerged in 1964, but paintings, inscriptions and other objects had been removed during rescue excavations. They preserved parts of the building’s history for study after the walls themselves became inaccessible. Conservation can save clues as well as beautiful pictures.

Nobatia joined Makuria, but the timing remains debated. Proposed dates extend from the seventh century into the early eighth. This ended separate kingship while northern Nubian communities continued under changed institutions. The map’s 800 endpoint is a coverage boundary, not a verified conquest or disappearance of the population.

sectionTitles: Read the atlas as evidence about the atlas
A horde that was a political network, not a blob
Power, famine and splintering in the sixteenth century
Between Kalmyks, Crimea, the Ottomans and the steppe
The 1770s ending was conquest, negotiation and movement
Herds, markets, raids and the work of moving
Families, rank and childhood, what we can and cannot see
Learning, belief and a letter whose original is missing
Health, water, toilets, games and honest blank spaces

passages.text: Imagine a government that could move with its herds, argue through family alliances, send huge embassies on horseback and stretch influence across the Volga to Ural steppe. That was the sixteenth-century Nogai Horde at its strongest. Yet the atlas keeps one Nogai label from 1530 to 1783, long after civil war, famine, Muscovite conquest and Kalmyk pressure scattered its political center. Great Nogai, Lesser Nogai, Altıoğul, Budjak, Yedisan, Yedichkul, Dzhambuiluk and Kuban communities followed different leaders and bargained with Russia, Crimea, the Ottomans and neighboring steppe powers. Their world joined mobile pastoral skill to markets, grain growing, books, diplomacy, warfare and painful captive trading. This card follows those branching histories, then enters homes, work, food, learning, health, water and play, marking later ethnography when early sources fall silent. Russia's 1783 annexation of Crimea explains the atlas ending; it did not erase Nogai people, language or memory.

passages.title: Read the atlas as evidence about the atlas
passages.text: The exact id is nogai-horde, labeled “Nogai Horde” and indexed circa 1530 to 1783. The index supplies no alias, historical link or author-written summary. The coverage register calls it a state and records five border intervals, but those database fields do not prove one government lasted unchanged for 253 years.

passages.title: Read the atlas as evidence about the atlas
passages.text: At 1492 the exact id is absent. Tested Astrakhan and lower-Volga places sit in a broad golden-horde polygon; Emba, Aktobe, Mangyshlak and Orenburg sit in white-horde; Kuban, Azov and Crimea sit in an Ottoman feature labeled Crimean Khanate. This predecessor seam is already a rough editorial patchwork.

passages.title: Read the atlas as evidence about the atlas
passages.text: The 1530 layer contains two separate nogai-horde Polygons. The larger, unlabeled one has 99 positions and spans roughly 28.09° to 61.00° east, 44.44° to 58.21° north. It includes tested Astrakhan, lower Volga, Atyrau, Yaik, Emba, Aktobe, Orenburg and even Kazan, an enormous locator rather than a defensible frontier.

passages.title: Read the atlas as evidence about the atlas
passages.text: The other 1530 polygon has 92 positions, spans roughly 37.47° to 48.22° east and 41.20° to 46.81° north, and covers tested Kizlyar, Terek, Stavropol, Cherkessk and Kuban. Its embedded label says “Astrakhan Khanate,” yet Astrakhan itself lies outside it. That is an explicit id-label-geometry collision.

passages.title: Read the atlas as evidence about the atlas
passages.text: From 1600 through 1783 the target shrinks to one 33-position polygon around tested Atyrau, Emba and Aktobe. Lower-Volga and western Nogai worlds disappear from the id. At 1783 the polygon vanishes into Russian, Ottoman and generic Central Asian features. The redraw cannot be read as a complete migration diary.

passages.title: A horde that was a political network, not a blob
passages.text: Nogai political leadership grew from Edige's Manghit descendants. Because they were not Chinggisids, a biy could lead the confederation but could not simply claim the khan's sacred dynastic rank. Offices, councils, wing leadership and relationships with Chinggisid princes turned a family network into government without copying a European crown.

passages.title: A horde that was a political network, not a blob
passages.text: Nogai leaders drew legitimacy from Manghit tribal custom and descent from Edige. Crimean khans answered with Chinggisid töre, while Ottoman sultans stressed Islamic sovereignty. The result was not a tidy ladder: the same leader might bargain with Moscow, serve a Crimean khan on campaign and still defend his own ulus's right to move.

passages.title: A horde that was a political network, not a blob
passages.text: The terms Great Nogai and Lesser Nogai describe branches formed during dispersal, not two halves cut neatly by a ruler. Great Nogai remained mainly east of the Volga under growing Moscow pressure; Lesser Nogai gathered around Azov and Kuban in the Crimean sphere. Altıoğul groups followed another route near Emba.

passages.title: A horde that was a political network, not a blob
passages.text: Internal names multiplied because people followed leaders, kin and pasture opportunities. Ulu, Kiçi, Urumbet, Şıdak, Mansurlu, Çobaneli, Nevruzeli and Deveyli were among groups recorded in the seventeenth century. A modern viewer should imagine overlapping camps and allegiances, not colored provinces with border posts at every edge.

passages.title: A horde that was a political network, not a blob
passages.text: Some Nogai nobles entered Muscovite service and founded durable elite lines, including families later known as Yusupov and Urusov. Their careers, marriages and estates show one kind of continuity: political incorporation could transform status while preserving genealogy. It did not mean every ordinary herding household shared an aristocrat's choices or rewards.

passages.title: Power, famine and splintering in the sixteenth century
passages.text: Musa's turn-of-the-sixteenth-century confederation reached from the lower Volga and Yaik toward western Kazakhstan and influenced Astrakhan, Kazan and Kazakh politics. Saraychik was a capital and caravan place, but mobile rulers governed through people, pasture routes and negotiated submission. Calling the polity borderless would be wrong; drawing it like a fenced farm would also be wrong.

passages.title: Power, famine and splintering in the sixteenth century
passages.text: Muscovy conquered Kazan in 1552 and Astrakhan in 1556, planting its power on the Volga corridor that Nogai diplomacy and trade depended upon. Ismail cooperated with Ivan IV against rivals, yet Russian officials, Cossacks and neighboring leaders continually altered the bargain. “Ally,” “subject” and “enemy” could change faster than a herd changed pasture.

passages.title: Power, famine and splintering in the sixteenth century
passages.text: In the later 1550s civil war, ruined routes, flood, severe winter and long famine killed livestock and people and drove communities outward. Requests for seed, grain and relief survive in diplomacy. This crisis helps explain political dispersal much better than a story in which one decisive battle suddenly shattered a perfectly united state.

passages.title: Power, famine and splintering in the sixteenth century
passages.text: Lesser Nogai emerged around Azov and Kuban under leaders who entered the Crimean sphere, while groups reaching Budjak could fall more directly under Ottoman authority. Those migrations did not erase autonomy: Nogai mirzas continued to argue from tribal custom, choose patrons and sometimes raid the very partners who claimed to command them.

passages.title: Power, famine and splintering in the sixteenth century
passages.text: The atlas's long end date hides this central fact: by the early seventeenth century there was no single polity matching its surviving eastern polygon. Great Nogai, Lesser Nogai, Altıoğul and other communities had different leaders and neighbors. The card therefore tracks a Nogai political world after the original horde's unity had broken.

passages.title: Between Kalmyks, Crimea, the Ottomans and the steppe
passages.text: Oirat groups called Kalmyks pushed west in the early seventeenth century and struck Great Nogai communities hard in the 1630s. Some Nogais submitted, some fought, and many moved toward the North Caucasus or Black Sea. Migration was a strategy of survival, but every route also placed families inside new political and ecological negotiations.

passages.title: Between Kalmyks, Crimea, the Ottomans and the steppe
passages.text: Evliya Çelebi's later travels found Nogai groups from the Danube and Budjak through Azov and Kuban to Circassia and the lower Volga. His dramatic descriptions require criticism, yet the broad pattern matches other observers: Nogai life had become a transregional network after Kalmyk pressure, not a single camp east of Astrakhan.

passages.title: Between Kalmyks, Crimea, the Ottomans and the steppe
passages.text: Crimean khans expected Nogai cavalry on campaigns and claimed the authority of Chinggisid descent. Ottoman officials also relocated groups, negotiated directly with mirzas and sometimes disciplined khans who acted without permission. Nogai communities could therefore be Crimean vassals, Ottoman dependents and active political bargainers at the same time.

passages.title: Between Kalmyks, Crimea, the Ottomans and the steppe
passages.text: Sixteenth-century heroes such as Qazi and Karasai entered later Nogai epic traditions alongside memories of struggles involving Crimea, Russia, the Ottomans and Safavids. Oral poetry preserves political meaning, not a stenographic transcript. Historians compare variants and documents before using a heroic song to reconstruct a particular march or speech.

passages.title: Between Kalmyks, Crimea, the Ottomans and the steppe
passages.text: In the Pontic steppe Nogai hordes, Crimean rulers, Cossacks, Polish-Lithuanian authorities, Ottoman officers and Russia shared and contested the same grasslands and river corridors. Later Russian settlement did not enter empty land. It reordered an inhabited frontier whose residents already traded, fought, moved and claimed routes in different ways.

passages.title: The 1770s ending was conquest, negotiation and movement
passages.text: During the Russo-Ottoman war of 1768 to 1774, Nogai leaders became essential to both sides. Some allied with Russia, others stayed with Crimean or Ottoman patrons, and allegiances shifted as armies moved. Russian commanders used oaths, gifts and steppe diplomatic habits; calling every oath permanent loyalty would misread the bargaining world that produced it.

passages.title: The 1770s ending was conquest, negotiation and movement
passages.text: The 1774 Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca declared the Crimean Khanate independent of Ottoman authority but left it under powerful Russian influence. Nogai hordes did not become one independent nation in the process. They faced rival khans, resettlement schemes, military pressure and new demands to fit imperial categories designed elsewhere.

passages.title: The 1770s ending was conquest, negotiation and movement
passages.text: Russia annexed Crimea in 1783, making that year a logical atlas cutoff for the Crimean political system that encompassed many western Nogais. It is not the death date of all Nogai organization. Budjak remained Ottoman, Trans-Kuban resistance continued, and eastern Nogai communities followed histories the Crimea-centered endpoint cannot contain.

passages.title: The 1770s ending was conquest, negotiation and movement
passages.text: After annexation, Giray and Nogai resistance continued from Budjak and Trans-Kuban centers into the nineteenth century. The atlas transfer to a Russian polygon therefore records an imperial claim and major military change, not instant consent. People could cross a cartographic seam while still fighting the government whose color had appeared beneath them.

passages.title: The 1770s ending was conquest, negotiation and movement
passages.text: Later displacement carried Crimean and Nogai Tatars into Ottoman Anatolia and the Balkans, while other Nogai communities remained in the North Caucasus, lower Volga and steppe. Today Nogai language and identity continue in several Russian regions and diasporas. A state ended; a people, language and memory did not.

passages.title: Herds, markets, raids and the work of moving
passages.text: Seasonal pastoralism organized much of sixteenth-century life. One major cycle linked winter grounds near the lower Syr Darya with summer pastures by the Yaik; another linked lower-Volga winters with northern summer grounds. Routes belonged to communities and mirzas, and redistributing pasture could produce political quarrels as serious as arguments over titles.

passages.title: Herds, markets, raids and the work of moving
passages.text: Sheep, horses, cattle and camels supplied milk, meat, hides, felt, transport and exchange value. Winter cold, deep snow and livestock disease could destroy wealth quickly, because a herd was also pantry, wardrobe and vehicle fleet. The 1550s disaster was therefore not merely “bad business”; it attacked the machinery of daily survival.

passages.title: Herds, markets, raids and the work of moving
passages.text: Nogai embassies were also enormous logistical events. A 1556 report counted a mission and trading party with hundreds of people, thousands of horses and sheep; records track feed, lodging, safe conduct and market access. Such numbers are claims recorded by officials, not a census, but they reveal diplomacy traveling on hooves.

passages.title: Herds, markets, raids and the work of moving
passages.text: Seventeenth-century Nogai economies also included grain. Evliya reported Çobaneli and Budjak groups using two-humped camels to pull plows and carts and sowing wheat, barley and millet. That evidence punctures the cartoon of people who only followed animals; mobile herding and cultivation could work together in one regional economy.

passages.title: Herds, markets, raids and the work of moving
passages.text: Trade and raiding both moved wealth. Nogais supplied livestock products and horses, taxed or protected routes, and sold captives; they were also captured and sold by enemies. A child-readable history must say plainly that slavery harmed real people. It was an economic institution, not a colorful adventure attached to fast cavalry.

passages.title: Families, rank and childhood, what we can and cannot see
passages.text: Diplomatic books constantly name brothers, sons, nephews, wives, daughters and foster kin because households linked politics. Ismail tried to bind younger relatives to his agreements, while rival branches moved with women and children. Elite family evidence is vivid, but it cannot tell us the average household size or everyone's private feelings.

passages.title: Families, rank and childhood, what we can and cannot see
passages.text: Later Nogai ethnography describes households ordered by age and gender, marriage payments, parental negotiation and strong obligations among relatives. It also records women's work and authority inside families. Because those observations come from the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the card treats them as possible continuity, never as a sixteenth-century household census.

passages.title: Families, rank and childhood, what we can and cannot see
passages.text: Children learned the skills a moving household needed: tending animals, handling materials, recognizing kin obligations and listening to stories. That is a cautious reconstruction from the pastoral economy and later childrearing record. The sources do not give a Nogai child's hour-by-hour timetable, age at first riding or a universal division of chores.

passages.title: Families, rank and childhood, what we can and cannot see
passages.text: Women's lives varied sharply by wealth, age, marital status, captivity and location. A mirza's marriage could make an alliance; an enslaved woman had radically less freedom; ordinary pastoral work demanded knowledge and endurance. Later family research helps name domestic roles, but it cannot turn all women across three centuries into one character.

passages.title: Families, rank and childhood, what we can and cannot see
passages.text: Rank mattered. Biys and mirzas commanded followers and large herds; religious specialists and envoys carried knowledge; ordinary ulus members bore much of the herding and moving; captives faced coercion. Mobility offered communities political choices, yet poverty or violence could strip that choice away. “Nomad” was never a single social class.

passages.title: Learning, belief and a letter whose original is missing
passages.text: Nogai Muslim learning was real even though schools are poorly mapped. A 1550 letter mentions a foster brother who went to Crimea to learn writing. Another request sought the poet and interpreter Muhammad Yar. These are named cases of mobile education and court literacy, not proof that every camp had a classroom.

passages.title: Learning, belief and a letter whose original is missing
passages.text: Nogai leaders cited the Qur'an, the Gospels and the words of learned men in diplomacy. In 1538 a biy requested paper, saffron and six colors, evidence consistent with book production. Learned advisers, mullahs and interpreters connected oral politics to written Islamic and chancery worlds across the steppe.

passages.title: Learning, belief and a letter whose original is missing
passages.text: Evliya identified Nogais as Muslims and described a Nogai scholar who became a Qur'an commentator and hadith expert within Ottoman society. He also assigned legal schools rather too neatly to many groups. His testimony proves learned careers existed; it does not establish the exact beliefs or religious practice of every household.

passages.title: Learning, belief and a letter whose original is missing
passages.text: The safest short written sample is an archival form: “Исмаиль мирза белому князю поклон.” Transliteration: “Ismail' mirza belomu knyazyu poklon.” Translation: “Ismail Mirza sends a bow, or greeting, to the White Prince.” It appears in a letter delivered in July 1551 and copied into Muscovite embassy books.

passages.title: Learning, belief and a letter whose original is missing
passages.text: That sample is Early Modern Russian chancery language, not a surviving Nogai autograph. Muscovite scribes recorded a translated diplomatic message; the lost incoming document may have used a Turkic written register. Labeling the copied language honestly is better history than manufacturing Arabic-script Nogai words that no checked contemporary manuscript preserves.

passages.title: Portable homes, clothes and supper
passages.text: Later ethnography records two Nogai portable felt-home forms: a collapsible lattice-framed terme and a smaller otav that could be carried whole. Wooden frames, felt covers, roof openings and central hearths made houses movable and repairable. This helps explain pastoral logistics, but the detailed description is later evidence, not a photograph of 1551.

passages.title: Portable homes, clothes and supper
passages.text: Felt turned sheep's wool into walls, rugs, bags, straps, footwear and outer clothing. Household production demanded sorting, wetting, rolling and smoothing wool, with different quality for different uses. A portable house was therefore a craft project as well as shelter; its walls began as many hours of skilled work.

passages.title: Portable homes, clothes and supper
passages.text: Clothing visible in seventeenth-century testimony included sheepskin coats, lambskin caps, colored cloth garments, belts, boots and riding gear. Dress varied with wealth, trade and regional neighbors. The funny-looking part to a modern child may be packing your wall and wardrobe from the same flock; the historical point is material efficiency.

passages.title: Portable homes, clothes and supper
passages.text: Evliya listed millet bread and gruel, dried dairy foods, soups, horse meat and boza among Nogai foods, while later food studies document a broad dairy-and-meat repertoire plus grains and preserved products. His claim that people never drank water is rhetorical exaggeration, especially beside records of drought and desperate well digging.

passages.title: Portable homes, clothes and supper
passages.text: Meals changed by season, herd health, market access, wealth and region. Dairy could be processed when animals were milking; meat and grain could be stored or traded; famine wrecked every plan. No source supports one universal daily menu. “Nogai food” names a repertoire, not a lunchbox issued to everyone for 253 years.

passages.title: Health, water, toilets, games and honest blank spaces
passages.text: Sixteenth-century sources document hunger, exposure, drowning, wounds, illness and livestock disease far more often than treatment. The great famine brought malnutrition and death; an ill biy appears in correspondence, but no clinical notes survive. We can discuss health risks securely without inventing a Nogai pharmacy or claiming an unrecorded cure worked.

passages.title: Health, water, toilets, games and honest blank spaces
passages.text: Later Nogai ethnography records respected healers, practical remedies, ritual treatment and veterinary knowledge, plus sayings linking cleanliness and health. Those traditions may preserve older elements, but their recorded nineteenth- and twentieth-century form cannot simply be dated to 1530. The card separates continuity evidence from contemporary proof.

passages.title: Health, water, toilets, games and honest blank spaces
passages.text: Water followed rivers, seasonal camps, wells and weather. In the 1550s drought, one account says people dug deeply and still found little; a flood then ruined Saraychik fields. These crises show why route knowledge mattered. They do not prove ordinary water quality, who fetched it or a standard treatment before drinking.

passages.title: Health, water, toilets, games and honest blank spaces
passages.text: The checked sixteenth- and seventeenth-century sources do not securely describe a Nogai camp toilet, latrine, sewer or waste-disposal rule. Later dwelling and medicine studies also focus elsewhere. The honest answer to “where did people poop?” is that people certainly did, but this evidence set cannot document the arrangement without guessing.

passages.title: Health, water, toilets, games and honest blank spaces
passages.text: Recorded modern Nogai childlore includes counting-out, drawing lots, game choruses, teasing, jokes, tongue twisters and song appeals. Collected Edige epics add heroic performance and memory. Both repertoires changed through transmission, so neither source tells us exactly what a child heard or shouted beside the Yaik in 1600.

The 1783 endpoint is an atlas handoff tied to Russia's annexation of Crimea and expanding claims across the steppe. No single Nogai Horde had survived intact until that date. Nogai resistance, migration and community life continued in Budjak, Trans-Kuban, the North Caucasus, lower Volga, Ottoman lands and elsewhere.

sectionTitles: Norwegian farms, food and useful things
Swedish farmyards, water and health questions
Communities, craft and the limits of writing

passages.text: Although its name sounds Viking, this imported record is dated 200 to 100 BCE and covers much of southern Norway and Sweden. Those dates belong to the Pre-Roman Iron Age, roughly a millennium before the Viking-age Northmen. The outline should not be read as a proven ethnic border or a united Norse kingdom. Archaeological communities, their farms and their changing skills provide the soundest starting point.

passages.title: Norwegian farms, food and useful things
passages.text: At Forsandmoen in southwestern Norway, charred grains from the Pre-Roman Iron Age include barley, wheat and oats. Barley dominates the identified grains from this phase, while oats appear toward its later part. Burnt food and crop remains can preserve the agricultural history that ordinary unburnt plants leave behind.

passages.title: Norwegian farms, food and useful things
passages.text: Six Forsandmoen houses of one Pre-Roman type averaged about fifteen metres long and six metres wide. Researchers interpret space for both people and cattle, although the original stall partitions are missing in these houses. Estimates of household and animal numbers are calculations from the available space, not an ancient census.

passages.title: Norwegian farms, food and useful things
passages.text: Forsandmoen’s finds include a curved iron knife from one house, a horse bit from another and complete pottery vessels from two more. Each object adds a different activity to the settlement’s picture: cutting, handling horses and using containers. The assemblage belongs to the broader Pre-Roman period, not one precisely dated year.

passages.title: Norwegian farms, food and useful things
passages.text: A Forsandmoen cairn also preserves evidence that older monuments could be reused. The researcher interprets pottery concentrations as an original early Pre-Roman burial and at least one later burial from the same broad period. A mound could remain important to successive generations rather than serving only one funeral.

passages.title: Swedish farmyards, water and health questions
passages.text: At Skälby near Västerås, a 2019 investigation found houses, fences, work areas and wells belonging to one or more farms of the late Pre-Roman and early Roman Iron Ages. The wells place access to water alongside buildings and boundaries in the reconstruction of everyday farm life.

passages.title: Swedish farmyards, water and health questions
passages.text: Across Skälby’s longer Iron Age history, wet ground became pasture and hay meadows through work and gradual land uplift. Researchers describe scattered settlement and an important role for livestock. This regional landscape history spans more centuries than the map’s narrow 200 to 100 BCE window.

passages.title: Swedish farmyards, water and health questions
passages.text: Some Skälby wells were reused as rubbish pits or places for ritual deposits after people stopped drawing water from them. Archaeologists also asked whether intensive manuring and watering near homes encouraged intestinal parasites. That is a research question in the cited field report, not proof that every household suffered from them.

passages.title: Swedish farmyards, water and health questions
passages.text: At Klinga near Norrköping, postholes and hearths helped identify a small Pre-Roman Iron Age farm with a yard. Excavators also recorded cooking pits, a possible well and a pile of cleared stones. Much of this vanished home survives as changes in the soil where its working parts once stood.

passages.title: Communities, craft and the limits of writing
passages.text: Two cairns at Sømme in southwestern Norway have been interpreted as ritual constructions connected with settlement expansion and changing landscapes. Their broad date spans the Late Bronze and Pre-Roman Iron Ages. The interpretation reminds us that a heap of stones may have held meanings beyond clearing a field or marking a grave.

passages.title: Communities, craft and the limits of writing
passages.text: For a neighboring comparison outside this outline, the Danish village of Hodde had individually fenced farms inside a common enclosure. At its largest, it contained 27 farms and 53 buildings. Unequal farm sizes suggest differences in wealth within a community that also maintained a shared boundary.

passages.title: Communities, craft and the limits of writing
passages.text: Hodde was occupied for about 150 years before ending around the beginning of the Common Era. Farms moved to another village, and the old settlement ground became fields. This is a local change of land use in neighboring Denmark, not evidence that all Scandinavian communities disappeared together.

passages.title: Communities, craft and the limits of writing
passages.text: Around 100 BCE or shortly afterward, highly skilled goldwork appears in the Nordic region. Fine wires and tiny gold grains were soldered onto ornaments using techniques also known around the Mediterranean. The museum’s comparisons with the Havor and Vittene neck rings illuminate craft connections at and beyond this record’s endpoint.

passages.title: Communities, craft and the limits of writing
passages.text: No securely attested local sentence from 200 to 100 BCE is established by the sources used here. The early runestone fragments from Svingerud in Norway come from contexts dated between 50 BCE and 275 CE, already later than this map interval. Their discovery helps investigate writing’s beginnings without supplying an invented Viking-age phrase for a much older population.

The imported 100 BCE endpoint is not a known conquest or extinction. Scandinavian communities continued into the Roman Iron Age, conventionally beginning around the turn of the era, with changing settlements and connections. This broad archaeological record has no single ruler whose fall would explain its ending.

sectionTitles: Building a city from fibers, earth and stone

passages.text: Norte Chico refers here to Peru’s north-central coastal valleys and their early monumental societies, including Caral-Supe. Large centers flourished especially around 3000 to 1800 BCE, connecting farming and fishing communities. The imported 4000 to 1500 BCE span is broader than Caral’s dated development, and its outline stretches far beyond the core valleys.

passages.title: Building a city from fibers, earth and stone
passages.text: Caral’s monumental plan includes large platform mounds and sunken circular courts. These spaces were built and modified over generations. Organizing their construction required sustained cooperation and authority, long before pottery became common in these communities.

passages.title: Building a city from fibers, earth and stone
passages.text: Builders filled woven plant-fiber bags, called shicras, with stones and placed them inside platforms and foundations. A bag was both a way to handle material and part of the finished structure. Some of the city’s engineering is hidden inside what looks like solid earth.

passages.title: Building a city from fibers, earth and stone
passages.text: Researchers interpret the flexible stone-filled bags, together with stepped walls and other structural choices, as helping buildings respond to earthquakes. That is an engineering interpretation of surviving construction, not a promise that any ancient building was earthquake-proof.

passages.title: Building a city from fibers, earth and stone
passages.text: Caral’s homes differed in size, materials and location. Small rooms in the peripheral residential sector stood between the city’s core and cultivated land. Archaeologists interpret these differences as evidence of social ranking, while the rooms also held domestic, productive and ritual activities.

passages.title: Building a city from fibers, earth and stone
passages.text: House walls could use a plant framework or stone, coated with clay and painted red, white or yellow in different periods. The excavation report also describes burning waste near residences to reduce its volume. Even a monumental city had household rubbish to deal with.

passages.title: Building a city from fibers, earth and stone
passages.text: A complex offering from the Gallery Pyramid included a cord object identified by excavators as a quipu. Its hanging, knotted cords may have recorded information. No readable sentence has been established for this particular object, so there is no responsible original-language translation to supply.

passages.title: Food, music and changing landscapes
passages.text: Research at thirteen sites in the Pativilca and Fortaleza valleys found maize pollen and microscopic plant traces. Eleven of fourteen tested stone tools carried maize starch on working surfaces. Ordinary scraping, pounding and grinding left evidence too small to see without laboratory equipment.

passages.title: Food, music and changing landscapes
passages.text: Preserved human feces also contained maize remains, while fish, especially anchovies, contributed protein. It is an unusually direct clue to meals. Archaeology sometimes finds its best dinner evidence at the other end of dinner.

passages.title: Food, music and changing landscapes
passages.text: The relative contribution of farming and marine foods has been debated. The 2013 study argued that maize was a regular major food in its sampled valleys, rather than an occasional ceremonial ingredient. That conclusion concerns specific evidence and does not make every coastal household’s diet identical.

passages.title: Food, music and changing landscapes
passages.text: At Caral’s Amphitheater complex, excavators recovered a group of thirty-two transverse bone flutes near a sunken circular plaza. They were arranged in a bounded deposit, not scattered like casual rubbish. Their context links musical instruments with the ceremonial landscape.

passages.title: Food, music and changing landscapes
passages.text: The flute study identifies pelican bones as the material and investigates the instruments’ acoustic possibilities. A coastal bird became part of high-level craft and sound-making inland. Surviving instruments let researchers study how sound could be produced, even when the tunes are unknown.

passages.title: Food, music and changing landscapes
passages.text: At Áspero, late deposits include flood silts separated by windblown sand; at Caral, displaced architecture has been interpreted as earthquake damage. Researchers propose that earthquakes, flooding and coastal sediment changes disrupted livelihoods. The deposits are evidence; a complete explanation of regional change remains debated.

Caral’s principal development is dated roughly 3000 to 1800 BCE, followed by abandonment and much later limited reuse. Environmental disruption is one researched explanation for change in the early Supe settlements. Different communities and technologies continued in the Andes; neither a single conquered empire nor a vanished population should be inferred from the map’s endpoint.

sectionTitles: Read the giant umbrella label carefully
Discover local histories with several kinds of evidence
Work with ocean, river, forest, oakland and fire
Catch, gather, preserve, cook and share food
Shape wood, fibre, stone, shell and boats
Build homes, store supplies and organize work
Live with family, women, children and teachers
Care for health, water, waste and bathroom needs
Respect ceremony, images, language, conflict and coercion
Celebrate achievements, expose seams and follow continuity

passages.text: This card’s extra-long label is a warning. From 1500 BCE, the atlas stretches four disconnected polygons from southeast Alaska and British Columbia through Washington, Oregon and much of California. It calls everyone inside “North American Pacific foraging, hunting and fishing peoples.” Real communities shared oceans, rivers, forests, trade routes and food technologies, but they were never one people, language, government or identical culture. A Tlingit camp, a Coast Salish village, a Makah community, a Nuxalk family, a Yurok river settlement and a Chumash island voyage need their own names and evidence. The map accidentally agrees: it shrinks southward in 800 CE, explodes into many named layers in 1492, returns as a smaller northern umbrella in 1500 and disappears in 1530. Those are editing seams, not mass migrations or extinction. Archaeology stays local: ancient DNA identifies salmon choices in Burrard Inlet, wet sites preserve fibre and wood, and stone-walled clam gardens reveal active sea farming. Families built homes, stored food, traveled by canoe, traded, taught children and held ceremonies. No shared pre-1530 script is securely attributable to this umbrella. Living Indigenous Nations continue; the atlas label does not.

passages.title: Read the giant umbrella label carefully
passages.text: The exact record is a circa culture entry from 1500 BCE to 1530 CE with 26 observed intervals and no existing card or summary. Its phrase describes three activities, not an Indigenous nation. Fishing, hunting and gathering were practiced by many politically and linguistically distinct peoples.

passages.title: Read the giant umbrella label carefully
passages.text: The opening geometry is one MultiPolygon with four disconnected parts and 268 positions. One part covers Prince of Wales Island, another Haida Gwaii, another Vancouver Island, and a huge mainland strip reaches California. Water between shapes did not create one government, and the outlines are not treaty boundaries.

passages.title: Read the giant umbrella label carefully
passages.text: The atlas leaves tested Prince Rupert, Victoria, the Columbia mouth, Point Reyes, San Francisco and Santa Barbara outside even when nearby places are inside. It also assigns some California points to “anasazi” in 800. These mismatches expose a rough imported basemap, not missing Indigenous history.

passages.title: Read the giant umbrella label carefully
passages.text: At 1492 the umbrella yields to dozens of names. Even “Coast Salish” means more than forty independent Nations and over twenty related but distinct languages and dialects. The dense atlas mosaic is more specific than the umbrella, yet its overlaps and modern-looking borders still require caution.

passages.title: Read the giant umbrella label carefully
passages.text: British Columbia alone contains extraordinary Indigenous language diversity, and a language-family map is an evolving community-informed depiction rather than an ancient border chart. The full Pacific footprint also includes unrelated language families farther south and north. One economy label cannot supply everybody with one vocabulary or identity.

passages.title: Discover local histories with several kinds of evidence
passages.text: Olympic Peninsula sequences show changing local emphases through time: marine foods and flaked stone in some layers, then larger cedar-plank villages and differing reliance on salmon, flatfish or sea mammals. Archaeologists compare dated layers; they do not use one “Northwest Coast package” as a timeless checklist.

passages.title: Discover local histories with several kinds of evidence
passages.text: Kiix̣in preserves nearly three thousand years of Huu-ay-aht occupation in middens and house remains. Its standing village and fortress architecture is nineteenth-century, however. The site brilliantly joins oral history, archaeology and archives, while its different dates prevent a later defensive structure from being mislabeled 1000 BCE.

passages.title: Discover local histories with several kinds of evidence
passages.text: At Ozette, a mudslide sealed part of a Makah village and preserved wood, fibre, fishing gear and household objects that usually rot. The Makah Cultural and Research Center cares for and interprets the collection. Exceptional preservation reveals ordinary work without turning one village into a coast-wide template.

passages.title: Discover local histories with several kinds of evidence
passages.text: Ancient DNA from salmon bones at four ancestral Tsleil-Waututh settlements, dated about 400 BCE to 1200 CE, identified species and sex. Two sites favored male chum. That is strong local evidence for selective harvesting; the study’s laboratory methods do not authorize claiming every river used the same rule.

passages.title: Discover local histories with several kinds of evidence
passages.text: Clam-garden walls are difficult to date because beaches move sediment and old shell can be redeposited. Researchers combine radiocarbon samples, barnacle scars, shells, sea-level history and sediment evidence. On northern Quadra Island, results support about 3,500 years of use, squarely overlapping this atlas interval.

passages.title: Work with ocean, river, forest, oakland and fire
passages.text: This footprint crosses stormy island coasts, fjords, salmon rivers, rain forest, estuaries, redwood country, oak woodland and drier California interiors. A Makah whaling ground, lower Columbia root place and Pomo seasonal camp demanded different calendars and skills. “Pacific” never meant one environment or identical menu.

passages.title: Work with ocean, river, forest, oakland and fire
passages.text: Northern Quadra Island sea gardens used rock walls low in the intertidal zone to trap sediment, flatten beach terraces and expand clam habitat. They were engineered food landscapes, not untouched “wild” shore. Dating remains local, so the card never paints a clam wall onto every Pacific bay.

passages.title: Work with ocean, river, forest, oakland and fire
passages.text: A coast-wide radiocarbon study compiled 511 dates from more than 200 wooden fish traps. Building and maintaining large traps demanded cooperation and long investment, and patterns changed with settlement and climate. The compilation reveals varied histories; it does not prove one central authority directed every fishery.

passages.title: Work with ocean, river, forest, oakland and fire
passages.text: California peoples tended plants for food, medicine, shelter, clothing, tools and baskets. Acorns needed collecting, drying, pounding and repeated freshwater leaching, which is skilled processing rather than passive “foraging.” Historical syntheses help identify tasks, but individual plant use must be localized instead of projected northward.

passages.title: Work with ocean, river, forest, oakland and fire
passages.text: Lower Columbia communities linked river villages, prairies, wetlands and travel corridors. Plants supported foods, medicines and artefacts, while trade moved east and west. Families followed seasonal opportunities without wandering aimlessly. Routes were social landscapes full of named places, responsibilities, partners and boundaries that this polygon cannot show.

passages.title: Catch, gather, preserve, cook and share food
passages.text: Salmon mattered enormously in many northern and river communities, but species, runs, gear and rules differed by watershed. Around Sitka, archaeological and oral histories describe weirs, summer fishing camps and storage. Calling the entire coastline “salmon people” would erase whale, shellfish, acorn, seed, deer and other food systems.

passages.title: Catch, gather, preserve, cook and share food
passages.text: Makah evidence from Ozette includes whale bones and harpoon barbs dating back about two thousand years. Specialized shafts, toggling heads, floats, ropes, paddlers, towing and butchering made whaling coordinated expertise. This is securely Makah evidence, not permission to award every coastal household a whaling canoe.

passages.title: Catch, gather, preserve, cook and share food
passages.text: For local Miwok communities, acorns could be dried in tall granaries, pounded in mortars, leached until bitterness washed away, then cooked with hot stones in watertight baskets. It is a splendid reminder that “gathered food” can require storage engineering, chemistry, patience and a lot of stirring.

passages.title: Catch, gather, preserve, cook and share food
passages.text: Chumash island middens preserve abalone, mussel, fish, bird and marine-mammal remains with tools and shell beads. Some water-poor islands supported seasonal visits rather than permanent villages. Bones and shells reveal meals and work, while the exact menu, sharing rule and recipe still require local context.

passages.title: Catch, gather, preserve, cook and share food
passages.text: Fun fact: eulachon carry so much oil that a dried fish can burn like a candle, hence “candlefish.” Northern communities valued them more seriously as seasonal food and trade grease. The joke practically writes itself: useful fish, terrible birthday scent. Biology and later records do not prove identical ancient use everywhere.

passages.title: Shape wood, fibre, stone, shell and boats
passages.text: Makah canoe makers hollowed cedar logs, added hot water and fire-heated stones, then spread the softened hull while preserving strong grain. Replaceable hardwood gunwales protected edges. Canoes ranged from small practice craft to ocean whalers, and navigation joined weather, stars, swells, sounds and landmarks.

passages.title: Shape wood, fibre, stone, shell and boats
passages.text: Chumash tomols used carefully fitted planks, plant-fibre cord and asphaltum-based sealant rather than one hollowed log. They supported island-mainland travel and exchange, including shell beads drilled with Santa Cruz Island chert. Two excellent boat traditions demonstrate why a coast-wide “canoe type” would be false.

passages.title: Shape wood, fibre, stone, shell and boats
passages.text: Coast Salish weavers later documented coiling, twining and plaiting cedar root, cedar bark, cattail, grasses and other fibres into containers, mats and garments. Some baskets held water or cooked food with heated stones. These named regional techniques are comparison, not a universal ancient craft manual.

passages.title: Shape wood, fibre, stone, shell and boats
passages.text: Haida community history describes cedar canoes moving between villages, relatives, trading partners and sometimes enemies. Archaeological features include house depressions, shell middens, bark-stripped trees and lithics. Canoe travel connected sea and land, but exchange routes did not dissolve the distinct laws and identities of participating Nations.

passages.title: Shape wood, fibre, stone, shell and boats
passages.text: Ozette’s wet preservation reminds us how biased survival can be. Stone and shell often last; baskets, cord, handles, wooden boxes and clothing usually disappear. When waterlogged objects survive, the “stone age” picture suddenly fills with carpentry and fibre skill. Missing wood is often rotten evidence, not missing technology.

passages.title: Build homes, store supplies and organize work
passages.text: At Kiix̣in, house outlines and middens document long occupation, while surviving big-house frames belong to much later centuries. Substantial timber architecture required tree selection, carpentry, transport, raising beams, repairs and shared decisions. A permanent-looking house could still belong to a seasonal round linking several resource places.

passages.title: Build homes, store supplies and organize work
passages.text: Later Makah accounts describe winter villages with several cedar-plank longhouses, each sheltering extended families and multiple generations. Summer camps sat nearer fishing, whaling and gathering places. This local pattern shows mobility and rooted villages working together, rather than a choice between “nomad” and “settled.”

passages.title: Build homes, store supplies and organize work
passages.text: Chumash tribal history describes large dome-shaped homes made with willow branches and increasingly permanent villages supported by storage, boats and skilled work. This southern architecture differed from northern plank houses. Families used materials suited to place, so cedar should never become the umbrella card’s compulsory building code.

passages.title: Build homes, store supplies and organize work
passages.text: At Sitka, a rectangular hearth and structure dated about 1153 to 1228 CE may represent a summer house or smokehouse. Nearby pits invite several interpretations, including food caches. Radiocarbon, stratigraphy and consultation narrow possibilities, but a pit does not arrive with a label saying whose berries were inside.

passages.title: Build homes, store supplies and organize work
passages.text: Daily work included fetching water and fuel, checking tides, cutting fish, drying or smoking food, tending storage, repairing nets and traps, shaping wood, twisting fibre, preparing plants and maintaining homes. Particular people divided work differently. Archaeology preserves results more often than jokes, arguments, rest or the planning that made work possible.

passages.title: Live with family, women, children and teachers
passages.text: Makah tribal history places several generations of extended family within local longhouses. Other Nations organized houses, clans, lineages, villages and leadership differently. Kin could structure access to places, names, songs or work, but this umbrella has no single marriage rule, inheritance system, chief or coast-wide family tree.

passages.title: Live with family, women, children and teachers
passages.text: Nuxalk community maps connect families with villages of descent, crests, songs, dances and Smayustas, their histories. That evidence belongs to Nuxalk people and Country. It demonstrates why family knowledge matters, while refusing to lend Nuxalk ancestry or governance to unrelated neighbours inside the atlas polygon.

passages.title: Live with family, women, children and teachers
passages.text: Women’s work and authority varied. Pomo women became celebrated basket makers; Chumash tribal history records women as chiefs and ceremonial specialists; fisheries and food work could involve many ages and genders. Late descriptions illuminate possibilities but cannot assign one gender chart to three millennia and thousands of kilometres.

passages.title: Live with family, women, children and teachers
passages.text: Children learned language, places, safety, materials and relationships by listening, watching, helping and practicing with relatives. Modern Nuxalk camps and schools are explicitly present-day evidence of cultural renewal after colonial schooling disrupted family teaching. They show living pedagogy, not a reconstructed timetable for every ancient child.

passages.title: Live with family, women, children and teachers
passages.text: Makah canoe makers produced small practice canoes for children as well as ocean craft. That gives play and learning a wonderfully concrete object: a learner could paddle, imitate and experiment at safer scale. The evidence is locally documented and later recorded, so no imaginary coast-wide “canoe class” appears here.

passages.title: Care for health, water, waste and bathroom needs
passages.text: Smoke, sharp tools, cold water, storms, falls, burns, injury, infection and food shortages were possible risks, but health varied by place and century. At later Tlingit sites, spruce pitch is documented for fire starting, boat repair and medicine. That useful local comparison is not a coast-wide pharmacy.

passages.title: Care for health, water, waste and bathroom needs
passages.text: California plant knowledge included medicines as well as food and fibre, yet broad plant lists can flatten careful expertise. A remedy depends on species, preparation, dose, season and the people authorized to use it. This card does not invent one healer title, surgery or prescription shared from Alaska to California.

passages.title: Care for health, water, waste and bathroom needs
passages.text: Fresh water came from springs, streams, rivers, lakes, rain and carried supplies. Anacapa’s lack of dependable fresh water helps archaeologists interpret Chumash visits as seasonal; it does not reveal the exact container or ration. Water access shaped camps and voyages, but no single purification routine is securely documented here.

passages.title: Care for health, water, waste and bathroom needs
passages.text: Middens can hold shell, bone, charcoal, broken tools and food-processing remains, sometimes building into house terraces. Archaeologists study layers, seasonality and species rather than calling every deposit a careless trash heap. Waste placement was patterned, but one midden cannot provide a universal hygiene code or daily sweeping schedule.

passages.title: Care for health, water, waste and bathroom needs
passages.text: No built toilet, latrine, sewer or umbrella-wide bodily-waste practice is securely attributable across this exact record. People handled bathroom needs somehow, yet those traces rarely preserve or have not been identified consistently. The honest toilet report is simple: detailed fishing gear survives; a shared plumbing plan does not.

passages.title: Respect ceremony, images, language, conflict and coercion
passages.text: Haida community accounts join ancestors, living beings, land, sea, villages and stewardship. Other Nations hold their own teachings, restricted knowledge and ceremonial responsibilities. The card can acknowledge spiritual relationships without translating every carving, burial or landscape feature into one generic “nature religion” invented for the umbrella.

passages.title: Respect ceremony, images, language, conflict and coercion
passages.text: Coast Salish carvings and basketry have archaeological depth, including Hoko River basketry about 2,500 years old. Some objects are understood as ancestors rather than Western-style “art.” Material skill, story and ceremony can meet in one object, while meaning remains with its community and context.

passages.title: Respect ceremony, images, language, conflict and coercion
passages.text: Contemporaneous written-language sample: none is securely attributable to this exact umbrella and interval. Rock markings can carry messages, memory or sacred meaning, but they are not automatically phonetic script. Borrowing a modern Haida, Nuxalk, Lushootseed, Yurok or Samala spelling would falsely make one Nation speak for all.

passages.title: Respect ceremony, images, language, conflict and coercion
passages.text: Conflict was real but not constant or uniform. Kiix̣in includes a nineteenth-century fortress above a site occupied since about 1000 BCE; its late date prevents backdating that structure. Defended places, weapons and trauma require local study, while trade, marriage and diplomacy also connected communities.

passages.title: Respect ceremony, images, language, conflict and coercion
passages.text: Later lower Columbia records document raiding, captivity and hereditary slavery, a serious form of coercion. Practices and status differed across communities, and written evidence largely postdates this card. Naming the harm matters; projecting that later system unchanged across the entire coast and all 3,000 years would also be wrong.

passages.title: Celebrate achievements, expose seams and follow continuity
passages.text: Achievements were plural: selective fisheries, fish traps, clam gardens, food storage, ocean navigation, plank and dugout boats, fibre work, shell exchange, architecture, art and intergenerational law. They arose through particular communities rather than an umbrella government. Skilled abundance was produced and maintained, not simply collected from an effortless coast.

passages.title: Celebrate achievements, expose seams and follow continuity
passages.text: In 1492 the atlas suddenly replaces the target with a crowded mosaic of named layers. That view usefully signals diversity but mixes Nations, communities and overlapping modern-style categories. No eight-year cultural explosion occurred. The underlying peoples did not wait for a map editor to receive names, languages, laws or homelands.

passages.title: Celebrate achievements, expose seams and follow continuity
passages.text: In 1500 the umbrella returns as three northern components with 121 positions. Many Oregon and northern California points move beneath a broad “coqs” polygon, while Pomo owns farther-south points. The contraction is database reclassification, not a northward retreat, conquest or disappearance of coastal communities.

passages.title: Celebrate achievements, expose seams and follow continuity
passages.text: At 1530 the exact id vanishes. Kwakwaka’wakw, Eyak, Athabaskan, Kijkitat, Pomo, Patwin, Miwok, Costanoan and Chumash labels own some tested places, while others are blank. No synchronized fall occurred. Later epidemics, missions, land seizure and forced schooling caused real devastation, but on later local timelines.

passages.title: Celebrate achievements, expose seams and follow continuity
passages.text: Living Nations continue. Nuxalk families teach language on their own terms; Chumash children learn Samala and basketry; Chinook families sustain canoe and salmon traditions despite a recognition struggle. Continuity includes recovery, innovation and political work. The atlas id ends, while Indigenous peoples emphatically do not.

The exact umbrella id disappears in 1530 as the atlas redistributes parts of the Pacific coast among named and sometimes badly overbroad labels. That file seam is not a fall, migration wave or extinction. Later colonial epidemics, missions, violence, land seizure, forced schooling and resource restrictions devastated particular Nations on different timelines. Their descendants and governments remain: they protect Country, renew languages, fish, carve, weave, paddle, teach children and correct museum and map stories today.

sectionTitles: Making art and learning in caves
A written voice and a changing world

passages.text: Northern Liang was a regional kingdom along the Hexi Corridor of northwestern China, established in 397 and later ruled by the Juqu family. Its position connected important routes between China and Central Asia. The atlas displays a Gansu outline from about 400 to 500, but the kingdom there ended in 439. A later Juqu continuation around Gaochang lay farther west, outside this polygon.

passages.title: A kingdom between powerful neighbors
passages.text: In 397, Juqu Mengxun’s rebellion helped place Duan Ye on the throne. Mengxun later removed him and became ruler himself. By 412 he held Guzang, near modern Wuwei. Northern Liang’s beginning was therefore a sequence of shifting alliances and rulers, rather than one peaceful founding ceremony.

passages.title: A kingdom between powerful neighbors
passages.text: Hexi offered a comparatively sheltered destination for people escaping warfare farther east. Scholars carried books and learning with them, while Buddhist monks traveled through the corridor. Northern Liang’s cultural influence grew partly from welcoming skills and traditions already developed elsewhere.

passages.title: A kingdom between powerful neighbors
passages.text: Political loyalties can hide inside a date. Northern Liang artifacts sometimes use the reign names of the neighboring Xia or Northern Wei rulers. A clothing inventory dated 436 uses a form of the Northern Wei era name. These small written choices help historians trace the kingdom’s efforts to accommodate stronger powers.

passages.title: Households, food and family hopes
passages.text: In contemporary Turfan, farther west than the map’s Gansu outline, silk production grew as migrants arrived through Hexi. Northern Liang-period tax records calculate silk obligations using land holdings and household population. Family size could therefore matter to an official as well as to whoever was counting bowls at dinner.

passages.title: Households, food and family hopes
passages.text: A fragment from Kara-Khoja Tomb 91 in the Turfan region records wheat owed as land rent during the first half of the fifth century. It connects fields, a staple food and official accounting. Grain was useful enough to be collected directly; these fragments preserve part of the farming economy behind long-distance trade.

passages.title: Households, food and family hopes
passages.text: A small stupa from Jiuquan, dated 434, records Bai Shuangju’s hope that relatives and ancestors from seven generations would eventually encounter Maitreya, the future Buddha. This was a religious wish, not a report of something observed. Family remembrance could reach much farther back than grandparents.

passages.title: Households, food and family hopes
passages.text: The donor of a different Jiuquan stupa, dated 429, remembered parents and a ruler together. Such dedications made personal family obligations visible in religious objects. A stone monument could preserve the concerns of a named patron whose ordinary conversations have vanished.

passages.title: Making art and learning in caves
passages.text: Bai Shuangju’s 434 stupa survives in three stacked portions: an eight-sided base, a cylindrical body and a rounded shoulder. A projecting tenon underneath shows that it once fitted into another support. Even a sacred monument needed a practical way to hold its pieces together.

passages.title: Making art and learning in caves
passages.text: The same stupa combines carved scripture with Buddha and bodhisattva figures. The museum explains the images as linking past, present and future, including Maitreya. Text and sculpture worked together to express Buddhist teachings, so the decoration carried meaning beyond making the stone look impressive.

passages.title: Making art and learning in caves
passages.text: Dunhuang’s cliff rock contains loose sand and pebbles, making it unsuitable for elaborate stone carving. Artists instead made painted clay figures and murals. The landscape helped shape the technique: a cliff full of Buddhist images did not mean that every image was carved from the cliff itself.

passages.title: Making art and learning in caves
passages.text: Mogao Cave 268 belongs to an early design with a main chamber and tiny adjoining meditation cells. The Dunhuang Academy describes these cells as just large enough for a person to practice inside. This was a setting for concentrated religious training, with very little room for pacing about.

passages.title: Making art and learning in caves
passages.text: Researchers dated plant material from the clay cores of statues and from wall plaster in three early Mogao caves. Straw, reeds and chaff can preserve a construction clue long after their builders are forgotten. Materials hidden inside an artwork can be as informative as the painted surface.

passages.title: Making art and learning in caves
passages.text: A 2018 study combined radiocarbon results with archaeological evidence and a statistical model, placing the early construction of Caves 268 and 272, together with Cave 275, around 410 to 440. This supports a fifth-century setting while leaving room for uncertainty and alterations. The result is a date range, not an inscription naming a single opening day.

passages.title: Making art and learning in caves
passages.text: A surviving Sixteen Kingdoms manuscript fragment copies letters by Pan Yue, an earlier writer. Displayed by the Gansu museum, it illustrates the broader Five Liang region’s interest in literature. Copying a respected author kept both his words and the work of handwriting alive during political upheaval.

passages.title: A written voice and a changing world
passages.text: The 429 Jiuquan stupa includes the Chinese phrase “為父母君王”, meaning “for parents and the ruler”. These characters are shown in modern scholarly transcription of the inscription, not as a facsimile of its carved handwriting. A short phrase carries a very human list of people the donor wanted to honor.

passages.title: A written voice and a changing world
passages.text: Northern Wei’s conquest in 439 uprooted Northern Liang communities. People were forcibly resettled around Pingcheng, modern Datong. Juqu relatives escaped westward and continued resisting from Gaochang, where they controlled important routes. Military victory changed where people lived and worked, as well as who collected their allegiance.

passages.title: A written voice and a changing world
passages.text: Craft workers moved to Pingcheng after the conquest and helped make Buddhist temples and images there. Northern Liang’s government had lost power, but its artistic skills traveled with people. The small stupas and caves of Hexi belong to a history that continued beyond the kingdom’s borders and lifetime.

Northern Wei conquered Northern Liang’s Gansu kingdom in 439. The Juqu family’s western continuation around Gaochang survived until Rouran conquest in 460. Neither event ended the region’s communities or Buddhist artistic traditions. The atlas’s 500 endpoint is a coarse map cutoff, not a further Northern Liang reign.
