sectionTitles: Herds, meals and one extremely tough cat
Belief, learning and a voice on the page

passages.text: Across the lower Syr Darya, Aral shores and northern Caspian steppe, Oghuz clans made a political world that could move: herds, tents, chiefs and armed followings traveled while Yengi-kent anchored a winter court and caravan town. This was a loose, unequal confederation, not a modern nation or one uniform people. Its yabghu bargained with nobles and commanders, raised tribute, traded with oasis cities and joined alliances that shifted power across Inner Eurasia. The atlas’s 900 to 1000 date is only a display slice, and its polygon is wildly oversized, reaching from the Caspian almost to Lake Baikal. Read it as a locator for the western Oghuz Yabghu world, not verified control.

passages.title: First, read this map carefully
passages.text: The exact atlas record is approximate: one 900 to 1000 interval, one border file, and no earlier card. Those dates describe this imported display feature; they are not a founding certificate or an extinction date.

passages.title: First, read this map carefully
passages.text: The decoded shape is one polygon with three rings and 595 positions. Its box runs from 50.3267°E to 116.9634°E, an implausible span from the Caspian region to far beyond the historically defensible Oghuz core.

passages.title: First, read this map carefully
passages.text: Point tests put Yengi-kent, lower-Syr country, Ustyurt and Mangystau inside, but also enormous lands across Siberia and Mongolia. Bukhara, Samarkand, Merv, Gurganj, Kashgar, Balkh and the Khazar capital Itil test outside. The boundary is a drawing artifact, not a frontier survey.

passages.title: First, read this map carefully
passages.text: “Oghuz” did not always name the same coalition. The relationship between western Oghuz on the Syr Darya and earlier Toquz Oghuz groupings in Mongolia remains disputed, so this card does not quietly merge them with the Uyghur Khaganate.

passages.title: First, read this map carefully
passages.text: The project also has separate records for the later Seljuk Empire, an `oghuz` shape in 1100 to 1200, the Cuman-Kipchak confederation, Khwarazmian dynasty and modern Turkmenistan. They are historical neighbors or continuities, not spare pieces of this card.

passages.title: Power, argument and inequality
passages.text: The supreme ruler carried the title yabghu. Succession favored leading paternal lines, yet formal choice still mattered; rare popular assemblies and a noble council called the känkäsh meant rule depended on negotiation, not a button the yabghu could press.

passages.title: Power, argument and inequality
passages.text: An heir was an inal and an atabeg tutored him. A ruler’s wife held the title khatun and could matter at court; a sü-bashï commanded the army and might openly oppose the yabghu. That is elite education and court power, not evidence that all children attended school.

passages.title: Power, argument and inequality
passages.text: Officials collected tribute from mobile and settled communities, sometimes backed by mounted force. Society distinguished free full members from enslaved or dependent people, while hereditary begs and military households ranked above many pastoral families.

passages.title: Power, argument and inequality
passages.text: Warriors could make regional history, but “the Oghuz army” was not a permanent national force. Ibn Fadlan instead met commanders and leading households who consulted other elites and assembled armed followings.

passages.title: Power, argument and inequality
passages.text: A hard truth belongs beside the cavalry: enslavement was part of this world. Research at Dzhankent links the town to north to south traffic in livestock, furs and enslaved people; the evidence is serious, although one unusual enclosure remains an archaeological hypothesis.

passages.title: Town, road, market and work
passages.text: Yengi-kent, “New Town,” identified with Dzhankent/Jankent, sat near the lower Syr Darya, cultivated oasis economies and routes running north and east. It let a mobile court winter near merchants, grain, craft goods and river-delta resources.

passages.title: Town, road, market and work
passages.text: Archaeology complicates the capital story in a useful way. Dzhankent had older settlement beneath its Oghuz-era walls, dense tenth-century houses and several pottery traditions, but no proven palace or monumental “nomad capital” plan. Townspeople were culturally mixed.

passages.title: Town, road, market and work
passages.text: Pastoralists exchanged skins, wool, pelts and livestock for grain and crafted goods. At Jand, Muslim merchant communities probably received products arriving from steppe and forest zones. The frontier was a marketplace as well as a battle line.

passages.title: Town, road, market and work
passages.text: Cooking pots came in hand-built and wheel-thrown forms, and their recipes for clay and temper were not all the same. That variety points toward households, mobile traditions and southern workshops meeting in one town; the pottery classification is still unfinished.

passages.title: Town, road, market and work
passages.text: Finds include glass, coins, a bronze vessel, querns and storage jars. None is a magic label saying “owned by an Oghuz family”: each object instead shows what could circulate through a fortified town shared by local, Khwarazmian, Turkic and Muslim-linked communities.

passages.title: Home, family, friends and clothes
passages.text: On the move, families used transportable haircloth tents and shifted camp with animals and pasture. Ibn Fadlan saw only part of Oghuz country in 922, so his roadside snapshot is precious without being everybody’s floor plan.

passages.title: Home, family, friends and clothes
passages.text: In town, a main room could have raised sufa platforms around the walls, one or two built-in tandirs, a central hearth and a pantry with jars sunk into the floor. Imagine a warm multipurpose room: cooking, sitting, sleeping, talking and work crowded together.

passages.title: Home, family, friends and clothes
passages.text: Fun hearth fact: some ceramic fireplace supports ended in paired ram heads. A family could heat dinner beside an object that was practical, decorative and perhaps meaningful, basically a very old kitchen gadget with horns.

passages.title: Home, family, friends and clothes
passages.text: Hospitality could create a cross-cultural safety net. Ibn Fadlan says a visiting merchant might form a reciprocal bond with an Oghuz host who supplied lodging and sheep; the visitor brought desired goods. Friendship here also did the work of travel insurance.

passages.title: Home, family, friends and clothes
passages.text: Textiles, caps, leather boots, silk, spices, nuts and grain appear in elite gift exchanges. They reveal taste and trade, but a diplomatic gift table is not an ordinary family wardrobe or shopping list. Some leaders were visibly richer than others.

passages.title: Home, family, friends and clothes
passages.text: Evidence for ordinary marriage, childcare and girls’ education is thin. Ibn Fadlan’s account notices elite households and a few sensational encounters, but later epics and modern customs cannot be pasted unchanged onto every tenth-century family.

passages.title: Herds, meals and one extremely tough cat
passages.text: A 2026 isotope study of sixteen Dzhankent sheep found different birth seasons and feeding histories. Some animals grazed near the Syr Darya; others may have arrived from farther away. The city’s food system depended on many herders, not one synchronized super-flock.

passages.title: Herds, meals and one extremely tough cat
passages.text: Staggered lambing may have lengthened the seasons when milk and meat were available, and winter fodder may have included summer-cut plants or millet by-products. Those are careful scientific inferences, not a recovered weekly menu.

passages.title: Herds, meals and one extremely tough cat
passages.text: Sheep and goats dominate studied animal remains, with cattle, horses, camels, fish, birds and wild species also present. Bones show provisioning and work animals; they do not prove that each household ate every species or that meat was equally shared.

passages.title: Herds, meals and one extremely tough cat
passages.text: Querns, hearths, tandirs, cooking pots and large storage jars make daily labor visible: grinding, heating, baking, simmering, carrying and keeping supplies safe. Archaeology preserves the chores that victory lists forget.

passages.title: Herds, meals and one extremely tough cat
passages.text: Best resident: an adult tomcat dated about 775 to 940 survived broken bones, damaged teeth and other injuries while eating a rich protein diet and moving little. Researchers think sustained human care helped him live. We cannot name his owner, or prove he respected the pantry.

passages.title: Belief, learning and a voice on the page
passages.text: In 922 many Oghuz people Ibn Fadlan met followed non-Islamic Turkic traditions. Islam spread unevenly through merchants, towns, alliances and leaders; the Seljuk family was Muslim by 992, while Yengi-kent’s ruling family appears to have converted around 1003.

passages.title: Belief, learning and a voice on the page
passages.text: Written-language sample: `بير تنكرى ,  bir täŋri ,  “one God.”` Ibn Fadlan heard Oghuz speech and wrote these words in Arabic script. This is an authentic tenth-century speech sample preserved by an outsider, not proof that Oghuz communities normally wrote Turkic this way.

passages.title: Belief, learning and a voice on the page
passages.text: Coins, Arabic graffiti, decorated lamps and a signet reading Muhammad show Islamic-linked writing in Dzhankent’s contact zone. An inscribed object could belong to a resident or arrive by trade, gift or war, so it cannot count every reader or believer.

passages.title: Belief, learning and a voice on the page
passages.text: Three eggs were discovered inside a pot with Arabic writing on their shells. The project reported that the words were still undeciphered. History occasionally hands archaeologists an inscribed egg and refuses to include the answer key.

passages.title: Belief, learning and a voice on the page
passages.text: There is no evidence here for universal schooling. Atabegs trained elite heirs; wider written culture came through towns and merchants. Kashgari’s great eleventh-century dictionary records Turkic life and Oghuz words, but its sole manuscript was copied in 1266: valuable later evidence, not a tenth-century schoolbook.

passages.title: Illness, water, washing and toilets
passages.text: Ibn Fadlan says a sick person of means could be placed in a tent apart from the household while servants cared for him until recovery or death. That is evidence for social response and isolation, not proof of germ theory or a formal clinic.

passages.title: Illness, water, washing and toilets
passages.text: His next detail is cruel: an enslaved or poor sick person might be abandoned. Care depended on status. The same passage that hints at practical isolation also exposes how sharply unequal survival could be.

passages.title: Illness, water, washing and toilets
passages.text: No source in this research set securely documents an Oghuz physician, pharmacy, hospital or standard treatment. People surely tended wounds and illness, but naming herbs or cures without evidence would replace history with a costume drama.

passages.title: Illness, water, washing and toilets
passages.text: One Dzhankent house had a tiled area draining dirty washwater into a buried jar or soakaway called a tashnau. That is real household sanitation, and specifically not a proven toilet, flush system or city sewer.

passages.title: Illness, water, washing and toilets
passages.text: Ibn Fadlan complained that Oghuz people did not perform the post-toilet and ritual washings he expected, especially in winter. His religious standard and disgust shape the sentence. It cannot prove that everyone avoided washing, or that nobody had a latrine. Archaeology has not yet supplied a secure Oghuz-period toilet.

passages.title: How this political world changed
passages.text: Late in the tenth century, attempts at regular taxation helped provoke revolt among mobile communities. Seljuk-associated leaders used that anger against Yengi-kent’s rulers. The crisis came from inside political relationships as well as outside enemies.

passages.title: How this political world changed
passages.text: The Seljuk branch did not represent every Oghuz person. It moved south, adopted Islam, recruited followers and eventually won an empire. That astonishing sequel grew from Oghuz history, but later Seljuk palaces and art cannot be back-projected into a 922 steppe camp.

passages.title: How this political world changed
passages.text: The older Yengi-kent polity survived past 1000. War with Seljuk rivals weakened it, and Kipchak pressure helped break it apart around the mid-eleventh century. The clean atlas endpoint is therefore a data handoff, not the night a civilization vanished.

passages.title: How this political world changed
passages.text: Oghuz-speaking groups continued across Central Asia, Iran, the Caucasus and Anatolia. Modern Turkish, Azerbaijani and Turkmen belong to the Oghuz language branch. That is powerful linguistic continuity, not a claim that every modern speaker has one simple tenth-century ancestry.

passages.title: How this political world changed
passages.text: What ended was one confederated center of power. Oghuz speech and identity continued through changing communities. The story is less a falling curtain than a road splitting into many roads, with no single modern population serving as a frozen copy of the year 1000.

The year 1000 ends this atlas geometry, not the Oghuz. Yengi-kent’s yabghu polity continued into the eleventh century, then fractured through tax revolt, Seljuk rivalry and Kipchak pressure. Some Oghuz communities remained across the steppe; others moved south and west, and the Seljuk branch built a new empire. Oghuz languages and identities continued in changing forms. The ending is therefore political transformation and dispersal, with no single extinction year.

sectionTitles: Power, diplomacy and the map’s short window
Horses, markets and a glimpse inside a camp
Later Oirat households and practical rules, in 1640
Later books, discoveries and a small Oirat word

passages.text: Oirat leaders built changing alliances within the Mongolian world, sometimes challenging its khans and sometimes cooperating with them. This atlas shows only 1492 to 1530. Its outline is displaced far north into Siberia and misses much of the Altai and Dzungarian setting; it should not be read as a reliable boundary. Earlier power under Esen and later Oirat cultural achievements are dated separately below.

passages.title: Power, diplomacy and the map’s short window
passages.text: The membership of the “Four Oirats” changed. Powerful chiefs lacked descent from Chinggis Khan, which mattered in disputes over their right to become khans.

passages.title: Power, diplomacy and the map’s short window
passages.text: Before this map phase, Esen’s forces defeated the Ming army at Tumu in 1449 and captured the emperor Zhu Qizhen. Capturing an emperor was an extraordinary political opportunity, but it did not turn the Oirats into rulers of all China. The episode reveals how dangerous a mobile northern coalition could be to an enormous settled empire.

passages.title: Power, diplomacy and the map’s short window
passages.text: In 1453 Esen announced his own claim to the Yuan throne. A letter recorded by Ming officials invoked the old dynasty, its people and its imperial jade seal. Historian Hidehiro Okada uses this document to show that the loss of China in 1368 had not ended claims to Yuan legitimacy. A seal could be a powerful political argument.

passages.title: Power, diplomacy and the map’s short window
passages.text: The 1492 to 1530 map window belongs to a different balance of power. By about 1510, Dayan Khan had reunited the eastern Mongols and removed the taishi office that strongmen had used to dominate khans. Oirat communities survived these reversals; later sixteenth-century campaigns against them continued.

passages.title: Power, diplomacy and the map’s short window
passages.text: Diplomacy involved competing descriptions of authority. In 1488 Dayan Khan sent a Mongolian letter demanding reception for his envoys and calling himself Grand Khan of the Great Yuan. Ming records preserve that claim. Reading such letters alongside later chronicles helps historians separate contemporary assertions from stories written generations afterward.

passages.title: Horses, markets and a glimpse inside a camp
passages.text: Fifteenth-century Oirat missions brought horses, camels and furs to Ming China and received valuable textiles. At Beijing’s Huitongguan guesthouse, envoys could exchange luxury rewards for everyday necessities. Diplomacy therefore carried shopping lists as well as grand titles. Muslim merchants also travelled with these missions, connecting Oirat power to Hami and wider Central Asian trade.

passages.title: Horses, markets and a glimpse inside a camp
passages.text: An official horse market opened near Datong in 1438. Trade also included items Ming authorities tried to restrict, such as ironware and weapons. A horse breeder, a merchant and a government official could want very different things from the same market. Commercial restrictions were part of the rivalry that preceded Esen’s invasion.

passages.title: Horses, markets and a glimpse inside a camp
passages.text: The Ming interpreter Ha Ming, later called Yang Ming, describes life around the captive emperor in 1449. He and his father obtained a skin bag of mare’s milk, searched for rice and flour, and exchanged clothing for a sheep. These are unusually concrete glimpses of camp provisions, although an imperial prisoner’s meals were not an ordinary family’s daily ration.

passages.title: Horses, markets and a glimpse inside a camp
passages.text: His Chinese account calls the milk container “馬乳一皮袋”, translated here as “one skin bag of mare’s milk”. In modern Mandarin reading, that is mǎ rǔ yī pí dài. The phrase records an object in an Oirat camp through a Ming servant’s Chinese narrative; it is not an Oirat-language sentence. A flexible bag made more sense on a journey than a kitchen cupboard.

passages.title: Later Oirat households and practical rules, in 1640
passages.text: The Mongol-Oirat Great Code of 1640 belongs more than a century after this map ends. Its household provisions discuss respect for elders and assistance between relatives at weddings. Family relationships carried economic duties, as well as affection and ceremony. These are rules lawmakers wanted people to follow, not proof that every household behaved identically.

passages.title: Later Oirat households and practical rules, in 1640
passages.text: The later code rewarded someone who extinguished a fire left at an abandoned camp with a sheep. It also provided rewards for rescuing people, livestock and felt tents from danger. Moving camp did not make a neglected fire someone else’s harmless problem.

passages.title: Later Oirat households and practical rules, in 1640
passages.text: Another 1640 rule addressed help during childbirth or illness: a successful helper should receive the promised reward, or a horse if none had been agreed. The same section rewards rescuing animals stuck in mud. It records the value placed on practical assistance, but supplies neither a medical recipe nor evidence for camp toilets.

passages.title: Later books, discoveries and a small Oirat word
passages.text: Zaya Pandita developed Clear Script in 1648, long after this atlas phase. It supported Buddhist translation into Oirat and became an important literary medium. It must not be placed in a scene dated 1500. Cambridge’s cultural-heritage project documents readers and collectors who still discuss and preserve this tradition.

passages.title: Later books, discoveries and a small Oirat word
passages.text: At the later monastery of Ablaikit, excavations in 2016 to 2019 recovered small birch-bark manuscript fragments. Three belong to a Heart Sutra book measuring about 5 by 10 centimetres, written in black ink. It was almost pocket-sized. Its proposed early date, 1648 to 1657, depends on deliberate burial during construction; disturbed deposits allow a later date, possibly into the 1710s.

passages.title: Later books, discoveries and a small Oirat word
passages.text: A tiny writing sample from that Oirat Heart Sutra is “tegēd”, meaning “after that”. This is the scholar’s Latin-letter transcription of Clear Script on folio 13 recto, line 10, rather than a recreation of its damaged letters. The same word and translation are identified in another seventeenth-century manuscript, Mong. K 38. The sample belongs to later Oirat literary history, not 1492.

passages.title: Later books, discoveries and a small Oirat word
passages.text: Ablaikit’s surviving books also reveal people learning from other people’s handwriting. In one manuscript, the pen changes between an Oirat style and a more formal Mongolian style. Yampolskaya suggests that one scribe was demonstrating a technique and another trying to copy it. This is an interpretation of the strokes, a rare possible glimpse of a lesson rather than a school attendance register.

passages.title: Changing states and surviving communities
passages.text: The later fortified monastery was founded by the Khoshut leader Ablai in the 1650s. Research on its archives places his dealings with Muscovy within hopes of profiting from trade with China. Oirat politics still involved several competing leaders; calling every local ruler “Dzungar” can conceal Khoshut power. Later visitors found books among the ruins, while settlers reused building materials.

passages.title: Changing states and surviving communities
passages.text: Oirat political history continued through different seventeenth-century centres, including Dzungaria, the Khoshut realm around Qinghai, and the Kalmyk polity near the Volga. Their laws changed with migration, rulers and relations with neighbouring empires. Those branches should be studied in their own periods, rather than stretched backward into one unchanging confederation.

The map’s cutoff in 1530 is not a documented collective disappearance. Oirat coalitions endured military setbacks, regrouped and developed new political centres. Communities of Oirat ancestry and cultural affiliation continue in Mongolia, China and Russia.

passages.text: Olmec names a group of early Mesoamerican societies, especially those of Mexico's Gulf Coast. Their monumental building projects and stoneworking joined local farming communities to far-reaching networks of materials and artistic ideas.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: At San Lorenzo, communities cooperated to build large earthen platforms and mounds. These were shared construction projects beyond the needs of individual households.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Artists worked both enormous volcanic-stone sculptures and small, finely finished jade objects. Those materials could travel from distant sources.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Maize farming helped sustain communities in Gulf Coast river valleys, although many details of San Lorenzo's households remain under investigation.

passages.title: Games
passages.text: Rubber balls recovered at El Manati provide early evidence for the place of ballgames in Olmec life.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: La Venta's carvings connect rulers with watery environments and agricultural fertility. Their imagery draws on the surrounding landscape.

passages.title: Change over time
passages.text: La Venta flourished especially between 1000 and 500 BCE and was apparently abandoned by 400 BCE. That local sequence does not establish one universal fall for all Olmec societies.

sectionTitles: A river power and its households
Health, rights and a living voice

passages.text: The Omaha, or Umoⁿhoⁿ, are a distinct people of the Missouri River region whose communities continue in Nebraska and Iowa. Their history includes migration, powerful trading villages and the survival of tribal government. The imported 1492 and 1530 outlines place them in Nebraska too precisely for those early dates: migration accounts are broad, and these shapes should not be read as securely dated borders.

passages.title: A river power and its households
passages.text: In the late eighteenth century, Chief Blackbird helped make Omaha Big Village an important center of the upper Missouri fur trade. James Mackay established the nearby Spanish trading post Fort Charles in 1795. Goods and political relationships moved together through this busy river world.

passages.title: A river power and its households
passages.text: Smallpox devastated Big Village around 1800 and killed Blackbird. When expedition members visited in 1804, they described burned houses and were told survivors were away hunting bison. Their account records catastrophe, but also a community still organizing its food supply; estimates of the deaths differ.

passages.title: A river power and its households
passages.text: Dorsey’s late-nineteenth-century account describes Omaha women building earth lodges from timber supports, closely spaced willow rafters, grass and an outer covering of soil. Smoke escaped through a roof opening. A covered entrance with hanging buffalo hides helped separate the house’s interior from the weather outside.

passages.title: A river power and its households
passages.text: Housework needed more than one broom. In that same account, bundled sticks swept the lodge floor and ground outside, while goose or turkey feathers cleaned the hearth. Even before a cupboard full of cleaning gadgets, different messes called for different tools.

passages.title: A river power and its households
passages.text: Corn processing took muscle. Omaha women used wooden mortars and long, heavy pestles, commonly made from elm or oak. A smaller mortar could have a pointed base driven into the ground to hold it steady. A meal began well before anything reached the cooking pot.

passages.title: A river power and its households
passages.text: Clan membership organized responsibilities and marriage relationships. On communal bison hunts, clans occupied particular places in the camp circle, and ceremonies depended on cooperation between groups. The museum’s account describes a social arrangement in which no single clan could do every essential job alone.

passages.title: Health, rights and a living voice
passages.text: The 1854 treaty ceded extensive Omaha lands west of the Missouri while reserving a northern homeland, with a provision for an alternative acceptable location. It also promised payments and support. Reading the actual boundaries matters: the treaty did not simply say that Omaha people surrendered every place west of the river.

passages.title: Health, rights and a living voice
passages.text: Susan La Flesche Picotte finished first in her medical-school class and returned to care for her people. After marrying and having two sons, she continued practicing and sometimes took the children on house calls. Her work joined professional achievement with the everyday difficulty of reaching scattered patients.

passages.title: Health, rights and a living voice
passages.text: Picotte taught sick patients to use separate washing basins and towels from other family members to reduce the spread of illness. She sometimes cooked for families and stayed overnight with very ill patients. Healthcare involved clean household routines and food as well as medicines.

passages.title: Health, rights and a living voice
passages.text: Her public-health work included drinking fountains in schools, examinations for schoolchildren and local health inspections. In January 1913, her hospital opened at Walthill, serving Indigenous and white patients. Its maternity and operating rooms, kitchen and bathrooms made organized care available nearer to home.

passages.title: Health, rights and a living voice
passages.text: Picotte also helped neighbors understand wills and recover unpaid rent. In 1911, more than sixty Omaha gathered at her home to discuss a bill protecting wives’ and children’s inheritance rights. She addressed her community in Omaha, connecting language, law and the practical needs of families.

passages.title: Health, rights and a living voice
passages.text: Omaha researcher Francis La Flesche helped preserve voices using wax-cylinder recording. The Library of Congress explains that he probably made most of the Omaha recordings in his collaboration with Alice Fletcher. The surviving cylinders preserve performances as sound, beyond what musical notes or a written description can capture.

passages.title: Health, rights and a living voice
passages.text: The Sacred Pole returned from Harvard’s Peabody Museum to Omaha care in 1989, after more than a century away. The tribal council arranged the return, celebrated at the powwow. The university museum’s account presents it as an important renewal of community relationships and responsibility.

passages.title: Health, rights and a living voice
passages.text: The Tribe’s October 2024 newsletter prints “Táxti kigthígthoⁿi-kʰe”, translated there as “When the Deer Rut”. The seasonal expression refers to the deer mating season. This is an attested modern Omaha spelling in a community publication, rather than a sentence invented for the early map period.

passages.title: Health, rights and a living voice
passages.text: That newsletter also explains the language department’s aim of making Umoⁿhoⁿ part of daily life. It describes gathering resources and planning with community programs so people have more opportunities to speak. Preserving a word in a document and using it with another person are connected kinds of work.

The map’s cutoffs do not end Omaha history. Epidemics, land cessions and federal policies changed the community’s territory and institutions, but the Omaha Tribe continues. Its families and programs keep working on health, language, cultural responsibilities and the next generation’s wellbeing.

sectionTitles: One map label, several very different political orders
Indian Ocean power, cultural exchange and coerced labour
Forts, government, learning and water engineering
Homes, harvests, markets and school days
Two excellent kid facts, and the atlas’s misleading finish line

passages.text: This card covers atlas id oman, an approximate 1530-1914 sequence of eleven display intervals. It is not a single unchanging state: the range crosses Portuguese-held Muscat, the Ya‘ruba imamate, Al Bu Said rule, an overseas empire and a diminished coastal sultanate. The identical 1530-1715 polygon excludes every tested Omani city, including Muscat and Nizwa. From 1783 to 1914 the shapes include only Nizwa and Duqm among the tested domestic sites; they still omit Muscat, Sohar, Sur, Salalah, Mirbat, Khasab and Buraimi. No oman shape includes tested Hormuz, Gwadar, Zanzibar, Mombasa, Lamu, Pemba or Kilwa. The later oman-1945 modern geometry finally includes most tested core cities. These are poor locators, not control maps. The 1530 start is not a founding date, and 1914 is not dissolution. Separate muscat-and-oman (1938-1945) and oman-1945 (1945-open) records leave an atlas gap from 1914 to 1938.

passages.title: One map label, several very different political orders
passages.text: The atlas opens in 1530, but “Oman” was not founded that year. Portuguese forces had appeared at Muscat in 1507 and later held fortified coastal positions, while inland towns, tribal coalitions and imams followed their own politics. A 1915 British compilation is useful for the sequence, yet its categories and spellings come from an imperial archive. The safest reading is a region with overlapping power, not a neat national polygon waiting to become modern Oman.

passages.title: One map label, several very different political orders
passages.text: In 1624 Nasir bin Murshid was elected the first Ya‘ruba imam. He fought to unite rival communities and weaken Portuguese positions; his successor Sultan bin Saif captured Muscat in 1650. The achievement was political and military, not a magic moment when every corner of today’s Oman instantly obeyed one administration. It also explains a major atlas failure: the 1650 shape does not even contain the tested point for Muscat.

passages.title: One map label, several very different political orders
passages.text: Victory at Muscat helped Ya‘ruba rulers build naval power toward East Africa. A disputed succession fed factional war, and Persian expeditions occupied parts of Oman in 1737-1744. Ahmad bin Said, governor of Sohar, emerged from the crisis, drove out Persian forces and was elected imam, beginning the Al Bu Said era.

passages.title: One map label, several very different political orders
passages.text: Al Bu Said rule changed titles and centres without erasing the older imamate ideal. Muscat grew as the dynastic and commercial capital, while claims to elected Ibadi leadership remained powerful in the interior. A treaty with Britain in 1798 and another with the United States in 1833 expanded diplomacy and commerce. Those connections brought opportunity, but they also gave foreign powers more tools to shape Omani finance and politics.

passages.title: Indian Ocean power, cultural exchange and coerced labour
passages.text: Said bin Sultan’s realm connected Muscat, ports on the Iranian and Makran coasts and a growing East African domain. Around 1840 he made Zanzibar his main court; the Omani National Museum calls this a capital transfer. Ships, sailors and merchants moved dates, fish, grain, ivory, cloves, timber and manufactured goods around the ocean. Authority was uneven and depended on ports, local partners and maritime routes, so “empire” never meant one uniform administration painted solidly across every coast.

passages.title: Indian Ocean power, cultural exchange and coerced labour
passages.text: Stone Town was not simply “Oman overseas.” UNESCO describes a Swahili trading city whose coral-rag houses, narrow streets, courtyards and carved doors blended African, Arab, Indian and European practices. Omani dynastic rule and foreign merchants reshaped it, but Swahili residents and builders were agents in its history. Its surviving architecture records exchange, inequality and local creativity; it should not be credited to a single sultan or treated as a copy of Muscat.

passages.title: Indian Ocean power, cultural exchange and coerced labour
passages.text: The empire’s prosperity carried a brutal cost. The Zanzibar nomination dossier says that by the mid-nineteenth century more than 20,000 enslaved people were being imported, with about half absorbed by island clove plantations and many others re-exported. Omani Arab owners were prominent, though not the only slaveholders. People seized from African communities produced wealth under coercion; describing cloves and ivory as ordinary “trade goods” without them would hide the human machinery of the economy.

passages.title: Indian Ocean power, cultural exchange and coerced labour
passages.text: An 1845 agreement, effective in 1847, promised to stop slave exports from the sultan’s African dominions and imports into his Asian possessions, and let British ships seize some offending vessels. Yet it explicitly excepted transport within a broad East African zone including Zanzibar, Pemba and Mafia. This was a restriction, not emancipation: it neither freed people already enslaved nor immediately ended plantation labour or trafficking. The treaty itself shows why a proclamation date must not be mistaken for lived freedom.

passages.title: Indian Ocean power, cultural exchange and coerced labour
passages.text: Said bin Sultan died in 1856, and his sons Thuwaini and Majid held Muscat and Zanzibar respectively. Lord Canning’s 1861 British arbitration declared the two inheritances distinct and required Zanzibar to pay Muscat an annual subsidy. That settlement ended the united dynastic realm; it did not end Omani families, language, religious networks or memories in East Africa. Later Zanzibar history, including the final closure of its slave market, belongs to Zanzibar’s separate political record.

passages.title: Indian Ocean power, cultural exchange and coerced labour
passages.text: After separation, the sultans of Muscat were officially independent yet increasingly depended on British money and force. In 1891 the sultan pledged not to cede, sell, mortgage or otherwise place territory under another power except Britain. Britain later supported coastal rulers against interior opponents. “Independent” and “under strong imperial influence” can both be true; calling Oman either a simple British colony or completely unconstrained misses the documented relationship.

passages.title: Forts, government, learning and water engineering
passages.text: Jabreen, built in 1675 for Imam Bil‘arab bin Sultan, was more than a battle box. Its plan joined residence, government and learning: meeting rooms, a courtroom, living quarters, kitchen, date stores, guardrooms and spaces associated with administrative and religious study. It also had prisons and nasty defensive openings for pouring boiling oil or date molasses. Kid verdict: a castle where homework, court cases, dinner and extremely sticky defence could happen under one roof.

passages.title: Forts, government, learning and water engineering
passages.text: Bahla Fort is a useful warning against giving every old building to the period on this card. UNESCO dates the oasis’s great Banu Nebhan phase to the twelfth through fifteenth centuries, before the atlas’s 1530 start. Later rulers repaired and occupied parts of the complex, but the mud-brick fort, family compounds, market, mosques, sablas, bath houses and falaj form a layered settlement. It is heritage located in Oman, not a construction project of the modern sultanate or one dynasty.

passages.title: Forts, government, learning and water engineering
passages.text: Aflaj made permanent settlement possible in dry country by carrying groundwater or spring water downhill through surface and underground channels. Communities divided flow in timed shares, sometimes read against a sundial, and maintained the system together. Water supported date palms, other crops and domestic use; access was therefore economic and political power. UNESCO’s roughly 3,000 functioning systems demonstrate endurance, but its ancient origin evidence does not mean every channel visible today was dug in 500 CE, or by the rulers on this card.

passages.title: Forts, government, learning and water engineering
passages.text: A heritage description of Fiqain Fort records a seven-metre well connected through the floors and a washing or bathing basin on each level. That is clever vertical water access inside a fortified elite building, not evidence of taps in every village house. The source does not identify a universal household toilet system. When evidence is thin, the honest answer is “we do not know one standard”, much better than installing imaginary palace plumbing with a historian’s wrench.

passages.title: Homes, harvests, markets and school days
passages.text: At Harat al-Sulaif, founded in the Ya‘ruba era, people shifted residence with the agricultural calendar: during the date harvest many lived among the palm gardens, returning to the fortified settlement afterward. Houses were often two-storey mud-brick buildings with courtyards and decorated rooms. The market had livestock auctions, vegetable sellers, tailors, blacksmiths and weapon makers. This is one documented community, not a template for coastal sailors, Dhofari pastoralists, enslaved workers or every Omani family.

passages.title: Homes, harvests, markets and school days
passages.text: Homes could double as family archives. At the eighteenth-century al-Bait al-‘Aod, generations wrote births, deaths and other important events upstairs; its windows and doors came from India. In Musandam, one-room lock houses stored food and water in jars too large to fit through the finished doorway, so the jars went in during construction. These museum examples show family memory, seasonal movement and ocean trade in wood and craft, plus the ancient truth that storage planning matters before you build the door.

passages.title: Homes, harvests, markets and school days
passages.text: From the seventeenth through nineteenth centuries, many children’s first formal lessons took place in kuttab, where Qur’an recitation anchored elementary learning. Students who completed that stage could join mosque circles in centres such as Nizwa, Rustaq, Bahla, al-Mudhaibi and al-Hamra for religious, literary and historical subjects. This was not a universal public-school system: access, duration and curriculum varied, and the museum account does not justify assuming that all children, girls and boys, studied alike.

passages.title: Homes, harvests, markets and school days
passages.text: An authentic written sample appears on a copper coin minted in 1894: فيصل بن تركي بن سعيد امام مسقط وعمان. Arabic reads right to left. Editorial transliteration: Fayṣal bin Turkī bin Saʿīd, imām Masqaṭ wa-ʿUmān. Close translation: “Faisal bin Turki bin Said, Imam of Muscat and Oman.” It is the reverse legend of the Baisa al-Jalali, alongside English, not a sentence from everyday conversation. The title on a coin expresses rulership; it does not prove control of every place claimed.

passages.title: Healing, hospitals, water and sanitation
passages.text: Most healing happened long before a public biomedical system existed. A Ministry of Health-authored review documents oral plant knowledge passed by elders and healers, with remedies prepared as infusions, pastes, poultices or smoke; frankincense was among the plants used. Its evidence comes from later fieldwork, so it supports continuity of inherited practice rather than proving that every listed remedy had the same recipe in 1600. “Traditional” also does not automatically mean safe or clinically effective.

passages.title: Healing, hospitals, water and sanitation
passages.text: Nineteenth-century biomedicine arrived unevenly: visiting practitioners and court physicians came first, then a small British Agency hospital after 1861, the Arabian Mission from 1893 and a Muttrah clinic in 1904. Services clustered around Muscat and often favoured troops, foreigners or elites before missionary care widened access. Cholera struck in 1821, 1864 and 1899; plague was reported in Muttrah in 1899-1900. The medical history links epidemic risk to population movement, poor sanitation and unreliable clean water. Fort baths existed, but a flush-toilet fairy had not visited every home.

passages.title: Two excellent kid facts, and the atlas’s misleading finish line
passages.text: The Sultanah was built in Bombay in 1833 and sailed from Zanzibar to New York with an Omani envoy and gifts in 1840. The crossing took 87 days; two years later the ship carried another mission to London. A museum reconstruction also shows a nineteenth-century fishing badan with planks stitched using coconut rope. Kid challenge: imagine trusting your lunch, letters and diplomatic presents to a wooden ship for almost three months, with zero airport snacks.

passages.title: Two excellent kid facts, and the atlas’s misleading finish line
passages.text: In 1913 supporters of an elected Ibadi imam under Salim bin Rashid al-Kharusi rose against the sultan. Interior centres including Nizwa, Izki and Awabi came under their control, while British Indian troops and ships backed the sultan’s coastal position. The archive calls the movement a “rebellion”; the card names the competing political claim instead of treating the imperial label as the only viewpoint. This conflict was active when the atlas polygon stops in 1914.

The oman atlas record ends in 1914, but Oman did not. Fighting between the coastal sultanate and the interior imamate continued; the 1920 Treaty of As Sib left the sultan governing Muscat and coastal towns and the imam governing an autonomous interior. Later consolidation, oil-era conflict and the 1970 change from “Sultanate of Muscat and Oman” to “Sultanate of Oman” belong with the later muscat-and-oman and oman-1945 cards. The dataset has no Oman record for 1914-1938, so its blank is a coverage gap, not a vanished country or people.

sectionTitles: A sultanate through conflict, reform and succession
Oil, work and inventions inherited from deep history
Coffee signals, dancing daggers and family craft
School, health, clean water and toilets that children notice

passages.text: This is the modern Omani sultanate record, not a state created in 1945. It continues the older Sultanate of Muscat and Oman represented by the distinct muscat-and-oman record through 1945; the separate oman record covers a still earlier imported interval. Five broad MultiPolygon snapshots run from 1945-1960 through 2010-2020 while the indexed lifetime remains open. Point tests place Sohar, Nizwa, Duqm and Mirbat inside the first shape, but Muscat, Khasab, Sur, Salalah and Buraimi outside it; later snapshots still omit several major coastal points. Treat the outline as approximate atlas coverage, not a surveyed border or a claim that those cities were outside Oman.

passages.title: A sultanate through conflict, reform and succession
passages.text: The atlas begins in 1945 during Sultan Said bin Taymur’s rule, when the state was called the Sultanate of Muscat and Oman. It was politically divided between the coast and a contested interior, and later faced a rebellion in Dhofar. Said restricted travel, education and development even as oil income began to arrive. These conditions explain why many Omanis remember 1970, rather than 1945, as the great political and social turning point.

passages.title: A sultanate through conflict, reform and succession
passages.text: On 23 July 1970, Qaboos bin Said replaced his father in a palace coup. A contemporary UN report records the change and the shortening of “Sultanate of Muscat and Oman” to “Sultanate of Oman.” Oman joined the United Nations on 7 October 1971. The new name and international membership marked a new phase of government, not the sudden invention of an Omani people.

passages.title: A sultanate through conflict, reform and succession
passages.text: The Dhofar war did not end with the 1970 coup. Qaboos’s forces, backed by Britain, Iran and regional allies, defeated the insurgency by 1975 while oil revenue funded roads, wells, schools and clinics intended to win support as well as develop the country. A U.S. diplomatic memo also warned that nearly all export earnings and government revenue then came from petroleum. Modernization and counterinsurgency were intertwined, and the new state was financially vulnerable.

passages.title: A sultanate through conflict, reform and succession
passages.text: Oman built a foreign policy around maintaining relations with rivals. Its foreign ministry points to constructive neutrality during the Iran-Iraq war, participation in the Gulf Cooperation Council from 1981, later border settlements and mediation between states that were not speaking directly. “Friend to all” is the government’s slogan, but the documented achievement is practical: keeping channels open when neighbouring governments quarrel.

passages.title: A sultanate through conflict, reform and succession
passages.text: Under the current Basic Law, the sultan is head of state and holds central executive authority. A Council of Ministers assists him, while the Council of Oman has an appointed State Council and an elected Shura Council. Citizens elect the lower chamber, but that does not make the cabinet answerable to a parliamentary majority. The system combines consultation and elections with concentrated monarchical power.

passages.title: A sultanate through conflict, reform and succession
passages.text: A short sample of official written Arabic is سلطنة عمان دولة عربية إسلامية مستقلة ذات سيادة تامة. It means, “The Sultanate of Oman is an Arab Islamic independent state with full sovereignty.” This is Article 1 of the 2021 Basic Law. Arabic is read right to left, so the sentence begins at سلطنة عمان, “the Sultanate of Oman.” It is a modern legal sample, not a claim that every Omani speaks or writes in exactly the same way.

passages.title: Oil, work and inventions inherited from deep history
passages.text: Oil paid for much of Oman’s modern infrastructure, but dependence remains a constraint. The IMF’s 2025 review found continuing non-oil growth while judging diversification behind some Gulf peers and estimating youth unemployment at 12.5 percent. A fall in oil prices can still squeeze public finances and jobs. New sectors, private employment and useful skills matter because a pipeline cannot employ every young person forever.

passages.title: Oil, work and inventions inherited from deep history
passages.text: A 2023 social-protection law provides 14 weeks of job-protected maternity leave and seven days of paternity leave at full pay for employed Omani and non-Omani parents. The ILO also says key provisions were to be phased over three years and describes migrant-worker inclusion as gradual. That caveat matters: passing a law is the start of changing a family’s budget during a new baby’s first weeks, not proof that every eligible worker immediately received the benefit.

passages.title: Oil, work and inventions inherited from deep history
passages.text: At Bat, Al-Khutm and Al-Ayn, archaeologists study settlements, towers and large stone tombs from the third millennium BCE. Cuneiform records connect ancient Magan with copper production and trade. The stones stand inside modern Oman, but their builders lived roughly five thousand years before this atlas record and did not call their country the Sultanate of Oman. This is inherited archaeological heritage, not a post-1945 national invention.

passages.title: Oil, work and inventions inherited from deep history
passages.text: Oman’s aflaj move spring or groundwater downhill through channels without pumps. UNESCO counted about 3,000 systems still operating when the heritage site was nominated. Communities divide flow by time shares, sometimes measured with a sundial, so water management joins engineering, law and neighbourly negotiation. Some irrigation evidence in Oman reaches back to about 2500 BCE, while the listed systems’ origins may be much later. Falling groundwater is a modern threat.

passages.title: Coffee signals, dancing daggers and family craft
passages.text: Arabic coffee has a tiny piece of hand-language. At a gathering, the server offers elders and guests first and uses the right hand. A guest who wants no more gently shakes the little cup; otherwise it may be refilled. Congratulations, you can now say “my caffeine tank is full” without a sentence. UNESCO lists this as a shared regional tradition, so Oman participates in it but did not invent it alone.

passages.title: Coffee signals, dancing daggers and family craft
passages.text: Al-Bar’ah is a Dhofari music-and-dance tradition performed at weddings and festivities. A semicircle of men and women claps and sings while drums and a flute play; two men holding khanjars dance at the centre. UNESCO notes participation across age and social background. The blades are part of a controlled performance, not an invitation to improvise sword-fighting at cousin Ahmed’s wedding.

passages.title: Coffee signals, dancing daggers and family craft
passages.text: The Omani khanjar is a curved dagger assembled from several crafts: a handle and blade, a scabbard, belt and decorated cover using materials such as wood, leather, cloth and silver. Men wear it for major national, religious and family occasions, including weddings. Craftspeople pass specialized skills through families and workshops. It is a ceremonial symbol and carefully made object, not everyday playground equipment.

passages.title: School, health, clean water and toilets that children notice
passages.text: In 1970 Oman had only three formal schools, serving 909 boys. By 2005 the UNESCO-UNEVOC report counted 1,045 government schools and more than half a million pupils, including girls. That expansion is one of the clearest changes after 1970. Numbers of desks and buildings do not by themselves measure teaching quality, but they show how quickly formal education moved from a tiny male system toward mass schooling.

passages.title: School, health, clean water and toilets that children notice
passages.text: Geography can make a school journey an adventure before the lesson begins. Kumzar, at the tip of Musandam, is reachable only by boat. At another remote school in Lima, UNICEF visitors watched pupils use hydroponics to grow plants and learn about farming with little soil. These are individual child-friendly-school examples, but they show teachers adapting science and access to mountain-and-sea communities rather than assuming every pupil lives beside a highway.

passages.title: School, health, clean water and toilets that children notice
passages.text: Access is still uneven for children with disabilities. UNICEF estimated about 16,000 Omani children with disabilities in 2023 and reported that specialist services were concentrated in cities, with shortages of trained teachers and social workers and gaps in early identification and consistent data. A legal promise of inclusion needs ramps, transport, skilled adults and good records before it becomes an ordinary school day.

passages.title: School, health, clean water and toilets that children notice
passages.text: Oman introduced the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness approach in 1999. It trains primary-care workers to look at a child as a whole: several possible illnesses, nutrition, vaccination, caregiver advice and referral, rather than one symptom in isolation. That is useful where the same fever may need very different responses. A national programme, however, cannot guarantee that every family reaches a clinic quickly or receives identical care.

passages.title: School, health, clean water and toilets that children notice
passages.text: UNICEF reported that child mortality had fallen by about 70 percent since 1990 by the time of Oman’s 2017 national nutrition survey. The same survey measured continuing problems such as anaemia and unhealthy growth patterns. Children surviving at much higher rates is a major achievement; making sure they grow well is a different task. Public health can celebrate one graph while still worrying about the next one.

passages.title: School, health, clean water and toilets that children notice
passages.text: UNICEF’s SDG profile estimated that in 2022 about 92 percent of people used at least basic drinking water, 91 percent used safely managed drinking water and 99 percent used basic sanitation; reported open defecation was near zero. These national percentages are high, but they do not mean every remote settlement has the same supply reliability or that every school toilet is child-friendly.

passages.title: School, health, clean water and toilets that children notice
passages.text: In schools examined for a UNICEF child-friendly-school evaluation, observers found pupil toilets clearly labelled and participants described them as kept clean; respondents also noticed more monitoring of drinking-water quality. That is a modest but meaningful finding. Children cannot concentrate on fractions if they are calculating how long they can avoid a filthy toilet. The evaluation covered selected schools, so it should guide improvement rather than stand in for a nationwide toilet census.

Oman continues as a sovereign sultanate under Haitham bin Tarik. The atlas’s final geometry interval ends in 2020 because the imported border series stops there, not because Oman ended. The central transition inside this record came in 1970: a new sultan, a shorter official name, the opening of schools and services, and the final years of the Dhofar war. Today’s state carries older Omani communities, trade routes, water institutions and archaeological landscapes forward while facing the practical limits of oil dependence, jobs, inclusion and scarce water.

sectionTitles: Paddles, nails and a raised palace
Later accounts: festival errands and town work

passages.text: Opobo was a Niger Delta trading kingdom established by Jaja after conflict at Bonny. The map’s 1878 to 1914 window spans royal control, British intervention and colonial rule. Its rivers connected producers and Atlantic merchants.

passages.title: Households that were also institutions
passages.text: A Niger Delta trading House was more than one building. It combined relatives, dependants and enslaved people within an organization that conducted trade and exercised local authority. Family membership, work and politics overlapped, but members did not all enjoy equal freedom or power.

passages.title: Households that were also institutions
passages.text: Jaja rose from enslavement to become a powerful House head and king. His extraordinary career shows that social advancement was possible in this system. It does not erase slavery: other people remained controlled as labourers, and their freedom became a major political question under colonial rule.

passages.title: Paddles, nails and a raised palace
passages.text: A Smithsonian photograph catalogued between 1877 and 1895 describes roughly thirty paddlers in Sam Yubis’s canoe at Opobo. Moving such a vessel required a crew working together. The archive’s old caption calls them canoe boys, but does not establish their ages or whether they were free.

passages.title: Paddles, nails and a raised palace
passages.text: An 1886 visitor reported a forge where four men made nails. One worked two skin bellows alternately to feed the fire, while the metal was hammered into shape. Nails may seem a small achievement until a boat, roof or wooden house needs to stay together.

passages.title: Paddles, nails and a raised palace
passages.text: The same visitor described Jaja’s painted wooden palace standing on piles about eight feet high, with a surrounding veranda. Craftspeople from Accra had built it. The account connects an Opobo royal building with skilled workers travelling along the West African coast.

passages.title: Paddles, nails and a raised palace
passages.text: At the royal meal, the visitor described goat, fish and fowl served in large clay bowls, with palm oil and spices. This was a particular banquet for guests, rather than a menu for every family. It offers a rare, dated glimpse of hospitality at Jaja’s court.

passages.title: Treaties, writing and colonial coercion
passages.text: The 1873 agreement recognized Jaja as king and restricted European trading establishments in Opobo. Later British demands to enter inland markets challenged those arrangements. Control of the river meant control of commercial access, making treaty language economically important.

passages.title: Treaties, writing and colonial coercion
passages.text: In an English letter dated 26 March 1886, Jaja defended “our laws, rights and privileges of our markets”. In plain language, he insisted that British protection should not cancel Opobo’s authority over its own commerce. This is an attested diplomatic transcription, not a claim that Jaja personally wrote the surviving words by hand.

passages.title: Treaties, writing and colonial coercion
passages.text: British officials detained Jaja in 1887 despite assurances surrounding the meeting. An inquiry at Accra preceded his exile. The process helped impose imperial power while falling short of the protections that British authorities claimed to value in their own legal system.

passages.title: Treaties, writing and colonial coercion
passages.text: Colonial government did not immediately free everyone in trading Houses. The 1901 Native House Rule Ordinance strengthened restrictions on people leaving them. Lagos campaigners challenged this protection of coerced labour, reminding us that African opposition to slavery also confronted British colonial legislation.

passages.title: Later accounts: festival errands and town work
passages.text: Royal accounts from the 1940s record preparations for a harvest festival, including messengers chasing late deliveries of yams and corn. Hiring Benedict’s small canoe cost two shillings. Even a royal celebration needed somebody to sort out the food delivery; these are later records, well after the map window.

passages.title: Later accounts: festival errands and town work
passages.text: The same account book records payments for rubbish clearance and boat-dock repairs, alongside purchases of newspapers and books. Named workers and modest expenses reveal activities that grand political histories often miss. Opobo’s community institutions and practical responsibilities continued long after Jaja’s removal.

Jaja was exiled to the Caribbean and died at Tenerife in July 1891 before returning home. British control displaced his sovereignty, but Opobo’s Houses, residents and royal institution continued beyond the map’s 1914 endpoint.

passages.text: The Orange Free State was a white-ruled republic between the Orange and Vaal rivers. Bloemfontein became its administrative centre, while the struggle over land drew Basotho and other African communities into conflict with the settler state. Its imported map interval also covers later British rule.

passages.title: A republic with contested boundaries
passages.text: Britain recognized the new republic at the Bloemfontein Convention in 1854 without consulting African chiefdoms. The agreement did not settle the frontier with Moshoeshoe’s Basotho kingdom. Political recognition on paper therefore left fundamental disputes over who possessed the land.

passages.title: A republic with contested boundaries
passages.text: The Free State’s expansion cost Basotho communities much fertile land. Conflict concerned fields, grazing and livestock, not an empty strip between two colored shapes. Basotho farming and political life continued beyond the republic’s borders and within the wider region.

passages.title: A republic with contested boundaries
passages.text: The First Raadsaal began in 1849 as a school and also served as a church. In 1854 it became the republic’s assembly hall and offices. A building could host lessons, worship and government in succession: the rooms did not insist on just one career.

passages.title: A republic with contested boundaries
passages.text: When the assembly moved to larger premises in 1856, the old building returned to schooling until 1877. Today it is restored as a museum. Its changing uses provide evidence for the institutions of a growing town without making its present display an untouched classroom.

passages.title: Water, houses and the road
passages.text: Before a piped supply, Bloemfontein households and businesses relied on streams, fountains, wells, dams and boreholes. Water had to be carried in buckets. A drink, a wash and cooking a meal all began with somebody moving a heavy load.

passages.title: Water, houses and the road
passages.text: Water shortages became critical in 1894. The Modder River scheme, approved in 1896, brought water to town in 1899 through pumping facilities and pipes around Naval Hill. This changed urban infrastructure, though the account does not show every home receiving equal service.

passages.title: Water, houses and the road
passages.text: Freshford House, completed in 1897, preserves the setting of an affluent Bloemfontein household. Red brick walls, bay windows, a carved wooden veranda and cast-iron details show the materials and decorative choices of this home. Its comfort should not stand in for the lives of the town’s poorer residents.

passages.title: Water, houses and the road
passages.text: Bloemfontein’s Wagon Museum holds ox wagons, transport wagons, a stagecoach, mule wagons and smaller carts. These different vehicles remind us that carrying freight and carrying passengers presented different problems. The collection also discusses transport used by Black people in the early twentieth century.

passages.title: Water, houses and the road
passages.text: Earlier ox wagons could slow down with metal skidpans chained beneath their rear wheels. The wheels stopped turning while the shoes dragged along the ground. It was an effective answer to a very serious downhill question: how do you persuade a loaded wagon to stop?

passages.title: Writing, learning and restricted lives
passages.text: A Dutch phrase from the 1893 pass law is “verblijf brief”, meaning “residential pass”. The law required Black location residents over sixteen, women as well as men, to carry one. This small writing sample came from paperwork that could determine whether somebody was arrested.

passages.title: Writing, learning and restricted lives
passages.text: Contemporary newspapers reported police raids in Waaihoek, including arrests of residents without passes. One resident complained about officers entering houses and dragging out older women. These accounts restore African households to a city history too easily told only through presidents and public buildings.

passages.title: Writing, learning and restricted lives
passages.text: The National Museum was founded in 1877 and opened in 1878. Its first honorary curator, Hugh Exton, sought public donations, and collections grew until the old Raadsaal needed extensions. Collecting natural and human history became another form of organized learning in the republic.

passages.title: Writing, learning and restricted lives
passages.text: During the South African War, British scorched-earth operations destroyed farms, and camps imprisoned Boer families and Black civilians. Poor food, water and sanitation caused terrible suffering. The Treaty of Vereeniging in 1902 ended the war, after Britain had already proclaimed annexation in 1900.

The independent republic was defeated in the war ending in 1902. Its territory became the Orange River Colony, which joined the Union of South Africa in 1910. The peoples and settlements continued; the map record’s 1914 endpoint does not extend republican independence to that date.

sectionTitles: Giant wheels and objects from a palace
A written Saturday and a changing kingdom

passages.text: This Orissa record spans later Eastern Ganga rule, the expansion of the Gajapati kingdom, and subsequent regional and imperial governments in Odisha. Puri’s Jagannath temple helped rulers express their authority. The atlas dates, 1279 to 1650, are coverage limits rather than one dynasty’s lifetime. Its coarse western outline actually omits Cuttack, Puri and Konark, important centres discussed here; it should not be read as their kingdom’s complete boundary.

passages.title: Royal power reached beyond Odisha
passages.text: Kapilendra took power in 1435, replacing the Eastern Ganga ruling line. He initially faced resistance from local chiefs as well as neighbouring powers. His kingdom had to be built through political struggle: a coronation did not automatically make every regional lord obedient.

passages.title: Royal power reached beyond Odisha
passages.text: A Telugu inscription at a Warangal gateway records the capture of the fort by Ambira-deva, also known as Hamvira, a son of Kapilendra. Its date corresponds to 2 February 1460. This surviving local record gives a concrete foothold for Gajapati expansion into Telangana, far beyond the Odisha coast.

passages.title: Royal power reached beyond Odisha
passages.text: An inscription at Puri records Kapilendra remitting taxes on salt and cowries in favour of the god Purushottama. Revenue and religion met in a written royal order. This was a specified temple concession, rather than evidence that everyone in the kingdom stopped paying those taxes.

passages.title: Royal power reached beyond Odisha
passages.text: Another Puri inscription records the king giving a sari cloth called Pundarika gopa to Jagannath. The order passed through a named storekeeper and superintendent. Even a royal religious gift needed someone to receive instructions and look after the goods.

passages.title: Meals, weddings and learning
passages.text: Sarala Dasa’s fifteenth-century Odia Mahabharata brought the epic into an Odia literary world. In historian Pravakar Sethi’s reading, its food descriptions include boiled rice, pulses, vegetables, milk sweets and occasional plantain-leaf plates. These are glimpses through literature, whose surviving versions vary, rather than a menu proven for every family.

passages.title: Meals, weddings and learning
passages.text: Sethi also describes wedding scenes in Sarala’s work: relatives arrive at the bride’s home, roads are cleaned, walls decorated, and young women collect water from seven houses for the couple’s ritual bath. A wedding could become a neighbourhood project. The detail belongs to the literary account, not a rule for every community.

passages.title: Meals, weddings and learning
passages.text: A 1291 inscription at Simhachalam records an endowment supporting teachers of Vedic texts, grammar, poetry and drama. It belongs to the Eastern Ganga world inherited by later rulers. A temple could support demanding study as well as worship, although this example tells us about a particular learned institution.

passages.title: Meals, weddings and learning
passages.text: The scholar Divakara’s Laksanadarsa retells the Pandavas’ story while illustrating grammatical points in its sections. Adventure and grammar could share the same page. Subrahmanyam discusses it among the literature associated with Prataparudra’s learned world.

passages.title: Meals, weddings and learning
passages.text: A short Sanskrit drama, Parasurama Vijaya, is attributed to Kapilendra. The work indicates that it was performed during a festival at the Jagannath temple before 1458. Courtly literature could be heard and watched by an audience, rather than remaining only in a manuscript.

passages.title: Giant wheels and objects from a palace
passages.text: The Sun Temple at Konark was already standing before this map record begins. Built under Narasimha Deva I in the thirteenth century, it presents the sun god’s chariot through monumental stone architecture. Its 24 carved wheels are about three metres across: a wheel taller than many adults, with no chance of fitting on a bicycle.

passages.title: Giant wheels and objects from a palace
passages.text: Konark’s sculptors carved musicians, dancers and scenes of social life into the temple. Its surviving dance hall and audience hall help show how architecture, performance and worship belonged together. Stone preserves gestures and instruments that would otherwise vanish when the music stopped.

passages.title: Giant wheels and objects from a palace
passages.text: At Barabati Fort in Cuttack, excavators identified a large pillared hall and adjoining courtyard in the fifteenth- and sixteenth-century phase. The hall’s surviving width is about twenty metres. Its foundations offer firmer evidence for royal space than the conflicting later stories about a many-storeyed palace.

passages.title: Giant wheels and objects from a palace
passages.text: Debris filling that hall included Chinese porcelain dated around the sixteenth century, coloured lime plaster and small beads shaped like areca nuts. The fragments bring imported objects and bright decoration into an otherwise ruined room. A broken plate can preserve evidence of a connection much farther away than the palace walls.

passages.title: Giant wheels and objects from a palace
passages.text: A sculpture recovered from Barabati’s moat shows a couple on a swing. Archaeologists assigned it stylistically to the Gajapati period and suggested it may have decorated a temple. Its playful subject survives, although the displaced carving cannot tell us the names or everyday routines of a real family.

passages.title: A written Saturday and a changing kingdom
passages.text: The 1460 Warangal inscription supplies a tiny language sample: Vadda-varamu, meaning “Saturday.” This is the editor’s Roman-letter rendering of a word in a Telugu inscription, not an image of its original letters. It formed part of the date recording a military capture. The kingdom’s surviving records therefore include languages used beyond its Odia-speaking core.

passages.title: A written Saturday and a changing kingdom
passages.text: After the 1568 conquest, Ramachandra Deva of the Bhoi line established a smaller kingdom at Khurda and restored Jagannath worship at Puri. Successive rulers retained a role supervising the temple. Political authority had contracted, but royal ritual and local institutions continued.

passages.title: A written Saturday and a changing kingdom
passages.text: Under Mughal administration from 1592, Odisha’s revenue organization included the districts of Jaleswar, Bhadrak and Kataka, with Puri in Kataka. Collecting and organizing revenue became part of an imperial framework. The atlas’s final date of 1650 does not mark the disappearance of Odisha’s towns, languages or communities.

The large independent kingdom was broken by dynastic struggles and the Afghan conquest of 1568. Smaller Khurda and continuing temple institutions survived; Mughal administration followed in 1592. The imported 1650 endpoint is a map cutoff, not the end of Odisha’s people or regional identity.

sectionTitles: Water, milk and sharing the work

passages.text: Oromo communities transformed the Horn of Africa through migration, farming, herding, commerce and varied forms of government. This broad map label is not one empire: Gadaa institutions and later Gibe kingdoms represent different political histories. The imported southern outline cannot show the full distribution of Oromo people.

passages.title: Movements, markets and learning
passages.text: Historian Mohammed Hassen places Oromo expansion within the wider sixteenth-century wars that weakened neighboring Christian and Muslim states. Migration involved settlement and new alliances as well as fighting; it was not a single army following one permanent ruler.

passages.title: Movements, markets and learning
passages.text: Gibe rulers benefited from customs duties and gifts carried along organized caravan routes. Products moved north through Gojjam and east through Shawa; commerce connected the kingdoms with much larger networks.

passages.title: Movements, markets and learning
passages.text: The Gibe kingdoms also became important centers of Islamic study. Their combination of agriculture, commerce and scholarship reminds us that Oromo history includes towns and classrooms as well as cattle and migration.

passages.title: Movements, markets and learning
passages.text: Cooperation across political boundaries could restore trade. Ishikawa’s study of the Gondar period finds that migrant communities south of Lake Tana worked with Oromo groups south of the Blue Nile, helping revive long-distance exchange.

passages.title: Gadaa: governing and remembering
passages.text: In UNESCO’s account of living Gadaa institutions, five classes take turns in authority, with leadership changing every eight years. A governing class includes a chairperson, officials and an assembly. Power comes with a timetable, not an automatic lifetime appointment.

passages.title: Gadaa: governing and remembering
passages.text: Participation is structured by gender and family. Men enter classes to which their fathers belong; women are consulted on decisions protecting women’s rights. Calling this a democratic tradition should not hide these particular rules of membership.

passages.title: Gadaa: governing and remembering
passages.text: Oral historians teach law, history, calendars, ritual and conduct. Meetings may gather under a sycamore tree, while children learn at home and school. A tree can shade a serious political classroom without needing a blackboard.

passages.title: Water, milk and sharing the work
passages.text: Borana communities, one part of the Oromo world, manage ancient tula wells in southern Ethiopia. Research published in 2011 traced a system operating for more than five centuries. Its survival depends on customary rules, repairs and surrounding grazing land, not just a hole in the ground.

passages.title: Water, milk and sharing the work
passages.text: A 1994 research synthesis describes chains of workers passing buckets up deep well shafts, then onward to livestock troughs. Other people regulate the queue, clear manure and repair clay troughs. Getting cattle a drink can require an entire shift of water engineers.

passages.title: Water, milk and sharing the work
passages.text: In the same research, Borana women rotated market duty: one carried dairy products to sell for her friends. Sharing the journey saved other households a long walk and left time for their own demanding work.

passages.title: Water, milk and sharing the work
passages.text: In the same late twentieth-century research, a gorfa milk container was woven from asparagus-root fibers, smoked inside, then used for souring and churning milk. A golondi was carved from wood and carried by herders. Clever containers served different jobs, just as a lunchbox differs from a mixing bowl.

passages.title: A little written Oromo
passages.text: “Umurii” means “Age,” and “Mallattoo” means “signature.” These Oromo words appear beside English translations on the community consent form submitted for UNESCO recognition of Gadaa. They show contemporary Oromo in Latin letters; they are not presented as a text from the map’s early centuries.
The map stops at 1815, but Oromo history continues. Gadaa remained a living institution recognized by UNESCO in 2016; later kingdoms and communities followed different political paths.
