passages.text: Pergamon, above modern Bergama in western Turkey, became the Attalid dynasty’s capital and a celebrated center of learning and art. Its hillside buildings joined royal ambition with impressive engineering. This card follows the late kingdom and its transition into the Roman world.

passages.title: Kings, cities and the map
passages.text: The imported outline shows a restricted area of western Anatolia between 200 and 100 BCE. It does not show the Attalids’ full expanded territory. Its final decades also fall after the dynasty’s bequest to Rome: a changing regional history is hidden behind one map label.

passages.title: Kings, cities and the map
passages.text: Pergamon’s ruling family emerged from the struggles after Alexander the Great. Philetairos gained substantial independence in 281 BCE. Attalos I later took the royal title after defeating Galatian opponents. The kingdom was already generations old when this map record begins.

passages.title: Kings, cities and the map
passages.text: The settlement at Apameia in 188 BCE rewarded Rome’s Attalid ally with extensive former Seleucid lands. Holding them required further wars and cooperation with local communities. The new kingdom included Greek cities and diverse inland Anatolian populations.

passages.title: Kings, cities and the map
passages.text: The capital climbed a steep hill. Builders used terraces for sanctuaries, colonnades and public buildings, while the theatre fitted the slope. Looking impressive here required serious work with the landscape: a royal building project could also be a stair-climbing project.

passages.title: Homes, water and everyday objects
passages.text: Courtyards shaped domestic space. Monika Trümper’s survey counted 18 courtyard houses and 21 houses with columned courtyards at Pergamon, including palaces; most originated in the Hellenistic centuries. These different-sized homes give a much broader picture of residents’ surroundings than the royal monuments alone.

passages.title: Homes, water and everyday objects
passages.text: A bathroom in every house? The same survey identified no securely Hellenistic bathroom in those 39 dwellings. Some large houses gained elaborate bathing rooms much later, from the late first century BCE. Ancient washing could use portable basins; absence of a dedicated room does not mean absence of washing.

passages.title: Homes, water and everyday objects
passages.text: Everyday clay objects depended on nearby craftspeople. Research covering Hellenistic and Roman Pergamon finds that regional workshops supplied most pottery. Archaeologists compare clay under magnification and use chemical analysis to separate local products from imports. A broken pot can preserve a surprisingly useful workshop address.

passages.title: Homes, water and everyday objects
passages.text: Water reached the hill through ambitious pipelines. The Madradağ system, dated around 180 to 160 BCE, ran approximately 42 kilometers. Engineer Günther Garbrecht estimated that it required about 200,000 individual pipe sections. Supplying a city also meant supplying potters with clay, fuel and an enormous production job.

passages.title: Homes, water and everyday objects
passages.text: Pipe fragments still raise questions. A 2022 field report describes pieces with different clay fabrics, shapes and stamps near an aqueduct. Some marks resemble those of other known pipelines. Researchers are testing how the pieces belong together, rather like solving a plumbing puzzle with most of the instructions missing.

passages.title: Homes, water and everyday objects
passages.text: A large cistern near the palaces measured roughly 4.55 meters across and 6.20 meters deep. One engineering study interprets it as a water reserve for fighting fires. In that reconstruction, people passed water along human chains: an emergency service powered by neighbors and buckets.

passages.title: Learning, exercise and healing
passages.text: Eumenes II’s gymnasium spread over three terraces, with running tracks and an open exercise court. A public fountain stood by its western entrance. Streets of the expanding city led toward it, making exercise and civic gathering a central part of Pergamon’s urban plan.

passages.title: Learning, exercise and healing
passages.text: The royal treasury supported the gymnasium’s oil fund. After the dynasty ended, responsibility passed to the gymnasium’s official. Physical training required a budget as well as enthusiasm; this institution was a meeting point between royal finance and civic life.

passages.title: Learning, exercise and healing
passages.text: At Metropolis, another city in the kingdom, inscriptions record an annual royal allocation of 500 drachmas for lessons for freeborn young people, alongside a separate oil fund. Education had its own line in the budget, though this was not schooling available equally to everyone.

passages.title: Learning, exercise and healing
passages.text: The library displayed a large marble Athena modeled on the famous gold-and-ivory goddess in Athens. The Pergamene version, from the second century BCE, linked books and scholarship with a deity of arts and knowledge. Royal learning was also public image-making: the kings wanted their city compared with Athens.

passages.title: Learning, exercise and healing
passages.text: People seeking healing could visit the sanctuary of Asklepios outside the city. A sleeping or incubation area developed in the third century BCE; worshippers hoped for the god’s help through dreams. Early in the second century, colonnades enclosed the sanctuary and a sacred road connected it with Pergamon.

passages.title: Art, writing and international connections
passages.text: The Great Altar, dated approximately 180 to 160 BCE, carried a dramatic carved battle between gods and giants. Another frieze told the story of Telephos, the city’s mythical founder. The monument joined religious offerings, spectacular storytelling and a royal claim to an impressive ancestry.

passages.title: Art, writing and international connections
passages.text: Palace mosaic-makers used tiny cut stones, colored stones and glass instead of relying only on pebbles. Fine picture panels could be made in a workshop and inserted into a floor afterward. One royal mosaic includes a vividly colored parakeet: luxury decoration at your feet.

passages.title: Art, writing and international connections
passages.text: A real Greek signature survives in the Hephaistion mosaic from Palace V: ΗΦΑΙΣΤΙΩΝ ΕΠΟΙΕΙ, meaning “Hephaistion made [it].” These are modern printed letters transcribing the Hellenistic mosaic inscription. They preserve a craftsperson’s name, not just a king’s.

passages.title: Art, writing and international connections
passages.text: The signature is itself a visual joke. Its letters appear on a little piece of parchment represented in stone, held down at the corners, with one corner curling upward and casting a shadow. The floor pretends to have a loose note on it. Please do not tidy away the artwork!

passages.title: Art, writing and international connections
passages.text: Attalos II also paid for a great market building in Athens during his reign, 159 to 138 BCE. It had two storeys, each with 21 shops behind a colonnade. Such gifts let a king’s reputation travel abroad while providing real places to trade, walk and meet.

Attalos III’s bequest in 133 BCE did not create a peaceful instant handover. Aristonikos rebelled before Roman provincial rule was established after 129 BCE. Pergamon itself was not destroyed in that transition and retained civic privileges under Rome. The kingdom ended, but the city and its cultural life continued beyond the map’s 100 BCE endpoint.

Pictures and a Persian writing sample

passages.text: Persia here means Iran during Qajar consolidation and rule. Its imported dates, 1783 to 1920, are map coverage limits: Qajar consolidation continued through 1794 and the founder’s coronation in 1796, while the dynasty ended in 1925. Some outlines extend too far into the Caucasus for their displayed dates. They should not be treated as precise borders after the nineteenth-century wars with Russia.

passages.title: How power changed
passages.text: Qajar power emerged through a prolonged struggle after the Zand era. Agha Mohammad Khan defeated Lotf Ali Khan in 1794 and took the crown in 1796. His assassination in 1797 brought his nephew Fath Ali Shah to power. The dynasty’s beginning is therefore better understood as a sequence than as a single map date.

passages.title: How power changed
passages.text: Wars with Russia transformed the northern frontier. The treaties of Golestan in 1813 and Turkmenchay in 1828 confirmed major losses of Iranian-held territories in the Caucasus. Communities and trade routes were divided by a new international boundary. Several imported atlas outlines fail to keep pace with these changes.

passages.title: How power changed
passages.text: The Constitutional Revolution brought merchants, clerics and reform-minded intellectuals into a struggle to limit arbitrary royal power. The first Majles assembled in 1906. Constitutional government faced a royal coup in 1908, was restored in 1909, and suffered another major reversal when the second Majles was dissolved in 1911. Agreement on a parliament did not mean agreement on every reform.

passages.title: How power changed
passages.text: World War I brought foreign troops into Iran and further weakened the state. In 1921, Reza Khan’s Cossack forces entered Tehran and he became the dominant military figure. These events belong to the final Qajar years, even though this particular map record stops in 1920.

passages.title: Families, food and getting through the day
passages.text: Extended families could share a compound, with married sons, their spouses and children living alongside older relatives. Wealth shaped the space: a rich household might have separate private and reception sections, while poorer families shared buildings and used curtains to divide a room. Family life did not look identical behind every doorway.

passages.title: Families, food and getting through the day
passages.text: In the urban houses described by historian Shireen Mahdavi, toilets stood off the courtyard, with a water pitcher for cleansing. Wealthy compounds could have their own baths; other residents used public bathhouses. Water storage rooms could also keep perishable food cool. Plumbing arrangements depended strongly on the household’s resources.

passages.title: Families, food and getting through the day
passages.text: Rooms changed jobs during the day. Bedding was folded away in the morning; at mealtimes, food was served on a cloth spread on the floor. Water and a basin were brought for washing fingers before and after eating. Bread could help scoop up food: part of the meal also did the work of a utensil.

passages.title: Families, food and getting through the day
passages.text: A korsi made winter gatherings cozy: a low wooden frame stood over a heat source beneath a large quilt, with people sitting around it and warming their feet underneath. Tea, meals and games could occupy the top. It was a gathering place as well as a heater, and its history began long before the Qajars.

passages.title: Families, food and getting through the day
passages.text: The new Russian frontier cut across Shahsevan winter pastures in the Moghan plain. Families and herds continued crossing it, provoking disputes with border authorities. Russia’s closure of the frontier to these nomadic groups in 1884 disrupted an established seasonal way of life. A line drawn between states could become a very practical problem for finding grazing.

passages.title: Families, food and getting through the day
passages.text: Kerman’s expanding carpet industry linked local work to distant buyers. Its workshops employed people displaced from the countryside and many children under harsh conditions. Merchants often captured much of the profit, while imported textiles undermined other crafts, including shawl-making. Beautiful exported objects could conceal very unequal working lives.

passages.title: Learning and health
passages.text: Dar al-Fonun opened in Tehran in December 1851. Its subjects included military sciences, engineering, mining, medicine and pharmacy. The first recruitment notice sought teenage sons of elite families, but the actual intake was more mixed and students arrived with very different preparation. Some needed basic language and mathematics instruction before tackling advanced work.

passages.title: Learning and health
passages.text: The college provided a free daily lunch and two sets of clothes each year, one for summer and one for winter. Uniform colors distinguished students in different disciplines. Studies also included Persian, Arabic and French. School life combined new technical subjects with language learning, exams and a distinctly military sense of discipline.

passages.title: Learning and health
passages.text: Girls’ education followed several paths. Some attended traditional maktabs or learned at home; Assyrian, Armenian, Jewish, Zoroastrian and other communities developed schools, alongside new Muslim girls’ schools. A 1911 report counted 47 girls’ schools in Tehran with 2,187 pupils. These opportunities mattered, but they were far from universal access.

passages.title: Learning and health
passages.text: Smallpox vaccination developed unevenly. Crown Prince Abbas Mirza had his family vaccinated and encouraged medical learning; a Persian translation of John Cormick’s vaccination tract was printed in Tabriz in 1829. Print could carry practical health information as well as poetry and news. Acceptance and administration remained difficult, so publication alone did not guarantee protection.

passages.title: Learning and health
passages.text: By 1916, a vaccination center at Dar al-Fonun combined treatment with teaching. Medical students vaccinated people under professors’ supervision, learning techniques and possible complications while serving the city. Public-health administration was changing, although this one clinic cannot tell us how easily a family in a distant village obtained care.

passages.title: Pictures and a Persian writing sample
passages.text: Qajar artists adopted lithography and photography while also changing older forms such as painted portraits. These technologies widened the ways pictures could be made and circulated. Royal images could look back to Iran’s earlier dynasties while presenting the ruler as a patron of new techniques and reform.

passages.title: Pictures and a Persian writing sample
passages.text: By the late nineteenth century, large religious paintings appeared in coffeehouses. Their subjects included the martyrdom of Husain at Karbala, also commemorated in Shiite passion plays. These portable canvases brought ambitious storytelling to public gathering places beyond the royal palace.

passages.title: Pictures and a Persian writing sample
passages.text: A painting now in the Metropolitan Museum shows Nasir al-Din Shah beside a cannon. Made in Iran around 1850 with watercolor, ink and gold on paper, it combines a carefully presented ruler with military equipment. The combination can be read as a display of royal authority, using paint and precious metal to give the ruler a commanding presence.

passages.title: Pictures and a Persian writing sample
passages.text: A silver coin from Isfahan, dated 1244 AH (1828-29), carries this Persian inscription: سكه فتحعلى شه خسرو صاحبقران. The Ashmolean translates it as “the coin of Fatḥ ‘Alī Shāh, Caesar of the fortunate conjunction.” The grand title linked the ruler to auspicious astrology. This wording survives on museum coin HCR18505.

The map stops in 1920, but Qajar rule ended in 1925. On 31 October, the Majles deposed the dynasty; on 12 December, a constituent assembly transferred the crown to Reza Shah and his male heirs. The Pahlavi dynasty replaced the ruling house. Iran’s population, languages and communities continued through that political change.

passages.text: Peru proclaimed independence in 1821, decades before this map record begins. The republic encompasses coastal, Andean and Amazonian communities whose histories extend far beyond the state. Its story includes railways and libraries, living textile and pottery knowledge, and the difficult work of confronting political violence.

passages.title: Making, learning and everyday skill
passages.text: Awajún potters in northern Peru use grinding and polishing stones, wooden tools and brushes made with human hair. They collect materials, shape, fire, decorate and finish their vessels. Designs draw on plants, animals, mountains and stars, turning careful observation into useful objects.

passages.title: Making, learning and everyday skill
passages.text: Awajún pots serve for cooking, drinking and sharing food as well as ceremonies. Elder women known as Dukúg pass knowledge to other women in their families. Growing the plants used in production is part of the work, so the craft reaches from garden to hearth.

passages.title: Making, learning and everyday skill
passages.text: On Taquile in Lake Titicaca, men and women make textiles as an everyday activity. Garments may be knitted or woven on four-stake ground looms. A knitted chullo keeps ears covered; a wide calendar belt depicts agricultural and ritual cycles.

passages.title: Making, learning and everyday skill
passages.text: Taquile’s crafts school helps younger people learn textile skills. Makers have also introduced contemporary images while retaining established techniques. Tourism supplies income, but greater demand can change materials and meaning, a handmade tradition has to negotiate a changing market.

passages.title: Making, learning and everyday skill
passages.text: The National Library opened in September 1822 with more than eleven thousand volumes, including books from former Jesuit collections and private gifts. San Martín donated about six hundred. The early republic invested in a place where knowledge could be collected and consulted.

passages.title: Making, learning and everyday skill
passages.text: After wartime looting in 1881, Ricardo Palma sought donated books through letters to writers abroad. A devastating fire followed in 1943. Jorge Basadre’s rebuilding effort included professional staff training and a National School of Librarians in 1944: recovering a library required people as well as shelves.

passages.title: Making, learning and everyday skill
passages.text: The 1821 founding decree described the library as devoted “a la ilustración universal”, “to universal enlightenment.” The National Library reproduces this Spanish phrase from San Martín’s decree of 28 August. It captures an early republican ambition to support independence through learning.

passages.title: Connections, money and remembrance
passages.text: A railway between Lima and Callao opened in 1851, linking the capital and its port. Railway building later reached other regions: the first locomotive entered Cusco in September 1908. Travel and shipping were being reorganized, but connection arrived at different times in different places.

passages.title: Connections, money and remembrance
passages.text: The Lima mint produced eight-real coins under both royal and republican authority in 1821 to 1822. Their different shields make political change visible in objects used for payment. A person examining two coins can see a revolution in the designs without reading a whole proclamation.

passages.title: Connections, money and remembrance
passages.text: Peru participated in the Peru to Bolivian Confederation from 1836 until its dissolution in 1839. That short-lived arrangement belongs between independence and the later republic. National political structures changed even while towns, farms and trading relationships carried on.

passages.title: Connections, money and remembrance
passages.text: The Truth and Reconciliation Commission documented killings, disappearances and other abuses during the 1980 to 2000 conflict, committed by insurgent organizations and state agents. Rural and Indigenous-language communities suffered disproportionately. Its investigation made those unequal experiences central to the national account.

passages.title: Connections, money and remembrance
passages.text: Families of disappeared people organized to seek information and justice, often with women sustaining the effort through years of uncertainty. The commission recognized their persistence. Public memory was built through the work of relatives and communities, not only through official hearings.

Peru continues as a republic. Changes of government, the nineteenth-century confederation and the internal armed conflict altered its institutions without ending the country or its diverse peoples. The map’s 1878 start is a coverage date, not the beginning of Peruvian society.

passages.text: The Petun, also called Tionontati, were Iroquoian-speaking communities south of Georgian Bay. The map’s 1492 to 1500 label is earlier than the well-documented Petun villages discussed here, which developed in the late 1500s and 1600s. Archaeologists debate their earlier origins. Their descendants helped form later Wyandot communities; this early map cutoff is not their disappearance.

passages.title: Communities, neighbors and visitors
passages.text: Researchers associate the historic Petun with two groupings conventionally called Wolf and Deer. Their earlier origins are debated: proposals connect them with communities in the Humber Valley or farther southwest in Neutral country. Pottery connections help investigate movement, but do not turn either proposed route into a certainty.

passages.title: Communities, neighbors and visitors
passages.text: Charles Garrad noticed that several Petun village sites occur in pairs: a larger settlement close to a smaller one. The Deer settlements were especially close together. He interpreted these patterns as relationships between communities with different functions, rather than assuming every cluster of houses operated independently.

passages.title: Communities, neighbors and visitors
passages.text: Garrad proposed that some smaller settlements accommodated visitors, including Odawa people who spent winters among the Petun. Different artifact and animal-bone patterns supported his investigation. This offers a picture of villages with guests and seasonal connections, while the exact role of each settlement remains a research question.

passages.title: Food, trade and practical discoveries
passages.text: When Champlain visited in January 1616, he described people growing maize and living in permanent settlements. His hosts supplied meat and fish for a feast during his visits among neighboring villages. The account connects farming with hospitality: welcoming travelers meant sharing a meal as well as discussing friendship.

passages.title: Food, trade and practical discoveries
passages.text: At Plater-Fleming, copper-kettle fragments were plentiful while pottery was comparatively scarce. Garrad interpreted this as evidence that imported kettles had replaced some clay cooking vessels at that particular late Petun settlement. Changes in trade could therefore alter the objects used to prepare everyday food.

passages.title: Food, trade and practical discoveries
passages.text: Glass beads also help investigate Plater-Fleming’s date. Its small recorded assemblage included red tubular beads, a style useful for comparison with other late contact-period sites. A bead was an ornament to its owner; centuries later, its material and shape also help archaeologists compare settlements.

passages.title: Food, trade and practical discoveries
passages.text: Animal remains make beaver processing particularly visible at Petun sites. Garrad compared bone assemblages from named villages and found beaver among the most common identified mammals. Those remains record intensive work with animals linked to the fur trade; percentages of bones are not percentages of people’s dinner.

passages.title: Food, trade and practical discoveries
passages.text: Modern experiments by J. Allan Blair tested whether native tobacco could grow near old village sites. Carefully weeded and fenced plants matured, while open-field plantings failed. The experiment highlights the effort of protecting young plants from weeds and hungry animals, without proving exactly how every Petun garden was arranged.

passages.title: Dispersal, families and language today
passages.text: The Wyandotte Nation explains that the Tionontati were separate from the old Huron-Wendat confederacy. They received refugees, then suffered Haudenosaunee attacks. Survivors joined with Attignawantan and Wenro people in 1649 and 1650, forming a new community while drawing on several earlier identities.

passages.title: Dispersal, families and language today
passages.text: The modern Wyandotte Nation’s shield recalls twelve clans, including several turtle clans as well as Wolf, Bear and Deer. These names form part of the Nation’s own account of family and community identity today; the shield is not a diagram of the earlier Petun village map.

passages.title: Dispersal, families and language today
passages.text: A short modern Waⁿdat example is “aža?áha,” meaning “she is a child.” Beci Wright printed it in the Wyandotte Nation’s newspaper in August 2022, with linguistic support credited to Craig Kopris. This sample belongs to a descendant community’s language teaching, rather than an unchanged sentence documented in Petun country in 1492.

passages.title: Dispersal, families and language today
passages.text: That 2022 language column paired written examples with audio recordings and invited learners to online practice sessions. Children, elders and adults appeared together in its vocabulary of age. A modern classroom can reach families living far apart, helping language learning fit into ordinary community life.

passages.title: Dispersal, families and language today
passages.text: The same newspaper invited artists to a 2022 community showcase with separate youth and adult divisions. Categories included beadwork, pottery, basketry, textiles and mixed media. Younger artists could show their work alongside older makers, giving creativity and shared learning a place in the gathering.

Attacks dispersed Petun communities in 1649 and 1650. Survivors helped form the later Wyandot people, whose communities continue. Political upheaval and new shared identities, rather than extinction at the map’s 1500 cutoff, explain this transition.

passages.text: This is the atlas's 1492 to 1530 teaching label for parts of the archipelago. There was no country called the Philippines and no single archipelago-wide government in this period. The name Filipina was coined only in 1543, while the imported outline skips many major islands and must not be read as a real border.

passages.title: Read the label before reading the history
passages.text: The exact atlas record is id philippines, dated approximately 1492 to 1530. Those years describe imported map coverage. They do not mark national founding and extinction, because no state with this name governed the archipelago then.

passages.title: Read the label before reading the history
passages.text: The 1492 feature runs to 1500. It has eight separate polygons, 279 vertices and bounds from about 117.129 to 126.374 east and 5.488 to 18.552 north. Its many digits measure the file, not historical certainty.

passages.title: Read the label before reading the history
passages.text: The 1500 feature runs to 1530. It again has eight polygons and 279 vertices, with bounds differing from the first by only tiny fractions of a degree. That near repetition is a cartographic interval, not evidence that political borders froze for thirty years.

passages.title: Read the label before reading the history
passages.text: Point tests expose the outline's limits. Both versions include Manila, Vigan and Cotabato, yet omit tested points at Puerto Princesa, Iloilo, Cebu, Tacloban, Davao, Zamboanga, Jolo and Basco. The archipelago has become a map-shaped colander, so use it only as a locator.

passages.title: Read the label before reading the history
passages.text: The label is anachronistic. Villalobos applied Filipina to an island in 1543, after this card ends, and the name later widened to the archipelago. Using Philippines here is modern catalog shorthand, not the name people across the islands shared in 1492.

passages.title: Read the label before reading the history
passages.text: No matching Philippines feature appears at 1530 or 1600. A different record, philippines-1650, begins in 1650 and already has its own detailed card. The 120-year blank is an atlas gap, not a claim that people, ports or polities vanished.

passages.title: Many centers connected by water
passages.text: There was no archipelago-wide capital or government. The NCCA account gives 1450 as the traditional founding date of the Sulu sultanate, but that chronology comes through genealogies and later historical reconstruction. It belongs in this story as a powerful southern polity, not as ruler of every island.

passages.title: Many centers connected by water
passages.text: A separate NCCA survey says Muslim communities existed in Sulu by the late thirteenth century and attributes an early mosque tradition to Makhdum Karim in the fourteenth. Its words such as probably and attributed matter: perishable buildings and remembered genealogies do not behave like a modern dated registry.

passages.title: Many centers connected by water
passages.text: The same institutional history places Sharif Kabungsuwan's arrival near Malabang in 1515 and calls a Maguindanao sultanate in 1516 possible. These traditional dates show political change within the atlas period, while their uncertainty prevents a pretend exact coronation calendar.

passages.title: Many centers connected by water
passages.text: Underwater archaeology supplies a different kind of evidence. Wrecks at Pandanan, Lena Shoal and Santa Cruz carried ceramics from China, Thailand, Vietnam and Myanmar, plus metals, pottery, gongs, a weighing scale and even crocodile teeth. The sea joined communities that the map turns into isolated blobs.

passages.title: Many centers connected by water
passages.text: The Santa Cruz wreck dates to 1488 to 1505, almost perfectly overlapping this card's opening. Excavators recovered about 15,000 objects, including thousands of intact ceramics, cooking pots, stoves, cauldrons, beads, bracelets and small cannon. Trade cargo carried both beautiful dishes and very practical kitchen hardware.

passages.title: Many centers connected by water
passages.text: Older heritage gives the networks a deeper past. Butuan's lashed-lug boats date from the late eighth to early tenth centuries, and the Laguna Copperplate records a contract in an Early Kawi-related script in 900 CE. These discoveries show regional connections centuries before 1492, not one ancient Philippine nation.

passages.title: What archaeology can and cannot show
passages.text: More than 1,000 burials excavated at Calatagan date around the fifteenth century. Their grave goods include local pottery, ceramics from China, Vietnam and Thailand, spindle whorls, ornaments, iron tools and shells. A single cemetery can therefore reveal trade, craftwork and mourning without telling us the deceased person's whole biography.

passages.title: What archaeology can and cannot show
passages.text: The Calatagan graves were unequal: some contained richer assemblages than others, part of a broader increase in burial stratification before 1521. Archaeology can reveal social differences, but grave wealth is not a tidy salary chart and should not be converted into fixed classes for every community.

passages.title: What archaeology can and cannot show
passages.text: Earthenware survives where words often do not. The National Museum collection includes cooking stoves and fourteenth-to-sixteenth-century Calatagan vessels. Shape, residue and find location help reconstruct cooking, trade and ritual, although no pot gets to stand up in court and explain who used it.

passages.title: What archaeology can and cannot show
passages.text: Goldworking was an old achievement rather than a gift of European arrival. Butuan objects date around the eighth century, and the National Museum places the strongest ornament tradition in the ninth to fourteenth centuries. Sixteenth-century Manila still had native goldsmiths, evidence of skills continuing into a changing world.

passages.title: What archaeology can and cannot show
passages.text: Fourteenth-to-fifteenth-century graves beneath Cebu's Plaza Independencia included rare gold covers for the eyes, nose and mouth. That is spectacular evidence from some high-status burials, not proof that everybody went to the afterlife wearing a shiny face mask.

passages.title: What archaeology can and cannot show
passages.text: One National Museum article uses a 1640 report and archaeological remains to discuss infant head shaping in parts of the Visayas. Because the written description is much later than 1530, it can only be a cautious clue about some childhood practices, never a rule for all babies in this card.

passages.title: The 1521 encounter was diplomacy and violence
passages.text: Pigafetta was not an invisible camera. He took part in negotiations and joined the expedition whose actions he described. His manuscript was composed around 1525, after the voyage. It is precious eyewitness evidence, but its Christian labels and judgments reveal the author's position as much as local life.

passages.title: The 1521 encounter was diplomacy and violence
passages.text: Enrique of Malacca, an enslaved Malay-speaking interpreter, made conversations possible. Sources disagree on whether he came from Malacca, Sumatra or Maluku, and there is no sound basis for turning him into a secret Cebuano. Malay worked as a regional contact language among multilingual rulers and traders.

passages.title: The 1521 encounter was diplomacy and violence
passages.text: Humabon, ruler of Cebu, received the expedition on 7 April 1521. He permitted a cross and a Christian baptism ceremony, and he and members of his household took Spanish names on 14 April. Alliance, trade, religion and local rivalry became entangled within days.

passages.title: The 1521 encounter was diplomacy and violence
passages.text: The visitors also coerced. Pigafetta wrote that his group burned a neighboring hamlet because its inhabitants would not obey Humabon or the expedition. He later described threats against chiefs. Baptism and alliance cannot be narrated honestly without the guns, intimidation and destroyed homes beside them.

passages.title: The 1521 encounter was diplomacy and violence
passages.text: Lapulapu and his Mactan force rejected the attack. On 27 April 1521 they drove off Magellan's landing party and killed Magellan. Calling this a local victory is supported; pretending Lapulapu commanded a modern Filipino nation would put a later nation-state into his boat.

passages.title: The 1521 encounter was diplomacy and violence
passages.text: Pigafetta says Magellan's men burned twenty or thirty houses during the Mactan assault before retreating under fire. The battle was no clean duel between two famous men. It endangered residents, destroyed homes and involved large groups whose names the European account mostly did not preserve.

passages.title: The 1521 encounter was diplomacy and violence
passages.text: The alliance then ruptured. The NHCP chronology says Humabon supported the Mactan assault, faced a threat from Mactan afterward and led the killing of expedition officers at a banquet on 1 May. Local choices changed quickly after Magellan's defeat; no Spanish conquest followed in 1521.

passages.title: The 1521 encounter was diplomacy and violence
passages.text: The first circumnavigation did not end at Mactan. The Victoria reached Spain on 6 September 1522 after Magellan's death, with Pigafetta among eighteen returnees. The achievement belonged to a battered, multinational crew and depended on Asian interpreters, ports and provisions as well as European ships.

passages.title: Homes, food, dress, work and family
passages.text: At Mazaua and Cebu, Pigafetta described wooden or bamboo houses raised on large posts and entered by ladders, with palm mats for sitting and sleeping. In one account animals stayed beneath the floor. The front door came with a short climb, but this eyewitness scene cannot define every island's architecture.

passages.title: Homes, food, dress, work and family
passages.text: Coconut palms supplied drink, food, oil, milk-like liquid, vinegar, fiber for boat ropes and palm wine in Pigafetta's account. Rice, fish, pork, bananas, ginger and sugarcane also appear at meals or in exchange. One tree was doing the work of a pantry, bottle shop and hardware drawer.

passages.title: Homes, food, dress, work and family
passages.text: Elite display could be dazzling. Pigafetta described a Butuan ruler with gold spots on each tooth, while archaeology confirms deep goldworking traditions. His smile could literally flash, but one ruler's dental fashion is not a population-wide description of health or wealth.

passages.title: Homes, food, dress, work and family
passages.text: Tattooing existed before Spanish rule, but meanings and methods differed by community, age, gender and achievement. The National Museum's Kalinga discussion preserves that specificity. A modern child-friendly label such as cool body art would miss warfare, maturity and community identity embedded in the practice.

passages.title: Homes, food, dress, work and family
passages.text: At Cebu's court, Pigafetta described embroidered cotton and silk on rulers, palm or bark cloth on other people, and young performers playing a drum and several gongs before a dance. This was one court scene through a visitor's eyes, not everybody's wardrobe or job. That much metal probably made whispering tricky.

passages.title: Homes, food, dress, work and family
passages.text: A 1589 Spanish friar described Tagalog barangays as small groups led by datus, linked by kinship and friendship rather than one chain of command. He also recorded nobles, commoners, enslaved people and required service. This is later, Tagalog-focused and colonial evidence, not a template for Sulu, Cebu or every upland community.

passages.title: Homes, food, dress, work and family
passages.text: The same late Tagalog account discusses marriage, inheritance, children and debt slavery, showing that households were legal and economic units as well as affectionate ones. Its categories came through a missionary writing for colonial officials, so children and enslaved people are heard mostly through an outsider with power.

passages.title: Learning, writing, health, water and toilets
passages.text: A beautiful writing sample survives just after this card's period. The 1593 Doctrina prints ᜀᜋ ᜈᜋᜒ in Baybayin. Its syllabic reading is a-ma na-mi; the facing Roman text reads Amá namin, meaning Our Father. Traditional Baybayin normally left the final n sounds unwritten, so readers supplied them from language and context.

passages.title: Learning, writing, health, water and toilets
passages.text: Baybayin is an Indic-derived alphasyllabary used by Tagalog speakers before Spanish arrival and afterward. The sample is a colonial Christian publication from Manila, sixty-three years after this card ends. It proves a writing tradition and adaptation to print, not one script, faith or literacy rate for the whole archipelago.

passages.title: Learning, writing, health, water and toilets
passages.text: Pigafetta also wrote a 1521 Visayan word list in Latin letters. One entry is tubin, water; his editors compare it with tobig or tubig. It records a European ear and Italian spelling, not an Indigenous manuscript. Still, it lets a period voice peek through a very imperfect notebook.

passages.title: Learning, writing, health, water and toilets
passages.text: No source used here demonstrates a standardized archipelago-wide school system in 1492 to 1530. Children likely learned many skills within households and communities, but that is an inference. The Baybayin print, trade weights, weaving tools and boat technology show knowledge; they do not give enrollment totals or a universal classroom.

passages.title: Learning, writing, health, water and toilets
passages.text: Plasencia's later Tagalog account names ritual specialists and ceremonies seeking recovery from illness, safe childbirth and successful voyages. He called Indigenous religions devilish, so his categories need care. The evidence shows that health could involve ritual experts; it does not inventory medicines or prove identical practice elsewhere.

passages.title: Learning, writing, health, water and toilets
passages.text: Pigafetta saw fresh water collected, coconut water offered and food prepared in earthen pots, but his surviving descriptions do not establish one water-supply system. Wells, springs, rain, rivers and carried water would have varied by island and settlement. A travel diary is a poor plumbing survey.

passages.title: Learning, writing, health, water and toilets
passages.text: Toilets are the honest blank in this card. The museum earthenware summary identifies cooking and burial vessels, yet no securely identified household latrine or archipelago-wide waste system for 1492 to 1530. History cannot flush evidence into existence, so this card says unknown instead of inventing a bathroom.

passages.title: Learning, writing, health, water and toilets
passages.text: A 1640 description says some Visayan families shaped infants' heads toward a locally admired form, and archaeology finds modified skulls in several central and southern sites. This is later and regional evidence. It reminds us that children had bodies, beauty standards and family care, while warning against one childhood story for thousands of islands.

passages.title: What came after the atlas stopped
passages.text: The map ends at 1530, but no government called Philippines collapsed that year. Communities continued trading, farming, governing, worshipping and arguing. The empty 1530 and 1600 snapshots record a database gap, not an empty archipelago.

passages.title: What came after the atlas stopped
passages.text: Villalobos introduced the name Filipina in 1543, after this card. That expedition did not create an archipelago-wide state; the name itself widened later.

passages.title: What came after the atlas stopped
passages.text: Legazpi founded a permanent Spanish settlement at Cebu in 1565, outside this card. Spanish rule belongs in the separate philippines-1650 card, where colonial power, coercion and resistance can be explained at proper length.

passages.title: What came after the atlas stopped
passages.text: U.S. colonial rule, Japanese occupation, independence, dictatorship and People Power are also outside a 1492 to 1530 record. They are important, already covered in the later card and should not be squeezed into a finale that makes four centuries look like an afterthought.

In 1530 the atlas label simply stops. Distinct peoples, ports, sultanates, barangays and inland communities continued, and the very name Philippines still lay thirteen years in the future. The next atlas record starts only in 1650, after permanent Spanish settlement began, so continuity belongs to people and places rather than to one imagined state line.

passages.text: This map label spans Spanish colonial rule, revolution, American rule, Japanese occupation and an independent republic. Its 1650 starting point marks imported map coverage, not the birth of one continuous government.

passages.title: An archipelago through changing governments
passages.text: The imported outline remains almost unchanged across centuries. It cannot show the uneven reach of Spanish power, especially among Muslim and highland communities. Nor does this simplified land outline decide modern maritime claims. The earlier map record called Philippines, covering 1492 to 1530, is kept separate.

passages.title: An archipelago through changing governments
passages.text: Spanish Manila became the colonial capital in 1571, well before this map begins. Officials governed partly through existing local leaders, while Catholic religious orders developed considerable influence. Indigenous communities nevertheless retained varied relationships with the colonial administration.

passages.title: An archipelago through changing governments
passages.text: From 1565 to 1815, the Manila galleon route connected the Philippines with Acapulco in Mexico. Asian silk, porcelain and other goods crossed the Pacific, while American silver traveled toward Asia. A ceramic dish could therefore belong to a trading story stretching far beyond the kitchen where it eventually landed.

passages.title: An archipelago through changing governments
passages.text: The San Jose wrecked near Lubang Island in 1694 after seeking shelter from a storm. Excavators in 1986 found ceramics, glass buttons, copper rings, lead sheets and ammunition. The collection places humble fittings beside cargo and weapons: a ship was also a crowded working place, not just a line on a trade map.

passages.title: An archipelago through changing governments
passages.text: Researchers returned to the San Jose site in 2019 and recovered more ceramics, including four intact miniature bottles. They also documented anchors. Returning to a known wreck can reveal fresh evidence; archaeology is often repeated, patient work rather than a single dramatic treasure discovery.

passages.title: An archipelago through changing governments
passages.text: The revolution against Spain began in 1896. Spain subsequently ceded the Philippines to the United States in the 1898 Treaty of Paris, although Filipino revolutionaries sought independence. Fighting between Filipino and American forces began on 4 February 1899. Changing colonial flags did not settle who should govern.

passages.title: An archipelago through changing governments
passages.text: The First Philippine Republic was inaugurated at Barasoain Church in Malolos on 23 January 1899. This was a Filipino republican project, distinct from both Spanish colonial government and the American administration that fought it.

passages.title: An archipelago through changing governments
passages.text: American forces captured Emilio Aguinaldo in 1901. The United States declared the war over in 1902, but armed resistance continued in several areas. Civilians suffered severely from violence, hunger and disease. The republic lost its struggle for control; the desire for independence did not disappear with it.

passages.title: An archipelago through changing governments
passages.text: The Jones Law of 1916 established a Philippine Senate and House, but some legislation still required American approval. The Commonwealth, inaugurated on 15 November 1935, expanded self-government while remaining under U.S. sovereignty. Its legislature was initially one chamber; constitutional changes restored two chambers in 1940.

passages.title: An archipelago through changing governments
passages.text: Japan attacked in December 1941 and occupied Manila in January 1942. Guerrilla movements resisted occupation, while a Japanese-backed government claimed authority. Allied forces returned in 1944; Japan surrendered in 1945. These wartime governments should not be mistaken for an uninterrupted independent republic.

passages.title: An archipelago through changing governments
passages.text: On 4 July 1946, the United States formally recognized Philippine independence and signed a treaty relinquishing its sovereignty claims. This date concerns the end of American colonial sovereignty; it is different from the revolutionary declaration of independence in 1898.

passages.title: An archipelago through changing governments
passages.text: Ferdinand Marcos imposed martial law in 1972. Political repression and media censorship restricted everyday freedoms. The People Power uprising of 1986, joined by defections within the military, brought down his regime. Remembering this transition means remembering the citizens who challenged authoritarian power, as well as political leaders.

passages.title: An archipelago through changing governments
passages.text: Martial law was formally lifted on 17 January 1981, but Marcos remained in power until 1986. That distinction matters: ending a legal proclamation and ending a dictatorship were different events.

passages.title: An archipelago through changing governments
passages.text: The constitution ratified on 2 February 1987 places sovereignty in the people and describes a democratic republic. It protects family life, recognizes women’s equality before the law and requires free public elementary and secondary education. These are legal commitments against which government can be judged, rather than proof that everyone enjoys identical opportunities.

passages.title: Homes, kitchens and children
passages.text: Casa Manila is a museum reconstruction of an affluent late-colonial home, with a facade modeled on an 1850s house in Binondo. Its mezzanine evokes rooms for extended family and guests, including grandparents, aunts and uncles. This is one wealthy urban setting, not a model for every island household.

passages.title: Homes, kitchens and children
passages.text: The Casa Manila guide describes small sliding panels beneath the windows, called ventanillas. They admitted extra air and let children watch processions in the street below. One architectural feature could help cool a room and provide a child-sized view of the neighborhood.

passages.title: Homes, kitchens and children
passages.text: The Casa Manila kitchen includes a slatted food cupboard, the paminggalan, and an icebox called a nievera. Imported American ice made the latter a nineteenth-century luxury. Leftovers had their own furniture long before an electric refrigerator could hum in the corner.

passages.title: Homes, kitchens and children
passages.text: In the same museum, roof gutters feed an aljibe, a cistern whose water passed through gravel, sand and charcoal. The azotea accommodated washing and other messy chores. The toilet display explains that large houses could have several seats together: the historic bathroom did not always promise modern-style privacy.

passages.title: Homes, kitchens and children
passages.text: A Spanish educational decree in 1863 called for primary schools for boys and girls in each town and a school for training male teachers. Under American rule, the 1901 education law created a centralized public system and authorized recruiting 600 American teachers. The Thomasites expanded teaching, but education in the islands had a much longer history.

passages.title: Homes, kitchens and children
passages.text: Food scientist Maria Orosa developed ways to preserve local produce and presented preserved foods, including a whole canned mango, at the 1925 Manila Carnival. In the 1930s she developed banana ketchup. A familiar condiment could be the result of laboratory work on how to use locally available ingredients.

passages.title: Homes, kitchens and children
passages.text: Orosa also adapted an earthenware cooking pot into a palayok oven that could bake over a fire without electricity. Her extension work taught food preservation and practical household skills. Kitchen equipment, gardens and community lessons formed part of the same effort to improve nutrition and food supplies.

passages.title: Homes, kitchens and children
passages.text: In Aklan, piña weavers extract fibers from pineapple leaves and prepare them for weaving into fine cloth. UNESCO’s 2023 account describes weighing fibers with an old coin as a unit. Children learn by watching relatives, while community schools teach the craft too. The pineapple contributes clothing as well as a snack.

passages.title: Homes, kitchens and children
passages.text: Bohol’s asin tibuok salt looks like a white egg inside a brown shell. Makers soak coconut husks in seawater, dry and burn them, prepare brine with the ash, and boil it in clay pots. UNESCO’s 2025 account describes knowledge passed within families. The egg-like object on the table is salt, not breakfast waiting to hatch.

passages.title: Farming, health and useful science
passages.text: At the International Rice Research Institute in Los Baños, IR8 rice underwent trials in the Philippines and other Asian countries in 1965 and 1966. Its short, sturdy stems helped plants stay upright under productive growing conditions. Released in 1966, it became an important example of breeding crops for higher yields, with results still depending on farming conditions.

passages.title: Farming, health and useful science
passages.text: An IRRI history records farmers arriving by bus, bicycle and on foot to collect two kilograms of IR8 seed after leaving their names and addresses. More than two thousand farmers received seed in the second half of 1966. A major agricultural change began, for many participants, with a small package to try at home.

passages.title: Farming, health and useful science
passages.text: Pediatrician Fe del Mundo worked on more than hospital treatment. The National Academy’s 1988 biography emphasizes her training of doctors, other health workers and lay helpers, together with extension into remote rural areas. Caring for children also required sharing knowledge with people who could reach families beyond major hospitals.

passages.title: Farming, health and useful science
passages.text: The Universal Health Care Act of 2019 provides automatic enrollment of Filipino citizens in the National Health Insurance Program. WHO described reforms intended to coordinate services and improve access. Insurance rules, local facilities and trained staff are all parts of getting care to a patient; passing the law was a step in that work.

passages.title: Farming, health and useful science
passages.text: A UNICEF report from May 2024 visited Pagasinan Elementary School in Bongao, Tawi-Tawi. Pupils brought drinking water from home; handwashing pipes needed a container supply. Of three toilets, one was broken and another reserved for teachers, leaving one for pupils. This named school shows why usable water and toilets remain part of the education story.

passages.title: Farming, health and useful science
passages.text: Diwata-1 was launched in March 2016 and deployed from the International Space Station that April. Filipino engineers trained in Japan as part of the project. A 2026 Philippine Space Agency account links it to lessons from Typhoon Yolanda: satellite images could become maps useful in disasters, once teams learned to obtain and process them.

passages.title: A short written voice
passages.text: A 13 February 2023 Civil Service Commission announcement quotes “ang wikang pambansa ng Pilipinas ay Filipino”: “the national language of the Philippines is Filipino.” This Latin-script Filipino passage reproduces Article XIV of the 1987 constitution, which also recognizes English and regional languages.

Colonial sovereignty ended, and the Marcos dictatorship later fell, but the Philippines did not disappear. The constitutional republic continues; this open-ended map record should be read through its changing governments rather than assigned a single fall date.

sectionTitles: A child’s small chariot and a very large meal
Names in stone, dates in wood

passages.text: Phrygian communities built an influential Iron Age kingdom in Anatolia, with Gordion as its principal royal centre. Their monumental buildings, workshops and burials preserve evidence of power and daily work. The map’s broad 1500-500 BCE span is not the documented lifetime of that kingdom: its start is much too early, and the same large outline cannot show changing political control. This card focuses on the better-attested Iron Age society and its later continuity.

passages.title: Power beyond the golden-touch story
passages.text: The historical Midas appears as Mita in late-eighth-century Assyrian records. He was a significant opponent of Assyrian ambitions in Anatolia. The later tale that everything he touched became gold is a myth; excavated palaces and the diplomatic record provide firmer evidence for his kingdom’s wealth and influence.

passages.title: Power beyond the golden-touch story
passages.text: Gordion’s monumental gateway still has stone walls standing about ten metres high. A visitor approaching it would have encountered a carefully built statement of royal strength. Behind the defences stood large halls, workshops and the institutions needed to sustain a major Iron Age centre.

passages.title: Power beyond the golden-touch story
passages.text: Elite buildings at Gordion contained early coloured pebble mosaics, with stones arranged into lively geometric patterns. The builders also tackled long timber roof spans. These achievements depended on planning and skilled construction, extending royal display from the city’s massive entrance to the floor under a visitor’s feet.

passages.title: Making bread, thread and furniture
passages.text: In the Terrace Building and nearby workshops, cooking areas stood beside rooms with grinding platforms and textile tools. Workers turned grain into flour while others prepared thread and cloth. The repeated layouts point to organized production on a substantial scale, although the tools alone cannot identify each worker’s social status.

passages.title: Making bread, thread and furniture
passages.text: Archaeologists inventoried more than a thousand spindle whorls at Gordion. These small clay weights helped spinners make thread. Other clay weights kept hanging threads taut on upright looms. Some of the city’s grandest economic achievements depended on very small objects doing their jobs over and over.

passages.title: Making bread, thread and furniture
passages.text: Outside the citadel, excavated homes had hearths, ovens, grinding benches and plastered storage bins. Some rooms had stone paving and mud-brick walls strengthened with wooden posts. Preparing food and making textiles were part of life here too, beyond the monumental spaces associated with rulers.

passages.title: Making bread, thread and furniture
passages.text: Wooden objects from Gordion’s elite tombs include tables, stools, bowls and spoons, as well as elaborately decorated furniture. Dry, relatively stable tomb interiors helped them survive. Craftspeople chose woods such as boxwood, juniper and walnut, combining different materials with carving, inlay and bronze decoration.

passages.title: Making bread, thread and furniture
passages.text: Wooden plates from Tumulus W preserve early, securely dated evidence for lathe work. Turning wood allowed craftspeople to shape a piece as it rotated. Careful study of tool marks can recover a workshop technique even when the workshop and its tools have disappeared.

passages.title: A child’s small chariot and a very large meal
passages.text: The rich child burial called Tumulus P contained a small toy quadriga, a four-horse chariot. This is a glimpse of an object placed with one privileged child, not a catalogue of every child’s playthings. Its miniature horse equipment became the subject of detailed archaeological study.

passages.title: A child’s small chariot and a very large meal
passages.text: Most people did not receive a vast burial mound. In Gordion’s Common Cemetery, excavators catalogued 112 graves, and only 34 contained even modest offerings. Comparing these burials with lavish tumuli reveals differences in wealth and funerary treatment that the royal monuments alone would hide.

passages.title: A child’s small chariot and a very large meal
passages.text: Residues in vessels from Tumulus MM suggest a funeral meal of meat and legumes, with a fermented drink combining grape wine, barley beer and honey. The proposed menu comes from chemical analysis. It describes an exceptional royal occasion, rather than what every Phrygian family ate for dinner.

passages.title: A child’s small chariot and a very large meal
passages.text: The funeral equipment included three large cauldrons, each capable of holding about 150 litres, and animal-headed pouring vessels. Serving tables and drinking bowls helped researchers reconstruct how the mourners were supplied. This was a meal requiring serious organization, not simply one oversized cup.

passages.title: A child’s small chariot and a very large meal
passages.text: The man in Tumulus MM lay in a log coffin on dyed textiles. The excavators observed purple and brown traces when the chamber was opened. Furniture and fabrics accompanied the burial, preserving evidence of care, ceremony and costly craftsmanship even where organic materials normally decay.

passages.title: Names in stone, dates in wood
passages.text: At the rock-cut Midas Monument near Yazılıkaya, the Phrygian inscription includes “midai lavagtaei”, meaning “for Midas the leader”. This is a modern Latin-letter transcription of the ancient alphabet. The sixth-century BCE monument is later than the famous eighth-century king; which Midas it invokes remains a historical question.

passages.title: Names in stone, dates in wood
passages.text: The same monument belongs to the worship of Matar, the Phrygian Mother Goddess. Its façade and niche connected a divine presence with the named people who commissioned work. A dedication could preserve a patron’s ambitions alongside a community’s religious setting.

passages.title: Names in stone, dates in wood
passages.text: Tree-ring research moved Tumulus MM’s construction to around 740 BCE. Since Assyrian records still place Midas in power in 709 BCE, its occupant cannot readily be the famous king himself. The label “Midas Mound” survived a major change in what archaeologists think the tomb represents.

passages.title: Names in stone, dates in wood
passages.text: Excavations began with the Körte brothers in 1900 and expanded under Rodney Young from 1950. Investigators uncovered citadels, tombs and earlier settlement layers. Separating those layers matters: people lived at Gordion before the Phrygian kingdom, and continued using the site after its independence ended.

passages.title: Names in stone, dates in wood
passages.text: Phrygian writing continued far beyond the map’s 500 BCE cutoff. In Roman-period funerary inscriptions, Greek might record a dead person’s details while Phrygian supplied a warning against disturbing the grave. These later bilingual texts show a continuing language in a changed political and social world.

The independent kingdom gave way to Lydian dominance and then Persian rule in the sixth century BCE. Gordion remained an important district centre. Phrygian communities and their language continued under later powers, so neither a single destruction layer nor the map’s 500 BCE endpoint marks the disappearance of the people.

passages.text: Pictish communities and kingdoms occupied parts of early medieval Scotland. Their history survives in carved stones, workshops, food remains and outside accounts. The evidence reveals connected regional societies, not a single unchanged state. Political authority and language changed as Alba emerged, without a securely established single date when all Picts disappeared.

passages.title: Peoples, places and evidence
passages.text: Written references to Picts begin in the late third century. This first surviving name is not a secure founding date for a people or kingdom.

passages.title: Peoples, places and evidence
passages.text: Fortriu, a powerful kingdom by the seventh century, is now located around the Moray Firth. Its full extent and relationship with smaller regions remain debated.

passages.title: Peoples, places and evidence
passages.text: Rhynie's fifth- and sixth-century settlement had successive ditches and a larger timber palisade. The Craw Stane stood near an entrance. These excavated relationships connect symbol stones with an inhabited, repeatedly remodelled place.

passages.title: Making, exchange and ordinary work
passages.text: An iron axe-shaped pin from Rhynie resembles the axe on the Rhynie Man stone. Clay moulds for comparable pins establish local manufacture, linking a carved image to the work of metalworkers.

passages.title: Making, exchange and ordinary work
passages.text: Rhynie's ditch deposits contained imported amphora fragments, continental glass, crucibles and metalworking tools. The vessels demonstrate exchange connections, while production debris shows that the settlement also made valuable objects.

passages.title: Making, exchange and ordinary work
passages.text: Around 700, Portmahomack's workers carved stone, worked metal and glass, and processed hides interpreted as parchment production. Combined with its burial pattern and infrastructure, this supports identification as a monastery.

passages.title: Making, exchange and ordinary work
passages.text: Cattle bones dominate Portmahomack's animal remains. The researchers connect cattle with food, possible dairying and hides for parchment. Supporting a religious community required husbandry and skilled processing as well as prayer.

passages.title: Making, exchange and ordinary work
passages.text: After the monastic phase, a Portmahomack workshop became a kiln barn with an upper floor and flue. Its alteration, together with grain remains, makes a change in everyday work visible in the buildings.

passages.title: Making, exchange and ordinary work
passages.text: Charred barley and evidence for oats and wheat at Lairg document cultivation from about 450 onward. Such environmental traces reveal food production even where early medieval houses are difficult to identify.

passages.title: Images, learning and change
passages.text: The Hilton of Cadboll cross-slab, erected around 800, places a woman prominently in a hunting scene. The original was later cut and reused as a grave marker; the stone at the site today is a replica.

passages.title: Images, learning and change
passages.text: Bede reports that King Naiton asked Ceolfrid for guidance on Easter and builders for a stone church. His account shows royal interest in religious calculation and imported expertise, although it presents these exchanges through Bede's Christian viewpoint.

passages.title: Images, learning and change
passages.text: Burning and broken sculpture mark Portmahomack's destruction around 800. A Viking raid is a proposed explanation, not an identified attacker. Workers subsequently cleared debris and resumed metal and glass production.

Pictish power centres shifted during the later ninth century, and Alba extended uneven authority into the Highlands in the tenth. This was a prolonged political and cultural transformation. The evidence does not support one conquest date or the disappearance of an entire population.
