sectionTitles: First, catch the map making a two-century mistake
How an empire reached Kannauj before this card begins
A royal umbrella folds between 1000 and 1036
Government lived in grants, ranks and local memory
War, diplomacy and the danger of giant border blobs
Fields, water, workshops and money kept the world moving
Temples, sculptures, books and a very useful zero
Families, ranks, lessons and a copper voice
Homes, meals, clothes, markets and time off
Health, water, washing, toilets and what continued

passages.text: Picture a giant royal umbrella folding while dozens of smaller umbrellas pop open beneath it. Around 1000 CE, the Gurjara-Pratihara court still claimed Kannauj, but its great ninth-century empire had already lost powerful lords, forts and provinces. Mahmud of Ghazni raided Kannauj in 1018; Rajyapala fled and was killed after a Chandela-led response. Trilochanapala then issued a copper grant near Prayaga in 1027, and a Yashapala inscription dated 1036 may mark a last flicker, though that family link is disputed. The atlas makes the puzzle stranger: its separate id pratiharas runs from 1000 to 1200, misses Kannauj, Gwalior and Jhusi, and stretches east across Gorakhpur and Patna. This card follows the historical line only to its cautious early-eleventh-century ending, then explains the people, temples, farms, markets and successor powers that continued. Inscriptions favor kings and donors, so gaps about children, healers and toilets are labeled instead of filled with guesses.

passages.title: First, catch the map making a two-century mistake
passages.text: The exact imported record is id “pratiharas,” name “Pratiharas,” circa 1000 to 1200. The earlier id gurjara-pratihara is separately indexed from 800 to 1000 and already has its own card. This bundle creates a standalone continuation card; it does not alias, replace or duplicate that earlier record.

passages.title: First, catch the map making a two-century mistake
passages.text: At 1000 the target is one Polygon, one ring and 29 positions. Its bounds are 77.061° to 94.154° east and 25.106° to 32.309° north; coordinate SHA-256 is 610039ec6650844e94ac104e78125ae6df7620a406eca047ffb2bc94e7f416b3. Ayodhya, Gorakhpur and Patna test inside, while Kannauj and Gwalior do not.

passages.title: First, catch the map making a two-century mistake
passages.text: At 1100 the polygon remains one ring but changes to 31 positions, bounds 77.061° to 94.370° east and 25.105° to 32.309° north, SHA-256 936e72e00c7635bc64be188b5fa2fc5341c63ab8bc0e16884b5e0d7958d1959f. It still contains Ayodhya, Gorakhpur and Patna while excluding Kannauj, Gwalior, Prayaga, Jhusi and Kara.

passages.title: First, catch the map making a two-century mistake
passages.text: The 1000 polygon overlaps rajput-kingdoms at Ayodhya and Gorakhpur and overlaps palas at Patna. At 1100, the atlas gives Kannauj and Varanasi to chandellas, Gwalior to its misspelled paramas layer, and Patna solely to pratiharas. These graphics cannot be read as clean or mutually exclusive frontiers.

passages.title: First, catch the map making a two-century mistake
passages.text: At 700 the exact target is absent. At 800 and 900, the earlier gurjara-pratihara polygon includes Kannauj, Gwalior and major western or central centers. At 1200, pratiharas disappears and broad Delhi Sultanate and rajput-kingdoms layers take over many tests. The abrupt eastward jump at 1000 is a data-model break, not measured territorial history.

passages.title: How an empire reached Kannauj before this card begins
passages.text: Pratihara histories begin with more than one branch and several debated origin stories. Inscriptions linked the royal family to Lakshmana, Rama’s brother and legendary door guardian. Historians treat that genealogy as political prestige, not a birth certificate reaching back into an epic age.

passages.title: How an empire reached Kannauj before this card begins
passages.text: The label “Gurjara-Pratihara” has generated modern arguments about ethnicity, region and dynasty. One late subordinate inscription uses the compound explicitly, while imperial records vary. A careful card preserves the historical name without pretending that one word identifies every subject’s ancestry or a modern community unchanged across twelve centuries.

passages.title: How an empire reached Kannauj before this card begins
passages.text: Nagabhata II captured Kannauj, and Mihira Bhoja and Mahendrapala later ruled the dynasty at its height. Competition with Pala and Rashtrakuta rulers is often called a tripartite struggle, but campaigns, alliances and regional lords changed repeatedly. A triangle on a school diagram should not become three permanent colored teams.

passages.title: How an empire reached Kannauj before this card begins
passages.text: Imperial government depended on subordinate rulers, officers, landed beneficiaries and local communities. Kings could proclaim universal power, yet practical control varied by road, fort, town and season. When strong lords stopped cooperating, the empire contracted without every plough, workshop or shrine waiting for a single command from Kannauj.

passages.title: How an empire reached Kannauj before this card begins
passages.text: The earlier gurjara-pratihara card covers the high imperial phase from 800 to 1000. This target begins at an atlas seam just when the historical empire was weakest. Its job is therefore to connect the last Kannauj rulers to that predecessor while refusing to stretch their government all the way to 1200.

passages.title: A royal umbrella folds between 1000 and 1036
passages.text: Rajyapala ruled Kannauj as former feudatories controlled much of the older empire. Mahmud of Ghazni’s 1018 campaign reached the city, and accounts differ on whether Rajyapala fled or submitted. Either way, the episode shows a vulnerable court; it does not prove that every community in northern India suddenly changed rulers that morning.

passages.title: A royal umbrella folds between 1000 and 1036
passages.text: Chandela records celebrate Rajyapala’s killing after the raid and credit Arjuna, a subordinate of the Chandela ruler. This is evidence of a coalition policing royal honor and exploiting weakness. It is also victory writing, so the exact motives and choreography cannot be recovered as if an eyewitness filmed the meeting.

passages.title: A royal umbrella folds between 1000 and 1036
passages.text: The 1027 Jhusi plate names Trilochanapala after Rajyapala and Vijayapala and gives him very grand titles. It was issued on the Ganges near Prayaga, far from a restored continent-sized empire. Magnificent titles could travel on a shrinking royal letterhead; geography and effective power still require separate evidence.

passages.title: A royal umbrella folds between 1000 and 1036
passages.text: The Kara gateway inscription dated 1036 records Yashapala granting Payalasa village in Kausambi-mandala to Mathura Vikata of Pabhosa, with customary dues, royalties, taxes, gold and tithes. It is an unusually late administrative glimpse, but whether this Yashapala certainly belonged to the imperial Pratihara family remains debated.

passages.title: A royal umbrella folds between 1000 and 1036
passages.text: By the later eleventh century, records place Kalachuri and then Gahadavala rulers around Varanasi and Kannauj. The Pratihara political ending was a fragmentation and replacement, not a vanishing population. Farmers, merchants, ritual specialists, artisans and scribes continued while royal names above them changed.

passages.title: Government lived in grants, ranks and local memory
passages.text: Pratihara rule worked through layered relationships. A royal court recognized regional lords; those lords sponsored temples and managed local forces; village elites and corporate groups handled resources on the ground. The system could expand quickly through alliances, but the same structure let powerful subordinates become independent when the center weakened.

passages.title: Government lived in grants, ranks and local memory
passages.text: Gwalior’s 876 inscription names cultivators Dallaka and Memmaka and describes two fields by the amount of barley seed needed to sow them. Boundaries used rocks, another field and a water channel. Grand endowments still needed neighbors to know exactly which patch of dirt the elegant Sanskrit meant.

passages.title: Government lived in grants, ranks and local memory
passages.text: Pehowa’s 882 record describes horse dealers contributing fees to maintain temples at Pehowa and Kannauj. Merchants, animals, toll-like payments and religious institutions met in one organized arrangement. It reveals administration through a commercial community, not simply royal tax collectors appearing everywhere with identical forms.

passages.title: Government lived in grants, ranks and local memory
passages.text: Royal grants were social instructions as well as documents. Courts depended on ranked officers, village leaders, landholders and recipients to recognize new rights and obligations locally. A copper plate could announce authority, but its commands still had to be understood, remembered and enforced by people on the ground.

passages.title: Government lived in grants, ranks and local memory
passages.text: Yashapala’s possible last grant was made to an individual rather than securely identified as a Brahmana religious gift. Historians have read it as a service grant, perhaps to a literate Kayastha official, but that social identification is an inference. The inscription securely gives the grantee’s name, place and revenue package.

passages.title: War, diplomacy and the danger of giant border blobs
passages.text: Pratihara rulers had fought Palas in the east and Rashtrakutas in the Deccan for influence around Kannauj. Those wars were not one continuous three-way match. Kings died, branches split, feudatories shifted sides and campaigns followed routes and forts; large zones of claimed authority contained communities with very different local histories.

passages.title: War, diplomacy and the danger of giant border blobs
passages.text: The 1018 invasion tied north Indian politics to Ghazni, but the response was also deeply regional. Chandela power, a Gwalior subordinate and the diminished Kannauj court all mattered. “Foreign invasion” and “internal rivalry” were happening together, which is why one arrow on a map cannot explain Rajyapala’s fall.

passages.title: War, diplomacy and the danger of giant border blobs
passages.text: After the Pratiharas, Kalachuris, Chandelas and Gahadavalas competed in the Ganges-Yamuna region. Farther west, Chauhans, Paramaras, Chaulukyas and other houses had their own courts. These were not obedient pieces waiting to reunite; each formed alliances, patronized institutions and claimed status for itself.

passages.title: War, diplomacy and the danger of giant border blobs
passages.text: Premodern power often followed nodes, roads, river crossings and negotiated relationships rather than a surveyed line. That model fits the inscriptions better than the atlas’s polygon reaching almost to 94° east. A royal title at one camp or a land grant in one district cannot fill every pixel between them.

passages.title: War, diplomacy and the danger of giant border blobs
passages.text: No single atlas successor matches the Pratihara dissolution. At 1200, Delhi Sultanate and rajput-kingdoms polygons absorb many tested points, while Chandelas, Chauhans and Palas have separate indexed histories. The structured ending therefore names no one-to-one successor, even though the target records a predecessor link to gurjara-pratihara.

passages.title: Fields, water, workshops and money kept the world moving
passages.text: The Gwalior endowment required oil workers and guild leaders from several towns to provide measured oil from every press each month for temple lamps. A glowing shrine depended on crushing seed, maintaining presses, measuring liquid and organizing deliveries. The miracle here was partly a dependable supply schedule.

passages.title: Fields, water, workshops and money kept the world moving
passages.text: A rock inscription from about 942 to 943 credits Vinayakapala with irrigation work on the Urvasi River and names Bhailadaman, son of Krishnaraja, as writer. Water engineering involved embankments or channels, labor and maintenance; public memory also required somebody trained to compose and write the record.

passages.title: Fields, water, workshops and money kept the world moving
passages.text: Early medieval northern farms produced wheat, barley, rice, millets, pulses, sesame, mustard, sugarcane, cotton and other crops in different ecological zones. This list describes regional possibilities, not one family’s dinner or one village’s field. Rain, rivers, wells and local soils decided what could actually grow.

passages.title: Fields, water, workshops and money kept the world moving
passages.text: Trade joined market towns, pilgrimage places and rural producers. Horse dealers at Pehowa are unusually visible, while other merchants moved salt, cloth, grain, oil, metal goods and ritual supplies. Historians debate whether every early medieval town declined, so the card avoids both a golden-age bazaar and an empty-city myth.

passages.title: Fields, water, workshops and money kept the world moving
passages.text: A debased silver Gurjara-Pratihara coin in the British Museum weighs 3.18 grams and imitates an older Indo-Sasanian design: a rough ruler bust on one face and a fire altar with attendant on the other. Long-lived imagery made money recognizable even when the portrait would never win a drawing contest.

passages.title: Temples, sculptures, books and a very useful zero
passages.text: At Gwalior, officer Alla commissioned the Caturbhuj temple under Mihira Bhoja. Workers cut its interior from living rock rather than stacking every wall. The inscription ties architecture to a named official, while the finished space points to planners, quarrying skill, tool makers, stone cutters and many laborers the text leaves unnamed.

passages.title: Temples, sculptures, books and a very useful zero
passages.text: Pratihara-style temples experimented with plans, wall projections, doorways, towers and sculpture as temple building expanded across early medieval India. The tall Teli-ka-Mandir at Gwalior is exceptional, while Bateshwar and Amrol show related but varied forms. “Pratihara style” is an art-historical family resemblance, not proof that one king personally designed every chisel mark.

passages.title: Temples, sculptures, books and a very useful zero
passages.text: A tenth-century Malwa sandstone goddess in the British Museum is over a meter tall. Her lotus seat and powerful divine body belonged to a carefully carved sacred image, not an ordinary portrait. Museum labels can locate style and material, but missing excavation context limits what one sculpture says about its first worshippers.

passages.title: Temples, sculptures, books and a very useful zero
passages.text: A central Indian Gauri sculpture places Ganesha on a lotus in the goddess’s hand and an iguana-like creature near her feet; smaller women are interpreted as donors. Divine family imagery and human patrons meet in one object, but elite religious sculpture cannot serve as a candid photograph of everybody’s clothes or home.

passages.title: Temples, sculptures, books and a very useful zero
passages.text: The 876 Gwalior inscription writes small circular zeros in 270 and 50 while measuring a flower garden and its daily garlands. Zero was doing practical paperwork, not posing alone on a chalkboard. The record is famous because its date and place are secure, though Indian place-value notation had a longer history.

passages.title: Families, ranks, lessons and a copper voice
passages.text: Court poet Rajashekhara served Mahendrapala, and his wife Avantisundari was credited with opinions on literary criticism that he quoted. This learned couple offers rare evidence for an elite woman’s intellectual work. It cannot prove that girls of every caste or village had equal access to books and teachers.

passages.title: Families, ranks, lessons and a copper voice
passages.text: Early medieval society combined Brahmanical varna ideals with many regionally specific jatis, occupations and status claims. Landholding, court service, craft, gender and ritual rank shaped opportunity. Sources written by elite men describe hierarchy more clearly than children, servants or laborers speaking in their own voices, so certainty is uneven.

passages.title: Families, ranks, lessons and a copper voice
passages.text: Written sample, in readable modern Devanagari normalization: “ॐ स्वस्ति । श्रीप्रयागसमीपगङ्गातटावासे ... श्रीमत्त्रिलोचनपालदेवः”. The 1027 Jhusi plate is Sanskrit in Nagari characters, while an earlier Gwalior record uses Siddhamatrika. This display regularizes the editor’s Roman text; it is not a facsimile of the copper letters or their original spacing.

passages.title: Families, ranks, lessons and a copper voice
passages.text: Transliteration: “oṁ svasti | śrī-prayāga-samīpa-gaṅgā-taṭāvāse ... śrīmat-trilocanapāladevaḥ”. Translation: “Om. Fortune! Residing on the bank of the Ganges near illustrious Prayaga ... the illustrious Trilochanapala.” The ellipsis skips royal genealogy, so the sample is an opening fragment, not a complete sentence. It locates the issuing court before naming its ruler.

passages.title: Families, ranks, lessons and a copper voice
passages.text: Convention links the plate to late Kannauj Pratiharas because it names Vijayapala, Rajyapala and Trilochanapala, but its first editor noted that no dynasty is named. This teaches real evidence with a real limit: genealogy alone does not erase doubt for historians.

passages.title: Homes, meals, clothes, markets and time off
passages.text: At Anai in the middle Ganges plain, a 700 to 1000 layer preserved a mud house, ovens, red-ware cooking pots, storage jars, spouted vessels, iron objects, glass bangles, cowries and miniature vessels. This nearby settlement is regional comparison, not proof that every Pratihara household owned the same objects.

passages.title: Homes, meals, clothes, markets and time off
passages.text: Possible meals drew on wheat or barley flatbreads and porridge, rice where water allowed, millets, pulses, oils, sugarcane products, fruit, vegetables and dairy or meat according to place, wealth and custom. Crop lists cannot reconstruct a fixed menu, and feast food was not the same as a laborer’s everyday bowl.

passages.title: Homes, meals, clothes, markets and time off
passages.text: Stone deities and donors wear jewelry, arranged hair and draped garments that display sculptors’ ideals and elite presentation. Cotton cultivation and craft records support textile production, but cloth rarely survives in the region’s soil. The safest clothing picture combines fibers, tools and images while admitting that colors and everyday patches are mostly lost.

passages.title: Homes, meals, clothes, markets and time off
passages.text: Markets brought cultivators, oil pressers, potters, metalworkers, cloth sellers, carriers, money handlers and animal dealers into exchange. Pehowa’s horse merchants show that traders could organize collective payments. A child might see impressive horses there, but no source says every market was a permanent fairground.

passages.title: Homes, meals, clothes, markets and time off
passages.text: Rajashekhara imagined an aspiring poet reading and writing in the morning, discussing poetry after lunch and socializing in the evening. It is elite advice, not an average timetable. Songs, stories and performance surely mattered, but the consulted Pratihara evidence does not securely identify a particular children’s board game or toy.

passages.title: Health, water, washing, toilets and what continued
passages.text: The wider Susruta tradition discusses anatomy, surgery, medicines and learning from a teacher, but its textual layers and dates are debated. It gives Indian medical background rather than a patient chart from Kannauj. Household caregivers, herbal specialists and learned physicians probably served people unequally, yet direct Pratihara clinic evidence is sparse.

passages.title: Health, water, washing, toilets and what continued
passages.text: Early medieval learning included mathematics, astronomy, medical and technical texts, while craftspeople also learned through practiced work. The written zero, precise stone cutting and irrigation records show skills in action. A surviving achievement does not reveal one universal school system; most children probably learned duties within households and occupations.

passages.title: Health, water, washing, toilets and what continued
passages.text: Jhusi’s archaeological list records a tank and deep stone-lined wells at a settlement beside the Ganges. Those structures supplied water that could serve drinking, ritual, washing or bathing, but the source does not assign every use. Nor does it tell us how often each person washed or how clean the water remained.

passages.title: Health, water, washing, toilets and what continued
passages.text: The Anai report describes a mud house, ovens, vessels and nearby wells but no securely identified household latrine in its 700 to 1000 layer. The directly Pratihara records consulted here are equally silent. Wells, drains, pits or ring structures must not be renamed toilets without archaeological evidence; sanitation probably varied household by household.

passages.title: Health, water, washing, toilets and what continued
passages.text: The Pratihara court dissolved around the 1030s, but fields, waterworks, temples, craft knowledge, Sanskrit record keeping and local communities continued under other rulers. The atlas keeps the id until 1200 and then redraws the region again. Political endings change institutions and risks; they do not switch ordinary life off like a lamp.

Around 1036, the last possible inscriptional trace of a Pratihara ruler appears at Kara, although Yashapala’s connection to the imperial family is disputed. The Kannauj-centered empire had already broken apart, and no continuous Pratihara state can be demonstrated through the atlas endpoint of 1200. Chandelas, Kalachuris, Gahadavalas, Chauhans, Palas, Paramaras and other powers shaped different parts of the old political world. Farms, markets, temples, waterworks, crafts and families continued under those changing authorities. This card therefore ends the polity around the 1030s, leaves structured successors empty rather than inventing one heir, and treats the remaining atlas interval as a documented map error and afterlife.

sectionTitles: Earlier town life beneath the kingdom

passages.text: Roman Mstyslavych united Galicia and Volhynia in 1199, creating a powerful state in southwestern Rus. His successors negotiated between local nobles, neighbouring kingdoms and Mongol overlords. Its towns supported crafts and ambitious builders. The imported outline’s southern extent is uncertain and should not be treated as a precise historical border.

passages.title: A kingdom between stronger neighbours
passages.text: Danylo accepted a crown from Pope Innocent IV in 1253 while seeking military help against the Mongols. A crown could advertise royal standing, but it could not supply an army by itself. The hoped-for western assistance did not arrive in the form Danylo needed.

passages.title: A kingdom between stronger neighbours
passages.text: Danylo had already visited Batu Khan’s court and acknowledged his supremacy in 1246. Later Mongol pressure forced the dismantling of fortifications. The kingdom’s survival therefore involved uncomfortable compromises as well as victories; paying homage and surrendering defences limited what its rulers could do.

passages.title: A kingdom between stronger neighbours
passages.text: Trade connected the principality with other Rus lands, Poland, Hungary, Bohemia, Lithuania and the Byzantine world. Merchants crossed political and linguistic frontiers that a coloured map can make look much more solid than they were in everyday commercial life.

passages.title: Stone, books and ingenious builders
passages.text: At Danylo’s residence in Kholm, now Chełm in Poland, excavators have recovered walls and architectural fragments made with green local stone. The chronicle also describes white and green building materials. The remains give archaeologists a way to test a written description against an actual building site.

passages.title: Stone, books and ingenious builders
passages.text: The green stone was relatively easy to carve into mouldings and intricate reliefs. Its beauty came with a practical drawback: wet, freezing conditions could damage it. Medieval builders had to juggle appearance, workability and durability, much as builders still do when choosing materials.

passages.title: Stone, books and ingenious builders
passages.text: Researchers studying white building pieces from the residence identified a material they interpret as an artificial, marble-like stone. Their analysis suggests chalk and silica from horsetail plants, hardened under hot, wet conditions. This proposed recipe makes the building site look surprisingly experimental, with plants contributing more than garden decoration.

passages.title: Stone, books and ingenious builders
passages.text: The Galician-Volhynian Chronicle combines narratives centred on Danylo with a later Volhynian section. Its authors favoured strong princes and criticized rebellious nobles. They were skilled storytellers with political loyalties, so their descriptions are valuable evidence that historians compare with archaeology and other texts.

passages.title: Stone, books and ingenious builders
passages.text: Volodymyr Vasylkovych, a later thirteenth-century ruler in Volhynia, supported churches, literature and ecclesiastical art and assembled a substantial library. The chronicle praised his learning. Books required expensive materials and skilled labour, making a princely library both a personal interest and an important act of patronage.

passages.title: Earlier town life beneath the kingdom
passages.text: Zvenyhorod was already an important town before the union of 1199. Its wet ground preserved wooden building remains, wooden dishes and leather footwear that often decay elsewhere. These earlier finds let us picture kitchens, feet and household work, instead of seeing the region only through its rulers.

passages.title: Earlier town life beneath the kingdom
passages.text: Archaeologists identified craft and household areas along the Bilka River and recovered many ornaments, including glass jewellery. Together, the workshop landscape and personal possessions reveal a town where skilled production and dressing up were parts of life long before the united principality was founded.

passages.title: Earlier town life beneath the kingdom
passages.text: A birchbark letter from around 1120 to 1140 records Goven’s widow demanding sixty kunas connected with a boat. She threatens to bring a prince’s official if the debtor refuses. The message preserves a woman pursuing a household claim, with the distinctly unromantic problem of collecting money owed.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: The same earlier Zvenyhorod letter opens “ѿ говѣновое : ко нѣжьньцю”, meaning “From Goven’s widow to Nezhenets”. This is the catalogue’s historical Cyrillic transcription with editorial word divisions; “widow” is supplied from the interpretation. It illustrates local writing before the kingdom’s foundation, rather than a thirteenth-century royal document.

The death of Yurii II Boleslav in 1340 ended the united state’s dynastic phase and brought prolonged competition between Polish and Lithuanian rulers. Its territories were divided through subsequent struggles. The map’s 1279 cutoff is a coverage limit, not the kingdom’s historical ending.

sectionTitles: A river city and its workshops
Useful objects and places of learning

passages.text: Kyiv’s regional principality remained important after the wider Rus world divided among competing dynasties. Its river trade, craft neighbourhoods and religious buildings connected it to distant places. The Mongol attack of 1240 devastated the city, but political and urban life continued in changing forms.

passages.title: A river city and its workshops
passages.text: Kyiv stood where north-south and east-west trade routes met. Competing dynasties fought for its prestigious throne. This regional principality covered only part of the wider Rus world that had earlier acknowledged Kyiv’s leadership.

passages.title: A river city and its workshops
passages.text: Podil, the lower riverside district, contained a harbour, customs house and large marketplace. Potters, pitch makers and tanners worked in different quarters. Merchants arriving by water entered a busy working landscape below the upper town, where goods had to be unloaded, assessed and exchanged.

passages.title: A river city and its workshops
passages.text: Archaeologists have identified glass-working complexes in twelfth- and early thirteenth-century Podil. Workshops belonged to household properties, with small furnaces inside wooden buildings. Their locations near waterways made practical sense where hot work and timber walls created a serious fire risk.

passages.title: A river city and its workshops
passages.text: Some glass workers reheated ready-made glass rather than making every ingredient from scratch. Crucibles, lumps of glass, damaged products and furnace deposits help identify the process. A broken bead can therefore be valuable evidence: a modern excavator may be delighted by what a medieval craftsperson threw away.

passages.title: A river city and its workshops
passages.text: Podil’s workshops produced beads, bracelets and rings in different colour ranges. One workshop’s products emphasized blue, pale blue and green; another used yellow, green, pale blue and violet. These were ornaments made in batches for a market, bringing colour into the archaeological record without revealing each buyer’s wealth.

passages.title: Useful objects and places of learning
passages.text: A study of the middle Dnipro region shows that bone and antler tools remained useful in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries. Craftspeople used them for work involving leather, fur and textiles. Pointed pieces had several functions, so calling every sharp bone an awl would oversimplify the evidence.

passages.title: Useful objects and places of learning
passages.text: The same regional study examines bone skates used for moving over snow and ice. Wear on some examples suggests that they instead served as tools. Archaeologists compare working surfaces carefully: an object shaped like a skate does not automatically prove that its owner spent the afternoon skating.

passages.title: Useful objects and places of learning
passages.text: Saint Sophia’s eleventh-century interior still preserves mosaics and frescoes made with Byzantine and local participation. The Virgin Orans raises her hands in prayer, while other compositions show Christ and the apostles. These older images remained part of the religious environment inherited by the later principality.

passages.title: Useful objects and places of learning
passages.text: The Kyiv-Pechersk monastery began in the eleventh century and developed around caves overlooking the Dnipro. It became a major religious and cultural centre. Its familiar skyline includes much later rebuilding, so the large Baroque complex visible today is not a photograph of what thirteenth-century Kyiv looked like.

passages.title: Useful objects and places of learning
passages.text: Saint Sophia’s walls preserve notes made by clergy as well as visitors. Researcher Viacheslav Korniienko describes names accompanied by tally marks that counted services performed for particular people. The cathedral thus holds traces of practical record-keeping alongside its grand religious paintings.

passages.title: Useful objects and places of learning
passages.text: Korniienko also identifies writing exercises and drawings that he interprets as pupils’ caricatures of teachers. Wax tablets were available for writing, yet some marks ended up on the cathedral walls. Students finding an unofficial extra surface for their work may sound rather familiar.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: “Господи, помози” means “Lord, help”. These words begin a common medieval prayer formula scratched into Saint Sophia’s walls, quoted by the reserve’s researcher. They are shown in his normalized Cyrillic transcription of the historical Church Slavonic wording, rather than copied from one individual graffito’s letter shapes.

Kyiv’s political status changed repeatedly after 1240. Under Lithuanian rule the principality was abolished, later restored, and finally replaced by Kyiv voivodeship in 1471. The city survived these changes. Its imported map endpoint of 1279 is not the date when Kyiv ceased to exist.

passages.text: Polotsk was a Rus principality centred on the Western Dvina in what is now northern Belarus. River connections supported Baltic trade, while rival branches of its ruling family shared and contested power. Its surviving art and excavated household objects reveal both ambitious religious patronage and busy urban communities.

passages.title: Rivers, patrons and buildings
passages.text: Connections along the Western Dvina and Neman linked the Polotsk lands with Baltic trading centres. Important towns included Minsk, Vitebsk and Drutsk. Political authority was divided among princely relatives, so the region’s economy cannot be reduced to a single ruler sitting in one capital.

passages.title: Rivers, patrons and buildings
passages.text: Saint Sophia Cathedral was built in the eleventh century, before the map’s displayed phase. Parts of its foundations, apses, masonry and wall paintings survive beneath and within later rebuilding. The cathedral visible today therefore contains several historical buildings’ worth of change, rather than an untouched medieval exterior.

passages.title: Rivers, patrons and buildings
passages.text: Euphrosyne of Polotsk founded a women’s religious community and became an important patron of sacred art. The twelfth-century Saviour church and the cross commissioned in 1161 connect a named woman with major artistic work. Her influence is visible in expensive objects and architecture, not only in later stories about her.

passages.title: Rivers, patrons and buildings
passages.text: The Saviour church’s medieval builders used thin bricks, lime mortar and specially shaped bricks for curved details. A staircase runs within the western wall, leading to an upper gallery with small chapels. Such compact planning made a relatively small building contain several distinct spaces for worship.

passages.title: Rivers, patrons and buildings
passages.text: The church preserves extensive twelfth-century wall painting beneath much later decoration. Modern conservators separated later painted layers and transferred them to new supports while revealing the older frescoes. Restoring this building meant saving more than one period of art, rather like carefully keeping every layer of a very fragile cake.

passages.title: Food, animals and games
passages.text: Polotsk excavations produced large wooden pestles and parts of barrels used in household work. A thirteenth-century barrel base even retained a cucumber seed. It is a tiny piece of later evidence, but a useful reminder that food storage depended on containers somebody had to make and maintain.

passages.title: Food, animals and games
passages.text: Archaeologists found livestock buildings and manure in towns of the Polotsk lands. Thirteenth-century deposits at Polotsk were particularly rich in it. Animals belonged inside the urban economy, bringing food and useful materials along with a smell that no reconstruction painting can quite deliver.

passages.title: Food, animals and games
passages.text: Wooden spades from Polotsk were cut from single pieces of timber and lacked iron edges. Their shape suited softer ground. These plain tools put gardening and digging beside the finer crafts usually displayed in museums: much of daily work involved ordinary materials and repeated effort.

passages.title: Food, animals and games
passages.text: Twelfth- and thirteenth-century chess pieces were found in Polotsk and neighbouring towns. Many were abstract forms carved or turned from bone, rather than tiny realistic kings and horses. A surviving piece preserves the possibility of an evening’s game, although it cannot tell us who won.

passages.title: A jeweller’s work and words
passages.text: Lazar Bogsha’s cross of 1161 had a wooden core covered with gold and gilded silver plates, with settings for gemstones and relics. The precious surface depended on a carefully assembled structure beneath it. Surviving photographs document an object that combined carpentry, metalwork and religious devotion.

passages.title: A jeweller’s work and words
passages.text: Its enamel images were made directly on the cross’s own plates, an important detail in Alekseev’s study. They were designed for this commission rather than simply attached as ready-made decorations. Saints and plant-like ornaments turned a small surface into an exceptionally intricate composition.

passages.title: A jeweller’s work and words
passages.text: One word in the cross’s inscription is “злото”, meaning “gold”. This is the historical word in Alekseev’s Cyrillic transcription, with our literal English translation. The longer inscription recorded the gift and its value and warned against removing it: the beautiful object also carried its own instructions.

Polotsk was incorporated into the Grand Duchy of Lithuania in 1307 and retained a measure of autonomy afterward. Its political institutions changed while the city continued. The imported map ends this record in 1200, well before that transition.

sectionTitles: Documents and buildings that travelled through time

passages.text: Vladimir-Suzdal became a leading power in northeastern Rus, supported by fertile agricultural districts and connections to Volga trade. Its princes sponsored distinctive white-stone churches, while townspeople made tools, ornaments and household goods. Political power later fragmented and came increasingly under Mongol and Muscovite control.

passages.title: Fields, towns and political change
passages.text: The fertile Suzdal Opolye supplied an agricultural base, while the Volga connected the region with eastern trade. Rulers benefited from both food production and movement along rivers. Their power rested on working landscapes and transport routes as well as soldiers and impressive stone buildings.

passages.title: Fields, towns and political change
passages.text: Archaeology shows that Suzdal continued growing after the princely centre shifted to Vladimir in 1157. Some nearby rural settlements lay only a few hundred metres from its developed areas. Fields, gardens and town streets formed a close patchwork, with no neat modern boundary between urban and rural life.

passages.title: Fields, towns and political change
passages.text: By the later thirteenth century, the territory directly controlled by the grand prince had shrunk as separate principalities multiplied. Mongol khans awarded the right to hold the senior title. A grand-sounding title therefore did not always mean that its holder directly governed every town coloured into the older region.

passages.title: Getting ready for the day
passages.text: Suzdal’s excavated combs include many from twelfth- and early thirteenth-century layers. Double-sided examples often had closely spaced teeth on one edge and wider teeth on the other. Hair care had its own equipment, and an ordinary morning could begin with a familiar battle against tangles.

passages.title: Getting ready for the day
passages.text: Most identifiable comb material in Baranov’s study was dense deer antler, with animal bone used less often. Some combs were cut from one piece; others were assembled from separate parts. Making a useful comb required selecting suitable material and cutting a row of small, regular teeth.

passages.title: Getting ready for the day
passages.text: Workshop evidence links Suzdal’s bone and antler workers with combs, small crosses and knife handles. Unfinished and defective pieces help identify production rather than just ownership. A broken object can be especially useful to an archaeologist when it reveals what a craftsperson was trying to make.

passages.title: Documents and buildings that travelled through time
passages.text: A lead seal found in Suzdal carries a princely sign attributed to Yuri Dolgoruky. Such seals were attached to documents, which could disappear while the metal survived. The find helps connect the town’s archaeological remains with the ruler whose administration made it an important centre before Vladimir’s rise.

passages.title: Documents and buildings that travelled through time
passages.text: Another seal belonged to Gregory, a notary, and dates to an earlier phase around Vladimir Monomakh’s time. Its Greek text contains errors that researchers use to discuss where its stamp was made. A tiny object preserves contact with Byzantine documentary habits, although Gregory’s exact employer remains uncertain.

passages.title: Documents and buildings that travelled through time
passages.text: The region’s buildings were faced with carefully worked blocks of white limestone. Their stone carving made walls into places to look closely, not simply surfaces that held up roofs. Saint Demetrios in Vladimir is among the best-known surviving examples of this decorated architecture.

passages.title: Documents and buildings that travelled through time
passages.text: Vladimir’s Assumption Cathedral preserves a medieval building with important later painting, including work associated with Andrei Rublev in 1408. Its different layers should be read separately: a twelfth-century structure can carry art made long after the powerful pre-Mongol principality had changed.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: An inscription on the cathedral at Pereslavl-Zalessky records Prince Andrei’s assassination in 1174 and names people blamed for it. Researchers used detailed photographs and three-dimensional modelling to improve the reading. They propose that it was carved in 1175 or 1176, making it a near-contemporary response to political violence.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: The inscription includes “Овому вѣчная память”, meaning “Eternal remembrance to him”. This follows the scholarly edition’s simplified historical Cyrillic transcription, with our English rendering based on its Russian translation. The words commemorate the dead prince; they are part of a political and religious message carved into a church wall.

Vladimir’s grand-princely authority gradually passed into the hands of Moscow’s rulers. In 1389 Dmitry Donskoy transmitted it to his son as an inheritance. This was a long political transformation; the map’s 1279 endpoint is only a coverage boundary.

sectionTitles: Money and the work of exchange
A later letter brings us closer to a person

passages.text: Wallachia occupied a position between the Danube and Carpathian trading routes. Princes, merchants, farmers, craftspeople and religious communities supported its economy. Coins and monastery buildings reveal early-fifteenth-century activity, while a later letter preserves the concerns of a named person communicating across the mountains.

passages.title: Money and the work of exchange
passages.text: In Mircea the Elder’s time, Wallachian ducats and smaller bani circulated alongside coins of earlier rulers. A change of prince did not require every older coin to vanish. Surviving money shows a layered everyday economy.

passages.title: Money and the work of exchange
passages.text: Foreign currency entered Wallachia while local issues travelled abroad. Coin finds make exchange visible, although a coin’s presence alone cannot identify its owner. Trade connected the principality with wider Danubian and Central European routes.

passages.title: Money and the work of exchange
passages.text: The ruler needed money for troops as well as commerce. The museum links increased minting with both demands. A coin could help purchase goods or finance military power; its meaning depended on how it was used.

passages.title: Money and the work of exchange
passages.text: A study of 66 early coins of Mircea held in Budapest uses X-ray analysis to investigate their metal composition. Researchers combine measurements with hoard histories. Where an old collection’s findspot is uncertain, the study identifies that limitation.

passages.title: Markets, supplies and skilled building
passages.text: Wallachia’s routes carried cloth, tools, weapons, spices and other goods between different markets. Merchants required local transport and provisioning. Imported objects therefore depended on many workers who never travelled the full distance themselves.

passages.title: Markets, supplies and skilled building
passages.text: Brașov supplied agricultural tools and manufactured goods to neighbouring regions and received their products. Its borderland position made it a meeting place for traders. Cross-mountain exchange could matter to a household’s tools as much as to a prince’s revenue.

passages.title: Markets, supplies and skilled building
passages.text: Cozia Monastery stands beside the Olt. Its late-1380s foundation and 1388 charter precede this atlas segment but explain a major institution already present in 1400. Buildings and documents can establish different parts of the same history.

passages.title: Markets, supplies and skilled building
passages.text: Cozia’s early interior painting is dated to 1390 to 1391. Producing such an interior required organized craft work as well as patronage. The surviving church should be read in layers, because later repairs changed parts of its appearance.

passages.title: Markets, supplies and skilled building
passages.text: Carved window surrounds and rosettes at Cozia belong to its early decoration. The church record also dates painting renewal and a fountain to 1517. Attractive details seen together today need not all have been made at the same time.

passages.title: A later letter brings us closer to a person
passages.text: In 1521 Neacșu of Câmpulung warned Johannes Benkner of Brașov about Ottoman preparations. This is later than the map’s 1492 endpoint. A named letter writer lets us see information moving through personal contacts, not only royal proclamations.

passages.title: A later letter brings us closer to a person
passages.text: Ипак дау щире (Ipak dau știre) means “And again, I give notice.” This Cyrillic-script sample reproduces the opening formula of Neacșu’s 1521 letter in a modern transcription. A Slavonic linking phrase introduces Romanian words; the message illustrates the difference between a language and the letters used to write it.

passages.title: A later letter brings us closer to a person
passages.text: Neacșu asks the recipient to keep his words private and refers to reports from other people, including a relative. The letter exposes a chain of information and uncertainty: its warnings tell us what the writer had heard, not everything that actually happened.

Wallachia did not disappear at the atlas’s 1492 endpoint. Its later political history continued for centuries. In 1859 Wallachia and Moldavia elected the same ruler, Alexandru Ioan Cuza, creating the union from which the modern Romanian state developed. This later institutional union is distinct from the medieval interval shown here.

passages.text: “Proto-Altaic pastoralists” is the atlas’s modern umbrella for an enormous zone from the eastern Tian Shan and Tarim Basin to Mongolia, Transbaikal and the Pacific between about 1500 and 323 BCE. It was never one named civilization, state, ethnic group or border. Archaeology instead finds overlapping regional traditions, including Deer Stone-Khirigsuur communities, Ulaanzuukh and Slab Grave burials, Altai groups, forest-steppe hunters and many local settlements. Herding, dairying, riding, hunting, metallurgy, exchange and monument building changed at different speeds. Even ancestry was diverse: people could adopt livestock and milk without wholesale population replacement. The label is especially risky because “Altaic” also names a disputed language-family proposal. Scholars disagree over whether similarities among Turkic, Mongolic, Tungusic, Koreanic and Japonic reflect common descent, ancient contact or both. Archaeological pots and graves cannot settle that argument or identify the language of their makers. This card therefore treats the map shape as a coverage layer, then follows securely dated evidence within it. At 400 BCE the atlas abruptly reallocates most of the same landscape to Xiongnu and Donghu labels while leaving a northern scrap. That seam is not proof that one people vanished overnight.

passages.title: Read the giant map shape with care
passages.text: The 1500 BCE polygon stretches roughly from 81 to 141 degrees east and 39 to 60 degrees north. Tested points inside include Urumqi, Ulaanbaatar, both sides of Lake Baikal, Harbin and Vladivostok. No Bronze Age survey found a wall or government around that spectacularly enormous shape; it is an atlas generalization.

passages.title: Read the giant map shape with care
passages.text: The 1500, 1000 and 700 BCE snapshots reuse exactly the same 63-position geometry, down to an identical coordinate hash. Neighboring map labels change while this one stays frozen. That is useful evidence about the dataset’s construction and terrible evidence for a real border remaining perfectly motionless for eight centuries.

passages.title: Read the giant map shape with care
passages.text: At 500 BCE the polygon keeps the same bounds, position count and tested membership, but its coordinate hash changes slightly. The safe reading is minor topology editing rather than a documented frontier adjustment. Ancient mobile communities did negotiate access to pasture and water; this file cannot show where those negotiations ran.

passages.title: Read the giant map shape with care
passages.text: The 400 BCE layer performs a dramatic cartographic costume change. Ulaanbaatar, the Tarim test points and Lake Baikal shift into an atlas Xiongnu polygon, Harbin shifts toward Donghu, and the old label survives only in a seven-point northern remnant. Real identities did not update like phone software at midnight.

passages.title: Read the giant map shape with care
passages.text: At 323 BCE the target disappears and many tested places are not covered by any obvious replacement layer. The index endpoint therefore records the end of one atlas feature, not the death, defeat or departure of every community once drawn inside it. This card leaves “fell” empty and invents no successor genealogy.

passages.title: Separate language debate from ancient people
passages.text: “Altaic,” now often reframed as “Transeurasian,” is a disputed proposal connecting several established language families. One major study argues for shared descent and prehistoric farming dispersals; a detailed response challenges its word comparisons, archaeological links and genetic interpretation. A fair card reports the dispute instead of promoting either model as settled fact.

passages.title: Separate language debate from ancient people
passages.text: Some historical linguists have defended an Altaic relationship and objected to claims that the proposal is simply dead. Their case reminds us that scholarly controversy is real. It still does not authorize drawing a Bronze Age nation across six thousand kilometers, because a proposed language genealogy is not a territorial census.

passages.title: Separate language debate from ancient people
passages.text: A permutation study found that proposed basic-vocabulary matches among Turkic, Mongolic and Tungusic performed better than randomized comparisons, but it called its support partial and left inheritance versus ancient borrowing unresolved. Statistics can test patterns in reconstructions; they cannot tell us which language an uninscribed grave’s occupant spoke.

passages.title: Separate language debate from ancient people
passages.text: Alexander Vovin’s famous review argued that proposed Altaic etymologies and sound correspondences failed comparative-method tests. Other specialists disagree, which is precisely why the atlas label needs quotation marks in our heads. Similar grammar or vocabulary can spread through long contact, and contact is especially plausible across connected pastoral landscapes.

passages.title: Separate language debate from ancient people
passages.text: Contemporaneous written-language sample: none is securely attributable to this atlas category. The securely interpreted early Mongolic Bugut and Khuis Tolgoi inscriptions date around the sixth and early seventh centuries CE, and famous Old Turkic inscriptions are later still. Borrowing their words here would time-travel nearly a millennium and pretend the debate is solved.

passages.title: Discover the past with several toolkits
passages.text: Radiocarbon dates turn monument styles into testable timelines. Bayesian models show horse-centered Deer Stone-Khirigsuur practices spreading rapidly around 1200 BCE and overlapping with other traditions. Dates come with probability ranges, reservoir questions and sample histories, so a neat phase boundary is a research model rather than an ancient New Year celebration.

passages.title: Discover the past with several toolkits
passages.text: Ancient DNA reveals repeated mixture and at least three differently structured Bronze Age populations across Mongolia. All could participate in dairying despite different ancestry. Genes track biological relationships among sampled people; they do not carry labels saying “culture,” “tribe” or “language,” and cemeteries never sample everyone who lived nearby.

passages.title: Discover the past with several toolkits
passages.text: Milk proteins trapped in calcified dental plaque identify sheep, goat, cattle or horse dairy even when bowls and animal bones are scarce. The method is powerful but personal: a positive result shows what one sampled mouth encountered, while a negative result may reflect preservation. It does not supply an entire community menu.

passages.title: Discover the past with several toolkits
passages.text: Strontium, oxygen and carbon measured along horse teeth act like a travel diary written during enamel growth. Seven horses buried together in the Mongolian Altai included four with a shared pattern of frequent movement, suggesting cyclical herding by a small community. Isotopes reveal landscapes, not the riders’ names.

passages.title: Discover the past with several toolkits
passages.text: Domestic sites are elusive because mobile camps can leave thin, scattered layers while stone monuments shout across millennia. Khanuy Valley researchers combine large-area excavation with animal bone, seed, sediment and modern-camp comparisons to find quieter evidence. “Few houses found” therefore means an archaeological visibility problem, not people living without homes.

passages.title: Eat, herd and adapt to difficult country
passages.text: Dry grasslands can feed animals where dependable grain harvests are difficult. Late Bronze Age sites show sheep, goats, cattle and horses, but herd balance varied with altitude, pasture and season. Pastoralism means skilled management of living animals, births, fodder, water and risk; it is much more than wandering randomly with woolly luggage.

passages.title: Eat, herd and adapt to difficult country
passages.text: At northern Mongolian burials dated about 1380 to 975 BCE, proteins from sheep, goat and cattle milk survived in human dental calculus. Most sampled people lacked the genetic variant that lets many adults digest fresh milk easily. Processing and microbial cultures may have helped, but the exact Bronze Age recipes did not survive.

passages.title: Eat, herd and adapt to difficult country
passages.text: Horse milk appears directly in calculus from about 1200 BCE, alongside evidence for mounted herding. Calling it modern airag would go too far because no recipe, fermentation vessel or flavor review survives. Still, milk turned a mobile animal into recurring food without slaughtering it, an impressive economic achievement in a severe environment.

passages.title: Eat, herd and adapt to difficult country
passages.text: Millet reached many steppe regions, but isotope and seed evidence show very uneven adoption. In Mongolia, intensive consumption was delayed until late in the first millennium BCE, though some people ate small amounts earlier. A pot of grain could be traded food, ritual material or a crop; it does not automatically prove local fields.

passages.title: Eat, herd and adapt to difficult country
passages.text: Herding never erased hunting. Melting ice patches in high mountains preserve arrows and animal remains that ordinary open sites lose, showing continued use of wild resources. These finds also expose preservation bias: a wooden shaft survives in ice by luck, while a thousand equally useful wooden objects may vanish from dry camp deposits.

passages.title: Transform horses into partners, transport and power
passages.text: Around 1200 BCE, bridling damage, heavy exertion and monument deposits make mounted riding increasingly visible in Mongolia. Riding could help locate animals, move between pastures and carry messages. It did not instantly turn every herder into a cavalry warrior, and some horses still provided meat, milk, traction or ritual value.

passages.title: Transform horses into partners, transport and power
passages.text: Horse care included startlingly practical dentistry. One young horse had an erupting milk tooth deliberately sawn around 1150 BCE; by about 750 BCE, some handlers removed painful “wolf teeth” that interfered with metal bits. The early attempt was not perfect, but it records observation, experimentation and veterinary knowledge without a written manual.

passages.title: Transform horses into partners, transport and power
passages.text: Age profiles in horse-head deposits include juveniles, prime adults and an elderly mare, a pattern compatible with breeding-herd management rather than random hunting. Ritual selection distorts the sample, however. A cemetery herd is not a complete stable roster, and researchers cannot convert twenty-five skulls into a census of every horse outside.

passages.title: Transform horses into partners, transport and power
passages.text: Cut marks and missing soft tissue show that many sacrificed horses were slaughtered and dismembered before selected heads and hooves entered small mounds. People may have eaten or distributed the removed meat during ceremonies. The evidence joins solemn ritual to practical butchery, which ancient participants may not have regarded as contradictory.

passages.title: Transform horses into partners, transport and power
passages.text: Ancient horse genomes from Uushgiin Uvur and other sites let researchers track maternal lineages and management over thousands of years. DNA can reveal breeding histories that shape alone misses. It still cannot tell whether a particular horse was gentle, stubborn or famous for escaping whenever someone fetched the bridle.

passages.title: Carve, cast, trade and make portable beauty
passages.text: Deer stones stand up to four meters high and carry stylized flying stags, belts, tools and weapons. About 1,500 are known across the Eurasian steppe, with more than eighty percent in Mongolia. Selecting, moving, erecting and carving stone demanded planning and skill, even though no inscription names the artists.

passages.title: Carve, cast, trade and make portable beauty
passages.text: The Mongolian-Smithsonian project records deer stones singly, in groups and beside khirigsuur mounds. Low-relief antlers flow across hard stone with remarkable control. Their concentration in grassy northern landscapes links art to gathering places, but “deer equals one god” is not a translation. Images can carry layered meanings we cannot recover.

passages.title: Carve, cast, trade and make portable beauty
passages.text: Excavations find east-facing horse heads, shallow human burials, charcoal, ceramics and burned sheep or goat bones around some monuments. These patterns support ceremonies and feasting. Poor preservation and ancient looting leave many central graves almost empty, so missing grave goods cannot prove that the buried person owned nothing.

passages.title: Carve, cast, trade and make portable beauty
passages.text: Bronze and early iron objects moved through both production and exchange. Slag, casting leftovers and microstructure can distinguish local working from imported finished pieces, while alloy chemistry traces copper, tin and recycling. A shiny dagger may have traveled far, but its metal recipe does not automatically identify its maker’s language.

passages.title: Carve, cast, trade and make portable beauty
passages.text: Portable art suited lives in motion: harness fittings, belt ornaments, garment plaques, weapons and vessels carried animal images in bronze, gold, silver and jade. “Portable” does not mean simple. Tiny objects concentrate casting, engraving, fastening and visual storytelling into things that could ride on a person or horse.

passages.title: Build a home, dress and complete the day’s work
passages.text: Many Late Bronze Age camps sat at or near later seasonal camps, exploiting familiar pasture and water. Some movements may have been only several kilometers; others were longer. Mobility was planned and tethered to animals, weather and grazing, not endless motion. A family could revisit places while leaving a light archaeological footprint.

passages.title: Build a home, dress and complete the day’s work
passages.text: At several earlier western Mongolian sites, excavators found circular structures with stone foundations or upright supports around central hearths. Elsewhere shelters may have used poles, felt, hide, brush or other perishable materials. The record does not justify giving everyone the later standardized ger, complete with furniture and a convenient gift-shop diagram.

passages.title: Build a home, dress and complete the day’s work
passages.text: Fire meant heat, cooking and craft, but treeless country makes fuel a daily problem. Ethnoarchaeology shows that wood, bone and dried dung can all burn on the steppe. Those modern observations help archaeologists recognize residues; they are analogies, not proof that every Bronze Age hearth used the same fuel recipe.

passages.title: Build a home, dress and complete the day’s work
passages.text: Deer-stone belts and hanging tools suggest clothing systems that carried equipment, while metal plaques and ornaments show how garments could be fastened or displayed. Cloth, felt, leather and sinew usually decay, so no universal outfit survives. Warm layers are sensible in Mongolia; an exact cut, color or gender rule needs direct evidence.

passages.title: Build a home, dress and complete the day’s work
passages.text: Daily labor included guarding births, moving herds, milking, processing food, fetching water, gathering fuel, repairing tack, shaping tools and watching weather. Altai protein evidence shows ruminant dairy sustained communities before horse milk grew prominent. Beautiful monuments were only possible because less glamorous jobs kept builders and animals alive.

passages.title: Grow up, learn and belong without stereotypes
passages.text: Genomes show that people with different ancestry could share dairy pastoralism, while neighboring groups with related ancestry could use different burial customs. Biological family, household, camp and ritual community were not necessarily identical circles. We should not turn a genetic cluster into a tribe or assume everyone buried alike married alike.

passages.title: Grow up, learn and belong without stereotypes
passages.text: Large monuments required quarrying, transport, food and coordinated work among people who otherwise lived at dispersed camps. Such gathering could build alliances and make leadership visible. Archaeologists debate whether the result was hierarchy, communal cooperation or both; impressive stonework alone does not produce a king, tax office or standing army.

passages.title: Grow up, learn and belong without stereotypes
passages.text: Women, men and children all lived within these economies, but tools rarely arrive with reliable job labels. Assigning all riding or metalwork to men and all milking or sewing to women would import later stereotypes. Sexed skeletons, wear patterns and graves can test roles only where samples and contexts are strong enough.

passages.title: Grow up, learn and belong without stereotypes
passages.text: Children likely learned through observation, imitation and gradually riskier tasks: approach a calm animal, keep a fire, twist cord, recognize weather, remember routes. Skilled herding and carving required teaching, yet no schoolroom or lesson list survives. A small object may be a toy, tool or offering; size alone cannot decide.

passages.title: Grow up, learn and belong without stereotypes
passages.text: Rock art shows herds, hunters, carts, riders and changing landscapes over many periods. It offers vivid scenes but not speech bubbles, ages or classroom schedules. Children surely played and adults surely joked, yet tag and teasing are archaeology’s escape artists. The honest fun fact is how much ordinary life refuses to fossilize.

passages.title: Handle health, medicine, water and the toilet question
passages.text: A study of twenty-five northern Mongolian skeletons found little visible infectious or chronic disease, while trauma, spinal changes and joint wear suggested riding and some interpersonal violence. Twenty-five people are a tiny and preservation-filtered sample. Most fevers, stomach troubles and soft-tissue illnesses leave no mark on bone.

passages.title: Handle health, medicine, water and the toilet question
passages.text: No human medical text survives from this atlas category. Healed injuries can show survival and perhaps care, but not the remedy. Horse teeth provide unusually direct evidence for attempted treatment, which proves close observation of animals. It does not let us invent a human surgeon, herbal pharmacy or bedside ritual.

passages.title: Handle health, medicine, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Camps needed dependable water for people and several animal species, so rivers, springs, snow and seasonal pasture structured movement. The Orkhon and other valleys later became enduring corridors partly because water and shelter mattered. No evidence here supports municipal pipes; carrying, timing and herd access were the infrastructure.

passages.title: Handle health, medicine, water and the toilet question
passages.text: No standard Bronze Age steppe toilet or sewer is securely identified for this enormous atlas category. At light camps, human waste may have been deposited beyond living and water areas, scattered, buried or later erased, but exact practice is unknown. Archaeologists find hearths more readily than bathrooms, because toilets are terrible at becoming monuments.

passages.title: Handle health, medicine, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Dental calculus is mineralized plaque, which makes it an archaeological treasure rather than proof that an individual never cleaned their teeth. It traps dietary proteins for millennia. Researchers also study cavities, wear and lost teeth, but hygiene tools made of fiber or wood could disappear, leaving good manners and bad toothaches equally unrecorded.

passages.title: Gather, compete, change and continue
passages.text: Khirigsuurs, deer stones and satellite mounds organized ceremonies across visible landscapes. Some complexes contain hundreds of horse offerings, signaling access to animals and coordinated labor. Scale may express status, alliance or generosity, but grave robbing and sparse domestic data make any exact political ladder uncertain. No evidence joins the whole atlas polygon under one ruler.

passages.title: Gather, compete, change and continue
passages.text: The spread of Slab Grave ancestry and burial practice changed central Mongolia after long coexistence among distinct herding groups. “Expansion” need not mean one simple invasion: movement, marriage, demographic growth and cultural adoption can overlap. New data sharpen the story while also making the old single-population atlas label less defensible.

passages.title: Gather, compete, change and continue
passages.text: Stable isotopes show millet consumption increasing around and after 800 BCE in some Mongolian samples, foreshadowing the more diversified economies that later supported steppe empires. Herding remained crucial. The achievement was flexibility: animals, hunted foods, exchanged grain and craft networks could be combined rather than obeying a single “pure nomad” rule.

passages.title: Gather, compete, change and continue
passages.text: Gobi rock art includes riders, camels, carts, cattle and rare plowing scenes, but the panels accumulated over long periods. They reveal contact among different economic worlds, not a census of one culture. Images of weapons also show that violence was imaginable; they cannot measure how often a household fought or suffered coercion.

passages.title: Gather, compete, change and continue
passages.text: The atlas endpoint at 323 BCE is followed by gaps and later labels, while archaeology shows communities and pastoral knowledge continuing. Xiongnu political formation drew on several eastern-steppe ancestries and networks rather than replacing a mythical Proto-Altaic nation. The responsible ending is continuity through reorganization, with no fabricated fall or single successor.

The atlas stops this exact label at approximately 323 BCE, after already shrinking it to a small northern residual polygon at 400 BCE. That is a map-classification endpoint, not evidence that a Proto-Altaic people, language or state fell. Across eastern Eurasia, pastoral households, hunters, craftspeople and exchange networks continued, while Xiongnu and other political formations drew together communities with varied ancestry and histories. Because the original category is disputed and overbroad, naming one successor would repeat its mistake.

passages.text: This chapter follows the designed landscapes and museum ambitions associated with Prussia in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. It focuses on architects, craftspeople and the institutions that organized their work.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Frederick II commissioned Sanssouci between 1745 and 1747. The palace later hosted the French writer Voltaire.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, Potsdam's parks combined architecture with landscape gardening. Builders, painters, sculptors and gardeners contributed to the ensemble.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: During the nineteenth century, Peter Joseph Lenne planned changes to the Havel landscape around Potsdam. Designed parkland linked water, buildings and views.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Museum Island project in Berlin began in the nineteenth century. It treated museum architecture and the display of art and archaeology as a connected public undertaking.

sectionTitles: A trading place on the edge of several worlds
A language survives in later pages

passages.text: Medieval Prussians were Western Baltic communities, distinct from the later German kingdom. Regional groups had different histories. Trading settlements, burials and later writings illuminate particular places and periods.

passages.title: A trading place on the edge of several worlds
passages.text: At Truso, near modern Elbląg, excavators found rows of timber houses and working areas. Most evidence dates before or around 1000. The port connected Scandinavian and Baltic networks; it should not stand for every Prussian village.

passages.title: A trading place on the edge of several worlds
passages.text: Some Truso houses had three rooms, with hearths and loom remains indicating different activities. Households needed space for work and storage as well as sleep. The archaeological plans reveal arrangements that written accounts rarely describe.

passages.title: A trading place on the edge of several worlds
passages.text: The port preserved remains of clinker-built boats, whose overlapping planks were joined with iron rivets. Surviving details suggest vessels around nine to eleven metres long. Boatbuilding knowledge supported the movement of goods and people.

passages.title: A trading place on the edge of several worlds
passages.text: Truso’s combs and weights can be compared with finds from other Baltic ports. Matching types help investigate connections and chronology, but a familiar object design does not identify an individual owner’s birthplace or language.

passages.title: A trading place on the edge of several worlds
passages.text: The settlement’s drainage ditch removed excess water and divided areas of activity. The nearby stream was also regulated. Keeping a working waterfront usable required routine control of water, as well as boats and successful trading.

passages.title: A trading place on the edge of several worlds
passages.text: Truso smiths used imported iron bars and local bog iron to make tools and weapons. Weaving traces occur in many buildings. Manufacturing belonged inside the settlement’s daily work; trade was not simply waiting for a foreign ship to unload.

passages.title: Communities beyond the port
passages.text: An illustrated mid-eleventh-century grave assemblage from Irzekapinis in Sambia includes weapons, horse equipment, pottery and parts of weighing equipment. Their association records one burial’s treatment. It does not tell us what every person owned during life.

passages.title: Communities beyond the port
passages.text: Regional groups included Sambians, Natangians and Bartians. Local leadership and assemblies varied; one atlas colour simplifies communities that did not share a centralized national government.

passages.title: Communities beyond the port
passages.text: Missionaries Adalbert and Bruno died in 997 and 1009 during missions in the region or its borderlands. Christian accounts preserve these events through the particular viewpoints of missionary writers.

passages.title: A language survives in later pages
passages.text: Kayle rekyse is an Old Prussian greeting, translated “Hello, mister!” in the study of the Basel Epigram. It appears on folio 63ra of manuscript F.V.2 beside a text dated 1369. This attested sample is later than the atlas’s 1000 to 1200 interval.

passages.title: A language survives in later pages
passages.text: The epigram’s handwriting and several readings are debated. Comparing letter shapes and paper watermarks helps scholars test interpretations. Its playful greeting belongs to a particular manuscript setting, not a reconstructed conversation invented for medieval Prussians.

passages.title: A language survives in later pages
passages.text: Longer Old Prussian texts survive in sixteenth-century Christian catechisms; the Elbing vocabulary records words with German equivalents. These later documents preserve language knowledge while also reflecting the religious and educational purposes of their compilers.

The Teutonic Order conquered the Prussian lands during the thirteenth century, after the atlas segment ends. War, displacement and unequal rule transformed communities, but people and their language survived for generations. Later language loss and assimilation were processes, not a disappearance of everyone in one conquest year.
