passages.text: Pskov was a northwestern Rus city with its own civic institutions, law and coinage. Its builders developed a distinctive church architecture beside the Velikaya River. Moscow ended its republican government in 1510, although local crafts, buildings and urban life continued.

passages.title: Buildings, government and money
passages.text: Pskov’s builders combined compact, roughly cubic church bodies with domes, porches and open belfries. Their use of local building materials and restrained decoration gave the city a recognizable architectural character. The school reached particular prominence in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

passages.title: Buildings, government and money
passages.text: Churches stood within gardens, walls and fences rather than appearing as isolated monuments. UNESCO recognizes ten surviving religious monuments representing this architectural tradition. The whole group spans several centuries, so its oldest and newest buildings should not all be imagined standing together in republican Pskov.

passages.title: Buildings, government and money
passages.text: The veche, or civic assembly, was an important institution of Pskov’s republic. Its bell could call people together and became a powerful symbol of local government. In January 1510, Vasily III ordered the bell removed and the assembly and elected posadnik offices abolished.

passages.title: Buildings, government and money
passages.text: Pskov began issuing its own coins in 1425, including the denga and a smaller denomination called the chetverettsa. Different principalities still used their own monetary systems. A merchant therefore needed to recognize more than a coin’s shine before agreeing that a payment was sufficient.

passages.title: Buildings, government and money
passages.text: Some Pskov coins show Prince Dovmont holding a sword, while others carry a leopard on the reverse. The museum dates the leopard design from 1460. These images made civic identity portable: a little piece of Pskov could travel in somebody’s money pouch.

passages.title: Buildings, government and money
passages.text: The Judicial Charter survives in manuscript copies made after the republic’s ending. Its text combines several layers of law, and scholars debate its compilation dates. Modern editors divide it into 120 articles covering courts, property, inheritance and offences, a remarkably detailed window into the disputes people expected to face.

passages.title: Work, family and merchants’ worries
passages.text: The charter allowed a master craftsman to sue for unpaid wages. It also recognized certain property claims by dependent workers and herdsmen. Making something useful and actually getting paid could be separate problems, familiar enough to need written rules.

passages.title: Work, family and merchants’ worries
passages.text: Women could inherit property and make wills. If a husband died without a will, his widow could use his property while she remained unmarried. These rules tell us how lawmakers organized household security; they do not establish that every widow could easily enforce her rights.

passages.title: Work, family and merchants’ worries
passages.text: The charter required children to support their parents or risk losing their inheritance. Family care thus appeared in property law as well as personal obligation. It is a practical reminder that medieval households had to plan for ageing relatives, just as they had to plan for children.

passages.title: Work, family and merchants’ worries
passages.text: An earlier birchbark letter from Kiurik and Gerasim asks Onfim to send squirrel skins because customers want them. It also complains that a man named Ksinofont has damaged their business. The catalogue places the letter around 1260 to 1280: medieval commerce came with impatient messages and troublesome partners.

passages.title: Work, family and merchants’ worries
passages.text: Another letter asks Vatsiuta to load cloth promptly onto a boat and present it as his own. The sender promises to settle the transport charge. This late thirteenth- or early fourteenth-century message makes river transport tangible, down to the awkward question of who would pay for the journey.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: Pskov letter 6 begins “ѿ кюрика и ѿ герасима”, meaning “From Kiurik and from Gerasim”. These are historical Cyrillic forms in the scholarly transcription, with word divisions added by editors. The greeting introduces an ordinary commercial letter, rather than a royal proclamation or a church service.

Vasily III of Moscow ended Pskov’s republican institutions in 1510 and replaced their authority with his governors. Pskov remained an inhabited and productive city. The map’s 1530 endpoint is an imported coverage boundary, not the republic’s ending date.

passages.text: The Ptolemies governed Egypt from Alexandria as Macedonian monarchs and Egyptian pharaohs. Their kingdom brought Greek-speaking rulers into a society with enduring Egyptian languages, temples and crafts. Surviving decrees and estate papers reveal both royal institutions and everyday work.

passages.title: Discoveries and what they reveal
passages.text: The Rosetta Stone preserves a priestly decree honoring Ptolemy V in 196 BCE. Soldiers found it reused in a fort at el-Rashid in 1799, so its discovery location is not the original setting of the decree.

passages.title: Discoveries and what they reveal
passages.text: Hieroglyphic Egyptian, Demotic Egyptian and Greek versions address different readers of the same royal decree. This is evidence of multilingual administration and priestly authority, not three different spoken languages.

passages.title: Discoveries and what they reveal
passages.text: Villagers digging for fertilizer uncovered the Zenon archive near ancient Philadelphia in 1914 to 1915. The documents illuminate a third-century BCE estate, but their exact original findspot was not recorded.

passages.title: Daily life and agricultural work
passages.text: A lease copied in a lawsuit prepared by Zenon required tenants to grow wheat and barley and deliver grain rent at Philadelphia. Clauses about seed advances and outstanding debts reveal how agricultural work depended on both produce and credit.

passages.title: Daily life and agricultural work
passages.text: The same document allowed recovery from debtors, their guarantors and their property. Read beside its crop instructions, it shows the unequal bargaining power behind estate production, rather than an idyllic picture of farming.

passages.title: Daily life and agricultural work
passages.text: A papyrus dated 7 May 254 BCE records a stolen donkey. This small dispute survives because estate papers were kept, giving a glimpse of transport animals and ordinary losses outside royal histories.

passages.title: Science and learning
passages.text: Eratosthenes worked at the Alexandrian library in the third century BCE. He compared summer-solstice shadows at Syene and Alexandria with an estimated distance between them to calculate Earth's circumference.

passages.title: Science and learning
passages.text: His original measurement treatise is lost; the method survives in later authors. Uncertainty about the length of the stadium makes a single modern claim for his percentage accuracy misleading.

passages.title: Science and learning
passages.text: The sieve associated with Eratosthenes identifies prime numbers by removing multiples. It is a concrete example of mathematical reasoning connected with Alexandria's scholarly world.

passages.title: Arts and religious life
passages.text: Temple workshops made faience vessels and colorful glass inlays. Egyptian and Greek forms coexisted, and royal portraits could combine Greek hair with Egyptian poses.

passages.title: Arts and religious life
passages.text: Egyptian temples remained centers of scholarship and worship, supported by rulers who also promoted their own royal cults.

passages.title: Trade and correspondence
passages.text: Zenon's files include letters about shipments of wheat and wine as well as official and personal business. Their survival connects agricultural production with transport and administration, rather than treating trade as an abstract royal achievement.
Roman takeover in 30 BCE ended the dynasty after Cleopatra VII's defeat. Egyptian religious and artistic traditions continued beyond the change of rulers.

passages.text: Pueblo societies comprise distinct communities and histories. Chaco Canyon and Mesa Verde preserve ancestral building and farming landscapes; Taos Pueblo is a living community with its own traditions and government.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: At Chaco, builders planned multistory Great Houses whose construction could span generations. Their masonry and shared layouts mark a regional architectural tradition.

passages.title: Science and landscape
passages.text: Many Chaco structures were oriented toward solar, lunar or cardinal directions. Their placement linked buildings to a meaningful surrounding landscape.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Mesa Verde preserves farming terraces, check dams, reservoirs and ditches as well as houses. These remains document the engineering of everyday subsistence.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Roads connected Chaco Great Houses across the region. Some major buildings may have hosted periodic ceremonies and exchange rather than dense permanent populations.

passages.title: Living architecture
passages.text: At Taos, families maintain adobe homes by renewing earthen plaster. Taos describes that work as an ongoing connection between ancestors and the present.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: Changes in ancestral settlements did not end Pueblo life. Mesa Verde remains a living connection to present-day Pueblo peoples, and Taos continues as a sovereign community.

sectionTitles: Discoveries: spaces for gathering and living

passages.text: Puerto Rico’s history includes knowledge passed through hands, families and neighbourhoods. Hammock makers work plant fibres, coffee farmers teach younger growers, and dancers exchange ideas with drummers. These living practices belong to an island shaped by Indigenous, African and European histories and a wider Puerto Rican diaspora.

passages.title: Discoveries: spaces for gathering and living
passages.text: At Caguana in Utuado, a ceremonial centre dating broadly to 1200 to 1500 CE, excavators uncovered rows of limestone slabs around a levelled plaza. Some bore carved faces. Builders cut into the hillside to create the flat gathering space. The remains show organised construction and a setting for communal ceremonies, although every activity cannot be reconstructed from the stones alone.

passages.title: Discoveries: spaces for gathering and living
passages.text: Between two of Caguana’s courts, excavators recorded postholes outlining a circular wooden building, along with two hearths, decorated pottery and a carved stone cemí, a spiritual object. A piece of Spanish glazed pottery appeared with Taíno objects in an undisturbed context. This association suggests activity into the contact period, rather than a perfectly clean break between two worlds.

passages.title: Homes, water and learning
passages.text: Smithsonian researchers documented an elderly Puerto Rican woman making hammocks with fibres from the maguey plant. Textile specialist Soraya Serra Collazo helped the team find this living craft tradition. Turning a tough plant into a place to rest takes considerable skill. A good nap can begin with somebody else’s hard work.

passages.title: Homes, water and learning
passages.text: The builders of Castillo San Cristóbal designed the fort to collect rain. Five cisterns beneath its plaza stored water for use inside. Those underground reservoirs were part of the engineering that made the eighteenth-century fortress workable. Beneath the impressive courtyard lay a practical answer to a very ordinary problem: everyone gets thirsty.

passages.title: Homes, water and learning
passages.text: A January 1942 photograph by Jack Delano shows children outside a wooden building in Aibonito. Above the doorway, the sign reads “Comedor Escolar,” meaning school dining room. Open shutters and a corrugated roof are visible. School history includes places to eat as well as classrooms, although this photograph does not tell us what lunch tasted like.

passages.title: Health, food and practical knowledge
passages.text: In the early twentieth century, Bailey Ashford and Pedro Gutiérrez worked on Puerto Rico’s hookworm problem. Their programme combined investigation and treatment with teaching about infection and improving waste disposal to reduce contact with contaminated soil. The historical account shows that caring for health extended beyond a doctor’s consulting room into public facilities and everyday surroundings.

passages.title: Health, food and practical knowledge
passages.text: In a 2022 interview, filmmaker Russell Oliver described learning about farming at Hacienda Masini in the mountains of Yauco. He met older coffee farmers who wanted to pass their knowledge to the next generation. His team’s documentation project grew from those relationships. Behind a cup of coffee are people learning about plants, land and the work of growing a crop.

passages.title: Music, family and social life
passages.text: In bomba, the lead drummer responds to a dancer’s movements, turning gestures into rhythms. Your feet can give the drummer homework. Singing often uses call and response, while barrel-shaped drums, a maraca and wooden sticks contribute different sounds. The tradition developed among African-descended communities in Puerto Rico and continues through performances and workshops on the island and in its diaspora.

passages.title: Music, family and social life
passages.text: Margarita “Tata” Cepeda’s bomba dress entered the story told by the Smithsonian’s Latino museum in its 2023 exhibition rotation. The museum connects the garment to the Cepeda family’s work performing and teaching bomba and plena. Clothing can preserve a history of movement and family learning, as well as fabric and colour.

passages.title: Freedom, government and living heritage
passages.text: Puerto Rico’s March 22, 1873 abolition law declared an end to slavery, yet required freed people to enter labour contracts lasting at least three years. Former enslavers received compensation, while full political rights for the freed people were delayed. The law’s clauses show why a legal declaration of freedom did not immediately remove every coercive restriction on daily life.

passages.title: Freedom, government and living heritage
passages.text: Voters approved a Puerto Rican constitution in 1952, followed by congressional approval. It organised the island’s internal government, including elected leaders and courts. Constitutional self-government and independent national sovereignty are different things: Puerto Rico continued within the United States territorial system.

passages.title: Freedom, government and living heritage
passages.text: Caguana is also a place of living spiritual meaning. In a 2007 account, Taíno advocates described their campaign for ceremonial access and a voice in caring for the site, including a 2005 protest. Their perspective reminds us that an archaeological park can be someone’s sacred place. Present-day communities have their own knowledge, responsibilities and views about its future.

Spanish rule ended in 1898, followed by United States administration and later commonwealth government. Puerto Rico remains a U.S. territory. Its communities and Indigenous heritage continue through changing institutions and cultural practices.

sectionTitles: Floors, food and the people who made them
Pyu words in a later royal dedication

passages.text: Pyu cities and communities developed in the dry Irrawaddy basin of present-day Myanmar. This shared card follows their urban history and later cultural legacy, not one uninterrupted kingdom. The atlas repeats the same broad outline for 800 to 900 and 1100 to 1279, enclosing Halin, Beikthano, Sri Ksetra and also Pagan. The later interval belongs to the Pagan period: surviving Pyu writing does not establish a separate Pyu state then. These imported dates and borders cannot serve as a founding date, conquest date or precise political frontier.

passages.title: Cities, rulers and changing power
passages.text: Halin, Beikthano and Sri Ksetra preserve brick walls, moats, religious monuments and waterworks. UNESCO places their broader urban tradition between about 200 BCE and 900 CE. Craftspeople worked iron, precious metals, terracotta and semiprecious stones, linking monumental building with many kinds of skilled work.

passages.title: Cities, rulers and changing power
passages.text: Four inscribed burial urns discovered near Sri Ksetra’s Payagyi stupa in 1911 preserve names and dates, probably of rulers. But which calendar starts the year count? Scholars disagree, and another urn complicates the supposed family sequence. Turning a carved number into a modern date can require a whole historical detective story.

passages.title: Cities, rulers and changing power
passages.text: At Sri Ksetra’s Bawbawgyi monument, tablets bearing the eleventh-century Pagan ruler Anawratha’s name provide evidence of later royal involvement. Hudson and Lustig interpret the deposit as a growing kingdom marking its territory ritually. The tablets themselves do not prove the much later chronicles’ story that he destroyed the city.

passages.title: Floors, food and the people who made them
passages.text: In 2015, excavators at Sri Ksetra’s Yahanda mound discovered that an apparently natural hard layer was a stack of human-made work floors. People mixed sandy silt, clay, tiny potsherds, gravel and water, then let the sun harden it. The dated sequence runs from the mid-fifth through late-seventh century, probably into the eighth.

passages.title: Floors, food and the people who made them
passages.text: Those floors held food spills, cooking charcoal, iron nails and fragments of plain and cord-marked household pottery. A kitchen mess had become archaeological evidence! Across repeated rebuilding, the hard surfaces accumulated to about 60 to 70 centimeters in thickness. These earlier traces reveal household activity before the atlas’s 800 start.

passages.title: Floors, food and the people who made them
passages.text: A still older, pre-fifth-century dwelling at Yahanda had a wooden floor and postholes above a burial terrace. One posthole reached a cremation burial. Living and burial spaces could overlap here, although this single example cannot identify relatives or prove exactly why the builders chose that spot.

passages.title: Floors, food and the people who made them
passages.text: Brickmakers drew fingers through soft clay before drying and firing it, commonly leaving two or three parallel grooves. Such bricks occur at Pyu and Mon sites. The marks preserve a shared craft, rather than reliably identifying a maker’s language.

passages.title: Floors, food and the people who made them
passages.text: A study of rice chaff in 82 old brick samples found rounded, early-maturing grains prominent at Pyu sites and Pagan. The samples lacked independent dating. Even building materials can preserve food clues, though they cannot reconstruct everyone’s meals.

passages.title: Water and far-traveling silver
passages.text: Outside Sri Ksetra’s western and southern walls, researchers traced a drainage channel running parallel to them for eight kilometers. Walls and moats helped manage water as well as shape the city. This is landscape drainage evidence; it does not establish household sewers, flushing toilets or a particular washing routine.

passages.title: Water and far-traveling silver
passages.text: A silver coin catalogued by the British Museum as Pyu, around the sixth century, is only 20 millimeters across and weighs 2.28 grams. It carries a rising sun and an auspicious srivatsa design. This museum object predates the atlas interval; its record does not give a secure excavated findspot.

passages.title: Water and far-traveling silver
passages.text: A 2025 study compared 245 full-unit Rising Sun/Srivatsa coins from regional museum collections. Matching tiny details can identify coins struck with the same die. One match links a coin found in eastern Bangladesh with another from Oc Eo in Vietnam, revealing far-reaching circulation. A shared coin design does not mean those places formed one Pyu empire.

passages.title: Pyu words in a later royal dedication
passages.text: The early twelfth-century Myazedi pillars at Pagan preserve a royal dedication in Pyu, Old Burmese, Old Mon and Pali. Comparing their versions helps scholars decipher Pyu. These are evidence for skilled multilingual writing; they do not tell us that every family could read or that children all followed one school curriculum.

passages.title: Pyu words in a later royal dedication
passages.text: The Pyu face opens “siri”, glossed “Glory!”; line 4 contains “saḥ”, meaning “son”. These are scholarly Latin transliterations of the early twelfth-century inscription, not reproductions of its original letterforms. Miyake identifies siri as a Pali borrowing. Two little words connect religious praise and family relationships.

passages.title: Pyu words in a later royal dedication
passages.text: The dedication recalls Prince Rajakumar making a gold Buddha image for his sick father, King Kyansittha. It also records the endowment of three villages with enslaved workers. Family devotion, religious merit and coercive labor appear together in this Pagan-era document; the account does not establish a medical treatment or cure.

passages.title: Pyu words in a later royal dedication
passages.text: The associated Kubyaukgyi temple has a dark central shrine and a corridor lit through perforated stone windows. Builders shaped a visitor’s experience with light as well as brick. This is a Pagan-period setting for the Pyu-language dedication, rather than a building assigned to an independent twelfth-century Pyu kingdom.

Pyu urban communities did not disappear together at a single atlas cutoff. Pagan authority became visible at older sites, while Pyu remained a written language in an early twelfth-century royal dedication. The map’s 900 and 1279 endpoints therefore should not be read as two documented falls of one Pyu kingdom.

sectionTitles: A kingdom of routes, markets and water
At home: meals, names and games
Sanctuaries, ancestors and a surviving name

passages.text: Qataban was an ancient South Arabian kingdom centred on Wadi Bayhan in today’s Yemen. Its capital Timna linked irrigated farming communities with incense caravans. The imported map covers 323 to 1 BCE, only part of a history extending into the early centuries CE. Its broad southern-Yemen outline includes places outside the kingdom’s documented heartland and should not be read as a surveyed frontier. Saba and Hadramawt were neighbouring kingdoms with their own histories.

passages.title: A kingdom of routes, markets and water
passages.text: Timna’s location on Wadi Bayhan helped connect Indian Ocean commerce with routes towards the Mediterranean. The excavation project places Qataban among southern Arabia’s leading powers from the sixth to first centuries BCE. Incense traffic relied on a substantial urban and agricultural hinterland.

passages.title: A kingdom of routes, markets and water
passages.text: A granite pillar in Timna’s market carries royal commercial regulations on all four sides. Nearby excavations uncovered ten houses. Government could make its rules physically present where merchants worked: a stone noticeboard was much harder to misplace than a loose sheet.

passages.title: A kingdom of routes, markets and water
passages.text: The stone-paved Najd Marqad road linked the commercial corridor between Timna and Haribat. Yemen’s heritage submission describes this surviving mountain route alongside settlements, fields and caravan facilities. Trade required a connected landscape, including the difficult ground between cities.

passages.title: A kingdom of routes, markets and water
passages.text: Farmers diverted seasonal floodwater into fields through branching channels. Water usually involved local management, but stronger kings also regulated distribution and commissioned major works. Controlling the flow could determine which downstream fields received a drink after the rain.

passages.title: A kingdom of routes, markets and water
passages.text: A fifth-century BCE decree discussed by Charbonnier ordered an upstream area kept clear of obstructions so floodwater could reach land below. This predates the map’s first snapshot. Another inscription records a father and son digging a well in their palm grove: water infrastructure could also be a family undertaking.

passages.title: At home: meals, names and games
passages.text: Plant remains at Hajar Ibn Humayd include barley, millet, cumin, sesame, flax and grapevine, according to Charbonnier’s archaeological synthesis. These are clues to the valley’s crops across its ancient occupation, rather than the contents of one dated dinner. The menu was much more varied than incense!

passages.title: At home: meals, names and games
passages.text: Some Timna houses advertised their names in façade inscriptions, including bayt Yaʿūd. Stone bases supported upper construction of mudbrick and timber lattice. Charred uprights date some building work to the late fourth or early third century BCE. A house name could survive long after its roof collapsed.

passages.title: At home: meals, names and games
passages.text: House Yafash yielded containers, a burned comb and a stone die. These small objects bring grooming, storage and gaming into a picture often dominated by temples and kings. The house’s destruction belongs to the first century CE in the Smithsonian account, after this map record ends.

passages.title: At home: meals, names and games
passages.text: Two bronze lions from House Yafash each carry a small boy on their backs. The museum dates them to about 75 BCE to 50 CE. Artists cast the lions and riders separately using the lost-wax technique. These were extraordinary decorations; actual children were not being issued lion transport.

passages.title: At home: meals, names and games
passages.text: The bronze bases name Thuwayb and Aqrab of the Muhasni family as the people who decorated Yafash. Archaeologists therefore have both objects from a home and words identifying its patrons. The names help turn an anonymous ruin into a place where particular people made choices.

passages.title: Sanctuaries, ancestors and a surviving name
passages.text: In Timna’s northwestern sector, inscriptions identify a courtyard sanctuary of Athirat. Founded around the fourth or third century BCE, it was repeatedly altered. Its rear wall also formed part of the city perimeter: religious buildings and the settlement’s boundary could share the same masonry.

passages.title: Sanctuaries, ancestors and a surviving name
passages.text: Another monumental building, TT1, was first called an Athtar temple because of one inscription. The Metropolitan Museum’s later catalogue considers a palace more likely. Revising a building’s label can change our picture of royal and religious space without moving a single stone.

passages.title: Sanctuaries, ancestors and a surviving name
passages.text: At Hayd ibn Aqil, large family tombs had central corridors and long chambers with shelves for the dead. Some funerary stelae survived in place despite ancient looting elsewhere. Relatives were remembered together in deliberately arranged spaces, giving archaeologists evidence about commemoration as well as carving.

passages.title: Sanctuaries, ancestors and a surviving name
passages.text: A third-century BCE alabaster figure now in Toledo Museum of Art is about 47 centimetres tall and has inlaid shell eyes. Its likely origin is the cemetery near Timna, but that findspot is not securely documented. The luminous stone and carefully treated eyes made a striking memorial.

passages.title: Sanctuaries, ancestors and a surviving name
passages.text: The same statue’s base carries a South Arabian inscription transcribed by the museum as “ʾbydʿ ḏ-Ḏmrʾl”, translated “Abī-yadaʿ son of Damar’ali”. This is a scholarly Latin-letter rendering of the ancient writing, not modern Arabic or the original letter shapes. It preserves a person’s name and lineage from the third century BCE.

Qataban did not fall at the map’s 1 BCE cutoff. Hadramawt eventually annexed the kingdom. Published summaries differ between the first and second centuries CE, so a single exact year would mislead. Timna’s destruction and the political annexation are separate questions. The loss of Qataban’s kingship was not the disappearance of southern Arabia’s farming communities or commercial traditions.

sectionTitles: Treaty, independence and changing constitutional rules
Pearls, hydrocarbons and the people behind the boom
Home, hospitality and learning to listen

passages.text: This card follows the Qatari polity from its late British-protected period through independence in 1971 and the continuing State of Qatar. The approximate 1938 atlas onset points toward the oil era, not national founding; the first oil strike actually came at the end of 1939. Six topology files generate seven displayed intervals, and world-1938.json contains the Qatar feature twice. Every imported outline includes the tested point at Doha but excludes tested points at Al Zubarah, Dukhan, Abu Samra and Al Ruwais, so the repeated peninsula shape is conspicuously too narrow in the west and clipped in the north. It is a classroom locator, not a legal boundary record.

passages.title: Treaty, independence and changing constitutional rules
passages.text: Qatar's 1916 treaty placed foreign and defence relations within a British-protected framework. A renewed agreement and oil concession followed in 1935. Oil was struck at the end of 1939, but the Second World War stopped exploration just as cultured pearls and global recession were already hurting the older diving economy. The atlas date of 1938 catches this economic hinge, not a birth certificate for Qatar.

passages.title: Treaty, independence and changing constitutional rules
passages.text: Qatar declared independence on 3 September 1971 when its treaty relationship with Britain ended. The United States recognized it two days later and established diplomatic relations in 1972. Independence changed external sovereignty; it did not make the peninsula, its towns or its families suddenly appear. The official record is especially useful here because it separates declaration, recognition and diplomatic relations into three different events.

passages.title: Treaty, independence and changing constitutional rules
passages.text: A draft permanent Constitution won 96.6 percent of votes cast in the April 2003 referendum and was issued in June 2004. In November 2024 another referendum approved amendments with 90.6 percent of valid votes. Official percentages report the announced results; they do not by themselves measure the openness of debate or how institutions operate after a legal change.

passages.title: Treaty, independence and changing constitutional rules
passages.text: Thirty of the 45 Shura Council members were elected in 2021. Amendments approved in 2024 required at least 45 appointed members; Decree No. 42 of 2025 appointed 49, who held their first plenary session on 21 October. The Amir's 2024 speech argued that appointment better served unity and equal citizenship. That is the government's rationale, not an independent judgment about representation.

passages.title: Treaty, independence and changing constitutional rules
passages.text: A short sample from current constitutional Article 1 is قطر دولة عربية ذات سيادة مستقلة, “Qatar is an independent sovereign Arab state.” Arabic is read right to left; an editorial transliteration is Qaṭar dawlah ʿarabiyyah dhāt siyādah mustaqillah. This is formal Modern Standard Arabic in a legal document, not a claim that every resident speaks the same dialect or uses Arabic in every setting.

passages.title: Pearls, hydrocarbons and the people behind the boom
passages.text: Al Zubarah flourished for about fifty years in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries as a pearling and trading town linked to the Indian Ocean, Arabia and western Asia. Sand preserved streets, courtyard houses, fishermen's huts, walls and water works after abandonment. UNESCO inscribed the archaeological site in 2013. Its story is an antecedent to the modern state, and its pearl weights make trade visible without pretending diving was easy.

passages.title: Pearls, hydrocarbons and the people behind the boom
passages.text: The first crude shipment left Dukhan through Mesaieed on 31 December 1949. North Field natural-gas production began in 1991, four decades after oil exports started. These projects supplied revenue and energy for rapid urban change. They were major engineering and organizational achievements, but they depended on international technology, capital and workers as well as resources beneath Qatari waters and land.

passages.title: Pearls, hydrocarbons and the people behind the boom
passages.text: Hydrocarbon wealth remains both strength and constraint. In February 2026 IMF staff linked Qatar's outlook to expanding liquefied-natural-gas capacity and growing non-hydrocarbon activity, while also listing climate stress and possible future LNG oversupply among the risks. The same review urged a knowledge-based economy with stronger skills, private enterprise and trade. A giant gas field can finance choices; it cannot make diversification automatic.

passages.title: Pearls, hydrocarbons and the people behind the boom
passages.text: Much of modern Qatar was built and serviced by migrant workers. An ILO review in 2022 recorded job-change reforms, online complaints and elected worker representatives in some companies. It also found continuing obstacles: employer retaliation, unpaid wages, slow recovery of money and incomplete protection for domestic workers. Skyscrapers and stadiums are achievements only when the people who build and clean them are kept in the story.

passages.title: Home, hospitality and learning to listen
passages.text: A majlis is a sitting place where people receive guests, exchange news, settle problems, pay condolences and celebrate weddings. Carpets, wall cushions and hot drinks make the setting comfortable, but the social skill is listening. Children learn manners and oral traditions by accompanying older relatives. UNESCO also notes women's majlis, including academic and literary gatherings. This is a living shared practice, not a floor plan required in every home.

passages.title: Home, hospitality and learning to listen
passages.text: Arabic coffee turns hospitality into a tiny choreography. Beans may be roasted and ground for guests; elders and guests are served first, the server pours with the right hand, and a drinker shakes the little cup to say “enough.” Poetry and memories may accompany it. Useful child fact: before asking for a seventh refill, learn the cup wiggle. The custom is shared across several Arab countries, not uniquely Qatari.

passages.title: Home, hospitality and learning to listen
passages.text: Falconry grew from hunting into a social and recreational practice. Families, mentors and clubs teach how to handle, train and care for birds, while modern practitioners also work to protect falcons, prey and habitat. UNESCO's multinational listing includes Qatar and emphasizes trust between bird and handler. A falcon is not a feathery remote-controlled airplane; training begins with patient care and reading an animal's behaviour.

passages.title: Home, hospitality and learning to listen
passages.text: Family life in Qatar is diverse because residents come from many countries. The Education Ministry's published snapshot described more than 300 private schools alongside public schools, with different curricula serving many nationalities. That means classmates may bring different languages, foods and school traditions into the same small country. National culture matters, but no single majlis, meal or household arrangement represents everyone who lives there.

passages.title: Classrooms, clinics, pipes and toilets
passages.text: Qatar's Education Ministry oversees public and private schooling, sets standards and invests in teacher training. Its published snapshot paired large public enrolment with a similarly large private-school population and described higher-education institutions serving local and international students. This is an institutional achievement with an ongoing homework assignment: resources and impressive campuses still have to produce strong, inclusive learning for very different pupils.

passages.title: Classrooms, clinics, pipes and toilets
passages.text: Primary medical care developed alongside the oil-era population boom. A WHO-hosted account traces clinics to 1954 and, in its 2013 snapshot, describes centres providing general treatment, dentistry, pregnancy care, vaccination, pharmacy services, laboratory tests, health education, home visits and hospital referrals. Medicine was therefore organized as more than a hospital building: prevention, babies' care, teeth and medicines all met families closer to home.

passages.title: Classrooms, clinics, pipes and toilets
passages.text: UNICEF's comparable 2022 estimates put safely managed sanitation at 100 percent, safely managed drinking water at 97 percent and open defecation at zero. Translation for the toilet-curious: nearly everyone was counted as using a system that safely handles waste, which is much more informative than saying bathrooms exist. National percentages still cannot promise that every toilet, worker accommodation or pipe is equally reliable.

passages.title: Classrooms, clinics, pipes and toilets
passages.text: That water success has an environmental bill. Qatar's 2025 climate submission says extreme aridity, low rain and high evaporation make desalination vital, while hotter and saltier seas can raise treatment costs. Coastal plants face sea-level rise and storms, and more desalination can demand more energy and produce more emissions. In a desert, every dependable tap is an engineering triumph connected to climate, electricity and the sea.

Qatar remains a continuing sovereign state; the atlas's open future interval is a data convention. Independence in 1971 ended the British treaty relationship. Decree No. 42 of 2025 appointed 49 Shura Council members, and the Council reported completing its first ordinary session on 6 July 2026. This establishes institutional status only through that dated check; families and communities have histories beyond constitutional dates.

passages.text: Qin began as a frontier state of the Zhou in the Wei River valley in 770 BCE and grew, by reform and conquest, into the power that unified China in 221 BCE. The empire created a centralized bureaucratic state that replaced feudal fragmentation. Though the dynasty lasted only fifteen years, its institutional innovations became the foundation of all subsequent Chinese empires.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Shang Yang's reforms in the state of Qin reward farming and soldiering, punish by fixed law and break the power of the old nobility, the Legalist programme the empire would follow.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Legalism becomes state orthodoxy, emphasizing strict laws, harsh punishments and absolute state power.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Books of rival philosophies are ordered burned, and by tradition scholars are executed the next year.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The First Emperor seeks immortality through alchemy and travels to sacred mountains.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Standardization of weights, measures, axle widths and written script across the empire.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Construction of the Great Wall begins, connecting earlier defensive walls along the northern frontier.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Terracotta Army, some 8,000 life-size soldiers, is completed to guard the First Emperor's tomb; work had begun on his accession in 246 BCE.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bronze mirrors, crossbow mechanisms and standardized coinage show unified artistic standards.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: The small seal script standardized for official use, later replaced by clerical script.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The empire divided into thirty-six commanderies governed by appointed officials rather than hereditary lords.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Corvée labor conscripted for massive public works: roads, the Lingqu canal linking the Yangzi and Pearl river systems, and the Epang palace.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Harsh legal code applied uniformly across the empire.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Standardized bronze coins in round shape with square hole become the empire's currency.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Imperial highways facilitate military movement and commercial exchange.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The name China probably derives from Qin, by way of Sanskrit and Persian.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Centralized bureaucratic administration replaced feudalism in all subsequent dynasties.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Standardized writing enabled cultural unity across linguistic diversity.
After the First Emperor's death, popular rebellions and civil war led to the dynasty's collapse in 206 BCE; Liu Bang, the victor of the wars that followed, founded the Han.

sectionTitles: A vast empire and its public image
Feeding households and earning a living

passages.text: Hong Taiji proclaimed the Qing dynastic name in 1636, and Qing rulers established their court in Beijing in 1644. Their empire brought many peoples under a Manchu ruling house. The dynasty ended with abdication in 1912. The imported 1650 to 1920 range therefore extends beyond imperial rule. Its early Taiwan features also group the separately labelled Middag Kingdom under Qing; these coarse shapes must not be treated as evidence of continuous Qing control.

passages.title: A vast empire and its public image
passages.text: Qianlong’s empire extended across Tibet and large areas of Central Asia. He presented himself differently to different subjects: as a learned patron to Han Chinese scholars, as a steppe prince to Mongols, and as a Buddhist sacred figure to Tibetans. These were deliberate claims to authority over varied communities, rather than evidence that everyone welcomed Qing rule.

passages.title: A vast empire and its public image
passages.text: The artist Wang Hui supervised great painted scrolls commemorating Kangxi’s southern inspection tour of 1689. They included the emperor’s arrival at Mount Tai and entry into Suzhou. Roads, boats, cities and crowds fill these court-sponsored images. They are valuable pictures of a landscape and a powerful ruler’s preferred public image, rather than a neutral opinion poll about his popularity.

passages.title: Feeding households and earning a living
passages.text: Qing officials used grain reserves and trade to respond to harvest failures. River transport could bring food into some regions relatively easily; inland districts were harder and more expensive to supply. Emergency granaries were especially important where markets and transport could not quickly fill the gap. Storing money was useful, but a hungry family still needed actual grain.

passages.title: Feeding households and earning a living
passages.text: In some prosperous, densely settled districts, women devoted more work to spinning and weaving cloth for sale. Households could buy goods they previously made themselves, using money from textile production. Officials promoted cotton-growing and weaving instruction; illustrated materials showed stages such as picking cotton and working a loom. Domestic work could connect a family closely to distant markets.

passages.title: Feeding households and earning a living
passages.text: Yin Yu Tang, built around 1800 for a merchant family in Huizhou, had sixteen bedrooms around shared spaces and a central courtyard. Carved lattice windows overlooked fish ponds. The house survives today at the Peabody Essex Museum after being moved from China. Its long occupation continued beyond the Qing, so furnishings and alterations belong to several generations of family history.

passages.title: Feeding households and earning a living
passages.text: In Huizhou’s merchant families, boys might leave in their early teens to apprentice with relatives or family contacts in another city. Women, younger children and elders kept the household going while merchants spent long periods away. Family reunions at the Mid-Autumn Festival could therefore carry special meaning. Commercial success had a very personal cost in time spent apart.

passages.title: Study, health and games
passages.text: A silk fragment dated around 1875 is covered with tiny writing in black and red ink. Powerhouse Museum identifies it as a concealed aid for an imperial examination candidate: passages from the Chinese classics worn as garment lining. Its width is only 16.5 centimetres. Preparing for exams took learning and practice; this object records someone’s plan for an unauthorized shortcut.

passages.title: Study, health and games
passages.text: A manuscript from around 1805 describes smallpox vaccination as practised at Guangzhou, then often called Canton. Surgeon Alexander Pearson prepared the account, George Thomas Staunton translated it for Chinese readers, and a local merchant helped publish it. The Royal Society preserves the English manuscript. Sharing a medical technique depended on translators, publishers and local networks as well as doctors.

passages.title: Study, health and games
passages.text: A nineteenth-century shuttlecock from Shanghai, now in the British Museum, was made from cotton and feathers. Players kicked it with their feet to keep it airborne. The surviving toy gives a wonderfully simple glimpse of recreation: feet did the work usually given to a racket. The museum dates this example broadly to the 1800s.

passages.title: Writing and inventive workshops
passages.text: A porcelain ritual vessel in the Royal Collection carries “大清乾隆年製”, meaning “Made in the Qianlong reign of the Great Qing”. This is Chinese written on its base in seal script, transcribed here in ordinary modern type. The eighteenth-century vessel, RCIN 58813.1, was made at Jingdezhen. Its mark connects a workshop’s product with an imperial reign.

passages.title: Writing and inventive workshops
passages.text: A vase dated 1744 in the National Palace Museum contains another vase inside it. Turning the neck rotates the inner vessel, allowing its blue lotus decoration to move behind openings in the outer shell. Yellow enamels and gold details decorate the outside. Firing and fitting the separate porcelain parts demanded precision: this is a moving artwork powered by a hand, not a hidden motor.

passages.title: A changing nineteenth century
passages.text: The later Qing period brought devastating rebellions and foreign wars, alongside striking changes in everyday communication. Photography and lithographic printing expanded the ways people could make and encounter images. Telegraphs, railways and electricity also entered a society still containing many older forms of work and transport. These changes were uneven, rather than a simultaneous transformation of every town and village.

The Wuchang uprising of October 1911 was followed by provinces withdrawing their allegiance to the Qing government. On 12 February 1912, the emperor abdicated, ending the dynasty’s imperial rule as a republic replaced it. Communities, families and many cultural practices continued amid further political upheaval. The map’s 1920 endpoint is a coverage error, not an additional eight years of Qing government.

sectionTitles: Building and governing a steppe power
Moving home and making a living
Water, schools and life in southern towns

passages.text: The Kazakh Khanate emerged from the post-Mongol steppe world in the fifteenth century and became a major Central Asian power. Its rulers governed mobile pastoral communities and competed for southern towns. “Quazaq” is this map’s spelling of Kazakh. The imported 1530 to 1783 span is neither its full lifetime nor a period of uniform control: the broad outline conceals changing alliances, contested towns and several regional khans.

passages.title: Building and governing a steppe power
passages.text: Kasym Khan strengthened Kazakh power in the early sixteenth century, before this map begins. His successors faced serious internal conflicts, followed by renewed expansion under Hak-Nazar. Southern towns mattered because control of grazing country and control of markets were connected. Rival khans repeatedly fought for the oases along the Syr Darya.

passages.title: Building and governing a steppe power
passages.text: In 1598, Tauekel’s army seized several southern cities but failed to take Bukhara. He died after being wounded. The subsequent settlement left Tashkent, Sairam and Turkestan with the Kazakhs, while Samarkand was relinquished. A large campaign could therefore end in negotiation and a reshaped frontier, rather than permanent possession of everything an army reached.

passages.title: Building and governing a steppe power
passages.text: The Senior, Middle and Junior juz were large regional groupings, each with its own leaders. Their origins cannot be pinned to a securely documented founding ceremony. By the later khanate, a single coloured area on a map hides overlapping loyalties and rulers whose authority depended on cooperation with other influential people. Dzungar attacks from 1723 forced many Kazakhs to flee toward neighbouring territories, creating a human crisis and encouraging rulers to seek outside protection.

passages.title: Building and governing a steppe power
passages.text: A bi was a judge valued for knowledge of customary law and persuasive speech. Traditions associated with Tauke Khan describe an oral body of rules covering disputes, marriage and other obligations. Scholars reconstruct this system partly from later accounts, so a neat modern “law code” would give the wrong impression of how rules were remembered and argued.

passages.title: Moving home and making a living
passages.text: Pastoral households used different grazing areas through the seasons. Winter shelter, spring growth and summer pasture created a working calendar for people and animals. Herds supplied food, transport and materials, and animals could be exchanged for goods. Moving was skilled economic planning, with familiar destinations, rather than simply wandering until somewhere looked pleasant.

passages.title: Moving home and making a living
passages.text: Early-sixteenth-century writer Ruzbihan described both portable dwellings and impressive homes mounted on carts. Some elite wagons had wooden walls, felt coverings and windows, and were pulled by camels. Smaller dwellings served ordinary herders. For some travellers, “moving house” was almost literal: the house came along for the ride.

passages.title: Moving home and making a living
passages.text: Summer gatherings could also be social occasions. Muhatova’s study, citing Ruzbihan’s early-sixteenth-century account, describes weddings, horse races, wrestling and contests involving singers and storytellers on the summer pastures. The pastoral year made room for celebration as well as work, although this account does not describe every family or every region.

passages.title: Moving home and making a living
passages.text: In a letter received in 1772, Abulfeiz explained that a blocked route toward Tashkent had interrupted supplies. He specifically needed flour and rice. This is a useful correction to a picture of steppe meals made entirely from meat and milk: pastoral communities also depended on agricultural neighbours and safe trading routes.

passages.title: Moving home and making a living
passages.text: Cloth shopping had strong opinions attached. In 1773, traders complained through Abulfeiz that they had been pushed into exchanging animals for fabrics they did not want. Qing records show demand for white and red cotton. The historian relates these colours to shrouds and clothing, and to wedding textiles. A bolt of cloth could matter at several turning points in family life.

passages.title: Water, schools and life in southern towns
passages.text: Sauran belonged to the southern urban world contested by Kazakh and neighbouring rulers. Its farms used both surface channels and kariz, underground galleries that collected groundwater. Summer shortages made this especially valuable: spring streams alone could not reliably supply fields and gardens through the hottest part of the year.

passages.title: Water, schools and life in southern towns
passages.text: Aerial photographs helped researchers identify chains of kariz traces around Sauran. Combining archaeology with geology showed that Sauran and nearby Mirtobe had separate water systems. That finding challenged an older reading of a written description. Archaeology can correct a famous traveller as well as illustrate one.

passages.title: Water, schools and life in southern towns
passages.text: Sauran’s excavated madrasa had a courtyard surrounded by small residential rooms, a teaching hall and an entrance marked by two minarets. Excavators identify it with a school described in 1515. It was built before this map’s opening year and before later Kazakh control: the khanate inherited an urban tradition of learning, rather than inventing all of its buildings.

passages.title: Water, schools and life in southern towns
passages.text: The school’s remains preserve practical details as well as grand architecture. Rooms had wall niches and brick floors. Later occupants installed stoves with flues running through raised platforms, changing the original floor arrangement. These alterations show people adapting rooms to everyday needs; the report does not establish one exact year for each modification.

passages.title: Letters, languages and diplomatic skill
passages.text: A 1769 letter from Abulfeyz Sultan to the Qing military governor includes “تيم قوانديم”, transcribed tim quwandïm and translated by its editors as “I was rather pleased.” This is Turki in Arabic script, shown here in modern typesetting from the scholarly edition. He was responding to an imperial document about travel and negotiation over territory. It is a specific diplomatic voice, not a sample of modern standard Kazakh.

passages.title: Letters, languages and diplomatic skill
passages.text: Kazakh correspondence crossed several language boundaries. Some letters used Turki; others used Oirat and its Clear Script. Envoys also explained matters in person because Qing officials did not always understand the written Turkic documents fully. A letter, its seal and a messenger’s spoken explanation could work together to carry a ruler’s message.

passages.title: Letters, languages and diplomatic skill
passages.text: Diplomacy did not mean that the khans simply obeyed every foreign demand. In 1775, Ablai requested Qing troops while offering revenue claimed from Tashkent. Qing officials refused and disputed the terms of his proposal. Such exchanges reveal bargaining, competing claims and sharp disagreement behind the polite titles used in official letters.

passages.title: Changing sovereignty, continuing communities
passages.text: Abulkhair and a group of supporters took an oath to Russia in 1731. The relationship did not instantly place every Kazakh community under direct Russian administration. The parties had different ambitions, and later imperial expansion involved further political pressure and administrative changes. The eighteenth-century khanate cannot be reduced to a single all-or-nothing moment of “joining”.

passages.title: Changing sovereignty, continuing communities
passages.text: After the map ends, Russian reforms abolished the khan’s office in the Middle juz in 1822 and the Junior juz in 1824. New districts and officials replaced important parts of regional government. These were losses of political authority, not the disappearance of Kazakh families, language or cultural life, which continued under changed and increasingly colonial conditions.

The map stops in 1783, but Kazakh khans and communities continued. Russian expansion gradually dismantled regional khanly institutions, including reforms in 1822 and 1824. There was no single nationwide fall in 1783, and Kazakh cultural and community life survived the loss of sovereignty.

sectionTitles: Letters and people beyond a ruler

passages.text: Rabih Fadlallah built a military state through conquest and enslavement, eventually occupying Borno in 1893. This map’s eastern polygon lies far from his later capital, Dikwa: it cannot show the full extent of his changing power.

passages.title: Power and its costs
passages.text: Rabih had served the slave-trading forces associated with Zubayr and his son Sulayman. After their defeat, he and followers moved west; commanders elected him amir in 1879. His mobile force preceded the later state centred on Dikwa.

passages.title: Power and its costs
passages.text: Raiding devastated communities in southern Chad and northern Central Africa. Captured people could be forced into Rabih’s army, so military growth also meant families separated and people deprived of freedom. Resistance to French conquest does not erase these harms.

passages.title: Power and its costs
passages.text: Military commanders supervised local rulers and collected resources through enlarged territorial holdings. Rabih retained some experienced Borno officials, but their room to act depended on submission to his authority.

passages.title: Food, homes and markets
passages.text: Before the invasion, weekly markets connected farmers and townspeople through grain, milk products, fish, meat and building materials. War and neighbouring states’ blockades damaged those networks. The loss was felt in ordinary shopping and meals, not just in royal income.

passages.title: Food, homes and markets
passages.text: Food shortages worsened by 1898. Areas such as Gujba, which escaped some destruction, became important sources of grain. An army could capture a capital quickly; rebuilding the farming that fed it was much harder.

passages.title: Food, homes and markets
passages.text: Travelling toward Dikwa after Rabih’s defeat in 1900, Émile Gentil first mistook newly planted fields for empty plains. He then noticed channels designed to hold rainwater. The apparent emptiness was a visitor’s misunderstanding of farming.

passages.title: Food, homes and markets
passages.text: Gentil’s June 1900 journey also records local people bringing fresh milk and butter. Millet fields and livestock supported settlements along his route. These are observations from just after the war, rather than a menu for every household.

passages.title: Food, homes and markets
passages.text: Dikwa’s palace builders bundled smaller timbers into supporting pillars where large wood was scarce. Gentil described thick walls, several courtyards and plastered surfaces: practical engineering on a grand scale.

passages.title: Food, homes and markets
passages.text: In the market Gentil saw local cotton alongside imported fabrics, sugar, coffee, tea and metal goods. His account describes a busy city after conquest; it does not cancel the evidence of severe wartime disruption elsewhere.

passages.title: Letters and people beyond a ruler
passages.text: A letter of 28 November 1894 from al-Sanusi al-Bakr proposed trade on behalf of Rabih and the ruler of Wadai. It discussed animals, textiles and guns, but also trading enslaved people. Diplomatic paperwork exposes coercion behind the word commerce.

passages.title: Letters and people beyond a ruler
passages.text: Writing sample: “الحمد لله”, meaning “Praise be to God,” appears in that 1894 Arabic letter’s opening. This is a normalized transcription from the published edition. The author was al-Sanusi, writing about Rabih’s trade interests; these are not words from a verified Rabih autograph.

passages.title: Letters and people beyond a ruler
passages.text: Rabih’s death did not make his followers disappear. His son Fadlallah led a surviving force, and families moved with the defeated army. Their later negotiations and flight belong to the story too, beyond a map’s single ending date.

Rabih died in the battle near Kousseri on 22 April 1900. Fadlallah and other survivors continued resisting and negotiating into 1901. Colonial partition followed; the peoples and communities affected by these wars continued their own histories.

Learning, skilled hands and a surviving word
Water, food and carved social scenes

passages.text: The atlas’s 800 to 900 label points toward early ruling networks in northwestern India, not one Rajput state. Its polygon is misplaced in mainland Southeast Asia, including Chiang Mai and Vientiane, and cannot represent Indian territories. None of the Indian sites described here lies inside it. This card provides historical context for the label, without identifying Southeast Asian communities as Rajput. Rajput identities developed over centuries; later kingdoms and named dynasties retain separate cards.

passages.title: Ruling houses and family claims
passages.text: Historian Irfan Habib connects the development of Rajput status with military service and control of agricultural land. The word and the social groups it described changed over time. Reading later clan identities straight back into every ninth-century village would flatten that history.

passages.title: Ruling houses and family claims
passages.text: The Pratihara family around Mandor was a regional ruling house, distinct from the imperial Pratihara court at Kanauj. Its inscriptions supply unusually concrete local examples for this broad label. Shared dynastic names should not make every king or settlement part of one undivided government.

passages.title: Ruling houses and family claims
passages.text: Bauka’s inscription, dated about 837, boasts that he rescued his position when allies fled and enemies attacked. It celebrates a ruler’s victory, rather than giving a neutral account. Such claims show how a local house advertised its power.

passages.title: Ruling houses and family claims
passages.text: That inscription also presents Bauka’s ancestors as descendants of Harichandra and Bhadra, described as Brahmana and Kshatriya. This is the ruling family’s own genealogy. It records how they explained their ancestry, rather than proving a single origin for all Rajputs.

passages.title: Ruling houses and family claims
passages.text: A Buchkala inscription of 815 credits queen Jayavali with building a temple and making an unspecified installation. It names mason Panchahari, son of Deia, linking royal patronage with craft work.

passages.title: A market and several kinds of worship
passages.text: In 861, Kakkuka established a market at Ghatiyala and promised livelihoods to invited settlers. The inscriptions single out privileged groups, so their prosperity claims cannot stand for every resident.

passages.title: A market and several kinds of worship
passages.text: Ghatiyala’s sandstone pillar was assembled from three parts: two shaft pieces and a capital with four Ganesha images facing the compass directions. Whichever side someone approached, there was another elephant face. The 1907 survey recorded weathering that had damaged several of them.

passages.title: A market and several kinds of worship
passages.text: Nearby, Kakkuka also supported a Jain temple. Its Prakrit inscription identifies the building’s Jain purpose, although later visitors knew the ruins by a goddess-related name. A monument’s later name can conceal an earlier religious history.

passages.title: Learning, skilled hands and a surviving word
passages.text: Bauka’s court praised his father Kakka for grammar, logic, astronomy and poetry. That is a royal ideal of learning, not evidence that every child studied those subjects. A warrior’s public image could include being good with words as well as weapons.

passages.title: Learning, skilled hands and a surviving word
passages.text: “उत्कीर्ण्णा” (utkīrṇṇā) means “engraved” in the Sanskrit inscription dated about 837. This is a modern Devanagari rendering of the published transcription, not a facsimile. The closing line names engraver Krishnesvara and his father Vishnuravi, a goldsmith.

passages.title: Learning, skilled hands and a surviving word
passages.text: The same inscription resurfaced around 1892 in Jodhpur’s city wall, reused upside down. Someone had treated a ruler’s carefully written praise as building stone. Its position helped later researchers recognize that it had been moved from an earlier setting.

passages.title: Water, food and carved social scenes
passages.text: At Abhaneri, Chand Baori’s steps form repeating geometric patterns as they descend underground. Official heritage descriptions date the well to the eighth or ninth century. Fetching water called for serious stair design! The monument does not establish everyone’s washing habits or prove that houses had toilets.

passages.title: Water, food and carved social scenes
passages.text: Charred barley, rice and wheat from Chandravati reveal a varied plant economy. These samples belong to the broad 800 to 1300 archaeological phase, not securely just the ninth century. A burnt grain can preserve a food clue, but it cannot tell us one family’s complete dinner menu.

passages.title: Water, food and carved social scenes
passages.text: At Abhaneri’s Harshat Mata temple, carvings show music, dance, garden recreation and affectionate couples. ASI assigns the temple to the eighth century, before this atlas interval. Its art imagines an enjoyable social world, rather than documenting how every household spent its evening.

passages.title: Water, food and carved social scenes
passages.text: Excavation at Mandor revealed a temple rising over three terraces, reached by stairs from several sides. ASI dates its core to the seventh or eighth century, with repairs in the ninth and tenth and again in the twelfth. People maintained and altered inherited buildings across changes of rulers.

There was no collective collapse in 900. Regional houses changed fortunes separately, while Rajput identities and landholding networks continued developing over later centuries. The atlas cutoff closes a map slice, not a people’s history.

sectionTitles: A giant building site left unfinished
A town of crops, crafts and worshippers
What continued after the atlas label

passages.text: The atlas alternates two broad labels: “Rajput kingdoms” in 1000 to 1100 and 1200 to 1279, and “Hindu kingdoms” in 1100 to 1200. This shared page covers regional ruling networks, not one empire or everyone’s religion. The middle outline covers the northwest; the later one misleadingly reaches southern India. These are unreliable borders. Examples complement separate dynasty cards; Bhojpur and Chandravati lie outside the middle-century outline.

passages.title: Power, families and political relationships
passages.text: Forts anchored control over surrounding farmland as well as military defence. IGNOU’s historical survey connects regional strongholds with rural property and landed authority. A king needed food and people behind the walls, and connections beyond them.

passages.title: Power, families and political relationships
passages.text: Marriage between ruling clans helped create political alliances and social standing. Rajput identity developed through changing relationships among families, warriors and landholders; it was not a single unchanged ancestry shared by everyone living in these territories.

passages.title: Power, families and political relationships
passages.text: At Kiradu in 1161, Somesvara’s praise inscription placed a local Paramara ruler within the power of the Chaulukya king Kumarapala. Such records reveal layered authority: an ambitious regional lord could advertise victories while acknowledging a more powerful king.

passages.title: Power, families and political relationships
passages.text: An early twelfth-century Jalor inscription credits Queen Melaradevi, wife of Visala, with furnishing a Shiva temple with a golden cupola. Royal women could commission highly visible religious gifts in their own names. This is one queen’s documented patronage, not a description of every woman’s opportunities.

passages.title: A giant building site left unfinished
passages.text: At Bhojpur, the eleventh-century Paramara king Bhoja is associated with an enormous Shiva temple that was never completed. Its surviving hall has four columns about 12 metres tall. The unfinished structure lets researchers investigate decisions that a completed building might have hidden.

passages.title: A giant building site left unfinished
passages.text: Builders scratched architectural drawings onto the surrounding rock: plans, pillars, doorways, capitals and measurements for spacing columns. These were working aids at the construction site. Imagine doing your geometry homework on the ground, then using the answer to position a giant stone pillar.

passages.title: A giant building site left unfinished
passages.text: Carved blocks still lie around Bhojpur, and surviving earthen ramps help explain how heavy building materials could be raised. Nearby dam remains show that the project also reshaped the Betwa river landscape. ASI excavations in 1950 investigated the temple area, adding excavation evidence to the visible ruins.

passages.title: A town of crops, crafts and worshippers
passages.text: Excavations at Chandravati from 2013 to 2016 uncovered remains of a town with substantial religious buildings. Researchers describe temple platforms built in brick and the use of marble from the Ambaji area. Stone arriving from a quarry had to pass through the hands of transport workers, builders and sculptors.

passages.title: A town of crops, crafts and worshippers
passages.text: A Chandravati panel dated to the twelfth or thirteenth century shows worshippers queued before a Jain image. The excavators interpret objects in their hands as possible water pots for ritual bathing of the image. Even a carved medieval crowd seems familiar: everyone waiting for a turn.

passages.title: A town of crops, crafts and worshippers
passages.text: Another sculpture of the same broad period shows a woman adjusting her anklet. Religious art could include recognizable gestures of dressing and adornment. This little action gives a more personal glimpse than a list of royal victories, although an idealized sculpture is not a household photograph.

passages.title: A town of crops, crafts and worshippers
passages.text: Charred crop remains from Chandravati’s roughly 800 to 1300 phase include barley and rice; the researchers also illustrate wheat from that phase. Winter and summer crops both appear. These are actual traces of the plant economy, though surviving seeds cannot tell us precisely what every family ate for dinner.

passages.title: A town of crops, crafts and worshippers
passages.text: Researchers dated charred grain, seeds and wood, then compared the town’s evidence with pollen from nearby Mandovari Lake. They interpret the diverse medieval crops alongside relatively favourable monsoon conditions. Burnt food can be a disaster for a cook and a useful clue for an archaeologist.

passages.title: Learning and words that survive
passages.text: A twelfth-century Sarasvati from Pallu, now in the National Museum, stands about 77 centimetres high and carries symbols including a book and rosary. The museum identifies her as the Jain goddess of learning. Books mattered in this religious imagery, but the statue cannot tell us how many children attended lessons.

passages.title: Learning and words that survive
passages.text: Kiradu’s Sanskrit inscription says “प्रशस्तिमकरोदेतां”, here rendered in modern Devanagari from the scholarly transcription praśastim akarod etāṃ: “composed this eulogy”. The next words name Narasimha acting at the king’s order. These are words from a specific 1161 court monument, not a sample of everyone’s everyday speech.

passages.title: Learning and words that survive
passages.text: The Kiradu record survives on a temple pillar and has been studied through impressions and successive editions. Some letters have been lost or damaged. The modern edition marks restored passages with brackets; the short sample above avoids those restorations.

passages.title: What continued after the atlas label
passages.text: Later Rajasthan forts enclosed temples, homes, markets and palaces, with water-harvesting systems that helped sustain these communities. Jaisalmer remains inhabited. These buildings developed over many centuries, so its present-day streets and reservoirs should not all be assigned to the map’s 1000 to 1279 interval.

passages.title: What continued after the atlas label
passages.text: Chandravati’s excavations show occupation continuing into the late seventeenth century. Its eventual decline was much later than this atlas cutoff. The study considers environmental stress alongside historical and institutional changes, rather than giving every settlement in the region one shared disaster story.

There was no collective collapse in 1200 or 1279, the endpoints of these imported labels. Regional dynasties faced different wars, successions and changing alliances, while Rajput courts and communities continued for centuries. Rajasthan’s surviving fort traditions extend into the eighteenth century and include later interactions with Sultanate and Mughal architecture.
