sectionTitles: Government, defence and getting an education
Books and a small sample of Sardinian
Families, illness and evidence from teeth

passages.text: This Sardinia record covers the island kingdom under the Spanish crown during 1530 to 1700. Sardinians lived with local institutions, maritime dangers, religious learning and recurring epidemics. The island-shaped outline is reasonable as a regional frame; its dates are a map window within a much longer history.

passages.title: Government, defence and getting an education
passages.text: Sardinia’s parliament had three estates, or stamenti: clergy, nobles and representatives of the seven royal towns. It negotiated taxes and proposed legislation for royal approval. This gave organized groups a bargaining role, but was not an assembly elected by every adult on the island.

passages.title: Government, defence and getting an education
passages.text: In Cagliari, the estates could meet in different buildings: church representatives at the archbishop’s residence or cathedral sacristy, nobles at the church of the Speranza, and town representatives at the municipality. Delegates carried messages between them and the viceroy. Government involved plenty of walking as well as talking.

passages.title: Government, defence and getting an education
passages.text: Philip II established the Royal Administration of the Towers in 1587 to organize coastal defenses, soldiers and supplies. Guards watched for hostile ships. For coastal communities threatened by raids, keeping watch over the sea was a serious, organized job.

passages.title: Government, defence and getting an education
passages.text: A tower’s entrance could stand about four to six metres above the ground. Guards reached it by a wooden or rope ladder and then pulled the ladder inside. Reaching the rooftop lookout could require another ladder through a hatch or stairs built into the thick walls.

passages.title: Government, defence and getting an education
passages.text: Early-sixteenth-century Cagliari and Sassari supported public grammar schools. Language could be political: in 1567, Philip II required the Jesuits at Sassari’s college to use Castilian in teaching and even in preaching in the city. Local elites wanted their sons to master it alongside their humanistic studies.

passages.title: Government, defence and getting an education
passages.text: Cagliari’s university received papal authorization in 1607 and a royal foundation privilege in 1620; arrangements for teaching were still being implemented in 1626. The proposed funding split costs between church and city. Establishing a university meant finding rooms and money as well as signing an impressive parchment.

passages.title: Government, defence and getting an education
passages.text: The papal authorization envisaged subjects including medicine, law, philosophy and Latin, Greek and Hebrew. In the royal arrangements, Cagliari’s council would select the rector for a three-year term, while the archbishop could confer degrees. These documents reveal how civic and church authorities shared responsibility for higher learning.

passages.title: Books and a small sample of Sardinian
passages.text: Nicolò Canelles established a printing shop in Cagliari in 1566. Copies preserved in the University Library document this early local printing enterprise. Books could now be produced on the island through a durable workshop, adding a new craft to its cultural life.

passages.title: Books and a small sample of Sardinian
passages.text: Gerolamo Araolla’s collection of 1597 mixed Sardinian, Italian and Spanish poetry. Its original printed heading includes “RIMAS DIVERSAS SPIRITUALES”, meaning “Various spiritual poems”. This is a transcription of an attested title, recorded by the modern editor from the surviving Cagliari copy, not a newly composed example of Sardinian.

passages.title: Families, illness and evidence from teeth
passages.text: During Alghero’s plague outbreak of 1582 to 1583, the physician Quinto Tiberio Angelerio organized restrictions later published as fifty-seven instructions. One rule allowed only one member of a household to go shopping, with permission. Another required people outside to carry a six-foot cane to keep their distance.

passages.title: Families, illness and evidence from teeth
passages.text: The rules also told physicians to visit patients regardless of wealth: richer people would pay, while the city would cover poor patients. Pharmacies had to maintain supplies. These prescriptions show an effort to organize public help during a crisis, although the surviving rules cannot prove that every patient received it.

passages.title: Families, illness and evidence from teeth
passages.text: Some prescriptions came from mistaken explanations of disease: bells and artillery were supposed to purify the air. The same programme used isolation and heated objects and textiles. Angelerio worked before the bacterium and flea transmission were understood; his booklet combined observation with the medical ideas of his time.

passages.title: Families, illness and evidence from teeth
passages.text: Teeth offer a different window into life. Researchers examined 160 people from Alghero’s plague cemetery, including 79 children or adolescents. Cavities, tartar and tooth loss suggested substantial carbohydrate consumption and poor oral hygiene. This is an inference from one burial population, not a menu for every Sardinian family.

The map ends in 1700, but Spanish rule did not instantly end then. Sardinia passed to Austrian control in 1708, was retaken by Spain in 1717, and came under the House of Savoy in 1720. Its institutions and communities continued through these changes of dynasty.

sectionTitles: A capital powered by water and work

passages.text: The House of Savoy governed a changing collection of Alpine and Italian territories, with Turin becoming its capital in 1563. Its rulers acquired the Sardinian crown in 1720. The three map labels belong to successive phases of this dynastic state, although “Sardinia-Piedmont” is premature for the map’s 1650 starting date.

passages.title: A capital powered by water and work
passages.text: When Marguerite of France formally entered Turin on 7 February 1563, municipal officials arranged a canopy and prepared the streets. City accounts record the work and expense behind the ceremony. A royal welcome required ordinary people to build, organize and pay, not simply wave at a procession.

passages.title: A capital powered by water and work
passages.text: Turin’s municipal mills used water from the Dora to grind grain. In 1679 the city expanded their capacity as population and demand grew. Bread depended on machinery, water management and decisions about shared infrastructure as well as on farmers’ harvests.

passages.title: A capital powered by water and work
passages.text: Silk production connected mulberry growing and silkworm keeping with skilled processing. In the 1660s Turin supported a water-powered silk mill associated with Galleani. The technology improved production, but luxurious cloth still depended on the labor of people far removed from the court wearing it.

passages.title: A capital powered by water and work
passages.text: A silk works commissioned at Venaria in 1670 included machinery and a professional training school. Visitors could see the work from the street. Industrial skill was something to teach and display: this royal neighborhood offered a glimpse of manufacturing as well as grand architecture.

passages.title: A capital powered by water and work
passages.text: Before mechanization, silk thread was largely processed by hand, with women providing much of that labor. The machines produced a finer, stronger and more consistent thread. The change affected working routines as well as the appearance and value of the finished material.

passages.title: Schools, land and care
passages.text: In Sardinia, eighteenth-century reforms changed the language of schools and official business from Spanish to Italian. The universities at Cagliari and Sassari reopened in 1764 and 1765. These were major institutional changes, not evidence that every island household immediately changed its everyday language.

passages.title: Schools, land and care
passages.text: The 1820 enclosure edict encouraged private landholding, but access to land was already woven into pastoral and village life. Closing land could disrupt shared grazing and other uses. Property reform brought conflict as well as promises of agricultural improvement.

passages.title: Schools, land and care
passages.text: The 1847 administrative fusion applied mainland institutions to Sardinia. An island already sharing a monarch with the mainland had retained distinct arrangements. A shared crown and a single administrative system were therefore different things, with practical consequences for how people were governed.

passages.title: Schools, land and care
passages.text: In 1832 Giuseppe Cottolengo began a new charitable institution at Valdocco in a modest building with a stable, hayloft and an upstairs room. It welcomed poor sick people who could be excluded by other hospitals. The hospital complex grew from these very ordinary premises.

passages.title: Schools, land and care
passages.text: Turin’s wells and fountains could supply too little water, and some water was polluted. A new distribution network brought water from the Val Sangone. Its 1859 inauguration activated the fountain in Piazza Carlo Felice, making an engineering project visible in a familiar public space.

passages.title: A constitution in Italian
passages.text: Charles Albert granted the Statuto in 1848 after pressure for constitutional reform. It established a framework with a king and two parliamentary chambers. The document changed government, but the monarch still appointed the Senate; constitutional government did not mean everyone could vote.

passages.title: A constitution in Italian
passages.text: Article 24 reads “Tutti i regnicoli, qualunque sia il loro titolo o grado, sono eguali dinanzi alla legge.” It means “All subjects of the kingdom, whatever their title or rank, are equal before the law.” The Italian legal text states a principle; it does not prove equal political participation.

In 1861 the monarchy became the Kingdom of Italy, with the Savoy dynasty continuing on its throne. This was a transformation into a larger state, not the disappearance of its people or institutions. The map’s 1878 endpoint should not be read as the end of an independent Sardinian kingdom.

sectionTitles: Everyday belongings and the people behind them
A feast, skilled metalworkers and an elite necklace
Later villages and a real written message

passages.text: Sarmates is this map’s name for Sarmatian peoples, a varied Iranian-speaking world associated with the Pontic-Caspian steppe. The imported outline for 100 to 1 BCE is an approximate regional label, not the frontier of a single state. Earlier Lower Volga evidence and later communities in Hungary and Roman Britain are identified separately below; neither the people nor their history stopped at the map’s endpoint.

passages.title: Everyday belongings and the people behind them
passages.text: Dating Sarmatian arrivals in the Lower Don is an archaeological puzzle. A stamped Rhodian amphora, black-glazed drinking cups and molded bowls helped Glebov and Dedyulkin place some early complexes in the middle decades of the second century BCE. Imported containers can act as time clues when a grave has no written date.

passages.title: Everyday belongings and the people behind them
passages.text: Lower Don graves of the second and first centuries BCE contain large metal mirrors with raised rims and projecting handles, as well as smaller flat disks without handles. Many retained traces of cases; one had a stand. Looking at your reflection could involve a carefully protected portable object rather than a bathroom wall.

passages.title: Everyday belongings and the people behind them
passages.text: Only about a fifth of the mirrors in that study survived whole. Some were cut, bent or broken, and the author interprets much of this damage as part of funerary rituals. A broken mirror in a grave therefore need not mean its owner was simply careless with their belongings.

passages.title: Everyday belongings and the people behind them
passages.text: An earlier Lower Volga study examined fifty-eight children and adolescents from burials dated 400 to 100 BCE. Researchers recorded dental tartar, including deposits on baby teeth, and one case of tooth decay in a teenager. Such small traces let children enter a history often dominated by warriors and wealthy adults.

passages.title: A feast, skilled metalworkers and an elite necklace
passages.text: At Sadovy Kurgan near Novocherkassk, excavated in 1962, a burial lay in a rectangular pit beneath wooden planks and reeds. Scholarly discussion places the assemblage broadly in the first century BCE. Although robbers had entered the grave, equipment deposited around it still preserved traces of the funeral gathering.

passages.title: A feast, skilled metalworkers and an elite necklace
passages.text: Two bronze cauldrons at Sadovy were blackened with soot. The excavator connected them with cooking for the funeral feast. Eight silver bowls had been stacked upside down and covered with a larger silver vessel. Even a lavish ceremony involved the practical business of cooking and gathering the dishes together.

passages.title: A feast, skilled metalworkers and an elite necklace
passages.text: Sadovy’s large decorative roundels were made from hammered silver covered in gold leaf. Griffins and feline animals filled their surfaces. Thin precious layers could create a brilliant effect without making every part solid gold. Their construction records the work of specialists in shaping, covering and joining metal.

passages.title: A feast, skilled metalworkers and an elite necklace
passages.text: A later gold collar from Khokhlach, another burial mound near Novocherkassk, belongs to the first century CE. It had three joined rings, turquoise settings and pairs of facing lions. The Metropolitan Museum’s example is a nineteenth-century electrotype copy; the ancient original is in the Hermitage. The distinction matters when following an object’s story.

passages.title: Later villages and a real written message
passages.text: Centuries later and west of this map’s outline, Sarmatian communities farmed on the Great Hungarian Plain. At Rákóczifalva-Bagi-földek, fourth- and fifth-century CE plant remains emphasize cereals, while animal remains are dominated by cattle. These villagers combined crops and livestock in a landscape of fields, grassland, floodplain woods and river.

passages.title: Later villages and a real written message
passages.text: At the same Hungarian site, researchers identified twelve grape pips from four pits. They suggest contacts with Roman food traditions and possibly food exchange with Roman provinces. A few seeds can raise interesting questions about meals, but they do not establish that every household owned a vineyard.

passages.title: Later villages and a real written message
passages.text: Writing sample: “DEO SAN” opens a stone inscription from Ribchester in Britain dated 31 August 241 CE. Expanded as “Deo sancto,” it means “To the holy god.” The dedication concerns Apollo Maponus and a Sarmatian cavalry unit. This later Roman military text is Latin, not an example of the Sarmatians’ own language.

passages.title: Later villages and a real written message
passages.text: The same inscription names Aelius Antoninus, a Roman officer from Melitene near the Euphrates. His dedication links an officer from the eastern empire, a unit carrying a Sarmatian name and a fort in Britain. The surviving stone is part of a monument’s pedestal, with a relief of Apollo beside the text.

There was no single Sarmatian state to fall in 1 BCE. Communities continued through the Roman centuries. Later Hunnic expansion broke up Alanic political alliances within this wider world, while different groups moved, joined new coalitions or continued in regions such as the Caucasus. Political labels and communities changed along different paths.

sectionTitles: Read the painted label before the history
Why Khosrow sent Vahrez so far
Power, war and the limits of a distant empire
Homes, clothes, crafts and a little music
Faith, languages and who could learn
Illness, water, and the missing toilet
Conquest, successor states and what continued

passages.text: The atlas paints “Sasanian dependencies” across Yemen from 600 to 800, but the real story is a lightning-fast imperial arrival followed by two centuries of change. Persian troops under Vahrez crossed the sea around 570, defeated an Aksumite-backed ruler, installed a tributary king and later kept governors and soldiers near Sana'a. Those settlers formed families with local women; their descendants were called Abna. When the Sasanian state collapsed after 628, Badhan and other leaders accepted Islam, and Yemen entered the world of the first caliphs. The Persian dynasty itself ended in 651. This card therefore treats the 700 layer as an atlas afterimage. It follows Yemen's older dams, farms, scripts and faiths; Persian strategy and mixed families; plague, trade, clothes, music and water; then Umayyad and Abbasid successors. The polygon stays still, but history races underneath it.

passages.title: Read the painted label before the history
passages.text: The exact atlas id is sasanian-dependencies, displayed as “Sasanian dependencies.” It is a circa state covering 600 to 800 and has no aliases, summary or linked historical article in the index. That plural label invites caution: it describes an editorial map category, not the name of a single dynasty or Yemeni kingdom.

passages.title: Read the painted label before the history
passages.text: In 500 the target does not exist. The atlas puts Najran, Sana'a, Marib and Shibam/Hadramawt inside himyarite-kingdom, while Ctesiphon, Istakhr, Gundeshapur and other Iranian or Iraqi tests belong to a separate sasanian-empire feature. The later dependency card therefore concerns Yemen, not the Persian imperial heartland.

passages.title: Read the painted label before the history
passages.text: In 600 the target is one Polygon, one ring and 57 positions, with a bounding box from about 41.20° to 52.36° east and 12.61° to 19.18° north. Najran, Sana'a, Marib and Shibam/Hadramawt test inside; Aden, Socotra, Mecca, Oman, Iraq and Iran test outside.

passages.title: Read the painted label before the history
passages.text: The 700 target is byte-for-byte the same 57-position polygon with the same bounding box and SHA-256. The atlas also continues a separate sasanian-empire shape over much of Iran. Both are historical afterimages: Yemen changed allegiance around 631 to 632, and the Sasanian dynasty ended in 651, long before this layer closes.

passages.title: Read the painted label before the history
passages.text: At 800 the dependency id vanishes. The atlas assigns tested Najran, Sana'a, Marib and Shibam/Hadramawt to abbasid-caliphate, and does the same for tested Ctesiphon, Istakhr and Gundeshapur. This is an editorial handoff, not a conquest in exactly 800; the real political transitions happened in several earlier stages.

passages.title: The Yemen that Persia entered
passages.text: Aksumite forces crossed from northeast Africa in 525 during a conflict in which a Jewish Himyarite king had attacked Christians. Their inscriptions presented conquest through Christian language and Ethiopian identity. That matters because Persian intervention around 570 displaced an Aksumite-backed order; it did not arrive in an empty or religiously uniform land.

passages.title: The Yemen that Persia entered
passages.text: Late pre-Islamic Yemen included Jewish and Christian communities alongside older South Arabian traditions. The Persian colony's own religious path is surprisingly unclear: the best account says we do not know whether it retained Zoroastrian practice, joined local Christianity or otherwise assimilated. A Sasanian flag cannot serve as a faith census.

passages.title: The Yemen that Persia entered
passages.text: Marib's dam and canals created an enormous artificial oasis in a dry landscape. Cities, temples, walls and inscriptions reveal centuries of local organization and engineering extending to Islam's arrival around 630. Persian governors inherited this achievement; describing every canal as “Sasanian technology” would erase the Yemeni builders who made and maintained it.

passages.title: The Yemen that Persia entered
passages.text: An inscription records the Great Dam's rupture in 547, an outbreak of plague that halted repair, and work resuming when the outbreak eased. Tribes completed major stone construction before Abraha returned to Sana'a in 548. It is rare, vivid evidence for labor, disease and public works just before the Persian conquest.

passages.title: The Yemen that Persia entered
passages.text: A short line from CIH 541, carved at Marib in March 548, reads 𐩨𐩭𐩺𐩡 𐩥[𐩧]𐩵𐩱 𐩥𐩧𐩢𐩣𐩩 𐩧𐩢𐩣𐩬𐩬. Editorial transliteration: “b-ḫyl w-[r]dʾ w-rḥmt rḥmnn”; translation: “By the power and [a]id and mercy of Raḥmānān.” It is a normalized Old South Arabian script rendering, not a facsimile, and directly represents Yemen's Christian Sabaic tradition immediately before Persian rule.

passages.title: Why Khosrow sent Vahrez so far
passages.text: A Yemeni prince, Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan, sought outside help against Masruq's Ethiopian-backed regime. Khosrow I eventually sent Vahrez with a small force by sea. After victory, Sayf ruled as Persia's tributary vassal. The arrangement began as client kingship, not an instant Persian province with identical rules everywhere.

passages.title: Why Khosrow sent Vahrez so far
passages.text: When Sayf was killed after only a few years, Vahrez returned with a larger force. Persian soldiers and officials then remained near Sana'a under successive governors. This second intervention explains why the atlas has a dependency at all, but the record still names local rulers, allies and resistance rather than total control from village to village.

passages.title: Why Khosrow sent Vahrez so far
passages.text: Yemen stood beside routes joining India, the Red Sea, northeast Africa and the Mediterranean. Persian and Ethiopian competition therefore involved shipping, customs, prestige and access as well as religion. Ships carrying valuable goods make a better explanation for distant imperial interest than the idea that Khosrow simply liked collecting faraway colors on a map.

passages.title: Why Khosrow sent Vahrez so far
passages.text: Across Arabia, Sasanian rulers mixed methods: direct garrisons in some strategic places, treaties or tributary rulers in others, and tribal alliances that could change. Yemen's Persian force fits that wider pattern. “Dependency” is therefore a useful atlas shorthand only if readers remember that negotiated influence and military settlement were not the same thing.

passages.title: Why Khosrow sent Vahrez so far
passages.text: The Lakhmid kings at Hira guarded desert approaches, negotiated with Arab groups and fought for Sasanian interests. Khosrow II abolished their dynasty before the final crisis, weakening one long-used client system. Their story helps explain the term dependency, but Hira is outside this card's Yemen polygon and must not be folded into its geography.

passages.title: Power, war and the limits of a distant empire
passages.text: The Sasanian state in Iran could mobilize courts, armies, taxation, priestly institutions, coinage and long traditions of kingship. Its rulers fought Rome and Byzantium on an enormous scale. Yemen's garrison drew prestige from that empire, yet a few governors at Sana'a were never a miniature copy of Ctesiphon's whole government.

passages.title: Power, war and the limits of a distant empire
passages.text: A dependency could send tribute, host troops or follow an imperial ally without every local decision traveling to Persia. Archaeology across Arabia is uneven, so written stories can make imperial reach look cleaner than it was. The card separates documented garrisons and governors from unprovable claims about continuous control of the entire painted polygon.

passages.title: Power, war and the limits of a distant empire
passages.text: The Persian settlement changed through contact. One governor's son, Khurra Khosrow, was reportedly so arabized that the king replaced him. The same source records mountain unrest over Persian financial demands. Those clues show adaptation and resistance together: becoming locally connected did not make taxes cheerful or imperial orders easy.

passages.title: Power, war and the limits of a distant empire
passages.text: Persian strategy around the southern seas also aimed to protect shipping and collect customs. Ports and overland communities did not all depend on the same road, season or political bargain. Trade made Yemen valuable, while Yemen's mountains and local leaders made it hard to command, a combination empires often discover the expensive way.

passages.title: Power, war and the limits of a distant empire
passages.text: Sasanian law in the imperial core classified people by freedom, citizenship, religion, social rank, gender and age. That reveals a sharply unequal world, but no checked source proves the same courts applied every rule identically in Yemen. It is safer to say the garrison carried status ideas than to invent a province-wide legal code.

passages.title: Families, ranks and unequal choices
passages.text: Persian soldiers and officials settled around Sana'a and married local Arab women. Their children and descendants were called Abna, “sons.” This is the clearest family evidence for the dependency: homes and kinship turned a foreign garrison into a locally rooted community whose members remained visible during the first Islamic century.

passages.title: Families, ranks and unequal choices
passages.text: In Sasanian Iran, a free adult noble Zoroastrian man held legal advantages that women, children, enslaved people, foreigners and religious minorities did not share. Yemen had its own norms and rulers, so this is imperial background rather than a household census. Either way, power was distributed very unequally by birth and status.

passages.title: Families, ranks and unequal choices
passages.text: A much earlier Marib decree regulated sales, loans and the enslavement of people. Its third-century date means it cannot be quoted as law in 600, but it proves that written rules and slavery belonged to the region's inherited social history. Hard truth: some households' comfort depended on other people's constrained labor.

passages.title: Families, ranks and unequal choices
passages.text: Early Islamic political organization reshaped what “Yemeni” meant, and later writers remembered little of the old polyglot, terraced and incense-trading past. Families did not wake up in 632 with one new identity. Tribal connection, town, faith, language, Persian ancestry and loyalty could overlap or change across generations.

passages.title: Families, ranks and unequal choices
passages.text: Wahb ibn Munabbih came from a Yemeni family with Persian connections and became a major early transmitter of historical and religious lore. His career shows learning inside a mixed post-conquest society. It also warns us that stories preserved later are interpretation, not a video recording of his grandparents' daily life.

passages.title: Fields, caravans, ships and supper
passages.text: Yemen's position linked Indian Ocean cargoes with Red Sea and overland routes. Sailors, port workers, camel drivers, guards, brokers and tax collectors all helped goods move, though the sources spotlight rulers more than laborers. Commerce did not erase risk: changing alliances, storms and demands for customs could interrupt a profitable journey.

passages.title: Fields, caravans, ships and supper
passages.text: The Marib system diverted seasonal water through canals to cultivate a vast oasis. Farmers and water managers had to clear, repair and negotiate access to this inherited infrastructure. The achievement belongs to centuries of South Arabian practice, not one governor. A polygon can change color faster than a field learns to drink.

passages.title: Fields, caravans, ships and supper
passages.text: A Shabwa incense burner pictures a camel rider, while the museum record explains the animal's value for transport, milk and hair as well as meat. The object is third-century, so it supplies earlier regional context rather than a 600 menu. Camels carried economies; they were not merely scenery behind battles.

passages.title: Fields, caravans, ships and supper
passages.text: Shabwa also earned income from salt and sat on routes toward Najran and the coast. Salt, animals, cultivated produce and imported goods could meet in markets, yet no checked source gives an average family's shopping list for 600 to 800. Food likely varied sharply by altitude, season, wealth and access to irrigation.

passages.title: Fields, caravans, ships and supper
passages.text: After the conquest, Yemen remained part of a Red Sea zone of economic and social interaction rather than becoming isolated. Connections ran toward the Hejaz and northeast Africa while wider caliphal trade patterns changed. Political rulers changed more quickly than sailors' knowledge of winds, ports and trustworthy partners.

passages.title: Homes, clothes, crafts and a little music
passages.text: At earlier Shabwa, crowded tower houses had thick rectangular stone foundations with upper parts of wood and unfired mudbrick; inscriptions even mention several storeys. This is excellent regional building evidence but predates the card. It helps explain why masonry survives while roofs, mats and ordinary upstairs belongings often disappear.

passages.title: Homes, clothes, crafts and a little music
passages.text: Dhafar's landscape preserves rock-cut and built structures beside farms, dams and cisterns. Households depended on careful use of seasonal rain in a highland environment without perennial water. The surviving monumental features reveal setting and skill, while most bedding, baskets, toys and everyday wooden tools left a much fainter trace.

passages.title: Homes, clothes, crafts and a little music
passages.text: An eighth to ninth-century shawl attributed to Sana'a is cotton embroidered with wool. Its survival shows skilled textile work during the Umayyad-Abbasid successor period, just after this atlas interval. It cannot dress every earlier resident for us, but it proves that cloth production remained a celebrated Yemeni craft.

passages.title: Homes, clothes, crafts and a little music
passages.text: A tiny first to second-century bronze shows a seated woman playing a lyre. Museum curators stress that evidence for pre-Islamic Yemeni music is fragmentary, although lyres, lutes and drums appear in images and later reports. It suggests performance at feasts or ceremonies, not mandatory lyre lessons for every child in 650.

passages.title: Homes, clothes, crafts and a little music
passages.text: Excavation and mapping at Zafar keep finding important sixth-century material, but erosion, later building and destruction have removed context. That makes ordinary play especially hard to recover. Children surely did more than watch adults work, yet the checked archaeology does not supply a securely dated toy box or game rulebook.

passages.title: Faith, languages and who could learn
passages.text: Zoroastrian institutions were closely linked to Sasanian kingship in Iran, while Christians, Jews, Manichaeans and others also lived across the empire. Yemen's religious history followed its own path. A Persian officer may have known Zoroastrian practice, but the colony's actual beliefs are too poorly documented to label every Abna household.

passages.title: Faith, languages and who could learn
passages.text: The Marib invocation uses Sabaic in Ancient South Arabian script for Christian language, while Aksumite conquerors also erected Ge'ez inscriptions. Scripts and languages carried political identity. By the seventh century Arabic grew more important, but an alphabet change was gradual and did not make everybody literate overnight.

passages.title: Faith, languages and who could learn
passages.text: Later Muslim-era communities often could not read the old South Arabian inscriptions around them, and early Arabic literature preserved only fragments of the polyglot past. That is a useful lesson about education: knowledge can be lost even when stones survive. No checked source gives a universal school system for dependency-era children.

passages.title: Faith, languages and who could learn
passages.text: Wahb ibn Munabbih and other Abna-associated scholars became known for religious traditions and stories in the early Islamic period. Learning could travel through families, teachers and scholarly circles. Their visibility cannot be turned into a literacy rate: farmers' children, servants and elite sons did not receive equal time, books or instruction.

passages.title: Faith, languages and who could learn
passages.text: The Sana'a shawl carries an Arabic inscription translated by the museum as “In the name of God. Blessing from God. Of what was made in the tiraz of Sana'a.” It dates to the eighth to ninth century and identifies a textile workshop, so it is successor-era evidence for writing woven into work, faith and prestige.

passages.title: Illness, water, and the missing toilet
passages.text: The 547 plague outbreak stopped work at Marib's dam; leaders dismissed assembled tribes, and repairs resumed after the outbreak eased. The inscription records disruption and timing, not symptoms or a cure. It proves that epidemic disease could reorganize labor while leaving us almost nothing about bedside care for an ordinary child.

passages.title: Illness, water, and the missing toilet
passages.text: Gondeshapur in Khuzestan became famous for medical learning and later transmission of Galenic traditions. It belonged to the Sasanian imperial core, not this Yemen polygon, and scholars debate the exact shape of its early hospital. It would be exciting, but false, to place a Gondeshapur clinic in every town the atlas colors.

passages.title: Illness, water, and the missing toilet
passages.text: At Dhafar, open reservoirs served irrigation and animals, while enclosed cisterns stored drinking water. This distinction shows practical attention to water quality in a seasonal-rain landscape. It does not prove germ theory or pipes in every house; carrying, storing and rationing water remained household work with unequal burdens.

passages.title: Illness, water, and the missing toilet
passages.text: Archaeologists at Zafar recover strong walls more readily than timber, wattle, daub or small household fittings. In the sources checked, no securely dated Sasanian or early Islamic Yemeni household latrine has been identified. That is an evidence statement, not proof that people had no private ways to manage waste.

passages.title: Illness, water, and the missing toilet
passages.text: Marib's sluices and Dhafar's cisterns managed precious water, but neither is automatically a sewer. Water engineering deserves admiration without turning every channel into plumbing. Put less politely: a dam has an outlet, not a giant toilet seat. The joke follows the archaeology, the sanitation hardware itself remains undocumented here.

passages.title: Conquest, successor states and what continued
passages.text: By 628 Byzantine victories and civil crisis left Persian agents across Arabia without reliable support. Badhan and leading Abna accepted Islam around 631. That local switch came before Muslim armies conquered the Sasanian heartland, so Yemen's dependency ended through isolation and changed allegiance rather than one battle at Sana'a in 651.

passages.title: Conquest, successor states and what continued
passages.text: The years around 632 were violent. Rival Yemeni leaders challenged Badhan's successors and targeted Abna families; Firuz and allies resisted, and a force sent by Abu Bakr helped restore Muslim authority. Persian-descended residents survived as neighbors, soldiers and scholars even though their imperial chain of command did not.

passages.title: Conquest, successor states and what continued
passages.text: In Iran, Muslim forces won at Qadisiyya in 636, took Ctesiphon in 637 and defeated another major army at Nihavand in 642. Yazdegerd III was killed in 651, ending the dynasty. Those dates make the atlas problem unmistakable: a Sasanian dependency cannot remain politically Sasanian through 800.

passages.title: Conquest, successor states and what continued
passages.text: Under the Umayyads, Yemen was divided between a northern region centered on Sana'a and a southern one around al-Janad. Abbasid rulers after 750 found the region difficult to control because of distance and tribal politics. These are successor administrations inside the atlas's unchanged old polygon, not a revived Persian dependency.

passages.title: Conquest, successor states and what continued
passages.text: A silver drachm minted at Yazd in 662 still shows Khosrow II's bust and a fire altar under Arab-Sasanian authority. The coin comes from Iran, not Yemen, but it offers a perfect continuity lesson: governments can fall while money designs, officials and habits continue. Political ending is not cultural amnesia.

The 800 endpoint is an atlas handoff to abbasid-caliphate, not the fall of a still-living Sasanian dependency. Persian rule in Yemen had changed into Muslim allegiance around 631 to 632, and Yazdegerd III's dynasty ended in 651. Abna families, administrative habits and Persian cultural forms continued, while Yemen's local farming, trade and social networks adapted under Umayyad and Abbasid power.

passages.text: The Sasanian dynasty ruled a major Iranian empire from 224 to 651, competing with Rome and Byzantium across western Asia. Its cities, crafts and scholarship connected Mesopotamia, Iran and Central Asia. This map imports an approximate 300 to 800 interval: the outline after 651 is an error in historical coverage, not evidence that Sasanian emperors still ruled.

passages.title: Power, belief and exchange
passages.text: Ardashir I defeated the Parthians around 224. His successor Shapur I captured the Roman emperor Valerian near Edessa in 260: a striking reversal for Rome and a demonstration of Persia’s military reach.

passages.title: Power, belief and exchange
passages.text: Zoroastrianism received royal support, while Jewish and Christian communities also sustained important centers of learning in Mesopotamia. The Babylonian Talmud developed in this Sasanian setting. One imperial border could contain several religious and intellectual worlds.

passages.title: Power, belief and exchange
passages.text: The silver drahm weighed roughly four grams. Copper coins served smaller transactions, while taxes and exchanges could also use goods rather than cash. A market economy involved more than a glittering pile of royal silver.

passages.title: Waterworks and households
passages.text: At Shushtar, engineers developed an integrated hydraulic system during the third century, building on older knowledge. Diverting the Karun River into canals let the same water network serve a town, irrigated land and watermills. Coordinating its parts was the achievement: a canal alone was only one piece of the machine.

passages.title: Waterworks and households
passages.text: The Gargar canal fed tunnels supplying mills; water then continued toward agricultural land. Moving water could do useful work before reaching fields. The surviving Shushtar system includes later repairs and alterations, so its present appearance is a long engineering history rather than a perfectly preserved Sasanian snapshot.

passages.title: Waterworks and households
passages.text: Excavators at Erk-Kala, ancient Merv, studied a residence occupied in the sixth and seventh centuries. Ovens in a small rear room suggest a kitchen. Builders mixed chaff into mudbrick to limit cracking as it dried, then protected many wall faces with mud plaster. Straw helped hold the house together.

passages.title: Waterworks and households
passages.text: Those Merv householders probably swept and washed their floors regularly. Compacted surfaces and thin layers between successive floors led the excavator to that interpretation. Broken material was moved outside rather than conveniently left for future archaeologists. Keeping a room tidy can make its history harder to recover!

passages.title: Waterworks and households
passages.text: Numerous spindle whorls from Erk-Kala show household spinning. Plant remains also document cotton cultivation, while animal evidence suggests sheep and goats supplied useful secondary products. Clothing and furnishings began with labor at home as well as with merchants: someone had to turn fibers into thread.

passages.title: Crafts, learning and care
passages.text: A glass bowl now in the Met, dated to the sixth or seventh century, has four rows of carefully cut facets. After shaping the glass, craftspeople cut and polished these surfaces with a wheel. Its original pale green color has weathered into an iridescent surface over the centuries.

passages.title: Crafts, learning and care
passages.text: Similar faceted bowls traveled remarkably far: examples survive in Japan, including the Shōsō-in treasury assembled in the eighth century. The museum suggests Persian merchants or embassies as possible carriers. An attractive drinking vessel could cross a continent and remain treasured after the empire that made its style had fallen.

passages.title: Crafts, learning and care
passages.text: A sixth-century house at Umm ez-Za’tir near Ctesiphon had decorative stucco friezes around a large courtyard. Molds repeated leaves and pearl-like borders across the walls. Craftspeople could make an elaborate pattern recur neatly without carving every leaf from scratch: a practical shortcut with a grand result.

passages.title: Crafts, learning and care
passages.text: A Middle Persian literary account describes an elite child learning writing, religious texts, physical skills and courtly accomplishments. Other accounts include riding, archery, music and board games. Such sources tell us most about wealthy families and specialist training; they cannot give every Sasanian child the same school timetable.

passages.title: Crafts, learning and care
passages.text: Gondēšāpur became famous for medicine, but the dates matter. The earliest testimony about medical learning there concerns a medical and philosophical debate around 610. A specific hospital is first mentioned in connection with events in 765, after Sasanian rule. Doctors and learned families crossed the boundary between dynasties.

passages.title: Writing and what survived
passages.text: A silver coin of Khusrau II, minted at Bishapur around 626, carries a crowned portrait on one side and a fire altar with attendants on the other. Stars and crescents surround the designs. At just 3.2 centimeters across, it squeezed royal identity and religious imagery into a very small announcement.

passages.title: Writing and what survived
passages.text: Try a tiny piece of Middle Persian writing: “hptsyh,” meaning “37.” This is the British Museum’s scholarly transliteration of the Pahlavi inscription on that coin, identifying the ruler’s thirty-seventh regnal year. It counts years of a reign, not the year 37 in our calendar.

passages.title: Writing and what survived
passages.text: Imperial warfare reached ordinary supplies. A Coptic letter written on a pottery fragment during the Persian occupation of Egypt, dated 618 to 629, discusses grain. It brings the enormous contest with Byzantium down to the level of food and deliveries.

Muslim conquests ended Sasanian imperial power, and Yazdegerd III died in 651. People and skills remained: early Islamic rulers used Sasanian-style coins, sometimes adding Arabic, while stucco, silverwork and textile traditions continued. Dynastic defeat did not erase the societies of Iran and Mesopotamia.

passages.text: Picture a map label that is also a historical puzzle. “Satavahanihara” was not the normal name of a five-hundred-year empire. An inscription from Myakadoni uses a related word for a Satavahana district, while the Satavahana dynasty itself ruled much of the Deccan roughly from the second century BCE into the early third century CE. Its kings fought Western Kshatrapas, issued lively coins, supported trade routes, and shared an age of Buddhist stupas, caves and Prakrit inscriptions. Farmers grew many grains and pulses; artisans made beads, iron tools, pottery and dazzling gold jewelry. Women, nuns, merchants and whole families appear as donors. Then royal power fragmented, but towns, farms, shrines and the district name continued under new rulers. The atlas stretches one huge polygon from 1 BCE to 500 CE, leaves famous western Satavahana centers outside it, and keeps the old label long after the dynasty ended. This card preserves that odd identity while showing what the evidence actually says.

passages.title: First, decode the strange atlas name
passages.text: The exact indexed id is “satavahanihara,” labeled “Satavahanihara” with the alias “Satava.” and an approximate span from 1 BCE to 500 CE. It is absent at 100 BCE. No separate indexed Satavahana, Andhra, Abhira, Ikshvaku or Chutu identity exists. The spelling and interval are preserved rather than silently repaired.

passages.title: First, decode the strange atlas name
passages.text: Satavahanihara has genuine epigraphic roots. The Myakadoni inscription calls a locale sātavāhanihāra, understood as a Satavahana ahara or district. Scholars warn that this one district name cannot prove the dynasty’s original homeland, much less turn the district into a five-century empire.

passages.title: First, decode the strange atlas name
passages.text: At 1 BCE, 100, 200 and 300 the atlas repeats exactly one Polygon, one ring and 51 positions. Its bounds are about 73.032° to 84.754° east and 12.975° to 21.352° north; the coordinate SHA-256 is 3da3734817b8ece4c666ceffc6f5c91514af3339b827a2a388917e5db7bddfa4.

passages.title: First, decode the strange atlas name
passages.text: The repeated polygon contains Tagara, Nagardhan, Sannati, Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Kondapur and Kotalingala. It excludes Paithan, Nashik, Naneghat, Junnar, Karle, Kanheri, Sopara, Bharuch, Ujjain, Vidisha, Ajanta and Kanchipuram. Several excluded sites are central to Satavahana history. Point tests describe the atlas artwork, not surveyed ancient borders.

passages.title: First, decode the strange atlas name
passages.text: The atlas assigns Paithan, Nashik, Naneghat, Junnar, Karle, Kanheri, Bharuch and other western centers to the separate saka-kingdom polygon through 300. At 400, gupta-empire takes those centers and Amaravati while Satavahanihara shrinks to 21 positions. These are major historical and geographic mismatches.

passages.title: Kings, rivals and the limits of royal stories
passages.text: Satavahana chronology is unusually slippery. Puranic lists, inscriptions and coins do not line up into one uncontested sequence, and scholars differ about the dynasty’s start and original center. Dates in this card use broad phases; a precise-looking year is never smuggled in where the evidence only gives a range.

passages.title: Kings, rivals and the limits of royal stories
passages.text: Kings often used matronymics such as Gotamiputa and Vasithiputa, names connecting them to their mothers. Succession still ran through men, so a mother’s name did not create a matriarchy. The pattern reveals important elite kin identities while leaving ordinary family naming much less visible.

passages.title: Kings, rivals and the limits of royal stories
passages.text: A Kanaganahalli eulogy praises Gautamiputra Satakarni with sweeping virtues and territorial claims. Such inscriptions tell us how courts wished a ruler to be remembered. Historians can use them, but royal praise is closer to a campaign poster carved in stone than a neutral field report.

passages.title: Kings, rivals and the limits of royal stories
passages.text: Gautamiputra’s restriking of Nahapana’s silver coins is hard evidence of conflict and recovery in the west. Instead of melting every captured piece, authorities stamped a new message onto familiar money. Coin circulation and overstrikes reveal political change, although one coin cannot draw the frontier on a map.

passages.title: Kings, rivals and the limits of royal stories
passages.text: Rudradaman’s Sanskrit inscription claims two victories over a Satakarni and says kinship spared the defeated king. That boast demonstrates rivalry and marriage-linked diplomacy between Western Kshatrapas and Satavahanas. It also comes from Rudradaman’s monument, so its heroic framing belongs to the victor’s public image.

passages.title: Districts, officials, taxes and money
passages.text: The ending -ahara in Satavahanihara identifies an administrative or territorial district in the Myakadoni record. This is the strongest explanation for the atlas word. It does not identify the district’s exact boundaries, and the record cannot support the enormous polygon drawn from the Arabian Sea side toward the Bay of Bengal.

passages.title: Districts, officials, taxes and money
passages.text: The Myakadoni text records a tank made by a householder named Samba or Samha during a Pulumavi’s reign. Readings of the regnal year and which Pulumavi is meant have differed. The durable facts are the local water work, the named donor and the district word, not a perfectly fixed modern date.

passages.title: Districts, officials, taxes and money
passages.text: A later Pallava charter addresses princes, commanders, district officers, village headmen, cattle keepers, guards and other royal agents. The list shows administration reaching through several kinds of official. It belongs to a new dynasty, but it helps explain how the old Sātāhani territorial name could survive inside another government.

passages.title: Districts, officials, taxes and money
passages.text: The same charter grants shares of land, a house plot, a threshing floor and workers to Brahmin recipients. It exempts the grant from demands for milk, curds, salt, sugar, bullocks, grass, wood, vegetables, flowers and forced labor. A tax exemption list is an accidental window into everyone else’s burdens.

passages.title: Districts, officials, taxes and money
passages.text: A late first-century copper alloy coin of a Satakarni weighs 11.72 grams and carries an elephant, a tree, fish or moat imagery and a four-orbed Ujjain symbol. Coins joined authority with recognizable pictures, but their findspots and circulation must be studied before treating each piece as a royal border marker.

passages.title: Roads, ports, towns and working networks
passages.text: The Periplus describes Barygaza as a difficult port where strong tides and narrow channels required local pilots. Its author was an anonymous Greek-speaking merchant in the mid-first century CE. His attention follows profitable cargo, so it illuminates trade while overlooking most farmers, children and inland daily routines.

passages.title: Roads, ports, towns and working networks
passages.text: From Barygaza, the merchant guide places Paithana about twenty days inland and Tagara another ten days east, with wagons moving cotton cloth and other goods. Distances are practical travel estimates, not modern survey measurements. Paithana lies outside the atlas target even though it is central to this Satavahana-era network.

passages.title: Roads, ports, towns and working networks
passages.text: Traders, caravan leaders and craft associations called srenis could organize production, credit and gifts. Inscriptions show merchants supporting religious establishments, which offered trusted meeting places along routes. These networks connected courts with working towns without making every merchant a royal employee or every monastery a bank.

passages.title: Roads, ports, towns and working networks
passages.text: Coins, pottery, inscriptions and imported objects reveal busy exchange among western ports, plateau towns and eastern river valleys. Revenue from long-distance trade mattered to rulers, yet local markets also moved grain, salt, tools and cloth. Trade routes were branching human networks rather than one straight “Silk Road” line.

passages.title: Roads, ports, towns and working networks
passages.text: A merchant’s son at Kanaganahalli made a religious gift together with his mother, brothers and sons, dedicating merit broadly. The inscription joins commerce, family and belief in one act. It also warns against picturing trade as only male travelers: household relationships stood behind public donations and business reputations.

passages.title: Fields, water and practical technology
passages.text: Charred plant remains from Satavahana levels at Mungi include wheat, rice, pearl millet, sorghum, pea, Bengal gram, pigeon pea and safflower. This varied crop list suggests farmers balanced cereals, pulses and an oilseed. It comes from one excavated site and should not be turned into everybody’s daily menu.

passages.title: Fields, water and practical technology
passages.text: Farm work depended on seasonal rain, soils, animals, stored seed and access to water. Landholders and laborers did not share rewards equally, while rulers claimed revenue from agricultural production. Inscriptions favor donors and elites, so the many people who weeded, harvested, carried and threshed usually remain unnamed.

passages.title: Fields, water and practical technology
passages.text: At Peddabankur, excavators reported brick enclosures, a well and drainage features in Satavahana levels. These finds show planned construction and water management at a settlement. They do not prove that every home had piped water, and a drain’s exact job must be established from its archaeological context.

passages.title: Fields, water and practical technology
passages.text: The Myakadoni tank donation shows that storing water could earn public credit and be dated by a king’s regnal year. A tank supported people, animals or fields depending on its setting. The short record celebrates a useful local project, not a dynasty-wide water department with identical systems everywhere.

passages.title: Fields, water and practical technology
passages.text: Iron implements, pottery kilns, bead drilling, brickwork and coin striking required trained hands and dependable fuel or raw materials. Museum collections preserve the finished objects more often than the workers’ voices. Technology here means accumulated practical skill, not a sudden invention credited to a single king.

passages.title: Beliefs, stupas, caves and visual storytelling
passages.text: Satavahana-era communities supported Buddhist stupas and rock-cut caves while Brahmanical rituals and other traditions also continued. Patronage came from rulers, merchants, craftspeople, monks, nuns and families. A donation inscription records one act of devotion; it cannot tell us that an entire town shared one belief.

passages.title: Beliefs, stupas, caves and visual storytelling
passages.text: Amaravati grew through centuries of building, carving and repair. Prakrit inscriptions in Brahmi name donors from different walks of life, and some slabs were recut or reused around 250 CE. The monument is therefore a layered community project, not a palace-style commission completed in one king’s reign.

passages.title: Beliefs, stupas, caves and visual storytelling
passages.text: A limestone drum slab from Amaravati, dated about 200 to 240 CE, carries narrative carving for the great stupa. Sculptors made stone seem crowded with movement, bodies and architecture. Its survival teaches art history, while its museum journey also reminds us that many pieces left their original monument.

passages.title: Beliefs, stupas, caves and visual storytelling
passages.text: Kanaganahalli’s stupa developed from roughly the first century BCE into the third century CE. Inscriptions name rulers and donors, including the nun Dhammasiri. Architecture, sculpture and writing worked together there, letting visitors encounter sacred stories while walking around the monument.

passages.title: Beliefs, stupas, caves and visual storytelling
passages.text: At Kanheri, a market councillor from Kalyan donated a cistern to a cave community. Rock-cut cisterns captured precious monsoon water near residences and worship spaces. The inscription links urban trade and monastic infrastructure, but Kanheri sits outside this atlas polygon and belongs to the excluded western evidence.

passages.title: Families, women and an unequal social world
passages.text: Royal mothers mattered visibly in names, yet royal sons inherited. Queens often kept their fathers’ gotras, and some marriages joined people from the same gotra despite Brahmanical rules that advised otherwise. Real elite practice was more complicated than prescriptive social texts, and non-elite families remain less fully recorded.

passages.title: Families, women and an unequal social world
passages.text: A Kanheri cave inscription gathers father, mother, brother and elders around a donor’s religious act. Another Kanaganahalli record includes mother, brothers and sons. These public family lists show kinship as a source of identity and merit, although they cannot reveal every affection, quarrel or household arrangement.

passages.title: Families, women and an unequal social world
passages.text: Women were not absent from public life. Inscriptions name female donors, and the nun Dhammasiri funded work at Kanaganahalli. Donating required resources or influence, so these women are especially visible because they could sponsor durable monuments. Poorer women’s labor is much harder to hear in stone.

passages.title: Families, women and an unequal social world
passages.text: At Amaravati, inscriptions identify women acting alone and with relatives, including wives, sisters, daughters and grandmothers. A family could build merit across generations. These names are precious snapshots, but a donor wall is not a household census and says little about people unable to commission stonework.

passages.title: Families, women and an unequal social world
passages.text: Social ideals ranked Brahmanas, rulers, cultivators, craft workers and laborers, while actual communities also organized around occupation, locality, kin and wealth. Gautamiputra’s court presented him as a defender of social order, yet marriages, donations and guild activity show people navigating rules rather than living inside neat textbook boxes.

passages.title: Children, learning and voices in Brahmi
passages.text: There is no evidence for universal childhood schooling in this district. Children probably learned much work by watching and helping relatives, while specialists learned scripts, accounting, ritual, craft skills or monastic texts through teachers and practice. That is a cautious reconstruction; no Satavahanihara school register survives.

passages.title: Children, learning and voices in Brahmi
passages.text: Inscriptions required a chain of learned work: someone planned the wording, a scribe wrote or prepared it, and a craftsperson cut it into stone or metal. The Hirahadagalli charter even closes by addressing writer, reader and listeners. Literacy could therefore be shared aloud beyond the small group who wrote fluently.

passages.title: Children, learning and voices in Brahmi
passages.text: A directly relevant sample comes from Dhammasiri’s Kanaganahalli inscription, in Middle Indo-Aryan or Prakrit and Southern Brahmi: “𑀦𑀫𑁄 𑀪𑀕𑀯𑀢𑁄 𑀲𑀫𑀲𑀩𑀼𑀥𑀲”. This is a readable Unicode Brahmi normalization made from the critical Roman edition, not a facsimile of the weathered letter shapes.

passages.title: Children, learning and voices in Brahmi
passages.text: Transliteration: “namo bhagavato samasabudhasa.” Translation: “Homage to the Blessed One, the perfectly and completely awakened Buddha.” The spelling represents regional Prakrit rather than classical Sanskrit. Keeping the original grammar matters because inscriptions record how patrons chose to speak publicly, not merely what later editors expected.

passages.title: Children, learning and voices in Brahmi
passages.text: The text dates itself to regnal year 35 of Vasisthiputra Siri Pulumavi and names the nun Dhammasiri’s gift, made with parents and a preceptor for the welfare of all beings. Its absolute year remains debated because Satavahana royal chronology is debated; the regnal date is the secure label.

passages.title: Meals, clothes, homes, work and play
passages.text: The Mungi crops could become boiled grains, breads, porridges, pulse dishes and oil, but archaeology rarely preserves recipes. The Periplus also lists food commodities moving through trade. Cargo lists and charred seeds tell us what was available; they do not prove one standard “Satavahana dinner” for rich and poor alike.

passages.title: Meals, clothes, homes, work and play
passages.text: Cotton textiles moved along routes through Tagara and Paithana. Relief sculpture shows draped garments, while actual cloth usually decays. People could distinguish status with fabric, jewelry and grooming, but stone bodies and elite gifts overrepresent those who could afford display. Everyday patched clothing almost never reaches a museum case.

passages.title: Meals, clothes, homes, work and play
passages.text: A first-century gold ear ornament in the Met combines tiny granules with an elephant and winged lion. It demonstrates extraordinary metalworking and elite taste, not what every ear wore. Jewelry also existed in shell, glass, stone and terracotta, making adornment available at very different prices.

passages.title: Meals, clothes, homes, work and play
passages.text: Brick structures, pottery, iron implements, ivory combs, shell bangles and beads reveal homes filled with useful and personal things. Archaeologists usually recover broken, lost or discarded objects rather than a complete room. A comb can hint at grooming, but it cannot introduce us to the person who pulled it through their hair.

passages.title: Meals, clothes, homes, work and play
passages.text: Dice and terracotta figurines survive from regional Satavahana sites. They may reflect games, storytelling, ritual or decoration; dice were certainly not reserved for children. Human figurine fragments from Peddabankur add faces to the material world, but direct evidence for specific children’s games remains delightfully and frustratingly thin.

passages.title: Health, washing, toilets and what followed
passages.text: Early Indian medical traditions associated with the Susruta Samhita describe anatomy, surgery, medicines and teacher-pupil training. The text evolved over time and its precise dates are debated. It shows a wider learned medical world in the early centuries CE, not a patient chart from Myakadoni or proof of equal access to care.

passages.title: Health, washing, toilets and what followed
passages.text: Wells, tanks, cave cisterns and drains helped communities collect water and move runoff or waste. People bathed and washed using stored or carried water, but the consulted target-area reports do not identify a standard private bathroom. Water infrastructure varied by settlement, season, wealth and purpose.

passages.title: Health, washing, toilets and what followed
passages.text: No securely identified Satavahana-period household toilet from Satavahanihara itself appeared in the consulted excavation reports. Drains and ring-like wells should not automatically be renamed latrines. The honest answer is that direct toilet evidence is sparse, while disposal practices probably differed between dense towns, monasteries and farms.

passages.title: Health, washing, toilets and what followed
passages.text: Satavahana imperial power fragmented around the early third century as regional houses asserted independence. That political change did not empty the Deccan: people still farmed, traded, made objects and supported shrines under new rulers. A dynasty can end while the communities and routes that sustained it keep changing.

passages.title: Health, washing, toilets and what followed
passages.text: At 500 the atlas drops Satavahanihara. Its Vakataka polygon then contains many tested Deccan centers while Gupta and Pallava polygons take others; at 600 Chalukya and Pallava labels replace most of that picture again. These are separate identities and later contexts, so this card adds no appliesTo alias or invented single successor.

By about the early third century CE, the Satavahana imperial line had fragmented into several regional political stories rather than passing intact to one successor. Communities, routes, farms, workshops and religious institutions continued under changing rulers. The atlas instead keeps Satavahanihara as one nearly unchanged polygon through 400 and removes it at 500. Vakataka, Pallava, Gupta, Saka and other records belong to separately carded identities; none is mapped here as the sole heir. This ending marks political transformation around 225 while retaining the atlas interval as metadata, not as a claim that one government ruled for five centuries.

materialEvidence.question: Does a concrete finding have an identifiable context, date, interpretation and evidence limit?

dailyLife.question: Does the account explain ordinary practices with evidence rather than only rulers?

artsScienceTechnology.question: Are achievements concrete and correctly attributed to this polity and period?

chronologicalPhases.question: Are source-supported phases distinguished from map snapshot dates?

endingContinuity.question: Does the narrative identify what ended or continued, with dates, mechanism and uncertainty?

uncertainty.question: Are uncertainties attached to particular claims rather than a blanket disclaimer?

sectionTitles: A kingdom, discoveries and global influence

passages.text: Saudi Arabia is the kingdom proclaimed in 1932, joining regions with different urban, farming and pastoral histories. This imported record begins in 1938. Its first outline wrongly includes Sana’a in Yemen, while all six snapshots omit Dammam. Available polygons end at 2020 even though the index continues to the present. Those map defects are not political events, and the older Nejd and Hejaz records remain separate.

passages.title: A kingdom, discoveries and global influence
passages.text: The Basic Law issued in 1992 describes an Islamic monarchy, with succession among the founder Abdulaziz’s sons and descendants. The king supervises general policy and commands the armed forces. Royal institutions hold extensive authority; this is not a system in which voters elect the national ruler.

passages.title: A kingdom, discoveries and global influence
passages.text: A 1933 concession brought American oil exploration to the Eastern Province. After difficult early drilling, Dammam No. 7 began commercial production in 1938. Geologists searched for promising sites while drilling crews tested them. The oil industry began with investigation and repeated setbacks, not a ready-made fountain of wealth.

passages.title: A kingdom, discoveries and global influence
passages.text: Saudi guide Khamis ibn Rimthan helped exploration teams navigate unfamiliar desert country. Aramco’s historical account describes him leading large camel caravans by the early 1940s, when motor transport was still limited. Knowledge of routes and terrain mattered alongside geological instruments: an expedition needed to reach its destination before it could investigate it.

passages.title: A kingdom, discoveries and global influence
passages.text: The 1,212-kilometre Trans-Arabian Pipeline, completed in 1950, connected eastern Saudi oilfields with the Mediterranean export route. In 1980 the Saudi government increased its ownership of Aramco to 100 percent. Transport infrastructure and ownership changed together as oil became a much larger source of state power.

passages.title: A kingdom, discoveries and global influence
passages.text: Saudi Arabia was one of five states that founded OPEC at Baghdad in September 1960, alongside Iran, Iraq, Kuwait and Venezuela. Abdullah al-Tariki represented Saudi Arabia among the founders. The organization gave oil-producing governments a forum for coordinating policies that affected customers far beyond the region.

passages.title: A kingdom, discoveries and global influence
passages.text: During the 1973 Arab-Israeli War, Saudi Arabia and other participating Arab oil exporters restricted supplies to the United States and other supporters of Israel. The embargo contributed to a wider energy crisis and intense diplomacy before it was lifted in March 1974. Oil prices also reflected other economic pressures; one decision did not explain the whole crisis.

passages.title: Homes, hospitality and food
passages.text: In Asir, women traditionally decorate guest-room walls with al-Qatt al-Asiri painting. Female relatives of different ages help, drawing geometric forms and symbols on a usually white gypsum base. Children can learn by watching and practising alongside older relatives. Here the family artwork can be an entire wall, not just a drawing attached to the refrigerator.

passages.title: Homes, hospitality and food
passages.text: Arabic coffee is part of hospitality in Saudi Arabia and neighbouring countries. UNESCO’s account describes serving elders and guests first, sharing poetry and conversation, and shaking the cup to signal that one has finished. A small movement saves a long explanation: the cup has its own polite vocabulary.

passages.title: Homes, hospitality and food
passages.text: Al-Ahsa’s oasis is a working landscape of springs, wells, open canals, gardens and settlements. Water distribution links farms to one another, and drainage is part of the system too. Its agricultural history long predates the modern kingdom. The greenery is the result of sustained work with water, rather than the desert simply deciding to become a garden.

passages.title: Homes, hospitality and food
passages.text: UNESCO’s Al-Ahsa listing describes about 2.5 million date palms, but dates are not the only crop. A local red rice variety also survives. Historic souks and modern markets distribute farm produce and handicrafts. An oasis meal and a market basket can therefore reveal more variety than a picture of palms alone suggests.

passages.title: Homes, hospitality and food
passages.text: Historic Jeddah preserves late nineteenth-century merchant tower houses built before the Saudi kingdom. Ground floors could serve business, while rooms accommodated pilgrims travelling to Mecca. Such buildings brought work, lodging and household life under one roof. The city’s Red Sea connections carried people, food and ideas from Africa and Asia.

passages.title: Homes, hospitality and food
passages.text: Jeddah’s wooden roshan projections create shaded extensions to living rooms. The nomination describes people sitting or sleeping there and placing clay water pots in the shade and airflow. Louvred panels admitted breezes. A window could be a small living space as well as an opening to look through.

passages.title: Learning, health and changing opportunities
passages.text: King Saud University was established in 1957. Its institutional history records an initial Arts intake of twenty-one male students. Women began entering in 1381 AH, approximately 1961 to 1962; the first group in English comprised four Saudi women. These small cohorts put human scale on the expansion of university education.

passages.title: Learning, health and changing opportunities
passages.text: Building a public girls’ school system also required teachers. The King Saud Library records a women’s teacher-training institute in 1380 AH and fifteen girls’ primary schools in the 1380 to 1381 academic year, around 1960 to 1962. These were milestones in public schooling, not the beginning of all learning among Saudi girls.

passages.title: Learning, health and changing opportunities
passages.text: WHO validated Saudi Arabia’s elimination of trachoma as a public health problem in January 2022. Trachoma can damage sight. The achievement involved connecting eye care with local health services and cooperation with education, water and agriculture authorities. The precise milestone matters: it did not mean that no future patient could ever develop the disease.

passages.title: Learning, health and changing opportunities
passages.text: The ban on women driving ended on 24 June 2018, a change welcomed by the UN Secretary-General. Yet Human Rights Watch had reported the arrest of women’s-rights campaigners the previous month, including Eman al-Nafjan and Loujain al-Hathloul. New opportunities and repression occurred in the same period; the reform did not erase the campaigners’ experiences.

passages.title: Arabic words in everyday money
passages.text: SAMA’s Arabic announcement dated 4 October 2020 contains “خمسة ريالات”, transliterated khamsat riyālāt, meaning “five riyals”. This is a short modern Arabic writing sample from the announcement’s first paragraph, with its meaning confirmed by the parallel English version. It identifies the denomination of a new banknote; it is not an ancient inscription.

passages.title: Arabic words in everyday money
passages.text: The new five-riyal note was made of polymer and scheduled to circulate from 5 October 2020 alongside cotton notes. Its front showed King Salman and the Shaybah oilfield, while the back showed wildflowers. A transparent window carried decorative motifs. Everyday money put petroleum and small desert flowers in the same pocket.

Saudi Arabia continues as a kingdom. The last available map snapshot is not a fall date. Royal institutions and distinctive regional communities have continued through extensive economic and social change.
