sectionTitles: Read the border as an atlas artifact
Replace one label with many regional histories
Plan life around rains, fires, rivers and floods
Gather, hunt, fish, cultivate and cook many menus
Make tools, pots, paths and exchange relationships
Build shelter, clothing and an ordinary workday
See families, women, children and learning carefully
Face illness, medicine, water and the toilet question
Honor beliefs while naming conflict and coercion
Celebrate discoveries and continue past the map ending

passages.text: Imagine one map color spread across a chunk of South America bigger than many countries, then call everyone inside “Savanna hunter-gatherers.” The exact atlas shape begins in 1500 BCE across much of central and eastern Brazil, the Pantanal, the Gran Chaco and nearby southern lowlands. It is a leftover map category, not one people, language, state or way of life. Archaeology instead finds small camps, rock shelters, wetland mounds, villages, pottery traditions, gardens, fishing places and long-distance relationships that changed by region and century. Cerrado families could combine wild fruits, hunting and fishing with crops; Pantanal communities engineered durable high places beside seasonal water; Chaco peoples followed their own mobile and horticultural histories. Around 800 CE the atlas suddenly hands a huge eastern area to “Tupis,” although real change was messier. The label briefly vanishes in 1492, returns in 1500, splits after 1650 and disappears in 1783 beneath Portuguese and Spanish colonial colors. None of those edits means everybody moved or vanished. There is no honest written-language sample for this umbrella because it had no common language or script.

passages.title: Read the border as an atlas artifact
passages.text: The exact record is id “savanna-hunter-gatherers,” kind “culture,” circa 1500 BCE to 1800 CE, generated from historical basemaps. Its coverage ledger routes it to South America and records 31 border files. The id is absent at 2000 BCE, then appears suddenly at 1500 BCE without a demonstrated ethnogenesis event.

passages.title: Read the border as an atlas artifact
passages.text: From 1500 BCE through 700 CE, seventeen exact snapshots reuse one 117-position polygon with coordinate hash 18f91a88d8d1b404e38e8765de6fb36ab2fbdc40d7dd378226715fd5a2cce680. Its bounds stretch roughly from 69.320 degrees west to 34.890 west and 31.824 south to 4.393 south. Repetition that perfect signals basemap reuse, not cultural stillness.

passages.title: Read the border as an atlas artifact
passages.text: At 800 CE the shape drops from 117 to 46 positions and its eastern edge jumps west from about 34.890 to 48.469 degrees west. Brasília, Goiás, Belo Horizonte and Lagoa Santa move to a Tupi polygon, while ten tested western and southern points remain. That is an abrupt classification seam, not a measured migration front.

passages.title: Read the border as an atlas artifact
passages.text: The smaller polygon drifts by fractions of a degree from 1000 through 1400. At 1492 the exact id vanishes and several named Indigenous labels appear; at 1500 the generic shape returns with a slightly narrower western bound. A real people cannot sensibly cease for eight years and restart, so the card preserves the gap as atlas metadata.

passages.title: Read the border as an atlas artifact
passages.text: At 1650 the feature becomes two polygons with 66 positions; at 1715 it keeps two fragments but only 43 positions. At 1783 it disappears while the index still runs to 1800. Spanish and Portuguese ownership colors replace it. Those seams trace atlas editing and imperial claims, never a synchronized Indigenous surrender or extinction.

passages.title: Replace one label with many regional histories
passages.text: “Savanna hunter-gatherers” is a modern English description, not a recovered self-name. The early polygon joins Cerrado plateaus, river valleys, Pantanal wetlands, Chaco woodland and southern grasslands. Archaeologists name local sites and material traditions, but a shared stone-tool style does not automatically reveal language, ethnicity or political membership.

passages.title: Replace one label with many regional histories
passages.text: Central Brazilian sequences include rock shelters and open sites associated with Itaparica and Serranópolis technologies, followed much later by several ceramic and horticultural traditions. Those categories were built from artifacts and dates. They should not be treated as ancient passports, and none maps neatly onto the atlas’s enormous residual polygon.

passages.title: Replace one label with many regional histories
passages.text: The Pantanal record contains hunter-gatherer contexts, ceramic occupations and thousands of durable mounds beside channels, lagoons and floodplains. Its archaeology follows water rather than a neat savanna border. Calling all those residents the same as communities in dry Chaco scrub would erase different building methods, foods and seasonal calendars.

passages.title: Replace one label with many regional histories
passages.text: Historical Chaco sources distinguish Guaycuruan, Matacoan and other peoples with their own names, languages, alliances and movements. The atlas polygon partly overlaps their homelands, but the umbrella is not “the Chaco people.” Even the later labels Toba, Wichí, Abipón or Mbayá describe specific histories, never safe aliases for every earlier resident.

passages.title: Replace one label with many regional histories
passages.text: Large circular or horseshoe-shaped villages appear in parts of Central Brazil around 800 CE, occupied by pottery-making agriculturalists. Their plazas and house arrangements reveal organized communities, not a single regional capital. The atlas’s simultaneous Tupi recoloring is too coarse to identify who built any particular ring village.

passages.title: Plan life around rains, fires, rivers and floods
passages.text: The broad polygon crosses vegetation that Brazil’s mapping agency separates into Cerrado savanna, Pantanal savanna-steppe and southern grasslands, with gallery forests and wetlands threaded among them. Seasons did not offer one shared calendar. A family on a floodplain planned around rising water; a plateau community watched rains, fruiting and dry-season fire.

passages.title: Plan life around rains, fires, rivers and floods
passages.text: Later Xavante evidence shows carefully timed burning connected with collective hunting and ceremonial life. Researchers found these local fires could help maintain open savanna mosaics rather than simply destroy them. This is a useful comparison for landscape skill, not proof that every archaeological community used the same flames, rules or ritual.

passages.title: Plan life around rains, fires, rivers and floods
passages.text: A broader set of later Indigenous case studies connects burning with tortoise hunts, festivals, courtship, youth initiation and learning. Fire could therefore be ecology, work and social life at once. The funny modern shortcut is “ancient lawn mower,” but the serious point is that timing and responsibility mattered more than simply lighting a match.

passages.title: Plan life around rains, fires, rivers and floods
passages.text: Pantanal mounds created or enlarged dependable high ground near floodwaters. Later Guató knowledge links a mound’s excavated depression and connecting channel to fish habitat and travel. Archaeology and community memory together show engineered wetland places, though the exact age and builders of each feature must be established site by site.

passages.title: Plan life around rains, fires, rivers and floods
passages.text: Rivers were drinking sources, travel corridors, fishing grounds and boundaries, but also brought floods and biting insects. Archaeology rarely preserves a rulebook for safe water. People could choose springs, flowing channels or seasonal camps, yet this umbrella supports no claim for shared wells, aqueducts, filtration system or water authority.

passages.title: Gather, hunt, fish, cultivate and cook many menus
passages.text: Pequi and buriti are nutritious native Cerrado fruits with edible pulp, oils and other useful parts. An Embrapa study documents their modern food importance, while archaeology must establish ancient use separately. It is reasonable to teach the landscape’s possibilities; it is not reasonable to place the same pequi recipe in every household for 3,300 years.

passages.title: Gather, hunt, fish, cultivate and cook many menus
passages.text: Una-related sites in Central Brazil preserve evidence associated with maize, beans, peanuts, gourds and cotton, alongside hunting and gathered foods. Other traditions favored different crops and settings, including manioc in some regions. “Hunter-gatherer” therefore becomes badly misleading inside the target interval: many communities mixed cultivation, foraging and exchange instead of choosing one economic team.

passages.title: Gather, hunt, fish, cultivate and cook many menus
passages.text: Pantanal residents could fish lagoons, rivers and seasonal channels while hunting and collecting wetland plants. Mounds made repeated occupation safer above floods and placed people near aquatic resources. Fish availability changed with water levels, so successful meals depended on knowing when a “road” for canoes would become grass or mud.

passages.title: Gather, hunt, fish, cultivate and cook many menus
passages.text: Later Toba and Wichí accounts describe mobile or semimobile lives combining hunting, fishing, wild fruit, honey, tubers and limited horticulture. They help imagine Chaco seasonality only when clearly labeled comparison. Twentieth-century nutrition change cannot be projected backward, and one people’s division of foods cannot stand for another’s ancient kitchen.

passages.title: Gather, hunt, fish, cultivate and cook many menus
passages.text: Near the polygon’s western edge, archaeologists recover tiny starch grains, phytoliths, charred plant remains and residues trapped on stone tools. These methods reveal plant processing that bones alone would miss. Forest-island excavations likewise show foragers repeatedly using stable places, challenging the cartoon that gathering always meant wandering without homes or gardens.

passages.title: Make tools, pots, paths and exchange relationships
passages.text: Stone technology at Serranópolis required choosing rock, planning flakes, maintaining edges and knowing when a portable tool was worth extra work. Similar designs across sites may record shared concepts and contact networks, yet local differences matter. A point or scraper is evidence of skilled decisions, not a barcode for one tribe.

passages.title: Make tools, pots, paths and exchange relationships
passages.text: Pottery let people boil, store and serve foods, but ceramic traditions vary in shape, surface and temper. Pantanal archaeologists combine vessel study with settlement context rather than treating pots as ethnic name tags. A broken sherd can reveal technology and use; it cannot introduce its potter without additional evidence.

passages.title: Make tools, pots, paths and exchange relationships
passages.text: Phytoliths and starch residues survive after soft foods disappear. Researchers sample soil and microscopic traces on stone edges, compare forms with reference plants and use radiocarbon dates to anchor layers. The method can detect plant processing, but contamination and uncertain identification demand caution. Even microscopic evidence needs a trustworthy address and date.

passages.title: Make tools, pots, paths and exchange relationships
passages.text: Circular villages with central plazas represent building, gardening and social coordination at scales the generic label never predicts. House rings also created paths, sightlines and gathering space. Archaeologists compare size and layout through time to study demographic and political change, while avoiding the claim that every plaza hosted identical ceremonies or councils.

passages.title: Make tools, pots, paths and exchange relationships
passages.text: Ancient DNA now adds another kind of evidence, but Brazilian sampling remains sparse and tropical preservation is difficult. Genomes from coastal and Lagoa Santa contexts reveal population relationships and change, not a “savanna hunter-gatherer gene.” DNA, language, pottery and identity can follow different paths, so none should automatically name the others.

passages.title: Build shelter, clothing and an ordinary workday
passages.text: Shelters ranged from rock overhangs to houses made with posts, thatch, leaves and fiber. Perishable walls often vanish, leaving postholes, hearths and artifact patterns. Older Smithsonian comparisons describe poles, mats and mobile shelters across South America, but their broad categories are clues, not blueprints for every target household.

passages.title: Build shelter, clothing and an ordinary workday
passages.text: Clothing rarely survives tropical soils. Fiber, hide, feathers, body paint and ornaments could all carry practical or social meaning, yet the exact mix was local. Chaco ethnography offers later examples of woven bags, nets and dress; the card uses them as comparison and refuses to assign a single costume to the umbrella.

passages.title: Build shelter, clothing and an ordinary workday
passages.text: Daily labor included collecting fuel, carrying water, processing plants, cooking, maintaining tools, watching children, tending gardens, hunting, fishing and repairing shelter. Wetland households also managed canoes, landing places and mound surfaces. Archaeology sees the durable results more easily than the hundreds of small jobs that kept dinner and dry feet possible.

passages.title: Build shelter, clothing and an ordinary workday
passages.text: Recent Wichí observations describe women taking long forest trips for fruit, wood and plants while men hunt, fish and make wooden objects. This is one modern community, not an ancient universal. It shows how adults and children can learn through accompanying real work, with a forest serving as classroom, pantry and hardware aisle.

passages.title: Build shelter, clothing and an ordinary workday
passages.text: Later Central Brazilian fire festivals connect collective hunting with singing, courtship, initiation and community memory. Work and play were not necessarily separate boxes. A demanding hunt could also be a social event, while children learned timing and responsibility by watching and joining. Specific dances or games remain undocumented for the atlas umbrella.

passages.title: See families, women, children and learning carefully
passages.text: Houses, hearths and food debris show people living together, but they do not identify a modern nuclear family. A dwelling might hold an extended family, visitors or a work group, and arrangements could change by season. Kinship rules certainly mattered somewhere, yet no single marriage or inheritance system belongs to this atlas bucket.

passages.title: See families, women, children and learning carefully
passages.text: Later Toba research shows women’s health shaped by diet, mobility, land access, reproductive work and colonial or market pressure. It also warns against treating “women” as one timeless job category. Archaeological tools usually lack a reliable gender label, so the card names women’s likely importance without assigning every pot, basket or plant to them.

passages.title: See families, women, children and learning carefully
passages.text: A modern Qom feeding study shows that children’s meals are tied to caregiving, household resources and ideas about proper growth, not just calories. As later comparison, it reminds us that ancient children were active social members. It cannot tell us the target’s weaning ages, favorite snacks or who got the last honeycomb.

passages.title: See families, women, children and learning carefully
passages.text: Wichí caregiver-infant research observes learning inside multiparty interactions, including careful watching, shared attention and participation rather than constant spoken instruction. That makes a useful alternative to imagining a formal schoolhouse. For the target record, there is no securely identified school system, curriculum or continent-wide coming-of-age rule.

passages.title: See families, women, children and learning carefully
passages.text: Village plazas could host gatherings, work, ceremonies and children’s play, but archaeology rarely preserves the joke somebody told or the rules of a game. Miniature objects, footprints or wear can sometimes suggest childhood, yet none supports an umbrella-wide claim here. Learning probably mixed storytelling, observation, correction, practice and participation in daily tasks.

passages.title: Face illness, medicine, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Paleoparasitology turns ancient fecal traces and preserved bodies into health evidence. A Peruaçu Valley mummy carried intestinal parasite evidence in a context with Una ceramics and cultivated plants. That tells us infection existed at one place and time; it does not reveal a universal diagnosis, cure or cleanliness standard.

passages.title: Face illness, medicine, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Teeth record diet, wear and disease. Modern Xavante research, paired with bioarchaeological comparisons, shows how greater reliance on cariogenic farm or market foods can raise cavity risk, while fibrous diets can wear teeth heavily. Dental health was therefore not simply “good” or “bad”; different menus produced different problems.

passages.title: Face illness, medicine, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Modern Mbyá-Guarani specialists describe plant medicines, careful diagnosis and spiritual dimensions of healing, including knowledge for pregnancy and children. This belongs to named present communities and appears only as comparison. The atlas umbrella offers no safe list of ancient remedies, healer titles or doses, so the card will not invent grandma’s miracle leaf.

passages.title: Face illness, medicine, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Water and waste were practical camp and village problems. People could place activity areas away from living floors, discard bones and sherds in middens, and shift a shelter when refuse or flooding became troublesome. Yet no shared sewer, bathhouse, drainage code or water-treatment technology is securely attributable across this enormous target.

passages.title: Face illness, medicine, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Toilets leave surprisingly tricky evidence. Archaeologists can find latrine pits, parasite eggs or concentrated waste when preservation is kind, but none establishes an umbrella-wide built toilet here. The safest answer is wonderfully unglamorous: people had bodily-waste routines, probably local and changing, while the exact locations and rules remain unknown.

passages.title: Honor beliefs while naming conflict and coercion
passages.text: Rock art, burials, special objects and village space can show that places and bodies carried meaning, but interpretation must stay local. Serranópolis materials belong to layered occupations, not one atlas religion. A painted figure might relate to story, ritual, memory or teaching; without secure context, choosing only one meaning turns evidence into fan fiction.

passages.title: Honor beliefs while naming conflict and coercion
passages.text: Later Indigenous fire practices could link hunting with ceremony, initiation and responsibility to the landscape. They demonstrate that ecology and belief need not be separate. The comparison supports respect for sophisticated knowledge, while avoiding a claim that all target communities worshipped fire or followed one calendar of sacred burns.

passages.title: Honor beliefs while naming conflict and coercion
passages.text: Conflict existed before Europeans, including feuds, raids and competition, but the generic polygon supplies no single army or war history. In the colonial Chaco, horses, metal goods, missions and shifting alliances transformed warfare. Some peoples resisted Spanish advances for centuries, moved strategically or entered and left mission settlements.

passages.title: Honor beliefs while naming conflict and coercion
passages.text: Portuguese bandeiras sought Indigenous captives as forced labor and tied inland expansion to enslavement, demographic destruction and displacement. The harm was organized, not a natural fading of “hunter-gatherers.” Families fled, fought, negotiated, regrouped and formed new communities, actions hidden when the map simply repaints territory as Portuguese Brazil.

passages.title: Honor beliefs while naming conflict and coercion
passages.text: Colonial authorities sometimes labeled attacks “just wars,” describing Indigenous communities as savage to justify expeditions, captivity and forced pacification. Those documents reveal the colonizers’ legal language and goals, not neutral portraits of their targets. The atlas’s 1783 recoloring must therefore never be narrated as peaceful, complete or inevitable control.

passages.title: Celebrate discoveries and continue past the map ending
passages.text: The greatest achievement was not one monument but thousands of years of regional problem-solving: reading rains and floods, maintaining paths, selecting plants, building mounds and villages, making tools and pots, sharing food and teaching children. Calling these societies a leftover category misses how deliberately they shaped homes and landscapes.

passages.title: Celebrate discoveries and continue past the map ending
passages.text: Archaeologists now combine survey, excavation, stratigraphy, radiocarbon dating, microscopic plant residues, human and animal remains, stable chemistry and ancient DNA. Each method sees a different slice. Strong conclusions come from agreement among several lines of evidence, while gaps remain especially large where tropical soils destroy bone, fiber, wood and food.

passages.title: Celebrate discoveries and continue past the map ending
passages.text: Forest-island settlements, Pantanal mounds and Central Brazilian villages overturn an old picture of people merely passing through “empty” nature. Repeated occupation, burials, earth building and managed resources show deep attachment and accumulated knowledge. Mobility could be planned within a known homeland rather than endless wandering across someone else’s blank map.

passages.title: Celebrate discoveries and continue past the map ending
passages.text: Contemporaneous written-language sample: none is securely attributable to this atlas record. “Savanna hunter-gatherers” was not one language community, and no common self-authored inscription or manuscript spans its shape and dates. Colonial Portuguese, Spanish or mission Guarani text belongs to specific writers and settings; borrowing it would fake a voice the umbrella never had.

passages.title: Celebrate discoveries and continue past the map ending
passages.text: When the polygon disappears in 1783, people do not. Boe, Guató, Xavante, Kayapó, Terena, Qom, Wichí, Guarani and many other named peoples have distinct histories continuing beyond the map, despite invasion and land loss. They are not interchangeable descendants of one atlas civilization, but living nations whose names deserve precision.

At 1783 the atlas removes “Savanna hunter-gatherers” and assigns tested interior locations to Portuguese or Spanish imperial colors. That seam neither proves effective colonial control nor marks a people’s fall. Named Indigenous communities continued, resisted, moved, regrouped and preserved distinct identities. The card ends the imported umbrella here, while recording that the index’s nominal 1800 endpoint contains no exact target geometry.

sectionTitles: A capital powered by water and work

passages.text: The House of Savoy governed a changing collection of Alpine and Italian territories, with Turin becoming its capital in 1563. Its rulers acquired the Sardinian crown in 1720. The three map labels belong to successive phases of this dynastic state, although “Sardinia-Piedmont” is premature for the map’s 1650 starting date.

passages.title: A capital powered by water and work
passages.text: When Marguerite of France formally entered Turin on 7 February 1563, municipal officials arranged a canopy and prepared the streets. City accounts record the work and expense behind the ceremony. A royal welcome required ordinary people to build, organize and pay, not simply wave at a procession.

passages.title: A capital powered by water and work
passages.text: Turin’s municipal mills used water from the Dora to grind grain. In 1679 the city expanded their capacity as population and demand grew. Bread depended on machinery, water management and decisions about shared infrastructure as well as on farmers’ harvests.

passages.title: A capital powered by water and work
passages.text: Silk production connected mulberry growing and silkworm keeping with skilled processing. In the 1660s Turin supported a water-powered silk mill associated with Galleani. The technology improved production, but luxurious cloth still depended on the labor of people far removed from the court wearing it.

passages.title: A capital powered by water and work
passages.text: A silk works commissioned at Venaria in 1670 included machinery and a professional training school. Visitors could see the work from the street. Industrial skill was something to teach and display: this royal neighborhood offered a glimpse of manufacturing as well as grand architecture.

passages.title: A capital powered by water and work
passages.text: Before mechanization, silk thread was largely processed by hand, with women providing much of that labor. The machines produced a finer, stronger and more consistent thread. The change affected working routines as well as the appearance and value of the finished material.

passages.title: Schools, land and care
passages.text: In Sardinia, eighteenth-century reforms changed the language of schools and official business from Spanish to Italian. The universities at Cagliari and Sassari reopened in 1764 and 1765. These were major institutional changes, not evidence that every island household immediately changed its everyday language.

passages.title: Schools, land and care
passages.text: The 1820 enclosure edict encouraged private landholding, but access to land was already woven into pastoral and village life. Closing land could disrupt shared grazing and other uses. Property reform brought conflict as well as promises of agricultural improvement.

passages.title: Schools, land and care
passages.text: The 1847 administrative fusion applied mainland institutions to Sardinia. An island already sharing a monarch with the mainland had retained distinct arrangements. A shared crown and a single administrative system were therefore different things, with practical consequences for how people were governed.

passages.title: Schools, land and care
passages.text: In 1832 Giuseppe Cottolengo began a new charitable institution at Valdocco in a modest building with a stable, hayloft and an upstairs room. It welcomed poor sick people who could be excluded by other hospitals. The hospital complex grew from these very ordinary premises.

passages.title: Schools, land and care
passages.text: Turin’s wells and fountains could supply too little water, and some water was polluted. A new distribution network brought water from the Val Sangone. Its 1859 inauguration activated the fountain in Piazza Carlo Felice, making an engineering project visible in a familiar public space.

passages.title: A constitution in Italian
passages.text: Charles Albert granted the Statuto in 1848 after pressure for constitutional reform. It established a framework with a king and two parliamentary chambers. The document changed government, but the monarch still appointed the Senate; constitutional government did not mean everyone could vote.

passages.title: A constitution in Italian
passages.text: Article 24 reads “Tutti i regnicoli, qualunque sia il loro titolo o grado, sono eguali dinanzi alla legge.” It means “All subjects of the kingdom, whatever their title or rank, are equal before the law.” The Italian legal text states a principle; it does not prove equal political participation.

In 1861 the monarchy became the Kingdom of Italy, with the Savoy dynasty continuing on its throne. This was a transformation into a larger state, not the disappearance of its people or institutions. The map’s 1878 endpoint should not be read as the end of an independent Sardinian kingdom.

sectionTitles: A farm was a cluster of buildings
A later voice in Old Saxon

passages.text: The continental Saxons were communities in northern Germany whose leaders and settlements formed a loose political network. This card follows their early medieval world and conquest by the Franks. The imported 500 outline stretches implausibly far into Jutland; it is not a reliable kingdom boundary, and this record is distinct from the kingdoms of Anglo-Saxon England.

passages.title: A farm was a cluster of buildings
passages.text: At Warendorf, seventh- and eighth-century farmsteads included a large living hall, barns, stores and smaller buildings. Archaeologists reconstructed these layouts from excavated traces. A household’s work spread across a whole yard, with places for animals, equipment, supplies and making things.

passages.title: A farm was a cluster of buildings
passages.text: Successive buildings occupied the same ground several times. Timber posts could decay or buildings could burn, so a farm needed repair and replacement. Those overlapping post-holes help archaeologists recover the settlement’s history, rather than treating every mark as a building that stood at once.

passages.title: A farm was a cluster of buildings
passages.text: Warendorf stood beside a crossing of the Ems. Its sunken buildings are interpreted mainly as spinning and weaving workshops, with other possible uses. The evidence connects household craft with a settlement positioned on a route for people and goods.

passages.title: A burned loom leaves clues
passages.text: At nearby Milte, an early medieval workshop contained charred timber and clay loom weights. Fire had destroyed the wooden loom, but left enough evidence to recognise textile work. The excavation report does not yet give the loom a narrow date within the early medieval period.

passages.title: A burned loom leaves clues
passages.text: Excavators recovered seven complete weights and fragments of twelve more. Fragile examples were lifted inside blocks of soil so conservators could expose them carefully. These objects once kept threads under tension, part of the patient work needed to turn yarn into cloth.

passages.title: The kitchen’s pottery collection
passages.text: Warendorf’s everyday ceramics included bowls, rounded vessels and early globular pots. Some had holes below the rim for suspension; others had broad handles. A pot’s shape could preserve clues to handling and use even when only broken pieces survived.

passages.title: The kitchen’s pottery collection
passages.text: Most pottery was relatively coarse, but some vessels had fine clay and carefully smoothed surfaces. Pottery imported from the Rhineland also reached the settlement. A rural household’s material world could include objects made beyond its own region.

passages.title: Power, belief and opportunity
passages.text: Saxon society was unequal. Nobles enjoyed privileges, while other people were free, partly dependent or unfree. The absence of one permanent king did not mean that everybody had the same rights or control over their own work.

passages.title: Power, belief and opportunity
passages.text: War with Charlemagne’s Franks began in 772 and continued in repeated campaigns until 804. Incorporation changed political rule and strengthened Christian institutions. Families experienced these decades through conflict and disruption, while subsequent generations lived under the new order.

passages.title: Power, belief and opportunity
passages.text: Some Saxon aristocratic families made marriage connections with Frankish elites and sent children into monasteries. Such institutions created paths into religious life and learning for privileged households. That evidence does not establish universal schooling for Saxon children.

passages.title: A later voice in Old Saxon
passages.text: The Heliand preserves the words “gesidos mine”, meaning “my companions”. They appear in a speech by Jesus in section 56. This is a scholarly transcription in Latin letters of attested Old Saxon, from a poem that retells Gospel stories in alliterative verse.

passages.title: A later voice in Old Saxon
passages.text: The poem was composed in the first half of the ninth century, after the independent period shown on the map. A major manuscript was copied around or shortly after 850. Its survival shows how Saxon language and poetic traditions continued within a Christian literary setting.
Frankish conquest was completed through campaigns ending in 804, just beyond the map’s endpoint. Saxon communities continued within the Carolingian realm.

sectionTitles: A music lesson from the nineteenth century

passages.text: Saxony became a kingdom in 1806, after the beginning of this map record, and lost substantial territory in 1815. Its nineteenth-century story includes constitutional conflict, technical education, manufacturing, railways and music. The kingdom’s institutions and population continued beyond the map’s 1878 endpoint until the monarchy ended in 1918.

passages.title: Learning useful skills
passages.text: After unrest in 1830, Saxony adopted a constitution in 1831. The elderly King Anton shared government with his nephew Friedrich August during this transition. Reform grew out of political pressure and negotiation rather than a smooth royal decision to modernize everything at once.

passages.title: Learning useful skills
passages.text: The constitution provided a route to challenge administrative decisions through law. That mattered because government affected property and livelihoods. It was a step toward legal restraints on administration, not a guarantee that everyone enjoyed the political rights available in a modern democracy.

passages.title: Learning useful skills
passages.text: Chemnitz’s Royal Technical School opened in 1836 in response to demand for technically trained workers. Local manufacturing needed people who could understand materials and machinery. Education was increasingly connected to the practical problems of workshops and industry.

passages.title: Learning useful skills
passages.text: The school’s early library collected books on machinery, chemistry and textiles alongside geography, surveying and road building. Technical education crossed subject boundaries. A future engineer might need a map and a chemistry book as much as a drawing of a machine.

passages.title: Learning useful skills
passages.text: At Dresden, Carl Gustav Carus directed the royal midwives’ school from 1814 and taught obstetrics. Training people who assisted births was a concrete form of medical education. It concerned the care of mothers and babies, although the existence of a school does not measure access for every family.

passages.title: Steam, bricks and difficult ground
passages.text: Museum researchers date Carl Julius Borcherdt’s first Chemnitz steam engine to 1836 using nineteenth-century accounts. They question an older 1829 claim. Industrial history depends on checking records, not repeating an impressive “first” until it becomes accepted by habit.

passages.title: Steam, bricks and difficult ground
passages.text: The Göltzsch valley railway bridge was built between 1846 and 1851. Weak ground forced engineers to rethink its central supports and use larger openings. A design that looks orderly today preserves a response to awkward conditions discovered during construction.

passages.title: Steam, bricks and difficult ground
passages.text: The viaduct used roughly 26 million bricks, with local clay helping make that choice practical. Granite was used where stresses required it. Its great size depended on repeated small components and careful material choices, not simply on making everything out of the strongest-looking stone.

passages.title: Steam, bricks and difficult ground
passages.text: Construction employed an average of about 770 workers. The 1851 opening connected the finished structure to a wider railway route. Behind the celebrated engineering were years of quarrying, brickmaking, transport and work at height, tasks hidden when a train crosses in a few moments.

passages.title: A music lesson from the nineteenth century
passages.text: Felix Mendelssohn helped establish Leipzig’s conservatory, which opened in 1843. Organized musical training became one of the city’s enduring institutions. Music was both an art heard in performance and a craft learned through sustained instruction.

passages.title: A music lesson from the nineteenth century
passages.text: Robert Schumann’s published advice urged young musicians to train their ears, listen attentively and avoid reducing practice to mechanical finger exercises. These are instructions aimed at learners, not a description of every Saxon child’s upbringing. Access to an instrument and lessons was uneven.

passages.title: A music lesson from the nineteenth century
passages.text: One rule says “Spiele immer, als hörte dir ein Meister zu.” It means “Always play as though a master were listening to you.” The German appears in the 1850 first printing of Schumann’s advice. An imaginary expert could apparently help with practice even before recorded lessons existed.

The Saxon monarchy ended in 1918, when the king relinquished the throne during the revolution. Saxony continued under republican institutions. Neither the 1815 loss of territory nor this map record’s 1878 endpoint meant that its people, industry or cultural life disappeared.

sectionTitles: What a town ate and threw away

passages.text: The later kingdom of Scotland joined regions with different languages, traditions and political histories. Its surviving record includes trading towns, universities, churches and royal documents. The atlas interval 1000-1715 is map coverage: political union with England occurred in 1707, and Scotland's communities continued afterward.

passages.title: What a town ate and threw away
passages.text: Waterlogged deposits in medieval Perth preserved plant remains from floors, rubbish pits and latrines. Many come from the 1100s-1200s. Things discarded in a damp backyard can be better evidence for dinner than a royal chronicle.

passages.title: What a town ate and threw away
passages.text: Perth's plant remains include oats and barley, with less wheat, alongside berries, apples and hazelnuts. Figs, grapes and walnuts point to imported foods. Their presence shows access, not that every household enjoyed the same menu.

passages.title: What a town ate and threw away
passages.text: Moss was gathered for several purposes, including bedding and toilet hygiene. Archaeologists must use context to distinguish those activities. Medieval shopping lists could include useful plants that a modern supermarket would put nowhere near the food aisle.

passages.title: What a town ate and threw away
passages.text: Perth's narrow property plots accommodated households and urban trades, including work on animal skins. The town's river crossing and overseas connections linked local labour to distant customers. This urban evidence cannot stand for all Scottish homes.

passages.title: Games, crafts and connections
passages.text: The Lewis hoard contains 93 gaming objects, including pieces from at least four chess sets. Most were carved from walrus ivory, probably in Norway around 1200; some used whale teeth. Their thrones, clothing and faces preserve a carver's close attention to detail.

passages.title: Games, crafts and connections
passages.text: Lewis belonged to the Norwegian kingdom when the chess pieces were probably buried. The Isles passed to Scotland in 1266. Including them here shows the changing regional history, not that a Scottish royal workshop necessarily made them.

passages.title: Games, crafts and connections
passages.text: No one securely knows who buried the pieces or why. A merchant's stock and a local powerful owner's possessions are possibilities. The discovery accounts also conflict. Treasure can produce excellent questions without supplying a complete adventure story.

passages.title: Books, buildings and public claims
passages.text: Teaching began at St Andrews in 1410, and papal documents formally established its university in 1413. Organized higher learning was an achievement, but admission to such study was far narrower than access to a modern school.

passages.title: Books, buildings and public claims
passages.text: St Andrews Castle preserves a mine and countermine associated with its 1546-47 siege. Attackers dug toward the defenses while defenders dug to intercept them. The surviving tunnels make military engineering visible beneath a former bishop's residence.

passages.title: Books, buildings and public claims
passages.text: The Protestant Reformation of 1560 changed church institutions and worship. St Andrews Castle's history includes religious conflict before that turning point. Religious change was lived through buildings, communities and authority, not simply one ruler choosing a new label.

passages.title: Books, buildings and public claims
passages.text: The 1320 Declaration of Arbroath appealed to the pope on behalf of the kingdom's political community. It argued for independence under Robert Bruce. A forceful diplomatic letter states its authors' case; it is not a survey of every inhabitant's opinions.

passages.title: Books, buildings and public claims
passages.text: The letter's Latin includes propter libertatem solummodo, “for freedom alone.” This follows the National Records of Scotland's scholarly text of the 1320 letter. The archive distinguishes that edition from an exact transcription of its surviving document; Latin was an international language of diplomacy.

On 1 May 1707 Scotland and England became the kingdom of Great Britain with a shared parliament. Scotland retained important legal institutions, and its people, languages and regional identities continued. The atlas's 1715 boundary is not the date of this union and should not be presented as Scotland's disappearance.

sectionTitles: A small book with several lives

passages.text: Here Scots means early Gaelic-speaking western communities associated with Dál Riata and its successors, rather than all modern Scottish people or speakers of the later Scots language. Dunadd and island monasteries reveal craft, food, learning and sea connections.

passages.title: Royal power needed skilled hands
passages.text: Excavations at Dunadd found moulds and debris from a seventh-century workshop making fine metalwork. Brooch production involved planning, heating and finishing. This earlier evidence shows the skills behind the ornaments worn by powerful households.

passages.title: Royal power needed skilled hands
passages.text: Some Dunadd brooch designs adapted Anglo-Saxon forms. Imported pottery and glass also reached this Argyll hillfort. Objects crossed political and language boundaries; a foreign-looking ornament does not by itself identify its wearer's birthplace.

passages.title: Royal power needed skilled hands
passages.text: The early excavations recovered 54 stone querns used to grind grain. Feeding a gathering required repeated physical work before anyone sat down to a feast. A royal meeting also needed someone to make the flour.

passages.title: Royal power needed skilled hands
passages.text: Dál Riata contained several kindreds with their own territories. Scholars have suggested that Dunadd offered a meeting place between them. The footprint carved near its summit is interpreted as an inauguration feature, not a surviving royal footprint pressed into wet rock.

passages.title: Monasteries were places of work
passages.text: Iona was connected to Ireland and mainland Scotland by boat. Its island position could help communication rather than simply isolate its community. The standing thirteenth-century abbey is much later than Columba's sixth-century foundation.

passages.title: Monasteries were places of work
passages.text: Adomnán's Life of Columba, written before 704, mentions fishing nets, deer traps and salt stores. This earlier monastic account gives specific glimpses of obtaining and preserving food; it is also a saint's biography with a religious purpose.

passages.title: Monasteries were places of work
passages.text: The same account mentions harvest labour, book satchels and ink horns. Monastic learning depended on farming and supplies as well as prayer. A beautifully written page had a working community behind it.

passages.title: Monasteries were places of work
passages.text: At Inchmarnock, excavators recovered slates carrying trial letters, designs and scraps of text. Some are interpreted as pupils' work. Reusable stone offered a surface for practice before committing writing to costly parchment.

passages.title: Monasteries were places of work
passages.text: The Inchmarnock collection includes Latin and Gaelic writing, with ogham examples dated broadly to the seventh-ninth centuries. Other slates are much later. Finding several scripts together does not make every inscription contemporary.

passages.title: A small book with several lives
passages.text: The Book of Deer is a small parchment Gospel book, about 16 by 11 centimetres. Cambridge's catalogue dates its main production to the late 800s or early 900s and cautiously suggests Scotland. Its compact size contrasts with the labour of preparing skin, copying and painting.

passages.title: A small book with several lives
passages.text: The book contains a service for visiting the sick alongside Gospel texts. This is evidence of religious care, not proof of an effective medical treatment. Gaelic notes about Deer's property were added in the 1100s, well after the main book.

passages.title: A small book with several lives
passages.text: In principio, “In the beginning,” appears at the opening of John on folio 42r of the Book of Deer. It is Latin written in an Insular manuscript, not a sample of everyday Gaelic speech. The short phrase introduces a sacred text.

Dál Riata’s political world changed, but Gaelic-speaking communities continued through later kingdoms and island societies. The map changes labels at 1000; that is not an extinction date or proof of an unbroken independent western state.

sectionTitles: More than life in the saddle
A ruler’s name and a changing political world

passages.text: Scythian communities north of the Black Sea included powerful rulers, horse riders, farmers and craftspeople. This map isolates 400 to 323 BCE, within a much longer history. Its sweeping outline reaches far beyond Pontic Scythia and omits important southern areas; it should not be read as the border of one empire. The examples below distinguish fourth-century objects from earlier settlements and later changes.

passages.title: More than life in the saddle
passages.text: Bilsk in today’s Ukraine was a substantial settlement complex in the wider Scythian-era world. Fortifications linked several settlements, and excavators found pottery ovens, metalworking installations, granaries and different kinds of houses. Its earlier history gives horse-centered stories some useful neighbors: potters, metalworkers and people keeping grain dry.

passages.title: More than life in the saddle
passages.text: Millet, wheat and barley were cultivated around Bilsk, alongside animal husbandry. Granaries made harvested food something that could be stored rather than eaten immediately. Farming and herding belonged together here; a family’s food supply depended on more than whatever could fit in a saddlebag.

passages.title: More than life in the saddle
passages.text: A study of Ukrainian sites dating broadly between 700 and 200 BCE used chemical signatures in teeth to investigate movement. All fifteen sampled Medvin teeth, and twenty-one of twenty-five from Mamai Gora, fell within the researchers’ estimated local strontium ranges. Many sampled people therefore appear to have spent childhood locally.

passages.title: More than life in the saddle
passages.text: The same study found differences in diet between communities. Millet contributed more strongly at Bilsk and Medvin than at Mamai Gora. One Mamai Gora man had different strontium signatures in teeth formed at different ages, suggesting movement during childhood. Staying near home was common in the sample, but it was not everyone’s story.

passages.title: More than life in the saddle
passages.text: At Bilsk’s Tsaryna Mohyla sector, pottery from the late seventh to early fifth centuries BCE preserves an earlier kitchen history. Handmade cooking pots often carried raised clay bands; bowls, ladles and large storage vessels could have polished surfaces. Later layers brought more jugs, mugs and small vessels. Even cupboard fashions changed.

passages.title: Tiny animals and astonishing goldwork
passages.text: A gold griffin ornament at the Metropolitan Museum, dated to the fifth century BCE, is only 2.7 centimeters high. A small loop on its back allowed attachment to clothing. Its bird head, wings and feline body made a miniature fantastic animal wearable. Its reported northern Black Sea origin is less certain than its surviving construction.

passages.title: Tiny animals and astonishing goldwork
passages.text: On 21 June 1971, Borys Mozolevskyi discovered the famous gold pectoral at Tovsta Mohyla, near present-day Pokrov in Ukraine. It lay in the passage leading to the central grave. This fourth-century BCE neck ornament weighs 1,149 grams and measures 30.6 centimeters across: spectacular craftsmanship with considerable weight behind it.

passages.title: Tiny animals and astonishing goldwork
passages.text: The pectoral’s makers formed four hollow gold rods to look like twisted ropes. They cast tiny figures using the lost-wax process and soldered them into the composition. The museum counts forty-eight figures. Hollow construction and careful joining helped turn metalworking knowledge into an intricate object rather than a solid lump.

passages.title: Tiny animals and astonishing goldwork
passages.text: Look closely at the pectoral’s upper register and everyday animal care appears among the gold. A boy milks a sheep; a foal nurses beside its mother. These are crafted scenes, not a census of children’s chores, but they bring feeding and tending animals into an object made for an exceptionally wealthy setting.

passages.title: A ruler’s name and a changing political world
passages.text: Writing sample: “ΑΤΑΙΑΣ” is the Greek-letter name “Ataias,” usually called Ateas in English. It appears on silver coins catalogued for this fourth-century BCE Scythian ruler. This is a real ancient written name in Greek lettering, not a surviving sentence in the Scythian language.

passages.title: A ruler’s name and a changing political world
passages.text: One of Ateas’s silver coins pairs the head of Heracles in a lion skin with a mounted archer shooting while his horse gallops. The combination brought a Greek heroic image and steppe-style horsemanship onto the same small object. Coins could advertise a ruler while circulating through exchange.

passages.title: A ruler’s name and a changing political world
passages.text: Ateas died fighting Philip II of Macedon in 339 BCE. His activities are particularly associated with the western steppe, and scholars question whether he ruled all Scythia. A king’s defeat therefore cannot stand in for the disappearance of every community covered by a much larger map label.

The map stops in 323 BCE, not at a demonstrated collective collapse. Major steppe changes followed in the early third century BCE; their causes remain debated. Later Scythian communities developed in Crimea and the lower Dnieper, with different settlements and political arrangements.

sectionTitles: Read the map before riding into the story
Names, peoples and evidence with labels attached
Kings, cities, wars and negotiated power
Homes, work, meals and long-distance trade
Families, children, women and unequal lives
Gold, cloth, ceramics and clever portable messages
Learning and the written voices that survive
Health, possible remedies, water and the toilet question

passages.text: The atlas calls three far-flung map clusters “Scythians” between 200 BCE and 200 CE: Bactria and a huge zone reaching into Central Asia, then a smaller Central Asian footprint, and later Crimea and the lower Don. That is a clue, not a marching border. The English name came through Greek, while related Saka names appear farther east; archaeology shows different local communities, kingdoms and mixtures. Follow this card and you meet mounted rulers, herders, grain growers, fortress builders, coin makers, traders, parents and children. In Crimea, a settled and strongly Hellenized kingdom centered on Scythian Neapolis fought Chersonesos before life continued under new powers. Farther east, the atlas umbrella gathers related communities whose local histories must be kept distinct. The atlas even drops the exact id at 1 BCE. So this is a connected history of changing groups, not one nation teleporting across the map. Its 200 CE endpoint marks atlas coverage, not extinction.

passages.title: Read the map before riding into the story
passages.text: At 200 BCE, the exact id occurs three times, not once. One 53-position polygon is labelled Bactria; a 64-position two-part feature is labelled Bosporan Kingdom; and a 519-position three-part feature stretches from the Black Sea deep into Central Asia. These are display geometries, not a surveyed frontier.

passages.title: Read the map before riding into the story
passages.text: The 100 BCE snapshot keeps the id but replaces those three features with one three-part MultiPolygon of 328 positions between about 46.87 to 68.56°E and 37.52 to 51.03°N. Khiva and Bukhara test inside; Balkh, Crimea and Tashkent do not. The shift is an atlas reclassification, not a proven mass journey.

passages.title: Read the map before riding into the story
passages.text: At 1 BCE the exact id vanishes completely. A blank map layer cannot make people vanish, especially when coins, burials and settlements continue in the historical record. The card treats this as a coverage gap and refuses to draw a neat collapse line through a missing polygon.

passages.title: Read the map before riding into the story
passages.text: At 100 CE the id returns as a single 79-position polygon around Crimea and the lower Don, roughly 31.93 to 41.24°E. Kherson and Rostov test inside while Balkh, Bukhara and the Crimean sites of Neapolis and Chersonesos fall just outside this particular outline. Even famous places can miss a simplified border.

passages.title: Read the map before riding into the story
passages.text: The id is absent in both the 300 BCE predecessor and 200 CE successor snapshots. Its indexed dates therefore describe imported map coverage, not the birth and death of a civilization. Separate records for earlier Scythians, Saka polities, Sarmatians and Alans remain separate; this card never aliases them.

passages.title: Names, peoples and evidence with labels attached
passages.text: “Scythian” came through Greek and Latin, while eastern Iranian and Indian sources used Saka for related mobile peoples. Ancient authors, modern archaeologists and this atlas do not always draw the same group boundaries. A familiar label may connect evidence without proving that every community shared one ruler, dialect or ancestry.

passages.title: Names, peoples and evidence with labels attached
passages.text: The 200 BCE map’s “Bactria” label does not settle who occupied every valley. Saka and Yuezhi groups both figure in the end of Greek power there, and assigning nomadic material at Ai Khanum to one named people remains hypothetical. Pots cannot introduce themselves, even when historians would find that very convenient.

passages.title: Names, peoples and evidence with labels attached
passages.text: “Indo-Scythian” is a modern dynastic label for Saka-origin rulers in parts of Afghanistan and northwest South Asia. Their sequence begins around the late second century BCE, but the dates and relationships of rulers such as Maues, Azes and Azilises remain debated because coins carry more evidence than surviving chronicles.

passages.title: Names, peoples and evidence with labels attached
passages.text: The Crimean Late Scythian culture was new in important ways: it mixed Scythian, Taurian and Greek traditions and became increasingly settled. Calling it “Late Scythian” records ancient and scholarly connections, but it should not turn its inhabitants into unchanged copies of fourth-century BCE steppe nomads.

passages.title: Names, peoples and evidence with labels attached
passages.text: No continuous book in an indigenous Scythian language survives. Linguists work mainly with personal and place names, short glosses and words recorded by outsiders, and they may be dealing with several related Iranian dialects. That evidence supports careful reconstruction, not a fictional native paragraph written for modern readers.

passages.title: Kings, cities, wars and negotiated power
passages.text: Skilurus ruled a Hellenized Crimean kingdom from Scythian Neapolis in the later second century BCE. Coins minted at Olbia in his name carried familiar Greek civic and divine imagery alongside bows, grain and other symbols. Coinage made authority portable, but one coin cannot map every village that obeyed him.

passages.title: Kings, cities, wars and negotiated power
passages.text: A Greek decree from Chersonesos praises the general Diophantos and names Palakos and the Scythians. It is close political evidence for campaigns around 110 to 107 BCE, yet it speaks in the victory language of the winning city. Reading the inscription means learning both what it records and whose applause shaped it.

passages.title: Kings, cities, wars and negotiated power
passages.text: Diophantos’s forces defeated Palakos and seized Scythian fortresses, including Neapolis. That ended a phase of independent royal power, not every household, farm or local identity. The settlement continued under new political conditions, which is why “conquest” and “disappearance” belong in different boxes.

passages.title: Kings, cities, wars and negotiated power
passages.text: Farther east, rulers issued bilingual money and adapted earlier Hellenistic royal forms. A mounted king on one side and a deity or animal on the other could communicate rank across communities with different languages. The achievement was political translation through objects people handled, weighed and recognized.

passages.title: Kings, cities, wars and negotiated power
passages.text: In the 60s CE, Scythian forces besieged Chersonesos until Roman troops under Plautius Silvanus intervened. The episode shows that local powers could still threaten a Greek city centuries after Skilurus. It also shows why the map’s missing 1 BCE feature cannot be read as a historical obituary.

passages.title: Homes, work, meals and long-distance trade
passages.text: Scythian Neapolis had defensive walls, stone-and-mudbrick houses, courtyards, a granary and a wine-making complex. That is a settled capital with stored food and specialized work, not a camp frozen in horseback stereotypes. Greek-style building methods mingled with local plans rather than replacing every older practice.

passages.title: Homes, work, meals and long-distance trade
passages.text: Ust-Alma covered more than six hectares near Crimea’s western coast and combined a settlement with a large burial ground. Its residents occupied a coastal landscape tied to farming, herding and exchange. Archaeology identifies structures and goods more securely than the exact job title of every person who lived there.

passages.title: Homes, work, meals and long-distance trade
passages.text: North of the Tianshan, Saka-period communities combined cattle breeding with farming. Children would have watched adults manage animals, fields, weather and storage, learning by repeated work; that education is a reasonable inference from the economy, not evidence for a standard school, timetable or graduation ceremony.

passages.title: Homes, work, meals and long-distance trade
passages.text: Isotopes from people dated 700 to 200 BCE show varied mobility and diets, including millet, near this card’s opening edge. The sample warns against a single “Scythian menu”: some people moved little, and crops joined animal foods. These results do not automatically describe a Crimean child living two centuries later.

passages.title: Homes, work, meals and long-distance trade
passages.text: Teeth at Chervony Mayak carry heavy calculus consistent with substantial protein intake, while caries patterns suggest carbohydrates also mattered and changed with age. Burial type may track dietary differences between social groups. Teeth preserve trends, not recipes, so the stew, bread or dairy proportions remain unknown.

passages.title: Families, children, women and unequal lives
passages.text: Tillya Tepe held six richly furnished first-century CE graves, one associated with a man and five with women. The arrangement is often described as a chieftain’s household, but the exact kin relationships and group identity remain uncertain. Grave proximity can suggest a social unit without handing archaeologists a family tree.

passages.title: Families, children, women and unequal lives
passages.text: Children’s ornaments and clothing in Late Scythian graves helped adults display age, rank and hoped-for social roles. Researchers warn that beads or costume pieces do not prove a child’s ethnicity. Funerals show how survivors presented children; they cannot recover every game, friendship, fear or ordinary school-less afternoon.

passages.title: Families, children, women and unequal lives
passages.text: Early Ust-Alma crypts had built chambers reused for multiple burials, with pottery, brooches, buckles, bracelets and beads. Shared tomb architecture may reflect family or household groups, but biology was not tested in every case. “Buried together” is evidence of relationship, not an automatic DNA result.

passages.title: Families, children, women and unequal lives
passages.text: One Ust-Alma warrior received a sword, bow and arrows, gold ornaments, vessels and imported goods in the mid-first century CE. Such a spectacular burial marks elite status and martial display. It cannot stand for every adult man, and grave weapons show an identity claimed in ritual, not a complete work diary.

passages.title: Families, children, women and unequal lives
passages.text: Gold garment plaques from Chervony Mayak burial 128 show that a woman’s clothing could carry wealth and visual status. Modern looting and war have scattered parts of the archaeological record, making reconstruction harder. Elite jewelry makes women visible, but it should not hide poorer women whose clothes left fewer traces.

passages.title: Gold, cloth, ceramics and clever portable messages
passages.text: A gold crown from Tillya Tepe was built in sections that could fold for travel. Tree-like forms and birds turned thin metal into a tall, glittering sign of rank, while turquoise added color. Portable engineering suited mobile elite display, though one royal tomb cannot tell us what ordinary herders wore.

passages.title: Gold, cloth, ceramics and clever portable messages
passages.text: Tillya Tepe ornaments combine steppe animal forms with imagery and techniques from Iranian, Greek, Indian and other traditions. Baltic amber, lapis lazuli, turquoise and garnet reveal far-reaching connections. Materials may have changed hands many times, so “long-distance trade” does not require one traveler to walk the whole route.

passages.title: Gold, cloth, ceramics and clever portable messages
passages.text: Alma Kermen yielded about 350 terra-sigillata vessels alongside beads, rings, wooden containers and grooming utensils. Imported red tableware reached a Late Scythian fortress through Black Sea exchange. The assemblage also reminds us that a fashionable bowl can travel farther than the person eating from it.

passages.title: Gold, cloth, ceramics and clever portable messages
passages.text: A copper coin of Azilises pairs Greek and Kharoshthi legends with an elephant and a humped bull. Metalworkers and die engravers compressed royal identity into a tiny, repeatable object. Animals, scripts and titles could cross language boundaries even when listeners pronounced the ruler’s name differently.

passages.title: Gold, cloth, ceramics and clever portable messages
passages.text: A coin in the British Museum, attributed in the name of Azes II and found at the Bimaran stupa complex, shows a mounted king and carries Greek and Kharoshthi inscriptions. Its archaeological findspot links royal money to a religious landscape, while the ruler attribution remains a numismatic convention open to revision.

passages.title: Learning and the written voices that survive
passages.text: No standard Scythian classroom is documented. In herding and farming households, young people still had to learn animal care, routes, planting, tools, manners and obligations by watching and practicing. That apprenticeship model is inferred from recorded work, so the card does not invent school ages, teachers or alphabet lessons.

passages.title: Learning and the written voices that survive
passages.text: Authentic written sample: “ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩΣ ΒΑΣΙΛΕΩΝ ΜΕΓΑΛΟΥ ΑΖΟΥ” means “of the Great King of Kings Azes.” It appears as a Greek royal legend on an Indo-Scythian coin around 48 to 25 BCE. This is an external Greek public language, not a sentence in an indigenous Scythian tongue.

passages.title: Learning and the written voices that survive
passages.text: The reverse of the same coin gives a comparable title in Kharoshthi-script Gandhari, transliterated “Maharajasa Rajarajasa Mahatasa Ayasa.” Bilingual coinage let a ruler address overlapping reading communities. Gandhari was another public language of rule, so neither side proves which language Azes spoke at home.

passages.title: Learning and the written voices that survive
passages.text: The Chersonesan decree for Diophantos preserves names and events in Greek because a Greek civic community carved it. It is an authentic contemporary voice, but not a neutral transcript of Scythian debate. Children learning history can ask the useful question carved into every monument: who paid for these words?

passages.title: Learning and the written voices that survive
passages.text: Scythian-language reconstruction rests on scattered names and glosses recorded by others, not a surviving library. Similar Iranian name forms help linguists test relationships among dialects, but spelling through Greek ears can distort sounds. The responsible sample is therefore the labelled bilingual coin, with its language limits plainly visible.

passages.title: Health, possible remedies, water and the toilet question
passages.text: A dental study examined 106 people from Chervony Mayak. Calculus, cavities, tooth loss and wear reveal diet and health stresses across age and burial groups. They do not identify the healer, pain relief or treatment a person received. Skeletons often preserve the ache more clearly than the attempted cure.

passages.title: Health, possible remedies, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Cinnabar, a bright red mercury mineral, appeared in two female burials at Chervony Mayak. Researchers discuss pigment, cosmetic, ritual and body-preservation possibilities, but none is certain. Calling it medicine would outrun the evidence, and mercury can be poisonous, so the card records an intriguing substance rather than a prescription.

passages.title: Health, possible remedies, water and the toilet question
passages.text: No medical handbook or securely identified treatment kit from these target communities appears in the reviewed sources. Dental disease shows health; cinnabar shows a puzzling material; neither proves a healthcare system. Remedies may have existed without surviving, but naming herbs, doctors or operations here would turn possibility into fiction.

passages.title: Health, possible remedies, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Ust-Alma occupied a coastal landscape near essential water and transport routes, yet the reviewed site account does not reconstruct a universal water-supply system. Residents obviously needed water for people, animals and crops, but wells, carriers and seasonal sources cannot be assigned to every household from silence.

passages.title: Health, possible remedies, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Toilets remain an honest unknown. The Alma Kermen study lists vessels, jewelry, containers and grooming equipment but does not securely identify a household latrine or sewer. Its “toilette utensils” are personal-care objects, not toilets. Waste practices surely existed; the evidence reviewed here cannot map them.

passages.title: Burials, discoveries and what continued
passages.text: Scythian Neapolis came back into scholarly view after carved reliefs and Greek inscriptions were found in 1827. Later excavation exposed walls, houses, a mausoleum and a granary. Discovery dates describe modern research, not when local people first knew the place; archaeology often “discovers” what nearby landscapes never forgot.

passages.title: Burials, discoveries and what continued
passages.text: Tillya Tepe’s six first-century princely tombs preserved a dazzling concentration of gold objects shaped by steppe, Iranian, Greek, Indian and other traditions. The discovery transformed study of Bactria, but its wealth is socially selective. Gold speaks loudly because poverty rarely gets a display case.

passages.title: Burials, discoveries and what continued
passages.text: Chervony Mayak pairs a hillfort with a large cemetery on the lower Dnieper. Excavations make settlement and burial practice visible together, while damage and theft remove relationships between objects and bodies. Context is part of the evidence: a jewel without its exact burial position loses much of its historical sentence.

passages.title: Burials, discoveries and what continued
passages.text: Late Scythian burial customs changed over time and differed among sites, ages and ranks. Children, elite warriors and richly dressed women appear most clearly because funerals selected objects for display. Those choices reveal social values, yet they are performances by survivors rather than candid photographs of daily family life.

passages.title: Burials, discoveries and what continued
passages.text: There was no single Scythian ending. Crimean royal independence changed after Diophantos, Roman power intervened later, eastern dynasties gave way to other states, and communities mixed with neighbors. Farming, herding, craft, trade and family life continued as names and rulers changed. The atlas’s 200 CE cutoff closes a layer, not a lineage.

The atlas stops drawing this exact id at 200 CE, but no source records a single Scythian people falling in that year. Crimean settlements and cemeteries continued into the third century, and people lived under changing powers and alongside new neighbors. Political independence, names and burial fashions shifted while families, farming, herding, craft and exchange continued. The endpoint is therefore an editorial handoff and transformation, not extinction.

sectionTitles: Trade, skilled work and military adaptation
Diplomacy and the human cost of empire
Sites, sources and what remains uncertain

passages.text: Samori Ture built a state through conquest, trade and Islamic authority in the later 1800s. Often called the Wassoulou or Samorian empire, it shifted eastward under French military pressure. “First” and “Second Samori Empire” describe different territorial phases of the same ruler’s state. Its independent history ended with his capture in 1898, not with the 1900 to 1914 interval currently attached to those two map labels.

passages.title: Trade, skilled work and military adaptation
passages.text: Samori’s armies depended on supply networks. Earlier muskets came chiefly through Freetown, while horses came from the northwestern Sudan. These routes connected inland politics with coastal commerce.

passages.title: Trade, skilled work and military adaptation
passages.text: In 1891 to 1892, negotiations with Freetown traders brought breechloading and repeating firearms. Legassick also records a local firearms industry established by this period. Adaptation meant acquiring weapons and developing skilled work to support them.

passages.title: Trade, skilled work and military adaptation
passages.text: After French advances restricted western supplies, Samori sought weapons through the Ivory Coast and Gold Coast and horses through Mossi country. Existing African trade routes became crucial to the state’s survival.

passages.title: Trade, skilled work and military adaptation
passages.text: The Buré goldfields mattered to Samori’s economy. When French forces occupied Buré in 1885, his armies drove them back. Control of a resource region could be as consequential as control of a capital.

passages.title: Diplomacy and the human cost of empire
passages.text: Samori sought an agreement with the British authorities in Sierra Leone and also negotiated treaties with France. His strategy combined fighting and bargaining; African rulers were participants in diplomacy, not merely spectators to European decisions.

passages.title: Diplomacy and the human cost of empire
passages.text: Trade also carried a terrible cost: Samori captured and sold people to help finance guns and horses. Resistance to French conquest did not mean freedom for everyone living under his own expanding power.

passages.title: Diplomacy and the human cost of empire
passages.text: Yves Person’s chronology records a decision in 1892 to move east with a substantial part of the population. A moving state meant uprooted households as well as marching soldiers. The chronology establishes the displacement without telling us every family’s experience.

passages.title: Diplomacy and the human cost of empire
passages.text: The same chronology records scorched-earth tactics in 1891. Destroying resources could obstruct an advancing army while making civilian life more precarious. Military success and the welfare of local people cannot be treated as the same thing.

passages.title: Sites, sources and what remains uncertain
passages.text: Sordi’s fortified settlement in northern Côte d’Ivoire became part of the struggle between Kénédougou, Samori’s forces and French expansion. Historian M’Brah identifies occupation by Samori’s sofa troops from 1896 to 1898. A single site reveals overlapping rulers and local experiences.

passages.title: Sites, sources and what remains uncertain
passages.text: M’Brah traces Diawala’s growth to people dispersed from Sordi and to exiles returning after Kénédougou’s defeat in 1898. Related families reunited and organized a new settlement. Political defeat changed where people lived; it did not erase their family connections.

passages.title: Sites, sources and what remains uncertain
passages.text: Accounts of Samori need careful comparison. Legassick’s article explicitly warns that some French visitors’ descriptions were imaginative or unreliable. Historians use local traditions and archival evidence together instead of treating an officer’s vivid story as automatic fact.

passages.title: Sites, sources and what remains uncertain
passages.text: This dossier has not verified a short original-script passage from a securely identified Samorian document. Arabic scholarship belonged to the wider region, but substituting an unrelated manuscript would give a false impression. Household sanitation and specific medical routines also remain unestablished by the sources used here.

passages.title: Capture and continuing communities
passages.text: French forces captured Samori on 29 September 1898. He was exiled to Gabon and died in 1900. His death date is therefore not the date a “first” or “second” empire began; those map labels need chronological correction.

Samori’s capture by French forces in 1898 ended his independent state. Exile and his death in 1900 followed. The region’s communities continued under colonial rule; the changing imperial labels describe political power, not the appearance or disappearance of a people.
