sectionTitles: Mining towns and the tools of authority
Books, textiles and a riverside capital

passages.text: This card concerns medieval Serbian principalities, the Nemanjic kingdom and empire, and later successor lordships. Their borders and institutions changed over time. Quarry settlements, burnt food, fish bones, illuminated books and a seal-maker's tool reveal work and learning beyond royal campaigns. Evidence from a monastery or court describes that setting, not every household.

passages.title: Building, labour and painted spaces
passages.text: Near Studenica, marble quarries and remains of a workers' settlement connect the Church of the Virgin with the people who extracted and shaped its stone. The monastery's finely finished surfaces depended on a wider landscape of skilled and demanding labour.

passages.title: Building, labour and painted spaces
passages.text: Studenica's Church of the Virgin combines a domed interior with an exterior drawing on Romanesque architecture. Its design became a model for other monasteries. Builders adapted forms circulating across the Adriatic and Byzantine worlds rather than working within a sealed national tradition.

passages.title: Building, labour and painted spaces
passages.text: Paintings made in the Church of the Virgin in 1208 and 1209 organise religious figures through expressive gestures and carefully conceived space. Their surviving setting lets historians study images as part of a building used for worship, rather than as detached museum pictures.

passages.title: Food recovered from the ground
passages.text: Charred remains from twelfth- and thirteenth-century buildings at Ras include bread wheat, rye, barley, oats and millet. Wheat was most abundant in the studied samples. Weeds mixed with grain, including corncockle, preserve traces of crop handling as well as the crops themselves.

passages.title: Food recovered from the ground
passages.text: The Ras study also identified a round piece of burnt bread, cereal remains in a pot and fragments of peach stones. These finds bring prepared food and fruit into view. They document particular deposits, not a complete menu or the quantities eaten by every resident.

passages.title: Food recovered from the ground
passages.text: Waste deposits at Studenica from the fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries contained catfish, carp and pike alongside migratory sturgeon. The researchers connect the sturgeon with the distant Danube. Feeding a monastery could involve both nearby fishing and longer supply routes.

passages.title: Food recovered from the ground
passages.text: Studenica's fish bones preserve information about body parts, size and cutting. The authors suggest that some large fish arrived whole, perhaps dried or salted. Preservation methods are an interpretation of the remains; the bones do not supply a surviving recipe.

passages.title: Mining towns and the tools of authority
passages.text: Excavation at Drenje in Rudnik revealed secular buildings and three churches, two Orthodox and one Catholic, in a settlement flourishing during the fourteenth and early fifteenth centuries. These remains suggest a varied religious landscape. Identifying the area specifically as the medieval market remains an interpretation.

passages.title: Mining towns and the tools of authority
passages.text: A seal-die from a pit at Rudnik bears Prince Lazar's name and a helmet with horned ornament. Dated to his rule there between 1373 and 1389, it is a tool for producing official impressions. No matching impression was known to the study's authors.

passages.title: Books, textiles and a riverside capital
passages.text: The late twelfth-century Miroslav Gospel combines writing on parchment with gilding and painted decoration. Its illuminations draw on Italian and Byzantine artistic traditions. The manuscript shows bookmaking as a collaboration of textual, material and visual skills shaped by connections beyond one court.

passages.title: Books, textiles and a riverside capital
passages.text: The Miroslav Gospel arranges readings for liturgical use rather than simply presenting an unbroken narrative. Its language and spelling also preserve evidence of a regional scribal tradition. A book could guide repeated communal worship while carrying the choices of the people who copied it.

passages.title: Books, textiles and a riverside capital
passages.text: An embroidered priestly stole, or epitrachelion, from the Church of Saints Peter and Paul near Novi Pazar preserves another demanding craft. The National Museum dates its style to the late fourteenth or early fifteenth century. This ceremonial garment cannot stand for ordinary clothing.

passages.title: Books, textiles and a riverside capital
passages.text: Smederevo's new court was built at the meeting of the Danube and Jezava in 1428 to 1430. Its builders faced shortages of local stone, bringing material from farther away and reusing older masonry. The fortress records transport and salvage as well as defensive planning.

Ottoman conquest of Smederevo in 1459 ended the remaining Serbian despotate. The medieval empire had fragmented much earlier; 1389 was not the date when all Serbian political institutions vanished. Settlement at Smederevo and religious communities such as Studenica continued under changed conditions. The imported map endpoint of 1300 is not a historical fall date.

sectionTitles: Political participation and care during war

passages.text: This record follows Serbia after international recognition of its independence in 1878, through its kingdom and the First World War. Banks, water systems, museums and universities developed alongside parliamentary conflict and devastating war. It ends around the transition into a larger South Slav state, not the end of Serbian communities.

passages.title: Water, streets and money
passages.text: Before Belgrade’s water-supply system opened in 1892, Knez Mihailova Street depended on courtyard wells and the Delijska Fountain. Fetching water was part of household work. The new system changed a practical daily task, not merely the city’s appearance.

passages.title: Water, streets and money
passages.text: Electric street lighting arrived in Belgrade in 1891, with an early lantern at the corner of Kralja Petra and Knez Mihailova. Lighting a street extended useful public space after dark, although one lamp does not prove every household had electricity.

passages.title: Water, streets and money
passages.text: After recognition of independence, Serbia minted gold twenty-dinar coins in 1879. In 1884 its new national bank issued hundred-dinar notes payable in gold. Paper money depended on confidence in an institution as well as the paper’s printed design.

passages.title: Water, streets and money
passages.text: The bank began operations in July 1884, following legislation passed the previous year. It supplied credit and handled currency issuance. Establishing an institution required rules and staff, not simply printing an impressive-looking note.

passages.title: Water, streets and money
passages.text: Привилегована Народна банка Краљевине Србије means “Privileged National Bank of the Kingdom of Serbia.” This Serbian Cyrillic title is attested in the bank’s catalogue of a book published in Belgrade in 1909, covering its first twenty-five years.

passages.title: Studying, calculating and preserving
passages.text: Milutin Milanković joined the University of Belgrade in 1909 and shared an office with Mihailo Petrović. One taught applied mathematics and the other theoretical mathematics. A scientific community grew through colleagues teaching and exchanging ideas.

passages.title: Studying, calculating and preserving
passages.text: In 1912 Mladen Berić defended the university’s first doctoral dissertation in mathematical sciences before a commission including Petrović and Milanković. Advanced education required teachers able to train a new generation, not just individuals making discoveries alone.

passages.title: Studying, calculating and preserving
passages.text: Petrović constructed a hydro-integrator in 1900, a calculating instrument using water, and received a bronze medal at the Paris exhibition. Mathematical work could take the form of a physical device as well as equations on a blackboard.

passages.title: Studying, calculating and preserving
passages.text: The National Museum had been founded in 1844 to collect and preserve antiquities, before this map interval. Its continued work made objects available for study. A museum collection is assembled through choices, rather than being a complete sample of everyone’s past.

passages.title: Political participation and care during war
passages.text: The constitutions of 1888 and 1903 shaped parliamentary life and the role of parties. The Assembly’s history records changes in the balance between monarchs, governments and representatives. Rules about participation had consequences for how power could be challenged.

passages.title: Political participation and care during war
passages.text: Assembly meetings took place in several buildings and cities, including a school in Niš. During wartime, public institutions had to adapt their location and routines. Parliamentary history therefore includes ordinary rooms temporarily used for extraordinary decisions.

passages.title: Political participation and care during war
passages.text: Nurse Ljubica Luković cared for wounded people from Serbian and opposing armies. A Red Cross notice records that she worked at Valjevo during the 1915 typhus epidemic and died after becoming infected. Her story shows the human labour behind wartime healthcare.

Serbia entered the new South Slav kingdom in 1918. Its independent kingdom was incorporated into a larger state, while communities and institutions continued in a changed framework. The atlas extends this label to 1920; that endpoint should not turn the 1918 transition into two additional years of unchanged sovereignty.

sectionTitles: Conflict and the limits of a map

passages.text: This record begins while Serbia was part of a federation with Montenegro. The state union changed in 2003 and ended in 2006, after which Serbia continued separately. Modern Serbian life includes family celebrations, skilled pottery, education and public institutions, alongside the consequences of conflict and contested political boundaries.

passages.title: A changing state framework
passages.text: The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia entered the United Nations in November 2000. Its official name changed to Serbia and Montenegro in 2003. These dates explain why a map labelled Serbia in the 1990s needs a federal context.

passages.title: A changing state framework
passages.text: Montenegro declared independence in June 2006. Serbia continued the former union’s United Nations membership, while Montenegro joined separately. A change in international representation is one documented way to follow the institutional transition.

passages.title: A changing state framework
passages.text: Serbia’s new constitution was approved by referendum in October 2006 and proclaimed in November. It defines state institutions and legal rights. A constitution is evidence of stated rules; it is not proof that every rule is fulfilled in practice.

passages.title: Family tables and useful clay
passages.text: Some Orthodox families celebrate Slava in honour of a patron saint, gathering relatives, friends and neighbours. UNESCO’s 2014 record describes a decorated cake, wine and a candle. This is a specific religious family tradition, not a universal Serbian custom.

passages.title: Family tables and useful clay
passages.text: Knowledge of Slava is passed through families, with women playing a major teaching role in the documented practice. Preparing food and welcoming guests help transmit social knowledge as well as religious meaning.

passages.title: Family tables and useful clay
passages.text: Zlakusa potters mix clay with calcite and shape vessels on a wheel turned by hand. Making a pot takes several stages over seven to ten days, including drying and firing. The cooking vessel has already required patience before dinner begins.

passages.title: Family tables and useful clay
passages.text: The craft produces pots and pans suited to cooking and serving, with shapes adapted to modern kitchens. Learners work alongside experienced makers; school classes and public demonstrations also help. Tradition here includes practical adaptation.

passages.title: Messages and public services
passages.text: Народна банка Србије means “National Bank of Serbia.” The name appears in Serbian Cyrillic and Latin letters on the 2003 hundred-dinar note. Its official design specification supplies a precise witness for this short sample of modern written Serbian.

passages.title: Messages and public services
passages.text: The note’s Nikola Tesla imagery includes an electromagnetic engine. Its specification also describes features visible under infrared and ultraviolet light. Scientific commemoration and anti-counterfeiting technology share the same everyday object.

passages.title: Messages and public services
passages.text: The floods of 2014 damaged schools and disrupted healthcare. Some schools became temporary shelters and others ended the year early. UNICEF’s account shows why protecting children’s routines includes safe buildings, clean surroundings and functioning public services.

passages.title: Conflict and the limits of a map
passages.text: Fighting in Kosovo in 1998 to 1999 displaced civilians and destroyed homes; NATO began air strikes against Yugoslavia in March 1999. The United Nations documented humanitarian consequences. A political map cannot convey the experiences of families forced to move.

passages.title: Conflict and the limits of a map
passages.text: Kosovo declared independence in 2008. The International Court of Justice concluded in 2010 that the declaration did not violate international law. That narrow finding was not a ruling requiring every state to recognize Kosovo, and does not by itself validate this atlas’s borders.

Serbia continues as a state after the 2006 end of its union with Montenegro. Its present-day institutions and communities did not begin from nothing at the atlas’s 1994 starting snapshot. Kosovo’s separate declaration and international legal debate require explicit treatment rather than a claim that one map colour resolves them.

sectionTitles: A large settlement on the Psel
Pots, crops and the work of feeding people
Later neighbours and what excavation corrected
Tribute and a later written name

passages.text: The Severians, or Siverianians, were East Slavic communities associated with the Desna and the upper Seim, Sula, Psel and Vorskla regions. This imported 700 to 800 outline omits substantial territory farther east. Bytytsia and Novotroitske, discussed below, lie beyond its eastern edge and provide regional comparisons. Archaeological traditions and chronicle names do not establish a single kingdom with surveyed borders.

passages.title: A large settlement on the Psel
passages.text: At Bytytsia, east of this imported outline, a fortified settlement stood high above the Psel. Excavator Oleg Sukhobokov dates it from the middle of the eighth century to the turn of the ninth. Its area exceeded seven hectares, making it an unusually substantial site among the Volyntseve settlements associated with this region.

passages.title: A large settlement on the Psel
passages.text: Excavation at Bytytsia uncovered more than sixty dwellings, around 250 metal objects and two hoards containing ornaments and tools. These discoveries bring domestic work and valued possessions into the story. They are totals from archaeological investigation, rather than a headcount of families living there on one particular day.

passages.title: A large settlement on the Psel
passages.text: Sukhobokov interpreted Bytytsia’s contrasting material traditions as evidence of Slavic and Turkic inhabitants with different economic backgrounds. That proposed mixture helps explain why the site is discussed as a meeting place. Objects support an interpretation of cultural contact; they do not reveal each household’s spoken language.

passages.title: Pots, crops and the work of feeding people
passages.text: Volyntseve pottery included both handmade vessels and locally produced wheel-made pottery. Sukhobokov stresses that handmade pots and bowls still formed the main part of the assemblage. A skilled new technique could coexist with familiar ways of making everyday containers.

passages.title: Pots, crops and the work of feeding people
passages.text: The wheel-made vessels were distinctive enough in shape and decoration to provoke debate about their origins and connections. Researchers compared them with neighbouring and earlier traditions. Even an ordinary pot can raise a big historical question: who taught the potter to make it that way?

passages.title: Pots, crops and the work of feeding people
passages.text: Sergiy Gorbanenko’s study of impressions at Bytytsia identified millet, barley, bread wheat, rye, emmer and oats, with rarer traces of other wheats. The marks preserve evidence of crops after the plants themselves decayed. A dent in clay can turn out to be a tiny record of farming.

passages.title: Pots, crops and the work of feeding people
passages.text: The same study identified weed impressions as well as crops. Gorbanenko used them to argue for repeatedly cultivated ground and crops with different seasonal cycles. These are interpretations of botanical clues, rather than a surviving farming calendar, but they help reconstruct the work behind a household’s food supply.

passages.title: Later neighbours and what excavation corrected
passages.text: Novotroitske, another site east of the imported outline, provides a ninth-century comparison after this card’s map interval. Lyapushkin excavated more than fifty partly sunken houses and about a hundred utility structures. These accumulated during the settlement’s occupation; the totals do not mean every building stood at once.

passages.title: Later neighbours and what excavation corrected
passages.text: Older books imagined such settlements as networks of homes connected by covered passages. At Novotroitske, Lyapushkin found separate houses, even where they stood close together, and no connecting corridors. Careful excavation corrected an appealing picture that had been repeated as fact.

passages.title: Later neighbours and what excavation corrected
passages.text: Ninth-century Novotroitske also yielded iron axes, adzes and spoon-carving tools, along with bone points and animal knucklebones bearing geometric marks. These objects offer glimpses of woodworking and small things people handled. The marked bones alone cannot tell us precisely who used them or whether a particular one was a toy.

passages.title: Tribute and a later written name
passages.text: The Primary Chronicle says that Prince Oleh subdued the Severians in 884, imposed a light tribute and stopped their payments to the Khazars. This later account describes a change in political obligations. It belongs after the map’s eighth-century window.

passages.title: Tribute and a later written name
passages.text: In the Laurentian Chronicle manuscript of 1377, the account placed under 859 names them among people paying tribute. The National Library of Russia’s transcription has “на северех”, meaning “from the Severians” here. This is a later chronicle witness, not a contemporary eighth-century text written by the mapped communities.

The map stops at 800, but Severian communities continued into the history of Rus’. The chronicle name is last reported in 1024, while related regional names survived much longer. The end of recorded use of a tribal name is not a date when its people disappeared.

sectionTitles: Reading the evidence on stone and paper

passages.text: The Shan states were a changing network of principalities, not one kingdom. Valley towns and upland communities had different rulers and relationships with neighbouring courts. The imported outline includes Guwahati in Assam but omits Kengtung; regional examples below extend beyond its shading. This 1530 to 1783 record cannot reliably show individual boundaries or independence. Its dates are map coverage, not the birth and disappearance of Shan people.

passages.title: Courts, conquest and trade
passages.text: Northern Tay or Shan forces took Ava in 1527, shortly before this map begins. Historian Ken Kirigaya connects that victory with competition for a valuable river trading centre. Rubies, jade, amber and musk linked the inland region to southern ports and wider markets. These principalities could shape lowland politics as well as respond to it.

passages.title: Courts, conquest and trade
passages.text: A large surviving bell at Shwezigon in Bagan preserves Bayinnaung’s own account of expansion. Its Burmese, Mon and Pali texts record the capture of Ava in 1555 and campaigns against Mong Mit, Hsipaw, Mohnyin and Mogaung in 1557. The bell is a contemporary royal claim, to be read with the conqueror’s viewpoint in mind.

passages.title: Courts, conquest and trade
passages.text: Conquest could leave a local royal house in place. U Thaw Kaung’s study describes Bayinnaung reinstating defeated rulers after they swore allegiance and retaining ministers. Rebellion could instead bring removal. A town might therefore keep its court while its ruler owed service to a stronger king.

passages.title: Courts, conquest and trade
passages.text: From the seventeenth century, frontier commerce benefited from rulers who maintained recognition at both Chinese and Burmese courts. Jingli Bai’s study follows tea and cotton moving outward, and metals and spices arriving through caravans and rivers. Its Sipsong Panna case illustrates the wider Tai commercial world, rather than proving that every place shaded here belonged to one government.

passages.title: Courts, conquest and trade
passages.text: In the Konbaung period, these polities included both valley farmers growing wet rice and upland communities cultivating cleared plots in shifting cycles. Feeding a town involved different landscapes and kinds of work. Calling the whole region simply a land of mountain farmers misses the productive valleys between the hills.

passages.title: Reading the evidence on stone and paper
passages.text: Two British Library rubbings turned out to preserve different pieces of the same stone. In 2025, epigrapher Nuttapong Punjaburi matched its fragmented faces. The original 1537 inscription, in Tai Khoen and Fak Kham script, records instructions for lay followers at Wat Pa Mai. Fak Kham means tamarind pod, a deliciously memorable name for curved letters.

passages.title: Reading the evidence on stone and paper
passages.text: A text added to that stone in 1600 records a donation to Wat Phiang Sri of 400 rice fields with people or farmers, plus a Buddha image valued at three baht. The wording places agricultural labour alongside temple wealth. The people supplying food were part of the institution’s economy, although this fragment cannot tell us their individual family arrangements.

passages.title: Reading the evidence on stone and paper
passages.text: The poet and monk Sao Dhammadinna, traditionally dated 1541 to 1640, helped make Buddhist teaching accessible in Shan verse. His Sutta Nibbāna means Discourse on Nibbāna. In an introduction he admired his teacher at Wan Khang monastery. That personal acknowledgement gives us a glimpse of a learning relationship behind the finished text.

passages.title: Reading the evidence on stone and paper
passages.text: Dhammadinna’s work continued to be copied for families remembering the dead. A manuscript now at the Rylands Library preserves a message that donating a book earns merit but does not replace living well. Its completion note gives 6 January without a year, so the surviving copy cannot be assigned to the poet’s lifetime.

passages.title: Reading the evidence on stone and paper
passages.text: That Rylands volume also explains why books need not look like books on our shelves. Its extremely thin paper has writing on only one side; the leaves are folded double, sewn along the top and stored rolled up. Such suspended books are called pap kin. The paper is probably bamboo paper, rather than securely identified by laboratory testing.

passages.title: Reading the evidence on stone and paper
passages.text: A dated later writing sample is ဗုဒ္ဓါနူဿတိ, transliterated Buddhānūssati, meaning recollection of the Buddha. This Pali title labels a Shan Buddhist manuscript, British Library Or 12040, dated 1885. The Burmese-script characters follow the curator’s transcription, rather than reproducing the handwriting. The text concerns mindful recollection of the Buddha’s qualities.

passages.title: Reading the evidence on stone and paper
passages.text: Later Shan folding books could resemble gold bars when closed. Craftspeople lacquered and gilded their covers, sometimes adding raised decoration and coloured mirror glass. Or 14572, dated 1894, weighs more than two kilograms. Not exactly a pocket book!

passages.title: Later windows into ordinary life
passages.text: These household observations are later than the map. In her 1910 book, Leslie Milne describes mothers packing rice and curry separately in banana leaves for children tending cattle, tying the parcels with bamboo strips. Some children had only rice. A leaf could do the job of a lunch box, but this account also records uneven access to food.

passages.title: Later windows into ordinary life
passages.text: Milne also described preparing bamboo for houses: stems were soaked for days or weeks, and builders chose an auspicious day to begin. Her account estimates sixty or seventy large bamboos and at least a hundred smaller ones for a small house. This is a colonial-era observation of building work and belief, not a standard blueprint for every earlier Shan home.

passages.title: Later windows into ordinary life
passages.text: Surviving Shan manuscript collections include texts about healing, charms and tattooing alongside Buddhist teaching, history and stories. SOAS researchers are cataloguing this varied knowledge. The collection does not by itself establish which remedies were used in a particular sixteenth-century village, and these texts are evidence of practices and beliefs rather than proof that a treatment worked.

passages.title: Later windows into ordinary life
passages.text: A Penn Museum report published in 1961 describes Hopong’s market recurring every fifth day. Pa-oh neighbours brought produce from surrounding hills, including garlic and strawberries in May, and bought manufactured goods. This later scene shows different communities sharing a regional economy after princely powers changed. It is not evidence that the same produce filled a market stall in 1530.

Nothing in the evidence identifies 1783 as a collective fall of the Shan states. Principalities continued under changing overlords and later colonial rule. By the 1961 Hopong account, the government had purchased most sawbwas’ old powers, while a ruling family still occupied its residence. Political institutions changed; Shan communities and their neighbours continued.

passages.text: The Shang is the first Chinese dynasty confirmed by contemporary written records, surviving on oracle bones and bronze inscriptions. Centered in the Anyang region, it controlled a network of towns and dependent settlements through ritual authority and bronze technology.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Oracle bone script, the direct ancestor of modern Chinese characters, carved on turtle plastrons and cattle shoulder blades to record the king's divinations. The earliest inscriptions date from the reign of Wu Ding.

passages.title: Inventions
passages.text: Horse-drawn chariots appear in Shang burials at Anyang, adopted from the steppe, and are used for hunting, display and war.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Piece-mold bronze casting reaches its peak. The Houmuwu ding from Anyang, the heaviest bronze vessel known from the ancient world, weighs 832 kg.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: A ten-day week and the sixty-day cycle of ten stems and twelve branches, still used in the Chinese calendar, organized Shang time; oracle bones are dated by the cycle.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Taotie masks and dragon motifs on bronze vessels show sophisticated design principles.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Jade carvings, marble sculptures and pottery figurines from royal tombs; the undisturbed tomb of Fu Hao, a consort of Wu Ding, held 755 jades and 468 bronzes.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Musical instruments including bronze bells and stone chimes found in Anyang excavations.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The supreme deity Di ruled over lesser spirits and royal ancestors who mediated between heaven and earth.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Royal divination addressed questions of war, harvest, weather, illness and the king's activities.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Human sacrifice accompanied royal burials, with dozens or hundreds of victims in major tombs.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Millet farming, with rice and wheat as lesser crops, supported urban populations at Anyang and other centers.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Silk production, evident from the impressions of silk wrappings preserved on bronze vessels.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: The king hunted from chariots with bows and bronze-tipped arrows.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Cowrie shells from the Indian Ocean, given by the king as rewards and buried with the dead as wealth.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Tin and copper for bronze imported from distant sources.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Chinese writing system preserved in continuous use to the present day.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Bronze ritual vessel forms influenced Chinese metalwork for two thousand years.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The concept of a central royal authority over subordinate territories took root.
King Wu of Zhou defeated the last Shang king, Di Xin, at the Battle of Muye, ending the dynasty.

passages.text: Picture a river capital where copper grants clinked onto rings, gold coins showed Shiva riding a bull, monks studied near busy landing places, and officials measured fields by ditches and ponds. The atlas calls this realm `Shaskanka`; historians call its seventh-century ruler Shashanka or Śaśāṅka and usually call his kingdom Gauda. From Karnasuvarna in Bengal, he rose after Gupta power weakened, fought in the dangerous contest around Kanauj and held enough influence that a ruler in coastal Odisha named him overlord in 619 or 620. Hostile court stories later blamed him for murder and attacks on Buddhism, yet a major Buddhist monastery flourished beside his capital, so careful readers keep accusation and proof apart. Shashanka died by the late 630s and his realm fragmented. The atlas stretches his personal label to 700, then hands most of the region to the Palas decades too early. Coins, charters and archaeology let us rebuild a bright, incomplete picture without pretending every colored border is exact.

passages.title: First decode the atlas name, shape and date seams
passages.text: The exact indexed id is `shaskanka`, and its display label is “Shaskanka.” Neither is the usual historical spelling: inscriptions and scholarship use Shashanka or Śaśāṅka. The row is marked circa 600 to 700, generated from historical basemaps, with no alias or authored link. Coverage records one border file, a missing card and three unreviewed audits.

passages.title: First decode the atlas name, shape and date seams
passages.text: At the 500 snapshot the target does not exist. One sweeping `gupta-empire` feature owns all twenty tested places, from Karnasuvarna and Pundravardhana to Nalanda, Ganjam and Kanauj. That digital predecessor is far broader than secure late Gupta control, so a colored owner at this scale is a locator, not proof of uniform government.

passages.title: First decode the atlas name, shape and date seams
passages.text: At 600 the target appears exactly once as an unlabeled Polygon: one part, one ring and 54 positions. Its bounds are 83.98343983439833° to 91.68391683916838° east and 19.60571058531461° to 26.45034275546749° north. The coordinate-array SHA-256 is `227c9296079964ab3eff1b002200fd6a54925cec46b39ccaba91f1bd16801df2`, an exact file fingerprint rather than a historical claim.

passages.title: First decode the atlas name, shape and date seams
passages.text: The 600 polygon contains Karnasuvarna, Gaur, Pundravardhana, Samatata, Tamralipta, Pataliputra, Nalanda, Bodh Gaya, Cuttack and Bhubaneswar, yet misses Rohtasgarh and Ganjam, both important to Shashanka's evidence. Its raw arcs are `[[[-53,-40,-46,54]]]`, shared with `kanauj`, `kamarupa` and `hindu-kingdoms`. The shape simplifies both reach and rivalry.

passages.title: First decode the atlas name, shape and date seams
passages.text: At 700 `shaskanka` vanishes and `palas` immediately owns most eastern audit points; at 800 that Pala blanket remains. Historically, Shashanka had died decades before 700, but Gopala's Pala kingdom did not arise until the mid-eighth century. One seam is late and the next is early, leaving a missing century of shifting powers between them.

passages.title: Meet Shashanka, and learn what the surviving evidence can say
passages.text: The atlas spelling points to a person, not a dynasty called Shaskanka. Śaśāṅka means “moon” in Sanskrit, while inscriptions style him a great king of kings. Modern historians usually call the realm Gauda. Because names, titles, regions and dynasties are different things, this card keeps the exact database id but corrects the history in every explanation.

passages.title: Meet Shashanka, and learn what the surviving evidence can say
passages.text: A seal found at Rohtas uses a title usually read as “Śrī Mahāsāmanta Śaśāṅka,” suggesting an early phase as a powerful subordinate. The object does not supply a tidy biography, employer or accession date. It is safest to say he emerged from the post-Gupta political world, then became independent, rather than inventing a royal childhood or dramatic coronation.

passages.title: Meet Shashanka, and learn what the surviving evidence can say
passages.text: The Indian Museum's Egra copper plate is a palm-sized government archive in metal: roughly 24 by 17 centimetres, with a seven-centimetre seal, twenty lines on one face and seventeen on the other. It probably records a land grant under Shashanka. Copper survived where everyday letters on leaves, bark or cloth usually did not.

passages.title: Meet Shashanka, and learn what the surviving evidence can say
passages.text: Karnasuvarna was Shashanka's capital near today's Murshidabad. Excavated monastery seals from Rajbadidanga identify Raktamrittika and help locate the capital's neighborhood. Archaeologists have not uncovered a complete royal-city plan, so the capital should be imagined as a river landscape of settlement clusters, landing places and institutions, not one perfectly excavated palace grid.

passages.title: Meet Shashanka, and learn what the surviving evidence can say
passages.text: Written evidence is lopsided. Royal charters preserve donations and titles; coins preserve names and sacred images; hostile courts preserve accusations; archaeology preserves what happened to survive. Farmers' conversations, children's jokes and most women's voices were not engraved on copper. A strong reconstruction combines these evidence types while leaving blank spaces visible instead of filling them with certainty.

passages.title: A dangerous game of alliances, armies and rival courts
passages.text: Around 606, politics linked Gauda to Malwa and Kanauj. Shashanka opposed the Maukhari-Pushyabhuti bloc and became a chief rival of Harsha. Coin scholarship places his issues inside this struggle involving Rajyavardhana and Bhaskaravarman. Alliances could turn a distant succession dispute into marching armies, sieges and bargaining across much of northern India.

passages.title: A dangerous game of alliances, armies and rival courts
passages.text: Harsha's court author Bana blamed Shashanka for Rajyavardhana's death, and later traditions sharpened the villainous portrait. A court biography praises its patron and attacks enemies, so it cannot be read like a security camera. Shashanka may have been involved, but exactly who planned, invited, trapped or struck the fatal blow remains disputed.

passages.title: A dangerous game of alliances, armies and rival courts
passages.text: Bhaskaravarman of Kamarupa allied with Harsha against Shashanka, creating pressure from west and northeast. The atlas makes `kamarupa` a shared-arc neighbor, but this clean border hides mobile armies and contested influence. Diplomacy joined rulers through envoys and promises; it did not freeze every village into one permanently colored side.

passages.title: A dangerous game of alliances, armies and rival courts
passages.text: The firmest dated sign of Shashanka's southern reach comes from Ganjam. In 619 or 620, Madhavaraja II of Kongoda issued a charter while acknowledging Shashanka as overlord. That shows suzerainty in part of coastal Odisha; it does not prove that officials from Karnasuvarna personally ran every field, port or household there.

passages.title: A dangerous game of alliances, armies and rival courts
passages.text: Power had layers. A subordinate ruler could keep his capital, officers and grants while recognizing a mightier king; frontier chiefs might obey only when an army was close. This is why Shashanka's political reach cannot be reduced to the 600 polygon, which includes places without equally strong proof and excludes Ganjam despite its dated vassal charter.

passages.title: Copper charters turn fields, offices and favors into records
passages.text: A copperplate grant was both legal memory and political theater. A ruler or subordinate authority announced a donation, named officials and recipients, described land and attached a seal. The durable plate told future tax collectors to respect the arrangement. It also advertised the donor's generosity and rank, so its praise language must be separated from its practical instructions.

passages.title: Copper charters turn fields, offices and favors into records
passages.text: The Egra plate probably concerns a grant in coastal Bengal, and its thirty-seven written lines show how much administration could fit on one object. The exact local geography is difficult to reconstruct, but the record proves scribes, engravers, witnesses and seal-making knowledge. A grant required many hands even when the king's name received the largest spotlight.

passages.title: Copper charters turn fields, offices and favors into records
passages.text: Madhavaraja's Ganjam charter granted a village to a learned Brahmin on the occasion of a solar eclipse. The plates name Kongoda, use Sanskrit and carry a bull seal. Religious merit, land revenue and royal hierarchy met in one transaction: the sky event supplied an auspicious moment, while the charter supplied lasting administrative instructions.

passages.title: Copper charters turn fields, offices and favors into records
passages.text: Land boundaries were described through features people could recognize: neighboring holdings, ditches, posts, paths, watercourses or ponds. Such lists show officials walking and remembering a working landscape, not drawing a modern satellite map. Floods, moved markers and disputes could still make a supposedly precise boundary troublesome; medieval paperwork did not magically stop arguments.

passages.title: Copper charters turn fields, offices and favors into records
passages.text: Grants helped build a ladder of authority: king, subordinate lord, provincial officer, village intermediaries and privileged recipient. Broad early medieval studies connect such gifts with tax rights and growing landed power. That model explains the offices on plates, but it cannot tell us that every Gauda village had identical ranks or that social ideals always matched daily behavior.

passages.title: Coins, symbols and one authentic line of royal Sanskrit
passages.text: Shashanka issued gold and silver coins, a major sign that he claimed independent kingship. Surviving examples link money to the same political world as Harsha and the Maukharis. Coin finds cannot calculate the size of his treasury or prove that every market used royal gold, but they show controlled designs, skilled dies and a name meant to travel.

passages.title: Coins, symbols and one authentic line of royal Sanskrit
passages.text: Many Shashanka types show Shiva with the bull Nandi on one side and a seated goddess, usually identified as Lakshmi, on the other. A large digital study groups hundreds of Gauḍa coin images into recurring classes. The pictures express royal religion and legitimacy; they are not photographs of ordinary clothing, cattle gear or household furniture.

passages.title: Coins, symbols and one authentic line of royal Sanskrit
passages.text: An additional gold coin carries short Brāhmī readings including `Śaśā` and `Jaya` near the Shiva-and-bull design. Tiny letters could announce victory and identity without a long paragraph. Because dies wear, metal cracks and readings differ, numismatists compare many specimens rather than trusting the blurriest single coin like a perfectly printed textbook page.

passages.title: Coins, symbols and one authentic line of royal Sanskrit
passages.text: Moon imagery on some issues may play on the ruler's name, which means “moon,” while the goddess and Shiva-bull imagery connect kingship with prosperity and devotion. Older catalogues remain useful records of specimens, yet interpretations can change as new coins appear. Numismatic evidence is strongest for designs and legends, weaker for reconstructing motives inside the king's mind.

passages.title: Coins, symbols and one authentic line of royal Sanskrit
passages.text: The 619 or 620 Ganjam plate says, in normalized editorial Devanagari, `महाराजाधिराजश्रीशशाङ्कराज्ये शासति`; transliteration: `mahārājādhirāja-śrī-śaśāṅkarājye śāsati`; translation: “while the illustrious great king of kings Shashanka was ruling.” This is formal Sanskrit from a land-grant charter, not street conversation. The actual copperplate uses acute-angled transitional Gupta-to-Nagari letters, so the Devanagari line is a clearly labeled modern normalization.

passages.title: Shaiva kingship beside a thriving Buddhist monastery
passages.text: Shiva and Nandi dominate Shashanka's coin imagery, while his title and bull seals fit a strongly Shaiva court style. Royal devotion mattered politically: sacred symbols linked the king with power and recognizable tradition. They do not tell us that every subject worshipped the same deity or followed one identical ritual calendar.

passages.title: Shaiva kingship beside a thriving Buddhist monastery
passages.text: Raktamrittika Mahavihara stood near Karnasuvarna. Xuanzang says distinguished and learned monks gathered there, and excavators found platforms, stairways, stupa bases, sacred sealings and a monastery seal naming its community. This is direct evidence that an important Buddhist institution flourished in the capital region across Shashanka's century.

passages.title: Shaiva kingship beside a thriving Buddhist monastery
passages.text: The same site produced a sealing referring to a `guhyacakra`, perhaps an early clue to esoteric ritual. One small object cannot map every monk's beliefs, but it warns against treating seventh-century Buddhism as one unchanging package. Monasteries contained study, ritual, patrons and debates, not rows of people all thinking precisely alike.

passages.title: Shaiva kingship beside a thriving Buddhist monastery
passages.text: Xuanzang's tradition accuses Shashanka of damaging the Bodhi tree and persecuting Buddhists. Scholars debate these reports because the pilgrim wrote within Buddhist memory and because hostile royal politics shaped the story. The accusation belongs in the card, but it must sit beside the flourishing Raktamrittika evidence instead of becoming an unquestioned empire-wide policy.

passages.title: Shaiva kingship beside a thriving Buddhist monastery
passages.text: A monastery beside a Shaiva ruler's capital does not prove modern-style tolerance, and a persecution story does not erase every monastery. The evidence supports a mixed religious landscape where institutions could prosper, compete, receive patrons or face violence at different moments. Archaeology can correct literary exaggeration, while literature can ask questions bricks alone cannot answer.

passages.title: Families, rank, women, children and paths to learning
passages.text: Court society placed kings and subordinate rulers at the top, then officials, landholders, religious specialists and local intermediaries, with cultivators and laborers carrying much of the material burden. Varna language shaped ideals, yet broad social research warns that region, occupation, status and negotiation complicated daily life. No single ladder fits every household in Gauda.

passages.title: Families, rank, women, children and paths to learning
passages.text: A later seventh-century charter from Karnasuvarna says its donor sought merit for his mother, father and himself. That elite formula reveals family memory inside public religious giving, although it cannot describe an average kitchen or inheritance argument. It is successor-era evidence: useful for continuity after Shashanka, but too late to quote as his own family policy.

passages.title: Families, rank, women, children and paths to learning
passages.text: Most surviving Gauda records name male rulers, officers, monks and Brahmin recipients, leaving women largely indirect. Wider north Indian evidence describes patriarchal marriage and unequal access to property and advanced learning, with important variation by class and community. The honest lesson is both inequality and silence: no source gives a census of Shashanka-era girls' lives.

passages.title: Families, rank, women, children and paths to learning
passages.text: Women in early medieval India could hold forms of personal property and also work in fields, herding and household production, especially below elite ranks. Those regional patterns make women economically visible, but they do not justify assigning every Gauda woman the same chores. Palace women, cultivators, craft workers, servants and nuns would have faced very different choices.

passages.title: Families, rank, women, children and paths to learning
passages.text: Learning was specialized, not universal schooling. Raktamrittika gathered celebrated monks, while a successor charter names a learned Samaveda student as land recipient. Children probably learned many tasks in households and workshops, but direct Gauda childhood records are absent. Excavated balls and game objects are intriguing; we cannot label their players, rules or songs with confidence.

passages.title: Rice stores, river work, workshops and long-distance exchange
passages.text: At Rajbadidanga, a granary contained burnt rice and wheat. These charred grains are rare direct evidence for stored food near Karnasuvarna, though they span an archaeological phase wider than one reign. Rice suited the deltaic world; wheat also moved through stores. The find does not reveal portions, recipes or whether rich and poor ate alike.

passages.title: Rice stores, river work, workshops and long-distance exchange
passages.text: Excavators recovered bowls, dishes, lids, sprinklers and many pottery sherds, along with iron nails, copper, bronze and shell objects. Pots point to cooking, serving, storing and pouring; material variety points to craft and exchange. A broken vessel cannot identify its owner's favorite dinner, and monastery rubbish is not automatically a sample of every village cupboard.

passages.title: Rice stores, river work, workshops and long-distance exchange
passages.text: The Bhagirathi connected Karnasuvarna with other Bengal waterways, ports and the Bay of Bengal. Boats could move people, grain, cloth, ritual goods and messages more efficiently than muddy overland paths in many seasons. River trade made a capital powerful, but floods, shifting channels and sandbanks meant sailors and carriers earned their keep the hard way.

passages.title: Rice stores, river work, workshops and long-distance exchange
passages.text: Archaeological comparisons connect Bengal to Southeast Asian maritime networks, yet identical-looking objects do not always prove a direct voyage from one named port. Goods could pass through several merchants and harbors. The safe picture is an outward-facing delta linked to Bay routes, while exact cargo lists, ship schedules and Shashanka's customs rates remain unknown.

passages.title: Rice stores, river work, workshops and long-distance exchange
passages.text: Merchant sealings at Rajbadidanga show commercial people interacting with the monastery, perhaps as travelers, patrons or suppliers. That does not turn the monastery into the entire marketplace. Farmers, boat crews, potters, metalworkers, scribes and builders all supported the capital region, but official inscriptions make their daily negotiations much harder to hear than a king's title.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, medicine, water and the missing bathroom tour
passages.text: Floodplain settlements often used perishable wood, bamboo, reeds, earth and thatch, while the monastery invested in brick and other durable construction. This survival gap makes elite or sacred masonry look more common than ordinary homes were. Cloth survives poorly too, so coins and terracotta figures cannot supply a standard Gauda outfit or prove what every child wore.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, medicine, water and the missing bathroom tour
passages.text: Vāgbhaṭa's seventh-century `Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya` shows that learned Ayurvedic medicine organized diagnosis, regimen, drugs and bodily care in Shashanka's wider South Asian world. It does not prove the author visited Karnasuvarna or that a clinic stood beside the palace. Households, healers and religious specialists likely offered varied care, but local rosters do not survive.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, medicine, water and the missing bathroom tour
passages.text: The National Library of Medicine dates Vāgbhaṭa's activity to the seventh century and identifies his Sanskrit medical authorship. That secure comparison tells children written medical learning existed in the same broad era. It cannot reveal which remedies reached Gauda, how much treatment cost or whether a sick farm worker and a king received comparable attention.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, medicine, water and the missing bathroom tour
passages.text: Karnasuvarna depended on the Bhagirathi and on ponds or tanks that caught rainwater; low groundwater and floods shaped settlement choices. Checked excavations do not provide a secure Shashanka-era sewer map or labeled household latrines. Archaeology has not handed us Shashanka's bathroom tour, so the card reports water management and negative evidence without inventing royal plumbing.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, medicine, water and the missing bathroom tour
passages.text: Yijing, who traveled in India from 671 to 695, later described Buddhist ideals such as tooth sticks, washing after defecation, separating clean and dirty water and filtering water from rivers, ponds or wells. These are valuable later monastic prescriptions, not proof that every Raktamrittika monk, or any palace household, followed every rule under Shashanka.

passages.title: Death, successor states and what continued after the king
passages.text: The last secure dated anchor is the Ganjam grant of 619 or 620. Reconstructions often place Shashanka's death around 625 or as late as 636 or 637, and the exact year remains unsettled. This card uses circa 637 as a practical transformation marker, not a claim that a witnessed death certificate survives from one particular day.

passages.title: Death, successor states and what continued after the king
passages.text: After Shashanka, Bhaskaravarman issued a grant from a victory camp at Karnasuvarna, showing that the old capital had passed into a rival's political orbit. Harsha also gained influence. “Realm fragmented” is more accurate than drawing one instant successor arrow: conquest, temporary occupation and local survival could overlap across different parts of Gauda.

passages.title: Death, successor states and what continued after the king
passages.text: Jayanaga later ruled from Karnasuvarna and used provincial officers, a sealed copper charter and carefully listed riverbed and reservoir boundaries. His record proves administrative habits and the capital place continued after Shashanka. It does not prove descent from him, an unbroken dynasty or control over the atlas's entire 600 polygon.

passages.title: Death, successor states and what continued after the king
passages.text: Gopala's Pala rule belongs to the middle of the eighth century, traditionally around 750 to 756, after a long period of regional instability. The atlas moves most of eastern India to `palas` at 700, several decades too soon. The Pala kingdom is an important later continuity of Bengal-based power, but not Shashanka's immediate documented heir.

passages.title: Death, successor states and what continued after the king
passages.text: What lasted was not one unchanged empire: Karnasuvarna remained a political place, Raktamrittika remained a learned Buddhist institution, charters kept recording land and river boundaries, and Bengal's waterways kept carrying people and goods. What remains unknown includes Shashanka's family tree, most common speech, ordinary songs, exact toilets and a year-by-year frontier. Those are excellent reasons to keep investigating.

Shashanka died after the securely dated 619 or 620 Ganjam charter and probably by the late 630s. No well-documented heir kept his whole realm together. Bhaskaravarman and Harsha gained influence, Jayanaga later ruled at Karnasuvarna, and other regional powers filled the gaps. The atlas endpoint of 700 therefore marks a delayed label change, not the ruler's death or an immediate Pala succession.

dailyLife.question: Does the account explain ordinary practices with evidence rather than only rulers?

chronologicalPhases.question: Are source-supported phases distinguished from map snapshot dates?

endingContinuity.question: Does the narrative identify what ended or continued, with dates, mechanism and uncertainty?

uncertainty.question: Are uncertainties attached to particular claims rather than a blanket disclaimer?

sectionTitles: Removal, children and recovering practical knowledge

passages.text: Shawnee communities have deep ties to the Ohio Valley and histories of movement across eastern North America. Today distinct Shawnee nations continue. This map’s 1530 to 1783 outline is a regional snapshot, not the complete territory of every Shawnee community or the lifetime of the people.

passages.title: Towns, work and diplomacy
passages.text: Lower Shawneetown stood near the meeting of the Ohio and Scioto rivers and became a major diplomatic and trading centre in the mid-eighteenth century. Shawnee hosts negotiated with other Native peoples and European representatives. Its river location connected local households to political decisions across a much wider region.

passages.title: Towns, work and diplomacy
passages.text: At the Bentley part of Lower Shawneetown, pebble-lined post settings outlined a building at least 30 feet wide and 50 feet long. Nearby rubbish included Native pottery alongside imported knives, scissors and mouth harps. People used new goods while continuing local manufacturing traditions: old and new could share a kitchen.

passages.title: Towns, work and diplomacy
passages.text: The Eastern Shawnee history describes summer villages of bark-covered houses, with a larger council house for gatherings. In autumn, extended families moved into smaller hunting camps. This seasonal pattern linked farming, stored food and hunting rather than fitting everyone into a single permanent village.

passages.title: Towns, work and diplomacy
passages.text: Agriculture helped organize the ceremonial year. The Eastern Shawnee account describes a spring bread dance around planting, a green corn dance as crops ripened, and an autumn bread dance around harvest. The food calendar was also a calendar for coming together.

passages.title: Towns, work and diplomacy
passages.text: In 1808, the brothers Tenskwatawa and Tecumseh established Prophetstown near the Wabash and Tippecanoe rivers. Tenskwatawa’s religious renewal movement and Tecumseh’s diplomacy drew people from several nations. The settlement became a centre for a confederation opposing further loss of Native land.

passages.title: Towns, work and diplomacy
passages.text: Shawnee leaders did not all choose the same strategy. Black Hoof favoured peaceful adaptation, while Tecumseh sought a wider alliance to resist US expansion. American troops burned Prophetstown after the 1811 battle; Tecumseh continued seeking allies until he died at the Thames in 1813.

passages.title: Removal, children and recovering practical knowledge
passages.text: The 1831 removal agreement for Wapakoneta and Hog Creek Shawnees transferred their remaining Ohio reserve lands to the United States. The treaty promised a more secure western home. Reading its provisions alongside removal history shows what officials pledged, rather than proving that every family freely welcomed the journey.

passages.title: Removal, children and recovering practical knowledge
passages.text: The Shawnee Indian Mission Manual Labor School opened at Fairway, Kansas, in 1839. Shawnee children lived there, and three substantial brick buildings survive. The Shawnee Tribe has worked to recover the children’s history and assess the site, bringing family and community questions into its interpretation.

passages.title: Removal, children and recovering practical knowledge
passages.text: In a 2022 preservation statement, Chief Ben Barnes described children sleeping in the mission’s attic after work in its fields. The buildings hold evidence of a demanding residential-school routine. Investigating them is also about understanding what children experienced, beyond the institution’s name and architecture.

passages.title: Removal, children and recovering practical knowledge
passages.text: A modern pottery project brought Shawnee citizens and scholars together with Wyandotte potter Richard Zane Smith. A replica Fort Ancient vessel was used to cook corn and venison. Making and using a pot can test practical questions about food preparation while researchers investigate its relationship to Shawnee ancestral traditions.

passages.title: Writing and present-day learning
passages.text: The Shawnee Sun began publication in 1835 using a printing system developed by missionary Jotham Meeker. A surviving November 1841 sheet is held by the University of Missouri-Kansas City. It is evidence of nineteenth-century Shawnee-language printing within a missionary setting, not an ancient alphabet or universal literacy.

passages.title: Writing and present-day learning
passages.text: “Hato Caakiwiyeefa” means “Hello everyone”. Roy Baldridge used the greeting in the Shawnee Tribe’s Fall 2024 message from its chiefs, where the English meaning is printed alongside it. This is an attested modern Shawnee sample in Latin letters, from a community publication addressed to its readers.

passages.title: Writing and present-day learning
passages.text: When language classes moved online during the pandemic, the Shawnee Tribe could reach learners living far apart. Its immersion program worked with first-language speaker George Blanchard and emphasized listening and speaking in small classes. Digital lessons supported a goal that was very personal: using Shawnee in everyday conversation.

The destruction of towns, the collapse of Tecumseh’s wartime alliance and forced removal caused profound losses. They did not end Shawnee life. The Eastern Shawnee Tribe, Absentee Shawnee Tribe and Shawnee Tribe are distinct contemporary nations; the map’s 1783 cutoff is only a coverage boundary.
