sectionTitles: Read the economic label and archaeological evidence carefully
Build landmarks in moving lagoons, dunes and estuaries
Eat fish, shellfish, plants and terrestrial foods in varied proportions
Engineer fishing gear, stone tools, containers and art
Organize living space, fires, water and waste without inventing plumbing
See households, women, age groups and cooperation without stereotypes
Follow babies, children, learning and play through careful clues
Investigate health, medicine, food safety and hygiene without diagnosis games
Honor burials and beliefs without translating silent objects
Celebrate discoveries, changing traditions and living continuity

passages.text: The atlas calls this broad patch “Shellfish gatherers,” but that is an economic label, not a people's name. Its polygon follows parts of southeastern and southern Brazil while sweeping inland. Archaeologists call local shell sites sambaquis, a later Tupi-derived term. They were far more than clam-dinner heaps. Layers can contain fish bones, plants, hearths, tools, ornaments and burials; enormous mounds became landmarks of memory. Fish often supplied more protein than shellfish, while dental calculus, teeth and stone tools reveal important plants. Communities around Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Paraná and Santa Catarina did not form one timeless culture, language or government. Genomes likewise reveal regional diversity and later contact despite similarities in mound building. Near this card's final centuries, some sites changed from shell-rich layers to darker fish-rich deposits, and pottery appears in particular contexts. The atlas polygon narrows sharply in 800 and disappears in 900. Those are map seams, not proof that coastal families vanished. Distinct Indigenous peoples live across these regions today, and no living nation should be treated as the automatic name or voice of every ancient mound builder.

passages.title: Read the economic label and archaeological evidence carefully
passages.text: “Shellfish gatherers” is the atlas editor's category, not a recovered self-name. It risks reducing people to one ingredient. The card retains the exact id for software compatibility while treating each mound, bay and dated community separately. Fishing, plants, hunting, ceremony, construction and exchange all belonged in the wider picture.

passages.title: Read the economic label and archaeological evidence carefully
passages.text: The early polygon follows the Atlantic coast from around Rio de Janeiro toward Santa Catarina, yet its northwestern edge cuts far inland. Its boundary excludes some famous eastern Rio shellmound areas while including interior cities. That geometry cannot be a surveyed ethnic, language or archaeological frontier.

passages.title: Read the economic label and archaeological evidence carefully
passages.text: Soil micromorphology at Rio Preto I separates shell deposits, burning, organic movement and later soil formation. This matters because roots, animals, rain and chemistry alter a mound after people leave. Archaeologists do not simply count visible shells; they study thin sections, elements, layers and radiocarbon context.

passages.title: Read the economic label and archaeological evidence carefully
passages.text: Contemporaneous written-language sample: none represents this exact atlas umbrella. Original script: unavailable. Transliteration: unavailable. Translation: unavailable. “Sambaqui” is a later Tupi-derived archaeological term, not a surviving sentence written by these builders. Rich speech and oral knowledge certainly existed, but no secure text identifies their languages.

passages.title: Read the economic label and archaeological evidence carefully
passages.text: Small inland shellmounds in the Ribeira highlands have different materials, foods and chronologies from monumental coastal sites. Capelinha diet evidence is terrestrial despite shell and coastal connections. Shared shell construction can signal contact or similar choices without proving one ancestry, political system, language or migration route.

passages.title: Build landmarks in moving lagoons, dunes and estuaries
passages.text: Ground-penetrating radar beneath a southern mound found archaeological layers over an old lagoon margin and wind-built sediments. The method maps contrasts without digging away the whole site. It helps reconstruct why a once-watery edge may now look dry, inland or buried beneath later landscape change.

passages.title: Build landmarks in moving lagoons, dunes and estuaries
passages.text: A mound's shells could be food remains, building material, grave covering or several things at different moments. Human isotopes sometimes disagree with what the most visible shells suggest. The useful question is not “trash heap or temple?” but which activities built each layer and how they changed.

passages.title: Build landmarks in moving lagoons, dunes and estuaries
passages.text: Araujo II in Paraná contains stratified shell, ash, stone and bone objects and burials. Recreio, beyond the polygon's southern edge, preserves a separately dated coastal sequence. Older excavations remain valuable, but a layer is not a calendar page unless its context stays intact.

passages.title: Build landmarks in moving lagoons, dunes and estuaries
passages.text: Late southern routes connected mound sites, discrete camps and Jê-associated contexts across wetlands, dunes and higher ground. Least-cost paths are models of possible movement, not footprints. They help compare terrain and access while leaving room for boats, seasonal water, social permission and routes archaeologists cannot recover.

passages.title: Build landmarks in moving lagoons, dunes and estuaries
passages.text: Many sambaquis were quarried for lime, damaged by construction or exposed by erosion. IPHAN protects archaeological heritage, while museums preserve collections and site records. Conservation is an achievement in the present because a mound cannot be re-excavated after bulldozing, and an unlabeled box can lose nearly as much history as a destroyed layer.

passages.title: Eat fish, shellfish, plants and terrestrial foods in varied proportions
passages.text: Isotope models at Piaçaguera and Moraes show different mixtures of marine, freshwater and terrestrial foods, plus differences among individuals. The numbers are estimates shaped by baseline animals and tissue turnover. They defeat the idea that every mound builder ate the same seafood plate merely because shell preserves spectacularly.

passages.title: Eat fish, shellfish, plants and terrestrial foods in varied proportions
passages.text: At Morro do Ouro, cavities, bone chemistry and plant microremains point to carbohydrate-rich foods. Possible yam, sweet potato, palm and other plants appear, but identification and domestication status need caution. Tropical plant foods often vanish unless charred or trapped in dental calculus, making the surviving shell pile an unfairly loud witness.

passages.title: Eat fish, shellfish, plants and terrestrial foods in varied proportions
passages.text: Ilha Grande fish assemblages represent reef, estuary and open-water habitats, while thousands of bone artifacts help test capture methods. Species lists can reveal seasonal and environmental choices, but fish bones also reflect screen size, preservation and which parts reached the mound. Fishing skill was ecological knowledge plus technology.

passages.title: Eat fish, shellfish, plants and terrestrial foods in varied proportions
passages.text: Mollusk shells identify habitats and collection choices, but people may have carried shell for building as well as food. Tarioba biodiversity research uses many species to reconstruct coastal conditions. A giant mound is therefore not one enormous restaurant receipt; it is a time-layered human construction with ecological clues.

passages.title: Eat fish, shellfish, plants and terrestrial foods in varied proportions
passages.text: Marine mammals, birds and reptiles contributed meat, bone, teeth and symbolic materials at southern sites. Zooarchaeologists examine species, cut marks, burning and artifact manufacture before deciding how an animal was used. A whale bone tool does not by itself prove the animal was hunted rather than found stranded.

passages.title: Engineer fishing gear, stone tools, containers and art
passages.text: Saquarema Lagoon sites east of much of the decoded polygon provide a labeled regional comparison: worked fish spines and bone points represent different fishing technologies. Their exact targets remain debated. Similar-looking points elsewhere require local wear, context and fauna before researchers assume the same technique or cultural identity.

passages.title: Engineer fishing gear, stone tools, containers and art
passages.text: At Camboinhas, researchers identify fish more precisely and ask how bodies were processed. The site lies outside or near the map's northeastern seam, so it cannot silently stand for the entire target. It is useful comparison showing how better taxonomy changes stories about capture, season and disposal.

passages.title: Engineer fishing gear, stone tools, containers and art
passages.text: Prainha stone artifacts preserve an operational sequence: choosing raw material, shaping edges, using tools and sometimes reworking them. A finished ax hides those steps. Reconstructing the chain shows planning and learned technique, while no stone flake tells us whether the teacher was a parent, specialist or patient friend.

passages.title: Engineer fishing gear, stone tools, containers and art
passages.text: Grinding stones, mortars and dental microremains make plants technologically visible. Processing could crush fibers, nuts, roots or seeds, but tool form alone does not name a recipe. Different residues and wear patterns matter. Food technology included knowledge of what decays, even when museums end up displaying mostly durable stone and shell.

passages.title: Engineer fishing gear, stone tools, containers and art
passages.text: Southern sites produced polished stone or bone animal sculptures called zooliths, as well as ornaments and practical tools. Their realism can delight children, but an animal-shaped bowl is not a captioned myth. It demonstrates design, patient grinding and shared conventions while its spoken story remains unknown.

passages.title: Organize living space, fires, water and waste without inventing plumbing
passages.text: Postholes, hearths and activity deposits imply built spaces, yet tropical wood, thatch and fiber usually decay. Geophysical survey can find buried features without exposing them all. The evidence supports shelters and planned activity areas, not one standard house drawing for every coastal region and century.

passages.title: Organize living space, fires, water and waste without inventing plumbing
passages.text: Microscopic charcoal anatomy identifies woods burned in funerary areas and distinguishes some depositional sequences. Fire supplied heat, light, cooking and material transformation, but a charcoal fragment needs context before becoming a domestic hearth. Smoke management, fire tending and fuel collection were learned household work even when roofs disappear.

passages.title: Organize living space, fires, water and waste without inventing plumbing
passages.text: Shell beads and ornaments placed with a child at Cabeçuda show adornment and careful mortuary treatment. They do not preserve a full wardrobe. Plant fiber, hide and feathers may have served clothing or carrying needs but rarely survive; the honest card avoids dressing everyone in one speculative costume.

passages.title: Organize living space, fires, water and waste without inventing plumbing
passages.text: Lagoon water could be salty or brackish, so communities still needed reliable fresh drinking water. Site location, hydrology and containers matter, but no reviewed source documents one umbrella-wide well or plumbing system. Changing barriers and sediment could alter water access within a family's lifetime.

passages.title: Organize living space, fires, water and waste without inventing plumbing
passages.text: No reviewed excavation identifies a shared toilet, latrine or sewer. Mounds contain food refuse, ash, broken objects, human burials and deliberate construction layers, sometimes carefully separated. That organization is evidence for spatial rules, but calling any dark patch a bathroom would be funny for the wrong reason and scientifically reckless.

passages.title: See households, women, age groups and cooperation without stereotypes
passages.text: At Corondo, east of the polygon's strongest coastal core, grave goods were interpreted as showing differences by age, gender and status, including changing female prestige. This is one mortuary study, not a constitution for all sambaqui societies. Burial treatment can express identity without mapping daily authority exactly.

passages.title: See households, women, age groups and cooperation without stereotypes
passages.text: A broader Rio de Janeiro review found burial goods were not exclusively assigned to one gender, even when some tendencies appeared. That warns against labeling fishing points “men's tools” or plant equipment “women's work” by habit. Bones may estimate biological sex; objects do not automatically reveal gender identity or job.

passages.title: See households, women, age groups and cooperation without stereotypes
passages.text: Funerary contexts vary so much that researchers use gender as a question rather than a ready answer. Women, men and people whose identities do not fit modern binaries all require evidence-based treatment. The safest conclusion is social diversity, not an invented universal division of coastal labor.

passages.title: See households, women, age groups and cooperation without stereotypes
passages.text: Repeated burial clusters and meals at Jabuticabeira II suggest groups returned to honor particular dead and renew relationships. Archaeologists may discuss affinity groups, but a burial cluster is not automatically a biological family. Adoption, marriage, friendship and ritual belonging cannot be read from proximity alone.

passages.title: See households, women, age groups and cooperation without stereotypes
passages.text: Building a visible mound required coordinated carrying, fishing, gathering and ceremony across generations. That is a social achievement. It does not prove enslaved labor, a king or compulsory taxation. Regional reviews debate hierarchy and heterarchy because cooperation, prestige and inequality can coexist without a centralized state.

passages.title: Follow babies, children, learning and play through careful clues
passages.text: Isotopes from Jabuticabeira II suggest supplementary foods began near six months for sampled children and complete weaning often occurred around two to three years. These are modeled averages from particular bones and teeth, not parenting instructions or a fixed rule. Feeding a child joined biology with family care and available foods.

passages.title: Follow babies, children, learning and play through careful clues
passages.text: Growth disruptions and bone lesions at Jabuticabeira II show that some children experienced physiological stress or infection, while survival to later ages records resilience and care. Skeletal stress is not a report card on parenting. Disease, food, environment and preservation interact, and the sample represents people who were buried there.

passages.title: Follow babies, children, learning and play through careful clues
passages.text: A carefully ornamented child's burial at Cabeçuda makes childhood visible without reducing the young person to an age category. Shell adornments show investment and remembrance. They cannot tell whether the child wore them in life, who made them, or what words mourners spoke beside the grave.

passages.title: Follow babies, children, learning and play through careful clues
passages.text: Children probably learned knots, balance, tide timing, plant recognition and tool safety through watching and helping, but no excavated object is automatically a lesson. A small point might be practice, a finished tool or a broken adult object. Production sequences reveal skill levels more securely than invented schoolrooms.

passages.title: Follow babies, children, learning and play through careful clues
passages.text: The Joinville museum teaches with tens of thousands of artifacts and protects knowledge recovered from damaged sites. Modern museum learning is not an ancient classroom, yet it makes a good continuity lesson: asking, drawing, comparing and caring for context are skills too. Archaeology has no secure sambaqui board game or recess schedule.

passages.title: Investigate health, medicine, food safety and hygiene without diagnosis games
passages.text: High cavity rates at Morro do Ouro support substantial carbohydrate consumption, while neighboring groups show different patterns. Teeth preserve diet and disease together. A cavity does not identify one plant or prove poor hygiene; texture, processing, mouth bacteria, age and sampling all matter.

passages.title: Investigate health, medicine, food safety and hygiene without diagnosis games
passages.text: Ancient DNA from Jabuticabeira II reconstructed treponemal bacteria related to diseases in the same family as syphilis, but the genomes represent an ancient non-venereal lineage. Researchers combine lesions, molecules and dates rather than diagnosing from appearance alone. Pathogen history is not a reason to stigmatize the buried community.

passages.title: Investigate health, medicine, food safety and hygiene without diagnosis games
passages.text: Jabuticabeira II children show non-specific stress indicators, which can form after many kinds of hardship. They do not name a fever, famine or treatment. Evidence of survival may imply feeding and caregiving, yet the bones cannot identify a healer, medicine bundle or exact household response.

passages.title: Investigate health, medicine, food safety and hygiene without diagnosis games
passages.text: Cabeçuda and Arapuan samples showed low observed levels of trauma interpreted as interpersonal violence, but sample sizes and preservation limit the conclusion. Low injury prevalence is not proof that conflict never happened; it simply rejects a cartoon of constant fighting and demands local, dated evidence.

passages.title: Investigate health, medicine, food safety and hygiene without diagnosis games
passages.text: No securely attributable medical recipe survives for this umbrella. Plant remains may represent food, fuel, offerings or medicine, and healed bones can show recovery without naming treatment. Clean water, waste placement, fire and food processing affected health, but no single hygiene code can be reconstructed from shell layers.

passages.title: Honor burials and beliefs without translating silent objects
passages.text: At Jabuticabeira II, repeated fish-rich feasts and burials helped construct the mound. Meals may have joined mourners and ancestors, but archaeologists infer ceremony from patterned deposits rather than a written liturgy. One cemetery's sequence should not become the religion of every mound along two thousand kilometers of coast.

passages.title: Honor burials and beliefs without translating silent objects
passages.text: Carbonized seeds and palm nuts in funerary features could be feast remains, offerings or both. Charring improves survival, so preserved plants are a biased sample of everything used. Their position beside hearths and burials narrows possibilities without providing the name of a spirit, dish or ritual specialist.

passages.title: Honor burials and beliefs without translating silent objects
passages.text: Thousands of fish otoliths, the hard “ear stones” that help fish balance, occur in Jabuticabeira II funerary contexts. Researchers ask whether some were selected beyond food disposal. Fun fact: a tiny fish balance stone can become a human clue, but it still does not whisper its meaning to archaeologists.

passages.title: Honor burials and beliefs without translating silent objects
passages.text: Burial goods and body treatment vary across Rio de Janeiro sites. Some patterns relate imperfectly to biological sex or age, while none supplies a universal gender rule. Respectful interpretation keeps biological estimates, social gender, personal identity and archaeologists' own assumptions from collapsing into one label.

passages.title: Honor burials and beliefs without translating silent objects
passages.text: Mound scale proves sustained work, not the political method used to organize it. No palace archive records orders, and no laborer's testimony survives. Cooperation, obligation, grief, prestige and unequal influence are all possibilities. Claims of coercion require stronger evidence than “this monument was difficult to build.”

passages.title: Celebrate discoveries, changing traditions and living continuity
passages.text: Marine foods can distort radiocarbon ages because old dissolved carbon enters food webs. At Cabeçuda, paired shell, charcoal and human bone let researchers estimate and correct the reservoir effect. That detective work is an achievement: the best date is not always the number a laboratory first prints.

passages.title: Celebrate discoveries, changing traditions and living continuity
passages.text: Geophysical surveys can reveal buried layers and hearth-like anomalies before excavation, letting teams target small areas and preserve more of a site. Non-destructive technology does not replace careful digging; it adds a map of possibilities. The mound stays mostly intact while researchers decide which questions justify disturbance.

passages.title: Celebrate discoveries, changing traditions and living continuity
passages.text: Ancient genomes reveal that southeastern and southern mound communities were not one genetically uniform population. Contact with inland peoples increased in late periods, but ancestry is not language or culture. Genetic similarity cannot turn present Kaingang, Guarani, Laklano-Xokleng or other nations into automatic descendants of every excavated person.

passages.title: Celebrate discoveries, changing traditions and living continuity
passages.text: Collections at Joinville preserve tools, animal remains and records from sites that lime quarrying and development damaged. Museums also inherit older collecting problems, including lost context and human remains. Preservation today should involve ethical care, transparent records and Indigenous participation, not simply locking attractive objects in cases.

passages.title: Celebrate discoveries, changing traditions and living continuity
passages.text: In 900 the atlas removes this economic umbrella; people and coastal knowledge do not end. Late shellmounds show continuity, pottery and new relationships rather than one sudden fall. Living Kaingang cultural work is one present example, not a claim of sole succession. Every living Indigenous nation keeps its own name and history.

The exact atlas layer contracts in 800 and disappears in 900, but no synchronized cultural fall is documented. Coastal mound traditions had already changed in different ways through fish-rich deposits, ceramics, mobility and contact. Later Indigenous histories are regionally specific, and living nations retain their own identities; the override therefore keeps fell null and invents no single successor chain.

sectionTitles: Which Shewa are we looking at?
Beads, families and words that survive

passages.text: This imported Shoa record covers 1279 to 1492, but its outline lies far northeast of the Shewa sites discussed here. Medieval Shewa included different Muslim, Christian and Indigenous communities. The card presents regional evidence; it does not claim that one independent kingdom ruled this entire area throughout the map interval.

passages.title: Which Shewa are we looking at?
passages.text: An Arabic chronological record describes the fall of the Makhzumi dynasty to the Walasma in 1285. Researchers still cannot securely locate the places named in those annals. The better-documented town of Nora belongs to later Ifat history, providing regional context rather than an identified old Shewa capital.

passages.title: Inside a medieval town
passages.text: At Nora, builders used local volcanic stone: mostly rhyolite, with some cut ignimbrite blocks. They levelled house interiors and laid clay floors, moulding ovens into the clay itself. The kitchen was partly built into the floor, rather than assembled entirely from movable appliances.

passages.title: Inside a medieval town
passages.text: Nora’s small rectangular rooms had walls roughly 40 to 50 centimetres thick. Their dimensions could support short beams beneath flat earth-covered roofs, the excavators suggest. Narrow doors, windows and wall niches made these substantial houses more than empty stone boxes.

passages.title: Inside a medieval town
passages.text: Grinding equipment occurs throughout Nora’s archaeological levels and surrounding landscape. It points to the repeated work of processing crops. Nearby terraces and reservoirs are intriguing, but the 2024 excavation report says their medieval date remains unproved: an old-looking waterwork still needs dating.

passages.title: Inside a medieval town
passages.text: Animal bones from Nora include cattle, sheep and goats. Butchers left cuts on some bones, and broken long bones preserve traces of food preparation. Researchers examined material from houses and a rubbish heap: yesterday’s discarded scraps can become tomorrow’s evidence about dinner.

passages.title: Inside a medieval town
passages.text: Some cattle lived long enough to develop heavily worn teeth. The animal specialist suggests they may have supplied milk or traction before slaughter. A cow could therefore contribute much more than meat, although the bones alone cannot tell us which household milked it or what it pulled.

passages.title: Washing, worship and portable courts
passages.text: Beside a small Nora mosque stood a large basalt stone. Archaeologist Stéphane Pradines interprets it as a footrest used during washing before prayer, comparing similar arrangements elsewhere. This is a specific proposed use for a surviving object, not proof of a fully excavated public bathhouse.

passages.title: Washing, worship and portable courts
passages.text: The same mosque’s prayer room measured about 19 square metres and had a central column supporting its roof. It served worship on a much more intimate scale than a vast cathedral. Its courtyard and carefully arranged entrances show how a small building could organize communal activity.

passages.title: Washing, worship and portable courts
passages.text: In the Christian kingdom, royal camps could contain separate areas for the ruler’s household, soldiers, officials and livestock, sometimes divided by palisades. Researchers have explored a possible fifteenth-century royal camp in Menz, northeastern Shewa. A travelling court required space for both political business and animals.

passages.title: Beads, families and words that survive
passages.text: Shay communities lived in this wider region from about the ninth to fourteenth centuries. At Meshala Maryam, a burial mound contained human remains, pottery, beads and metal ornaments. Repeated use suggests a family tomb. Their distinct burial traditions should not automatically be labelled Christian or Muslim because of nearby states.

passages.title: Beads, families and words that survive
passages.text: A 2023 study analysed 34 glass beads from two Shay burial sites. Their chemistry connects the glass with several manufacturing traditions, including the Middle East, Egypt and the Indian Ocean world. Tiny ornaments reveal wide trading connections, even when the route taken by a particular bead remains unknown.

passages.title: Beads, families and words that survive
passages.text: “هذا قبر” means “This is the tomb.” These Arabic words open the published transcription of tomb T9 at Awfat, dated April to May 1364. The inscription commemorates a religious scholar associated with the Walasma. It is a later Ifat writing sample in regional context, not a Makhzumi royal document.

The old Muslim Shewa dynasty ended in 1285, but this imported record extends to 1492 without a securely identified corresponding fall. Regional communities continued under changing powers. Nora’s excavated urban history itself reaches into the early sixteenth century, so 1492 should not erase its inhabitants.

passages.text: Shona describes related language communities and historical societies, not one kingdom lasting from 1878 to 1914. This imported outline sits largely north of Zimbabwe and misses the heartland of many examples below. The card follows the named communities; its dates and polygon are not reliable cultural boundaries.

passages.title: Work, skills and food security
passages.text: In the late nineteenth century, Njanja ironworkers in central Zimbabwe used small furnaces supplied with air by bellows through clay pipes. They worked with ore from the Hwedza Mountains. Their achievement lay in controlling a demanding process and producing useful iron tools, not simply finding a rock that looked metallic.

passages.title: Work, skills and food security
passages.text: Ironworking also taught skills. Young men could apprentice to Njanja ironmasters, contributing labor while learning the craft. These specialists still farmed, and their workshops depended on relatives and wider networks. A skilled smith could gain followers and influence as well as produce hoes for the next agricultural season.

passages.title: Work, skills and food security
passages.text: Nineteenth-century grain storage in southern Zimbabwe offers a regional comparison involving several neighboring peoples, including Karanga and Kalanga communities. At the Homba Hills, builders combined wooden poles and reeds with clay plaster to make bins in protected caves. Keeping a harvest safe required construction skills as well as successful farming.

passages.title: Work, skills and food security
passages.text: Some Homba Hills bins were repaired by covering cracks with another layer of clay. This suggests repeated care and reuse. The study links concealed storage with both food security and conflict, but archaeology cannot tell us whether a particular bin was always full or exactly which household depended on it.

passages.title: Inside a household
passages.text: Manyika pottery research brings cooking into view. Accounts from 1941, 1947 and 1965 describe smaller cooking vessels used for children’s porridge and larger pots for meat or vegetable relish. These are later observations from eastern Zimbabwe, not a claim that every family in the nineteenth century owned an identical kitchen set.

passages.title: Inside a household
passages.text: The same study describes potters, mainly women, carefully selecting clay from streams and riverbanks. Researchers combined archives with knowledge shared by Manyika elders and potters. That lets a broken vessel tell a richer story than its shape alone: someone had to recognize suitable clay, prepare it and turn it into a useful container.

passages.title: Inside a household
passages.text: At Chief Mugabe’s homestead near Great Zimbabwe in the late nineteenth century, travelers Theodore and Mabel Bent were given a kitchen rondavel for the night. It also contained a chicken enclosure. Their account gives one unusually specific glimpse of a room serving several purposes, with feathered fellow lodgers included.

passages.title: Inside a household
passages.text: A much later study, published in 1981, describes sun drying as an important way rural Shona households preserved food across the year. Its author also noted seasonal shortages of fresh produce. Food history therefore includes the work between harvest and dinner: drying and storing supplies mattered alongside growing them.

passages.title: Language, learning and political change
passages.text: Written language sample: “nhanga” means “pumpkin.” George Fortune’s 1979 study reproduces this entry from the 1974 Standard Shona Dictionary. The same written form also names a house for unmarried girls in Zezuru usage. Context matters: a dictionary can keep you from mistaking a bedroom for a vegetable.

passages.title: Language, learning and political change
passages.text: Printed dictionaries appeared during the colonial period: Hartmann’s English-Mashona Dictionary in 1894 and Elliot’s dictionary in 1897 used different selections and spellings. Fortune’s later review shows why these books must be read critically. Recording a language on paper did not mean its local varieties suddenly became identical.

passages.title: Language, learning and political change
passages.text: British South Africa Company settlers entered Mashonaland in 1890. Colonial demands for labor and taxes, together with seizures of livestock and land, disrupted existing authority and livelihoods. This was a political takeover affecting distinct communities, not the peaceful beginning of society in a previously empty place.

passages.title: Language, learning and political change
passages.text: Shona communities resisted Company rule during the wars of 1896 to 1897. Colonial forces destroyed crops and grain stores as part of their campaign. Those attacks show why the history of a war is also a history of family food supplies: losing a field could matter long after soldiers had moved away.
Colonial conquest reduced the independence of Shona communities during the 1890s; 1914 is only this map record’s endpoint. Their languages, households and traditions continued and changed.

passages.text: Shoshoni is an older spelling of Shoshone. This broad map entry covers communities across the Great Basin and Rocky Mountains, rather than a single kingdom. Its outline combines regional homelands, while the dates mark imported map coverage. The examples below identify particular communities so that one family’s history does not become everybody’s story.

passages.title: Homes, food and practical knowledge
passages.text: Some regional bands were identified by foods strongly associated with their home areas, such as salmon or pine nuts. These names reflected local knowledge and relationships. The Northwestern Band’s history describes many smaller family groups, a useful reminder that this enormous map shape never had one royal capital.

passages.title: Homes, food and practical knowledge
passages.text: In the Bear River and Cache Valley region, winter camps used dense willows and brush for protection from wind and snow. The Northwestern Band also describes nearby hot springs, fish and game. Choosing a campsite meant knowing a whole neighborhood of useful places, not simply finding an empty patch of ground.

passages.title: Homes, food and practical knowledge
passages.text: In August 1805, expedition observers described Lemhi Shoshone fishing barriers made from poles and willows. Basket traps caught fish moving in both directions. Narrow basket ends could be untied to remove the catch: river engineering with a built-in opening for dinner.

passages.title: Homes, food and practical knowledge
passages.text: Cameahwait explained the landscape to Meriwether Lewis by drawing rivers on the ground and making small mounds to represent mountains. His account warned of difficult routes. In this 1805 meeting, the visitor’s notebook depended on a local expert’s knowledge of the country.

passages.title: Homes, food and practical knowledge
passages.text: Lewis also recorded Shoshone women making and repairing his party’s moccasins. He described hide robes that served as daytime clothing and nighttime covers. Those August 1805 observations preserve a glimpse of the skilled work that kept travelers shod and warm.

passages.title: Homes, food and practical knowledge
passages.text: Yellowstone archaeologists associate a pottery tradition called Intermountain Ware with Shoshone presence roughly seven centuries ago. Fragments of cooking vessels can preserve traces of everyday activities long after their owners’ camps have disappeared. This is a regional archaeological clue within a much longer history of people using Yellowstone.

passages.title: Loss, leadership and keeping knowledge
passages.text: Eastern Shoshone leader Washakie worked through a period of expanding settlement and military pressure. The tribe’s history connects treaties in 1863 and 1868 with the eventual Wind River reservation. Washakie favored a place familiar as a wintering area, tying political negotiations to lived knowledge of the landscape.

passages.title: Loss, leadership and keeping knowledge
passages.text: On January 29, 1863, United States troops attacked Northwestern Shoshone families at Bear River. The massacre devastated this community. Its later history includes the return of land: the Northwestern Band purchased a substantial part of the massacre site in 2018, strengthening its role in caring for the place.

passages.title: Loss, leadership and keeping knowledge
passages.text: Mae Timbimboo Parry began writing down elders’ histories while she was still in high school. Her grandfather had survived Bear River as a child. She later challenged accounts calling the massacre a battle, helping bring community testimony into the public history of the event.

passages.title: Loss, leadership and keeping knowledge
passages.text: For Timbisha Shoshone families in Death Valley, houses built in the 1930s came without indoor plumbing or electricity, and residents shared a water tap. Their seasonal travel out of the heat later became an excuse for officials to destroy empty houses. A home could be occupied seasonally and still be somebody’s home.

passages.title: Loss, leadership and keeping knowledge
passages.text: Timbisha women including Pauline Esteves and Barbara Durham helped lead the struggle for a secure homeland. Federal recognition in 1983 and the Timbisha Shoshone Homeland Act in 2000 were major steps. This southern community has its own history, rather than serving as a stand-in for every Shoshone nation.

passages.title: Loss, leadership and keeping knowledge
passages.text: A recorded Duck Valley expression is “Hakanni e?”, translated “How are you?” in the University of Utah’s Shoshoni dictionary. Its entry credits Crum, Crum and Dayley’s 2002 work. This is an attested modern spelling of a spoken expression, offered with its regional attribution.

passages.title: Loss, leadership and keeping knowledge
passages.text: The Shoshoni Talking Dictionary grew through collaboration with communities and young learners. Its history describes work with Ely Shoshone beginning in 2008 and later recordings involving youth and elders. A digital dictionary can carry pronunciation as well as print, preserving differences between speakers and communities.

passages.title: Loss, leadership and keeping knowledge
passages.text: At Fort Hall, the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes’ language and culture program describes archives supporting family history, land claims and language learning. Shoshone and Bannock instruction are identified separately. Family records can therefore help both a child asking about relatives and a nation documenting its rights.

The map’s 1783 cutoff is not an ending for Shoshone peoples. Distinct communities and governments continue, including Eastern Shoshone, Northwestern Shoshone and Timbisha Shoshone. Their histories include losses of land and lives, but also continuing language work, leadership and claims to home.

passages.text: Shu Han claimed legitimacy as the true successor to the Han dynasty, ruling Sichuan under Liu Bei and his famous chancellor Zhuge Liang. Though the smallest of the Three Kingdoms, it became the most romanticized in later literature.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The repeating crossbow, known since the Warring States, was improved under Zhuge Liang by tradition, along with the wooden ox, a wheelbarrow-like cart for carrying supplies over mountain roads.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Sichuan's irrigation, built around the Dujiangyan works of the third century BCE, was kept up and extended to feed the state.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Confucian legitimacy theory justified resistance to Cao Wei.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Loyalty and righteousness became central virtues in Shu Han ideology.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Zhuge Liang became the archetype of the brilliant but tragic loyal minister in Chinese culture.
Cao Wei general Deng Ai led a surprise attack through mountain passes and captured Chengdu, forcing Liu Shan to surrender.

passages.text: The atlas colors a patch of Ecuadorian Amazonia “Shuar” from 1279 to 1878, but it was never one kingdom with a border. Shuar-speaking households lived among rivers, forest, gardens and neighboring Chicham-language communities, including Achuar, Wampis and Awajún. Kin ties, visiting, marriage, exchange and conflict connected settlements; authority usually rested closer to household and local alliance than palace or capital. Families planted manioc and plantains, fished, hunted, made pottery and baskets, shared chicha, told stories and taught children by participation. Later observations help us ask about these activities, yet they cannot be photocopied into the Middle Ages. Spanish miners, forced labor, disease, missions and military expeditions brought devastation. Allied communities expelled colonial settlements in 1599 and defended substantial autonomy, although captives and frontier violence complicate any heroic cartoon. The famous tsantsa must be discussed as human remains whose meanings changed under a colonial collectors’ market, never as a spooky mascot. Archaeology reveals much older Upano settlements beneath this landscape but cannot simply name their builders Shuar. No securely attributable Shuar text survives from 1279 to 1878; today’s written tradition is later. The map ends when Ecuador and Peru replace Indigenous layers, while Shuar people, language, organizations and knowledge continue.

passages.title: Reading the map without inventing a kingdom
passages.text: The live index calls this record “Shuar,” dates it approximately 1279 to 1878 and labels its source historical basemaps. The coverage ledger calls it a state, but that database type is a drawing bucket, not evidence for a king, capital, tax system or single government.

passages.title: Reading the map without inventing a kingdom
passages.text: Shuar Chicham is one language in the Chicham family. Glottolog records its modern identifiers and alternate names; linguistic research distinguishes Shuar from Achuar, Wampis and Awajún. Related languages and overlapping histories do not turn all their speakers into one interchangeable ancient people or government.

passages.title: Reading the map without inventing a kingdom
passages.text: The polygon contains audited points around Macas, Sucúa, Méndez, Taisha, Morona, the Upano valley and Santiago River. Gualaquiza usually lies just outside. A crude seven-vertex outline cannot represent seasonal travel, marriage networks, gardens, river routes or locally understood territories and boundaries.

passages.title: Reading the map without inventing a kingdom
passages.text: Historical Shuar political life was strongly household- and kin-centered, with leaders and alliances assembled for particular needs rather than a permanent centralized state. Modern identity and territorial politics developed under new pressures. The atlas color therefore signals a research topic, not sovereign uniformity.

passages.title: Reading the map without inventing a kingdom
passages.text: The major Shuar federation dates to 1964, long after this card. Missions, schools, land pressure and the Ecuadorian state helped shape that organization, while Shuar leaders made it their own. It is living political achievement, but it cannot govern backward over people in 1279.

passages.title: Deep landscape, discoveries and how evidence works
passages.text: Lidar and excavation revealed platforms, plazas, roads, canals and fields in the Upano valley, with occupation beginning about 500 BCE and major abandonment centuries before this atlas layer. The discovery proves Amazonian landscape engineering, not that archaeologists found a medieval Shuar capital.

passages.title: Deep landscape, discoveries and how evidence works
passages.text: Researchers combined laser mapping with ground survey and excavation: lidar can see shape beneath vegetation, while soil layers, artifacts and dates test what a shape means. Museum reporting makes the achievement vivid without turning every platform into a palace or every road into an empire.

passages.title: Deep landscape, discoveries and how evidence works
passages.text: Ecuadorian heritage archaeology adds local site records, ceramics and regional context. Objects can reveal making, cooking, movement and exchange, but ethnic names rarely sit conveniently on a potsherd. Connecting a site to later Shuar history requires dated, contextual argument rather than visual resemblance.

passages.title: Deep landscape, discoveries and how evidence works
passages.text: “Lost city” headlines can make lidar look like a magic camera that instantly identifies a civilization. Archaeological-methods research warns that publicity often skips uncertainty and ground checking. A better kid question is, “What evidence would change this interpretation?”, the engine of real discovery.

passages.title: Deep landscape, discoveries and how evidence works
passages.text: Eastern Andean volcanoes, steep slopes, flood-prone rivers and humid forest create dramatic ecological variation. UNESCO documents rapid river-level changes, while today’s Kutukú research records extraordinary bird diversity and Shuar stewardship. Modern conservation evidence shows continuity of care, not an unchanged medieval ecosystem.

passages.title: Households, alliances, outsiders and changing power
passages.text: Authority often rested in capable household heads, healers, speakers and alliance builders. Influence depended on relationships and could shift with marriage, residence, reputation or danger. Calling every respected man a “chief” imports a permanent, rigid office that historical sources do not consistently support.

passages.title: Households, alliances, outsiders and changing power
passages.text: Spanish frontier projects sought gold, labor, souls and routes. A Science Panel synthesis places eastern Ecuador within wider colonial invasion and Indigenous resistance. Colonial records are indispensable but interested documents: miners and missionaries described obstacles in language designed to justify their own plans.

passages.title: Households, alliances, outsiders and changing power
passages.text: Archival reconstruction records mines from the 1550s, forced labor, tribute and epidemics before the 1599 uprising. Allied communities attacked colonial settlements after years of abuse. “Allied” matters: coordination can be powerful without proving one timeless nation, commander or bureaucratic state.

passages.title: Households, alliances, outsiders and changing power
passages.text: After 1599, repeated resistance constrained intensive colonial settlement and resource extraction for generations. Long environmental history connects that political autonomy to reduced deforestation. The outcome was not untouched wilderness: communities gardened, traveled, exchanged, fought and actively made this inhabited landscape together.

passages.title: Households, alliances, outsiders and changing power
passages.text: Jesuit missions in Maynas and later Salesian projects belonged to different centuries and strategies. Missionaries sought conversion and settlement; Indigenous people visited, negotiated, rejected, reinterpreted or avoided them. Modern federation politics grew partly through mission-era institutions, yet Shuar agency cannot be reduced to mission design.

passages.title: Gardens, food, fishing and hunting
passages.text: Later Shuar fieldwork describes household gardens centered on manioc and plantains, plus fruit and other crops. These observations illuminate durable Amazonian techniques, but the exact medieval crop mix still needs dated plant remains. Gardens were skilled, managed landscapes rather than scraps carved from “wild” forest.

passages.title: Gardens, food, fishing and hunting
passages.text: Contemporary research records women as major guardians of garden diversity and planting knowledge in particular Shuar communities. That is strong evidence for living expertise, not a rule assigning every past task by sex. Historical labor could change with household need, age, absence and local custom.

passages.title: Gardens, food, fishing and hunting
passages.text: Manioc could be cooked and made into chicha for nourishment, hospitality and cooperative work. In later accounts, chewing cooked manioc helps saliva turn starch toward fermentable sugars, a kitchen science fact that may earn an “eww!” from kids. Exact recipes and meanings varied by place and occasion.

passages.title: Gardens, food, fishing and hunting
passages.text: Hunting supplied some meat and knowledge of animal behavior, paths and seasons. One modern study measured trips and harvests in a single community; another notes women and children also hunted in studied settings. Neither result licenses a medieval stereotype that every Shuar man was always a hunter.

passages.title: Gardens, food, fishing and hunting
passages.text: Fishing brought people to streams and rivers, sometimes in cooperative groups that included children. Catch, water level and technique changed seasonally. Later ethnography helps picture social learning, but named fish, poisons, hooks or nets should not be assigned to 1279 without site-specific evidence.

passages.title: Pottery, tools, routes and exchange
passages.text: Historical material-culture research follows vessels, weapons, ornaments and imported goods across the sixteenth to nineteenth centuries. Objects were not passive markers of “contact”: people selected, repaired, exchanged and repurposed them. A metal tool could be useful without transferring its maker’s political authority.

passages.title: Pottery, tools, routes and exchange
passages.text: Pottery required finding clay, preparing temper, shaping walls, decorating, drying and firing while judging heat without a thermostat. Shuar-authored documentation preserves living knowledge and teaching. It provides questions for older ceramics, not permission to date every current design to the atlas interval.

passages.title: Pottery, tools, routes and exchange
passages.text: River corridors and footpaths connected homes, gardens, hunting places, neighboring communities and Andean markets. Loads moved by human effort and canoe where water allowed. Routes were social infrastructure: safe passage depended on knowledge, kin, hosts and negotiation as much as compass direction or distance.

passages.title: Pottery, tools, routes and exchange
passages.text: After Ecuadorian independence, state claims still exceeded routine control. Traders exchanged tools, cloth, fishhooks and other manufactures through fragile networks. New goods could save labor or create dependence, and their movement shows exchange across boundaries rather than a sudden switch from “traditional” to “modern.”

passages.title: Pottery, tools, routes and exchange
passages.text: From about 1850, firearms and a growing outside market for curios changed conflict and incentives. Late-century quinine and rubber extraction intensified trade in manufactured goods. These processes began near this card’s end and accelerated later, so they should not be projected across all six centuries.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, work, music and play
passages.text: Later architectural studies describe large open Shuar houses with named and sometimes gender-associated zones, built from forest materials and maintained by household labor. That comparison helps ask about ventilation, smoke and hospitality; it does not supply one floor plan for every family since 1279.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, work, music and play
passages.text: Daily work joined gardening, cooking, carrying water and fuel, pottery, basketry, childcare, fishing, hunting, visiting and house repair. Tasks overlapped: a child watching a pot also listened to stories, and a fishing trip taught river judgment. Historical documents record crises more readily than ordinary competence.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, work, music and play
passages.text: Clothing and ornament changed with climate, work, trade and occasion. Imported cloth appears increasingly in nineteenth-century exchange, but it supplemented rather than instantly erased locally made items and body arts. The atlas supplies no uniform, because there was no centralized Shuar army or official dress code.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, work, music and play
passages.text: Cooperative work could be supported by food, drink, visiting and reputation. Modern anthropology examines how sharing and inequality now change together. Similar cooperation may have older roots, yet the exact rules, obligations and power differences in 1400 cannot be recovered by simply copying a present-day minga.

passages.title: Homes, clothing, work, music and play
passages.text: Recorded Shuar songs, dance music and children’s experiences show that daily life included humor, rhythm, stories and play as well as work. Smithsonian recordings preserve modern performances, not a medieval playlist. A responsible card can celebrate living music without inventing ancient lyrics or pretending styles stood still.

passages.title: Family, women, children and learning
passages.text: Households and kin networks organized production, care, visiting, marriage and protection. Residence and alliances could change, so one isolated dot cannot represent a community. Later research finds cooperation among related households while also documenting difference, disagreement, inequality and new economic pressures.

passages.title: Family, women, children and learning
passages.text: Women’s garden and pottery knowledge are highly visible in contemporary Shuar-authored and scholarly work. Those skills carry intellectual authority: choosing seed, reading soil and controlling a firing are expert decisions. Women’s lives also varied, and neither “equal forest society” nor “unchanging gender roles” fits the evidence.

passages.title: Family, women, children and learning
passages.text: Children learned by listening, watching, helping, imitating and being corrected. Contemporary childhood research records growing participation in household work, food gathering and social life. For earlier centuries this is comparison, not a timetable: age, skill, personality and family circumstances shaped what any child did.

passages.title: Family, women, children and learning
passages.text: Mission schools and alphabetic instruction came much later than the first atlas centuries and carried religious and colonial aims. Families could value literacy while resisting other demands. Education is broader than school: river routes, plants, kin histories, speech, safety and craft all required rigorous learning.

passages.title: Family, women, children and learning
passages.text: Living community health research shows Shuar settlements today differ greatly in roads, markets, schooling and services. This warns against a single daily-life template even now, much less across 599 years. The best historical reconstruction keeps families active and knowledgeable while naming what sources cannot resolve.

passages.title: Health, plant knowledge, healing and belief
passages.text: Care began with observation, food, rest, cleaning wounds, social support and knowledge of the environment. Archaeology and colonial records preserve only fragments of those choices. We should describe skilled care without promising that every old remedy worked or treating Indigenous medicine as either magic or modern pharmacy.

passages.title: Health, plant knowledge, healing and belief
passages.text: A Shuar-produced book about tsentsak and healing specialists preserves interviews and community explanations on their own intellectual terms. It is contemporary evidence with historical depth, not a transcript from 1500. Translation also matters because English words such as “shaman” can flatten distinct roles and theories.

passages.title: Health, plant knowledge, healing and belief
passages.text: Ethnobotanical research across five communities and a local study in Shimpis record many plant names, preparations and reported uses. Variation between communities is itself a finding. Scientific documentation does not automatically verify clinical effectiveness, dosage safety or continuous use since the Middle Ages.

passages.title: Health, plant knowledge, healing and belief
passages.text: Illness also came through colonial contact. Archival histories describe epidemic loss alongside mining and forced labor before 1599. Disease was not a neutral natural disaster: forced movement, crowding, hunger, violence and unequal access to food and care shaped exposure, recovery and survival.

passages.title: Health, plant knowledge, healing and belief
passages.text: Current co-produced research treats Shuar ecological knowledge as expertise and community members as research partners. It documents gardens, fishing, cooking and plants while recognizing climate change. That method offers a model for studying continuity: ask living people, share authority and avoid mining knowledge like another resource.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets and the honest evidence gap
passages.text: Rivers and streams supplied travel, food, washing and water in a landscape where rain and flood levels could change quickly. Water carried risk as well as life. Choosing a landing, keeping paths passable and knowing when a river was dangerous were forms of practical education.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets and the honest evidence gap
passages.text: Households had to carry water, manage ash, food scraps, broken pots and other refuse, and keep living areas usable. Yet the cited archaeology does not identify a standard Shuar waste system for 1279 to 1878. Ordinary cleaning often disappears unless excavation records deposits carefully.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets and the honest evidence gap
passages.text: No securely excavated, date-specific Shuar toilet is established by these sources. People certainly urinated and defecated, but a tidy claim about a special latrine, wiping material or universal forest rule would be invention. The accurate bathroom fact for kids is that evidence can be missing.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets and the honest evidence gap
passages.text: A modern health study records real variation in household water and latrines and relates conditions to infection and child growth. It cannot tell us how a family managed waste in 1600. It does show why sanitation matters and why present infrastructure should never be mistaken for timeless culture.

passages.title: Water, waste, toilets and the honest evidence gap
passages.text: Modern settlements with schools, roads, tanks, pipes, clinics or latrines reflect community decisions, public policy and unequal investment. Living Shuar people are not museum exhibits. Historical continuity includes innovation: adopting safer water or toilets changes infrastructure without making language, kinship or identity less Indigenous.

passages.title: Violence, tsantsa, writing, achievements and continuity
passages.text: Warfare and feuding had social histories; outside trade later altered their scale and rewards. Tsantsa carried meanings tied to relationships and power, then colonial collectors’ demand encouraged killing, trafficking and fabrication. Treating the practice as a timeless Shuar personality repeats the market’s dehumanizing gaze.

passages.title: Violence, tsantsa, writing, achievements and continuity
passages.text: Tsantsa in museums are possible human remains, not spooky props. Imaging and provenance studies can help distinguish human, animal and commercial examples, but scientific authentication does not settle ownership. Ethical work includes consultation, careful handling, transparent provenance and potential repatriation rather than curiosity alone.

passages.title: Violence, tsantsa, writing, achievements and continuity
passages.text: Pitt Rivers Museum education asks students to examine colonial collection and community consultation. This shifts the fun-house question “How was it made?” toward better questions: Whose relative may this be? How did it leave? Who decides display, research or return?

passages.title: Violence, tsantsa, writing, achievements and continuity
passages.text: Written-language sample: none can be responsibly shown for this exact 1279 to 1878 layer. Shuar Chicham was transmitted orally, while sustained Shuar authorship, dictionaries and standardized alphabetic practices belong mainly to later mission, school and Indigenous writing histories. Borrowing a modern sentence would fake a contemporaneous voice.

passages.title: Violence, tsantsa, writing, achievements and continuity
passages.text: Achievements include sustaining gardens and kin networks, navigating rivers, making pottery, preserving language and knowledge, building alliances, defeating exploitative settlements and later organizing politically. The 1878 map replacement by Ecuador and Peru is editorial. Shuar communities and institutions live, adapt and defend land today.

At 1878 the exact Shuar feature disappears and audited core points switch to Ecuador, while Peruvian points farther south switch to Peru. That is an atlas taxonomy change, not annexation completed on one day and certainly not the end of Shuar people. Communities, Shuar Chicham, local knowledge and later federations continued amid stronger state, mission and extractive pressure.

materialEvidence.question: Does a concrete finding have an identifiable context, date, interpretation and evidence limit?

dailyLife.question: Does the account explain ordinary practices with evidence rather than only rulers?

artsScienceTechnology.question: Are achievements concrete and correctly attributed to this polity and period?

chronologicalPhases.question: Are source-supported phases distinguished from map snapshot dates?

endingContinuity.question: Does the narrative identify what ended or continued, with dates, mechanism and uncertainty?

uncertainty.question: Are uncertainties attached to particular claims rather than a blanket disclaimer?
