sectionTitles: An independent country and children’s lives

passages.text: These two map records follow Sierra Leone through British colonial government and independence on 27 April 1961. The later label begins in 1960, one year too early to represent an independent state. Earlier coastal outlines also must not be read as control of the entire later country: Britain declared the inland protectorate only in 1896.

passages.title: Ports, coercion and learning
passages.text: Britain made Sierra Leone a colony in 1808, but its later national territory was not one uniform colony from that date. The hinterland became a protectorate in 1896. Keeping those categories separate helps explain why an early map outline can exaggerate the reach of a colonial administration.

passages.title: Ports, coercion and learning
passages.text: Bunce Island preserves the walls of a slave-trading complex used from the late 1600s to 1807. Its merchants’ quarters, gunpowder store, cookhouse and captive holding yard made a connected system. These ruins show how buildings helped organize the imprisonment and forced transport of people across the Atlantic.

passages.title: Ports, coercion and learning
passages.text: Rice-growing expertise traveled under terrible circumstances. Captives from this West African rice-growing region were sought by plantation owners in South Carolina and Georgia. Their agricultural knowledge was valuable, although the people who possessed it were denied freedom and the rewards of their work.

passages.title: Ports, coercion and learning
passages.text: Fourah Bay College began in 1827. Its later waterfront building opened in 1848 on a site previously connected with slave trading; the heritage survey records that its roof used timber from condemned slave ships. The material of a coercive trade was literally reused in a place of learning.

passages.title: Cloth, language and everyday ingenuity
passages.text: A Mende country cloth made before 1899, now catalogued in Brighton, has sixteen blue strips sewn into a large textile. Makers spun cotton into thread, dyed it and wove narrow lengths on a tripod loom before joining them edge to edge. A big cloth did not require a giant loom.

passages.title: Cloth, language and everyday ingenuity
passages.text: Country cloth could communicate wealth and prestige as well as keep a body covered. The same catalogue records the Brighton example as 1.55 metres wide and 3.7 metres long. Its seams preserve the practical decisions of spinners, dyers, weavers and stitchers, even though the maker’s name is unrecorded.

passages.title: Cloth, language and everyday ingenuity
passages.text: A short written Krio sample is “fes di it kam”, translated “Bring the food here.” It appears as example 27 in Malcolm Awadajin Finney’s 2013 linguistic survey. This is a modern scholarly transcription in a Latin-based script, not a colonial inscription; the sequence of verbs is a normal grammatical construction.

passages.title: Cloth, language and everyday ingenuity
passages.text: Krio has a history of educational exclusion as well as creativity. Finney describes pupils once being punished for speaking it at school, followed by its later inclusion in education and extensive use in radio, television and political speech. A language can flourish in public life after institutions have tried to silence it.

passages.title: An independent country and children’s lives
passages.text: Independence came on 27 April 1961, not at the atlas’s 1960 label change. The diplomatic record marks that day explicitly. A new international status changed who governed the country; it did not replace its communities, local languages or accumulated knowledge with a completely new population.

passages.title: An independent country and children’s lives
passages.text: After a devastating civil war, disarmament helped make elections possible in May 2002. The United Nations account emphasizes Sierra Leoneans’ own determination to secure peace, alongside international support. Rebuilding involved restoring local administration and helping former fighters return to civilian work, not simply announcing that shooting had stopped.

passages.title: An independent country and children’s lives
passages.text: At Services Secondary School in Freetown, UNICEF reported in February 2023 that girls met weekly with trained peer mentors to discuss menstruation. Kits included reusable pads, underwear, soap and instructions; teachers and boys also joined the effort to reduce stigma. Ordinary supplies and accurate information can determine whether a pupil feels able to attend lessons.

passages.title: An independent country and children’s lives
passages.text: A 2022 account from Jui gives a family example: Abdul Sesay used his school peer-mentor training to reassure his sister Daniella when her first period made her afraid to attend school. He encouraged her to speak with their grandmother and explained how to obtain pads. Education could travel home in a brother’s schoolbag.
Colonial rule ended in 1961. The war’s end and elections in 2002 opened another period of rebuilding; neither change meant the disappearance of Sierra Leone’s people or languages.

passages.text: Picture Lahore in 1801: horsemen crowd a gate, silver rupees ring at a mint, Persian clerks bend over account books, and Ranjit Singh is proclaimed Maharaja. He had taken Lahore in 1799 and was turning Sikh misls into the State of Lahore, later called the Sikh Empire. The atlas labels its 1800 polygon “Sikhs,” but a faith and a people are not the same thing as a government. Muslims, Hindus and Sikhs lived in the mapped territory and served its court and army. Nor is the map a reliable conquest diary: it includes Multan, Kashmir, Peshawar and Cis-Sutlej states years before, or despite, their political relationship with Ranjit Singh. During the real 1800 to 1815 story, the ruler secured Lahore and Amritsar, issued Nanakshahi coins, experimented with infantry and artillery, signed the 1809 Treaty of Amritsar, took Attock in 1813 and failed repeatedly at Multan. In 1815 the atlas suddenly paints Punjab Maratha, an impossible seam. The Sikh Empire did not fall then. It expanded afterward, survived Ranjit Singh until 1839, and ended under British annexation in 1849, while Sikh communities and traditions continued.

passages.title: Audit the exact atlas identity first
passages.text: The live record is exact id “sikhs,” imported label “Sikhs,” circa 1800 to 1815, with one state feature and no card when first audited. Its imported summary defines followers of Sikhism, but its geometry is territorial. This card preserves the id while correcting the subject to Ranjit Singh's early state.

passages.title: Audit the exact atlas identity first
passages.text: At 1800 the target is one Polygon with one ring and 35 positions. Its bounds are 67.445° to 81.449° east and 27.710° to 35.989° north. The exact coordinate SHA-256 is 2cd9186c13755098f800c6d299b2c5001c9b57b4a8eab40d00cd2f2820f187b5. These numbers identify imported display geometry, not surveyed sovereignty.

passages.title: Audit the exact atlas identity first
passages.text: Point tests put Lahore, Amritsar, Gujranwala, Sialkot, Kasur, Multan, Peshawar, Rawalpindi, Attock, Jammu, Srinagar, Kangra, Ludhiana, Patiala, Firozpur and Tarn Taran inside, but exclude Anandpur Sahib and Delhi. A polygon test cannot tell who paid tax, held a fort or practiced Sikhism.

passages.title: Audit the exact atlas identity first
passages.text: The shape is badly ahead of events. Multan fell only in 1818, Kashmir in 1819 and Peshawar was annexed in 1834; the Cis-Sutlej states were not absorbed after the 1809 treaty. Meanwhile Anandpur Sahib, a crucial Sikh place, falls outside. The border must never be read as exact rule in 1800.

passages.title: Audit the exact atlas identity first
passages.text: The preceding 1783 snapshot calls much of the central region “Lahore,” with Multan and Cis-Sutlej areas separate. In 1815 the exact id vanishes and the atlas absurdly assigns every tested Punjab point to “maratha.” Neither seam supplies a trustworthy predecessor, conqueror or successor for the State of Lahore.

passages.title: Keep faith, community and state distinct
passages.text: Sikhism and Sikh communities began centuries before this map window and continued long afterward. The plural atlas label can accidentally turn every inhabitant into a Sikh and every Sikh into Ranjit Singh's subject. Both moves are wrong: the empire was religiously diverse, and Sikh communities also lived beyond its authority.

passages.title: Keep faith, community and state distinct
passages.text: The Khalsa was founded in 1699 as a collective of initiated Sikhs bound by shared discipline and ideals. It helps explain later political language and military identity, but it was not created in 1800 and was not identical to every soldier, taxpayer, villager or institution inside the State of Lahore.

passages.title: Keep faith, community and state distinct
passages.text: Before Ranjit Singh, Sikh misls were shifting warrior confederacies with their own leaders, territories and alliances. They could cooperate, compete or fight. Calling them a ready-made unitary empire hides the negotiations and coercion required to build a stronger Lahore-centered state at the end of the eighteenth century.

passages.title: Keep faith, community and state distinct
passages.text: Ranjit Singh entered Lahore on 7 July 1799 after local invitation and political maneuvering, then used the city as his capital. That event is a better historical opening than the atlas date 1800, which merely marks the first border snapshot containing the exact id.

passages.title: Keep faith, community and state distinct
passages.text: Persian chroniclers called the government Sarkar Khalsaji, while historians also use State of Lahore and Sikh Empire. Each name highlights something different: Khalsa legitimacy, the capital, or later imperial reach. The indexed id remains “sikhs,” but the card names the mapped polity rather than redefining a whole religion.

passages.title: Follow consolidation without a victory montage
passages.text: Ranjit Singh was proclaimed Maharaja in 1801. His new coinage did not simply stamp “Ranjit rules” across Punjab. Nanakshahi legends invoked the Gurus and divine grace, helping the ruler claim legitimacy while presenting authority as larger than his personal name.

passages.title: Follow consolidation without a victory montage
passages.text: Taking Amritsar in 1802 brought a major sacred and commercial center under his control. It also brought the Zamzama cannon, nicknamed Bhangian di Top. Famous objects make memorable stories, but one giant gun could not replace powder makers, gunners, oxen or horses, road crews and repair shops.

passages.title: Follow consolidation without a victory montage
passages.text: Kasur was taken in 1807 after earlier pressure and conflict. Such expansion mixed sieges, tribute demands, appointments and negotiated submission. A town could be attacked more than once, and a local chief's promise was not the same thing as uniform administration across every farm beyond its walls.

passages.title: Follow consolidation without a victory montage
passages.text: The Treaty of Amritsar was signed on 25 April 1809. Ranjit Singh accepted a boundary to his ambitions south of the Sutlej, while the East India Company promised not to interfere north of it. The agreement frustrated one direction of expansion but gave him room to consolidate elsewhere.

passages.title: Follow consolidation without a victory montage
passages.text: Attock came under Ranjit Singh's power in 1813, strengthening access to the Indus corridor. Yet repeated Multan expeditions had failed by 1815. The record is therefore one of real expansion mixed with stubborn limits, not the smooth, continent-sized success suggested by the atlas polygon.

passages.title: See how the Lahore state worked
passages.text: Ranjit Singh supervised diplomacy, war, appointments, revenue and petitions closely. Power remained personal and court-centered rather than divided into modern ministries with printed rulebooks. Provincial governors, commanders, revenue officers, local chiefs and village institutions linked Lahore decisions to places where the ruler could not be present.

passages.title: See how the Lahore state worked
passages.text: Sikh elites held many important posts, yet Hindu and Muslim officials, soldiers and landholders also served the state. Religious grants crossed community lines. It is safer to describe strategic, plural patronage than to paste a modern label onto the court or assume equal power for every faith and rank.

passages.title: See how the Lahore state worked
passages.text: Khalsa Darbar records survive in Persian from 1811. They track income, expenditure, troops, establishments and orders, revealing an administration that counted resources rather than governing by heroic speeches alone. Surviving files are uneven, however, and an account total is not a complete census of the whole kingdom.

passages.title: See how the Lahore state worked
passages.text: Jagirs assigned rights to collect revenue, sometimes in cash and sometimes in kind, in return for service or support. Grants could be temporary or last for life; they were not always private farms owned forever. This system tied commanders and officials to the ruler while leaving room for bargaining and abuse.

passages.title: See how the Lahore state worked
passages.text: Thousands of Bhandari papers preserve Persian correspondence, court orders, deeds, mortgages, grants and revenue documents. Their very variety is an achievement: rule required scribes, seals, archives and people who knew local custom. They also show why one court chronicle cannot explain every dispute or transaction.

passages.title: Build an army, then check the dates
passages.text: Early state forces combined irregular cavalry with growing infantry and artillery. Some infantry learned drill from deserters who had served the East India Company. Soldiers came from different religious and regional backgrounds, so equipment, pay and loyalty could vary. A parade-ground army was still being made during this card's window.

passages.title: Build an army, then check the dates
passages.text: The 1811 records list 2,852 regular infantry and 1,209 artillery personnel, a useful dated glimpse rather than a final total. Hindustanis, Gurkhas, Afghans, Sikhs and others appear in recruitment evidence. Numbers in one account category should not be stretched into every fort, retainer or irregular horseman.

passages.title: Build an army, then check the dates
passages.text: Workshops cast or repaired guns and made ammunition, while horse-drawn artillery improved movement. Cannons still demanded skilled crews, measured powder, shot, draft animals and dry storage. The noisy blast was only the exciting final second of a much longer supply chain.

passages.title: Build an army, then check the dates
passages.text: Diplomacy mattered beside battle. The 1809 treaty lowered the chance of immediate war with the East India Company but protected Cis-Sutlej rulers from Ranjit Singh. Maps showing Ludhiana and Patiala inside his polygon erase exactly the political boundary that the treaty formalized.

passages.title: Build an army, then check the dates
passages.text: European officers Allard and Ventura arrived only in 1822, after the atlas interval, and helped develop the later Fauj-i-Khas. The early army was already changing, but dressing every 1805 soldier like the famous later European-drilled corps would be a costume-history mistake.

passages.title: Trace fields, trade, money and art
passages.text: Most wealth ultimately depended on land, crops, herds and the people who worked them. Revenue demands passed through layered rights and local power. Punjab produced grain and other crops, while pastoral communities also paid tribute. “Farmer” covered owners, tenants and laborers whose security could differ sharply.

passages.title: Trace fields, trade, money and art
passages.text: Routes linked Punjab westward and toward Kashmir and the plains. Recorded trade included rice, sugar, indigo and white cloth moving outward, with horses, fruit, lead and spices coming in; Kashmir exchanged shawls and saffron. Lists of goods show movement, not what every child ate or wore.

passages.title: Trace fields, trade, money and art
passages.text: Lahore began striking silver rupees in 1801 and Amritsar followed in 1805 to 1806. Coins standardized payments and broadcast sacred-political messages. They also reveal mints and metalworking, although finding a coin far away can show trade or saving rather than direct rule by the issuing state.

passages.title: Trace fields, trade, money and art
passages.text: The court stored gifts in its toshakhana and rewarded loyalty through robes, jewels, weapons and other objects. A celebrated gold throne was made around 1805 to 1810 by Hafiz Muhammad Multani, a Muslim goldsmith. Its glitter records specialist craft and court power, not an ordinary Punjabi chair.

passages.title: Trace fields, trade, money and art
passages.text: Ranjit Singh sponsored marble and gilded decoration at the Harimandir Sahib, later called the Golden Temple. The shrine long predated him, and work continued in stages. Crediting his patronage is accurate; pretending he founded the whole sacred complex in 1800 is not.

passages.title: Read several languages and kinds of learning
passages.text: Persian served the court and much administration, while Punjabi was widely spoken and Gurmukhi was central to Sikh scripture and community learning. Gurmukhi use spread in administration under Ranjit Singh, but no single language or script reached every village, office, trader and religious institution in the same way.

passages.title: Read several languages and kinds of learning
passages.text: Education formed a multilingual landscape. Maktabs and madrasas taught through Islamic institutions, pathshalas used Sanskritic curricula, Gurmukhi schools served Sikh learning, and Landa scripts helped some merchant boys. Categories overlapped, access varied by place and family, and attendance was never universal.

passages.title: Read several languages and kinds of learning
passages.text: Retrospective studies describe children beginning with alphabets, copying, recitation and practical arithmetic, while elite families could hire tutors. Some girls and women learned too, but evidence is patchier and opportunity unequal. These reports illuminate Sikh-period traditions without providing an 1805 enrollment census.

passages.title: Read several languages and kinds of learning
passages.text: Religion shaped patronage, calendars and learning, yet the state population was not one congregation. Gurdwaras, mosques, temples, shrines and teachers served different communities. Court grants could support several traditions, partly from devotion and partly because rulers built alliances through respected local institutions.

passages.title: Read several languages and kinds of learning
passages.text: Persian files and coin legends survive more often than a child's exercise sheet. That survival bias makes courts look more literate than kitchens or workshops. Historians compare archives, objects and later educational reports, then say plainly when they cannot calculate ordinary literacy or reconstruct a typical lesson.

passages.title: Meet families, ranks, women and children carefully
passages.text: Ranjit Singh's household was a political institution. Queens, mothers, sons and in-laws could command property, patronage, alliances and succession claims. Priya Atwal's dynastic history restores women and princes to the story, while warning us that royal family power says little about an ordinary farm household.

passages.title: Meet families, ranks, women and children carefully
passages.text: Society contained rulers, jagirdars, religious specialists, merchants, artisans, cultivators, pastoralists, servants and laborers, with status also shaped by caste, clan, gender, wealth and locality. Sikh teachings challenged inherited pride, but ideals did not erase hierarchy, dependence or unequal access to land and office.

passages.title: Meet families, ranks, women and children carefully
passages.text: Female singers and dancers worked at the Lahore court, sometimes winning reward or influence and sometimes facing exploitation. Their visibility proves that women made culture and politics, not that all women shared court performers' opportunities. Sources written by male courtiers and visitors also filtered what later readers can see.

passages.title: Meet families, ranks, women and children carefully
passages.text: Children learned through households as well as schools: watching work, caring for animals, memorizing prayers, practicing letters or arithmetic and joining a family trade. Exact chores differed by rank, gender, place and season. No surviving source supplies one universal “day of a Sikh child” for 1800.

passages.title: Meet families, ranks, women and children carefully
passages.text: A British Library album from about 1860 shows couples working together, a woman spinning, another winnowing, a herder's wife holding a calf and children buying clay toys. It is valuable comparative material, but it was commissioned after annexation and cannot be silently backdated sixty years.

passages.title: Reconstruct daily life without pretending certainty
passages.text: Lahore contained a fortified core, lanes, markets, religious sites, gardens and elite havelis, while rural homes followed local materials and means. Ranjit Singh repaired defenses and encouraged rebuilding. Direct evidence for a standard 1800 house plan is thin, so palace rooms must not stand in for every mud-brick home.

passages.title: Reconstruct daily life without pretending certainty
passages.text: Rice, sugar, fruit, spices, curd, vegetables and sweets appear in trade lists or later Punjab images, but availability and daily meals differed by wealth, season, religion and locality. The sources do not justify serving every family one identical “traditional plate,” however delicious that imaginary dinner might be.

passages.title: Reconstruct daily life without pretending certainty
passages.text: Shawls, white cloth, robes of honor, turbans, jewelry and uniforms appear in trade, court and military evidence. Materials, cut and decoration signaled work, wealth and rank. Court textiles were portable politics; they should not become a universal costume pasted onto farmers, craft workers and children.

passages.title: Reconstruct daily life without pretending certainty
passages.text: A later painting places Ranjit Singh among merchants, mendicants, soldiers and townspeople in a bazaar. It helps us imagine crowded exchange, but the artist reused stock figure types and worked around 1830 to 1840. It is composed art, not a camera pointed at an 1805 street.

passages.title: Reconstruct daily life without pretending certainty
passages.text: The circa 1860 Lahore album shows potters, weavers, water carriers, vegetable sellers, sweet makers, cloth merchants and a seller of earthen toys to children. These tools and trades offer cautious continuity clues. They do not prove that play, wages or caste roles were unchanged since Ranjit Singh's first decade.

passages.title: Test medicine, water, writing and the ending
passages.text: Direct evidence for ordinary treatment in 1800 to 1815 is sparse. The later court physician Johann Martin Honigberger described overlapping European, homeopathic, Ayurvedic and Unani practice after arriving in 1829. That proves medical plurality later in the reign, not a doctor, diagnosis or remedy in every earlier village.

passages.title: Test medicine, water, writing and the ending
passages.text: Court sources mention sacred bathing at Amritsar and Tarn Taran. A later Lahore album shows a well, water carrier, Persian wheel and laundry. Ritual bathing, irrigation, washing and drinking water are different uses. Neither source demonstrates safe water at every home or a citywide pipe network in 1810.

passages.title: Test medicine, water, writing and the ending
passages.text: No consulted authoritative source securely identifies an ordinary Sikh-period household toilet, sewer network or regular waste-removal system. Lahore formed a sanitation committee in 1858 and opened municipal waterworks in 1882; formal preventive-health policy grew after 1860. Those later dates expose, rather than fill, the 1800 to 1815 evidence gap.

passages.title: Test medicine, water, writing and the ending
passages.text: An 1801 Lahore silver rupee carries the Persian clause “سکه زد بر سیم وزر فضل سچا صاحب است”. Transliteration: “Sikka zad bar sim wa zar, fazl sacha sahib ast.” Translation: “The coin struck in silver and gold by the grace of the true Lord.” This is a normalized readable transcription, not a facsimile of one tiny, worn die strike; spelling mixes Persian form with Sikh-Punjabi vocabulary.

passages.title: Test medicine, water, writing and the ending
passages.text: The 1815 atlas disappearance is not a fall. The kingdom expanded, Ranjit Singh ruled until 1839, later regencies fought the First Anglo-Sikh War, and Britain annexed Punjab on 29 March 1849 after the Second. The state ended; Sikh families, faith, language, institutions and political life did not.

The exact atlas feature stops in 1815 and replaces the audited Punjab region with a Maratha polygon, but that seam is historically impossible. Ranjit Singh's State of Lahore continued and survived his death in 1839. Political instability and the two Anglo-Sikh wars eventually brought British annexation on 29 March 1849. Even 1849 ended a state, not Sikh people or Sikhism. The structured ending is therefore continuity at the atlas endpoint, with fell set to null and no false link to Maratha or the East India Company.

sectionTitles: Homes, food, families and useful bamboo
Health and learning, with dates attached
A word for home, and continuing knowledge

passages.text: This atlas record covers Sikkim from 1815 to 1878, during growing British intervention. Its single outline includes Darjeeling even after the 1835 cession, so it cannot represent changing borders accurately. The imported label “Indian princely state” is shorthand for changing relationships with British India, not membership in independent India. Sikkim’s kingdom and diverse communities had histories far beyond this map interval.

passages.title: Rulers, borders and unequal treaties
passages.text: The 1817 Treaty of Titalia restored hill territory between the Mechi and Teesta rivers to Sikkim’s ruler. It also required him to submit disputes to British arbitration and assist British troops. Restored territory therefore came with political obligations.

passages.title: Rulers, borders and unequal treaties
passages.text: The 1861 Treaty of Tumlong followed a British invasion. Its clauses required support for a trade road and rest houses, permitted surveys, and limited dealings with neighboring states. These were concrete restrictions on royal authority, not merely a friendly exchange of promises.

passages.title: Rulers, borders and unequal treaties
passages.text: Trade rules affected travelers as well as rulers. Tumlong capped customs on goods passing toward Tibet, Bhutan or Nepal at five percent and required a pass after payment. That piece of paperwork was meant to prevent another charge farther along the route.

passages.title: Homes, food, families and useful bamboo
passages.text: During his late-1840s travels, Hooker described Lepcha workers making temporary waterproof shelters with leaf or bamboo thatch, plus tables and sleeping platforms, using heavy knives. A skilled builder could turn nearby plants into a furnished camp: flat-pack furniture, forest edition.

passages.title: Homes, food, families and useful bamboo
passages.text: Hooker recorded bamboo stems used as water vessels and leaves used for roofing around Darjeeling. Some young shoots were eaten. Choosing the right bamboo mattered: a plant useful for a sturdy container was not necessarily the best one to split into fine strips.

passages.title: Homes, food, families and useful bamboo
passages.text: His account of Lepcha families describes marriage arrangements involving either payments or labor for the bride’s family, followed by a public feast. Household work, farming and family obligations were closely connected. This is one outsider’s nineteenth-century report, not a rule for every family.

passages.title: Homes, food, families and useful bamboo
passages.text: A surviving nineteenth-century Lepcha basket base is woven from light-brown and red bamboo strips. It is about twenty centimeters across and weighs only fifty-five grams. Light materials could still require careful, patient work: every strip had to fit the pattern.

passages.title: Homes, food, families and useful bamboo
passages.text: The basket’s catalogue lists Sikkim or Darjeeling as possible origins, with question marks. Its collection history is unknown. This makes it valuable evidence of a named craft tradition, but it cannot tell us which household made it or exactly where that family lived.

passages.title: Health and learning, with dates attached
passages.text: Hooker reported strong fear of smallpox and demand for vaccination in the Darjeeling area. Doctors Pearson and Campbell provided it. This belongs to the British settlement after the cession; it does not establish that every remote Sikkimese village had access to vaccination.

passages.title: Health and learning, with dates attached
passages.text: Buddhist teaching centers long predated the atlas’s opening. Sikkim’s ecclesiastical history connects their foundation with the royal consecration of 1642 and subsequent patronage. Monasteries linked learning, religious authority and government; this did not mean that every child attended a monastery.

passages.title: Health and learning, with dates attached
passages.text: Later developments must stay later: historian Alex McKay places the growth of Western-style schools within Sikkim from the 1880s, followed by a supply of locally trained medical workers. Those institutions belong beyond the map’s 1878 endpoint, not in its earliest villages.

passages.title: Plants, knowledge and imperial power
passages.text: Hooker’s plant collecting depended on Lepcha assistants who knew the forests, gathered specimens and dried them. Botanical discovery was collaborative labor. Plants newly described for European science were often already familiar to the people who helped the visiting botanist find them.

passages.title: Plants, knowledge and imperial power
passages.text: The first part of The Rhododendrons of the Sikkim-Himalaya appeared in 1849, while Hooker was still away. Walter Hood Fitch turned field sketches into published botanical pictures. A flower could travel as a dried specimen and a carefully painted scientific image.

passages.title: Plants, knowledge and imperial power
passages.text: Collecting was entangled with power. Sikkim’s leaders worried that surveying visitors could help outsiders control their country. Hooker and Campbell crossed a prohibited frontier and were imprisoned in 1849; British threats secured their release, followed by territorial punishment for Sikkim.

passages.title: A word for home, and continuing knowledge
passages.text: Here is a Lepcha word printed in Mainwaring’s 1876 grammar: ᰜᰧᰶ, li in simplified Roman transcription, meaning “house.” The original page shows the Lepcha letters beside the English gloss. This is an attested nineteenth-century printed example, reproduced here with modern Unicode characters.

passages.title: A word for home, and continuing knowledge
passages.text: The same grammar distinguishes words for an older brother and older sister, while younger siblings can be specified with additional gender terms. A grammar book preserves more than rules for sentences: it can reveal distinctions speakers make when talking about their families.

passages.title: A word for home, and continuing knowledge
passages.text: Long after this map interval, Gangtok’s Namgyal Institute of Tibetology opened in 1958. Its collections preserve texts, printing blocks, paintings and ritual objects. These surviving materials connect historical learning with research by living communities, rather than treating Sikkim’s traditions as things that ended in 1878.

passages.title: A word for home, and continuing knowledge
passages.text: The institute added a Tibetan medicine department in 2018. That dated example shows continuing study of Sowa-Rigpa alongside changing educational institutions. It should not be mistaken for a nineteenth-century medical college or evidence that a historical remedy was clinically effective.

The 1878 endpoint is only a break in this atlas record. Sikkim’s monarchy continued beyond it; much later, in 1975, Sikkim became a state of India. Its communities, languages, religious institutions and knowledge continued through those political changes.

passages.text: Silla began as the smallest of Korea's Three Kingdoms, in the southeast around Gyeongju, and by 676 had brought most of the peninsula under one rule. Its bone-rank aristocracy, gold crowns, Hwarang youth bands and Buddhist temples made a distinctive civilization that lasted nearly a thousand years.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Gold crowns with tree and antler uprights, hung with jade and gold spangles, from the royal mound tombs of Gyeongju.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bulguksa temple and the Seokguram grotto, with its granite Buddha facing the sea, were begun; UNESCO listed both in 1995.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Cheomseongdae, a stone tower built in the reign of Queen Seondeok (632 to 647), is among the oldest surviving astronomical observatories in the world.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The bone-rank system fixed a person's rank, office and even the size of their house by birth.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Hwarang, bands of aristocratic youths, trained in arms, song and Buddhist and Confucian teaching, and led Silla's armies.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Buddhism became the state religion after the martyrdom of Ichadon, and temples rose across the kingdom.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Gyeongju grew into a planned capital of palaces, temples, markets and tiled houses, with the Anapji pleasure pond laid out in 674.

passages.title: Daily life
passages.text: Court culture prized refinement, poetry in the hyangga form and Buddhist devotion.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Gyeongju Historic Areas were listed by UNESCO.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Unified Silla's administration, Buddhism and script laid the foundations of later Korean culture.
The last king, Gyeongsun, surrendered to Goryeo in 935, ending nearly a millennium of Silla rule counted from its traditional founding in 57 BCE.

sectionTitles: Learning, festivals and a visitor far from home
Objects, art and a voice in writing

passages.text: The map’s Simhala label covers Sri Lanka from about 500 BCE to 800 CE, a span of changing rulers and regional communities. Anuradhapura became a major capital and Buddhist center. Its island-shaped outline is not proof that one state controlled every district throughout these centuries; neither endpoint marks the beginning or disappearance of Sri Lankan civilization.

passages.title: Cities, rulers and sacred places
passages.text: Anuradhapura’s history lies in layers of rebuilt buildings and discarded objects. A trench only ten meters square descended through roughly ten meters of deposits. Excavations show an urban settlement and trade networks already developing before the third-century BCE missions traditionally associated with Ashoka.

passages.title: Cities, rulers and sacred places
passages.text: Buddhist tradition remembers the nun Sanghamitta bringing a cutting of the Bodhi tree from India in the third century BCE. The tree became a living focus of pilgrimage at Anuradhapura, connecting generations of worshippers with the story of the Buddha’s enlightenment.

passages.title: Cities, rulers and sacred places
passages.text: The second-century BCE king Dutthagamani was remembered for monumental building, including the Ruvanvelisaya stupa and the Brazen Palace. Anuradhapura’s huge stupas made sacred relics visible in the cityscape: rounded monuments set on circular foundations, sometimes surrounded by rings of stone columns.

passages.title: Cities, rulers and sacred places
passages.text: Royal support could divide monasteries as well as enrich them. Around the late third century, Mahasena withdrew support from the Mahavihara and founded Jetavana; materials from Mahavihara were taken for Abhayagiri. His son restored relations, and all three communities continued receiving patronage.

passages.title: Cities, rulers and sacred places
passages.text: Between 477 and 495, Kashyapa made Sigiriya his royal stronghold amid a struggle with his brother Moggallana. Palaces, gardens and defenses transformed the rock and its surroundings. Kashyapa’s defeat ended this brief royal episode; the place subsequently served Buddhist monastic life again.

passages.title: Water, kitchens and families
passages.text: Reservoirs, often called tanks, stored water for dry-zone farming. Their history includes local chiefs, families, individual owners and royal patrons. An inscription might donate part of a tank’s income or water rights to a monastery, rather than hand over every field and every drop.

passages.title: Water, kitchens and families
passages.text: Water management required people with practical responsibilities. Second-century BCE inscriptions name a flow operator, a canal officer and an irrigation officer. Their precise job descriptions have not survived, but the titles show that directing water was organized work, not simply a king ordering a lake into existence.

passages.title: Water, kitchens and families
passages.text: A woman named Anulabi, daughter of Mitaya, appears in a roughly third-century rock inscription. She gave income from a share of her family’s reservoir to monks at Gagapavata. This unusually personal record shows family property and a woman making a substantial religious gift.

passages.title: Water, kitchens and families
passages.text: Some excavated bowls have shallow bodies, wide mouths and scratched interiors. Archaeologists compare them with the nambiliya, a bowl used to separate grit from rice. Examples in early settlements around Anuradhapura bring food preparation into view: someone still had to keep unwanted crunch out of dinner.

passages.title: Water, kitchens and families
passages.text: Another rock inscription, assigned to the fifth or sixth century, records a family’s effort to overcome slavery. Aba’s elder brother paid one hundred kahavanas to secure Aba’s freedom. The payment and the hope that it would earn religious merit are preserved; the brothers’ wider life stories are not.

passages.title: Learning, festivals and a visitor far from home
passages.text: The Chinese monk Faxian visited in the early fifth century. At Abhayagiri, the sight of a merchant offering a white silk fan brought him to tears after years away from familiar people and places. His account preserves homesickness beside descriptions of spectacular religious buildings.

passages.title: Learning, festivals and a visitor far from home
passages.text: Faxian describes preaching halls at four important streets. On designated days, people laid out carpets and raised a pulpit; monks and lay listeners gathered to hear teaching. Learning could happen through a public spoken gathering, rather than only through reading a manuscript.

passages.title: Learning, festivals and a visitor far from home
passages.text: During his two-year stay, Faxian obtained Buddhist disciplinary and scriptural texts unavailable in China. He carried them away by sea. When a storm threatened the ship, he feared the merchants would throw his books overboard with the cargo: a scholar’s luggage could be precious indeed.

passages.title: Learning, festivals and a visitor far from home
passages.text: For the tooth-relic festival, Faxian reports an announcement made from an elephant ten days ahead. The route displayed scenes from the Buddha’s past lives; devotees brought flowers and incense and lit lamps. Processions brought religion into shared streets and involved far more people than the clergy.

passages.title: Health, sanitation and practical ingenuity
passages.text: A chronicle credits King Upatissa I, in the fourth to early fifth century, with establishing maternity homes. This is literary evidence for care around childbirth. Surviving hospital ruins often belong to later centuries, so their detailed floor plans cannot simply be assigned to his reign.

passages.title: Health, sanitation and practical ingenuity
passages.text: Toilet engineering also survives at Abhayagiri, although the study does not securely date these particular structures before 800. Clay pipes led urine into stacks of bottomless pots, with traces suggesting sand, lime and charcoal filters. It is a revealing comparison from Anuradhapura’s longer history, not a model of every household bathroom.

passages.title: Health, sanitation and practical ingenuity
passages.text: The chronicles also credit the eighth-century king Aggabodhi VII with investigating medicinal plants and their effectiveness. In this account, royal concern for health extended beyond paying for buildings: it included curiosity about what remedies could do.

passages.title: Health, sanitation and practical ingenuity
passages.text: At Samanalawewa, ironworkers placed furnaces where monsoon winds could supply air to the fire. Archaeologists found evidence reaching back to the seventh century. Replica experiments produced high-carbon steel, demonstrating a sophisticated process in which careful furnace design made seasonal winds part of the workshop.

passages.title: Health, sanitation and practical ingenuity
passages.text: Sigiriya’s water gardens linked pools and fountains through underground conduits. Circular limestone plates formed fountain outlets, and some fountains still work when rainfall supplies sufficient water. The spectacle depended on engineering hidden beneath visitors’ feet, not just the beauty of the pools.

passages.title: Objects, art and a voice in writing
passages.text: Pottery jars from Anuradhapura’s layers dated 300 to 600 held a chemical clue to distant trade. Their waterproof bitumen lining was traced to Susa in Iran. The jars carried liquids, but analysis did not identify the contents: their shape alone cannot tell us what anyone drank.

passages.title: Objects, art and a voice in writing
passages.text: Sigiriya’s surviving paintings show richly adorned women, but their identities remain debated: royal figures, celestial beings and religious interpretations have all been proposed. Looking closely at the paintings reveals skill and courtly display; it does not establish that every pictured woman was one of Kashyapa’s wives.

passages.title: Objects, art and a voice in writing
passages.text: Anulabi’s inscription lets us read a real personal introduction: “Mitayaha jita Anuḷabi,” meaning “Anulabi, daughter of Mitaya.” This is a scholarly Latin-letter transliteration of an inscription originally carved in Brahmi letters, dated approximately to the third century. The original letter shapes differ from modern Sinhala script.

The map label stops at 800; Anuradhapura did not. Its later decline involved disrupted economic networks and political conflict, while other centers grew. Communities adapted, and Buddhist institutions, farming and Sri Lankan societies continued beyond this record’s boundaries.

passages.text: The atlas labels one 900 to 1000 layer “Sindh,” but its decoded 16-position polygon is not the lower Indus region or today’s Pakistani province. It includes tested Umarkot, Mithi, Nagarparkar, Bhuj, Lakhpat, Gandhidham, the central Rann, Barmer, and Tharad. It excludes Mansura, Aror, Banbhore, Thatta, Karachi, Hyderabad, Sehwan, Larkana, and Sukkur. Read the color as an editorial bucket across the Thar-Kutch corridor, not a surveyed border or uniform state. The historical doorway was more complicated: Habbarid emirs ruled from Mansura; Multan followed a separate political and religious course; ports connected inland producers to the Indian Ocean; and Kutch had its own changing settlement and environmental history. Archaeology recovers streets, houses, a reservoir, workshops, ceramics, and imported wares, while tenth-century geographers describe named cities, crops, clothing, trade, and languages. Their urban and court-facing reports do not speak for every farmer, pastoralist, fisher, craft worker, woman, or child. At 1000 the exact id disappears and most tested polygon points become “rajput-kingdoms.” Habbarid rule did not demonstrably fall that year, so this card treats the endpoint as a map seam and keeps communities in view.

passages.title: Read the polygon before trusting its name
passages.text: The exact index has one generated state id, “sindh,” named “Sindh,” with approximate dates 900 to 1000. It is present in one border file and still lacks a researched summary, card, review, or accepted override. The imported summary describes the modern province, so it is unsafe medieval copy.

passages.title: Read the polygon before trusting its name
passages.text: The 900 target is one Polygon with one ring, 16 decoded positions, and bbox 68.07128071280712, 22.777107514890602 to 73.42813428134284, 27.15540484530348. Its decoded geometry SHA-256 is 4fe97d38b91de7376dfb4be244cd046ac5f297b8a0814e291d9feea462193e1d. Those are reproducible display-data facts from a coarse digital shape, not historical survey coordinates or proof of control.

passages.title: Read the polygon before trusting its name
passages.text: Tested Umarkot, Mithi, Nagarparkar, Bhuj, Lakhpat, Gandhidham, the central Rann, Barmer, and Tharad lie inside. Mansura, Aror, Banbhore, Thatta, Karachi, Hyderabad, Sehwan, Larkana, Sukkur, Mirpur Khas, and Badin do not. The label therefore misses the Indus core normally central to medieval Sind history.

passages.title: Read the polygon before trusting its name
passages.text: At 800, the exact id is absent. The future polygon’s tested points are split among the atlas’s “hindu-states” and “vallabhi” layers, while Indus urban probes fall under “abbasid-caliphate.” At 900 those same Indus probes become “saffarids,” yet they remain outside the new Sindh polygon.

passages.title: Read the polygon before trusting its name
passages.text: At 1000, the target disappears. Most former member probes become “rajput-kingdoms,” while surrounding points divide among other atlas layers. By 1100, Indus centers sit in “soomra-emirate,” but Kutch and Thar probes again divide. Neither seam licenses a claim that one population vanished or changed identity overnight.

passages.title: Rulers, capitals, and power with boundaries attached
passages.text: The Habbarid family established independent authority at Mansura around the mid-ninth century. The reviewed archaeological monograph credits Umar with expanding the great mosque and building the government palace and other structures. That court history belongs to lower Sind, especially Mansura, which the atlas polygon itself excludes.

passages.title: Rulers, capitals, and power with boundaries attached
passages.text: A Pakistan Archaeology synthesis says caliphal authority assigned Sind to the Saffarids in 871 and that Samanids replaced them around 900, but neither exercised effective control. Its conclusion is two almost independent principalities, Mansura and Multan. The atlas instead colors different places and must not overwrite that distinction.

passages.title: Rulers, capitals, and power with boundaries attached
passages.text: Al-Masudi traveled through the Indus region in 915 to 916. A modern historical study associates his Mansura account with Umar ibn Abdullah but warns that a solitary report cannot settle every political question. Even impressive army, elephant, and village figures should be read as transmitted claims, not audited statistics.

passages.title: Rulers, capitals, and power with boundaries attached
passages.text: Religion and politics were not synchronized across the region. MacLean’s study treats Ismailism in Multan separately from religious life in Habbarid Mansura and from Hindu and Buddhist communities. A ruler’s sermon, judge, or mosque can reveal an institution without revealing the belief of every household beyond its walls.

passages.title: Rulers, capitals, and power with boundaries attached
passages.text: A British Museum authority file knows Muhammad, amir of Sind, principally through coins and dates him only broadly between 800 and 1000. That is a useful warning about ruler lists: a name on silver is strong evidence for authority, but a broad catalogue date cannot supply an exact reign or border.

passages.title: Trade, farming, river routes, and the Indian Ocean
passages.text: Banbhore occupied an old Indus-channel setting near the coast. The Government of Sindh describes a long-lived early Islamic port site, but the identification with written Debal remains a scholarly proposal rather than a settled fact. Its location still makes it crucial evidence for exchange between river country and sea routes.

passages.title: Trade, farming, river routes, and the Indian Ocean
passages.text: Banbhore’s museum inventory includes eighth-century storage jars, glass from the Muslim-period sequence, and Chinese pottery dated broadly from the ninth through twelfth centuries. Those ranges cross this card’s interval but extend beyond it. They prove long-distance material connections more safely than they date any single family’s cupboard.

passages.title: Trade, farming, river routes, and the Indian Ocean
passages.text: Ibn Hawqal compares Multan with Mansura: Multan was smaller and fortified, its produce cheap and its territory fertile, though cultivated less carefully. This is useful evidence for urban markets and farming contrasts, but one geographer’s comparison cannot be pasted onto inland farmers, desert pastoralists, port workers, or Kutch settlements.

passages.title: Trade, farming, river routes, and the Indian Ocean
passages.text: Al-Istakhri records date palms, sugar cane, a very sour apple-sized fruit, and mango-like fruit around Mansura. Cheap abundance in a geographic text signals productive cultivation and markets, though it gives no farm sizes or labor shares. Please resist inventing a medieval fruit salad recipe from a crop list.

passages.title: Trade, farming, river routes, and the Indian Ocean
passages.text: A specialist irrigation history proposes that Habbarid stability supported restored inundation channels, expanded cultivation, and urban surpluses. The author reconstructs rather than directly measures this system, so the cautious conclusion is dependence on shifting Indus water and managed flood flows, not a precise tenth-century canal map or acreage total.

passages.title: Homes, food, clothing, and ordinary work
passages.text: A departmental Mansura excavation report identifies a numbered house measuring 370 by 196 feet. Its exceptional scale proves that substantial residential architecture existed, not that every family occupied anything similar. Excavated urban buildings are especially visible; huts, temporary shelters, rural compounds, and mobile pastoral homes survive less generously.

passages.title: Homes, food, clothing, and ordinary work
passages.text: A 1981 Mansura field diary indexes wheat, animal and bird bones, a cooking furnace, storage jar, copper bowl, grinding or rubbing equipment, and household fittings. Because an index is not a finished stratigraphic synthesis, these finds illuminate tasks and foods at the site without guaranteeing that all belong to 900 to 1000.

passages.title: Homes, food, clothing, and ordinary work
passages.text: The 1982 diary adds fish bones, cock bones, eggshell, date-palm material, a grinding stone, fireplaces, jars, and rubbish pits. That is excellent evidence for people cooking, eating, storing, and discarding things. It is poor evidence for a universal menu, and the published index alone cannot assign every item a precise decade.

passages.title: Homes, food, clothing, and ordinary work
passages.text: Al-Istakhri compares ordinary clothing at Mansura to Iraqi dress while saying rulers adopted hair and tunic styles he considered Indian. The contrast suggests connected fashions and deliberate elite display. It does not tell us how women, laborers, children, pastoralists, or people in Kutch dressed across seasons and social ranks.

passages.title: Homes, food, clothing, and ordinary work
passages.text: Habbarid silver was tiny: the State Bank Museum describes fractional dammas of about 0.5 gram and says the mint, Mansura or Multan, is not named. Small coins made daily exchanges possible, but their survival favors durable money over perishable wages, baskets, cloth, and lunch. Archaeology always keeps odd receipts.

passages.title: Families, social life, belief, and unequal voices
passages.text: Mansura excavators recorded residential rooms, verandas, courtyards, partitions, and water fittings. These spaces hosted repeated domestic activity, probably by households, but walls cannot disclose whether residents formed nuclear, extended, servant-containing, or workshop households. Architecture supplies a stage for family life, not a complete cast list.

passages.title: Families, social life, belief, and unequal voices
passages.text: Excavated bangles, beads, rings, jewelry, and decorated objects show bodily adornment and personal possessions. A 1966 diary also records shell and glass bangles and a copper finger ring. Assigning each object automatically to women or to one faith would turn modern expectation into evidence, so the card leaves owners open.

passages.title: Families, social life, belief, and unequal voices
passages.text: MacLean reconstructs Muslim, Hindu, Buddhist, and other religious lives from uneven textual traces. Conversion unfolded over time, and named scholars or rulers are more visible than villagers. The responsible social picture is plural and changing, with disagreement and coexistence, rather than a sudden replacement of everybody’s practice after conquest.

passages.title: Families, social life, belief, and unequal voices
passages.text: The congregational mosque, government complex, market areas, streets, workshops, and residential quarters at Mansura structured different kinds of gathering and authority. Archaeology makes institutions visible but rarely records who was excluded, who swept the floors, or who cared for children nearby. Social life must be described with those silences intact.

passages.title: Families, social life, belief, and unequal voices
passages.text: Government excavations across fourteen seasons recovered coins, artifacts, jewelry, and other objects over ruins extending several kilometers. Their variety suggests rulers, craftspeople, traders, worshippers, and households sharing an urban landscape. The short official summary does not sort those finds by gender, status, religion, or exact century, so neither does this card.

passages.title: Children, education, languages, and a written sample
passages.text: The 1966 Mansura diary indexes children’s teeth, a toy rattle, a toy grinding mill, animal figurines, game objects, and small balls. These are rare direct openings onto childhood and learning through imitation or play. Mixed deposits and object labels prevent assigning every toy to a particular child or decade.

passages.title: Children, education, languages, and a written sample
passages.text: No surviving source in this packet provides enrollment lists, lesson schedules, or a typical child’s school day. MacLean can identify scholars, hadith study, judges, and religious networks, but that is adult institutional history. Children likely learned through households, work, worship, and play; exact curricula would be speculation.

passages.title: Children, education, languages, and a written sample
passages.text: Tenth-century geographers report Arabic and Sindhi at Daybul, Mansura, and Multan. That statement supports multilingual urban life, not one standardized Sindhi spelling system or universal fluency. Ports and courts needed language crossing, while many spoken varieties, occupational vocabularies, and rural speech communities remain invisible in the brief reports.

passages.title: Children, education, languages, and a written sample
passages.text: An Indira Gandhi National Open University unit reports that a Hindu ruler commissioned an Arabic scholar from Mansura in 886 to translate the Quran into a local language. The episode matters for translation, but no manuscript is presented here, and “local language” should not be silently converted into a known modern Sindhi text.

passages.title: Children, education, languages, and a written sample
passages.text: Written-language sample, about 985, Mansura: Arabic “المنصورة هي قصبة السند ومصر الإقليم” (al-Manṣūra hiya qaṣabat al-Sind wa-miṣr al-iqlīm), literally “Mansura is the capital of Sind and the metropolis of the province.” This is al-Muqaddasi’s learned geographic prose, not a sample of every resident’s speech; recensions and spellings vary.

passages.title: Medicine, health, diet, and honest absences
passages.text: This packet found no securely dated 900 to 1000 Mansura hospital, physician’s kit, prescription, or medical school. That absence in reviewed evidence does not mean nobody treated illness. It means the card should not import Baghdad’s famous medicine into Sind without a local source, however tempting the golden-age shortcut may be.

passages.title: Medicine, health, diet, and honest absences
passages.text: Urban access to water mattered for health even though medieval builders did not know germ theory. Archaeology describes wells, covered drains, channels, baths, and a lake-side source at Banbhore and Mansura. Such systems sustained neighborhoods but also required upkeep. They identify infrastructure, not water-quality tests or equal access.

passages.title: Medicine, health, diet, and honest absences
passages.text: Mansura’s 1966 excavation index includes a bathing tub, water outlet, terracotta drainpipe, soak pipe, and soak pit. These features show people managing water and dirty runoff. Their precise dates and household relationships require fuller stratigraphic publication, so they are evidence of site practice rather than a citywide sanitation guarantee.

passages.title: Medicine, health, diet, and honest absences
passages.text: Wheat, fish bones, bird bones, eggshell, animal remains, and date-palm material can help reconstruct diet, seasonality, and environment. The 1982 diary lists them but does not provide a complete quantified food study. Bones also preserve better than porridge, so the surviving menu is biased toward the crunchy evidence.

passages.title: Medicine, health, diet, and honest absences
passages.text: Al-Muqaddasi calls Mansura’s air mild and winter easy, yet also emphasizes severe heat and many mosquitoes. That memorable complaint is period evidence for discomfort, not a diagnosis of malaria or another disease. Apparently even a tenth-century geographer knew that mosquitoes can review a city without being invited.

passages.title: Water, waste, baths, and the toilet question
passages.text: Treccani’s archaeological synthesis describes Mansura blocks with independent water supply through wells and drainage through underground channels. Residences had wells, often with terracotta collars, plus covered lined drains. This is substantial urban engineering evidence, but coverage varied by block and cannot be extended to villages or the Thar-Kutch polygon.

passages.title: Water, waste, baths, and the toilet question
passages.text: A 1977 to 1978 field diary records water supply, a terracotta pipe, drains, rubbish, pits, and ash among residential remains. These features show maintenance and disposal work, the unglamorous engineering that lets a city function. The diary index does not prove a unified municipal sewer or identify who cleaned it.

passages.title: Water, waste, baths, and the toilet question
passages.text: Banbhore’s fortified town bordered a lake or reservoir used as a major water source, while access routes connected the city to it. Such storage helped a port survive dry periods and crowded activity. It also demanded protection from silt and waste, although the archaeological plan cannot tell us a daily cleaning schedule.

passages.title: Water, waste, baths, and the toilet question
passages.text: Near Banbhore’s mosque, channels may have served ritual washing and latrines; the interpretation is explicitly uncertain. Archaeologists also report baths elsewhere at the site. So the safest toilet answer is “possibly here, with plumbing,” not a claim that every home owned a private bathroom or that the drain smelled delightful.

passages.title: Water, waste, baths, and the toilet question
passages.text: Mansura’s 1982 diary separately indexes a terracotta soak pit, rubbish pits, a covered drain, and street surfaces. Together with other seasons, this shows multiple strategies for water and waste. Because features come from excavated portions and mixed occupation phases, citywide access and tenth-century dating remain open questions.

passages.title: Craft, architecture, discovery, and achievement
passages.text: Four bronze door knockers found near Mansura’s government complex bear Arabic religious text and a Habbarid ruler’s name. Archaeological comparison argues for local manufacture and a thriving metalworking bazaar. Their fierce faces and petal-shaped rings made an official doorway announce itself before anyone even knocked.

passages.title: Craft, architecture, discovery, and achievement
passages.text: A British Museum Mansura coin weighs only 0.50 gram and measures 11 millimeters. Its Arabic inscriptions occupy several lines, with a crescent and dot among the designs. Minting legible authority onto such a tiny silver surface was a technical achievement, although catalogue dating remains broadly 800 to 1000.

passages.title: Craft, architecture, discovery, and achievement
passages.text: Banbhore excavators recovered more than 4,000 carved ivory, animal-bone, and shell fragments linked to jewelry and furniture manufacture. Other materials were locally made or imported from Iran. The concentration reveals skilled work and Indian Ocean connections, while the project cautions that the site’s identification with written Debal remains debated.

passages.title: Craft, architecture, discovery, and achievement
passages.text: Glass fragments at Banbhore are being studied compositionally to distinguish raw materials, technologies, and possible links with Middle Eastern and eastern production. That scientific caution matters: a pretty shard is not automatically an import. Archaeometry can test whether craftspeople remelted, copied, traded, or locally produced materials.

passages.title: Craft, architecture, discovery, and achievement
passages.text: A recent Banbhore synthesis records ivory and bone-working waste, glass, metallurgy, mother-of-pearl objects, vessels, and Chinese porcelain in later sequences. These finds show production, distribution, and redistribution, not merely consumption. Their broad stratigraphy crosses centuries, so individual pieces should not all be stamped “tenth century” for convenience.

passages.title: Conflict, environmental change, and the 1000 seam
passages.text: Al-Masudi’s report portrays Mansura’s ruler fighting Med groups and maintaining soldiers, cavalry, and elephants. A historical thesis reproduces the figures but notes how thin the evidence is. Warfare affected frontier communities, animals, food supply, and labor, not only rulers; exact force totals remain claims rather than verified rolls.

passages.title: Conflict, environmental change, and the 1000 seam
passages.text: Banbhore’s heavy walls, bastions, and gates materialize defense, while Mansura diaries record arrowheads, spearheads, daggers, and sling balls. Weapons prove preparation and episodes of danger more readily than a particular battle. Fortification also redirected everyday movement, taxation, work, and refuge for people living inside and beyond the walls.

passages.title: Conflict, environmental change, and the 1000 seam
passages.text: The Indus delta and Rann changed physically. Historical geography describes silting that transformed an open bay near Badin toward salt marsh by the eleventh century. Such change altered channels, pasture, cultivation, and access to ports. It did not respect the straight chronological boundary of an atlas snapshot.

passages.title: Conflict, environmental change, and the 1000 seam
passages.text: Sources disagree on the Habbarid ending. The State Bank museum gives 1010; the reviewed archaeological monograph gives Mahmud of Ghazna’s conquest in 1025. Neither supports a fall in 1000. The difference should stay visible because compressing it into a confident date would hide the limits of the evidence.

passages.title: Conflict, environmental change, and the 1000 seam
passages.text: The 1000 map removes “sindh” and assigns most former member probes to “rajput-kingdoms”; by 1100, the atlas separately colors a Soomra emirate on the Indus plain. These are editorial layers across a century gap. Farmers, traders, craft workers, families, languages, and water systems continued through the software seam.

At 1000 the exact “sindh” feature disappears. Most tested Thar-Kutch member points become “rajput-kingdoms,” while the historically central Indus probes, outside the target all along, change from “saffarids” to other atlas layers. The map encodes no conquest or population break at this boundary. The override therefore leaves fell null and names no single successor. Ports, farms, workshops, households, languages, religious communities, and water systems continued through the editorial seam.

dailyLife.question: Does the account explain ordinary practices with evidence rather than only rulers?

chronologicalPhases.question: Are source-supported phases distinguished from map snapshot dates?

endingContinuity.question: Does the narrative identify what ended or continued, with dates, mechanism and uncertainty?

uncertainty.question: Are uncertainties attached to particular claims rather than a blanket disclaimer?

passages.text: These two atlas records cover late medieval Sri Lanka from 1279 to 1530. Their near-island-wide outlines are regional umbrellas: they do not show one Sinhala-speaking state ruling every district throughout that time. Royal centers shifted through Yapahuwa, Kurunegala and Gampola, while Kotte became powerful in the fifteenth century and divided in 1521. The Tamil kingdom of Jaffna, hill-country rulers and local communities had distinct histories. The simplified coast even clips the modern Colombo, Galle and Jaffna points, although their connections matter to this history. This card joins the two consecutive map phases while keeping earlier Anuradhapura-era and later named-state records separate.

passages.title: Royal centers and their limits
passages.text: Yapahuwa combined a high rock stronghold with walls, ramparts and moats below. Bhuvanaikabahu I made it a royal center in the late thirteenth century and housed the Buddha’s Tooth Relic there. Custody of that revered object helped support claims to kingship. A Pandyan attack in the 1280s carried the relic to South India, ending Yapahuwa’s brief prominence as a capital.

passages.title: Royal centers and their limits
passages.text: Yapahuwa’s ornamental stairway is still crowded with carved beings: mythical makaras, small supporting figures and dancers. Stoneworkers combined a practical ascent with an elaborate setting for royal and religious authority. Rock-cut cisterns collected rainwater elsewhere in the fortress. Reaching the top required legs; keeping people there also required a dependable water supply.

passages.title: Royal centers and their limits
passages.text: Kotte’s strength began with its landscape. Waterways and marshes around the Kolonna Oya and Diyawanna Oya helped protect the fortress associated with Alakeshwara. Proximity to Colombo linked the inland court with maritime commerce. The early fifteenth-century kingdom grew from this defended setting, rather than appearing fully formed across the whole island on one foundation day.

passages.title: Royal centers and their limits
passages.text: Royal family conflict reshaped the later map phase. In 1521, three brothers divided Kotte’s territories: Bhuvanaikabahu held Kotte, Mayadunne ruled from Sitawaka, and Raigam Bandara received Raigama. Their competing ambitions influenced alliances and war. Jaffna and the hill-country rulers cannot be folded into that family partition as if they were merely districts of an uncontested kingdom.

passages.title: Building, farming and household obligations
passages.text: The Gadaladeniya inscription, dated 1344, names Dharmmakirtti as the founder and Ganesvaracari as the leading master artisan. It describes payments in money and paddy to craftspeople skilled in architecture and making images. The shrine’s South Indian connections are visible in its design and the architect’s name, although a name alone does not reveal every worker’s origin.

passages.title: Building, farming and household obligations
passages.text: Temple donations could leave room for a donor’s family. Gadaladeniya’s long grant list includes Anura Attara’s land with a reservation allowing his relations to enjoy it while paying customary dues and tithes. Other gifts included a house and garden. Such clauses show how religious endowments intersected with continuing household livelihoods, rather than simply removing land from everyday use.

passages.title: Building, farming and household obligations
passages.text: At nearby Lankatilaka, a 1344 inscription describes artisans receiving paddy, gold, silver and cloth for constructing the image-house. It also credits the minister’s sons and women of his household with a pavilion containing a bronze image. The record presents building as a collaboration involving rulers, officials, religious communities, craftspeople and an elite family.

passages.title: Building, farming and household obligations
passages.text: The same foundation depended on unequal labor. Lankatilaka’s records list 200 enslaved men and women, some inherited or received through marriage and others purchased, alongside cattle and buffaloes. They also prescribe a small annual contribution from each household for offerings and ceremonies. The inscriptions praise generosity, but the people assigned as property could not choose freely how to work.

passages.title: Building, farming and household obligations
passages.text: Lankatilaka’s land grants describe improving fields with a new dam, removing stumps and making embankments. Rice-producing land supported offerings, lamps, flowers and festivities at the shrine. The grand building therefore depended on less glamorous tasks beyond its walls: cultivating fields, tending animals and keeping water under control. The record does not establish plumbing or toilets in ordinary homes.

passages.title: Building, farming and household obligations
passages.text: Around 1500, Colombo traded cinnamon, areca nuts, gems and elephants for imported goods including cloth and rice. The port was culturally and religiously diverse. Its exchange networks connected producers, carriers and traders with the royal economy at Kotte. Colombo lies just outside this particular simplified polygon, so its importance should not be mistaken for evidence that the drawn coastline is accurate.

passages.title: Poetry, learning and written evidence
passages.text: A bird could deliver a very important message in Sinhala poetry. Around 1450, the monk Sri Rahula composed the Selalihini Sandeshaya, imagining a journey from Kotte to Kelaniya to ask a deity to grant a princess a son. Its author headed Vijayabahu Pirivena, a monastic learning institution. This was literary invention and royal aspiration, not a report of a working bird-post service.

passages.title: Poetry, learning and written evidence
passages.text: The poem also describes women singing Tamil hymns at a Hindu shrine and female dancers at Kelaniya. Those scenes illuminate how a Sinhala Buddhist poet imagined public worship and performance. They cannot tell us what every woman was permitted to do, but they preserve a richer social picture than a list containing only kings and battles.

passages.title: Poetry, learning and written evidence
passages.text: For a small Sinhala sample, verse 7 uses “සුරපුර,” glossed by translator Dharshani Lakmali Jayasinghe as “city of gods.” The poet compares Kotte with a celestial city. These are modern printed Sinhala letters representing a word in the fifteenth-century poem, not a photograph of an original medieval manuscript. The praise belongs to poetry, not a measured city ranking.

passages.title: Poetry, learning and written evidence
passages.text: A very different written object was found at Galle in 1911: a stone bearing Chinese, Tamil and Persian texts and the date 1409. Brought by Zheng He’s expedition, it records religious offerings and is now in the Colombo National Museum. This foreign-sponsored inscription reveals Indian Ocean connections; it is not a Sinhala royal proclamation or proof that everyone spoke all three languages.

passages.title: Commerce and an unfinished transition
passages.text: Portuguese influence did not arrive as complete territorial control. A fort and cinnamon trading post were established at Colombo in 1518, but the fort was dismantled in 1524. Bhuvanaikabahu later sought military support against Sitawaka. Trading arrangements, local rivalries and changing garrisons shaped the relationship long before direct colonial government replaced Kotte’s court.

passages.title: Commerce and an unfinished transition
passages.text: Cinnamon profits encouraged attempts to control routes and supply. Historian C. R. de Silva describes a Portuguese Crown monopoly decision for the oceanic trade route in 1520 and a 1524 order directing cinnamon cargoes through Cochin. He also reports the destruction of surplus cinnamon to support prices. A fragrant ingredient could sit at the center of coercive commercial policy, far from the kitchens where it was used.

Neither 1492 nor 1530 marks the disappearance of these communities. Kotte had already divided in 1521, and later conflict drove its court to Colombo in 1565. The Kotte royal line continued under Dharmapala until 1597, while other states and communities followed different paths. The map’s two intervals capture parts of that transition, not a single island-wide fall.
