sectionTitles: Living, bathing and learning in monasteries

passages.text: This map label covers Sri Lanka from 800 to 900, especially the Anuradhapura monarchy and the communities, monasteries and ports around it. It is one century within a much longer history, not the lifetime of a single dynasty. The coarse island outline clips parts of the coastline and does not demonstrate equal royal control everywhere. Royal and monastic claims to land and labour could compete. Earlier Simhala and the much later Sinhalese-kingdom records have separate cards or map entries.

passages.title: Kings, monasteries and public authority
passages.text: Sena I’s reign included a damaging Pandyan raid from southern India. A later inscription identifies this ruler, using his title Salamevan, as the founder of Ritigala monastery. The combination of inscription and chronicle places renewed royal patronage after the raid. Scholars use different absolute chronologies for these kings, so a precise modern year should not be invented from a regnal title alone.

passages.title: Kings, monasteries and public authority
passages.text: Under Sena II, an army departed through Mahatittha, now called Mantai, for a campaign in the Pandyan kingdom. The same harbour could receive merchandise or launch a military expedition. Historian Wijerathne Bohingamuwa cautions that chronicles emphasize warfare, so archaeology is essential for understanding the port’s less dramatic but persistent commercial work.

passages.title: Kings, monasteries and public authority
passages.text: A rough pillar at Viyaulpata records privileges for a monastic dwelling, issued by the heir-apparent Mahinda in Sena II’s first regnal year. Two officers, Kaṇṇā and Rāvaṇā, assembled local notables before setting up the pillar and proclaiming the order. A written command also needed people to hear about it; carving a stone was only part of making government work.

passages.title: Kings, monasteries and public authority
passages.text: Inscriptions from the Sigiriya-Dambulla area, dated from the middle of the ninth century into the tenth, describe competing claims over fields, water, labour and produce. Monasteries could control substantial resources, while royal officials intervened in those arrangements. For farming households, an endowment could change who claimed their work or part of their harvest.

passages.title: Food, materials and movement
passages.text: Dry-zone communities stored seasonal rain in large reservoirs and smaller, gravity-fed chains of tanks. Canals linked these supplies with settlements and fields. This infrastructure had developed over generations before the ninth century. Maintaining it connected people’s farming work with the wider landscape.

passages.title: Food, materials and movement
passages.text: Anuradhapura’s early medieval residential layers contain shallow, internally grooved bowls called nambiliya. Researchers associate them with separating grit from rice. Their increasing presence suggests more city residents were processing rice themselves as supply networks changed. Those grooves helped keep unwanted crunch out of dinner.

passages.title: Food, materials and movement
passages.text: Excavations at Mantai recovered ninth-century Changsha pottery from China alongside locally made wares and other imports. A broken bowl can therefore connect an island port to kilns thousands of kilometres away. Its arrival need not mean that a Chinese potter or merchant lived in the particular house where it was eventually discarded.

passages.title: Food, materials and movement
passages.text: Mantai’s deposits, spanning the early centuries CE into medieval times, contain rice, wheat, pulses and millets. Researchers think much of the rice reached the port in its husk, while wheat arrived already cleaned, probably through trade. These finds reveal provisioning and varied food traditions across several centuries; they are not a single ninth-century household’s shopping list.

passages.title: Food, materials and movement
passages.text: Microscopic plant remains at Mantai point to the importance of palms. The excavators interpret their abundance as evidence for palm leaves used in buildings, and suggest fibres could also have supplied ropes for boats and port work. A palm could contribute to shelter and transport as well as food, although each proposed use leaves different amounts of archaeological evidence.

passages.title: Food, materials and movement
passages.text: Sri Lankan gold kahavanu circulated between roughly the eighth and eleventh centuries. Their designs show a standing figure on one side and a seated figure on the other, with a short Nagari inscription. Scholars have proposed several readings of that legend. These coins are surviving evidence for skilled metalworking and exchange, without telling us how many coins an ordinary family possessed.

passages.title: Living, bathing and learning in monasteries
passages.text: The Western Monasteries near Anuradhapura and related sites such as Ritigala contain paired stone platforms linked by a narrow gangway. Rear platforms preserve evidence of roofs, partitions and doorways; front platforms were generally open. Scholars associate this architecture with communities devoted to meditation. The surviving arrangement helps distinguish a place to live from an open area used for other activities.

passages.title: Living, bathing and learning in monasteries
passages.text: These monastic complexes also had paths interpreted as meditation walkways and buildings for hot-water bathing. Bathhouses could include a fireplace, water containers and seats. The remains make monastic life more tangible: thought and teaching took place in bodies that also needed washing, rest and movement. The larger complexes shared some facilities among several residential units.

passages.title: Living, bathing and learning in monasteries
passages.text: Some monastic urinals were unexpectedly fancy. Carved stone slabs had foot supports, a collecting depression and an outlet, with architectural decoration showing a building. Separate latrines could be plainer and farther from the living rooms. Why decorate a urinal so elaborately? Scholars disagree about the symbolism, but the practical need is easy to recognize.

passages.title: Living, bathing and learning in monasteries
passages.text: The hospital at Mihintale is dated to the ninth century through its inscriptional and archaeological context. Rooms opened onto an inner courtyard and are interpreted as accommodation for patients. The outer area included a refectory and spaces associated with preparing and storing medicines. Caring for sick people required food, supplies and organized space as well as a healer.

passages.title: Living, bathing and learning in monasteries
passages.text: Mihintale also preserves a stone trough hollowed into a shape that fits a human body, interpreted as a medical bath. It is one of the objects helping identify the site as a hospital. The trough shows that treatment could involve immersion; it cannot by itself establish which ingredients were used for every patient or how effective a treatment was.

passages.title: Written voices and rediscovery
passages.text: A short ninth-century Sinhala phrase from the Kivulekada inscription is transcribed “Riṭgal-aram kärū Salamevan Rajpahi”, referring to King Salamevan as the builder of Ritigala monastery. These are scholarly Latin letters representing the inscription’s language, rather than a reproduction of its carved Sinhala letters. A royal title and a building project help scholars identify Sena I behind the name.

passages.title: Written voices and rediscovery
passages.text: A medieval visitor to Sigiriya left a wonderfully human note. Nimal de Silva transcribes its opening as “Budalmi”, meaning “I am Budal”. Budal explained that so many people had already written songs that he did not write one. He wrote to explain why he was not writing a poem. His individual date is uncertain within the broader medieval graffiti tradition.

passages.title: Written voices and rediscovery
passages.text: Sigiriya’s graffiti preserve visitors’ names, places, titles and responses to its paintings. Scholars have read both polished poems and much shorter notes. They reveal people choosing words for an audience, not merely copying a royal command. The surviving writers were a selected literate group, so their words cannot measure how many children elsewhere learned to read.

passages.title: Written voices and rediscovery
passages.text: The Kivulekada inscription nearly had a second career holding up a granary. When it was recorded in 1892, a local official said he had dug out the slab to use as a support. A researcher visiting in 1928 found it half-buried with its writing face down. Ordinary reuse helped determine which clues later archaeologists could find.

The map stops at 900, before Anuradhapura lost its role as the chief capital. Chola conquest changed the political landscape around the end of the tenth century; UNESCO dates a destructive attack to 993. Polonnaruwa became a successor capital, preserving monuments from Chola and later Sri Lankan rulers. Political institutions changed while communities and religious traditions continued.

passages.text: These two atlas records cover late medieval Sri Lanka from 1279 to 1530. Their near-island-wide outlines are regional umbrellas: they do not show one Sinhala-speaking state ruling every district throughout that time. Royal centers shifted through Yapahuwa, Kurunegala and Gampola, while Kotte became powerful in the fifteenth century and divided in 1521. The Tamil kingdom of Jaffna, hill-country rulers and local communities had distinct histories. The simplified coast even clips the modern Colombo, Galle and Jaffna points, although their connections matter to this history. This card joins the two consecutive map phases while keeping earlier Anuradhapura-era and later named-state records separate.

passages.title: Royal centers and their limits
passages.text: Yapahuwa combined a high rock stronghold with walls, ramparts and moats below. Bhuvanaikabahu I made it a royal center in the late thirteenth century and housed the Buddha’s Tooth Relic there. Custody of that revered object helped support claims to kingship. A Pandyan attack in the 1280s carried the relic to South India, ending Yapahuwa’s brief prominence as a capital.

passages.title: Royal centers and their limits
passages.text: Yapahuwa’s ornamental stairway is still crowded with carved beings: mythical makaras, small supporting figures and dancers. Stoneworkers combined a practical ascent with an elaborate setting for royal and religious authority. Rock-cut cisterns collected rainwater elsewhere in the fortress. Reaching the top required legs; keeping people there also required a dependable water supply.

passages.title: Royal centers and their limits
passages.text: Kotte’s strength began with its landscape. Waterways and marshes around the Kolonna Oya and Diyawanna Oya helped protect the fortress associated with Alakeshwara. Proximity to Colombo linked the inland court with maritime commerce. The early fifteenth-century kingdom grew from this defended setting, rather than appearing fully formed across the whole island on one foundation day.

passages.title: Royal centers and their limits
passages.text: Royal family conflict reshaped the later map phase. In 1521, three brothers divided Kotte’s territories: Bhuvanaikabahu held Kotte, Mayadunne ruled from Sitawaka, and Raigam Bandara received Raigama. Their competing ambitions influenced alliances and war. Jaffna and the hill-country rulers cannot be folded into that family partition as if they were merely districts of an uncontested kingdom.

passages.title: Building, farming and household obligations
passages.text: The Gadaladeniya inscription, dated 1344, names Dharmmakirtti as the founder and Ganesvaracari as the leading master artisan. It describes payments in money and paddy to craftspeople skilled in architecture and making images. The shrine’s South Indian connections are visible in its design and the architect’s name, although a name alone does not reveal every worker’s origin.

passages.title: Building, farming and household obligations
passages.text: Temple donations could leave room for a donor’s family. Gadaladeniya’s long grant list includes Anura Attara’s land with a reservation allowing his relations to enjoy it while paying customary dues and tithes. Other gifts included a house and garden. Such clauses show how religious endowments intersected with continuing household livelihoods, rather than simply removing land from everyday use.

passages.title: Building, farming and household obligations
passages.text: At nearby Lankatilaka, a 1344 inscription describes artisans receiving paddy, gold, silver and cloth for constructing the image-house. It also credits the minister’s sons and women of his household with a pavilion containing a bronze image. The record presents building as a collaboration involving rulers, officials, religious communities, craftspeople and an elite family.

passages.title: Building, farming and household obligations
passages.text: The same foundation depended on unequal labor. Lankatilaka’s records list 200 enslaved men and women, some inherited or received through marriage and others purchased, alongside cattle and buffaloes. They also prescribe a small annual contribution from each household for offerings and ceremonies. The inscriptions praise generosity, but the people assigned as property could not choose freely how to work.

passages.title: Building, farming and household obligations
passages.text: Lankatilaka’s land grants describe improving fields with a new dam, removing stumps and making embankments. Rice-producing land supported offerings, lamps, flowers and festivities at the shrine. The grand building therefore depended on less glamorous tasks beyond its walls: cultivating fields, tending animals and keeping water under control. The record does not establish plumbing or toilets in ordinary homes.

passages.title: Building, farming and household obligations
passages.text: Around 1500, Colombo traded cinnamon, areca nuts, gems and elephants for imported goods including cloth and rice. The port was culturally and religiously diverse. Its exchange networks connected producers, carriers and traders with the royal economy at Kotte. Colombo lies just outside this particular simplified polygon, so its importance should not be mistaken for evidence that the drawn coastline is accurate.

passages.title: Poetry, learning and written evidence
passages.text: A bird could deliver a very important message in Sinhala poetry. Around 1450, the monk Sri Rahula composed the Selalihini Sandeshaya, imagining a journey from Kotte to Kelaniya to ask a deity to grant a princess a son. Its author headed Vijayabahu Pirivena, a monastic learning institution. This was literary invention and royal aspiration, not a report of a working bird-post service.

passages.title: Poetry, learning and written evidence
passages.text: The poem also describes women singing Tamil hymns at a Hindu shrine and female dancers at Kelaniya. Those scenes illuminate how a Sinhala Buddhist poet imagined public worship and performance. They cannot tell us what every woman was permitted to do, but they preserve a richer social picture than a list containing only kings and battles.

passages.title: Poetry, learning and written evidence
passages.text: For a small Sinhala sample, verse 7 uses “සුරපුර,” glossed by translator Dharshani Lakmali Jayasinghe as “city of gods.” The poet compares Kotte with a celestial city. These are modern printed Sinhala letters representing a word in the fifteenth-century poem, not a photograph of an original medieval manuscript. The praise belongs to poetry, not a measured city ranking.

passages.title: Poetry, learning and written evidence
passages.text: A very different written object was found at Galle in 1911: a stone bearing Chinese, Tamil and Persian texts and the date 1409. Brought by Zheng He’s expedition, it records religious offerings and is now in the Colombo National Museum. This foreign-sponsored inscription reveals Indian Ocean connections; it is not a Sinhala royal proclamation or proof that everyone spoke all three languages.

passages.title: Commerce and an unfinished transition
passages.text: Portuguese influence did not arrive as complete territorial control. A fort and cinnamon trading post were established at Colombo in 1518, but the fort was dismantled in 1524. Bhuvanaikabahu later sought military support against Sitawaka. Trading arrangements, local rivalries and changing garrisons shaped the relationship long before direct colonial government replaced Kotte’s court.

passages.title: Commerce and an unfinished transition
passages.text: Cinnamon profits encouraged attempts to control routes and supply. Historian C. R. de Silva describes a Portuguese Crown monopoly decision for the oceanic trade route in 1520 and a 1524 order directing cinnamon cargoes through Cochin. He also reports the destruction of surplus cinnamon to support prices. A fragrant ingredient could sit at the center of coercive commercial policy, far from the kitchens where it was used.

Neither 1492 nor 1530 marks the disappearance of these communities. Kotte had already divided in 1521, and later conflict drove its court to Colombo in 1565. The Kotte royal line continued under Dharmapala until 1597, while other states and communities followed different paths. The map’s two intervals capture parts of that transition, not a single island-wide fall.

sectionTitles: Read the label and shape before the story
Language, ancestry and artifacts are different evidence
Homes, clothes, daily work and a fashion fossil
Families, women, children, learning and play

passages.text: “Sinic” is the atlas’s label for a very odd 1500 to 500 BCE polygon, not the name of one ancient nation. The identical shape survives across three map snapshots, looping from parts of the middle Yangzi and south China through Lanzhou to sections of northeast China while excluding Anyang, Xi’an, Luoyang, Nanjing and modern Beijing. Those gaps are crucial: famous Shang and Zhou capitals and the Anyang oracle-bone archive sit in neighboring atlas layers, so their history cannot simply fill this card. Sinitic properly names a branch of the Sino-Tibetan language family. Linguists reconstruct earlier sounds from inscriptions, rhymes, later pronunciations and related languages, but archaeology cannot hear what every potter, miner or farmer spoke. Inside the shape, named communities built Panlongcheng’s walled center, fired high-temperature stoneware at Wucheng, worked copper around Tonglüshan, farmed rice and millet, exchanged bronzes and lived in very different southern, northwestern and northeastern landscapes. A cheerful detective clue: a bronze spiral pattern may preserve the look of vanished woven cloth, a fashion fossil in metal. Evidence for ordinary medicine, schooling and toilets is much thinner than evidence for walls, tombs and elite vessels. The map deletes “Sinic” at 500 BCE; local people and languages continued.

passages.title: Read the label and shape before the story
passages.text: The live index records “Sinic” as an approximate culture layer from 1500 to 500 BCE. Coverage contains three consecutive intervals and no imported summary or card. The id is kept for app compatibility, but its label is interpreted cautiously rather than expanded into “all ancient Chinese people.”

passages.title: Read the label and shape before the story
passages.text: At 1500 BCE the exact feature is one ring with 95 coordinate positions, bounded roughly by 102.41 to 131.51°E and 23.04 to 44.19°N. The coordinate checksum stays exactly the same in 1000 and 700 BCE. A frozen drawing over one thousand years is editorial, not an observed language frontier.

passages.title: Read the label and shape before the story
passages.text: Tested points owned by the target include Lanzhou, Wuhan, Panlongcheng, Changsha, Wucheng, Nanchang, Guilin, Shenyang and Changchun. The shape therefore joins distant southern, northwestern and northeastern zones. Calling all of them one people would hide the strongest fact: their archaeological histories differ.

passages.title: Read the label and shape before the story
passages.text: Anyang, Yinxu, Zhengzhou, Luoyang, Xi’an, Beijing and many other Central Plain points sit in Zhou layers; Nanjing and Shanghai sit in Wu; Chengdu in Tibetans; southern coast points in an Austro-Asiatic label; Korea and the far northeast have still other owners. The exact polygon is not “China.”

passages.title: Read the label and shape before the story
passages.text: At 500 BCE the id vanishes. Many eastern points become “Zhou states,” while Lanzhou, Changsha, Wucheng, Shenyang and Changchun are unowned at the tested coordinates. This is a taxonomy switch, not proof of conquest, mass migration, language death or the fall of a Sinic empire.

passages.title: Language, ancestry and artifacts are different evidence
passages.text: Sinitic is a branch of the Sino-Tibetan language family, containing many Chinese varieties rather than one timeless tongue. Modern Mandarin, Cantonese, Hakka, Min and others cannot simply be projected backward unchanged. “Sinic” is also not a biological category or a synonym for every society within modern China.

passages.title: Language, ancestry and artifacts are different evidence
passages.text: Old Chinese pronunciations are reconstructed from several evidence streams: early graphs and phonetic series, ancient rhymes, later dictionaries and comparison with related languages. A reconstruction is a testable scholarly model, often marked with an asterisk. It is not an audio recording and does not automatically locate speakers inside this polygon.

passages.title: Language, ancestry and artifacts are different evidence
passages.text: One Bayesian study models a northern Late Neolithic origin and a broad 4,200 to 7,800-year divergence range for Sino-Tibetan. That result depends on lexical data, calibrations and tree assumptions. It cannot transform a Panlongcheng workshop, Wucheng potsherd or Upper Xiajiadian grave into a language label.

passages.title: Language, ancestry and artifacts are different evidence
passages.text: Ancient genomes reveal changing ancestry in Yellow River, West Liao and Amur regions as farming, herding and mobility changed. Genetic clusters measure biological relationships among sampled individuals; they do not reveal self-names or speech. Fifty-five genomes across millennia cannot stand for everyone in this far larger polygon.

passages.title: Language, ancestry and artifacts are different evidence
passages.text: Southern coastal genomes also show layered population histories and movement. Archaeology, genes and language may illuminate one another only when their dates and places genuinely match. None moves as a single package: people can change language, foods can travel without people, and craft styles can be copied.

passages.title: How archaeologists uncover local histories
passages.text: Stratigraphy records which deposits lie above or below others, while radiocarbon dates organic remains in probability ranges. Survey maps settlements beyond spectacular tombs. These methods reveal that Panlongcheng, Wucheng, Tanheli, Tonglüshan and later Chu centers followed overlapping but unequal timelines, not three neat map blocks.

passages.title: How archaeologists uncover local histories
passages.text: Modern Panlongcheng fieldwork combines excavation, landscape mapping and laboratory training. Decades of research have identified walls, large foundations, cemeteries, workshops, pottery, jades and bronzes. Each object matters most with its layer and feature; an unprovenanced museum treasure loses much of the evidence that makes history testable.

passages.title: How archaeologists uncover local histories
passages.text: Lead-isotope ratios and alloy chemistry help compare bronze metal batches and possible ore zones. They rarely provide a simple mine-to-vessel address, because metal could be mixed, recycled or exchanged repeatedly. Panlongcheng’s relationship to southern copper is therefore investigated through several methods, not one magic chemical fingerprint.

passages.title: How archaeologists uncover local histories
passages.text: Microscopes and experiments reveal scratches, drilled points, abrasives and polishing sequences on bronze and jade. Sand, whetstones, fibers, leather and carefully controlled motion transformed cast surfaces. Such traces recover expert hands and teaching even when the craftsperson’s name, gender and spoken language are unknown.

passages.title: How archaeologists uncover local histories
passages.text: Regional survey in northeast China compares settlement size, spacing, fortifications and access to fields rather than treating a pottery style as a whole ethnic group. That approach is essential here because the atlas’s northeastern lobe reaches Shenyang and Changchun but bypasses many supposed “core” places.

passages.title: Landscapes, farming, animals and meals
passages.text: The shape crosses humid middle-Yangzi lowlands, lake and river systems, subtropical hills, the drier Lanzhou region and colder northeast. Floods, growing seasons, soils and wild resources differed. Environmental opportunities shaped choices, but no climate mechanically created one language, ethnicity or political system.

passages.title: Landscapes, farming, animals and meals
passages.text: Rice had a deep history in the Yangzi basin, while broomcorn and foxtail millet were important farther north and in mixed farming zones. Archaeobotanists identify charred grains, husks, weeds and phytoliths through flotation and microscopy. A crop’s presence does not tell us the farmer’s language.

passages.title: Landscapes, farming, animals and meals
passages.text: People boiled and steamed grains, made porridges, cooked meat and fish, gathered plants and stored seasonal foods. Cuisine varied by ecology and access. Even millet grain size can reflect cooking preferences; crops moving between regions did not necessarily carry identical pots, recipes or social meanings.

passages.title: Landscapes, farming, animals and meals
passages.text: Northeastern households combined cultivation with hunting, herding and mobility in changing proportions. Earlier Lower Xiajiadian fortified villages and later Upper Xiajiadian lifeways should not be collapsed together. Ancient DNA from only fourteen Dadianzi people illustrates movement questions but remains far too small to define a population.

passages.title: Landscapes, farming, animals and meals
passages.text: Stable carbon and nitrogen isotopes preserve broad dietary pathways, while cavities and tooth wear track starch and food processing. Regional datasets show millet, wheat, barley and rice mixtures changing through time. Individual diets still varied with age, movement, status, season and what happened to preserve.

passages.title: Homes, clothes, daily work and a fashion fossil
passages.text: Panlongcheng had a rammed-earth citadel, moat, substantial buildings, workshops and cemeteries within a much larger occupied landscape. Nearby communities also used local house forms and ceramics. Monumental construction demanded coordinated labor, but it does not prove that every builder belonged to one imported population.

passages.title: Homes, clothes, daily work and a fashion fossil
passages.text: Wucheng’s large enclosure, kilns and workshops supported high-fired stoneware often called proto-porcelain. Tanheli used a different wall technique and developed bronze and jade craft. These southern centers selected, remade and combined technologies rather than merely copying a single northern civilization.

passages.title: Homes, clothes, daily work and a fashion fossil
passages.text: Clothing was made from perishable fibers, so complete outfits almost never survive this interval. Loom weights, tools, impressions and patterns transferred into durable media offer indirect clues. A bronze spiral from Panlongcheng may echo woven design, a delightful “fashion fossil” left after the original cloth disappeared.

passages.title: Homes, clothes, daily work and a fashion fossil
passages.text: Most work used wood, stone, bone, bamboo, fiber and pottery even when bronze dazzles museum visitors. Farming, fishing, carrying water, tending animals, firing kilns, repairing walls and preparing food consumed countless hours. Elite tombs preserve expensive objects disproportionately and make ordinary labor too easy to overlook.

passages.title: Homes, clothes, daily work and a fashion fossil
passages.text: Houses organized cooking, storage, sleep, craft and care, yet a room’s function needs hearths, residues, tools and wear patterns rather than imagination. Household size is equally hard to infer: several generations might share work, while temporary residents, servants or unrelated dependents leave ambiguous traces.

passages.title: Copper, bronze, exchange and achievement
passages.text: Tonglüshan preserves timber-supported mine workings, stone, wood, bamboo and metal tools, and huge quantities of slag. Secure exploitation begins around the eleventh century BCE and grows later. Miners solved ventilation, water, rock removal and collapse risks long before electric lamps or steel helmets.

passages.title: Copper, bronze, exchange and achievement
passages.text: Bronze production joined prospecting, mining, fuel making, smelting, alloying, ceramic mold production, casting and finishing. No lone genius performed the entire chain. Workshops depended on teams and supply networks, while elites controlled many finished ritual objects and weapons used in ceremonies and warfare.

passages.title: Copper, bronze, exchange and achievement
passages.text: Hanzhong bronzes combine technical and stylistic links with Panlongcheng and Central Plain traditions alongside local production. More than seven hundred objects show that “periphery” is a misleading word: mountain and river corridors could be active workshops and exchange hubs, not passive edges awaiting civilization.

passages.title: Copper, bronze, exchange and achievement
passages.text: Metal technologies, horses and chariots moved through contact with northern frontier and steppe communities, then were transformed locally. Adoption was selective rather than wholesale. A borrowed wheel, casting method or ornament does not prove that its user changed ancestry, language or political loyalty.

passages.title: Copper, bronze, exchange and achievement
passages.text: The period’s achievements belong to many named communities: southern high-temperature kilns, deep mines, bronze and jade workshops, fortified centers, regional food systems and long exchange routes. Presenting them as one “Sinic invention” would steal credit from the very diversity that archaeology makes visible.

passages.title: Families, women, children, learning and play
passages.text: Burials sometimes group people by status, lineage or affiliation, but grave proximity alone does not prove a nuclear family. Biological kin can now be tested with ancient DNA when preservation allows; social parenthood, adoption, fosterage, marriage alliances and chosen bonds can still remain invisible.

passages.title: Families, women, children, learning and play
passages.text: Inscribed Zeng bronzes identify named marriages among elites and show women participating in interstate kin networks. That evidence is valuable but narrow: elite marriage politics cannot define every woman’s life. Women also farmed, crafted, traded, managed homes and cared for others, though task-by-gender assignments require local proof.

passages.title: Families, women, children, learning and play
passages.text: Children learned speech, manners, farming, cooking, fishing and craft by watching and practicing. Apprenticeship is strongly implied by the technical sequences behind pottery, weaving and casting, but no standardized “Sinic school” has been excavated. A clumsy object may be a learner’s work, or simply damaged.

passages.title: Families, women, children, learning and play
passages.text: Writing schools are documented most clearly around literate courts, but famous Anyang diviners sit outside this exact map footprint. Wucheng potters incised short sign sequences that may be writing, yet they remain undeciphered. We cannot name the teachers, lessons or language behind those marks.

passages.title: Families, women, children, learning and play
passages.text: People surely joked, sang, danced and played, but archaeologists cannot label every small figurine, pebble or noise-maker a toy. Context matters. Music and performance appear strongly in later elite bells and ritual equipment, while children’s games and ordinary songs mostly vanished without being written down.

passages.title: Health, medicine, water and toilets
passages.text: Bones and teeth can record healed injuries, joint strain, childhood stress and dental disease, but most infections leave no skeletal mark. Burial access and preservation create bias. A cemetery sample should never be treated as a health census for miners, farmers, craftspeople, children and mobile herders.

passages.title: Health, medicine, water and toilets
passages.text: People treated wounds, fever, pain and difficult births with practical care, food, rest, plants and ritual, but no securely readable medical manual belongs to this exact umbrella. Identifying a remedy requires residues, preparation context or text; a plant near a hearth may simply be food or fuel.

passages.title: Health, medicine, water and toilets
passages.text: Settlements needed dependable water for drinking, cooking, crops, animals, clay, cooling and metalwork. Rivers and lakes aided travel but also flooded. Wells, ditches, drains and storage pits must be distinguished by shape, sediment, location and contents; calling every channel a sewer invents evidence.

passages.title: Health, medicine, water and toilets
passages.text: No toilet design can be assigned to every community in this polygon. People could use pits, middens, fields, pig areas or spaces beyond walls, while organic waste decayed. Archaeologists look for fecal chemistry, parasite eggs and repeated deposits before confidently identifying a latrine.

passages.title: Health, medicine, water and toilets
passages.text: Later Hubei mummies and a Han-period Gansu latrine preserve parasite eggs and even hygiene sticks. They show what paleoparasitology can discover when context survives, but both are after this card. They are method comparisons, not permission to equip Panlongcheng or Wucheng with the same toilets.

passages.title: Belief, inequality, violence and coercion
passages.text: Bronze and pottery vessels in graves helped mourners display rank and conduct ceremonies with the dead. Their shapes and placement reveal action, not a universal creed. Communities could share vessel forms while understanding ancestors, spirits and obligation differently, especially across this scattered atlas footprint.

passages.title: Belief, inequality, violence and coercion
passages.text: Panlongcheng elite tombs contained rich bronzes and, in some cases, sacrificed people. Walls, controlled craft and unequal burials show concentrated power alongside ordinary households. Whether control came through kin hierarchy, alliance, threat or direct administration may have shifted; “colony” and “empire” remain debated models.

passages.title: Belief, inequality, violence and coercion
passages.text: Weapons, fortifications and traumatic injuries can document conflict, but a wall may also display authority, guide movement or resist floods. The northeast’s double stone walls and towers demanded major labor. Their builders were organized communities, yet defensive architecture alone does not reveal ethnicity or language.

passages.title: Belief, inequality, violence and coercion
passages.text: Early Chu and Zeng became competing and cooperating named polities around the middle Yangzi. Texts and inscriptions illuminate elites, while villages and border communities remain less visible. “Chu” itself can mean a state, region, archaeological style or identity, so those meanings must never be swapped silently.

passages.title: Belief, inequality, violence and coercion
passages.text: Later scientific work on elite Chu burials combines isotopes, ancient DNA and artifacts to study movement. Because those graves mainly postdate 500 BCE, they are not direct evidence for this card. Their value here is methodological: even lavish objects and ancestry results require exact dates and local context.

passages.title: Writing, change and continuity
passages.text: Contemporaneous written-language sample: none is responsibly attributable to this exact atlas category and footprint. Wucheng signs are too small and undeciphered for secure script, transliteration and translation. A decorative mark or possible sign sequence cannot become speech merely because it resembles writing.

passages.title: Writing, change and continuity
passages.text: Anyang oracle bones do preserve early Chinese language during part of this interval, recording royal divinations on cattle shoulder blades and turtle plastrons. Yet Anyang and Yinxu are outside the exact polygon in neighboring Zhou layers. Borrowing even a famous short phrase would violate the map audit.

passages.title: Writing, change and continuity
passages.text: Oracle-bone dates and readings require archaeological context, genealogy, scribal groups, radiocarbon and paleography. Roughly 1,200 of more than 4,500 graph forms have been deciphered in one scholarly accounting. Even at Anyang, experts do not pretend every sign or fragment is understood.

passages.title: Writing, change and continuity
passages.text: Panlongcheng was abandoned around 1400 to 1300 BCE without clear violent destruction; later southern centers expanded and remade bronze networks. In the first millennium, Zeng and Chu rose while northeast and northwest communities changed differently. No single ending fits all lobes of the atlas shape.

passages.title: Writing, change and continuity
passages.text: At 500 BCE the map removes “Sinic,” but farming, mining, language, family, craft and local polities continued. The app’s new owners are not automatic conquerors or descendants. Later written Chinese, Chu texts and imperial histories deserve their own correctly bounded cards rather than being pulled backward.

The exact “sinic” id disappears at 500 BCE after three snapshots with identical geometry. Tested locations then become Zhou-states territory or fall outside any polygon, but no matching collapse joins the middle Yangzi, Lanzhou and northeast. Chu, Zeng, mining districts, farmers, craftspeople and speech communities continued on local timelines. Because this atlas layer is a linguistic umbrella rather than a state, the packet records no fall and names no automatic successor. Later texts and polities must be handled through their own dated, geographically grounded evidence.

sectionTitles: Families, work and messages from far away

passages.text: The Sixteen Kingdoms were competing states across northern China during 304 to 439. Their rulers, soldiers, merchants and monks came from many backgrounds. This map combines them into one outline; its surviving 400 to 500 border interval outlasts the period, and it omits western communities discussed here.

passages.title: Rival states and fortified capitals
passages.text: The number sixteen is a historical convention: historian Charles Holcombe counts as many as twenty-two significant states. Some were large, multiethnic conquest empires whose rulers claimed the title of emperor; others were independent governors who still professed loyalty to Jin. Sharing a map color did not mean sharing a government.

passages.title: Rival states and fortified capitals
passages.text: In 383, Former Qin ruler Fu Jian tried to conquer Eastern Jin in the south. His army was defeated at the Fei River near Bagongshan. The battle illustrates how quickly an ambitious court could lose its advantage. Eastern Jin was a separate southern state, not another name for the whole northern collection.

passages.title: Rival states and fortified capitals
passages.text: Helian Bobo’s Xia state built its capital at Tongwancheng, in present-day northern Shaanxi. Its remains include an outer city and two inner-city divisions, with the palace area in the west. Towers, projecting defenses, protected entrances and moats made this a carefully organized urban stronghold. A ruler associated with steppe peoples could also commission a substantial city.

passages.title: Rival states and fortified capitals
passages.text: What held Tongwancheng’s pale walls together? Researchers tested samples from the west city and identified lime, sand and clay, with organic additives including peach gum. Their experiments suggest that lime, light river clay and surface calcium carbonate helped produce the whiteness. The familiar “white city” nickname has a material story beneath it.

passages.title: Families, work and messages from far away
passages.text: Around 313 to 314, a Sogdian woman named Miwnay wrote from Dunhuang to her mother Chatis. Abandoned by her husband, she lacked money and clothing and depended on a priest’s charity. In another letter, her daughter Shayn added her own account of tending animals. The surviving pages let a mother and child speak across sixteen centuries.

passages.title: Families, work and messages from far away
passages.text: The same letter collection names pepper, musk, silver and cloth moving along trade routes. Merchants had to find partners, arrange transport and wait for news over enormous distances. One abandoned commercial partner had to return from Dunhuang to Guzang. Trade meant worried correspondence as well as valuable cargo.

passages.title: Families, work and messages from far away
passages.text: A merchant’s letter to Samarkand reported famine and the burning of Luoyang in 311. He also complained that news from associates had stopped arriving. This is a contemporary report, with the writer’s own uncertainties: warfare appears through broken communication and concern for absent people, rather than only a list of victories.

passages.title: Families, work and messages from far away
passages.text: At Leijiacun near Xianyang, excavators found miniature wells, granaries, stoves and mills in tombs, alongside pottery animals and carts. These objects supplied the deceased with an imagined household. Even in the afterlife, somebody apparently expected the grain to be stored and dinner to be prepared.

passages.title: Families, work and messages from far away
passages.text: One Leijiacun burial contained piglet skulls; another had skulls above a stone covering a small pit of millet remains. Excavators interpreted these as funeral offerings. The grain survived as fragile pale husks, a reminder that food history can begin with something far less glamorous than a royal banquet.

passages.title: Families, work and messages from far away
passages.text: Two bronze seals from Leijiacun carried military office titles. Together with twelve tombs arranged in two planned rows, they led excavators to suggest a military family cemetery. Names and biological relationships were not established by the report. The discovery connects army service with household objects and remembrance of relatives.

passages.title: Music, memory and skilled hands
passages.text: Four seated female musician figures from Pingling tomb M1 wear painted clothes and flat black headdresses. Three retain identifiable instruments: a zheng zither, a drum and a pipa lute. The fourth looks ready to blow an instrument, but that object is missing. Archaeology occasionally delivers the band with one instrument lost.

passages.title: Music, memory and skilled hands
passages.text: In the Xianyang and Xi’an area, many cemeteries used neat parallel rows, with tombs placed at regular intervals. Archaeologists identify these as planned family burial grounds. Remembering relatives involved organizing space as well as arranging ceremonies; a cemetery could preserve a family’s connections over successive burials.

passages.title: Music, memory and skilled hands
passages.text: A brick from Wenlin tomb M49 names a woman of the Zhang family as the wife of Zhu Yi and dates the burial to 378. Such a short inscription helps archaeologists compare and date other graves. An individual woman’s memorial becomes a chronological landmark for a much larger regional history.

passages.title: Music, memory and skilled hands
passages.text: Try reading a dated object: 建武四年 means “fourth year of the Jianwu reign era,” here 338. These characters open the surviving inscription on a gilded bronze Buddha from Later Zhao, now in San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum. This is the museum’s transcription in standard Chinese characters, rather than a reproduction of the original letterforms.

passages.title: Music, memory and skilled hands
passages.text: A technical study found that the 338 Buddha was cast in sections of a clay mold fitted around a core, leaving space for molten bronze. Bronze spacers helped hold the arrangement. A gold surface finished the object; the mercury gilding used for it produced dangerous fumes. Religious splendor depended on demanding workshop labor.

passages.title: Music, memory and skilled hands
passages.text: The Buddha has clues to missing decorations: a projection behind its head probably held a halo, while holes on the base may once have supported a lotus and lions. Looking carefully turns an apparently complete museum statue into a small reconstruction puzzle.

passages.title: Learning across languages
passages.text: Kumarajiva, a Buddhist scholar born in Kucha, reached Chang’an in 401 after years of captivity. Later Qin ruler Yao Xing commissioned translations of Buddhist scriptures into Chinese. Dozens of translations are attributed to him, helping establish major traditions of Chinese Buddhism. This influential exchange of learning took place amid coercion and warfare as well as royal support.

Northern Wei reunited northern China in 439, the conventional endpoint of the Sixteen Kingdoms period. This ended the era of rival regional courts, not the lives of their inhabitants. Their cities, religious communities, crafts and family traditions form part of the history that followed.

sectionTitles: Learning, care and actual written words

passages.text: “Slavic tribes” and “Slavonic tribes” are broad map labels for many communities speaking related languages, not one kingdom. Their combined coverage runs from 800 to 1000. The earlier outline stretches implausibly far across different populations and is not a reliable ethnic frontier; the later outline is narrower. Local examples below come from western and central Europe and the eastern Alps. They do not represent every community inside either outline.

passages.title: Many communities and changing homes
passages.text: Slavic languages developed through connected dialects whose boundaries were often fluid. Later written languages grew around different political and cultural centres. Shared vocabulary therefore connects people without making their villages, rulers, customs or later national identities interchangeable.

passages.title: Many communities and changing homes
passages.text: At ninth-century Groß Raden in present-day northeastern Germany, earlier houses had woven walls and measured about 4 by 5 metres. A hearth stood on the sandy floor. The archaeological remains give a sense of compact living spaces where heat, light and everyday activity gathered around the fire.

passages.title: Many communities and changing homes
passages.text: Later Groß Raden houses were built from stacked logs and could cover up to 45 square metres. They probably had two rooms, and most had a domed oven. This was a local change in household architecture, visible because later floor plans overlap earlier ones.

passages.title: Many communities and changing homes
passages.text: An oak-plank path ran through Groß Raden towards an island. Houses stood along both sides in a pattern the museum interprets as planned. The wooden route linked domestic space with the wider settlement, a reminder that streets could be built from trees long before they were paved with asphalt.

passages.title: Tools, food and water
passages.text: Excavators at Groß Raden found textile-making equipment and waste left by comb makers, barrel makers, woodturners and smiths. Such leftovers reveal work that finished objects alone might conceal. A scrap beside a workshop can tell us where something was made, rather than simply where it was eventually used.

passages.title: Tools, food and water
passages.text: Wet conditions also preserved a wooden harrow, an oil press and other equipment at Groß Raden. A harrow helped work the soil; the press shows another stage of processing useful plant materials. These discoveries bring farming and food-related work into a story that might otherwise be dominated by walls and weapons.

passages.title: Tools, food and water
passages.text: At ninth- and tenth-century Raddusch in Lower Lusatia, archaeologists uncovered four wells inside the fort. They supplied water for people and animals. A refuge needed more than strong walls: the people sheltering there still had to drink, prepare food and care for livestock.

passages.title: Tools, food and water
passages.text: A study of 91 adults buried near Church VI at ninth- and tenth-century Mikulčice compared tooth and bone chemistry from the same people. The researchers inferred more millet and less animal protein during childhood than adulthood. Childhood meals were reconstructed from adult remains, giving a glimpse of changes within individual lives.

passages.title: Tools, food and water
passages.text: The Mikulčice study also examined cavities and tooth wear. Dietary differences were associated with differences in dental health, and higher-status people had consumed more animal protein from childhood. These are patterns within this cemetery sample, not a claim that all Slavic children ate the same meals or had the same teeth.

passages.title: Belief and a settlement rebuilt
passages.text: A carved oak plank interpreted as a sacred figure ended up in a Raddusch well during the tenth century. It is now a particularly important museum object. The find preserves a physical trace of local religious practice; the circumstances and intentions behind putting it into the well are less certain.

passages.title: Belief and a settlement rebuilt
passages.text: Groß Raden burned around 900 and was quickly rebuilt with larger log houses and a new island sanctuary. The museum considers the fire probably unrelated to an enemy attack. A burned layer records a destructive event, but identifying an enemy requires evidence beyond charcoal.

passages.title: Learning, care and actual written words
passages.text: The Freising Manuscripts contain two confession texts and a sermon in early Slovenian. Scholars place their writing probably shortly before 1000 and connect their use with Upper Carinthia. They preserve one regional Slavic language in Latin letters, showing how religious teaching could use a local language alongside Latin.

passages.title: Learning, care and actual written words
passages.text: The first manuscript begins “GLAGOLITE PO NAƷ REDKA ZLOUEZA·”. Translation: “Say after us [these] few words.” This is Igor Grdina’s transcription of folio 78r, retaining the medieval Latin-letter spelling. The instruction invites listeners to repeat the prayer, offering a direct glimpse of teaching through spoken participation.

passages.title: Learning, care and actual written words
passages.text: The second Freising text praises giving meals and clothing to people in need, visiting the sick and offering shelter to strangers. It is a sermon urging good conduct, rather than proof that every community provided these services. Its examples nevertheless show the kinds of everyday care that a preacher wanted listeners to recognise.

The year 1000 ends this map interval, not Slavic-speaking society. Communities continued within different states and religious traditions, and their dialects developed into several written languages. Some local languages later disappeared, while others remain spoken today. There was no single collective fall or successor kingdom.

sectionTitles: Art, school and skills passed between generations

passages.text: The modern Slovak Republic became independent on 1 January 1993 when Czechoslovakia divided peacefully. This is the republic that continues today, not the separate Slovak state of the Second World War. The map starts its modern label in 1994, after the actual founding.

passages.title: Small spacecraft, large waterworks
passages.text: Slovakia’s first satellite, skCUBE, launched on 23 June 2017. The Slovak Organisation for Space Activities worked with universities and companies, and more than sixty volunteers contributed. A small spacecraft could bring together students, engineers and radio enthusiasts.

passages.title: Small spacecraft, large waterworks
passages.text: skCUBE suffered a problem shortly after launch, but ground stations in Slovakia continued receiving its transmissions. It operated for 569 days without a restart before stopping in January 2019. Engineering history includes learning from a mission that did not work exactly as planned.

passages.title: Small spacecraft, large waterworks
passages.text: The Danube dam dispute inherited by Slovakia began with a 1977 treaty between Hungary and Czechoslovakia. The project combined electricity generation, navigation and river engineering. Changing a river shared with a neighbor raised questions about water flows and the environment as well as machinery.

passages.title: Small spacecraft, large waterworks
passages.text: In April 1997, judges of the International Court of Justice visited the dam sites. It was the Court’s first site visit in its fifty-year history. Sometimes deciding an international legal case means putting down the paperwork and going to look at the river.

passages.title: Art, school and skills passed between generations
passages.text: The Danubiana museum opened in September 2000 on a peninsula at the Čunovo reservoir, south of Bratislava. Dutch collector Gerard Meulensteen and Slovak gallery founder Vincent Polakovič helped create it. A waterside setting became a meeting place for Slovak and international contemporary art.

passages.title: Art, school and skills passed between generations
passages.text: Danubiana’s collections include paintings by international artists, contemporary Slovak work and outdoor sculpture. Its history records a move into a nonprofit public institution with majority state participation in 2012. Caring for modern art involves collections, buildings and long-term public support.

passages.title: Art, school and skills passed between generations
passages.text: Puppetry in Slovakia includes families who carve figures, make costumes, write stories and perform them. Children can meet the craft through workshops and performances, while experienced puppeteers teach newcomers. One small wooden character may require several different people’s skills.

passages.title: Art, school and skills passed between generations
passages.text: The fujara is an unusually long wooden pipe with just three finger holes, associated with shepherds in central Slovakia. Makers often decorate their instruments individually. The older pastoral tradition continues through musicians and craftspeople, giving this very tall instrument a life beyond the sheep pasture.

passages.title: Art, school and skills passed between generations
passages.text: Traveling tinkers once repaired damaged kitchen vessels using wire and tin. Today, the Považské Museum at Budatín presents both older work and contemporary wire designs. A practical skill for keeping a pot useful became a craft that could also make decorative objects.

passages.title: Art, school and skills passed between generations
passages.text: The education ministry describes ten years of compulsory school attendance, lasting through the school year in which a pupil reaches sixteen. This is the modern educational system. Children’s learning has its own timetable, quite separate from the much older history of the region.

passages.title: Art, school and skills passed between generations
passages.text: On 1 January 2009, Slovakia replaced the koruna with the euro. For the first sixteen days, people could pay using either currency. Shops and families had to learn new prices, with one euro officially equal to 30.1260 koruna.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: Slovak, article 1 of the constitution: “Slovenská republika je zvrchovaný, demokratický a právny štát.” Translation: “The Slovak Republic is a sovereign, democratic state governed by law.” This wording is taken from Parliament’s official 2019 consolidated edition of the constitution originally adopted in 1992.

The Slovak Republic continues as an independent state. Its modern beginning was the agreed division of Czechoslovakia in 1993, rather than a conquest or the disappearance of the communities that had lived together in the federation.

sectionTitles: Spacecraft and the things a town needs

passages.text: Slovenia declared independence from Yugoslavia on 25 June 1991, following the independence plebiscite of December 1990. It adopted a new constitution that December and joined the European Union in 2004. Its continuing republic combines modern research and public services with older local crafts and communal traditions.

passages.title: Families, craft and community
passages.text: Photographs of Ljubljana during the 1991 war show shopping for supplies, air-raid warnings and parents appealing for their sons’ safety. The City Museum preserves these alongside official events. Independence was experienced in households and streets as well as in government buildings.

passages.title: Families, craft and community
passages.text: Slovenian beekeeping often places wooden apiaries close to family homes. Beekeepers work with the native Carniolan bee and pass practical knowledge between generations. Looking after the hives can be part of a household’s yearly routine, involving observation, patience and respect for the bees.

passages.title: Families, craft and community
passages.text: Painted panels on beehives carry religious images and scenes from everyday life. The paintings form a recognizable part of Slovenian beekeeping culture. A row of hives can double as a miniature outdoor picture gallery, with a very busy workforce living behind it.

passages.title: Families, craft and community
passages.text: Bobbin lacemakers twist and cross threads wound around wooden bobbins. A paper pattern is attached to a cylindrical pillow, supported in a basket or wooden base. The finished lace can become clothing decoration or household textiles. Those apparently tangled threads have a carefully organized plan.

passages.title: Families, craft and community
passages.text: Lacemaking knowledge moves through families and neighborhood groups, often from older women to younger learners. Gathering to work also creates time for conversation and friendship. UNESCO’s account describes a social activity as well as the skill needed to produce a fine pattern.

passages.title: Families, craft and community
passages.text: The Škofja Loka Passion Play brings a large community into the streets to perform a religious drama in older local language. UNESCO’s nomination described about nine hundred performers and four hundred helpers. Costumes, scenery, music and rehearsals make it a shared undertaking well beyond the acting.

passages.title: Spacecraft and the things a town needs
passages.text: Slovenia’s NEMO-HD satellite launched in September 2020. The sixty-five-kilogram spacecraft was designed for Earth observation using video and several bands of light. Ground stations and image-processing systems were part of the project, because pictures from orbit still need people and computers back on Earth.

passages.title: Spacecraft and the things a town needs
passages.text: The same launch carried TRISAT, a five-kilogram satellite developed by the University of Maribor and SkyLabs. Its mission was designed to test miniature space electronics and an optical sensor. Small satellites can provide a demanding test bench for very small components.

passages.title: Spacecraft and the things a town needs
passages.text: Ljubljana’s Reuse Centre opened in 2013 to repair and repurpose objects, while providing employment opportunities. One example in the city’s environmental report is a shoe cupboard made from an old gaming machine. An object could retire from one job and start another.

passages.title: Spacecraft and the things a town needs
passages.text: Ljubljana’s regional waste centre combines mechanical sorting and biological treatment with facilities for treating liquid that drains from landfill. The mid-2010s project deals with several different problems hidden inside the ordinary act of throwing something away.

passages.title: Spacecraft and the things a town needs
passages.text: Slovenia’s basic school lasts nine years and usually begins at age six. The government also describes after-school programs for the first five years, including study, play and other activities. For working families, the school day can involve more than classroom lessons.

passages.title: Spacecraft and the things a town needs
passages.text: In 2016, Slovenia added a right to drinking water to its constitution. The provision treats water resources as a public good and gives household drinking-water supply priority. This records a public commitment about how an everyday necessity should be managed.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: Slovenian, article 1 of the 1991 constitution: “Slovenija je demokratična republika.” Translation: “Slovenia is a democratic republic.” The wording is preserved here in the official legal database’s consolidated text, rather than a photograph of the first printed edition.
Slovenia continues as an independent republic. Its historical starting point is independence in 1991; the map’s first modern Slovenia snapshot in 1994 should not be read as its founding year.

sectionTitles: Lessons that traveled to the students
A written greeting and a political ending

passages.text: The Sokoto Caliphate grew from the Islamic reform movement and warfare begun by Usman dan Fodio in 1804. The atlas labels its earlier Nigerian phase “Fulani Empire” and its later phase “Sokoto Caliphate”; these are connected parts of one political history, not two unrelated civilizations. Scholarship, textile production and an economy relying heavily on enslaved labor all shaped its society.

passages.title: Lessons that traveled to the students
passages.text: Nana Asma’u, 1793 to 1864, wrote, taught and managed a large household. Mack and Boyd describe her work in Arabic, Fulfulde, Hausa and Tamachek. She belonged to a family of scholars, but her teaching reached beyond that family.

passages.title: Lessons that traveled to the students
passages.text: Asma’u trained traveling women teachers called jajis. They took verse lessons to women in other communities, including learners taught at home. A lesson could travel with its teacher instead of requiring everyone to reach one school building.

passages.title: Lessons that traveled to the students
passages.text: Recitation and memorization helped lessons spread to relatives and neighbors. Written poetry and oral teaching worked together; listening to a poem could make someone a participant even without owning a manuscript.

passages.title: Lessons that traveled to the students
passages.text: The surviving Admonition poem is in Hausa Ajami, with vowel marks helping readers sound out the text. Boston University dates its composition between 1855 and 1857. The reproduced copy is an undated printed witness, not a sheet known to be in Asma’u’s hand.

passages.title: Family, kindness and keeping clean
passages.text: Asma’u’s elegies remember women’s practical care. Zaharatu assisted at births; Aisha helped orphans and widows. Such named work shows that community history included caregiving, not only the careers of male rulers.

passages.title: Family, kindness and keeping clean
passages.text: Admonition treats obtaining food and seeking education as legitimate reasons for women to leave home. It also asks wives to follow lawful marital obligations. This was a religious argument made within her society, not a claim that its rules matched modern equality.

passages.title: Family, kindness and keeping clean
passages.text: The poem tells believers to observe ritual washing, while allowing dry ablution during illness. The editors explain that earth or sand could be used when water was unavailable or a person was sick. This concerns religious practice; it does not establish a citywide plumbing system.

passages.title: Family, kindness and keeping clean
passages.text: It also encourages charity and extra help for people in need. Alongside prayer and study, generosity belonged in the moral life Asma’u was teaching. Her verses are evidence of ideals being urged, not proof everyone always lived up to them.

passages.title: Hands, crops and unequal power
passages.text: Plantations around Sokoto, Kano, Zaria and other towns supplied food and raw materials. Salau lists millet, sorghum, cotton and indigo among the goods tied to this economy. Everyday eating and dressing depended on large amounts of agricultural work.

passages.title: Hands, crops and unequal power
passages.text: That work often came from enslaved people. Salau distinguishes supervised labor gangs, work alongside owners and arrangements requiring payments to owners. Different arrangements did not remove the fundamental denial of freedom.

passages.title: Hands, crops and unequal power
passages.text: Muhammad Bello promoted agricultural settlement as part of consolidating the state. Lovejoy connects these policies with textile production in southern Kano and northern Zaria: fields, spinning, weaving, dyeing and trade belonged to an interconnected economy.

passages.title: Hands, crops and unequal power
passages.text: No single plantation export crop dominated the whole caliphate. Food markets and textile making were both important. This helps explain why a history of the state must include workshops and farms, not just armies.

passages.title: A written greeting and a political ending
passages.text: “بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم” means “In the name of God, the Compassionate, the Merciful.” This Arabic invocation opens the scanned printed witness of Admonition, before its Hausa Ajami verses. Here it is shown without vowel marks. The surviving printed copy is not known to be in Asma’u’s own hand.

passages.title: A written greeting and a political ending
passages.text: British forces took Kano and Sokoto in 1903 amid the wider European partition of the caliphate’s territories. Loss of independent government did not end Muslim scholarship or the communities whose lives had made the state.

passages.title: A written greeting and a political ending
passages.text: Asma’u’s educational work remained influential long after her lifetime. SOAS’s account of her writings and Jean Boyd’s scholarship documents a continuing legacy of women teaching women, rather than a tradition that simply stopped when the state was conquered.

Colonial conquest ended the independent Sokoto Caliphate in 1903. Its territories were divided under European rule, while Muslim communities and traditions of scholarship continued. The later 1914 map endpoint is not the end date of independent Sokoto.

sectionTitles: A kingdom ran on records as well as armies
Food cargoes, family gifts and a port’s income
Learning, unequal households and surviving words

passages.text: The Solankis, also called the Chaulukyas of Gujarat, governed a major western Indian kingdom from Anahilapataka, modern Patan. This is a different dynasty from the Chalukyas of the Deccan. The imported 1100 to 1200 interval captures an influential century within a longer history. Its broad Gujarat, Rajasthan and eastward outline simplifies changing conquests and subordinate rulers; it is not a surveyed boundary held unchanged for a hundred years.

passages.title: A kingdom ran on records as well as armies
passages.text: The kingdom’s reach could extend beyond Gujarat. Inscriptions associated with Kumarapala’s officers occur at Udayapura near Bhilsa in Malwa. Such records help historians trace political power beyond the capital, while reminding us that local officers and subordinate rulers mattered alongside the king.

passages.title: A kingdom ran on records as well as armies
passages.text: Royal copper-plate grants became more standardized around the beginning of the twelfth century. Historian Masahiko Mita connects this change with the emergence of a document office in the late eleventh century. Keeping consistent records was one of the quieter achievements of government, with consequences for land and revenue.

passages.title: A kingdom ran on records as well as armies
passages.text: In these royal grants, the king appeared as donor, announcer and issuer. Mita distinguishes this regular form from documents issued by subordinate rulers. A copper plate was therefore more than a durable receipt: its wording displayed who claimed the right to grant land.

passages.title: Water, memory and remarkable stonework
passages.text: Rani-ki-Vav at Patan was built in the eleventh century, before the displayed map interval, and is traditionally attributed to Queen Udayamati, wife of Bhima I. Its memorial purpose joined family remembrance to a substantial public water structure. Royal women could leave their mark on a city’s practical landscape.

passages.title: Water, memory and remarkable stonework
passages.text: The stepwell descends through seven levels of stairs and carved panels toward stored water. More than five hundred principal sculptures mix sacred and secular subjects. The builders made the descent itself an architectural experience: getting water could involve walking down into an extraordinary stone world.

passages.title: Water, memory and remarkable stonework
passages.text: UNESCO’s account links the well’s later silting to thirteenth-century flooding and changes to the Saraswati riverbed. Burial helped preserve much of its sculpture for centuries. The same environmental change that ended its original water function helped shelter evidence of the craftspeople who built it.

passages.title: Water, memory and remarkable stonework
passages.text: Another Patan water project, Sahastralinga Talav, renewed an earlier reservoir during Siddharaja Jayasimha’s reign. The district’s monument account notes that both rulers and citizens sponsored lakes, wells and reservoirs. Supplying water depended on repeated maintenance and patronage, not just one spectacular new building.

passages.title: Water, memory and remarkable stonework
passages.text: At Modhera, an eleventh-century Sun temple combines a shrine, an assembly hall and a stepped tank. Sculptors filled its surfaces with gods, musicians, birds and animals; ceiling scenes draw on the Ramayana and Mahabharata. Architecture provided space for gathering while its carvings carried stories and religious imagery.

passages.title: Food cargoes, family gifts and a port’s income
passages.text: A Mangrol inscription from the mid-1140s records a temple named for Sahajiga, father of the donors Somaraja and Muluka. Muluka assigned revenue to support its worship. This family memorial connected kinship, local leadership and the continuing costs of maintaining a religious institution.

passages.title: Food cargoes, family gifts and a port’s income
passages.text: The same record lists dues on grain carts, bullock and donkey loads, camels carrying betel leaves, and salt production. These are useful glimpses of working lives: growers, carters, pack-animal handlers and sellers kept goods moving. A temple’s accounts can unexpectedly turn into a map of everyday trade.

passages.title: Food cargoes, family gifts and a port’s income
passages.text: Leading people at Choravad also dedicated a tree-lined well near a village road, with royal permission. The inscription describes an existing, bounded property. Water facilities could be shared civic assets whose support and ownership were carefully recorded, rather than merely holes somebody dug and forgot.

passages.title: Food cargoes, family gifts and a port’s income
passages.text: Cambay’s maritime importance depended on its inland connections. Research links the rise of Chaulukya power with routes joining the coast, agricultural districts and intermediary markets. A twelfth-century Jewish business letter also records a voyage through Diu toward Aden. Gujarat’s economy connected inland growers with people travelling far across the sea.

passages.title: Learning, unequal households and surviving words
passages.text: Hemachandra composed a work in 1160 that illustrated grammar through praised deeds of royal patrons, including Kumarapala. Language lessons could also tell readers how a ruler wished to be remembered. This was learned courtly literature; its survival does not tell us that every child attended school.

passages.title: Learning, unequal households and surviving words
passages.text: A surviving copy made in 1428 shows Hemachandra teaching Kumarapala. The monk carries a cloth to avoid swallowing insects and a broom to protect small creatures in his path. This later illustration preserves a Jain ideal of avoiding harm, while remaining a later artistic portrayal rather than an eyewitness portrait.

passages.title: Learning, unequal households and surviving words
passages.text: The Lekhapaddhati preserves actual and model documents used by scribes, including credit agreements, mortgages and private letters. Its materials span several centuries of Gujarat’s history. Forms for everyday obligations show why trained writers mattered: making a promise about property or money could require specialized language.

passages.title: Learning, unequal households and surviving words
passages.text: Some documents in that collection concern enslaved girls and reveal the power their owners exercised over their work and treatment. Courtly learning and magnificent temples existed alongside deep household inequalities. These records help recover people whose choices were sharply restricted and whose own voices rarely survive.

passages.title: Learning, unequal households and surviving words
passages.text: नमः शिवाय, namaḥ śivāya, means “Salutation to Shiva.” This Sanskrit phrase opens the Mangrol stone record dated Vikrama Samvat 1202, in the mid-1140s. It appears here in modern Devanagari type, following the published transcription of the inscription, rather than reproducing the stone’s individual carved letters.

The 1200 map cutoff does not mark the dynasty’s end. During the thirteenth century, Vaghela leaders accumulated authority, and Visaladeva established independent supremacy in the 1240s. This was a transfer of ruling power within a continuing regional society. Gujarat’s water monuments, trade and learned traditions outlived the Solanki court.
