passages.text: The exact atlas id “south-russia” spans 1920 to 1930, but its only decoded feature is Crimea, not the Russian south. The polygon includes tested Simferopol, Sevastopol, and Kerch while excluding Rostov-on-Don, the Kuban, Donbas, Odesa, the North Caucasus, and lower Volga. Historical “South Russia” meant Pyotr Wrangel's anti-Bolshevik military government, defeated and evacuated from Crimea in November 1920; it did not rule through the mapped decade. From October 1921 the peninsula instead formed the Crimean Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic within the Russian SFSR, then the USSR. Residents included Crimean Tatars, Russians, Ukrainians, Jews, Germans, Greeks, Armenians, Bulgarians, Karaites, Krymchaks, and others, with sharp differences among ports, steppe farms, mountain villages, and resort towns. Civil-war terror and the 1921 to 1923 famine scarred families. NEP brought partial recovery, markets, national schools, Tatarization, Jewish agricultural settlement, sanatoria, theatre, archaeology, and new infrastructure, alongside coercion and unequal access. By 1928 repression and forced collectivization were closing that opening. In 1930 the atlas wrongly recolors Crimea as “white-russia.” The Crimean ASSR continued; the seam proves neither conquest nor a modern territorial claim.

passages.title: Read the atlas label as Crimea, not a southern empire
passages.text: The live index contains one exact “south-russia” record named “South Russia,” approximately 1920 to 1930. One border snapshot carries it, but its researched card and override are missing. The imported summary correctly ends Wrangel's White South in 1920, so it cannot explain the atlas feature's extra decade.

passages.title: Read the atlas label as Crimea, not a southern empire
passages.text: The only decoded target is one Polygon with one component, one ring, 39 positions, and bbox 32.50292502925029, 44.491549258420484 to 36.520565205652076, 46.192463742475915. Its geometry SHA-256 is 27eb507d7271400ebe45a546b0d4c05d8fc1a3ff7df60e56f225f4a4bdb01824. That footprint is Crimea, not all southern Russia. It audits a simplified software shape, not a surveyed historical frontier.

passages.title: Read the atlas label as Crimea, not a southern empire
passages.text: Tested Simferopol, Sevastopol, and Kerch fall inside. Rostov-on-Don, Novocherkassk, Taganrog, Krasnodar, Novorossiysk, Sochi, Stavropol, Armavir, Maykop, Elista, Tsaritsyn, Astrakhan, Donetsk, Mariupol, Kharkiv, Kyiv, Odesa, Makhachkala, Grozny, and Vladikavkaz do not. The label's geographic mismatch is therefore measurable, not merely semantic.

passages.title: Read the atlas label as Crimea, not a southern empire
passages.text: In 1914 every tested Crimean and southern point is assigned to “russian-empire.” In 1920 only the three Crimean probes enter “south-russia”; Rostov and Krasnodar are already “ussr,” while Donetsk and Odesa are “ukraine.” The sudden categories describe atlas design, not a uniform founding, border treaty, or popular allegiance.

passages.title: Read the atlas label as Crimea, not a southern empire
passages.text: At 1930 the target vanishes and every sampled Soviet point, from Crimea to Moscow and Baku, is misassigned to “white-russia.” By 1938 and 1945 all tested Crimean and Soviet comparators return to “ussr.” The endpoint is a broad atlas failure, not Belarusian rule, White restoration, or Crimean collapse.

passages.title: Follow war, evacuation, terror, autonomy, and Union rule
passages.text: Wrangel's Government of South Russia was a White military and civilian regime centered on Crimea during 1920, not a stable country lasting to 1930. Its archives show attempted land reform and administration under severe military pressure. Municipal politicians could oppose it, and residents were never one ideological camp.

passages.title: Follow war, evacuation, terror, autonomy, and Union rule
passages.text: Red forces breached Perekop in November 1920, and Wrangel ordered evacuation from Crimean ports. Ships carried soldiers, officials, families, refugees, foreign personnel, and supplies toward Constantinople. Numbers vary by source, so the card emphasizes the documented movement and separation rather than pretending that every evacuee shared one motive or fate.

passages.title: Follow war, evacuation, terror, autonomy, and Union rule
passages.text: After the White defeat, Soviet security organs screened prisoners and civilians and carried out mass executions from November 1920 into 1921. Archival historians debate totals and categories. The secure conclusion is organized lethal repression on a large scale; disputed numbers should never become a gruesome scoreboard or erase individual victims.

passages.title: Follow war, evacuation, terror, autonomy, and Union rule
passages.text: The 1921 Crimean constitution placed the republic inside the Russian SFSR. Its institutions used Soviet congresses, executive committees, and commissariats, while autonomy and Tatarization emerged through negotiation and coercion. This was neither Wrangel's government nor an independent nation-state, and constitutional words did not guarantee equal power or safety.

passages.title: Follow war, evacuation, terror, autonomy, and Union rule
passages.text: When the USSR was declared in December 1922, Crimea did not join as a union republic. It remained an autonomous republic within the Russian SFSR, one of the new Union's constituent republics. Moscow gained extensive federal authority, while local institutions continued under layered party and state control that residents encountered unevenly.

passages.title: Meet a multilingual peninsula and contested national policies
passages.text: The 1926 census and local city studies show Crimea as multiethnic and multilingual: Crimean Tatars, Russians, Ukrainians, Jews, Germans, Greeks, Armenians, Bulgarians, Karaites, Krymchaks, and others lived in different proportions across towns and countryside. Census labels are valuable evidence, but mixed homes, changing language, migration, and self-identification resist tidy boxes.

passages.title: Meet a multilingual peninsula and contested national policies
passages.text: Tatarization promoted Crimean Tatar personnel, schools, publications, and public-language use during the 1920s. It partly recognized an Indigenous population marginalized by empire and war, yet operated inside a one-party system. National institutions created real opportunities without making every Crimean Tatar supportive, every official bilingual, or every village equally served.

passages.title: Meet a multilingual peninsula and contested national policies
passages.text: Veli Ibrahimov, a Crimean Tatar communist and republic leader, defended land and staffing priorities that increasingly clashed with central policy. His 1928 arrest and execution marked a decisive assault on Tatarization's leadership. Treating the case simply as factional politics would miss the fear carried into offices, schools, villages, and families.

passages.title: Meet a multilingual peninsula and contested national policies
passages.text: Muslims, Orthodox Christians, Jews, Karaites, Krymchaks, Catholics, and other communities maintained worship, family rites, calendars, charity, and social networks. Soviet authorities regulated, taxed, closed, or repurposed religious institutions while promoting atheism. Practice varied by locality and generation; neither “religious Crimea” nor “atheist Crimea” describes everyone.

passages.title: Meet a multilingual peninsula and contested national policies
passages.text: National village councils and schools could make language and representation visible, while settlement schemes redistributed land and resources. Jewish agricultural colonists built new cooperatives with Soviet and overseas aid; Crimean Tatar leaders protested allocations they considered unjust. Both communities had diverse interests, so conflict must not be recast as timeless ethnic hostility.

passages.title: Work farms, vineyards, ports, markets, and new settlements
passages.text: Crimean agriculture differed sharply by ecology. Steppe districts emphasized grain and livestock; foothills mixed crops; mountain and south-coast zones supported orchards, vineyards, and tobacco. War, famine, animal losses, land redistribution, weather, and access to tools changed each household's choices. One peninsula-wide peasant routine would be fictional.

passages.title: Work farms, vineyards, ports, markets, and new settlements
passages.text: NEP restored limited legal trade, cooperatives, leasing, and some hired labor after War Communism, helping markets and farms recover. It did not restore prewar ownership or remove taxes and state procurement. Traders, artisans, porters, shopkeepers, seasonal workers, and farmers navigated changing rules whose enforcement differed across districts.

passages.title: Work farms, vineyards, ports, markets, and new settlements
passages.text: Ports including Feodosiia and Yevpatoriia connected shipping, fishing, military facilities, salt, grain, fruit, wine, and passengers. Rail and cart routes tied harbors to Simferopol and rural producers. Port activity also meant inspections, dangerous loading, irregular employment, and family separation, not simply bustling prosperity.

passages.title: Work farms, vineyards, ports, markets, and new settlements
passages.text: From 1924 Agro-Joint and Soviet bodies supported Jewish farming settlements with land plans, machinery, credit, agronomists, health work, and schools. Colonists had to learn unfamiliar soils and farm routines. Calling northern Crimea “empty” hides earlier users, landless Crimean Tatars, ecological limits, and political disputes over allocation.

passages.title: Work farms, vineyards, ports, markets, and new settlements
passages.text: A 1924 to 1925 Crimean budget basket lists rye and wheat flour, millet, potatoes, meat, butter, milk, vegetable oil, herring, sugar, cloth, kerosene, soap, tobacco, and firewood. It describes priced necessities for university staff, not everyone's pantry, but restores ordinary purchasing decisions to economic history.

passages.title: Enter families, homes, meals, clothes, and social life
passages.text: Families absorbed demobilization, death, exile, famine, migration, unemployment, and new wage work. Adults and older children combined paid labor with cooking, fuel gathering, care, repairs, and queues. Interwar household studies reveal gendered and age-graded work, but a Soviet average cannot replace evidence for each Crimean Tatar village, port family, or settler household.

passages.title: Enter families, homes, meals, clothes, and social life
passages.text: Soviet law expanded civil marriage, divorce, women's formal equality, children's legal status, and access to abortion. Those rules mattered, but paperwork, housing, income, childcare, religion, kin expectations, and local officials shaped actual choices. Legal emancipation did not wash dishes, find wages, or make an unsafe partner disappear.

passages.title: Enter families, homes, meals, clothes, and social life
passages.text: Housing ranged from rural farmsteads and Crimean Tatar village homes to port rooms, divided urban apartments, barracks, sanatorium wards, and repurposed villas. Crowding and fuel shortages could turn privacy into a luxury. Evidence from Moscow hygiene campaigns is only a comparator, not permission to assign communal apartments to every Crimean household.

passages.title: Enter families, homes, meals, clothes, and social life
passages.text: Meals reflected grain, potatoes, dairy, vegetables, fruit, fish, meat, oil, and local or religious practice, but access varied drastically. Contemporary price lists record goods, not what every family ate. During famine even familiar foods became unobtainable, and relief rations cannot be mistaken for a normal Crimean diet.

passages.title: Enter families, homes, meals, clothes, and social life
passages.text: Clothing marked occupation, gender, age, faith, wealth, and setting. Crimean Tatar dress changed under urban fashion and Soviet campaigns, while work clothes faced salt, soil, grease, weather, and repeated mending. Photographs and costume debates preserve selected appearances; they rarely inventory the patched shirt worn to exhaustion.

passages.title: Grow up, teach, learn, and navigate changing rights
passages.text: War, evacuation, famine, epidemic disease, and adult death left children hungry, displaced, or without dependable caregivers. Schools and orphanages faced overwhelming demand and weak supplies. General Soviet evidence documents institutional scarcity; Yalta evidence confirms severe local population loss. Neither source permits a precise peninsula-wide count of homeless children.

passages.title: Grow up, teach, learn, and navigate changing rights
passages.text: National-language schools, literacy classes, teacher training, clubs, and libraries expanded, but buildings, books, trained staff, and attendance remained uneven. Census analysis reports high Crimean literacy relative to many regions, yet urban and rural opportunity differed. Reading ability also ranged from signing a form to handling complex literature.

passages.title: Grow up, teach, learn, and navigate changing rights
passages.text: Crimean Tatar women worked as teachers and cultural organizers while journals debated education, consent in marriage, property, leisure, and public participation. These debates reveal women speaking and acting, not a single “traditional” position. Formal rights still met childcare burdens, poverty, patriarchal authority, state surveillance, and differences among families.

passages.title: Grow up, teach, learn, and navigate changing rights
passages.text: Artek opened in June 1925 as a small sanatorium camp for medically selected children. Archival files preserve selection letters, schedules, transport reports, and photographs. That evidence illuminates some children's meals, rest, outdoor routines, and supervision, but it describes an exceptional institution, not an average Crimean summer vacation.

passages.title: Grow up, teach, learn, and navigate changing rights
passages.text: Children learned in secular schools, Crimean Tatar institutions, families, farms, workshops, religious settings, youth groups, and workplaces. Soviet educational experiments sought mass access while teacher and orphanage shortages narrowed delivery. A timetable can show official hopes; it cannot reveal every child's fear, curiosity, chores, language switches, or missed class.

passages.title: Read law, scripts, newspapers, theatre, and archaeology
passages.text: Written-language sample, Simferopol, 1924 publication of the 1921 constitution: “Конституция Крымской Советской Социалистической Республики.” Transliteration: “Konstitutsiya Krymskoy Sovetskoy Sotsialisticheskoy Respubliki.” Translation: “Constitution of the Crimean Soviet Socialist Republic.” This is a Russian legal title in Cyrillic, securely cataloged by the Presidential Library, not everyday speech.

passages.title: Read law, scripts, newspapers, theatre, and archaeology
passages.text: Crimean Tatar, Russian, Ukrainian, Yiddish, German, Greek, Armenian, and other languages circulated in homes, schools, administration, worship, trade, and print. Crimean Tatar writing moved from reformed Arabic script toward Latin letters in 1928. Script reform changed literacy work and access; it did not instantly change speech or erase older readers.

passages.title: Read law, scripts, newspapers, theatre, and archaeology
passages.text: The Crimean Tatar State Drama Theatre opened in Simferopol in 1923 and employed writers, actors, directors, musicians, costumers, stage workers, and ticket staff. Theatre could support language and public culture while serving Soviet institutions. A state logo never performed a play by itself; people did the rehearsing, sewing, hauling, and remembering.

passages.title: Read law, scripts, newspapers, theatre, and archaeology
passages.text: The Muslim journal Asriy Musulmanliq discussed women's education, consent, property, leisure, and civic participation between 1924 and 1927. Newspapers and magazines created argument rather than automatic consensus. Editors, subscribers, teachers, religious thinkers, secular activists, and readers could disagree, and surviving print does not measure what every household believed.

passages.title: Read law, scripts, newspapers, theatre, and archaeology
passages.text: Crimean archaeologists and museum workers excavated, cataloged, protected, and published sites during the 1920s, including Chersonesos. Their work preserved knowledge and trained specialists, yet institutions also fought for land, buildings, funds, and authority. Archaeology was an achievement produced by field crews and archives, and it could also serve state narratives.

passages.title: Face famine, epidemics, medicine, resorts, and earthquakes
passages.text: Famine weakened bodies already affected by war, displacement, cold, and disease. Yalta histories record severe loss, while relief archives show food and medicine moving through international systems. Typhus, relapsing fever, typhoid, and other infections traveled with hunger and crowding. Survival depended on locality, timing, connections, and aid access.

passages.title: Face famine, epidemics, medicine, resorts, and earthquakes
passages.text: The Soviet health system emphasized unified administration, prevention, vaccination, sanitation, and campaigns against tuberculosis, venereal disease, and alcoholism. These were ambitious public-health tools rather than proof of universal treatment. Clinics still needed trained staff, beds, drugs, transport, trust, clean water, and time that famine-stricken families might not have.

passages.title: Face famine, epidemics, medicine, resorts, and earthquakes
passages.text: Sevastopol rebuilt a city health department and medical institutions after war, but shortages constrained services. Hospitals, outpatient care, sanitary work, and epidemic response reached a strategic port with unusual needs. Evidence from Sevastopol cannot represent a mountain village, and formal availability does not prove affordable, timely, or culturally trusted care.

passages.title: Face famine, epidemics, medicine, resorts, and earthquakes
passages.text: Nationalized villas, estates, and palaces supported plans for a “workers' health resort.” Sanatoria combined rest, diet, climate, supervision, and ideology, while admission depended on referrals, categories, beds, and budgets. NEP brought more flexible financing. The achievement expanded treatment, but a Crimean address did not give every resident a seaside bed.

passages.title: Face famine, epidemics, medicine, resorts, and earthquakes
passages.text: The 1927 Crimean earthquakes damaged southern settlements and produced recorded Black Sea waves. Instrumental stations began operating at Yalta, Feodosiia, Simferopol, and Sevastopol, improving regional observation. Better measurement was a scientific achievement, but families first encountered shaking through falling masonry, interrupted sleep, damaged homes, frightened animals, and uncertain repairs.

passages.title: Carry water, mend pipes, manage waste, and discuss toilets honestly
passages.text: Yalta inherited municipal waterworks and a separate sewer system, but war brought broken crossings, leaks, inflation, and unstable tariffs. In 1921 local rules made communal water use and household pipe or sewer repair free. The decree mattered; still, water pressure, distance, maintenance, and building connections shaped what reached a kitchen.

passages.title: Carry water, mend pipes, manage waste, and discuss toilets honestly
passages.text: Sevastopol's 1925 water trust confronted a network able to supply only limited daily volume. Some residents collected water from public booths, and summer shortages were acute. Repair and finance improved parts of the system, but a strategic port still rationed convenience by neighborhood. Pipes, rather stubbornly, did not repair themselves.

passages.title: Carry water, mend pipes, manage waste, and discuss toilets honestly
passages.text: Simferopol opened a sewer system in 1925 with biological treatment, yet the network had not reached full capacity. That is a real sanitation milestone, not proof that every street or dwelling was connected. Sewers also required drains, pumping, treatment, workers, fees, repairs, and habits that changed more slowly than an opening ceremony.

passages.title: Carry water, mend pipes, manage waste, and discuss toilets honestly
passages.text: Reviewed sources do not provide a reliable 1920 to 1930 inventory of Crimean household toilets. City sewers imply connected fixtures somewhere, while public water booths and incomplete networks imply very unequal plumbing. The card therefore does not assign flush toilets, privies, chamber pots, or waste collectors uniformly. “Unknown” is useful plumbing information.

passages.title: Carry water, mend pipes, manage waste, and discuss toilets honestly
passages.text: Health campaigns urged clean homes, safe water, ventilation, washing, inspections, and disease prevention, but domestic labor and underfunded facilities limited compliance. Women and cleaners often carried the burden while officials blamed habits. Sanitation involved hauling, scrubbing, fuel, soap, drainage, and municipal work, not simply posters telling microbes to behave.

passages.title: Weigh achievements, human costs, and the false 1930 ending
passages.text: International relief joined American food and medicine with aid mobilized from Turkey and other networks. Kitchens, warehouses, transport, medical supplies, translators, and local distribution saved lives, although politics shaped access and publicity. Relief deserves credit without turning catastrophe into an uplifting adventure or hiding why households had become dependent on it.

passages.title: Weigh achievements, human costs, and the false 1930 ending
passages.text: Sanatoria and Artek developed new combinations of preventive medicine, climate therapy, children's routines, and collective care. They became influential models and employed many workers. Their benefits remained selected and unequal, especially beside famine and poor rural access. Achievement is clearest when the people admitted, excluded, cooking, cleaning, and caring remain visible.

passages.title: Weigh achievements, human costs, and the false 1930 ending
passages.text: Crimean Tatar theatre, museums, archaeological fieldwork, and new earthquake stations widened cultural and scientific work. None arose from a single “civilization.” Actors, excavators, technicians, librarians, students, and audiences built them across communities, often while negotiating censorship, funding, language reform, institutional rivalry, and political danger.

passages.title: Weigh achievements, human costs, and the false 1930 ending
passages.text: The late 1920s ended much of the NEP compromise and accelerated forced collectivization, grain procurement, and campaigns against alleged kulaks. These policies cost property, livelihoods, freedom, and lives. Modernization statistics cannot cancel coercion, and later catastrophe should not be read as inevitable from every choice made in 1920.

passages.title: Weigh achievements, human costs, and the false 1930 ending
passages.text: At the 1930 seam “south-russia” disappears, yet the Crimean ASSR, its towns, villages, institutions, families, and ecological regions continue. The atlas's “white-russia” replacement blankets places far beyond Belarus and is corrected to “ussr” by 1938. This software sequence offers no historical argument about sovereignty or present-day borders.

At 1930 the atlas removes “south-russia” and assigns Crimea, Rostov, Donbas, Odesa, Moscow, and every other tested Soviet point to “white-russia.” By 1938 those probes are “ussr.” No White government returned and Crimea did not become Belarusian. The Crimean ASSR continued inside the Russian SFSR; forced collectivization changed life without making society vanish.

sectionTitles: A new country with older histories
Saving records and making history public
School, water and skilled local work

passages.text: South Sudan became independent from Sudan on 9 July 2011 after a referendum. This map’s modern-country layer begins only in 2020, so its first displayed year is not the country’s founding date. Older communities and histories also extend across the border separating the two modern states.

passages.title: A new country with older histories
passages.text: The 2005 Comprehensive Peace Agreement set the path toward a vote on southern Sudan’s future. In January 2011, voters overwhelmingly chose separation, and independence followed that July. South Sudan and Sudan therefore became distinct countries, while families and historical connections continued across the new international boundary.

passages.title: A new country with older histories
passages.text: Fighting broke out in December 2013, only two years after independence. The United Nations strengthened its mission’s civilian-protection role. A revitalized peace agreement was signed in September 2018, but signing a document was one step in a difficult process of making communities safe.

passages.title: A new country with older histories
passages.text: Here is Juba Arabic in the scholarly spelling recorded by linguists: “ána kan déru áynu akú tái”, translated “I wanted to see my brother.” The Latin letters and accents reproduce an attested modern transcription. This small family sentence offers a language sample without pretending it is an ancient inscription.

passages.title: Saving records and making history public
passages.text: War left many administrative records damaged, scattered or stored in sacks in damp rooms. Archivists and their partners worked to clean, sort, box and digitize surviving papers from the colonial period through the 1980s. Sometimes preserving history starts with the distinctly unglamorous job of rescuing a pile of paper.

passages.title: Saving records and making history public
passages.text: In November 2017, the Tarikh Tana radio series brought archival documents into public conversation. South Sudanese panelists discussed a different document each week on Eye Radio, alongside exhibitions. History could be heard on a radio as well as read in an archive, reaching people beyond a reading room.

passages.title: School, water and skilled local work
passages.text: A 2021 education case study describes repairs to girls’ latrines and installation of handwashing facilities at two schools in Torit County. These changes helped pupils manage everyday needs, including menstruation. Returning to class after COVID-19 closures involved usable toilets and privacy as well as reopening school gates.

passages.title: School, water and skilled local work
passages.text: The same programme supported mothers’ groups and girls’ clubs. Older female pupils trained to encourage others to return to school and to speak up about education. Learning was supported by relationships across generations: classmates and mothers could help address concerns that a textbook alone could not solve.

passages.title: School, water and skilled local work
passages.text: Yei’s upgraded water system opened in May 2023 with five boreholes, 59 water kiosks and about 33 kilometres of pipe. Solar power ran the system, and chlorination helped keep the water safe. Water services need pumps, treatment and maintenance together; sunshine alone cannot make a dirty cup clean.

passages.title: School, water and skilled local work
passages.text: At Boma Hospital, solar equipment installed in late 2022 supplied lights and reliable power for vaccine storage. In a May 2023 report, staff described easier night-time deliveries and better temperature control. Electricity changed very practical tasks: seeing a patient clearly and keeping essential medicines appropriately cool.

passages.title: School, water and skilled local work
passages.text: In a 2025 account from Mangaten, 21-year-old Veronica interpreted for a women’s support group while studying international relations in Juba. The programme combined emotional support with skills such as making soap and weaving baskets for sale. Her story shows education, care and earning a living meeting in one person’s working week.

passages.title: A sporting first
passages.text: At the Paris 2024 Olympic tournament, South Sudan’s men won their first Olympic basketball game, defeating Puerto Rico 90 to 79 in Lille. Nuni Omot scored the country’s first Olympic basketball points. A young state could now add an international sporting achievement to the stories told about it.

passages.title: A sporting first
passages.text: The win required more than one star. Carlik Jones recorded 19 points, seven rebounds and six assists, while four teammates also scored at least ten points. South Sudan collected 55 rebounds against Puerto Rico’s 37. A missed shot was often the beginning of another chance, not the end of the play.

South Sudan continues as an independent country. In April 2025, UN officials warned that renewed military confrontation threatened the peace process. That dated warning shows why the 2018 agreement should not be presented as a complete end to violence, even as citizens continue schooling, research, work and cultural life.

sectionTitles: Stone families and brick picture puzzles

passages.text: Southern Qi ruled from Jiankang, today’s Nanjing, between 479 and 502, after Liu Song and before Liang. The Xiao imperial family governed a southern realm while Northern Wei held much of the north. This record’s imported outline appears only for 500 to 502 and is a coarse reconstruction, not a reliable frontier for every year. Household records, poetry, medicine and monuments reveal its short history.

passages.title: Power, households and social rank
passages.text: Princes received provincial military commands, but document clerks watched over their households and affairs. Managing a prince’s paperwork gave these officials knowledge of his resources and plans. Family appointment did not mean that the emperor trusted relatives without supervision.

passages.title: Power, households and social rank
passages.text: Emperor Wu reviewed household registers to identify families liable for taxes and labour service. Registration could change a household’s obligations, so it was a matter of livelihoods as well as paperwork. The campaign helped provoke resistance, including Tang Yuzhi’s rebellion.

passages.title: Power, households and social rank
passages.text: Ancestry mattered when elite families arranged marriages and sought office. Yet the boundaries were negotiable: daughters of the prestigious Wang clan became Qi empresses, while Wang and Xie men married imperial princesses. Family connections could join established social prestige to a newer ruling house.

passages.title: Stone families and brick picture puzzles
passages.text: A Buddhist stele dated 483 was found in Mao County, Sichuan, in 1921. Its surviving fragments carry figures, small shrines and a dated dedication. It is now in Sichuan Museum. This securely dated object helps scholars compare southern Buddhist carving styles without dating every similar-looking sculpture to the same year.

passages.title: Stone families and brick picture puzzles
passages.text: A different carving from Xi’an Road in Chengdu dates to 490. Its inscription says that the monk Fahai and his mother made an image for his deceased father, extending their wish to relatives and other beings. Religious dedication preserved the memory of a particular family, including a mother’s participation.

passages.title: Stone families and brick picture puzzles
passages.text: Try a tiny piece of that 490 inscription: “与母为亡父”, meaning “with his mother, for his deceased father”. In modern Mandarin it reads yǔ mǔ wèi wáng fù. These are the museum’s modern transcribed Chinese characters, not a facsimile of the carved handwriting; the modern pronunciation is not a reconstruction of fifth-century speech.

passages.title: Stone families and brick picture puzzles
passages.text: At Danyang, tomb builders made huge pictures by assembling moulded relief bricks. Audrey Spiro’s study distinguishes three Qi-period tombs, only one securely identified as Xiao Daosheng’s reburial monument. Different moulds produced similar pictures of famous cultivated men. Think of a heavy picture puzzle whose pieces also make a wall.

passages.title: Stone families and brick picture puzzles
passages.text: The Danyang tomb decoration also includes a three-legged crow inside the sun and a hare holding a pestle in the moon. These are symbolic images, not a record of local wildlife! Spiro reconstructs the decorative programme from damaged remains across the tombs, rather than pretending one complete room survived.

passages.title: Food, schooling and skilled work
passages.text: An order recorded for 491 specified favourite foods for offerings to deceased royal relatives. The list includes bamboo shoots and duck eggs for one empress, and tea and grilled fish for another. Remembering someone could include remembering what they liked to eat. This is evidence for royal ritual and tastes, rather than a menu for every household.

passages.title: Food, schooling and skilled work
passages.text: The same history records an order in 485 to establish a school with 200 students recruited from the children of officials. Buildings had to be prepared, and officials debated the proper ceremonies for honouring earlier teachers. This was education tied to elite status, with its own arguments about how school should begin.

passages.title: Food, schooling and skilled work
passages.text: Writing between 492 and 498, Tao Hongjing complained that doctors relied on medicine sellers, who in turn relied on gatherers and suppliers. A plant passed through many hands before reaching a patient. Recognizing the right substance, and spotting poor or adulterated supplies, required practical knowledge that could be lost along the way.

passages.title: Food, schooling and skilled work
passages.text: Court poets such as Shen Yue, Wang Rong and Xie Tiao explored how words could evoke sounds, sights and sensations. Meow Hui Goh’s study connects Yongming poetry with Buddhist ideas about perception and the poets’ lives as courtiers. Literary skill was part of being seen and heard in this competitive social world.

passages.title: Food, schooling and skilled work
passages.text: Zu Chongzhi served both Liu Song and Southern Qi; his son Zu Geng also became a mathematician and astronomer. Their calendar story crosses dynasties: the father proposed the Daming calendar in 462, and the son helped secure its adoption in 510 under Liang. Important research could outlast the rulers who first heard about it.

passages.title: Food, schooling and skilled work
passages.text: Zu Chongzhi also worked out how to use a midday shadow to determine the winter solstice, and placed pi between 3.1415926 and 3.1415927. These achievements belong to a career spanning the later fifth century; the source does not assign each result to a specific Qi year. A shadow could be a measuring instrument.

In 502, the general Xiao Yan, a distant member of the ruling family, replaced the last Qi emperor and founded Liang. Southern Qi’s imperial house lost the throne; southern communities and much of their cultural life continued under the new dynasty.

sectionTitles: First, inspect what the atlas actually draws
A southern branch formed before this map begins
Politics ran through kin, gifts and watchful neighbors
Rebellions and Xianbei power changed the frontier
The chanyu office ended, but people did not
Herds, grain, markets and the work behind them
Families, rank and children lived inside unequal worlds
Homes, clothes and objects crossed cultural lines
Learning, health, play and an outside written voice
Water, toilets and an honest blank space

passages.text: At 100 CE, the Southern Xiongnu lived inside a dangerous bargain. Their chanyu ruled through royal kin and marriage clans, guarded Han’s northern frontier and received grain, livestock, silk and gold, while Han officials watched him and elite sons went to Luoyang as hostages. This was not the enormous empire of earlier Xiongnu rulers. It was a smaller, divided world of herders, cavalry, markets, forts, farm country and families navigating two political traditions. Rebellions repeatedly shook the alliance. Xianbei power rose independently across the outer steppe, and a disastrous 177 expedition proved that yesterday’s great name did not guarantee tomorrow’s victory. In 188 rebels killed the chanyu; in 216 Cao Cao replaced his office with Five Divisions under imperial supervision. Yet people did not evaporate when the title ended. Communities continued in Ordos and Shanxi, joining Wei and Jin armies, courts and economies. The atlas makes the story trickier: its polygon sits far west around Alxa, missing the documented settlement core. Read it as a locator with a warning label, not a hoofprint-perfect border.

passages.title: First, inspect what the atlas actually draws
passages.text: The exact record is southern-xiongnu, labelled “Southern Xiongnu” and indexed circa 100 to 300 CE. Coverage records two intervals, 100 to 200 and 200 to 300, and showed no card before this packet. The dates describe imported map coverage, not the polity’s birth and death certificates or a modern territorial claim.

passages.title: First, inspect what the atlas actually draws
passages.text: At both 100 and 200 the target is one Polygon with one ring and 20 coordinate positions. Its bounds are [98.29358293582936, 39.41380788564797, 106.35766357663579, 42.82299046120785], and both coordinates hash to eb99737ebad52a00066b46c0925c947a0a38598b34652faa036b2a83bb48bfca. The repeated outline is exact, not an estimate from a screenshot.

passages.title: First, inspect what the atlas actually draws
passages.text: Point tests put Ejin/Khara-Khoto, the Badain Jaran and northern Alxa inside, but Ordos, Hohhot, Shuofang, Datong, Taiyuan, Pingyang, Ye and Luoyang outside. Historical sources place Southern Xiongnu communities around Ordos and later Shanxi, so the polygon is seriously displaced westward.

passages.title: First, inspect what the atlas actually draws
passages.text: The same snapshots draw Han over Ordos, Hohhot, Shuofang, Datong, Taiyuan and Pingyang. Overlapping labels can be useful, because Southern Xiongnu communities lived within Han frontier commanderies; here, however, the target polygon misses those tested settlements instead of showing the political overlap.

passages.title: First, inspect what the atlas actually draws
passages.text: The target vanishes at 300 and remains absent at 400. Jin and the separate han-zhao feature appear in different places, while the exact Southern Xiongnu shape is gone. That seam is an atlas decision: Cao Cao ended the chanyu office in 216, and Han-Zhao began only after Liu Yuan’s revolt in 304.

passages.title: A southern branch formed before this map begins
passages.text: Bi broke with the northern ruler Punu, established an Ordos base, and took the chanyu title in winter 48/49. In spring 50 he secured Han alliance, moved his headquarters to Meiji in western Ordos and accepted close supervision. The atlas begins half a century later.

passages.title: A southern branch formed before this map begins
passages.text: At the split, Bi could claim only eight tribal divisions and perhaps 100,000 people. Han valued them as a frontier buffer, but subsidies, an official supervisor and a chanyu’s son held at Luoyang made the bargain unequal. “Ally,” “vassal” and “hostage” all belong in the same complicated sentence.

passages.title: A southern branch formed before this map begins
passages.text: The court history says the new chanyu received a seal, carriage, weapons, silk, grain, cattle and sheep, while clerks and guards attended his camp. These were resources for an elite political system and its followers. They are not a shopping list for every family on the frontier.

passages.title: A southern branch formed before this map begins
passages.text: Southern forces joined Han campaigns that destroyed the northern royal line in 89 to 92. Xianbei groups then occupied much former northern territory. That makes three distinct histories: the older imperial confederation, the Han-aligned Southern polity and a rising Xianbei world, not one people changing labels on command.

passages.title: A southern branch formed before this map begins
passages.text: The earlier atlas ids xiongnu and xiongnu-bc200 remain separate. Southern Xiongnu is absent at 100 BCE and 1 BCE, then appears at 100 CE; no appliesTo alias is added. The card can explain institutional inheritance without swallowing two earlier histories or borrowing their enormous steppe borders.

passages.title: Politics ran through kin, gifts and watchful neighbors
passages.text: The chanyu’s royal clan and four leading non-royal houses were tied by marriage. Ranked “horn” princes stood in a succession order, while other offices varied with power and the number of followers. This was government through people and relationships, not departments neatly filed in identical tents.

passages.title: Politics ran through kin, gifts and watchful neighbors
passages.text: The same Chinese account says Huyan, Lan and Xubu nobles heard cases and reported decisions orally to the chanyu, without written dockets. That detail describes an outsider’s view of elite justice. It does not prove that nobody remembered precedents, used marks, negotiated locally or disagreed with a verdict.

passages.title: Politics ran through kin, gifts and watchful neighbors
passages.text: Each New Year, the chanyu sent memorials and hostages; Han returned gold, silk and prized foods distributed among the queen mother, consorts, princes and senior lords. Gifts held the coalition together, but the named recipients also reveal rank. Diplomacy could arrive wrapped in brocade and political obligation.

passages.title: Politics ran through kin, gifts and watchful neighbors
passages.text: Frontier markets mattered as much as battlefields. In 84, Northern Xiongnu traders reportedly brought more than ten thousand cattle and horses; Southern forces then attacked them for captives and livestock. Trade, raiding and alliance were competing ways to obtain resources, sometimes in the same season.

passages.title: Politics ran through kin, gifts and watchful neighbors
passages.text: Later Han control increasingly depended on bargaining: Xiongnu and Wuhuan auxiliaries defended districts where Han civilian populations had fallen. A chanyu could receive imperial backing yet fail to command every clan. Calling the Southern polity a simple puppet misses both coercion and the room local leaders still had.

passages.title: Rebellions and Xianbei power changed the frontier
passages.text: Northern refugees rebelled in 94, and in 109 the Southern chanyu joined a rising during the great Qiang war; by 110 it had failed. Xiongnu units later fought again for Han, and another mutiny came in 124. Loyalty was repeatedly renegotiated, not permanently switched on in 50.

passages.title: Rebellions and Xianbei power changed the frontier
passages.text: In 140 a Southern Xiongnu revolt spread across the frontier. Han officials blamed the chanyu Xiuli for failing to control it; pressured and humiliated, he killed himself. Han then abandoned much of the Ordos. The episode shows how a title could survive even while its practical reach collapsed.

passages.title: Rebellions and Xianbei power changed the frontier
passages.text: Tanshihuai united a powerful Xianbei coalition across the northern steppe. In 177, a Han expedition including Southern Xiongnu cavalry followed him too far and suffered a crushing defeat; sources claim three quarters did not return. Xianbei were independent rivals and occasional partners, never an alias for Southern Xiongnu.

passages.title: Rebellions and Xianbei power changed the frontier
passages.text: Archaeology adds another warning. Scholars note that named Xiongnu events or communities can rarely be matched securely to a material “Xiongnu culture.” Mixed graves near a fluid frontier may show interaction without supplying the deceased person’s political membership. Pottery is excellent evidence and a terrible passport.

passages.title: Rebellions and Xianbei power changed the frontier
passages.text: In 188, Xiuchuge mutineers killed chanyu Qiangqu. His son Yufuluo sought help, but Han itself dissolved into civil war; refused a stable return, he became a wandering military leader until 195. Huchuquan inherited the claim, not a reunited confederation. Fragmentation had become the political reality.

passages.title: The chanyu office ended, but people did not
passages.text: The Xiuchuge submitted to Cao Cao in 214. In 216 he kept Huchuquan at court and installed Qubei over five divisions along the southern Ordos and Shanxi frontier. No new chanyu followed Huchuquan. That is the strongest political endpoint for the Southern Xiongnu state inside this atlas interval.

passages.title: The chanyu office ended, but people did not
passages.text: Cao Wei’s Five Divisions were an administrative framework for communities already fragmented by war and migration. Leaders could serve imperial armies, bargain for rank or resist. The arrangement preserved group names and organization under another government; it did not restore the old chanyu’s sovereignty with a new office sign.

passages.title: The chanyu office ended, but people did not
passages.text: The later Jin history places five Xiongnu divisions around the Fen River and Jinyang during the Taikang era of the 280s. That is far east and south of the atlas polygon. It supports a Shanxi settlement story, but the text was compiled centuries later and favors elite political lineages.

passages.title: The chanyu office ended, but people did not
passages.text: Liu Yuan appears in the same later source as a Xiongnu elite educated in the Poetry, Documents, Changes, Zuo tradition, histories and military texts while linked to the Jin court. This is striking evidence for one aristocrat’s learned path, not a school timetable for every Southern Xiongnu child.

passages.title: The chanyu office ended, but people did not
passages.text: Liu Yuan founded his own Han regime only in 304, after this card ends; the atlas represents Han-Zhao separately at 300 to 400. Descent claims gave the later court legitimacy, but successor identity is not uninterrupted statehood. The 216 office ending and the 304 rebellion belong on opposite sides of that distinction.

passages.title: Herds, grain, markets and the work behind them
passages.text: Pastoralism remained fundamental: households and followers managed horses, sheep, goats and cattle, moving skills and animals through a frontier of pastures, forts and farms. Earlier Xiongnu states also used agriculture. The balance varied by place; “mobile” never meant nobody planted grain or stayed beside a town.

passages.title: Herds, grain, markets and the work behind them
passages.text: Elite gifts of cattle, sheep, grain and silk were political fuel. Keeping, dividing, transporting and redistributing them required herders, drovers, cooks, guards, weavers and storekeepers whom the court text rarely names. A royal list proves resources changed hands; it cannot calculate an ordinary household’s yearly income.

passages.title: Herds, grain, markets and the work behind them
passages.text: Earlier and mostly northern Xiongnu isotope studies find millet alongside animal foods, showing a mixed economy rather than an all-meat cartoon. Because those samples are not securely Southern Xiongnu households of 100 to 300, this card uses them as inherited background and refuses to print one universal frontier menu.

passages.title: Herds, grain, markets and the work behind them
passages.text: Dairy processing had a very long eastern-steppe history before the Southern polity. Milk from managed animals could become durable food through fermentation, but direct residues from a Southern Xiongnu kitchen in this interval are scarce. “They certainly drank this exact recipe” would be a tastier sentence than the evidence allows.

passages.title: Herds, grain, markets and the work behind them
passages.text: At Budongdou in Inner Mongolia, nine graves assigned by excavators to a Southern Xiongnu context held pottery, many iron objects and offerings including horse, ox and sheep skulls. Burial food and animals reveal ritual and wealth; they are not a photograph of Tuesday dinner or proof of equal access.

passages.title: Families, rank and children lived inside unequal worlds
passages.text: Steppe communities often organized around families and clans that herded and hunted together. The Southern court’s marriage houses and ranked princes fit that wider pattern, but political kinship was not the whole household world. Sources barely record adoption, divorce, care work, typical family size or ordinary disagreements.

passages.title: Families, rank and children lived inside unequal worlds
passages.text: A paired man-and-woman burial at Budongdou makes one relationship archaeologically visible, but it does not identify their names, marriage rules or feelings. Other graves held single bodies, and status differed through goods and offerings. One cemetery cannot be promoted into a census of all Southern Xiongnu families.

passages.title: Families, rank and children lived inside unequal worlds
passages.text: Court sources name a queen mother, consorts, princes and powerful marriage clans, showing that elite women mattered in succession and distribution. They say much less about women who herded, made clothing, prepared food or raised children. Absence from the annals is a documentary bias, not evidence of inactivity.

passages.title: Families, rank and children lived inside unequal worlds
passages.text: Children could inherit very different futures. A chanyu’s son might be sent to Luoyang as a political hostage and receive classical training, while pastoral children learned animals, routes and tools through work. Both are education, but only the elite pathway enters surviving court narratives with names and titles.

passages.title: Families, rank and children lived inside unequal worlds
passages.text: Rank depended on royal birth, marriage connections, office and the size of a leader’s following. Farmers, craftworkers, captives, guards and pastoral dependents are harder to place precisely. The evidence supports hierarchy but not a complete class chart, and it certainly does not tell us where every child sat at supper.

passages.title: Homes, clothes and objects crossed cultural lines
passages.text: No reviewed source provides a standard Southern Xiongnu house plan. Some families remained mobile; others lived near Han forts, commandery towns or later Fen-valley settlements. Archaeology shows several ways of living, so assigning everybody the same round tent, or the same tiled courtyard, would replace uncertainty with furniture.

passages.title: Homes, clothes and objects crossed cultural lines
passages.text: Han northern frontier archaeology finds a four-level hierarchy of walled settlements shaped by imperial planning and local variation. Southern Xiongnu communities lived within this political landscape, but a Han county wall is not automatically their home. Administrative space and domestic identity must stay analytically separate.

passages.title: Homes, clothes and objects crossed cultural lines
passages.text: Earlier elite Xiongnu graves at Noin-Ula preserved caftans, trousers, leggings, felt, fur and imported silk. They demonstrate skilled textile work and long exchange, not the exact wardrobe of a Southern Xiongnu shepherd two centuries later. Ordinary patched clothing is much less likely than luxury cloth to survive.

passages.title: Homes, clothes and objects crossed cultural lines
passages.text: Budongdou’s pottery, iron goods and animal offerings mix practices scholars call Xiongnu with objects circulating through Han territory. The material record can show contact and skilled making without assigning a single ethnicity to every jar. Frontier objects had careers; they did not politely remain in modern museum categories.

passages.title: Homes, clothes and objects crossed cultural lines
passages.text: Even “Ordos style” is a risky shortcut. A scholarly review warns that finds from multiple styles and sometimes different named groups have been bundled under broad labels. The atlas polygon’s Alxa location makes restraint even more necessary: attractive bronzes cannot repair a misplaced map or identify their owner by silhouette.

passages.title: Learning, health, play and an outside written voice
passages.text: For most children, no Southern Xiongnu curriculum survives. Pastoral work required learning animal behavior, weather, water, routes, riding and social obligations; that is a reasoned inference from the economy, not proof of a fixed starting age or identical training for girls and boys. Homework sometimes had hooves.

passages.title: Learning, health, play and an outside written voice
passages.text: Liu Yuan’s reported classical education belongs near the end of this card and near the top of society. His reading across canonical, historical and military texts shows elite cultural crossing under Jin. It cannot establish mass literacy, village classrooms or equal access for daughters and sons.

passages.title: Learning, health, play and an outside written voice
passages.text: A study of 104 Xiongnu-period skulls and 1,394 teeth from Mongolia found caries and calculus, with regional variation and evidence for carbohydrate consumption. Teeth document illness more securely than treatment: no Southern Xiongnu medical handbook, healer’s kit, hospital or reliable cure list survives in the reviewed evidence.

passages.title: Learning, health, play and an outside written voice
passages.text: The Book of Later Han says Southern assemblies met three times a year for sacrifices, state discussion and horse and camel races. That joins religion, politics and play in one elite gathering. It is wonderful evidence for organized sport, but it does not name children’s games or prove every village held the same event.

passages.title: Learning, health, play and an outside written voice
passages.text: An Eastern Han chronicle records “單于歲祭三龍祠，走馬鬥橐駝，以為樂事。” Modern Mandarin: “Chányú suì jì Sān Lóng Cí, zǒu mǎ dòu tuótuó, yǐ wéi lèshì.” Translation: “Each year the chanyu sacrificed at the Three Dragons shrine, raced horses and held camel contests for amusement.” This is authentic Classical Chinese external testimony, not Xiongnu speech or an indigenous script.

passages.title: Water, toilets and an honest blank space
passages.text: Water governed pasture movement, animals and settlement along the Yellow River and Fen valley, but the reviewed evidence does not identify a Southern Xiongnu well, pipe network or drinking-water rule for 100 to 300. A river on a historical map proves access to water, not purity, distance, ownership or who carried it.

passages.title: Water, toilets and an honest blank space
passages.text: A first-century Eastern Han tomb model in the Smithsonian shows a glazed latrine joined to a pigsty. It proves that such an arrangement was imaginable in Han China. It does not prove that Southern Xiongnu households used it, that the model copies one real building, or that waste handling was hygienically safe.

passages.title: Water, toilets and an honest blank space
passages.text: A rare Eastern Han mural at Yinan shows a railed privy, water container, urinal jar and a servant cleaning. A Dunhuang relay-station latrine yielded hygiene sticks, some with faecal traces. Both are valuable Han evidence from other settings; neither is a Southern Xiongnu toilet in Ordos or Shanxi.

passages.title: Water, toilets and an honest blank space
passages.text: No reviewed excavation securely identifies a Southern Xiongnu latrine, cesspit, drain or sewer for this interval. People necessarily managed waste, but mobile camps, frontier villages and elite compounds may have differed. Calling any convenient pit a toilet would be archaeology by hopeful sniffing, so the answer stays unknown.

passages.title: Water, toilets and an honest blank space
passages.text: Political collapse did not stop eating, herding, washing, caring for children or disposing of waste. It mostly changed who claimed taxes, hostages and military service. Daily continuities are historically likely, but exact routines remain unevenly documented because court annals followed chanyus and rebellions more eagerly than water buckets.

The Southern chanyu office effectively ended in 216 when Cao Cao retained Huchuquan at court and reorganized Xiongnu communities into Five Divisions. Pastoral work, families, group names and military networks continued under Cao Wei and Western Jin, especially around Shanxi’s Fen valley. Liu Yuan’s later regime began in 304 and belongs to the separately indexed Han-Zhao story; Xianbei confederations were distinct powers, not renamed Southern Xiongnu. The atlas carries this id to 300, so the last 84 years describe supervised communities and institutional afterlives rather than an independent chanyu state.

passages.text: Architecture and painting show different sides of Spain's sixteenth- and seventeenth-century culture: a royal monastery organized around worship and learning, and pictures shaped by observation and international exchange.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Philip II founded El Escorial in 1563. Juan Bautista de Toledo designed the complex, and Juan de Herrera completed the work after Toledo's death.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: El Escorial combined a monastery, church, palace, school, seminary and royal library around courtyards. Religious life, royal authority and study occupied one complex.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Early in his seventeenth-century career, Velazquez painted kitchen scenes known as bodegones and studied figures directly from life.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Velazquez became painter to Philip IV in 1623. Later at Madrid, Venetian paintings and contact with Rubens helped shape his art.

sectionTitles: Learning, language and a later ending

passages.text: The imported Spanish Guinea outline covers mainland Río Muni, not the whole island-and-mainland colony. In the late nineteenth century Spanish claims greatly exceeded effective control. The 1900 Treaty of Paris recognized a mainland territory, but much of its interior remained outside colonial occupation into the twentieth century.

passages.title: Claims, borders and unequal rule
passages.text: The 1900 settlement between France and Spain did not make everyone within the new border Spanish subjects under effective daily administration overnight. Spanish presence remained coastal, and occupation of the interior continued into the 1920s. The colored outline gets ahead of control on the ground.

passages.title: Claims, borders and unequal rule
passages.text: A 1902 order treated European people and African converts to Christianity under the Spanish penal code, while directing other African cases toward local custom and general legal principles. Religious classification helped determine legal treatment: colonial courts were not a system of equal citizenship.

passages.title: Claims, borders and unequal rule
passages.text: Colonial officials made local chiefs responsible for maintaining villages, receiving European travelers and pursuing fugitives. Chiefs also supplied workers for public projects and plantations. These duties could turn an existing community office into an instrument of coercion, although chiefs sometimes protested the demands imposed on their people.

passages.title: Dinner, pottery and practical skill
passages.text: A Fang plate from the Bata district shows how a meal could begin with basketry. Collected in the 1880s, it is woven from melongo fibre and measures about 24.5 centimetres across. The museum explains that diners placed leaves over this kind of plate before eating.

passages.title: Dinner, pottery and practical skill
passages.text: The same type of woven plate could work as a hand-turned support for making pottery. Men made these plates; women also used them for ceramic work, according to the museum. A useful object could have two careers: dinner service and pottery workshop.

passages.title: Dinner, pottery and practical skill
passages.text: Preparing melongo for basketry meant cutting, peeling and drying the plant material, then splitting it into strips of suitable thickness. The catalogue connects that skill to baskets, plates and crab traps. Changing the weave could change a bundle of fibre into a household tool or a way to catch supper.

passages.title: Dinner, pottery and practical skill
passages.text: A Balengue comb collected during the 1884 to 1886 expedition has 27 bamboo teeth held together by woven plant fibre. It is less than nine centimetres tall. The object brings history down to a familiar scale: somebody had to deal with their hair before starting the day.

passages.title: Dinner, pottery and practical skill
passages.text: The comb catalogue also describes Fang women and men oiling their hair with palm oil before combing, with the intention of avoiding lice. This is evidence of a recorded grooming practice and its purpose, not a modern test of how well it prevented parasites.

passages.title: Dinner, pottery and practical skill
passages.text: Ossorio’s collection includes a nineteenth-century tool from the Río Congüe catalogued as a carpenter’s plane. Alongside the decorated household objects, it preserves evidence of skilled woodworking. The museum record names the locality and collector, but leaves the individual craftsperson anonymous.

passages.title: Learning, language and a later ending
passages.text: Bata had a complicated school history: French Spiritan missionaries taught in Spanish and remained there until 1919. From the 1910s, rural teaching expanded through African catechists and colonial-guard interpreters. Schooling trained clerks and other assistants while also pressing children toward Spanish language and colonial loyalties.

passages.title: Learning, language and a later ending
passages.text: Elsewhere in the same colony, on Bioko rather than this mainland outline, Banapá’s school taught printing, shoemaking, tailoring, carpentry and masonry. Its press produced La Guinea Española from 1903. The biography of pupil Joaquín Sialo records workshops, a band and an experimental farm: education involved tools as well as books.

passages.title: Learning, language and a later ending
passages.text: A short Fang language sample in the museum’s present-day spelling is “along ncueng”, translated as “make a basket.” It accompanies the nineteenth-century woven plate in the catalogue. These Latin letters record spoken Fang; the phrase is a modern explanatory transcription, not writing discovered on the plate.

passages.title: Learning, language and a later ending
passages.text: For period writing, a Spanish military map published in 1900 bears the catalogued title “Mapa de la Guinea Española”: “Map of Spanish Guinea.” Its main scale is 1:500,000, with a much more detailed Río Muni inset. Survey information helped officials turn claims into lines on paper.

passages.title: Learning, language and a later ending
passages.text: Equatorial Guinea gained independence on 12 October 1968. Spanish colonial rule ended decades after this map label stops.
Spanish rule continued beyond the 1914 map cutoff. Equatorial Guinea became independent on 12 October 1968; mainland communities continued within the new state.

sectionTitles: Government, resistance and a written sample
Health, everyday movement and continuing craft

passages.text: This record represents Spain’s northern protectorate in Morocco, created by the Franco-Spanish agreement of November 1912 and ended in 1956. The map shows only 1914 to 1920, a short slice of that history. Its northern outline should not be confused with Spanish Sahara or the separate southern protectorate zone. Formal colonial boundaries also concealed areas where Moroccan resistance prevented effective Spanish control.

passages.title: Government, resistance and a written sample
passages.text: The protectorate kept Moroccan authorities while placing them under Spanish supervision. The 1916 regulations empowered the high commissioner to authorize or suspend the khalifa’s decrees and control his government’s official foreign contacts. The legal machinery makes the imbalance of power clearer than the reassuring word “protectorate.”

passages.title: Government, resistance and a written sample
passages.text: The official gazette of 6 December 1912 prints “Convenio entre España y Francia,” meaning “Agreement between Spain and France.” The phrase occurs in a decree seeking parliamentary authorization to ratify the agreement of 27 November. It is an attested Spanish administrative sample from the creation of the protectorate.

passages.title: Government, resistance and a written sample
passages.text: Spain’s defeat at Annual in 1921 exposed the gap between a claimed protectorate and control on the ground. The later Alhucemas landing in 1925 formed part of a joint Franco-Spanish offensive. Fighting continued until 1927, so the map’s disappearance of this label in 1920 is especially misleading.

passages.title: Government, resistance and a written sample
passages.text: During the Rif War, Abdelkrim sought recognition for a local Red Cross or Red Crescent and appealed for outside medical assistance. French and Spanish resistance obstructed these projects. A planned international mission was overtaken by his surrender in 1926: caring for civilians was entangled with arguments about who had the right to govern.

passages.title: School desks and workshop benches
passages.text: Early Spanish schools did not always have trained teachers or a settled curriculum. Soldiers, officials and consular staff sometimes taught, and facilities could be poor. A teaching board created in 1913 tried to organize this uneven system. Opening a classroom and providing a dependable education were two different achievements.

passages.title: School desks and workshop benches
passages.text: Inspectors in 1914 recommended paying Spanish-language teachers in the Alliance Israélite schools of Tetouan and Larache. Their report also proposed improving Muslim teacher training and secondary education; many recommendations waited years. The document reveals distinct Jewish and Muslim educational institutions, alongside Spanish ambitions to shape what children learned.

passages.title: School desks and workshop benches
passages.text: Tetouan’s Dar Sanaa craft school opened in 1919. Antonio Got’s plan proposed free instruction and materials, entry from age twelve, and places reserved mainly for local pupils. Its workshops covered wood, leather, metal, cloth and ceramics. Learning could mean making a useful object rather than filling another page of exercises.

passages.title: School desks and workshop benches
passages.text: The same workshop plan respected Muslim prayer times and anticipated Muslim, Jewish and Christian pupils sharing the school. It recognized that agreeing on a weekly rest day would be tricky. Masters were to keep records of each apprentice’s materials and working time, turning skilled handwork into a carefully documented education.

passages.title: Health, everyday movement and continuing craft
passages.text: Clinic reports from Nador and Zoco El Had describe vaccination campaigns that included schoolchildren. The Nador report recorded 998 vaccinations in 1913. These records give a concrete glimpse of attempts to prevent smallpox, while remaining reports by colonial doctors rather than a count of every child protected across the Rif.

passages.title: Health, everyday movement and continuing craft
passages.text: The same doctors treated wounds, fractures and other surgical problems using local anesthesia. Patients needing major operations were sent to the hospital at Melilla. They also performed dental work. A small clinic therefore depended on a wider network: some problems could be handled locally, while others required a difficult journey.

passages.title: Health, everyday movement and continuing craft
passages.text: The protectorate’s public-health organization assigned officials such tasks as checking drinking water, studying underground sanitation and considering healthier housing. These were formal responsibilities, not proof that every household received clean water. They show how staying well depended on streets, buildings and water supplies as well as doctors.

passages.title: Health, everyday movement and continuing craft
passages.text: The independence agreement of April 1956 also changed ordinary travel: its additional protocol abolished visas and administrative formalities for moving between Morocco’s zones. Political reunification could therefore affect a family journey or a trader’s trip, as well as the names on government offices.

passages.title: Health, everyday movement and continuing craft
passages.text: Dar Sanaa outlived the protectorate. Morocco’s culture ministry describes its continuing work training students from Tetouan and nearby places in threatened traditional crafts, alongside a museum of handmade objects. Skills passed from teacher to learner are a living part of the region’s heritage, not simply souvenirs of colonial rule.

Spain recognized Moroccan independence on 7 April 1956 and agreed to transfer its authorities’ powers to the Moroccan government. This ended the northern protectorate. Communities, workshops and schools continued within independent Morocco; the imported 1920 endpoint marks neither independence nor disappearance.
