sectionTitles: A kitchen discovery that changed its job

passages.text: Thrace was a region of different peoples, towns and kingdoms, rather than one state lasting throughout the map’s 1500 to 500 BCE interval. Its imported outline extends too far west to serve as a reliable political boundary. Bronze Age treasures belong to the earlier story; the homes, inscriptions and famous tombs below are explicitly later evidence.

passages.title: Metalworkers and a buried treasure
passages.text: The Valchitran treasure includes gold vessels, lids and a striking three-part container. The surviving group weighs more than twelve kilograms. Broadly assigned to the Late Bronze Age, it gives this earlier period a tangible achievement: highly skilled workers could shape and join precious metal into elaborate forms.

passages.title: Metalworkers and a buried treasure
passages.text: Two brothers discovered the treasure while working in a vineyard in 1924. Thirteen objects eventually entered the museum collection, after damage and disturbance. Scholars have proposed drinking and ritual uses for the vessels; their exact original arrangement and ceremony remain uncertain.

passages.title: Life in a trading town
passages.text: At Adzhiyska Vodenitsa, usually identified as Pistiros, houses had mud-brick walls, timber elements and tiled roofs. A planned settlement developed during the fifth century BCE. These buildings belonged to a Greek trading community in inland Thrace, illustrating the region’s mixture of communities.

passages.title: Life in a trading town
passages.text: One excavated house contained large storage jars and many drinking cups. Its excavators suggest that it may have served as a tavern. That is a plausible interpretation of the equipment, rather than an ancient sign saying that drinks were for sale.

passages.title: Life in a trading town
passages.text: A coin hoard lay beneath the floor of that house. Three sheep knucklebones were placed on top of its container; such bones were used for games. Money and gaming pieces ended up together in a hiding place that its owner never successfully emptied.

passages.title: Life in a trading town
passages.text: Molds and production waste show local work in bronze, silver and gold. Imported wine containers and fine pottery connect the settlement with Aegean markets. Its workshops and shops operated within long-distance networks rather than relying only on products made next door.

passages.title: A kitchen discovery that changed its job
passages.text: Some unusual clay objects from the settlement were long described as nozzles for metalworking bellows. A 2026 study instead identifies them as movable cooking supports, comparing their shapes with examples from Greek settlements elsewhere. An apparent workshop tool can turn out to belong beside dinner.

passages.title: A kitchen discovery that changed its job
passages.text: Several of these supports came from residential areas with sunken houses dated to the first half of the fourth century BCE; others came from sealed household rubbish deposits. Their contexts strengthen the kitchen interpretation. They help identify cooking practices without telling us precisely what was in each pot.

passages.title: Words and pictures that survived
passages.text: Writing sample: a Greek charter found near Vetren contains “τοῖς ἐμπορίταις,” meaning “to the merchants,” in line 8. The text dates after 359 BCE. This is the inscription’s wording in a modern scholarly transcription with accents, and an example of Greek used in the region, not a translated Thracian sentence.

passages.title: Words and pictures that survived
passages.text: The charter protected traders and described their dealings with Thracian rulers and communities. It preserved privileges associated with the earlier king Kotys. Because the stone was reused as building material, scholars debate the precise location of its Pistiros; the trading rights are clearer than the stone’s original address.

passages.title: Words and pictures that survived
passages.text: The tomb at Kazanlak, built near the end of the fourth century BCE, has a narrow corridor and a circular burial chamber decorated with paintings. Funeral scenes preserve clothing, gestures and ceremonial display. They show how an elite burial was imagined, rather than an ordinary family’s dining room.

passages.title: Words and pictures that survived
passages.text: At Sveshtari, a third-century BCE Getic tomb has ten carved female figures whose bodies merge with plant forms. Some original ochre, brown, blue, red and lilac coloring survives. Ancient stone interiors could be brightly painted; today’s pale museum sculptures can give a misleading impression.

Thrace did not end at the map’s 500 BCE cutoff. Later kingdoms, cities and communities continued through repeated changes of rule. Rome organized Thrace as a province around 46 CE, while local traditions survived within the imperial world.

passages.text: Picture an atlas label that cannot decide where it lives. From 800 to 1200 CE, its “Thule” polygon sits mostly across southern Alaska. In 1279 it suddenly adds twelve Arctic pieces reaching toward Greenland while keeping a duplicate Alaska feature. In 1492 only a Greenland-shaped remnant remains; in 1500 a broad Arctic shape returns. The imported summary makes matters stranger by describing the ancient Greek and Roman idea of a far-northern place called Thule. This card rejects that mismatch. Archaeologists use “Thule tradition” for material patterns connected with the ancestors of Inuit who moved rapidly eastward from Alaska across Arctic Canada and into Greenland, especially during the thirteenth century. It was never one state, ruler or frozen culture. Communities differed by coast, island, season and century. They read sea ice, built sod-covered houses, traveled by skin boat and dog sled, tailored warm clothing, stored food and hunted seals, fish, caribou, birds, walrus and whales. Whaling could demand remarkable teamwork, while some families lived far from bowhead grounds. Living Inuit peoples inherit distinct regional histories; they are not museum labels. The map ends in 1530, but their histories continue.

passages.title: Repair the identity before reading the map
passages.text: The live record is exactly “Thule,” id “thule,” circa 800 to 1530 CE, generated from historical basemaps. The coverage ledger calls it a state, routes it to North America, lists ten intervals and reports an imported summary but no card or review. Archaeology supports a tradition label, not a state with borders or one ruler.

passages.title: Repair the identity before reading the map
passages.text: The imported summary is about Pytheas and the classical literary place “Thule” somewhere north of Britain. That is a different subject sharing a name. The card rejects the text rather than mixing Greek geography with Inuit ancestry. A Greek or Latin quotation would therefore be a false written-language sample for this record.

passages.title: Repair the identity before reading the map
passages.text: From 800 through 1200 the atlas target is a 200-position southern Alaska polygon, covering tested Bethel, Dillingham, Naknek, Anchorage and Cordova but missing Utqiagvik and western Canadian Arctic sites. This conflicts with careful archaeological use of “Thule,” so the geometry is documented as basemap evidence, not accepted as a cultural boundary.

passages.title: Repair the identity before reading the map
passages.text: At 1279, 1300 and 1400 each file contains two independent features with the same id: one enormous Arctic multipolygon and one southern Alaska polygon. Duplicate ids are not two Thule governments. They expose layered map construction and make it essential to audit every component rather than stopping after the first match.

passages.title: Repair the identity before reading the map
passages.text: The 1492 file keeps only four components around Greenland while named Inuit, Inupiat and Inuvialuit layers occupy most tested Arctic places. The 1500 file restores thirteen target components, and 1530 removes them. No population can sensibly vanish, return and vanish on that schedule; these are atlas taxonomy seams.

passages.title: Trace archaeology without freezing identities
passages.text: Birnirk at Piġniq near Utqiagvik is a type site: its artifact patterns help archaeologists compare other places. NPS dates the Birnirk tradition roughly 500 to 900 CE and describes it as ancestral to later Thule archaeology and northern Alaskan Iñupiat history. A type site organizes evidence; it does not name every ancestor.

passages.title: Trace archaeology without freezing identities
passages.text: At Wales, Henry Collins found Birnirk artifacts low in a midden, transitional material above and Thule material higher up. Harpoon heads and ceramics supported a developmental sequence, while Punuk influences complicated it. Stratigraphy is powerful because lower layers usually came first, but every named phase remains an archaeological interpretation open to revision.

passages.title: Trace archaeology without freezing identities
passages.text: New radiocarbon dates from Nelson River and Washout strengthen a thirteenth-century date for the rapid movement into Arctic Canada, later than the once-common 1000 CE story. Two sites cannot date every journey, but they show why a confident textbook timeline may change when short-lived samples are measured carefully.

passages.title: Trace archaeology without freezing identities
passages.text: An early-migration study argues that small groups moved astonishing distances toward Lancaster Sound, perhaps attracted by rich bowhead grounds, without simply following a warm-climate conveyor belt. The journey required knowledge, scouting and social decisions. Climate opened or closed possibilities; it did not push identical people east like pieces on a board.

passages.title: Trace archaeology without freezing identities
passages.text: Dorset and Thule are separate archaeological traditions, not stages of one state. Qajartalik’s carved faces belong to Dorset history, while some eastern areas show chronological overlap. Similar dates or nearby sites cannot prove a meeting, battle or transfer of knowledge. Contact, avoidance and displacement must be tested locally rather than assumed.

passages.title: Read ice, water, animals and seasons
passages.text: Sea ice could be road, hunting platform, barrier and danger, changing with wind, current, snow, temperature and season. Modern Inuit hunters describe testing ice and reading its sound, texture and movement. That living expertise is a labeled comparison, not a word-for-word reconstruction of every Thule traveler’s rules centuries ago.

passages.title: Read ice, water, animals and seasons
passages.text: Bowhead whales live with seasonal ice, carry exceptionally thick blubber and can break breathing holes with massive skulls. Their movements respond to changing ice and food. Hunters needed to know leads, floe edges and migration timing, but whale biology differed by sea; one successful technique could not simply be copied everywhere.

passages.title: Read ice, water, animals and seasons
passages.text: Around Auyuittuq, Parks Canada describes regional diets including ringed seal, caribou, fish, waterfowl, narwhal, walrus and bowhead whale. Season decided which routes and animals were available. This is a useful eastern example because it breaks the “everyone ate whale all year” stereotype without inventing one Arctic menu.

passages.title: Read ice, water, animals and seasons
passages.text: North Water research finds early whaling settlements and later smaller, more dispersed communities using walrus, small whales, ringed seals and fjord resources as conditions changed. Adaptation meant reorganizing social and economic relationships, not merely swapping one animal for another. Regional flexibility is a stronger achievement than a frozen “Thule lifestyle.”

passages.title: Read ice, water, animals and seasons
passages.text: Fresh water still mattered in a land surrounded by salty ocean. Archaeology rarely preserves a household’s exact drinking routine; snow, freshwater ice, lakes and streams were locally available at different seasons. The record supports no target-wide water-storage rule, purification method or claim that people casually drank sea ice without testing its salt and condition.

passages.title: Hunt, fish, share and store food
passages.text: Open-water whaling required a seaworthy skin boat, paddlers, a steerer, harpooner, lines, floats, lances, favorable weather and people ready to tow and process an enormous animal. NPS calls Thule hunters successful whalers, artists and traders. The achievement was coordinated work and knowledge, not one dramatic throw by a lone hero.

passages.title: Hunt, fish, share and store food
passages.text: A toggling harpoon head turns sideways after entering an animal, while an attached line and sealskin float help hunters track and tire prey. University of Alaska Museum evidence links floats and specialized gear to larger marine animals. The system joined carving, strong cordage, boat handling and calm teamwork under dangerous conditions.

passages.title: Hunt, fish, share and store food
passages.text: Whales were never the whole economy. Birnirk deposits include seals, fish, birds, caribou and smaller land mammals, and whales were rare there before later whaling emphasis. Elsewhere walrus or caribou could dominate. Animal bones reveal meals and craft material, but preservation and excavation choices can exaggerate the largest species.

passages.title: Hunt, fish, share and store food
passages.text: At Many Caches, fitted limestone slabs formed vaulted stores for caribou meat. Researchers think coastal people repeatedly traveled inland in summer and fall to hunt and fish, then returned coastward. Only two bones supplied reported radiocarbon dates, so the whole cache field cannot be assigned one construction day or one household.

passages.title: Hunt, fish, share and store food
passages.text: Whale butchering and household refuse could alter even Arctic ponds. Sediment chemistry beside a central Arctic site records nutrients entering the water from processing and discarded organic material. That is an environmental footprint, not proof of carelessness: a large cooperative harvest concentrated enormous amounts of bone, fat and waste in one place.

passages.title: Build homes and travel across land and sea
passages.text: Early regional winter houses around Auyuittuq used stone, sod and whale bone, with a partly sunken room reached through a low tunnel. Sleeping platforms and storage sat toward the rear; side platforms held oil lamps for heat, cooking and drying clothes. Architecture turned limited materials into a warm, organized interior.

passages.title: Build homes and travel across land and sea
passages.text: Coastal Alaskan builders collected driftwood delivered by rivers, currents, storms and ice. Cape Espenberg houses used large logs for walls, posts, floors and benches, later reusing smaller pieces as supplies changed. Preserved cut marks show carpentry choices. Treeless tundra did not mean people lacked wood or woodworking expertise.

passages.title: Build homes and travel across land and sea
passages.text: Birnirk preserved parts of a roughly thousand-year-old umiak, including baleen lashings and decorative ivory inlays. Kayaks served individuals while larger skin boats carried crews, families or cargo; dogs and sleds opened winter routes. Each vehicle depended on repair, fitted parts and knowledge of ice, water and weather.

passages.title: Build homes and travel across land and sea
passages.text: A qulliq oil lamp supplied controlled light and warmth where open wood fires were impractical, and Parks Canada links this technology with sea-ice camping. Snow knives and dog sleds expanded other possibilities. A toolkit did not “conquer” the Arctic; skilled people continually judged whether a route, camp or flame was safe.

passages.title: Build homes and travel across land and sea
passages.text: Not every dwelling was a monumental whalebone house. A Melville Island survey recorded small tent features, hearths and temporary hunting camps, including one charred-bone date near 1110 CE. Summer structures could leave only rings of stone. Mobility and repeated winter settlement were compatible parts of the same regional life.

passages.title: Sew clothing and make everyday tools
passages.text: Tailored clothing was life-support technology. Fine bone needles and awls pierced prepared skins; fitted layers reduced gaps where wind could enter. Regional garments used seal, caribou, bird or gut skin for different properties. A tiny needle may look modest beside a harpoon, yet one failed seam could make travel dangerously cold.

passages.title: Sew clothing and make everyday tools
passages.text: Proteomic analysis of fourteenth-century Nuulliit garments identifies animal materials from fragile gut skin, edging and sinew thread. Researchers cleaned samples to reduce museum-treatment contamination and preserve irreplaceable objects. The study reveals deliberate material selection while showing how modern laboratory methods can refine, rather than replace, careful visual archaeology.

passages.title: Sew clothing and make everyday tools
passages.text: Lamps, cooking containers, ulus, engraving tools, combs, needle cases and clothing scraps bring daily maintenance into view. Labrador collections include a wooden doll and a miniature baleen scraper or ulu, reminding us that households contained grooming, repair and play alongside hunting gear. Archaeology becomes richer when it notices small objects.

passages.title: Sew clothing and make everyday tools
passages.text: Fun fact: a Canadian Museum snow knife dated to about 1400 or later is roughly 41 centimetres long and combines whale bone, mammal ivory and sinew. That is nearly forearm length. Its “ingredient list” sounds unusual to us, but every material answered a construction problem in a metal-scarce environment.

passages.title: Sew clothing and make everyday tools
passages.text: Permafrost can preserve wood, baleen, skin and cordage that normally vanish, yet thaw and coastal erosion now expose or destroy sites. Cape Krusenstern beach ridges help sequence occupations, while changing shorelines complicate them. Archaeologists must record quickly without pretending that the best-preserved coast represents every inland or summer activity.

passages.title: Live in families, crews and learning communities
passages.text: Large-looking winter-house fields may combine ruins from different years. Demographic research warns that visible houses need not have been occupied together. Archaeology can estimate floor area and rebuilding, but it cannot give this entire tradition one household size, marriage rule, inheritance system or clan map. Families varied through region and time.

passages.title: Live in families, crews and learning communities
passages.text: Whaling could link several households in production and sharing, and artifact differences suggest that some Classic Thule households held more prestige or specialized equipment. Researchers debate how much hierarchy existed. A successful crew needed leadership and cooperation, but that does not establish one target-wide class system, chief title or permanent government.

passages.title: Live in families, crews and learning communities
passages.text: A wooden doll and miniature tools from Labrador make childhood archaeologically visible without revealing a complete game. Children probably learned by observing, helping and practicing with safer or smaller objects, while stories carried knowledge that does not fossilize. No evidence supports one universal Thule school, lesson schedule or age of adulthood.

passages.title: Live in families, crews and learning communities
passages.text: At Qilakitsoq, six women and two boys buried around 1475 represented three closely related generations. Their carefully layered clothing, extra skins and shared graves reveal kinship and care at one Greenland place. They cannot define every family, but they prevent the past from becoming a story containing only adult male hunters.

passages.title: Live in families, crews and learning communities
passages.text: Living Inuit hunters describe sea-ice knowledge as learned through generations and updated through direct observation. That later testimony helps explain why education could be practical, social and lifelong. It remains comparison: archaeological Thule communities had no single curriculum, and living Inuit knowledge belongs to its holders rather than serving as a frozen ancient textbook.

passages.title: Care for bodies, water, waste and toilets
passages.text: Greenland mummies preserve evidence that ordinary skeletons cannot: soot exposure in lungs, lice and, in one child, a parasite associated with raw meat. Such findings reveal risks, not a universal health condition or cause of death. Cold, injury, smoke, hunger and infection varied with household, season and individual circumstance.

passages.title: Care for bodies, water, waste and toilets
passages.text: Soil from four early Thule winter houses contained hundreds of preserved lice, distributed in patterns researchers interpret as localized delousing activity. That is unusually direct hygiene evidence. It does not mean every house was equally infested or that one cleaning method governed the Arctic; insects survive only under favorable archaeological conditions.

passages.title: Care for bodies, water, waste and toilets
passages.text: People surely treated wounds, pain and illness, but this atlas record preserves no shared healer title, diagnosis system or medicine list. Lamps, warmth, food, sewn protection and family care supported health in visible ways. Beyond that, the card keeps uncertainty instead of borrowing later regional remedies and projecting them unchanged into earlier centuries.

passages.title: Care for bodies, water, waste and toilets
passages.text: Clean drinking water required local judgment about snow, freshwater ice, streams and lakes; sea ice can contain salt, especially when young. The archaeological sources do not preserve one water rule or treatment device. Household lamps could heat and cook, but claiming a universal snow-melting routine would outrun the specific evidence.

passages.title: Care for bodies, water, waste and toilets
passages.text: No built toilet or target-wide sewer is securely attributable. People managed bodily waste somehow, but exact outdoor spots, containers or disposal habits rarely survive. Middens, pond nutrients and house insects reveal refuse and cleaning indirectly. Saying “unknown” is more accurate than placing a modern bathroom inside every sod house.

passages.title: Respect belief, art, conflict and encounters
passages.text: Qilakitsoq’s dead were fully clothed, wrapped in skins and accompanied by extra garments and amulets for a journey after death. Facial tattoos may have expressed kinship or status, although details remain uncertain. These burials illuminate one Greenland community’s care and belief, not a target-wide religion or priesthood.

passages.title: Respect belief, art, conflict and encounters
passages.text: Ivory inlays, engravings and carefully shaped tools show that beauty and function could share one object. Archaeologists should not decode every motif as a sentence or universal myth. Images may carry personal, social or sacred meanings, but this record supplies no securely deciphered writing system or target-wide symbol dictionary.

passages.title: Respect belief, art, conflict and encounters
passages.text: Copper and ivory slat armor from western contexts suggests real danger and possible conflict. Armor alone cannot measure how often people fought, why, or who participated. The evidence supports no common army, fortification system, prison, tribute rule or captive policy across Alaska, Canada and Greenland, and resource competition is not an automatic explanation.

passages.title: Respect belief, art, conflict and encounters
passages.text: Dorset disappearance and Thule expansion overlap chronologically in some regions, but nearby dates do not prove a battle. Archaeologists test contact through artifacts, settlement sequence and genetics while debating alternatives. The card avoids calling living Inuit “invaders” and does not turn a complex population history into a simple victory story.

passages.title: Respect belief, art, conflict and encounters
passages.text: Norse and Thule materials occur in overlapping Greenland landscapes, and projects at Sandhavn investigate possible interaction. A few traded objects cannot reveal whether every encounter was friendly, hostile or indirect. Norse runes belong to Norse writers, not to Thule households, so they cannot supply the missing written-language sample.

passages.title: Recognize discoveries, achievements and continuity
passages.text: “Thule culture” became an archaeological term through early twentieth-century expeditions and comparison, then researchers refined it with stratigraphy, radiocarbon dates and regional variants. Wales and Walakpa show how interpretations were built from artifact layers. The label is a research tool with history, not an ancient nation’s official name.

passages.title: Recognize discoveries, achievements and continuity
passages.text: Today researchers combine radiocarbon dating, animal-bone analysis, lake chemistry, insect remains, proteins, cut marks and spatial mapping. Each method sees a different slice of life, and all have sampling limits. The strongest discovery is often a correction: a later migration date, fewer simultaneous houses or a garment material nobody recognized by eye.

passages.title: Recognize discoveries, achievements and continuity
passages.text: Major achievements include rapid long-distance movement, skin boats, dog transport, toggling harpoons, fitted clothing, sod-and-bone houses, controlled oil lamps, storage, carpentry and detailed seasonal knowledge. No single inventor or capital directed them. Communities adapted a shared repertoire to local ice, animals and materials while maintaining families and exchange across enormous distances.

passages.title: Recognize discoveries, achievements and continuity
passages.text: Contemporaneous written-language sample: none is securely attributable to this exact archaeological record. The later history of written Inuktut includes nineteenth-century missionary systems and modern Inuit-led standardization. Borrowing those forms, classical Greek text or Norse runes would create an anachronistic voice, so the card supplies no fabricated script, transliteration or translation.

passages.title: Recognize discoveries, achievements and continuity
passages.text: After 1530, European traders, commercial whalers, missionaries, disease and colonial governments affected Arctic regions on different schedules. Living Inuit peoples continued and continue with distinct languages, homelands and institutions. The Inuit Circumpolar Council is a modern representative body, not the heir to an ancient Thule state that never existed.

At 1530 the exact atlas id is absent and tested places receive other broad or named labels. That seam ends an archaeological map category, not Inuit life. The target was never one state capable of falling, and the 1492 remnant plus 1500 return already expose unstable atlas taxonomy. Distinct Inuit peoples continued through regional adaptation, trade, colonial disruption and living self-determination, so no predecessor or successor chain is invented.

sectionTitles: Building a city high in the Andes

passages.text: Tiwanaku was a major highland city near Lake Titicaca and the center of far-reaching religious and political connections during the first millennium CE. Its communities also settled lower valleys. “Tiahuanaco” is an older spelling. The broad imported outline is not proof of uniform imperial control, and its 1279 endpoint substantially outlasts the city’s main occupation.

passages.title: Building a city high in the Andes
passages.text: At roughly 3,850 meters above sea level, Tiwanaku stood in a demanding highland environment. Most buildings were made of earth, while major ceremonial structures used stone. The spectacular monuments are only the visible fraction of a much larger lived-in settlement.

passages.title: Building a city high in the Andes
passages.text: Akapana had seven terraced levels and an internal drainage system. Managing rainwater mattered even in monumental ceremonial architecture. Carefully built channels helped water leave the structure instead of simply soaking through it.

passages.title: Building a city high in the Andes
passages.text: Pumapunku masons shaped andesite blocks with precise recesses and finished details before assembly. Small holes helped workers grip and position some blocks. Their achievement becomes more impressive when studied as skilled human work, with identifiable building techniques.

passages.title: Building a city high in the Andes
passages.text: Modern researchers have made small three-dimensional models of the scattered Pumapunku stones to test how they fit. Reassembly is difficult because many pieces were removed or broken after abandonment. A convincing model must work with the surviving blocks, rather than an imagined perfect temple.

passages.title: Building a city high in the Andes
passages.text: Residential compounds grouped smaller buildings around open patios. Stone foundations helped protect adobe walls from rising moisture. Excavated cooking and storage pottery, bone tools and food remains recover the ordinary work that kept households going beside the famous monuments.

passages.title: Building a city high in the Andes
passages.text: Some Tiwanaku homes incorporated burials beneath living areas. The placement brought certain dead relatives or ancestors into the spaces used by later residents. Archaeologists therefore study domestic buildings as places of family memory as well as cooking and sleeping.

passages.title: Meals, fields and shared symbols
passages.text: Food remains vary among neighborhoods. Quinoa was widespread, with tubers and maize also present. Maize was not confined to the grandest residences: its differing distribution suggests that household connections and access mattered alongside social rank.

passages.title: Meals, fields and shared symbols
passages.text: At Cerro San Antonio in Peru’s Locumba Valley, plant remains show that Tiwanaku settlers retained familiar highland foods, including quinoa and related plants, in a lower-altitude setting. Moving house did not mean forgetting what tasted like home.

passages.title: Meals, fields and shared symbols
passages.text: Raised fields around Lake Titicaca placed crops on elevated beds separated by channels. Erickson’s research emphasizes that such systems could be built and maintained in manageable local units. Their scale does not by itself prove that a ruler commanded every farming household.

passages.title: Meals, fields and shared symbols
passages.text: Keros were flaring cups used for chicha, a fermented corn drink, at ceremonies and everyday gatherings. They could be made from wood, clay or precious metal. Sharing drinks helped sustain relationships; the container could also advertise its owner’s standing.

passages.title: Meals, fields and shared symbols
passages.text: One wooden kero, dated 500 to 1000 CE, carries four winged staff-holding figures carved around its surface. Two have feline faces and two have bird-of-prey heads. The cup turns in the hand like a small gallery of powerful beings.

passages.title: Meals, fields and shared symbols
passages.text: No securely readable Tiwanaku sentence survives for an original-language sample and translation. Carved figures on monuments and vessels carried meaning, but they are not a deciphered written text. Even applying the later name Viracocha to Tiwanaku’s central staff-bearing figure remains uncertain.

A 2023 radiocarbon study places rapid urban collapse around 1010 to 1050 CE, before the later drought often blamed for it. This finding concerns Tiwanaku itself: traditions continued in other communities, and visitors returned afterward. Its urban institutions changed dramatically, but its people did not vanish. The imported 1279 map endpoint is not a supported collapse date.

passages.text: Between 1000 and 1783, Tibet developed influential monastic, artistic and medical traditions under changing regional rulers and relationships with Mongol and Qing powers. This atlas outline represents a broad plateau region, not one government continuously controlling every place inside it. It is distinct from the earlier Tibetan Empire and cannot establish later sovereignty.

passages.title: Changing centers of power
passages.text: Around 1042, the Indian teacher Atisha arrived in central Tibet. Teaching journeys, new monasteries and exchanges of texts helped renew Buddhist learning. Monasteries became important economic and political institutions as well as places of worship, so an argument over religious leadership could also affect land and authority.

passages.title: Changing centers of power
passages.text: During the thirteenth century, Sakya leaders gained predominance through their relationship with Mongol rulers. Tibetan religious teachers also served at the Yuan court. This was a connection between religious influence and imperial power, rather than a single isolated mountain kingdom.

passages.title: Changing centers of power
passages.text: In 1354, Changchup Gyeltsen of Pakmodru took control of central Tibet and ended Sakya hegemony there. His successors later faced internal conflict. The following centuries therefore need several regional histories, rather than a straight list of rulers governing the entire plateau.

passages.title: Changing centers of power
passages.text: In 1642, the Fifth Dalai Lama and Mongol allies consolidated power after civil wars. The Ganden Podrang administration employed both monastic officials and secular nobles. Religious leadership and government were closely connected, but running the state also required offices, records and administrators.

passages.title: Changing centers of power
passages.text: Dzungar forces invaded in 1717; Qing and Tibetan forces drove them out in 1720. In 1727, Qing representatives called ambans became resident in Lhasa. Tibetan religious and political institutions continued within this changing relationship with the Qing empire.

passages.title: Buildings, workers and religious diversity
passages.text: The rulers of Gyantse sponsored an extraordinary monument: the Kumbum, built around 1427 to 1442 beside Pelkhor Chode monastery. Its regional patrons show that ambitious cultural projects flourished outside Lhasa. Political geography was a patchwork, and several towns could become important centers of learning and art.

passages.title: Buildings, workers and religious diversity
passages.text: Gyantse’s Kumbum contains 73 chapels and more than 20,000 images of deities. The arrangement follows an organized hierarchy of Buddhist teachings. Moving through the building was therefore also a journey through a religious curriculum: a library of painted rooms, with rather more stairs than a book.

passages.title: Buildings, workers and religious diversity
passages.text: Bon remained an active religious tradition. A fifteenth-century painting of its deity Trowo Tsochok Khagying survives on cloth with ink, color and gold. Organized Bon institutions developed during the tenth and eleventh centuries in interaction with Buddhism while drawing on older traditions. Tibet’s religious life was never only one school.

passages.title: Buildings, workers and religious diversity
passages.text: The Potala’s White Palace rose from 1645 to 1648; the Red Palace followed from 1690 to 1694. Thousands of artisans, engineers and conscripted laborers contributed. Its impressive walls also represent compulsory work, not simply the wishes or achievements of rulers.

passages.title: Buildings, workers and religious diversity
passages.text: Norbulingka began with the Uya Palace in 1751; the Gesang Palace followed in 1755 with a debate courtyard. It became the Dalai Lamas’ summer residence. The heritage account describes government departments moving there seasonally too: the paperwork had a summer address along with the ruler.

passages.title: Learning, families and medicine
passages.text: Medical students had spectacular revision aids. Desi Sanggye Gyatso commissioned 79 medical paintings from 1687 to 1697, alongside his commentary on the Four Tantras. Chakpori Medical College opened in 1696. Branching diagrams turned knowledge into memorable trees; many surviving illustrations are later copies of these designs.

passages.title: Learning, families and medicine
passages.text: The medical pictures include ordinary work: farmers and pastoralists milk animals, people prepare food together, and different water sources appear. Another painting shows fetal development and childbirth. These are unusually detailed windows into activities that grand portraits of rulers usually leave out.

passages.title: Learning, families and medicine
passages.text: Painting 64 illustrates examination of urine in bowls. Doctors also assessed the pulse and tongue. A patient’s pee could become a medical lesson! These images document historical diagnostic practices; they do not establish that every explanation or treatment was effective.

passages.title: Learning, families and medicine
passages.text: Anatomical disagreements could lead to investigation: the account of painting 49 describes examining human remains to settle questions about bones. The medical tradition included observation and debate alongside inherited texts. Even an authoritative book could prompt the question: does the body actually look like that?

passages.title: Learning, families and medicine
passages.text: Chokyi Dronma, born into a royal family in 1422, married and had a child before becoming a nun. She received full ordination, unusual for a Tibetan woman, and became the first figure in the Samding Dorje Pakmo incarnation line. Her story reveals a remarkable female religious leader with an earlier family life.

passages.title: Learning, families and medicine
passages.text: The young Lobzang Yeshe, recognized as a Panchen Lama, received a tutor for basic reading and writing after his enthronement at Tashilhunpo. His education then developed into years of religious study. This is evidence for one highly privileged child’s schooling, rather than a school timetable for every Tibetan household.

passages.title: Learning, families and medicine
passages.text: During the turmoil of the late 1720s, Lobzang Yeshe avoided face-to-face meetings because of the danger of smallpox, while continuing to communicate through messengers. The precaution shows disease affecting political and religious business. It was an attempt to reduce contact, centuries before email could rescue a cancelled meeting.

passages.title: Books, stories and Tibetan writing
passages.text: A surviving 1538 printing of Milarepa’s life was made at Ron Wosel Puk in Gungtang. Carving wooden printing blocks demanded skilled labor, paper and ink, but allowed multiple copies. It is the earliest surviving print of this biography, not the beginning of Tibetan printing.

passages.title: Books, stories and Tibetan writing
passages.text: Milarepa’s famous biography was composed by Tsangnyon Heruka in the late fifteenth century, long after the teacher’s lifetime. Its spiritual adventures helped make him widely known. The distance matters: a beloved religious life story is also literature, rather than a contemporary reporter’s transcript of every event.

passages.title: Books, stories and Tibetan writing
passages.text: A short Tibetan title is རྒྱུད་བཞི་, transliterated rgyud bzhi, meaning “Four Tantras.” The Grolier Club catalogue supplies this original-language title for a medical book dated around 1750, probably produced in Beijing. The witness shows Tibetan learning traveling beyond the plateau; the script here follows the catalogue’s transcription.

passages.title: Books, stories and Tibetan writing
passages.text: The same medical book’s cloth wrapper is called a na bza’, a “robe,” and its cord a ska rags, a “belt.” A book could be dressed with the vocabulary used for a monk’s clothing. The catalogue connects this careful treatment with reverence for the teacher and the teachings embodied in the text.

The map stops in 1783, not at Tibet’s disappearance. Under changing political arrangements, the Ganden Podrang remained central Tibet’s government until 1959, when the Dalai Lama fled to India. Tibetan communities, language and religious traditions continued; neither this date nor the atlas polygon can settle modern sovereignty.

A government trying to change without agreeing on how fast
From Chamdo to 1959: military campaign, agreement and rupture

passages.text: This card covers the atlas’s approximate Tibet record from 1914 to 1994, not the earlier Tibetan Empire or medieval Tibet cards. Six imported polygons keep almost the same broad outline even though the period crosses a de facto self-governing Tibetan administration, contested international status, the 1950 PLA campaign, the 1951 Seventeen-Point Agreement, the 1959 uprising and flight of the Dalai Lama, direct rule by the People’s Republic of China, the 1965 Tibet Autonomous Region, Cultural Revolution and 1980s revival and protest. The map shape is therefore a regional locator, never proof of one unchanged state, one government, or an agreed border. Tibetan communities, language and religion also extend beyond this polygon.

passages.title: First, read the atlas label without mistaking it for a verdict
passages.text: The 1914 feature is a single 162-vertex polygon. It contains the tested points for Lhasa, Shigatse, Gyantse, Tsetang, Nagqu, Chamdo and Gartok, while tested Leh, Xining, Lanzhou, Chengdu, Kathmandu and Thimphu fall outside. Its boundary meets imported features labeled British Raj, Nepal, Bhutan, Xinjiang and Qing dynasty. Those tests explain what the software draws. They cannot tell us who collected tax in a valley, which language a family spoke, or whose claim international law accepted.

passages.title: First, read the atlas label without mistaking it for a verdict
passages.text: By the 1960-1994 snapshot, the target is still a 162-vertex polygon with almost the same bounding box and exactly the same thirteen point-test results. It now meets an imported China feature as well as India, Nepal, Bhutan and Burma. The political world changed profoundly while this locator barely moved. That mismatch is the card’s central warning: a stable shape can hide conquest, agreement, revolt, administrative reorganization and disputed sovereignty.

passages.title: First, read the atlas label without mistaking it for a verdict
passages.text: From 1912 until 1951, the Lhasa government exercised de facto independence across much of central and western Tibet, but it won little general recognition as a sovereign state and never controlled every Tibetan-speaking district. Republican China continued to claim sovereignty; Britain used the deliberately fuzzy term “suzerainty.” Modern writers still choose different legal labels. The honest map answer is therefore specific: this polygon locates a region and one imported identity, not an internationally agreed state border.

passages.title: First, read the atlas label without mistaking it for a verdict
passages.text: The 1913-1914 Simla talks joined British, Tibetan and Chinese representatives, but Britain also wanted a buffer protecting colonial India. British and Tibetan negotiators advanced an “Outer” and “Inner” Tibet scheme and a boundary in the east; China did not accept the final convention. That history explains why a neat atlas outline is especially dangerous here. Diplomats drew proposals while empires pursued strategy, and communities on the ground were not taking part in a modern border referendum.

passages.title: A government trying to change without agreeing on how fast
passages.text: The Thirteenth Dalai Lama returned after the Qing collapse and supported a stronger army, a government postal network, paper money, telegraphy and a state printing press. Shol Press even produced translated military manuals as well as religious texts. Reform was expensive and politically risky: senior monasteries and officials resisted measures that threatened money or authority, and revenue was limited. “Modernization” was therefore a contest inside Tibetan society, not a magic lever one ruler could pull.

passages.title: A government trying to change without agreeing on how fast
passages.text: After the Dalai Lama died in 1933, the Kashag cabinet, regents, monastic blocs and aristocratic officials struggled over appointments and policy while a search identified the child who became the Fourteenth Dalai Lama. Some officials owned radios or received foreign newspapers by the 1940s, yet the state’s army and finances remained weak. A child could be the sacred focus of government while adults around him argued fiercely about who would actually rule: divine prestige did not cancel office politics.

passages.title: A government trying to change without agreeing on how fast
passages.text: Tibetan paper notes are physical evidence of this reform era. The earliest issues date to 1913; designs and numbers were printed from carved blocks, and tiny changes in a date block help numismatists reconstruct the sequence. Officials limited the quantity and later stored imported gold as backing. It was ambitious money-making without a modern central bank. Fun fact: a banknote’s suspicious little carved gap can tell historians which batch came first, rather like spotting a typo in history’s wallet.

passages.title: A government trying to change without agreeing on how fast
passages.text: The government also adapted an older relay system into public mail. Twelve stations served central routes; a letter could travel roughly 130 kilometers between Lhasa and Gyantse in about two and a half days. Tibetan stamps worked inside the network, while mail going overseas had to transfer into the British Indian system. A simple Lhasa-Gyantse telegraph added speed. In other words, the plateau had “last-mile delivery” before anyone called it that, but international mail still needed a border handoff.

passages.title: From Chamdo to 1959: military campaign, agreement and rupture
passages.text: In October 1950, the People’s Liberation Army defeated Tibetan forces around Chamdo. Tibetan appeals produced debate abroad but no intervention capable of reversing the military result. A contemporary US diplomatic record says Tibetan leaders felt they had to accept Beijing’s demands after receiving no effective answer from the United Nations or other governments. That document also reflects Cold War strategy, so it helps reconstruct what diplomats believed, not every Tibetan or Chinese motive.

passages.title: From Chamdo to 1959: military campaign, agreement and rupture
passages.text: The May 1951 agreement did two things at once. It declared Tibet part of the PRC and authorized PLA entry, yet promised regional autonomy, protection of the existing political system, status of the Dalai and Panchen Lamas, religious freedom and reforms only when Tibetan leaders and people wanted them. Beijing’s official account says the delegates had full powers and Lhasa later accepted the text; Tibetan exile accounts say signatures came under military coercion without authority. The promises are primary text. The legitimacy dispute is not solved by quoting only one government.

passages.title: From Chamdo to 1959: military campaign, agreement and rupture
passages.text: For several years, two systems uneasily occupied the same political space. PLA and central-government offices arrived, while the Dalai Lama’s administration, monasteries, aristocratic households and estate obligations continued in central Tibet. Chinese leaders initially pursued gradual change rather than immediate land reform there. Cooperation was real in some offices and mistrust was real too. This was neither untouched independence nor instant total uniformity; it was a negotiated arrangement under overwhelming military imbalance.

passages.title: From Chamdo to 1959: military campaign, agreement and rupture
passages.text: By 1959, fighting in eastern Tibetan regions, refugee movement, armed resistance, reform fears and failures by leaders on both sides had poisoned that coexistence. On 10 March, crowds gathered around the Norbulingka amid rumors the PLA planned to seize the Dalai Lama. Talks collapsed; he fled Lhasa on 17 March and later repudiated the agreement in India. Beijing dissolved the old government. The uprising involved monks, officials, ordinary residents, fighters and foreign covert support, so a one-villain version will not survive the evidence.

passages.title: From Chamdo to 1959: military campaign, agreement and rupture
passages.text: The United Nations General Assembly responded later in 1959 by calling for respect for Tibetans’ fundamental human rights and distinctive cultural and religious life. The resolution matters as an international record of alarm, but read its limits: it neither recognized an independent Tibetan state nor supplied a border. Its wording cannot be used as a magic sovereignty certificate, just as the atlas polygon cannot. It does show that religion and culture had become central international concerns immediately after the uprising.

passages.title: Socialist transformation, cultural assault and guarded recovery
passages.text: After 1959, authorities broke up the old estate order, redistributed land, separated religious and governmental authority and replaced the Tibetan cabinet with PRC institutions. Beijing calls this “democratic reform” and emancipation from feudal serfdom; many Tibetans remember violence, imprisonment and the loss of political and religious institutions. Both the end of hereditary estate obligations and coercive state campaigns are historical facts. The Tibet Autonomous Region was formally inaugurated on 1 September 1965 inside the PRC.

passages.title: Socialist transformation, cultural assault and guarded recovery
passages.text: The Cultural Revolution attacked monasteries, images, scriptures, clothing, rituals and people associated with the “old.” Yet local history was not simply Tibetans on one side and outsiders on the other. Tibetan students, villagers and cadres joined rival revolutionary factions; the 1969 Nyemo killings grew from that factional struggle as well as spiritual and local tensions. Acknowledging Tibetan participation does not shrink the destruction. It makes the tragedy harder and more human: political campaigns could recruit neighbors to damage their own inheritance.

passages.title: Socialist transformation, cultural assault and guarded recovery
passages.text: Hu Yaobang’s 1980 visit triggered decollectivization, economic relief and a limited cultural opening. Families could reconnect across India and Tibet; monasteries reopened or were repaired, religious activity returned and Tibetan books appeared. Declassified diplomats also reported deep poverty, weak technical capacity and a job market where Chinese-language education brought advantage. Revival therefore meant real breathing room inside continued one-party control, not a rewind button that restored 1950.

passages.title: Socialist transformation, cultural assault and guarded recovery
passages.text: Field researchers in the 1980s found Changtang herders once again owning household livestock after commune rules were reversed. They saw sheep, goats and yaks, black yak-hair tents, traditional dress and prayer flags. That continuity surprised scholars who had expected Cultural Revolution policies to have erased everything. It should not be romanticized: pastoralists remembered deprivation and were adapting to markets and state programs. Still, the tent, herd and prayer flag are strong evidence that political rupture did not make Tibetan life vanish.

passages.title: Socialist transformation, cultural assault and guarded recovery
passages.text: Beginning in 1987, demonstrations in Lhasa demanded independence, religious freedom or human rights; some episodes included violence, and security forces used lethal force and mass detention. Beijing imposed martial law on 8 March 1989, officially saying it needed to protect unity, people and property, and lifted it in May 1990. Reported death and detention totals vary and no independent inquiry settled them. The careful lesson is the event and crackdown, not a confidently repeated internet number.

passages.title: Estates, families, work and the danger of two propaganda cartoons
passages.text: Old central Tibet had government, monastery and aristocratic estates. Many lay households inherited obligations to a lord or estate, paid produce or labor and needed permission for some moves; categories and local practice also allowed negotiation and mobility. Goldstein calls the structure pervasive serfdom, but other scholars have challenged parts of his command-and-choice model. “Everyone was a happy free peasant” and “everyone was a chained slave” are rival cartoons. Children deserve the harder truth: inequality was institutional, experiences differed, and historians argue over the best comparison word.

passages.title: Estates, families, work and the danger of two propaganda cartoons
passages.text: Marriage was not one-size-fits-all. In some landholding households, brothers married one wife so farmland and obligations could remain with one corporate family instead of splitting each generation. Other Tibetans practiced monogamy, other plural arrangements or celibate monastic life. Polyandry was neither universal nor merely an exotic romance; it was tied to property, rank, inheritance and household strategy. The study concerns central Tibet, so it cannot describe every pastoral camp, town, class or Tibetan-speaking region.

passages.title: Estates, families, work and the danger of two propaganda cartoons
passages.text: Tsering Wangmo remembered a pastoral household where parents, children and relatives shared a camp. Before sunrise, people milked female yaks, churned butter, dried cheese, roasted barley, spun and wove wool, grazed animals and carried firewood. Children worked too. Meals included tsampa dough, tea, dairy, meat and noodle soup; thick wool and sheepskin fought the cold. Evenings could bring spinning, stories, songs and dance, especially at weddings and Losar. She described both exhausting work and joyful gatherings. One woman’s 2007 memory, though wonderfully specific, is not a census of Tibet.

passages.title: Estates, families, work and the danger of two propaganda cartoons
passages.text: Phurbu Chogba’s life shows why social change cannot be scored with one slogan. Born poor in 1949, she said her mother’s family fled heavy estate obligations; at seven or eight she had to replace her mother in service, carry fertilizer and glean grain under threat of beating. After 1959 she returned home and entered a community school, learning Tibetan literacy and later mathematics. She welcomed those openings, then recalled commune shortages, political campaigns and swollen faces from inadequate food. The same witness remembered liberation, pressure, hope and hunger.

passages.title: Estates, families, work and the danger of two propaganda cartoons
passages.text: The evidence itself is an achievement. The Library of Congress archive preserves almost 700 interviews: common folk from many strata, former officials and monks from Drepung. People recall ordinary work, taxes, jokes, quarrels, ritual, fear and political campaigns in Tibetan and Chinese, with English transcripts. Memories can conflict or age, so historians compare them with documents and objects. But without this archive, a map card might contain only rulers and armies. A grandmother explaining a wooden bowl or a clerk remembering a tax can change the questions history asks.

passages.title: Childhood, learning and healing
passages.text: Before 1959, learning depended strongly on family, wealth, place and monastic connections. Lobsang Thardho remembered beginning lessons around age five or six at the Potala with an uncle who was also an opera singer, then entering Ganden monastery at thirteen for religious study and a demanding daily routine. That path tells us what was possible for one connected boy, not that every child attended a school. Phurbu’s forced childhood service shows the opposite end of the opportunity ladder.

passages.title: Childhood, learning and healing
passages.text: State schooling expanded after 1959. In 1980, officials promised more primary schools, teacher training, Tibetan textbooks and Tibetan-language study; border-area pupils could receive food, clothing and lodging. Those measures opened classrooms to many rural children. The source is a PRC government history, however, and its enrollment and spending figures do not independently measure teaching quality, family choice or whether Tibetan or Chinese carried more power beyond the classroom. Education can be both a door and a contest over whose words unlock it.

passages.title: Childhood, learning and healing
passages.text: The Thirteenth Dalai Lama founded a Lhasa medicine clinic, school and pharmacy in 1916, now remembered as Men-Tsee-Khang. Students learned Sowa Rigpa, a Tibetan medical system using pulse and urine examination, diet, behavior, external therapies and compound medicines within its own theory of bodily balance. That was a major institution for preserving and teaching medical knowledge. Historical diagnosis is evidence of careful observation and a living intellectual tradition; it is not proof that every remedy worked or a substitute for present-day medical advice.

passages.title: Childhood, learning and healing
passages.text: PRC state records report rapid growth after 1959: by 1965, 193 medical institutions, 1,631 beds and 2,947 health workers. Those numbers document administrative construction, not equal care. Phurbu recalled villagers carrying a man with appendicitis about 30 kilometers on a door because no vehicle was available; the county facility then sent him onward to Shigatse for surgery and a blood transfusion. A hospital could exist on paper while mountains still made the trip an emergency expedition.

passages.title: Water, washing and the toilet evidence we actually have
passages.text: Wangmo remembered fetching river water in a pastoral region and, in the frozen months, breaking ice, loading blocks onto yaks and melting them over a fire. Bathing meant cold flowing water; she laughed grimly that children shivered and cried. Her memory should not become “Tibetans never washed” or “all water was pure.” It reveals one household’s priorities when fuel, labor, winter and distance mattered. Drinking water came first, and a hot bath required enough fire to turn solid water into a luxury.

passages.title: Water, washing and the toilet evidence we actually have
passages.text: A former Tibetan official remembered Lhasa household toilets receiving ash each day to control odor. The contents were allowed to rot and later used as fertilizer. He contrasted that with PLA gardeners in the early 1950s mixing fresh human waste with water for remarkably large vegetables. This is an interview memory, not a sanitary engineering survey, and handling untreated waste carries disease risk. Still, it answers the children’s practical question: yes, the toilet could feed the field, and no, nobody needed to pretend the job smelled like roses.

passages.title: Water, washing and the toilet evidence we actually have
passages.text: Systematic sanitation evidence is thin inside this card’s period. A 1997 conservation study, just after the 1994 atlas cutoff, found toilets among the weakest parts of traditional old-city buildings. Some housing built around 1990 used cesspits whose liquid drained toward the river while solids were usually emptied by hand; the project added pipes and repaired an old stone drain. That does not prove every earlier Lhasa toilet worked the same way. It proves why honest history sometimes ends with “we have a close, late snapshot, not a century-long bathroom census.”

passages.title: Money, mail, newspapers and Tibetan on the page
passages.text: Printing tied reform to older book skills. Government workers carved blocks for banknotes, stamps, proclamations and manuals, while monasteries and workshops continued religious publishing. These were not simply copies of foreign gadgets: Tibetan artists and scribes adapted local paper, script, symbols and carving practice to new state jobs. A paper note or postal cancel is tiny compared with a palace, but it survives with a date, denomination and route. For historians, the pocket-sized evidence can be wonderfully bossy.

passages.title: Money, mail, newspapers and Tibetan on the page
passages.text: A small written-language sample is `ཡུལ་ཕྱོགས་སོ་སོའི་གསར་འགྱུར་མེ་ལོང་`, transliterated *Yul phyogs so so’i gsar ’gyur me long*: “Mirror of News from All Sides of the World.” This is the documented Tibetan title of the Tibet Mirror, printed in Kalimpong from 1925 to 1963 and read by people traveling to or living in Tibet. The Unicode line is a modern editorial transcription of the masthead, not an invented chatty sentence. Its pages carried global war, Indian independence and regional news into a scarce vernacular media world.

passages.title: Money, mail, newspapers and Tibetan on the page
passages.text: Writing did not belong only to monks or ministers. After 1959, Phurbu’s village class used Tibetan reading, writing and newspapers before she studied mathematics. During the 1980s opening, new Tibetan literary, academic and religious works appeared even as Chinese fluency often brought greater access to jobs and higher education. A script can survive while its social power changes. The important question is therefore not merely “Could someone read Tibetan?” but “Where could Tibetan reading take them next?”

Nothing “fell” in 1994. The atlas simply stops drawing this Tibet ID then. The pre-1959 Tibetan government had already ended in Lhasa. The Tibet Autonomous Region continued as a province-level jurisdiction of the PRC; the Dalai Lama, refugee settlements and a Tibetan political-administrative system continued in India. These were different institutions on different sides of a conflict, and neither meant that Tibetan people or culture had stopped. The Library of Congress uses separate jurisdiction headings before and after 1 September 1965, a useful catalog distinction rather than a sovereignty judgment. A map ID can end even when people do not. This card therefore ends with transformed institutions and continuing people, not extinction.

passages.text: The Tibetan Empire rose under Songtsen Gampo in the seventh century and for two hundred years matched Tang China and the Arab caliphate for control of the Silk Road, from the Tarim Basin to the Himalaya. It gave Tibet its script, its first monasteries and its Buddhism.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Songtsen Gampo married Princess Wencheng of Tang, who brought a Buddha image and texts to Lhasa; a Nepalese princess, Bhrikuti, is remembered as his other Buddhist queen.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The Tibetan script was created, by tradition by Thonmi Sambhota, from an Indian script of the Gupta type.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Samye, the first Tibetan Buddhist monastery, was completed under Trisong Detsen, and Buddhism spread beside the native Bon rites.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Jokhang temple was built in Lhasa and became Tibet's holiest shrine.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Tibetan armies fielded armored cavalry and took fortified towns with methods learned from China and Central Asia.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Tibet held the Tarim oases and, from 786 to 848, Dunhuang, taxing the Silk Road between China, India and Central Asia.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: A Tibetan army occupied the Tang capital Chang'an for about two weeks.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: A peace treaty with Tang was carved in Tibetan and Chinese on a pillar that still stands outside the Jokhang.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Tibetan script is in use today across Tibet, Bhutan and the Himalaya.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Buddhism became the core of Tibetan identity and culture.
The emperor Langdarma was assassinated in 842 and the empire broke into rival kingdoms, the Era of Fragmentation, that lasted until the eleventh century.
