passages.text: This card’s “Tibetans” label belongs to the atlas, not to a known Bronze Age nation. From about 1500 to 500 BCE, the map paints one enormous shape across the Tibetan Plateau and far beyond. Archaeology instead reveals many local communities in valleys, grasslands, basins and Himalayan corridors. At sites such as Qugong, Changguogou, Bangga and Gepaseru, people combined crops, herds, hunting, craft and exchange in different ways. Barley and wheat tolerated cold highlands; sheep, goats, cattle, horses and eventually securely identified domestic yak helped turn grass into food, fiber, transport and fuel. Tiny clues do surprising work: charred seeds reveal meals, animal teeth track movement, and hardened dental plaque preserves milk proteins, an ancient snack record no toothbrush could erase. The evidence does not name everyone’s language, government or beliefs. Tibetan writing, the Tibetan Empire and state-supported Buddhism appear more than a thousand years after this card ends, so they must not be pasted backward. At 500 BCE the atlas polygon simply disappears. People, farms, herds, routes and regional cultures continued; only this broad editorial category stopped.

passages.title: Read the map before imagining a country
passages.text: The live index calls this exact record “Tibetans,” classifies it as a culture and assigns approximate dates of 1500 to 500 BCE. Those fields identify an atlas feature. They do not establish an ancient self-name, census, capital, government, common language or surveyed border.

passages.title: Read the map before imagining a country
passages.text: The old imported summary describes present-day population totals and modern administrative regions. That information is centuries out of place for a Bronze and early Iron Age card. The replacement begins with dated archaeology and clearly separates modern Tibetan identities from unnamed prehistoric communities.

passages.title: Read the map before imagining a country
passages.text: At 1500 and 1000 BCE the target geometry is byte-for-byte identical: one simple polygon stretching from near Hotan and Leh to Chengdu and Xining. A thousand kilometres of mountains, basins and valleys cannot be treated as a single excavated cultural zone because a digital outline encloses them.

passages.title: Read the map before imagining a country
passages.text: At 700 BCE one coordinate changes and the geometry hash changes, yet every tested target point remains inside. At 500 BCE the id is absent everywhere tested. These are cartographic seams; neither a one-point edit nor feature deletion proves migration, conquest, ethnic replacement or collapse.

passages.title: Read the map before imagining a country
passages.text: The atlas previously labels parts of the region “Tibeto-Burmanese” and later applies “Proto-Tibetan cultures,” but archaeology cannot certify a tidy relay between those categories. Pots, genes and crops can show contact or descent patterns; none records the map-maker’s sequence as an ancient family tree.

passages.title: How discoveries become evidence
passages.text: Archaeologists excavate layer by layer, record where objects lie and date short-lived material such as charred grain. At Bangga, flotation recovered tiny plant remains, while pottery, stone tools, animal bones and architecture were studied together. A loose bronze object without context answers far fewer questions.

passages.title: How discoveries become evidence
passages.text: Direct radiocarbon dates on barley and wheat matter because an undated seed might have slipped into an older layer. Large site syntheses then compare altitude, crop species and domestic animals. Their famous “after 3600 BP” pattern is a regional trend, not one exact settlement date for the entire plateau.

passages.title: How discoveries become evidence
passages.text: Surface stone artifacts are especially hard to date because wind, water, trampling and burial move them. Optically stimulated luminescence can estimate when a stone surface was buried, but researchers also study sediment and landforms. The clever machine does not cancel the need for careful context.

passages.title: How discoveries become evidence
passages.text: At Nwya Devu, Chusang and Baishiya, stone tools, footprints, sediment, fossils, proteins and DNA show much older high-altitude visits or occupation. They are essential background, but their makers lived thousands to more than one hundred thousand years before this card; they cannot be renamed “Tibetans” here.

passages.title: How discoveries become evidence
passages.text: Ancient DNA can compare sampled individuals, estimate close kinship and reveal ancestry change. It cannot hear a dead person speak or read their political loyalties. Plateau genome studies show continuity and repeated interaction, so this card reports population history without turning a genetic cluster into a nation.

passages.title: Thin air, cold ground and many environments
passages.text: The plateau is not one endless snowy table. Cold desert, dry steppe, alpine meadow, warmer river valleys, basins and forested eastern margins offer different water, fuel, crops and pasture. Later ecological surveys help describe that variety, but they are environmental comparison rather than a Bronze Age land-use census.

passages.title: Thin air, cold ground and many environments
passages.text: At roughly 4,000 metres, each breath contains much less oxygen than at sea level. Present-day Tibetan populations carry strongly selected high-altitude variants, including a Denisovan-related EPAS1 haplotype. That deep inheritance illuminates biology, yet it cannot identify which excavated potter carried it without ancient DNA.

passages.title: Thin air, cold ground and many environments
passages.text: Cold, aridity and surprise snow made resilience a household problem. Communities could spread risk across crops, grazing, stored food, dairy and exchange instead of trusting one harvest. Pollen, charcoal and other environmental proxies show mountain landscapes changing through long interaction between climate, vegetation and people.

passages.title: Thin air, cold ground and many environments
passages.text: Warm valleys could support fields while broad uplands offered seasonal pasture. Mobility models suggest repeated farmer to herder interaction corridors, but their pathways are calculated possibilities checked against artifacts, not GPS tracks from 800 BCE. Real routes shifted with grass, snow, water, kin and exchange partners.

passages.title: Thin air, cold ground and many environments
passages.text: The giant atlas polygon includes places with sharply different rainfall and growing seasons, even though its outline barely changes for centuries. Archaeological evidence therefore works best as a mosaic: a claim about Qugong or Qaidam stays local unless several independently dated sites justify a broader pattern.

passages.title: Fields, herds and dinner
passages.text: At Changguogou, researchers identified naked barley, wheat and foxtail millet. Their coexistence matters: western-origin wheat and barley met an eastern millet tradition in central Tibet. People were choosing a mixed menu and crop-risk strategy, not instantly replacing every older plant with one “Tibetan” staple.

passages.title: Fields, herds and dinner
passages.text: Barley and wheat tolerate colder growing conditions than millet and helped farming reach higher elevations. Regional evidence after about 1600 BCE combines these grains with sheep and other livestock. Elevation still mattered: some communities farmed valleys, while people in non-arable highlands depended more heavily on animals.

passages.title: Fields, herds and dinner
passages.text: Dental calculus, the hard plaque a dentist scrapes away, preserved milk proteins in ancient mouths. At Gepaseru, goat-milk protein dates to about 1500 to 1312 BCE. That is a wonderfully unglamorous archive: somebody’s stubborn tooth crust became a tiny, scientifically readable receipt for dairy consumption.

passages.title: Fields, herds and dinner
passages.text: Grinding stones at Qugong, Changguogou and Bangga could turn barley or wheat into flour. Bangga vessel forms and tool assemblages suggest flour-based cooking, but no surviving recipe says “make this exact bread.” Porridge, dough or roasted flour remain possibilities only where residues or cooking traces support them.

passages.title: Fields, herds and dinner
passages.text: Plant and animal finds also leave room for hunting, fishing and gathering alongside farming and herding. Their proportions changed by region. A family in a productive valley, a mobile highland camp and a basin settlement did not necessarily eat alike, even if the atlas colors them identically.

passages.title: Animals, movement and useful dung
passages.text: Sheep and goats converted short highland grasses into meat, milk, hides and fiber. Their bones occur widely, while animal genomes help trace long dispersals. A sheep lineage is still not a human ethnicity: animals can be traded, stolen, exchanged at marriage or moved between communities speaking different languages.

passages.title: Animals, movement and useful dung
passages.text: Qugong animal remains suggested possible yak and sheep in the second millennium BCE, but secure domestic-yak evidence is later. At Bangga around 2500 BP, ancient DNA identifies domestic yak, taurine cattle and hybrids. The card preserves that sequence instead of granting every earlier large bovine a yak passport.

passages.title: Animals, movement and useful dung
passages.text: Bangga herders kept sheep, goats, cattle, yak or hybrids and horses. Different animals supplied different combinations of meat, milk, fiber, traction and transport, buffering bad weather or disease. Manure in a corral also became fertilizer or fuel, the least glamorous part of the herd could still keep a hearth useful.

passages.title: Animals, movement and useful dung
passages.text: Qaidam surveys found smaller, sometimes ephemeral high-altitude structures with barley, wheat, grinding tools and bones of horses, cattle, sheep and dogs. This supports flexible agro-pastoral mobility in that basin. It does not prove that every household moved seasonally or followed the same annual circuit.

passages.title: Animals, movement and useful dung
passages.text: Upper Mustang’s Kali Gandaki corridor links plateau and South Asian lowlands, while modeling identifies other likely corridors across grasslands and valleys. Goods, animals, stories and marriage partners could travel in stages. Calling these links a prehistoric “Silk Road” would be catchy but chronologically misleading.

passages.title: Homes, pots, cloth and metalwork
passages.text: Bangga preserves stone foundations, rooms, enclosures and a corral-like area rather than a palace or city grid. Architecture suggests repeated agropastoral occupation, but building use can change. Archaeologists compare floors, hearths, dung, artifacts and repairs before deciding whether a space sheltered people, animals or supplies.

passages.title: Homes, pots, cloth and metalwork
passages.text: Qugong’s second-millennium ceramics include finely polished black wares and distinctive ring-footed forms; first-millennium Bangga pottery differs while retaining a few local practices. Pots therefore reveal skilled choices and contact, not an ethnic barcode. The same household could imitate, trade or reject a neighboring style.

passages.title: Homes, pots, cloth and metalwork
passages.text: Spindle whorls and rare fabric traces from the southeastern plateau show people spinning fiber and weaving. Some later Bronze Age graves contain more costly textile tools, hinting at status differences. Because cloth decays easily and graves are selective, archaeologists cannot reconstruct one standard outfit for all communities.

passages.title: Homes, pots, cloth and metalwork
passages.text: Cold-weather clothing probably required layered plant fiber, wool, hair, hide or fur, but exact combinations must remain site-specific. Animal management made fiber and skins available; textile tools show production. A modern yak-hair tent or robe may inspire questions, yet it cannot serve as a photograph of 1000 BCE.

passages.title: Homes, pots, cloth and metalwork
passages.text: Copper, bronze, iron and mixed-metal objects enter different plateau regions on uneven schedules. Composite objects and imported forms show experimentation and exchange. Metal did not erase stone or bone tools overnight, and a bronze style cannot by itself identify a migrant, ruler or language community.

passages.title: Families, women, children and learning
passages.text: No household list names parents, grandparents or adopted children in this interval. Houses, shared work areas, graves and ancient DNA can test possible relationships, but each captures only part of social life. The safest picture is cooperating households and networks whose exact kin rules remain unknown.

passages.title: Families, women, children and learning
passages.text: Milk proteins occur in women and men, adults and children, and both richer and plainer burials. That result gives people of different ages and statuses a rare presence in food history. It does not tell who milked, churned or controlled herds, so those jobs should not be assigned automatically by gender.

passages.title: Families, women, children and learning
passages.text: Spinning tools show substantial textile labor, and differences among graves may reflect organized production or status. Some workers were likely highly practiced, but the objects do not announce “women’s work” or “men’s work.” Sexed skeletons, use-wear and workshop context are needed before making that claim.

passages.title: Families, women, children and learning
passages.text: Children had to learn animal behavior, safe routes, crop timing, tool handling, food preparation and local social rules. There is no evidence for a Bronze Age school or Tibetan alphabet lesson. Skill probably grew through watching, helping and practice, an inference from household production rather than a surviving timetable.

passages.title: Families, women, children and learning
passages.text: Burials include people of different ages, and cave or cist traditions vary across the plateau and Himalayas. A child buried with objects is not a simple measure of affection, rank or inheritance. Mortuary choices concern survivors and ritual as well as the dead, so comparisons require dates and local context.

passages.title: Health, medicine, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Thin air, cold, smoke, injuries, childbirth, infection and food shortage all posed risks, yet this card has no contemporary medical manual. Healed bone can show survival after injury and teeth can preserve disease or diet. It cannot name the herb, helper or ritual used during recovery.

passages.title: Health, medicine, water and the toilet question
passages.text: High-Himalayan skeletons show that dental disease and childhood stress differed between sites rather than following one altitude rule. Those studied communities span other dates and places, so they offer method and comparison. They cannot be pasted wholesale onto Qugong or every person inside the atlas polygon.

passages.title: Health, medicine, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Dental calculus can preserve food proteins as well as the microbial mineral layer itself. Researchers sampled it carefully, checked preservation and identified peptides. Finding milk protein proves consumption far more securely than guessing from a pot shape; failing to find it, however, does not prove someone never drank milk.

passages.title: Health, medicine, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Settlements depended on springs, streams, rivers, snowmelt and seasonal water, but published evidence does not establish one managed water system for this umbrella. Households had to separate drinking, cooking, animals and refuse somehow. The exact containers, rules and daily fetching duties vary or remain archaeologically invisible.

passages.title: Health, medicine, water and the toilet question
passages.text: No securely identified toilet, latrine or sewer is attributable to this exact atlas category and interval. Corrals and manure deposits show that people managed at least some animal waste, but human sanitation leaves weaker traces. It would be irresponsible to invent either palace plumbing or a universal “go outside” rule.

passages.title: Belief, status, conflict and political limits
passages.text: Stone-cist, cave and other graves, animal offerings and selected objects show that death carried social and ritual meaning. Archaeology can describe placement, bodies and grave goods; it cannot recover a complete theology. Different burial customs may coexist without representing separate religions or ethnic groups.

passages.title: Belief, status, conflict and political limits
passages.text: Some graves contain rarer ornaments, metalwork or animals, suggesting unequal access and public display. Inequality does not automatically equal a kingdom, hereditary caste or tax state. Researchers need settlements, storage, fortifications, production and repeated mortuary patterns before scaling status into political institutions.

passages.title: Belief, status, conflict and political limits
passages.text: Weapons and defended positions occur in wider plateau records, and trauma can sometimes document violence. This atlas interval offers no evidence for one army controlling the drawn polygon. Raiding, feud, defense and coercion are possible, but naming commanders, enemies or imperial campaigns would be fiction.

passages.title: Belief, status, conflict and political limits
passages.text: Tibetan Buddhism is not an in-period explanation. Museum and textual chronologies place royal patronage, monasteries and Buddhist manuscript culture mainly in the seventh century CE and later, more than a millennium after this card ends. Prehistoric graves should be studied on their own terms rather than called Buddhist.

passages.title: Belief, status, conflict and political limits
passages.text: The Tibetan Empire is also later: its political formation, armies, court records and territorial expansion belong to roughly the seventh through ninth centuries CE. Imperial burial mounds are valuable evidence for that later world, but they cannot supply kings, borders or beliefs for 1500 to 500 BCE.

passages.title: Achievements, language and what continued
passages.text: The outstanding achievement was not a single monument. Communities combined frost-tolerant crops, dairy, varied livestock, mobility, storage, grinding, pottery, textiles and exchange to make lives at altitude. Different solutions fit different valleys and grasslands, which is precisely why one civilization label fits poorly.

passages.title: Achievements, language and what continued
passages.text: Craft was inventive as well as practical: polished ceramics, decorated stone tools, spun fibers and composite metal objects required learned sequences and aesthetic judgment. Similarities reveal communication; differences reveal local choices. Neither pattern needs a plateau-wide ruler issuing designs from one capital.

passages.title: Achievements, language and what continued
passages.text: Modern Tibetic languages form a diverse family derived from Old Tibetan, and many Tibetan-speaking communities have distinct identities. Historical linguistics can model deeper relationships, but this record predates attested Old Tibetan. Archaeological objects inside the polygon cannot tell us exactly which languages their makers spoke.

passages.title: Achievements, language and what continued
passages.text: Contemporaneous written-language sample: none is securely attributable to this atlas category between 1500 and 500 BCE. Tibetan script and the earliest surviving Old Tibetan historical records belong to the imperial era. Supplying Tibetan letters, transliteration and translation here would borrow a voice from more than a thousand years later.

passages.title: Achievements, language and what continued
passages.text: At 500 BCE the exact atlas id disappears; at 400 BCE other broad labels cover many tested places. That editorial switch is not a fall. Farms, herds, routes, households and local traditions continued changing, and much later states and Tibetic literary culture emerged through histories that this polygon cannot summarize.

The atlas removes this exact id at 500 BCE. One century later it draws “Proto-Tibetan cultures” across many tested plateau locations and “Zhangzhung kingdom” over several western points, but those are later atlas classifications, not proven successors to one earlier state. The target was never a demonstrated polity, so it did not “fall” as a unit. Local communities, crops, herds, routes and traditions continued and changed. Tibetan script, empire and Buddhist institutions arose much later; none should be used to manufacture a neat ending for this prehistoric umbrella.

materialEvidence.question: Does a concrete finding have an identifiable context, date, interpretation and evidence limit?

dailyLife.question: Does the account explain ordinary practices with evidence rather than only rulers?

artsScienceTechnology.question: Are achievements concrete and correctly attributed to this polity and period?

chronologicalPhases.question: Are source-supported phases distinguished from map snapshot dates?

endingContinuity.question: Does the narrative identify what ended or continued, with dates, mechanism and uncertainty?

uncertainty.question: Are uncertainties attached to particular claims rather than a blanket disclaimer?

sectionTitles: Unpaint the map before meeting the people
Thin air, cold ground and many environments
Homes, water, fire and the toilet question
Tools, pots, cloth and practiced hands
Movement, exchange and conflict without an empire

passages.text: The atlas paints “Tibeto-Burmanese” across a huge slice of High Asia from 2000 to 1500 BCE. That catchy label is the map editor’s umbrella, not the name of a known people, country, language, or border. Its polygon includes Nagqu, Qamdo, Nyingchi, Yushu and even Hotan, yet leaves out Lhasa, Kathmandu and much of the eastern Himalaya. Archaeology is patchier and more interesting. Near and beyond that outline, communities fished cold lakes, hunted, tended millet fields, adopted barley and wheat, managed sheep and goats, shaped stone and bone, made pots, and exchanged materials along valleys and grasslands, but never all in the same way. A fun scientific clue comes from ancient tooth crust: proteins can reveal milk, although the first direct goat-milk result here dates just after the card ends. New radiocarbon work can also ruin a neat tale in the best possible way: Qugong, once assigned to this span, now dates around 1400 to 1300 BCE. Language-family trees remain debated, and no object tells us its maker’s speech. At 1500 BCE the atlas replaces this shape with several other labels. People and lifeways continued; only the oversized category vanished.

passages.title: Unpaint the map before meeting the people
passages.text: The live index names this exact record “Tibeto-Burmanese,” calls it a culture, and gives approximate dates of 2000 to 1500 BCE. Those are database fields, not ancient testimony. No inscription, ruler list, capital, census or self-name establishes a society by that name.

passages.title: Unpaint the map before meeting the people
passages.text: The sole polygon is one nine-point shape spanning about 73.5° to 99.7°E and 25.2° to 37.8°N. It owns sampled Nagqu, Qamdo, Nyingchi, Yushu and Hotan, yet excludes Lhasa, Shigatse, Kathmandu and much territory where related languages are spoken today.

passages.title: Unpaint the map before meeting the people
passages.text: At 1500 BCE the exact id vanishes. Sampled places are redistributed among atlas labels such as “Tibetans,” “Burmese,” “Dravidians” and others, often with radically changed coverage. That redraw is not evidence of conquest, migration, language replacement or four clean successor peoples.

passages.title: Unpaint the map before meeting the people
passages.text: “Tibeto-Burman” is a linguistic classification with hundreds of diverse languages and disputed internal branching. Even scholars who accept a Sinitic versus Tibeto-Burman split do not thereby create one prehistoric people. Languages can spread through learning, marriage, trade and political change.

passages.title: Unpaint the map before meeting the people
passages.text: Archaeologists instead work from named sites, layers, objects, bones, plants and dates. The current synthesis treats transformations after 2000 BCE as regional processes. This card follows that method: every example keeps its locality and never turns a language-tree branch into a territorial border.

passages.title: How discoveries change the story
passages.text: Radiocarbon dates estimate when once-living material stopped exchanging carbon with the atmosphere. Researchers calibrate results and compare them with stratigraphy. A date belongs to the sampled seed, bone or charcoal, not automatically to every artifact, wall or person found nearby.

passages.title: How discoveries change the story
passages.text: Qugong once anchored a 2000/1750 to 1500 BCE story. Seven new dates plus stratigraphic Bayesian modeling now place its relevant deposits around 1400 to 1300 BCE, after this card. Science did not “lose” a site; it gained a sharper clock and exposed how inherited chronologies can mislead.

passages.title: How discoveries change the story
passages.text: Optically stimulated luminescence can date when mineral grains were last exposed to light before burial. It is especially helpful when stone artifacts lack charcoal, but sediment movement and landform history matter. A glowing laboratory signal still needs a secure archaeological context.

passages.title: How discoveries change the story
passages.text: Ancient DNA can reveal biological relationships and population interaction. Plateau genomes show strong regional structure as well as shared ancestry. Genes do not encode pottery style, political loyalty or spoken language, so “genetically related” must never be rewritten as “the same Tibeto-Burman people.”

passages.title: How discoveries change the story
passages.text: At Mabu Co, excavation, isotopes, animal and plant remains, tools and DNA combine to reconstruct a lake-centered life around 2450 to 2050 BCE. The site is just before this interval and outside the strict polygon; it supplies a nearby predecessor case, not a universal opening scene.

passages.title: Thin air, cold ground and many environments
passages.text: The polygon crosses high steppe, cold desert, river valleys, basins and eastern mountain margins. Water, snow, growing season and fuel differ enormously across those settings. A later ecological survey helps describe the physical mosaic, but it is comparison rather than a Bronze Age census.

passages.title: Thin air, cold ground and many environments
passages.text: Nwya Devu lies inside the mapped shape and preserves high-altitude stone-working tens of thousands of years earlier. Its importance is deep human experience on the plateau, not direct ancestry for a 2000 BCE community. A very old campsite cannot name a much later language.

passages.title: Thin air, cold ground and many environments
passages.text: Chusang hand- and footprints show another much earlier episode of central-plateau use. Competing date interpretations remind us that spectacular traces still require careful geology and chronometry. The prints are human and moving; they are not signatures saying what their makers called themselves.

passages.title: Thin air, cold ground and many environments
passages.text: Present-day high-altitude physiology includes a Denisovan-related EPAS1 variant, and ancient research places selected variants deep in plateau history. That explains biological adaptation at population scale. Without a sampled genome, it cannot identify the breath, ancestry or language of an individual potter.

passages.title: Thin air, cold ground and many environments
passages.text: Pollen, charcoal and sediments record vegetation, fire and landscape change over long spans. They show that agropastoral landscapes emerged through repeated human-environment interaction over centuries. They do not reveal a single arrival day when everyone suddenly became a farmer or herder.

passages.title: Dinner came from several strategies
passages.text: Karuo near Qamdo preserves houses, roads, ash pits, pottery, stone and bone tools, millet and animal remains, but its accepted range ends around 2100 BCE. It is a close predecessor inside the polygon, useful for inherited skills and questions, not proof that identical households survived unchanged.

passages.title: Dinner came from several strategies
passages.text: Near the northeastern plateau margin, directly dated barley appears around 2000 BCE. Crop genetics suggests several possible eastward routes. One grain can establish presence at a site; it cannot by itself reveal whether seed arrived through migrating farmers, neighbors, exchange or experimentation.

passages.title: Dinner came from several strategies
passages.text: Millet favored warmer lower valleys, while barley and wheat later made colder elevations more farmable. Archaeobotanical syntheses nevertheless show mixed systems and large gaps across seasons. Families could combine crops rather than swap one complete “civilization package” for another overnight.

passages.title: Dinner came from several strategies
passages.text: Domestic sheep are directly dated in the Tao River Valley around 1900 to 1750 BCE, with goats later. Animals provided meat, hides, fiber and perhaps milk, but this evidence lies east of much of the map. A traveling sheep carries no tiny passport naming its owner’s language.

passages.title: Dinner came from several strategies
passages.text: Gepaseru offers the interval’s funniest serious clue: hardened tooth plaque survived when food did not. The earliest individual, dated about 1883 to 1691 BCE, lacked enough preserved calculus for milk-protein testing; nearby sheep and goat skulls suggest possible milking, while direct goat protein is later.

passages.title: Homes, water, fire and the toilet question
passages.text: No excavated floor plan represents every community inside this polygon. Karuo’s earlier substantial buildings contrast with mobile or poorly preserved traces elsewhere, and later Qaidam sites include small structures. Houses may have used stone, earth, timber or perishable materials according to local supply.

passages.title: Homes, water, fire and the toilet question
passages.text: Cold households needed fuel for cooking and warmth. Charcoal and combustion studies can identify burned woody plants, shrubs or dung-like materials, but choices varied with ecology. A hearth assemblage records what reached one fire; it is not a plateau-wide fuel rule.

passages.title: Homes, water, fire and the toilet question
passages.text: Water came from rivers, springs, lakes, snowmelt and stored supplies, depending on season and place. The archaeological sources do not document one in-period canal or household water code for this umbrella. Fetching, protecting and sharing water were necessary, but exact duties remain unknown.

passages.title: Homes, water, fire and the toilet question
passages.text: Ash pits and refuse deposits help archaeologists reconstruct food, fuel and broken tools. Their contents can mix through cleaning, animals or later disturbance. A rubbish hollow is valuable evidence, yet it is not automatically a kitchen, ritual deposit or carefully engineered sanitation system.

passages.title: Homes, water, fire and the toilet question
passages.text: No securely dated toilet, latrine or sewer belongs to this exact atlas layer. Human waste may have been deposited away from living and water areas, but no universal practice is preserved. The honest answer is less glamorous than invented plumbing: archaeologists have not found enough.

passages.title: Families, women, children and learning
passages.text: No text lists households, marriages or inheritance rules. Graves and genomes can sometimes identify biological relatives, while settlements show shared work, but neither captures adoption, friendship or every kind of family. Household organization almost certainly varied among valleys, camps and generations.

passages.title: Families, women, children and learning
passages.text: Women and men both contributed to survival, yet tools rarely announce a worker’s gender. Later textile evidence shows skilled spinning and weaving, but spindle whorls alone cannot prove who spun. Tasks may have followed age, ability, season, household custom or status.

passages.title: Families, women, children and learning
passages.text: Children learned safe routes, weather signs, animals, plants, tool handling, cooking and social obligations by watching and practicing. No school building, alphabet lesson or timetable survives for this layer. Learning is a strong household inference, while formal education would be an unsupported invention.

passages.title: Families, women, children and learning
passages.text: Mabu Co’s bone needles, fish-gorge hooks, pottery and stone tools reveal sequences that require teaching and repeated practice. Because the site predates the card, it demonstrates available regional knowledge without proving that every 1800 BCE child learned fishing or sewing.

passages.title: Families, women, children and learning
passages.text: Ancient genetic samples show regional continuity and interaction, not sealed bloodlines. Marriage could have linked communities, but genomes do not disclose affection, consent, residence rules or spoken language. A biological connection is one strand of social history, never the whole family story.

passages.title: Tools, pots, cloth and practiced hands
passages.text: Stone remained useful beside new metals. Knappers selected raw material, struck flakes and resharpened edges; polished tools demanded grinding. Luminescence, use-wear and residue studies can date or test activities, but a tool type alone cannot supply its maker’s ethnicity or mother tongue.

passages.title: Tools, pots, cloth and practiced hands
passages.text: Pottery stored, cooked and carried food and water. Similar forms can spread by exchange, imitation or shared practical needs, while local clays and tempers expose different production choices. Archaeologists compare whole assemblages and layers rather than treating one decorated sherd as an ethnic badge.

passages.title: Tools, pots, cloth and practiced hands
passages.text: Spindle whorls and fabric traces from the southeastern plateau show that spinning and weaving were skilled technologies, although much evidence belongs later. Cloth decays, so the surviving sample is biased. Wool, hair, hides and plant fibers remain possibilities only where direct traces support them.

passages.title: Tools, pots, cloth and practiced hands
passages.text: Copper and bronze appear unevenly across northwest and eastern plateau regions. Qijia-associated metallurgy changed from early copper-working to more tin bronze around 1700 to 1500 BCE, but different local sequences overlap. Metal knowledge traveled; it did not draw this atlas polygon.

passages.title: Tools, pots, cloth and practiced hands
passages.text: At Changguogou, reported barley, wheat and foxtail millet show demanding knowledge of planting, harvesting, storage and processing. The site’s position outside the strict polygon and uncertain older chronology make it regional comparison. Its crops cannot feed every household painted on the map.

passages.title: Movement, exchange and conflict without an empire
passages.text: Valleys and grassland passes linked ecological zones. Crop varieties, livestock, pottery ideas and stone or metal materials could move in stages between neighbors. Geospatial models propose interaction corridors; they are testable reconstructions, not recorded roads, borders or royal transport plans.

passages.title: Movement, exchange and conflict without an empire
passages.text: Zongri combines foraging evidence, cultivated plants, animal remains and ceramics that reflect exchange near the northeastern margin. That mixture shows people could borrow foods and objects without becoming one identical culture. Contact leaves overlapping traces rather than tidy color blocks.

passages.title: Movement, exchange and conflict without an empire
passages.text: Barley and wheat followed different routes and flowering adaptations across Eurasia. Their arrival on plateau margins belongs to crop history, not a single human migration. Seed can travel through many hands, and farmers can adopt a plant while retaining other languages and traditions.

passages.title: Movement, exchange and conflict without an empire
passages.text: Metal weapons eventually appear in neighboring regions, but no army is shown controlling this polygon between 2000 and 1500 BCE. Hunting gear, personal defense, raiding and organized warfare can overlap materially. Without trauma, fortifications or settlement patterns, scale and coercion remain uncertain.

passages.title: Movement, exchange and conflict without an empire
passages.text: The map reaches Hotan while excluding many Himalayan and southeastern places associated with related languages today. That odd seam itself disproves literal reading. It is a modern editorial shortcut across exchange zones, not a surveyed frontier that ancient families guarded or crossed at checkpoints.

passages.title: Health, care, death and belief
passages.text: Thin air, cold, smoke, falls, infection, hunger and childbirth could harm people. Ancient bones and teeth can show stress, injury or disease, while healing suggests survival with time and perhaps care. They rarely identify the herb, food, helper or ritual that aided recovery.

passages.title: Health, care, death and belief
passages.text: Dental calculus preserves proteins because plaque mineralizes. Laboratory controls distinguish ancient peptides and assess preservation in one sample. Direct evidence is powerful, but absence is tricky: the earliest Gepaseru calculus was too poorly preserved, so “no detected milk” cannot become “no dairy.”

passages.title: Health, care, death and belief
passages.text: Baishiya Cave animal bones and proteins demonstrate how zooarchaeology and proteomics can reconstruct subsistence in deep time. Those Denisovan-era findings are vastly earlier than this card. They teach a method, not a belief system or direct family line for Bronze Age communities.

passages.title: Health, care, death and belief
passages.text: Burials may preserve body position, offerings, ornaments and relationships among graves. Later Sding Chung cave evidence proves mortuary practices varied across the plateau. It cannot be pasted backward as this interval’s religion, and grave goods never translate themselves into a complete theology.

passages.title: Health, care, death and belief
passages.text: Sheep or goat remains beside a burial may reflect food, offering, herd wealth or several meanings. At Gepaseru, skulls help establish animal presence but do not name a god or ritual sentence. Belief must stay an open question when texts and secure repeated patterns are absent.

passages.title: Language, writing, achievements and continuity
passages.text: Language phylogenies reconstruct relationships from systematic sound and vocabulary correspondences. One model estimates a northern farming-linked origin around 7200 years before present; another favors a later mean near 5900 years. Neither can place a named language inside this exact polygon in 1800 BCE.

passages.title: Language, writing, achievements and continuity
passages.text: A third clock analysis produces a very broad root-age interval and different subgroup support. That disagreement is useful: models depend on language samples, cognate judgments, calibrations and tree assumptions. “Proto-Tibeto-Burman” is a reconstruction, not a recorded speaker community or archaeological culture.

passages.title: Language, writing, achievements and continuity
passages.text: Contemporaneous written-language sample: none is responsibly attributable to this record between 2000 and 1500 BCE. Old Tibetan documents begin in the imperial era, and the earliest Burmese texts are later still. Borrowing either script, a modern phrase or an oracle-bone character would fabricate a voice.

passages.title: Language, writing, achievements and continuity
passages.text: The real achievements were plural: surviving altitude, combining foods, tending animals, reading seasons, crafting stone, bone, pottery and cloth, and maintaining exchange across difficult terrain. These accomplishments belonged to many local communities, including people whose languages and names remain unknown.

passages.title: Language, writing, achievements and continuity
passages.text: At 1500 BCE the atlas removes one umbrella and paints several new ones. No archaeological evidence shows that one Tibeto-Burmanese civilization fell. Households, routes, crops, herds and local traditions continued changing, while much later Tibetan, Burmese and other language histories developed on their own timelines.

The exact atlas id disappears at 1500 BCE, when its sampled territory is redistributed among several other broad labels. That is a cartographic seam, not the fall of a state or disappearance of a people. Archaeological communities, routes, farming, herding and foraging continued locally. Newly dated Qugong deposits and direct goat-milk proteins mostly begin after this endpoint, illustrating why later evidence must not be pulled backward. No automatic predecessor or successor is defensible for an anachronistic language-family umbrella.

sectionTitles: Towns, families and a coastal pantry
What excavations reveal about mission life
A written language and later lives

passages.text: Timucua names several peoples and chiefdoms linked by related speech across northern Florida and southern Georgia, including the Saturiwa, Utina and Potano. It was not one unified empire. The imported 1492 to 1650 outline groups a broad region; local political boundaries differed, and Timucua history continued after that map cutoff.

passages.title: Towns, families and a coastal pantry
passages.text: In 1565, Seloy was the principal chief in the St. Augustine area. Archaeologists located his town on the grounds of today’s Fountain of Youth Archaeological Park, where settlement extended across more than twelve acres. Finding its material remains puts a Native town back into a story often told mainly through Spanish buildings.

passages.title: Towns, families and a coastal pantry
passages.text: The St. Augustine communities were organized into chiefdoms: several allied settlements recognized hereditary leadership. Descent and inheritance followed the female line. Family relationships therefore helped shape political authority as well as household life, although individual Timucua-speaking regions had their own histories.

passages.title: Towns, families and a coastal pantry
passages.text: Circular homes had conical roofs thatched with palm leaves. Woven walls could be sealed with clay, and some villages stood behind wooden defenses. Larger settlements included ceremonial squares for festivals and dancing. A village needed places for public gatherings as well as sheltered spaces to sleep and cook.

passages.title: Towns, families and a coastal pantry
passages.text: A shell could become part of a toolbox. St. Augustine Timucua craftspeople used whelk shells for implements and made ornaments from shell, bone and teeth. Cooking and storage vessels belonged to the St. Johns pottery tradition. Everyday materials reveal skill in working several very different substances.

passages.title: Towns, families and a coastal pantry
passages.text: Fishing, shellfish collecting and farming worked together. People planted maize, beans and squash, while discarded oyster and other shells accumulated in middens over generations. Archaeologists examine these food remains to learn what people caught and ate. Yesterday’s rubbish can become tomorrow’s evidence.

passages.title: Towns, families and a coastal pantry
passages.text: Healing and religious practice were closely connected. The National Park Service describes healers using local plants and helping women during childbirth, as well as giving blessings connected with work and travel. These are accounts of historical beliefs and care, not instructions for trying an old remedy today.

passages.title: What excavations reveal about mission life
passages.text: After Spanish attacks displaced the Potano in 1585, a new village developed near present-day Gainesville. A friar arrived in 1606, establishing Mission San Francisco de Potano, which was abandoned in 1706. Excavated turtle, freshwater fish and turkey bones show foods eaten at this particular community.

passages.title: What excavations reveal about mission life
passages.text: Students excavating that mission found a small intact pot, a rare discovery because discarded vessels are usually broken. Its faint scorch marks might come from manufacture or warming food beside a fire. Without the interior coating often left by cooking, its precise job remains uncertain: even a complete pot does not tell its whole story.

passages.title: What excavations reveal about mission life
passages.text: At the seventeenth-century Baptizing Spring mission settlement, archaeologists found traces of Native houses alongside hearths, storage pits and rubbish pits. Glass and copper beads and a religious medal occurred among mostly Native-made tools and pottery. Households incorporated some imported belongings while continuing familiar crafts and domestic routines.

passages.title: What excavations reveal about mission life
passages.text: Mission communities supplied the Spanish colony with food and labor. Some crops were taken as tribute, and people could be drafted as carriers, couriers, cattle workers and river pilots. Religious instruction therefore came within a system that also made substantial demands on families’ time and harvests.

passages.title: What excavations reveal about mission life
passages.text: Women could hold chiefly authority during the mission period. Doña Ana governed Nombre de Dios when its first full-time friar arrived in 1587, and her daughter Doña María later succeeded her. Their recorded leadership gives names to the women behind broad descriptions of matrilineal politics.

passages.title: What excavations reveal about mission life
passages.text: During the 1650s, chiefs and nobles led a revolt against Spanish military authority, seeking to recover power over their communities. Some participants came from San Juan del Puerto. The rebellion failed, showing that acceptance of missionaries did not necessarily mean acceptance of colonial governors or their labor demands.

passages.title: A written language and later lives
passages.text: Francisco Pareja’s 1613 confession manual records “Tola, ucuchua nacaqui binaqechu, naquosobicho?” The Library of Congress translates: “The ceremony of the laurel that is made to the devil, have you performed it?” The hostile description reflects the missionary’s judgment of a Timucua ceremony. The original words survive through a colonial religious text.

passages.title: A written language and later lives
passages.text: In 1702, forces led by Carolina governor James Moore destroyed San Juan del Puerto on Fort George Island. Attacks forced people to seek refuge near St. Augustine. Destroying a mission displaced its residents; it did not make everyone disappear.

passages.title: A written language and later lives
passages.text: Eighteenth-century records preserve families that crossed colonial categories. María Magdalena Chrisístomo-Balthazar had a Mocama Timucua mother and an enslaved African father; she and her sister were born free in their mother’s village. Her later marriages connected Native, African and European backgrounds in the changing society around St. Augustine.

passages.title: A written language and later lives
passages.text: When Spain transferred Florida to Britain in 1763, the remaining Native residents of Nombre de Dios and Tolomato left for Cuba with the Spanish. These communities included refugees from different peoples. Following their departure avoids turning the collapse of Florida’s mission settlements into a claim that every family line simply vanished.

Timucua chiefdoms lost autonomy through colonization, disease, warfare and mission reorganization. The imported 1650 cutoff predates later resistance and refugee communities. The 1763 move to Cuba marks the end of this Florida mission chapter, not proof that every descendant disappeared.

sectionTitles: Read the map without letting it fool you
Work, markets and what was for dinner
Learning, books and a line of real Persian
Remarkable things people made and passed on
Clothes, games and ways to have fun
Medicine, water, baths and the toilet question

passages.text: In 1492 the Timurid world was no single, tidy empire. Sultan Husayn Bayqara ruled a brilliant court at Herat, while princes of Timur’s family competed across Fergana and Transoxiana. Babur inherited Fergana as a boy, repeatedly won and lost Samarkand, then made Kabul his base in 1504. Muhammad Shaybani’s Uzbek coalition captured Herat in 1507; Shah Ismail’s Safavids defeated Shaybani in 1510, but Timurid restoration in Central Asia did not last. Babur carried a Timurid court tradition east and founded Mughal rule in northern India after Panipat in 1526. The map’s broad 1492 to 1530 shape therefore joins several rival courts and changing frontiers. Its real continuity lies in people, books, gardens, workshops, family networks and administrative habits that survived political defeat and traveled into Safavid, Uzbek and Mughal worlds.

passages.title: Read the map without letting it fool you
passages.text: The atlas index calls this feature “Timurid Emirates,” marks every date circa, and gives it a 1492 to 1530 interval. That is a map identity, not proof that one government controlled every colored place for thirty-eight years. The plural name is a useful warning: rival members of one dynasty held separate courts and frequently fought one another.

passages.title: Read the map without letting it fool you
passages.text: At the 1492 snapshot, the exact target polygon has one ring with 53 positions and stretches roughly from 53.88° to 72.03° east and 26.51° to 46.26° north. Herat, Mashhad, Balkh, Kabul and Bukhara test inside; Samarkand and Fergana test outside. These point tests explain the imported shape, not historical border precision.

passages.title: Read the map without letting it fool you
passages.text: The 1500 target also has one ring and 53 positions. Its coordinates differ from 1492 by at most about 0.00123 degrees, a tiny topology-scaling change. Politics were anything but static during those years, so nearly identical outlines show that the atlas is a broad locator, not an annual frontier animation.

passages.title: Read the map without letting it fool you
passages.text: The 1400 predecessor called “Timurid Empire” is far larger: its ring has 362 positions and reaches much farther west and east. The switch to this card at 1492 is an editorial period boundary. It should not be read as a sudden founding event, because Timurid courts and family struggles crossed that year.

passages.title: Read the map without letting it fool you
passages.text: By the atlas’s 1530 snapshot, pieces of the old locator sit under Safavid, Mughal, Khiva and “Bukara Khanate” features. The file even uses the historical-basemap spelling “Bukara.” That mosaic suits the history better than a single fall date: Herat fell in 1507, Kabul’s branch continued, and Babur’s descendants ruled in India.

passages.title: Courts, rivals and dramatic escapes
passages.text: Husayn Bayqara ruled Herat for most of 1470 to 1506 and patronized Persian and Chaghatay literature, painting and architecture. Yet his sons held territories, rebelled and competed for succession. After his death, two sons attempted joint rule. A dazzling court could therefore coexist with a family structure that made unified command very difficult.

passages.title: Courts, rivals and dramatic escapes
passages.text: Babur inherited Fergana in 1494 while only about eleven. Samarkand, Timur’s famous capital, seemed worth enormous risk: he captured it more than once and repeatedly lost it. Family members and former allies changed sides. His memoir turns these reversals into vivid personal history, but ordinary soldiers, farmers and townspeople paid for each siege and march.

passages.title: Courts, rivals and dramatic escapes
passages.text: Muhammad Shaybani assembled Uzbek followers and exploited Timurid divisions to capture Bukhara, Samarkand and, eventually, Herat. His movement had its own political traditions and was not merely a faceless “invader” in somebody else’s story. Its victories created the Shaybanid power that reshaped Central Asia after the Timurid princes were displaced.

passages.title: Courts, rivals and dramatic escapes
passages.text: Kabul, taken by Babur in 1504, became refuge, capital and launching ground. Revenue was limited for the large body of relatives, retainers and soldiers who expected support, which helped push campaigns toward richer lands. This was state building by movement: the court carried memories, skills and ambitions across mountains instead of simply vanishing after losing Samarkand.

passages.title: Courts, rivals and dramatic escapes
passages.text: Herat surrendered to Shaybani in 1507 after Husayn’s heirs failed to cooperate. The conquerors retained some former Timurid dignitaries, while other courtiers scattered. That detail matters: a captured city did not instantly lose every administrator, poet, craftsperson or household. Political replacement and human continuity happened at the same time.

passages.title: Government, war and consequences
passages.text: Timurid government mixed a Turko-Mongol ruling house and military elite with Persian administrative practice. Land revenues and endowed property supported courts, institutions and learning. Princes treated territories as inheritances, which encouraged rivalry. “Empire” could therefore mean overlapping household claims and negotiated loyalties rather than one neat ladder of officials.

passages.title: Government, war and consequences
passages.text: Shah Ismail’s Safavid army defeated Muhammad Shaybani near Merv in 1510 and moved into Herat. Babur briefly regained Samarkand with Safavid help, but the restoration did not stick. The old Timurid heartlands were becoming part of Uzbek and Safavid imperial contests, with religious and political change layered over local continuities.

passages.title: Government, war and consequences
passages.text: Babur’s 1526 victory at Panipat began a new problem: conquering was quicker than governing. His Central Asian followers found Hindustan unfamiliar, and some wanted to go home. Babur had to distribute rewards, secure roads and persuade an army and household to stay. The Mughal state grew from that fragile settlement, not from effortless triumph.

passages.title: Government, war and consequences
passages.text: Babur’s memoir could be charmingly observant, but his wars were brutal. At Bajaur he ordered mass killing and a tower of heads, and captives were enslaved. Children should meet both sides of the evidence: gardens and poems do not cancel violence, and a conqueror’s own storytelling never supplies the victims’ full account.

passages.title: Government, war and consequences
passages.text: When Babur died in 1530, Humayun inherited northern India, but succession among Timurid princes was not automatic in the later European first-son sense. Brothers and other male relatives could expect territories and make claims. The family system kept several capable princes in politics, and also kept producing dangerous arguments about who should command everyone else.

passages.title: Work, markets and what was for dinner
passages.text: Most people lived from land and animals rather than palace art. Irrigated fields produced wheat, barley, rice, pulses and vegetables; orchards offered grapes, melons, apricots and nuts. Maintaining canals demanded organized labor. A blocked channel could matter more to a farming family’s dinner than whichever prince had most recently entered a distant capital.

passages.title: Work, markets and what was for dinner
passages.text: Herat’s bazaars linked farmers, herders, craft workers and merchants. Caravans moved expensive goods across Iran, Central Asia, India and China, while ordinary exchange remained local. Shops and workshops turned raw materials into cloth, metalware and other necessities. Long-distance glamour depended on porters, animal handlers, repairers and food sellers doing less celebrated work.

passages.title: Work, markets and what was for dinner
passages.text: Babur praised Fergana’s grapes and melons and Kabul’s many fruits, sometimes comparing varieties with comic seriousness. Such lists are clues to orchards, trade and taste, but they reflect an elite traveler with access. A laborer’s bowl, a pastoral family’s dairy food and a court banquet belonged to very different food worlds.

passages.title: Work, markets and what was for dinner
passages.text: During one desperate winter retreat, Babur’s party slaughtered and roasted a horse because food had run out. That grim meal punctures the jeweled-court image: rulers and followers could be cold, lost and hungry in mountain passes. It also reminds us that horses were transport, military power, wealth, and, in an emergency, supper.

passages.title: Work, markets and what was for dinner
passages.text: Ali Shir Navai’s endowed Ikhlasiyya complex reportedly joined a mosque, school, Sufi lodge, hospital, bath, garden and kitchen. Its soup kitchen fed more than a thousand people on stated occasions. This was one wealthy foundation, not universal welfare, but it shows how food charity, worship, study, medicine and reputation could share a single institutional network.

passages.title: Families, friendships and awkward adolescence
passages.text: Babur listened to senior women in his family. He records seeking advice from women relatives and obeying his mother, Qutlugh Nigar Khanum. His sister Khanzada also became a political intermediary. Elite women’s influence often worked through households and kinship, but that was real political work, especially when a dynasty was scattered.

passages.title: Families, friendships and awkward adolescence
passages.text: At seventeen, Babur married Aisha Sultan Begum and became so shy that his mother had to make him visit his wife about once a month. His memoir also frankly remembers an adolescent crush on a boy and the poetry it inspired. Dynastic marriage was serious politics, yet the teenager inside the prince could still be spectacularly awkward.

passages.title: Families, friendships and awkward adolescence
passages.text: Royal and aristocratic women commissioned buildings and appeared at major public occasions. A report from 1506 places women gathering at Husayn Bayqara’s madrasa during mourning. These examples do not describe every woman’s freedom; they show that the familiar idea of all women being invisible from public cultural and religious life is too simple.

passages.title: Families, friendships and awkward adolescence
passages.text: Babur remembered outings at Istalif with companions who talked, recited poetry, heard music and sometimes drank wine. Gardens gave courts a stage for friendship, diplomacy and showing off. They also generated jobs for gardeners and water workers. The fun was unequal, but a picnic with songs is more recognizable than a list of battles.

passages.title: Families, friendships and awkward adolescence
passages.text: A late Timurid model petition asks authorities to help a family whose girl was being forced into marriage after an abduction. Because it is a model letter, it cannot measure how common the event was or guarantee justice. It does reveal a problem officials expected petitioners to describe and a family trying to use written procedure.

passages.title: Learning, books and a line of real Persian
passages.text: Elite education prized poetry, history, calligraphy, theology and polished conversation. A noble might be judged by how well he recognized beautiful handwriting or composed a verse. This was not schooling for every child: learning also happened through families, religious teachers, apprenticeships and work, while access varied sharply by wealth, gender and place.

passages.title: Learning, books and a line of real Persian
passages.text: Navai’s Herat foundation included a madrasa with lecturers and students alongside Quran readers, a Sufi lodge and hospital. Endowments paid for a structured community of learning. Children should not picture a modern public school with grades and buses; this was advanced religious and literary study supported by a powerful patron.

passages.title: Learning, books and a line of real Persian
passages.text: Nasta‘liq, celebrated for flowing diagonals and balanced curves, became a prized script for Persian poetry. Sultan Ali Mashhadi worked at Husayn’s Herat court, while artists could also cut letters from paper and mount them as qita‘i compositions. Imagine doing perfect handwriting with scissors, then remember that one slip had no “undo” button.

passages.title: Learning, books and a line of real Persian
passages.text: One Timurid Persian petition begins “توفیق رفیق باد” (Tawfīq rafīq bād), “May success be your companion.” It is an authentic formal line, reproduced here in modern type, from a letter attributed to Jami. Persian was a major written language of court and administration; it was not necessarily the language spoken in every home.

passages.title: Learning, books and a line of real Persian
passages.text: Babur wrote his memoir chiefly in Chaghatay Turkish, often simply called Turki in his setting. Later, Akbar’s court commissioned a Persian translation and lavish illustrations. The text’s travels matter as much as its author: a Central Asian prince’s personal prose became a multilingual Mughal family history and a source read around the world.

passages.title: Remarkable things people made and passed on
passages.text: A poetry collection by Sultan Husayn was copied at Herat in 1500 on colored papers with gold decoration. Its poems are in Chaghatay Turkish, and the calligrapher was Sultan Ali Mashhadi. The manuscript makes a political point too: a ruler could present himself as a writer and patron, not only a commander.

passages.title: Remarkable things people made and passed on
passages.text: Husayn Vaiz Kashifi composed the Persian Anvar-i Suhayli, or “Lights of Canopus,” at Herat around 1499 to 1500 for a Timurid amir. Its nested animal fables reworked older Indian and Persian storytelling traditions to discuss cleverness, justice and rule. A court book could therefore be both entertaining and a disguised advice manual.

passages.title: Remarkable things people made and passed on
passages.text: A brass ewer made at Herat bears the astonishingly exact date 11 April 1498. Its maker signed it, and artisans inlaid its surface with silver and gold inscriptions and patterns. That precision lets one workshop object sit inside this card’s interval almost like a timestamp, and gives a craftsperson a trace beside famous princes.

passages.title: Remarkable things people made and passed on
passages.text: Court workshops coordinated calligraphers, painters, illuminators, paper cutters and binders. Bihzad became the era’s most famous painter, but a finished manuscript depended on many specialized hands. When a museum label praises one master, children can play detective: who prepared pigments, polished paper, ruled lines, mixed glue and repaired mistakes?

passages.title: Remarkable things people made and passed on
passages.text: Babur carried Timurid garden ideas into South Asia: ordered enclosures, straight channels, reservoirs, fruit trees and carefully chosen views. Local builders, plants and climates changed the results. Gardens were not simply copied templates; they became places where Central Asian memory met Indian materials, labor and weather, influencing Mughal landscapes for generations.

passages.title: Clothes, games and ways to have fun
passages.text: People wore layered shirts, trousers, robes, belts, boots and many forms of headgear, made from wool, cotton, silk and other textiles according to means and setting. Paintings are useful clues but not photographs, and few garments survive. A bright court robe cannot stand in for a shepherd’s work clothes or a child’s mended tunic.

passages.title: Clothes, games and ways to have fun
passages.text: Horse racing could be recreation, training and a display of nerve. Babur describes racing with companions and records a nasty fall in which he struck his head and briefly could not understand speech. Even princes ignored the modern instruction “wear a helmet”, and the memoir preserves the painful reason that would have been excellent advice.

passages.title: Clothes, games and ways to have fun
passages.text: Hunting trips pursued deer, birds and other game and trained riders to move together outdoors. Babur records them in great detail, sometimes mixing sport, travel and military reconnaissance. These were elite pursuits involving many helpers and animals, not carefree nature walks; the same landscape meant work or danger to nearby communities.

passages.title: Clothes, games and ways to have fun
passages.text: In Kabul, Babur laid out more than a dozen gardens and adjusted channels so water would run through terraces and pools. The spaces hosted receptions, robe presentations, celebrations and recovery from illness. A garden was part park, part political theater and part engineering project, beautiful only because someone kept clearing the channels.

passages.title: Clothes, games and ways to have fun
passages.text: Music, improvised verse and teasing conversation animated elite gatherings at Istalif. Babur’s record also includes wine, even though religious rules and personal practice could conflict. Treat the scene as one circle of companions, not everybody’s weekend. Still, humans five centuries ago also wanted shade, snacks, jokes and a song that everyone knew.

passages.title: Medicine, water, baths and the toilet question
passages.text: A medical manuscript copied in Herat in 1491, just before this card opens, contains two Arabic works and about 200 images, with headings and important terms in red ink. It proves that medical knowledge circulated in carefully made books. It does not tell us how often a village family could see a trained physician.

passages.title: Medicine, water, baths and the toilet question
passages.text: A later historian named five hospitals in Timurid Herat, and evidence connects students and physicians with the hospital founded by Ali Shir Navai. Medical learning could combine texts, observation and supervised practice. Survival is patchy, however, so named urban institutions should not be mistaken for a complete health system reaching everyone.

passages.title: Medicine, water, baths and the toilet question
passages.text: Timurid bathhouses used changing and resting rooms, warm and hot spaces, water tanks, furnaces and drainage; some plans include foot-washing and a small toilet. They were places to wash and socialize, with workers hauling fuel and managing heat. Many reconstructions rely on incomplete remains, so details varied by building and town.

passages.title: Medicine, water, baths and the toilet question
passages.text: Yes, there is a sewage story. A model complaint says a house had been flooded by dirty outflow from a hammam and asks officials to stop the damage. The document cannot map a citywide sewer system, but it reveals drains, neighboring buildings and the ancient truth that nobody enjoys someone else’s bathwater entering the living room.

passages.title: Medicine, water, baths and the toilet question
passages.text: Water made Kabul’s gardens possible. Babur redirected streams, used springs and arranged terraces so channels could feed pools and planting. The display depended on practical engineering and constant maintenance. Clean drinking water, irrigation and decorative water were related but not identical needs; an elegant cascade did not guarantee safe water for every household.

There was no single Timurid-Emirates “fall” in 1530. Herat’s independent Timurid court had ended in 1507; Uzbek Shaybanids and Safavids then contested the old heartlands. Babur’s Kabul branch continued and, after 1526, became the Mughal dynasty in India. The atlas handoff at 1530 coincides conveniently with Babur’s death and Humayun’s succession, but it is a cartographic endpoint rather than an extinction date. Persianate administration, Chaghatay memory, books, gardens, craftspeople and family claims continued across Safavid, Uzbek and Mughal societies. A Herati physician even dedicated a Persian hygiene poem to Babur in 1530, an apt reminder that people and knowledge crossed the map’s colored boundaries.

passages.text: Timur established his power in Transoxiana in 1370 and made Samarkand his capital. His conquests created a vast but unstable empire; after his death in 1405, descendants governed changing territories and rival courts. The imported 1400 to 1492 polygon cannot show those shifts and greatly overstates continuous control across that whole period. It also stops before the loss of Herat in 1507. This card distinguishes Timur’s conquests from the later communities and courts that inherited his dynasty’s name.

passages.title: Power and its human costs
passages.text: Timur’s campaigns devastated many towns and displaced people through killing, enslavement and forced relocation. Skilled artisans were taken to Samarkand, enriching the capital while damaging workshops elsewhere. Later rulers rebuilt parts of the economy. The monuments and beautiful objects that survive belong alongside this harder history of families losing homes, livelihoods and freedom.

passages.title: Power and its human costs
passages.text: Gowhar-Shad, Shah Rukh’s wife and the mother of Ulugh Beg and Baisunghur, played an active role in politics and public building. She commissioned a major mosque at Mashhad, completed in 1418, and a mosque and college complex at Herat. Her influence ran through family relationships, court allies and foundations that supported institutions beyond her own household.

passages.title: Food, water and community life
passages.text: Farming paid much of the state’s bills. Under Shah Rukh, damaged irrigation in the Marv oasis was repaired to restore production. Fifteenth-century histories and a later agricultural manual describe cereals, legumes, vegetables, fruit, nuts and flowers in the wider Khorasan region. The food supply depended on farmers, water management and seasonal work as much as on royal decisions.

passages.title: Food, water and community life
passages.text: Around Herat, the Juy-e Soltani canal was dug on Abu Sa‘id’s orders in 1467 to 1469. It improved irrigation for agricultural districts on both sides of the river south of the city. Water also helped extend gardens and leisure grounds. A canal could help grow dinner and create a pleasant place to spend an afternoon, although access and benefits were unequal.

passages.title: Food, water and community life
passages.text: Shah Rukh’s government restored and enlarged Herat’s bazaar and promoted manufacturing and trade. Towns were places where settled farmers and craftspeople exchanged goods with pastoral communities. Long-distance caravans also carried valuable products such as silk and porcelain between Central Asian and Iranian centres and India and China. Market life connected very different ways of making a living.

passages.title: Food, water and community life
passages.text: The poet and statesman Ali Shir Navai supported a complex at Herat with a college, a Sufi meeting and residential institution, a hospital and a bathhouse. Its kitchen also fed people in need. Teaching, worship, healthcare, washing and food could therefore be supported within one network of charitable buildings. This was a particular endowed foundation, rather than a service available equally everywhere.

passages.title: Learning, stories and workshops
passages.text: A manuscript painted at Herat in 1431 or 1432 shows the storybook lovers Laila and Majnun meeting as children at a mosque school. Colourful tiles, patterned surfaces, writing and figures fill the page. Commissioned for Prince Baisunghur, it shows how an older Persian poem could become an elaborate illustrated book. Its classroom is a literary scene, not a survey of every child’s schooling.

passages.title: Learning, stories and workshops
passages.text: A workshop progress report from around 1430, attributed to Ja‘far al-Tabrizi at Baisunghur’s court, tracks the work of several kinds of makers. It mentions book illustrators, illuminators and binders alongside stonecutters, tent-makers and people supplying designs for saddles. A royal library could be a busy production centre. Beautiful books emerged from coordinated labour, with plenty of unfinished jobs to report.

passages.title: Learning, stories and workshops
passages.text: Ulugh Beg’s observatory at Samarkand used a huge measuring instrument with a radius of about forty metres, partly set below ground. Astronomers including al-Kashi, Qadi-zada and Ali Qushji worked on observations and calculations. Their programme checked and corrected the positions of more than a thousand stars. This was a team achievement built from careful measuring, calculation and comparison.

passages.title: Learning, stories and workshops
passages.text: Al-Kashi’s letters to his father describe Ulugh Beg joining scholarly discussions and taking an interest in appointments. One report has the ruler performing difficult astronomical calculations while riding a horse. We cannot watch the ride ourselves, but the letter preserves a memorable contemporary claim. Mathematics at this court involved conversation and teaching as well as impressive instruments.

passages.title: Written words and precious objects
passages.text: A copper coin of Shah Rukh, Ashmolean HCR16074, begins its inscription “السلطان الاعظم”, meaning “the supreme sultan”. The museum dates it broadly to 1405 to 1446 and identifies the mint as Ta’us. This is Arabic language in Arabic script, transcribed here in modern type. Such titles proclaimed authority; they do not establish which language everyone spoke at home.

passages.title: Written words and precious objects
passages.text: Ulugh Beg owned a white jade jug now in the Gulbenkian Museum. Its dragon-shaped handle was made separately and attached with gold rivets; specialists disagree about whether that handle was original or added later. Later Mughal owners added their own inscriptions. One treasured vessel can therefore carry several centuries of ownership, alterations and claims to an illustrious family past.

passages.title: Written words and precious objects
passages.text: A glazed bowl dated 1419 or 1420 carries a repeated Persian blessing that the museum translates as wishing for a good outcome or good fortune. A spread-winged bird fills its centre, while lotus leaves run around the outside. The maker used lustre decoration on stonepaste. Even a vessel’s decoration could combine a kindly wish with a display of skilled craftsmanship.

The empire broke into competing territories rather than falling everywhere at once. In 1507, Muhammad Shaybani’s forces took Herat, ending its Timurid court; some former officials continued serving under the new rulers. The dynasty’s descendants and cultural traditions survived. Babur, a descendant of Timur, founded Mughal rule in India in 1526. The map’s 1492 cutoff is therefore a coverage boundary, not the dynasty’s disappearance.
