sectionTitles: Read the atlas as an imported locator, not a border treaty
A Roman successor state shaped by mountains and the sea
Rulers, factions and the hard work of staying in power
Diplomacy, tribute, war and the 1461 conquest
Caravans, ships, coins, fields and skilled work
Families, women, children and unequal social worlds
Orthodox worship, learning and words from the period
Churches, books, clothing, ceremony and remembered sound
Food, houses, markets and the texture of an ordinary day
Plague, medicine, water, toilets and honest unknowns

passages.text: Imagine a green ribbon of coast squeezed between Black Sea waves and steep Pontic mountains. From 1204 to 1461, the Grand Komnenoi ruled there from Trebizond, a walled Roman and Orthodox capital where caravans from Iran met ships from Genoa, Venice and neighboring ports. Its rulers survived by paying tribute, guarding passes, minting silver, marrying Georgian and Turkmen dynasties, sponsoring brilliant churches and books, and sometimes fighting bitterly among themselves. Farmers in mountain valleys supplied a rich hinterland; sailors, merchants, monks, painters, soldiers and interpreters linked their small state to a huge world. Plague could break families, while worship and festivals filled churches with crowds and chant. The atlas paints Trebizond from 1279 to 1492, but Mehmed II conquered the empire in 1461. Ottoman Trabzon continued with changed rulers, resettled people and enduring Christian communities; the map's late endpoint is a handoff, not an extra thirty-one-year empire.

passages.title: Read the atlas as an imported locator, not a border treaty
passages.text: The exact id is trebizond, labeled simply “Trebizond” and indexed circa 1279 to 1492. It has no alias, historical link or authored summary. Coverage calls it a state, records three border intervals and marks every review missing or unreviewed. Those database fields identify the map object; they do not establish historical dates.

passages.title: Read the atlas as an imported locator, not a border treaty
passages.text: At 1200 the exact id is absent. The imported Byzantine feature owns most audited Pontic interior tests, Georgia owns Tbilisi and Kutaisi, and an Armenian feature owns Kars and Ani; several exact coastal city points fall through polygon gaps. The historical Trebizond state began in 1204, so this is a predecessor seam.

passages.title: Read the atlas as an imported locator, not a border treaty
passages.text: The 1279 target is one unlabeled MultiPolygon with three parts, three rings and 41 positions, spanning 31.0341° to 41.4850° east and 40.1507° to 42.0433° north. Its eastern strip contains tested Ordu and Giresun; two detached western slivers sit around the Sinope to Samsun and western Black Sea coasts. Exact Trabzon, Sinope, Samsun and Rize points miss it.

passages.title: Read the atlas as an imported locator, not a border treaty
passages.text: At 1300 and 1400 Trebizond becomes one 17-position Polygon, about 37.25° to 41.49° east. Georgia lies northeast; imported Rum and Ilkhanate or Timurid shapes lie south and east; Byzantine, then Ottoman shapes lie west. The 1400 layer oddly keeps a Sultanate of Rum id long after that sultanate's political collapse, another warning against literal reading.

passages.title: Read the atlas as an imported locator, not a border treaty
passages.text: At 1492 the exact target vanishes. Ottoman geometry takes tested Ordu, Giresun and the Anatolian interior; Georgia retains Batumi and Kutaisi; Aq Qoyunlu geometry takes Erzurum and eastern Caucasian tests. The same seam persists at 1500. Since Trebizond surrendered in late summer 1461, the map cutoff trails conquest by thirty-one years.

passages.title: A Roman successor state shaped by mountains and the sea
passages.text: Alexios and David were grandsons of the Byzantine emperor Andronikos I Komnenos. With the support of their Georgian relative Queen Tamar, they seized Trebizond and nearby territory in 1204 as crusaders captured Constantinople. Their new regime was both a local Pontic power and one claimant to the Roman imperial inheritance.

passages.title: A Roman successor state shaped by mountains and the sea
passages.text: Early expansion westward did not last. Nicaean forces removed David's western conquests, and the Seljuks captured Sinope in 1214, cutting the capital off from its most ambitious western reach. Trebizond thereafter depended on a narrow coastal core, mountain valleys and scattered influence rather than commanding the whole southern Black Sea shore continuously.

passages.title: A Roman successor state shaped by mountains and the sea
passages.text: The city's steep ravines, fortified ridges, harbor approaches and Pontic mountains helped a small court endure, but geography was no magic shield. Roads crossed difficult passes toward Bayburt and Erzincan, and ships joined coastal settlements. Political control varied greatly between the capital, valleys, castles and far western outposts.

passages.title: A Roman successor state shaped by mountains and the sea
passages.text: Georgia was neither a permanent parent state nor a simple enemy. Royal marriages joined the houses, while frontier influence changed. The Grand Komnenoi also married Byzantine, Turkmen and western families, using kinship as a diplomatic road where armies and mountain tracks could fail.

passages.title: A Roman successor state shaped by mountains and the sea
passages.text: People at court described themselves within the Roman and Orthodox world, while modern historians use “Empire of Trebizond” for clarity. John II's court adjusted its imperial style after the Palaiologoi regained Constantinople. Titles expressed rank and rivalry; they do not mean two giant empires occupied the same coastline like transparent map layers.

passages.title: Rulers, factions and the hard work of staying in power
passages.text: The atlas opens in 1279 during George I's final year. John II succeeded in 1280, married Eudokia Palaiologina and negotiated Trebizond's place beside the restored Constantinopolitan empire. His reign shows that imperial language, marriage and ceremony could be instruments of foreign policy just as surely as tribute, fortresses or cavalry.

passages.title: Rulers, factions and the hard work of staying in power
passages.text: A surviving silver asper was minted at Trebizond under Alexios II in 1297. It weighs 2.15 grams, measures 21 millimetres and names sacred and imperial figures in its inscriptions. The small object made government, devotion and dynastic memory portable whenever it moved from hand to hand.

passages.title: Rulers, factions and the hard work of staying in power
passages.text: After Alexios II, short reigns, killings, exiles and rival aristocratic groupings destabilized the state. Empresses such as Irene Palaiologina and Anna Anachoutlou were political actors, not decorative names in a family tree. The surviving narrative is court-centered, so its quarrels reveal elite power more clearly than ordinary opinion.

passages.title: Rulers, factions and the hard work of staying in power
passages.text: Alexios III took the throne in 1349 and ruled until 1390. He traveled on campaigns, faced internal challengers, arranged marriages and spent heavily on religious patronage. A 1374 charter portrays him beside Empress Theodora and promises silver and annual Trebizond aspers to Dionysiou, making power visible in ink, image, seal and cash.

passages.title: Rulers, factions and the hard work of staying in power
passages.text: Manuel III, Alexios IV, John IV and David carried the dynasty through Timur's age and rising Ottoman pressure. Their successions were entangled with sons, brothers, spouses and exiles. Genealogy helps untangle those relationships, but it should never turn every reported rumor of murder or adultery in hostile travelers into established fact.

passages.title: Diplomacy, tribute, war and the 1461 conquest
passages.text: After Sinope's loss, Trebizond accepted Seljuk superiority at times; after the Mongol victory over the Seljuks at Köse Dağ in 1243, Mongol power reordered Anatolia. Tribute was a survival tool, not proof that local government vanished. The court could acknowledge a stronger overlord while still minting, judging, marrying and fighting locally.

passages.title: Diplomacy, tribute, war and the 1461 conquest
passages.text: Mongol rule also opened and protected long-distance routes that made Trebizond valuable as a gate toward Iran and inner Asia. That prosperity carried risk: a port tied to caravan traffic depended on peace beyond its borders, and later Ilkhanid decline weakened the conditions that had enriched Alexios II's generation.

passages.title: Diplomacy, tribute, war and the 1461 conquest
passages.text: Fourteenth-century warfare with Aq Qoyunlu leaders gave way to marriage diplomacy in 1352, when Alexios III's sister Maria married Qutlu. Later unions renewed the relationship. In the 1450s Uzun Hasan married Theodora of Trebizond and joined an anti-Ottoman alliance, but kinship did not guarantee rescue against Mehmed II.

passages.title: Diplomacy, tribute, war and the 1461 conquest
passages.text: Genoese and Venetians sought privileges, quarters and favorable taxes while competing across the Black Sea. Trebizond's emperors bargained with both and sometimes fought them. The Italians were powerful commercial communities, yet “they controlled everything” is too simple: local rulers, landholders, sailors, artisans and caravan traders also shaped the economy.

passages.title: Diplomacy, tribute, war and the 1461 conquest
passages.text: Mehmed II isolated Trebizond before attacking in 1461. His campaign combined an army crossing Anatolia with a fleet blockading the capital; artillery sharpened the imbalance. David surrendered rather than gamble the city on absent allies. This was the empire's political ending, whatever the imported map continued to display until 1492.

passages.title: Caravans, ships, coins, fields and skilled work
passages.text: Trebizond connected Black Sea shipping to the overland road toward Tabriz and beyond. Silk, spices and other high-value goods mattered, but the port was never merely a pipe carrying exotic cargo westward. Customs, provisioning, warehousing, interpretation, animal handling and credit created work wherever ships met caravans.

passages.title: Caravans, ships, coins, fields and skilled work
passages.text: Shipping joined the capital to smaller Pontic ports and foreign markets. Local vessels and crews operated beside Genoese and Venetian shipping, while timber-rich coasts supported boatbuilding and repair. Storms, reefs, piracy and political embargoes made sailing a skilled and risky occupation rather than an effortless blue highway on a map.

passages.title: Caravans, ships, coins, fields and skilled work
passages.text: Clavijo's embassy reached Trebizond in 1404 before taking pack animals across steep mountain roads toward Erzincan. His journey makes the transport chain concrete: sea passage, interpreters, court permissions, guides, animals and safe-conducts all had to connect. A luxurious cargo could still spend its day bumping over rocks behind a mule.

passages.title: Caravans, ships, coins, fields and skilled work
passages.text: The silver asper was both payment and political messaging. Alexios II's 1297 issue bears sacred and imperial names and images, showing the city maintained its own minting tradition. One museum coin cannot reveal a worker's daily wage or every market price, so the card uses it as an object, not a complete medieval budget spreadsheet.

passages.title: Caravans, ships, coins, fields and skilled work
passages.text: Vazelon monastery records reveal fields, orchards, threshing floors, watermills and tools for plowing, reaping and digging. They mention walnuts, hazelnuts, pears, apples, plums, medlars, hemp and honey. These documents illuminate Matzouka's rural labor and produce, though monastic property paperwork cannot count every crop or independent farmer.

passages.title: Families, women, children and unequal social worlds
passages.text: At the top, dynastic families treated marriage as alliance-making. Princesses connected Trebizond to Georgia, Constantinople and Turkmen courts; empresses could sponsor institutions, mediate succession or become factional centers. These political marriages mattered enormously, but they are not a template for how a village couple chose partners or divided chores.

passages.title: Families, women, children and unequal social worlds
passages.text: Vazelon acts show women buying, selling, mortgaging or inheriting land and appearing in disputes. Dowry and family transmission gave some women recognized property interests, though power varied by wealth, marital status and kin. A named land transaction proves legal action in that case, not equal rights for every woman in the empire.

passages.title: Families, women, children and unequal social worlds
passages.text: One 1302 document records a father selling a field for one hundred aspers to ransom his captured child. It offers a sharp glimpse of parental obligation, warfare and money in one family. The same source warns against inventing an average household: words translated as homestead or holding can include tenants and several related people.

passages.title: Families, women, children and unequal social worlds
passages.text: The court chronicle names members of the imperial household, titled officials, soldiers and church leaders. Their ranks and family ties overlapped rather than forming a simple pyramid. That source is socially lopsided: people near the palace and institutions that preserved parchment are far more visible than dockworkers, servants or isolated farmers.

passages.title: Families, women, children and unequal social worlds
passages.text: Children learned first through households, work and worship, but the checked sources do not provide a Trebizond-wide school system, attendance rate or standard childhood timetable. Elite boys could pursue advanced religious and literary study; rural children likely learned practical tasks. The difference between those statements is the difference between evidence and guesswork.

passages.title: Orthodox worship, learning and words from the period
passages.text: Orthodox Christianity organized calendars, patronage and public space. Hagia Sophia, built under Manuel I, used architecture, sculpture and painting to present an imperial identity. Its decoration drew on Byzantine traditions while also engaging forms familiar in Seljuk Anatolia and the Caucasus, a local visual argument made from several artistic languages.

passages.title: Orthodox worship, learning and words from the period
passages.text: Alexios III's 1374 chrysobull funded Dionysiou Monastery on Mount Athos and promised annual Trebizond aspers. In return, monks commemorated the imperial family and welcomed visitors from Trebizond. Piety, family memory, diplomacy and money met in one enormous document with colored writing, portraiture and a dangling gold seal.

passages.title: Orthodox worship, learning and words from the period
passages.text: Bessarion was born in Trebizond around 1400, then pursued religious, literary, scientific and philosophical study elsewhere. His later donation ultimately brought hundreds of Greek and Latin manuscripts to Venice. His career proves exceptional pathways for advanced learning and manuscript rescue; it does not prove that every Trapezuntine child read Plato.

passages.title: Orthodox worship, learning and words from the period
passages.text: Gregory Chioniades returned from Persia with astronomical and medical material that entered Greek scholarly circulation at Trebizond. A source calls him an iatrosophist, a learned medical teacher or scholar, but historians explicitly lack proof that he practiced as a physician. Books traveled; a documented city hospital does not follow automatically.

passages.title: Orthodox worship, learning and words from the period
passages.text: Written-language sample, court chronicle, learned administrative setting, September 1347. Original: `ἐγένετο αἰφνίδιος θάνατος, ἡ πανούκλα`. Editorial transliteration: `egeneto aiphnidios thanatos, hē panoukla`. Translation: “there came sudden death, the plague.” Michael Panaretos wrote medieval Greek; this is historical prose from a court official, not a transcript of ordinary street speech.

passages.title: Churches, books, clothing, ceremony and remembered sound
passages.text: Hagia Sophia's dome, porches, carved surfaces and painted biblical cycles were built for movement, worship and imperial memory, not as a silent art gallery. Eastmond reads contrasts between exterior sculpture and interior painting as choices about identity. Viewers brought different languages and experiences, so a motif need not carry only one meaning.

passages.title: Churches, books, clothing, ceremony and remembered sound
passages.text: The Grand Komnenian palace stood within Trebizond's inner citadel, but its surviving fabric is fragmentary and the complex has never yielded a complete, secure floor plan. It was an elite fortified setting, not a model ordinary house. Responsible reconstruction marks missing rooms instead of furnishing them from imagination.

passages.title: Churches, books, clothing, ceremony and remembered sound
passages.text: A fourteenth-century Greek Alexander Romance probably made for the Trebizond court contains about 250 miniatures attributed to three painters. The pictures weave eastern elements into an ancient adventure story. It demonstrates specialized scribes, painters, pigments and wealthy patronage, while telling us nothing certain about how many market children knew the tale.

passages.title: Churches, books, clothing, ceremony and remembered sound
passages.text: Clavijo described Manuel III and his son in imperial robes, tall hats, gold cords, a crane-feather plume and marten fur. Church festivals added processions and chant to public life. These sources preserve court costume and sacred performance far better than children's games; no exact playground rules or tavern lyrics survive here.

passages.title: Churches, books, clothing, ceremony and remembered sound
passages.text: A Florentine painted panel made after 1461 turned Trebizond's conquest into visual memory far away. Museum analysis now cautions that the painted front and chest may not form one untouched original object. That detective work is useful: art can preserve reactions to an event while its own assembly history still needs testing.

passages.title: Food, houses, markets and the texture of an ordinary day
passages.text: Pontic meals could draw on orchard fruit, nuts, honey, grain, fish and game. Sources mention partridges at an elite diplomatic meal and abundant regional produce. That menu is evidence of available foods, not permission to serve every villager an emperor's feast every Tuesday.

passages.title: Food, houses, markets and the texture of an ordinary day
passages.text: Tafur called the land around Trebizond fruitful and the city strongly walled, but his population estimate and political gossip came from a brief outsider visit in 1437. Travelers noticed supplies, harbors, danger and rulers because those affected their journey. Their silences cannot measure every neighborhood, workshop or household meal.

passages.title: Food, houses, markets and the texture of an ordinary day
passages.text: Coastal settlements probably relied heavily on timber construction, while stone survives disproportionately in walls, churches, castles and elite buildings. Rural records name holdings and farm structures without providing a universal floor plan. Houses likely varied from capital to valley; archaeology's stone skeleton should not make ordinary medieval streets entirely stone.

passages.title: Food, houses, markets and the texture of an ordinary day
passages.text: Markets joined local produce to imported goods and travelers. Tafur arrived by ship, sought an audience, received provisions and moved onward through a network of Genoese routes. His tale also exposes violence and enslavement elsewhere in the Black Sea system, a reminder that trade's bustling variety could rest beside coercion and captivity.

passages.title: Food, houses, markets and the texture of an ordinary day
passages.text: Manuscript making required prepared writing surfaces, inks, pigments, planning and several skilled hands. The Alexander Romance's three painters make that teamwork visible. This was luxury craft near the court, not the whole urban economy. Most craftspeople left objects or repaired buildings more often than they left signed biographies.

passages.title: Plague, medicine, water, toilets and honest unknowns
passages.text: Panaretos says the 1347 plague caused sudden death and that people lost children, spouses, siblings, mothers and other relatives; he says it lasted seven months. The entry records grief more clearly than symptoms or treatment. It therefore supports a family-centered account of disaster, not a modern diagnosis for each person who died.

passages.title: Plague, medicine, water, toilets and honest unknowns
passages.text: One modern study proposes that northern grain shipments may have helped plague reach Trebizond and Constantinople at nearly the same time after Black Sea embargoes lifted. The author presents a route and timing model, not an eyewitness certainty. Ships could carry food, news and invisible biological danger together.

passages.title: Plague, medicine, water, toilets and honest unknowns
passages.text: Scientific and medical recipes crossed languages through scholars such as Chioniades, but the surviving Trebizond evidence does not document a routine clinic, staffing roster, common cure or childbirth practice for this period. General Byzantine hospitals elsewhere cannot simply be moved to Trabzon by analogy. Here, uncertainty is more accurate than a confident imaginary doctor.

passages.title: Plague, medicine, water, toilets and honest unknowns
passages.text: A modern Trabzon survey catalogs surviving aqueducts, fountains, baths and bridges, but says most examples are Ottoman and some older works were repaired later. Those structures prove long investment in moving and storing water; they do not establish a standard Trapezuntine household supply, fetching routine or drinking-water treatment.

passages.title: Plague, medicine, water, toilets and honest unknowns
passages.text: The checked monument survey does not securely identify a Trapezuntine household toilet, latrine network, sewer or waste rule. One later bath was probably a medieval church before Ottoman conversion, so it cannot fill the gap. People obviously relieved themselves; medieval evidence simply declines to give us the hoped-for bathroom tour.

Trebizond surrendered to Mehmed II in late summer 1461 after a combined land-and-sea campaign. David and his court lost sovereignty, and Ottoman policies removed and resettled inhabitants. Christian communities, churches, Pontic Greek culture and regional trade continued under changed rule. The 1492 atlas endpoint is a delayed geometry handoff, thirty-one years after conquest.

sectionTitles: Discoveries: tools and a kitchen under the sea
Learning by doing, and political change

passages.text: Trinidad and Tobago have distinct island histories, brought together in one country. Their everyday creativity includes stone tools, skilfully tuned steel, cooking traditions and community teaching. Each example below identifies its place and period.

passages.title: Discoveries: tools and a kitchen under the sea
passages.text: At Banwari Trace in southern Trinidad, a settlement dating to around 5000 BCE, archaeologists found stone pestles, grinders, an axe and cutting flakes. Layers of discarded shells also survive. The tools and refuse reveal practical work and food gathering. A midden, archaeologists’ name for accumulated rubbish, can preserve an excellent record of everyday life, though it is nobody’s idea of a tidy kitchen.

passages.title: Discoveries: tools and a kitchen under the sea
passages.text: At wreck site TRB-5 in Tobago’s Rockley Bay, a 2014 excavation recovered bricks still joined with mortar, copper sheet and wood fragments. Researchers interpreted these as possible remains of a ship’s galley, or kitchen. The finds date broadly to the seventeenth century; association with the 1677 battle is supported, but the vessel’s exact identity remained uncertain in the report.

passages.title: Discoveries: tools and a kitchen under the sea
passages.text: The same test trench yielded four forks and five spoons. These small objects bring eating aboard ship into view alongside the cannon. They show that studying a wreck can recover traces of meals as well as battles. The report does not identify the diners, their food on a particular day, or whether everyone aboard had similar utensils.

passages.title: Food, households and family records
passages.text: NALIS’s account of Indian heritage in Trinidad names a belna, a rolling pin; a chauki, a board for working dough; and a sil and lorha, stones used for grinding. Such equipment accompanied cooking knowledge reshaped in Caribbean homes. Familiar foods involve practiced movements and specialised tools. The kitchen has its own vocabulary, and learning a word can also mean learning a skill.

passages.title: Food, households and family records
passages.text: Chinese shopkeepers became part of village life in Trinidad. NALIS describes a credit arrangement called trusting: customers could take groceries and pay later, while the shopkeeper recorded purchases and repayments in a copy book. A small notebook connected household needs with a local business. This is a documented practice, rather than a claim that every shop offered identical terms.

passages.title: Food, households and family records
passages.text: Trinidad’s immigration registers can record a person’s village in India, relatives, ship and assigned estate. These documents help descendants piece together family histories across oceans. Archivist Helena Leonce also describes missing records and arrivals through other Caribbean colonies. A gap in one register is a research problem, not evidence that a family has no history.

passages.title: Food, households and family records
passages.text: At Christmas, parang musicians visit homes with instruments such as the cuatro, guitar and maracas, while hosts offer food and drink. NALIS recalls nighttime visits that sometimes woke relatives and friends. It gives the idea of an alarm clock a much more musical interpretation. The account describes a particular festive tradition, not a rule followed by every household.

passages.title: Making music and sharing traditions
passages.text: Steelpan developed through experimentation in Trinidad during the 1930s and 1940s. Makers shaped metal containers and tuned parts of the playing surface to different pitches. Earlier tamboo-bamboo groups made percussion music with cut bamboo tubes. The new instrument grew through many people’s work; accounts disagree about assigning its invention to a single person.

passages.title: Making music and sharing traditions
passages.text: A steelband’s engine room is its percussion section, which helps keep the music moving together. NALIS lists bottle and spoon, maracas and assorted iron among its instruments. Here the engine runs on rhythm. The phrase is a useful reminder that a musical ensemble depends on timing and coordination as well as the performers carrying the tune.

passages.title: Making music and sharing traditions
passages.text: In January 2023, Trinidad’s Santa Rosa First Peoples Community helped present the Caribbean Ties exhibition. Community members added baskets, hammocks, ceremonial clothing, photographs and foods including cassava. An ajoupa, a tapia hut, housed the exhibition. People shared their own knowledge and heritage in a community setting, showing that Indigenous history includes living voices as well as excavated objects.

passages.title: Making music and sharing traditions
passages.text: Tobago’s Moriah Ole Time Wedding, documented in July 2017, recreated an older wedding celebration at the village’s Moravian church. A procession then carried the celebration through Moriah with participants and onlookers. It was a heritage performance, using humour and participation to share memories of social life. The staged ceremony should not be mistaken for a record of one historical couple’s marriage.

passages.title: Learning by doing, and political change
passages.text: In a 2015 project concluding at Speyside Secondary School in Tobago, students built solar ovens from boxes, reflective material, insulation and clear plastic wrap. They tested the ovens with bread dough. The winning design baked its loaf all the way through. The exercise turned energy science into something visible and practical, with a result rather easier to inspect than an invisible sunbeam.

passages.title: Learning by doing, and political change
passages.text: Independence and becoming a republic happened in different years. In 1962, Trinidad and Tobago became independent while retaining the monarch as head of state. In 1976, a president replaced that role. The distinction helps explain how a country can govern itself while still sharing a monarch with other countries.

British colonial rule ended at independence in 1962; republican status followed in 1976. Trinidad and Tobago continues as a country. Its communities keep creating and sharing traditions, including First Peoples’ knowledge, music and food.

sectionTitles: A port connected to several worlds

passages.text: Tripolitania was the western Libyan region centered on Tripoli. During much of this map interval, the Karamanli family ruled with considerable autonomy while acknowledging Ottoman authority. Direct Ottoman administration returned in 1835. The coastal outline is not the full territory claimed by Tripoli’s governors, and neighboring Cyrenaica has a separate history.

passages.title: A port connected to several worlds
passages.text: By the late seventeenth century, Tripoli already brought together Arabic-speaking townspeople, Ottoman soldiers and their families, Jewish merchants and craftspeople, and European consular communities. Enslaved people brought from south of the Sahara and captured at sea were also part of this unequal urban society.

passages.title: A port connected to several worlds
passages.text: Yusuf Karamanli’s demands for increased payments helped trigger war with the United States in 1801. The 1805 treaty included a ransom for prisoners but ended American tribute to Tripoli. Maritime diplomacy concerned real sailors’ freedom as well as state revenues.

passages.title: A port connected to several worlds
passages.text: After 1835, Ottoman governors operated through provincial and district officials, with local leaders advising at lower levels. Control remained uneven, especially away from towns. A neatly organized administrative chart was easier to produce than obedience across a large region.

passages.title: Schools, fountains and an inscription
passages.text: The eighteenth-century Ahmad Pasha Karamanli mosque formed a complex with a school and cemetery. Its entrances opened toward nearby markets. Religious learning, commerce and family remembrance occupied neighboring spaces in the working city.

passages.title: Schools, fountains and an inscription
passages.text: An inscription at the Ahmad Pasha mosque praises its patron for providing flowing water at a public fountain. Flowering tile panels surround the lettering. The monument advertised useful urban provision as well as a ruler’s piety and prestige.

passages.title: Schools, fountains and an inscription
passages.text: “بسم الله الرحمن الرحيم” means “In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Compassionate.” This Arabic opening appears on the Ahmad Pasha mosque’s eighteenth-century foundation inscription. The sample is a normalized transcription, without the original calligraphic layout and vowel marks.

passages.title: Schools, fountains and an inscription
passages.text: In the early nineteenth century, naval captain Mustafa Gurgi commissioned another richly decorated mosque complex. Researchers used its 1844 waqf deed, an endowment document, to study the building’s setting. Architecture leaves both stonework and a paper trail.

passages.title: Households, hospitality and health
passages.text: In a letter dated 9 September 1783, Miss Tully describes roof rainwater draining into cisterns beneath courtyards. Flat roofs also served for drying fruit. The house could help collect tomorrow’s water and prepare the pantry.

passages.title: Households, hospitality and health
passages.text: Tully describes affluent women turning courtyards into reception rooms for celebrations: mats and carpets covered the floor, cushions supplied seats, and an awning provided shade. Outdoor space became a room for a special occasion.

passages.title: Households, hospitality and health
passages.text: At bathhouses, Tully observed wealthy women attended by enslaved women who washed their hair with orange-flower water and arranged elaborate braids. The luxurious routine depended on other women’s coerced labor.

passages.title: Households, hospitality and health
passages.text: A travelers’ inn funded by the ruler’s wife offered rooms, storage, a courtyard well and space for pack animals. Tully reports simple sleeping mats and gates locked overnight. Hospitality required practical arrangements for people and cargo.

passages.title: Households, hospitality and health
passages.text: During plague in May 1785, Tully’s consular circle prepared household quarantine. New servants had to bathe and remain isolated for two weeks. This records one privileged community’s precautions amid a frightening epidemic.

Karamanli rule ended in 1835, before the imported 1878 endpoint. Ottoman government continued until Italy’s invasion in 1911 and the 1912 settlement. Colonial conquest met prolonged local resistance; Tripolitania’s communities and regional identity continued.

passages.text: Tsimshian communities belong to the Skeena River and northern British Columbia coast, with a later community at Metlakatla, Alaska. Related Gitxsan and Nisg̱a’a peoples remain distinct neighbors. This map outlines part of a diverse homeland; its 1492 to 1500 interval is coverage, not a people’s lifetime.

passages.title: Village traces and regional power
passages.text: On Pike Island, three former village sites and two petroglyph sites lie along the protected waters of Metlakatla Pass. Trails connect settlement remains; carved images survive on shoreline boulders. The largest village area, used both before and after European contact, measures about 211 by 70 metres.

passages.title: Village traces and regional power
passages.text: Around the wider pass, archaeological remains include house depressions, canoe landing places and shell middens. Parks Canada identifies a particularly dense sequence of winter villages from about 500 to 1770. These traces connect homes, boats and meals across a worked coastal landscape.

passages.title: Village traces and regional power
passages.text: Kitselas Canyon guarded a route between the coast and the interior. Its surviving evidence includes five village sites, carved poles, caches and house depressions. In the nineteenth century, the fortified village of Gitlaxdzok and another permanent village occupied positions from which residents could influence trade through the Skeena corridor.

passages.title: Village traces and regional power
passages.text: The Nine Tribes of Lax Kw’alaams built power through alliances, strategic marriages and military action. Their trade connections followed routes carrying valuable eulachon oil into the interior. Community history emphasizes these relationships and decisions, rather than explaining political power simply as a result of plentiful fish.

passages.title: Village traces and regional power
passages.text: In 1834, the Hudson’s Bay Company built Fort Simpson at Lax Kw’alaams on a site controlled by the Gispaxlo’ots leader Legex. He required payments for trading there. Tsimshian people also supplied wood and labor; their seasonal activities shaped how the fort could operate.

passages.title: Kinship, harvesting and feasts
passages.text: Tsimshian clan membership comes through the mother. The four clans are associated with Killer Whale, Wolf, Eagle and Raven. Crests can identify a clan or an extended family and carry histories and inherited rights; they are much more than decorative animal pictures.

passages.title: Kinship, harvesting and feasts
passages.text: At Metlakatla potlatches, guests witness proceedings such as naming and succession. Hosts feed them and provide gifts in thanks. Dance, masks and family histories help make those rights publicly known, so a feast also performs serious political and legal work.

passages.title: Kinship, harvesting and feasts
passages.text: Gitga’at families travel to Kiel camp on Princess Royal Island for spring harvesting. Their Nation’s 2024 account describes collecting red laver seaweed in May and preserving food for later months. Harvesting joins practical work with time together and opportunities for younger relatives to learn.

passages.title: Kinship, harvesting and feasts
passages.text: The same account describes slicing halibut thin for drying after returning to Hartley Bay, then smoking heads and backbones for soup. It also recalls exchanging harvested seaweed at Kitamaat for eulachon grease. A fishing trip could supply several kinds of meal and goods for trade.

passages.title: Kinship, harvesting and feasts
passages.text: A 2023 Gitga’at food guide describes dayks, a dessert of berries with whipped grease, snow or water and sugar. The recipe illustrates the community’s living food traditions, including later ingredients. Snow can enter the dessert bowl, but this modern description is not evidence for sugar in a precontact kitchen.

passages.title: Migration, public health and teaching
passages.text: William Duncan’s mission at Metlakatla, British Columbia, began in 1862. In 1887, he and part of the Tsimshian community moved to Alaska; others remained in British Columbia. Metlakatla Pass and Pike Island retain their connection to the Canadian Metlakatla First Nation, so the move did not empty an entire homeland.

passages.title: Migration, public health and teaching
passages.text: The Alaska community’s 1944 constitution records the establishment of its Annette Islands reserve in 1891. It provided for a twelve-member council, elected officials and community management of land. These institutions belong to a particular Tsimshian community, not to a government ruling all Tsimshian peoples.

passages.title: Migration, public health and teaching
passages.text: Public health had its own place in that constitution. A three-member committee was to help preserve birth and death records, cooperate with health officials, maintain sanitary conditions and enforce quarantine rules. Community government included the everyday work of keeping households and public spaces healthy.

passages.title: Migration, public health and teaching
passages.text: A modern Sm’algya̱x language exhibit prints “‘Niit, nda wila waan”, translated “Hello, how are you doing?” The museum credits the Ts’msyen language authority, Sarah Booth and the Haayk Foundation for its language material. This is an attested contemporary spelling, not a claimed fifteenth-century inscription.

passages.title: Migration, public health and teaching
passages.text: At Gitxaała’s Lach Klan School, education from early childhood through Grade 12 includes language, culture and learning on the land alongside provincial requirements. Its published programs also include breakfast, snacks and fruit and vegetables. Teaching and feeding children are part of the same daily community work.

passages.title: Migration, public health and teaching
passages.text: Canadian Metlakatla’s heritage staff combine elder interviews, community mapping and archival research, storing knowledge in digital maps for land and marine decisions. They also monitor archaeological resources such as canoe runs, fish traps and culturally modified trees. New tools help communities care for inherited places.

The map’s 1500 cutoff is not an ending. Colonial missions, settlement and restrictions changed Tsimshian lives, while distinct First Nations in British Columbia and the Metlakatla Indian Community in Alaska continued. Their governments, cultural teaching and stewardship remain active; no single successor state replaces them.

passages.text: The Moscow-centred Russian state became a tsardom when Ivan IV was crowned in 1547. It endured a severe succession crisis, then continued under the Romanovs. Expansion, printing and skilled crafts accompanied deep social inequality. Peter I adopted the imperial title in 1721, marking its transition into the Russian Empire.

passages.title: Power, expansion and unequal lives
passages.text: Ivan IV’s coronation took place in the Kremlin’s Dormition Cathedral on 16 January 1547. Religious ritual and royal regalia presented his authority as sacred. The ceremony matters because the map’s imported label begins earlier, when Moscow’s ruler still held the grand-princely title.

passages.title: Power, expansion and unequal lives
passages.text: Saint Basil’s Cathedral was built in Moscow from 1555 to 1561 to commemorate victory over the Kazan Khanate. Its clustered churches turned a military conquest into a major architectural commission. The complex changed afterwards; the church dedicated to Basil the Blessed was added in 1588.

passages.title: Power, expansion and unequal lives
passages.text: The early seventeenth-century Time of Troubles brought famine, political breakdown, rival claimants and foreign intervention. In 1613 an assembly chose the young Mikhail Romanov as tsar. Establishing a dynasty did not instantly repair ruined farms and towns, but it restored a continuing line of rulers.

passages.title: Power, expansion and unequal lives
passages.text: The law code adopted in 1649 tied privately owned peasants and their descendants to their landlords’ estates. It also removed time limits on pursuing fugitives. For these families, moving away to seek a better life could bring forced return; the state’s growing strength did not mean growing freedom for everyone.

passages.title: Power, expansion and unequal lives
passages.text: During the seventeenth century, Russian expeditions crossed Siberia and reached the Pacific. Fur tribute, called yasak, helped drive this expansion. Historian Denis Shaw emphasizes coercion and violent conflict as well as journeys and geographical knowledge: these were inhabited lands whose peoples faced new demands from an expanding state.

passages.title: Books, food and practical inventions
passages.text: Ivan Fedorov and Petr Mstislavets completed the Apostle in 1564, Moscow’s first precisely dated printed book. It contained biblical Acts and Epistles and took about eleven months to produce. The edition carried features useful for church reading as well as reading at home or in a monastic cell.

passages.title: Books, food and practical inventions
passages.text: Printing red and black on the same page required careful work. For the Apostle, the letters intended to print in red were raised above the rest, printed, then removed before the black text was added. A misaligned sheet could spoil the effect; attractive pages depended on workshop skill.

passages.title: Books, food and practical inventions
passages.text: Moscow’s Kislovskaya quarter housed suppliers of sour cabbage, soaked apples, pickled cucumbers and kvass for the court. Preserving food made winter supplies possible. Archaeologists found cellar pits in the neighbourhood, connecting the written history of its food workers with the spaces in which they worked.

passages.title: Books, food and practical inventions
passages.text: Seventeenth-century layers in that quarter yielded green-glazed stove tiles, a miniature ceramic jug and an enamelled copper-alloy cross. These finds bring colour into an otherwise earth-brown excavation. They also help distinguish the tsardom’s neighbourhood from the larger eighteenth- and nineteenth-century estates built over it.

passages.title: Books, food and practical inventions
passages.text: Kolomenskoye’s water tower, built in the 1670s, raised water from a source beneath it to a large barrel above. Water then travelled through wooden pipes to palace buildings. Researchers describe pumps or a bucket mechanism: even a royal water supply needed somebody’s machinery to do the lifting.

passages.title: Books, food and practical inventions
passages.text: In 1654 the Apothecary Chancery organized a school to train medical practitioners. Thirty musketeers and musketeers’ sons were assigned to foreign medical teachers, with interpreters helping lessons along. Graduates served with army regiments or the chancery. This was a small specialist programme, far from healthcare for every household.

passages.title: Books, food and practical inventions
passages.text: Karion Istomin’s 1696 primer taught letters, syllables, numbers and religious texts. Only twenty copies were printed for an edition intended for Tsarevich Alexei. A surviving proof copy bears editorial corrections, while red letters in a poem spell out the author’s name. Even a royal schoolbook needed proofreading.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: The primer addresses “к юношам учитися хотящим”, literally “to young people wishing to learn”. This is its historical Church Slavonic wording in the library’s normalized Cyrillic transcription, rather than a reproduction of the printed letter shapes. The greeting makes a seventeenth-century textbook sound pleasantly welcoming.

Peter I accepted the title emperor in 1721 after the Treaty of Nystad ended the Northern War with Sweden. The tsardom became the Russian Empire through a change of political title and institutions, not the disappearance of its population. The imported 1530 to 1783 map range spans both earlier and later phases.

passages.text: The Tuʻi Tonga were paramount chiefs associated with Tongatapu and wider Pacific relationships. This import’s 500 to 700 dates are far too early for their medieval state: earlier settlements do not establish a Tuʻi Tonga empire then. Its broad outline across island groups also cannot distinguish direct rule from exchange or influence. This card therefore describes the later polity and clearly dated continuities, rather than certifying the imported borders or timeline.

passages.title: A built island landscape
passages.text: Many earth mounds on Tongatapu supported homes. Coring near Lapaha and Talasiu found constructed floors and, in some mounds, shells, stone flakes and oven stones. Repeated floors suggest people renewed dwelling places over generations. Some mound construction predates the Tuʻi Tonga state by centuries, so an ancient house foundation cannot by itself identify the dynasty that governed its builders.

passages.title: A built island landscape
passages.text: At Lapaha, chiefly tombs known as langi were faced with stone slabs. Quarrying, transporting and arranging them demanded substantial community work. Oral genealogies remember a long sequence of Tuʻi Tonga, but the names of some tombs and their occupants differ between recorded accounts. Archaeology and inherited knowledge both matter, without making every remembered identification equally certain.

passages.title: A built island landscape
passages.text: Even small grave stones could travel far. A study of volcanic kilikili placed on royal graves traced a tradition of collecting them from islands in central Tonga, involving voyages of about 150 kilometers. Their placement marked the end of public mourning. The researchers found this practice extending across roughly seven centuries, linking ceremonies with repeated work at sea.

passages.title: A built island landscape
passages.text: The Lapaha Kolotau was an earthwork fort at the chiefly center. Researchers mapped it, excavated it and combined radiocarbon evidence with traditional history to place its construction in the fourteenth century. They interpret the defenses as evidence that political centralization was contested. Grand royal monuments and fortifications belonged to the same changing landscape of power.

passages.title: Meals, movement and family rank
passages.text: Chemical traces in human remains from the ʻAtele burial mounds, broadly dating to about 1450 to 1800, suggest diets rich in starchy plants and marine foods. Yam, taro and breadfruit fit the plant evidence, alongside fish and other sea resources known from historical accounts. The two burial groups differed in their food proportions; researchers could not reduce those differences to one simple ranking of rich and poor.

passages.title: Meals, movement and family rank
passages.text: Teeth also offered clues to childhood movement. At ʻAtele, one woman had an unusual strontium signature that could indicate an origin on a larger island such as Fiji’s Viti Levu. That is a possibility, not a named birthplace. Sea spray can make different small islands chemically similar, and only parts of the burial mounds were excavated.

passages.title: Meals, movement and family rank
passages.text: Among chiefly families, a person’s standing depended on more than holding a title. Ancestry through mothers and fathers, marriage connections and the relative seniority of kin groups could affect succession. Some heirs even stepped aside for relatives judged to have higher rank. Royal marriages therefore shaped public responsibilities and political competition as well as the lives of the families involved.

passages.title: Meals, movement and family rank
passages.text: William Mariner’s early nineteenth-century account describes an annual offering of first fruits to the Tuʻi Tonga. An early-growing yam variety was planted for the ceremony before most other yams. The crop was therefore both food and part of a sacred calendar. This is evidence from the dynasty’s late history, not a securely dated description of farming in 500.

passages.title: Clothing, grooming and learning
passages.text: An eighteenth-century ornamental comb at Te Papa uses 20 dried coconut-leaf midribs lashed together with fine fiber. Such combs could project from the back of the head or decorate a beard. The museum notes that distinguished chiefs had hair attendants. The object may have come from Cook’s voyages, but that collecting connection is less certain than its construction.

passages.title: Clothing, grooming and learning
passages.text: In Mariner’s account, people bathed in the sea or a pond, or had water poured over them from coconut shells. He also describes cleaning teeth with husk or charcoal and applying scented oil after washing. These are an observer’s reports from the early 1800s, not medical advice. A coconut shell could serve as a very portable water container.

passages.title: Clothing, grooming and learning
passages.text: Barkcloth connects old collections with living makers. A sample book assembled by Alexander Shaw in 1787 includes Tongan cloth collected during Cook’s voyages. At a 2023 workshop, ngatu maker Sulieti Fieme‘a Burrows described learning from her parents and passing the practice to her daughter. Looking at old patterns became a conversation across generations, rather than proof that the craft had ended.

passages.title: Clothing, grooming and learning
passages.text: During the nineteenth-century political transition, reading and printing acquired new importance. An 1828 mission school enrolled boys and girls, and a small press arrived in 1831. Lessons used Tongan as well as Christian texts. This schooling was connected to missionary activity and changing chiefly power; it was not the beginning of all Tongan knowledge or education.

passages.title: A dated written-language sample
passages.text: “Máló felow my.” is translated “Welcome (your) voyage hither.” in the 1817 account edited by John Martin from William Mariner’s recollections. It opens a reported conversation between two young chiefs at Vavaʻu. This preserves that book’s early Roman-letter spelling, not modern Tongan orthography or a medieval inscription. Earlier Tuʻi Tonga history relies heavily on archaeology and oral traditions.

Chiefly authority changed through rivalry and marriage rather than one conquest ending Tongan life. After the last Tuʻi Tonga, Laufilitonga, died, the title was not reappointed and effectively lapsed. The 1875 constitutional settlement recognized Kalaniuvalu as a representative of that line within the new order. Descendants and Tongan communities continued; the map’s 700 endpoint is unrelated to this much later transformation.

sectionTitles: Monuments and the evidence for power
Changing institutions and a living legacy

passages.text: The Tu'i Tonga chiefly line was associated with monumental centers on Tongatapu and far-reaching Pacific relationships. Excavated stone tools, royal tombs and collected household objects reveal different aspects of this history. Sacred chiefly rank, practical government and overseas exchange changed over time; they should not be compressed into a single unchanging empire.

passages.title: Monuments and the evidence for power
passages.text: At Heketa in eastern Tongatapu, fieldwork recorded house and seat platforms, a tiered tomb and the Ha'amonga trilithon. Their arrangement joined domestic, ceremonial and chiefly spaces. Clark and Reepmeyer interpret this complex as part of a new political order taking shape in the fourteenth century.

passages.title: Monuments and the evidence for power
passages.text: Ha'amonga is built from two upright coral-limestone slabs supporting a third slab across the top. Tonga's heritage submission links it to Tu'itatui through oral tradition. The monument demonstrates large-stone construction; a proposed astronomical purpose is less securely established.

passages.title: Monuments and the evidence for power
passages.text: The langi at Lapaha are raised burial platforms faced with carefully fitted stone. Moving, shaping and placing those blocks required coordinated labor. The structures preserve evidence of chiefly funerary practice, while continued care connects them with living communities.

passages.title: Voyaging, tools and exchange
passages.text: A 2014 study compared the chemistry of stone tools from Tongan chiefly centers with Pacific stone sources. Many pieces came from Samoa or Fiji, and one adze was traced to the Society Islands. The findings show material moving over long sea routes.

passages.title: Voyaging, tools and exchange
passages.text: In that study, 29 of 44 analyzed adzes and flakes from the state-period sample were nonlocal. The authors interpret the concentration of imports at chiefly centers as evidence of intensified exchange and political connections. Imported stone alone does not establish conquest of its source island.

passages.title: Households and skilled work
passages.text: A wooden kali in the Cook-Forster collection has a narrow head support carried on curved legs. Eighteenth-century observers described Tongans using these objects while sleeping. This household object shows careful woodworking directed toward an ordinary bodily need.

passages.title: Households and skilled work
passages.text: A food hook in the Pitt Rivers Museum retains an original wooden disk painted with bird figures. The hook attached to it is a later replacement. Reading that repair history matters: the whole object on display cannot be treated as untouched evidence from the collecting voyage.

passages.title: Households and skilled work
passages.text: Te Papa's account of eighteenth-century Tonga describes ngatu barkcloth used for bedding and clothing as well as other everyday purposes. Making useful cloth from inner bark connected plant cultivation, beating, joining and decoration with household life.

passages.title: Households and skilled work
passages.text: Clark and Reepmeyer connect Heketa's ceremonial spaces with kava drinking and presentation of first fruits to chiefs. In their interpretation, cultivated food and formal gatherings helped express the sacred standing of the Tu'i Tonga.

passages.title: Changing institutions and a living legacy
passages.text: The Tu'i Ha'atakalaua and Tu'i Kanokupolu lines exercised governing authority as the Tu'i Tonga retained sacred rank. Their relationships developed through succession, marriage and conflict. A list of Tu'i Tonga titleholders is therefore not a complete list of rulers exercising the same powers.

passages.title: Changing institutions and a living legacy
passages.text: Laufilitonga, the last Tu'i Tonga titleholder, died in 1865. George Tupou I's constitutional government followed in 1875, but the earlier transfer of power was a process rather than a single foreign conquest.

passages.title: Changing institutions and a living legacy
passages.text: At Lapaha, community leaders and researchers have worked together to repair stone structures and train residents in conservation. The tombs remain places of cultural responsibility, with archaeological research contributing to their protection.

The Tu'i Tonga title ended with Laufilitonga's death in 1865, after governing power had already shifted among chiefly lines. Tonga developed a constitutional monarchy under George Tupou I in 1875. Tongan communities and their heritage continued; neither date marks their disappearance.

passages.text: Tuareg communities speak related Amazigh languages and have lived across the central Sahara and its southern margins. These three map labels are broad cultural snapshots, not one empire. Their outlines are unreliable: one reaches the Nile region and another the Atlantic. The dated examples below distinguish medieval trading places from later Tuareg towns and living traditions.

passages.title: Caravans and towns
passages.text: At medieval Tadmekka in northeastern Mali, stone compounds, mosques, caravan lodgings and livestock enclosures crowded a town of roughly 125 acres. Arabic gravestones and Tifinagh inscriptions survive nearby. This mixed trading centre offers a concrete setting for Saharan exchange during the map’s medieval centuries.

passages.title: Caravans and towns
passages.text: Excavators at Tadmekka found a tiny piece of Chinese porcelain and silk whose embroidery was probably added locally. Goods moved through chains of markets across enormous distances. Ordinary pottery mattered too: jars and bowls served cooking, storage and the transport of food.

passages.title: Caravans and towns
passages.text: Agadez grew in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, after the dates shown by these map labels. As Tuareg groups settled, the boundaries of their camps helped shape the town’s eleven irregular neighbourhoods. A street plan can preserve the memory of a campsite.

passages.title: Caravans and towns
passages.text: Agadez builders worked with earthen bricks for houses, religious buildings and the sultan’s palace. The mosque’s minaret rises about 27 metres. Maintaining such buildings requires continuing craft knowledge; UNESCO’s 2013 assessment describes neighbourhood authorities participating in their care.

passages.title: Homes, work and social life
passages.text: A twentieth-century wooden tent pole from Niger shows that portable homes could contain carefully made decoration. Its upper part has seven projecting flanges, with geometric patterns cut into the wood. The Smithsonian preserves it as an example of Tuareg household craftsmanship.

passages.title: Homes, work and social life
passages.text: In the Peabody Museum’s Tuareg collection, women’s leather travelling bags held personal possessions, while decorated locks protected large bags. Another object is a hollow ring filled with seeds: moving a hand makes it rattle. Jewellery could supply its own tiny soundtrack.

passages.title: Homes, work and social life
passages.text: Tuareg societies included powerful nobles, herders, specialist artisans and enslaved people whose labour sustained households. Their experiences differed sharply. The fine objects in museum collections also reflect that inequality: wealth and freedom were not shared equally.

passages.title: Music and learning
passages.text: UNESCO’s 2013 account describes women making the imzad from half a dried gourd, stretched skin and a wooden bridge. One string and an arched bow produce its music. The player rests the instrument on her knees while accompanying poetry and songs.

passages.title: Music and learning
passages.text: Imzad skills pass through watching, listening and practice. Performances bring together women musicians, men singing or reciting poems, and other participants calling out. Music is also played for sick people as part of local healing beliefs, offering comfort and a shared social occasion.

passages.title: Music and learning
passages.text: At Ghat in the mid nineteenth century, traveller James Richardson described children reciting Qur’anic lessons after dark. He also reported that the governor’s daughters learned to read. The account even mentions sand being used as a surface for writing practice.

passages.title: A written language sample
passages.text: “Wăr tatəw ăssukăr.” means “Don’t forget the sugar.” This is the editors’ normalized Latin reading of a Tuareg phrase recorded in Arabic script at Ghat in 1850, in a manuscript associated with Muhammad Sharif. It preserves a later local voice, not medieval wording.

passages.title: A written language sample
passages.text: The phrasebook also contains a delicious translation accident. An Arabic instruction to shut a tent door was read as a statement putting sugar at its entrance. Similar-looking words caused the mix-up; the editors trace it to the Arabic teaching text used in 1850.

The map’s 1300 endpoint is not an ending for Tuareg peoples. Colonial conquest, drought, migration and new national borders transformed their lives. Communities continued, including town residents, musicians, craftspeople and pastoral families.

sectionTitles: A library was part of the state’s wealth
Work, families and the cost of campaigns
A political ending, not a vanished people

passages.text: The atlas’s “Tukular Caliphate” is the Umarian or Toucouleur state associated with al-Hajj Umar Tall and his successors. Its nineteenth-century conquests brought different communities under changing rulers. Ségou’s library and treasury preserve unusually concrete evidence of scholarship, craft, warfare and the repeated seizure of wealth.

passages.title: A library was part of the state’s wealth
passages.text: Umar began collecting manuscripts by about 1841. After his death in 1864, his son Ahmadu continued enlarging the collection. The BnF describes 518 bound volumes, mostly gathered into a consecutive manuscript series.

passages.title: A library was part of the state’s wealth
passages.text: The library was seized during France’s conquest of Ségou in 1890 and transferred to Paris. Later binding and cataloging changed its physical organization. Its survival is therefore also a history of conquest and displacement, not simply a peaceful museum acquisition.

passages.title: A library was part of the state’s wealth
passages.text: Cataloging this material required researchers from several countries. The 1985 inventory and microfilming made the contents more accessible. Scholarship can help reconnect a dispersed collection with the African history from which it was removed.

passages.title: A library was part of the state’s wealth
passages.text: “رماح حزب الرحيم” means “Lances of the party of the Merciful.” These are the opening words of Umar al-Futi’s Arabic book title, preserved in a 1876 Tunis edition catalogued by Tunisia’s national library. The printed edition is later than Umar’s lifetime, not his original manuscript.

passages.title: Beautiful objects with difficult journeys
passages.text: The Treasure of Ahmadu includes ornaments of gold, silver and leather, dated to the late 1700s or early 1800s. Many objects were older than the Umarian state itself. Their survival shows the work of earlier craftspeople as well as later royal collecting.

passages.title: Beautiful objects with difficult journeys
passages.text: Umar had seized precious objects from the treasuries of Tamba, Kaarta, Bamana Ségou and Masina. French troops later removed the collection from Ahmadu’s palace. The same object can tell more than one story of conquest.

passages.title: Beautiful objects with difficult journeys
passages.text: A famous sabre long connected with Umar offers a warning about labels. The Musée de l’Armée now explicitly calls that attribution false. Its return to Senegal does not prove that Umar personally carried it.

passages.title: Work, families and the cost of campaigns
passages.text: Before Umar’s conquest, the Middle Niger around Ségou already supported grain and cotton production and river commerce. Somono boat crews carried goods between routes bringing salt, cattle and horses from the north and products from farther south. The new rulers entered an existing economy.

passages.title: Work, families and the cost of campaigns
passages.text: The 1859 to 1861 campaign needed practical specialists: carpenters repaired gun carriages and smiths made cannonballs. Military technology relied on craft knowledge and maintenance, not merely possession of imported weapons.

passages.title: Work, families and the cost of campaigns
passages.text: Women and children accompanied the army, including relatives and enslaved dependants. When supplies became inadequate at Markoya, Umar ordered many back west. Robinson describes the resulting hunger and remembered suffering. These families were part of the story, although they rarely led the armies.

passages.title: Work, families and the cost of campaigns
passages.text: The checked collection records do not establish how every family ate, treated illness or used toilets. Books and royal ornaments illuminate particular institutions; they cannot stand in for an excavated ordinary household.

passages.title: A political ending, not a vanished people
passages.text: French forces took Ségou in 1890, ending Ahmadu’s rule there. Resistance and other power centers continued afterward; Person’s chronology places the wider dismantling in 1893. The map’s 1914 endpoint should not be read as evidence of an independent state surviving to that year.

French conquest removed Ahmadu from Ségou in 1890 and dismantled the wider state during the following years. Its communities and religious traditions continued. The library’s surviving manuscripts record intellectual life that cannot be reduced to the political map’s final date.

sectionTitles: Dinner, clothing and making a living

passages.text: The Tunica built influential trading connections along the lower Mississippi and its tributaries. The map’s 1492 to 1783 outline is only a broad regional snapshot: communities moved repeatedly, eventually settling around Marksville, Louisiana. Their history continues within the Tunica-Biloxi Tribe, whose members also have other distinct ancestral heritages.

passages.title: River routes and political choices
passages.text: In 1699, the missionary La Source described Tunica settlements near the Yazoo River as scattered villages totaling about 260 cabins. Archaeologist Jeffrey Brain connects these accounts with an agricultural society on a major river corridor. The figure belongs to that visitor’s account, rather than a census of everyone shown inside the map polygon.

passages.title: River routes and political choices
passages.text: Another early French observer, Gravier, described Tunica men clearing fields, planting and harvesting, while women made pottery and clothing. This is a useful reminder that neighboring peoples did not all organize household work in the same way. The account describes a particular historical setting, rather than rules for every later family.

passages.title: River routes and political choices
passages.text: Salt was valuable cargo. Tunica trading parties traveled into northeastern Louisiana to boil brine and obtain salt, which they distributed through regional exchange networks. River junctions helped them connect communities over long distances. A small ingredient in dinner could become a substantial reason to travel.

passages.title: River routes and political choices
passages.text: At Trudeau Landing, occupied from 1731 to 1764, Tunica traders exchanged horses and salt with the French. Colonists needed horses for farm work and military transport, and regional trade was cheaper than importing them from France. Tunica influence depended on useful goods as well as strategic river access.

passages.title: River routes and political choices
passages.text: Tunica alliances changed as European empires fought over Louisiana. In 1779, Tunica warriors joined Bernardo de Gálvez’s Spanish forces against British posts at Manchac and Baton Rouge. Gálvez subsequently invited the Tunica and their allies to settle on the Avoyelles Prairie, near present-day Marksville.

passages.title: River routes and political choices
passages.text: The modern Tunica-Biloxi Tribe developed through alliances and the gradual coming together of Tunica, Ofo, Avoyel and part of the Biloxi population. Federal researchers documented this process across the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Sharing a later tribal government does not make those earlier peoples interchangeable.

passages.title: Dinner, clothing and making a living
passages.text: The tribal museum’s collections include copper cooking kettles and brass bells used on clothing, blankets and cradles. Rolled metal cones could decorate bags, boots and belts with a tinkling sound. Imported materials became part of objects that people cooked with, carried and wore.

passages.title: Dinner, clothing and making a living
passages.text: Tunica-Biloxi women sold dyed rivercane baskets to earn money. By the middle of the twentieth century, weavers also used longleaf pine needles, which had become easier to obtain than cane. A change in available plants could alter the material while skilled weaving continued.

passages.title: Dinner, clothing and making a living
passages.text: Around the beginning of the twentieth century, families at the village farmed, hunted and fished. Cotton, garden produce, chickens and harvested pecans brought small earnings, while corn remained a staple. After cotton prices collapsed in 1919, some people sought wage work in lumbering and moved to Texas.

passages.title: Dinner, clothing and making a living
passages.text: In 1938, the community raised money to send a delegation to Washington. Its members sought help with lost land, schooling and economic conditions that had pushed families away. The visit led to an investigation by anthropologist Ruth Underhill. Access to education was part of a broader struggle to keep a community together.

passages.title: Recovering belongings and teaching children
passages.text: In 1968, a looter disturbed more than a hundred graves at Trudeau Landing and removed burial belongings. The collection later became known as the Tunica Treasure. Tribal efforts to recover it challenged the treatment of ancestors and their possessions as objects outsiders could simply take away.

passages.title: Recovering belongings and teaching children
passages.text: After taking possession of the collection in 1989, the Tribe created an unusual conservation laboratory from two refrigerated truck trailers. Specialists trained tribal members to care for fragile objects. A new laboratory opened in 2011. Refrigerated trailers are not the usual museum building, but they helped bring conservation work home.

passages.title: Recovering belongings and teaching children
passages.text: A documented written Tunica phrase is “Taluhchi Yoroni Woruhk’iti,” translated by the tribal language program as “We are learning the Tunica language.” It is the heading of a modern account by John Barbry. The spelling belongs to contemporary language teaching, not to an eighteenth-century inscription.

passages.title: Recovering belongings and teaching children
passages.text: A 2011 children’s story collection drew on narratives recorded from Sesostrie Youchigant. A tribal artist illustrated the book, and three young people recorded themselves telling the stories. Their recordings became gifts for elders: children were helping return family stories in a new form.

passages.title: Recovering belongings and teaching children
passages.text: The Tribe’s 2023 language textbook grew from older recordings and written documentation, including work by Mary Haas and Sesostrie Youchigant. Its opening material recalls Chief Joseph Pierite asking Haas to preserve recordings for descendants. A request made for future generations became part of lessons those generations could use.
The map’s 1783 endpoint is not the end of the Tunica. Federal recognition of the Tunica-Biloxi Tribe came in 1981, and language teaching, cultural work and self-government continue.

passages.text: The Tunis entry covers a North African regency ruled by beys within the Ottoman political world. Its interval crosses Muradid rule and the Husainid dynasty established in 1705. Mosques, family houses, craftwork and nineteenth-century reforms reveal a society broader than its ruling household.

passages.title: Buildings and the state
passages.text: Hammuda Pasha’s mosque in Tunis is dated by an inscription to 1655. Its prayer hall measures about 24 by 17 metres and uses 48 columns to support its vaulted interior. Architecture supplies evidence for both religious life and organized building work.

passages.title: Buildings and the state
passages.text: The mosque joined worship with dynastic memory: Hammuda Pasha and his family were buried in a square mausoleum beside it. Green glazed roof tiles and contrasting marble decoration made the burial building conspicuous within the complex.

passages.title: Buildings and the state
passages.text: An eastern gallery included an outdoor prayer niche for summer worship. That small practical detail matters: a religious building also had to accommodate bodies, seasons and the need for usable space.

passages.title: Buildings and the state
passages.text: The 1861 constitution kept succession hereditary within the Husainid family, ordered by age. It also required two official registers recording the ruling family. Reform here meant defining and recording royal government, not immediately replacing monarchy with elected rule.

passages.title: Inside a Tunis household
passages.text: Dar Ben Abdallah is an eighteenth-century residence later made into a museum. Its reconstructed scenes focus on comfortable urban households of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. They are useful evidence for that social setting, not a model of every home in the regency.

passages.title: Inside a Tunis household
passages.text: The museum’s nineteenth-century room presents embroidery, belt weaving and chechia-cap knitting as women’s work. These were skilled activities producing things to wear, not merely decorative hobbies.

passages.title: Inside a Tunis household
passages.text: A childhood display shows a skilled embroiderer teaching two girls, alongside children’s clothes and toys. It offers a concrete example of knowledge being learned within household settings, while remaining a museum reconstruction.

passages.title: Inside a Tunis household
passages.text: The reconstructed kitchen occupies a small open courtyard, with sheltered areas for preparing food and cooking. Pottery, copper and wooden utensils show a kitchen assembled from several materials. The pots had jobs before they became museum exhibits.

passages.title: Inside a Tunis household
passages.text: Wedding displays include combs, mirrors, powder boxes, jewellery and clothing. These objects help explain preparations for a major family occasion; they do not establish one uniform wedding ceremony for all Tunisians.

passages.title: Writing, reform and record keeping
passages.text: A short Arabic sample from the 1857 Fundamental Pact is “اختلاف الأديان والألسنة والألوان”, meaning “differences of religions, languages and colours”. It appears within the first article’s promise of security for inhabitants regardless of these differences, reproduced here in typed Arabic from the ministry’s transcription.

passages.title: Writing, reform and record keeping
passages.text: The pact also addressed equality in taxation and customs duties, trading and work. These were promises about how government should treat people and property; the existence of a written guarantee alone does not prove equal treatment in everyday practice.

passages.title: Writing, reform and record keeping
passages.text: A dedicated archive service was created within the Grand Ministry in 1874. Preserving and organizing correspondence made government decisions retrievable. Behind a grand constitution stood the decidedly less glamorous but essential task of keeping the paperwork.

The map entry ends in 1878, before a decisive change: France invaded and imposed the protectorate in 1881. The beys remained under colonial constraints, while Tunisia’s cities and communities continued into a different political order.
