sectionTitles: From coalition to the first great steppe empire
Work moved with grass, animals and seasons
Dinner, homes, water and the toilet question
Families, children, women and social rank
Clothes, art, bows and clever hands
Learning, health, play and written words
Belief, burials, exchange and evidence traps
Endings, continuities and the Huns question

passages.text: The atlas plants the word “Xiongnu” across the eastern steppe in 400 BCE, long before the securely documented empire. This card follows the harder and more interesting story: diverse herders, riders, farmers and craftspeople built wider networks while northern Chinese states pushed toward the grasslands; the name appears in surviving Chinese history in 318 BCE; and Modu’s victories around 209 BCE turned those connections into Inner Asia’s first great nomadic empire. Archaeology restores lives that hostile court texts flatten, seasonal pasture work, millet and dairy meals, pit houses, iron smelting, bright felt and silk, influential women, children inside unequal families, cavities, horse races and the stubborn mystery of toilets. It also sets limits: no indigenous Xiongnu book survives, genes do not name languages, elite tombs do not represent everybody, and the 17-point map outline is not a surveyed border. The endpoint is transformation into the later imperial card, not disappearance.

passages.title: First, fix the time machine
passages.text: The exact missing record is xiongnu, indexed circa 400 to 323 BCE. Its single decoded polygon has one ring and only 17 positions, yet stretches from about 81.4°E to 132.3°E. That is a broad teaching shape, not a surveyed frontier, tax map or proof of one government controlling half a continent.

passages.title: First, fix the time machine
passages.text: At 500 BCE, the same tested steppe points sit inside an atlas feature called proto-altaic-pastoralists. That linguistic-looking umbrella is also an interpretation, not a people’s own border. The switch to “Xiongnu” at 400 BCE shows a cartographic category change; it cannot establish that everybody inside changed identity on New Year’s morning.

passages.title: First, fix the time machine
passages.text: At the 323 BCE seam, the xiongnu polygon disappears and the tested Mongolian core is simply uncovered. The first explicit textual mention usually cited comes in 318 BCE, five years after the map stops showing it. This delightfully awkward sequence is excellent evidence that atlas endpoints are not birth and death certificates.

passages.title: First, fix the time machine
passages.text: The later imperial confederation has its own id, xiongnu-bc200, and appears in the 200 BCE topology as a different 20-position polygon. Southern Xiongnu is another separate record in 100 CE. This card therefore ends with Modu’s imperial consolidation rather than stealing two later cards’ histories and wearing them as one very oversized coat.

passages.title: First, fix the time machine
passages.text: Ulaanbaatar, the Khangai, south Baikal and the eastern Altai test inside the 400 BCE shape; Ordos, Hohhot, Kashgar and Beijing do not. Those tests document only what the imported geometry draws. They say nothing certain about allegiance, seasonal range, language, ancestry or where any modern border ought to be.

passages.title: How many communities became “the Xiongnu”?
passages.text: Archaeologists find fourth to third-century BCE tombs in northern and western Mongolia that combine older slab-grave practices with features later called Xiongnu. Scholars describe an early process of “xiongnuization,” not the replacement of one pure people by another. Pots and grave plans can reveal connections; they do not carry ethnic ID cards.

passages.title: How many communities became “the Xiongnu”?
passages.text: Metal objects at Tamiryn Ulaan Khoshuu include bronze alloys used mainly for ornaments and cast-iron household objects. Radiocarbon ranges reach the fourth century BCE, suggesting connected material traditions earlier than once assumed. A shared buckle style can signal exchange or political relationship without proving that its owner spoke one specific language.

passages.title: How many communities became “the Xiongnu”?
passages.text: Ancient DNA shows that populations contributing to the later empire came from deeply different eastern and western steppe ancestries, with additional connections across Eurasia. This supports coalition and movement, but genes cannot pronounce a word. Calling one ancestry “Turkic,” “Mongolic” or “Iranian” without linguistic evidence would turn a laboratory result into fan fiction.

passages.title: How many communities became “the Xiongnu”?
passages.text: Only rival or neighboring literate societies left continuous written narratives. Chinese historians used categories shaped by frontier politics, while archaeological cultures are modern classifications built from material patterns. The two records illuminate one another, but neither lets us match every named group to every grave or every skeleton to a political faction.

passages.title: How many communities became “the Xiongnu”?
passages.text: The safest picture is plural: herders, riders, farmers, metalworkers and local leaders were connected through alliance, competition, marriage and exchange. Their growing networks eventually supported a state that mobile people built in mobile ways. It was not a failed city-state waiting for someone to invent enough bricks.

passages.title: From coalition to the first great steppe empire
passages.text: Around 209 BCE, Modu transformed steppe politics through rapid conquests and a more centralized confederation under the chanyu. That imperial achievement belongs at the ending of this origins card and the beginning of xiongnu-bc200. The map’s 400 BCE label must not quietly promote Modu’s empire by nearly two centuries.

passages.title: From coalition to the first great steppe empire
passages.text: The imperial regime paired offices and territories of the left and right beneath the chanyu, linking royal kin, commanders and dependent leaders. It coordinated people and resources across enormous distances without copying a sedentary bureaucracy wholesale. Centralized authority could travel by horse; it did not need a marble reception desk.

passages.title: From coalition to the first great steppe empire
passages.text: Sima Qian’s Shiji preserves stories of Touman, Modu, campaigns, diplomacy and succession. It is a primary historical source, but it was written in Classical Chinese within a Han imperial world. Read it for what a brilliant historian recorded, and keep one eyebrow raised when an enemy’s court narrates steppe motives as if it heard every tent conversation.

passages.title: From coalition to the first great steppe empire
passages.text: Xiongnu rulers sought control of animals, grain, luxury goods and human followings, not empty colored acreage. Raiding, trade, gifts, tribute and negotiation all belonged to political economy. Silk or grain crossing a frontier might be diplomatic payment, exchange, redistribution or loot; a shiny object cannot explain the whole transaction by itself.

passages.title: From coalition to the first great steppe empire
passages.text: Empire did not erase local difference. Frontier cemeteries show extraordinary genetic diversity, while political authority linked communities with very different ancestries and material habits. “Multiethnic” here means a state joined varied populations; it does not mean ancient residents filled out a modern census form with boxes matching ours.

passages.title: Work moved with grass, animals and seasons
passages.text: Many households managed sheep, goats, cattle and horses by moving between seasonal pastures. Mobility was skilled work: families had to read weather, grass, water and animal condition, coordinate labor, protect newborn stock and avoid exhausting a pasture. “Nomad” did not mean wandering randomly until dinner happened to moo nearby.

passages.title: Work moved with grass, animals and seasons
passages.text: Isotope studies suggest established winter-grazing routines and mostly local circulation punctuated by long-distance movement. That pattern fits pasture knowledge and political connections rather than constant migration by everyone. Some people traveled far; others spent childhood near the same valleys where their livestock fed.

passages.title: Work moved with grass, animals and seasons
passages.text: Settlement survey at Egiin Gol found ceramics, cultivation and a hierarchy of habitation sites alongside pastoralism. The evidence dismantles a cartoon choice between “mobile herder” and “settled farmer.” A household, community or empire could depend on both, and could move people, grain and animals through the same regional system.

passages.title: Work moved with grass, animals and seasons
passages.text: Ivolga preserves semi-subterranean dwellings, storage, cereals, animal bones and specialized work within a fortified settlement. Some residents may have been farmers, craftspeople, captives or semi-vassals under nomadic political dominance. Archaeologists debate their exact statuses, so the card does not assign every potter one legal label.

passages.title: Work moved with grass, animals and seasons
passages.text: Ironworkers controlled carbon through carburization and used bloomery traditions distinct from Han cast-iron production. Later furnaces grew more efficient with altered designs, tuyères and charcoal use. The achievement was local technical knowledge embedded in steppe communities, though the best-dated furnaces belong after this card’s early map interval.

passages.title: Dinner, homes, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Milk and meat from managed herds were central resources, and protein preserved in dental calculus shows that dairy traditions on the eastern steppe were already ancient. Neighboring texts later mention fermented horse milk. We cannot reconstruct one universal breakfast, but a milk-based meal was technology too: microbes made a seasonal liquid easier to keep and share.

passages.title: Dinner, homes, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Human isotope evidence reveals millet and other crops mixed with animal foods, while Ivolga produced wheat, rye, barley, fish and domestic-animal remains. Diet differed by region and status. So the truthful menu is broader than “meat, more meat, and a dramatic final garnish of meat,” even if livestock remained enormously important.

passages.title: Dinner, homes, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Most mobile homes leave faint traces, but excavated settlements add another picture: Ivolga had pit houses with hearths, and later elite graves preserved felt rugs and cover-like textiles. Those burial textiles suggest sophisticated felt craft, not that every family owned the same decorated dwelling. Ordinary tents rarely RSVP to the archaeological record.

passages.title: Dinner, homes, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Water shaped movement and settlement. Ivolga stood by an old channel of the Selenga; many excavated settlements cluster in better-watered forest-steppe and river valleys, while herders also had to plan seasonal access for people and stock. No evidence supports one empire-wide plumbing system, and a river location is not proof that its water was always safe.

passages.title: Dinner, homes, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Toilets are an honest blank spot. Published Ivolga summaries describe 54 dwellings and hundreds of household pits, but the reviewed evidence does not securely identify a Xiongnu latrine or tell us how mobile camps managed human waste. Calling an unlabeled pit a toilet would be archaeology by wishful sniff test, so the card leaves the answer unknown.

passages.title: Families, children, women and social rank
passages.text: DNA from frontier cemeteries shows close relatives buried near people with very different ancestries. Families and alliances helped knit distant groups into the empire, but biology was not the only glue. Fosterage, marriage, political loyalty, adoption and status can shape a community even when they leave weaker genetic fingerprints.

passages.title: Families, children, women and social rank
passages.text: High-status graves on the western frontier were disproportionately associated with women, some buried with prestigious belt plaques and other signs of authority. That evidence makes women visible as political actors in expansion and integration. It does not mean every woman was powerful; status differences among women were sharp.

passages.title: Families, children, women and social rank
passages.text: At Tamir, selected adults were sometimes accompanied by spouses and young children who died before marriageable age. Other close relatives were buried elsewhere, and burial location followed power as well as kin. A cemetery can preserve grief and family ties while still functioning like a highly exclusive guest list.

passages.title: Families, children, women and social rank
passages.text: One Tamir woman may have continued her lineage when her father lacked a male heir; her burial treatment differed from others. Researchers present this as an interpretation, not a recorded biography. It is a useful reminder that patrilineal systems could bend, and that archaeology sometimes finds a rule precisely where someone negotiated an exception.

passages.title: Families, children, women and social rank
passages.text: Ivolga’s graves show marked wealth differences among men, women and children, and scholars interpret settled farmers and craftspeople as lower in status than nomadic elites. Some may have been captives or tribute-paying dependents. Children inherited unequal worlds long before they could saddle a horse or object to the seating plan.

passages.title: Clothes, art, bows and clever hands
passages.text: Noin-Ula elite clothing combined locally worked felt, coarse cloth, fur and birch bark with imported wool and Han silk. Caftans, trousers, leggings and felt shoes were assembled in the steppe, probably by skilled craftswomen. These splendid pieces show creative combination, not the everyday wardrobe of every herder.

passages.title: Clothes, art, bows and clever hands
passages.text: One set of leggings joined Mediterranean wool, Chinese silk embroidery, steppe sewing and birch-bark soles. That is a wearable map of long-distance exchange. It is also an elite burial object, so the fun fact has a price tag attached: most children were not galloping around in international luxury pants.

passages.title: Clothes, art, bows and clever hands
passages.text: A bronze belt plaque now at the Met shows fighting horses in relief. Animal-combat designs made belts into moving art, visible when bodies and clothing moved. We know this object’s material, date range and collection history; we do not know the exact joke, story or status signal its first wearer associated with the scene.

passages.title: Clothes, art, bows and clever hands
passages.text: Composite bows from Xiongnu to Xianbei-period sites used wood cores strengthened with horn plates in carefully placed sections. Such construction stored substantial energy in a portable weapon suited to mounted use. The surviving examples are later than 400 BCE, so they illuminate an imperial technology rather than prove the exact kit of the earliest communities.

passages.title: Clothes, art, bows and clever hands
passages.text: Tomb construction itself was a major engineering feat: deep chambers, satellite graves and paired-stone ritual lines required planning and coordinated labor. Horse gear, chariots, weapons, tools and food offerings survived inside. Monumental graves display elite organization, though the quiet laborers who dug them rarely receive names.

passages.title: Learning, health, play and written words
passages.text: No Xiongnu school curriculum survives. Children in pastoral households still had a formidable education: managing animals, routes, weather, tools and social obligations required repeated practical learning. That is an inference from the documented economy, not evidence for a standard age, classroom or lesson plan. The steppe supplied homework with hooves.

passages.title: Learning, health, play and written words
passages.text: A dental study examined 110 skulls and 1,394 teeth. It found caries in 17.3 percent of examined individuals and connected higher rates than earlier populations cautiously with greater carbohydrate consumption. Cavities are tiny archives: millet and other foods can leave an ache long after the recipe and the annoyed patient are gone.

passages.title: Learning, health, play and written words
passages.text: Bones and teeth reveal workload, nutrition and disease better than they reveal treatment. No Xiongnu medical handbook or securely identified medicine kit survives in the sources reviewed here, so naming herbs, doctors or cures would be invention. Similar male and female food access in one skeletal sample is valuable evidence, but it is not a healthcare system.

passages.title: Learning, health, play and written words
passages.text: A later account says Southern Xiongnu assemblies included horse and camel racing for enjoyment alongside sacrifice and political business. That sounds like a spectacular sports day, but it belongs to a later branch centuries after this card begins. It cannot prove what a 400 BCE child played at home, which remains unknown.

passages.title: Learning, health, play and written words
passages.text: Authentic written sample: “匈奴列傳” is the Classical Chinese heading of Shiji chapter 110, usually translated “Account” or “Biographies of the Xiongnu.” The characters 匈奴 are an outsider’s written name, pronounced Xiōngnú in modern Mandarin, not a sample of the lost Xiongnu language. No securely demonstrated indigenous Xiongnu script survives.

passages.title: Belief, burials, exchange and evidence traps
passages.text: Elite cemeteries preserve animal offerings, chariots, weapons and fine textiles because mourners deliberately buried them and tomb conditions sometimes protected them. They are not frozen living rooms. A golden buckle survives more eagerly than a patched work sock, so archaeology naturally gives the wealthy better lighting.

passages.title: Belief, burials, exchange and evidence traps
passages.text: Excavated stone lines held burnt and unburnt animal remains from distinct ceremonial events. Sheep and cattle parts could represent offerings, feasting, fuel or several acts combined. Researchers can reconstruct placement and burning more securely than the exact words, emotions or theology of participants.

passages.title: Belief, burials, exchange and evidence traps
passages.text: Chinese lacquer, Central or West Asian textiles and Mediterranean glass reached elite Xiongnu graves. Those objects reveal far-reaching routes and redistribution, but not necessarily one merchant traveling end to end. Goods could change hands many times, collecting stories, scratches and markups on a steppe supply chain.

passages.title: Belief, burials, exchange and evidence traps
passages.text: The cemetery complexes demanded labor and made social rank visible, yet UNESCO stresses that much about their rites remains unknown. Looting and decay removed context from many tombs. A careful card can be exciting without pretending the missing pieces whispered their answers to the excavator.

passages.title: Belief, burials, exchange and evidence traps
passages.text: Permanent architecture and production sites do exist, but mobile lives often leave low archaeological visibility. Survey teams therefore study whole landscapes, seasonal camps, cemeteries and scattered ceramics, rather than waiting for a capital to appear. The discovery is methodological: an empire can be legible in relationships between small traces.

passages.title: Endings, continuities and the Huns question
passages.text: This origins card ends around 209 BCE because Modu’s imperial consolidation changes the scale of the story and the atlas already has xiongnu-bc200 for it. That is a narrative handoff, not a collapse. Families, herds, craft knowledge and political relationships continued through the transition.

passages.title: Endings, continuities and the Huns question
passages.text: The later empire weakened amid Han pressure and internal struggles, then divided into northern and southern formations. Those events belong to the later cards, but they show why “the Xiongnu ended” is too simple. Governments split and titles shifted while communities persisted, moved and entered new alliances.

passages.title: Endings, continuities and the Huns question
passages.text: A later Southern Xiongnu polity operated under heavy Han influence and is represented separately in the atlas. Its assemblies, offices and races preserve continuity and adaptation rather than a museum-perfect copy of Modu’s state. Political descendants change because survival is usually an improvisation, not a reenactment.

passages.title: Endings, continuities and the Huns question
passages.text: Some scholarship links Xiongnu names or political traditions to later Huns; other researchers emphasize the lack of direct archaeological, linguistic or population continuity. Similar names are clues, not time-travel visas. The card leaves this debate open and refuses to turn Attila into Modu’s documented great-great-great-grandson.

passages.title: Endings, continuities and the Huns question
passages.text: Their clearest legacy is less a single bloodline than a political demonstration: mobile pastoral communities could create durable hierarchy, long-distance diplomacy, specialized production and continent-spanning exchange. Later steppe empires developed their own institutions, but the Xiongnu made sedentary historians confront a state whose center could move.

Around 209 BCE, Modu’s conquests created the imperial confederation followed by the separate xiongnu-bc200 card. The early Xiongnu did not vanish at that handoff; communities, families, herds, skills and alliances were reorganized on a larger political scale. The atlas had already dropped the exact early polygon at 323 BCE, so neither 323 nor 209 should be read as an extinction date. This is a change of chapter, from uncertain origins and coalition-building to documented empire, not the end of the people who made it.

passages.text: The Xiongnu were the first great steppe empire, united by Modu Chanyu in 209 BCE and ruling Mongolia and the lands to its west for three centuries. Their mounted archers, tribute treaties with Han China and left-and-right administration set the pattern for the Turkic and Mongol empires that followed.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Composite bows of horn and sinew, shot from the saddle, made every herdsman a warrior.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Bronze and iron for weapons and harness; gold plaques of animals in combat for the elite.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: The chanyu ruled under Heaven, Tengri, with shamans and seasonal gatherings to sacrifice to ancestors, heaven and earth.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Elite tombs at Noin-Ula held Chinese silks, lacquer and Bactrian textiles beside the dead.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The heqin treaties from 198 BCE brought Han princesses, silk, grain and wine to the chanyu as the price of peace.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: The Xiongnu taxed the oasis towns of the Tarim Basin and traded horses and furs to China.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Xiongnu model of steppe empire was followed by the Turkic khaganates and the Mongols.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: Their name may lie behind the Huns of European sources, though the link is unproven.

The confederation split into southern and northern halves in 54 BCE. Han armies broke the Northern Xiongnu at Ikh Bayan in 89 CE, and by 93 the Xianbei had taken over the steppe; the Southern Xiongnu lived on as Han clients inside the Great Wall.

sectionTitles: A state of trade, languages and skilled builders
Learning, books and a few Tangut characters

passages.text: Xixia, or Western Xia, was the Tangut imperial state in western China, conventionally dated 1038 to 1227. This imported map record instead runs from 1000 to 1279. Its broad, nearly repeated outlines are approximate and chronologically misleading: the early interval precedes the imperial proclamation, while the final interval extends well beyond Mongol conquest. It must not suggest that an independent Western Xia still existed in 1279.

passages.title: A state of trade, languages and skilled builders
passages.text: Western Xia brought Tangut rulers and communities into a state also inhabited by Han Chinese, Tibetans, Uyghurs and other peoples. Its royal burial landscape lies beside the Helan Mountains in Ningxia. The tombs combine Chinese imperial planning with Buddhist forms and local choices, leaving evidence of a court that drew on several cultural traditions.

passages.title: A state of trade, languages and skilled builders
passages.text: In eleventh-century diplomacy, Western Xia used its position on trade routes toward Central Asia to bargain with the Song court. Historian Jeongwon Hyun finds that benefits could arrive as official return gifts. A ceremonial exchange between rulers could therefore also be a commercial negotiation, with access to valuable goods at stake.

passages.title: A state of trade, languages and skilled builders
passages.text: Builders at the imperial cemetery worked with rammed earth, brick and timber. They also created flood defenses: the surviving system includes 26 dikes and six drainage ditches. Protecting royal monuments meant thinking about moving water as well as impressive walls. These drains served the burial landscape; they are not evidence for toilets in ordinary houses.

passages.title: Fields, households and working agreements
passages.text: Land-sale contracts from Khara Khoto describe farms by their canals, water supplies and neighboring plots. Households built homes on their own farmland, producing a scattered settlement pattern. In this dry region, canals brought water from the Black River to crops. A field’s value depended on more than its size: getting water to it mattered.

passages.title: Fields, households and working agreements
passages.text: A grain-loan document from 1217 names the borrower’s wife as a co-borrower. Other surviving contracts also record wives sharing responsibility for repayment. Such papers bring a household into view: borrowing food could create obligations for more than one family member. Signing alongside a spouse had financial consequences.

passages.title: Fields, households and working agreements
passages.text: An employment contract drawn up at the end of 1219 arranged nine months of work in the following year, from the first month to the tenth. Part of the payment was due immediately. The agreement covered the agricultural season from sowing through harvest. Advance payment and a written work schedule were already practical matters.

passages.title: Fields, households and working agreements
passages.text: Khara Khoto’s surviving papers now help researchers recover names and activities that royal chronicles often overlook. The British Library’s Tangut collection includes material recovered during Aurel Stein’s 1913 to 1916 expedition. The site’s documents span the tenth to fourteenth centuries, so scholars must date individual pieces before assigning them to independent Western Xia.

passages.title: Learning, books and a few Tangut characters
passages.text: In 1190, Gule Maocai compiled a Tangut-Chinese wordbook known as the Pearl in the Palm. It put two languages together for learners who needed to cross a linguistic boundary. The surviving book has 37 leaves. Its usefulness was very practical: knowing one language did not automatically make the neighboring language readable.

passages.title: Learning, books and a few Tangut characters
passages.text: That wordbook also preserves the work of printers and bookbinders. Its butterfly binding folded sheets with their printed faces inward and attached their blank backs. Lotus decorations filled otherwise awkward spaces in the layout. Even a serious vocabulary book had room for a little visual flair, while its construction shaped how readers turned the leaves.

passages.title: Learning, books and a few Tangut characters
passages.text: A late eleventh-century Da’an coin offers a tiny writing sample: “𘜶𗵐𘏨𘔭,” meaning “precious coin of the Da’an reign period.” This is a modern character transcription of its Tangut inscription, following Andrew West’s reading. On the coin, the four characters run clockwise from the top. The National Museum of China catalogues a Da’an example only 2.4 centimeters across.

passages.title: Learning, books and a few Tangut characters
passages.text: Western Xia’s Buddhist printing needed organized craft work. Under royal patrons including Emperor Renzong and Empress Luo, institutions handled the production of sacred books; a character-carving bureau worked with Tangut texts. Surviving illustrated front pages let historians examine the people and techniques behind those books, beyond simply counting how many titles existed.

passages.title: Gatherings, families and care
passages.text: A major Buddhist gathering in 1189 at Dadumin Monastery combined the distribution of sacred texts with public acts of generosity. The account describes food for monks and poor people, the release of captive animals and pardons for prisoners. The ceremonies continued for ten days and nights. Religious patronage could involve meals and crowds as well as books.

passages.title: Gatherings, families and care
passages.text: A ritual banner found in Yinchuan’s Hongfo pagoda names Zhao Zhong and his family as donors. Their home was in neighboring Jin territory, in Zhenrong Prefecture. Dated between 1190 and 1227, the banner records a family’s religious connection across a political border. An object offered at a temple could carry the names of people living elsewhere.

passages.title: Gatherings, families and care
passages.text: Three Tangut medical prescriptions preserved in Russia concern sores on children’s heads. Modern researchers translated them and compared them with Chinese medical writings in a study published in 2016. These small texts document attention to children’s health and the exchange of medical knowledge. They preserve attempted treatments; the manuscripts alone cannot tell us whether those treatments helped.

passages.title: Gatherings, families and care
passages.text: Tangut writing continued after the kingdom’s conquest. At Mogao, a stele erected in 1348 commemorated Prince Sulaiman and his family’s support for a temple. Its Buddhist mantra appeared in six scripts, including Tangut. This later monument belongs to the Mongol era and shows why the end of a government is not automatically the end of its written culture.

Mongol conquest ended independent Western Xia in 1227. The map’s 1279 endpoint is not a later fall date. Tangut texts and the 1348 Sulaiman stele show that language and religious traditions continued under changed political rule; conquest did not make the population or its culture disappear.

passages.text: Yakama communities belong to the Columbia Plateau of present-day Washington. The map’s Yakima and Yakama labels show differently sized regional outlines, not the boundaries of a single ancient state. The fourteen tribes and bands confederated under the 1855 treaty had distinct earlier identities. This card follows Yakama history into that later nation; its institutions should not be projected into the map’s 1492 or 1530 scenes.

passages.title: Homelands, leadership and change
passages.text: Before Fort Simcoe became the first formal Yakama agency in 1859, the place was Mool-mool, a seasonal camp with bubbling spring water. Families stopped there while hunting, fishing, gathering roots and picking huckleberries. A later military and administrative location had an older life as a busy food-gathering crossroads.

passages.title: Homelands, leadership and change
passages.text: Chief Kamiakin’s garden in the Upper Ahtanum Valley grew corn, peas, potatoes, squash, melons and wheat before the 1855 war. A ditch about a quarter-mile long brought water to it. Gardening was part of his community’s changing economy alongside seasonal fishing and gathering.

passages.title: Homelands, leadership and change
passages.text: Signed on June 9, 1855, the treaty named fourteen tribes and bands as a confederated nation and ceded extensive lands to the United States. It set aside a reservation. Ratification followed in March 1859, nearly four years after the signing.

passages.title: Homelands, leadership and change
passages.text: War followed in 1855 amid settler encroachment and killings. Kamiakin helped lead resistance, and his forces initially drove back an American military expedition. Colonel George Wright’s 1858 campaign broke organized resistance. Kamiakin stayed away from the reservation and eventually lived at Rock Lake.

passages.title: Homelands, leadership and change
passages.text: The treaty’s practical details reach right into family life. Article 3 reserved fishing at customary places and hunting and gathering on open, unclaimed land. Article 5 promised schools, a hospital, medicines and a physician. These were written government commitments, not proof that every promised service arrived.

passages.title: Homelands, leadership and change
passages.text: The tribal council formally established in 1944 has fourteen members, recalling the treaty’s fourteen signers. The museum describes a General Council of adult members electing representatives by raised hands. The nation officially adopted the spelling Yakama in 1994; older records commonly say Yakima.

passages.title: Food, family and skilled hands
passages.text: The seasonal round was a moving food calendar. A historical reconstruction describes spring root digging, summer fishing and travel to cooler high ground, followed by mountain huckleberry gathering. Knowledge of when different foods were ready helped families use several landscapes across the year.

passages.title: Food, family and skilled hands
passages.text: Winter brought families back to sheltered valley camps with stored roots, berries, salmon and venison. People repaired homes, made tools and clothing, and visited one another. The pantry had been assembled over many months; winter preparation involved much more than one enormous shopping trip.

passages.title: Food, family and skilled hands
passages.text: In a 1995 cultural-resources memorandum, Florence Aguilar explained meals beginning with water, followed by salmon, deer or elk, roots and berries, and ending with water. Her account connects eating with gratitude and responsibility for the waters that sustain salmon.

passages.title: Food, family and skilled hands
passages.text: A Yakama basket in the National Museum of the American Indian combines cedar roots, beargrass, sedge and hide thong. Its maker used coiling and imbricated decoration, layering materials into a patterned surface. The museum received it in 1957, but does not know its maker or manufacture date.

passages.title: Food, family and skilled hands
passages.text: At the intertribal fishery of Celilo Falls, Yakama and other fishers worked from platforms above dangerous currents. Raymond Matheny’s 1952 notes describe long-handled nets and compulsory safety ropes. Some fishers worked in groups and divided the proceeds from the fish they sold.

passages.title: Food, family and skilled hands
passages.text: On March 10, 1957, water backed up behind The Dalles Dam and submerged Celilo Falls. The government paid compensation for flooded fishing sites, but did not buy away treaty fishing rights. Losing the falls damaged a place of work, trade, family memory and ceremony.

passages.title: Language and restoration
passages.text: A small written sample of modern Ichishkíin is “Shix̱ iwá wyáx̱ayx̱t”, translated “Life is Good”. It appears as a storybook title on the Yakama language program’s page, credited to the Northwest Indian Language Institute and recorded by the nation’s program. This is contemporary teaching material.

passages.title: Language and restoration
passages.text: Language lessons can accompany the busiest moments of parenting. The Yakama program offers resources for nursing, babyboards and diapering through meet-ups with Ttáwax̱t Birth Justice Center. Its handwashing poster and video bring language into hygiene routines too. Even changing a diaper can have vocabulary practice attached.

passages.title: Language and restoration
passages.text: The nation’s 2017 coho restoration plan reported fish returning to Wenatchee and Methow watersheds and reproducing naturally. It also reported that local broodstock had replaced reliance on transfers from the lower Columbia. Building self-sustaining populations remained a long-term project, with monitoring as well as hatchery work.

The imported map cutoffs do not mark the disappearance of Yakama people. The later nation continues through its government and treaty relationship, while language programs help families carry Ichishkíin into everyday life.

passages.text: The Yamato period covers the rise of a single Japanese state from the chiefdoms of the Kofun age. Great keyhole-shaped tombs mark the power of the early rulers; in the sixth and seventh centuries the court took Buddhism, writing and Chinese-style government from Korea and China.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Keyhole-shaped kofun mounds for rulers; the largest, the Daisen Kofun near Osaka, is 486 meters long.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Haniwa clay figures of warriors, horses, houses and dancers stood on the mounds.

passages.title: Arts
passages.text: Bronze mirrors, iron swords and gilt-bronze horse trappings came from Korea and China and were buried with the chiefs.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Buddhism arrived from Baekje, and the Soga and Mononobe clans fought over whether to accept it.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Prince Shotoku's Seventeen-Article Constitution set out Buddhist and Confucian principles for officials.

passages.title: Ideas and beliefs
passages.text: Native kami worship, later called Shinto, continued alongside Buddhism and Confucian learning.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Iron tools and weapons improved through smiths and ore from the Korean kingdoms.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Chinese writing was adopted for court records; the inscribed sword from Inariyama, dated to 471, is among the earliest texts written in Japan.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: The Taika Reform began to remodel the court and its land system on Tang lines.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The imperial line that emerged in this period continues to the present.

passages.title: Legacy
passages.text: The Mozu-Furuichi Kofun Group was listed by UNESCO.
The court moved to a permanent capital at Heijo-kyo in 710, the start of the Nara period.

sectionTitles: Children and the people around them
What science can tell us, and what remains a question

passages.text: Yamnaya names widespread communities of the late fourth and third millennia BCE, known especially from burial mounds and animal herding. They were not one kingdom. The imported map’s 3000 to 2000 BCE span and outline are a rough regional display, not the full chronology or distribution: important early evidence predates it, and related sites extend farther west.

passages.title: Milk remembered by teeth
passages.text: A 2021 study found dairy proteins in fifteen of sixteen Early Bronze Age samples of hardened dental plaque from the steppe. This material, called dental calculus, can trap traces of meals for thousands of years. An ancient tooth sometimes keeps a better food diary than its owner ever could.

passages.title: Milk remembered by teeth
passages.text: Some proteins identified milk from sheep, goats and cattle. They establish dairy consumption, but not a particular recipe. Fresh milk, fermented drinks and processed foods remain possibilities. The researchers emphasize that regular dairy use could coexist with the rarity of the genetic variant associated with digesting milk easily in adulthood.

passages.title: Homes, work and changing pastures
passages.text: In southern Kalmykia, surveys found early third-millennium burial sites beside lowland rivers and on nearby higher ground. Differences in the seasons when graves were built helped researchers reconstruct movements between pastures. Their picture is of groups returning through a local landscape, rather than wandering without a route.

passages.title: Homes, work and changing pastures
passages.text: The same Kalmykia research describes braided mats made from reeds, reed mace and wormwood, interpreted as insulation for portable homes. Plant fibers required gathering and skilled work even where stone buildings were scarce. A movable home still needed someone to make it comfortable.

passages.title: Homes, work and changing pastures
passages.text: Small bone pins from Yamnaya graves in Kalmykia have hammer-shaped heads and finely cut decoration. Their survival shows attention to small crafted objects alongside large burial mounds. We can admire the engraving without pretending to know exactly what each pattern meant to its maker.

passages.title: Homes, work and changing pastures
passages.text: Mykhailivka, on the lower Dnipro, preserves a different side of this world. Its middle and upper layers, attributed to the Yamnaya cultural community, contained workshops for metal, stone and bone objects, surrounded by substantial stone walls and deep ditches. Herding traditions could coexist with places where craftspeople repeatedly gathered and worked.

passages.title: Wooden wheels and journeys
passages.text: Real wooden vehicle parts survive in Yamnaya graves. A 2021 survey collected forty-three well-described examples containing wagons or their components, often wheels. Most vehicles were heavy and had four wheels. These finds document substantial woodworking and transport technology; they are not evidence that everyone owned a wagon.

passages.title: Wooden wheels and journeys
passages.text: People sometimes dismantled a wagon before placing it in a grave: wheels stood separately, while the body could form a bed or a cover. At Izobilnoe near the Urals, clay copies of wheels were arranged like those of a real vehicle. Practical transport also had a place in ceremonies for the dead.

passages.title: Children and the people around them
passages.text: At Boldyrevo-4 in the Southern Urals, archaeologists studied three children, each about six years old, buried in two graves beneath early mounds. The complex dates to around 3300 to 3100 BCE, before this map entry begins. A much larger mound for adults later covered the earlier children’s burials.

passages.title: Children and the people around them
passages.text: The Boldyrevo children’s graves contained pots similar in shape and decoration but made by different techniques. Their burial mats also used different organic materials. Researchers suggest related but distinct groups contributed these objects. Such differences let archaeologists investigate connections between communities without having a written family tree.

passages.title: What science can tell us, and what remains a question
passages.text: Ancient DNA has changed the scale of the story. A major 2015 study found substantial Yamnaya-related ancestry in sampled Corded Ware people from Germany, supporting large movements from the steppe into central Europe. Genetic connections reveal ancestry; they do not by themselves identify someone’s language, personal loyalties or membership in a kingdom.

passages.title: What science can tell us, and what remains a question
passages.text: Writing and language: no attested written sentence from Yamnaya communities is available to quote. Researchers investigate possible Indo-European language connections by comparing later languages alongside archaeology and biological evidence. A reconstructed ancient word can be useful scholarship, but it would not be an inscription that a Yamnaya person left for us.

passages.title: What science can tell us, and what remains a question
passages.text: Did Yamnaya people ride horses? Researchers disagree about how securely the evidence answers that question. A 2024 review warns that skeletal changes attributed to riding could also reflect wagon travel or other activities. A 2026 response argues for early riding using several kinds of evidence. The debate concerns how to recognize an activity that leaves no simple label.

Yamnaya traditions changed at different times across a very large area. In Kalmykia, distinctive Catacomb burial practices overlapped with late Yamnaya groups by the middle of the third millennium BCE. The map’s 2000 BCE endpoint does not mark the fall of a kingdom or the disappearance of its descendants.

passages.text: Yanomami communities live across the forested upper Amazon and Orinoco region in Brazil and Venezuela. The name embraces related peoples and languages, including Sanöma and Ninam. The imported 1492 to 1500 outline is an approximate regional label; it cannot establish every community’s boundary in that period, and its cutoff does not mark their disappearance.

passages.title: Forest histories and threatened territory
passages.text: Oral histories and early documents identify the Serra Parima as an important historical centre. Movement toward surrounding lowlands probably accelerated in the early nineteenth century. Exchange with neighbouring peoples helped bring new crops and metal tools before regular direct encounters with Brazilian officials or missionaries.

passages.title: Forest histories and threatened territory
passages.text: From the 1940s into the 1960s, missions and government posts made outside contact more regular. They supplied manufactured goods and sometimes medical help, but also became sources of measles, influenza and whooping-cough outbreaks. A new trading connection could bring a dangerous new infection.

passages.title: Forest histories and threatened territory
passages.text: Construction of the Perimetral Norte road began in 1973. Communities near its workers suffered infectious disease, while mineral surveys and mining invasions drew outsiders deeper into the forest. The late 1980s brought particularly intense mining pressure, damaging both community health and the land that supplied food.

passages.title: Forest histories and threatened territory
passages.text: Brazil recognised the Terra Indígena Yanomami in 1992, covering about 96,650 square kilometres in Amazonas and Roraima. This Brazilian legal territory is only part of the wider cross-border homeland. It is also home to Ye’kwana, a distinct people whose language belongs to the Karib family.

passages.title: Homes, children and forest materials
passages.text: A UNICEF teaching portrait of a boy named Kiko describes a large circular communal house. Each family had its own cooking fire and hammock space, opening toward a shared centre. An opening in the roof let smoke escape. Several households could have their own corners under one enormous roof.

passages.title: Homes, children and forest materials
passages.text: In the same portrait, a propped-up blackboard marked a new classroom inside the house. Kiko learned fishing, food gathering and beadwork from people around him, and attended afternoon language lessons. Reading his own language and Portuguese joined skills learned through everyday participation.

passages.title: Homes, children and forest materials
passages.text: The Smithsonian catalogues a 1974 film, made from a 1971 project, in which a village headman weaves a cotton hammock while his wife and infant watch. This small domestic scene preserves patient craftwork and family company, a useful reminder that historical records can show ordinary afternoons as well as conflicts.

passages.title: Homes, children and forest materials
passages.text: Women at Maturacá helped researchers identify the fungus Marasmius yanomami, whose shiny black strands decorate baskets. Their association Kumirãyôma documented collecting and using it in a bilingual book with research partners. Something that looks like dark thread can be part of a fungus: forest knowledge becomes visible in a basket.

passages.title: Homes, children and forest materials
passages.text: Hutukara’s 2025 basket catalogue distinguishes different jobs and forms: women make elongated baskets for travelling or storing food, while Sanöma men make certain tubular kitchen utensils and sieves. Baskets sent for sale through the association help obtain goods requested by communities. The catalogue describes an organised community exchange, with different crafts serving different needs.

passages.title: Food knowledge, writing and care
passages.text: Sanöma teachers in Awaris helped produce a 2016 book about local edible mushrooms. Many grow on decaying wood in gardens and in vegetation returning after gardens are left to regrow. The book records local names alongside scientific identifications, bringing experienced forest observers and laboratory specialists into the same conversation.

passages.title: Food knowledge, writing and care
passages.text: A short written sample is “Ana amopö”, the Sanöma title translated on the book’s cover as Portuguese “Cogumelos”, meaning “Mushrooms”. Sanöma is one language within the Yanomami family. This is attested modern Indigenous publishing from 2016, rather than a surviving written label from the map’s fifteenth-century snapshot.

passages.title: Food knowledge, writing and care
passages.text: A Fiocruz study reported in 2024 found mercury in all 287 hair samples examined from nine Ninam villages in the Alto Rio Mucajaí region. Samples had been collected in October 2022, including from children and older people. The findings document a serious local health consequence in an area affected by illegal gold mining.

passages.title: Food knowledge, writing and care
passages.text: In August 2025, a programme in Palimiú and Maloca Paapiú trained community participants to use drones for territorial monitoring. It combined technical practice with local knowledge and safety planning. The aim was to identify threats while reducing direct encounters with intruders, giving communities another way to watch over their forest.

Yanomami peoples continue living across Brazil and Venezuela. Mining, disease and pressure on food supplies have caused grave harm, but the map’s 1500 endpoint is not an ending. Contemporary community publishing and territorial-monitoring initiatives show people preserving knowledge, organising collectively and defending a future on their land.

passages.text: Msiri’s Yeke kingdom developed in nineteenth-century Katanga, with Bunkeya as a major political and trading centre. Nyamwezi migrants and local communities built connections around copper, ivory and other goods. Enslavement and armed coercion were also central to its power.

passages.title: Trade and political power
passages.text: Msiri’s power depended on routes linking inland producers with Atlantic and Indian Ocean commerce. European expeditions followed established routes used by African traders. They arrived in a connected political landscape, not a blank space waiting to be discovered.

passages.title: Trade and political power
passages.text: Sanga resistance disrupted caravans moving toward the Atlantic, and Msiri’s forces tried to restore control. Local opposition mattered alongside European pressure. A royal claim to a large territory did not mean that everyone within it accepted the ruler’s authority.

passages.title: Trade and political power
passages.text: The museum’s regional history describes migrants arriving in different caravans, marrying into surrounding communities and incorporating young people of varied origins. Yeke society took shape through these relationships. A common political identity did not require every family to have the same birthplace.

passages.title: Copper: skill, heat and exchange
passages.text: Copper production in the wider region long predated Msiri. The Bunkeya research project notes evidence reaching back to the fifth century. His kingdom drew on an established field of knowledge and resources; it did not invent the region’s metallurgy.

passages.title: Copper: skill, heat and exchange
passages.text: Nicolas Nikis describes later demonstrations by experienced Yeke smelters near Likasi. They used a two-stage process of smelting and refining in temporary structures, then collected molten copper in a crucible. These recorded demonstrations help recover practical expertise that political documents rarely explain.

passages.title: Copper: skill, heat and exchange
passages.text: Those smelters poured copper into open molds made from clay or termite-mound material, commonly producing rectangular ingots for further working. A useful mold could begin with carefully chosen local earth. The result was a transportable material that other craftspeople could reshape.

passages.title: Copper: skill, heat and exchange
passages.text: Oral traditions recorded among smelters credited Sanga specialists with teaching copperworking to Yeke newcomers. Learning a craft crossed community boundaries. The story identifies skilled local teachers instead of giving every technical achievement to a conquering ruler.

passages.title: Copper: skill, heat and exchange
passages.text: Research on nineteenth-century trade distinguishes copper used in wider exchange from ivory over which Msiri sought tighter control. Copper could also decorate prestigious equipment. The same material moved between practical trade, skilled production and displays of status.

passages.title: Families, songs and recovering Bunkeya
passages.text: Maria de Fonseca, one of Msiri’s wives, belonged to a Portuguese trading family. Her image survives in an 1893 European travel publication discussed by historian Rachel Taylor. Such pictures are evidence of how observers represented women, and need interpretation alongside the women’s political and family connections.

passages.title: Families, songs and recovering Bunkeya
passages.text: A short sample from a modern printed Yeke song collection is “Linumba”, translated there as “The Great House”. The title appears in the royal heritage site’s bilingual collection. It is continuing written cultural expression, not an inscription securely dated to Msiri’s reign.

passages.title: Families, songs and recovering Bunkeya
passages.text: The Bunkeya Plurielle project combines archaeology, documents and oral accounts, working with local communities and artists. It also trains students from the University of Lubumbashi. These are research aims, and they promise ways to study households and crafts beyond the familiar story of Msiri’s death.

passages.title: Families, songs and recovering Bunkeya
passages.text: After Msiri’s death, his successor Mukanda Bantu accommodated Congo Free State rule. The shift preserved a form of Yeke leadership but redirected it within a violent colonial order. Survival of a ruling family was not the same thing as continued independence.
Msiri was killed during the Stairs expedition on 20 December 1891. Congo Free State domination followed; Yeke communities continued. The map’s 1914 endpoint extends beyond the independent kingdom.

passages.text: This map label covers parts of medieval Yemen from about 1000 to 1530, not one state lasting five centuries. Sulayhid rulers, Zaydi imams, Ayyubids, Rasulids and Tahirids held different territories at different times. The broad outline and its changing eastern edge cannot show those divisions accurately. The Rasulids were especially influential in the southern highlands, coastal plain and maritime trade.

passages.title: Courts, towns and competing rulers
passages.text: Queen Arwa, also known as Sayyida Hurra, moved the Sulayhid seat from Sanaa to Dhu Jibla. She built a palace and converted an older one into a mosque. Her future mother-in-law Asma had helped educate her and had herself participated in government. This was an exceptional courtly story of women exercising political and religious authority, not evidence of equal opportunities for every woman.

passages.title: Courts, towns and competing rulers
passages.text: Ayyubid expansion began in the 1170s. The Rasulids emerged as independent rulers around 1228 or 1229 and remained powerful until 1454. Their records show officials organizing territory and markets, alongside scholars writing about history, astronomy, medicine and agriculture. Yet northern Zaydi leaders remained important rivals: one colour on this map hides a much more complicated political landscape.

passages.title: Courts, towns and competing rulers
passages.text: Aden linked the Red Sea with the Indian Ocean. Ships and merchants connected Yemen to distant markets, and the Rasulids made overseas commerce an important part of their power. Inland agriculture and coastal exchange belonged to the same economy: the busy port depended on routes and communities beyond its harbour.

passages.title: Farms, seasons and household responsibilities
passages.text: Farmers used more than one way to obtain water. Irrigation along major wadis worked alongside rainfall and the collection of runoff. A tax register compiled for the Rasulid sultan al-Muayyad, who died in 1321, even preserves a plan of irrigation along Wadi Zabid. Such records connect channels and fields with the government’s interest in harvests and revenue.

passages.title: Farms, seasons and household responsibilities
passages.text: Al-Ashraf’s late-thirteenth-century farming book covered planting times, grain, pulses, fruit, fragrant plants, vegetables and pests. Royal interest could reach right into the garden. Rasulid horticultural experiments included roses and grapevines; agricultural learning was partly about practical cultivation, not only impressive books on a shelf.

passages.title: Farms, seasons and household responsibilities
passages.text: Some crop names remembered a season. Medieval Rasulid sources describe a sorghum variety called baynt, planted in January and harvested in late March. Al-Afdal explained its name by planting between particular stars of the Great Bear. These were local timing traditions, and the elaborate twenty-eight-marker calendar documented much later should not be projected intact into medieval Yemen.

passages.title: Farms, seasons and household responsibilities
passages.text: Long voyages affected the people left at home. Before travelling from Egypt to Yemen, the Jewish merchant Moses ben Yefet arranged money and wheat for his wife Sitt al-Fakhr, their family and a maidservant in Fustat. Their twelfth-century legal agreement specifies 25 dinars and five measures of wheat. He also provided a conditional divorce deed in case he failed to return.

passages.title: Farms, seasons and household responsibilities
passages.text: Moses did reach Aden: his name appears on a letter sent from there in 1156. That letter described a ship lost on the voyage from Aden to India’s Malabar Coast. The documents reveal the risks behind commercial journeys and why families made careful legal arrangements. They survive because papers accumulated in a synagogue storeroom in Cairo.

passages.title: Learning, instruments and written words
passages.text: A brass astrolabe made in Yemen in 1291 names the Rasulid prince Umar ibn Yusuf as its maker. The future sultan wrote about constructing scientific instruments, and a surviving manuscript includes his teachers’ certifications of his skill. An astrolabe brought measurements of the sky into work on time and prayer. Even a prince could need his teachers to sign off on his work.

passages.title: Learning, instruments and written words
passages.text: A scientific text by al-Ashraf tells the maker of a compass bowl to label its rim “شمال جنوب مشرق مغرب”, meaning “north, south, east, west”. This Arabic sample follows Petra Schmidl’s normalized scholarly edition of a manuscript copied in Yemen in 1293, now in Cairo. The directions occur at folio 144v; they are words from an identified medieval witness, rather than a modern invented phrase.

passages.title: Learning, instruments and written words
passages.text: Al-Ashraf’s compass used a magnetized steel needle crossed with a light plant stem and floated on water. His text explains how to protect it from wind and use its approximate alignment to work out the direction of prayer. The author valued a device that could function under clouds or at night, when sighting the sun or stars was difficult.

passages.title: Learning, instruments and written words
passages.text: One fourteenth-century royal manuscript contains a remarkable six-language glossary: Arabic, Persian, Turkic, Greek, Armenian and Mongol, all written in Arabic letters. Vocabulary includes clothing, animals, foods and household equipment. It even explains chopsticks as two pieces of wood used for eating noodles. That entry reveals a compiler’s wide interests; it does not tell us that chopsticks sat on every Yemeni dinner table.

passages.title: Learning, instruments and written words
passages.text: Zabid was an important centre of Islamic learning. UNESCO identifies fourteen surviving madrasas from the Rasulid period, with brick buildings and, in some cases, elaborate carved brick and stucco. Students came for religious knowledge and other sciences. The town’s institutions made education part of its urban identity, although their existence does not establish that every child attended school.

passages.title: Water, medicine and later transformations
passages.text: Books preserved interests in both plant and animal health. Al-Afdal’s agricultural treatise included medicinal plants, while al-Ashraf wrote a separate veterinary work that also discussed fodder crops such as sorghum. These texts show subjects that scholars investigated. They do not prove that every remedy worked or that every household could consult a trained practitioner.

passages.title: Water, medicine and later transformations
passages.text: The Tahirid ruler Amir ibn Abd al-Wahhab founded the Amiriya madrasa at Rada in 1504. Its complex combined a richly decorated, six-domed prayer space with living quarters and facilities for students. Water channels supplied the ablution area, and a large open basin stood beside the building. Keeping a school functioning involved water and accommodation as well as lessons.

passages.title: Water, medicine and later transformations
passages.text: Modern restoration of the Amiriya revived the making of qudad, a waterproof material using lime and crushed volcanic aggregate. Craftspeople tested mixtures when the exact proportions were no longer readily remembered. Conservators also uncovered painted decoration hidden beneath dust, soot and whitewash. The work recovered evidence of historical building skills while training a new generation of specialists.

passages.title: Water, medicine and later transformations
passages.text: The Tahirid defeat in 1517 did not bring all Yemen under one new government. Zaydi rulers expanded from the north, Tahirid remnants held Aden and some fortresses, and military governors based at Zabid claimed Ottoman allegiance. Coins of the last Tahirid prince at Aden include dates in 1529 and 1534. The latter is already beyond this record’s 1530 cutoff.

The map’s 1530 endpoint is not Yemen’s disappearance or the end of one continuous kingdom. Rasulid power had ended in 1454, and the Tahirid sultan was killed in 1517 while smaller Tahirid authorities continued. Ottoman forces took Aden in 1538, beyond this map’s span; Zaydi power and Yemeni communities continued through changing regimes.

sectionTitles: How one atlas label became a united republic
Tall houses, old schools and remarkable nature
Families, neighbours and going to school
Medicine, clean water and public health

passages.text: This card follows the atlas record called “Yemen,” but that single label hides several different political maps. Its 1920 to 1938 shape misses Sana’a and much of the northern highlands as well as British Aden and Socotra; later shapes add the highlands but still omit Aden and Socotra. In history, an independent northern imamate/kingdom emerged after Ottoman rule, a northern republic began in 1962, and the British-ruled south became independent in 1967. The two sovereign states united on 22 May 1990 as the Republic of Yemen. The atlas has no geometry after 2020, while the continuing republic has long been divided by war and rival de facto administrations. Treat the outline as a navigation aid, not a legal border or a claim about who controls each place.

passages.title: How one atlas label became a united republic
passages.text: The atlas begins this record in 1920, but there was no single state covering its modern-looking label then. Much of the north was ruled by an imamate that later used the name Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen. Britain controlled Aden and protectorates in the south. This is why a map reader should not project the 1990 republic backward over everybody living inside today’s borders.

passages.title: How one atlas label became a united republic
passages.text: A revolution proclaimed the Yemen Arab Republic in the north in September 1962. Fighting between republicans and royalists quickly drew in Egypt and Saudi Arabia; the United Nations created an observation mission in 1963. A “republic” on paper therefore did not mean that stable nationwide government arrived overnight.

passages.title: How one atlas label became a united republic
passages.text: Southern Yemen became independent from Britain on 30 November 1967 and was renamed the People’s Democratic Republic of Yemen in 1970. For more than two decades, the Yemen Arab Republic in the north and the southern republic were separate sovereign states, each with its own government and international relationships.

passages.title: How one atlas label became a united republic
passages.text: The two governments signed a unification agreement in Sana’a on 22 April 1990, and it entered into force on 22 May. In its authentic Arabic, the new state is named «الجمهورية اليمنية» (al-Jumhūriyya al-Yamaniyya), “the Republic of Yemen.” Arabic is written from right to left; this is a real legal phrase, not decorative pseudo-script.

passages.title: How one atlas label became a united republic
passages.text: Unification did not settle every struggle over power and resources. The transition included power-sharing and a 1993 election, then collapsed into war in 1994. Southern leaders declared secession, but no state recognized it; northern forces captured Aden in July, and the Republic of Yemen legally remained one state while postwar rule became more centralized.

passages.title: How one atlas label became a united republic
passages.text: Houthi forces and allies seized Sana’a in September 2014. President Hadi later moved to Aden, and a Saudi-led coalition began military operations on 26 March 2015 at his request. The United Nations has continued mediation, but a negotiated nationwide settlement had not restored unified administration by 2026.

passages.title: How one atlas label became a united republic
passages.text: Control today needs a date attached. A World Bank project document prepared in January 2026 described a Sana’a-based Houthi authority and an Aden-based internationally recognized government, with duplicated institutions, currencies and rules. A UN statement on 30 January 2026 likewise referred to “Houthi de facto authorities” in Sana’a-controlled areas and the internationally recognized government in Marib. These descriptions report control; they do not create a new international border.

passages.title: Tall houses, old schools and remarkable nature
passages.text: Old Sana’a sits about 2,200 metres above sea level. Its decorated multi-storey tower houses, dense lanes, mosques and green bustans were shaped over centuries with local stone, fired brick and earth. Fun fact: from a rooftop, the city can look like a gingerbread skyline dusted with white icing, but the white patterns are carefully worked architectural decoration, not frosting.

passages.title: Tall houses, old schools and remarkable nature
passages.text: Shibam’s mud-brick towers rise as high as seven storeys inside a compact walled plan, which is why it is often nicknamed a desert “skyscraper city.” The towers are brilliant climate-and-space engineering, but mud walls need constant care. UNESCO also warns that modern water supplies without equally good drainage have harmed buildings and sanitation, a reminder that adding taps without planning where wastewater goes can backfire.

passages.title: Tall houses, old schools and remarkable nature
passages.text: Zabid was a major centre of Islamic learning, with mosques, madrasas and an old university embedded in a market town of shaded streets and courtyard houses. Courtyards helped families combine airflow, household work and privacy. This scholarly and architectural heritage predates the modern Republic of Yemen; preserving it is a modern responsibility, not evidence that today’s state built it.

passages.title: Tall houses, old schools and remarkable nature
passages.text: Socotra’s isolation produced an extraordinary living laboratory: UNESCO records 825 plant species, of which 307, about 37 per cent, occur nowhere else. The umbrella-shaped dragon’s blood tree is the celebrity, but the whole archipelago matters. Biodiversity evolved over deep time, so it is not a government “invention”; conservation is the achievement people can choose now.

passages.title: Tall houses, old schools and remarkable nature
passages.text: A small UNDP-backed experiment trained women and young people to install and manage solar microgrids in three frontline communities. UNDP reported that local electricity costs fell by 65 per cent and that women became technicians and business managers. That is clever, practical wartime problem-solving, but three communities are a pilot, not proof that Yemen’s national power crisis has been solved.

passages.title: Families, neighbours and going to school
passages.text: Family and neighbourhood life varies enormously among highland cities, coastal towns, islands, farms and displacement camps. Historic courtyard houses could screen domestic life from a busy street, while Shibam’s vertical homes stacked rooms upward inside a tight city wall. Architecture gives clues about privacy and social life, but it cannot tell us that every family lived, or lives, the same way.

passages.title: Families, neighbours and going to school
passages.text: In Jader village, children once walked about an hour to a distant school and crossed a dangerous road. Parents and neighbours helped establish a closer learning space; UNICEF supported a new school. The story shows how education can be a family logistics puzzle as much as a classroom lesson. In 2025 UNICEF estimated 3.7 million children aged 5 to 17 were out of school nationwide.

passages.title: Families, neighbours and going to school
passages.text: Bathrooms can decide whether a child stays in class. Mohamed, a student with diabetes, used to carry a 1.5-litre bottle because his school lacked safe water and usable toilets. Girls sometimes went home or avoided drinking because there was no privacy. After repairs brought running water and separate facilities, school became easier. In 2017 UNICEF-supported work improved WASH facilities in 232 schools, substantial, but far from every school.

passages.title: Families, neighbours and going to school
passages.text: In displacement sites in Al Jawf, some women and children collected water by donkey, missed lessons and had to use open ground as a toilet. Emergency water points and latrines improved privacy and cleanliness. Kid fact with a serious point: a toilet is a small room with a huge job, it protects dignity, school attendance and drinking water all at once.

passages.title: Medicine, clean water and public health
passages.text: Community midwives often connect remote families to the health system. In Marib, midwife Warda provided antenatal and postnatal checks, health education and family-planning counselling, and arranged referral when care was beyond what she could safely handle. Her story shows skilled local care and quick judgment; it does not mean every village has a trained midwife or a functioning referral route.

passages.title: Medicine, clean water and public health
passages.text: At Habil Jabr clinic in 2025, families brought children for vaccines, vitamins and treatment of fever and other common illnesses. UNICEF reported supplying 288 primary-health-care kits to supported facilities in late 2024 and early 2025. Kits keep routine care moving, but they cannot repair an entire health system, pay every worker or end shortages caused by war.

passages.title: Medicine, clean water and public health
passages.text: Vaccination teams achieved an important but limited result in southern governorates: WHO reported in March 2026 that transmission of circulating vaccine-derived poliovirus type 2 had been interrupted there, supported by vaccination and surveillance training. “In the south” matters. It would be wrong to turn this into a claim that all polio risk had disappeared throughout Yemen.

passages.title: Medicine, clean water and public health
passages.text: Clean-water lessons can be lifesaving science. In 2024, 6,448 pupils at 20 schools in Lahj learned why handwashing matters and how open defecation, uncovered wells and contaminated water can spread cholera and other disease. The funniest bathroom lesson may be the truest: germs do not care whether a toilet topic feels embarrassing, so asking good questions beats pretending toilets do not exist.

passages.title: Medicine, clean water and public health
passages.text: The emergency remained severe on 24 September 2026. WHO reported that about 60 per cent of assessed health units were fully functioning, and only 6 per cent offered trauma care, amid new displacement and disease outbreaks. These are dated operational figures, not a permanent description of Yemen. They explain why small successes, one stocked clinic, repaired toilet or trained vaccinator, matter so much.

The Republic of Yemen has not “ended.” It remains the single internationally recognized UN member created by the 1990 merger, while rival authorities exercise de facto control over different areas and war has fragmented institutions. The atlas stops drawing the country after 2020 because its basemap coverage stops, not because Yemen vanished. As of 24 September 2026, conflict and humanitarian need were still changing conditions on the ground, so any present-control description should be read with its date attached.

passages.text: Yolngu peoples maintain distinct clan identities in Arnhem Land. Country, law, food, ceremony and art remain connected, while institutions at Yirrkala carry knowledge through contemporary media.

passages.title: Worldview and institutions
passages.text: Dhuwa and Yirritja are complementary moieties connecting people, places and other living beings. In Miwatj, art and ceremony express relationships to fresh and saltwater Country.

passages.title: Food and seasons
passages.text: Seasonal food gathering draws on both land and sea, including yams, fruit, fish and shellfish. Traditional owners connect these practices with law and ceremony.

passages.title: Art and diplomacy
passages.text: Artists framed the Yirrkala petitions with clan designs in ochre, charcoal and pipeclay. These designs expressed relationships to land alongside text in English and Yolngu Matha.

passages.title: Political history
passages.text: Yolngu presented bark petitions to the Australian Parliament in 1963 in response to mining plans made without adequate consultation. They understood the documents as a diplomatic offering between equal powers.

passages.title: Digital knowledge
passages.text: The Mulka Project combines a recording studio, production house, learning centre and cultural archive under Yolngu law and elder leadership. It trains community members and returns audiovisual records to communities.

passages.title: Continuity
passages.text: A bark petition formerly held privately was formally returned to Yolngu at Yirrkala in 2023. Its return forms part of continuing cultural custody.
