sectionTitles: Courts, cities and the people who sustained them
Learning useful skills, making cloth and moving food
Warm water, food and children at play
Porcelain, family hopes and surviving writing

passages.text: The Yuan was the Mongol ruling dynasty proclaimed in China in 1271; the Southern Song fell in 1279. Its courts connected Chinese cities and farming regions with a wider Eurasian world. The imported map repeats a vast outline through 1492, although Yuan rule in China ended in 1368. That later outline must not be read as continued Yuan control of the same territory.

passages.title: Courts, cities and the people who sustained them
passages.text: At Dadu, now Beijing, Mongol emperors used Chinese administrative practices while governing a population with many languages and backgrounds. Yuan China was part of the wider story of Mongol expansion, but it was not the same political unit as every Mongol khanate across Eurasia.

passages.title: Courts, cities and the people who sustained them
passages.text: Xanadu, or Shangdu, was a summer capital on the grasslands. Its remains combine a planned palace city with spaces for encampments and royal hunting. The court could live among substantial walls and buildings while keeping room for practices associated with mobile steppe life.

passages.title: Courts, cities and the people who sustained them
passages.text: The remains of Xanadu’s Tiefan’gan Canal show that even a magnificent capital needed practical water management. Archaeologists have also investigated palace and temple mounds, with some remains reburied for protection. The famous city is more than a traveller’s story: its layout can still be studied in the ground.

passages.title: Courts, cities and the people who sustained them
passages.text: Rural cooperatives were organized around roughly fifty households and a village leader. Their tasks included farming, planting trees, reclaiming land and flood control. These groups also counted households and watched for opposition to the government. Village cooperation and state supervision could arrive in the same package.

passages.title: Courts, cities and the people who sustained them
passages.text: Cooperative granaries could help widows, orphans and older people when harvests failed. Yet major projects also required labour recruited from farming households: canals, postal stations and the capital took time and effort away from fields. Useful public works could carry a heavy cost for the families building them.

passages.title: Learning useful skills, making cloth and moving food
passages.text: Wang Zhen’s Agricultural Treatise, completed in 1313, paired explanations with drawings of equipment such as harrows, watermills and silk-reeling machines. Officials could use this information to teach practical methods. A drawing helped a carpenter see how parts fitted together: instructions were becoming something you could build from.

passages.title: Learning useful skills, making cloth and moving food
passages.text: Wang also recorded cotton-processing tools, including gins, bows and spinning wheels, at a time when their use was spreading. Cotton needed different handling from silk or hemp. The achievement lay partly in collecting and sharing existing skills, so useful knowledge could travel beyond the people who already knew it.

passages.title: Learning useful skills, making cloth and moving food
passages.text: The Grand Canal had centuries of history before the Yuan. By the thirteenth century its connected artificial waterways extended for more than 2,000 kilometres, linking major river basins. Grain transport and storage helped feed cities, troops and the court. A capital’s impressive skyline depended on boats carrying very ordinary rice.

passages.title: Learning useful skills, making cloth and moving food
passages.text: Marco Polo described Suzhou as a city of silk production, brocade, craftspeople and merchants using paper money. His account gives a traveller’s view of busy urban work, alongside its enthusiasm for wealth and grandeur. Making cloth meant skilled hands behind the luxurious clothes seen at court.

passages.title: Warm water, food and children at play
passages.text: Polo also described coal dug from mountain seams, saying a well-lit fire could still be burning the next morning. He connected this fuel with the demand for hot baths, including private baths among wealthy households. Heating the bath was a substantial job before anyone could complain that the water was getting cold.

passages.title: Warm water, food and children at play
passages.text: In 1330 the court nutritionist Hu Sihui compiled the Yinshan Zhengyao, a work joining food and medicine. It advised moderation and avoiding spoiled meat, while also containing medical beliefs particular to its time. This was advice for a courtly setting, not a record of what every family ate.

passages.title: Warm water, food and children at play
passages.text: The same book brings together Chinese food knowledge with Central and West Asian dishes. Many recipes use sheep or noodles, while another section gives medicinal soups, drinks and syrups. Its pages preserve a meeting of cuisines within the Yuan court; their historical interest does not make every old remedy effective.

passages.title: Warm water, food and children at play
passages.text: A fourteenth-century red lacquer tray shows two women supervising boys playing in a garden. Some children hide, some ride hobbyhorses, and others stage a pretend procession of officials. One carries a parasol for their important-looking playmate. Apparently, acting like a very grand grown-up has been entertaining for quite a while.

passages.title: Warm water, food and children at play
passages.text: On that same tray, three boys bathe in a shallow tub. The carved scene includes a pond, rocks and a veranda, with patterns distinguishing different surfaces. It is an idealized image of comfortable garden life, and also evidence of the skill needed to carve an intricate picture into lacquer.

passages.title: Porcelain, family hopes and surviving writing
passages.text: In 1351 Zhang Wenjin offered a pair of porcelain vases and an incense burner to a Daoist temple. The vase inscription asks for his family’s protection and his children’s peace. Alongside emperors and battles, a named person left us this very recognizable hope: please keep my family safe.

passages.title: Porcelain, family hopes and surviving writing
passages.text: A short phrase on the vase reads “子女平安”, meaning “peace for sons and daughters”. These are Chinese characters from the dated 1351 dedication, copied from the museum’s transcription. The words are part of the donor’s prayer, rather than a modern saying added to decorate the story.

passages.title: Porcelain, family hopes and surviving writing
passages.text: The vases were made at Jingdezhen with cobalt-blue decoration beneath the glaze. Elephant heads form their handles, and dragons, phoenixes and plants fill the surfaces. Their dated dedication helps researchers place this accomplished ceramic work in time; 1351 is the offering’s date, not the invention of blue-and-white porcelain.

passages.title: Porcelain, family hopes and surviving writing
passages.text: A merchant ship travelling from China to Japan sank near Sinan, off Korea, in the early fourteenth century. Its recovered cargo includes ceramics from the Longquan kilns, alongside personal possessions of passengers and crew. A small celadon vase with dragon-like handles makes that long trading route tangible: useful and beautiful things crossed the sea.

Rebellion and political crisis brought Yuan rule in China to an end in 1368, when the Ming took power. Mongol rulers and communities continued farther north, and some Mongol officials and soldiers served the Ming. The atlas’s 1492 endpoint and repeated outline do not mark a historical survival of Yuan government across China.

sectionTitles: Start with the exact atlas feature and its giant warning label
The chronology is a twelve-year window inside a four-century polygon
Historical geography points east of the atlas shape
A ruler, envoys and a clever alliance come into view
Rouran conflict is vivid, but the chronicle likes a good story
Herding, craft and exchange are regional clues, not a Yueban inventory
Families, ranks and learning mostly hide behind court politics
Hair could shine; houses, meals and play are harder to see
Medicine, water, bathing and toilets need separate answers
The surviving sentence is Chinese testimony about Yueban

passages.text: Imagine trying to find a kingdom that appears on a map for four centuries but steps into surviving history for only twelve years. Yueban is that puzzle. A later Chinese history traced its people to Northern Xiongnu followers left north of Kucha after a defeat around 89 CE, yet modern source study securely sees the name only from 437 to 448. In 437 envoys reached Northern Wei. In 448 they asked that empire to squeeze their Rouran enemies from the east while Yueban pressed from the west. The chronicle also preserves shiny buttered hair, frequent washing, sulfur used as medicine, weather-making claims and drum-and-dance rhythms adopted at the Wei court. These wonderful details still come through an outsider’s pen. Then Yueban disappears from dated records; theories linking it to Avars or Hephthalites disagree. The atlas makes the mystery bigger: one tiny unchanged polygon sits west of Lake Balkhash at 100, 200, 300 and 400, far from many historical placements around Ili, Chu, Tarbagatai or north of Issyk-Kul. Read it as a display shape, not a four-hundred-year border certificate.

passages.title: Start with the exact atlas feature and its giant warning label
passages.text: The exact id is yueban, labelled “Yueban” and indexed circa 100 to 500. Initial coverage calls it an approximate state with no card and four intervals: 100 to 200, 200 to 300, 300 to 400 and 400 to 500. Those intervals describe imported map files, not four centuries of documented government.

passages.title: Start with the exact atlas feature and its giant warning label
passages.text: At 100 the target is one Polygon with one ring and nine coordinate positions. Its bounds are [71.41931419314193, 44.50546215401255, 75.33615336153363, 47.772249836919286], its raw coordinate SHA-256 is d5fce106a2f8d45ea140352a79c7db162273d47b573c146e5d47906126447ad2, and its canonical geometry hash is c3bbdc5b2d998c0a00c5c47d341e5155b01198a4ba1cf343b45ac0161fe8f6bc. Every count comes from decoded TopoJSON coordinates, not a screenshot.

passages.title: Start with the exact atlas feature and its giant warning label
passages.text: Point tests place only the western Lake Balkhash test point inside. Tacheng, the Emil valley, Tarbagatai, Bortala, the Dzungarian Gate, Ili/Yining, Issyk-Kul, Suyab, eastern Balkhash, Altai, Urumqi, Turfan, Kucha, Kashgar, Tashkent, Fergana, Otrar and Dunhuang all fall outside. The result is geometric, not historical.

passages.title: Start with the exact atlas feature and its giant warning label
passages.text: The 100, 200 and 300 snapshots have exactly the same raw coordinate hash. The 400 raw hash changes to b1d3e85fa37e2661e1bba78461e366f7b4aa5d1709acc90cbfe8e56357fc1766 only because the closed ring starts at another vertex; rotation- and direction-independent canonical hashes prove all four outlines are geometrically identical.

passages.title: Start with the exact atlas feature and its giant warning label
passages.text: The exact target is absent at 1 BCE, 500 and 600. The index separately names earlier Xiongnu, Southern Xiongnu and later ruanruan; it contains no actual Xianbei, Kidarite or Hephthalite id. Map labels are separate data identities, and none should be silently merged into Yueban.

passages.title: The chronology is a twelve-year window inside a four-century polygon
passages.text: The Wei Shu origin story looks back to Dou Xian’s defeat of the Northern Xiongnu in 89 CE and says weaker followers stayed north of Kucha. Because the history was compiled centuries later, this is retrospective ancestry, not a contemporary certificate that a Yueban state began in 100.

passages.title: The chronology is a twelve-year window inside a four-century polygon
passages.text: A modern multilingual sourcebook says Yueban appears in Chinese history only in 437 to 448. That narrow statement matters: earlier residents, ancestors or archaeological cultures may have existed, but the name and polity cannot be followed securely through the atlas years 100, 200 or 300.

passages.title: The chronology is a twelve-year window inside a four-century polygon
passages.text: In 437 Yueban was among western states whose envoys reached Northern Wei. The annal record does not supply the envoys’ names, route or conversations. Even the first appearance therefore cannot become a cinematic scene we pretend to reconstruct for readers today.

passages.title: The chronology is a twelve-year window inside a four-century polygon
passages.text: The last securely dated notice is 448: Yueban envoys came twice, requested a coordinated attack on Rouran from east and west, and offered court marvel stories. “After this they often sent tribute” may be a conventional closing formula; it supplies no list of later years, rulers or places.

passages.title: The chronology is a twelve-year window inside a four-century polygon
passages.text: Older UNESCO synthesis associates a Yueban realm near Balkhash with Northern Xiongnu migration and treats its roots as early. That is a historiographical reconstruction, not equal evidence to dated embassies. This card keeps the origin possibility while refusing to manufacture annual events from 100 to 436.

passages.title: Historical geography points east of the atlas shape
passages.text: Wei Shu calls Yueban northwest of Wusun and gives a court-distance figure from the Northern Wei capital. Such directional geography is approximate and depends on what “Wusun” meant to the compiler; it does not plot a survey line or justify a modern national boundary.

passages.title: Historical geography points east of the atlas shape
passages.text: Yu reconstructs a move from north of Kucha into former Wusun land in the Ili and Chu river valleys after Rouran pressure pushed Wusun toward the Pamirs. He repeatedly marks parts of this reconstruction as probable or possible, so the route belongs on a dotted line.

passages.title: Historical geography points east of the atlas shape
passages.text: Selbitschka locates the small Yueban polity north of Issyk-Kul in modern northeastern Kyrgyzstan. That differs in detail from Ili and Chu valley or Tarbagatai placements, but all lie well east or southeast of the atlas polygon west of Lake Balkhash. Sources agree only approximately.

passages.title: Historical geography points east of the atlas shape
passages.text: Rouran was a separate imperial confederation founded in 402. Kradin reconstructs its western reach to the Ili River and Tarim depression, with a core, dependent groups and military hierarchy. The 400 atlas likewise draws a huge ruanruan polygon distinct from tiny Yueban.

passages.title: Historical geography points east of the atlas shape
passages.text: At 400 the separate Ruanruan feature contains Tacheng, Emil, Tarbagatai, Bortala, the Dzungarian Gate, Ili, eastern Balkhash, Altai, Urumqi and Turfan, while Yueban contains only western Balkhash. The imported display therefore reverses much of the historical placement and deserves an explicit geography warning.

passages.title: A ruler, envoys and a clever alliance come into view
passages.text: Wei Shu reports more than 200,000 people over several thousand li and says Liangzhou people called the ruler “Chanyu King.” These are outsider estimates and remembered titles, not census sheets or proof of an unbroken imperial office. They do show a ranked leadership recognizable to Chinese informants.

passages.title: A ruler, envoys and a clever alliance come into view
passages.text: Northern Wei “tribute” was active diplomacy rather than automatic surrender. Selbitschka shows that foreign courts used gifts and embassies to negotiate peace and help. Yueban’s 448 offering strengthened a practical request: pressure Rouran from two directions before more raids arrived.

passages.title: A ruler, envoys and a clever alliance come into view
passages.text: The 437 embassy placed Yueban in a broad Western Regions network reaching the Northern Wei court. We do not know the envoys’ names, exact route, cargo or spoken language. Their arrival still demonstrates organized messengers, elite authorization and knowledge of a distant political opportunity.

passages.title: A ruler, envoys and a clever alliance come into view
passages.text: In 448 Yueban asked Northern Wei to attack Rouran from the east while Yueban acted from the west. The emperor accepted, ordered forces ready and appointed a vanguard. This is the clearest Yueban political achievement: using distance, timing and a stronger partner as strategic tools.

passages.title: A ruler, envoys and a clever alliance come into view
passages.text: Northern Wei forces drilled, toured north and stored supplies, but did not meet the Rouran force in the recorded expedition. Yu concludes that the court acted “to some extent” in cooperation, while the joint action lacked the expected effect. Alliance paperwork was real; victory remains unproved.

passages.title: Rouran conflict is vivid, but the chronicle likes a good story
passages.text: Shelun created the Rouran imperial confederation in 402, organized forces by hundreds and thousands and expanded toward Ili and the Tarim. Kradin also identifies a grave Rouran crisis from 438 to 470. Yueban diplomacy belongs inside this larger contest, not in an empty steppe.

passages.title: Rouran conflict is vivid, but the chronicle likes a good story
passages.text: Wei Shu says Yueban first allied with Rouran, then a Yueban king visited with thousands, mocked Rouran washing customs and fled before pursuers caught him. Treat this as hostile court ethnography and a moralizing origin tale for war, not a hidden camera recording everyone’s cleanliness.

passages.title: Rouran conflict is vivid, but the chronicle likes a good story
passages.text: The same passage says Yueban ritual specialists summoned rain, wind, snow and flood against raiders. It proves that envoys reported supernatural protection and that a Chinese textual tradition preserved the claim. It does not prove weather control; storms remain weather, even when diplomats give them excellent publicity.

passages.title: Rouran conflict is vivid, but the chronicle likes a good story
passages.text: No reviewed source securely inventories a Yueban bow, saddle, armor or army size. Mounted warfare is plausible in the political setting, but borrowing every Xiongnu or Rouran weapon would erase differences. The safe military picture is raids, pursuit, envoys and planned pincer action: nothing more precise.

passages.title: Rouran conflict is vivid, but the chronicle likes a good story
passages.text: After 448, scholars have variously connected Yueban with European Avars or Hephthalites, while others reject those routes. Kidarites ruled Tokharistan and Gandhara and Hephthalites built a different later power. Similar “Hun” labels are clues for research, not permission to fuse dynasties.

passages.title: Herding, craft and exchange are regional clues, not a Yueban inventory
passages.text: Modern archaeology rejects the cartoon in which every Central Asian “nomad” ate only meat and moved constantly. Eastern Kazakhstan and western Xinjiang show mixed herding, farming and craft production with varied mobility. Yueban may have shared that landscape, but no excavated economy bears its name tag.

passages.title: Herding, craft and exchange are regional clues, not a Yueban inventory
passages.text: Begash in eastern Kazakhstan has a Phase 4 dated about 70 to 550, conventionally called Wusun. It shows intermittent use by smaller groups, with hearths and trash pits rather than a permanent Yueban capital. The overlap in time and region makes comparison useful; attribution remains explicitly non-Yueban.

passages.title: Herding, craft and exchange are regional clues, not a Yueban inventory
passages.text: Phase 4 finds at Begash include broken or unfinished spindle whorls, an iron rivet, ceramic slag and a cut bronze plate. They reveal spinning, repair and small-scale production in a regional pastoral setting. They cannot identify Yueban women, workshops or uniforms without inscriptions or stronger context.

passages.title: Herding, craft and exchange are regional clues, not a Yueban inventory
passages.text: Dental calculus and isotope research in the eastern Dzhungar Mountains finds long traditions of ruminant dairy, horse products and millet, with more agrarian food after the era of Han and Xiongnu rivalry. That makes a mixed menu possible around Yueban’s world, but it is regional evidence, not their dinner receipt.

passages.title: Herding, craft and exchange are regional clues, not a Yueban inventory
passages.text: Yueban envoys also carried knowledge: the Northern Wei court ordered Yueban drum-and-dance rhythms placed in its Music Bureau. That is a real cultural transfer and a rare achievement visible in the text. We have the adoption notice, not the melody, choreography or surviving Yueban instrument.

passages.title: Families, ranks and learning mostly hide behind court politics
passages.text: The surviving record distinguishes a king, accompanying followers, envoys, reported specialists and a large unnamed population. It does not explain councils, clans, taxes, property or succession. “Chanyu King” indicates remembered prestige, while actual power probably depended on followers and alliances we cannot enumerate.

passages.title: Families, ranks and learning mostly hide behind court politics
passages.text: No secure Yueban source gives household size, marriage rules, inheritance, pregnancy care or women’s named roles. Regional pastoral economies required extensive household labor, but assigning every task by gender would be modern guesswork. Women and families mattered; the archive simply does not describe them fairly.

passages.title: Families, ranks and learning mostly hide behind court politics
passages.text: No Yueban school, primer, teacher or child’s exercise survives. Children may have learned herding, spinning, routes and diplomacy by joining household work, yet that is an inference from regional activities. The honest lesson plan has many blank spaces and no made-up “typical school day.”

passages.title: Families, ranks and learning mostly hide behind court politics
passages.text: The embassy stories imply specialist learning: messengers navigated distant courts, performers knew music and dance, ritual experts knew ceremonies, and healers claimed plant knowledge. Sources never tell us who trained them, at what age or whether skills stayed inside families, so apprenticeship remains possible rather than proven.

passages.title: Families, ranks and learning mostly hide behind court politics
passages.text: A reported population above 200,000 is too round and too distant to treat as a modern census. It may signal that Northern Wei writers imagined a substantial polity. It cannot calculate family count, childhood survival, social percentages or the number of people living inside the atlas polygon.

passages.title: Hair could shine; houses, meals and play are harder to see
passages.text: Regional comparison at Begash suggests repeatedly used winter camps near pasture rather than aimless wandering. During the Yueban-era phase, earlier houses were mostly out of use and smaller periodic occupations left hearths and refuse pits. No structure there is securely a Yueban family home.

passages.title: Hair could shine; houses, meals and play are harder to see
passages.text: Wei Shu says people cut hair level with the eyebrows and rubbed it with clarified butter until it shone. That unforgettable detail may preserve real grooming, but it comes through an outsider’s ethnographic contrast. It is not proof that every age, gender and season followed one hairstyle.

passages.title: Hair could shine; houses, meals and play are harder to see
passages.text: Clarified butter appears in the hair report, not on a Yueban menu. Regional science makes dairy, meat and millet plausible foods, while mixed-economy archaeology allows grain and plant products too. Exact dishes, cooking pots, feast rules and children’s portions remain unknown; shiny hair is not a cookbook.

passages.title: Hair could shine; houses, meals and play are harder to see
passages.text: Hearths, spindle whorls, iron pieces and trash pits show cooking, textile work, repair and waste disposal in the wider region. Yueban musicians supplied drum-and-dance patterns admired at court. Together they suggest busy work and performance, while no securely Yueban toy or game rule has been found.

passages.title: Hair could shine; houses, meals and play are harder to see
passages.text: The sources record embassies but no Yueban market list, coin series or caravan tariff. People and gifts moved far, so elite exchange clearly occurred. Ordinary barter, animal sales and craft circulation remain possibilities; the evidence cannot price even one sheep for us.

passages.title: Medicine, water, bathing and toilets need separate answers
passages.text: Wei Shu describes a southern “Fire Mountain,” melted-looking rock and material people collected as medicine, identifying it as stone sulfur. The observation may join volcanic geography with mineral use, but the location is uncertain and the text gives no recipe, dose, illness or test of benefit.

passages.title: Medicine, water, bathing and toilets need separate answers
passages.text: A 448 embassy brought a performer or healer who claimed to stop terrible bleeding with herbs after cutting throats or crushing heads. The emperor reportedly tested the method on condemned prisoners. This is a sensational court marvel story and an ethical horror, not clinical proof or safe medical advice.

passages.title: Medicine, water, bathing and toilets need separate answers
passages.text: Weather-makers, sulfur collectors and herb specialists show that the chronicle associated Yueban with practical and ritual knowledge. It does not preserve diagnosis, childbirth care, wound cleaning or common remedies. Families certainly faced sickness and injury, but everyday medicine remains mostly outside the written spotlight.

passages.title: Medicine, water, bathing and toilets need separate answers
passages.text: Begash stood beside a spring-fed stream that still carries water year-round, illustrating why seasonal camps favored dependable water. Yueban reconstructions also cluster around major valleys. Neither fact proves pipes, wells or household storage, and the atlas polygon’s western-Balkhash position cannot answer a plumbing question.

passages.title: Medicine, water, bathing and toilets need separate answers
passages.text: The famous line says they bathed and rinsed three times daily before eating. It may express admired cleanliness through an outsider’s moral comparison. Bathing and mouth-rinsing are not toilet systems: no secure Yueban latrine, sewer, drain or waste rule has been identified, while regional trash pits are not privies.

passages.title: The surviving sentence is Chinese testimony about Yueban
passages.text: The Book of Wei was compiled by Wei Shou and presented in 554, more than a century after the 448 embassy. Its Western Regions chapter preserves earlier reports but speaks in an outside court’s Classical Chinese voice. Genre, distance and later compilation all matter when reading daily-life claims.

passages.title: The surviving sentence is Chinese testimony about Yueban
passages.text: Authentic written sample transmitted for the Yueban notice: “日三澡漱，然後飲食。” These eight Classical Chinese characters belong to an external Chinese textual tradition about Yueban. They are directly relevant evidence, but they are not an indigenous Yueban inscription, manuscript, alphabet, authorial voice or community self-description.

passages.title: The surviving sentence is Chinese testimony about Yueban
passages.text: Modern Mandarin pinyin: “Rì sān zǎo shù, ránhòu yǐnshí.” Translation: “Three times a day they bathed and rinsed; only afterward did they eat and drink.” The pinyin helps present readers pronounce today’s Chinese reading; it is not a reconstruction of sixth-century pronunciation or Yueban speech.

passages.title: The surviving sentence is Chinese testimony about Yueban
passages.text: Wei Shu says Yueban customs and language resembled Gaoche, but no securely Yueban-authored text survives and scholars disagree about early Hunnic languages. Names and outsider comparisons cannot invent a vernacular script. The sample must remain labelled external Classical Chinese court testimony.

passages.title: The surviving sentence is Chinese testimony about Yueban
passages.text: The weather story shows reported ritual specialists, yet no named Yueban deity, temple or shared creed survives. After 448 the political name fades; people, families and practices may have joined later groups, but Avar, Kidarite, Hephthalite or other continuities remain hypotheses rather than a documented royal succession.

Yueban has no documented final battle or extinction. The last secure dated action is the 448 alliance request; the atlas continues the unchanged polygon to its 500 seam, where the feature disappears. Later scholars proposed movement toward Europe, an Avar connection or identification with Hephthalites, but interdisciplinary work finds the bridges uncertain, while Kidarite and Hephthalite dynasties have their own southern settings and evidence. This bundle therefore marks 448 as the last attested political record, not the day families or communities vanished.

endingContinuity.question: Does the narrative identify what ended or continued, with dates, mechanism and uncertainty?

sectionTitles: The atlas under a magnifying glass
A migration forced by rival powers
Health, water and the toilet question

passages.text: The Yuezhi story crosses a continent. Chinese histories place them near Dunhuang and Gansu, where Xiongnu victories in 176 and 162 BCE drove the greater group west. After another displacement near the Ili valley, they crossed Central Asia and became overlords of Bactria by about 130 BCE. There they met walled towns, farmers, merchants and Greek-style coins; migration did not turn every resident into Yuezhi. Zhang Qian found their royal camp north of the Oxus and reported that they declined a Han alliance. Later sources describe five regional chiefs. In the first century CE, Kushan chief Kujula Kadphises brought those domains together and began a much larger empire. The atlas gets this journey badly out of step: its only Yuezhi polygon, from 200 to 100 BCE, still covers Dunhuang and the Hexi corridor, then paints an enormous Kushan realm too early. Read those shapes as rough locators. The clearest material evidence comes later, from Khalchayan art, coins, inscriptions and successor cities, while Yuezhi language, ordinary schooling, medicine and toilets remain poorly documented.

passages.title: The atlas under a magnifying glass
passages.text: The exact atlas target is id “yuezhi,” labeled Yuezhi and indexed circa 200 to 100 BCE. Its only feature is one Polygon with one ring and 26 coordinate positions. The decoded bounds run from about 72.280° to 106.044° east and 30.175° to 48.408° north.

passages.title: The atlas under a magnifying glass
passages.text: Point tests make the mismatch easy to see. Dunhuang and a central Hexi corridor point fall inside the 200 BCE shape, but the Ili valley, Issyk-Kul, Kashgar, Ferghana, Samarkand, Balkh, Termez, Kabul and Merv all fall outside. Geometry precision does not rescue historical timing.

passages.title: The atlas under a magnifying glass
passages.text: At 100 BCE the atlas replaces Yuezhi with a huge Kushan polygon covering tested places from Kashgar to Merv and Kabul. At 1 BCE Kushan disappears, then a smaller Kushan feature returns in 100 CE. That flicker is a dataset seam, not two documented imperial collapses.

passages.title: The atlas under a magnifying glass
passages.text: There is no yuezhi feature in the 300 BCE snapshot and no exact feature after 200 BCE. Appearance and disappearance therefore say only how this imported atlas grouped its snapshots. They do not date the people’s origin, migration, conquest of Bactria or transformation into Kushan rule.

passages.title: The atlas under a magnifying glass
passages.text: Older scholarship often equated the Yuezhi with the Tocharians, but archaeology and language do not make that identity automatic. No surviving Yuezhi sentence tells us what language the migrating confederation spoke. Genetic labels, later manuscripts and similar names cannot be snapped together like puzzle pieces without evidence.

passages.title: A migration forced by rival powers
passages.text: In 176 BCE, Xiongnu ruler Maodun defeated the Yuezhi in Gansu. This is a political and military event preserved by outside historians, not a census of every Yuezhi family. Some people moved, some may have followed later, and movement across such distances cannot be reduced to one arrow on a map.

passages.title: A migration forced by rival powers
passages.text: Around 162 BCE, Laoshang again crushed Yuezhi refugees in the Ili valley and pushed the greater group southwest. The two dated defeats explain why the journey came in stages. They also show why the atlas’s single 200 BCE shape cannot represent one stable homeland or surveyed state.

passages.title: A migration forced by rival powers
passages.text: The Shiji says a smaller group unable to follow took refuge among Qiang communities near the southern mountains and became known as the Little Yuezhi. “Great” and “Little” are labels in Chinese records. They should not be turned into neat, biologically separate peoples.

passages.title: A migration forced by rival powers
passages.text: Chapter 123 of the Shiji centers on Zhang Qian’s mission to the Dayuezhi. A rare-book witness preserved by Toyo Bunko now has page images and DOI metadata online. The archive notes that his observations informed later Han action and that a second western mission followed in 116 BCE.

passages.title: A migration forced by rival powers
passages.text: Zhang Qian found that the Yuezhi had conquered fertile Bactria and no longer wanted revenge badly enough to march east for Han. Their refusal shows political choice after catastrophe: leaders weighed distance, safety and new resources rather than obediently following the alliance plan imagined in Chang’an.

passages.title: Power in Bactria
passages.text: Greek and Roman writers name several nomadic groups in Bactria, while Chinese histories foreground the Yuezhi. Saka studies warn that pottery and invasions cannot always be assigned to one ethnicity. The end of Greco-Bactrian rule was a tangled regional change, not a clean handover between two uniform nations.

passages.title: Power in Bactria
passages.text: Around 130 BCE, Zhang Qian described Yuezhi camping grounds north of the Oxus and many Bactrian city principalities south of it under Yuezhi domination. Mobile rulers and settled subjects could exist together. Calling the whole population “Yuezhi” would erase Bactrian farmers, traders and local chiefs.

passages.title: Power in Bactria
passages.text: The Hou Han Shu later names five xihou or yabghus: Xiumi, Shuangmi, Guishuang, Xidun and Dumi. Scholars debate the places behind those transcriptions. What matters for this card is the political structure: several regional chiefs shared the Yuezhi-Bactrian world before one Kushan branch became dominant.

passages.title: Power in Bactria
passages.text: Coin hoards from Kunduz and Ai Khanum contain posthumous imitations of Eucratides and Heliocles. New rulers reused familiar Greek royal designs instead of inventing money from nothing. The coins reveal continuity in workshops and exchange, though a copied portrait does not identify the ethnicity of every maker or user.

passages.title: Power in Bactria
passages.text: More than a century after the migration, Kujula Kadphises of Guishuang overcame the other chiefs and styled himself king. His coins gradually replaced earlier names and adopted larger titles. This was the political formation of Kushan rule, usually placed around 30 CE, not an event in 100 BCE.

passages.title: What archaeology can actually show
passages.text: At Ai Khanum, handmade bottle-shaped pots have been proposed as Yuezhi and goblets on stands as Saka. Yet only a small quantity of “nomadic” ware appeared beside continuing Greco-Bactrian pottery, and scholars caution that exact ethnic labels remain hypothetical. A pot shape is evidence, not a passport.

passages.title: What archaeology can actually show
passages.text: Khalchayan in southern Uzbekistan preserves the clearest named Yuezhi-Kushan setting used here. Excavations from 1959 to 1963 uncovered a palace with painted, almost life-size clay figures. The palace is often dated to the mid-first century BCE, but its precise date and ruler remain disputed.

passages.title: What archaeology can actually show
passages.text: The Khalchayan palace was a one-story rectangle with a small aiwan portico, a throne room and corridors leading to surrounding rooms. Those walls turn “rule” into a built place where visitors, guards, attendants and elites moved, although the plan tells us little about ordinary tents or farmhouses.

passages.title: What archaeology can actually show
passages.text: Dalverzin Tepe grew from a small fortified place into an extensive walled town in the first century BCE and is proposed as a Yuezhi capital. Its best-described administrative, residential, religious and manufacturing zones belong mainly to the later Kushan city. The identification is useful, but not certain enough to redraw the atlas.

passages.title: What archaeology can actually show
passages.text: At first-century CE Tillya Tepe, archaeologists found a nomadic chieftain and women buried with thousands of gold objects. The cemetery belongs to the region’s post-migration nomadic world, but the museum does not securely call its occupants Yuezhi. It is comparative evidence, not a family photograph of this atlas label.

passages.title: Art, belief and public spectacle
passages.text: Khalchayan’s throne-hall sculptures show rulers and aristocrats under deities drawn from Iranian, West Asian and Hellenistic traditions. One surviving head may represent an ancestor. These are elite claims about protection and legitimacy, carefully staged in a palace, not a complete list of what every household believed.

passages.title: Art, belief and public spectacle
passages.text: The battle, hunting and enthronement scenes at Khalchayan used Hellenized sculptural methods for Iranian and Central Asian themes. That combination is an achievement of adaptation: artists learned an inherited technique, changed its subjects and made a visual language for new rulers instead of merely copying Greek art.

passages.title: Art, belief and public spectacle
passages.text: Other Khalchayan walls showed festivals and religious ceremonies with musicians, masked performers and comedians. A palace image cannot prove how often ordinary people attended or performed, but it is vivid evidence that elite public culture included music, costume and laughter as well as battle scenes.

passages.title: Art, belief and public spectacle
passages.text: Tillya Tepe jewelry mixes steppe animals, Greek cupids, Indian motifs and Chinese-looking dragons. Goldsmiths did not live inside sealed cultural boxes. Because these graves date to the first century CE and their occupants are not securely identified, the objects illuminate a connected Bactrian world rather than a uniquely Yuezhi style.

passages.title: Art, belief and public spectacle
passages.text: Later Kushan coins show Iranian, Hindu and Buddhist divine figures and royal clothing beside inherited Greek forms. Scholars read this broad pantheon as a strategy for ruling culturally different regions. It demonstrates political creativity by the successor empire, while remaining too late to define Yuezhi belief in 200 BCE.

passages.title: Families, rank and learning
passages.text: The Shiji says the Xiongnu killed a Yuezhi king and the people later established his heir. That single royal succession proves that a dynasty mattered at one crisis. It does not reveal a complete inheritance law, the authority of ordinary parents or a general gender system for Yuezhi families.

passages.title: Families, rank and learning
passages.text: At Khalchayan, a king and queen sit among Bactrian and Parthian princes and warrior nobles. The arrangement displays rank, dynasty and alliance. It tells us that elite family relationships mattered to royal imagery, but says nothing reliable about the household size, marriage rules or authority of ordinary families.

passages.title: Families, rank and learning
passages.text: Tillya Tepe placed a male chieftain at the mound’s highest central point and female graves around him. Different goods may mark status, but the women’s relationship to him and their causes of death are uncertain. The cemetery cannot supply a universal Yuezhi family tree.

passages.title: Families, rank and learning
passages.text: No schoolroom, primer or Yuezhi child’s exercise securely appears in the sources reviewed for this card. Later coins and multilingual inscriptions prove that some specialists learned scripts, formulas and die-cutting. They do not reveal where children studied, who taught them or how widely literacy reached.

passages.title: Families, rank and learning
passages.text: Khalchayan’s artists mastered modeling, paint, large compositions and several visual traditions. Those skills had to be learned through practice, but no named teacher or apprentice survives. “Workshop learning” is a cautious inference from skilled production, not evidence for a formal academy run by Yuezhi rulers.

passages.title: Food, clothing and work
passages.text: Zhang Qian described the Great Yuezhi as moving with their herds and changing camps. That supports pastoral mobility, but his short report does not list species, recipes, milking, meal times or who cooked. A child-friendly story still has to stop where the menu disappears from the evidence.

passages.title: Food, clothing and work
passages.text: Bactria was different from an empty pasture. Economic history contrasts the mobile Yuezhi with settled agricultural regions, then follows later Kushan canals, markets and workshops. Political conquest changed who received obedience without instantly turning every farmer or craft worker into a nomad.

passages.title: Food, clothing and work
passages.text: Later Kushan-period excavations found millet, barley, wheat, fruits, grapes, melons, sesame, fodder and cotton. These finds show what the broader region could grow and make after Yuezhi settlement. They are not a grocery receipt for the migrating confederation, and direct early Yuezhi food remains stay sparse.

passages.title: Food, clothing and work
passages.text: Elite figures at Khalchayan wear belted mantles over shirts, long trousers or leggings, boots and shoulder cloths. Women are shown in layered floor-length dresses, shoes and tiaras or crowns. Sculpture preserves dress choices, but court art should not become a uniform for every child, herder or farmer.

passages.title: Food, clothing and work
passages.text: Tiny gold and turquoise plaques from Tillya Tepe were sewn onto hats and robes. Turquoise, carnelian and amethyst point toward several supply regions, and wear on objects shows some were used before burial. These dazzling clothes belonged to a later nomadic elite, not everyone living under Yuezhi rule.

passages.title: Health, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Direct evidence for a Yuezhi physician, remedy or medical school has not been established in the sources reviewed here. A later Kushan inscription connects a dedication with a wish for a king’s health, but records no diagnosis or treatment. Anything more specific would be invention, not medicine history.

passages.title: Health, water and the toilet question
passages.text: The museum account says no evidence shows how the Tillya Tepe people died. Sickness, environment and sacrifice have all been suggested, but none is demonstrated. This is a useful lesson in archaeological restraint: rich graves can preserve jewelry brilliantly while preserving a life story very poorly.

passages.title: Health, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Bactrian farming depended on water long before and after the migration. In the Kushan era, canal irrigation and animal-drawn ploughs expanded. That later infrastructure shows rulers and communities managing an arid landscape, but it cannot prove that a named Yuezhi inventor designed each canal or farming tool.

passages.title: Health, water and the toilet question
passages.text: At the later Kushan sanctuary of Surkh Kotal, an inscription and excavated works record a failed water supply followed by a lined well and assigned caretakers. It is unusually concrete evidence for maintenance and clean water in the successor state, many generations after the atlas’s 200 to 100 BCE window.

passages.title: Health, water and the toilet question
passages.text: Published descriptions of Khalchayan’s portico, throne hall, corridors and surrounding rooms do not identify a latrine, sewer or toilet. That means this card cannot tell children what a Yuezhi toilet looked like. It does not prove that people lacked waste practices; the direct evidence is simply sparse.

passages.title: Writing, exchange and continuity
passages.text: The names Yuezhi and Great Yuezhi reach us through Chinese writing, not through a surviving self-description in a Yuezhi language. Later Kushan rulers used several regional languages and scripts. None proves the language spoken by every family during the migration from Gansu to Bactria.

passages.title: Writing, exchange and continuity
passages.text: An authentic successor-period sample, in the published diplomatic capitals, is OOHMO KAΔΦIΣHΣO ϷAO, read “Vima Kadphises the king.” It represents Bactrian in Greek-derived script and survives in the Rabatak genealogy, composed after about 132 CE. It is Kushan royal writing, not a Yuezhi sentence from 200 BCE.

passages.title: Writing, exchange and continuity
passages.text: Kushan coins made writing portable. A British Museum coin of Kanishka bears a Bactrian inscription, while earlier rulers had used Greek legends and inherited designs. Coins joined portrait, title, deity and metal in a tiny political message that could travel far beyond a palace wall.

passages.title: Writing, exchange and continuity
passages.text: Zhang Qian’s Yuezhi mission helped begin recorded direct contact between Han China and Iranian lands near the end of the second century BCE. The exchange network had older paths and many local middlemen. It is clearer to say the mission expanded official knowledge than to claim one traveler “invented” the Silk Road.

passages.title: Writing, exchange and continuity
passages.text: Yuezhi political organization became part of a Kushan state that blended local Bactrian, Hellenistic, Indian and nomadic practices. Later empires and dynasties changed again. The old label faded, but towns, farms, families, craft knowledge, languages and memories continued through every shift in royal name.

The Yuezhi did not disappear when the atlas id stops at 100 BCE. Its instant Kushan successor polygon is chronologically premature. Historical accounts instead place several Yuezhi domains in Bactria and say that, more than a century after the migration, Kujula Kadphises of the Kushan branch overcame the other chiefs and called himself king, usually placed around 30 CE. That transformation ended a separate Yuezhi political arrangement, not its communities. Kushan rulers adopted Bactrian and other regional institutions, expanded south and built a diverse empire. Later Kushan fragmentation ended particular courts; descendants, subjects, towns, farming and artistic traditions continued under changing powers.

sectionTitles: Work, international connections and difficult histories

passages.text: Founded in 1918, the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes became Yugoslavia in 1929. After wartime partition and conflict, a six-republic socialist federation emerged in 1945.

passages.title: Homes, objects and growing cities
passages.text: Rapid urban growth created a serious need for housing after the Second World War. Architects used prefabricated construction to build on a large scale. The resulting apartments were also experiments in arranging limited space for ordinary activities such as sleeping, eating and family gatherings.

passages.title: Homes, objects and growing cities
passages.text: Yugoslav apartment designs could include rooms with several uses, flexible layouts and balconies extending living space outdoors. Architects compared ideas through competitions and published plans. A modest flat still required careful thought about where people would cook, work, rest and spend time together.

passages.title: Homes, objects and growing cities
passages.text: The 1963 earthquake devastated Skopje, in the Yugoslav republic of Macedonia. Its reconstruction brought together local and international planners, including Japanese architect Kenzo Tange. New buildings and city plans emerged through this collaboration, making rebuilding both an urgent practical task and an architectural experiment.

passages.title: Homes, objects and growing cities
passages.text: Davorin Savnik designed the ETA 80 telephone for Iskra in 1979. Its unusually flat, clean shape attracted attention in industrial design. The Museum of Architecture and Design preserves the model, a reminder that an object used for an ordinary phone call could also be carefully designed.

passages.title: Homes, objects and growing cities
passages.text: Niko Kralj’s folding Rex lounge chair dates to 1956. Cuts in its plywood help the wood curve into the seat and back, while the whole chair folds away. It solves two domestic problems at once: somewhere comfortable to sit and somewhere to put the chair afterward.

passages.title: Homes, objects and growing cities
passages.text: Branko Ćopić’s children’s story first appeared as Ježeva kuća in 1949, illustrated by Aljoša Josić. The museum catalogue records a print run of five thousand and an Italian translation in 1951. A story associated with generations of childhood reading could travel across languages quite quickly.

passages.title: Work, international connections and difficult histories
passages.text: Youth work actions combined organized labor with group life. The Museum of Yugoslavia describes competitions between brigades in work, sport and cultural activities, as well as shared songs and greetings. Their surviving objects and memories connect construction projects with the experiences of young participants.

passages.title: Work, international connections and difficult histories
passages.text: Workers’ self-management became a central idea in Yugoslav socialism. The constitutional law of 1953 assigned management rights to workers and producers. These legal arrangements aimed to give workplaces a role in running enterprises, within a system that still had Communist political leadership.

passages.title: Work, international connections and difficult histories
passages.text: Belgrade hosted the first summit of the Non-Aligned Movement in 1961. Yugoslavia sought international relationships beyond membership in either of the Cold War’s rival military blocs. The meeting placed the country in a network with states across Africa, Asia and other regions.

passages.title: Work, international connections and difficult histories
passages.text: Economic changes in the 1960s brought both opportunities and unemployment. More Yugoslav citizens went abroad for work. Migration connected household income and family decisions with foreign labor markets, even while relatives and homes remained in the federation.

passages.title: Work, international connections and difficult histories
passages.text: During the Second World War, the Ustaša regime operated the Jasenovac camp system in the Axis-aligned Independent State of Croatia. Serbs, Jews, Roma and political opponents were persecuted and killed there. This wartime regime must be distinguished from both the earlier Yugoslav kingdom and modern Croatia.

passages.title: A small sample of writing
passages.text: Serbian in Cyrillic, article 1 of the 1946 constitution: “Федеративна Народна Република Југославија је савезна народна држава републиканског облика”. Translation: “The Federal People’s Republic of Yugoslavia is a federal people’s state of republican form.” This excerpt follows the Archives of Yugoslavia’s edition of the historical text.

The six-republic federation dissolved in 1991 and 1992 amid war and displacement. Serbia and Montenegro formed a smaller Federal Republic of Yugoslavia in April 1992, with different territory and membership. Map coverage ends in 1994, later than the federation.

sectionTitles: A homeland and its changing government
Meals, houses and a river highway
Learning and caring for a living landscape

passages.text: Yurok communities belong to the lower Klamath River and neighbouring Pacific coast of northern California. Their history joins river travel, fishing, redwood craftsmanship and continuing self-government. The imported 1492 to 1500 polygon is an approximate homeland snapshot; it is neither the present reservation boundary nor the lifetime of the Yurok people.

passages.title: A homeland and its changing government
passages.text: The Tribe’s history recalls more than fifty villages across its ancestral territory. River and coastal places mattered deeply to identity: people distinguished neighbours living upstream, downstream and along the coast. A broad name on a map can conceal a much more detailed geography of homes and relationships.

passages.title: A homeland and its changing government
passages.text: The 1850 Trinity River gold rush brought a devastating influx of settlers into northwestern California. Indigenous communities faced expulsion, enslavement and massacres; state payments rewarded some attacking militias. Treaties intended to reserve land were not ratified. These events explain major losses of land and security, rather than any disappearance in 1500.

passages.title: A homeland and its changing government
passages.text: The constitution’s historical preamble recalls confinement to the Klamath River Reserve in 1855, later land allotments and boarding schools that punished children for speaking their language. It also records the legal battles that reaffirmed fishing rights in the 1970s and 1980s. Language teaching and river stewardship respond to that difficult history.

passages.title: A homeland and its changing government
passages.text: The Yurok constitution was ratified in 1993. It establishes tribal government and sets out responsibilities toward people, land and cultural inheritance. Its preamble connects present institutions to ancestors and future generations. This constitutional government belongs to a modern phase of a much longer Yurok history.

passages.title: Meals, houses and a river highway
passages.text: Salmon, sturgeon and candlefish from the Klamath-Trinity system were important foods. The coast and inland country added mussels, seaweed, acorns, deer, elk and berries. The Tribe describes food gathering as a responsibility to future generations: a good harvest also leaves the next harvest possible.

passages.title: Meals, houses and a river highway
passages.text: Dentalia shells served as money for purchases, debts and marriage payments. The Tribe records that men’s arm tattoos could measure the shell strings. Measuring valuable money could therefore involve holding it against an arm, an unusually portable ruler.

passages.title: Meals, houses and a river highway
passages.text: The National Park Service describes north-coast plankhouses made from boards split from fallen redwoods. Houses stood over pits, with the ledge beside the pit forming a bench. In this regional tradition, a home was understood as a living presence, tied to the sacred character of redwood.

passages.title: Meals, houses and a river highway
passages.text: A canoe carved in 1968 by Dewey George and Jimmy James, with helpers, survives as a park display. It is eighteen feet long and was made from half a redwood log. Water kept inside the displayed canoe helps prevent drying and splitting. For this wooden boat, a little water inside is useful maintenance.

passages.title: Meals, houses and a river highway
passages.text: Canoe builders placed the denser inner wood at the bottom of the hull. Travellers used paddles going downstream and poles along banks and eddies upstream. Both women and men navigated these boats. Boatbuilding knowledge included the tree’s structure, the shape of the river and how a loaded craft would behave.

passages.title: Meals, houses and a river highway
passages.text: A Yurok cooking basket in the National Museum of the American Indian is twined from willow, conifer root and beargrass. Helen Culver Kerr donated it in 1926; the catalogue does not date its manufacture or name its maker. The interlaced plant materials preserve the work of a skilled craftsperson.

passages.title: Learning and caring for a living landscape
passages.text: The Cultural Fire Management Council describes planned burns that encourage hazel sticks for basketry, tanoak acorns for food and forage for grazing animals. Fire is part of tending the landscape. The useful basket plant and the meal begin well before someone gathers them.

passages.title: Learning and caring for a living landscape
passages.text: The council’s family-burning programme helps households prepare land and includes children in passing on knowledge. Its plant programme takes photographs, surveys vegetation before and after burns, and collects native seed. These projects bring observation, practical work and family learning together across generations.

passages.title: Learning and caring for a living landscape
passages.text: The Tribe’s curriculum prints “Kee-tue skuue-lek'!” with the translation “I'm going to school!” This is contemporary written Yurok used for teaching. The same page offers preschool and school lessons alongside work preserving elders’ recordings and earlier language records. A short school-day sentence sits beside generations of knowledge.

passages.title: Learning and caring for a living landscape
passages.text: In January 2022, the Tribe reported language-learning events built around gathering acorns and making eel hooks. Participants learned the words while doing the work. Its Planting Seeds programme sought to bring Yurok into homes, workplaces and community events, extending learning beyond a classroom lesson.

passages.title: Learning and caring for a living landscape
passages.text: In October 2024, the Tribe reported that in-river dam removal work had finished and salmon were again travelling above the former Iron Gate site. Yurok crews sowed native plants on exposed reservoir ground. Vegetation stabilised soil and supported insects eaten by young fish: rebuilding a river also meant planting its banks.

Yurok people continue as a living nation with constitutional government, language education and stewardship of their homeland. The map’s 1500 cutoff is only imported coverage. Recent river restoration and community teaching belong to an ongoing history shaped by survival, renewed authority and responsibilities to future generations.

sectionTitles: Music and cities imagined in miniature

passages.text: This record follows Congo-Kinshasa, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, from the late colonial period into independence. Zaire was its name from 1971 to 1997; it is a different state from neighboring Congo-Brazzaville.

passages.title: Names, government and written words
passages.text: The successive names Congo-Leopoldville, Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zaire do not identify three vanished populations. The UN’s country-name record tracks changes in official terminology. Keeping the dates straight also prevents confusion with the separate Republic of the Congo across the river.

passages.title: Names, government and written words
passages.text: The independence crisis brought the first UN peacekeeping operation in 1960. Later wars in 1996 to 1997 and 1998 to 2003 involved regional forces and armed groups. The UN’s 2025 history describes continuing violence and displacement, a serious part of modern life alongside cultural achievement.

passages.title: Names, government and written words
passages.text: Article 1 of the constitution, in its 2011 edition, prints the motto “Justice - Paix - Travail”: “Justice - Peace - Work”. This is a short attested French writing sample. The same article recognizes Kikongo, Lingala, Swahili and Tshiluba as national languages, showing that official French is only part of the linguistic picture.

passages.title: Music and cities imagined in miniature
passages.text: Congolese rumba belongs to communities in both Congo states and their diaspora. Musicians perform it at celebrations and in mourning, in homes, public spaces and religious settings. Its social life extends far beyond the concert stage or a famous recording.

passages.title: Music and cities imagined in miniature
passages.text: Younger musicians learn through neighborhood clubs, schools and community organizations. Established performers train apprentices in playing and making instruments. A musical tradition survives through rehearsal, teaching and practical work as well as moments when an audience gets up to dance.

passages.title: Music and cities imagined in miniature
passages.text: Kinshasa-based artist Bodys Isek Kingelez built dazzling architectural models from paper, packaging, plastic, cans and bottle caps. Everyday discarded materials became towers and public spaces. His creations ask viewers to imagine how cities might serve people better.

passages.title: Music and cities imagined in miniature
passages.text: In Kimbembele Ihunga, made in 1994, Kingelez reimagined his home village with a stadium, banks, restaurants and skyscrapers. Ville Fantome, from 1996, pictured a peaceful city that needed neither police nor doctors. These were artistic hopes, not claims that real communities had solved every problem.

passages.title: Food, school and care
passages.text: An IITA project launched in 2023 sought to strengthen cassava growing and processing in the DRC, including flour for breadmaking. The plan linked farmers, processors and bakeries. A familiar crop could become part of an effort to reduce dependence on imported wheat.

passages.title: Food, school and care
passages.text: The cassava project also addressed processing and access to buyers. Growing a crop is only one part of getting food onto a household table: roots must reach the right place in usable condition, and farmers need customers as well as harvests.

passages.title: Food, school and care
passages.text: At Chirhavanyi Primary School in Walungu, a new water supply and hygienic toilets arrived in 2021. Fourteen-year-old Asifiwe later described being able to wash her hands at school. An ordinary school break no longer needed to revolve around finding water.

passages.title: Food, school and care
passages.text: At nearby Izenge Health Centre, Chinama described previously leaving her sick daughter to fetch water far away. A water point close to the rooms changed that task. Infrastructure matters at the scale of one parent trying to care for one child, as well as in national statistics.

passages.title: Food, school and care
passages.text: Doctor Denis Mukwege shared the 2018 Nobel Peace Prize for work against sexual violence in war. At Panzi Hospital in Bukavu, his team cared for injured women and girls. Their achievement joined skilled medicine with advocacy for survivors’ dignity and protection.
The state continued after the end of Mobutu’s regime and the name Zaire in 1997. Subsequent wars and continuing armed violence did not erase Congolese communities, institutions or creative life.

sectionTitles: Woodworking in the very distant past
A game board with room for thought
Making dinner could be a group project
Learn the dance by joining in
Building a university, then training teachers

passages.text: Zambia’s regional history includes extraordinary traces of early woodworking and the ordinary skills of preparing and sharing food. Archaeological finds and local accounts reveal different kinds of knowledge, separated by immense stretches of time.

passages.title: Woodworking in the very distant past
passages.text: Excavations at Kalambo Falls in 2019 uncovered two logs joined through a deliberately shaped notch. Their waterlogged deposits were dated to roughly 476,000 years ago, with a margin of uncertainty. Researchers interpret them as parts of a wooden construction. A platform, walkway or foundation is possible; the find is not a complete house with a known floor plan.

passages.title: Woodworking in the very distant past
passages.text: The wet conditions at Kalambo helped wood survive where it would usually decay. The researchers also had to protect it after excavation. They used photographs and digital models to examine the shaping marks while keeping the pieces submerged. Studying an ancient wooden object could mean photographing it in a bath, rather than simply drying it and putting it on a shelf.

passages.title: A game board with room for thought
passages.text: A wooden cisolwa board in the British Museum has four rows of eight holes. The catalogue attributes it to Lala makers in Zambia and dates it approximately between 1957 and 1972. It is more than a metre wide. This game took up rather more space than a phone screen. The object preserves a material trace of play, even though its catalogue does not explain every move.

passages.title: Making dinner could be a group project
passages.text: Sociologist Mwizenge Tembo describes preparing maize meal with help from children, relatives and neighbours. After kernels were removed from the cobs, women and girls pounded the maize, sometimes accompanying the work with songs. His account draws on fieldwork in 1980, 1985 and 1993, especially around eastern Zambia. It makes the labour behind a meal visible, alongside the cooperation involved.

passages.title: Making dinner could be a group project
passages.text: Tembo explains how nshima, a thick porridge, is eaten with another dish that might contain vegetables, beans, meat or fish. Diners shape a small portion in one hand and dip it into the accompanying dish. Conversation and hospitality form part of his account too. The meal is a social occasion as well as a way to satisfy hunger.

passages.title: Recipes can have a calendar
passages.text: A 2016 Bioversity International project in the Barotse Floodplain brought people together in cooking groups. Its description records recipe sharing, cookbooks and seasonal food calendars, connecting available ingredients with family meals. The calendar helped make a practical question visible: what food is available at this time of year? This example concerns the participating communities, rather than one menu followed across Zambia.

passages.title: Learn the dance by joining in
passages.text: Kalela developed in colonial-era Luapula and was taken up by mine workers. UNESCO describes dancers moving in two or three lines, singing as they go forwards and backwards around central drums. Lead singers and dancers help guide the group. The performance depends on people coordinating movement, rhythm and voice, making it both skilled work and a shared occasion.

passages.title: Learn the dance by joining in
passages.text: Kalela skills are passed on through songs, poetry, watching and participation. Some groups also organise lessons with experienced drummers when they need new musicians. Performances belong to occasions ranging from weddings to public celebrations and funerals. There is more than one way to learn: sometimes a lesson has a teacher at the front, and sometimes it has a drumbeat in the middle.

passages.title: Building a university, then training teachers
passages.text: The University of Zambia began its first academic session at Lusaka’s Ridgeway Campus on 17 March 1966. That first day followed a commission, planning, legal establishment and recruitment of staff. The university’s own history separates the start of classes from the later July ceremonies. A school’s beginning can have several important dates, depending on whether we mean its paperwork, its buildings or its students.

passages.title: Building a university, then training teachers
passages.text: The School of Education opened in April 1966 with forty-two graduates studying for a postgraduate teaching certificate. By 1969 its programmes also included training for primary teachers and courses in library studies. Preparing people to teach, and people to organise books and information, helped extend the work of learning beyond the university’s own classrooms.

British rule ended on 24 October 1964, when Northern Rhodesia became independent as Zambia. The republic continued through later changes in its political system, including the return to multiparty elections in 1991. The earlier map intervals are not dates when Zambian communities disappeared.

sectionTitles: A house around a patch of sky
What was here before the fort?
Someone drew boats on the wall
Royal plumbing, including the less glamorous part
A bench, a floor and the work behind cloves

passages.text: Zanzibar’s history includes Swahili communities, Omani royal government and connections with India, Arabia and Europe. Stone Town’s streets and buildings preserve that mixture. Palace life, shopkeeping and plantation labour offer very different views of the same society.

passages.title: A house around a patch of sky
passages.text: Stone Town’s historic houses often used coral limestone, mangrove timber and lime mortar. Many larger houses arranged long, narrow rooms around an open courtyard. The building’s shape helped organise domestic space around that opening. A handsome carved entrance belonged to a practical building, not merely a decorative front.

passages.title: A house around a patch of sky
passages.text: The town also included simpler single-storey Swahili houses and Indian bazaar buildings centred on a duka, or shop. Those differences matter: a palace cannot stand in for everybody’s home. Shop spaces are reminders that urban life involved buying, selling and making a living as well as royal ceremonies.

passages.title: What was here before the fort?
passages.text: Excavations in the Old Fort’s western courtyard in 2017 and 2018 traced occupation back to an eleventh-century Swahili settlement beside the beach. Imported ceramics helped researchers investigate long connections with the Gulf. A broken pot can reveal a trading relationship, although it cannot by itself tell us the language or birthplace of its owner.

passages.title: What was here before the fort?
passages.text: The same site later held a Portuguese trading establishment and an Augustinian mission. Omani builders reused the church within a square fort; nineteenth-century expansion produced two courtyards. A place can preserve several political histories in its walls. The present fort therefore does not represent one untouched building from a single moment.

passages.title: Someone drew boats on the wall
passages.text: Researchers recorded ship drawings scratched into dry plaster at the Old Fort, especially inside its southwestern tower and along its ramparts. Hulls, masts and rigging appear in the marks. Building history and vessel types suggest a mid- to late-nineteenth-century date. The drawings are material traces of somebody looking closely at ships.

passages.title: Someone drew boats on the wall
passages.text: Who held the sharp point? The researchers suggest members of the fort’s garrison, who had access to these spaces and could see shipping nearby. Their makers remain unidentified.

passages.title: Royal plumbing, including the less glamorous part
passages.text: At Mtoni palace, researchers excavated a water channel in 2008. Their architectural study connects the palace’s water supply with a nineteenth-century aqueduct from the Chem Chem spring. This is practical evidence behind a grand residence: bringing water to the household required planned structures, not just a good view of the sea.

passages.title: Royal plumbing, including the less glamorous part
passages.text: Mtoni’s bathing complex included cold-water bathhouses and a separate heated bath. The latter had cold, warm and hot rooms with a boiler. These were facilities of a royal household, not evidence that everyone in Zanzibar had such a bathroom. Even within the palace, different bathing arrangements served different residents.

passages.title: Royal plumbing, including the less glamorous part
passages.text: The cold-water bathhouses also had latrines that were emptied through hatches at the rear. Channels ran beneath the bathing complex, while raised back rooms accommodated washing and toilet use. Royal architecture needed arrangements for waste as well as impressive reception rooms. Somebody still had to do the emptying.

passages.title: School on a veranda
passages.text: Princess Salme, later known as Emily Ruete, remembered lessons in the royal household on an open veranda. Children used bamboo pens, homemade ink and cleaned camel shoulder blades as writing surfaces. Enslaved people prepared the bones. This was her recollection of an elite nineteenth-century childhood, not a description of every Zanzibar school.

passages.title: School on a veranda
passages.text: Before lessons, Salme recalled children wrestling and climbing a balustrade. A lookout coughed when the teacher approached, and everybody hurried to sit down. The account comes from memory, but the scene is wonderfully recognisable: an unusually well-coordinated effort to look as though absolutely nothing had been happening.

passages.title: School on a veranda
passages.text: In her household, girls were taught reading while boys also learned writing. Salme secretly copied characters onto a bone, then learned more with help from an enslaved writing teacher. Her story records both a girl pursuing an excluded skill and knowledge held by a person whose own freedom was denied.

passages.title: A bench, a floor and the work behind cloves
passages.text: At the nineteenth-century plantation site of Mgoli on Pemba, a 2004 excavation uncovered a partly dismantled baraza, a bench outside a stone house. Beside it lay a packed-rubble floor interpreted as a place for drying cloves. A working floor at Bweni and local residents’ knowledge supported that interpretation.

passages.title: A bench, a floor and the work behind cloves
passages.text: Freshly picked cloves had to dry before export, and enslaved workers supplied the plantation labour. Croucher suggests that a bench beside the drying area could let owners watch that work while also serving as a social space. The bench and floor were excavated; this explanation of surveillance is an interpretation of their position.

passages.title: A clinic downstairs, homes upstairs
passages.text: Merchant Tharia Topan commissioned the building later called the Old Dispensary; its foundation stone was laid in 1887. After his death, his wife Janbai oversaw the project, but the completed building still needed money for equipment and staff. A fine building alone did not make a working clinic. It began operating under new ownership in 1900.

passages.title: A clinic downstairs, homes upstairs
passages.text: The early dispensary treated patients in three ground-floor rooms used for consultations, treatment and pharmacy services. Apartments occupied the upper floors. After later closure and restoration, the building returned to healthcare use as the Aga Khan Health Centre. Its history joins medical work, housing and the challenge of adapting an old building to a new purpose.

The sultanate ended in the revolution of 12 January 1964, which replaced the monarchy with a republic. Zanzibar united with Tanganyika on 26 April that year. Its communities continued, and Zanzibar later developed its own House of Representatives within Tanzania. The map’s endpoint in 1914 is not this political ending.

passages.text: Monte Alban was an important Zapotec capital in the Oaxaca Valley. Its history of urban planning, water management and carved inscriptions is one part of the much wider history of Zapotec societies.

passages.title: Technology
passages.text: Builders reshaped hillsides with terraces, dams and conduits. Water management and the creation of level spaces were integrated into urban development.

passages.title: Architecture
passages.text: Temples and platforms framed a long ceremonial esplanade. Open spaces were as important to the layout as the buildings themselves.

passages.title: Writing and arts
passages.text: Carved reliefs with hieroglyphic inscriptions survive alongside tombs and temples, giving evidence of visual art and record making.

passages.title: Public life
passages.text: The ceremonial center included a ball court. Its built spaces supported activities beyond the palaces and burial places of elites.

passages.title: Trade and exchange
passages.text: Monte Alban maintained relations with Teotihuacan. Those contacts connect Oaxaca's history to other contemporary Mesoamerican centers.

passages.title: Change over time
passages.text: UNESCO dates Monte Alban's long florescence from about 500 BCE to 850 CE, followed by decline. This is the trajectory of a city, not an extinction date for Zapotec peoples.
